reports.headline: Stellwagen Basin holding haddock on the mud, gravel edges still giving up cod at 110 feet
reports.subhead: Bluefin are still working the mackerel schools on top of the Bank, but the fleet's split on where the best grade of groundfish is sitting this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-eight degrees on the surface over the Basin, dropping into the low 50s once you punch through the thermocline around 90 feet — that's the number that matters right now on Stellwagen. The top of the water column is still carrying summer heat, but underneath it the Bank is behaving like it should for early September: cod tucked into the gravel on the edges, haddock spread out on the mud in the deeper basin, and bluefin still working the surface wherever the mackerel bunch up tight enough to get pinned.

The warm signature that's carried this whole summer hasn't cracked yet. We flagged it last week — said if that warm water held, the pattern would hold with it — and it has. Boats running deep-drop gear for swordfish have been finding fish farther north into Gulf of Maine water than is typical for this time of year, working the drop-offs toward Carter Canyon in 500-plus feet. That's not a groundfish signal, but it's confirmation the warm regime is still sitting on top of us. It won't last forever. Once that layer breaks down — and it will, probably with the first real cool front of the month — expect the whole Bank to reset toward a more typical fall pattern fast.

Until then, the groundfish bite is steady but not blow-the-doors-off. Cod are coming off the gravel patches on Stellwagen Edge, mostly in 100 to 130 feet, with the better fish running 8 to 15 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts that need to go back. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a squid strip is still outfishing bait on the drift — a 12-ounce diamond with a single mackerel-belly strip, worked with a short hop off bottom, has been the go-to for boats staying disciplined about keeping the jig ticking the gravel instead of ripping it too high. Bait soakers doing clam or herring on a high-low rig are getting fish too, but they're working harder for it — the cod have been more willing to chase a moving bait than sit and wait on this warm water.

Haddock are the more consistent story. The mud bottom in Stellwagen Basin, running 180 to 220 feet, has been giving up a steady grade of haddock in the 2 to 5 pound class, with the occasional 8-pounder mixed in to keep things interesting. Standard haddock rigs — a two-hook high-low with clam bellies or squid, fished right on bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current — are doing the work. The bite window has been tide-dependent more than time-of-day dependent: the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood have been producing the tightest bunches of bites, which tracks with how haddock stack up on structure when the current is moving enough to keep bait suspended but not so hard it's pinning gear sideways.

Pollock have been scattered along the steeper drop-offs near Tillies Bank, mostly suspended 40 to 60 feet down over deeper water, and they've been a bonus fish more than a target — a few boats jigging bucktails or heavy diamond jigs for cod have picked off pollock to 10 pounds on the same drops. Hake reports have been thinner this week; a few boats working the deeper current lines off the Basin at night have scratched out a few, but it hasn't been consistent enough to call it a pattern yet.

The bluefin story is the one everybody at the dock wants to talk about, and it's mixed. When the mackerel schools bunch up tight on top of the Bank — usually mid-morning once the sun's had a chance to push bait up — the tuna show and the bite can turn into a genuine spectacle for twenty or thirty minutes before it shuts back off. Chunking with fresh mackerel over a slick has worked when boats can find and hold on a school, and a few jig-and-pop guys throwing stickbaits into visible surface activity have connected on smaller fish in the 60 to 100 pound class. But it's not a bite you can plan a whole trip around yet — more than one boat has spent hours running the Bank without finding fish committed enough to feed. Patience and mobility matter more than gear right now.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern holds if the warm water holds — light winds and a building moon into the weekend should keep the Bank fishable and the tide cycles workable for both the gravel bite and the mud bite. If there's a shift worth watching, it's the same one we flagged before: any real cool front pushing through New England in the next week to two weeks is going to start knocking that surface layer down, and when it does, expect the cod to push shallower onto the edges as the water column evens out, and expect the tuna bite to either sharpen up on a final feed before the mackerel scatter, or shut down hard if the bait pushes out ahead of the cold. For now, if there's only one day to spend on the Bank, split it — work the gravel on Stellwagen Edge early on the last of the ebb for cod, then swing to the Basin mud for haddock once the tide turns, and keep an eye on the horizon for birds working bait in case the bluefin decide to show.

reports.headline: Billingsgate on the Building Moon: Bass Glued to Bait, Blues Filling the Gaps
reports.subhead: Stripers are stacked tight to mackerel and bunker but still won't commit to a blitz — the building moon should change that soon.
reports.body_markdown:
The Bay is carrying more bait right now than it has all summer, and that's both the good news and the reason the striper bite has stayed frustrating for a lot of boats this week. Mackerel schools are thick off Race Point, peanut bunker are working their way along Sandy Neck and into Barnstable Harbor, and every drift through the rip turns up marks on the sounder that look like a school bus stacked on bait. But the fish underneath them are still sluggish about actually feeding hard. Water out there is holding onto its late-summer warmth, and warm water this time of year tends to keep bass content to sit under the bait and pick rather than blow it up on top. That's exactly the pattern the fleet has been talking about at the ramps in P-town and Barnstable all week — plenty of fish, not much urgency.

That's going to change, and soon. The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and every year around here that's when the tide starts running harder and those loose bait schools get squeezed into tighter, more nervous balls. Once that happens, the switch usually flips fast. We flagged this exact setup last week — said the early tide stages would keep producing while everything built toward a bigger push — and that's held up almost to the hour. The best fish of the week have come in the first two hours of the ebb off Race Point and the top of the flood pushing onto Peaked Hill Bars, right when the current starts stacking bait against the structure.

Race Point remains the best bet for size. Boats working the rip on the last of the slack into the first stage of the ebb are getting bass into the 20s and 30s on live mackerel, drifted naturally off a 3-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that washing-machine current. A few better fish — high 30s, one report of a fish pushing 40 — came off live bunker fished the same way, just fished a little deeper in the guts of the rip where the bigger fish like to sit out of the heaviest wash. Depth there runs 20 to 35 feet depending on where you catch the tide, and the fish are moving with the bait, not holding on a fixed piece of structure, so staying mobile on the drift matters more than anchoring up.

Peaked Hill Bars has been a tube-and-worm and umbrella rig show, worked slow on the troll through the sandy troughs in 15 to 25 feet. It's a slower bite than the rip but a more consistent one — fewer giants, more keeper-class fish in the mid-20s to low 30s, and it's been holding up through the middle of the day when Race Point goes quiet on the higher stages of the tide.

Bluefish have been the one thing you can count on without much thinking. Sandy Neck and the mouth of Barnstable Harbor have had steady blitz activity on peanut bunker, especially in the last two hours of daylight when the bait gets pushed up against the beach. Poppers and 1-ounce metal have both worked — the blues aren't picky right now, they're just showing up in numbers and staying aggressive, which tracks with what's been reported basin-wide this summer. Expect that to hold through Labor Day week as long as the bait stays put.

Fluke have thinned out the way they always do this time of year. Billingsgate Shoal and the flats off Barnstable are still giving up keeper fish, but the doormats that were around in July have mostly slid off toward deeper structure, and the numbers game just isn't what it was a month ago. If you're still chasing them, work the edges of the shoal on the drift with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and don't expect to grind through many shorts to find a keeper — the ratio has flipped.

Cod are still a step behind. The deeper structure north of Race Point and off the backside of Peaked Hill Bars — 90 to 130 feet — is starting to hold a few fish, but the water hasn't cooled enough yet to bring them up in real numbers. That bite typically builds through the rest of September and really turns on once the surface temps drop into the mid-50s. Worth a scout trip with diamond jigs if you're already out there, but it's not worth planning a whole day around yet.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep rewarding the same pattern — early ebb and early flood at Race Point, midday on Peaked Hill Bars, dusk blitzes off Sandy Neck. If the moon does what moons do and tightens that bait up over the next week, look for the first real surface blitz activity to break loose right around the rip. Keep an eye on wind direction heading into the weekend — anything out of the northeast will stack more bait against Race Point and could be the trigger that turns this steady pick into the kind of push everyone's been waiting on.

reports.headline: Quick's Hole Turns Bonito Green — Albies Stacking Right Behind Them
reports.subhead: Bait's balled up tight in the Elizabeth Island rips and the first real albie push of the season is riding the building moon into Buzzards Bay.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait told the story all week before a single rod bent. Peanut bunker and silversides have been getting squeezed into fists in the rips off Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole, pinned against the current by bonito working underneath and gulls marking the surface from above. That's the setup we flagged a week ago — said the bonito and albie signals were building alongside the striper and bluefish pattern, and here it is, right on schedule, with bonito now showing consistently through the Elizabeth Islands chain and the first legitimate false albacore reports trickling in behind them.

Water's still holding in the low-to-mid 70s through Buzzards Bay and Vineyard Sound, which is exactly the kind of warm, current-scrubbed water that keeps bait schools tight and predators committed rather than scattered. The moon's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the number to watch — bigger tidal swings mean harder-running water through Woods Hole, Robinson's Hole, and Quick's Hole, and harder-running water is what turns loosely balled bait into the kind of pinched, panicked schools that get albies and bonito to commit instead of just cruising through.

The rip fishing itself has been honest work, not a gimme. Bonito are showing best on the last two hours of the ebb through Robinson's Hole, when the current funnels bait out of Buzzards Bay into the Sound and stacks it against the western shore of Naushon. Small profile is the difference-maker right now — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in green-and-white or bone, and Deadly Dicks in the smaller sizes, are outfishing the bigger metal that worked earlier in the summer. These fish are eating small right now, likely keyed on tiny silversides rather than anything with size to it, so if you're throwing standard Hopkins or Kastmasters and getting refusals, drop down before you give up on the spot.

False albacore reports are still spotty rather than steady — a few fish busting through Quick's Hole on the last of the outgoing, a handful more working the rip off Cuttyhunk near Sow and Pigs Reef on slack into the first of the flood. That's honest albie behavior for this early in September: they're here, they're feeding, but they're not locked in yet. The pattern usually tightens fast once that full moon current gets moving, so the next week is when this typically flips from occasional to reliable. Albie Snax in bone or pink-and-white, and small Deceivers in the 2-inch range on 20-pound fluorocarbon leader, have been the better calls when the fish do show — these are line-shy, fast-moving targets and a long cast into the boil beats working the edges.

Striped bass are still mostly a bait story rather than a blitz story in this zone. Bunker pods are thickening up inside Buzzards Bay, particularly off the mainland side toward New Bedford and down through the Bay proper, but the fish sitting under them are staged and non-committal rather than smashing the surface — same pattern playing out from Raritan Bay to Narragansett Bay right now. That should change as nighttime temps start dropping through September and the building moon tightens those bunker schools further. Worth working live bunker on a fishfinder rig or bucktailing the edges of visible pods around Cuttyhunk and the western Elizabeth Islands, but don't expect the top-water chaos yet — that's a look-ahead item, not a this-week item.

Bluefish have been the one bite you could count on without qualification. Blues are running thick through Woods Hole and along the south side of the Vineyard, chopping up peanut bunker and taking anything shiny thrown into the melee — poppers, small metal, bucktails, doesn't much matter. This has been consistent basin-wide through Labor Day week, and there's no reason to think it slows before the water starts dropping into the 60s.

Fluke are on the expected early-September fade. Back-bay and inlet numbers are thinning as the bigger fish slide out toward deeper structure ahead of the fall push. Vineyard Sound edges and the deeper water off Woods Hole are still worth a drift with a white Gulp swimming mullet on a bucktail if fluke is the priority, but this bite is winding down, not building — treat any keeper as a bonus rather than the plan.

Scup remain the reliable bread-and-butter fish for anyone who wants a bent rod without chasing moving targets. Oak Bluffs pier and the Woods Hole drawbridge current have both been producing steady scup on squid strips and small pieces of clam, mixed with snapper blues for anyone fishing bait on the bottom.

Looking ahead: the next several days should sharpen the albie and bonito bite as the moon builds. If the tide lines up right — start the ebb at Robinson's Hole two hours before dead low, or hit Quick's Hole on that same window — the odds of connecting go up considerably. Best case, the current strengthens enough by midweek to turn these scattered albie sightings into a real, sustained bite through the Elizabeth Islands chain. If the fish slide off the pace, Cuttyhunk's rip and the Menemsha side of the Sound are the backup plays. Either way, keep the small profile jigs rigged and ready — that's been the difference this week, and it's not likely to change until the bait size changes with it.

reports.headline: Great Point Rip: Terns Working Blues Hard, Albies Still Playing Games
reports.subhead: Bluefish have committed on the Sound's rips while the albies tease at the edges — and the bonito push west is finally close enough to matter.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood at the Great Point rip Tuesday morning watching a hundred terns work a bait ball the size of a pickup truck, diving so hard some of them were going under. Under that was blitzing bluefish, slashing bunker peanuts into confetti on the ebb. No albies busting through the middle of it — not that morning. That's been the story of the Sound the last ten days: the blues are locked in and violent, the albies are around but noncommittal, and everybody's watching the calendar for the bonito to finally show up in numbers.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefish would stay aggressive and widespread right through Labor Day week, and that's exactly what's playing out. Warm water in the low-to-mid 70s across the Sound has kept them fired up on peanut bunker and sand eels from Great Point down through Monomoy, and the reports out of the fleet match what the Canal and Montauk crowd are seeing too. This isn't a finicky bite. Bluefish to eight and nine pounds are hitting fast-retrieved metal — Deadly Dick or a 2-ounce Kastmaster in the epoxy jig finish — and topwater poppers when they're up busting on the surface, which has been most mornings on the last two hours of the ebb at Great Point and along the Sankaty side when the current stacks bait against the beach.

The albies are the frustrating part, and it's worth being straight about it: they're here, but they're not fully committed. Boats working Monomoy Rip and the water off Chatham are marking fish and getting shots, but the bite has been start-stop — a pod comes up, feeds for ninety seconds on something microscopic, and vanishes. That tells you they're likely tucked into bay anchovies or tiny silversides rather than committing hard to bigger forage, which is why the standard 00 Deadly Dick and Albie Snax have been outfished lately by smaller profile stuff — half-ounce epoxy jigs, small Game On Chick minnows, or a size 2 Clouser on the fly for the guys working the rips out of a skiff. If you're marking fish and getting refused on a 3-inch lure, cut down to something closer to 1.5 inches before you give up on the spot.

Bonito are the story to watch over the next week. They've been thick at Block Island and Point Judith and are pushing west into the Race and Fishers Island Sound, which puts them within realistic striking distance of Nantucket Sound proper. Historically when that push gets rolling this time of year, Nantucket Shoals and the water off Great Point start seeing scattered bonito mixed in with the albie pods within a week to ten days. Worth keeping a rod rigged with smaller Deadly Dicks or green machine feathers just in case that shows up sooner than expected — bonito this far into the run tend to be just as fussy about profile size as the albies have been.

Striped bass are around but staged, not blitzing, which tracks with what's happening up and down the coast right now. Bunker schools are still building rather than fully concentrated, and until that tightens up — which the building moon toward full on September 6-7 should help with — the bass are going to keep feeding more on structure and current edges than on the surface in big showy blitzes. Horseshoe Shoal has been holding fish on the drop of the tide, working sand eels and small bunker over the humps in 15 to 25 feet. Bucktails in the 1-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid or a white Gulp swimming mullet have been the better producer there over straight metal, worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb. Monomoy's outer rips are still worth a pass on the southwest wind — that wind stacks bait against the elbow and pushes current hard through the cut, and bass have been sitting under the blitzing blues picking off cripples on bucktail and umbrella rig drops.

Black sea bass remain the most dependable structure bite in the whole zone right now. The stretch between Craigville and Osterville has been holding fish consistently over rock and mussel bottom in 20 to 35 feet, and kayak guys working that inshore structure have been doing just as well as the boat fleet — jigs tipped with squid strips or a Gulp swimming mullet on a light jighead, fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide. Fluke, by contrast, are on their expected early-September fade. The doormats have mostly cleared out of the back-bay structure for deeper ocean-side bottom, and while there are still fish to be had around Monomoy's deeper holes, the numbers are thinning fast and this isn't the bite to plan a trip around anymore.

Looking at the next few days: wind stays manageable, tides are building toward the full moon push, and that stronger flow should start tightening up the bait and forcing some decisions out of both the albies and the bass. If the first real cool front of the season slides through behind that moon — which is the thing to watch on the forecast — expect the bluefish to stay locked in, the bass to get more aggressive on the rips as bait concentrates, and a real shot at the bonito at Great Point and the Shoals before Labor Day closes out. Best bet for the next 48 hours: work the ebb at Great Point early for blues and shots at albies, then swing down to Monomoy on the afternoon southwest wind for the rip bite underneath the birds.

reports.headline: Nahant to Deer Island: Bass Holding on Mackerel, Blues Running the Bait Off the Rocks
reports.subhead: The harbor islands are still the safer bet than the open rocks this week, but the first real cool nights are lining up to change that fast.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one or two days this week, the call is the harbor islands first, the North Shore rocks second. That's not a knock on Nahant or Gloucester — it's a read on where the bait is holding tightest right now, and bait is still the whole story in early September. Boston Harbor's islands — Deer Island, Spectacle, the flats off President Roads — are stacking pogies and mackerel on the tide changes, and the bass are staged on them rather than actively blitzing. That's a pattern we flagged last week: the bunker and pogie schools needed to concentrate further before the bass would commit in numbers, and that's exactly the stage we're in now. Water's still sitting warm, low-to-mid 70s inshore, which keeps fish comfortable enough to spread out and feed on their own schedule instead of balling up and busting bait on the surface. The moon builds to full around September 6-7, and that's the mechanism that should start tightening things up — bigger tidal swings, stronger current, bait pinned harder against structure. Until then, this is a mixed, honest bite: good fish around, but you have to find the seam.

The harbor program right now centers on the last two hours of the flood into the top of the ebb around Deer Island and the Nahant flats. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a chunk of pogie fished on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet off the Deer Island drop, has been the most consistent producer for keeper-class bass, with a scattering of fish pushing over 30 inches on the deeper edges where the flat drops into the channel. Light-tackle guys working bucktails — 1 to 1.5 ounce white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom on the last of the ebb — are picking at fish too, but it's not a wide-open bite. You're working for your fish, not covering water blind and expecting them to show up.

Bluefish are the more dependable target basin-wide right now, and that's held true here as well. The warm water that's kept them aggressive up and down the coast all summer hasn't broken yet, and the harbor and North Shore rocks are both giving up blues in the 3-to-6-pound range on any incoming bait push. Nahant's outer rocks and the ledges off Gloucester and Cape Ann have both been holding bluefish tight to structure, chopping up pogies and mackerel schools that get pinned against the rocks on the last of the flood. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything in the half-ounce to two-ounce range worked fast over the top of the school — have been the go-to when the blues are up and feeding visibly. When they're not showing on top, a bucktail bounced along the base of the ledge in 10 to 20 feet has been just as effective, sometimes better, because you're not competing with every other angler casting into the same boil.

Flounder are still around on the harbor flats — Deer Island and the flats off Winthrop have been giving up a few keepers on sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, best on the slower stages of the tide when the current isn't ripping the bait off bottom. It's not a numbers game right now, more a bonus fish while you're anchored up working bass or bait, but worth a rod in the spread if you're set up on the flats anyway.

Cod and haddock are the harder call this week. The deeper ledges off Cape Ann and out toward Stellwagen have produced sporadically, but with water still warm and no major cooling trend through the water column yet, the bottom bite hasn't turned on in a serious way. If you're making the run out there, treat it as a bonus stop rather than the primary plan until nights start cooling consistently — that shift usually shows up in the codfish first once the thermocline starts to break down.

Looking at the next few days: wind and tide look manageable, nothing disruptive on the horizon, and that stability is actually working against a hard blitz trigger — it takes a real push, usually the first legitimate cool front of the season, to jam bait against structure hard enough to set off sustained surface feeding. We don't have that yet. What we do have is a building moon tightening the tides through the weekend, which should concentrate bait further in the harbor and along the North Shore ledges. If you're picking a window, the outgoing tide at Deer Island in the first two hours of light, or the last of the flood at Nahant's outer rocks in the evening, are the two best bets right now. Keep working live bait and bucktails rather than blind-casting for blitzes — this is a stage-and-wait week, not a run-and-gun one. If the first real cool night hits before next weekend, expect that to be the trigger that turns the staged bass into the fall pattern everyone's waiting for, and Plymouth and Duxbury Bay should start lighting up on the same schedule as the bait pushes south.

reports.headline: Monhegan Pollock, Eastern Egg Mackerel, and Bass Still Parked on the Bait
reports.subhead: Warm water is keeping the bay's stripers content to sit on bunker instead of blitzing, but the groundfish and mackerel are making up for it in open water.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty Septembers on this water teach you the same lesson every year before the calendar admits it: the first week of the month always looks like summer and fishes like a question mark. The water's still holding warm out past the islands, the bait's scattered instead of balled up, and the fish know a change is coming before anybody standing on a dock does. That's exactly where Penobscot Bay and the Midcoast sit right now — warm, restless, and not quite ready to tip over into the fall pattern everybody's waiting on.

The warm regime that's carried this whole summer offshore is still sitting on top of Gulf of Maine water, and it's showing up in strange ways — deep-drop swordfish gear working farther north than usual is one sign of it, and closer to home it means the striped bass are staged rather than committed. They're stacked around the river mouths — the Kennebec, the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta — sitting on schools of peanut bunker and pogies without the kind of tightly-wound blitz behavior that shows up once the nights turn cold. We flagged this pattern last week, calling for a gradual slide toward fall structure with no sudden turnover, and that's precisely what the bay's giving back. Nothing dramatic yet. The bass are there, they're just not in a hurry.

The moon's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's worth watching closely over the next several days. Bigger tidal swings mean more current through the river mouths and the thoroughfares, and that current is what eventually organizes scattered bait into something a bass will commit to hard. Best window right now is the last two hours of the ebb at first light — slack water and bright sun just push these fish deeper and less interested. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig off Pemaquid Point and at the mouth of the Damariscotta have been drawing slot fish in the 28 to 34-inch range, and chunk bunker soaked on the bottom near the Sheepscot's ledges is picking off a few bigger stragglers after dark. Topwater at first light off the outer islands near Boothbay has produced some fish too, but it's a short window before the sun gets up and shuts it down.

Bluefish are the one thing that hasn't slowed a bit. Warm water's kept them aggressive and spread wide all summer, and that's held true straight through the last week — we said it would carry through Labor Day week, and the reports off Damariscove and the outer ledges near Boothbay back that up. Diamond jigs and Deadly Dicks worked fast on the retrieve are taking blues in the 3 to 6-pound class, often mixed right in with the mackerel schools, which makes for a busy rod if you're not paying attention to what just ate your jig.

Speaking of mackerel — that's been the most dependable bite in the zone all week. Eastern Egg Rock and the water around the Cuckolds have both had thick schools working the surface most mornings, easy pickings on mackerel trees or small Swedish pimples jigged fast through 15 to 30 feet of water. It's meat-and-potatoes fishing, but it's produced when the bass have made you wait, and it's also filling coolers with fresh bait for anyone planning to soak eels or chunks for stripers that evening.

Groundfish remain the steadiest hand in the deck right now, and that's not changing anytime soon. Pollock have been stacking up and surface-feeding around Monhegan's White Head ledges most mornings on the last of the incoming tide, chasing bait right up into visible boils — a fast-sinking diamond jig worked with a sweeping retrieve through the top thirty feet has been the go-to, and fish in the 8 to 15-pound class aren't uncommon out there this time of year. Deeper in the bay, cod and a scattering of haddock are still holding in the channels east of Isle au Haut and around Matinicus, 150 to 250 feet of water, taken on bait rigs and heavier jigs bounced right off bottom on the tail end of the drift. It's not a numbers fishery the way it was decades back, but for a boat willing to run the distance and fish it slow and patient on the tide change, there's still enough down there to make the trip worthwhile.

Looking at the next several days, the building moon is the thing to watch. As the tidal flow strengthens through the weekend, expect the bait at the river mouths to organize a little tighter, which usually pulls the bass into shorter, more aggressive feeding windows rather than the lazy, spread-out pattern they've shown lately. If the first real cool nights show up in the back half of September like they typically do, that's the trigger that pushes stripers off the bait schools and into blitz behavior along the outer shorelines and river mouths — worth keeping an eye on overnight temperatures heading into next week. Until then, the mackerel and bluefish are the sure thing inshore, and the pollock at Monhegan and the deep channel cod and haddock around Matinicus and Isle au Haut are the better bet if a boat's looking for something with more backbone than a bay full of staged, unhurried stripers.

reports.headline: East end on the 5:41 ebb: bluefish stacked, bass still playing coy
reports.subhead: The moon's building toward full and the current's tightening up the bite windows on both ends of the ditch — the blues are all in, the bass are still feeling it out.
reports.body_markdown:
Max ebb at the east end ran right around 5:41 this week, and for the last ninety minutes of that stage the water off Sandwich was doing exactly what it's supposed to do in early September — stacking bait against the rip and turning bluefish into a chopping machine. That's been the story on both ends of the Canal for the better part of ten days now: the ebb is the tide to fish, the blues are eating everything that moves, and the bass are around in real numbers but still playing the coy game they've been playing since the water sat in the low 70s through August.

We flagged this last week — said the building moon would tighten current strength and sharpen the bite windows through the Canal — and that's exactly what's happened. With the moon pushing toward full on the 6th and 7th, the current at both ends has picked up noticeably off the neap lull from ten days back. Max ebb and max flood are both running harder, the rip lines are holding shape longer instead of collapsing into slop, and that extra push is exactly the kind of current that turns bait-holding water into feeding water. The next 48 to 72 hours should only sharpen that further as the moon tops out.

East end remains the show. The rip off the power plant and the stretch down toward the Sandwich side of the canal mouth have had bluefish stacked on peanut bunker and mackerel schools pushing through on the last two hours of the ebb, right into the top of slack. Boats and shore guys working that window with Ava 27s and 47s, tins like Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters in the 2- to 3-ounce range, and topwater poppers during the last hour of light have had steady action — blues to 8 and 9 pounds, some genuine chopper-class fish mixed in, and that bite has held up better than the bass bite for most of the week. Striped bass are in that same water, but they're not committing the way the blues are. Best luck on bass has come to guys slowing down — bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, bounced along bottom on the last of the ebb, or a tube-and-worm trolled slow through the seam where the rip meets the flat water. Fish have been mostly schoolie-to-mid-20s class, with the occasional better fish, but nobody's calling it a blitz yet.

West end tells a similar story with different scenery. The current seams off Mashnee Island and around Hog Island have been the go-to for guys chasing bass on the flood, particularly the middle two hours when the seam sets up clean and holds bait against the edge instead of blowing it through. Wings Neck and the mouth of Phinneys Harbor have had some quality fluke still coming off sandy bottom on Gulp in white and pink, 3- to 4-inch paddletails on light jigheads, though that bite is thinning out fast the way it does every year this time — doormats are already sliding toward deeper structure outside, and what's left inside is mostly keeper-class fish, not the numbers game July and August gave up. If fluke is the target, the west end drift on the last of the incoming, working slow along the drop where the channel meets the flat, is still worth the trip, just don't expect it to last much past the middle of the month.

Bait-wise, the canal's getting a healthy push of peanut bunker and mackerel through both ends right now, which is exactly what's holding the bluefish so tight to the rips. Striped bass are clearly feeding on that same bait — you can see it in the marks and in the fish that are coming up — but the water hasn't cooled enough yet to flip them from scattered feeders into the kind of tight, aggressive schools that blitz on top. That's consistent with what's happening basin-wide right now: bunker schools building in the bays and sounds to the south still need a real cool-down to trigger that switch, and the Canal usually follows that same clock, just compressed because the current does half the work for the fish that the bays have to do with water temperature alone.

No albacore or bonito reports worth hanging a hat on inside the Canal itself yet — that push is still working its way west through the Sound and Buzzards Bay approaches, and if it reaches the west end mouth in the next week or two, expect it to show first around Wings Neck and the outer edge of Phinneys Harbor where clean water meets the current. Worth keeping small profile epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks in the bag on the off chance a pod shows on the surface near the west end breakwater.

Looking ahead, the building moon through the weekend should keep tightening these bite windows — expect max current speeds a touch stronger each day through the 7th, which means the rip lines will hold their shape longer and the feeding windows around slack will be shorter but more concentrated. If there's only one tide to fish this week, make it the evening ebb at the east end — that's where the bait's thickest and the current's doing the most work. West end guys should target the flood's middle two hours around Mashnee for the better bass shots. If overnight temps start dropping the way the calendar suggests they should, the first real bass commitment of the fall could show up in the Canal within the next week to ten days — right on the heels of whatever breaks loose in the bays to the south.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock on the Slack: Bass Staged on Pogies, Groundfish Holding
reports.subhead: The bay's bait is thickening ahead of the full moon, and the ledges are giving up steady fish to anyone willing to work the tide right.
reports.body_markdown:
Halfway Rock wears its early-September look this week — flat granite standing out of a near-slack tide, gulls working nervous, tight-balled pogie schools off the northeast corner instead of diving hard and committed. That hesitation, more than any single catch, tells you where the bay sits right now. The bait is here and building. The predators know it. But nobody's fully committed to the feed yet, and that's the pattern to understand before you plan your next few days on the water.

Water around the outer islands has held in that comfortable late-summer range, and pogies — menhaden, if you want the textbook name — have been pushing into the bay in thickening pods, staging off Jewell Island, the back side of Peaks, and up toward the mouth of the Presumpscot. Striped bass are stacked on that bait rather than blitzing it, which is exactly what you'd expect with water still carrying summer warmth and the moon still four days from full. We flagged this continuity call a week ago, and it held — the bay's late-summer rhythm carried straight through, with the same ledges fishing the same tide windows they did seven days back. That's useful information: it means the milk run from last week is still the milk run this week.

The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the mechanism worth watching closely. Bigger tidal swings mean more current push across the ledges, which concentrates bait against structure instead of letting it drift loose across open water. When that happens here, the bass stop shadowing pogie schools passively and start working current seams hard — river mouths on the dropping tide, the down-current side of ledges on the last two hours of ebb. If the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, expect the next real uptick in bass aggression to show up right around that full moon push, not before it.

For now, the better bass have been coming off the ledges around Jewell and Cliff Island on live pogies fished under a slip float, or on white and pink soft-plastic swimbaits — 6- to 8-inch paddle tails on a 3/4-ounce jighead — worked slow along the drop-offs on the last hour of the ebb. Fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch range have been the rule, with a scattering of bigger fish pushed up tight to structure at first light before the sun gets on the water. Bluefish have been mixed into the same schools, which is no surprise given how warm and forage-rich the whole coast has run this summer — expect that to stay strong through Labor Day week, with choppers hitting mackerel-imitation jigs and diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve right through the same pogie balls the bass are shadowing.

Groundfish have been the more dependable story of the week, if less dramatic. Halfway Rock continues to hold cod and haddock in 90 to 120 feet on the down-current side, and the bite there has been steady rather than spectacular — diamond jigs and bait-tipped jigs working best on the slack around the tide change, when boats can hold position over structure without fighting a hard drift. Haddock in the 3- to 6-pound range have been coming up consistently on clam-baited hooks fished just off bottom, with the occasional keeper cod mixed in on bigger diamond jigs worked with a slow lift-and-drop. The ledges off Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small have produced similarly — not a stacked bite, but a reliable one for boats willing to fish the tide change patiently rather than drift through it.

Mackerel, which the bay hard back in May, have thinned considerably as a target species — what's left now is mostly forage for the bass and blues rather than a dedicated bite, though small pods still show up on Sabiki rigs around the harbor moorings early in the morning if you need fresh bait for the ledges.

Looking at the next several days, the setup favors patience over aggression. Wind has stayed manageable, which has kept water clarity decent around the outer islands — not gin-clear, but fishable, with enough visibility for the bass to key on bait balls without getting spooked by dirty water. If the forecast holds calm into the weekend, the building tidal push from the approaching full moon should tighten those pogie schools further, and that's when the bass typically stop shadowing and start feeding hard. The window to watch is the two days bracketing the full moon itself — the 6th and 7th — fishing the last two hours of the ebb at river mouths and ledge structure where current concentrates bait.

If there's only one trip in the next few days, start at first light on the down-current side of a ledge like Jewell or the backside of Peaks, working live pogies or large swimbaits through the last of the outgoing water. Keep a jig rod rigged for haddock as a backup if the bass stay quiet — Halfway Rock has been giving up fish reliably enough on the slack that it's a solid fallback rather than a consolation prize. The bay isn't blitzing yet, but the pieces — bait, moon, tide — are lining up the way they usually do right before it does.

reports.headline: Bunker Stack the Bay, Bonito Knock on Napatree's Door
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker are thickening from Sakonnet to Watch Hill and the first bonito have crossed the state line — the albies won't be far behind.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait tells the story on this shore before the fish ever do, and right now the story is bunker. Peanut schools that started the summer scattered and thin along the rocks have thickened into real bodies of bait working Sakonnet Point, Second Beach, and the mouth of the breachways at Charlestown and Weekapaug. Narragansett Bay has been pushing bunker out through the East and West Passages for two weeks now, and that spillover is exactly what's been loading up the water along Newport and Jamestown. Silversides are still in the wash on the calm mornings, and bay anchovies are showing thick enough in the breachway currents that the smallest fish in the food chain are finally worth paying attention to.

We flagged the bonito push last week, said the surge out of Block Island and Point Judith would keep spreading along the shoreline — and that's exactly what's happening. Bonito have crossed into Rhode Island water in real numbers now, working past Point Judith and showing up on the troll off the Sakonnet breakwater and outside Newport Harbor. They're still mostly an outside-the-breachway fish for now, but that westward creep toward Fishers Island Sound and the Race means Napatree and Watch Hill should start seeing them mixed with the bait balls any day. Albies haven't committed yet in this stretch — a few scattered reports of fish showing outside Sakonnet Point, nothing consistent enough to call a push into the breachways. September is when that flips, and with bait this dense, it won't take much.

Water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range, warm enough to keep the striped bass staged rather than blitzing. That's the honest read right now — bass are on the bunker, but they're not organized. Boats working the mouth of the Sakonnet River and the rips off Newport are marking fish under the bait pods but getting more follows than committed strikes, which is a classic late-summer pattern before the water starts to slide. The moon builds to full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the trigger to watch. Tighter tidal flow around the full moon tends to bunch these loose bunker schools into something a striper can actually pin against structure, and that's usually when the first real blitz breaks open on this shore. If the pattern holds like it usually does, look for that within the next week to ten days rather than this weekend.

Bluefish have been the one bite you can set a watch by. Choppers are working peanut bunker and silversides hard off Second Beach, Sachuest Point, and the rocks below Fort Adams, and that's held steady through the warm stretch without any signs of slowing. Bucktails and metal — 1 to 2-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — worked fast through the surface wash are getting hit as soon as they land when the blues are up. Chunked bunker fished on the bottom off the same rocky points is picking up bigger fish for anyone who wants to sit still instead of casting all morning. With bunker density building the way it is, expect the blue bite to carry through Labor Day week without much drop-off.

Fluke are doing what they do this time of year — thinning out of the back stretches. The upper Sakonnet River and the calmer stretches inside Jamestown have gone quiet compared to July, with the better fish sliding out toward deeper structure off Beavertail and the outside grounds near Newport. Anyone still chasing them should be working white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 30 to 40 feet rather than the flats, and expect fewer fish for more effort from here into October.

On the rock structure itself, it's still a scup and bergall show more than a tog bite — green crabs dropped into the cracks around Beavertail, Brenton Point, and the outer ledges at Sakonnet Point are getting picked apart fast by scup and cunner, which is normal for early September before the blackfish really settle onto that structure. Worth scouting now, because once the water starts to slip into the 60s, those same ledges turn over to tog holding tight in the same cracks on the slack tide, and that bite builds through the fall.

Looking at the next few days, wind and tide matter more than anything else on this coast. If it stays light out of the south and southwest, work the breachways — Napatree and Watch Hill first — on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed and concentrated against the rocks and any albies or bonito working the area have current to hunt in. Early morning remains the best window before boat traffic and sun push bait deeper. The bass game right now is patience: work bunker schools with a bucktail or a soft-plastic swim shad worked slow along the edge rather than through the middle, since fish holding under bait tend to peel off the sides rather than commit through open water. If the moon does its usual work and a cool night or two slides in behind it, expect the scattered stripers to organize fast, and the first real blitz of the fall to break open somewhere along this shore within the next week to ten days. Until then, this is a bait-first bite — find the peanut bunker, and everything else follows.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 180 feet: haddock working the mud, cod tight to the gravel edge
reports.subhead: The bottom is doing exactly what it should for early September — the question this week is whether the tuna show early on the ledge or wait for the usual October push.
reports.body_markdown:
One-eighty feet of water on the northern end of Jeffrey's Ledge, soft mud bottom, and the haddock have been sitting right where they're supposed to be for this time of year. That's the read from the fleet this week, and it's holding steady. Move a half mile east onto the gravel patches where the bottom hardens up and the depth comes up into the 130-to-150 range, and that's where the cod have been stacking — not thick, but consistent, which is the more honest way to describe most of this beat's groundfish action right now.

The pattern is textbook late-summer Gulf of Maine. Haddock don't want the hard stuff. They sit on mud and clay bottom where the worms and small crustaceans live, and they'll hold in loose pods that move with the tide rather than camping on one piece of structure. Cod are the opposite — they want the transition zones, gravel-to-boulder edges where bait gets pinned against structure on the drift. Both patterns have been repeating themselves day after day on Jeffrey's, which tells you the water column hasn't been kicked around by much weather lately. Stable conditions mean stable fish behavior, and that's exactly what's been showing up trip after trip.

Platts Bank has been the more interesting stop for boats willing to run the extra distance. The pollock have been sitting up off bottom on the sonar in 20-to-40 feet off the peak, which usually means they're chasing bait suspended mid-water rather than glued to the structure itself. Diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieat through that suspended layer have been outproducing straight bottom bouncing this week — when pollock come up off the rock, you have to meet them where they are instead of fishing the bottom like it's cod.

Tillies Bank has been quieter than Platts, and that's not unusual for early September. The hake bite there tends to wait for evening and the first hour after dark, when they slide up off the mud flats to feed. Boats staying out late with cut bait or squid strips on a two-hook bottom rig in 150-to-180 feet have picked at decent whiting-class hake, but it's not a daytime program right now.

Scantum Basin continues to be the deep-water wild card. The mud there runs deeper than most of the ledge, and the haddock that hold in that basin tend to run a little larger on average — probably because fewer boats bother making the run. Anyone fishing clam or squid on a standard high-low rig in that basin has reported solid average-size fish, though the numbers haven't been eye-popping. It's a quality-over-quantity spot this week.

On the tuna side, there's chatter worth flagging without overselling it. A few boats working the deeper edges off Jeffrey's toward Stellwagen Bank's northern approaches have reported some scattered bluefin interest — nothing like the giant class fish this ledge is known for in October, but enough surface activity and bait balling to suggest warmer water is nosing further into the Gulf of Maine than typical for early September. That lines up with what's been reported from deep-drop swordfish activity pushing further north than usual this year. Whether that warm filament holds through Labor Day week and starts pulling real numbers of giants up onto the ledge early, or fades back south with the first real cool front, is the single biggest question for the next two weeks. Historically the giants don't show in consistent numbers until October, when the mackerel and herring bunch up tight over the ledge and hold there through the fall. Right now it's mackerel schools, not giant bluefin, doing most of the work — solid jigging on small diamond jigs and Sabiki rigs in 60-to-100 feet along the western edge of Jeffrey's has kept bait tanks full for anyone bottom fishing gravel for cod.

Weather-wise, it's been a clean stretch — light winds, moderate swell, water color holding clear enough on the ledge that sight-casting to surface activity has actually been possible on calm mornings. That's a gift this time of year. The moon is building toward full over the next several days, which should tighten up tidal flow on the ledge and could concentrate both bait and groundfish along the sharper edges — worth watching Jeffrey's gravel-to-mud transition zones closer than usual as that current strengthens.

Looking at the next few days, if the wind stays out of the south and southwest like it has been, expect the haddock-on-mud, cod-on-gravel pattern on Jeffrey's to hold without much change. The better bet for anyone chasing something different is the run out to Platts for pollock working that suspended bait layer, or a late trip to Tillies for hake after dark. On the tuna question, there's no reason yet to change the game plan — keep working bait and structure for groundfish, but keep an eye on the ledge's deeper edges toward Stellwagen. If that warm water holds through the week, this could be one of the earlier starts to giant season this beat has seen in a few years. If it breaks down with the first real cool front, it'll be back to the usual October timeline, and there's no sense burning gas chasing a bite that hasn't committed yet.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack Near 9:40: Bonito Thick, Bass Still Ghosting the Bunker
reports.subhead: The Block's bonito run is peaking on schedule while striped bass sit on bait and wait for the moon and cooler nights to push them.
reports.body_markdown:
SW Ledge has been fishing its tide the way it should this time of year — the last hour of the ebb into that 9:30 to 9:50 slack window has been the money stretch, with bonito stacking on top of the structure in 15 to 25 feet as the current eases off and bait gets pinned against the rip line. That window has been consistent enough over the last five days that the charter fleet is setting watches by it instead of guessing. The bonito arrived off the Block right on the calendar this year, and now that westward push everyone expected has them showing at Sandy Point, North Light, and pushing bait around Clay Head on the making tide too — not just the Ledge. We flagged this exact move last week, said the leading edge would build as more fish stacked in behind it, and that's exactly what's happened. The run has thickened, not thinned.

Water's still holding warm out here — low-to-mid 70s inshore, which is part of why the bonito bite has stayed hot while the striped bass side of the ledger has been slower to develop. Bass are around. They're just not committing the way they will in three weeks. Bunker schools are thickening up in Narragansett Bay right now, same story playing out on the LI south shore and Raritan Bay, but the water's still too warm for those schools to tighten into the kind of dense, panicked balls that trigger real blitz behavior. Fish are staged on bait, not attacking it. That changes as the moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th — stronger tidal push should start squeezing those bunker schools, and the first real fall blitz activity in this region is likely within the next week to ten days, not this week.

On the bonito, the fish have been finicky in the way late-summer bonito always get once they've been picked at for a few weeks — they're clearly on micro-bait, probably bay anchovies or tiny silversides, and that's made small-profile presentations outfish the standard metal. Half-ounce and 3/8-ounce Deadly Dick and Hogy epoxy jigs in bone or olive have been the better call over the bigger Point Jude wobblers, worked with a fast, erratic retrieve right through the surface wash where the bait's getting pushed. Fly guys working the North Light rip on the making tide have done well with small Clouser-style patterns in olive-over-white, cast into the boils and stripped fast. The key at SW Ledge specifically is fishing the transition — the last twenty minutes of ebb through slack — because that's when the current stops ripping the bait out of the zone and the bonito can actually pin it against structure instead of chasing it through open water.

Striped bass fishing around the Block has been a mixed bag, which is the honest read. There are fish scattered along the rips off Southwest Ledge and out toward the deeper structure past Block Island, holding on bunker and peanut bunker pushing through, but they're not schooled tight enough yet for a reliable pattern. Jigging bucktails — 2 to 3 ounce, white or chartreuse — dropped to the bottom on the deeper edges of the Ledge on the last of the flood has produced some quality fish in the 20 to 30 pound class, but it's been a "put your time in" bite, not a sure thing. Live-lining bunker off Sandy Point on the outgoing has also worked for the boats willing to soak baits and wait rather than run-and-gun.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going in these waters right now, and that's tracking with what's happening basin-wide — strong reports out of Montauk, the Canal, and Nantucket Sound all point to the same thing, which is bluefish riding the bunker and peanut density hard through Labor Day week. Off Point Judith and around the Block, blues in the 4 to 8 pound class have been mixing right in with the bonito on the same small metal, and when a school of peanuts gets pushed up shallow near Clay Head, both species show up in the same five minutes of surface chaos.

Black sea bass are still holding true to form on the deeper structure around the Block — 60 to 90 feet on the rock piles and the drop-offs off the southwest side — and that bite has stayed steady all summer while fluke has done its predictable early-September fade. Fluke numbers are thinning fast as the doormats abandon the shallower structure for deeper ocean-side water ahead of their fall push, and while there are still a few keeper-class fish coming off the deeper drops, it's not the kind of bite worth planning a whole day around anymore.

Looking at the next few days, the bonito window at SW Ledge should hold through the building moon, with the slack tide timing sliding earlier each day — worth checking a current tide table before running out, since that window moves fast this time of year. The bigger story to watch is the bass. Once the bunker schools in Narragansett Bay tighten up behind this full moon push and the first real cool nights hit, that's when the switch flips from scattered bait-stagers to an honest blitz. Right now, if there's only one trip in the schedule this week, fish the SW Ledge slack for bonito and keep a bucktail rigged for any bass showing along the edges — the blitz isn't here yet, but it's close enough to start paying attention every morning.

reports.headline: Isles of Shoals cod still there for those who look, bluefish own the coast
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles doesn't sound like much until you fish it like a hundred and thirty — groundfish on the ledges, blues everywhere else.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to talk about. That's fine by me — means less pressure on water that fishes like a lot more than it looks on a map. Between the Piscataqua's current lines, the Isles of Shoals humps sitting eight miles offshore, and every rockpile from Odiorne to Great Boars Head, there's enough structure out here to keep a small boat busy through Columbus Day if you're willing to run early and read the tide right. This week proved that out again. Nothing spectacular, nothing to write home about on the striper side, but steady enough groundfish work on the Shoals and a bluefish bite that hasn't quit since August.

Water's still sitting warm for early September, upper 60s to low 70s depending where you check, and that's kept the striper schools loose rather than balled up and blitzing. They're around — bait's around too, pogies pushing into Hampton Harbor and mackerel schools working the mouth of the Piscataqua — but with the water this warm the bass aren't committing hard. We flagged this pattern last week and said not to expect a shift yet, and that's exactly what played out. The moon builds to full over the next couple days, which should tighten the tidal push, and the first real cool nights of the month are the piece still missing. Once nighttime temps start dropping into the 50s, that's when these scattered schools start acting like fall stripers instead of August stripers.
bluefish never got that memo. They've been the most dependable thing on this stretch of coast all week — steady action off Rye Harbor, around the Boars Head rip, and out past White Island at the Shoals, chopping through pogy schools with the same aggression they've shown since the water turned warm. That lines up with what we called last week too — warm water, wide open blues, and no sign of it backing off before Labor Day weekend wraps.

On the groundfish side, the Isles of Shoals are still doing what they do this time of year for the guys willing to make the run. Cod to eight pounds are coming off the ledges around Appledore and the backside of Star Island, mostly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current settles enough to hold bottom with a jig. Diamond jigs and bucktails tipped with squid strips are getting it done in 60 to 90 feet, right on the edges where the rock drops into mud. Haddock have been mixed in on the same drifts, nothing to fill a cooler fast but enough to make the trip worthwhile if you're patient and keep moving the boat rather than sitting on one mark. Mackerel are thick enough around the Shoals and off Odiorne Point that a rig with three or four small jigs can load up in minutes — good for the table, better for bait if you're planning to soak one for a bass or a bluefish afterward.

Stripers are still showing in the Piscataqua, particularly around the bridge pilings and the deeper bends where current stacks bait against structure. Fishing there has been a tide game — the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing are producing the most consistent action, with swimming plugs and soft plastic paddletails worked slow along the seams. Nothing overslot to speak of this week, mostly schoolies and a few keepers mixed in, but enough activity to keep rods bent if you're working the right stage of the tide. Hampton Harbor has been a similar story — pogies pushing in on the flood are drawing bass up into the channel, especially around the inlet mouth and along the marsh edges where current cuts hard against the bank. Live-lined pogies or a big paddletail worked through that seam has been the better bet over blind-casting the flats.

Bluefish continue to be the fish you can count on right now, and that's not changing in the next few days. Look for them anywhere bait is stacking — off Rye Harbor, around the Boars Head rips, and scattered through the Shoals grounds — on cut mackerel, pogy chunks, or metal jigs worked fast through the top of the water column. They're not picky and they're not leaving until the water cools enough to push them south, which by the current trend probably means they stick around through most of September.

Looking at the next several days, the setup favors patience over hero trips. The moon pushing toward full will strengthen the tidal flow, which should help tighten up those loose bunker and pogy schools in the harbor and river systems — that's usually the trigger that gets bass to commit rather than just shadow the bait. If a cool front comes through behind that full moon and knocks nighttime temps down, that's the combination worth watching closely; that's when the first real blitz activity typically breaks open on this coast. Until then, the safer bet is running out to the Shoals early on a calm morning for cod and haddock while the tide's still working the ebb, then working back in toward Rye Harbor or the Piscataqua on the way home for an evening bluefish or striper pass. Keep an eye on wind — anything out of the southeast over 15 knots turns the water off the Shoals into a bad idea fast, and that stretch of open water doesn't forgive a small boat caught out there when it turns.

reports.headline: Blues Won't Quit at Higgins — Bass Stacking on Mackerel at the River Mouths
reports.subhead: Bluefish are chewing through peanut schools from Pine Point to Prouts Neck while stripers hold tight on bait, waiting on the moon and the first cool nights to trigger.
reports.body_markdown:
Higgins Beach threw up another good one Tuesday morning — gulls stacked over a peanut bunker school just outside the second sandbar, blues in the 4-to-8 pound range busting bait so hard it looked like rain on flat water. That's been the story up and down this stretch for going on two weeks now, and we flagged it last week: warm water was going to keep the bluefish aggressive and spread out right through Labor Day, and that's exactly what's happening. Pine Point's had the same show on the morning tides, and Prouts Neck picked up a run of blues Thursday on a light southwest wind that pushed bait tight against the rocks.

The bass are a different animal right now. They're around — thick, even — but they're staged on mackerel and sand eels at the river mouths rather than committing to any real blitz pattern. Biddeford Pool is holding fish on the last two hours of the incoming, same as it always does this time of year, but the bite is more of a mackerel-school-and-pick than a wide-open feed. Water's sitting in that low-to-mid 60s range at the river mouths — Saco, Kennebunk — and that's textbook early fall staging. Bass push up on the flood to work the mackerel pods, then slide back out with the ebb into the deeper cuts off the Pool. It's not blitz behavior yet. It's setup behavior.

The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the piece that should tighten this whole thing up. Bigger tides mean harder current, which means bait gets pinned instead of scattered, which is when Biddeford Pool stops being a pick and starts being the best hour in the state again. If you can only fish one tide this week, make it the incoming at the Pool the evening of the 6th or morning of the 7th — that's when the moon and the bait density are most likely to line up.

On the plugging side, this has been a Danny/darter week at night and a pencil popper/Polaris popper week at first light. The Pool's north side, working the current seam off the sandbar as it floods, has given up bass to 28 inches on black Danny surface swimmers fished slow with a wide wobble — don't rush the retrieve, let the current do the work and just keep tension. Prouts Neck on that southwest wind has been a bucktail-and-popper combo game: white bucktail with a curl-tail trailer worked off the rocks on the down-current side for the bass holding in the wash, then switch to a pencil popper for the bluefish running through on top. Cape Elizabeth's ledges have had sporadic bass activity on the outgoing, mostly smaller fish in the 20-to-26 inch range, taken on green mackerel-pattern SP minnows worked just under the surface.

Mackerel themselves have been thick enough at Wells Harbor and Ogunquit to jig up a bait supply in twenty minutes on small diamond jigs or a mackerel tree — worth doing before you head to the Pool or Pine Point, because live or fresh-dead mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig has been outproducing plugs for the bigger bass holding deeper in the current seams. If you want a shot at something over 30 inches, that's the play: live mackerel, light enough weight to let it swim naturally, fished on the last of the flood tight to structure.

Flounder are winding down fast — a few keeper-sized fish still coming out of Wells Harbor and the back channels at Ogunquit on bloodworms and sandworms fished on the bottom, but that bite is thinning by the day as the water starts its slow slide toward fall temperatures. Cod remain mostly a boat game well offshore this time of year and nothing worth detouring the surf report for.

Looking at the next few days: expect the southwest wind pattern to hold, which keeps Prouts Neck fishable and keeps bait pushed toward the beaches rather than blown offshore. That's good news for the bluefish, which should keep chewing through Labor Day week as the warm water keeps them aggressive — that part of the pattern isn't changing yet. The bigger question is whether the building moon and the first real overnight cooldown — forecasters are watching for the season's first legitimate cool front — start compressing those staged bass schools into the kind of tight, current-driven feeds that make Biddeford Pool's incoming the must-fish window of the whole Maine season. If the nights start dropping into the 50s over the next week, look for that shift to happen fast, and look for it to happen first at the river mouths before it ever shows up on the open beaches. Until then, work the tides, work the mackerel, and don't be surprised if the best fish of your trip comes on the last twenty minutes of a tide you almost gave up on.

reports.headline: 71.2°F on the Bight Buoy, 3.9-Foot Swell: Reef Bite Holds, Canyon Tuna Stay Put
reports.subhead: A sloppy sea state is keeping some boats tied up, but the sea bass on the reef wrecks and the offshore tuna bite both look exactly like they did a week ago — for the same reason.
reports.body_markdown:
71.2 degrees and a 3.9-foot swell running five seconds apart — that's the number off the NY Bight buoy this week, and it's the number that's been setting the schedule more than the calendar has. Five-second period swell is short and stacked, the kind that turns a comfortable ride to the reef wrecks into a washing machine for the first couple hours off the dock. It's not stopping the fleet, but it's editing the trip list. Boats that would normally be splitting time between the inshore reef structure and a run out toward the Klondike lumps have been picking one or the other, not both, and that's thinned out the numbers of trips reporting in on any single piece of bottom.

The tide is building toward full moon, and that's starting to show in current speed on the reef sites — drifts that were lazy two weeks ago are moving with purpose now, which matters for how much lead you're carrying on bucktails and how fast bait spins on the way down. Water color inshore has stayed reasonably clean given the wind, but there's enough push on the swell that anyone running structure inside 20 fathoms should expect some turbidity on the bottom third of the water column, especially right after a blow.

We flagged this a week ago — said the warm filament sitting on the canyon edges would keep the offshore tuna and billfish bite intact as long as nothing tropical came through the western Atlantic, and that call has held. Nothing in the tropics has pushed into this stretch of the Atlantic, and the warm water sitting off the canyon-adjacent grounds hasn't budged. That's kept the deep-water side of this beat productive on schedule, and it's the single biggest reason boats willing to run the extra distance are still finding tuna in the same general water they were finding them in ten days ago. The threat is still the same one we named then — a tropical system anywhere in the western basin would be the thing that ends this, not a cold snap or a moon phase.

Closer to the beach, the story is the reef and wreck network doing what it typically does in early September — which is to say, still holding black sea bass, but with the bite going mixed rather than steady depending on which piece of structure you're on and what stage of tide you hit it. Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef have both been fishable between weather windows, and the pattern on both has been the same one that's worked all summer on this stretch of bottom: Gulp or squid strips on a double-hook bottom rig, dropped tight to the high relief pieces on the up-current side, with enough weight to hold bottom against the building tide without dragging off the wreck entirely. The keeper-size fish have been coming from the tighter structure — the actual wreck iron and reef balls, not the open sand between pieces — and that's typical for this time of year as the bigger sea bass tuck into the highest relief they can find ahead of the fall push.

Shrewsbury Rocks and the Triple Wrecks have seen less traffic this week simply because of the ride, but the boats that have made it out are reporting the same story — decent numbers of sea bass in the 12 to 15-inch range mixed with plenty of shorts that need throwing back, and the occasional better fish coming off bucktails tipped with squid worked slow along bottom rather than bounced. Nobody's calling it a banner week on the inshore structure, and it wouldn't be honest to say otherwise — the bite is there, but it's a tide-and-timing game right now, not a wide-open one. Best window on most of these sites has been the last two hours of the incoming, when the current slows enough to hold bottom with reasonable weight but still moves enough to keep bait scent working.

Mahi have gone quiet on the pot lines that were holding fish through midsummer, which tracks with the calendar — that pattern typically winds down through late August into September as the pot buoys lose their thermal edge and the dolphin move on. Nothing wrong with checking floating structure on the way out if you're already running past it, but it's not worth building a trip around right now.

Farther out, the Klondike and Barnegat Ridge remain the pieces of bottom worth knowing the numbers to heading into fall — both hold bait and structure that draw tuna through this stretch as the season turns, and both are the kind of grounds where a logged waypoint two decades old still means something. Right now they're context more than confirmed action; the real heat is still out on the canyon-adjacent water where the warm filament sits.

Looking ahead, the moon keeps building toward full over the next several days, which should keep tightening up current on the reef structure and could either sharpen the sea bass bite or push it into shorter, more defined windows depending on how hard the tide runs. If the swell backs off even a foot, that's the window to get back out to Shrewsbury Rocks and the Triple Wrecks before the water starts its seasonal cooldown. Offshore, the call stays the same as it's been — as long as that warm water holds and nothing spins up in the tropics, the tuna and billfish bite on the canyon edges should keep running on the same clock it's been on all month.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Pile Into Oyster Creek — Blues Stay Steady, Fluke Fade at Double Creek
reports.subhead: The bait's building faster than the stripers are willing to commit, but bluefish, blowfish, and the last of the fluke are keeping the fleet busy from Barnegat Light to Tices Shoal.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty years back I was mate on a Point Pleasant boat the first week of September, and the skipper pointed out over the transom at a school of peanut bunker so thick it looked like the water had grown skin. He told me, "Gus, when they pile in like that before the first cold snap, mark the date — the bass show up right behind them, but not till the water tells them it's time." That lesson has held up every September since, and it's exactly what's playing out on Barnegat Bay right now. The bunker are here, thick as I've seen them in years, but the water hasn't given the signal yet.

We're sitting with bay temps still hanging in the low-to-mid 70s, which is plenty warm for stripers to stage on bait without committing to a real blitz. Bunker schools have been thickening up from the mouth of Toms River down through Oyster Creek and into the deeper stretch by Double Creek Channel, and every mate on the dock has a story about bass shadowing those schools without ever breaking the surface. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the bait needed to concentrate further before the bass would commit in blitz numbers, and that's precisely what's unfolding. The moon builds to full on the 6th and 7th, which is going to tighten that tidal flow and push those bunker schools into tighter, more nervous balls. That's the trigger everybody's waiting on. It just hasn't tripped yet.

Fluke are doing what fluke do this time of year — thinning out of the back bay as the bigger, egg-heavy females start their slide toward the inlet and the ocean-side structure. Double Creek Channel is still giving up keepers, but the numbers are down from where they were in July and August. The better drifts have been on the last two hours of the outgoing, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along the channel edges where the current cuts hard against the mud. A few boats working the deeper water off Barnegat Light — down in that 20 to 25 foot range near the inlet rocks — have found a better grade of fish, some pushing 4 and 5 pounds, staged there ahead of their run out through the inlet. If you want fluke this week, fish early and fish the deeper structure. The shallow grass flats that carried the summer bite are mostly picked over now.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and that's held true basin-wide through the warm water. Snapper blues are thick in the coves and marina basins from Forked River down to Manahawkin, and the adult blues have been chopping up peanut bunker pods around Tices Shoal and along the surf at Island Beach State Park. Small metal — half-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked fast through the froth has been the ticket, along with poppers on the surface when the blues are actively feeding on top, usually the first hour of light or the last hour before dark. This bite should hold right through Labor Day week as long as the bait stays put, and there's no reason to think it won't.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around on the sandy bottom stretches near Barnegat Light and along the edges of the channel markers south of Waretown, working bloodworm and squid strips on high-low rigs with small hooks. It's a steady, unspectacular bite — good for a family afternoon, not the kind of thing that fills a cooler fast, but reliable if you've got the patience for it.

As for weakfish, the sedges are quiet right now. That's a spring pattern here on Barnegat Bay, and by early September those fish have long since slid out past the inlet or scattered into deeper holes where nobody's really targeting them. If you're chasing weakfish memories, mark your calendar for May and put this week's effort into the bunker-and-blues game instead.

Looking at the next several days, the wind pattern and tide setup favor working the early morning outgoing at Double Creek for what fluke remain, then shifting over to Tices Shoal or the Island Beach surf for blues once the sun gets up and the bait starts moving. The real story to watch is whether we get any kind of overnight cooldown before the weekend. If nighttime temps start dropping even a few degrees, combined with that building moon tightening the bait, this is the week the first real striper activity could break loose inside the bay — probably starting as scattered surface swirls around the bunker schools near Oyster Creek and Toms River before it turns into anything you'd call a blitz. Until that front shows up, the smart play is fishing the edges where bait and current meet, staying mobile, and not wasting a whole tide sitting on water that looked good yesterday but has already emptied out today. The bay's setting up for something — it just hasn't decided to show its hand yet.

reports.headline: Little Egg reshapes on the moving sand — peanut bunker pull the first bonito, fluke slide off the bar
reports.subhead: The inlet cut is throwing new structure just as peanut schools show, and the back bay doormats are already gone to the ocean side.
reports.body_markdown:
The sandbar off the south end of Holgate has moved again.
