Anyone who's run a drone over that stretch in the last ten days can see it — the outer bar that held through most of August has slid west and pinched down, and there's a new gut forming on the inside edge that's dumping current straight into the wash on the back half of the ebb. That kind of reshuffle usually means one thing this time of year: it's grabbing peanut bunker and holding them against the beach, and that's exactly what showed up this week.

We flagged this last week — said with bonito and albies already working the coast north and south of LBI, this stretch was a good bet to light up within the week — and that's more or less how it played out. Scattered false albacore and a few bonito have been showing in the wash off Holgate and around the Little Egg Inlet rip on the last two hours of the outgoing, chasing peanut bunker that are getting pushed and squeezed by the new structure. It's not a blitz yet. It's flashes — a school comes through on the moving current, blows up for five or ten minutes, then goes quiet. Anyone throwing small — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Hogy epoxy jigs, or 3-inch Albie Snax on light spinning gear — has had shots. The window is tight and it's tide-dependent: the last two hours of the ebb through the start of the new flood at Little Egg has been the best of it, when the current is ripping hardest through that reshaped cut.

Bluefish are the more dependable player right now. They're mixing right into those same peanut bunker schools at the inlet mouth and along the Barnegat Light jetty rocks, and they'll eat almost anything metal — Ava jigs, Kastmasters, tin squids — worked through the rip on a moving tide. That consistency tracks with what's been happening basin-wide; warm water has kept blues aggressive and spread out all summer, and there's no sign of that changing before Labor Day weekend closes out.

Fluke is the other half of the story, and it's not a good-news half. Back bay fluke fishing on this stretch — Great Bay, the Mullica flats, the deeper holes off Graveling Point — is thinning out fast, right on the seasonal schedule. Water in the back is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, warm enough that the bigger fish have already started sliding out through Little Egg Inlet toward ocean-side structure. If you want a shot at a quality doormat right now, the better play is the deeper edges outside the inlet — the humps and hard bottom off Beach Haven and the drop-offs along the outer bar — rather than the bay itself. Bucktails tipped with Gulp in white or chartreuse, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 35 feet, are still producing, but the numbers game inside the bay is over for the season.

Striped bass are the fish everyone's asking about, and the honest answer is: not yet, but soon. Bunker schools are stacking up in the bigger staging areas to our north — Raritan Bay, the south shore beaches, up into Narragansett Bay — and that's the trigger everyone's watching. Locally, there's bass mixed in around bait pods staged off the inlet and in the deeper channel edges of Little Egg, but they're not committing to blitz behavior. Water's still carrying enough late-summer warmth to keep them scattered and non-committal rather than stacked and aggressive. The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should tighten tidal flow and start squeezing those loose bait schools into something more concentrated. That's usually the ingredient that flips the switch. If the first real cool front of the season lines up with that tide push in the next week to ten days, expect the first legitimate blitz activity to break — and when it does on this stretch, it'll likely start in the surf at Holgate and the deeper edges of Little Egg Inlet before it shows up anywhere in the back bay.

Worth watching alongside all of this: the finger mullet are starting to stage in the back creeks off the Mullica and around Graveling Point, which is the first real marker of the fall mullet run building. It's early — the heavy push usually doesn't show until the back half of September — but the bait's there, and once it starts moving out through Little Egg on the outgoing tides, that's historically when the bass bite in the surf really turns over for real. Rig accordingly: keep a bag with peanut bunker imitations for the albie/bonito window, tins for the blues, and start setting aside some bunker-profile swimmers and darters for when that mullet push gets underway.

If there's only one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of flood at Little Egg Inlet — that's where the new cut is concentrating bait, and it's the window that's produced the most consistent action on bonito, albies, and blues alike. Keep the plug bag light and organized, because these are fast-moving, tide-triggered windows, not all-day soaks.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues to 9 Pounds, Bass Still Ghosting the Bunker
reports.subhead: The jetty crowd is feeding on bluefish while everyone waits for the bunker schools to tip over into the first real striper blitz.
reports.body_markdown:
There were nine guys on the Manasquan Inlet south jetty an hour before sunrise Tuesday, and by the time the sky went from black to gray, at least six of them had a bluefish thrashing at their feet. Ava 27s with green tubes, a couple of white bucktails, one guy working a Yo-Zuri popper like he was still mad at it — didn't matter much what was tied on, the blues were stacked on the last of the outgoing and they weren't picky. That's been the story on this stretch for two weeks now, and it's not changing this week either.

Here's the read: bunker are thick from Sea Bright down through Belmar, pushed tight against the beach and piling into the inlets on the tide changes, and bluefish have been all over them — slashing, cutting bait in half, the whole show. Stripers are a different matter. They're in the neighborhood, no question, showing as marks under the bigger bunker pods and occasionally peeling one off at night, but the water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range that keeps big bass lazy and non-committal instead of aggressive. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the blues and the fluke would carry the load while cooler nights held the real striper trigger back — and that's precisely how it's played out. Nothing wrong with that call holding up, but it also means patience is still the name of the game for anyone chasing linesides.

The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the piece that matters most right now. Bigger tides mean more water moving through Shark River and Manasquan inlets, which tightens up those loose bunker schools and usually forces the issue. Once you get a night or two of genuinely cooler air behind a front, that's when this thing tips — Raritan Bay and the LI south shore are flagged as the most likely first triggers for a real fall blitz, and this stretch from Sea Bright to Manasquan sits right in the pipeline for that same bait to slide south. It's a matter of when, not if, but nobody should be planning a Saturday around a blitz that hasn't shown up yet.

Bluefish remain the sure thing. Sea Bright rocks have been holding fish on the first two hours of the incoming, with the jetty regulars doing well on bunker spoons and 3-ounce Ava jigs bounced through the wash. Asbury Park's jetties have given up blues in the 4-to-6-pound range on chunked bunker fished on a fish-finder rig in the trough, best in that gray hour before full light. Spring Lake's rock piles have been more hit-or-miss — good one morning, dead the next — which tracks with how scattered these bunker pods still are along the beach. Belmar's been steady on poppers worked over visible bait during the last two hours of the ebb; when the pogies bunch up tight against the jetty rocks, that's your window, and it usually closes fast once the tide slacks.

Fluke fishing is winding down the way it always does this time of year, and there's no sugarcoating that. The back-bay and inlet fish have mostly cleared out for deeper ocean structure ahead of the fall push south. Shark River Inlet is still giving up keeper-class fish on the last of the outgoing, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets along the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, but the numbers are down noticeably from three weeks ago. Manasquan Inlet's channel has produced a few decent fish drifting the deeper water off the Coast Guard station on the incoming, but this is closing-window fishing now, not a bite to build a trip around.

Blackfish season doesn't open here until October, so that's still a few weeks off, and porgies have been a quiet, reliable snack fishery off the Belmar and Manasquan Inlet jetties on bloodworms and clam for anyone bored between blitzes — nothing to write home about, but good for a bucket if the kids are along. No albie signs yet in this stretch; that push is still working its way west from the Rhode Island side and hasn't shown teeth down here.

Looking at the next several days, expect more of the same pattern that's held all week — bluefish active on the tide changes at the usual jetty spots, fluke thinning out but still catchable if you hit the right channel structure, and stripers staying non-committal until the water temperature drops a real notch. If there's only one window worth planning around, it's dawn on the building tide around the full moon — the extra water movement should concentrate bait harder against the rocks at Sea Bright and Manasquan, and that's exactly the kind of setup that's tipped bass into feeding mode in past Septembers when the bunker get squeezed into a tight current seam. Keep an eye on the overnight temperatures over the next week; the first real cool front is the trigger everyone up and down this beach is waiting on, and when it comes through, the jetty country from Sea Bright to Manasquan is as good a bet as anywhere on the coast for the first real blitz of the fall.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips picky, weakfish carrying the bay, first albies knocking on the door
reports.subhead: Fluke are sliding off the flats toward structure, the drum run is long gone, and there's early word of bonito working the beach south of us.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the week: C-plus on the ocean side, B-minus in the bay. That's about where early September usually sits around here, and this year's tracking to form. The rips have been picky — not dead, but you've got to work the tide stage right or you're soaking bait for nothing. Delaware Bay's carrying the week on the back of a strong weakfish bite that nobody's talking about loud enough.

Here's the read. Water in Delaware Bay is sitting in the mid-70s, which is warm enough to keep weakfish and kingfish active in the back bay but not warm enough to trigger any kind of aggressive feed on the ocean side. That's the story of this whole stretch — everything's a half-step slow because the water hasn't turned over yet. The building moon toward full on the 6th and 7th is going to tighten up bait schools everywhere from here to Raritan Bay, and when that happens the striper bite that's been scattered and non-committal all week should start to organize. It's not blitzing yet. Bunker and peanut bunker are thick around the reef sites and holding bluefish hard, but the bass are still staged on bait rather than actively working it over. IF the moon does what moons do this time of year and the tide flow picks up behind it, look for the first real push of activity within the next week to ten days, not this weekend.

We flagged this back at the end of August — said to keep an eye on the rips for bonito and false albacore working down the beach from the central Shore, and that's exactly what's starting to show. Nothing stacked yet off Cape May Point, but there's enough warm water sitting in this zone that it's a logical next landing spot, and a few scattered sightings off the Wildwood side back that up. Worth having a small metal rigged and ready — half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Got-Cha plug — if you're out on the rips this week and see any nervous water or diving birds working bait on the surface. Don't go looking for a blitz. Go looking for a window.

On the fluke side, the story is exactly what it should be for this time of year: the doormats are done with the back bays. They're pulling off the flats and sliding toward structure — the Wildwood ridge and the deeper edges of the rips — ahead of their move offshore. If you want a shot at a legit fish over four pounds, that's where to put your bucktail, not in the skinny stuff. Six-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a three-quarter-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb, has been the combination producing quality fish rather than just numbers. Numbers are thinning out fast across the whole shore, so don't expect a fifteen-fish day. Expect a couple of good ones if you're patient and fish the structure right.

Hereford Inlet has been steady, not spectacular. The current there is doing what it always does this time of year — pushing bait through the cut and holding bluefish tight to the edges on both the incoming and the first two hours of the outgoing. Bunker chunks or peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig, fished tight to the jetty rocks, has been the play. Cobia have shown up occasionally around the reef sites where the anchovies are thick — not a fishery you plan a trip around, but if you're bottom fishing bunker chunks near structure and something bulldogs off with your rod tip buried, don't be shocked.

Down in Delaware Bay, weakfish are the real story right now. Fortescue and the mud flats up toward Brandywine Shoal are holding fish on the drop of the tide, and they're eating shedder crab and Fishbites in the mid-70s water without much hesitation. Kingfish are mixed in on the same bottom, which makes for a nice change of pace if the weakfish go quiet for a stretch. As for black drum — that run's done. Won't see it again until May, and anybody telling you different this time of year is selling something.

Triggerfish have been showing around the rocks and wreck structure off the Cape May side, typical late-summer pattern when the water's warm and clean. Small pieces of clam on a light jig head, dropped right to structure, is the way to pick them off if you've got the patience for it.

Looking ahead: expect the rips to stay picky through the weekend unless that moon-driven tide flow kicks the bait density up a notch. The better bet for the next few days is the bay side — weakfish on the drop tide out of Fortescue, fluke pushed to structure on the ocean side, and bluefish still reliable around the reef sites wherever the peanut bunker are stacked. If there's only one window to fish this week, make it the last two hours of the outgoing at the rips or the Wildwood ridge, and keep a rigged metal rod on deck just in case that albie push finally makes the turn into Cape May water. It's close. It's just not here yet.

reports.headline: Bunker Stacking the Bay: Blues Feasting, Bass Still Staged, Fluke Thinning Fast
reports.subhead: The bait's here in numbers we called last week — now it's a waiting game for the water to cool enough to flip the switch.
reports.body_markdown:
This week the smart play is to work the bunker schools where they're thickest — the flats off Keyport running down toward Flynn's Knoll — and treat anything with fins under them as a bonus, not a guarantee. The bait's been piling in for two weeks straight, exactly the setup we flagged last week when the schools first started showing density in the bay. That call is holding: bunker are stacked thick from Keyport Flats out past Flynn's Knoll and around toward Romer Shoal, and the bluefish have found every pod of them. What hasn't happened yet is the full striper commitment, and the reason is simple — the water's still sitting in the low-to-mid 70s. That's warm enough to keep bass scattered and picky, hitting under the bait rather than exploding through it.

The moon is the thing to watch here. We're building toward full around September 6-7, and that means bigger tidal swings starting this weekend into early next week. More water moving through Chapel Hill and the reach off the Highlands will start squeezing these loose bunker schools into tighter, more nervous balls — and tighter bait means predators start feeding with less hesitation. If the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, the first real blitz activity in this bay is more likely to break in the next week to ten days than this weekend, but the pieces are lining up fast. Keep gear rigged and ready, because when this bay flips from staged to committed, it can happen inside of one tide.

Bluefish are the dependable story right now, and dock talk up and down the Amboy and Keyport waterfront backs that up — this is the most consistent bite in the system. Snag-and-drop off live bunker is producing chopper blues to 8-10 pounds around Flynn's Knoll and the deeper edge off Romer Shoal, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the current stacks bait against the shoal itself. Diamond jigs, half-ounce to two-ounce depending on the drift speed, worked with a jigging motion through the middle of the bait balls, are also connecting well for boats not wanting to mess with snagging gear. If you're marking bait on the sounder in 15 to 25 feet anywhere between the Knoll and the Hook, there's a good chance blues are underneath it.

Stripers are there, but call this a staged bite, not a blitz. The fish are sitting under and around the bunker pods rather than working through them, which means the best presentations are ones that put bait right in their face rather than counting on a surface eruption to find them. Bunker chunks fished on fish-finder rigs, 3-ounce sinkers, right along the bottom edges of the Chapel Hill Channel and around the mouth of the Navesink have been picking off keeper-class bass in the 26 to 32 inch range, mostly on the tail end of the outgoing when the current slows enough for the chunks to sit still. Live bunker on a circle hook, drifted just off the bottom near the Knoll on slack tide into the start of the flood, has also been worth the trouble for boats patient enough to wait out slow bites. The Shrewsbury and Navesink rivers are both holding bait and should be on the list for evening trips — weakfish have been mixed in on the dusk bite in the deeper holes off the Highlands side, though numbers are light and this is more a bonus fish than a target right now.

Fluke are winding down, and this is the part of the report where honesty matters more than hype. The doormat run through the back bays and inlet structure is basically over for the season — those big females have already started sliding out toward ocean-side structure ahead of the fall migration, and the numbers left in the bay are thinning fast. That said, there's still quality fish being pulled off the channel edges for anglere willing to work them properly. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where Keyport Flats spills into the main channel, in 20 to 30 feet of water on the outgoing tide, are still turning up fish in the 3 to 5 pound range. It's not the volume bite of June and July anymore — treat every keeper fluke this week as a good one, because the window on numbers is closing.

Looking at the next few days: expect winds and tides to behave close to what we've seen, with the building moon steadily increasing current strength through the weekend. That's good news for concentrating bait and bad news for anyone hoping for a lazy, easy drift — moving water is going to be the theme. If you only have one window this week, fish the last two hours of the incoming around Flynn's Knoll or Romer Shoal, when the tide is pushing hardest and the bait gets pinned against structure. That's where the blues are most reliable and where the staged bass are most likely to finally commit. Keep an eye on overnight air temps — the first real cool front of September is the piece still missing, and once that shows up alongside this building moon, this bay has the ingredients to go from a bait-and-blues story to a genuine fall bass blitz in short order.

reports.headline: Conimicut on the ebb: bunker stacking thick, bass still holding their cards
reports.subhead: The bait's arrived in force from Conimicut to Rocky Point, but the stripers are staged, not blitzing — yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk the piers off the Providence River this week and you can't miss it — bunker balled up thick enough to shadow the bottom, from the flats off Conimicut Point down through Greenwich Bay and around Nyatt Point. Guys working the bridges are seeing peanut bunker pushed up against the pilings on the last of the ebb, and there's talk up and down the docks that this is the heaviest bait has looked in the upper bay since the herring run cleared out of Buckeye Brook back in the spring. That's a different bite trigger than herring — this is bunker season, and it's the one that sets up the fall run every year.

The water hasn't cooled off enough to flip the switch yet. Numbers coming out of the Sound side — Kings Point running near 71, New London closer to 69 — line up with what the bay's holding right now, and that's still warm enough to keep stripers content to sit on the bait instead of running it down on top. We flagged this pattern building last week, said the bay's bunker schools were thickening up the same way they were in Raritan Bay and along the LI south shore, and here we are — the bait's arrived, but the blitz hasn't tripped off yet. That's the honest read. Anybody telling you the bay's exploding right now is getting ahead of the calendar.

What's going to change that is the moon. It's building toward full over the next couple days, and that means more water moving through the bay on every tide — Conimicut, the East Passage, the flats off Rocky Point are all going to see stronger current than they have in weeks. Stronger current concentrates bait. Concentrated bait is what turns staged bass into committed bass. If there's a cool night or two mixed in behind that moon, even better — that's usually the spark. Right now it's a matter of days, not weeks, before this tightens up into real surface activity somewhere in the bay. Conimicut Point and the mouth of Greenwich Bay are the first places worth checking when it does.

In the meantime, the fishing that's actually happening is solid if you work it right. Striped bass are there, they're just not stupid about it. The better bite has been on the last two hours of the ebb at Conimicut, working bucktails — half-ounce to an ounce, white or chartreuse — bounced along the bottom where the current pulls off the point into deeper water. Guys live-lining bunker off Nyatt Point on wire or a simple fish-finder rig have been picking off keeper-class bass in the 28 to 34-inch range on the front of the incoming, right where the current stacks against the rip. Snag-and-drop with a bunker on a treble is still the most reliable way to connect when the schools are balled tight and not chasing anything — snag one, let it flutter down, and hang on.

Fluke are on their way out of the upper bay, and that's right on schedule for early September. The back-bay numbers around Greenwich Bay and the Providence River flats have thinned out fast over the past two weeks as the bigger fish slide toward deeper structure down toward Prudence Island and out past the East Passage channel edges. There are still keeper fish being picked off drifting Gulp on bucktails in 20 to 30 feet along the channel drop-offs, but it's not the numbers game it was in July. If fluke's the target, the next couple weeks are the window before they clear out of the bay entirely for ocean-side structure.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going in the bay right now, and that tracks with what's happening basin-wide — blues are chewing hard wherever bunker sits, and the bay's no exception. Rocky Point and the rips off Nyatt Point have had steady action on bunker spoons and topwater poppers worked through the peanut bunker schools, especially on the tide change when the bait gets pinned against structure. These aren't giants, mostly 3 to 6 pounds, but they're aggressive and they're consistent, which is more than you can say for the stripers right now.

Scup are stacked on the rocky ledges the way they always are this time of year — around the Nyatt Point rocks and the drop-offs near Prudence Island, bloodworms or squid strips on a simple high-low rig near bottom on the last of the flood has been steady. Black sea bass are holding on the deeper structure around Prudence, still worth a stop if you're passing through with a few clam-baited jigs, though that bite's better suited to a mixed bag trip than a target run at this point in the season.

Looking ahead, the next several days are about watching the moon build and keeping an eye on the overnight air. If a real cool front slides through behind this full moon, the upper bay could tip into its first legitimate blitz window within the week to ten days — that's the pattern this setup usually follows. Until then, work the tide changes at Conimicut and Nyatt Point, stick with bunker imitations and live bait over anything flashy, and don't be surprised if the bass stay quiet on top even while they're feeding hard underneath. That's exactly what staged fish on heavy bait look like right before they commit.

reports.headline: Where did the fluke go? Ocean structure, and why your back-bay drops are coming up empty
reports.subhead: Doormats are pushing offshore ahead of the fall run, but the inlets are paying off in albies, bonito, and blues for anyone willing to switch gears.
reports.body_markdown:
Why are the fluke drops that produced all summer suddenly quiet? That's the question coming across the counter this week, and it's a fair one, because the sod banks behind Absecon and the deeper holes off Great Egg were holding fish through mid-August. The answer is the calendar. Early September is when doormat-class fluke abandon the back bay for ocean-side structure — reef sites, wrecks, and the deeper bars off Ocean City and Townsends Inlet — and that shift is happening on schedule this year. You'll still find keeper fluke, but the numbers game that defined July and August is over in the bay. If you want fluke this week, fish the structure, not the flats.

What's replacing that program is a genuinely strong inshore migration bite. Surf temps have held in the 73 to 75-degree range along the beachfront, and that warmth has kept false albacore and bonito working peanut bunker pods from Brigantine down through Sea Isle and into Townsends Inlet. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the warm filament pushing albies and bonito into Rhode Island waters would widen the window down the Jersey coast — and that's exactly what's playing out. The bite isn't guesswork anymore; it's showing up at the inlets on the right tide stage, consistently enough that the tackle counter is selling out of small metal by Thursday.

Striped bass are a different story, and it's worth being straight about it. Bunker schools are building in the back bays and along the beachfront, but with water still sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, the bass are staged on that bait rather than committing to real blitz behavior. That matches what the moon is telling us — we're building toward full around September 6-7, and a fuller moon means stronger tidal push, which is usually the mechanism that tightens scattered bait into a target bass can actually work efficiently. Until that happens, striper fishing in this zone is a stealth game: small numbers, mostly at first light, mostly on bait imitations worked slow along current seams rather than anything resembling a top-water blitz.

The albie and bonito bite is best worked on the outgoing tide at Absecon Inlet, particularly the last two hours of the ebb when peanut bunker get pushed out of the back channels and stack against the jetty rocks. Half-ounce epoxy jigs in bunker or silverside patterns, and small Deadly Dicks, are the go-to — fast retrieve, no hesitation, because these fish are chasing, not inspecting. Great Egg Inlet is fishing the same way off the Longport side, with the deeper cut holding fish on the last of the ebb into the first hour of the new flood. Townsends Inlet has been more of a bonito show than albie, with fish showing tight to the jetty rocks on calm mornings — small profile metal, 1/2 to 3/4 ounce, cast right up against the rocks and worked back with a steady jigging motion.

Bluefish remain the most dependable bite in the zone right now, and that's holding true to what warm water has been doing basin-wide all summer. Cocktail blues in the 2 to 4-pound range are mixing right in with the albie and bonito schools at all four inlets — Absecon, Great Egg, Townsends, and the surf off Stone Harbor — chewing through peanut bunker pods with the same aggression that's been consistent since July. If metal isn't producing on a given tide, a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig soaking in the wash off Ocean City or Stone Harbor beach will pick up blues reliably, especially in the two hours around high tide when bait gets pushed tight to the beach.

Weakfish have been a minor but real presence in the deeper holes of the back bay — Absecon Channel and the Great Egg back bay both giving up a few fish in the 16 to 20-inch class on Gulp swimming mullets fished on light jigheads, drifted slow along the channel edges on the last of the outgoing. Kingfish are still working the surf troughs at Ocean City and Sea Isle on bloodworm and Fishbites, a steady but modest bite typical for this point in the season. Triggerfish, when they show, are turning up around the inlet jetty structure and pilings at Absecon and Townsends — bits of clam or crab fished tight to the rocks will find them, though this remains an incidental catch rather than a target species most days.

Looking ahead, the next 48 to 72 hours should mirror what's already working: strong albie and bonito action at the inlets on the outgoing tide, steady bluefish, and striped bass that stay staged on bait rather than committed until that building moon tightens the bunker schools further. If a real cool front pushes through in the next week to ten days — and there's reason to think one is coming as we move deeper into September — that's the trigger that should finally break the first legitimate fall blitz open somewhere along this beachfront. Until then, the smart plan is simple: fish the inlets on the ebb for albies and bonito, work ocean structure for fluke, and treat any bass you find as a bonus rather than the main event.

reports.headline: The Race Running 4-Plus Knots: Bonito Push In, Bass Still Sitting on Bait
reports.subhead: Building tides ahead of the full moon are loading up Valiant Rock and Plum Gut while stripers wait for the bunker to bunch.
reports.body_markdown:
Four-point-two knots on the peak ebb through the Race this week, and climbing. That's not a guess — that's what the tide tables are showing as the moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and it's the number that matters most right now for anyone running gear through Valiant Rock or dropping into Plum Gut. Bigger tides mean harder current, harder current means tighter bait, and tighter bait is exactly what this zone has been missing for the last two weeks. The slack windows are getting shorter too — figure a 15 to 20 minute true slack at Valiant Rock on the last of the ebb, usually sliding into early-to-mid afternoon this week, and a similar short window on the front of the flood before the rip builds back up. That's your work zone. Miss it by half an hour either way and you're fighting current that'll sweep a bucktail sideways before it ever gets down.

The bigger regional story is the bonito. They've been stacking at Block Island and Point Judith for weeks, and the push west is now showing up in real numbers — Fishers Island Sound, the eastern approaches to the Race, and pockets around Little Gull and Great Gull Island. Water's cooperating: New London is holding around 69.4°F, Kings Point over in the western Sound is up near 70.9, and that gradient is exactly the kind of setup that funnels bait and predators together as they move down-Sound. The catch is that a lot of these bonito are locked onto micro-bait — bay anchovies, tiny silversides — and they're being fussy about it. Standard 2-ounce metals are getting looked at and refused more than they're getting bit. The boats doing damage are downsizing hard: quarter-ounce and 3/8-ounce epoxy jigs in the Gut, worked on 20-pound fluoro, fast retrieve with a pause. Same story with false albacore mixed into the same schools — they're keying on the same micro-bait, and the small profile stuff is out-fishing anything flashy two or three to one right now.

Striped bass are the tougher conversation. The bass are here, they're just not committed yet. Bunker schools are thickening up in Raritan Bay, the LI south shore, and Narragansett Bay, but the water's still warm enough — low-to-mid 70s in a lot of those staging areas — to keep those schools loose and the bass non-committal instead of blitzing on top. We flagged this exact pattern last week: said the trigger was bait density, and that once those bunker schools tightened up under a building moon, bass would start committing in blitz numbers within a week or two. That hasn't broken yet, but the ingredients are lining up fast, and the full moon this weekend is the next real catalyst. In the meantime, the better bass action in this zone is coming the old-fashioned way — wire line and bucktails worked deep and slow through Valiant Rock and the western edge of Race Rock on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current is still strong enough to hold bait but starting to ease off the boil. Bucktails in the 2 to 4-ounce range, white or olive, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker, dragged just off bottom in 40 to 60 feet. Fish are coming up mixed sizes — some slot, some pushing overslot — but nobody's filling a box in an hour. It's a program, not a blitz, right now.

Bluefish are the one bite in this zone that hasn't needed any qualifiers. They've been consistent through the Race and out toward the Sluiceway, feeding hard on peanut bunker and whatever else gets pushed through the rip on the tide change. We said last week the warm water would keep them aggressive and widespread through Labor Day week, and that's exactly what's happened — jumbo blues mixed in with the bass at Valiant Rock, and smaller choppers stacked thick enough in Plum Gut to keep light-tackle guys busy between albie and bonito runs. Poppers and metal-lip swimmers worked over the rip on the top of the tide are getting hit hard; don't be surprised if wire leader saves you a few rigs.

Black sea bass remain the dependable structure bite while everything else sorts itself out. Drops around Great Gull Island and the rockier stretches off Plum Gut are holding fish on squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs, 40 to 70 feet. Fluke, on the other hand, are winding down the way they always do in early September — the doormats have mostly abandoned the shallower structure for deeper ocean-side ground, and what's left inside is mostly short fish. Not worth building a whole trip around anymore in this zone.

Looking ahead: the full moon on the 6th and 7th is going to push tidal flow even harder through the Race and Plum Gut, which should tighten up bait further and could be the spark that finally gets the bass moving in earnest — though the more likely first blitz zones are still Raritan Bay or the LI south shore, where bunker density is thickest. If that breaks, expect the ripple effect to reach this zone within days as bass push east along the migration corridor. For the next 48 to 72 hours, the smart play is running the slack windows at Valiant Rock for bass and bluefish, then working the Gut with small profile jigs for bonito and albies on the stronger stages of the tide. Watch the wind — anything out of the southwest holds the bonito pattern together, while a hard northeast blow will stir the rip enough to shut the visual bite down fast.

reports.headline: Wicopesset Rock on the drop: bonito nosing into the Race, albies flickering early
reports.subhead: Micro-bait has the boulder fields full of finicky speedsters while the stripers stay parked on bunker, waiting on the moon to tighten things up.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait around the boulder fields this week has been small and nervous — silversides and rain bait pushed tight against the rocks off Ram Island and Wicopesset, getting worked over by fish that won't commit to anything bigger than a size 2 fly. That's the tell. When the bait shrinks down like this in early September, it usually means bonito and albies are in residence before the water's ready to give up a real blitz, and that's exactly the read on Fishers Island Sound right now.

We flagged the Race as a zone to watch for bonito last week given the cooler, current-driven water out there, and they've shown up — spotty, but real. The push out of Block Island and Point Judith has reached the western edge of the Sound, with fish working micro-bait hard enough that standard Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters are getting refused more than they're getting bit. Downsizing is the whole game right now. Half-ounce epoxy jigs in bone or pearl, size 1 and 2 Clousers in olive-over-white, small profile Albie Snax in the peanut size — that's what's connecting when the fish show. Best water has been the rip off Wicopesset Rock on the last of the ebb and the seam running off North Dumpling, where the current stacks bait against structure and gives the bonito something to commit to instead of just slashing through and moving on.

False albacore are mixed in but still inconsistent — showing on the same tide stages, same structure, but not holding the way they will once the water cools another few degrees. New London buoy readings have the Sound running around 69°F, with the western end closer to 71°F off Fishers Island. That's still warm enough to keep both species scattered rather than balled up. The pattern to watch is the moon — building toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should tighten the tidal push through the reefs and rock piles and start concentrating bait in a way that makes for a more reliable window instead of a lucky hour here and there.

Striped bass are the frustrating part of the report right now. There's bait around — bunker pods showing off Napatree and drifting into Little Narragansett Bay — but the fish are staged on it rather than actively working it. That's a warm-water problem more than a bass problem. Low-to-mid 70s water keeps stripers lazy and non-committal even with forage stacked up in front of them. The better approach has been eeling the rock piles at Wamphassuc Point and the boulder fields off Ram Island on the front half of the incoming, when the current starts moving fish and bait together instead of leaving them parked in open water. A few bass in the mid-20s to low 30s have come off bucktails worked slow along bottom in 15 to 20 feet, tight to the rocks where the current breaks. Nothing explosive, but a legitimate fish if you're patient with the retrieve and willing to grind through a tide without a bite before it turns on.

Blackfish are starting to show interest again on the Stonington Breakwater and the rock structure around Ram Island as the water eases past its summer high. Green crabs on the bottom in 20 to 30 feet, fished tight to the base of the boulders on slack tide, have been picking at a few tog in the 3 to 4-pound class — early-season fish, not the winter-run bruisers, but a sign the pattern's waking up. This bite will only build from here as the water continues to cool through September.

Fluke are on the same decline everyone up and down the coast is seeing — the back-bay and shallow-flat fish have mostly cleared out of the skinnier parts of Fishers Island Sound, pushing toward deeper structure near the Race and Watch Hill Reef ahead of their fall exit. There are still keeper-class fish to be had on white Gulp and bucktails drifted along the deeper edges, but the numbers are thinning fast and this window is closing. Black sea bass, by contrast, remain a dependable structure bite on the same rock piles — squid strips or Gulp on a light jig around Ram Island and the breakwater rubble continues to produce steady, if unspectacular, action in 20 to 35 feet.

Looking ahead, the next several days should bring more of the same setup — warm enough water to keep the stripers patient rather than aggressive, but a building moon that should start pulling bait tighter against the rocks and reefs. If the bonito push continues at the current pace, expect numbers in the Race and around Wicopesset to build through the weekend, with the first real albie consistency likely following close behind once nighttime temperatures start easing. The stripers are the wild card — once that first genuine cool front comes through and knocks water temps down even a couple degrees, the bunker schools building in Narragansett Bay and along the Sound's western reaches should tighten fast, and that's when the real fall bite through these boulder fields tends to break open. Until then, work the tide changes, downsize the profile, and be ready to move between spots rather than anchoring on one rock and waiting.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Flood: Bunker-Fed Blues, Porgies Thick on the Cows
reports.subhead: The reef bite is splitting by tide window this week — blues and bass on the bunker push, sea bass and scup holding tight to structure while the stripers wait on a cool front.
reports.body_markdown:
The call this week is Cockenoe Reef on the incoming, not Penfield. That's the read off the water temp split — Kings Point sitting at 70.9 on the western end of the Sound, New London down to 69.4 to the east. That gradient matters because it tells you the bait and the blues are still riding warm water on our side of the Sound, while any cooling influence is still miles off. Cockenoe sits in that warmer western pocket, and with bunker schools thickening up and down the coast this week, that reef is where the bait is stacking on the flood, and where the bluefish are camped on top of it.

The 44th Annual Surfside Hotel bluefish tournament fleet has been working these waters hard, and the reports back that up — chopper blues from 4 to 8 pounds are hammering peanut bunker pushed up against the rockpiles off Cockenoe and out toward Sheffield Island on the last two hours of the flood, when the current stacks bait against the structure instead of sweeping it past. Diamond jigs, 2 to 3 ounces, tin-side up, worked with a fast erratic retrieve through the froth, are outfishing bucktails right now — the blues want speed, not finesse. Anyone throwing bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig off the stern anchored just up-current of the reef is getting steady action too, though you're picking through smaller blues doing that versus the jig bite on the edges.

Stripers are the trickier read. We flagged this last week — said nighttime striper activity would gradually improve on structure as temps ease, and that's exactly the shape of it right now. Daytime bass are still mostly staged rather than committed, sitting on bait but not blitzing, because 70-plus degree water on our end of the Sound isn't forcing the issue yet. The building moon toward full on the 6th and 7th is going to tighten those bunker schools further, and once a real cool front finally shows up, that's when this turns into the first legitimate fall pattern. Until then, the better bass have been coming after dark off Greenwich Point and along the drop at the western edge of the Norwalk Islands, working bunker spoons and 6-inch swimshads slow along the rock edges on the last of the ebb, when current pulls bait off the structure into the deeper water bass are holding in.

Penfield Reef is still worth the trip, but the tide window there is unforgiving — you want the last two hours of the ebb, when the reef's rockpile sheds current hard enough to concentrate blackfish and porgies but not so hard you're fighting a boat full of Saturday traffic for swing room. Blackfish are just starting to wake up on that structure as the water eases from summer highs — nothing explosive yet, but fish to 4 and 5 pounds are coming off the deeper boulders in 20 to 30 feet on green crab and Asian crab, worked tight to bottom with a light enough sinker to feel the structure change. That bite should build through the month as the water keeps sliding down.

The more consistent structure bite right now is porgies and black sea bass. The Cows off Stamford are holding scup thick in 15 to 25 feet — small hooks, squid strips or sandworms on a simple high-low rig, and you don't need much weight in that lighter current. It's meat-and-potatoes fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good call for anyone trying to avoid the weekend boat parade around the Norwalk Islands, since the Cows see a fraction of the traffic. Black sea bass are holding on the same structure that's been good all summer — the rockier stretches off Cockenoe and the deeper edges around Sheffield Island, 25 to 35 feet, squid and butterfish strips fished on bucktail-and-teaser combos right on bottom. Sizes have been solid, plenty in the 14 to 16 inch range with a few bigger mixed in.

Fluke are on the seasonal slide everyone expects this time of year — the doormat-class fish are pulling out toward deeper ocean-side structure, and what's left inside is thinning fast. Still worth a drift through the channels between the Norwalk Islands on the last of an outgoing tide if fluke is the target, using 4-inch white Gulp on a 3/4-ounce bucktail dragged slow along the sand-to-rock transitions, but don't plan a whole trip around it. That bite's closing, not opening.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold this same split pattern — bluefish staying aggressive on bunker through Labor Day week as the tournament fleet keeps proving out, porgies and sea bass steady on the same structure that's carried the summer, and stripers building toward something real but not there yet. If the first real cool front of the season lines up with this building moon, expect the switch to flip fast — that's usually how it goes here, bass go from scattered to committed within 48 hours once the trigger hits. Until then, fish the tide windows tight: Cockenoe on the flood for blues, Penfield on the last of the ebb for tog, and the Cows anytime for a guaranteed bend in the rod without fighting for space.

reports.headline: East Wall Porgies Stack Up While Blues Crash the Bunker and Bass Wait Their Turn
reports.subhead: The bottom bite held steady all week on the New Haven and Milford rockpiles — bluefish are the loudest thing in the water right now, and the stripers are staging just behind them.
reports.body_markdown:
The bottom bite never blinked this week, and that's the real story out of Central Connecticut Sound heading into the long weekend. Porgies and sea bass have been steady on every piece of structure from the New Haven breakwalls out to Falkner Island, and that consistency is buying time while the bigger story — the fall striper turnover — keeps loading up offstage.

Water temps are still soft for early September, running in the low-to-mid 70s on the western end and cooling off toward the high 60s as you push east toward New London. That gradient matters. It's kept bait schools from tightening into the kind of dense, panicked balls that trigger a real blitz. Bunker are thick in the harbor mouths and along the beaches from Stratford to Hammonasset, but they're still swimming loose and unbothered more often than not. Stripers are on them — captains working the Charles Island bar and the mouth of the Housatonic are marking fish under the pods on the graph — but they're eating opportunistically, not committing in numbers. We flagged this pattern last week: bait density needs to build further before the bass tip over into blitz mode, and with the moon building toward full on the 6th and 7th, the tidal push is about to get a lot stronger. That's usually the ingredient that's been missing. Give it seven to ten days.

Bluefish, meanwhile, have had zero patience for subtlety. They've been the most reliable thing happening in the zone, tearing through peanut bunker schools off the New Haven Harbor breakwalls, the Charles Island rip, and the reef structure off Hammonasset. That's exactly what we called for Labor Day week — warm water keeping them aggressive and spread out — and it's held. Metal is the move: half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast through the froth, or bucktails with a strip of fresh bunker if you want to slow it down and pick off a bigger fish sitting under the chaos.

On the rockpiles, it's been a genuinely fun week for anyone who likes fishing light. The east wall at New Haven Harbor has been giving up porgies in the 10-to-12-inch class on the last two hours of the dropping tide, with high-low rigs baited on sandworms and green crab working best in 15 to 20 feet tight to the riprap. Sea bass are mixed right in with them, especially around the deeper pockets near the harbor entrance buoys — squid strips and Gulp swimming mullets on a bucktail teaser have been outproducing plain bait rigs when the current's got some push to it.

Falkner Island remains the money spot for anyone willing to make the run. The rockpiles on the north and west sides in 25 to 35 feet have been holding a mixed bag of porgies and sea bass all week, with the bigger sea bass — some pushing 3 pounds — coming on butterflied clam and squid combos fished on the bottom during the last of the incoming tide, when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without a half-pound of lead. Stratford Shoal is fishing similarly, though boat traffic has been heavier there with the holiday crowd, so early morning has been the difference between a full cooler and a picked-over pile.

Fluke are thinning out the way they always do this time of year, and that's not a surprise — this is the normal seasonal shuffle as the bigger fish slide out toward deeper structure ahead of the fall run, not a sign the bite's collapsed. There's still a window in the Milford Gulf and along the channel edges toward Charles Island, working white and chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails on the last of the ebb. Numbers are down from August, but a few keeper-class fish are still coming off the deeper humps for anyone putting in the drift time.

Looking ahead, the wind pattern's been cooperative — nothing but light southwest breezes and clean water, which has kept the structure bite consistent and the harbor entrances fishable on both tides. That should hold through the weekend. The bigger question is what happens once the full moon tightens up the tidal flow. If the bunker schools along the Milford and Stratford beaches start bunching up the way they have in past Septembers, the first real blitz activity of the fall could break open right off the breakwalls — and that's a much better problem than the slow build we've had. Until then, the smart play is simple: fish the structure early and often for porgies and sea bass, keep a bucktail rigged for blues when the bunker get nervous, and keep an eye on Charles Island. That sandbar is usually the first place in this zone to tell you the fall bite has actually arrived.

reports.headline: Race Sees First Bonito, Black Point Sea Bass Won't Quit
reports.subhead: Bluefish keep the rods bent while the stripers wait on bait to bunch up ahead of Sunday's full moon.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic drift boat mates at the tackle counter Tuesday and the first thing out of his mouth wasn't fluke or bass — it was bonito. Said a couple of the smaller center consoles working out toward the Race picked up their first false albacore-looking fish of the season skipping bait on the surface, and by his description they were bonito, not albies, pushing in off that Block Island wave everybody's been talking about all August. That's early for this stretch of water but it tracks — the whole Eastern Sound has been running warm, New London reading 69.4 on the surface, and that's plenty of water for bonito to keep working west along the reefs toward Fishers Island and into the mouth of our zone. Worth having a small metal or an epoxy jig rigged on light tackle if you're running out that way, because that push doesn't usually stick around long once it shows.

The bigger story for the weekend, though, is the moon. We flagged this last week — said the building moon toward full would tighten up feeding activity and strengthen the tide over the next 72 hours, and the fleet is starting to see it. Current's noticeably harder on both the flood and the ebb through Twotree Island Channel and around Hole-in-the-Wall, and that's pushing bait tighter against structure instead of letting it spread out over the flats. Full moon lands Sunday/Monday, and if the pattern holds like it usually does this time of year, the next few days should sharpen up the bite on everything holding near rock — sea bass, porgies, and the blackfish that are starting to show up on the drift boat bycatch.

Sea bass are the one thing nobody's complaining about right now. Black Point and the rock piles off McCook Point are holding fish in that 30- to 45-foot range, and the party boats working Hole-in-the-Wall have been putting together solid mixed bags — sea bass to 4 pounds mixed with keeper porgies on the same drift. Squid strips and clam belly on a high-low rig is still the standard, but a few mates are running Gulp Peanut Butter and jelly swimming mullets on light jig heads when the current's ripping and bites get finicky. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, when the current slows enough that a bait or jig actually sits still on bottom instead of getting swept sideways off the structure.

Fluke are doing exactly what they're supposed to do the first week of September — thinning out. Niantic Bay and the inside grounds near the river mouth gave up decent numbers all summer, but those doormat-class fish are sliding out toward the deeper structure around Twotree Channel and the edges off Hole-in-the-Wall ahead of the fall push offshore. Anyone still chasing them should be working 25 to 35 feet of water on the outgoing tide, dragging white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails slow along the bottom. The numbers are there if you find the right piece of structure, but it's not the wide-open June bite anymore — call it a grind-it-out fishery now, not a limit-out fishery.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going and that's held true right through the week. Peanut bunker and small bunker schools are still stacked up in Niantic Bay and along the edge off McCook Point, and the blues have been chopping through them most mornings and again toward dusk. Diamond jigs with a tube teaser, or bigger poppers thrown at working birds, have been getting bit consistently. This activity should hold strong right through Labor Day week — warm water's kept these fish aggressive and spread out all along the Sound, and nothing in the forecast suggests that changes soon.

Striped bass are the one piece still lagging behind where the calendar says they should be. Reports out of Black Point and the river mouth have fish around — guys marking bunker schools on the meter and picking off a few bass working the edges — but nobody's calling it a blitz yet. Water's still sitting in that high-60s range, warm enough to keep the bigger schools loose and non-committal instead of balled up and vulnerable. The building moon and the stronger current that comes with it should start squeezing those bunker schools tighter over the next several days, and once that happens the bass usually follow. If you want a shot at one now, live bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the bait schools at first light, or a bucktail worked slow along the current seam off Black Point on the last of the ebb, are the better bets.

Looking at the next few days: expect the sea bass and porgy bite to stay the most consistent thing in the zone, especially on that top-of-tide window at Hole-in-the-Wall and Black Point. Keep an eye on the bluefish schools tracking the bunker — that bite isn't going anywhere through the holiday. And if the moon does what it usually does, the stripers could start tightening up into something more aggressive by the weekend. Worth having a rod rigged for bunker just in case that switch flips.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Rips Turn Bunker Into Bluefish, Bass Still Watching From the Seams
reports.subhead: The ebb off Fort Trumbull is stacking bait against the current line, and the blues have committed — the stripers haven't, yet.
reports.body_markdown:
The ebb off Fort Trumbull has a different sound to it this week. Where the river current pinches against the fort wall and kicks out toward the Race, there's a hard seam forming on the back half of the tide — you can see it from the seawall, a visible crease where the darker river water meets the harbor green. That seam has been loaded with peanut bunker and silversides for about ten days now, and it's the best single read on what's actually happening in this system heading into the second week of September.

Water at the mouth is sitting around 69.4 degrees, a few clicks cooler than what's showing out west toward Kings Point near 71. That gradient matters. It's the same gap that's been holding bunker schools tight in Raritan Bay and along the Long Island south shore without tipping them into full blitz mode — the water's warm enough that bass don't need to commit hard yet, but cool enough on this end of the Sound that the bait is starting to stage instead of scatter. The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the mechanism that usually breaks this stalemate. Stronger tidal flow on the building moon tightens loose bait balls into something a predator can actually pin against structure. We flagged the bonito push toward Fishers Island Sound last week as something worth watching given the proximity, and the spillover has shown up — a handful of fish have been seen working bait on the surface out toward the Race and into the eastern approaches, which tells you the same warm-water regime that's been feeding Block Island and Point Judith all summer hasn't broken yet.

Bluefish are the story right now, no question. The mouth of the Thames, from the sub base pilings down through Fort Trumbull, has had steady blitz activity on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, timed almost exactly to when bait gets squeezed through that current seam. Blues from 3 to 6 pounds are hammering peanut bunker imitations — 1-ounce Deadly Dick or a chrome Kastmaster worked with a fast, erratic retrieve gets bit as soon as it lands near the surface commotion. Poppers work too when the fish are up and slashing, which has been most mornings this week around first light. Gold Star Bridge has produced the same pattern on the pilings themselves — blues stacking on the downtide side of the concrete on the ebb, feeding on bait getting swept through. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these fish are cutting off gear that isn't built for it.

Striped bass are around, but honest talk: they're staged, not committed. That matches what's showing up basin-wide — the fish are sitting on bait rather than actively working it over. In the Thames, that means bass are holding deep on the current breaks below Fort Trumbull and along the deeper pilings under Gold Star Bridge, usually 15 to 25 feet down on the last of the ebb, picking off stragglers rather than blitzing the surface. Live-lining a peanut bunker on a 4/0 circle hook with just enough weight to hold near bottom has been the most consistent way to connect, fished tight to the pilings where the current slows in the eddy pocket. Bucktails in the 1- to 1.5-ounce range, white or olive over white, worked slow along the bottom through the same seams have also picked up fish in the mid-20-inch class, mostly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current is still moving enough to hold the bait but has eased enough to fish it properly. Nobody's finding numbers yet. It's a quality-over-quantity bite, and it's going to stay that way until the bunker schools tighten enough that the bass stop watching and start feeding.

Porgies are still worth a stop if bass and blues aren't cooperating — the pilings around the harbor and the rocky stretch off Pleasure Beach are holding decent scup on squid strips and clam, fished on standard high-low rigs in 15 to 20 feet. Nothing dramatic, but a reliable box-filler while the bigger story plays out.

Looking ahead, the full moon on the 6th-7th is the hinge point. If the tidal push it generates does what it usually does this time of year, expect the bait currently staging at Fort Trumbull and along the bridge pilings to get squeezed into tighter, more vulnerable schools — and that's when the stripers usually stop sitting on the sidelines. The window for the first real fall blitz in this river is realistically seven to ten days out, in line with what's setting up basin-wide in Raritan Bay and the south shore. Until then, the smart play is working the ebb at Fort Trumbull for blues, dropping bunker or bucktails deep on the bridge pilings for the bigger, quieter bass, and keeping an eye toward the Race for any more bonito showing up on the surface — that push west isn't finished yet.

reports.headline: Marsh Grass Turning, Bunker Stacking the River Mouth — Blues Steady, Bass Still Waiting
reports.subhead: Goldenrod's up on Great Island and the first bunker pods are pushing into the lower river, but the stripers are staged, not committed — yet.
reports.body_markdown:
The marsh grass out at Great Island is starting to go from green to that early bronze it gets right before the real turn, and the osprey platforms along the flats have mostly emptied out — the young birds fledged weeks back and the adults are already drifting south. That's the calendar talking, not the thermometer, and this time of year the calendar usually gets there first. Down at the river mouth, the water hasn't caught up to the marsh yet. It's still summer-warm at Saybrook Point and off the breakwater, low-to-mid 70s by feel, and that's exactly why the striper bite has been a staging bite instead of a blitz bite for the better part of two weeks now.

Here's the pattern the fleet's been talking about at the ramp: bunker pods have been thickening up in the lower river and pushing in and out of the mouth on the tide, but the bass haven't organized into that tight, panicked, surface-erupting mode yet. They're under the bait, they're around the bait, but the water's still soft enough that nothing's forcing the issue. We flagged this exact setup last week — said conditions would hold stable with gradual cooling working in the background — and that's precisely what's played out. Nothing dramatic, just the slow tightening you'd expect heading into the first week of September.

What changes that is the moon and the nights. We're building toward full around September 6-7, and that means stronger tidal push through the mouth and around Calves Island and the flats off Great Island — more current means more concentration, and concentration is what turns staged bass into committed bass. Pair that with the first real drop in overnight air temps, which cools the shallow flats and the marsh creeks faster than the main river channel, and you get the setup for the first legitimate blitz activity of the fall. It's not here yet. But the ingredients are on the table in a way they weren't three weeks ago.

While the big bass sort themselves out, the bluefish have carried the zone, and they've been dependable the way blues get dependable in early September — aggressive, close to the bait, and not picky. Snapper blues have been thick in the coves and side channels around Old Lyme and up into the Essex flats, hitting small gold and silver spoons, quarter-ounce Kastmasters, and gold Rebel-style minnow plugs worked fast on light spinning gear. That bite's been best on the last two hours of the incoming, when the young blues push bait up into the shallower water off the marsh edges. Adult blues, the two- and three-pound class, have been working the harder current at the river mouth itself — off the Saybrook breakwater and the outer edge of the DEP Marina channel — chopping bunker chunks and peanut-sized swimming plugs on the outgoing tide, particularly the last of the ebb when bait gets pulled out of the marsh and funneled through the narrower water.

Striped bass, where they've shown, have come on live eels and fresh bunker chunks fished on the bottom near current seams — the edge where the main river channel meets the flats off Great Island, and along the deeper water off Saybrook Point where the outgoing tide sets up a real seam against the incoming Sound push. These aren't blitz fish. They're one-at-a-time fish, mostly schoolie-to-mid-twenties class, taken by anglers willing to sit on the seam through a full tide change rather than run around chasing surface activity that isn't there yet. Anyone who fishes the mouth this week should plan around the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood — that's when the current is strongest and the bait gets squeezed hardest.

White perch have quietly been one of the better bets for anyone who wants steady action without waiting on tide windows. The deeper holes up around Essex and the bends below Old Lyme have been giving up decent numbers on nightcrawlers and small chartreuse or white curl-tail jigs, fished slow along the channel drop-offs on light tackle. This is a fish that doesn't care much about the moon or the bunker schools building downriver — it's been a consistent producer through the whole late-summer stretch and should stay that way into fall.

Looking at the next several days, the smart play is patience with the stripers and reliability with the blues. If the nights keep cooling the way early September nights tend to, and the building moon does what building moons do to tidal flow, the bunker schools in the lower river should tighten up enough to trigger the first real blitz activity at the mouth sometime in the next week to ten days — that's the same window the regional bait-buildup pattern has been pointing to all along. Until that flips, work the current seams on the ebb, keep bunker chunks and eels in rotation for bass, lean on the blues for guaranteed bent rods, and watch the marsh. When Great Island finishes its turn to bronze, the river usually isn't far behind.

reports.headline: Porgies Steady, Blues Chewing, Bonito Rumor Worth Chasing at the Gut
reports.subhead: The bass are still sitting on bait instead of busting it, but the moon's building and the water's setting up for the first real fall push.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a fella who's clammed the flats off Rocky Point since before some of these young guides were born, and he called down to the shop Tuesday morning to say he'd seen something skipping bait out past the moorings that didn't look right for a bluefish and didn't look right for a bass either. Small, quick, gone before you could get glasses on it. Could've been nothing. Could've been the first bonito of the year working the edge of Plum Gut. We flagged that possibility last week — said this stretch sits close enough to the Race to catch the overflow once the Rhode Island push started sliding west — and here it is, a week later, showing up exactly where we said to watch for it. Doesn't mean there's a school of them stacked up yet. Means keep a small metal or an epoxy jig rigged on light wire in the boat, because if they show, they don't stick around long enough for you to go home and get one.

The rest of the week was a more familiar story. Water's still carrying the last of the summer warmth — Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound reading near 71, New London down around 69 and change, which tells you the whole Sound is still sliding cooler as you move east, same as it does every September. That gradient matters. It's why the bass out toward Orient and the Gut are behaving different than the fish getting worked over in the western Sound and down around the bay side. They're not blitzing. They're staged — sitting tight on bunker and peanut bunker schools that are still thick but not yet balled up tight enough to trigger the kind of top-water chaos everybody's waiting for. The moon's building toward full the sixth and seventh, and that's usually the mechanism that tightens bait up and gets stripers committing instead of just picking. We're not there yet on this beach. Give it the better part of a week to ten days, especially if a real cool front finally shows up behind this stretch of warm, sticky air.

Bluefish, though — that bite hasn't needed any encouragement. They've been chewing hard from Mattituck Inlet clean through to the Orient side, and it's about the most dependable thing going right now. Warm water's kept them wound up and spread out wide instead of bunched in one or two spots, which actually makes them easier for the average angler to find. Diamond jigs in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, bounced through the rips off Horton Point on the last of the ebb, have been drawing cutoffs and blues in the three-to-six-pound range pretty steady. Poppers at first light off the Rocky Point rocks have been drawing some too, though you'll lose a few to the leader if you're fishing anything lighter than 40-pound fluorocarbon. This ought to hold right through Labor Day week — the warm water isn't going anywhere fast, and neither is the bait they're chewing on.

Striped bass are there, they're just making you work for them. The better fish have been coming off the bottom rather than the surface — bucktails, three-quarter to one-ounce, white or chartreuse, dragged slow along the drop-off in front of Horton Point on the last two hours of the incoming, or worked the same way off the rocks at the Orient side closer to the Gut. A few slot fish, a couple of overslots mixed in, nothing that's going to make the six o'clock news but honest fishing for anybody willing to fish the tide change instead of the middle of it. Live eels at night off Mattituck Inlet have also been producing, which is the same trick that's worked there for sixty years and shows no sign of quitting.

Porgies are the one bite around here you can set a clock by, and this week didn't change that. The reef structure off Rocky Point and the rougher bottom approaching Plum Gut have been holding scup in good numbers on standard high-low rigs, squid strips or clam, fished right on bottom in twenty to thirty feet. Nothing fancy required. If you've got somebody in the boat who just wants bent rods and a fish fry, that's where you send them.

Fluke are thinning out the way they always do this time of year — the doormats that were sitting in the deeper holes off the inlet mouths are starting to slide toward the harder structure out toward the Gut, chasing the same baitfish that everything else is chasing. Still catchable on white Gulp swimming mullets tipped on bucktails, but the easy back-bay action is winding down and won't be back till next spring.

Weakfish have been a whisper more than a pattern — the odd fish mixed in with the porgy bite on bait, nothing worth planning a trip around.

Looking ahead, the next few days should run close to what we've had — southwest breeze most afternoons, water holding warm enough to keep the bass patient rather than desperate. If that first proper cool front finally pushes through behind the full moon, watch the bait density in the usual staging spots tighten up fast, and that's when the blitz switch tends to flip out here. Until then, fish the tide changes, keep an eye on the Gut for any more of those unexplained skipping baitfish, and don't be surprised if the bluefish are still the most honest bite on the board come next weekend.

reports.headline: Nine Days Running: The Hudson's Warm Edge Refuses to Break
reports.subhead: The filament that's carried the canyon bite through August is still sitting on the wall heading into Labor Day week — here's how long it can last.
reports.body_markdown:
Ninety fathoms to better than a thousand in under three miles — that's the drop along the east wall by the Claw, and it's exactly the kind of structure that holds a temperature break in place once one sets up on it. That break has been sitting there for the better part of nine days now, and as of this week it still hasn't moved. That's the whole story of the Hudson right now. We flagged this pattern last week — said the setup would hold through several more days of stable high pressure before any wind shift or cool front started pushing on that warm edge — and that's precisely what's happened. No front has come through strong enough to knock it loose, and the fleet running out of Shinnecock, Manasquan, and Jones has been cashing in on it.

What's holding this together is a Gulf Stream filament that's kept warm water pinned against the canyon wall since mid-August, and it's doing what these filaments do best — pushing bait up against the 100-fathom line and stacking it there instead of letting it scatter into open water. That's the difference between a mixed week and a week where boats are running lines out before the sun's fully up. The color along the edge has stayed clean blue where the filament sits, with the dirtier green water pushed well up onto the shelf, and that contrast is as good a visual cue as any SST chart — if you're running out and the water goes from green to that deep cobalt blue somewhere around the Dip, you've found the edge worth working.

Yellowfin have been the most consistent player all week, showing on the troll in that 60- to 100-fathom stretch off the Claw, mixed in with a scattering of small bigeye that are pushing the average size up on some boats. Green machines and cedar plugs in the smaller spread positions have been drawing strikes on the troll, with naked ballyhoo and horse ballyhoo skirted in blue-white and green-machine combos working the long riggers. Boats willing to slow-troll or drift-chunk butterfish after dark over structure near the canyon head have reported better-grade bigeye mixed in with the yellowfin, which tracks with what's typically expected once the filament has had time to concentrate bait for over a week straight — the bigger fish move up onto the structure once the small stuff is reliably stacked there.

Wahoo have been a bonus rather than a target this week, mostly picked off on high-speed presentations — bombers and Ilanders pulled at 12 to 15 knots through the temperature seam itself, right where the warm and cooler water meet along the wall. That seam is narrow, sometimes only a quarter mile wide, so it takes discipline to stay on it rather than run through it. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure or weed lines found drifting near the Dip, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 3- to 8-pound class, but worth a few minutes with light spinning gear and small skirted jigs if the trolling bite goes quiet for a stretch. White marlin sightings have picked up on the troll as well, mostly incidental with the tuna spread, and a few boats have swaped one long rigger over to a naked ballyhoo on a lighter leader once a marlin's been spotted working the spread — worth having that rod rigged and ready rather than trying to re-rig on the fly.

The deep-drop swordfish game during daylight hours remains a long-day proposition this time of year, and with the bait and structure situation holding the way it has, boats making that run have generally had better luck staying patient on one drop over the canyon structure rather than moving around chasing marks. It's not a numbers game right now so much as a quality one — one good bite on a well-placed drop beats three shallow marks worked halfway.

The next several days should look a lot like the last several, provided the pattern holds. High pressure has been the stabilizing force here, and as long as it stays put, there's no reason for that warm filament to break down or slide off the wall. The one thing worth watching closely is the calendar — this is peak hurricane season, and any tropical development spinning up in the western Atlantic is the single biggest threat to this setup. A storm track that pushes swell and wind into the Bight would mix that warm water down and scatter the bait that's currently stacked along the edge, and it wouldn't take much to undo nine days of a good pattern. Keep an eye on storm tracks through the week rather than just the local forecast — that's the bigger variable right now.

If the pattern holds through the weekend, the play is the same one that's worked all week: run to the temperature seam along the wall near the Claw or the Dip, work the troll early with a green-machine and ballyhoo spread, and be ready to switch to chunking butterfish if the bite goes quiet midday. If a front does start pushing through and the edge starts to break down, don't be surprised if the bite gets patchier and more mark-dependent rather than the wide-open structure-following pattern it's been. Either way, this filament has already outlasted expectations for early September — worth taking advantage of it while it's still sitting where it is.

reports.headline: A Lost Bigeye at Midnight and the Case for Staying the Course to Atlantis
reports.subhead: The fleet running out of Montauk, Block Island, and the Bay lost one at the leader this week — but the warm water holding the tuna in the east canyons hasn't budged.
reports.body_markdown:
The radio chatter out of the Montauk fuel dock Tuesday night told the story better than any log book could. A boat working the east wall at Atlantis had a big bigeye up on the shortest flat line at 11 p.m., worked it boatside under the spreader lights for the better part of twenty minutes, and lost it at the leader when the hooks pulled. No cursing, no drama on the channel — just a flat "that's the one that got away" and a request for someone to check the fuel dock hours before the 3 a.m. run home. That's the tenor of this week in the east canyons: fish are there, the work is real, and the margins are thin enough that one bad hook set turns a good trip into a long ride back with an empty fish box.

The warm-water regime that's carried this canyon bite since July hasn't broken down. That's the headline, and it's the one worth trusting through Labor Day week. We flagged this last week — said the tuna action would hold and that this stretch of ocean was worth watching as a bellwether for how far the warm water was pushing north — and here it is, still intact, with swordfish now showing on the deep drop gear pushing further into Gulf of Maine water than is typical for early September. That's not a coincidence. When the filament that's been feeding Atlantis, Veatch, Hydrographer, and Oceanographer starts pushing swordfish that far north, it tells you the warm signature has some staying power left in it.

The run math hasn't changed and it never will.
