Out of Montauk, Atlantis is the closer of the four — call it an eight-to-ten hour round trip depending on sea state, which makes it the default pick when the weather window is tight. Veatch and Hydrographer sit further east and are better played from Block Island or the Rhode Island ports — Point Judith and the Bay boats are looking at a longer commit, often a true overnight, but the fuel burn pays for itself when the fish are stacked tight to the wall. Oceanographer is the long ball from any of these ports and this week it wasn't the play — the better reports were concentrated closer to home water at Atlantis and the western edge of Veatch, where the canyon wall holds structure and the current seams have been setting up clean.

Yellowfin have been the bread-and-butter fish, running mixed sizes from schoolie-class up to 40-plus pounds, taken both on the troll and on the chunk once the boats shut down over showing marks. Spreader bars and cedar plugs pulled off the shelf and down the canyon wall accounted for the bulk of the daytime yellowfin, with green machines and small Ilanders in the shorts working the middle of the pattern. Once the sun got low, the chunk bite on butterfish took over — small chunks, no weight, drifted back on a slow current, has been the difference-maker on Atlantis for the bigger fish showing at dusk and through the first few hours of dark. That's exactly the pattern that produced the bigeye lost this week — boats shutting the engines down, setting up a slow chunk slick over structure on the wall, and working the bite methodically rather than covering water.

Bluefin have been mixed in with the yellowfin on the troll, mostly smaller school fish in the 40-to-80 pound class, though there have been a handful of reports of bigger fish breaking off gear rigged for yellowfin — a reminder to check hooks and leader wind knots before every set when working these grounds, because the fish showing up don't always match the tackle you brought for them. Bigeye have been an after-dark proposition almost exclusively, coming on the chunk or on deep-dropped baits worked below the thermocline once the sun's off the water.

Wahoo and mahi have been a bonus rather than a target, picked up on high-speed trolled lures worked over structure on the way out to the grounds — small blue-white and pink-white lures pulled fast over the drop-offs have accounted for a few wahoo in the 30-to-50 pound range. White marlin sightings have been sparse this week compared to earlier in the summer; a few boats reported raising fish on the troll but conversions have been low, which tracks with this point in the season as the marlin bite starts to thin out ahead of the fall transition.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward full, which should tighten up the tidal push through the canyons and could sharpen the bite windows over the next several days — worth planning trips around the stronger current stages rather than fighting slack water. The bigger variable sitting on the watch list is tropical development in the western Atlantic. Nothing organized is threatening the grounds as of this week, but that's the one thing that can shut this bite down fast regardless of how good the water looks right now. If the pattern holds and no storm intrudes, Atlantis and the western Veatch wall remain the better bets for boats running out of Montauk and Block Island through the holiday weekend — just budget the fuel and the sleep for a real offshore day, because nothing about this run gets shorter just because the fishing's good.

reports.headline: Shagwong to the Lighthouse: Blues Blitz While Bass Hold for the Moon
reports.subhead: The bunker wall along the ocean beaches is drawing blitzing bluefish and staged bass, and the bonito are finally within reach from the east.
reports.body_markdown:
Early September at the Point always feels like the top of a hill you can see over but haven't crested yet. The water off the Lighthouse is still holding in the upper 60s, bunker schools are thick and visible from the bluffs at Camp Hero down through the South side beaches, and everything about this week says the fall run is loaded and waiting on a trigger. That trigger is the moon. It's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and with it comes stronger tidal push through the rips at North Bar and off the Lighthouse — the kind of current that takes a scattered, non-committal bunker school and squeezes it into something a big bass can't ignore. We're not there yet. But we're close enough that this is the week to start paying attention every single tide.

Here's the honest read on where things stand. Striped bass are around in real numbers, but they're staged on the bait rather than blitzing it. Water in the low-to-mid 70s along the beaches is still warm enough to keep them lazy and scattered during daylight, which means the best action right now is a dawn and dusk game, not a mid-day one. Boats working the boulder field off the Point on the building tide are picking at bass in the 20 to 34-inch range on bucktails and swimming plugs, with the occasional better fish mixed in for those willing to work the deeper edges off Turtle Cove on the last of the ebb. Surf guys working the South side rocks at first light on bunker spoons and Danny plugs are connecting, but it's a fish-here, fish-there bite, not a wall of rods bent.

Bluefish are the one thing that hasn't needed an excuse this week. They've been the most dependable bite on the whole East End, and Montauk's version of it has been legitimate — schools working bunker pods from the Lighthouse rip down through Shagwong Reef, with blitzes breaking on the surface hard enough to see gulls diving from the bluff road. Poppers and 2-ounce bunker spoons trolled or cast into the boils have been drawing quick, violent strikes, and these aren't dink blues — plenty of 6 to 10-pound fish mixed through the schools. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, this is it. Work the edges of the bait, not the thickest part of the ball, and keep moving with the school because these blitzes don't sit still.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year, and Montauk's version is no exception. The doormat-class fish that were holding in Fort Pond Bay and around the harbor structure through August have started sliding out toward deeper ocean-side rubble and rock piles, which is the classic pre-migration move. There's still a fish to be had on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails worked slow along the drop-offs outside the harbor mouth, but the numbers are thinning fast and this bite has maybe another week or two of real relevance before it's mostly a memory until next spring. Porgies, on the other hand, remain a sure thing — Shagwong Reef and the rock piles off Frisbie's continue to give up steady catches on sandworms and clam bellies fished on the bottom, incoming water, and that's a bite that'll carry right through the fall with little drama.

We flagged this a week back — that the bait balls building along the beaches and a bonito push working in from the east would open this zone up to more variety, and that's exactly the shape things are taking. The bonito run out of Block Island and Point Judith has continued pushing west, and it's now within range of Block Island Sound and the Race, which puts Montauk in position to see them show in the next several days if the pattern holds. There's also squid building up in Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound water, and once that forage starts filtering into the Montauk rips, it tends to supercharge everything from bass to bonito to false albacore. None of that has fully arrived yet, but the ingredients are lining up the way they do right before this place turns into what it's famous for.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern to watch is the moon and the bait. If the bunker schools along the South side beaches and off the Point keep thickening while the tide strengthens toward the full moon, the odds of a real surface blitz — the kind where bass, blues, and maybe the first albies of the season all show at once — go up significantly by the weekend. Until that trigger fires, the smart play is working the bluefish blitzes for guaranteed action, hitting the boulder field and Turtle Cove on the early flood for bass, and treating the fluke bite as a bonus rather than a target. Keep an eye on Shagwong and the Lighthouse rip for the first real signs the variety is expanding — that's usually how it starts out here, one species at a time until the whole Point lights up with all of them at once.

reports.headline: Peconic holds in the low 70s — porgies thick off Shelter Island, bass staging for the Gut
reports.subhead: Bunker pods are building through the bay and the bass are riding along, not blitzing yet, while porgies and fluke keep the rods bent through the work week.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic runs on its own clock this time of year, and right now that clock says late summer, not fall. Surface temps are still sitting in the low 70s across Gardiners Bay and up into Noyack, warmer than the open Sound thanks to the shallow, protected geography that's made this water a nursery and a feeding ground for two centuries. That warmth is good news for porgies and fluke, which are still locked into their summer patterns, and it's the reason the striped bass moving through right now are riding on bait rather than blowing it up on the surface. Water this mild keeps predator and prey in a loose, unhurried relationship. That changes fast once the nights start cooling off, and with the moon building toward full on the 6th and 7th, the tidal flow is about to get stronger through every cut and gut in the system. That's usually the first ingredient in tightening up scattered bunker schools into something a striper can commit to.

We flagged this a week ago — said porgy and fluke action would hold steady through the stretch leading into scallop season, with bonito potential building at the inlets — and that's exactly the shape of things on the water now. Porgy fishing off Shelter Island remains the most dependable bite in the zone. Boats working Cornelius Point and the drop just outside Coecles Harbor are anchoring up in 20 to 30 feet on the last two hours of the flood, dropping high-low rigs baited with sandworm or clam. Fish are running a mix of scup-sized keepers with enough jumbos mixed in to make it worth soaking a second rod with bigger bait. This bite doesn't need much finesse — bring enough bloodworms or clam and let the incoming tide do the work.

Fluke are still stacked in the channels, though the pattern is starting to show the first cracks of the seasonal shift. Robins Island's east and west channels and the deeper cuts off Jessup's Neck are holding fish in 15 to 25 feet, with the better drifts coming on the back half of the outgoing tide when the current pulls bait off the flats and funnels it through the deeper water. White and chartreuse five-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails are outproducing bare bait rigs right now, especially worked slow with a hop-and-drag retrieve rather than a straight drag. Sizes are respectable — plenty of 17 to 20-inch fish, with a scattered doormat in the 24 to 26-inch class turning up on the deeper edges near the mouth of Noyack Bay. The bite isn't as thick as it was a month ago, and that's expected; the same warm water holding fluke in the back bays elsewhere on Long Island is starting to nudge Peconic fish toward the deeper structure out near Orient and the Gut ahead of their fall exit.

The striped bass story right now is about positioning, not aggression. Bunker pods are showing along the north side of Shelter Island, off Cedar Point, and staging in the deeper water toward Orient Point, and the bass are shadowing them without committing to the kind of surface blitz you'll see once the water cools another few degrees. The better approach right now is a bucktail worked deep along the edge of a bait school rather than a topwater plug thrown into the middle of it — a 1.5 to 2-ounce bucktail dropped to the bottom edge of a bunker pod and swum back with a slow, rhythmic retrieve has been drawing strikes from fish in the mid-20 to low-30-inch range, with the occasional overslot mixed in for boats willing to work the deeper edges near Plum Gut on the last of the ebb. Live-lining a bunker off a fish-finder rig in that same water is worth the patience for anyone hoping for something bigger.

Bluefish have been the most reliable action for anyone who just wants bent rods without overthinking it. Peanut bunker pushing into Three Mile Harbor and Sag Harbor Cove have brought choppers up top on calm mornings, and metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything that throws a long cast and flutters — is getting hit as soon as it lands. This bite should hold strong right through Labor Day week as long as the bait stays put, and there's no sign yet that it's thinning.

Weakfish are still showing as a bonus on the evening fluke drifts in Noyack and Three Mile Harbor, mostly smaller fish taken on sandworm rigs fished slow along channel edges after sundown, not a dedicated target yet but worth a look if the tide and light line up.

Looking ahead, the building moon into the weekend should start compacting those bunker schools tighter, which is the trigger everyone's watching for. If the pattern holds the way it usually does here, expect the first real surface activity from stripers working those tighter bait balls near Orient Point and through Plum Gut within the next week to ten days, especially if a real cool front finally pushes through and knocks a few degrees off the surface temps. Until then, porgies at Shelter Island and fluke in the channels remain the two bites you can plan a trip around with confidence, and the scallop season opener sitting on the horizon is starting to shift some boat traffic and attention toward the flats — worth keeping an ear open at the docks in Greenport and Sag Harbor for word on timing.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: B+ Week Offshore: Yellowfin Steady at Spencer and Lindenkohl, Poor Man's Still Waiting Its Turn
reports.subhead: The warm-water setup that's carried the canyon bite all summer is holding into Labor Day week, but the tropics are the one grade that could still change.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a B+ week across the four canyons. Not an A — the bite wasn't uniform, and Poor Man's stayed the quiet cousin again — but Spencer and Lindenkohl carried the boats that ran there, and the reasons why are worth understanding before you plan the next trip.

The short version: the warm-water regime that's driven this whole summer's canyon action is still intact. The Gulf Stream filament pushing eddies up against the shelf edge hasn't broken down, and that's the difference between a good week and a bad one out here. We flagged this exact risk last week — said the pattern would hold in the near term with the biggest threat being any tropical system disrupting that warm eddy structure — and here we are, still riding it into September with nothing organized in the western Atlantic to knock it off track. That's the good news. Keep an eye on the tropics anyway, because that's the only thing that ends this run on short notice.

Routing logic for the week was simple. Spencer and Lindenkohl had the better temp breaks and cleaner blue water pushing up onto the edge, and that's where the fleet that ran offshore put their spreads. Yellowfin and bigeye stayed steady on the troll along both canyons, working the 100-fathom curve out to the deeper drop-offs where the color changes from green to that ink blue. Standard spread — naked ballyhoo staggered behind a couple of cedar plugs, a small spreader bar or two in the shotgun and long rigger — is still doing the work, with the bite windows tightening up early and again in that last hour before dark. Boats that stuck around after the sun dropped and switched to chunking bunker and butterfish picked up bigeye through the night, drifting with the current instead of anchoring, letting the chunk line stretch out naturally.

Norfolk, being the run it is, only had a handful of boats make the trip, but the ones that did came back with a mixed bag — a few yellowfin mixed with some mahi found sitting under scattered weed lines and any floating debris on the way out. That's the pattern down there right now: less consistent than the northern two canyons, more of a scout-as-you-go situation, worth it if you've got the fuel and the weather window but not a guaranteed day.

Wahoo showed up sporadically for boats running high-speed spreads with wahoo bombs and Ilanders in that 12-to-15-knot range along the edge at Lindenkohl, mostly early morning before the trolling bite settled into the tuna pattern. If wahoo is the target, that's the window — first light, before the boat traffic and prop wash push them off the structure.

White marlin have been in the mix but not stacked. A few releases came off Spencer on the drop-back with ballyhoo and a circle hook, mostly fish found working bait balls pushed up by the current on the edge of the canyon wall. Not a blitz, but enough activity that it's worth keeping a pitch rod rigged if you're already trolling that water.

The other piece of the week that's worth talking about at the dock is the daytime swordfish bite. Boats deep-dropping live squid around 200 feet during daylight hours have had an excellent run of it, and that's mirroring what's being reported further up the coast right now. If you've got the gear and the patience for it, that daytime swordfish window is producing better than a lot of the overnight chunk trips, and it doesn't require the all-nighter. Squid and butterfish have both been showing heavy on the meters along these edges, which is exactly the bait signature you want stacked under a temp break holding tuna and swords both.

The moon is building toward full over the next several days, and that's going to tighten current flow on all four canyons. Stronger tide means better drift speed for the chunk boats and tighter bait concentrations along the edges — usually a net positive for this pattern, as long as the wind doesn't stack up against the current and turn the ride uncomfortable.

Looking at the next few days: expect the canyon tuna and billfish bite to keep running close to what it's been doing, with Spencer and Lindenkohl remaining the better bets over Poor Man's for consistency. If the moon-driven current bumps up bait density like it should, look for the chunk bite at night to sharpen up on both those canyons. Norfolk stays the wildcard — worth the run if the forecast is clean and you're prepared to scout, but not the pick if you only have one shot at getting offshore this week. The single biggest variable through Labor Day weekend remains any tropical development spinning up in the basin; nothing's organized as of now, but that's the one line item that can turn a B+ week into a scrubbed one with a few days' notice. Until that changes, the smart play is running when the window's clean and picking Spencer or Lindenkohl first.

reports.headline: North Rip Green and Ripping — Bonito Committed, Bass Still Playing Coy
reports.subhead: The bait is thick, the water's clean, and the fleet is watching the moon build toward full for the first real fall trigger.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a change in the air out here that you feel before you can point to it on a chart. The nights have started to carry a little bite to them, the wind's swinging more out of the north on the mornings, and out on the water the bait has that nervous, balled-up look it gets right before things start happening for real. Block Island in early September doesn't announce itself — it leans into you a little at a time, and this week it leaned hard.

The bonito showed up in real numbers, and they showed up right on schedule. Southwest Ledge has had them working the rips on the last of the ebb, chasing bay anchovies and rain bait so small that standard metal has been getting refused half the time. The fleet's been downsizing — quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in olive-over-white, small Deceivers, anything with a slim profile — and that's what's been connecting. North Rip has had the same story on the change of tide, green water, current stacking bait against the structure, bonito slashing through it in those quick, hard-to-predict pushes that make you burn a lot of gas for a few good minutes of work. That westward push everyone's been tracking is real — Point Judith's getting them now too, and the word out of Fishers Island Sound and the Race is that the pattern's spreading fast. We flagged the false albacore to follow the bonito within a week or two of that push starting, and while nobody's called albies in numbers yet, the timing lines up — worth checking the rips daily from here out, because that's usually how it goes once the bonito get established.

Striped bass are the harder read right now. There's plenty of bait around — bunker are thickening up in Narragansett Bay the same way they are on the mainland side — but the water's still sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range that keeps bass more interested in staying loose on the bait than committing to a real blitz. Southwest Ledge has still been giving up fish on the drop of the tide, working live eels and bunker chunks down deep, 25 to 40 feet, right where the ledge breaks off into the deeper water. Nothing has come easy this week — it's been a fish here, a fish there, mostly at first light or the last hour of daylight when the light drops and the bigger fish push up onto the structure. We said last week that the trigger for the first real blitz activity would be bait density tightening up as the moon builds and the tide flow increases, and that's exactly the pattern setting up now. The moon's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should start squeezing those bunker schools tighter over the next several days. Combine that with the first real cool front, and there's a good chance the switch flips on Narragansett Bay and around the island within the next week to ten days. Until then, treat the Ledge and the North Rip as places where a handful of quality fish are still very catchable, not a guaranteed blitz.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going. We called this one too — said the warm water would keep them aggressive through Labor Day week, and that's held up. Choppers in the 4 to 8 pound class have been running hard on bunker schools off Newport and in the rips around the island, and topwater poppers and diamond jigs with wire leader have been getting bit steadily through the middle of the day, not just the classic dawn-and-dusk windows. If you want fast action without overthinking the tide, this has been the most consistent bite on the whole beat.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year. The back bay fish have mostly cleared out for deeper structure, and while there are still keeper-class fish being picked off around deeper rock piles and current-swept bottom off the island, the bite has thinned out noticeably compared to a month ago. If fluke is the goal, this is the week to fish the deeper edges early in the day before the bite shuts down with the sun.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold close to what we've already seen — bonito active on the tide changes at Southwest Ledge and North Rip, bluefish reliable on the bunker schools, and bass fishable but not yet blitzing. If the wind stays out of the north and the nights keep cooling the way they have been, expect that first real fall trigger for the stripers to start showing itself right around the full moon, with Narragansett Bay and the mouth of the Bay the most likely places for it to break open first. Until then, the smart play is working the tide changes on the rips for bonito and bluefish, and treating the bass bite as a low-light, structure-specific game rather than an all-day proposition. That should change soon — but it hasn't changed yet, and there's no sense pretending otherwise.

reports.headline: September 4 and Washington Canyon Hasn't Slowed a Step Since August
reports.subhead: The filament that's carried this canyon's tuna and billfish bite all summer is still sitting right where it should be heading into Labor Day week.
reports.body_markdown:
Early September is when Washington usually separates itself from the rest of the canyon string, and this year is no different. Washington sits far enough west and shallow enough on the shelf break that it typically comes alive two to three weeks before its neighbors in June, and it typically holds that warm water regime two to three weeks longer into the fall. We're right in that back half of the window now, and the canyon is behaving exactly like it should for the calendar — which is to say, better than most people expect for a September that's already seen one round of tropical noise churn through the basin.

We flagged this pattern last week and the week before that — said to expect continuity with the stable warm water and the strong tuna and billfish activity carrying over, and that's precisely what's held. The filament pushing off the main Gulf Stream axis hasn't broken down, hasn't sheared off east the way it sometimes does once Labor Day hits. That's the single biggest driver of everything happening out here right now, and it's the thing to watch hardest over the next week to ten days, because if any tropical development spins up in the western Atlantic, that's what unravels this bite fast.

For now, the eddy structure on the canyon's western edge — the wall that typically holds the better water from June through September — is still doing its job. Boats working the 100-fathom curve down through the 600 to 900-foot range along that wall are finding a mixed bag that's about as good as early September gets around here: yellowfin in the 40 to 60-pound class, scattered bigeye on the night bite, and wahoo showing up in the spread with enough regularity that crews are starting to run a dedicated high-speed lure off the shotgun. White marlin activity has stayed consistent too — not a blitz, but enough encounters on the troll that boats running dedicated spreads for them are getting looks most trips out.

The morning troll bite has been the more reliable window. Ballyhoo behind Ilanders in blue/white and green/yellow combinations are still the bread-and-butter for the yellowfin, run at a modest 6 to 7 knots with the spread staggered — shotgun and long riggers pulled back into the second and third wake, short riggers tight. Where the water color has broken clean along the edge of that western wall, the bite has been better; where it's gone off-color or mixed with cooler shelf water pushing up from below, the tuna have pushed deeper and the troll bite has gone quiet until the sun's higher. Bigeye have been coming on the drop at night, chunking bunker or butterfish over a chum slick set up along the same wall structure, fished on circle hooks with just enough weight to get down through the thermocline without spooking the bite.

Mahi have been a bonus rather than a target this week — scattered fish holding on any floating structure or weed line crossing the canyon edge, and worth a few minutes with light spinning gear and small chunks of butterfish if the crew spots color or debris on the troll. Wahoo have been the more interesting story. They've shown up consistently enough on the high-speed gear — the deep-diving lures pulled at 10 to 12 knots off the corner riggers — that a few boats have started rigging a second wahoo bait specifically for that stretch of wall where the temperature break sets up tightest.

Tide and moon are cooperating without doing anything dramatic. We're building toward the full moon over the next several days, which means tidal flow on the surface will start tightening up bait concentrations, and that's generally a good thing for the troll bite because it keeps forage pinned against structure instead of scattered across open water. Wind has been the more manageable variable lately — nothing that's kept the fleet home, though anyone running out should still check the marine forecast morning of, because a building sea on top of a long run adds up fast this far out.

The honest read: this isn't a blowtorch bite where every spread gets crushed on the first pass. It's a solid, dependable September pattern — multiple hookups per trip on the better days, a mixed bag of species, and enough bigeye and wahoo mixed in with the yellowfin to make the run worthwhile. The days where the water color turns or the wind kicks up out of the wrong quadrant have been noticeably tougher, and crews that pushed through those stretches without adjusting the drift or the spread depth came home lighter.

Looking ahead, the next 48 to 72 hours should mirror what's already working — stable warm water along the western wall, a troll bite that turns on with the first real light and holds through mid-morning, and a night chunk bite for bigeye that's been worth the extra hours for boats willing to sit on the slick. The bigger question is Labor Day week itself and whatever's brewing in the tropics. If that filament holds, Washington keeps punching above its weight the way it always does this time of year. If a storm system starts organizing anywhere in the basin, that's the first sign the party's closer to ending than starting.

reports.headline: Ran the warm filament to Wilmington, split time trolling and chunking — worth the fuel both ways
reports.subhead: The canyon's still holding a strong yellowfin and white marlin bite heading into Labor Day, but the tropics are the only thing that can shut this down.
reports.body_markdown:
The call this week for anyone burning fuel to Wilmington is simple: troll the early morning temp break, then switch to the chunk bucket once the fleet starts marking bait and the sun gets up. That's the pattern that's been paying off, and there's no reason to overthink it while the warm water's sitting where it is.

The Gulf Stream filament that's been feeding this canyon all summer hasn't broken down, and that's the whole story right now. We flagged this last week — said conditions looked set to hold through the near term with tropical development the only real threat — and that's exactly how it's played out. No storms have pushed through to mix things up, so the warm tongue is still draped over the grounds, still holding bait, and still holding fish. That's the kind of stability you don't get every September, so anyone with a weather window and the fuel budget should be using it.

For boats running out of Cape May or Indian River, the math still works if you're planning a full troll-and-chunk day rather than a quick strike. Burn the run out early, get lines in on the temper break along the canyon edge before the sun's fully up, and work the color changes where the clean blue meets the greener inshore water. That edge has been holding yellowfin and white marlin both, and the temperature line is doing exactly what it's supposed to do this time of year — stacking bait against the drop and giving the tuna and billfish a reason to sit right on it instead of running the open water.

Spread-wise, nothing fancy is required. A dredge with mullet or squid rigs up the middle, ballyhoo naked and rigged behind Sea Witches on the long riggers, and a couple of small cedar plugs or Green Machines in the shorts has been enough to draw both species into the pattern. White marlin have been eating the naked ballyhoo pulled just outside the wake, and once you raise one, it's worth dropping back a pitch bait — a ballyhoo on a circle hook — rather than trying to keep trolling through a school. Yellowfin have shown a preference for anything with some flash and speed in the mix, so a spreader bar with cut-eye Ilanders on the corners has been earning its spot in a lot of spreads this week.

Once the sun's up and the morning troll bite slows, that's the cue to switch over. Boats sliding into a chunk pattern along the canyon drop-off have been doing well on butterflied bunker and diced-up bluefish chunks fished on 50s and 30s, slow-trolling or drifting right on the temp line. Bigeye have been part of that mix after dark for the boats willing to stay out and work a chunk slick into the evening, with 6/0 circle hooks on fluorocarbon leader picking up the better-grade fish that won't come up for a bar rig in daylight.

Wahoo have been a bonus rather than a target — a couple of boats picked up fish on high-speed trolled lures worked around structure and current breaks on the run out, in that 12 to 18 knot range with a straight wire leader. Mahi have been scattered around any floating debris or grass lines holding along the edge, and it's worth having a couple of rods rigged with small ballyhoo or a bucktail ready to pitch if you spot a color change or a patch of weed — they'll show up when you're not necessarily fishing for them, and it's an easy add to the fish box if the crew's willing to slow down for a few minutes.

Honest read on effort versus result: this has not been an easy-money bite where every trolling pass turns a fish. It's been a grind-it-out pattern where the boats putting in the hours on the temp break and staying disciplined about switching to chunk when the troll goes quiet are the ones coming back with a mixed bag of yellowfin, a white marlin release or two, and the occasional wahoo or mahi. The days of just running out and getting bit on autopilot aren't here — you're working for it, but the work is paying off often enough to justify the fuel.

Looking ahead through Labor Day week, there's no reason to expect a dramatic shift. The warm water isn't going anywhere on its own, and the tuna and billfish activity should stay strong as long as nothing spins up in the tropics to mix the canyon. That's still the single biggest variable — any tropical system tracking up the Atlantic basin could churn this setup and cool the surface temps fast, so keep an eye on the extended tropical outlook before committing to a multi-day trip. Absent that, the smart play through the holiday weekend is the same one that's worked all week: early troll on the edge, chunk bucket ready for when the morning bite fades, and enough fuel in reserve to work the drop-off until the fish tell you otherwise.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: the bunker's stacking up, the blitz isn't here yet
reports.subhead: Fluke are sliding toward the ocean side, blues are chewing on the bait schools, and the bass are staged and patient — for now.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood at the fuel dock Tuesday morning listening to a mate off one of the party boats tell anybody who'd listen that he'd never seen so much bunker sitting in the bay this early without stripers tearing through it. That's the whole story of this week in one sentence. The bait is here — thick pods of bunker rolling off Nicoll Bay, more pushing in through the inlet on the last of the flood — and the bass know it. They're just not committing yet. Water's still holding in that mid-70s range, warm enough to keep fish lazy and scattered rather than balled up and blitzing. That changes fast once the nights start cooling off, and with the moon building toward full on the 6th and 7th, the tide swings are already getting stronger. We flagged the bunker build last week as the trigger to watch for the first real fall blitz, and it's still building — the pieces are lining up, they just haven't clicked yet. My money says within the next week to ten days somebody's phone lights up with a report out of the bay or right off the beach that makes everybody drop what they're doing.

In the meantime, the fishing hasn't been bad, it's just been a patience game. Fluke are doing exactly what they do this time of year — thinning out of the back bay and the inlet and sliding toward the ocean-side structure ahead of the fall run. The Robert Moses bridges are still giving up keeper fish, but the numbers are down from August. Best drift has been 20 to 30 feet on the outgoing, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to the pilings and the rip lines where the current stacks bait against structure. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, work the deeper edge off Democrat Point where the inlet dumps into the ocean — that's the kind of structure the bigger doormats are staging on before they push out. Chunk shedder crab or squid strips on the bucktail if the Gulp isn't getting bit.

Striped bass are the story everybody's watching. They're in the bay, staged on the bunker rather than actively chasing it, which means the bite is there but it's not easy — you have to be in the right spot at the right moment. Dawn and dusk have been the windows, especially the last two hours of the incoming at Democrat Point and along the Fire Island Inlet seam where the current pushes bait against the rocks. Snag a live bunker off the surface schools and free-line it back into the current, or chunk fresh bunker on a fishfinder rig and let it sit on bottom in 15 to 25 feet. Patience pays — a lot of guys are marking bait all day and getting one or two real windows where the bass actually turn on. Nobody's complaining about the size of what's coming over the rail, just the consistency.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and that tracks with what's happening basin-wide right now — warm water's kept them aggressive everywhere from Montauk down through here. They're showing up wherever the bunker schools are thick, which this week has meant the inlet mouth and the stretch just outside Democrat Point. Diamond jigs worked with a fast retrieve or bunker spoons trolled behind the boat have been getting bit hard. If you're marking bunker on the finder and seeing birds working, don't overthink it — cast into the edge of the school, not the middle, and let the jig flutter down before you start working it.

Porgies have quietly been solid around the Robert Moses bridge pilings and the deeper holes off Captree, 15 to 20 feet, high-low rigs with bloodworms or clam strips. It's not glamorous fishing but it's been steady, and it's a good option on a day when the wind's up and the inlet's got some chop to it — which it has, honestly, more days than not this week. The ocean buoy off the coast has been reading close to 4-foot seas on a short period, choppy enough that the open beach hasn't been fishing well and the surf guys have mostly stayed home or worked the calmer stretches inside the inlet. Weakfish are turning up as incidental catches in the bay channels around dusk on bucktails and soft plastics — nothing to build a trip around, but worth noting if you're working the same water for bass and get a surprise.

Looking ahead, the wind and the moon are the two things to watch. If the wind lays down through the weekend, that's your window to be on the water for the bass — work the incoming at Democrat Point early, then slide into the bridges for fluke as the tide turns. If a front comes through and knocks the overnight temps down even a few degrees, don't be surprised if the bunker schools tighten up fast and the first real blitz breaks loose somewhere along this stretch. Keep the rods rigged for both scenarios — a bucktail for structure fish, a snagging outfit for the bait schools — because when this bay decides to turn on, it doesn't give you much warning.

reports.headline: Matinecock Bunker Balls Pull Blitzing Blues While Bass Sit on the Edges
reports.subhead: Bluefish are tearing up bait from Hart Island to Execution Rocks, but the bass are still staged and picky in water that hasn't quite turned the corner.
reports.body_markdown:
The talk at the counter this week wasn't about stripers, it was about blues. With the Surfside Hotel derby lines full of guys chasing tournament fish, the question everybody kept asking was the same one I've been asking myself since August: when does all this bunker turn into a bass blitz instead of a bluefish blitz? Right now the answer is patience. We flagged this last week — said the bluefish would stay elevated through the tournament window and that any bunker holding past Labor Day could start pulling stripers in behind them — and that's exactly the shape of things out there right now. The blues showed up. The bass are still circling.

Water's still carrying summer heat. Kings Point is reading just under 71 degrees, and even out toward New London it's holding in the high 60s, so you've got almost no thermal gradient pushing fish to do anything in a hurry. That's the story of the whole week — warm, stable, bait-rich, and stripers that are staged but not committed. They're sitting under and around the bunker schools rather than exploding through them. When the water's in the low-to-mid 70s like this, bass get lazy about it. They'll eat, but you have to put it right on their nose instead of waiting for the boil.

The bluefish don't have that problem. Bunker schools have thickened up nicely off Matinecock Point and along the flats toward Hempstead Harbor, and the blues have been running through them hard on the last two hours of the ebb, right as that bait gets funneled and squeezed by the current. Boats working bunker spoons and 2-ounce Deadly Dicks off the schools have had doubles and triples most mornings, fish in the 4-to-8-pound range with the occasional bigger one mixed in. If you'd rather chunk, anchoring up-current of a bunker ball with a chunk on a fish-finder rig and letting it settle has been just as effective, maybe more so on the days when the surface action goes quiet but the fish are still stacked underneath.

Stripers are there too, just working the margins. Execution Rocks has been the most consistent spot for them, particularly right as the tide turns to outgoing — that rip line off the rocks concentrates whatever bait gets pulled through the Stepping Stones corridor, and bass have been sliding up onto it to pick off stragglers rather than crash the main school. Slow-rolled swim shads in the 5- to 7-inch range, white or bunker pattern, fished just off bottom in that 20-to-30-foot stretch, have out-produced anything fast or flashy. Same story around Hart Island — fish are there on the drop-off, but you need to slow down and work it like it's October, not July.

Fluke are winding down, right on schedule for early September. Numbers are thinning as the bigger fish start sliding out toward deeper structure ahead of the fall run, but there are still keepers to be had on the last of the tide around the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings and out toward the mouth of Manhasset Bay, mostly on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on a light bucktail so you can feel bottom in that 25-to-35-foot depth. Don't expect the numbers you had in July, but there's still a fish or two worth keeping if you put in the drift time.

Porgies are steady and reliable, which this time of year is worth something. Stepping Stones reef and the rockpiles off Little Neck Bay have been giving up decent porgies on sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, best on the last of the incoming when the current slows enough for bottom fish to feed comfortably. Weakfish have been scattered and inconsistent — a few reports of fish mixed in with the fluke around the deeper edges of Hempstead Harbor, but nothing you'd plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, the moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the piece of the puzzle everybody's watching. More moon means more current, and more current is what tightens up loosely scattered bait into the kind of concentrated schools that get bass to commit instead of just shadow. If the bunker stays put through this lunar push — and there's no reason yet to think it won't — the next real shift in this pattern is a legitimate striper blitz breaking open somewhere between Matinecock and Execution Rocks within the next week to ten days. It won't happen on a calendar, it'll happen the first cool night that knocks a couple degrees off the surface water and gets those bass aggressive instead of lazy.

For now, if you've only got one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the ebb at Execution Rocks or off Matinecock Point — that's where the bait is thickest and where both the blues and the occasional committed bass are showing up together. Keep the bluefish gear rigged heavy in case the blitz swings your way, but don't be surprised if the striper bite stays a finesse game a little while longer. The ingredients are all there. It's just waiting on that first real push of cooler air to light the fuse.

reports.headline: Bonito Hit The Race — Bass Still Sitting on Bait
reports.subhead: The Block Island push finally crossed into New York water this week, but the striper bite stays staged and stubborn until the bunker schools tighten up.
reports.body_markdown:
The bonito showed. We flagged this last week — said the Block Island push would ride the current through The Race and Plum Gut within days, and that's exactly what happened. Small, fast, silver fish are working the rip edges off Fishers Island and the eastern face of The Race on the tail of the ebb, and the fleet that got the timing right this week connected. That's the headline. The rest of the zone is still working through late-summer inertia, and honesty matters more than hype right now: the striper bite is present but staged, not committed.

Water temps explain both stories. New London is reading 69.4, Montauk's holding at 69.1, and Kings Point over in the western Sound is up at 70.9 — a real gradient running west to east. That cooler eastern water is exactly what pulled the bonito through The Race this week, and it's also why squid are building around Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound as that water eases into the high 50s and low 60s in the protected coves. That squid show is the next domino. When it thickens up around Fishers Island and pushes bait into the rip, that's when the Race turns from a bonito run into a genuine mixed bag with big bass mixed in.

For now, striped bass in the eastern Sound are doing what they do in early September before the trigger flips — sitting tight on bunker schools instead of running them down on top. Bunker are building fast in Raritan Bay, the LI south shore, and Narragansett Bay, and once that bait tightens under the building moon toward full on the 6th and 7th, the tidal flow through The Race and Plum Gut will do the rest. Increased current means bait gets pinned against structure, and that's when bass commit instead of shadowing. We're not there yet. Expect that within the next week to ten days, not this weekend.

What's actually working right now: bluefish are the most dependable thing in the water. Fresh peanut bunker showing thick off Orient Point and along the Plum Gut rip line is drawing consistent blitz activity, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets squeezed through the gut and blues pin it against the surface. Poppers and 2-ounce metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins, anything that throws a long cast into moving current — are getting hit on nearly every retrieve when the birds are working. This lines up with what's happening basin-wide; the bluefish bite from here through Montauk and up into Nantucket Sound has been the most consistent story of the whole late-summer stretch, and there's no reason to expect that to slow down through Labor Day week.

Striper presentation needs to shift with the conditions. Fish are staged deep on bait rather than surface-feeding, so the move is dropping a 1.5 to 2-ounce bucktail — white or chartreuse — off the edges at Valiant Rock and Race Rock, letting it sink clean off the drop before working a slow, rhythmic bottom retrieve through the strongest push of current. That's the pattern producing slot and overslot fish right now, not blind-casting the surface hoping for a blitz that isn't here yet. Boats working the deep water on the moving tide at Plum Gut, particularly on the last of the incoming when current stacks bait against the eastern wall, are picking off better-grade bass mixed in with the bluefish.

Bonito tactics are simple and unforgiving — small profile, fast retrieve, right in the seam. Half-ounce to one-ounce metal, Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax in bone or silver, cast tight to the rip edge on the southwest side of Fishers Island and burned back through the moving water. These fish don't sit still and they don't forgive a slow presentation, so match the speed of the current or don't bother. The window has been tightest on the last two hours of the ebb when the rip is running hardest and bait gets funneled through the gut.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year — doormats abandoning the shallower structure for deeper ocean-side water ahead of the fall run. If you're still targeting them, focus deeper drops around the Gut on the moving tide rather than the flats, but don't expect the numbers of July.

Looking ahead: the next 72 hours should keep the bonito pattern building as more fish push west out of Block Island, and the building moon into the 6th and 7th is the number to watch for stripers. If overnight temps start dropping even a few degrees as we move through the second week of September, expect the first real blitz activity to break loose — most likely starting further west in Raritan Bay or the LI south shore before it works its way east into the Sound. Until then, the smart play in the eastern Sound is working the current edges at first light and the last of the ebb, staying mobile between Plum Gut and The Race, and treating the bonito as the bonus fish they are while the real striper trigger keeps building underneath.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hold Deep at the Inlet While Bonito Work the Jetty by Day
reports.subhead: Weakfish are still showing at the Ponquogue Bridge on the night tide, but the real story this week is bait — and who shows up to eat it first.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one window this week, take the outgoing after dark at the inlet over anything the daylight fleet is doing on the ocean side. Water's still sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, which is warm enough to keep striped bass lazy and non-committal during the day, but once the sun drops and the tide starts pulling hard out of the bay, those fish tuck into the current seams along the east and west jetties and feed with more purpose. That's been the pattern all week, and there's no reason to think it changes before the weekend.

The bigger story setting up is bait. Bunker schools are thickening up and down the south shore corridor, and while Shinnecock hasn't seen a true blitz yet, the pieces are lining up. The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, tidal flow strengthens with it, and that's usually the trigger that tightens up loosely scattered bunker into the kind of dense balls that get stripers committing instead of just picking at the edges. We flagged this zone last week as one to watch over the next few days, and the arrival of bonito working bait around the inlet mouth is exactly the kind of confirmation that tells you the water's turning over the way it should this time of year. Don't be surprised if the first real blitz activity on this stretch breaks within the next week to ten days rather than tomorrow.

At the inlet itself, the night bass bite has been steady if not spectacular. Working the outgoing starting about two hours before dead low, boats and surfcasters working the rocks on the ocean side of the east jetty have been picking at slot bass in the 26 to 34 inch range on bucktails — 1 to 1.5 ounce white or chartreuse, bounced slow along bottom in 8 to 15 feet where the current rips past the rock piles. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig near the deep hole inside the inlet, the one that drops to around 20 feet on the bay side of the Coast Guard station, have also been producing after midnight, especially on the darker nights around the new-to-first-quarter stretch. Once that moon fills in this week, expect the bite to shift earlier in the tide as the extra light pushes fish tighter to structure and shadow lines under the jetty rocks.

Daytime around the inlet mouth and outside the jetties has belonged to bluefish and now bonito. The blues have been the most dependable bite in the whole system right now — peanut bunker and rain bait pushing through the inlet on the ebb are getting jumped by choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range, and small metal like a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster in silver has been drawing both blues and the first wave of bonito working the same bait schools just outside the rocks. That bonito push has been building westward out of Block Island and Point Judith all summer, and its arrival here right on the calendar is worth paying attention to — fast retrieves with light wire or straight 20-pound fluoro leader, cast into the surface nervousness rather than blind-casting open water, has been the difference for the boats connecting.

The Ponquogue Bridge weakfish bite is still there but it's a tighter window than it was a month ago. Working the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing, after the sun's well down, bucktail-and-Gulp combinations — a 3/8-ounce jig with a pearl or chartreuse 4-inch swimming mullet — dropped tight to the concrete and worked with a slow lift-and-drop through 12 to 18 feet has been drawing keeper weakfish along with the usual bycatch of small bluefish. It's not a numbers bite, more a patience bite, and the boats staying out past midnight are doing better than the sunset crowd.

Fluke are doing exactly what fluke do in early September — thinning out fast. The doormat-class fish that were holding in the deeper holes of the bay through August are starting to slide out toward ocean-side structure ahead of the fall migration, and the drift inside the bay has gotten noticeably quieter. There's still some action to be had drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets over sand-to-mud transitions between Tiana Beach and the canal entrance on the last of the incoming, but don't expect the volume from earlier in the summer. If fluke is the target, this is the week to fish the ocean-side structure outside the inlet rather than the bay.

Porgies remain a solid bread-and-butter option for anyone wanting steady action without chasing tides too precisely — bay-side structure and the rocks along the canal have been holding fish on bloodworms and clam on light tackle, a good option for the daylight hours when the bass and weakfish bite is dead. Blackfish season is still ahead, but the canal itself remains the connector worth remembering — that stretch to the Peconic keeps moving bait and fish through on both tide changes, and it's worth a look if the ocean side gets blown out.

Looking ahead, watch the moon and watch the wind. If nights stay calm through the weekend, the outgoing tide at the inlet after dark is still the highest-percentage play for bass, and the bonito ought to keep pushing in daylight around the jetties as that westward migration continues. If a real cool front finally shows up behind this building moon, that's when the fall bass trigger could actually break loose — and when it does, the smart money says it happens on a night tide, same as it always does out here.

reports.headline: Fort Tilden Surf Access: Blues Blitzing While Bass Stack Behind Bunker
reports.subhead: The walk-in at Fort Tilden puts you on the bluefish blitz and the staging striper bite at the same time — here's why that's the smart play this week.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one shot at this zone in the next few days, the Fort Tilden walk-in — the beach access west of the parking lot, toward Breezy Point — is the smarter play over the Rockaway Beach boulevards right now. Reason is simple: the bunker pods pushing along this stretch of beachfront are thick enough that you can see them from the dune line on a calm morning, and where the bunker sit, the bluefish and the first serious striper interest are sitting right behind them. That's not true everywhere on this beach yet. It is true there.

Here's the rundown. Water's still running warm — low-to-mid 70s inside the bay and along the beachfront — which is keeping striped bass in that scattered, non-committal mode instead of true blitz mode. They're staged on bait, not yet stacked under it. Bluefish don't have that hesitation. They've been the most reliable bite in this zone for two straight weeks, and with the moon building toward full on the 6th and 7th, the bunker schools running Raritan Bay through the LI south shore corridor — including this stretch off Rockaway — are getting squeezed tighter with every tide cycle. We flagged this exact pattern last week: warm water keeping the blues aggressive and widespread through Labor Day week, and that's exactly what the beach has delivered. No reason to expect that to change through the weekend.

What that means for stripers is patience for another week to ten days. The building moon and tighter bait schools are the trigger — once tidal flow ramps up around the full moon and overnight air temps start easing off, that's when the scattered fish start committing in numbers. Right now they're there, but you have to work for them.

On the outgoing tide at Marine Parkway Bridge, that staging pattern is showing up clearly. Boat and kayak guys working the pilings and the rip line off the Rockaway side on the last three hours of the ebb are picking at striped bass in the 24-to-32-inch range, mostly on bucktails — white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce — bounced tight to the structure, and on live eels for the after-dark crowd fishing the deeper scour holes under the span. It's not a blitz. It's a fish here, a fish there, but the quality has been decent and the bite window is real if you're on the outgoing.

Surfside from Fort Tilden through Breezy Point, the bluefish have been the story — cocktail-size fish mostly, with some better ones mixed in, chopping bunker pods right in the wash. Bunker chunks fished on a simple fish-finder rig off the beach will get you in the game, but the more consistent action has been metal — half-ounce to one-ounce diamond jigs and Kastmasters worked through the peanut bunker showers when the birds start working. Early and late are still the windows; midday sun has been pushing the bait and the blues out a little deeper past the bar.

Inside the bay, fluke are doing exactly what they do this time of year — thinning out, not disappearing. The channels off Cross Bay Bridge and the deeper cuts around the Raunt and Ruffle Bar are still giving up keeper fish, mostly on the smaller side but with the occasional surprise. White or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the incoming, have been the better producer over bare bait rigs this week. This is a normal seasonal transition — the doormats are sliding toward ocean-side structure ahead of the fall run — and there's no reason to expect fluke to shut off completely before late September, but the days of easy limits inside the bay are behind us for the season.

Canarsie Pier remains the most practical access for anyone without a boat or kayak who still wants a crack at porgies, and that bite has held up fine on bloodworms and clam fished on the bottom around the pier pilings and the drop-off just off the rocks. Blackfish season isn't open yet in these waters, so leave that structure alone for now and focus effort where it's legal. Weakfish have been quiet — a few reports of fish taken after dark on the bay flats near Canarsie and the Raunt on soft plastics, but nothing worth planning a trip around specifically.

Looking ahead, the next few days should track close to what's already happening: bluefish staying aggressive on bunker and peanut bunker through the beachfront, striped bass staging tighter behind the bait as the moon fills, and fluke continuing their slow slide out of the bay. If the first real cool front of the season shows up in the next week to ten days like the pattern suggests it should, that's the trigger that turns the staging bass into an actual blitz — and when it does, Rockaway Beach and the inlet mouth off Breezy Point are going to be the first places it shows. Until then, work the tides you know — outgoing at the bridge for bass, first and last light on the beach for blues — and keep a rod rigged for whatever shows up in the wash.

reports.headline: Forget the Fluke Run — the Bluefish Are Tearing It Up at the Jones Rocks
reports.subhead: While the fleet chases scraps in Sloop Channel, the real action is bunker getting squeezed at the inlet mouth on the outgoing tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Every boat still limping out to Sloop Channel this week chasing one more fluke is burning gas on a bite that's already halfway out the door. I get it — muscle memory, everybody wants that last doormat before the season turns — but the fluke have been sliding out of the back bays and inlets toward deeper ocean structure for two weeks now, and the numbers out there are thinning fast. If that's all you're fishing right now, you're fishing last month's pattern. The real story this week is happening thirty yards off the jetty rocks, where the bunker schools are stacking up at the inlet mouth and the bluefish are cutting them to ribbons on every outgoing tide.

Here's the setup. Offshore, the ocean's been sloppy — better than three-foot swell on a short five-second period pushing in against the beach, water out there running in the low 70s. That kind of chop doesn't do surfcasters any favors on the open beachfront, but it does something else that matters: it pushes bait and bass off the exposed sand and packs them into the inlet channels and jetty structure where the water stays organized. Jones Inlet, Short Beach, the rocks off the Coast Guard station — that's where the bait is getting funneled and squeezed, and where the bites are actually happening. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said bluefish would keep being the most consistent producer through the weekend while bass activity built behind the bunker — and that's precisely what's playing out at the inlet mouth right now.

The bluefish bite has been the most honest thing going. Peanut bunker are showing thick along the beachfront and getting bottled up against the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the blues are hitting them so hard the water looks like it's boiling. Guys working the north side of the west jetty at Short Beach with metal — Deadly Dicks, 2-ounce Ava jigs, or a simple diamond jig with a tube teaser — are connecting on cocktail blues from three to six pounds, with some better fish mixed in on the deeper edge of the channel. If you'd rather chuck plugs, a white or bone Danny surface swimmer worked across the current seam right where the rip meets the calmer water inside the jetty has been drawing crushing strikes at first light and again right at dusk. Don't overthink the retrieve — these fish are eating anything that moves with urgency.

Striped bass are a different story right now, and I'll be straight with you: they're not blitzing yet. They're staged on the bait, not committed to it. Water's still holding in the low-to-mid 70s, which is warm enough to keep bass scattered and lazy rather than balled up and aggressive. You're seeing them show — a boil here, a swirl there, a fish or two mixed into the bluefish chaos at the jetty — but not the sustained surface mayhem everybody's waiting for. The building moon toward full around September 6th and 7th should start tightening that bait up, and once tidal flow strengthens behind it, I'd expect the first legitimate blitz activity to break loose sometime in the next week to ten days. That's not a guess pulled out of thin air — that's the same bunker-density trigger that's been building down the whole south shore, and Jones Inlet sits right in the middle of it.

Until that switch flips, the better bass have been coming off the bottom on bait rather than up top on top water. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in the deeper cuts along the Wantagh Bridge pilings, fished tight to structure on the last of the ebb, have produced some quality fish in the high 20s to low 30s — nothing epic, but solid, honest bass if you're willing to sit on it through a slow tide change. Live eels drifted along the edge of the inlet channel on the incoming have also been worth a mention from a couple of the regulars working the rocks at night.

Don't sleep on the weakfish, either. They've been making a real comeback in South Oyster Bay and the deeper holes off Freeport, and dusk has been the window — light jigheads with a 4-inch chartreuse or pink soft plastic worked slow along the bottom in eight to twelve feet of water on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Nothing to build a whole trip around yet, but enough fish coming over the rail that it's worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up back there anyway.

Looking ahead, the next few days should mirror what we've already got — bluefish remaining the most dependable target at the inlet and along the beachfront wherever bunker are getting pinched, with bass activity slowly building underneath it as that moon fills out. If a real cool front finally shows up behind it — and this is early September, so it's not far off — that's when I'd expect this whole thing to tip over into the first real blitz of the fall. Until then, work the outgoing at the jetty, keep your metal in the water, and don't waste your whole weekend looking for doormats that already left the building.

reports.headline: The West Rip Cut Deeper This Week — Bunker Stacked In It, Bass Still Won't Commit
reports.subhead: Moriches Inlet's sandbar has reshaped the drift lines again, and the bait is thick, but the stripers are staged, not feeding hard yet.
reports.body_markdown:
The west rip off Cupsogue has scoured out noticeably since the last blow — the sandbar that sits off the jetty has pushed the main channel current tighter against the rocks, and the hole there is running a couple feet deeper than it was in July. That matters because it changes where the bait stacks on the ebb. Bunker schools pouring through the inlet on the outgoing tide are now holding in that deepened pocket instead of spreading across the flat like they did earlier in the summer, and that concentration is exactly what's been drawing bluefish into tight, repeatable ambush zones rather than scattered pods.

The bigger story this week is bait density building everywhere from Moriches west, and that's the trigger everyone on the bay is watching. We flagged this last week — said the bunker schools stacking in the back bays and along the south shore corridor would need to tighten up before the stripers committed in numbers, and that's precisely the pattern setting up now. Water in the low-to-mid 70s is still warm enough to keep bass staged rather than blitzing. They're sitting under and around the bunker schools in the inlet and in the deeper guts off Tuthill Point, but they're not yet pushing bait to the surface with any consistency. That should change as the moon builds toward full on the 6th-7th — stronger tidal flow tightens loose bunker schools into the kind of dense, panicked balls that trigger real blitz behavior. Right now we're in the staging phase, not the eruption.

Bluefish are the one thing anyone can count on this week, and that's held true basin-wide. Choppers in the 3-to-6-pound class are running the inlet mouth and the rip off Cupsogue on both the last two hours of the incoming and the first two of the outgoing, hammering bunker spoons and 2-ounce diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the current seam. Some better fish, pushing 8 pounds, have come from the deeper cut on the west side of the inlet on cut bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig with 40-pound leader — the bluefish don't seem to care that the water's still warm, and that lines up with what we expected heading into Labor Day week. Anyone working peanut bunker imitations — 3-inch white or bunker-colored soft plastics on a 3/4-ounce jighead — through the same current edge has been getting cut off regularly, which tells you the blues are thick even when they're not visibly blitzing on top.

Striped bass action inside the bay has been a mixed bag, and it's worth being straight about that. The better fish — mostly mid-20s to low-30-inch, with a scattering of overslot models pushing 34 — are coming out of the deeper water off Tuthill Point and along the channel edge running past Smith Point on the last two hours of the ebb, when the outgoing current pulls bait out of the marsh creeks and funnels it past the deeper structure. Bucktails in the 1-to-1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, fished with a slow bottom bounce through that current seam have been the most consistent producer. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, drifted right along the drop-off where the channel meets the flat, has also worked for the bigger fish holding deeper and less willing to chase. But this isn't wide-open blitz fishing yet — most reports describe scattered fish that need to be worked methodically rather than schools you can run-and-gun on.

Fluke are winding down, as expected for early September, but they haven't disappeared. The better doormats have moved off the shallow back-bay flats and out toward the deeper structure near the inlet mouth and the ocean-side edges off Westhampton, exactly the seasonal shift we called out last week — normal transition, not a collapse. Boats working the deeper holes in 15 to 25 feet with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, are still picking off keeper-class fish in the 18-to-20-inch range, with an occasional fish pushing 4 pounds. The window for that pattern is narrowing fast as water temperatures ease down through the month, so anyone still chasing fluke here should treat the next two to three weeks as the tail end, not the middle, of the season.

Weakfish have been quiet, which tracks with typical early-September behavior in this system — most of what's being caught is incidental, mixed in with the bass bite along the deeper channel edges on bucktails and soft plastics. Porgies and blackfish are still mostly a structure game around the inlet rocks and the bulkheads at Tuthill Point, best worked on the last of the ebb with green crab or clam on a hi-lo rig, and that bite should firm up as water cools into fall.

Looking ahead, the next several days hinge on that building moon and whatever wind shows up behind it. If the tidal flow strengthens as expected and the first real cool nights start knocking water temps down even a degree or two, the bunker schools stacking in the inlet and along the ocean-side edges should tighten enough to trigger the first legitimate blitz activity of the fall — most likely first light or last light on the stronger ebb tides, right where that deepened west rip funnels bait past the jetty. Until that happens, the smart play is fishing the current seams methodically rather than waiting for surface chaos — the bass are there, they're just not desperate yet.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Piling Up on Stratford Shoal — Bass Are Watching, Not Yet Eating
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking hard through the Central Sound narrows this week, but the bass are still staged and picky while blues and building bonito rumors take center stage.
reports.body_markdown:
Start with the bait, because that's where this week's story actually is. Peanut bunker and silversides have been pushing through the Stratford Shoal funnel in thick, nervous pods for the better part of ten days, getting squeezed by the same geography that's made this stretch productive for a century — the Sound narrows here, the current accelerates, and everything with fins gets pinched into a smaller lane. Terns and gulls have been working tight, jittery circles over the rip on the last two hours of the ebb, which is usually the tell that something underneath is pushing bait to the surface rather than just cruising through it. Off Charles Island and along the Norwalk Islands, the mullet run has thickened noticeably since Labor Day, and mixed in with it are early showings of small bay anchovies that are drawing porgies and the occasional weakfish up onto the flats at first light.

The thermal picture explains a lot of the behavior right now. Kings Point on the western end is reading close to 71 degrees, New London out east closer to 69 — a real gradient across the Central Sound stretch, and it's keeping bait comfortable enough to hold in loose, spread-out schools rather than getting hammered into tight bait balls. That matters because striped bass are clearly staged on this bunker and mullet right now, not committed. Boats working the Norwalk Islands and the flats off Oyster Bay have been marking good numbers of fish sitting under and around the bait on sonar, but the blitz behavior — the kind where the whole surface goes white — hasn't materialized yet. We flagged this pattern last week: the trigger is bait density, and until these bunker and mullet schools get squeezed tighter by stronger tidal flow, the bass are going to keep shadowing rather than committing. The moon is building toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should start doing exactly that job over the next several days.

In the meantime, the more reliable meat-and-potatoes bite has been bluefish, and it's been a genuinely good week for them. With the Surfside tournament crowd working the Sound hard, reports out of the Norwalk Islands and off Middle Ground Light have blues running 3 to 6 pounds, some bigger, chopping through peanut bunker on top during the last of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing. Poppers and metal — 1-ounce Deadly Dicks and white bucktails with a curly tail trailer — have been the move when they're up and feeding visibly; when they sink back down, a bunker chunk fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 25 feet off the Norwalk Islands or along the edge of the Stratford Shoal rip has kept rods bent. This bite should hold strong through the rest of Labor Day week — the warm water isn't going anywhere fast, and the bunker supply isn't either.

Fluke are doing what fluke do in early September, which is thinning out of the shallow structure and sliding toward deeper water ahead of the fall migration. The back bay and inlet numbers around Oyster Bay and Port Jefferson Harbor have dropped off noticeably compared to August, but there are still keeper-class fish coming off the deeper humps around Stratford Shoal and the drop-offs near Middle Ground Light, mostly on white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the ebb in 30 to 40 feet. Don't expect the volume of a month ago, but the quality fish that are left are worth a drift or two if fluke is the target.

Blackfish season isn't quite in full swing yet for this stretch, but a few scouting reports off the rockier structure near Charles Island and the western Norwalk Islands have turned up decent-sized tog on green crab, a preview of what's coming once water temps drop another few degrees.

The wildcard worth watching closely is bonito. The push that's been building around Block Island and Point Judith has reportedly reached Fishers Island Sound and the Race, and if that westward creep continues at the pace it's been going, Central Sound waters off Port Jefferson and the eastern approaches to Stratford Shoal could see the first real bonito showings within the next week to ten days. Nothing confirmed in our zone yet, but the timing lines up with past Augusts and early Septembers when bonito have shown up on exactly this kind of bait and thermal setup.

Looking ahead, the next 72 hours should bring strengthening tidal flow as the moon builds toward full, and that's the mechanism that tightens scattered bunker and mullet into the kind of concentrated schools that actually trigger blitz behavior. If nighttime temps start trending down even modestly, expect the first real striper commitment to show up on that tightening bait sometime in the second half of next week — the Norwalk Islands and the Stratford Shoal rip are the two spots to watch first. Until then, the smart play is working the bluefish, which are dependable right now, keeping an eye on the fluke drops for a last quality fish, and paying attention to any bird activity east toward Port Jefferson that might be the first sign of bonito arriving early.

reports.headline: Forty Gallons to Veatch, a Bigeye at Boatside, and a Long Look at the Sky
reports.subhead: The eastern grounds are still holding warm water and hungry tuna, but every captain on the radio this week was talking storms before they talked fish.
reports.body_markdown:
A mate on the radio out of Montauk Tuesday night summed up the whole week in one line: "We got the bigeye at color, lost him at the leader, and then spent twenty minutes arguing about the five-day." That's about where the fleet's head is right now — one eye on the fish finder, one eye on the tropics. The fishing itself has been the easy part.

The warm-water setup that's had this zone buzzing all August hasn't gone anywhere. Veatch, Hydrographer, and Oceanographer are still sitting inside water that's carrying real color and real bait, and the eddy structure that's been feeding this bite has shown no sign of breaking down. We flagged this pattern last week — said the tuna action should hold as long as that eddy stayed put, and it has. Boats running out of Montauk, Block Island, and the Rhode Island ports are still connecting on multi-species days: yellowfin in the 40- to 60-pound class on the troll, scattered bigeye on the night drift, and enough mahi and wahoo mixed in on the color changes to keep a crew busy between tuna bites. White marlin have been showing on the troll spreads too, mostly as incidental releases behind the ballyhoo, which is a good sign the bait base is broad and healthy out there, not just one species stacked on structure.

The run itself is still the real cost of doing business out here, and nobody in this fleet needs reminding of that. Out of Montauk, Veatch and Atlantis are the closer targets, but "closer" still means the better part of the day burned just getting there and back at a sane cruise speed. Block Island and the RI ports have a slightly shorter reach into Hydrographer and Oceanographer, but the fuel math doesn't change much — you're planning a full tank, a weather window on both ends, and a crew that understands an early wake-up beats getting caught running home in building seas. This week that math got more complicated, because the forecast discipline mattered as much as the tuna bite.

What's actually working: natural baits and the jig bite both continue to produce, which lines up with what's been said on this beat for the better part of two weeks now. Butterfish and small mackerel fished dead-bait style on wind-on leader are still drawing bigeye and yellowfin on the drift, particularly overnight when the bite tends to concentrate. The jig program — 180-gram class speed jigs worked with a mechanical yo-yo retrieve — has kept producing yellowfin and the occasional bigeye on the drop, especially over structure edges where the current is stacking bait against the drop-off. Streaker-style rigged natural baits behind the spread have also been drawing strikes, adding a little insurance to straight ballyhoo spreads that can go quiet during slower stretches of current.
