Mahi have been the bonus fish all month, showing up under floating debris and around any temperature break a boat happens to cross running canyon to canyon. Nothing enormous, mostly schoolies in the 5- to 12-pound range, but a welcome distraction when the tuna bite goes cold for an hour. Wahoo have been sporadic — a fish here, a fish there, usually on a high-speed lure run through a rip line rather than the standard trolling spread. Worth having one rigged and ready, but not worth planning the whole day around.

The bigger story this week isn't really the fish, it's the sky. The warm filament pushing this whole pattern north has been unusual enough that it's turned this stretch of ocean into one of the more interesting canyon zones going right now, and the only real threat to it is tropical activity spinning up somewhere south and disrupting the setup that's been holding all month. Nothing organized enough yet to change plans, but every captain running this water is watching the tracks closely, because a storm doesn't have to make landfall here to wreck a canyon trip — it just has to churn up the water column and scatter the bait that's been holding this bite together.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern should hold if the tropics stay quiet. The moon is building toward full, which tends to increase current strength out at the canyons and can concentrate bait tighter along the edges — that's usually good news for the troll and the night bite alike, assuming the water stays clean. Expect the exotic mix — yellowfin, bigeye, mahi, wahoo, and the occasional white marlin release — to keep showing through the weekend and into the Labor Day run, with boat traffic picking up as the holiday brings more hulls out to the drop-off. If a system does organize in the western Atlantic, that's the wildcard that changes everything, and it's worth checking the track before committing to a long run rather than after you're already forty miles out with a full crew and a half tank.

For now: if the forecast holds clean, this is still one of the better windows of the season to make the run. Fuel up early, watch the five-day like it's part of your pre-departure checklist, and treat any hint of tropical development the way you'd treat a fouled prop — deal with it before you leave the dock, not after.

reports.headline: Stellwagen Edge holding at 110-130 feet: cod steady on the gravel, haddock working the mud in the Basin
reports.subhead: Bluefin are pinning mackerel schools along Tillies Bank as the pattern we called last week holds through the Labor Day run.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ten to one-thirty feet of water along the Stellwagen Edge, hard sand-to-gravel transition, and the fleet is marking cod stacked tight to the bottom third of the column. That's the number that matters this week. We flagged this pattern last Friday — said stable offshore conditions would hold through the near-term window — and that's exactly what's playing out. No fronts pushed through, the wind's been light out of the southwest most days, and the water column hasn't turned over. That kind of stability is what keeps groundfish locked onto structure instead of scattering.

The cod bite is concentrated on the gravel patches along the southwest corner of the Bank and down the Edge itself, where the bottom breaks from soft sand into that rougher, cobbled stuff cod like to sit tight against. Jigging diamond jigs — the 12 to 16-ounce range depending on drift speed — tipped with a squid strip is still outproducing bait rigs for anyone willing to work the jig actively. Boats anchoring up and fishing clam or squid on a standard cod rig are doing fine too, but the jig guys are covering more bottom and finding the better fish, several in the 15 to 20-pound class mixed with a lot of school-size fish in the 5 to 8-pound range. Bottom line: fish the transition zones, not the flat sand. The gravel edges are where the bait funnels and the cod know it.

Haddock have settled into their late-summer pattern on the mud in Stellwagen Basin, running in that 170 to 200-foot range where the bottom softens up and holds the worm beds haddock like to root through. This has been the more consistent bite of the two groundfish species this week — haddock don't seem to care much about the moon phase or the light southwest breeze, they're just on the mud and feeding. Standard high-low rigs with clam bait or squid strips, fished right on bottom with just enough weight to hold in the light current, have been steady. Sizes have been solid, plenty of fish in the 3 to 5-pound range with some better ones mixed in. If you want a full box without burning half a tank running around, the Basin mud has been the more dependable stop over the gravel edges the last several days.

The bluefin story is the one everybody at the dock wants to talk about. Mackerel schools have been thick on top of the Bank and pushing up toward Tillies Bank, and where the mackerel balls tighten up, the giants have been showing right underneath them. This is textbook late-August, early-September behavior — the bait gets nervous, balls up tight near the surface, and the big fish come up under it working it from below. Boats running the troll spread with cedar plugs and small tuna feathers have had shots when they crossed through active bird activity, but this has been more of a sight-fishing and jig bite than a straight troll program. Vertical jigging with Shimano Butterfly-style jigs in the 200 to 300-gram range, dropped right through the bait ball, has connected on fish when the mackerel pushed deep enough to hold them down. It's not an every-boat, every-day bite — more spotty than the groundfish pattern, with the better windows coming early morning before the wind fills in and pushes the bait balls apart. Anyone heading out for bluefin should plan to run and gun a little, working the edges of bait concentrations rather than sitting on one mark and waiting.

Water's been holding warm for this time of year, and there's a broader pattern worth watching — warmer filaments of Gulf Stream water have been nosing farther north than usual this summer, and while that's mostly a story for the canyon approaches and points south of the Cape, it's part of why the mackerel and the tuna that follow them have been staying active later into the season up here. If that warm signature holds through September, expect the bluefin window on the Bank to stay open longer than a typical year. If a tropical system tracks up the coast in the next couple weeks, that's the wildcard that could shut it down fast and push everything back to a more typical early-fall pattern.

Looking at the next few days: conditions should stay manageable through the weekend, light southwest wind, no major swell in the forecast, and the moon working toward a phase that should tighten up the tidal push a bit without blowing out the drift. That's good news for the gravel bite on the Edge and the mud bite in the Basin — both should stay productive as long as the wind stays cooperative. For bluefin, keep an eye on bird activity and mackerel schools working the surface between the Bank and Tillies; that's where the next shot is most likely to develop. With Labor Day traffic building, expect more boats on the water and more competition for the better marks, so getting out early and getting your jigs down before the fleet arrives is worth the extra effort. If you've only got one day this week, split it — work the gravel or mud first thing while it's calm, then swing up toward the bait schools once the sun's higher and the birds start working.

reports.headline: Egg Rock to the Graves: Bass Holding Deep, Bluefish Owning the Bunker
reports.subhead: The harbor's bunker schools are pulling bluefish into a frenzy while the bass slide off into deeper water during the day — here's where and when to find both.
reports.body_markdown:
If there's only one tide window this week, the call is the North Shore rocks over the harbor islands — Nahant, Egg Rock, and out to the Graves — fished on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, first light or last light. The harbor islands are still holding fish, but the daytime bite around Deer Island and Spectacle Island has gone quiet under a high sun, with bass sliding into the deeper holes off the flats and not committing again until the light drops. The North Shore's rocky structure holds shade and current all day, and that's where the bigger fish have been showing consistently.

We flagged this pattern last week and it's held — this is a summer holding pattern, not the fall run. Water temps are still comfortable, nights haven't cooled off enough to trigger the real push, and the striper population out there is spread thin but present, feeding on schedule around structure and current rather than blitzing open water. That changes once nighttime temps start dropping in earnest, likely mid-September, but for now the program is precision over volume.

Bluefish are the one species doing exactly what we said they'd do — tracking bunker density block for block. Pogy schools have been thick from President Roads down through the Winthrop side of the harbor and out past Deer Island Light, and the blues have been all over them, especially in the two hours around the top of the tide when the bait gets pushed up shallow. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in the 2- to 3-ounce range — worked over visible bunker balls have been drawing fast, violent strikes, and chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig soaking bottom near the Deer Island flats has been picking off the bigger blues that hang under the schools rather than crashing the surface.

Striper-wise, the better fish are coming from the North Shore ledges on live mackerel and eels fished after dark. Egg Rock and the rock piles off Nahant have been giving up bass in the high 20s to low 30-inch range on live mackerel drifted or slow-trolled just off the structure in 15 to 25 feet, best on the last of the outgoing when current pulls bait off the rocks into deeper water. A few boats working the Graves and out toward Gloucester's outer ledges have connected on bigger fish — mid-30s and a few pushing 40 — on eels fished on a slow drift at night, working the tide change specifically, when the current slacks and the fish move up onto the rock to feed rather than holding tight against it.

Cape Ann's rocky shoreline from Bass Rocks down through Good Harbor and Brace Cove has been a mixed bag — some evenings the bass show hard on topwater plugs worked over the ledges at dusk, other nights it's dead calm with nothing showing until well after dark. That inconsistency tracks with what's happening region-wide: the fish are here, but they're not concentrated enough yet to fish predictably in daylight. Patience and putting in the dusk-to-dark window are paying off more than daytime effort right now.

Flounder have been steady but unspectacular on the harbor flats — Deer Island and the flats off Spectacle Island have produced fish in the 12- to 15-inch range on sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bottom bounced slow on the last of the ebb when the water's clean and the current isn't ripping. Nothing to build a trip around, but a solid option if the wind's up and the rocks are unfishable.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same pattern rather than a shift. The moon is building toward full, which should start pulling bait tighter and increasing tidal flow — worth watching closely because that's usually the trigger that gets bass to commit in bigger numbers rather than picking at bait individually. If that bait concentration happens the way it typically does heading into Labor Day week, look for the North Shore ledges and the harbor's bunker zones to both get more aggressive over the coming week. Wind out of the southwest has kept the water on the North Shore relatively clean; if that holds through the weekend, the dusk bite off Nahant and Egg Rock should stay productive.

For boat traffic heading into the holiday weekend, expect more pressure on the known spots — Deer Island Light, the Graves, and the bunker schools inside President Roads will get worked hard. If you want fish to yourself, the Cape Ann ledges north of Gloucester Harbor are seeing less pressure right now and still holding fish on the same eel-and-plug program after dark. Plymouth and Duxbury Bay remain a fallback for calmer water if wind kicks up out of the north, though nothing this week suggests they're outproducing the harbor or North Shore pattern currently in play.

reports.headline: Race Point Rip Holds the Bass Through the Ebb, Cod Nosing Onto Peaked Hill Bars
reports.subhead: Bluefish are chewing peanut bunker off Sandy Neck while the first cod of the season start showing on the deeper humps north of Race Point.
reports.body_markdown:
The fleet out of P-town has been working the same rhythm for about ten days now, and it's held up better than most late-August weeks do. Race Point continues to be the anchor of the bite — the rip off the Point still has enough current and bait pushing through it on the tide changes to keep stripers stacked on the structure, and that's been the case whether the wind has cooperated or not. We flagged this last week — said the early tide stages would remain the best bet through the short-term stretch — and that's exactly how it's played out. First two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood at Race Point have outproduced the middle of either tide almost every day this week.

Water's still holding summer warmth in the Bay, but the nights are getting a jump on things. You can feel it on the ride out in the morning — there's a little more bite to the air, and that's the signal that starts pulling bait around and eventually pulls the bass and the first cod onto the deeper structure. Wind has been mostly out of the southwest, light to moderate, which keeps the west side of the Bay fishable most mornings before it builds into the afternoon. Moon's working toward full over the next several days, and that added tidal push should start concentrating bait tighter on the rips and shoals rather than letting it spread out over open water — that's usually when the better-grade fish show up in numbers rather than just a few here and there.

Striper fishing on the rip has been solid, not spectacular. Fish are running mostly mid-20s to mid-30-inch class, with enough better fish mixed in — high 30s, occasional low 40s — to keep boats making repeat drifts. The pattern that's working is live mackerel under a balloon or slow-trolled on a fishfinder rig, drifted right through the seam where the rip stands up against the current, usually 20 to 35 feet of water depending on where the bait's holding that day. Bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped to the bottom and worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the same water, have also been taking fish, particularly on the last of the ebb when the current starts to ease and the bass tuck tighter to bottom. Peaked Hill Bars has been more hit or miss — good when the swell's down and the bait's sitting on the bar, dead when there's any groundswell running, which has been the case a few days this week.

Bluefish have been the more dependable player right now, and that tracks with what we expected — bluefish activity following bait density, and the peanut bunker showing up thick along Sandy Neck has brought the blues right in tight to the beach. Surfcasters working the flats off Sandy Neck at first light have had steady action on metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked fast through the bait schools as they get pushed up against the beach on the last of the incoming tide. Boat guys working just outside the bar have done well with small umbrella rigs and Ava jigs in the same window. Sizes have been average, two to four pounds, with some better fish mixed in when the bait balls get pushed tighter.

Fluke are in that typical late-summer holding pattern — still catchable, but you have to work for it. Billingsgate has been giving up keeper-class fish on the deeper edges of the shoal, and Barnstable Harbor's channel has produced some decent fluke on the last of the ebb when the water's draining hard off the flats. Gulp in white or pink, three to four inches, on a light bucktail or a simple fluke rig with a strip of squid, worked slow along the channel edges in 15 to 25 feet, has been the go-to. Nothing wide open, but enough to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're patient and willing to move around.

Cod are the story to watch heading into September. A handful of boats working the deeper structure north of Race Point and along the edges toward Peaked Hill have started picking up a few fish on diamond jigs and clam bait, nothing consistent yet, but that's the usual pattern this time of year — as the surface layer cools and mixes down, cod start nosing back onto the humps and wrecks they abandoned back in June. Worth keeping an eye on over the next couple weeks as nights keep shortening.

Looking ahead, the moon building toward full should tighten up bait on the rips and give the striper bite at Race Point a real chance to improve rather than just hold steady. If the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't build too hard, the early tide stages there remain the play — first light on the ebb, or the top of the flood before the crowds show up for the holiday weekend. Sandy Neck should keep producing blues as long as that peanut bunker stays put, and Billingsgate's still worth a drift for fluke if you're not married to the idea of a bent rod every cast. Keep a rod rigged for cod if you're running north past the Point — the early signs are there, even if the numbers aren't yet.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole Bait Balls Tighten Up — Bonito Pushing East, Albies Right Behind
reports.subhead: The warm-water filament that built the Falmouth marlin story is stacking peanut bunker in the rips, and the bonito/albie push out of Rhode Island is aimed straight at the Elizabeth Islands.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk out on the Woods Hole ferry dock right now and watch the surface instead of the boats. Peanut bunker are balling up tight against the current seams, bay anchovies are pushing through Robinson's Hole in silver sheets on the last of the ebb, and the terns already know something the rest of us are just catching up to. That bait behavior — nervous, bunched, getting pushed hard by tide instead of spreading out lazy like it does in July — is the tell. It means predators are working it, and it means the water's carrying the kind of energy that turns Vineyard Sound rips into albie and bonito country by mid-September most years. This year it's arriving early.

The warm-water filament that put a blue marlin on the beach in Falmouth hasn't packed up and left. It's still leaning into these waters, and it's the same push responsible for the bonito that dropped into Block Island and Point Judith in real numbers over the past several days. That's close enough to matter — Block Island sits right at the mouth of the corridor these fish use to filter into Vineyard and Buzzards Bay water, and false albacore are already showing in Nantucket Sound and the Cape Cod side, even if they're finicky and clearly locked onto tiny bait rather than anything you can match easily. We flagged this exact setup last week — said bonito numbers would build as warm water and bait density both trended favorably — and that's precisely what's happening on the Rhode Island side. The next logical step is that push sliding west and south into Quick's Hole, Robinson's Hole, and the rips off Wasque and Squibnocket. It hasn't fully landed in our waters yet. But the ingredients are lined up.

Striped bass are in a holding pattern here, same as most of the region. There are fish around — working the edges of Woods Hole current, staged off Cuttyhunk, showing on the sand eel schools that haven't cleared out of the Elizabeth Islands rips — but this isn't the concentrated fall bite yet. The bunker schools that need to build before stripers commit in blitz numbers are still assembling, and with the moon pushing toward full over the next week, tidal flow is only going to increase, which is exactly the mechanism that packs bait into chokepoints like Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or olive, worked slow along the bottom through the deeper cuts on the west side of Naushon, have been the more consistent producer for stripers this week over topwater — the fish are eating but not committing to the surface show yet.

Bluefish are the one species in this zone that hasn't needed any qualifiers this week. They're aggressive, they're everywhere the bait is, and they've been the most dependable fish on the dock scale from Woods Hole down through Menemsha. Poppers and metal — Hopkins, Kastmasters, anything with flash worked fast — are getting hit hard on the outgoing tide anywhere current runs past structure. If the albies are being coy, the blues are more than happy to fill the net, and given how warm and bait-rich the water has stayed through late August, expect that to hold right through Labor Day week without much change.

Fluke have softened into the pattern you'd expect for this time of year — fair, not great, and increasingly concentrated on structure and channel edges rather than spread out over the flats. The bay side around Menemsha Bight and the deeper holes off Oak Bluffs are still giving up keepers on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow with a long pause on the bottom. This isn't a collapse, it's the seasonal shift — fluke will stay catchable through September before they start easing off the structure toward deeper water, so there's still time if that's the target, just don't expect the volume days of July.

For the next few days, the read is this: keep an eye on Nantucket Sound and the west end of the Vineyard for the first real albie showing inside our zone, because the bait's already staging for it. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and holds light, the rips at Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole on the last two hours of the ebb are the first places that push should show, since that's where the bay anchovies and peanut bunker get squeezed hardest by the current. Best case, the bonito wave that hit Block Island slides straight into Vineyard Sound over the coming week and the albies follow tight behind on the same bait — that's the pattern this time of year more often than not. If it stalls or slides east toward Nantucket instead, shift attention to working bluefish and staging striper spots around Cuttyhunk and the Elizabeth Islands cuts while the sound sorts itself out. Either way, the moon building toward full is going to tighten up tidal flow and concentrate bait through the middle of next week, which is usually when this fishery stops teasing and starts producing in earnest. Worth having lines rigged and ready — this is the window where the Vineyard rips turn over fast once they turn.

reports.headline: Terns Working Nervous Water Off Sankaty — Albies Are Around, Just Not Committed
reports.subhead: Bluefish are the sure thing this week from Craigville to Osterville while the albies feed on bait too small for most boxes and bonito stage just to the east.
reports.body_markdown:
There's been a good tell running off Sankaty most mornings this week — terns stacking tight and dropping hard into slicks of nervous water, then peeling off before the bait even breaks the surface. That's the signature right now: fish are there, they're working, but they're not committing to anything big or obvious. Get close enough and you can see why. The bait balled up under those birds is tiny — bay anchovies and rice-grain silversides, not the fall peanut bunker everyone's hoping shows up. That's the whole story of the albie bite in Nantucket Sound this week: present, active, and stubborn.

We flagged the bonito potential building a few days back on the back of the warm water sitting over the Cape and Islands, and that's exactly the direction this is heading. Block Island and Point Judith got run over with bonito this week, and that push doesn't stop at the Sound line — it walks west. Give it several days to two weeks and there's a real chance those fish show up hard around Great Point and the deeper cuts off Nantucket Shoals, the same water where albies are already teasing the fleet. Worth watching the outer edges — Great Point rip on the last of the ebb, and the deeper humps off the Shoals where the bait tends to stage before it gets pushed onto the flats.

The sure thing this week isn't the albies, it's the bluefish. Between Craigville and Osterville the blues have been dependable — mid-Sound structure, drifting bucktails and small metal (Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters) through bait schools on the moving tide, with black sea bass mixing in on the same structure for boats working bottom rigs with squid strips. That's the everyday catch right now, and it's been steady enough that it's worth building a morning around even when the more glamorous stuff is being difficult.

On the albie front, the fix is going smaller, not louder. Standard Albie Snax and 3-inch epoxy jigs are getting refused when the fish are locked onto anchovy-sized bait. Size 2 bay anchovy flies, small Deceivers, and the smallest Albie Snax in the box — the 2.5-inch, not the standard — have been the difference for guys willing to downsize. Same with spin gear: a 1/2-ounce epoxy jig retrieved fast and erratic beats a slow strip almost every time when the bait's this small. Best water has been off Sankaty on the ebb and around Great Point where the rip concentrates that fine bait against the current line. Patience matters here — these are pods that show, feed for a few minutes, and go quiet, so working a milk run of known rips beats parking on one spot and waiting.

Striped bass are still in that in-between stage the whole region's dealing with — around, catchable, but not yet grouped up tight enough to blitz. Monomoy and the rips off Chatham have had scattered bass on the last two hours of the ebb, mostly on soft plastics — 5-inch white paddletails on light jigheads — worked along the current seams where the sandbars break up the flow. Nothing to write home about yet, but the moon's building toward full over the next week, which means more water moving through those cuts and more bait getting pinned against structure. That's usually the trigger that turns a scattered bass pattern into a real one, so the next week to ten days is worth watching closely, especially around Monomoy Point and the Chatham inlet on a hard SW blow that stacks bait against the beach.

Fluke are doing what they do this time of year — softening, but not done. Horseshoe Shoal and the deeper channel edges around the Sound have still been giving up keeper fish on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the incoming when the water's had a chance to warm through the day. It's not a bent-rod-every-drift kind of bite anymore, but there's enough there to justify a stop before the season shifts fully to fall species.

Looking at the next few days: expect the bluefish to keep producing without much drama, expect the albies to stay frustrating until either the bait size changes or more fish push in behind the bonito wave building to the east, and keep an eye on Monomoy and Chatham as the moon fills and the tides get more current behind them. If there's only one window to fish this week, the ebb tide at Great Point or off Sankaty in the first hour of light is the one — that's when the bird activity has been tightest and the water's had all night to settle clean. Bring the small stuff regardless of what you're targeting; right now in the Sound, the fish are picky, not absent.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's Ledge, 190 feet: cod tight to the gravel, haddock spread thin on the mud
reports.subhead: The ledge is fishing like a normal late-August week — steady, not spectacular — while the fleet starts scouting for the first bluefin sign on top.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ninety on the sounder, hard gravel kicking back a clean mark, and that's been the number all week on the north end of Jeffrey's Ledge. Cod are holding right where they should be for this time of year — tucked into the gravel patches between 170 and 210 feet, not stacked deep in big pods but scattered in twos and threes along the harder bottom where the current breaks over the rise. That's typical late-August behavior. The big pushes of fish haven't shown yet, and they won't until the water starts cooling into September, but there's enough there to make a drift worth your time if you're working bait tight to bottom.

Haddock have been the more consistent producer, and that's no surprise — they want the softer mud basins off the west side of the ledge and in the deeper cuts toward Scantum Basin, typically 220 to 260 feet. The mud holds more worms and small crustaceans this time of year, and haddock will sit on it in loose schools that move with the tide rather than hold to one rock pile. Jigging has worked better than bait on the haddock lately — a 6- to 8-ounce diamond jig or a haddock rig tipped with a small strip of squid, worked with a short lift-drop right off bottom. When you mark them thick on the screen, mark the spot and make repeat drifts; they'll school up and thin out through the day depending on tide stage.

We flagged last week that conditions would hold stable through this stretch, and that's exactly what's played out — no fronts pushing through, no big wind events, water staying clean and green rather than churned up. That stability is why the pattern hasn't shifted much drift to drift. Southwest wind has stayed light most mornings, building a bit in the afternoons, which means starting early and getting your drifts in before the chop picks up is still the smart play. Tide-wise, the moon's coming off full and the currents are running a little stronger than average, which has actually helped concentrate the haddock on the mud basins rather than let them spread out — good news for anyone marking fish and trying to stay on them.

Platts Bank has been quieter than the ledge itself this week, but it's still worth a look if you're already running that direction — pollock have been mixed in with the cod on the rocky high spots, hitting diamond jigs worked a little faster through the water column, 20 to 40 feet off bottom, rather than right on it. Pollock like a moving jig more than a bait sitting still, so if you're marking suspended fish on the meter, speed up the retrieve before you give up on the spot.

Tillies Bank has been mostly a mackerel show right now — thick schools of mackerel showing on top and mid-water, which is a good sign for bait but hasn't translated into a heavy groundfish bite out there yet this week. If you need fresh bait for cod or want to jig mackerel for the smoker, that's the spot, but for targeted cod and haddock work, the ledge and the Scantum mud have been the better bet.

On the bluefin front — not yet, and that's expected. October is when the giants show up on the ledge in numbers, working the bait pushed up along the drop-offs near Cape Ann and out toward Thatcher Island. Right now we're still a month-plus out from that pattern setting up in earnest. A few boats have reported single fish sign — birds working bait balls, the odd blast of surface activity — but nothing consistent enough to call it a bite. Worth keeping an eye on if you're running that way anyway, but don't plan a trip around it yet. The mackerel schools building on Tillies are usually the first tell that the tuna are getting interested, so that's the piece to watch over the next couple weeks.

For the next few days, expect more of the same: stable weather, light morning winds building through the afternoon, clean water, and a groundfish pattern that rewards precision over volume. If you're targeting cod, work the gravel edges on the north ledge in that 170-210 foot band and fish bait — herring or clam — right on bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current. If haddock's the target, the mud basins toward Scantum Basin are producing better numbers, and jigging is outfishing bait right now. Either way, get there before the afternoon breeze fills in, because the morning tide stage has been the more productive window all week. Nothing dramatic setting up in the short term, but nothing falling apart either — just a solid, seasonal Gulf of Maine week, and that's usually when the fishing rewards the guys who know exactly where to put the anchor.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push the Ledges, Bonito Hit Point Judith, Albies Knock on the Breachways
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking tight to the rocks from Second Beach to Napatree, and the first false albacore and bonito of the season are working their way toward the breachway mouths.
reports.body_markdown:
Peanut bunker have been working down the ledges all week, tight to the rocks from Second Beach through Sachuest and around to Sakonnet Point, getting pushed and balled up by whatever's chasing them on the last two hours of the ebb. That bait movement is the story right now. It's what pulled the first bonito into Point Judith and Block Island in real numbers this week, and it's the same signal that has guys at Watch Hill and Napatree watching the breachway mouths a little closer than usual, because this is exactly the calendar window when albies start pushing into Charlestown, Quonnie, and Weekapaug on the morning tide.

We flagged this last week — said to expect steady, incremental improvement in the surf striper bite over the next several days — and the peanut bunker piling up along the ledges is backing that up. It's not a blitz yet. It's schoolies and a scattering of slot fish working the wash at first light and again at dusk, but the bait density is building the way it's supposed to this time of year, and that's the trigger everyone's waiting on for the real fall push to start.

Water's still warm for the season, running in the high 60s to low 70s depending on where you check, which keeps things in a holding pattern rather than an explosion. Bonito and albies like that kind of water, which is exactly why Point Judith before the Sakonnet side did — that structure sits a little further out, catches cleaner water off the reef, and the bait doesn't have to travel as far. Expect that push to keep spreading west over the next several days to two weeks as the pattern usually goes, which means Sakonnet Point, Second Beach, and the Newport ledges should start seeing scattered fish before the breachways do, and Watch Hill and Napatree picking it up last as the bait finally works its way down the south shore and funnels into those inlets.

On the bonito, the Point Judith and Block Island contingent is working small profile stuff — half-ounce epoxy jigs, Deadly Dicks, and Albie Snax in bone or pearl, worked fast on light fluoro, 15 to 20 pound leader, because these fish are locked onto tiny bait and won't touch anything that doesn't match the hatch. Same story creeping into Nantucket Sound with the albies — showing but finicky, feeding on something small enough that standard-size Deceivers are getting refused. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, downsize before you do anything else.

Striper fishing off the rocks is honest work right now, not a guarantee. The better window is that last hour of light into full dark, working white bucktails or three-inch swim shads through the pockets between the ledges at Beavertail, off the rocks below the Newport bridge, and along the Sachuest side. Incoming tide is pushing bait into those pockets and the fish are using the moving water to pin it against structure, so time your casts to the current, not the clock. A few better fish are coming on bunker chunks fished at night off the deeper Newport ledges, but daytime action is mostly schoolies and short slot fish mixed in with the peanut bunker.

Bluefish remain the most dependable player on the whole south shore. Choppers are working the bunker schools hard off Second Beach and around Sakonnet Point, and that activity should keep tracking with bait density straight through Labor Day week — wherever the bunker are thick, the blues are on them. Tin squids and single-hook poppers on wire leader are doing the damage; no finesse required, just get something shiny in front of them.

Fluke have settled into the pattern we called for — fair, not great, holding on structure and in the deeper channels rather than collapsing outright. The breachway channel edges at Charlestown and Quonnie are still giving up keeper fish on white Gulp paired with quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb when the water's pulling out through the cut. Jamestown's deeper holes off the west side are producing similarly — slow and steady beats aggressive jigging right now. Expect that fair-to-good pattern to hold through September before the fish start their move offshore.

On the blackfish side, it's early yet, but there's a feeler bite starting to show on the deeper ledges off Beavertail and around Fort Wetherill as water starts its seasonal cool. Nothing worth planning a trip around yet, but rock hoppers who like to be ahead of the season should start scouting which cracks are holding crabs on the slack tide, because that bite only gets better from here into October.

Looking ahead, the next several days should bring more of the same trend — bait continuing to concentrate along the ledges, bonito holding steady or building at Point Judith and Block Island, and the first real test of whether albies commit to the breachways before the moon builds toward full and tidal flow picks up. If the bait keeps pushing west the way it typically does this time of year, Watch Hill and Napatree are worth checking daily starting this weekend. Keep a Plan B on the striper side — the schoolie bite is real but not blitz-caliber yet, and it likely won't be until the bunker schools in Narragansett Bay get squeezed tighter by the tide.

reports.headline: Appledore boulders give up cod and haddock, bluefish chew the Piscataqua mouth
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coast doesn't need padding when the Shoals structure is loaded and the bunker schools are finally stacking the harbors.
reports.body_markdown:
Every summer somebody from away pulls into the state pier, looks at the chart, and asks where the real fishing is since New Hampshire's coastline barely cracks thirteen miles. That question gets answered the same way every year — point the bow six miles offshore to the Isles of Shoals and fish it like it's a hundred and thirty. The boulder fields off Appledore and White Island don't care how short the coastline is on a map. They fish like Jeffreys Ledge on a good day, and this week they did exactly that for the boats willing to run out early and work the drift right.

The pattern right now is a split one, and it's worth being straight about it. Offshore at the Shoals, the groundfish bite has been steady — not a blitz, but dependable, which this time of year is worth more. Inshore, the striper and bluefish game is still catching up to where it should be for Labor Day week. Bunker haven't fully concentrated in the harbors yet, and that's held the inshore bite to windows instead of all-day action. We flagged this pattern last week, calling for stability through the next several days with the real seasonal turn still a couple weeks out, and that's exactly how it's played. Bluefish activity has tracked bunker density almost point for point — thin bait, thin blitzes; when a pod of pogies pushes into Hampton Harbor or past Rye Harbor's breakwall, the blues show up on them within the tide.

At the Shoals, boats working the rock piles and ledges between Appledore, White Island, and Star Island are finding cod in the 40 to 70 foot range, with the better fish coming off bottom on jigs — diamond jigs and 4 to 6 ounce Norwegian-style jigs tipped with a clam strip — worked on the last of the ebb through the start of the flood, when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a mooring's worth of lead. Haddock are mixed in on the same structure but running smaller on average this month; most of the keeper-sized fish are coming from the deeper humps off White Island in 70 to 90 feet, still on clam belly or squid strips fished on a standard cod rig with a short dropper. Nothing has been what you'd call fast, but a two-to-three hour drift session at the Shoals is putting a mixed box of cod and haddock in the fish hold for boats that know which pieces of bottom hold fish on a given tide stage — the north side pieces fish better on the incoming, the south-facing rock tends to hold fish through the slack.

Mackerel have been schooling thick around the Shoals and pushing up into the mouth of the Piscataqua on the last of the flood, and that's been the saving grace for bait — small Swedish jigs or a mackerel tree worked through the school fills a bucket in minutes, and fresh mackerel strip has been outproducing frozen clam on the groundfish drifts by a wide margin this week.

Inshore, the striper story is patchy but not dead. Hampton Harbor is holding fish on the push — the channel edges near the Route 1A bridge and the deeper cuts by the Willows have given up schoolie-to-mid-slot bass on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets funneled through the inlet against the current. Live pogies under a slip float or a white paddletail swimming plug worked slow along the channel edge has been the better presentation over straight bucktails this week — the bass have been sluggish enough that a slower retrieve is closing more bites than a fast one. Great Boars Head has produced after dark on eels and darters fished tight to the rocks on the outgoing tide, though it's been a game of patience rather than volume. Rye Harbor's breakwall and the rocks off Odiorne Point have both given up bluefish in the 3 to 6 pound class on metal — Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks in chrome — worked through the surface froth when the blues show on bait, which has mostly been dawn and the last hour of daylight.

Flounder season in the harbors is winding down fast as the water starts its slow cool-off, but there are still fish to be had on bloodworms and clam in the deeper channel bends of Hampton Harbor and Rye Harbor on the slower stages of the tide, before the current picks up and blows the rig around.

The moon is building toward full over the next several days, which means more water moving through the inlets and, with it, better odds of bait finally concentrating the way it needs to for a real inshore push. If that bait shows up thick in Hampton Harbor or off Great Boars Head, expect the bluefish to answer within a tide cycle and the striper bite to sharpen behind it. Offshore, there's no reason to expect the Shoals groundfish bite to do anything but hold steady through the coming week — the structure doesn't change, and the fish sitting on it haven't shown any sign of leaving. If there's only one day to fish this week, run to the Shoals early on a dropping tide for the cod and haddock, then swing back inshore on the last of the flood to check Hampton Harbor's channel edges for bass working the bait push. Keep the eel bucket ready for after dark at Boars Head — that bite has been the most consistent thing going this week, small as the window is.

reports.headline: East end ebb at 5:40: bass hold the rip, blues crash bait through
reports.subhead: The moon's building fast now and the current's sharpening right on schedule — here's where the Canal is paying off and where it's still a grind.
reports.body_markdown:
The east tide started running hard out of Cape Cod Bay around 5:40 this past week, and that's the number that's mattered most. Not the moon, not the wind — the clock on the current. Thirty years watching this ditch and the lesson never changes: the Canal doesn't care what the calendar says, it cares what the water's doing between the Bourne and Sagamore bridges, and right now that water is moving with more push than it had two weeks ago. We flagged that last week — said the building moon would tighten current strength and sharpen the bite windows — and that's exactly what's happened. Full moon is coming up fast, and every tide between now and then is going to run a little harder, a little longer, and the fish know it before we do.

The pattern this week has been current-driven striper fishing, plain and simple. Bass are stacked on the seams where the fast water meets the slower water — the classic rip lines off the Railroad Bridge and down through the Sagamore side toward the power lines. These aren't blitzing fish jumping all over bait balls; this is a working bite, fish holding in the current and eating what gets swept past them. Swimming plugs — Red Fins and Danny-style plugs in bone and mackerel patterns — worked on the outgoing east tide have been the most consistent producers, especially in that last two hours of flow when the current really starts ripping and bait gets pinned against the rocks. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1.5 to 2 ounces depending on how hard it's running, dragged slow along bottom on the drop-off edges, have picked up fish in the 28 to 34-inch range mixed with shorts. Nobody's filling a cooler with overslots down here — this is a keeper-slot mixed bag, honest work for honest effort, not a blitz.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player of the two species this week, and that tracks with what we've been saying — bluefish activity follows bunker density, and there's enough peanut bunker and adult bunker pushing through both ends of the Canal right now to keep the blues committed. They're crashing bait on top during the stronger push of current, particularly at the west end near the Mashnee flats and around Hog Island, where the west-running tide funnels bait against the Buzzards Bay side structure. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — thrown into visible surface activity have been the play there, and it's been good enough that a few boats working out of Phinneys Harbor have made it a short-run pattern: hit the west end on the building west tide, work the bird activity, and be done by mid-morning before the current slacks off and the bite goes quiet.

Fluke are still around but this is the softening part of the season for them, right on schedule. The deeper channel edges near the Mashnee Island cut and the holes off Wings Neck have been giving up keeper fluke to white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow on the last of the ebb when the current eases enough to fish it properly without getting swept sideways. It's not a numbers game anymore — one or two keepers for an hour of drifting is realistic — but the fish are there and they'll stay catchable on structure through September before they start sliding toward deeper water.

The piece everybody at the shop is talking about is what's happening east of here. False albacore have started showing in Nantucket Sound and on the Cape Cod Bay side, and bonito have already crashed hard into Block Island and Point Judith. That's the leading edge of a push that typically works its way along the coast, and the Canal's east end mouth off Scusset Beach is exactly the kind of current-swept structure that pulls albies in once they commit to this stretch. Nothing confirmed yet inside the Canal itself — the reports so far are fussy fish on tiny bait outside the rips — but if that pattern follows its usual track, the next week to two weeks is when Scusset and the east end jetty could turn into an albie spot worth the long cast with a Deadly Dick or small epoxy jig on light tackle.

Looking ahead: expect the current to keep building as the moon rounds toward full over the next several days, which means longer, harder-running tides at both ends and potentially shorter, more defined bite windows rather than long lazy grazing periods. If there's only one tide to fish this week, make it the east end on the tail of the east-flowing current — that two-hour window before slack has been the most consistent for stripers holding the rip. West end anglers should watch the west tide push past Mashnee and Hog Island early, before the Labor Day boat traffic picks up and pushes the bite around. The bunker are still building in the bay systems on both sides of the Canal, and once those schools tighten up further with the stronger moon tides, this stretch of water usually turns from a working bite into something with real teeth. Not there yet — but the pieces are lining up.

reports.headline: Monhegan holds, Egg Rock feeds, and Penobscot cod stay down deep
reports.subhead: Late-August stability across Midcoast Maine keeps stripers at the river mouths and groundfish tucked into the Bay's cold channels.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty years of hauling gear out of Boothbay teaches you one thing about the last week of August: the water doesn't rush anything. Cod don't leave the bottom just because the calendar flips, and stripers don't quit a river mouth until the water tells them to. Back in the '90s there was a stretch of Augusts just like this one — flat, steady, boring on paper — that turned into some of the best September fishing this coast has seen once the nights cooled and the bait got nervous. That's the pattern setting up again.

We called this one last week — flagged stable, typical late-August conditions holding through the next 72 hours, and that's exactly what the fleet found. No abrupt shift, no warm-water stress pushing fish around like it's doing to waters south of here. Penobscot Bay and the outer islands have stayed clean and comfortable, water color holding good and green rather than milky, and that steadiness is why the bite, while not explosive, has been dependable enough to plan a trip around.

Striped bass are still working the river mouths — Kennebec off Popham, the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, and the Georges River mouth down at Port Clyde. The pattern hasn't changed much in three weeks: fish stack on the last two hours of the ebb where warm river water dumps into the cooler bay, and bait — pogies and small herring — gets pinned against the current seam. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, worked slow along bottom structure, have taken slot fish to 30 inches. Live mackerel under a slip float, drifted right on that seam, is still the more consistent producer for the bigger fish holding deeper in the channel. Eastern Egg Rock continues to hold bass around the ledges on the up-tide side, particularly on the last of the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the rock — small poppers early, then switch to soft plastics once the sun's up and the fish stop showing on top.

Monhegan is fishing true to form for this time of year. Pollock are up on the surface working bait schools at first light and again toward dusk, and anyone with a light spinning rod and a two-ounce diamond jig has been getting into them steady off the eastern ledges. Cod are holding deeper, 60 to 90 feet on the northwest side where the bottom drops off hard — jigging with a heavier diamond jig or a bait rig tipped with clam has produced fish in the 6 to 12 pound range, nothing to write home about but enough to keep interest up. The groundfish bite off Monhegan tends to hold through September before the fish slide deeper, so there's time yet.

Inside the Bay, the deeper channels between Islesboro and Vinalhaven, and the water off Stonington toward Isle au Haut, are still carrying cod and some haddock, though the haddock have thinned out compared to July. Boats working those channels are marking fish 80 to 110 feet down on structure — ledge edges and the old lobster-ground humps that every captain up here has scratched into a chart at some point. Jigging is out-producing bait rigs right now; a 6-ounce diamond or a Norwegian-style jig worked with a short, sharp lift-and-drop has been the difference-maker.

Mackerel remain the one truly reliable bite in the zone — schools have been thick off Boothbay Harbor's town landing and around Rockland breakwater, taking mackerel trees on light tackle with almost no effort. That abundance is exactly what's keeping the bass and pollock fed and staged where they are; when the mackerel move, everything else follows. Bluefish have made scattered appearances in the warmer pockets around Casco Bay's edge and into outer Boothbay waters, nothing like the numbers being seen to the south, but worth a cast if you're marking bait and see slashing on top.

Looking at the next several days, expect more of the same — no big weather disruption on the immediate horizon, tides building modestly toward the coming moon, which should tighten up the current seams at the river mouths and sharpen the bite window on the ebb. If there's only one day to fish this week, first light at a river mouth on the last two hours of the outgoing tide is the safer bet for stripers, with Monhegan's dawn pollock bite as a strong second option if the wind stays light enough to make the run out. The Bay's groundfish will keep holding deep and steady; no reason to expect a sudden change there until the water starts its real cool-down in a few weeks, which is when the cod tend to push shallower and get considerably easier to find.

reports.headline: Pine Point Blues Shred Mackerel While Biddeford Pool Bass Hold Through the Incoming
reports.subhead: Bluefish are running the coast right now — the bass are still here too, but you've got to work the tide to find them.
reports.body_markdown:
Mackerel showed up thick off Pine Point this week, and the blues found them fast. Guys working the jetty and the beach in front of the Pine Point Fishermen's Co-op were cutting off wire leaders left and right — 3- to 6-pound bluefish coming through in waves, tearing mackerel schools apart on the surface hard enough that you could see it from the parking lot. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch of coast: bluefish are the sure thing, bass are the puzzle you've got to work a little harder to solve.

We said last week that the cooler, more stable Gulf of Maine water would keep this fishery dependable while the water south of us cooks off — and that's exactly what's playing out. Nobody up here is dealing with dead water or stressed fish. The bite's been steady, not spectacular, which after a summer like this one, most of the regulars will take.

Biddeford Pool is still doing what it does best on the incoming — stripers stacking in the channel as the tide floods over the flats and pushes bait into the Pool. The first two hours of the incoming, especially with a rising moon overhead building toward full later this week, has been the most consistent window on this whole beat. Fish to the high 20s, a few pushing 30, have come on Danny-style swimmers in olive-over-white and on Doc's Goofy Jigs bounced slow along the channel edge. Nothing crazy in numbers — two or three good fish a tide if you put your time in and fish the structure right, not just chuck and hope. The last hour of the incoming into the first of the high slack has been the sweet spot; once it turns and starts draining back out, the bite shuts down fast.

Prouts Neck has been a southwest-wind spot all week, and it delivered. That wind pushes bait up against the ledges and gets the current working right for fish holding tight to the rocks. Pencil poppers — the bigger Gibbs Polaris in white or yellow — worked the outside edges at dusk have been drawing bass in the 20s, along with the occasional bluefish crashing the same water. Cape Elizabeth's rocky stretch has fished similarly after dark, big swimming plugs worked slow through the wash, best on a dropping tide when the current pulls bait off the ledges.

Higgins Beach is where the bluefish have really taken over. Between the mackerel schools running the beach and warm, bait-rich water pushing up against the sand, the blues have been chopping bait right in the wash during the last two hours of daylight. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader — 40-pound minimum — because these fish are not shy about cutting you off on topwater. Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast through the froth have been the ticket; slow it down and you'll just feed the school your lure. Anyone throwing a Whopper Plopper into that mess this week found out the hard way what a school of hungry blues does to soft plastic tails.

Mackerel themselves have been thick enough to jig right off the rocks at Wells Harbor and the Ogunquit breakwater — small Swedish Pimples or a mackerel tree will load you up in twenty minutes if you want live bait for the evening tide. A lot of the better bass this week came off live-lined macks fished on a fish-finder rig in the current seams outside Biddeford Pool, proof that when you've got the real thing swimming on your hook, the stripers still can't help themselves.

Flounder action has held up in the usual spots — Wells Harbor and the calmer water inside Cape Porpoise — bloodworms and clam bellies on a simple two-hook bottom rig working the mud on the last of the ebb. Nothing to write home about, but a fine way to fill a cooler on a slow tide when the surf isn't cooperating.

Cod remain mostly a boat story right now, party boats out of the deeper water off Kittery still finding fish on structure, but that's a different report than this beach-and-rock game.

Looking ahead, the moon builds through the week and that means more water moving, which should tighten up the bait and start pulling more bass into range at the Pool and along the Prouts Neck ledges. If the wind holds out of the southwest into the weekend, stick with the pattern — Biddeford Pool on the incoming, Prouts Neck and Cape Elizabeth at dusk on the outgoing. If it swings northeast and starts stacking swell on the open beaches, shift toward the harbors and let the flounder carry the day until it lays back down. Labor Day traffic is going to thicken the beaches, so an early alarm clock still buys you the best water with the fewest footprints in the sand.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:52: Bonito Flood the Rip, Bass Still Playing It Coy
reports.subhead: The bonito finally showed in numbers off Block Island this week, right on schedule — the bass push is close but not here yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack water hit SW Ledge at 6:52 this morning, and for about twenty minutes on either side of it the surface out there looked like it was boiling — not blitzing bass, bonito. That's the story of the week down here. We flagged it last week, said the bonito numbers would build as the days went on, and that's exactly what happened. The push that was flashing off the south side of Block Island a few days ago has thickened into a real bite, with fish showing consistently on the rips off SW Ledge, out past North Light, and along the tide lines running off Sandy Point on the last two hours of the ebb.

Water's still carrying summer heat — Montauk read 69.1 this week and New London 69.4, and the water around the Block has been tracking in that same range, which is exactly the kind of thermal window bonito like before they push further west. The bait's tiny — silversides and rain bait getting pushed around by the current — and that's why the standard albie game is working: half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in pink/white and bone, small metal like Deadly Dicks and Hogy epoxies, and soft plastics like Albie Snax on light leader, 20-pound fluoro max, because these fish get leader shy fast when the bait's this small. Cast into the boils, let it sink for a two-count, then work it back with a fast, erratic retrieve — anything too smooth gets ignored. The bite windows have been tight, mostly tied to the tide changes at the Ledge rather than time of day, which tracks — moving water concentrates the bait, and moving water is what's turning these fish on.

False albacore are starting to show the same pattern up in Nantucket Sound and off the Cape, and if the last few Augusts are any guide, that push works its way toward us before it works toward Long Island. Worth watching the water off Clay Head and the east side of the island over the next week — albies tend to show there first locally once they arrive, working the same small-bait pattern as the bonito but usually a touch fussier about presentation.

Striped bass are the one piece of this puzzle that hasn't fallen into place yet. There's fish around — some being picked off structure off SW Ledge on bucktails during the tide change, and reports of stray bass mixed in with the bluefish working bunker pods closer to Point Judith — but this isn't the fall push yet. The trigger for that is bait density, and right now the bunker schools building down through Narragansett Bay and along the south shore aren't concentrated enough to pull the bigger class of fish into a real pattern. The moon's building toward full over the next week, which means more tidal push, which is usually what tightens up those bunker schools and gets the bass committing in numbers. If you want a bass this week, the better bet is working bucktails — white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounces — slow along the bottom on the SW Ledge tide change, rather than expecting a blitz on top.

Fluke fishing has done what it typically does this time of year — it's softened. Boats working the deeper edges off Block Island and the channels near Galilee are still picking fish, but it's a fair bite, not a red-hot one. Warm bay water has pushed fluke toward the inlets and ocean-front structure where there's better oxygen and cooler bottom temps. Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink shad, paired with a half-ounce to one-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along channel edges and drop-offs, is still the most consistent combination. This window's closing as we move into September, so if fluke's the target, the next week or two is the time to fit it in before attention shifts fully to the fall run.

Bluefish have been the most dependable fish in the water all week, and that's not surprising with bunker schools thick from Narragansett Bay out past the Ledge. Warm water's kept them aggressive, and they've been busting up on top most mornings, especially where bait's getting pinned against structure on the last of the ebb. Poppers and metal lip swimmers work when they're up top; when they're not, diamond jigs bounced through the school get eaten fast. Black sea bass remain a solid, if unglamorous, bycatch on the deeper structure around the Ledge and out toward the Block — steady fishing on squid and clam baits fished tight to bottom, and that should hold into the early fall transition without much drama.

Looking at the next few days: the bonito bite should hold, and likely improve, as more fish filter down from the Cape and Nantucket Sound behind the leading edge already here — that's the pattern this species has followed for years, and there's no reason to expect different this time. The bass situation is the one to watch closely. If the moon-driven tidal push over the coming week concentrates bait the way it usually does heading into Labor Day, expect the first real signs of the fall bass bite to show up in the bunker-heavy stretches before it shows on the open rips. Until then, SW Ledge on the tide change is still the smartest use of a morning — bonito on top, bass and bluefish underneath, and enough happening to make the trip worth the fuel.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds its rhythm: pollock and bass steady while the mackerel start to thin
reports.subhead: Groundfish are still schooling the ledges on the slack, but cooling nights are nudging the bay toward its fall pattern.
reports.body_markdown:
Stand on the rail off Halfway Rock on a clear morning now and you can see the season turning without a thermometer. The water's still that deep green-blue of late summer, but there's a crispness to the light, and the terns that spent July working bait balls tight against the ledge are ranging wider, chasing mackerel schools that are starting to thin and scatter toward open water. That's the tell. Casco Bay in the last week of August is holding its pattern — but it's a pattern with an expiration date, and the smart money is already planning for what comes after Labor Day.

The groundfish bite around Halfway Rock and the outer ledges off Peaks and Bailey Island has been the most dependable thing going. Pollock in the 3-to-8-pound class are stacked over the rockpiles in 50 to 70 feet, and they're eating jigs — diamond jigs in the 2-to-4-ounce range, worked with a lift-and-flutter through the water column on the last of the ebb and into the early flood, when the current slows enough to hold bottom contact without a pound of lead. Cod have been mixed in with them, mostly shorts and a scattering of keeper-class fish in the 24-to-28-inch range, holding tighter to bottom structure than the pollock. Haddock have shown in modest numbers deeper off the Rock, out past 80 feet, but they're not thick — a fish or two on a drift rather than a program you can count on.

Striped bass have settled into the holding pattern we flagged last week — steady light-tackle action rather than blitz conditions, and that's exactly what's playing out. Fish are working the ledges off Bailey Island and around Cape Small on the moving tide, particularly the two hours either side of high, when current pushes bait against structure and bass pin it there. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig has been the go-to for the better fish, but soft plastics — 6-inch white or bone Slug-Go style baits on a light jighead — are drawing plenty of strikes for anglers working the rockier stretches around Harpswell's outer islands. Two Lights continues to produce from the rocks for surf guys willing to work the tide right; the bite there is best on the incoming, when bait gets pushed up against the ledge rock and stripers move in tight to ambush it.

Bluefish have been present but inconsistent in the bay itself — more of a factor closer to the mouth, around the outer islands where warmer water pushes in on the tide, than back toward Portland. When they show, they're chopping mackerel and small pogies on the surface, and a straight retrieve with a Kastmaster or a tin will draw fast strikes, but the window tends to be short and tied closely to bait presence rather than time of day.

The mackerel run itself, which the inner bay through May and June and carried through much of the summer, is doing what it does this time of year — thinning out and pushing toward deeper, cooler water outside the islands. Sabiki rigs are still producing around Peaks Island and in the channels near Portland Harbor, but the schools are looser and moving more, which means less standing on one spot and more covering water to find them. That mackerel movement matters beyond the bait bucket — it's mackerel density that keeps striped bass and bluefish committed to feeding in a given stretch of the bay, and as that bait pulls back toward the outer ledges and Halfway Rock itself, expect the predator activity to follow it out.

Looking at the next several days, conditions favor staying with what's working rather than chasing a shift that hasn't fully arrived. Nights are cooling, which will accelerate the bay's transition toward the fall groundfish and striper push, but that transition tends to happen in stages here, not all at once — a few degrees of surface cooling, then another push of bait, then another wave of fish moving toward structure. If there's only one day to fish this week, work Halfway Rock on the slack tide for pollock and cod, then swing over to the Bailey Island ledges on the incoming for stripers — that double-header has been the most consistent combination on the water this month. Watch the wind out of the northeast; a sustained blow will dirty up the shallower ledge water fast and push the bite deeper and further out toward the Rock. Absent that, the pattern holding steady through early fall looks like the safer bet, with the real question being how fast the bait keeps sliding toward the bay's mouth — because wherever the mackerel go this September, the bass and bluefish won't be far behind.

reports.headline: 68 to 90 Feet: Sea Bass Still Jumbo, Tuna Still Working the Ridges Past the 10
reports.subhead: The high pressure that parked over the Jersey grounds a week ago is still there, and so is the bite — from Axel Carlson Reef out to Barnegat Ridge.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-eight feet. That's the number in my book next to Axel Carlson Reef this week, and it's the depth where the better sea bass have been sitting tight to structure since the middle of the month. Ninety feet does the same job out on Sea Girt Reef. Neither number has moved much in ten days, which tells you almost everything about why the fishing has stayed consistent — the water hasn't been pushed around, the bottom temp hasn't crashed, and the bait hasn't scattered.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the warm filament sitting on the ridges and reef edges would hold the bite together as long as high pressure stayed put, and that's exactly what's happened. No fronts, no dirty water, no big wind events to blow the structure out. That kind of stability is rare for late August in this stretch of the Bight, and it's the reason the tuna work out on Klondike and Barnegat Ridge has kept producing instead of going quiet the way it usually does once the calendar flips toward Labor Day.

The sea bass grounds have been the most dependable part of the week. Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are both holding fish in the 60 to 90-foot range, and the better ones — 3 and 4 pounds, some pushing bigger — are coming off the high-relief pieces rather than the open sand between wrecks. Standard high-low rigs baited with clam and squid strips are doing the work; there's no need to get fancy right now, the fish are eating the bottom bait as fast as it goes down. Shrewsbury Rocks has been a touch spottier — good pockets of keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of short teasers, so it pays to move around rather than anchor on the first mark that shows fish on the sounder. Triple Wrecks has been the sleeper this week, producing some of the better mixed bags — sea bass stacked with the occasional ling — for boats willing to make the extra run and work the pieces methodically instead of drifting through once and leaving.

Offshore, the tuna picture has stayed better than it usually is this deep into summer. Yellowfin and some bluefin have been working the temperature breaks out past Klondike and along Barnegat Ridge, and the mix of species reported out there — with mahi mixed in around the color changes and current lines — is unusual for this time of year in water this close to the beach. Trolling small spreads of cedar plugs and green machines has been the more consistent producer over straight bird-and-ballyhoo rigs, and boats willing to chunk once they mark fish have had better luck closing the deal than the ones running-and-gunning all day. Mahi have been scattered around whatever current edges and floating structure hold bait — nothing stacked up in big numbers, but enough for a mixed cooler if you're willing to put in the running time and check a few lines rather than sit on one spot.

The moon is building toward full over the next several nights, and that's going to matter more than people think. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving across the reef structure, which usually tightens up bait concentrations rather than spreading them out — that's typically good news for the reef bite, less predictable for the open-water tuna work where bait can get pushed off the temperature lines. Expect the sea bass bite to hold or even improve slightly as the tide flow increases over the reefs; expect the offshore bite to stay a little more day-to-day as boats chase whichever line holds the warm water best.

With Labor Day weekend on the horizon, boat traffic is going to pick up fast across all of these grounds, and that's worth planning around. The reef structure — Axel Carlson, Sea Girt, Shrewsbury Rocks — gets crowded on a holiday weekend, and anchoring rights on the better pieces go to whoever gets there first. If you're set on fishing one of the wreck numbers rather than the open reef, get out early; the good pieces on Triple Wrecks only hold so many boats before the bite gets picked over.

Looking at the next 72 hours, the pattern should hold if the high pressure stays where it is. That's the wildcard worth watching — nothing organized in the tropics yet that threatens this stretch, but late August into early September is exactly the window when that can change fast. If the weather stays quiet, Barnegat Ridge and Klondike should keep producing tuna and mahi on the troll, and the reef network should keep giving up jumbo sea bass on bottom rigs through the holiday weekend. If a system starts spinning up in the western Atlantic, that's the signal to shift plans inside and work the closer wrecks rather than committing to a long run offshore. For now, the numbers in the book are holding steady, and that's about as good a sign as this time of year offers.

reports.headline: Where Did the Fluke Go? Follow the Cool Water to the Inlets
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is pushing the fluke program toward Absecon and Great Egg while the first real signs of the fall turn start to show at the inlet mouths.
reports.body_markdown:
The question I've gotten more than any other this week, from the rail at the Brigantine ramp to the phone calls after Sunday service, is some version of: "Where'd the fluke go?" Fair question for late August. The answer is the same lesson I've been teaching this beat for thirty years — when the back bay water gets warm and thin on oxygen, the fluke don't disappear, they relocate. Right now that means the mud flats and sod banks in the upper reaches of Absecon and Great Egg are fishing softer than they were three weeks ago, while the channel edges tight to the inlet mouths and the ocean-front structure off Ocean City and Townsends are holding up better.

That's the pattern we flagged coming — fluke staying catchable on structure and in the deeper channels through September rather than falling off a cliff, and that's exactly what the fleet is finding. It's not a bell-ringer bite anywhere right now, but it's a fair one if you fish the right water on the right stage of tide. Best producers this week have been white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the sod bank channels dump into the main inlet current — the last two hours of the outgoing at Great Egg has been the most consistent window, with fish stacking on that seam where warm bay water meets the cooler, moving inlet water. A few boats working bucktail-and-Gulp combos in 12 to 18 feet off the Rt. 52 causeway rubble in Ocean City have picked at keeper-class fish in that same 18 to 22 inch class, nothing spectacular in size, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you're patient and keep the boat moving.

Bluefish have been the most dependable predator in the mix, and that tracks with what the bait is doing. Bunker pods have been building along the beachfront from Brigantine down through Stone Harbor, and wherever those schools bunch up tight, the blues are on them — snapping bunker chunks and casting big straight-tail plastics into the melee has been producing fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, with some better ones mixed in off the Ocean City pier and the north end of Townsends Inlet on the last of the ebb. That's the call we made last week — bluefish activity tracking bunker density — and it's holding true almost to the letter. Watch those bunker schools closely over the next several days, because wherever they concentrate tight against the beach or stack up in the inlet mouths, that's your tell for the first real striper activity of the fall.

Speaking of stripers, there's finally something to write about there. It's early and it's not a blitz by any stretch, but a handful of school bass in the mid-20-inch range have started showing at first light around the Absecon Inlet rocks and the Great Egg jetty, working the bunker pods on the last hour of the incoming. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounces, cast up-current and swung through the seam, have taken a few. Don't build a trip around it yet — the real push is still a week or two off, tied to bait density concentrating further as the moon builds toward full and tidal flow strengthens — but it's worth a rod in the spread if you're already out there working blues or fluke.

Kingfish have been scattered but present in the surf from Ocean City down to Stone Harbor, biting best on bloodworms and Fishbites fished on a high-low rig in the wash during the middle of the outgoing tide, particularly in that sandy trough water that holds after a period of onshore wind. Weakfish have been quiet — a few reports of fish in the 16 to 18 inch range coming from the deeper holes inside Great Egg on soft plastics fished after dark, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. Triggerfish are showing up as a bonus around the Townsends Inlet jetty rocks and the Ocean City inlet structure, taking small pieces of clam or green crab fished tight to the rip-rap on light tackle — fun catch, not a program to plan around.

The bigger story for the week ahead is the warm-water visitors starting to work their way down the coast. With the same warm filament that's been pushing bonito and false albacore into play further north continuing to extend its influence south, the reef structure and open beachfront from Absecon to Stone Harbor is worth watching closely over the next several days — that's the call we made, and the ingredients are lining up. If that warm water holds and the bait stays thick along the beach, don't be surprised if the first bonito of the season show up working bait pods within casting range of the surf.

Looking at the next 72 hours: expect the fluke bite to hold in that fair-but-fishable range, best worked on the outgoing at the inlet channel edges rather than the upper bay flats. The bluefish should stay steady as long as bunker holds along the beach. The moon building toward full over the next week should start concentrating bait tighter into the inlet mouths, and that's the signal to watch for the striper pattern to take its next step. If you've only got one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the outgoing at Great Egg or Absecon — that's where the classroom says to be right now.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at First Light: Blues Chewing, First Bass Whispers
reports.subhead: The bluefish are keeping the jetty rats honest while the first teaser stripers start following bait into the wash.
reports.body_markdown:
Dawn patrol this week has a familiar late-August look to it — six, eight guys spread across the Sea Bright rocks and the Manasquan jetty before the sun clears the horizon, most of them throwing metal. Ava 17s, Kastmasters, the occasional guy still married to a needlefish out of habit more than results. The blues have been the honest fish. Cocktails to four pounds, some pushing five, chopping bunker pods that have been sliding down from Raritan Bay and settling along the beachfront from Monmouth Beach through Sea Bright on the outgoing tide.
