That bunker push is the thing to watch right now — when those schools get thick and pinned against the beach, that's usually the flare that lights the real fall bass run. We're not there yet, but the smoke's starting to show.

Ocean temps offshore are sitting around 71 degrees with a modest three-to-four-foot swell out of the south, which has kept the surf a little lumpy but not unfishable — just enough push to keep the white water working the front of the rocks at Sea Bright and Spring Lake without turning it into a washing machine. Inside the inlets it's calmer and that's where the fluke guys have been putting in the hours. Tides at Manasquan and Shark River are running normal late-summer cycles, and the better window for everything right now is that last hour of the outgoing into dead low, when bait gets pinned against structure and everything with fins lines up to eat.

We flagged this last week — said to expect steady but unspectacular blues and fluke through early September before any real striper signal shows, and that's exactly the shape of it right now. Fluke fishing has softened the way it always does this time of year. Warm water in Shark River and up in the Manasquan back bays is pushing the better fish out toward the inlets and the ocean-front sod banks looking for cleaner, cooler water. The bite isn't dead, it's just concentrated. Channel edges on the outside of the Manasquan Inlet rock piles, working four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along the bottom, have been the most consistent producers — fish to four pounds, nothing huge, but enough keepers mixed with shorts to make the drift worth running on a falling tide. Shark River Inlet has been similar, better on the last two hours of the ebb when the current pulls bait out past the Belmar side.

Bluefish remain the fish you can count on. They're stacked on bunker from Sea Bright down through Asbury Park, and the jetty game has been simple — get there before first light, throw something big and loud, and expect company. Poppers and bunker-pattern swimmers worked over white water at the tip of the Sea Bright rocks have drawn violent strikes at gray light, tapering off hard once the sun gets up over the dunes. Spring Lake and Belmar jetties have shown the same pattern on the right tide stage, generally the first two hours of the incoming when bait gets pushed up tight against the rocks. Bring pliers you don't mind losing — this bunch has been chewing through leader material like it's nothing.

Stripers are still the whisper, not the shout. A handful of schoolies and a few teeners have started showing at last light and first light around the Manasquan jetty and the Shark River Inlet rocks, working the edges of bluefish activity and picking off stragglers out of the bunker chop. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but it's notable — this is usually how it starts. Guys throwing bunker spooks and darters in the low light are picking up the occasional fish, and a couple of reports out of the Sea Bright stretch mention bass following bunker pods right into the wash on a north wind. If that Raritan Bay bunker keeps building and starts sliding south in real numbers over the next week or two, that's when this shifts from whisper to blitz — the moon's building toward full, tidal flow is picking up, and that combination is usually what flips the switch on the first real fall push.

Porgies have been a quiet, dependable side dish for anyone fishing bait rigs off the Manasquan Inlet rocks and the Shark River Inlet bridge — bloodworms and clam on standard porgy rigs in 15 to 20 feet, better on the tail end of the incoming. Nothing exciting, but a good way to fill a cooler while waiting on the bass to show real interest.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same shape: blues on the beachfront early, fluke holding tight to inlet structure and channel edges, and stripers staying in that tantalizing, not-quite-there mode. If you've only got one morning to spend, put it at first light on an outgoing tide at either the Manasquan jetty or the Sea Bright rocks, work bunker-imitation plugs through the wash, and don't be shocked if a bass shows up in the middle of a blitz. The albie run working its way west out of Rhode Island hasn't reached this stretch yet, but keep an eye on the horizon toward Shinnecock and the eastern Sound over the next week or two — when that shows, it tends to arrive here not long after.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: C-Plus Grade — Bluefish Steady, Fluke Fading, Drum Long Gone
reports.subhead: The rips are picky on the turn but honest on the ebb, while Delaware Bay panfish carry the back-bay rods and the first tuna-of-the-south-shore chatter starts turning heads toward Cape May Point.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the week: C-plus. That's the honest read on the Cape May Rips right now — not a bad bite, not a bite you plan a whole weekend around either. The water's warm, the current's still doing its job on the bigger tides, and there's enough bait moving through to keep things interesting, but the striper action out there is a holding pattern, not a blitz. Fishable, pickable, occasionally rewarding if you're on the right piece of the tide. That's where we sit heading into Labor Day week.

Here's the why. Delaware Bay is running warm — mid-70s warm — which is exactly the kind of water that shuts fluke down and turns on the panfish crowd instead. That's what's happened. The mouth of the bay and the reef sites are still giving up fluke, but it's softened the way it always does this time of year, bait scattering out in the heat instead of holding tight to structure. We flagged that shift a few days back and called it a normal seasonal transition, not a collapse, and that's holding up — there's still a fluke in the box for anglers working gulp and bucktail combinations slow along the channel edges, particularly the drop-offs near Brandywine Shoal on the last two hours of the ebb. Just don't expect the June numbers.

The rips themselves are current-dependent right now, and that's the piece anglers keep getting wrong. On slack water there's nothing doing out there — the bait's not concentrated, the bass aren't stacked, and you're just soaking bait in dead water. But get out to Cape May Point on a building tide, especially the last of the incoming pushing into the first hour of the outgoing, and the rip lines start setting up with real current seams. That's where the keeper bass have been coming from — mixed in with plenty of shorts, working bucktails and swim shads in 20 to 35 feet where the moving water stacks bait against the bottom structure. We also called the mackerel bite tide-dependent, best on the stronger moving water through the rips, and that's exactly what's played out — good pods of mackerel showing on the harder tides, dead on the slack.

Same story with croaker and kingfish in the back bay — we said that bite would hold steady with the high pressure sitting on us, and it has. Fortescue and the marsh creeks off the bay are producing weakfish spikes, croaker, and spot on simple high-low bottom rigs baited with bloodworm or Fishbites, worked on the bottom of the marsh drains on the outgoing. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's steady, it's a fish a drift most days, and it's keeping rods bent for anglers who don't want to fight the bigger water.

On the black drum — nothing to report, because there's nothing left to report. That run's done. May was the window, the fish pushed out of the bay weeks ago, and if anyone's telling you there's a late-season drum bite happening in Delaware Bay right now, they're selling you something. Save that trip for next spring and don't waste tide chasing a fish that's already gone.

Bluefish are the one predator out there behaving the way they're supposed to. Bunker schools are still working the mouth of Delaware Bay and along the Wildwood beachfront, and wherever that bait balls up, the blues are on it — hard, fast, aggressive, exactly the pattern we expected as bunker density built through late summer. Metal — Kastmasters and Hopkins spoons — worked through the surface wash off Hereford Inlet has been the go-to, and anglers throwing bait into visible slicks off the jetties at Cape May Point are getting steady action too. That should keep running through Labor Day week as long as the bunker schools stay put.

The striper situation is a wait-and-see. Fish are around — some being picked off the rips on the better tides, a few showing along the Wildwood beachfront on bait — but the real fall push hasn't started. The trigger is bait density, and it needs another week or two of building tidal flow behind the growing moon to concentrate those bunker schools tight enough to get stripers committing in numbers. Worth keeping an eye on, not worth betting the farm on just yet.

What's actually got the dock talking is the warm-water push working down the Jersey coast — bonito and false albacore have started showing along the central Shore beaches, and with the water sitting warm here at Cape May, this zone is a logical next stop if that push keeps sliding south. Nothing confirmed at the rips yet, but if you're the type who likes to be there first, small metal and a pair of eyes scanning for diving birds off Cape May Point over the next week wouldn't be wasted time.

Look-ahead: if you've only got one day, fish the rips on the stronger half of the tide — either side of the moving water, not the slack — with bucktails and swim shads for the bass and mackerel mix. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod, run to Fortescue and work the bottom rigs on the outgoing for weakfish, croaker, and spot. Watch the bunker schools off Hereford and Wildwood for the blues, and keep half an eye on the horizon for that first albie or bonito showing up where it hasn't been all summer.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point bunker balls thicken up, blues crash them, stripers still biding their time
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking in the upper bay just like we said it would — now it's a waiting game for the moon and the tide to flip the switch on the fall bass bite.
reports.body_markdown:
Stand on the state pier around first light and you don't need a fish finder to know what's building in this bay. The bunker balls off Field's Point and up toward the Point Street bridge have gotten noticeably thicker over the last ten days, dimpling the surface in that nervous, packed-in way that means something's pushing them. We flagged this last week — said menhaden and silversides were building in the upper bay, the same leading indicator we've watched pay off further south before the fall push — and here it is, thicker and tighter than it was even a few days ago.

What's eating them right now is mostly bluefish, and they're not shy about it. Chopper blues in the 3-to-6-pound class have been slashing through those bunker schools from Conimicut Point down through the mouth of the Providence River, and on the right morning you can see the whole thing happen from shore — bait skying, gulls dropping, blues crashing through white water. Poppers and metal — a 2-ounce Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick worked fast on top — have been the move at Conimicut and off the rocks below Rocky Point, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when current pulls that bait off the flats and funnels it past the points.

Stripers are still playing it cagey. There are fish around — guys working eels and bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs at Nyatt Point and in the deeper water off Conimicut have picked at slot bass on the last of the outgoing tide, mostly after dark — but nobody's calling it a real bite yet. That's normal for this stretch of the calendar. The bass know the bait's there, but with the moon still building toward full and tidal flow not yet at its peak, the concentration hasn't hit the tipping point where they commit in numbers. Buckeye Brook taught me that lesson years ago on the spring end of things — the herring don't run heavy until the water and the moon line up, and the bass show up right behind them. Same principle now, different bait, different season. When that bunker gets pushed into tighter, more desperate pods by bigger tides later this week, that's when the stripers stop sampling and start feeding hard.

Fluke have gone soft the way they always do this time of year. It's not a collapse, it's the seasonal handoff — warm surface water has pushed the better fish off the flats and into the channel edges and deeper holes where there's more oxygen and cooler water underneath. The Greenwich Bay channel and the drop-offs along the west side of Prudence Island have been giving up fair numbers, most fish in the 16-to-19-inch range with a keeper mixed in here and there. White or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom through the deeper cuts, have outfished the faster strip-bait presentations. This pattern should hold through most of September before the real offshore pull starts, so there's still time to put a few in the cooler if you fish it smart and stay on the deeper structure instead of the shallow flats.

Scup are exactly where you'd expect them — stacked on the rocky ledges around Prudence Island and the reef structure off Rocky Point, and they haven't slowed a bit with the warm water. Sea worms and squid strips on a simple high-low rig, dropped right to the rocks on the last of the incoming tide, will fill a bucket without much trouble. Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure, a little more scattered than midsummer but still a reliable bycatch anywhere there's broken bottom or old wreckage near the bay mouth.

Weakfish have been quiet — not much to report there, and with the water this warm they're not likely to show in numbers until things cool off in a few weeks.

Looking ahead, the next few days should look a lot like the last few: bluefish staying aggressive on the bunker schools as long as that bait holds together, fluke grinding out fair numbers on the channel edges, and scup staying dependable on the ledges. The bigger story is the moon. As it builds toward full over the coming days, tidal flow picks up, and that's exactly the mechanism that should tighten the bunker schools further and start pulling stripers into a real feeding pattern instead of the opportunistic pecking we're seeing now. If you can only fish one window this week, make it the last two hours of the ebb around Conimicut or Nyatt Point, right as that current pulls bait off the flats — that's where the blues are already committed, and it's the most likely spot for the first real striper blitz to show once the bait gets squeezed hard enough. Keep an eye on the evening temps too; a few cool nights on top of a building tide is usually the combination that flips this bay from waiting-game to game-on.

reports.headline: Holgate's New Cut Holds Bait — Fluke Sliding to the Inlets as the Bay Cooks Off
reports.subhead: The back bay is warm and soft, the ocean side is starting to whisper albie, and the real question this week is which cut holds the bait when the tide turns.
reports.body_markdown:
Flew a drone over the Holgate cut this week just to see what the last few blows did to the sandbar, and the read is worth passing along before we get into the bite. The outer bar off the Rip has slid north maybe forty yards since mid-August, and there's a new gut forming on the inside edge that's throwing a rip current visible from three hundred feet up. That kind of structure change matters right now because everything in this zone — fluke, blues, the first albie scouts — is keying on where current concentrates bait, and that cut is doing exactly that on the back half of the outgoing.

The bigger picture for LBI and Great Bay this week is a classic late-August hangover. Water in the back bay has stayed warm and soft, which is why the fluke bite has thinned out the way we said it would — this is the seasonal slide, not a collapse, and it's pushing fish toward the inlets and ocean-front structure where there's cooler, better-oxygenated water moving. We flagged this pattern last week, said the fluke bite would stay soft through the weekend until a real cool-down hits in September, and that's exactly what's playing out. Nothing dramatic, just a slow bleed of fish off the flats and into the current lines.

Fluke are still catchable, just work-for-it catchable. Best results are coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges at Barnegat Light Inlet and the deeper water off the Ship Bottom jetties. Little Egg Inlet is holding fish too, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current funnels bait out of Graveling Point and the Mullica flats and stacks it against the inlet's south edge. Depth there runs 15 to 20 feet with a hard sand bottom — keep the bucktail ticking, don't rip it, and expect keepers mixed with a lot of shorts.

Back in Great Bay and up the Mullica, the summer pattern is still humming — croaker, spot, and spike weakfish on live minnows fished on the bottom near Graveling Point and the deeper holes off Mott Creek. It's a soft bite, but it's a real one, and it's the kind of thing that keeps rods bent for kids and visiting anglers while the bigger fish sort themselves out elsewhere. That pattern typically holds into early September before the water starts to turn.

Bluefish remain the most dependable predator in the zone right now, and that's tracking exactly with what the bait is doing. Bunker schools are still showing along the ocean side beaches from Barnegat Light down through Beach Haven, and where the bunker balls up tight, the blues are all over them — chunking bunker off the beach at first light, or working diamond jigs and metal-lip swimmers through the pods when they're visible from the sand. Expect this to hold through Labor Day week as long as the bunker stay put, and there's no sign yet of them thinning out.

Stripers are still in a holding pattern here, which matches what's happening up and down the coast. There are fish around — some being picked off structure at the inlet mouths on bucktails and swim shads during the last of the outgoing — but the real fall push hasn't started. The trigger is bait density, and with the moon building toward full over the next week, tidal flow is going to increase and start concentrating bunker in the key zones. When that bunker gets thick enough in Little Egg and along the ocean beaches, that's when the bass start committing in numbers instead of picking at scraps. Watch for that shift to start showing in the next week to ten days, not this week.

The wildcard worth rigging for right now is albies and bonito. Both species are already active to the north and south of this stretch, and with warm water still sitting on the ocean side and bait pushed up tight against the inlets, there's a real chance they show inside Barnegat Light's rip or off the end of Holgate within the next several days. Keep a bag ready for a quick switch — small metal like a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Game Changer epoxy jig, light spinning gear, no wire. If the birds start working tight over bait balls off the Rip or the south end of the island, that's the tell.

Looking at the next few days, expect continuity more than change. The fluke bite stays soft and inlet-focused, bluefish keep pace with the bunker, and the back bay minnow bite holds for Great Bay and the Mullica. The bigger story to watch is the moon building toward full — that's going to push more water through the cuts, sharpen the current lines, and set the stage for the first real signs of the fall transition. If there's only one window worth prioritizing this week, it's the last two hours of the outgoing at Little Egg Inlet or Barnegat Light, right where the new structure is funneling bait. That's where the next move in this zone is going to show up first.

reports.headline: Bunker Density Builds on the Flats — Bluefish Cash In, Bass Still Waiting on the Moon
reports.subhead: Flynn's Knoll and the Verrazzano approaches are stacked with peanut bunker and blitzing blues, but the real striper trigger is still a week or two out.
reports.body_markdown:
If there's only one call to make on the bay this week, it's this: fish the bunker, not the moon. The peanut bunker schools that have been building in Raritan Bay all month have tightened up into real density now, especially off the Verrazzano approaches, on the flats south of the shipping channel, and around Flynn's Knoll. That's where the boat traffic is, that's where the birds are working, and that's where bluefish are cashing in daily. We flagged this last week — said the bunker schools were building fast and the blitzes on peanuts would become a daily occurrence off the Knoll and near the Verrazzano side — and that's exactly what the fleet is finding right now.

The decision for this week is simple: split your time between the bunker blitzes for blues and the channel edges for fluke, and treat the striper bite as a bonus, not the primary target. Water in the bay is still carrying summer heat, and stripers haven't committed to the bait the way they will once real tidal flow kicks in. The moon builds toward full on September 6, and that's the trigger to watch — more push on the tide means more bait getting corralled against structure, and that's when Raritan Bay stripers stop picking at the edges and start showing up in numbers on top.

Right now, Flynn's Knoll on the incoming tide is holding bluefish in the 3-to-6-pound class, working peanut bunker balled up in 8 to 15 feet of water. Metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked through the surface commotion is getting bit as fast as you can put them back in the water. If the blitz shows itself, don't overthink it: match the bunker size, keep the retrieve erratic, and expect follow-up strikes right at the boat. Topwater walkers like a Zara Spook or a Yo-Zuri Mag Popper will also draw blues up when the peanuts are pinned tight against the surface, which has been happening most mornings on the flats south of the channel near the Verrazzano side.

Stripers are mixed into those same blitzes but in smaller numbers and mostly on the shorter end of the slot. The better bass have been coming from the edges of the action rather than the middle of the chaos — working bunker spoons or white bucktails with a curly-tail trailer along the drop where the flat falls into the channel, particularly on the last two hours of the incoming into Flynn's Knoll and the flats off Keyport. If you want a shot at a better fish, work that transition zone slow, right where the bunker school thins out and the bigger predators sit and pick off stragglers.

Fluke fishing has settled into its typical late-August pattern — fair, not fast, and increasingly concentrated on structure and channel edges rather than open flats. The warm bay water has pushed fluke toward the deeper, better-oxygenated cuts: the edges of the Chapel Hill and Ambrose channels, the deeper water off Romer Shoal, and the drop-offs along Keyport Flats where the bottom falls from 15 feet down into the 25-to-35-foot range. Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink shad, paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the outgoing tide, have been the most consistent producer. This is a normal seasonal transition, not a collapse — fluke should stay catchable on those channel edges through September before the offshore migration really takes hold, so there's still time to put a few keepers in the cooler if you're willing to work the deeper structure instead of the shallow flats.

The Navesink and Shrewsbury rivers are quieter right now but worth a look on evening tides, especially for anyone chasing weakfish around the deeper holes and bridge structure — that bite has been sporadic, best described as a fish here and there rather than a pattern, and it's not worth building a whole trip around yet. Porgies and blackfish remain a backup play around Romer Shoal and the rockier stretches off the Hook, best fished on the bottom of the tide with clam or green crab when the wind allows for a clean drift.

Looking at the next few days, expect the bluefish blitzes to keep firing as long as the bunker stay concentrated, and that's likely through the holiday weekend given how tight those schools have packed in. The bigger story is what happens as the moon fills. If the tidal flow builds the way it should heading into September 6, look for the first real signs of the fall striper push — bigger fish showing up tight to the bunker schools instead of picking at the margins. That's the shift to watch for at Flynn's Knoll, the flats off Keyport, and the deeper edges around Romer Shoal. Until then, work the blitzes for blues, work the channel edges for fluke, and keep an eye on the tide charts leading into Labor Day weekend — that's when this bay usually tips from summer pattern into fall pattern, and this year looks right on schedule.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke Slide Toward the Inlet — Weakfish Spikes Working the Tices Shoal Flats
reports.subhead: Warm bay water has pushed the fluke bite toward Barnegat Inlet while bunker start showing near the rocks — the first real clue fall stripers aren't far behind.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty Augusts ago my uncle Nick used to say the bay gets "tired" this time of year — water sits too long under a high sun, the channels hold heat down deep, and every fish with a choice starts looking for a way out toward the inlet. He wasn't wrong then and he's not wrong now. That's exactly the pattern setting up on Barnegat Bay this week, and it's the same one we flagged a few days back — expect fluke fishing to stay modest until the nights cool enough to break up that warm layer sitting on the bottom. Well, the nights haven't cooled much yet, and the fluke have voted with their fins.

Through the back half of August the bay held onto its summer heat stubbornly, and that's pushed fluke out of the mid-bay flats and into the better-oxygenated water near Barnegat Inlet, Double Creek Channel, and the deeper cuts off Barnegat Light. Anybody working the shallow sod banks up around Toms River or the flats off Good Luck Point has been finding mostly shorts and the occasional keeper, but the real keeper activity has shifted down toward the inlet structure where the tide runs harder and the water stays cooler on the bottom. Boats working the edges of Double Creek Channel on the last two hours of the outgoing tide have had the better of it, dragging 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail right along the channel drop where the mud gives way to shell. Fish to four and five pounds have come from there, but it's not a bucket bite — you're working for every keeper, and the shorts still outnumber them three or four to one on most drifts.

Weakfish have been the pleasant surprise. The classic May pattern up at the sedge banks doesn't repeat itself in September the same way, but there's a real spike of weakfish working the grass edges around Tices Shoal and the flats south of there on the last of the incoming tide, particularly in that hour before the top when the current still has some push to it. These aren't the springtime spawners — smaller, feistier fish in the 14 to 18-inch range, but they're eating well on small pink or chartreuse Gulp shrimp fished on a light jighead, worked slow just off bottom in three to five feet of water. Anybody who remembers to slow down and let the bait sit a beat longer than instinct tells them has been doing better than the guys ripping it through.

Snapper blues are everywhere right now, which is normal for this stretch of summer into early fall — small blues chasing peanut bunker and spearing up in the skinny water off Island Beach and around the Oyster Creek outflow, where that warm discharge water still draws bait even this late in the season. Kids with a bobber and a strip of bunker under a dock at Forked River or up around Cedar Creek are having no trouble filling an afternoon. The bigger cocktail blues, three and four pounds, have been mixing into the bunker pods that are just starting to show near the inlet rocks — and that bunker buildup is the thing to watch closest over the next two weeks. It's early, but it's there, and that's usually the first domino before the fall striper run gets moving in this part of the bay. Nothing dramatic yet on stripers themselves — a few schoolies have shown around the inlet jetties on the last of the ebb, mostly incidental fish mixed in with the blues, nothing worth planning a trip around.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around the usual haunts — blowfish thick around the docks and bulkheads in Forked River and Waretown on clam bits fished on a high-low rig, kingfish working the surf troughs at Island Beach State Park on bloodworm or Fishbites during the calmer tide stages. Nothing exceptional, but steady if you've got the patience for small baits and light line.

Looking at the water and the calendar, this holding pattern probably continues through the first few days of September. Nights haven't dropped enough yet to flip that thermal layering in the bay, and until they do, fluke will keep favoring the inlet-adjacent structure over the open flats. If you've only got one day this weekend, fish the last two hours of the outgoing on Double Creek Channel for fluke, then slide over to Tices Shoal for the last hour of the incoming for weakfish and snapper blues — that covers both tide stages without burning the whole day running around. Keep an eye on the bunker schools near the inlet rocks; if they thicken up over the next week or two the way they usually do heading into September, that's your signal the first real fall striper push into the bay is close. Until then, this is patient-man fishing — work the edges, mind the tide, and don't expect a bucket, but there's enough moving to make the trip worthwhile.

reports.headline: Peanut bunker floods Ram Island rocks, stripers on the seams, Race still waiting on albies
reports.subhead: Stripers are working the boulder fields on peanut bunker and silversides while the fleet keeps one eye on the Race for the first bonito push.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait is stacking on the rocks before anything else happens, and that's the tell worth watching this week. Peanut bunker and silversides are pouring over the boulder fields between Ram Island and Wamphassuc Point, pushed tight to the structure by the building current as the moon works toward full. When you see bait pinned against granite like that, holding in the eddies behind the humps instead of running open water, something's about to commit to it. Right now that something is striped bass — schoolie to mid-twenties mostly, with a few better fish mixed in on the last of the ebb — but the water's telling the fleet a second story is coming too.

New London is reading around 69.4 degrees, still comfortable, not the trigger-cold that pushes bait into panic. But the Race stays several degrees cooler than the Sound proper because of the tidal mixing through there, and that's exactly why it's the first place anyone with a fly rod or a spinning outfit loaded with small metal should be checking daily right now. We flagged this last week — said the Race was the logical landing spot for the bonito push building at Block Island and Point Judith, given the cold, current-scrubbed water it runs — and the pattern hasn't changed. Bonito are stacked to our east in numbers. False albacore are showing in Nantucket Sound on tiny bait, finicky but present. Neither has committed to Fishers Island Sound yet, but the ingredients are lining up, and this is a check-daily window through Labor Day.

Striped bass are the honest bite right now, and it's a structure game more than a blitz. The boulder fields off Ram Island and the rock piles tight to Wamphassuc Point are holding fish on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current pulls bait off the shallows and funnels it through the guts between the rocks. Work those seams with a 3/4-ounce white or olive bucktail, short hops just off bottom, four to eight feet of water, and expect the takes right where the current breaks around a submerged boulder. Fly guys working the same water at first light with a sinking Clouser or a small white Deceiver are finding fish holding in the shadow lines off the ledge at Esker Point, especially on the slack before the tide turns. Nothing about this bite is fast — it's a fish here, a fish there, working through likely water and letting the structure do the sorting. But the sizes have been respectable, and a few fish pushing into the high twenties have come off the rocks on eels fished at dusk.

Today closes out the summer blackfish season in Connecticut waters, and a handful of boats worked the Stonington breakwater one more time on the last of the ebb, picking at tog in the four-to-six-pound range around the riprap on green crab. That fishery goes quiet now until the fall reopener, and the boulder fields that hold tog in October are the same rocks holding bass right now — worth remembering where you marked fish, because those same humps will be productive again once the season reopens.

Fluke have softened into the pattern you'd expect for the end of August — fair, not great, with fish sliding toward the deeper channel edges of Little Narragansett Bay and the cuts through Watch Hill Passage as the shallow water in the coves warms under the afternoon sun. This tracks with what we said last week — a normal seasonal shuffle, not a fluke collapse. Gulp and bucktail combos, white or pink, worked slow along the channel drop-offs on the last of the incoming, are still putting keeper-class fish in the boat, just not in the numbers you'd see in July. Black sea bass remain a dependable structure fish through this stretch — the rock piles and mussel beds off Fishers Island are holding them, and they'll stay a steady producer as the water cools into fall.

The next few days set up around the building moon and the tide swings that come with it. More tidal flow means more bait getting pushed and concentrated against structure, which is exactly the mechanism that turns a scattered striper bite into something closer to a real push. If the wind stays out of the south and southwest through the weekend, keep working the boulder fields on the outgoing and watch the Race every day for the first bonito or albie sign — small profile epoxy jigs and 00 Deceivers in the boat bag now, because when that push arrives here it tends to arrive fast, and the guys ready for it are the ones who get the first week of it. Labor Day traffic will be heavier on the water, so first light and the two hours around the tide change are worth prioritizing before the pressure builds. If there's only one window to fish this week, work the last of the ebb around Ram Island or Wamphassuc at daybreak — that's where the bait's been thickest and the bass have been most willing to show themselves.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Flood: Bluefish Corner the Bunker, Porgies Steady on the Cows
reports.subhead: With bunker schools pinned against the reef line, the bluefish bite is the sure thing this week — stripers and fluke are the projects.
reports.body_markdown:
The call this week is Cockenoe Reef on the last two hours of the flood, and here's the thinking behind it. Bunker schools have been working the reef complex from the Norwalk Islands east toward Penfield, and with the moon building toward full, tidal flow is picking up enough to pin those schools against structure instead of letting them wander open water. That's exactly the setup bluefish want — bait trapped, current running, an ambush point built right into the rock. Cockenoe sits in 12 to 20 feet with enough relief to hold gamefish underneath moving bait, and it's been the most consistent producer in the zone for the last week and a half.

The thermal picture backs this up. Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London 69.4, which keeps the classic west-to-east gradient intact — warmer water on our end of the Sound, cooler water building toward the Race. That gradient matters because it means the Western Sound reef system is still holding the most active feeding pattern in Connecticut waters right now, while the eastern stretch cools off first. Bunker density is still the engine driving all of it. The same bait push fueling the bluefish tournament fleet working schools down toward the city line is running right through our reef line too, and it should keep doing so through Labor Day week unless something scatters the bunker.

Bluefish are the reliable target. Cockenoe, the outer edge of the Norwalk Islands, and the flats off Sheffield Island have all been giving up bluefish in the 3 to 6 pound class, mixed with some cocktail-sized fish, on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet, and on poppers and metal — Kastmasters and Hopkins — worked over breaking fish when the blitzes show on top. Best window is that last stretch of the flood into the top of the tide, before boat traffic from the weekend crowd pushes fish off the structure. Weekday mornings are quieter and the bite holds longer without six boats circling the same school.

Stripers are still in a holding pattern, and that's not a surprise — we flagged this last week, said nighttime activity would gradually improve on structure as the heat eased off, and that's what the fleet is seeing. Nothing close to a blitz yet, but the Norwalk Islands' back channels and the rock piles off Greenwich Point are giving up scattered fish after dark on the last of the ebb, when warm water draining out of the shallows concentrates bait along the current seams. Bucktails in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the drop-offs, are outproducing anything cast blind into open water. The real push — the one where bait density finally forces stripers to commit in numbers — is still a week or two off. Bunker have to concentrate further first, and that's a process, not a light switch.

Fluke fishing has softened into the pattern you'd expect for the calendar. This is a normal seasonal transition, not a collapse — the channel edges between the Norwalk Islands and the deeper cuts off Sheffield Island are still giving up keeper fish, just fewer of them and more work per fish. Gulp and bucktail combinations, white or pink, dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the outgoing, are the play. Expect this to hold fair through September before the offshore push starts pulling fish out of the Sound entirely.

Penfield Reef is where the bottom bite lives right now. Blackfish are starting to show on the rockpile, still early-season numbers but real fish, and porgies are thick on the Cows off Stamford — hi-lo rigs with sandworm or green crab, fished tight to structure in 10 to 15 feet on the tail end of the ebb when current eases enough to hold bottom without getting swept off the rock. That window is short — maybe 90 minutes around dead low — but it's been productive every day the fleet has worked it this week. Black sea bass are mixing in as bycatch on the same structure, nothing to plan a trip around specifically but a welcome addition to the box.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same setup: bluefish the surest bet on the bunker schools working the reef line, best on the flood before weekend boat traffic thickens up. If you've only got one window this weekend, take the early flood at Cockenoe or the islands and get off the water before the Saturday parade of center consoles pushes through — Labor Day weekend traffic is going to be heavy everywhere from Greenwich Point east, and fish that get pressured off structure by 10 a.m. usually don't come back until the pressure lifts. The striper pattern is the one to watch closest. If bait keeps building through the week the way it has, the first real concentration could show along the reef edges by the weekend after next, and that's the window worth clearing the calendar for.

reports.headline: Marsh Grass Turning Gold, Bunker Pushing In — Blues Rule the River Mouth
reports.subhead: The shad run is a distant memory, but peanut bunker pouring off Great Island have turned the mouth into a bluefish highway while the stripers wait on cooler nights.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk the breakwater at Saybrook Point this week and you'll see it before you feel it — the marsh grass out toward Great Island has gone from green to that first dusty gold, and the ospreys that spent June and July hauling menhaden up to the nest platforms are mostly gone, fledged and off south already. That's the calendar telling you what the thermometer hasn't quite caught up to yet. The river's still carrying summer warmth on the surface, but the nights are cooling, and every guide who's run this stretch for a few decades knows what that combination means: bunker start balling up in the coves, and the blues find them before the stripers commit to anything serious.

That's exactly the pattern right now. Peanut bunker have flooded into the lower river — thick pods stacking along the edges off Great Island, working in and out of Calves Island and down toward the outer bar on the tide — and bluefish have taken that as an invitation. Boats working the mouth on the last two hours of the ebb have been finding blues busting bunker on top, sometimes visible from the Point itself, slashing through pods that get pinned against the current seam where the river dumps into the Sound. That's a sight worth chasing with a bucktail or a Kastmaster — 2 to 3-ounce, white or chartreuse, cast into the commotion and worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. No finesse needed. These blues, 3 to 6 pounds mostly with some better fish mixed in, are eating with intent, and a popper thrown right into a boil off the Saybrook breakwater or the flats below Great Island will get hit as fast as you can crank it.

Stripers are in the mix, but they're playing a different game than the blues right now, and that's worth being honest about. The bass are mostly holding under the bunker schools rather than crashing them on top, picking off cripples and stragglers on the drop rather than committing to a full blitz. That means the better program for bass has been working soft plastics and swimming plugs down through the water column rather than fishing the surface show. A white Al's Goldfish or a 5-inch white/pearl soft plastic swimbait, fished on the last two hours of the ebb along the channel edge off North Cove and down past Calves Island toward the mouth, has been picking up schoolies and some slot-class fish holding tight to the drop-off where the river current meets the harder Sound water. Depth's been in the 8 to 15-foot range along those edges, and the take is subtle — a soft pull rather than a slam — which tells you these fish aren't in a hurry yet.

White perch fishing has quietly been solid for anyone willing to slow down and fish deep. The holes below the Baldwin Bridge and up into the Essex reaches have been holding good numbers, and small bucktail jigs tipped with a piece of bloodworm or a sliver of shrimp, worked slow along bottom in 15 to 20 feet, have been steady producers on the last of the incoming. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's dependable, and it's a good option on the days when the wind kicks up out on the flats and makes the bunker chase uncomfortable.

We flagged last week that conditions in this stretch would hold stable through the near term, and that's exactly what's played out — no big shift in water temperature, no major push of new bait, just the same warm-water pattern grinding along with the bluefish carrying the show. That's typical for this river. It tends to lag the open Sound by a week or two on anything seasonal, whether that's the spring shad run coming in behind the rest of the coast or the fall transition arriving late. Out west in the Sound, the water's sitting in the low 70s and blues have been the most dependable predator around bait schools for weeks now — the same story that's playing out here at the mouth, just with a river current mixed in instead of open water.

Looking at the next several days, don't expect a wholesale changeover yet. The moon's building toward full, which should tighten up the tide and start concentrating bait more aggressively in the usual pinch points — the bar off Great Island, the seam below the breakwater, the mouth of North Cove. That's typically the first real trigger for stripers to shift from picking at scraps to committing harder, and if the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, look for that shift to show up in the next one to two weeks rather than this weekend. For now, the smart play is fishing the bluefish blitzes when they show — they're reliable and they're fun — while working the plugs and soft plastics underneath for the bass that are still playing it patient. If the wind stays manageable out of the south and southwest, early morning and the last two hours of the ebb remain the windows worth building a trip around, whether that's off the Point, down along Great Island, or working the deeper bends up toward Essex for perch when the top-water action goes quiet.

reports.headline: Terns Tight on the Rocks at Horton Point — Bluefish Behind Them, Bass Still Waiting
reports.subhead: Bunker pushed into the beach this week woke up the blues while stripers hang back for cooler water and a bigger moon.
reports.body_markdown:
Ray Tuthill's been tending the same string of oyster cages off Mattituck Inlet for going on thirty years, and he's got one rule he trusts more than any weather app: when the terns quit working the open water and start diving tight against the rocks, something's pushed the bait shallow. He called the bait shop Tuesday to report the birds were stacked up hard against Horton Point, working low and fast over the boulders. That's about as reliable a forecast as this stretch of Sound gives you, and it turned out right — a run of bunker got pinned against the beach there by midweek, and the bluefish showed up behind them like they'd been invited.

That's the story for the North Fork's Sound side this week: bluefish carrying the load, porgy holding steady as the sure thing, fluke thinning out the way it always does this time of year, and striped bass sitting on the sideline waiting for a signal that hasn't quite come yet. The water tells part of it. Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound is reading close to 71 degrees, New London down near the Race is running about 69.4, and that gradient runs right through this beat — warmer water piling up toward Mattituck, a cooler bite of it working in from Plum Gut east. Bass don't love either extreme this time of year. They want the bait concentrated, and the bait isn't quite there yet.

Bluefish don't share that problem. They've been the most dependable predator on this stretch straight through the month, tracking bunker schools that have been moving in pods along the beach from Mattituck to Rocky Point. When those schools get pinned against structure — a rock pile, a point, a current seam — the blues pile in and it turns into fast fishing for twenty minutes at a stretch. Diamond jigs in the one-to-two-ounce range worked with a fast retrieve have been doing the damage, and so have bunker chunks fished on wire leader for anyone who'd rather sit and let the current do the work. We flagged a couple weeks back that bluefish activity would track bunker density, and that's exactly the pattern playing out now — where the bunker balls are thick, the blues are thick behind them, and where the bait's thinned, so has the bite.

Porgy fishing remains the fallback that never seems to fail this time of year, and it hasn't changed. The rock piles off Horton Point and the drop-offs east of Rocky Point are holding good numbers of scup in the eight-to-twelve-inch class, with a scattering of better fish mixed in on the deeper structure. Small hooks, sandworms or squid strips, light sinkers — nothing complicated about it, and it's about the only bite around here you can set a watch by right now.

Fluke have gone soft, which is normal for the end of August and nothing to read too much into. The warm water sitting up in the shallows has pushed them out toward the inlets and deeper channel edges where there's a bit more oxygen and a bit less heat. Mattituck Inlet itself has been giving up a few keeper-class fish to white Gulp paired with a half-ounce bucktail, worked slow along the channel drop on the last of the outgoing. It's not the kind of fishing that fills a cooler fast, but patient anglers working the deeper edges are still connecting. We said this stretch would hold catchable fluke into September before the offshore push starts in earnest, and that's holding true — just don't expect the June numbers.

Striped bass are the one everybody's watching and nobody's catching much of yet. There's fish around — a few taken on bunker chunks at first light off Rocky Point, a handful more on eels worked slow through the Plum Gut approach on a strong tide stage — but it's spotty, not a pattern you can plan a trip around. The real trigger is bait density, and right now the bunker schools that will eventually pull bass into blitz mode are still scattered rather than balled up tight. That tends to change fast once the moon builds toward full and the tides start moving more water — probably another week to two weeks out, based on how this has gone in past seasons. When it turns, it usually turns quick, and Plum Gut is the place to be watching, since that's where the first pushes of bait and predator alike tend to funnel through on a strong tide.

Speaking of Plum Gut — keep an eye out there for something besides bass. There's bonito working the Race and the Rhode Island side of the Sound already, and this stretch sits close enough to catch the overflow if that push keeps drifting west. Nothing confirmed on this side yet, but small metal jigs and epoxy flies would be the play if they show.

Blackfish remain off the table, and that's no surprise — we said last week the bigger tautog story here is still weeks off, waiting on the Sound to cool down further, and nothing this week changes that read. For now, work the bunker-and-tern pattern for blues, hit the rock piles for a reliable bag of porgy, and if you want fluke, fish the channel edges slow rather than the flats. The next real shift on this beat is the bass turning on with the bigger tides — watch the moon, watch the bait, and watch Plum Gut closest of all.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Rip Still Turning: Bluefish Committed, Bass Staging Deep
reports.subhead: The seam off the fort is holding bait and blues on every ebb, while the striper bite waits on the bunker to bunch up.
reports.body_markdown:
The current off Fort Trumbull has been running hard and clean on the back half of the ebb all week, and that seam where the river water pours past the old fort wall into the harbor channel has been the most consistent read on this stretch of the Thames. Water off New London has been sitting in the high 60s, closer to 69 degrees, and that's warm enough to keep bait tight to structure rather than scattered across open water. That's the pattern that's been setting up for ten days now — bluefish committed and predictable, striped bass present but not yet organized into the kind of push that makes September memorable on this river.

We flagged this last week — said to expect stability through the short-term window with no major changes in this sheltered zone — and that's exactly what's played out. No fronts have come through to stir things up, the harbor has stayed clean, and the bite has held its shape day to day rather than swinging hot and cold. That kind of steadiness is a gift this time of year, because it means anglers can plan around known windows instead of chasing a moving target.

Bluefish are the dependable half of that equation right now, and they've been tracking bunker density just like we said they would. Peanut and adult bunker have been pushing through the Gold Star Bridge pilings on the last two hours of the ebb, and the blues have been parked underneath, working the pilings like a feeding station. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped tight to the concrete and swept with the current, have been drawing consistent strikes from blues in the 3 to 6-pound class. Chunk bunker fished on a fish-finder rig off the Fort Trumbull rocks has also been producing, particularly in the last hour of daylight when the current is still moving but the sun's off the water. Topwater has had its moments too — poppers worked off the rocks at Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach during the early morning slack have drawn some violent surface strikes when bait is visibly nervous on top.

Striped bass are the harder read. They're in the system — boats working the deeper current seams below the Gold Star Bridge and in the mouth of the harbor near the state pier have picked bass in the 24 to 30-inch range on the last two hours of the incoming, mostly on eels drifted along bottom structure or bunker chunks fished tight to the channel edge. But it's not a blitz pattern yet, and anyone expecting surface commotion is going to be disappointed. These fish are holding deep, tucked against current breaks and rock piles rather than chasing bait on top, which tracks with what the moon is doing right now. We're building toward full, and that means tidal flow is only going to get stronger over the next several days, which should start concentrating bait harder in the same zones where bluefish are already parked. When that bait finally bunches up tight enough, the bass tend to commit fast — that's the pattern up and down this whole stretch of coast right now, and there's no reason the Thames should be any different once it happens.

Porgies have stayed a reliable side dish for anyone fishing bottom rigs off Groton, particularly around the drop-offs near the state pier and the deeper stretches toward Sarah's Ledge, where sandworms and clam strips on a simple hi-lo rig have kept rods bent for anyone willing to sit on anchor through a tide change. Blackfish are starting to show a little more interest around the rock piles and jetty structure near Avery Point and the mouth of Fishers Island Sound, though it's still early-season picking rather than a full-blown tautog bite — green crabs on a jig head, worked slow along the rocks on the bottom of the tide, have taken a few fish in the 14 to 18-inch range.

One thing worth watching given how close this harbor sits to Fishers Island Sound: bonito have been showing signs of pushing west out of Rhode Island waters, and if that spillover reaches the Race or the eastern Sound approaches, this river mouth and the water off Ocean Beach would be a logical place for them to show up next. Nothing confirmed yet on this side of the line, but it's worth keeping a small metal or epoxy jig rigged on light tackle in the boat just in case that shows up over the holiday weekend.

Looking at the next several days, expect the bluefish pattern to hold — warm water, strong current, bait tight to structure, and blues willing to eat anything that swims through the seam. The striper situation is the one to watch closely as the moon builds toward full over Labor Day weekend; if the bunker schools in the harbor and river mouth tighten up the way they have elsewhere on the coast, the bass bite here could shift from a deep, patient game to something a lot more aggressive in a short window. Until that happens, the smart play is working the known current breaks — Fort Trumbull on the ebb, the bridge pilings on the last of the tide — rather than searching for fish that haven't organized yet.

reports.headline: Race Running 4.8 Knots: Bass Holding, Bonito Knocking on the Door
reports.subhead: Spring tides are loading Plum Gut with bait while the Block Island bonito push creeps toward the Sluiceway.
reports.body_markdown:
The Race is starting to run hard again — pushing into the 4.5 to 4.8 knot range on the max flood as the moon builds toward full over the next week. That's spring-tide strength, and it changes everything out there. Slack at Valiant Rock is tightening into a narrower window, maybe 20 minutes either side of the turn, and if you're not set up on the rock before the water goes still, you're fishing the wrong tide. That's the technical read for the week: bigger current, shorter slack, and a thermal gradient across the Sound that's still steering where the bait — and the bass — want to sit.

Kings Point is holding at 70.9 degrees, New London's at 69.4, and that three-quarters of a degree spread across the Sound matters more than it sounds like it should. Warmer water to the west is keeping bait mobile and spread out; the cooler eastern end around the Race and Plum Gut is where forage tends to stack up against structure once the tide starts to squeeze it. That's exactly what's happening at Valiant Rock and Race Rock right now — not a blitz, but a consistent grind of resident stripers working the eddies on the down-tide side once the current lays over.

Striped bass are in a holding pattern, and it's worth saying that plainly instead of dressing it up. The fish are here, they're catchable, but the true fall push — the one that turns the Race into a washing machine of birds and breaking bass — hasn't started. That trigger is bait density, and bunker schools from Raritan Bay to the LI south shore to Narragansett Bay need another week or two of tidal flow to concentrate before that switch flips. In the meantime, wire line trolled tight along the rock piles at Valiant Rock and Race Rock, or bucktails bounced through the seams off Little Gull Island on the last hour of the ebb, are producing keeper-class fish in the 28 to 34 inch range. Chartreuse and white 2-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of mackerel belly are getting bit better than plain jigs right now — something about that extra scent line in current this strong.

Bluefish remain the most dependable predator in the zone. They're chopping bait through the Sluiceway and along the Plum Gut rip on both stages of the tide, not just around the turn, which tells you they're not current-dependent the way the bass are — they're just following bait wherever it drifts. Diamond jigs in the 3 to 4 ounce range worked with a fast, erratic retrieve are the go-to, and there's no need to finesse it. Warm water has kept them aggressive and spread wide, and with the Surfside Hotel tournament crowd working the western Sound hard this week, that pressure is pushing some of that bluefish biomass east toward Gull Island and the Gut mouth. Expect this to hold through Labor Day.

The number everyone in the shop is talking about is the bonito. They crashed into Block Island and Point Judith in real numbers this week, right on the seasonal schedule we've been watching build. False albacore are showing in Nantucket Sound too, though they're feeding on tiny bait and staying finicky — small profile epoxy jigs and Albie Snax in the smallest sizes you own are the play if you find them. Neither species has committed to the Race or Plum Gut yet, but the historical pattern says this push spreads west into Fishers Island Sound and the eastern approaches within days to two weeks. Little Gull Island and the outer edge of the Sluiceway are the first places it'll show on our side — keep half an eye on the surface for nervous bait and diving terns anywhere along that stretch starting this weekend.

Fluke have softened into the typical late-August pattern — fair, not great, and thinning out as the bay water stays warm and the fish push toward cooler structure. Plum Gut's deep channel edges and the drop-offs along the Sluiceway are still worth a drift on the last of the incoming, working white Gulp paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail slow along bottom. Don't expect numbers, but the fish that are there are decent size. Black sea bass remain the steady bycatch on the reef structure around Race Rock and Valiant Rock — jigs tipped with squid strips are filling out coolers even on days when everything else is quiet.

We flagged this last week — said conditions would stay favorable for pelagic species through the near term — and the bonito arrival at Block Island is exactly that call playing out on schedule. The next 72 hours should hold that pattern: canyon and coastal pelagic activity staying strong, the bluefish grind continuing straight through the holiday weekend, and the first real test of whether that bonito push reaches the Race before Labor Day traffic hits the water. If it does, Valiant Rock and the Gull Island edge are where to be on the morning slack. If the bass are your priority instead, keep working the rock piles on wire and bucktail through the tide changes — the fall blitz isn't here yet, but the bait's building, and the moon's doing exactly what it needs to do to make that happen inside the next two weeks.

reports.headline: Bonito Talk Out of the Race Has the Niantic Fleet Watching — Bluefish Are Still Doing the Real Work
reports.subhead: Waterford and Niantic boats are grinding bluefish and sea bass while everyone keeps one eye on the Race for the first bonito to slide in from Block Island.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk into any tackle shop from Niantic to Waterford right now and the conversation starts the same way: has anybody seen a bonito yet? The word out of Block Island and Point Judith is that they've been thick for a couple weeks, and with the Race sitting right at our doorstep, the fleet's been half-expecting one of the drift boats to come back with a story. Nobody's confirmed it in this zone yet — but the water's set up for it. New London's reading around 69.4 degrees, and there's a real gradient running west to east, with Kings Point up near 71. That kind of stair-step is exactly how these fish walk west along the Sound, riding the warmer edge until they find bait to hold on. Keep an ear out over the next several days, because if bonito show up in Twotree Island Channel or off the Race, it'll be the first real sign the push has crossed the state line.

In the meantime, the bread and butter out here is bluefish, and they're not asking anybody's permission. Bunker schools have been thick in Niantic Bay and stacking up around Black Point, and the blues have been all over them — this is the pattern we flagged last week, that bluefish activity was going to track bunker density, and that's exactly what's playing out. Drift boats working bunker schools off McCook Point and along the mouth of the Niantic River have had steady action on diamond jigs and bunker spoons, with some boats doing well on cut bunker chunks fished on wire leader in 15 to 25 feet. These aren't monster blues across the board — there's a mix of 3- to 6-pound fish with some better ones mixed in — but they've been reliable enough that mates are steering people toward them when the rest of the bite gets picky. Topwater guys throwing poppers early in the morning around the bait schools have had some violent strikes, worth doing if you're on the water at first light before the boat traffic pushes the bunker deeper.

Fluke have softened up the way they always do this time of year, and it's fair to call it a mixed bag rather than a hot bite. The warm surface water in the back of Niantic Bay has pushed fish out toward better-oxygenated structure — Hole-in-the-Wall and the channel edges around Twotree have been holding better fish than the flats. Boats working 35 to 45 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, have been picking at keepers in that 18- to 20-inch class, with the occasional 4- or 5-pounder mixed in. This is exactly the transition we called last week — not a collapse, just fluke sliding toward structure and deeper water the way they do every late August. They'll stay catchable into September if you follow them off the flats and onto the drops.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable structure fish on the beat. Black Point reef and the rockpiles off McCook have been giving up decent numbers on squid strips and green crab fished on high-low rigs in 30 to 50 feet, with the better bite coming on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without needing a pound of lead. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts to sort through, but enough 14- to 16-inch fish in the mix to make a trip worthwhile if you're patient about moving around the structure.

Striped bass remain the wildcard, and right now they're still in a holding pattern rather than a blitz. There are fish around — some being picked off structure at Hole-in-the-Wall and along the current seams off Black Point on bucktails and swim shads — but the bunker haven't concentrated enough yet to trigger the kind of surface chaos everyone's waiting for. The moon building toward full over the next several days should start changing that. More current means bait gets pushed and squeezed into tighter pockets, and that's usually when the bass stop nibbling around the edges and start committing. If there's one thing worth watching closely heading into Labor Day week, it's whether the bunker schools in Niantic Bay start balling up the way they have in years past when the tide gets some teeth back in it.

For the next few days, the smart play is still bluefish and sea bass while keeping a rod rigged for a quick bucktail cast if stripers show themselves on bait. Wind and boat traffic will both pick up over the holiday weekend, so early starts matter more than usual — get out ahead of the fleet on the last of the ebb, work the bunker schools before they scatter, and don't be shocked if somebody radios in a bonito sighting near the Race before this week is out. The water's right for it. Whether the fish cooperate is the only question left.

reports.headline: New Haven Breakwalls Stacked With Porgies and Sea Bass, Blackfish Starting to Show
reports.subhead: The rockpiles are producing all day long while stripers work the Charles Island bar on the flood and bluefish chase bait everywhere else.
reports.body_markdown:
Three guys working the outer wall at New Haven Harbor Tuesday morning had a five-gallon bucket half full of porgies before nine o'clock, and mixed into that bucket were three sea bass pushing two pounds — the kind that make you check your knot twice before the next drop. That's been the story on the rockpiles all week: steady, dependable, the bread-and-butter bite that Central Sound structure fishing is built on, with the added bonus that blackfish are starting to nose into the mix as water temps ease off their summer peak.

The Sound's holding warm — Kings Point up around 71, New London closer to 69 — and that west-to-east gradient means the New Haven-to-Milford stretch is still fishing like late summer, not like the shoulder season yet. That's good news for porgies and sea bass, which want that stable warm water over structure, and it's part of why the bite on the breakwalls, Charles Island rockpile, and the Falkner Island reef complex has stayed so consistent through the back half of August. Blackfish are a step behind — a few keeper-class tog are coming off the deeper humps around Stratford Shoal on green crabs, but that's an early trickle, not the main event yet. Give it two, three more weeks of cooling water and that fishery turns on in earnest.

Stripers are the more complicated story right now, and honestly, they're behaving exactly the way we said they would last week — this is a summer holding pattern, not the fall run. Fish are stacked on the Charles Island sandbar, especially on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when current sweeps bait off the bar edge into deeper water. Live eels and chunked bunker fished on the drop-off have been drawing slot-class bass in the 26 to 34 inch range, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in after dark. But it's not blitz fishing — it's a tide-window bite, and if you show up at the wrong stage you'll wonder what everyone's talking about. The real push, when bunker schools finally concentrate enough to trigger blitz-level feeding, is still likely a couple weeks off, tracking the moon toward full and the first real drop in overnight temps come mid-September.

Bluefish, on the other hand, have been the most dependable predator in the zone, and that's tracking exactly with bunker density like we flagged — wherever the bait pods are thick, from the mouth of the harbor out past Charles Island to the pocket water off Hammonasset, the blues are on them. Casting metal — quarter to half-ounce Kastmasters, or bucktail-tipped diamond jigs — into visible pods has been producing fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, with some better ones mixed in off Falkner Island where the bait's been holding tighter. Poppers worked over the surface pods at first light have been just as effective and a lot more fun on light spinning gear.

Fluke have softened up the way they always do this time of year, and that's the seasonal transition we called for — not a collapse, just fish sliding off the open flats and tucking into structure and deeper channel edges looking for cooler, better-oxygenated water. The Milford Gulf has been the most consistent producer, with anglers working white and chartreuse Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails slow along the channel drop, picking through shorts to find the occasional keeper in the 18 to 20 inch range. It's fair fishing, not fast, and the window for it is closing as September moves in — worth a trip if you're patient, not worth planning a whole day around.

For the porgy and sea bass crowd, the program hasn't changed and doesn't need to: top-and-bottom rigs with sandworms, clam strips, or grass shrimp, dropped straight down over the rockpiles at New Haven's east and west breakwalls, the Charles Island reef, and the Falkner Island structure. High tide and the two hours around it have been the strongest window, with porgies stacking thick enough that doubles are common and sea bass mixed in on almost every other drop. Stratford Shoal is worth the run for boats that can handle the current — deeper water there is holding bigger sea bass, some pushing three pounds, on squid strips fished tight to bottom.

Looking into Labor Day week, expect more boat traffic and more pressure on all these spots as the holiday pulls people onto the water, but the underlying pattern should hold — warm water keeps the porgy and sea bass bite steady, bluefish stay locked to bait, and stripers keep working the Charles Island bar on tide rather than committing to anything bigger. Watch the moon build toward full over the next several days; as tidal flow increases, that's usually the trigger that starts concentrating bait harder in the back bays and bar edges, and that's when the striper bite tends to step up a notch. If you've only got one trip in you before the holiday, fish the breakwalls on the high and don't overthink it — that's where the guaranteed action is right now.

reports.headline: 71.2°F at the Bight, Warm Filament Holds — Yellowfin and Mahi Keep Coming on the Troll
reports.subhead: A stable warm-water tongue is still sitting over the canyon edge, and the fleet working the 100-fathom line, the Claw, and the Dip is cashing in before the moon and the tropics have a say.
reports.body_markdown:
71.2°F. That's the reading off buoy 44025 out in the Bight this week, with seas running 3 to 4 feet on a short 5-second period — nothing dramatic, but it tells you the surface layer is stable and the ride out hasn't been beating anybody up too badly. That number by itself isn't the story. The story is what's sitting on top of it: a warm filament pushing off the Gulf Stream that's been parked over the canyon edge for close to two weeks now, and it hasn't budged. We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold through several more days of stable high pressure before any wind shift or cool front started pushing on that warm edge — and that's exactly what's played out. No front has come through to knock it loose, and the fleet radioing in from the sword grounds and the tuna spreads is backing that up.

Yellowfin have been the most consistent player, and they're doing it the way late-August yellowfin usually do out here — working the color change and temp breaks along the 100-fathom line and pushing up onto the Claw when the current sets up right. Green machines and small Ilanders in the spreader bar, cedar plugs way back, and naked ballyhoo skipped off the corner have all been drawing strikes. Fish in the 20 to 40-pound class have been the bulk of it, with the occasional bigger one mixed in on the chunk once the trolling bite shuts down around midday. That's the pattern worth knowing — troll the break in the morning, then switch over to butterfish chunks anchored up or drifting near structure like the Dip once the sun gets high and the fish stop chasing iron.

Bluefin have been mixed in on some of those chunk drops, not consistent enough to call a sure thing but enough that boats are keeping a rod rigged with a 50 or 80-wide and a fresh butterfish chunk soaking on a slow current. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure — weed lines, debris, current seams where the warm water meets slightly cooler green — and small skirted ballyhoo or dink feathers pulled just off the temp break have been picking them off, mostly schoolies in the 3 to 8-pound range with the occasional bull mixed in near actual structure.

White marlin have shown consistently enough on the dink spread and naked ballyhoo pulled flat lines that it's worth running one dedicated teaser and a couple of light baits even on a tuna-focused spread. Nothing has been stacked wall to wall — this is a "keep working the temp break and stay ready" bite, not a "set it and forget it" one. Boats that ran the edge without adjusting to where the color and the break actually sat some mornings came back with a quieter day than the ones that worked the grid and found where bait was actually getting pushed up.

Swordfish have still been down deep during daylight, which hasn't changed with the season. Boats running daytime drops with squid strips and glow rigs on electric reels down in that 1,500 to 1,800-foot range have connected, though it's a grind — long soaks, patient drops, and reading the sound machine for that bottom layer of bait before committing a full drop. Worth the setup time if that's the target, but it's not a fast bite by any measure.

Here's the honest part: this bite depends entirely on that warm filament staying put, and the moon is about to complicate things. As it builds toward full over the next several days, expect tidal flow to increase and bait to start concentrating tighter around structure — which can actually help the canyon bite by pulling forage up onto the edge, but it also means current lines can shift fast and the color break that produced Tuesday might not be sitting in the same spot Friday. Run the SST overlay before you leave the dock, don't assume last week's numbers hold, and be ready to make a move of five or ten miles if the first pass over the 100-fathom line comes up quiet.

The bigger wildcard heading into Labor Day weekend is tropical activity. Peak hurricane season doesn't care about a good bite, and any system spinning up in the western Atlantic can push swell and mix that warm surface layer down before anyone gets a forecast update. As of now there's nothing forcing a change, and the pattern that's held through stable high pressure all month looks likely to carry through the next few days. Expect more boat traffic over the holiday weekend as word spreads that the canyon's producing, so get an early start if crowding on the good stretches of the edge is a concern. If the filament holds and the moon doesn't scatter the bait too hard, the next few days should look a lot like the last two weeks — yellowfin on the troll in the morning, chunk bite for bluefin and stragglers midday, and mahi wherever the debris and the color line up. Watch the storm tracks closely. That's still the single biggest thing that can end this run.

reports.headline: August 31 and Washington Still Hasn't Given Up the Warm Water
reports.subhead: The canyon's late-summer thermal setup is holding a beat ahead of the rest of the fleet, and the fish know it.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this date I start checking the calendar against the water instead of the other way around, and every year Washington tells me the same thing: this canyon runs on its own clock. By the end of August most of the mid-Atlantic grounds are starting to think about the shoulder season, but Washington sits close enough to the Gulf Stream's western edge that it holds a mature warm-water push later than its neighbors to the north. That's not a hot take, that's just how the geography works — the Stream meanders in tight to this stretch of the shelf, and when it does, Washington gets first crack at the good water and holds it longest. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said to expect continuity with stable warm water in place over the next 72 hours — and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing about the setup has broken down.

What that means practically: the color change and the temperature break that split shelf water from blue Gulf Stream water are still sitting in a productive spot along the edge, and the eddies spinning off that break are still doing their job of stacking bait against structure. Late August into early September is usually when Washington's yellowfin bite matures — the fish have had all summer to settle into a rhythm, and the bait has had all summer to build up along the walls. This is the stretch where a well-run spread pays for itself.

Trolling remains the primary tool out here and nothing about that changes this week. Ballyhoo behind Islanders in dark colors — purple/black, green/yellow — worked with naked ballyhoo mixed into the pattern, continues to be the standard yellowfin approach along the temperature breaks. Spreader bars in the middle of the pattern give the school something to commit to, and the outside baits fished long and staggered pick up the stragglers that won't come all the way to the boat. Mahi are riding the same warm water and showing up opportunistically around any floating structure or weed line the fleet crosses on the way out or back — a rigged ballyhoo or a small skirted lure tossed at a school holding under debris is still the move, and this time of year those mahi can run bigger than the June fish, some pushing into double digits.

Wahoo remain the wildcard piece of this puzzle. Late August is prime timing for a hookup on a high-speed bait run tight to the temperature break, particularly early and late in the day when the light angle is low. A planer or a downrigger rigged with a hard-diving lure run off the corner, separate from the main spread, is the way most of the boats working this pattern give themselves a shot without disrupting the tuna trolling.

Bigeye continue to be a night bite here, and that hasn't shifted. The chunk-and-drift approach after dark, working squid strips or butterflied squid on a slow bottom-bounce presentation near the drop-off, is still producing for boats willing to put in the overnight hours.
