It's a different kind of fishing than the daytime troll — patience-heavy, gear-heavy — but the canyon's structure along the wall gives bigeye a reason to hold there once the sun goes down and the bait pulls up off the bottom.

White marlin is the piece of this report I want to be straight about. This is typically the tail end of the strongest white marlin window for Washington — the bite that built through July and August starts to thin out as we move into September, not because the fish disappear overnight but because the pattern gets less concentrated and more scattered as the season turns. If billfish is the priority, this is closer to the last good stretch than the middle of it. Ballyhoo behind small Islanders, worked at a moderate troll speed with the spread pulled tight, is still the right presentation while the window holds.

Looking at the next several days, the setup argues for more of the same. The moon is building toward full, which should tighten up the tidal push and help concentrate bait along the edge rather than spreading it thin — generally a good sign for consistency on the troll. Barring any tropical development in the western Atlantic, which remains the one variable worth watching on the forecast models, there's no obvious reason for this pattern to break down in the near term. That's the biggest wildcard on the board right now, not the fish.

For boats planning a run this week, the read is straightforward: work the temperature breaks and color changes along the canyon edge early in the day for yellowfin and wahoo, keep an eye out for floating structure for mahi on the way out and back, and if billfish is the goal, don't wait — this window is closer to its end than its beginning. Washington has been ahead of the rest of the fleet all season. No reason to think that changes before Labor Day.

reports.headline: Trolled the Wilmington wall for six hours — bigeye, giant bluefin, and wahoo all showed up on the spread
reports.subhead: The run is long and the fuel bill isn't cheap, but late August has this canyon paying off in multiple species at once.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one shot before Labor Day traffic clogs the ramps and the marina lots, the call this week is simple: run to Wilmington Canyon and troll the temperature break rather than sit on the anchor and chunk. The eddy that's been spinning off the Stream has pinned a clean, blue-water push right up against the canyon wall, and that kind of setup rewards boats covering ground with a spread out — not boats waiting for fish to come find a chunk slick. Chunking still has its window here, but it's a late-afternoon and dusk play once the sun's off the water and the current slacks. For daylight hours right now, trolling is putting more species on deck.

The why is straightforward. Warm, clean water has been holding tight along the drop, roughly where the bottom falls from the 50- to 60-fathom curve down into the canyon proper, and that edge has stacked bait against structure the way it's supposed to in late summer. The moon's building toward full over the next several days, which is going to push more tidal flow through the canyon and concentrate that bait even tighter along the wall. That's usually a green light for the bite to hold or even improve heading into the weekend — but it's also the kind of window that can turn on you fast if a tropical system organizes anywhere in the western Atlantic. That's the one thing worth watching daily before you commit to the run. Right now there's nothing forcing a change of plans, but late August is late August, and this canyon's weather can flip in 48 hours.

On the troll, the mixed bag has been the story. Bigeye tuna are coming on ballyhoo-and-skirt combos pulled off the boat's long riggers, worked slow across the temperature break at first light and again in the last two hours before dark — that's when bigeye seem willing to come up and eat instead of holding deep. Boats working spreader bars with a naked ballyhoo trailer in the middle have had the better shots at bigeye specifically, versus straight skirted-ballyhoo spreads, which have leaned more toward yellowfin. Yellowfin have been scattered but present anywhere the water color goes from green to that blue-green break — 15 to 20 knots of trolling speed, cedar plugs and small green machines in the shotgun and short rigger positions picking off fish that miss the bigger baits.

Giant-class bluefin — the true elephants — are the headline fish this week, and they're not coming on the troll. The producing method has been live-lining once the fish are marked or a school is spotted working bait on top: bridled live bait, whether that's a bigger bunker imitation, a live mackerel, or whatever's around the boat, sent back on a long flat line or slow-trolled just off the surface. Patience matters more than gear here — boats willing to sit on marked fish and let a bait swim naturally are the ones connecting on the big bluefin, not the ones running and gunning.

Wahoo have shown up as a bonus on the high-speed presentations — planers and heavy trolling weights pulling single skirted lures or a Ilander/ballyhoo combo at 12 to 14 knots along the same temperature break that's holding the tuna. If you're not rigging at least one or two rods for wahoo speed, you're leaving fish on the table right now, because they've been mixed in more than usual for this time of year.

Mahi have been the consolation prize around any floating structure, weed lines, or current seams inside the canyon — small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 3- to 8-pound range, but eager, and a few gaffer-class fish have come off deeper structure edges. Small skirted ballyhoo or a dropped bucktail once you spot the pod will get bit fast.

White marlin are still in the mix on dredge teams — dark, natural-colored dredges with a spread of ballyhoo skirts and dredge teasers pulled just off the transom, matched with a light bait or naked ballyhoo pitch bait ready when a fish shows in the spread. It's not a stacked bite, more a few quality shots per trip for boats running a proper dredge program and staying patient when a fish shows interest but won't commit on the first pass.

Be honest with yourself about the economics before you run. This is not a nearshore trip — the fuel burn to reach the canyon and work the grounds properly adds up fast, and a slow bigeye bite doesn't offset that math the way a good yellowfin day does. Right now the multi-species mix — bigeye, giant bluefin, yellowfin, wahoo, mahi, and white marlin all realistically in play on the same day — makes the run worth it for boats set up to fish more than one program. If you're only rigged to troll, you're leaving the bluefin opportunity on the table; if you're only rigged to chunk or live-bait, you're missing the wahoo and mahi.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern should hold if the tropics stay quiet. Building tide into the full moon should tighten the bait concentrations along the wall and could sharpen the bigeye and bluefin bite even further heading into the holiday weekend. Expect more boat traffic on the grounds as Labor Day approaches — get an early start if you want clean water and room to work the spread before the fleet spreads out. Keep one eye on any tropical development between now and then; that's the single factor that could shut this window down fast.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Strong finish, scattered start: Norfolk wahoo and Spencer yellowfin carry the week
reports.subhead: The canyon run split into two speeds this week — slow mornings offshore, then a hot afternoon bite once the temp break sharpened up.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a B-plus week on the southern run. Monday and Tuesday were a grind — bait was thin on the meter and the marlin bite at Lindenkohl went quiet for most of the morning. But by Wednesday the fleet found the seam again, and Thursday through the weekend the canyons put up the kind of numbers that make the long ride worth it. Norfolk carried the back half of the week, Spencer held up the middle, and Poor Man's turned into the night-bite secret nobody wanted to talk about on the radio.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold as long as no tropical system knocked the warm eddy off its perch, and that's exactly how it played out. The Gulf Stream filament that's been parked off the shelf edge stayed put, the water stayed clean and blue, and the exotic mix — yellowfin, some bigeye, mahi, wahoo, and a scattering of white marlin — kept working the edges where that warm water folds against the canyon walls.

Spencer, out around the 38°34'N, 73°37'W range, has been the most consistent stop for boats running out of Cape May. The chunk bite there set up nicely once the current started ripping across the 100-fathom curve — butterfish chunks on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders, no weight, drifted back in the slick, and yellowfin in the 30-to-50-pound class came up steady through the afternoon. Mornings were slower, more like two or three fish before the sun got high, but the afternoon bite tightened up as the thermocline pushed the tuna shallower. A few boats working the troll early with green machines and small Islanders picked up mahi in the 8-to-15-pound range on the color changes north of the canyon head — nothing epic, but a solid bonus while waiting on the chunk to turn on.

Lindenkohl, up around 38°50'N, 73°22'W, was the disappointment early in the week — the white marlin that had been showing on the temp break went quiet Monday and Tuesday, likely pushed by a shift in the current line. By Thursday they were back, feeding on the surface in the mid-afternoon, and boats trolling a spread of horse ballyhoo behind Sea Witch skirts, staggered short and long, raised fish steadily in that 78-to-79-degree water where the break sharpens. Drop-back conversions were the difference-maker — hook baits rigged light so the circle hook could do its job on the pitch. Yellowfin showed there too, mixed in on the edge, but Lindenkohl this week was really a marlin story more than a tuna one.

Poor Man's, tucked in around 38°26'N, 73°48'W, turned into the bigeye play for boats willing to stay out after dark. The daytime bite there was spotty — a few yellowfin on the troll, nothing to write home about — but the overnight chunk with squid strips and glow sticks on the swim baits produced bigeye in the 80-to-150-pound class for boats that committed to staying on the drift through the middle of the night. That's a small window and it takes patience, but for boats set up for it, Poor Man's has been the highest-value stop per hour on the water this week.

Norfolk, the furthest run out of Cape May and Ocean City at roughly 37°23'N, 74°38'W, closed the week out strong. The wahoo bite there turned on hard Thursday and held through the weekend — high-speed spreads pulling Ilander/ballyhoo combos and cedar plugs at 14 to 18 knots across the canyon edge picked off wahoo in the 30-to-50-pound range, with a few pushing bigger. That canyon has been running warmer than the others, and the water color out there has stayed a clean cobalt blue that the wahoo clearly like. Bluefin showed up scattered in the mix, mostly smaller school fish in the 40-to-60-pound range, taking green machines off the long rigger.

The moon's building toward full over the next several days, and that's going to matter. Expect the tide push to tighten up bait concentrations along the canyon edges, which should sharpen the afternoon bite pattern that's already working at Spencer and Norfolk. If the current stays organized and the water color holds, the next 48 hours look like more of the same — strong afternoons, spotty mornings, and the chunk bite as the more reliable play over the troll until the fish commit harder to the surface.

The wildcard heading into the Labor Day stretch is the tropics. Nothing organized is close enough to worry about yet, but any system spinning up in the western Atlantic is the one thing that could scramble this eddy structure fast. Boat traffic is going to spike over the holiday weekend regardless, so expect more competition on the better drifts at Spencer and Lindenkohl. If there's only one shot to take this week, Norfolk's wahoo bite and Spencer's afternoon chunk are the two plays worth the fuel — just keep an eye on the tropical outlook before committing to the long run south.

reports.headline: Bluefin Holding Off the Lighthouse While the Point Waits on Its Bass
reports.subhead: Blues are running hard on bunker, fluke has thinned to the channel edges, and the real fall trigger is still a few tides away.
reports.body_markdown:
Late August at the Point is a waiting game, and anyone who's fished here more than a few seasons knows exactly what that feels like. The water off the Lighthouse is sitting around 69 degrees, still warm enough to hold summer patterns but cool enough that you can feel the calendar turning underneath it. The moon is building toward full, which means more water moving through the rips every tide, and that's the single biggest thing to watch this week — because more current means more bait getting pushed and pinned, and that's the trigger this whole system has been waiting on.

We flagged the bluefin holding off the Point last week, and the boats are still finding them close enough that it doesn't take a long run to get bit. That school hasn't broken up yet, and as long as the bait stays put out there, there's no reason to think it will. Worth a call to the local charter docks before you commit a day offshore, but right now Montauk is one of the few places on the whole Island where you can leave the harbor, catch a bluefin, and be back in time for the evening bass tide.

Striped bass are still in that in-between stage — present, catchable, but not yet doing what October Montauk does. Surfcasters working the boulder field on the ocean side of the Point are picking up fish on the building tide, mostly on bucktails and darters worked slow through the wash, with the better fish coming right at the edge of light — first gray of dawn and the last of dusk. North Bar has been giving up a mix of schoolies and a few respectable fish in the 20s on the incoming, especially when there's a push of sand eels or peanut bunker getting corralled against the bar. Nobody's talking about blitz numbers yet. The bunker schools further west haven't concentrated enough to pull big bass into a feeding frenzy at the Point, but that's the pattern building, not one that's arrived — give it the better part of the next two tide cycles as the moon fills and the water keeps moving.

Bluefish are the fish putting bends in rods right now, and that part of the season is not soft at all. Turtle Cove and the stretch of south side beach running toward the Point have had steady morning blitzes on bunker pods, blues in the 8-to-12-pound class crashing bait right in the wash, sometimes close enough to hit with a topwater popper on the first cast off the beach. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins — worked fast through the froth is still the simplest way to connect, and there's no shortage of fish willing to eat it. This bite tracks bait, plain and simple, and as long as bunker keep working the beach, the blues will keep showing up behind them.

Fluke have thinned out, which is normal for this point in the season and not a reason to panic. The Frisbee grounds and the drift off Shagwong Reef are still producing, but the better fish have slid into deeper water and channel edges chasing cooler, better-oxygenated flow — 25 to 40 feet is where the boats are finding keepers now instead of the shallower flats that were productive in July. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, are still the go-to combo, but it's a fair bite rather than a fast one. Expect this window to hold through most of September before those fish push offshore for good.

Porgies remain one of the more dependable meals of the week for anyone fishing the harbor or the inshore reef structure — sandworms and squid strips on the bottom in 20 to 30 feet, no complicated rig required, just patience and a good chum slick. Weakfish are around in scattered numbers but nothing worth planning a trip around specifically; if you're working the same grass edges as the porgies, don't be surprised if one shows up in the mix. Blackfish season hasn't opened yet, so leave the tog gear at home for now.

The next few days should hold mostly steady — winds look manageable, the tide push will keep building with the moon, and that combination usually starts concentrating bait tighter against structure like North Bar and the boulder field. If there's one thing to watch closely, it's the eastern approach: bonito have been working westward out of Rhode Island waters, and Montauk is typically next in line once that push reaches Block Island Sound. It hasn't shown here yet, but the conditions setting up — clean water, building current, squid and bait concentrating in the rips — are exactly what turns it on fast once it starts. Keep a bag of small metal or a bonito-weight bucktail rigged and ready, because when that bite arrives at the Point, it doesn't give much warning.

For anyone with one day to spend this week, the smart play is still bluefish in the morning off the south side beaches on the building tide, then a swing out to the boulder field at last light for bass. The bigger fall push isn't here yet — but every tide from here to the full moon is one step closer, and Montauk in early September is about as good a place as there is to be standing when it finally breaks loose.

reports.headline: North Rip Turns Cold and Green — Bonito Beat the Calendar to the Island
reports.subhead: The water changed color before the bonito showed, and by midweek the rips were full of them — bass and blues are still working on their own schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
You feel it before you see it out here. Sometime around Wednesday the wind swung out of the northeast for half a day, just long enough to push a clean, cold ribbon of water up against the Southwest Ledge, and the color went from that flat late-August green to something with more blue in it. That's usually the tell. Within 48 hours the bonito showed, and they showed in numbers — we flagged this exact move last week, said the warm water and building bait density would bring them in on schedule, and here they are, stacked on the north side of the Ledge and working the rip off North Light on the last of the ebb.

The bigger picture: the Sound to our west is still carrying real heat — Kings Point up around 71, New London a touch cooler at 69 — and that gradient is exactly what funnels bait and predators toward the island. Block Island sits right where that warm coastal water collides with the cleaner, better-oxygenated flow coming off the ledges and rips, and that collision is the whole reason this place fishes different than the beaches on either side of us. Bass and bluefish don't need to gamble on murky bay water here — they've got current, cold pockets, and bait getting squeezed into a smaller piece of real estate. That's the draw, every August, without fail.

Stripers are in what I'd call a holding pattern right now, and that's an honest read, not a sales pitch. There are fish on the Southwest Ledge and working the deeper edge of the North Rip, but they're not stacked the way they will be once the moon builds toward full over the next week and a half and the bunker schools in Narragansett Bay and up toward Newport get squeezed tighter. Right now the better bass are coming on live eels fished slow along the boulder fields on the Ledge during the last two hours of the incoming, and on bunker chunks anchored up in the rip on North Rip during a hard ebb. Nothing enormous reported this week — mostly mid-20s to low-30-inch fish, with a handful of upper-30s taken on umbrella rigs trolled tight to the bottom contour where the Ledge drops from 20 feet down into the 40s. If you want a shot at something heavier, that's still a nighttime program — dark, moving water, big profile bait, patience.

Bluefish have been the most dependable fish in the water this week, and that tracks with what bunker density usually does for them — where the bait balls up, the blues show up right behind it. Boats working bunker schools off Point Judith and along the Narragansett shoreline have had steady action on diamond jigs and bucktails, some fish pushing into the 8- to 10-pound class. Chunking has worked just as well as jigging when the schools sit still on the tide change — cut bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished on bottom in 25 to 35 feet, has been picking off the bigger blues while the smaller ones stay up top hammering topwater plugs.

Bonito are the story of the week, and they're behaving the way they always do this time of year — fast, aggressive, and completely uninterested in anything that doesn't match the tiny bait they're keyed on. Half-ounce epoxy jigs and small metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in silver or green mackerel pattern — worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the surface froth on the Southwest Ledge has been the ticket. Timing matters more than location right now: the window is short, usually the last two hours of the ebb when current compresses the bait against the ledge structure, and it can shut off as quick as it turns on. Fly guys working small Deceivers and Bonito Bunny patterns on intermediate lines have had good mornings when the wind lays down enough to see the nervous water.

Fluke have softened up, which is the normal late-August pattern and not a red flag. Boats working the channel edges around the Great Salt Pond entrance and the deeper structure off Old Harbor are still picking through legal fish on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing when the water's moving but not ripping. Expect this to hold through most of September before the real push offshore starts.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on what we're already seeing. If the water stays clean and that northeast breeze keeps nudging cooler water up against the Ledge, the bonito bite should hold or even improve, and false albacore won't be far behind — the pattern almost always follows that sequence once bonito are established this early. The moon is working toward full over the next week to ten days, which is the real trigger to watch for the bass — once that bunker in Narragansett Bay and along the Point Judith shoreline gets squeezed by tide and moon together, that's when the Ledge and the Rip start producing the kind of blitz mornings this island is known for. Until then, work the tide changes, keep the boat quiet on the drift, and don't be surprised if the best fish of the day comes in the last twenty minutes of light.

reports.headline: Peconic still running warm — porgies thick around Shelter Island, first bait pushes hint at the turn
reports.subhead: Bay water is holding onto summer while bunker schools start building for the fall run everyone's waiting on.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic hasn't gotten the memo that August is ending. Surface temps in the bay are still sitting in that warm, late-summer range, well above what the open Sound and ocean beaches are reading right now, and that lag is exactly why the porgy and fluke bite has stayed dependable while other zones start to wobble. The bay's shallow, protected geometry means it heats faster in spring and holds heat longer into fall — that's the whole reason this fishery runs on its own clock, a week or two ahead of the Sound in May and a week or two behind it when things finally cool off in October. Right now we're still on the summer side of that ledger, and the fishing reflects it.

Nights are starting to dip, though, and that's the thing to watch over the next several days. Cooler overnight air combined with the building moon means tidal flow is picking up, and that increased current is starting to concentrate bait — small bunker pods showing in the back of Three Mile Harbor and Noyack Bay, rain bait working the edges of the Greenport breakwater. Nothing dramatic yet, but it's the same mechanism that eventually triggers the fall striper push through Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip. We flagged this trend last week — said fluke and porgy action would hold steady through the scallop opener with bonito potential building at the inlets — and that's exactly the shape of things right now. No confirmed bonito yet inside Peconic waters, but the ingredients (warm bay water, tightening bait, building current) are lining up the way they usually do before that fish shows.

Porgy fishing remains the strongest, most consistent thing going in this zone. The reefs and rock piles off Shelter Island — Cedar Point, the rips off Hay Beach, and the drop-offs toward Coecles Harbor — are holding heavy numbers of scup in the 10-to-20-foot range, thickest on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing when current is moving but not ripping. Standard high-low rigs with size 6 or 4 hooks, tipped with squid strips or sandworm, are doing the damage, and there's no need to overthink bait presentation right now — the fish are eating anything that sinks with a little movement. Anchoring up-current and letting bait settle into the structure is outproducing constant drifting, since porgies here are holding tight to specific bottom contours rather than roaming.

Fluke are still in the game but showing the softer late-August pattern typical of this time of year — fair, not fast, and increasingly channel-bound as the shallow flats warm past their comfort zone. The deeper cuts through Noyack Bay, the Shelter Island ferry channels, and the mouth of Three Mile Harbor are holding keeper-class fish in 15 to 25 feet, best worked on the last of the outgoing when current stacks bait against the channel edges. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, are taking fish, along with the old standby of squid strip and spearing combos fished on a simple fluke rig with just enough sinker to hold bottom. This is a normal seasonal shift, not a collapse — expect fluke to keep producing on these deeper structures right through September before the real offshore migration pulls them out for good.

Bluefish remain the most aggressive predator in the bay system right now, and they're not subtle about it. Blitzes have been popping along the Orient Point rip and in Gardiners Bay off Cartwright Shoal, usually tied to the same bait pushes bringing bunker into the harbors. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything that throws flash — are getting hit hard when the blitzes surface, typically on a moving tide rather than dead slack. This bluefish activity should track bait density closely through the next couple weeks, and with bunker schools building, there's no reason to expect it to ease up before Labor Day.

Striped bass are present but still in that in-between phase — some fish working the current seams at Plum Gut and the North Race on the tide changes, a few holding around Shelter Island's deeper drop-offs, but nothing like the concentrated fall push that's coming. That trigger is bait density, and the bunker schools in the harbors need another week or two of building before the bass commit in numbers. Bucktails worked slow off the bottom at Plum Gut on the max of either tide are the way to find them right now, along with live bait — peanut bunker under a float — fished tight to structure in Noyack and Three Mile Harbor.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold this same pattern: warm bay water keeping porgies and fluke reliable, bluefish staying active wherever bait concentrates, and stripers slowly building toward the real transition. If the nights keep cooling and that moon-driven current keeps building, the first real signs of the fall run should start showing at Plum Gut and Orient Point within the next week to ten days. Until then, the smart move is working the bay's structure — the Shelter Island reefs, the harbor channels, the rip lines — while the water's still warm enough to keep everything biting.

reports.headline: Blues Blow Up The Race — Bass and Albies Still On Standby
reports.subhead: Bunker-fed bluefish are running the rip hard while the fleet waits on the first bonito sign and the bass hold their cards.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning at The Race looked like a war zone. Gulls stacked three deep over a bunker school getting hammered from below, blues to 12 pounds busting bait on top for the better part of an hour on the last of the ebb, with a handful of slot bass mixed in tight to the current seam where the rip folds back on itself. That's the read on Eastern Sound right now — bluefish are the engine, bass are riding shotgun, and everybody's watching for the first sign of false albies or bonito that hasn't landed yet.

The why is straightforward. Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London's sitting at 69.4, which puts a real thermal gradient across the Sound west to east — warmer water pushing bait and predators toward structure and current edges where the temperature break holds. The moon's building toward full, tidal flow is picking up day over day, and that combination is exactly what stacks bait in the pinch points — The Race, Plum Gut, the Orient Point rip, the reefs off Fishers Island. Bunker schools are getting squeezed into those funnels and the blues are all over them. We flagged bluefish tracking bunker density last week and that's exactly what's playing out — where the bunker sit, the blues show up in numbers, full stop.

Bluefish are the most dependable thing going right now, and they're not subtle about it. Poppers and 2-ounce Deadly Dicks worked on the up-current side of the rip at Plum Gut are getting hit on nearly every retrieve when the bunker are balled up. Ava 27s and 17s bounced through the lower third of the water column at The Race on the max of the ebb are producing better than most people expect this late in August — fish to 14 pounds reported off Fishers Island Sound on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 25 to 40 feet. If you want quality over quantity, work the edges of the blitz rather than the middle — the bigger fish tend to sit on the margins picking off cripples instead of fighting the pack.

Bass are in a genuine holding pattern. There's fish around — the surf has been giving up slot and overslot stripers on hard-running current edges from Orient Point down through the Fishers Island rips, mostly on bucktails worked slow off the bottom right where the flat drops into the channel. But this isn't blitz behavior yet. The bunker haven't concentrated enough to trigger the kind of feeding that turns individual fish into a wolf pack, and until that bait density builds — which the building moon and stronger tides over the next week or two should force — expect the bass bite to stay a game of right spot, right tide stage rather than a guaranteed thing. Best window has been the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the new flood, working eels or big soft plastics along the rock piles at Fishers Island and the drop-off at the east end of Plum Gut where the current stacks bait against structure.

Fluke have done exactly what late August fluke do — they've softened. This is the seasonal shift, not a crash, and we called that shift last week: fluke sliding into deeper channel structure and ocean-front edges as the shallow bay water loses its edge. The producing pattern right now is a slow drag with white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails along the deeper edges of Plum Gut and the channel drop-offs around Orient Point, fished tight to bottom on the last of the incoming when the current eases enough to hold bottom contact. Keeper-sized fish are still coming, but it's a pick, not a pile — expect two or three quality fish for an afternoon's work rather than a fast bag limit.

Porgies are still holding on the deeper rock and rubble bottom around Fishers Island and off Plum Gut in 30 to 50 feet, biting steady on bloodworms and squid strips fished on high-low rigs — a reliable fallback bite while everyone's attention is on the bigger stuff up top.

The thing everybody in the shops and on the radio keeps circling back to is the albie and bonito question. The Rhode Island push out of Block Island and Point Judith is close, and the current setup — building moon, stronger tidal flow, bait concentrating in the exact rip structure that mimics what's holding fish in Rhode Island right now — makes The Race and Plum Gut the logical next stop. It hasn't shown yet on this side of the line, so don't burn gas assuming it's happening; but if you're rigging up for the blitz anyway, keep a light spinning rod with small Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax rigged and ready on deck. When it turns on here it usually turns on fast and it doesn't wait around.

Look at the next several days through that lens. Wind stays manageable and the current keeps building toward the full moon, expect the bluefish bite to hold or improve at The Race and Plum Gut, the bass bite to stay a tide-specific pick along the rock structure at Fishers Island and Orient Point, and the albie watch to intensify — this is the window where it's most likely to break. If there's only one day to fish this week, work the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut with poppers ready for blues and a bucktail rigged for whatever else shows up in the wash. That's where the action's concentrated right now, and that's where it's most likely to change first.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Own the Deep Hole, Weakfish Still Working the Bridge
reports.subhead: Rough ocean has pushed the real action inside the inlet, and the night tide is where the numbers are.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one window this week, make it the last two hours of the outgoing tide after dark at Shinnecock Inlet. That's the call, and it's not close. The ocean side has been ugly — better than three-foot swell stacking up on a short period out front — which means the stripers and blues that would normally be working the bar and the jetty tips in daylight are tucking into the inlet itself, holding on the current seams and in the deep hole below the Coast Guard station. Daytime boat traffic and sun-bright water push them down and back. Slack water in the middle of the night with a hard outgoing push pulling bait past the rocks is when they come up and feed. That's been the pattern for two weeks now and there's no reason to think it flips before Labor Day.

The bigger picture: warm water sitting the length of the south shore has bait balled up and predator fish staged, waiting on the next trigger. Offshore, the moon's building toward full, and that means more water moving through the inlet and canal on every tide — which concentrates bait tighter against structure and usually kicks the bite up a notch as we get into the weekend. We flagged the inlet rips last week as the place to watch for the first bonito or albie of the season, with warm nearshore water and building bait setting the table, and that read still holds — the ingredients are all there, bunker and bay anchovies pushing through the inlet mouth, but nobody's iced one yet on this end. Worth rigging a spinning rod with small Deadly Dicks or epoxy jigs and keeping it within reach if you're working the rips, because when that push finally slides west from the Rhode Island side, it can happen fast.

Striped bass inside the inlet have been running mostly schoolie to mid-20-inch fish, with the occasional slot mixed in working the seam where the outgoing current collides with the incoming ocean swell just outside the rock pile. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom on the drift through the deep hole, have been the most consistent producer after dark. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, drifted naturally with the current rather than retrieved, are still taking the bigger fish that are holding tighter to the rock structure on the ocean side of the jetty. The window is short — really the two hours around max outgoing — but it's been repeatable most nights this week when the wind's been manageable.

Bluefish are the one species nobody's complaining about right now. They're pushing into the inlet on both tides, chopping up peanut bunker along the bay side flats near Tiana Beach and around the mouth, and they'll hit almost anything with flash — Hopkins spoons, bucktails, or bunker chunks fished on wire leader if you don't want your tackle shredded. This has been the most reliable bite of the week for anyone fishing daylight hours, and with bunker schools still building along the south shore, expect that to hold through the holiday weekend regardless of what the bass and fluke do.

Fluke fishing has softened the way it always does this time of year, but it hasn't collapsed — we said last week it would hold steady through the weekend while everyone starts checking the rips, and that's about right. Fair action, not fast, on channel edges throughout Shinnecock Bay, particularly the drop-offs near the canal entrance and the deeper cuts off Tiana. Warm, oxygen-thin bay water is pushing the better fish toward the inlet and ocean-front structure where there's more flow. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift in eighteen to twenty-five feet, have been outproducing bait-only rigs. Expect this pattern — fair fishing, concentrated near structure and current — to hold through most of September before the real fall exodus offshore begins.

Weakfish at the Ponquogue Bridge have been a night bite almost exclusively, which suits this column just fine. The pilings on the bay side, particularly the ones closest to the deeper channel water, have been holding fish that show up as the tide starts to move after dark — not necessarily max flow, but that first hour or two of current building either way. Bucktails tipped with strips of squid, or small soft plastics like three-inch Fin-S in white or bone, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right down in the current break next to the piling, have taken keeper weakfish along with the usual porgy bycatch. It's not a blitz-style bite — more a patient, one-or-two-a-drift kind of night — but it's been consistent enough to make the trip worthwhile if you're willing to fish the dark hours.

Porgies remain a solid backup throughout the bay, particularly around the canal and the deeper holes off Hampton Bays, taking sandworms and clam on standard bottom rigs pretty much any tide. Blackfish season is still off in the distance, but with cooler nights starting to show up, it's not too early to start thinking about the structure spots inside the inlet that'll turn on once that opens.

Looking ahead: the moon builds toward full over the next several days, which should tighten up the tidal push and, combined with the bait already staged along the coast, sets up the kind of conditions that trigger the first real blitz activity of the fall transition. Watch the inlet rips hard for bonito sign — breaking fish, diving birds, bait getting nervous on the surface — because if that push arrives from the east like it has in past seasons, Shinnecock is usually one of the first Long Island inlets to see it. Rough ocean conditions look likely to persist into the weekend, so keep leaning on the inside water and the night tide until that changes.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet's West Rip Deepened a Foot — Blues and Fluke Found the New Edge
reports.subhead: Storm-carved structure off Cupsogue is holding bait and predators while the bay waits on its first real bunker push.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk the west jetty at Moriches Inlet on a dropping tide right now and you can see it before you ever wet a line — the scour hole off the rocks has deepened noticeably since the last blow pushed through in mid-August, and the sandbar that usually pinches the channel down off Pattersquash has shifted maybe fifteen to twenty yards east. That's not a huge move by Moriches standards, this inlet has always been a living thing, cutting and filling depending on what storm energy hits it and from what angle. But it matters for where the fish are sitting right now. The new edge of that bar is holding a sharper drop-off than we've seen all summer, and current is ripping across it hard enough on the last two hours of the ebb to stack bait against the structure instead of just sweeping past it.

That's the mechanical reason the bite has concentrated so tightly around the inlet mouth and the Cupsogue side this week instead of spreading out into the open bay like it does in high summer. Water temps off the ocean beach are still running warm — the open Atlantic buoy off the Bight is reading in the low 70s with some wave energy mixed in, nothing dramatic, three to four foot at five seconds, enough to keep the surf a little sloppy but not enough to shut down the bar. Inside the bay, the shallow flats around Tuthill Point and up toward East Moriches are heating up hard on afternoon sun, which is exactly why the fish that can move are pulling toward the inlet where the water column stays mixed and cooler on the bottom third.

We flagged this pattern last week — said Moriches would keep fluke on structure near the inlet where the current does the mixing, snapper blues thick in the bay, and the first bonito or albie scouting reports within a week or two as the fall forage shift gets rolling. That's exactly how it's playing out. Nothing revolutionary, but it's tracking.

Fluke are the honest story right now — call it a fair bite, not a hot one. The keepers are coming off the channel edges on the west side of the inlet, in twelve to twenty feet where that new drop-off is cutting, and along the deeper stretch running past Tuthill Point toward the day markers. Three-quarter ounce white bucktails teamed with a five-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in white or chartreuse, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the ebb into the start of the flood, has been the most consistent combination reported dockside. Shorts are still thick in the bay proper — anybody fishing the flats around East Moriches or up in the Forge River is going to sort through a lot of them before finding a keeper. The window for fluke here is closing the way it does every late August; expect the bite to hold fair through September on structure and in the deeper channels before the real push offshore starts, but don't expect the numbers game of July anymore.

Bluefish are the one thing nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick in the bay — East Moriches docks, the flats off Smith Point, anywhere there's current and small bait, kids with a bobber and a piece of spearing are into them all afternoon. The bigger harbor blues, three to six pounds, are working the bunker pods moving through the inlet mouth itself and along the Cupsogue jetty. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce and one-ounce Ava jigs — worked on the surface at first light and again on the last hour of daylight have been drawing consistent strikes right off the rocks. That bunker movement through the inlet is modest right now, nothing like a full-blown push, but it's building, and bluefish activity is going to track directly with how dense those bunker schools get over the next couple weeks.

Weakfish are scattered and mostly a dusk-into-dark proposition — a few reports of fish coming off the deeper holes near the Moriches Inlet Coast Guard station on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow right along bottom on the last of an outgoing tide. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up after dark working fluke or bass water. Porgies are steady and underrated right now — the jetty rocks at Cupsogue and the riprap on the inside of the inlet are holding good numbers on small hooks baited with clam, an easy bite for anyone who wants dinner without overthinking it.

Striped bass remain the wildcard everybody's watching. There's nothing happening inside Moriches yet that looks like the fall push — that trigger is bait density, and the bunker schools staging up and down the south shore need to concentrate a lot more before stripers commit here in blitz numbers. With the moon building toward full over the next several days, tidal flow is going to increase, which should start pulling bait tighter into the inlet and setting the stage. If there's a day to check the inlet mouth on the last two hours of the ebb into the turn, this week and next is when that first real striper sign is most likely to show. Keep an eye on the west rip — that new scour hole is exactly the kind of structure stripers use to ambush bait once the bunker finally stack up against it.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier and Cross Bay Bridge: the two doors into Jamaica Bay right now
reports.subhead: Snapper blues and weakfish are keeping rods bent while the bunker build that should trigger the fall run keeps thickening in the back bay.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got a few hours this week, pick your access point by what you want to catch, because the bay is splitting into two different games right now. Canarsie Pier is the play for anyone fishing with light tackle or bringing a kid along — the rail there is loaded with snapper blues and blowfish, and it's also the best free seat in the house for watching bunker density build along the mud flats. Cross Bay Bridge and the Beach Channel side, whether you're working it from a kayak or a small boat, is where the fluke and weakfish game is still alive on the channel edges. Two different access points, two different reasons to use them, and both worth knowing depending on what your Saturday looks like.

The bigger story for the week is bait. Bunker schools have been building steadily in the back bay — off Ruler's Bar, in Grassy Bay, and pushing toward the Rockaway Inlet side — and that's exactly the pattern we flagged last week: those schools concentrating are what sets up the first real fall striper push. It hasn't tipped yet. Stripers in the bay are still in a holding pattern, scattered rather than schooled, which lines up with what's happening region-wide — bass are present but not committed anywhere until the bait balls up tighter. With the moon building toward full over the next several days, tidal flow increases, and that's usually the mechanism that finally squeezes bait into blitz-worthy pods. Watch the mouth of the inlet and the flats off Breezy Point closely over the next week to ten days. That's where this transitions from "scattered bass around bait" to something worth planning a trip around.

Fluke fishing has done what it typically does at the end of August — it's softened, not collapsed. Warm water sitting in the shallower flats has pushed the better fish toward the inlet and toward the deeper channel structure where there's more current and cooler, better-oxygenated water. That's a seasonal transition, not a sign the season's over — expect fluke to stay catchable on structure and in the deeper channels right through September before they slide out toward the ocean side for good. Right now the better drifts are along the edges of Beach Channel and the deeper cuts near Cross Bay Bridge, working white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. A few boats working the flats off Ruler's Bar Hassock have also picked at fluke mixed in with weakfish on the same presentation, just fished a little higher off bottom.

Weakfish have been the pleasant surprise piece of the bay puzzle this month, and they're still showing on those same channel edges — Grassy Bay, the flats off Big Egg Marsh, and the deeper water tight to the Cross Bay Bridge pilings. Small soft plastics on light jigheads, three to four inch pearl or bubblegum-colored paddletails, worked slow on the drift with the outgoing tide, have been drawing strikes. These aren't the big spring weakfish — mostly schoolies in the 14 to 18-inch range — but they're active and they're a nice change of pace when the fluke bite is soft.

Bluefish remain the most dependable predator in the bay right now, and that tracks with what's happening up and down the coast — warm water has kept them aggressive and spread out, and that's not likely to change through Labor Day week. Snapper blues are thick around Canarsie Pier and the Cross Bay Bridge shadow line, easy pickings on tiny Kastmasters or a sliver of spearing under a bobber, which makes for good action if you've got kids or you're breaking in someone new to the sport. Bigger bluefish, cocktail-sized and up, are working the Rockaway Inlet on the last of the ebb, chopping bunker on the surface some mornings. Poppers and bunker chunks fished on wire leader near the inlet mouth have been producing, especially in that first hour of light before the boat traffic picks up.

Porgies are still around if you want to put some fillets in the cooler — the structure at Beach Channel and around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings holds them on bloodworms or clam bait, fished on a simple high-low rig near bottom. Nothing spectacular, but a steady producer for anyone who wants a mixed bag day rather than chasing one species.

For the next few days, expect more of the same pattern — soft but catchable fluke on the channel edges, dependable snapper and cocktail blues inside the bay, weakfish holding on the flats, and bass still scattered rather than schooled. The moon and the building bunker are the two things to watch. If that bait tightens up the way it's trending, the first real blitz signs should start showing at the inlet and off Breezy Point within the next week to ten days — that's when Marine Parkway Bridge starts to matter again, working the swirling water under the span on the outgoing with bucktails or swimmers after dark. Until then, work the access points that are actually producing, and keep an eye on the bunker.

reports.headline: Forget the bunker watch — the blues and blackbacks are paying the bills right now
reports.subhead: While everyone stares at the horizon waiting for the bass blitz, the real action at Jones Inlet is bluefish on the rocks and porgies stacking the channel edges.
reports.body_markdown:
Half the guys at the bait shop this week are standing around talking about bunker schools that haven't shown up yet. I get it — everybody wants to be there when the blitz goes off. But if you're burning gas or shoe leather waiting on a striper blowup that isn't here yet, you're leaving fish on the table. Right now, at Jones Inlet, the bite that's actually feeding people is bluefish on the jetty rocks and porgies working the channel edges. That's not sexy, but it's real, and it's been steady for two weeks straight.

Here's the why. The ocean's been ugly — better than 3 to 4 feet of swell on a short period pushing onto the beach most of this week, which is enough to blow out the surf and shove bait and predators off the open front. Water out front is still holding in the low 70s, which is fine for feeding fish, but nobody wants to work a washing machine. So the activity has concentrated inside — the inlet channel, the rocks at the jetty, Short Beach flats, and up into the bay where the water's calmer and the current still does work. That's classic late-August Jones Inlet: when the ocean gets sloppy, the fish push into the structure, and the structure at this inlet is about as good as it gets on the south shore.

We flagged this pattern last week — said bluefish would keep being the most consistent producer while striper activity built slower behind it as bunker density increased. That's exactly what's playing out. The blues have been the one thing you can set a clock by. Guys working the north side rocks at the inlet and the tip of the jetty at Short Beach are getting into choppers in the 3 to 6 pound class pretty reliably on the outgoing, especially the first two hours of the ebb when bait gets pulled out of the bay and funnels past the rocks. Diamond jigs — the 2-ounce silver or gold — worked with a fast retrieve through the rip are doing the damage, and if you want to save your tackle, wire leader is not optional with these fish snapping bucktails in half.

Fluke has softened, the way it does every year right about now. It's still catchable, but it's not the June pattern anymore. Sloop Channel is still giving up keeper fish on the drift, mostly in that 25 to 32 foot stretch off the deeper bends, with 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails working better than bare bait rigs this week. Warm bay water has fish looking for the cooler, better-oxygenated water near the inlet mouth and the deeper cuts, so if you're marking bait but not getting bit in the shallower flats, slide toward the channel edges closer to the inlet itself. The window for good fluke numbers is closing fast — figure you've got through most of September before the bulk of them slide out to the ocean structure for the fall run.

Porgies are doing what porgies do this time of year — showing up in real numbers on the rock piles and channel edges around the inlet. Bloodworms and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, fished on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet around the jetty rocks and the deeper holes off Jones Beach, is producing steady action, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slows enough to hold bottom without getting swept into the rocks. Not glamorous, but it's a guaranteed bend in the rod for anybody bringing kids or somebody new to the game.

Weakfish are still the sleeper story in this bay. They're not showing in numbers yet that anybody's bragging about, but there's real chatter about fish being picked up on light jigs and soft plastics in the deeper holes off Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge, mostly at last light. If that comeback keeps building the way it has the past couple seasons, September evenings on the bay side could be worth your time — small bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the bottom near deeper mud holes, is the play if you want to check it out.

Stripers are the story everybody's waiting on, and the pieces are starting to come together but the trigger hasn't been pulled. Bait balls are building near the inlet, and there've been scattered fish showing under the birds early and late, but it's not the concentrated blitz pattern yet. The moon's building toward full over the next several days, which means more tidal push, which means bait gets squeezed harder into the inlet mouth and the flats around Short Beach. That's usually when this fishery flips from scattered to serious. If you're going to gamble on stripers this week, first light at the inlet on the last of the outgoing, working a bunker spoon or a big topwater plug along the rip line, is the highest-percentage play — just don't expect a blitz yet.

Looking at the next few days: expect the bluefish to keep grinding along the rocks and inlet current, porgies to stay steady on bait rigs, and fluke to keep giving up fish to patient boats working the channel bends. The real change to watch for is the bait density spike as the moon builds — if bunker schools tighten up around the inlet mouth like they're starting to, the striper switch could flip fast, maybe within the next week to ten days. Keep an eye on the birds working the inlet mouth on the morning tide — that's usually the first tell before this whole thing turns on.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Balling Up on Stratford Shoal — Blues Are All Over It, Bass Still Waiting Their Turn
reports.subhead: The bait tells the story this week: bunker schools tightening under bird activity from the Norwalk Islands to Middle Ground, and it's the bluefish cashing in first.
reports.body_markdown:
Watch the bait before you watch the boats and this week made its case again. Peanut bunker started balling tight off Stratford Shoal and around Middle Ground Light in the last ten days, pushed into nervous, flickering pods by everything underneath them. Gulls and terns have been working the surface in short, violent bursts — the kind of bird play that tells you blues are underneath punching through, not just picking. Get closer and you can see the bunker doing what bunker do when they're scared: balling tight, dimpling the surface, then scattering in a spray when something big comes through from below. That's been the read across the Central Sound rip line all week, from the Norwalk Islands stretching east across to the Connecticut shore and down toward Charles Island.

The water is still carrying summer heat. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and even out toward New London it's holding near 69 — that's a shallow, forgiving gradient that's kept bait comfortable and slow to push out, which is exactly why the bunker schools have had time to build density instead of scattering east early like some years. Warmer water on the western and central end of the Sound versus the cooler eastern stretch has essentially parked the biomass right in our zone, and the bluefish have noticed first.

That lines up with what the 44th Annual Surfside Hotel tournament fleet has been finding working the western Sound and pushing into Central Sound structure — bluefish have been the most consistent predator around all week, and they're not subtle about it. Boats working bunker schools off Stratford Shoal and out toward the Norwalk Islands have been getting into choppers in the 4- to 8-pound class, some bigger, on straight bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 20 to 35 feet, and on wire-leadered Ava jigs and diamond jigs worked through the middle of the bait balls on the last two hours of the ebb. When the tide's really ripping through the Stratford Shoal cut, a simple bucktail bounced off bottom and swung through the current seam has been drawing hits too — the blues are using that current the same way stripers do, sitting on the downcurrent edge and letting the tide do the work.

Stripers are a different story right now, and it's worth being straight about it — they're in a holding pattern. There are fish around Middle Ground and scattered through the Norwalk Islands, but they're not committing in blitz numbers yet, and the honest read is that the bait hasn't concentrated enough to force the issue. That should change. The moon is building toward full, which means more tidal push, which means these bunker schools currently spread loosely from the Sound's midline down toward the CT shoreline should tighten up further in the next week to ten days. When that happens, expect the stripers already staged nearby to commit hard, the way they always do once bait gets pinned against structure instead of drifting free. Until then, the better bass move has been working eel or bunker chunks on the bottom around Stratford Shoal on the tail of the ebb, or dragging a swimming plug through the rip when the tide is really moving — fish are there, but you're earning them one at a time rather than into a blitz.

Fluke have done exactly what late August fluke do, which is soften without disappearing. We said last week this looked like a normal seasonal slide rather than a collapse, and that's held — fluke are still coming off the deeper channel edges around Port Jefferson Harbor mouth and the drop-offs near the Norwalk Islands, mostly on white and chartreuse Gulp paired with a light bucktail, worked slow on the last of the outgoing when the current lays down enough to keep bottom contact. Sizes have been mixed, plenty of shorts mixed with keeper-class fish in the 18 to 21-inch range, and the bite window is tightening to that slower water rather than running all tide long. Porgies remain a dependable afternoon fill-in around the rockier structure off Charles Island and the Norwalk Islands on the incoming, small hooks and sandworms doing the job, and blackfish are still a touch early — worth checking again once the water starts to actually cool rather than just holding steady.

Looking at the next few days, don't expect a dramatic shift. The bluefish should keep tracking the bunker schools hard through Labor Day week — that's been the most reliable pattern in the zone all month and there's no reason for it to break unless the bait scatters. Watch Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground closely for signs the bait is tightening further as the moon builds; that's the tell that stripers are about to switch from holding pattern to feeding mode. And keep half an eye east — bonito have been pushing west out of Rhode Island waters, and if that continues, the Race and the eastern approaches to the Sound are the first place a Central Sound angler would see it show up. Nothing on the board yet locally, but that's exactly the kind of thing you catch by watching the bait, not the forecast.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: fluke sliding to the inlet, blues chewing bunker, bass still on hold
reports.subhead: The ocean's been sloppy all week and it's pushed the whole program — fluke, blues, and the first fall stirrings — into the inlet and the bay.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood at the scale house Sunday morning listening to a mate off one of the party boats tell anybody who'd listen that the ocean's been "lumpy as a bad mattress" all week, and he wasn't wrong. Wind swell's been running three to four feet with a short five-second period out front of the inlet, and that kind of chop doesn't destroy a bite so much as it moves it. Fish don't like getting tossed around any more than we do, so the whole program this week — fluke, blues, even the first whispers of fall bass — has been sliding out of the open ocean and tucking into the inlet, the bay channels, and anywhere there's a lee.

Water's still warm, low 70s out at the buoy line and not much cooler inside the bay, and that warmth is exactly what's been pushing fluke off the flats and into the deeper, better-oxygenated water around the Robert Moses bridges and the main inlet channel. We flagged this pattern last week — said fluke wouldn't collapse, just shift into structure and deeper channels through September before the real fall pullout — and that's precisely what the fleet's finding. It's not a bang-bang bite anymore, but there are still keeper-class fish stacking on the drop-offs.

The fluke bite right now is a patience game. Best water has been 25 to 35 feet on the flood tide around the east and west Robert Moses bridges, with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged dead slow along the bottom. A few boats working the deeper edge of the Fire Island Inlet channel, closer to Democrat Point, have been picking off fish up to 5 pounds mixed in with a lot of shorts, so you're culling more than you're keeping most trips. The pattern holds through the last two hours of the incoming and the top of the tide — once it starts ripping out hard, the fluke tuck tight to structure and go quiet.

Bluefish have been the one thing you can set a watch by. They're chewing on bunker schools that have been building along the beach and pushing into the inlet mouth, and the size has been solid — 3 to 6 pounds, with the occasional bigger cow mixed in when a school gets pinned against the Democrat Point jetty. Diamond jigs, white bucktails, or just chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig fished on the bottom near working birds has been the simplest way to connect. This is textbook — blues track bunker density, plain and simple, and with bait still thick along the south shore beaches there's no reason to expect that to slow down before Labor Day.

Striped bass are the one piece of this puzzle everybody's asking about and nobody's got a real answer for yet. They're around — a few slot fish have come off the bridge pilings at Robert Moses on bucktails worked at night, and the bay side has produced some schoolies up in the Patchogue and Sayville flats on bloodworms and small swimming plugs — but this is a holding pattern, not the fall run. The bait hasn't concentrated enough yet to trigger a real push. That usually doesn't happen until nighttime temps start dropping hard, and we're not there. Mid-September is the number to watch, not this week.

Weakfish have been mostly a memory this time of year in the bay, though a few incidental fish have shown up mixed in with the fluke around channel edges — worth a mention if you're jigging soft plastics and feel something with a little more give in the fight than a fluke usually offers. Porgies are still there for anyone who wants a bend in the rod without overthinking it — the humps off Democrat Point and the deeper holes inside the inlet have been giving up decent numbers on sandworms and clam bellies, bottom rig, incoming tide. Blackfish season's still off in the distance, but a few boats have been marking fish already stacking up on the rockier structure near the inlet jetties, which is worth remembering come October.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full over the next several days, and that's going to matter. More tidal push means more current to concentrate bait, and if the bunker schools tighten up the way they have from Raritan Bay on up the coast, the blues should stay locked in right where they are — working the surf line off Fire Island and the inlet mouth. The ocean chop should ease some by midweek if the wind pattern backs off like it's forecast to, and that would open the beach fluke and surf bass bite back up a little, especially at first light around Democrat Point and the Fire Island beaches west of the lighthouse.

If you've only got one shot this weekend, work the last two hours of the flood at the Robert Moses bridges for fluke, then swing over to the inlet mouth at first light or last light for the blues working bunker. Keep an eye on the surf for any sign of albies or bonito showing in the wash — the water's warm enough right now that it wouldn't shock anybody at the dock if one turned up before Labor Day. Nobody's seen one yet. But the setup's there.

reports.headline: Bunker Still Thick on the Western Sound, and the Blues Won't Leave Them Alone
reports.subhead: Execution Rocks to Matinecock Point, bluefish are working bait schools hard while stripers sit back and wait for the bunker to stack tighter.
reports.body_markdown:
Every third guy who came through the shop this week asked some version of the same question: where'd the bunker go, and why are the blues still all over them? Simple answer — the bunker never left. They're just moving around more, pushed by the tide and by every bluefish in the western Sound trying to eat one. That's been the story since the Surfside Hotel Greatest Bluefish Tournament kicked off, and 44 years running, that tournament tends to find where the bait is before anybody else does.

Water's still carrying summer heat. Kings Point was reading 70.9 the other day, and that number drops as you run east — New London down around 69.4 — which tells you the western end of the Sound is holding the warmth and holding the bait longer. That gradient matters. It's why Execution Rocks, Stepping Stones, and the water off Matinecock Point have stayed loaded with bunker pods all month while the eastern Sound starts to cool off and thin out. Wherever that bait sits, that's where the action is, and right now that's still squarely in our zone.

Stripers are a different conversation. They're around — nobody's saying they're not — but they're in what I'd call a holding pattern. A few fish come off the bunker schools early and late, usually chunk bait fished on the bottom in 20 to 35 feet off Execution Rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing, but it's not the kind of concentrated blitz activity you get once that bait truly balls up tight. We flagged this last week — said to watch the bunker school movement for the first read on where the fall striper bite would concentrate, and that's exactly the pattern setting up now. The bass are shadowing those bunker schools without committing hard yet. Give it another week or two of building moon and stronger tidal flow, and that changes.

Bluefish, meanwhile, are doing exactly what warm water and thick bait tell them to do — hammering bunker wherever the schools show on the surface. The tournament fleet has been finding fish blitzing from Throgs Neck Bridge out through Hart Island and up toward Matinecock, with the heaviest surface activity showing on calm mornings when the bunker pods get pushed shallow by tide and current. Bunker spoons trolled behind the boat, big poppers worked over visible slicks, and straight chunk bait fished on wire leader in 15 to 25 feet are all producing. These aren't dink blues either — plenty of 6 to 10 pound fish coming out of these schools, which is normal for late August when the bigger blues finally push through behind the smaller resident fish. If you're not fishing the tournament, the same spots are worth your time — Stepping Stones light on the last of the flood has been holding bait and blues both, and it's a short run from most of the marinas between City Island and Port Washington.

Fluke have softened into their typical late-August pattern, and there's no sugarcoating that. It's fair fishing, not great fishing. The bay water's warm enough that fluke are drifting toward the deeper channel edges and structure looking for cooler water and better oxygen — the channel off Hart Island and the deeper cuts inside Manhasset Bay have both given up a mix of keepers and shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished slow on 3/4-ounce bucktails right on bottom. Hempstead Harbor's deeper holes are worth a drift too if you're set up for it. This bite typically holds through September before the fish start their move offshore, so there's still time, but don't expect the fast counts you had in July.

Porgies and blackfish are quiet background noise right now — a few porgies coming off the rockpiles around Execution Rocks on bloodworms for guys soaking bait between bluefish drifts, nothing worth a special trip yet. Blackfish season's still a ways off in terms of real activity; that'll pick up once the water starts to turn in earnest.

Looking at the next few days, the moon's building toward full, and that means more tidal push through the rips at Stepping Stones and Execution Rocks — exactly the kind of current that starts concentrating bait instead of letting it spread thin. If the bunker schools that are scattered from Throgs Neck to Matinecock start balling up tighter under that increased flow, that's your signal the fall striper push is getting close. It hasn't happened yet, but the ingredients are lining up. For the next 48 to 72 hours, I'd keep working the bluefish pattern — it's the most reliable game in the western Sound right now, and it should stay that way through the holiday weekend as boat traffic and tournament pressure both pick up. If you've only got one trip in you before Labor Day, make it a bluefish trip on the bunker schools, and keep a bass rod rigged with a bunker chunk on bottom just in case one of those shadowing stripers decides to commit. That's usually how the first real fall bass shows up around here — not in a blitz, but as a bonus fish while you're doing something else.

reports.headline: Stellwagen edge in 130 feet: haddock thick on the mud, bluefin still working the Basin line
reports.subhead: Groundfish split the bank by bottom type this week while school bluefin held tight to bait pushed up against the Basin drop.
reports.body_markdown:
Eighty feet on the gravel, one-thirty on the mud, and a temperature break sitting right along the Stellwagen Edge where the bank falls into the Basin — that's the three-number summary of the week, and it explains most of what the fleet found and didn't find. Southwest wind held in the 8-12 knot range through most of the stretch, which is about as good as August gives you out here, and it kept the bank fishable four out of six days. The one blow that mattered came through on a weekday and scattered bait for about eighteen hours before things settled back down. That matters more than it sounds like, because both the groundfish and the tuna are following forage right now, not just structure.

Cod have been a scratch fishery on the gravel patches, the way they usually are in late August. Boats working the classic hard-bottom stretches on the northwest corner found fish in the 80 to 100-foot range, but you had to move to find them — jigging diamond jigs and Norwegian-style bucktails tipped with clam wasn't producing steady drifts, it was producing one or two keepers per good mark and a lot of marks with nothing on them. That's normal for this time of year. The cod aren't schooled up tight like they will be come November; they're spread thin over structure, sitting in the cooler pockets where the gravel breaks up the bottom current.

Haddock is where the real consistency has been. The mud bottom in that 110 to 140-foot band, particularly toward the deeper flats south of the main bank, has been holding fish willing to eat. Standard haddock rigs — two-hook bottom rigs with green or chartreuse tube teasers ahead of a clam or squid strip — have been putting decent numbers of keeper haddock in the box on the drift, especially on the last of the ebb when the current slows enough to fish straight up and down instead of getting blown sideways. Boats that worked the mud methodically, marking soft returns just off bottom and repositioning rather than sitting on one spot, did noticeably better than anyone who anchored and waited. Haddock this year have been mobile, and the mud isn't uniform — there are richer patches and dead patches within a few hundred yards of each other.

Bluefin have been the story worth calling ahead about. We flagged last week that the surface activity on the bank would likely hold as long as bait didn't scatter, and that's essentially what played out — the one wind event did knock things back for the better part of a day, but the school bluefin regrouped on the mackerel pushed up tight against the Stellwagen Edge and along the drop into the Basin. These are school-class fish, not giants, working bait balls close enough to the surface that jigging and casting have both been productive when boats can get on top of them without spooking the school. Green machines and small metal jigs worked fast through the upper thirty feet have drawn strikes, and where the fish were feeding hard on the surface, stickbaits and poppers cast into the boils did their job too. The pattern has been classic mackerel-driven bluefin behavior — tight to bait, moving with it, here one hour and a half mile away the next. Boats spending time scouting birds and bait showers before committing to a stop are the ones connecting; running straight to yesterday's numbers has been a mixed bag.

There's a secondary piece worth mentioning. The warm-water push that's been talked about around the Cape and Islands this month appears to be nudging a bit more life into these waters generally — nothing dramatic on the groundfish side, but the tuna activity has stayed livelier later into the season than a typical year, and that's consistent with a warmer regime holding offshore longer than usual. Whether that continues to bring anything unusual toward Tillies Bank or the approaches toward Carter Canyon and Cape Cod Tails remains to be seen, but it's the kind of signal worth watching if you're running that direction anyway for tuna or looking at fall groundfish prospects early.

Looking at the next few days, the wind pattern looks like it holds in a similar southwest groove, which should keep the bank fishable and keep the tuna bite from getting blown out. The moon is building toward full, and that typically sharpens tidal push on the bank — expect the haddock bite on the mud to concentrate into tighter windows around the tide changes rather than staying spread all day, so timing the drift to the last two hours of the ebb or the first two of the flood is the smarter play than fishing through the whole cycle. For cod, keep working the gravel edges methodically rather than committing to one mark; the fish are there but they're not schooled up enough yet to reward staying put. For bluefin, the call is the same as it's been — find the bait, not the boat you saw with fish yesterday. If the bait holds along the Stellwagen Edge and doesn't get pushed off by another wind event, the school bluefin bite should keep going through the week. If a front comes through and scatters the mackerel again, expect a day or two of hunting before things reset. Either way, worth having tackle rigged for both bottom fish and a surface pop before you leave the dock — this time of year on Stellwagen, you often need both in the same trip.

reports.headline: Great Point's Full of Bait and Boils — Just No Albies Yet
reports.subhead: Terns are working sand eels hard off the Point and stripers are underneath them, but the first false albacore of the year still hasn't turned the corner into the Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a push of sand eels stacked on the rip off Great Point right now thick enough that the terns can't leave it alone, working in tight circles low over the water on the last two hours of the ebb, and under that bait there's bass — good ones, mixed with cocktail blues — punching through the surface in short, violent bursts before going back down. It's the kind of sign that gets your pulse up expecting the first bonito or albie of the season to come ripping through that bait ball. They haven't yet. Not off the Point, not at Sankaty, not out on the Shoals. The water's plenty warm enough — this has been a summer of warm-water signals up and down the coast, with bonito already showing at Block Island and Point Judith and expected to keep pushing this way as September nears — but Nantucket Sound hasn't gotten its invitation yet. Give it another week to ten days before you plan a trip strictly around speedsters.

What you can plan around right now is a solid, honest late-August pattern: stripers in a daytime lull, feeding hard at first light and again after dark, bluefish filling in the gaps everywhere, and fluke that have gone soft and scattered with the warm water pushing them off the open flats and into anything with current and depth. That's the read from the docks in Nantucket and out of Chatham this week, and it lines up with what's happening from the Cape down through the Islands — surface temps are holding high enough that fish are avoiding the sun and doing their business in low light or down in structure.

Great Point is fishing best on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, with the rip stacking bait against the shoal and stripers holding on the down-current edge in 15 to 25 feet. Sand eel imitations are the call — 3-inch Albie Snax in bone or olive, or a slim epoxy jig worked with a fast, erratic retrieve to match the real thing skittering across the surface. Bluefish are mixed in and will happily eat the same lures, so don't be shocked when something with teeth shortens your leader. A few boats working wire or heavy fluoro up top have done better keeping bass in the mix instead of getting bit off every third cast.

Sankaty's rip has been quieter but more consistent — smaller fish, tighter to the bottom, better on bucktails than surface plugs right now.
