A half-ounce white bucktail with a chunk of curly-tail trailer, bounced slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been picking away at schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass in that stretch. Nothing to write home about, but steady, and steady beats nothing on a week like this.

Monomoy is where the better numbers are coming from. With the wind out of the southwest most of this week, the rips off the south end and around the elbow have been setting up clean — moving water pushing bait against structure, stripers stacked on the seams. Live eels fished after dark on the last two hours of the ebb have been the most reliable producer for the better-class fish, with a few reports of bass pushing past 30 pounds coming off the flats south of the island in the dark hours. During the day, the same water has been giving up bluefish steadily on top-water — a Rebel Jumpin' Minnow or a Hopkins No-Eql worked fast through the current seams will get bit as long as there's bait around, and there has been. Chatham's inlet and the harbor structure have had their share of snapper blues thick in the shallows, a reliable back-bay bite for anyone with kids or a slow afternoon to kill.

Fluke have been the tougher story. With water this warm, the fish have spread out across the flats instead of holding tight, and that's softened catch rates almost everywhere except the deeper edges — the channel drop-offs around Monomoy, the cuts near Nantucket Shoals, and the deeper water off Horseshoe Shoal where a cooler bottom layer still holds. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the incoming, have been the most dependable presentation. Don't expect to load the cooler — a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts has been the honest average this week.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full, which should sharpen up the tidal swings and tighten the bite windows at the rips over the next several days — good news for anyone working Great Point or Monomoy on a set tide stage rather than fishing around blind. Southwest wind looks likely to hold into the weekend, which keeps Monomoy's rips in good shape and should keep pushing bait tight against structure there. The bigger question is the exotics. With bonito already stacking up to the west and the warm-water regime showing no signs of breaking yet, the smart bet is that Nantucket Sound gets its first legitimate bonito or albie push sometime in the next one to two weeks, likely showing first out on the Shoals or off Great Point where the bait concentrates hardest. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with small metal in the rocket launcher just in case — when they show, they don't give much notice.

reports.headline: North Shore Rocks Beat the Harbor This Week: Blues on the Rip, Bass After Dark
reports.subhead: With the moon building to full Thursday, the current's tightening up bait from Nahant to Cape Ann while the harbor's bass slide into a night-bite pattern.
reports.body_markdown:
If the fleet's asking where to point the bow this week, the call is North Shore rocks over the harbor islands — at least during daylight. The moon builds to full tomorrow, and that's already tightening the tidal swings from Nahant down through Gloucester and Cape Ann. Stronger current means bait gets pinned against ledges and rock piles instead of spreading out over open water, and that's exactly the kind of squeeze that turns a mediocre bluefish bite into a good one. We flagged this pattern last week — said the moon building toward full would strengthen the current that concentrates bait — and that's precisely what's setting up right now.

Inside the harbor, the bass have settled into their late-August holding pattern. This isn't the fall push south, not yet — that starts once nighttime temps really start dropping, likely mid-September at the earliest. Right now the surface water's warm enough that stripers around Deer Island and Spectacle Island are doing most of their feeding low-light and after dark, sliding up onto the flats and channel edges once the sun's off the water. Dawn and dusk remain the most reliable windows, same as we called it — bait balls get pushed toward the surface in that first and last hour of light, and the bass follow them up. If you're working the Deer Island flats on the drop, live mackerel or a rigged eel drifted along the edge where the flat spills into deeper water has been the most consistent producer, especially the last two hours of the outgoing. Daytime bass are there but sulking tighter to structure — bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the drop-offs, will still pick up fish for anglers willing to grind it out in the heat.

Flounder are steady but unspectacular on the harbor flats around Deer Island and the flats south toward Squantum — sandworms and squid strips on a standard spreader rig, fished on the bottom during the slower stages of the tide, are filling coolers with keeper-sized fish, nothing huge but a dependable box if bass aren't cooperating.

The better energy this week is outside the harbor. Nahant's ledges are holding cocktail bluefish in good numbers, and they're not shy about it — tins like Deadly Dicks and Swedish pimples worked through the rips at first light are getting hit hard, with some fish pushing into the 3- to 5-pound class mixed in with plenty of smaller choppers. Mackerel schools are stacked around the same structure, and where you find the mackerel, the bigger blues and the occasional bonus striper aren't far behind. A mackerel jig dropped through a school, then swapped for a bucktail once you mark bigger arcs underneath, has been the move for boats working Nahant and pushing up toward Gloucester.

Cape Ann and the deeper ledges off Gloucester are worth the run for anyone chasing bottom fish. Cod and haddock have been showing on the deeper structure for boats willing to work jigs and diamond jigs tight to bottom — it's not the kind of numbers game you get in the spring, but there are fish there for patient anglers marking the right bumps on the bottom machine and holding position through the drift. Bring extra weight; the current out there this week is running harder than it has in a month, and that's a direct result of the moon building toward full.

Down south, Plymouth, Duxbury Bay, and Scituate are fishing about how you'd expect for late August — a mixed bag, honest work required. Bass are scattered across the flats in Duxbury Bay, most active on the last two hours of the incoming when warmer water floods back over the sand and pushes bait tight to the edges. Live mackerel or a topwater plug worked at first light along the Scituate rocks has drawn some blitz-style feeding, but it's short-lived — fifteen, twenty minutes of surface chaos and then it shuts down until the next tide stage. Flounder fishing in Duxbury and around Plymouth Harbor remains steady on the same sandworm-and-squid combo that's working up in Boston Harbor.

Looking at the next few days, expect the pattern to hold and likely sharpen. With the full moon Thursday, tidal current will keep building through the weekend, which should keep bait pinned to structure and the bluefish bite consistent at Nahant, Gloucester, and Cape Ann. Winds look manageable out of the southwest in the 8 to 12 knot range, which keeps the North Shore ledges fishable without the swell that can shut down a rock-fishing program. If there's only one window this weekend, make it the dawn bite on the North Shore rips — that's where the moon, the bait, and the blues are lining up. For bass, stick with the after-dark program in the harbor until nights start cooling — that shift, when it comes, will be the real signal the fall run is starting to stir.

reports.headline: Billingsgate on the last of the ebb: bass holding deep as the moon builds
reports.subhead: Warm surface water has the bay's stripers pinned to structure and night tides, while bluefish keep the rods bent through the heat of the day.
reports.body_markdown:
The fleet working Billingsgate and the deeper humps off Race Point this week has settled into a pattern that's become familiar this time of year — bass sliding down off the sand and holding tight to bottom structure through the heat of the day, then coming up to feed hard on the moving tides around first light and last light. Surface water in the bay has stayed stubbornly warm through most of August, and that's pushed the bigger fish into a late-summer holding mode rather than anything resembling a migration push. It's not a bad bite. It's a specific bite, and knowing when and where to show up matters more right now than it did in June.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the moon coming up on full August 28 would strengthen the current through the rips and tighten the bait concentrations, and that's exactly what's setting up now. The tide is running harder through Peaked Hill Bars and off the Billingsgate edge than it was two weeks ago, and where there's harder current there's more bait getting funneled and more bass willing to commit. The last two hours of the ebb off Billingsgate has been the standout window, with fish holding in 18 to 25 feet on the drop where the shoal falls into deeper water. Live mackerel on a light fish-finder rig, or a chunk of the same fished slow along bottom, has been the most consistent producer for fish in the 20- to 34-inch range, with a scattering of bigger fish pushing past 36 inches coming on the same presentation worked right at the base of the drop as the tide starts to slack.

Race Point itself has been more of a dawn program. The rip there sets up hardest on the early stages of the incoming, and boats working live mackerel or trolling large bunker-colored umbrella rigs through the moving water have connected with better-grade fish holding just off the main current seam, generally in 20 to 35 feet. Once the sun gets up and the tide slows, the bite there shuts down fast — this is a tide-window fishery right now, not an all-day proposition, and anyone planning a trip around midday slack is going to be disappointed.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick in Provincetown Harbor and up into Barnstable's inner reaches, keeping light-tackle anglers and kids on the docks busy on small Kastmasters and Gulp shrimp under a float. The bigger cocktail blues, fish in the 3- to 6-pound class, are mixing right in with the striper catches on the rips and on the troll — anyone dragging a spoon or a small tube-and-worm rig through Peaked Hill Bars this week has had to fight through blues to get to bass, which is not the worst problem to have in late August.

Fluke have been the soft spot in the mix, and it's the same story playing out from here down through the mid-Atlantic — warm, thin water has the fish spread out across the flats instead of holding tight, and that's softened catch rates everywhere except the channel edges and deeper structure where a cooler bottom layer still holds. Barnstable Harbor's main channel and the drop-offs along Sandy Neck have kept producing keeper fish to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing. Anyone working the open flats in the middle of the bay this week has mostly found short fish and a lot of nothing.

Cod are still a deep-water proposition and it's early yet for the real showing — that pattern typically doesn't build until the water cools further into fall — but there's been a scattered presence on the deeper structure off Race Point and along the edges of the Bars, fish in the 20-inch class coming up on diamond jigs worked slow along bottom in 60 to 80 feet during the slower tide stages. Worth a stop if you're already out there working the rip, not worth a dedicated trip yet.

Looking at the next several days, expect the pattern to hold and likely sharpen. The moon hits full on the 28th, which means bigger tidal swings and stronger current through all the rip structure — Billingsgate, Race Point, and Peaked Hill Bars should all fish a little harder on both the ebb and the flood as a result. That's good news for anyone working the tide-window program, less good news for anyone hoping for an all-day bite. Southwest winds in the 8- to 12-knot range should keep conditions comfortable for drifting through the weekend, with water color staying clean along the outer structure. The real change everyone's watching for — the first hint of falling nighttime temperatures that starts nudging bass into more aggressive daytime feeding — probably doesn't show itself for another two to three weeks. Until then, the smart play is the same one that's been working: fish the moving water, work the drop-offs and rip edges, and don't waste good tide on the flats.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole bait balls tighten as the marlin catch hints at warm water knocking on the door
reports.subhead: Sand eels and peanut bunker are stacking in the rips between the Elizabeth Islands and the Vineyard — bonito are close, but they're not here yet.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait tells the story right now, and the story is: almost. Sand eels are balling tight in the rip off Robinson's Hole on the last two hours of the ebb, with terns working nervous little knots of them against the current seam where the Vineyard side drops into deeper water. Quick's Hole has the same look on the morning outgoing — peanut bunker pushed thin and flickering along the edge, getting harassed but not yet by anything with a sickle tail. That's the tell. When the bait gets nervous like this in late August, something's supposed to show up and rip through it. Right now that something is mostly bluefish.

The bigger story for the week didn't even happen in these waters — a 1,260-pound blue marlin came over the rail off Falmouth on Tuesday, a new Massachusetts record and the biggest marlin this region has ever produced. Blue marlin have no business being anywhere near Buzzards Bay or the Vineyard under normal conditions. That fish is a signal, not a fluke — there's a genuinely warm, tropical filament of water sitting unusually close to the Cape and Islands right now, and warm water offshore has a way of leaking inshore through the rips. We flagged this exact setup last week — bonito activity was building to the west in Rhode Island waters, and we said this zone was a good candidate to see them next. That call is holding up. Block Island and Point Judith have their first fish. Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard haven't connected yet, but the ingredients — warm water, tightening bait, a moon building toward full that's about to sharpen every tide-driven bite window from here to Cuttyhunk — are lining up fast.

Striped bass are stuck in the pattern you'd expect for this time of year: a summer holding lull, not the fall push. Daytime bass have gone deep and lazy in the warm surface layer, which means the better fish are coming off structure at dawn and after dark rather than on the bright afternoon tide. The Cuttyhunk-side rips and the ledges off the Elizabeth Islands are still the play, but shift the clock — first light on the last of the ebb, or the top of the incoming after sundown, working the current seams with a 1.5-ounce bucktail dressed with a white or olive tube, cast across the rip and swum back with the tide rather than against it. Umbrella rigs and bunker spoons trolled tight to the Woods Hole side of the channel have picked up a few keeper-class fish on the last of the outgoing, but it's not the kind of bite you build a whole trip around yet — more a bonus if you're already out there for something else.

Bluefish are the one thing you can set a watch by. Snapper blues are thick in Menemsha basin and the Oak Bluffs harbor mouth, small enough that a bare gold hook and a strip of squid will get bit within a few casts — good for getting a kid or a first-timer tight to something that fights. The bigger cocktail blues, two to four pounds, are mixing right into the bass catches on the rips and the troll, hammering the same bunker spoons and tube-and-worm rigs. If the tide is ripping hard through Robinson's Hole or Quick's Hole and you're marking bait balls on the sounder, there's a real chance whatever's under them is blue, not bonito — worth knowing before you burn through a box of epoxy jigs.

Fluke are the softer story right now, and it's consistent with what's happening everywhere south of here — warm water has spread the fish out across the flats instead of concentrating them, and the bite has gotten patchy outside of the deeper structure. The better fish are still coming from the channel edges in Buzzards Bay proper and the deeper cuts through Vineyard Sound, where a cooler bottom layer holds even when the surface is running warm. Four-inch white Gulp on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, has been the more consistent producer than bait this week — the fluke are eating but they're not aggressive, and a slow drag beats a fast drift almost every time right now.

Looking ahead, the moon building toward full over the next several days means bigger tidal swings and sharper current through every rip in this zone — Robinson's, Quick's, the Hole itself. That's exactly the kind of current that pulls bait tight against structure and gives predators, whatever species shows up next, a reason to commit. If the bonito are going to make the jump from Rhode Island water into Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard, the next week to ten days is the window — bait's already staging, the water's warm enough, and the tides are about to get more aggressive. Worth carrying a small epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick in the boat bag on any trip to Robinson's Hole or Menemsha through early September, just in case that first fish shows early. Until then, work the bluefish on the rips, fish the bass at the edges of daylight, and drag the fluke slow over the deeper structure. The real fireworks are close, but they're not lit yet.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's Ledge at 190 feet: cod tight to gravel, haddock scattered on the mud
reports.subhead: A steady week on the ledge complex with groundfish holding to structure and the first bluefin sign showing on top as bait tightens up.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ninety feet of water on the east side of Jeffrey's Ledge tells you almost everything you need to know this week. Drop a marker there and the sounder shows two different worlds inside a quarter mile — hard gravel humps holding cod tight to bottom, and softer mud basins off to the side stacked with haddock sitting a few feet up off the floor. That split has been the story of the whole week, and it's the story that should hold into the weekend.

Gravel and mud aren't just bottom types out here, they're two different fisheries. Cod want the hard stuff — broken gravel, cobble, the transition edges where current sweeps bait against structure. Haddock want it softer, working the mud basins and the flatter grounds where sand fleas and worms concentrate. Jeffrey's has both inside a short run, which is why boats working it this week have been able to switch programs mid-drift instead of running miles to change species.

Weather's cooperated. Light southwest breezes, working tides, and clean green water on the ledge have kept boats out and drifts controllable — that matters more than people think, because a two-knot drift on the gravel puts your jig past the strike zone before it ever gets seen. Slower drift days have produced better, cleaner cod bites; the days with more push have leaned haddock, since those fish will chase a bait a little further off bottom.

Tactically it's been jigs and bait both working, depending on what the boat's targeting. For cod on the gravel, a 12- to 16-ounce diamond jig tipped with a strip of squid, worked with a short lift-and-drop right on bottom, has been the go-to — cod on the ledge this time of year don't want to chase, they want it presented slow and right in their face. Clam and herring chunk baits fished on a high-low rig, weight just ticking bottom, have also been picking off cod along the gravel edges where the current sweeps scent downcurrent into the structure.

Haddock over the mud have been coming on smaller jigs — 6- to 8-ounce, fished a few cranks up off bottom with a slow, steady retrieve rather than an aggressive jig stroke. Haddock feed up, not down, so working a bait or jig 3 to 6 feet off the mud has out-produced anything worked tight to the bottom this week. Clam bait on a bottom rig still takes its share too, especially on the slower tide stages when the fish aren't as willing to move for a jig.

Pollock have been mixed in over the higher relief pinnacles closer to the western edge of the ledge and around structure toward Platts Bank, holding up higher in the water column — 60 to 90 feet down over bottom pushing 150 to 180 — and they'll hit the same diamond jigs meant for cod if you let them flutter on the fall instead of working them tight to bottom. Mackerel schools have been showing on the sounder in patches across the ledge and out toward Tillies Bank, which is exactly the kind of bait signature that starts pulling attention from bigger fish.

That's the piece worth watching. We flagged the pattern building a couple weeks back — mackerel and bait tightening up on structure tends to draw bluefin activity before the real fall push arrives, and there's been scattered word of tuna showing on top over the ledge chasing bait, nothing sustained yet, more scouting behavior than a pattern boats can plan a trip around. It's early. The giants that make October worth circling on the calendar haven't shown in numbers, but this kind of surface activity in late August is the leading edge of that, not a fluke. Worth keeping a rod rigged and ready if you're already out there for groundfish, but not worth running offshore specifically for yet.

Scantum Basin has been holding its usual late-summer mud character — haddock scattered through there in decent numbers but not concentrated, which matches the broader read on the ledge complex right now: this is a solid, workable bite, not a blowout. Boats that put in the time on the right bottom and match their presentation to gravel versus mud have had good mixed bags. Boats running one program everywhere have had spottier results.

Looking at the next few days, the moon's building and tidal push should sharpen up, which typically tightens the bite windows rather than killing them — expect shorter, more defined pushes of activity around the tide changes rather than an all-day grind. If the wind holds out of the southwest in the 8 to 12 knot range like it's been running, drift control stays manageable and boats should keep splitting time efficiently between the gravel for cod and the mud basins for haddock. If it swings more westerly or picks up, I'd lean toward the gravel humps first thing, since cod tend to hold tighter and feed more predictably when conditions get a little sloppier on top. Either way, the ledge is fishing the way it's supposed to for late August — steady, structure-dependent, and worth the run if you're willing to work both bottom types instead of anchoring on just one.

reports.headline: West End Flood Seam Stacks Bass at Hog Island; Bonito Knocking at Wings Neck
reports.subhead: Warm surface water has pushed the real bite into the dark hours and the hardest current, with steady bluefish and the first bonito scouts working the Buzzards Bay side.
reports.body_markdown:
The Canal's running close to its top gear this week — call it 4 to 4.5 knots at the peak of the stronger tide stages, and with the moon building toward full over the next few days, that number's only going up. That current speed is the whole story right now. Surface water everywhere from the Sound up through Buzzards Bay is sitting warm, and that's pushed the daytime bite down and into the shade, but the Canal doesn't care what the surface temp says. When that current starts ripping, it stacks bait regardless, and that's why the ditch is still outfishing the open water on both ends.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the night bite would be the most reliable play through the coming tide cycle, especially on the bigger current stages, and that's exactly how it's playing out. East end and west end both, the money windows are running dusk through the first couple hours of dark, and again in that gray light before sunrise. Daytime hours are producing bluefish as the dependable bycatch — cocktail-sized blues chopping up top-water plugs and slicing leaders — while the bass have slid into deeper current and structure until the light drops.

On the east end, off Scusset Beach, the pattern's been the last two hours of the ebb into the top of the slack. That's when the rip off the point organizes and bait gets pinned against the seam instead of getting flushed straight through. Guys working that window after dark have done well on 9-inch Redfins and jointed swimmers fished slow and dead-drifted through the seam, letting the current do the work instead of fighting it. A few schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass have come off that rip on the last two nights, mixed with bluefish up to 8 pounds that keep grabbing gear meant for stripers.

West end is where the better fish have shown. The flood pushing into Buzzards Bay stacks current seams off Hog Island and along the edge toward Mashnee Island, and that's become the go-to for the bigger bass this week. Bucktails in the 2- to 3-ounce range, white or olive, tipped with a strip of sea worm or a 6-inch white Gulp swimming mullet, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the seam right as the flood builds, have been drawing the better bites — 30- to 38-inch fish, with a handful pushing over that mark on the stronger tide nights. The key there is working the inside edge of the seam, not the fast center current — the bass are sitting in the slower water tight against the disturbance, not fighting the main flow.

Fluke have had a rough go of it everywhere this summer with the warm, thin water spreading fish out instead of concentrating them, and the Canal's periphery is no exception. The flats around Mashnee and the channel edge off Hog Island are still the better bet — there's a cooler bottom layer holding there that the open flats don't have. Gulp in white or pink on a light bucktail, dragged slow along the channel drop, has picked at keeper fluke in the 18- to 21-inch range, but it's a pick, not a program. Anyone leaning hard on fluke this week should expect a mixed bag rather than a limit.

Bonito haven't shown inside the Canal itself yet, but the signs pointing that way are stacking up fast. Point Judith and Block Island already have fish, and the bait's been tightening along the beaches and rips on the Buzzards Bay side — Wings Neck and Phinneys Harbor are the places to watch first. We said last week to expect this push to move west toward Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard corridor as water temps peaked, and that's precisely the direction it's heading. If the pattern holds, the first Canal-adjacent bonito sightings should come off Wings Neck within the next week to ten days, likely on the same small silversides and bay anchovies the blues have been chopping.

Looking at the next few days, the building moon is going to sharpen everything. Bigger swings mean harder current, and harder current on the Canal means better-defined rip lines on both ends and less guesswork about when the bite turns on. If there's only one window to fish this weekend, make it the west end on the building flood after sunset — Hog Island seam, bucktail on the drop, patience through the slower water inside the disturbance. East end guys should lean on the last two hours of the ebb into slack at Scusset, working the rip with a slow presentation rather than a fast retrieve. Daytime hours will keep producing bluefish as a consolation prize while the real program stays after dark until the nights start cooling off in earnest, which is still a couple weeks out on the calendar.

reports.headline: Napatree Bait Tightens, Snappers Run the Salt Ponds, First Albie Flash Building
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker are packing into the breachways as the moon swings toward full — bass are holding tight to rock, blues are everywhere shallow, and the first false albacore signs are starting to show.
reports.body_markdown:
Walk the rocks from Beavertail down to Napatree this week and the story is written in the bait, not the boats. Peanut bunker are stacking thick against the ledges at Second Beach and pushing hard into the mouths of the breachways on the last of the ebb, with rain bait and silversides balling up tight to structure at Sakonnet Point and along the Jamestown shore. That's classic late-August behavior — the bait is compressing, and it's dragging predators with it, but the predators themselves are behaving like it's still summer, not fall.

Striped bass on the south shore are in the holding pattern we flagged last week — this is not the fall migration kicking off, it's fish parked on structure through the warm daytime hours and only really turning on in low light or on a hard-moving tide. Surface temps are still up in the high 60s to low 70s depending on where you check, and that keeps bass glued to rock piles, current seams, and the deeper cuts inside the breachways rather than roaming the open beach. The better program right now is a night or dawn bite worked tight to structure — Newport's bridge pilings and rock walls, the ledges off Jamestown, the boulder fields at Second Beach — with eels or bunker chunks fished on the slack around the tide change, then a switch to swimming plugs or soft plastics as the current builds. Nothing about this is a blitz. It's a quiet, structure-bound bite that rewards patience and local knowledge of which crack holds a fish on a given stage of tide.

What is building, and building fast, is current strength. The moon rounds to full on the 28th, and we called this one too — the swing toward full builds the tidal push that concentrates bait right where the breachways narrow. Watch Hill, Weekapaug, and the Charlestown breachway are all going to feel that extra shove over the next several days, and that's exactly the mechanism that tightens up a scattered bait field into something worth working. Expect the moving-water windows — the first two hours of a building tide, either direction — to be noticeably better than they've been, especially right at the mouths where the bait gets squeezed through the gut.

Bluefish are the one constant nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick in Ninigret and the other salt ponds behind Charlestown, snapping at anything small and flashy off the docks and the pond mouths, and that's a signal in itself — those juvenile blues follow the bait out of the back bays as the season turns, and adult cocktail fish are already riding shotgun with the striper schools on the peanut bunker pushes along the beachfront. If you're marking bass on the ledges and getting cut off, it's not always a bluefish being a nuisance — sometimes it's the tell that bait's balled up tight enough to hold both species on the same piece of structure. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — worked fast through the peanut schools will connect with both.

Fluke are the soft spot right now, and it's a regional problem, not a local one. Warm water has spread fish out across the flats instead of holding them concentrated, and catch rates off places like the Sakonnet River channel edges and the deeper drops around Jamestown have been inconsistent — some drifts stacking three or four keepers, others going empty. The fish that are biting are sitting on the cooler bottom layer in the deeper cuts, so if fluke are the target, work the channel edges and structure rather than the open flats, and don't be afraid to work a heavier bucktail — three-quarter to one ounce with a Gulp swimming mullet trailer — to hold bottom in the deeper water where the better fish seem to be sitting.

Tog talk is starting up dockside even though the real structure bite doesn't kick into gear until the water cools another notch. A few incidental fish are coming off the deeper ledges around Beavertail and the rock piles off Jamestown on green crabs fished tight to bottom on the slack, but it's early — worth noting for the next few weeks rather than planning a trip around right now.

The albie and bonito question is the one everyone's asking in the shops, and the honest answer is: not yet, but the pieces are lining up. Bait is tightening along the beachfront exactly the way it does before the first push, and the breachways — Watch Hill and Napatree specifically — are historically where those fish show first on the South Shore before they spread east toward Sakonnet. With the moon building the current and bait getting squeezed into the gut of every breachway from Weekapaug down to Napatree, the next week to ten days is prime timing for that first confirmed showing. Keep a bag of half-ounce epoxy jigs and small Albie Snax rigged and ready, and work the rips right at the breachway mouths on the outgoing.

Look for the next 48 hours to hold mostly steady — same warm-water regime, same structure-bound bass pattern — with the building tidal swing sharpening the bite windows at every breachway and current seam. Past that, keep an eye on overnight air temps; the first real cooldown is what finally nudges this from a summer holding pattern into the start of the actual fall push, and that's usually a mid-September story here, not a Labor Day one.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock on the push: cod hold steady, bass slide into the dark tide
reports.subhead: With the moon rounding to full, Casco Bay's current is sharpening — and the bite is moving toward the edges of light.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rail off Halfway Rock this week and watched the tide line stack up harder than it has all month — a clean seam of green water pushing against the darker water off the ledge, gulls working it tight. That's the tell. The moon rounds to full tomorrow night, and the current through the bay's ledges and channels has been building toward it for days. We flagged this pattern last week, that the push toward full moon would strengthen the current enough to concentrate bait against structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now from Halfway Rock down through the Harpswell ledges.

The broader picture for Casco Bay right now is a stable one, and stable is the right word for late August here. While water farther south sits in that thermally stressed, structure-and-night-bite holding pattern for striped bass, the Gulf of Maine's cooler water keeps our fishery on a more even keel. It's not blazing, but it's dependable — the kind of program where a careful angler who reads the tide correctly will out-fish someone running blind on a schedule that doesn't match the current.

Striped bass are in exactly the kind of late-summer lull you'd expect this time of year, but they haven't gone anywhere — they've just shifted their address to the structure and to the low-light hours. Daytime fish are holding tight to the ledges off Bailey Island and along the drop-offs on the west side of Peaks Island, sitting deep against rock in 20 to 35 feet through the heat of the day and sliding up onto the flats and eddies as the light fails. The evening flood tide, roughly two hours before and after the top, has been the most consistent window — bass working the current seams off Cape Small and around the back side of Halfway Rock on tube-and-worm rigs fished slow along bottom, or live mackerel drifted on a fish-finder rig where the ledge drops into deeper water. Sluggos in bone or bunker colors, worked slow on a jighead after dark near the Two Lights ledges, have also been drawing strikes from fish that won't touch anything moving fast in daylight.

Bluefish are mixing into that same program in patches — nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around, but cocktail-sized blues have been showing up on the troll and on bucktails intended for bass, particularly on the outgoing tide off Peaks Island and in the deeper water south of Halfway Rock. Worth keeping a wire leader rigged as insurance if you're throwing plugs in that zone right now.

Groundfish have been the more reliable story this week. Cod and pollock are holding on the deep ledges around Halfway Rock and off Bailey Island, typically in 80 to 120 feet, and the bite has been most productive on the slack around the tide change — not the dead slack itself, but the twenty minutes on either side when the current eases enough to hold bottom without three ounces of extra lead. Diamond jigs in the 4- to 6-ounce range, tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly, have been the go-to presentation, worked in a slow lift-and-drop just off bottom. Haddock have been mixed in on some of the deeper structure toward Cape Small, though they're spottier than the cod right now — worth a few drifts but not a spot to build a whole day around yet.

Mackerel, which usually make their loudest push through the bay back in May, have thinned out but haven't disappeared. Small schools are still showing around the Peaks Island wharf pilings and along the edges near Halfway Rock, enough to fill a bait bucket on a Sabiki rig if you catch them working the surface early in the morning before the wind picks up. That live mackerel is worth more to a bass angler than almost anything in the tackle box right now — a lively mackerel free-lined or fished on a fish-finder rig near ledge structure at dusk has been the most consistent producer of the bigger bass reported this week.

Looking ahead, the building tide toward tomorrow's full moon should sharpen these bite windows rather than blow them out. Bigger swings mean stronger current at structure like Halfway Rock and the Harpswell ledges, which typically means better bait concentration and a tighter window when the fish commit. If the wind stays out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 range as it has, expect the pattern to hold through the weekend — work the evening flood at the ledges for bass, hit the slack tide change on the deep structure for cod, and don't overlook an early-morning pass with the Sabiki rig before the mackerel schools scatter with the sun. The bigger question worth watching into September is whether this warm pulse in Maine's coastal water continues to hold or starts to retreat as nights cool — that shift, when it comes, will be the signal that the real fall program is starting rather than this holding pattern we're in now.

reports.headline: Monhegan to Matinicus: pollock thick on the ledges, bass tucked into cool coves
reports.subhead: Forty years of late August on Penobscot Bay says the pattern holds until the nights turn cold — this week did nothing to argue otherwise.
reports.body_markdown:
Ask any old-timer around Stonington what August looks like on Penobscot Bay and he'll tell you the same thing every year without missing a beat: the mackerel show first, the bass tuck into the coves and river mouths, and the groundfish sit tight on the ledges until the water finally cools enough to move them. Forty years of hauling traps and running charter trips out of these harbors hasn't changed that rhythm one bit, and this week proved it again. While the coast south of Cape Cod is dealing with warm-water stress pushing bass into structure and night programs, Midcoast Maine is sitting comfortable on the northern edge of all that — we flagged this last week, said conditions here would hold steady while the south cooked in it, and that's exactly what happened. Water temps in the bay and around the islands stayed in the range that keeps fish honest and predictable rather than lockjawed.

Striped bass have been working the classic late-summer program — river mouths, cove edges, and the mud flats where warm outflow meets cooler bay water. The Damariscotta and Bagaduce river mouths have both been giving up fish on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, with bass in the 24 to 32 inch range holding in 8 to 15 feet of water where the current pinches down. Live mackerel on a simple three-way rig has been the most consistent producer, but a white or bone RonZ worked slow along bottom on the drop has taken its share too, especially in the hour around dead low when the fish are less committed to chasing and more willing to eat something presented right in their face. Boothbay Harbor's inner coves have been holding smaller schoolies on the incoming, mostly a light-tackle affair with soft plastics and topwater walking baits at first light before the sun gets up and pushes them down.

Mackerel have been thick around Eastern Egg Rock, same as they've been all summer, and that's been doing double duty — feeding the puffins the birders come out to see and feeding the bass and bluefish that shadow the schools. Sabiki rigs and small Diamond jigs worked in 20 to 40 feet on the tide change have been filling coolers fast, and that fresh mackerel is exactly what's been going down on those bass rigs upriver. Bluefish have been mixed in with the mackerel schools around Egg Rock and off the Cuckolds, nothing huge, mostly 2 to 4 pound choppers, but enough of them to keep rods bent for anyone jigging bucktails through the bait.

The groundfish story is where this zone earns its keep this time of year, and Monhegan's ledges have been holding up their end. Pollock have been thick on top, busting bait right on the surface around the eastern side of the island on the last of the ebb, and a diamond jig or a big soft plastic swimbait worked through the boils has been good for fish in the 8 to 15 pound class, occasionally bigger. Drop below that, and cod have been coming off the deeper structure in 100 to 150 feet, mostly on cut mackerel or clams fished tight to bottom on a slow drift. Haddock have been mixed in on some of the deeper humps out toward Matinicus, though that fishery stays spottier than the pollock and cod — some days the fleet does well, other days it's a lot of jigging for not much to show. Isle au Haut's channels and the deeper water off Vinalhaven have both been producing pollock and the occasional cod for boats willing to work the tide change carefully, since the current runs hard enough through those cuts that timing matters more than location.

Wind's been the cooperative kind this week, mostly out of the southwest in the 8 to 12 knot range, which keeps the bay workable without kicking up the kind of chop that shuts down jigging over the ledges. That pattern looks to hold through the next couple of days, which means the pollock bite off Monhegan should stay dependable on the ebb, and the bass should keep working the same river-mouth program on the outgoing tide morning and evening. The moon's building toward full over the next week, and when that happens the tidal swings sharpen up — worth watching the river mouths a little closer as the current gets more current, because bass tend to stack tighter against structure when the water's really moving rather than spreading out over the flats.

Looking a few days out, there's no sign yet of the fall push starting up here — that's a mid-September story once the nights get properly cold and the bay starts shedding heat in earnest. For now this is a summer holding pattern, stable and readable, which after forty years on this water is about the best thing anyone can ask for in late August. If there's one day to plan around this week, make it the morning after the wind lays down following any afternoon southwesterly — clean water and a settling tide off Monhegan will put the pollock back on top where the jigs can reach them, and the bass will still be waiting in the coves when the boat comes back in.

reports.headline: SW Ledge's 9:10 slack: bass holding deep, first bonito flashing off Sandy Point
reports.subhead: The rip window is shrinking to twenty minutes on either side of slack, but the fleet worked it hard enough to confirm the first bonito of the season off Block Island.
reports.body_markdown:
The morning slack at SW Ledge has been running right around 9:10 this week, and that narrow stretch — call it twenty minutes before the turn and twenty after — has been the only reliable window worth fishing hard. Outside of it, the rip is either roaring too fast to hold a jig in the strike zone or it's dead flat with no current to push bait over the structure. That's a function of the moon building toward full, which is stacking more water through the Ledge on both the flood and the ebb and compressing the good fishing into tighter blocks. If you're planning a trip off Galilee this week, build the day around that slack, not the other way around.

Surface water is sitting in the high 60s to low 70s across the region — Kings Point up in the Sound reading 70.9, New London a touch cooler at 69.4, and Montauk holding 69.1 off to the west. That's warm enough to push striped bass into the classic late-August pattern: they're not gone, they're just not stupid. Daytime bites have gone quiet on the flats and open structure, and the better fish are sliding down onto the deeper edges of SW Ledge and the drop-offs east of the Point where there's still a cooler layer of water underneath the warm cap. Night tides and the gray light around dawn and dusk are outproducing the middle of the day by a wide margin right now, and that's not likely to change until the nights start cooling off in a couple weeks.

On the bonito — we flagged this last week, said Point Judith and Block Island would be among the first spots in the region to see them, and the fleet is now confirming fish showing off Sandy Point and along the rip lines north of North Light. They're still scattered and the window is short, but small pods have been popping bait on the surface in the first hour of daylight, chasing peanut bunker and rain bait that's been getting pushed tight against the beach by the current. Epoxy jigs in the 1-ounce range, small Deadly Dicks, and green-and-white Albie Snax on light spinning gear have been the go-to when the fish show — the mistake anglers keep making is throwing too big a profile at fish that are eating something the size of your pinky finger. Expect this pattern to build over the next week to ten days as more bonito filter in behind the bunker schools and water temps hold in this range.

Striped bass fishing itself has been a mixed bag, and it's worth being straight about that. The daytime bite on structure around SW Ledge has been spotty — a fish or two on a diamond jig worked slow along bottom in 40 to 60 feet on the last of the ebb, then long stretches of nothing. The better action has shifted to the night program, with eel-and-bucktail combinations and swimming plugs worked slow over the rocky stretches off Sandy Point and Clay Head after dark producing better numbers and better size. This is a summer holding pattern, not the start of the fall run — that push doesn't really get going until nighttime temperatures drop hard in mid-September, so there's no need to panic if the daytime bite feels thin right now. Patience and a headlamp are doing more work than a bigger boat.

Fluke have been the most disappointing story of the month, and the warm water is the reason. Fish have spread out across the open bottom instead of holding tight anywhere, which has softened catch rates everywhere except the channel edges and deeper humps where a cooler bottom layer survives. The better fluke this week have come from the deeper water off the Ledge and around the deeper cuts near Block Island, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Don't expect a bag limit — expect a keeper or two mixed with a lot of shorts if you're patient and stay on structure rather than drifting open sand.

Bluefish have been the one dependable player in the mix. Snapper blues are thick in Galilee's back channels and around the breachway, and cocktail-sized blues in the 3- to 6-pound range are showing up mixed into both the fluke drift and the striper program on structure, occasionally sawing through leaders meant for bass. Not glamorous, but steady, and a fine option for anyone who wants bent rods without needing the tide to line up perfectly.

Sea bass remain a solid secondary catch for anyone working the deeper wrecks and rock piles off the Point — nothing spectacular, but consistent numbers on squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs for boats willing to run a little farther and fish bottom instead of chasing the surface bite.

Looking ahead, expect the wind to stay out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 knot range through the next couple days, keeping the water clean and the SW Ledge slack fishable on schedule. As the moon fills out, tidal swings will keep sharpening, which should tighten up both the bass bite on structure and the bonito windows along the beaches. The real story to watch is temperature — once overnight lows start dropping into September, look for the daytime striper bite to wake back up on structure and for bonito numbers to build steadily rather than trickle in. For now, work the slack, fish it hard and short, and don't be surprised if the best fish of the week come after the sun goes down.

reports.headline: Higgins Beach blues chop mackerel to pieces, Biddeford Pool bass hold to the incoming
reports.subhead: Cooler Gulf of Maine water is keeping Southern Maine honest while the rest of the coast cooks — the pattern we called last week is holding.
reports.body_markdown:
There was a solid hour off Higgins Beach midweek when the water actually turned white — bluefish, three to five pounds, working a pod of mackerel right up against the sandbar on the last of the incoming. Guys in the parking lot said the birds gave it away twenty minutes before the blues did, gulls dropping straight down onto bait that had nowhere left to run. That's the story of the week up and down this stretch: mackerel schools pushing tight to the beaches, and everything with teeth taking advantage of it before the tide turns them loose again.

We flagged this last week — said the cooler, more stable Gulf of Maine water would keep this fishery clean while the water south of us cooked into a stress pattern, and that's exactly what's playing out. Southern Maine is sitting in the low-to-mid 60s, comfortable water, and it's kept both the bass and the bluefish feeding on a normal schedule instead of shutting down at midday like the fish are doing from the Sound on south. This isn't the fall run yet — nowhere close. It's the late-August holding pattern: fish still up here, still feeding hard, still using the same rocks and river mouths they've used since July, and they'll keep doing it until the nights start cooling off for real, which is usually a mid-September story around here, not a Labor Day one.

Biddeford Pool remains the best hour in the state when it's working right, and this week it worked more often than not. The bite builds on the first two hours of the incoming, when water starts stacking through the mouth and pushing bait — mackerel, pogies, the occasional school of peanut bunker — up against the sandbar and into the channel by the Pool itself. Guides working eels have done well in the deeper cuts on the drop, but the plug bite has been the more consistent story: black Slug-Go on a weighted swimbait hook worked slow along the current seams, and a Gibbs Danny or a Doc's swimming when there's enough push to make it walk right. Fish have been mostly schoolies and mid-twenties, but there've been enough 30-inch-plus bass mixed in on the last hour of the flood to keep rods bent. Once the tide tops out and goes slack, shut it down and wait — the bite dies hard at the top and doesn't turn back on until the ebb gets some current moving again.

Pine Point has been a flounder program more than anything else this week — sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig in the mud channels behind the point, best on the last two hours of the ebb when the water's draining out of the marsh and pulling bait with it. Nothing giant, mostly 12 to 15 inch fish, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you're patient and willing to move around to find where the bottom's holding the most bait.

Prouts Neck has been the better bass bet on any day with a southwest wind, which has been most of this week. That wind pushes bait tight against the rocks on the south side and gives the stripers a reason to sit right in the wash instead of roaming. A 2-ounce Rebel Jumpin Minnow or a bone-colored pencil popper worked through the white water at first light has been drawing strikes from fish in the 20-to-28-inch range, with the occasional bigger fish following a popper right to the rod tip before committing. Wear a belt and watch your footing — that ledge gets slick and the swell's been running enough this week to make it interesting.

Wells Harbor and Ogunquit have been mackerel country, which isn't glamorous but it's fun and it's filling bait buckets for everyone targeting bass with live bait elsewhere. Small Deceivers or a three-hook mackerel tree worked off the docks and jetties has been producing steady action, with snapper blues mixed in tight to the pilings on the last of the incoming. Cape Elizabeth has had a few cod reports from boats working the deeper rockpiles off the point, but that's a small-boat, know-your-numbers game this time of year — nothing a shore angler's going to stumble into.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds. Southwest wind in the 8-to-12 range is expected to stick around, which keeps Prouts Neck and the ocean-side beaches working and keeps that mackerel bait pinned tight to shore. The moon's building toward full over the next several days, which should sharpen the tide swings and tighten up the bite windows at the Pool and at the river mouths — meaning shorter, more concentrated pushes rather than an all-day grind. If there's only one tide to fish this weekend, make it the incoming at Biddeford Pool in the two hours before the moon's peak influence kicks in — that's where the numbers and the size have both been best. Keep the Prouts Neck rocks as the backup plan if the wind holds southwest, and don't be surprised if the mackerel show up somewhere new by midweek — they've been moving fast, and everything that eats them has been following close behind.

reports.headline: Appledore ledges holding cod to 6 pounds, bass stacked on Piscataqua mackerel
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coast, but the ledges off the Shoals and the current lines on the river are still doing all the work.
reports.body_markdown:
Thirteen miles of coastline sounds like nothing until you've spent enough dawns idling out past Whaleback with a chart of the Shoals memorized cold. Guys drive two hours to fish structure that's a twenty-minute run from Rye Harbor State Marina. The water off Appledore and White Island doesn't care how big your bay is — it holds cod, it holds bass, and this week it held both, which is more than most of the mid-Atlantic can say right now.

The pattern that's been running since mid-August hasn't budged. Surface water along the coast is sitting in that comfortable, slightly-too-warm-for-daytime-aggression range that pushes stripers and blues onto structure and into the current lines rather than roaming open water. High pressure has held, winds have stayed out of the southwest in the 8-12 knot range most days, and that's kept the ocean off the Shoals fishable — not glassy, but workable, two-to-three-foot swell with a long enough period that a 20-foot boat can sit on the ledges without getting knocked around. We flagged this pattern last week, said mackerel schools close to shore would keep driving the predator activity, and that's exactly what's held. The bait is thick enough around the Shoals and off Great Boars Head that nothing has needed to travel far to eat.

On the groundfish side, the Appledore ledges and the drop east of Star Island have been the honest producers. Depths in the 45 to 65-foot range, fished right on the slack or the first hour of the new tide, have given up cod in the 4 to 6-pound class with a few better fish pushing 8. Diamond jigs — the 4 and 6-ounce sizes — tipped with a strip of squid or fished bare with a fast lift-and-drop have outfished bait rigs this week, which tells you the fish are chasing, not scavenging. Haddock have been mixed in but thinner than a July report would show; the ones coming over the rail are running 18 to 20 inches, mostly on the same jigs worked a little slower off bottom. If you're marking bait balls on the sounder around 50 feet and the current's easing off, that's the window — don't waste time on max flood or max ebb out there, the drift gets unmanageable and the fish stop feeding as hard anyway.

Stripers have been the better story inshore, and the Piscataqua River is the reason. Mackerel pushing up through Portsmouth Harbor on the last two hours of the flood have pulled bass right up into the current seams below the Memorial Bridge and around the moorings off Peirce Island. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a 3-ounce bucktail with a chunk of mackerel belly dressed on the hook, worked slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet, has been the move. Fish in the 28 to 34-inch range are common there right now, with the occasional overslot showing on the harder tide changes. Hampton Harbor has been more of a dusk program — the inlet by the Route 1A bridge stacks bait on the outgoing, and bass have been sliding through there in the last two hours of ebb chasing peanut bunker and silversides, best worked with white or chartreuse soft-plastic swim shads on light jig heads so they stay in the strike zone without snagging bottom.

Bluefish have done exactly what bluefish do this time of year — shown up everywhere and annoyed everyone trying to fish for something else. Snapper blues are thick in Rye and Hampton Harbors, small enough to be more nuisance than target, but cocktail blues in the 2 to 4-pound range have been mixing into the striper bite off Great Boars Head and around the outer edge of the Shoals, hitting the same mackerel-imitating baits meant for bass. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for a kid on the boat, a small silver Kastmaster worked fast through a surface blitz off the Boars Head rocks will get eaten every time right now.

Flounder fishing has stayed quiet but steady for the handful of guys still bothering with it — Rye Harbor and the mud flats inside Portsmouth Harbor near the Route 1B causeway have given up winter flounder and a few blackback keepers on bloodworms and clam bellies, fished on a simple bottom rig in 10 to 15 feet on the last of the ebb when the current slows enough for a bait to sit still.

Looking at the next several days, expect more of the same rather than a turn. The moon's building toward full, which should sharpen the tide swings and tighten up the bite windows at the river mouths and around the Shoals ledges — instead of a long lazy bite you'll get a harder, shorter push right around the tide change, so timing matters more than usual. Southwest wind in the 8 to 12-knot range looks likely to hold, keeping the run out to Appledore and White Island manageable most mornings. The real shift — the one that sends bass moving with more urgency and cools that surface layer enough to open up daytime activity closer to the beach — is still probably two to three weeks out, once overnight temps start dropping consistently into September. Until then, the smart money stays on the same program: ledges on the slack for cod and haddock, river current seams on the mackerel-fed tides for bass, and the harbors at last light for anything willing to chase a blitz.

reports.headline: 65 Feet at Sea Girt Reef: Limit Sea Bass, Bluefin Back on the Barnegat Ridge Lumps
reports.subhead: The reef wrecks are stacked with keeper sea bass while a warm eddy pushes tuna and squid up onto the Klondike and Barnegat Ridge.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-five feet of water over Sea Girt Reef, water temp holding better than 71 degrees on the meter — that's the number that's mattered most this week. Sea bass season is open in New Jersey through the end of the month, and the reef network from Shrewsbury Rocks down through Axel Carlson has been paying off for anyone willing to work bottom instead of running past it looking for something flashier offshore.

High pressure has parked over the region for the better part of ten days, southwest wind in the 8 to 12 knot range most afternoons, and that's kept the reef boats fishing clean, slick-calm water on structure that gets ugly fast when the wind swings onshore. That stability is the whole story right now. Bottom temps on the reef sites are steady, bait is holding tight to the wrecks instead of getting pushed around, and the sea bass have settled into a predictable pattern — tight to structure on the up-current side, feeding hard on the first two hours of a moving tide and going quiet in slack water.

Sea Girt Reef and Axel Carlson Reef, both sitting in that 55- to 70-foot band, have been the most consistent producers in the fleet reports coming back to the dock. Green crab and clam on standard sea bass rigs are taking the numbers, but the better fish — the 15- to 18-inch class that make a trip worth the gas — are coming on 4- to 6-ounce diamond jigs tipped with squid strips, worked with a short, sharp jig stroke a few feet off bottom. Shrewsbury Rocks has been holding a similar grade of fish in slightly shallower water, 40 to 55 feet, and it's the better call on a sloppier day since it sits tighter to the beach.

Triple Wrecks, deeper and further out, has been the spot for size. That structure holds up better in a bit of leftover swell, and the sea bass running out there have been noticeably bigger — book-worthy fish in the 3- to 4-pound class mixed into the limits. It's not a fast bite the way the shallower reefs can be, but it's a quality bite, and worth the extra run if the forecast holds. Blackfish won't be legal again until the fall opener, so leave the crabs in the bucket for tog and stick to the sea bass program on these wrecks for now.

The bigger story this week has been offshore of the reef line. The warm eddy that's been sitting south of us and holding clean blue water has finally pushed up onto the shelf the way we flagged it would — we said last week that eddy water working the canyon edges would eventually spill onto the inshore structure and trigger a bite, and that's exactly what's showing up on the Klondike and Barnegat Ridge lumps right now. Bluefin have been working both areas, and there's been enough yellowfin mixed in to keep the trolling spreads busy on the better mornings. Ballyhoo behind cedar plugs and small Spanish flags have both scored, along with the 180-gram vertical jig program on marks that show bait stacked tight to the bottom structure.

What's driving it is squid. Jumbo squid have shown up inshore of the ridges this week, a classic late-August signal that the warm-water forage base has hit its peak and is starting to push shoreward ahead of the first real cool-down. Where the squid balls are thick on the Klondike lumps, the tuna have been sitting underneath them, and that's produced some of the better jigging windows — bait marks stacked from 80 feet down to bottom, tuna slashing through on the sonar, and a short window before the school moves off the structure. It's not a wide-open bite. Boats working the lumps have connected in bursts rather than steady action, so plan on covering water and being ready to drop fast when the marks show up rather than sitting on one spot all day.

Mahi have been scattered around the same warm structure, holding on current edges and any floating debris near the ridge, with fish coming to small spreads and to bucktails dropped near the color changes. It's a bonus fish more than a target right now — nothing like the wide-open pot bite this pattern can produce later in the season, but worth a look if the spread's already out and the water color is right.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward full over the next several days, which should sharpen the tidal swings on the reef sites and tighten up the bite windows — better to fish the first hour of a building tide than to grind through slack water hoping something turns on. The stable high pressure is forecast to hold through midweek, which should keep both the reef bite and the tuna window on the Klondike and Barnegat Ridge intact. If there's a change coming, it's later than that — early signs of cooler overnight air working into the region by the weekend, which won't touch these bottom temps yet but is worth watching as the calendar turns toward September. For now, the play is simple: reef wrecks for a solid box of sea bass, and the ridge lumps for tuna if the squid stay put and you're willing to run and watch the meter instead of parking on hope.

reports.headline: Romer Shoal to the Reach: the porgy-fluke combo fills the gap the bass left behind
reports.subhead: Snapper blues own the piers, bunker are stacking for the fall push, and the moon builds toward full Friday — here's where the bay is actually paying off right now.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one tide window this week, spend it on the channel edges off the Reach and down toward Romer Shoal, not chasing bass around the bay. That's the call right now, and it's not close. Striped bass are in the predictable late-August holding pattern — scattered, structure-oriented, mostly a dusk-and-dawn program if they show at all — while porgies and fluke are the two species actually cooperating on a consistent basis. We flagged this exact setup last week, saying the porgy-fluke combo would be the most reliable play through the stretch, and that's exactly how it's played out on the drop-offs from Chapel Hill Channel out past the Flats.

Water's warm across the bay, surface temps sitting in that mid-70s range that pushes bait and predators alike off the open flats and onto structure with a cooler bottom layer. That's why the channel edges are holding up better than the Reach's open water — 18 to 24 feet along the drop, moving water on the last two hours of the ebb, is where the bucktail-and-Gulp program keeps finding keeper fluke instead of the dinks that are thick everywhere else. White or chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom as the tide pulls off the flat and funnels into the channel — that's the presentation putting fish in the box. Sizes are modest, most fish 16 to 19 inches, but there's enough of a mix in there to make it worth the drift, especially with a few short flurries of keeper-class fish showing up right where the mud gives way to hard sand along the edge.

Porgies are honestly the more dependable half of that combo right now. Anchoring up on the same channel structure — the drop just off Flynn's Knoll, or the deeper stretch running toward Romer Shoal — with a standard porgy rig, size 4 or 6 hooks, clam or squid strips, is filling coolers while the fluke bite stays hit-or-miss. These fish are stacked tight to bottom in that cooler layer and they're not picky. If you want steady rod-bending action for the family or you're breaking in a kid on the rail, this is the move over grinding for stripers that mostly aren't home.

Speaking of stripers — the bass situation is exactly the summer lull we called out a few days back. This isn't the fall run starting early, it's the bay doing what it does in late August: warm surface water, minimal daytime activity, whatever bass are around holding tight to structure or feeding at night. What's more interesting is what's building underneath that lull. Bunker schools are thickening up in the bay ahead of the fall push, and that's the tell everyone on the docks in Keyport and the Highlands is watching. The moon builds to full on Friday, and that's going to strengthen the tidal current running through the bay's channels and pinch those bunker schools tighter against structure — the same mechanism we pointed to last week when we said this pattern would intensify as the moon filled out. Watch Flynn's Knoll and the mouth of the Navesink over the next several tides; if bass are going to show any real interest before the calendar turns to September, that's where the first sign will be — bunker balled up, birds working, maybe a swirl or two on the surface at first light.

Snapper blues remain the one thing you can count on no matter what the tide chart says. They're thick off the Highlands and Keansburg piers, chasing peanut bunker into water so shallow you can watch it happen, and they'll hit just about anything small and flashy — 1/8-ounce Kastmasters, bare gold hooks with a sliver of bunker, tiny bucktail teasers under a bobber for kids fishing off the rail. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as close to a guarantee as this bay offers right now, and it's a good way to keep a rod bent while you wait on the bigger patterns to develop.

Up in the Navesink and Shrewsbury, the story's quieter. Warm, slack water in the upper reaches isn't holding much beyond the occasional snapper push and a few small fluke working the deeper bends. Better water and better current are down in the bay proper right now — the rivers should perk back up once nights start cooling and that first real drop in water temp gets underway, which typically doesn't happen here until deeper into September.

Looking at the next few days: expect the warm-water regime to hold with the wind staying out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 knot range, which means stable but unspectacular conditions — no big weather to reshuffle the deck. The building moon into Friday's full phase should sharpen the tidal push through the channels, which is good news for the fluke-porgy program on the edges and worth watching closely at Flynn's Knoll for any early bass activity around the bunker. If there's only one day to fish this weekend, run the last two hours of the ebb on the channel edge off the Reach with bucktail-and-Gulp, then set up on the porgy rigs once the tide goes dead slack. Keep an eye on the bunker schools — when they start getting nervous and balling up tight against structure, that's the signal the fall pattern is closer than the calendar suggests.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point on the push: bass working structure as the moon crowds full
reports.subhead: Fluke are spreading thin in the warm water, but the tide swings building into Friday's full moon are about to sharpen every bite window in the bay.
reports.body_markdown:
Down at the Providence River piers this week the talk wasn't about big fish, it was about timing. Guys standing around the bait shop counter with a scoop of green crabs in one hand were all saying the same thing — the bass are here, but they're not dumb, and if you're not fishing the turn of the tide you're just casting at empty water. That's late August on this bay. The water's warm on the surface, the bait's shifted from the herring that ran up Buckeye Brook back in April to silversides and peanut menhaden working the flats and the edges of Greenwich Bay, and the fish know exactly when the tide is going to stack that bait against a rock pile or a bridge piling. Miss the window and you're watching gulls instead of hooking up.

The moon is closing in on full tomorrow night, and that's the story for the next several days. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving through the East and West Passages, which means the current seams off Nyatt Point, Rocky Point, and the north end of Prudence Island are going to load up harder and longer than they have the past couple weeks. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the push toward full moon would strengthen the current that pins bait against structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now. The guys working Rocky Point after dark have been getting into slot bass on the last two hours of the incoming, throwing bunker chunks and swimming plugs tight to the ledge rock, and that bite should only get better as the tide range opens up into the weekend.

Striped bass overall are in that predictable late-summer holding pattern — nobody's expecting a blitz with the surface water sitting where it is, but the structure bite is real if you fish it on the tide change instead of the middle of the day. Nyatt Point's rock pile has been giving up fish on the last of the ebb into the start of the flood, mostly schoolies to mid-20s with the occasional better fish mixed in, taken on white bucktails tipped with a swimming mullet or live eels drifted along the drop. Conimicut Point is still holding fish too, especially right at first light before the boat traffic picks up — that flat drops off fast on the east side and bass will sit right on that break waiting for bait to get pushed off the flat on the outgoing.

Fluke are the tougher story right now, and there's no sense pretending otherwise. The warm surface layer has spread them out across the flats instead of concentrating them, so the easy days of drifting anywhere in Greenwich Bay and connecting are over for the moment. The better fish are coming off channel edges and deeper water where there's still a cooler bottom layer holding — the mouth of Greenwich Bay where it drops into the main channel, and the deeper water off the west side of Prudence Island, have both been producing keeper-class fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom through the last two hours of the outgoing. Anybody fishing the shallow flats in the middle of the day is mostly finding shorts.

Bluefish are doing what bluefish do — filling in the gaps. Snapper blues are thick in the coves around Greenwich Bay and up in the quieter corners off Rocky Point, plenty of fun for kids off the dock on small Kastmasters or a strip of squid under a bobber. The bigger cocktail blues, a pound and a half to three pounds, are mixing right in with the striper catches on structure, so if you're bucktailing for bass off Nyatt Point don't be surprised when a blue cuts your leader instead.

Scup fishing has been steady on the rocky ledges, which is about as reliable as this bay gets in August. Rocky Point and the rock piles off Nyatt are stacked with them, especially on the slower parts of the tide when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold bottom. Sandworms and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, 12 to 20 feet of water, will fill a bucket without much drama. Black sea bass are showing as a bonus catch on the same deeper structure around Prudence Island, nothing to build a trip around but a welcome addition when they show up on the same bait.

The one thing generating real chatter down at the docks is bonito. Nothing confirmed inside the bay yet, but there's scouting talk filtering up from the lower bay and the breachways toward Newport — guys seeing bait get nervous and boils that don't look like bluefish. Worth keeping an eye on the East Passage mouth and the water off the south end of Prudence over the next week if that pattern firms up.

Looking ahead, the full moon tomorrow night should be the pivot point. Expect the tidal swings to keep building through the weekend, which will sharpen the structure bite on bass at Nyatt Point and Rocky Point and should push more bait through the channel edges where the fluke have been holding. If you can only fish one tide this week, make it the two hours around the top of the flood at Rocky Point after dark — that's where the current and the structure are lining up best right now.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at Dawn: Snappers and Cocktail Blues Carry the Session, Bass a No-Show
reports.subhead: Porgies fill the gap on the reefs while bass sit out the heat, and the first rainfish push has the northern inlets on albie watch.
reports.body_markdown:
First light on the Sea Bright rocks this week looked about how it's looked for two weeks straight — a handful of regulars working the north jetty with swimmers and darters, getting nothing but the occasional swirl and a lot of quiet water. Down at Manasquan Inlet the jetty crews were doing the same dance, tossing pencil poppers into the current seam off the north wall on the last of the ebb and coming up with blues instead of bass. That's the story right now up and down this stretch — bass fishing is sitting in the same summer holding pattern it's been stuck in since the middle of the month, and nobody working the rocks is going to tell you different.

We flagged this last week — said stripers would stay sparse until a real cool-down kicks the fall push into gear, and that's exactly what the rocks are showing. Water's still warm enough that the bass that are around are doing their business after dark or tucked into deeper holes, not chasing bait in the wash at sunrise. Until nighttime temps start sliding — and there's no sign of that happening in the next 72 hours with high pressure holding and southwest wind sitting in that 8-to-12-knot range — this pattern isn't breaking. The fish will show. Just not yet.

What's filling the gap, and filling it well, are porgies. The nearshore reefs off Shark River and Belmar have been stacking up with them, and boats working bottom rigs with clam and squid strips in 30 to 45 feet are having no trouble putting a mess in the cooler. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and with bass this quiet it's the best bet going right now if you want bent rods without waiting until midnight. Bring light tackle — these aren't the jumbo porgies of October yet, but there are enough keeper-sized fish mixed in to make the trip worthwhile.

Bluefish remain the backbone of this whole zone and that hasn't changed. Snapper blues are thick in Shark River and the Manasquan back bay, small enough that a kid with a bare gold hook and a piece of bunker will load up in twenty minutes off the Belmar bridge or the docks along the Shark River channel. The bigger cocktail blues, two to four pounds, are mixing into the surf catch on metal — Ava 27s and 17s worked with a jigging retrieve off the Sea Bright rocks and the Asbury Park jetties on the incoming tide have been the go-to. Trollers working bunker spoons off Long Branch and Sea Bright are also connecting with better cocktail-class fish, particularly in that 20-to-40-foot band just outside the surf line.

Fluke are the soft spot this week, and there's no sugarcoating it. The warm surface layer has spread these fish out across the flats instead of concentrating them, and catch rates everywhere except the deeper structure have gone flat. The exception is the channel edges — Manasquan Inlet's deeper cuts near the Coast Guard station, and the Shark River Inlet channel itself, are still holding fish tight to the bottom where a cooler layer persists. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges on the last two hours of the outgoing, are still producing keepers in the 18-to-22-inch range, but you're working for every fish. Don't expect the easy fluke bite of June — this is a grind pattern now, best worked with the tide doing the work for you rather than burning gas running spot to spot.

Bunker are still thick along this beachfront, rolling in tight pods off Belmar and Spring Lake, and every guy on the rocks with eyes has noticed it.
