The ingredients for a real blitz are sitting right there — bait pinned against the beach on a falling tide, blues already working it hard from underneath. What's missing is the bass showing up to finish the job, and until that water cools a notch, the blitzes we're seeing are blue-only affairs. Worth watching daily, because when the bass do slide in on top of that bait, it won't take much warning.

The other thing worth keeping an eye on: rainfish are starting to show tighter along the beachfront as the canyon action to the south pushes bait north, and that's exactly the setup that precedes the first false albacore and bonito showings at the northern inlets. Manasquan's inlet tip and the Shark River jetties are historically the first spots in this zone to get a look at albies once that bait shows in earnest — nothing confirmed yet, but the ingredients are lining up earlier than usual this year.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full over the next few days, which means bigger tidal swings and sharper current at the inlets — good news for anyone working the fluke edges or hoping to be in position when the first albie run finally announces itself. If you've only got one morning to give it this week, split time between the porgy reefs at first light and a couple hours working metal on the Sea Bright or Manasquan rocks behind it. The bass will be back. Right now, the rocks are just asking for patience.

reports.headline: Double Creek Channel Fluke Holding the Drop-Offs While Snapper Blues Take Over the Docks
reports.subhead: Warm, stratified bay water is spreading the fluke thin, but the edges are still paying off — and the snapper run is telling us exactly what comes next.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a certain kind of late-August week on Barnegat Bay that old-timers like me have seen more times than we can count — the surface goes glassy and warm, the bay stratifies top to bottom, and every species with a lick of sense starts hunting for the cooler layer down deep or the moving water at the edges. I've watched this pattern play out from Toms River clear down to the Light for forty years now, and this week fit the mold about as well as any I can remember. The bay's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s on top, the flats have gone thin and quiet in the heat of the day, and the fish that are still biting have pushed themselves onto structure — channel edges, drop-offs, the inlet itself — anywhere there's current keeping the water turning over and the oxygen up.

We flagged this exact pattern last week — said fluke fishing would stay modest until the nights cool enough to knock down the thermal layering, and that's precisely what's held. The flats themselves have been soft and scattered, fish spread out over acres of warm bottom instead of stacked where you can find them twice. But the channel edges are a different story. Double Creek Channel has been the most consistent producer in the system, particularly working the drop-offs on the last two hours of the incoming tide, when bait gets pushed up off the deeper water and onto the lip of the flat. Keeper fluke to five pounds have come off there on 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged dead slow along bottom so the jig ticks the mud without lifting off it. The bite window is short — an hour, hour and a half around that tide change — but it's been the difference between a slow day and a decent one.

Tices Shoal and the grass edges south of there are worth a look on the same tide stage if Double Creek gets crowded, though the fish there have been running smaller, more shorts mixed with the occasional keeper. The deeper water off Barnegat Light, where the inlet current keeps things stirred and cooler, has also been quietly productive for anyone willing to work bucktail-and-gulp combos or strips of squid on a fluke rig down in that 20-to-25-foot zone on the ebb.

Weakfish are around in modest numbers, which is about what you'd expect for this time of year, showing up on the same sedge-bank drifts that are holding croaker right now — that stretch of marsh edge from the mouth of Oyster Creek down toward Double Creek has given up a few keeper weakfish on Fishbites and small pieces of bloodworm fished on light tackle, bottom rig, incoming water. Nothing to build a trip around by itself, but a nice bonus if you're already anchored up working bottom for croaker or kingfish. Speaking of kingfish, the sandy stretches along Island Beach and the inlet flats have had a fair showing on bloodworm and Fishbites combos fished on a simple two-hook bottom rig — good action for anyone who wants a bucket of fish for the pan without much fuss.

The bigger story right now, and the one worth paying attention to for what's coming, is the snapper blues. They're thick in the back-bay creeks — thick enough that the docks and bulkheads from Forked River up through Toms River are loaded with kids and grandparents alike snapping them up on tiny gold spoons and bits of bunker under a bobber. We called this one too — said the heavy snapper showing was the leading indicator that the bigger bluefish would follow the bait out of the bay as the nights start cooling, and that's exactly the mechanism at work. Right now the adult cocktail blues are mixing into the fluke and weakfish catches out on the channel edges and around the inlet structure, nothing huge, two to four pounds mostly, but there are more of them showing every week, and that usually means the real fall run of blues isn't far behind once that water temperature starts sliding.

Striped bass are exactly where you'd expect them in this heat — in a holding pattern, not a migration. Daytime action has been next to nothing on the bay side; the better play has been working the inlet structure and the deeper holes off Barnegat Light after dark, when the current is still hard-running on the tide change but the sun's off the water. This is a summer pattern, not the start of the fall push — that real migration doesn't typically get going here until the nights turn consistently cool, likely not before mid-September.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full over the next several days, which should sharpen up the tidal swings and put a little more current through the inlet and the channels — good news for the fluke bite at Double Creek and around the Light, since stronger current means better oxygen turnover and a tighter bait push onto the drop-offs. Wind's expected to stay out of the southwest in the 8-to-12 knot range through the weekend, which keeps the bay calm enough to fish comfortably but won't do much to cool things down. If you've only got one day, the smart play is still the last two hours of the incoming at Double Creek Channel for fluke, with a stop at the sedges on the way in for a shot at weakfish and croaker. Keep an eye on the overnight lows next week — once they start dipping, this whole bay changes character fast, and that's when the real fall action starts to build.

reports.headline: New Moon Reworked the Holgate Cuts — Bottom Bite Owns the Inlet Right Now
reports.subhead: Croaker, spot, and spike weakfish are cleaning up on bait rigs while fluke scatter across warm flats and the mullet build offshore.
reports.body_markdown:
The new moon tides this week did some real work on the bars. Anybody who walked the beach at Holgate or checked the drone footage off the north end knows the cut that's been forming behind the second bar since the last blow has deepened another foot or so with the stronger swings. That's not an accident — bigger tidal range means more water moving through those gaps twice a day, and moving water carves structure. The same thing happened at the Little Egg Inlet edge, where the sandbar off the northern tip has pushed further west, tightening up the channel that dumps bay water past Graveling Point. We flagged this last week — said the inlet bite would sharpen as tide flow strengthened off the new moon — and that's exactly what's playing out along Little Egg and the Beach Haven side of the inlet complex right now.

The bigger story for LBI this week isn't stripers, though. It's the bottom bite. Croaker, spot, and a scattering of spike weakfish are dominating simple high-low rigs baited with bloodworms and minnows, and they're outfishing the gulp-and-bucktail fluke crowd by a wide margin. That tells you something about where the water's at. Back bay and inshore ocean temps are sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s, which is fine for those bottom species but tough on fluke, who don't like to sit tight in warm, thin-oxygen water. Instead of stacking up on structure the way they do in cooler months, the fluke have spread out thin across the flats in Great Bay and behind Beach Haven, which is softening catch rates almost everywhere except the channel edges and the deeper cuts where a cooler bottom layer still holds. If you're set on fluke this week, work the edges of the Intracoastal channel off Ship Bottom in 12 to 18 feet, or drift the deeper water inside Barnegat Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing — that's where the better grade fish are stacking against current, not out on the open flats.

The inlet itself is the smart play right now, and not just because of the new tidal range. On the outgoing, cooler bay water pushes out and mixes hard with ocean water at the mouth, and that mixing zone is where the activity concentrates. Fish croaker and spot on high-low rigs with squid or bloodworm strips in the deeper holes just inside Barnegat Light, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when that cold-warm seam is most defined. Weakfish are mixed into that same bite — mostly spikes in the 12 to 15 inch range, but worth soaking a bloodworm on light tackle if you want a change of pace from the croaker parade.

Striped bass are stuck in the pattern you'd expect for this time of year. Warm surface water is pushing daytime activity onto structure and shutting down the aggressive daylight bite almost everywhere from here up through the Sound. This is a summer holding pattern, not the start of the fall run — the real push south doesn't typically show until nighttime temps start dropping hard, which is usually a mid-September story on this stretch of coast. That means your best shot at a keeper bass right now is a night program: work the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light or the deeper holes along the Holgate stretch after dark with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, or swim a darter plug through the current seams off the inlet on the last of the ebb. Daytime bass are mostly holding tight to structure and not feeding heavy, so don't expect a repeat bite in the same spot at noon that you got at 5 a.m.

Bluefish are the one constant that hasn't slowed down. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks around the Mullica and Graveling Point, and they'll hit anything shiny on light spinning gear — small metal, Kastmasters, or a bare bucktail teaser. Cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound range are mixing into the fluke and striper catches out front, especially around any bait pod that shows up on structure. If you're marking bait on the meter near the Ship Bottom channel edges, there's a good chance blues are under it even if the fluke aren't biting.

The thing to watch over the next week to ten days is the mullet. Bait schools are building along the beachfront from Beach Haven down toward Holgate, and that's the pattern that typically ignites LBI's first real surf blitzes of early fall. It hasn't fully kicked yet, but the pieces are in place — tightening bait, cooling nights on the horizon, and bass starting to think about staging. Keep an eye on the surf for the season's first false albacore too; late August into early September is the historical window once the bait tightens up along the beach, and albies love working those tighter mullet schools right in the wash.

For the next few days, expect the bottom bite to hold steady in the inlets on the outgoing tide, fluke to stay soft and spread out except on the channel edges, and the night striper program to be the more reliable bass play. Watch the surf daily for mullet activity — once those schools compress, the blitz window opens fast and it doesn't always wait for you to notice.

reports.headline: Where did the fluke go? Warm water spreads the class out from Absecon to Great Egg
reports.subhead: Kingfish and spot are filling the surf bags while the doormats scatter — and the first bonito showed at the inlets right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
A reader asked me at the bait shop counter this week why his fluke numbers were down even though the water looked clean and the tide was moving right. Good question, and it's the same one I've been fielding since the middle of August. The answer is warm water, plain and simple. Surf temps have been sitting in the mid-70s from Atlantic City down through Ocean City, and that kind of warmth doesn't concentrate fluke — it spreads them out. Instead of holding tight to structure where you can pattern them, the fish are scattered across broad, thinly-oxygenated flats in the back bays. That's softened catch rates almost everywhere except the places where a cooler bottom layer still hangs on: channel edges, inlet mouths, and the deeper humps in 40 to 60 feet off the beach.

So class, here's the lesson for the week: fish the seams, not the flats. In Absecon Inlet, that means working the deeper channel edge off the Route 30 bridge and down toward the Coast Guard station, 25 to 35 feet, on the last two hours of the outgoing tide when the current is still pulling bait off the sod banks but hasn't gone fully slack. A four-inch white Gulp swimming mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along bottom, has been the most consistent producer. Great Egg Inlet is running the same pattern — the deeper hole just inside the rock jetty on the Ocean City side has been holding better-grade fish than the flats to the north, especially on the second half of the ebb.

While the doormats have gone quiet, the surf has turned into a different kind of classroom entirely. Kingfish, croaker, and spot have moved in thick on the beachfronts from Absecon Island down through Ocean City, a direct result of that same warm-water push riding up from the south. High-low bottom rigs with small pieces of bloodworm or synthetic bloodworm strips, cast just beyond the second bar, have been filling coolers for anglers willing to sit on a spike and work the tide. Stone Harbor and Townsends Inlet have shown the same signs — smaller hooks, size 4 or 6, seem to be outproducing the bigger stuff for kingfish, and croaker have been mixed in on the same rigs during the last of the incoming.

Bluefish remain the one species you can set your watch by. Snapper blues are thick in the back bays behind Ocean City and Sea Isle City, hammering small silver spoons and Gotcha plugs off the docks on any tide. Cocktail-sized blues, a pound and a half to three pounds, are working the tide changes at Absecon and Townsends Inlets as rainfish and peanut bunker begin staging up along the beachfront — an early tell that the seasonal transition is starting even while the surface water stays summer-warm. And here's something worth noting: the first small bonito have started showing at the inlets on those same tide changes, chasing the same bait. We flagged the mullet run coming in this column two weeks back, said it would flip attention toward bluefish and early surf interest, and that's exactly what's beginning to unfold along these beaches now.

Striped bass are in their predictable late-August holding pattern — daytime activity pushed to structure and deeper water, with the better action coming after dark around the inlet jetties and bridge lights at Brigantine and Longport. That said, the moon builds to full on August 28, and I've taught this lesson before: bigger tides mean stronger current, and stronger current concentrates bait against structure. Expect the swing at Absecon and Great Egg Inlets to sharpen over the next several nights as the tidal range grows. If you're fishing after dark, work bunker chunks or a bucktail dressed with Gulp on the leading edge of the current seam, right where the light meets the shadow line under the bridges. That's where the bass have been staging.

Weakfish have been quiet, as expected for this time of year, though a few keepers have come from the deeper holes in Great Egg Inlet on the early morning outgoing, fished with bucktails tipped with a strip of squid. Triggerfish continue to show around the reef sites and wreck structure off Ocean City and Absecon in that 40- to 60-foot range where fluke anglers are also finding their better fish — small pieces of clam or squid on a simple bottom rig will take them if you're marking structure and holding position.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold mostly steady — southwest winds in the 8- to 12-knot range, warm surface water, stable high pressure. That means the fluke pattern stays the same: work the channel edges and deeper structure, skip the open flats. The building moon should sharpen the inlet current over the coming nights, which is where I'd put my time if bass are the target. And keep an eye on the beachfront — with rainfish and peanut bunker staging at the inlets, the mullet run window is closing in, and that's when this whole zone flips its attention toward blues and the first real surf-bass interest of the fall.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips Grade: C-Minus in the Heat, Delaware Bay Gets an A for Croaker
reports.subhead: Warm water has the rips sluggish and spread out, but Fortescue and the bay flats are stacked with croaker, spot, and a surprise run of mackerel.
reports.body_markdown:
If I'm grading the rips this week, it's a C-minus. Fishable, not exciting, and you need to pick your window instead of just showing up and expecting the tide to do the work for you. Water temps on the ocean side have been sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s at the surface — and that's pushed the bass off the top of the structure and down into whatever cooler water they can find, which this time of year means night bites and the deeper edges around Cape May Point and the outer rip lines. Daytime, the fish are there but they're not stacked and they're not aggressive. This is a classic late-August holding pattern, not the start of the fall run — that push doesn't really get going until the nights start cooling off in earnest, which is usually a mid-September story for us, not a Labor Day one.

Delaware Bay is where the real grade this week is an A. The warm bay water has pulled in the annual southern pulse — croaker, spot, and now a legitimate run of small king mackerel and Spanish mackerel showing up along the beaches from Fortescue down toward the mouth. We flagged this exact pattern building last week and said it would hold as long as bay temps stayed up, and that's exactly what's happened — no cold front has come through to shut it off, so the bite's carried straight through. High-low rigs with bloodworm or fresh clam on size 4 or 2 hooks are the ticket for the croaker and spot, fished right on the bottom off Fortescue and the mouth of the Maurice River. Weakfish are mixing in with those croaker catches, which is a nice bonus — we haven't seen numbers like that on weakies out of the bay in a couple seasons, and most are keeper-class fish in the 16 to 19-inch range, though nobody's limiting out.

The Spanish mackerel showing up is the interesting wrinkle. Small block tin or Clark spoons, trolled behind the jetties on a clean incoming tide, have been connecting for anglers working the surf line and inlet mouths from Cape May up toward Wildwood. These fish follow bait, and as long as that warm plume holds in the bay and along the beachfront, expect them to keep pushing north toward Absecon. The window closes fast the day a real cold front pushes through and knocks the surface water down — so if you want a shot at mackerel on light spinning tackle, don't wait around.

Fluke have taken the hit everywhere this warm spell has touched, and Cape May and Hereford Inlet are no exception. Inside the bay, fluke have spread thin across warm, soft-bottom flats instead of holding tight to structure, which means fewer keepers per drift and a lot more short fish in the mix. The better bet right now is ocean-side — the reef sites and rip structure off Cape May Point where a cooler bottom layer still persists even with warm water up top. Drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has been the more consistent producer than bare bucktail alone, working the deeper edges of the rip on the last of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood, when current is strongest and bait gets funneled through the troughs.

Bluefish are the one thing you can count on right now, same as everywhere else on this stretch of coast. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks and around the Hereford Inlet docks, and cocktail-sized blues are mixing into both the fluke drifts and the mackerel spoons along the beach. If the rest of the day's slow, a bucktail or metal lip swimmer worked through a blitz of blues will save the trip.

On the black drum — the run that made our name up here wrapped up back in May like it always does, and there's nothing happening on that front worth chasing right now. Anybody asking about drum this week, tell them to circle late April on next year's calendar and be patient.

Looking ahead: the moon builds toward full on Friday, and that's going to strengthen the tidal push through the rips and around Brandywine Shoal — we called this coming last week, and it's the one piece of good news for rip fishermen this stretch. Stronger current means better bait concentration, which should tighten up the bass bite some around the moon, particularly on the night tides at Cape May Point. Weather looks stable through the weekend — southwest wind in the 8 to 12 knot range, no fronts on the immediate horizon — so expect the warm-water pattern in the bay to hold and the croaker/mackerel bite at Fortescue to keep rolling. If a front does slide through behind the full moon, that's when this whole picture flips fast, and the smart move is fishing the bay hard now while it's producing rather than waiting for the ocean side to sort itself out.

reports.headline: Stonington breakwater at first light: bass hunker in the shadows, bonito knocking from the east
reports.subhead: Warm water has the boulder fields playing a waiting game, but the tide swings building toward full moon are about to change the math.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait tells you everything before you ever see a fish. Right now around the boulder fields of Fishers Island Sound, the peanut bunker and silversides are still loose and scattered — not tight, not nervous, not pushed into the corners the way they get when albies or bonito show up and start working them. That's the read for this week: close, but not here yet. New London is holding at 69.4 degrees, which is cool enough on the eastern end of the Sound to keep things interesting but not cool enough yet to trigger the real turn. Kings Point to the west is running 70.9, and that gradient matters — it's the kind of west-to-east temperature drop that eventually funnels bait and predators toward the Race, and Fishers Island Sound sits right in that pipeline.

Striped bass are in their predictable late-August posture — daytime fish tucked deep against rock, feeding hard only in short windows around the tide change, and the better grade of fish sliding into a night program. This isn't the fall push. It's the holding pattern before it. We said as much a few days back — this stretch of summer has bass sitting tight rather than migrating, and that's exactly what the boulder fields are showing. Anyone fishing the granite structure off Ram Island or the rockpiles tight to Wamphassuc Point during daylight is finding fish, but they're finding them shallow-holding in the shade lines and current breaks, not roaming and feeding on top. Eels drifted slow along the drop-offs on the last two hours of the ebb have been the most consistent producer after dark, fished on light spinning gear so the eel can work naturally through the rocks instead of getting horsed over them. During the day, a bucktail in the 3/4- to 1-ounce range, white or olive, cast tight to the rock edges on the Stonington Breakwater and allowed to tick bottom on the retrieve has been picking off fish in the mid-20s to low-30s, mostly on the last of the outgoing when current pulls bait off the stone.

The breakwater itself has been the most dependable piece of structure in the zone all week — both the east and west walls are holding fish on the slack and the beginning of the new tide, when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold a jig down in the rock seams. Once the tide really starts moving, especially with the moon building toward full and the swings getting more aggressive over the next few days, that bite tightens into shorter windows but gets more concentrated. That's worth planning around — if you've only got one tide this weekend, fish the hour before and after the change rather than the peak of the flow.

Fluke are the disappointment of the month, and it's not just a Stonington problem — this warm-water stretch has spread fluke out across flats and open bottom from here down through Long Island rather than letting them stack. Little Narragansett Bay and the deeper cuts near the Mystic River channel are still worth a drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, but the fish are thin and scattered compared to a normal late August. The better fluke have been coming from the deeper humps inside Fishers Island Sound proper, where a cooler bottom layer persists even with the surface running warm — that's the pattern to lean on until temperatures break.

Blackfish are around the same rock piles they always are, but with water this warm they're not the target right now — they'll matter again once the fall bite firms up and the cooler water pulls them back onto the structure in earnest. Sea bass are a steady secondary catch on the deeper rock and reef structure scattered through the Sound, and that's held true all week — nothing spectacular, but a reliable fill-in while you wait on bigger things.

And the bigger thing everyone in Stonington is actually watching for is bonito and false albacore. Nothing's confirmed inside the Sound yet, but the early word out of Block Island and Point Judith has bonito showing, and that's precisely the signal we flagged — this stretch of warm water peaking and starting its seasonal slide was supposed to push that bite west into eastern Long Island Sound within a week or two, and the reports out of Rhode Island's south shore right now are the leading edge of exactly that. Fishers Island Sound sits close enough to the Race and its current to be next in line. Watch the bait around Esker Point and the open water off Watch Hill — when the silversides start balling up tight and nervous instead of scattered, that's the tell. Have a 2- to 3-inch epoxy jig or a Deceiver-style fly ready, because once albies show in this stretch they don't give you much warning and they don't stick around long once the tide turns against them.

Look for the next few days to hold mostly steady — light southwest wind, stable pressure, warm surface water — with the tide swings sharpening as the moon fills out. That's good news for the breakwater and rock-edge bass bite on the turns, and it's the kind of current strength that tends to pull bonito and albies in behind the bait once they're ready to move. If there's one window worth protecting this week, it's the last two hours of the evening ebb around the breakwater and Ram Island — that's where the structure, the tide, and the bait are lining up closest to right.

reports.headline: The Race Holds at 69.4°F: Bass Working the Ledges While Bonito Build to the East
reports.subhead: A five-degree spread between Kings Point and New London is steering the bite, and the current break at Valiant Rock is still the sharpest tool in the box.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-nine point four degrees at New London this week, five and a half degrees cooler than the 70.9 reading out at Kings Point. That gradient is the whole story for the eastern Sound right now. The western basin is running warm and soft, the kind of water that pushes stripers off the flats and into structure by mid-morning. Out here at The Race, Plum Gut, and the Sluiceway, the faster water and deeper thermal layer are keeping fish more honest through the day, even if the bite itself has settled into what late August usually gives us — a real but grinding pattern, not a blitz.

This is the summer holding pattern, plain and simple. We said it a few days back and it's holding true: the true fall push doesn't start until nighttime temps start dropping hard, likely mid-September. Until then, the bass in this zone are working the classic late-summer program — deep structure by day, current edges at first and last light, and a stronger night bite than most weekend anglers ever fish. Race Rock and the ledge running west off Valiant Rock remain the most consistent stretch. That bottom rises out of over a hundred feet of moving water to inside thirty on the shoal itself, and on a hard ebb the seam it throws is still the best current break in the region. Wire line trolled with bunker spoons and umbrella rigs is producing fish in the twenty-to-thirty-four inch range along that edge, with a scattering of better fish pushing forty holding tighter to the rock on the last two hours of the ebb, right before slack.

Bucktail guys working the drift with six and eight-ounce heads dressed in white or chartreuse tube are doing better tucking bottom bounces into the deeper pocket on the east side of Valiant, letting the jig ride the current down into the eddy rather than fighting straight against it. That eddy is where the bait's been stacking — mostly peanut bunker and juvenile menhaden pushed in tight by the faster water outside. Slack itself is short here, fifteen to twenty minutes at best on a strong moon tide, so anyone working wire or heavy jigs needs to be ready the moment the rip starts to soften, not after it's already running the other way.

Bluefish remain the one constant nobody's complaining about. Cocktail blues in the three-to-six-pound range are mixing right into the bass catch on the same wire spreads and bucktails, and snapper-sized fish are thick enough in the back coves off Fishers Island and around Plum Gut's inner edges to keep any kid with a bobber and spearing busy for an afternoon. If the striper bite goes quiet on a given tide, there's almost always blues willing to fill the gap.

Fluke are the softer story this week, and it's worth being straight about it — the warm surface layer has spread fish out across the flats rather than concentrating them, and catch rates on the open bottom have thinned out accordingly. The better numbers are still coming from the deeper cuts, particularly the channel edges inside Plum Gut and the deeper holes along the Sluiceway between Little Gull and Great Gull Island, where a cooler bottom layer persists even with the surface running warm. Four-inch white Gulp on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been the more dependable combination there. Sea bass are holding as a steady secondary catch on the same structure — small jigs tipped with squid strips working the rockier stretches around Race Rock in twenty-five to forty feet.

Now for the one everybody's been asking about at the dock. Bonito are not here yet, but the signal is building fast. Block Island and Point Judith have the first confirmed fish of the season, and that bait behavior — squid and small baitfish tightening up along beaches and rip lines — is exactly the pattern that tends to walk west. We flagged this trend last week, saying it would push toward eastern Long Island Sound and the Race corridor within one to two weeks as water temperatures peak and start easing off, and that timeline still lines up. Anyone rigging ahead of the run should have half-ounce epoxy jigs in bone and green mackerel pattern ready for the Gut, along with small metal for when the fish are up on top working bait balls in the rip.

Looking at the next few days, expect the pattern to hold rather than shift hard. The moon is building toward full, which means stronger tidal swings and sharper, shorter slack windows through the Race and the Gut — good news for anyone who can time the last hour of the ebb precisely, tougher for anyone fishing loose on the clock. If the overnight air keeps trending cooler into the weekend, look for the first hints of the eastern Sound's surface temperature easing down a notch, which should extend the daytime striper window slightly and could be the trigger that finally pulls the first bonito west into Fishers Island Sound. Until then, the safe bet remains wire line and bucktails on the Race Rock-to-Valiant stretch on the last two hours of the ebb, with a backup drift into the Gut's deeper cuts for fluke and sea bass when the current lays down.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Split: Sea Bass Carrying Black Point While Fluke Scatter in the Warm Water
reports.subhead: The moon builds to full Friday and the fleet is betting the current comes back strong enough to save a soft fluke bite and wake the bass up at night.
reports.body_markdown:
Talk at the counter this week has been mostly about what's not happening rather than what is. A couple of the Waterford captains have been saying the same thing separately, which tells you something — the fluke have quit stacking up the way they were in July. Water's still warm, New London reading in the high 60s and pushing 70 in spots, and that's just enough heat to spread the fluke out across the flats instead of holding them tight to structure where the boats can work them. The better fish are still there, they're just harder to find, and the fleet has adjusted by leaning hard into Black Point and the deeper edges off Twotree Island Channel where a cooler bottom layer holds up even when the surface is soup-warm.

The good news is sea bass have picked up a lot of the slack. Boats working the rock piles off Black Point and out toward Hole-in-the-Wall have been putting together respectable sea bass counts on Gulp squid strips and clam-tipped bucktails, fished tight to structure in 30 to 45 feet. That's been the more dependable half of the mixed bag this week — steady enough that a few skippers have started calling it before they even leave the dock, telling anglers to bring the heavier jigging setups because the sea bass are the play in the middle of the day while the fluke bite windows shrink down to first light and the last two hours of the outgoing.

Striped bass are exactly where you'd expect them for the tail end of August — not gone, just quiet during the day. This is the predictable late-summer holding pattern, not the fall push, and the smart money in the fleet has moved to structure and low-light programs rather than daytime blind-casting. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the current would tighten up and concentrate bait as the moon swung toward full on the 28th — and that's exactly the setup coming into play right now. The moon builds to full Friday, and that means bigger tidal swings starting to stack through Niantic Bay and around McCook Point. That extra push of water should sharpen up the current seams the bass like to sit on, particularly on the last of the ebb out of the Niantic River where warm water dumps out into cooler bay water and stacks bait against the edge. Anglers working live eels or bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs after dark around the river mouth and the bay-side rock structure have had the better shots at keeper bass, with a few overslot fish mixed in on the darker nights.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's arguing about. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay off the Niantic River, and cocktail blues in the two-to-four-pound class are mixing into both the fluke drifts and the striper spots, especially anywhere there's bait getting pushed around by current. If the fluke bite goes cold on a drift, it's not unusual for the rod to bend anyway courtesy of a blue jumping on a Gulp mullet meant for something else. Not glamorous, but it's kept a lot of otherwise slow mornings from being total blanks.

Porgies remain the honest bottom fishery this zone leans on, and that hasn't changed. Boats anchoring up on the rubble and mussel beds around Black Point and off McCook Point are still filling coolers on standard porgy rigs with squid and clam, fishing the bottom third of the water column on the slower stages of the tide. Worth watching over the next couple weeks — as the season starts to turn, this is usually when scup fishing gets even better before the first cold nights push everybody's attention toward blackfish season.

One more thing worth keeping an eye on for the guys who run farther east: the water off the Race and toward Fishers Island has historically been one of the earlier tells for bonito and false albacore showing up in Connecticut waters, and the current there is strong enough to hold bait tight even through a warm stretch like this. Nothing confirmed yet in this zone, but with squid already building around Rhode Island and the Cape, it's not a bad idea to keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small metal in the rocket launcher just in case something silver shows up chasing bait through the rip.

Looking at the next few days, expect the pattern to hold close to what it's been — southwest breeze in the 8 to 12 knot range, warm surface water, and fluke that reward patience over volume. The building moon into Friday should be the difference-maker for striper anglers willing to fish the dark hours around the river mouth and bay structure, and it should also sharpen the fluke bite windows around the tide changes even if it doesn't fix the spread-out pattern completely. If there's only one window to fish this weekend, the last two hours of the outgoing around McCook Point or Twotree Island Channel, right as the moon tips full, is the one worth building the day around. Keep the sea bass gear rigged as the backup plan — right now, it's the fishery not letting anybody down.

reports.headline: Falkner Rockpile Loaded with Porgies, Blackfish Sneaking Into the Mix
reports.subhead: The bottom bite is carrying Central Sound through the August lull while stripers wait for dark and a cooler tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Regulars working the outer New Haven breakwall Tuesday morning had green crab hi-lo rigs bouncing bottom in eighteen feet on the last of the flood and couldn't keep porgies off the hook long enough to check for sea bass — until a 15-inch black hit the same rig and settled the question. That's been the story on the rockpiles all week: a steady, unglamorous, very catchable bite that's carrying this stretch of Sound through a stretch of warm water that's put everything else on a slower clock.

The thermal picture explains a lot of what's going on right now. Kings Point is reading 70.9 degrees, New London down east is 69.4, and that west-to-east gradient means Central Sound is sitting in the warmest water on the beat. Warm surface water like that pushes daytime feeding down onto structure and shuts the door on much of the open-water action, which is exactly why the rockpiles at Falkner Island, the New Haven breakwalls, and Stratford Shoal have been the most consistent producers of the week while everything pelagic stays quiet until the sun goes down.

Striped bass are in their predictable late-August pattern — daytime fish holding tight to structure and river mouths, real activity waiting for dark. We flagged this a week ago: that the moon building toward full on August 28 would strengthen the current sweeping bait around the harder structure, and that's precisely what's setting up now. The tide swings at Charles Island and the bar off Milford Gulf have been building noticeably day over day, and the night crowd working bucktails and swim shads over the Charles Island sandbar on the last two hours of the ebb has been finding better numbers of schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass than they were two weeks back. This isn't the fall run yet — that push doesn't really get going until nighttime water temps start dropping hard, likely mid-September — but the current is doing its job concentrating bait, and that's worth chasing after sundown.

On the rockpiles, porgies remain the easy money. Falkner Island's boulder fields in 25 to 35 feet are holding good numbers on green crab and squid strips fished on a two-hook bottom rig with just enough weight to hold in the current — an ounce and a half on the last of the ebb, up to three ounces once the tide really gets moving with this building moon. The New Haven breakwalls, both the outer and the shorter inner wall, are producing similar action in 15 to 20 feet, and they're an easier pull for anyone without a long ride in them. Sea bass are mixing in as a bonus rather than a target right now — legal fish to 17 inches coming up on the same rigs, with the better ones tending to show on the deeper edges of the rockpiles rather than the shallow tops.

Blackfish are just starting to trickle into the conversation, which is the first real sign the season is beginning to turn even if the water hasn't caught up yet. Early fish are coming off the rockier stretches around Stratford Shoal and the deeper structure off Falkner on green crab, mostly incidental catches while working porgy rigs, but it's enough that a few boats are starting to rig heavier tackle and fish crab exclusively on the last hour of the tide. Give it two to three weeks of cooling water before that becomes a real target fishery, but it's worth keeping a rod rigged for it now.

Bluefish are doing what bluefish do — showing up everywhere and complicating everyone's leaders. Snapper blues are thick in New Haven Harbor and around the Milford docks, small enough to be more nuisance than target but a good sign for what's coming. Cocktail-sized blues in the 2- to 4-pound class are mixing into the porgy and sea bass catches on the rockpiles and occasionally crashing bait on the surface off Hammonasset in the evening, worth a few casts with a small metal if you see them working.

Fluke are the softest part of the report right now. The warm, thin water has spread fish out across the flats rather than concentrating them, and catch rates off Hammonasset and the shallower stretches near Charles Island have been inconsistent at best. The better fish have been coming from channel edges and deeper structure — the drop-offs around Stratford Shoal and the deeper cuts near the Gulf — where a cooler bottom layer is holding fish tighter. White Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow through those deeper edges on the outgoing tide, has been the more reliable approach than working the shallow flats.

Looking ahead, the moon goes full Wednesday and that should sharpen every tide-dependent bite window on the beat. Expect the current at Charles Island and the New Haven breakwalls to swing harder over the next few days, which should improve both the night striper bite and the rockpile bottom fishing as bait gets pushed and pinned against structure more aggressively. If overnight temperatures start easing even slightly by the weekend, look for the first hints of improved daytime striper activity — not a full turn, but an early crack in the summer pattern. Until then, the smart play is simple: porgies and sea bass on the rockpiles during the day, bass after dark on the structure, and a rod rigged for blackfish just in case the early ones keep showing up.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull current sharpens ahead of Thursday's full moon — bass working the seams after dark
reports.subhead: Tide swings are widening through New London Harbor, and the bite windows at the bridge and the fort are getting tighter and better defined.
reports.body_markdown:
The current off Fort Trumbull has a different feel to it this week. Stand on the seawall at the state park on a strong ebb and you can watch the rip line stretch further out into the channel than it did two weeks ago — the moon's building toward full on Thursday, and that means bigger tidal swings pushing more water through the harbor mouth. Anyone who's spent time on this river knows what that does: it tightens up the seams, concentrates the bait, and turns lazy structure fish into predictable current feeders. We flagged this pattern last week — said the zone would see a bump in activity as the moon built toward full and the current strengthened — and that's exactly what's setting up over the next several tides.

Water on this end of the Sound is running cooler than the western reaches, New London reading in the high 60s, which keeps this fishery in its typical late-August holding pattern rather than anything migratory. That's an important distinction for anyone expecting a fall-run bite already — it isn't here yet. The stripers working the Thames right now are residents and holdovers keying on current and bait concentration, not fish staging for a push south. That push doesn't usually start in earnest until the nighttime air really starts dropping, which for this river means mid-to-late September. Until then, the game is reading the tide and fishing the structure that funnels bait past a fixed point.

The most consistent word off the docks this week has been snapper blues — thick in the upper harbor around the marinas, off City Pier, and up into the mouth of the river past the Gold Star Bridge. These aren't the cocktail blues that show up on the troll offshore; they're the summer snappers that pile into New London Harbor every August, chasing peanut bunker and silversides in tight against pilings and floating docks. Small silver spoons, quarter-ounce Kastmasters, or a sliver of mackerel on a long-shank hook under a bobber will connect all day, but the best window is the last two hours of the incoming when the bait gets pinned against the bulkheads.

Porgies are holding to form on the deeper structure — the rock piles off Pleasure Beach, the drop-off along the Ocean Beach jetty, and the mussel-covered rip-rap under the Gold Star Bridge pilings in 15 to 25 feet. Sandworms or clam strips on a high-low rig, fished on the bottom during the slower stages of the tide, are still the go-to. The bite's been steady rather than spectacular — a mixed bag of keeper-class porgies with a few throwbacks mixed in, best worked slow with light line so you can feel the subtle pickup before they spit the bait.

Striped bass are the story worth watching closest right now, and they're doing what this river's bass do every summer when the current sharpens: sliding into the seams after dark. The Fort Trumbull rip on the back half of the ebb has been holding fish in 18 to 30 feet, stacked up where the fresh water dumping out of the Thames meets the harder salt current sweeping past the point. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or live eels drifted slow through the seam, have been the producers, mostly from an hour before high tide through the first three hours of the ebb. Under the Gold Star Bridge, the pilings themselves are worth working on the same stage of tide — bass tuck in tight to the structure waiting on baitfish getting swept through, and a bucktail bounced along the base of the piling on a slow retrieve, or a swimming plug worked the seam line where lit water meets shadow, has been drawing strikes after dark.

Hickory shad have been scarce this late in the season, which tracks — that's more of a spring pattern up this river, and by late August they've largely thinned out. Not worth planning a trip around right now.

Looking at the next several days, the widening tide swings heading into Thursday's full moon should keep sharpening these bite windows rather than flattening them out. If there's only one evening available this week, the smart play is the Fort Trumbull rip starting an hour before the top of the tide and fishing through the first real push of the ebb — that's when the current does the work and stacks bait against the point. Keep a bunker chunk rig as Plan A and a bucktail as Plan B in case the fish are holding tighter to structure than the open seam. Wind's been cooperative and shouldn't be the deciding factor; it's the tide and the moon doing the heavy lifting here. Once nighttime temperatures start easing off in a few weeks, expect this holding pattern to give way to the real fall movement — but for now, work the current, work it after dark, and don't expect the fishing to hand itself to you in daylight.

reports.headline: The swallows left Mattituck early this year, and the bass took the hint
reports.subhead: Warm water's got the stripers hugging structure by day, but Plum Gut's current is starting to whisper fall.
reports.body_markdown:
There's an old fellow used to clam the flats off Mattituck Inlet every dawn, rain or shine, and he told me once that you don't need a thermometer if you watch the swallows on the wires by the marina. When they start lining up early and heading off before the light's even good, he said, the water's turning before the calendar says it should. This week they left about four days ahead of schedule. Make of that what you will — I've learned not to argue with a man who's read tide charts with his feet in the mud for forty years.

What the swallows knew, the water confirmed. Kings Point is sitting at 70.9, New London's holding 69.4, and out at Montauk it's 69.1 — still plenty warm for late August, and that warmth is exactly why the bass fishing along our stretch has settled into its predictable late-summer pattern. Daytime, the fish want structure and shade — the riprap at Horton Point, the drop by Rocky Point, anywhere there's a current seam cutting cooler water up off bottom. Come dusk and through the night, that's when they spread out and feed with some confidence. If you're only fishing daylight hours right now, you're working against the fish, not with them.

We flagged this a few weeks back — said the Sound-side water staying warmer than the ocean side would keep bait tucked tight to structure, and that the stronger tidal push building toward the full moon would sharpen things up at first light. That's exactly what the fleet's finding. The moon's filling out now, current's got some shoulder to it on the bigger swings, and the bite windows at the inlets and current-swept spots have gotten noticeably tighter and better defined — short, but real, right around the tide change at first light.

Fluke are the soft spot in the report this week, and there's no sense dressing it up. With water this warm clear through the water column, fluke have spread thin across the flats instead of bunching up where you can find them twice in a row. The better fish are coming from the channel edges and deeper holes where there's still a cooler layer down low — the deeper stretch off Mattituck Inlet on the last of the ebb has been giving up keeper-class fish to bucktails tipped with strips of squid, worked slow along bottom rather than snapped. Inshore on the flats, you'll find plenty of shorts and not much patience required to catch them, which tells you what you need to know.

Bluefish haven't missed a beat and probably won't for another month yet. Snapper blues are thick in the coves and creek mouths from Mattituck down toward Orient — kids with a bobber and a sliver of spearing can fill a bucket in an hour most evenings. The bigger cocktail blues are mixing in with the striper bite on structure, chopping up bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off Horton Point, and they'll hit a metal jig worked fast just as happily as they'll hit bait. If you want a fish that doesn't care what the thermometer says, that's your fish this week.

Porgy fishing remains the one thing you can set a watch by. The rockpiles off Rocky Point and the drop-offs approaching Orient Point are holding good numbers of scup in the 12- to 14-inch range, and they're not fussy — clam, sandworm, squid strips on a high-low rig with a couple ounces to hold bottom will get bit steady through most of a tide. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's honest, and on a week when the marquee species are playing hard to get, honest counts for something.

Blackfish season proper is still ahead, but there's already talk of a few being picked up incidentally around the rockier stretches near Orient as the water starts its slow slide toward autumn temperatures. Nothing worth planning a trip around yet — that fishery sharpens up as September wears on and the bottom water finally cools off enough to pull them out of the deeper holes. Worth keeping a few green crabs in the bait tank if you're already out there for something else.

The piece of this report I'd keep an eye on is Plum Gut. That current doesn't care what the calendar says, and the Gut and the Race are usually the first water around here to show early bonito or false albacore once the bait gets tight and the rips start running hard on the building tide. Nothing confirmed yet, and I wouldn't send a man out there chasing ghosts, but the ingredients are lining up — squid pushing down from the north, current sharpening with the moon, water temps still warm enough to hold them if they show. If there's one spot on this whole stretch worth checking daily through the first half of September, it's the Gut.

For the next few days, expect more of the same: stable, warm, current-driven fishing where the tide change and the first hour of light do the heavy lifting. If you've only got one window this weekend, take the dawn tide change at Horton Point or the Mattituck Inlet flats, work bucktails and bait low and slow, and don't be surprised if the afternoon goes quiet. That's not bad luck — that's just where the fish are telling you they'd rather be.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Building Flood: Porgies Stacked, First Blackfish Show on the Cows
reports.subhead: The moon goes full tomorrow night and the current is already sharpening up the reef bite from Greenwich to Bridgeport.
reports.body_markdown:
Tomorrow night's full moon is the whole story for the next 72 hours on this stretch of the Sound, and the smart play right now is picking your reef around how much current you want to fight rather than how much you want to sit still. Cockenoe Reef and the rockpile off Sheffield Island are drawing the bulk of the porgy and blackfish talk this week because the building tide is finally giving those spots the push they've been missing through the flat, sticky stretch of August. We flagged this last week — said the current toward the full moon should sharpen the bite around the reef structure — and that's exactly what's playing out as the swings get bigger through the weekend.

Water's still warm for the calendar. Kings Point is reading 70.9, and that west-end number matters for this zone because Greenwich to Bridgeport sits right in that warmer pocket compared to the cooler water working its way in from the east end of the Sound. That temperature is what's keeping this fishery locked into its late-August personality — a porgy-and-snapper-blue program during the day, with striped bass activity mostly pushed to structure at night or into the last two hours of ebb when there's a current edge and some shade. Daytime bass on the reefs have been a grind. Nobody's saying otherwise. The fish are there, they're just not eager to chase in 70-degree water with the sun straight overhead.

Penfield Reef is fishing the classic late-summer split. On the last two hours of the ebb, working the deeper edge off the lighthouse in 18 to 25 feet, blackfish are starting to show — not thick yet, but enough 2-to-4-pounders on green crab and Asian crab to tell you the pattern is turning over a few weeks early. That's worth watching into September. The porgy program on Penfield is more reliable right now: sandworms and clam strips on the high-low rig, fishing bottom in that same 18-to-25 foot band on the tail of the flood, with fish running a half-pound to a pound and a half, occasionally better. Boat traffic on Penfield gets thick on weekend mornings with the marina crowd running out of Black Rock and Fairfield, so the better window there has been first light through mid-morning before the pleasure boats stack up on top of the structure.

The Cows, off Stamford, have been the most consistent porgy spot in the zone all week. Anchoring up-current of the rockpile on the last of the ebb and first hour of the new flood, with clam on a two-hook bottom rig, has been putting good numbers of porgies in the box, mixed with cocktail blues that are chasing the same bait balls. Those blues have been a dependable presence everywhere from the Cows to Greenwich Point — snapper-sized fish thick in the harbors and coves, with the occasional 2-to-3-pound cocktail mixing into the porgy catches out on the reef itself. If you want bluefish action for kids or for numbers, small metal or a bucktail teaser above the porgy rig will get bit constantly right now.

Striped bass are the harder conversation. The daytime bite on Cockenoe and the Norwalk Islands rockpiles has been soft, which lines up with what's happening across the whole region — warm surface water is pushing bass activity to the edges of the day. The better program has been working the Norwalk Islands and the rocks off Sheffield Island after dark, drifting or slow-trolling live bait — peanut bunker or a chunk on a fishfinder rig — tight to the structure on the last two hours of the ebb when the current is pulling bait off the rocks into deeper water. Fish have been mostly schoolie to mid-20s class, with the occasional better fish mixed in on nights with a strong tide push. Nobody's stumbling onto slot-and-up numbers consistently yet, and that's expected — the real fall push doesn't usually show here until nighttime temperatures start knocking the surface water down in earnest, likely mid-September.

Fluke have been the toughest read of the summer. Warm, thin water across the flats has spread the fish out instead of concentrating them, and that's held true here — the channel edges around the Norwalk Islands and the deeper drop-offs near Sheffield Island have been holding a cooler bottom layer and are outfishing the open flats by a wide margin. Gulp or squid strips on a bucktail, worked slow along the edge where the depth breaks from 12 to 20 feet, has been the more productive approach than drifting the shallow flats blind.

Looking ahead, the full moon tomorrow night is going to keep building the tidal swings through the weekend, and that should keep sharpening the reef bite on Cockenoe, Penfield, and the Cows — bigger current means more bait pushed off structure, and that's when the porgies and blues really pile up. If the pattern holds and overnight temperatures start trending down even slightly next week, expect the first real crack in the daytime striper lull. Until then, play the tide windows tight, fish the last two hours of the ebb on the deeper reef edges, and save the open flats for another few weeks.

reports.headline: Full Moon Tightens the River Mouth — Blues Stage, Bass Wait on the Dark
reports.subhead: Late-August current at Saybrook Point is doing exactly what fifty years of Augusts have taught this river to do, and the bluefish are the first sign fall is loading up.
reports.body_markdown:
The marsh grass on Great Island has that late-August bronze creeping into the green, and the ospreys are already thinning out along Old Lyme — a couple weeks early by the calendar most of us keep in our heads, but right on schedule for the water. That's the tell this time of year. Not a thermometer, not a tide chart. It's the birds leaving before the fish arrive. The river mouth is deep into its summer holding pattern, and the moon building toward full tomorrow night is about to put some teeth back into the current for the first time in weeks.

That's not a small thing on this river. When the moon swells, the tide swings harder through the gut between Saybrook Point and the outer bar, and that current is the whole engine of this fishery in August. It's the thing that stacks bait against the breakwaters, that turns a slack, soupy afternoon into a moving conveyor of silversides and peanut bunker getting squeezed through the funnel at the mouth. We flagged this pattern building last week — said to watch the current tighten as the moon came up on full — and that's exactly what the fleet is seeing set up now heading into the weekend.

Striped bass are still sitting in their predictable late-summer posture: deep, shaded, or nocturnal. Daytime water in the lower river and the flats off Great Island is warm enough that the bigger fish just don't want to work in the sun. The producing program right now is the same one that's worked every August I can remember — fish the last two hours of light into full dark, on the last of the ebb, with the current pulling bait out past the Saybrook Point breakwaters and the old lighthouse rocks. Live eels on a fish-finder rig, or chunked bunker fished on the bottom in eight to fifteen feet along the edge of the channel, are taking slot fish and the occasional bigger one. A few boats working the deeper holes off Essex after dark with white or bone bucktails, swimming them slow along bottom, have picked at fish that won't touch anything in daylight. It's not a banner bite. It's a night-shift bite, and if you're only fishing daylight hours right now you're going to work harder than you need to.

Bluefish are the more honest story this week, and they're the fish worth paying attention to if you're trying to read where the season is headed. Blues have been thick and reliable at the river mouth, working the rips where the outflow meets the Sound current, and that's exactly the kind of staging we called for two weeks back — adult bluefish showing up near the mouth ahead of the real fall push. That's happening now. Cocktail-sized blues in the two-to-four-pound range are blitzing bait on the surface around the outer bar and off Great Island on a strong tide change, and they'll hit almost anything moving fast — Kastmasters, Hopkins spoons, or a simple white bucktail retrieved with speed through the froth. Bring wire or a long fluorocarbon leader; these fish have been cutting mono clean.

White perch are still there for anyone working the upper stretches around Essex and the DEP Marina flats, particularly on the last two hours of the incoming tide when the water's pushed up warm and slightly stained from the tributary creeks. Grass shrimp under a small float, or a sliver of bloodworm on a light jig head, worked slow along the drop-offs near the marina moorings, is still producing perch in the eight-to-ten-inch class, with the occasional better one mixed in. It's a quiet fishery this time of year, but a dependable one, and it's a good option for anyone who wants action without waiting on the tide to swing hard.

Looking at the next several days, the building moon should sharpen everything at the river mouth through the weekend — stronger current, tighter bait concentrations, better tide-change windows for both the bass and the blues. Southwest winds in the eight-to-twelve range should keep the water clean and the mouth fishable without the chop that's made the outer bar sloppy on other weeks this month. The bass pattern isn't going to break wide open yet — this is still the summer holding game, not the real push south, and that shift won't show itself in earnest until nighttime air temperatures start dropping hard, likely not before mid-September. But the bluefish staging near the mouth is worth watching closely over the next two weeks. If that presence builds and adult fish start pushing further up past Saybrook Point toward Essex, that's usually the first real signal the fall run is loading behind it. For now, work the dark hours for bass, hit the rips on the tide change for blues, and keep an eye on those ospreys — when the last of them clear out of Old Lyme, that's usually when this river starts to turn.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Steady Week, No Drama: Warm Water Holds Spencer to Norfolk, Yellowfin and Mahi Keep Filling Coolers
reports.subhead: The canyon complex is riding the same warm-water regime it's had for weeks, and the fleet from Cape May and Ocean City is still finding fish — just working harder for the marlin.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a B-plus week. Nothing spectacular, nothing that had the radio with hero numbers, but four canyons in a row that put fish in the box for boats willing to run the extra miles and read the water instead of just running to the same number as last trip. Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, and Norfolk are all sitting under the same stubborn warm-water regime that's held the whole Mid-Atlantic complex together through most of August, and that consistency is exactly why the bite has stayed workable even as the calendar turns toward fall.

Here's the setup: stable high pressure has parked over the region, southwest winds running 8 to 12 knots most days, seas laying down enough to make the canyon runs comfortable out of both Cape May and Ocean City. That kind of weather window doesn't force anybody to change plans mid-trip, which matters this time of year because the fish are spread across four different pieces of structure and picking the wrong one costs you a whole day's fuel. The warm water sitting on the edges hasn't broken down or retreated, and until it does, the multi-species mix — yellowfin, some bigeye, mahi, wahoo, and a thinning but still-present white marlin bite — should keep showing up the way it has for weeks.

Spencer remains the go-to when boats want the shortest run with the most reliable yellowfin. The temperature break along the northeast edge has held tight, and the chunk bite there has been steady on butterfish and bunker chunks fished on circle hooks, slow-trolled or drifted right on the color change. Boats working sunrise and the last two hours of daylight have done best, with fish running 30 to 55 pounds mixed in with the occasional bigger class fish for those willing to soak a bait deeper on a fluorocarbon leader. Trolling spreads pulling naked and skirted ballyhoo have also connected, especially green-and-yellow and pink-and-white combinations worked just outside the temp break rather than dead center on it — the fish have been sitting on the edges of the warm water, not stacked in the middle of it.

Lindenkohl has fished almost as a mirror of Spencer this week, which makes sense given how the same warm tongue runs across both pieces. The mahi bite has been the story here — smaller fish, two to six pounds mostly, but plenty of them holding under any floating grass or debris line boats can find. Small spreader bars and cedar plugs pulled at moderate speed have worked to locate them, then a pitch bait or a bucktail tossed right into the pod once they show up under the boat has kept rods bent. Anybody running Lindenkohl this week without a pair of long-handled dip nets ready has been leaving fish in the water.

Poor Man's has been the tougher read of the four. The white marlin bite is still alive there, but it's thinned out compared to earlier in the month, and the boats connecting have needed to cover more water to find them — trolling ballyhoo dink baits and small Islanders along temperature seams rather than committing to one spot and waiting. Two or three releases on a good day is realistic right now; boats expecting double-digit marlin days like July are going home disappointed. That's the honest read — it's a fishery in transition, not a dead one, but it demands more running and more patience than it did a month ago.

Norfolk continues to be the play for boats willing to make the longer run and stay overnight. The bigeye bite on the deep drop and slow-troll has been the most consistent producer down there, particularly in the pre-dawn hours when boats have worked butterfish chunks and glow squid baits over the deeper structure. Wahoo have also turned up on the high-speed troll for boats running wire line and deep-diving lures like Ilanders rigged behind cedar plugs, typically picked off on the run out or run back rather than on a dedicated wahoo drop.

The moon is building toward full over the next several days, and that's going to tighten up the bite windows across all four canyons rather than spread them out. Expect the best action to concentrate around the tide changes and current edges as the moon strengthens, with slower stretches in between. If the southwest wind pattern holds through the next 48 hours as expected, boats have a genuine window to work any of the four canyons without weather forcing a bailout — that's the time to commit to the longer run to Norfolk if bigeye or wahoo are the target, or stick closer with Spencer and Lindenkohl if the goal is filling a fish box with yellowfin and mahi on a shorter day.

Looking three days out, the warm-water regime that's been carrying this whole complex should still be in place, keeping the tuna and mahi bite solid even as the white marlin fishery continues its slow seasonal fade. The bigger question for early September is how long that warm pool holds before the first real cool-down starts working its way south. Until it breaks, the smart play is the same one that's worked all week — run to whichever canyon matches the target species and be ready to move if the first stop doesn't produce inside an hour.

reports.headline: 71.2°F on the Bight Buoy — the Hudson's Warm-Water Regime Isn't Cracking Yet
reports.subhead: A steady southerly swell and a stubborn warm eddy are keeping yellowfin, bigeye, and mahi stacked along the canyon edges, but the bite is a puzzle you have to work, not a gimme.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-one point two degrees. That's the read off Buoy 44025 out in the Bight this week, riding on top of a 3.9-foot swell out of the south at a soft 5-second period. It's not a dramatic number by itself, but it tells the story of a surface layer that's stayed warm and stable all the way out to the shelf break, and that matters because the same warm eddy that's carried the Hudson all August still hasn't been pushed off. No front has come through strong enough to flip the water, and the southwest 8-to-12-knot wind pattern that's held for days now isn't the kind that stirs things up — it's the kind that lets blue water sit and settle in against the canyon wall.

That stability is exactly why the mixed bag has held together out here. Yellowfin, some bigeye, mahi, and white marlin have all been coming out of the same general water, which tells you the canyon's structure is doing its job — pushing bait up out of deep water and letting predators work it along a clean edge rather than a blown-out one. Squid showing up thick in the bait column is the tell. When squid stack in the water column over the canyon rim, tuna don't have to move far to eat, and that's been the pattern for a couple weeks running.

The better boats have been splitting time between the troll and the jig. Naked ballyhoo behind small green machines and cedar plugs is still the bread-and-butter spread for yellowfin working the 100-fathom line, especially where it bends around the eastern lip of the Claw. When the fish are sitting on bait rather than chasing the surface, that's when the vertical jig program takes over — butterfly-style jigs worked with a fast, erratic stroke down through 150 to 250 feet has been drawing strikes when the troll goes quiet, particularly over structure near the Dip where the bottom breaks sharp and bait gets funneled against the wall.

Mahi have been scattered but present anywhere there's a defined temp line or floating debris — weed clumps, lobster gear, the occasional pallet — holding just under the surface. A small skirted ballyhoo or a bare hook with a strip of squid drifted back near the transom while the spread is out has been picking off a few extra fish for boats willing to slow down and look. White marlin have shown on the troll in the same general water as the yellowfin, which is normal for this time of year when bait is dense and mixed species are working the same edge rather than separating by depth.

Bigeye have been a nighttime story more than a daytime one. Chunking butterfish on the drift after dark, fishing baits at staggered depths off the current, has produced fish in the same zone where the daytime troll bite has been happening — not a coincidence, since bigeye tend to sit deeper during daylight and rise with the bait column after dark. For boats running the deep-drop program for swordfish, the pattern hasn't changed much: baits fished on the bottom in the 1,200-to-1,600-foot range, squid strips with a glow stick or LED strobe near the hook, worked slow-and-steady drifts across structure near the Claw and the Dip where the bottom holds current-swept troughs. That's a grind more than a sure thing right now, and boats should treat it that way — a few fish a trip, not a pile.

Honest read on the week: this has been a solid, working bite, not a blowtorch. Some days the troll connects early and stays hot through the morning; other days boats have had to hunt, working the edges with the jig before finding fish stacked tighter than expected. The squid-driven bait base is keeping things interesting, but it's not evenly spread across the whole canyon, and boats that ran without checking the chlorophyll break before committing to a spot came home with a lighter fish count than the ones who worked the edge first.

Looking at the next 24 to 48 hours, expect more of the same — stable high pressure, that same light southwest wind, and no real push to move the warm-water regime off the canyon. That's good news for consistency; the pattern that's produced this week should hold through the weekend. The moon building toward full over the next two days will tighten up the tidal swings, and that usually sharpens the bite windows right at first light and again in the evening, when current movement against the canyon wall pulls bait up onto the structure hardest. By 72 hours out, the warm-water setup should still be intact, keeping the tuna and billfish bite going in the Mid-Atlantic canyons generally, Hudson included. The one thing worth watching is any hint of a cooler push working down from the north — nothing in the current pattern suggests it's close, but late August is exactly when that kind of shift starts to show up on the charts without much warning.

If there's only one day to make the run this week, the early window on the building tide — working the 100-fathom edge first, then sliding over toward the Claw or the Dip if the troll goes quiet — is the smart play. Keep the jig rigged and ready. When this bait-rich, stable pattern holds, the fish are there; the job is putting the spread or the jig in the right piece of water at the right hour, not hoping the whole ocean lights up at once.

reports.headline: Radio Call at 4 A.M., a Long Run South, and Bluefin Still Working the Jig
reports.subhead: The eddy that's been holding warm water over Atlantis and Veatch hasn't budged, and the fleet running out of Montauk and Block Island is still cashing in on it.
reports.body_markdown:
The radio traffic out of the Block Island and Montauk fleets this week has had a familiar rhythm: a captain calling in fish on the jig somewhere along the canyon edge, a course correction from the next boat back, and a third falling in behind on the same temperature line an hour later. That's not excitement talking — that's boats burning diesel efficiently, which is the whole game once you're running two, three, sometimes four hours each way to get to water that's actually holding fish. Nobody out here runs on hope. They run on what the last boat back to the dock told them, and this week that story hasn't changed much: the eddy sitting over Atlantis and Veatch is still there, still warm, and it's still stacking bluefin.

Stable high pressure held through the week, southwest wind in the 8-to-12 knot range most days, which is about as good as it gets for a long offshore run — flat enough riding out that a 32-to-38 footer can hold cruise speed without beating the crew up, which matters when the fuel math already has you thinking about the tank gauge before you clear the sea buoy. Boats out of Montauk are timing departures to be on the grounds by first light, working the water while it's calm, and turning for home before the afternoon sea breeze fills in. Out of Block Island and the Rhode Island ports, the run to Atlantis and Veatch eats a similar bite out of the day — long enough that most captains aren't making the trip on a maybe. They're going because the last two or three boats back confirmed fish, and that's exactly what's been happening.

The bluefin have been school-sized — footballs mostly, some pushing into the mid-range class — and they've been eating jigs cleanly along current edges where the warm water is folding against cooler stuff underneath. The go-to has been 180-gram-class jigs worked on a fast, erratic retrieve through the middle of the water column, with streaker-style natural bait rigs — ballyhoo or small squid strips dressed behind a skirted head — picking up fish that won't commit to straight metal. We flagged this a few days back, that the jig bite would hold as long as the eddy structure stayed in place, and it has. Same water, same pattern, same 180-gram jigs still doing the damage off Atlantis and Veatch. That's not a coincidence — warm-core eddies like this one don't dissolve on a schedule, they get pushed or pulled apart by something bigger, and nothing this week has come along to break it up.

Billfish have carried over from the same warm-water regime. White marlin have been showing along temperature breaks and weed lines on the troll, mixed in with the tuna spread more than targeted outright — a fish here, a fish there, not a bonanza, but enough that boats running dredge and daisy chain spreads through Hydrographer and Oceanographer have had shots. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure that's holding bait, which out here usually means a weed line or a piece of debris that's collected juvenile fish underneath it — nothing consistent enough to plan a whole trip around, but worth a look if you cross one on the troll and have a spinning rod rigged with a small bucktail or a chunk of squid ready to pitch.

What's kept this going is the moon building toward full, which has sharpened the current on the edges without blowing the structure apart. A stronger tide means bait gets pushed and pinned against the temperature break instead of drifting loose through it, and that's when the bluefin show up in numbers instead of ones and twos. It's the same logic that's been tightening bite windows closer to shore — Block Island and Point Judith should start seeing their first bonito of the season any day now as bait pulls tight along the beaches — but offshore, the effect is on the eddy itself: tighter current, tighter bait, better jig bite.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern holds if the weather does. Southwest wind in that same comfortable range should keep the ride manageable through the weekend, and there's no sign yet of the eddy sliding off Atlantis or losing its warm core.
