If that holds, the smart move is the same one the fleet's already making — run early, work the edges where the color changes from blue to green-blue, and stick with the 180-gram jigs until something tells you to switch. Where this gets interesting is the 72-hour window. Overnight temperatures up in the northern reaches are starting to nudge down a notch, which won't touch the canyons directly but is usually the first sign the season's turning behind the scenes. The warm-water regime offshore should hold through that window regardless — these eddies don't answer to a calendar the way the inshore water does — but it's worth watching whether that cooling trend starts pulling the whole system south and east over the next week or two. For now, if you've got the fuel and the weather window, Atlantis and Veatch are still paying off. Just don't leave the dock without knowing exactly how much diesel it takes to get home.

reports.headline: Trolled the Wilmington Edge All Week — Yellowfin Steady, White Marlin Scattered but Real
reports.subhead: The warm-water setup that's held for three weeks isn't breaking down yet, and boats running ballyhoo spreads are still finding fish on the color change.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one trip left in the budget this week, troll before you chunk. That's the call coming off the docks in Cape May and Indian River right now, and it's the right one. The water sitting over Wilmington Canyon has held its warm, sterile-blue character for three straight weeks — no real breakdown, no cold intrusion pushing through to mess with it — and that kind of stability rewards covering ground with a spread before committing to an anchor-up chunk bite. Find the temp break first, mark bait on the meter, then decide whether the day turns into a drift-and-chunk operation.

The pattern holding this canyon together is the same one that's been in place since early August: a warm eddy has set up shop off the canyon's edge, and the blue water riding on top of it is about as clean as it gets this time of year. That kind of water isn't always loaded with life — it can look gorgeous and fish empty — but this stretch has been holding yellowfin consistently, with bluefin mixed in on the better days and white marlin working the temp lines on the troll. Boats aren't finding wall-to-wall numbers, but the ones running the edge with a full spread are putting fish in the box on most trips, which for late August is a fair trade for fuel burned.

High pressure has been steady, winds out of the southwest in the 8 to 12 knot range, which is about as comfortable as this stretch of water gets in summer. That's kept sea state manageable for the run out and let boats work the drop methodically instead of getting bounced off the troll early. If that pattern holds through the next couple days — and there's no strong signal it's about to change — expect the canyon to keep fishing close to how it has been: not a blitz, but a dependable multi-species day for boats willing to put in the time on the troll.

Tactically, the spreads that have been producing are straightforward. A dredge teaser run short off the transom, ballyhoo — naked and skirted both — worked in a standard pattern with a couple of daisy chains for teasers, and a spreader bar or two run long for bigger fish. Yellowfin have been coming on smaller skirted ballyhoo in green machine and pink/white combinations, fished 30 to 60 feet back where the water still shows some color transition rather than dead flat blue. White marlin have been more selective — they're showing on the naked ballyhoo pulled behind the dredge, and hookup ratios have been decent but not great, which tracks with a scattered rather than concentrated marlin push this month. Bluefin have come mixed in with the yellowfin on the better mornings, usually on the same spread, no special adjustment needed other than making sure drags are backed off enough to handle a bigger fish if one decides to eat.

Once boats find bait stacked and marked well on structure along the canyon wall, the switch to chunking has been worth it. Butterfish chunks fished on a slow-sink rig, no weight or just enough to get it under the slick, have drawn yellowfin up in the chum line on the calmer days. The key has been patience — let the slick build for twenty, thirty minutes before expecting results, and keep the chunks small and steady rather than dumping the bucket. Boats that rushed the chunk without a real bait presence on the meter mostly wasted drift time; the ones that waited for marks to show before setting up did better.

Mahi have been a bonus rather than a target this stretch, showing under whatever scattered weed lines boats have crossed running out to the drop. Nothing consistent enough to plan a day around, but worth a couple of casts with a small skirted bait or a bucktail if you cross a good mat of grass with the usual dolphin signs — peanut mahi flashing under the edges. Wahoo have been quieter than they were earlier in the summer; a couple of incidental fish on the high-speed lures run off the outriggers, but nobody's targeting them specifically right now and the numbers don't justify dedicating a rod to it yet.

Looking at the next few days, the setup holding this bite together shows no sign of breaking. Stable high pressure and light southwest wind should keep conditions fishable and the warm-water regime intact through the near-term window. That means the same game plan should keep working — troll the edge early, watch for the color change and bait marks, and be ready to switch to the chunk if the meter lights up. Where this gets more interesting is the moon building toward full over the next several days, which typically sharpens current and can tighten up bite windows right at the edges and breaks. If that plays out the way it usually does, expect shorter but more intense windows rather than an all-day grind — worth adjusting the day around first light and the last couple hours before the tide change rather than fishing the whole clock at the same intensity. Fuel math still favors this trip for boats willing to work the troll patiently before committing to anchor.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Green and Cold Underneath, First Bonito Cutting the North Rip
reports.subhead: Bass have gone nocturnal on the Ledge, bluefish are the daytime constant, and Block Island's first bonito of the season are finally showing where we said they would.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a smell to the air out here this week that tells you more than any thermometer will — that heavy, almost sweet bait smell drifting off the pond at first light, the kind that means the peanut bunker have finally packed themselves into the coves in real numbers. The water on top is still summer-warm, sitting in the low 70s off the beaches, but anyone who's dropped a temp gauge down the face of the Southwest Ledge this week knows there's a cold, green layer sitting underneath that warm cap, and that's where the bass have gone. This is the pattern we flagged a few days back — that late August on the Block would settle into a holding pattern rather than a push, and that's exactly what's happening. The real fall run doesn't start until the nights cool off hard, and we're not there yet.

Wind's been mostly out of the southwest at 8 to 15 knots, which keeps the south side a little bounced around in the afternoon but leaves the rips workable on the changes. The moon's building toward full over the next several days, and that's already sharpening up the tide swings around the island — the Southwest Ledge and North Rip both pulling harder water on the last two hours of the ebb than they were a week ago. That's good news. Stronger current means better oxygen exchange over the structure, and it's pulling bait tighter to the edges instead of letting it spread out across the flat, soupy water that's been softening the fluke bite everywhere from here to the Cape.

Striped bass are there, but this is a structure-and-shadow fishery right now, not a run-and-gun one. The better boats are working the Southwest Ledge in 35 to 55 feet on the top of the tide and through the first hour of the drop, dropping live eels or fresh-cut bunker chunks down into the rock piles rather than trolling over them. Daytime action has been slow and scattered — the fish are sitting deep against the cold layer and not moving much until the light drops. The real program has shifted to the night bite: eels drifted slow along the Ledge's east face after dark, or bunker spider-rigged off the drift right at the change of tide, have been the two most consistent ways to connect with better fish, some pushing into the 20s and low 30s. The North Rip is still producing on the harder tide stages — big swirling current edges where a school bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to the boil line rather than out in open water, has taken a few genuinely heavy fish this week, including at least one report of something well into the 40-pound class worked out of that white water on a slow outgoing tide. That's the kind of fish that reminds you why this island pulls stripers from three states away every summer — the cold, clean, well-oxygenated water coming up over that ledge is simply a different animal than what most of the coast is dealing with right now.

Bluefish have been the dependable piece of the puzzle, same as everywhere else in the region this year. Cocktail blues in the 3- to 6-pound range are mixing right in with the bass on the Ledge and off Southeast Light, and they've been the saving grace on days when the stripers wanted nothing to do with anything moving fast. Bucktails and diamond jigs worked with a jigging stroke through the deeper water have both bait and blues stacked up, and if the bass shut down, the blues usually haven't.

And here's the news worth circling — bonito have shown up. Not thick yet, but real, with the first solid reports coming off the rips on the north and south sides of the island and off Point Judith as well, right where we said they'd turn up as the water settled into that low-70s sweet spot. Small epoxy jigs and half-ounce Deceivers worked fast on top, right in the white water where the tide is ripping bait against structure, have accounted for the first fish. This is a moving-tide, moving-boat fishery — find the nervous water, make the cast into the seam, strip it fast, and don't stop to admire it. Expect this to build over the next week or two as it typically does once it starts, spreading toward Newport and the eastern approaches to Narragansett Bay as bait continues to tighten along the beaches.

Fluke have been the soft spot of the week, same story as the rest of southern New England — warm, thin water has scattered them across the flats rather than holding them tight, and the better catches have come from deeper structure and channel edges rather than the open bottom. If fluke is the target, work the deeper edges around the island rather than the shallow sand.

Looking ahead, expect the pattern to hold through the next several days — southwest breeze, warm cap on top, cold water underneath, and a building tide that should keep sharpening the bite windows at the Ledge and the Rip as the moon fills. If there's only one window to fish this weekend, it's the last two hours of the ebb into dark at the Southwest Ledge, eel or bunker chunk down deep, with a rod rigged light for bonito on the side in case the rip lights up on top. The real turn toward fall bass fishing is still a few weeks off — this is the in-between stretch, and it rewards patience and the right tide more than raw effort.

reports.headline: August 27: Washington's Early Start Is Still Paying Rent
reports.subhead: The same warm-water setup that got Washington going ahead of the pack in June is still holding late in August, and the canyon is fishing like it knows it.
reports.body_markdown:
Late August is usually when a lot of the Mid-Atlantic canyons start showing their age for the season — the early push fades, the water cools a half-degree here and there, and the bite gets choppier. Washington doesn't play by that calendar, and this year is no different. This canyon typically gets its warm-water setup earlier than its neighbors because of where it sits relative to the Gulf Stream, and that head start built in June is still paying dividends heading into September. The regime that's been in place — stable high pressure, southwest winds sitting in that 8-to-12 knot window, warm water holding firm — hasn't broken down. That's the story of the last several days and it's the story for the next few, too.

What that means practically is the canyon is still fishing like mid-summer instead of easing into the fall turn. Yellowfin remain the bread-and-butter species working the temperature breaks and current edges, white marlin are still showing on the troll where the water color changes, and mahi are scattered around whatever floating structure and weed lines the fleet can find. It's not a banner week where every boat limits out — it's a solid, honest mixed-bag week, and that's worth saying plainly. Some days the walls are stacked with life and some days boats have to run and hunt before they find the right piece of water. That's normal for this stretch of the season. The fish are here; they're just not evenly distributed, and that's exactly what you'd expect with a warm-water regime that's held steady rather than one that's actively pushing new water and new bait into the canyon.

The pattern that's produced the best results has been working the temperature and color breaks along the eastern and western walls rather than blind-trolling open water. Boats anchoring up on bait schools holding tight to the edges have done well chunking butterfish and bunker chunks, drawing yellowfin up out of the deeper water into a chum slick worked over a couple hours of tide. That bite tends to build slow and then go off in a short window, so patience at anchor has been outproducing boats that keep picking up and moving every 20 minutes. On the troll, a standard spread of naked and skirted ballyhoo behind small to mid-size bird teasers has been the go-to for both yellowfin and white marlin, with marlin especially responsive to a dink ballyhoo pulled just off a spreader bar in that flat, glassy water that builds under the current high pressure. Wahoo have shown up as a bycatch on the high-speed gear — boards or planers pulling cedar plugs and small skirted lures at 12-plus knots along the drop-offs — but they've been more opportunistic than a targeted, reliable bite this week.

Mahi have been the wildcard, and honestly the most fun part of the report. Anywhere the fleet has found a real weed line or a patch of floating debris, there have been fish stacked underneath it — some short, some pushing better than 10 pounds. Small hookless teasers followed by spinning tackle pitching pilchards or a bit of chunk bait has been the standard approach, and it's produced some of the more consistent action of the week when the bigger pelagics went quiet for a stretch. If there's one thing worth telling anyone headed out — carry the spinning rods rigged and ready, because the mahi bite has been the difference between a mediocre day and a genuinely good one more than once this week.

The bigger picture explains why this is holding. Washington sits in a warm-water regime that's been stable for days now, and there's no sign of that breaking in the near term. High pressure isn't going anywhere fast, the southwest wind pattern keeps the surface calm enough for good trolling conditions, and the warm water that's been in place isn't showing the kind of cooling that starts to push these pelagics off the canyon edge. That's the Washington advantage again — this canyon got its warm-water setup weeks before some of its neighbors, and it's simply got more runway left before any seasonal cooling starts to matter.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same conditions-wise — steady high pressure, manageable southwest wind, warm water holding. The moon is building toward full, which should tighten up the current on the walls and sharpen the bite windows rather than spread them out, so boats that time their drift or anchor to the peak of the tide swing should see better concentrated action than boats fishing the slack. Longer range, there's some early chatter about cooler nights starting to nudge water temperatures down farther north, but that's a story for New England and the Sound right now, not for Washington. This canyon's warm-water window still has room to run. If there's only one day to make the trip this week, work the walls on the building tide around the moon, keep the chunk bags ready for the yellowfin, and don't leave the spinning rods below — the mahi have been too good to leave on the dock.

reports.headline: Bass Hold the Boulders, Bluefin Camp Southwest of the Light
reports.subhead: The Point is easing into its September posture early, with bass staged on structure, bluefin settled off the rips, and the first albie showing feels close.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a specific feel to Montauk in the last week of August, and anyone who's fished this rock long enough knows it when it arrives. The daytime crowds are thinning at the Point, the light's coming in lower and gold by six, and the water — 69.1 degrees off the Lighthouse — still carries summer's warmth but not its indifference. This isn't the fall run yet. It's the setup for it, and this year it looks like it's arriving a little ahead of the calendar.

Across most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England right now, striped bass are stuck in that predictable late-August pattern — warm surface layers pushing fish down and into structure during daylight, real activity saved for the edges of light. Montauk's not exempt from that physics, but the difference here is what the structure actually is. From North Bar out to Shagwong Reef and the boulder fields off the Lighthouse itself, there's current, cold seams, and bait funneling past on every tide — and that's kept the surf bite alive when other stretches of coast have gone quiet in the heat.

The reports off the rocks this week have bass mixed with big bluefish, staging tight to structure and hard-running current edges rather than roaming open water. That's a pattern worth understanding, not just following: with the surface warm, stripers are using the boulder fields and rip lines as thermal breaks, holding low and picking off bait that gets disoriented in the wash. The building tide at North Bar has been the most consistent window — start fishing an hour before the top of the flood, work a bucktail (1.5 ounces, white or chartreuse) across the seam where the white water meets green, let it sink clean off the edge of the bar, and work it back with a slow, rhythmic bottom retrieve. That's the exact presentation putting bass in the sand at Turtle Cove and off the Lighthouse rocks right now — not fast retrieves, not surface plugs at midday, but patient bottom-contact work on the leading edge of moving water.

Offshore and just southwest of the Point, the more interesting story of the week has been school bluefin tuna holding in a tight, repeatable pattern rather than passing through. Boats working out of Montauk Harbor have found them stacked on sand eel and mackerel against a thermal edge, and the jig bite has been legitimate — UVT Chief soft plastics scaled from 1.5 up to 10 ounces depending on the depth the fish are sitting at, and 5-ounce pink Ronz working just as well when the fish are higher in the water column. The fact that this bite has held for more than a week now, rather than flashing and disappearing, suggests these fish have settled into real structure and bait rather than just riding through on a push of water. Barring a hard wind event that scatters the sand eels, there's no obvious reason this pattern breaks in the next several days.

Fluke fishing, by contrast, is the soft spot on the report card right now, and there's no point dressing it up. The warm, thinned-out water that's spreading fluke out across flats from here to Delaware Bay is doing the same thing inside Fort Pond Bay and the harbor — fish are there, but scattered, and catch rates have dropped everywhere except the channel edges and deeper structure holding a cooler bottom layer. If fluke is the priority, work the deeper drops in the harbor channel and along the edges of Fort Pond Bay on the last of the ebb, when a cooler layer settles along bottom and concentrates what fish are left. White or chartreuse Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow, is still the right call — there's just less water worth covering with confidence than there was a month ago.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's arguing about. Snapper blues are thick in the harbor and Fort Pond Bay, and larger cocktail blues are mixing right into the striper catches on structure and on the troll off the south side beaches. If a rod's been sitting quiet, it's usually not staying that way long with blues around.

We flagged it last week and it's worth repeating: the warm-water signal running through the region — squid pushing into Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound, a sailfish sighting off Chatham — pointed toward the first bonito or false albacore showing at the Point any day now. Nothing's confirmed yet in the rips, but the bait is right and the water's right, and Montauk is almost always among the first spots in the region to get them. Anyone fishing the Point or the Elbow this week should have a small metal — a Deadly Dick or a Got-Cha — rigged and ready on a spare rod, because when they show, it's usually with no warning at all.

Looking ahead: the moon's building toward full, which means bigger tidal swings and sharper bite windows at North Bar, Shagwong, and the rip lines off the Lighthouse over the next several days. Expect the surf bass bite to get another push on the increased current, expect the bluefin to keep holding southwest of the Point as long as the bait stays put, and keep watching the boils east of the Lighthouse for the first sign of albie or bonito activity. If there's only one tide to fish this week, make it the building flood at North Bar in the last hour of daylight — that's where the structure, the current, and the bait are lining up most reliably right now.

reports.headline: Peconic stays warm and stretched thin — porgies still thick around Shelter Island, fluke sliding to the edges
reports.subhead: Bottom bite carries the bay through late August while bass wait for cooler nights, and scallop talk starts creeping into the shops.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic is running its classic late-August program, and if you've fished this system for any length of time, you know exactly what that means: the bay warmed up faster than the Sound back in May, and now it's holding that warmth longer into the fall, same as it always does. Surface temps are sitting in that mid-70s range across Shelter Island Sound, Noyack Bay, and up into Southold Bay, which is warm enough that fluke have quit stacking up and started spreading out across the flats. That's not a crisis, it's just biology — warm, thinner water holds less oxygen near bottom, and fluke respond by scattering rather than piling into tight pods. The ones still feeding hard are doing it where a cooler bottom layer survives: the channel edges off Jessup Neck, the deeper cuts running into Threemile Harbor, and the drop-offs on either side of Plum Gut where the tide keeps things scrubbed and oxygenated.

The moon is building toward full on Friday, and that's the piece worth tracking closest right now. We flagged this a week ago — that bait would start pushing toward the bay mouths as the tides tightened up heading into September — and that's exactly the pattern setting up. Bigger swings mean stronger current at the pinch points: Plum Gut, the Gut off Orient Point, the reef off Cedar Beach, the mouth of Coecles Harbor. Bait gets squeezed through those funnels harder on a big moon tide, and everything from snapper blues to weakfish to the occasional early-season striper starts stacking behind the bait rather than chasing it across open water. If you're planning your week around one tide, plan it around the peak of this building moon rather than the dead middle of a weaker cycle.

Porgy fishing remains the most dependable thing going in the bay right now, and Shelter Island is still the address. The rockpiles off Cedar Point, the drop-off outside Coecles Harbor, and the mussel bottom along the Sound side of the island are holding solid numbers of porgies in the 12- to 14-inch class, with a few chunkier fish mixed in on the better drifts. Standard bottom rig, size 4 or 6 hooks, a piece of clam or squid strip, fished right on bottom in 15 to 25 feet — nothing fancy needed, just patience and a chum pot if the current allows it. Slack tide and the first hour of either the incoming or outgoing tend to produce the steadiest action; once the current really starts ripping through the Sound side, the porgies tuck tighter to structure and the bite gets more technical.

Fluke are there, but call it a working bite rather than an easy one. Drift the edges of the channel running between Robins Island and North Sea, or work the deeper water off the mouth of Sag Harbor, using a bucktail-and-Gulp combination — white or chartreuse 4-inch swimming mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail — dragged slow along bottom on the last of the ebb, when the current is still moving enough to keep the bait ticking bottom but not so hard that you're bouncing off structure. Fish are running a mix of keeper-sized 18- to 20-inch fish and shorts, so expect to cull through some smaller ones to find your dinner fish. The days of just anchoring anywhere on the flats and hammering fluke are behind us for the season — the fish that are left have moved to where the water still makes sense for them.

Weakfish are mixing into those same bait drifts in modest numbers, mostly in the deeper holes off Threemile Harbor and around the mouth of Northwest Creek, taking small white bucktails and swimming plugs worked slow near bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Nothing to build a trip around specifically, but worth a few casts if you're already fishing that structure for fluke.

Bluefish continue to be the bay's most reliable performer, especially the snapper blues that have taken over the docks and bulkheads in Greenport, Sag Harbor, and Three Mile Harbor. Kids with a bobber and a sliver of spearing are having a field day most evenings around the tide change. Cocktail-sized blues in the 2- to 4-pound range are mixing into the fluke drifts along the channel edges too, which means anyone throwing bucktails should expect the occasional bitten-off leader.

Striped bass remain the quiet story right now — this is the predictable late-August holding pattern rather than any real push, with most bass tucked into deeper, cooler pockets during daylight and only showing consistently after dark around structure like the Plum Gut rips and the deeper drop-offs off Orient Point. That's expected. The real fall staging typically doesn't kick in until nighttime temperatures start dropping in earnest, likely mid-September this year given how warm the bay has run. Worth working the night tide at Plum Gut with bucktails or swimming plugs if you're set up for it, but don't expect a daytime bite to materialize yet.

One more thing worth flagging for the calendar: bay scallop season opener chatter is starting to circulate around the docks, right on schedule for this time of year. Nothing official to report yet, but if you're a scalloper, start paying attention to the sheds and the tackle shops over the next couple of weeks — that conversation always picks up steam as September approaches.

reports.headline: Eel Down, 38 Pounds Up — The Race Turns On at the Turn
reports.subhead: A big bass off Fishers Island confirms what the current's been telegraphing all week: the rip is loading up ahead of the fall push.
reports.body_markdown:
A 38-pound striper came over the rail at the top of the ebb off the western end of Fishers Island this week, taken on a live eel drifted tight against the rock on the down-current side of the rip. That's the fish the docks from Orient to New London are talking about right now, and it's not an outlier — it's a signal. The bait is stacking hard against structure in the Race and Plum Gut, and the current is doing exactly what it does this time of year: compressing everything into a tight window at the turn of the tide.

Water's still warm for the calendar. New London is reading 69.4°F, Montauk's holding at 69.1°F, and that's actually the cooler side of the Sound — Kings Point up west is pushing 70.9°F. That gradient matters. It means the eastern stretch, from Mount Sinai out through Wading River and into Orient, is running a few degrees cooler than the central basin, and cooler water out here means the bass and blues stay more active through the daylight hours instead of shutting down and waiting for dark like they're doing to the west. We flagged this exact stretch last week as an early fall-staging zone, and it's playing out — bait is tightening up along that shoreline, and both bluefish and stripers are following it in tighter to the beach than they were two weeks ago.

The moon's building toward full over the next few days, which means bigger tidal swings and sharper current through the Race and Plum Gut. That's the single biggest factor to plan around this weekend. When that current runs 4 to 5 knots at max ebb, the fish don't chase — they hold in the eddies and let the bait wash to them. The window that matters is the hour before and after the turn, when the water slows enough for a bass to commit without burning energy fighting the rip. Show up mid-tide expecting a bite and you'll be fishing dead water.

Striped bass are the story right now, and they're behaving like late-August bass should — daytime activity pushed onto structure and into the deeper eddies, with the real window opening up at the night bite. The boulder fields off Orient Point and the north side of Fishers Island are holding fish after dark on big pencil poppers and Danny-style swimmers worked slow across the surface at the first hour of the incoming. If you want numbers over size, live eels drifted through the western Race on the last two hours of the ebb are still the most consistent producer the fleet's reporting — start the drift up-current of the visible boil line and let it swing naturally into the slack pocket behind the rock.

Bluefish are the dependable piece of this puzzle. Jumbo cocktail blues to 12 pounds are mixing right into that same striper program on the rips, hitting everything from bunker chunks to metal-lip swimmers worked through the froth at Plum Gut. Snapper blues are thick in every harbor from Port Jefferson to Orient — small poppers and Kastmasters off the docks at dusk will keep a rod bent for anyone who wants an easy hour with a kid.

Fluke are the soft spot in the report, and there's no dressing it up. The warm surface layer has spread fish out across the flats instead of concentrating them, and catch rates have thinned out everywhere except where there's real depth and current to hold a cooler bottom layer. That means Plum Gut's deep channel and the drop-off on the New London side of the Race are still worth a drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail — 3/4 to 1 ounce depending on the stage of tide — but the days of stacking doubles on the flats are done for now. Fish deep, fish the seam, and don't expect volume.

Porgies are quietly one of the better bets in the zone right now. The rock piles and reef structure around Fishers Island and the north side of Plum Gut are holding good numbers in 20 to 40 feet, and sandworms or clam on a high-low rig will fill a cooler fast on the slower stages of the tide when the current's not ripping too hard to hold bottom.

Looking a few days out: expect the pattern to hold, maybe sharpen. As the moon fills, tidal exchange through the Race and Plum Gut should get more aggressive, which tightens the bite windows but also concentrates the fish harder against structure — that's good news if you can time it. There's also real reason to keep an eye on Fishers Island Sound and the water toward Block Island. Squid have started showing in numbers up in Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound, which is usually the first domino before bonito and albies push west along this stretch. Nothing confirmed on the dock yet, but the ingredients are lining up. If there's only one trip in you this week, make it the last two hours of the ebb at the Race with an eel in hand, or first light at Orient with a popper — those are the two windows with the best odds of a real fish on the end of the line.

reports.headline: Silversides Bunching Off Stratford Shoal — Porgy Steady While Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking in the rip and along the reefs, but the stripers won't commit until the sun goes down and the moon keeps building.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait tells the story before the boats do, and this week the story is silversides and peanut bunker pushing into tight, nervous pods along the edges of Stratford Shoal and down through the Norwalk Islands. Terns have been working short, choppy dives over these pods rather than the sustained blitzes you get when predators are underneath pushing bait to the surface — a sign the bass and blues know the bait is there but aren't committing hard in daylight. That matches what the thermometer is telling us. Kings Point is reading 70.9 degrees, New London down around 69.4, and that west-to-east gradient is exactly the kind of setup that keeps bait comfortable and spread out across the middle Sound rather than pinned into one obvious ambush point.

We flagged this pattern last week — said bass would hold in a summer pattern rather than break into fall migration until nighttime temps really start dropping, and that's precisely what the fleet is seeing. Daytime surface water is still too warm for stripers to feed with any consistency in open water, so the program has shifted almost entirely to structure and darkness. The better reports are coming after sundown on eels fished tight to current — around the bridge abutments and points from Oyster Bay through Port Jeff, and along the rock piles off Charles Island on the Connecticut side. Rigged eels or 6-inch swimming plastics worked slow on the drop, right on the current seam, are picking up fish in the 24 to 34-inch range on the front half of the incoming tide, when the water is still cool from the overnight low. Daylight hours have been mostly a stretch-and-wait game unless you're working deep structure — the Stratford Shoal rip itself, worked slow with a bucktail bounced off bottom on the tail of the ebb, has given up a few daytime fish, but it's not the kind of bite you can set your watch to right now.

Porgy and scup remain the most dependable meat-in-the-cooler fishery in the zone, and that consistency is holding exactly as expected. Party boats working the reefs off Middle Ground Light and the rock piles scattered through the Norwalk Islands corridor are still icing solid catches on standard high-low rigs with squid strips and sandworms, fished in 20 to 40 feet of water on the last two hours of the incoming. This is one of the more reliable programs in the region right now, and there's no sign of it slowing down heading into September.

Bluefish are filling in the gaps everywhere else. Snapper-sized fish are thick in the back bays and harbor mouths — Oyster Bay, Port Jeff Harbor, the Norwalk River mouth — giving kids and light-tackle guys steady action on small spoons and Kastmasters worked fast near the surface. Out on the drift over structure, cocktail blues in the 3 to 6-pound range are mixing into the fluke and bass catches, especially anywhere bait is bunching along a current edge. If you're marking bait on the sounder and getting nothing but blues, don't fight it — that's usually the sign to move rather than grind it out.

Fluke are the soft spot this week, and it's not for lack of effort. With water this warm spread across the flats, fluke have scattered rather than held tight to structure, which is softening catch rates across the board except in the places that still carry a cooler bottom layer — channel edges, deeper holes, and current-swept structure like the drop-offs around the Norwalk Islands and the deeper stretches off Middle Ground. Four-inch white Gulp paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow right on bottom through those deeper cuts, is still the most consistent producer, but the days of picking fish up anywhere shallow and sandy are on pause until the water cools.

The moon is building toward full, and that's already sharpening the tidal swings — we called this too, expecting the bigger current push to improve current-driven bites, and the last few days of stronger sets through the Stratford Shoal rip and around Charles Island back that up. Over the next 48 to 72 hours, expect that trend to continue: bigger tides, tighter bite windows, better current definition at the structure spots. Watch the bait closely through this stretch — if those peanut bunker and silverside pods start getting nervous and balling tight along the beaches near Port Jeff or the Norwalk Islands, that's often the first tell that bonito or false albacore have slipped into the middle Sound, and nobody will see it on a boat before the birds and the bait give it away first. Nothing confirmed yet this week, but the timing lines up and it's worth keeping an eye on.

Looking further out, the overnight air is starting to carry a slightly cooler edge, and if that holds through the coming week it should begin nudging surface temps down enough to stretch the striper bite later into the morning and earlier into the evening. That's usually the first real crack in the summer pattern before the fall push gets serious. For now, if you've only got one trip in you, fish the dark side of the tide on eels around structure for bass, hit the reefs on the incoming for a guaranteed box of porgy, and keep the bucktails ready in case those blues — or something faster — show up on the drift.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks After Dark: Eels and Bunker Chunks Still Owning the Ebb
reports.subhead: Daytime bass have gone quiet in the mid-70s water, but the night program off Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones is holding up as the moon builds toward full.
reports.body_markdown:
A regular at the bait shop on City Island asked me Tuesday why nobody's marking bass on the meter off Execution Rocks in the middle of the day anymore. Told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen this month: the fish didn't leave, they just went to work at night. Kings Point is reading 70.9 degrees on the surface, and that's warm enough to shut down the daytime bite on anything bigger than a schoolie. The bass that are still around — and there are still plenty around — have pushed down onto structure and slid their feeding windows to dusk, dark, and dawn. That's been the pattern through most of August and it's not breaking yet.

The moon goes full tomorrow night, and we flagged this coming — said the tide swings would sharpen up and the current would start concentrating bait harder as we built toward it. That's exactly what's happening at Stepping Stones and Execution Rocks right now. The extra push on the ebb is stacking peanut bunker and silversides against the rocks, and the bass that have been holding deep and lazy are getting more aggressive in those tighter current windows. If you've been struggling to get bit in the middle of the tide, the last two hours of a big ebb around the new full moon phase is where the switch flips.

Execution Rocks is still the most consistent night spot on this end of the Sound. The outgoing tide pulls hard around that light, and the rockpile on the northeast side holds bass that are using the structure to ambush bait getting swept through. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or bunker chunks fresh cut and fished on the bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current, are doing the damage. Depths in the 15 to 25 foot range right around the rocks, working the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, has been the most productive window. Fish are coming mixed — some short, some solidly in the slot, and a few reports of overslot fish pushing 30 inches that came on whole bunker fished tight to the base of the rocks after 10 p.m.

Stepping Stones is running the same program. That light has always been a spring highway for migrating stripers, but in late August it turns into a night ambush point instead. Live bunker, snagged fresh off the schools that are still stacked up around Matinecock Point, are the best bait when you can get them. If bunker aren't cooperating, chunked bunker on a standard fish-finder rig, fished on the bottom in 20 to 30 feet on the outgoing, has kept rods bending. Bluefish are mixed in with these bass most nights, and if you're getting your chunk baits shredded before the bass show up, that's your sign — the cocktail blues are working the same current seam.

Matinecock Point still has bunker stacked up thick, and that bait is the reason the western end of this zone keeps producing despite the warm water. Snapper blues are thick in Little Neck Bay and up into Manhasset Bay — small gold or silver Kastmasters and tiny bucktails on ultralight gear will keep kids busy for hours off any dock or bulkhead in those back bays, and it's about the most reliable action going right now if you want a guaranteed bend in the rod during daylight.

Fluke have been the tough one. With water this warm across the board, the fluke have spread out across the flats instead of holding tight, and that's softened catch rates almost everywhere except the channel edges and deeper structure where there's still a cooler bottom layer. The Throgs Neck Bridge pilings and the deeper cuts in Manhasset Bay channel are still worth a drift — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet on the last of the outgoing, have been picking at some keeper-class fish, but it's grind fishing right now, not a sure thing.

Porgies remain the bread-and-butter bite around Hart Island and the rockpiles off City Island. Sandworms and clam on a simple two-hook bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet of water is still filling coolers, and that fishery hasn't slowed a bit despite everything else going soft in the heat.

Blackfish are starting to trickle into the conversation, which is the first real sign the calendar's turning even if the thermometer hasn't caught up yet. It's early — most of what's being picked up is incidental on porgy trips over rocky structure — but expect that program to build through September as water temps start their seasonal slide.

Looking ahead, the next few nights around the full moon should be the best window this zone has seen in weeks for night-bite bass at Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones, with the stronger current doing the work of pinning bait against structure. Daytime fishing will likely stay soft on anything beyond snapper blues and porgies until nighttime air temps start knocking the surface water down, which the pattern suggests is still a couple weeks off. If you can only fish one tide this weekend, make it the last two hours of the ebb after dark on a rockpile, eel or bunker chunk in hand, and be patient — this bite rewards waiting on the right stage of the tide more than covering water.

reports.headline: Outgoing After 11: Full Moon Current Loads the Inlet, Bass Trail the Bait Downhill
reports.subhead: Daytime fluke are scattered and sulking on warm flats, but the building moon is stacking bass, blues, and weakfish behind the bait after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Full moon hits tomorrow night, and if you're only getting one shot at Shinnecock this week, that's the tide to build around — not the flood, the outgoing, and not at dinnertime, somewhere past 11 PM when the current really starts hauling. That's the decision that matters more than which lure is in the bag right now. Daytime fishing in the bay has gone soft and spread out with the water sitting warm on the flats, and the fish that are still eating with any conviction are doing it on structure, in the dark, on the stronger half of the tide. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the current concentrating bait would intensify as the moon built toward full — and that's exactly what's setting up at the inlet mouth right now.

The mechanics are simple. Warm surface water on the bay flats pushes fluke and bass off the shallow structure during daylight, and they don't reconcentrate until that outgoing tide starts ripping bait out of the back creeks and marsh edges and funneling it through the inlet. The bigger the tidal swing, the harder that current runs, the tighter the bait gets squeezed against the rocks — and the bass know it. A full moon means bigger swings than we've had in weeks, and the fleet working after dark has noticed the difference already, with better numbers on the last two nights of outgoing than anything in the daylight bite.

Striped bass are the headline, and the program hasn't changed in years because it doesn't need to — fish the east jetty and the deep hole off the Coast Guard station on the back half of the outgoing, working bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range tipped with a strip of fluke belly or a white 5-inch Gulp swimming mullet, bounced slow along bottom where the current edge meets the deeper cut. Slot fish are mixed with a decent number of overslots holding in that deep hole, and the ones being kept in the legal window are mostly 26 to 32 inches. Live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, slow-trolled or drifted right along the rocks after dark, have been the most consistent producer for the bigger fish — this is not a lure most guys reach for until the sun goes down, and there's a reason for that. Bass in that inlet current get cagey in daylight and reckless after dark, which is the whole case for fishing nocturnal here in late August.

Bluefish are riding shotgun with the bass the way they have all month, chopping up peanut bunker schools that are getting pushed out of the back bay on the same outgoing water. Cocktail blues in the 3 to 5-pound range are showing up in the same drifts as the bass, and if you're throwing bucktails or Deadly Dicks along the jetty rocks, expect to lose a few to blue teeth before the night's over. Snapper blues are still thick up in the canal and around the docks in Hampton Bays, which tells you the adult fish still have plenty of forage to stay parked on before they start sliding out toward the ocean side for fall.

Weakfish are the one that rewards patience at Ponquogue Bridge. The pattern there hasn't moved — fish the shadow lines under the bridge lights on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a bucktail-and-Gulp combo or a bare jighead tipped with squid strips slow along the bottom where the current sweeps past the pilings. These aren't blitz fish. It's a handful of quality weakfish in the 3 to 5-pound class on a good night, more shorts than keepers most nights, but the ones coming over the rail have been solid, healthy fish, and the bridge remains the most reliable spot on the south shore for them this time of year.

Fluke are the tougher sell right now, and there's no point pretending otherwise. The warm, thin-oxygen water sitting on the open bay flats has scattered them out instead of holding them tight to structure, which is softening catch rates almost everywhere except the channel edges and the deeper cuts near the inlet where a cooler bottom layer still persists. If fluke are the target, work the deeper water drifting past Tiana Beach into the inlet throat on the last of the incoming, white or chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp trailer, keeping the boat moving slow enough to hug bottom in 15 to 25 feet. It's not a numbers game right now — it's a quality-over-quantity game, and the biggest fish are coming from the deepest, coolest water available.

Porgies remain a dependable bread-and-butter option inside the inlet on bloodworms or clam, fished on the bottom around the jetty rocks on either tide, and worth keeping in your back pocket if the bass and weakfish go quiet on a given night.

Looking ahead, the building moon should keep sharpening these outgoing-tide windows through the weekend, and if the wind stays out of the southwest in the 8 to 12-knot range as it has been, water clarity at the inlet should hold clean enough for the eel bite to keep producing after dark. Watch the tide change at the inlet mouth on calm mornings too — bait is tightening up out there, and it wouldn't be a surprise to see the first false albacore push through on that clean water before Labor Day. For now, the smart move is simple: sleep through the heat, fish the dark, and let the moon do the work.

reports.headline: The West Cut at Moriches Inlet Is Holding the Only Cold Water Left
reports.subhead: Warm-water fluke scattered across the bay flats, but the channel edge by the west jetty is still stacking bait — and bass — on the last of the ebb.
reports.body_markdown:
The bottom of Moriches Inlet has been doing something worth watching this week. The scour hole on the ocean side of the west jetty — the one that deepened out after the last real nor'easter reworked the cut — is still holding a noticeably cooler bottom layer than the rest of the system, and it's become the only reliable current edge in the zone right now. Everything else, from the flats off Tuthill Point to the back stretches toward East Moriches, has gone soft and warm under this stretch of high pressure and light southwest wind. That thermal split is dictating almost everything happening out there this week.

Water in the open bay has been sitting warm and mostly slack on the tide changes, which is exactly the kind of regime that spreads fluke out instead of concentrating them. That's been the story for two weeks now — fish scattered thin across flats that would normally hold a tight pack, softer catch rates everywhere except where current keeps the bottom stirred and a touch cooler. The inlet channel, the west cut, and the deeper edge along Cupsogue are the exceptions, and they've been fishing accordingly better than the open bay. We flagged this pattern last week — said tide-driven windows would be the best bet through the stretch — and that's held up almost exactly. The bite hasn't gotten easier, it's gotten narrower, concentrated into the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood when the current is actually moving water across structure.

Striped bass are in their expected late-August holding pattern — not absent, just not aggressive in daylight. Warm surface temps push them tight to structure and into low-light programs. The better bass action has been coming off bunker schools working the ocean side off Cupsogue and Westhampton, where boats trolling bunker spoons and umbrella rigs in 15 to 25 feet have picked up cocktail-to-mid-20-pound fish mixed in with bluefish on the same schools. Inside the inlet itself, bucktails in the 1- to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked along the deep edge of the west cut on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been the more consistent play for anyone working from a boat or the jetty rocks. Let it settle into that scour hole, hop it slow along bottom — that's where the cooler water is holding both bait and fish.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick through the bay — Tuthill Point, the flats off Mastic, even up into the creeks — small enough that bait shops are selling out of tiny bucktails and Kastmasters just for that action. Cocktail-sized blues in the 2- to 4-pound class are mixing into both the fluke drift and the troll off the inlet, hitting anything moving with flash. If there's a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, it's a snapper blue off a bay dock on a strip of spearing.

Fluke are the honest disappointment of the week, but not a surprise given the water. The better fish — some to 4 and 5 pounds — are still coming from the channel edges near Moriches Inlet and the deeper cuts off Cupsogue, where boats drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, are working 12 to 18 feet of water on the last of the ebb. Away from that current-swept structure, it's mostly a shorts show. Weakfish have shown up sporadically in the same deeper holes near the inlet, mostly incidental fish on bucktails intended for fluke, nothing worth planning a trip around. Porgies remain a dependable bay fish over structure and shell bottom off Westhampton and the inlet rocks, taking clam and squid on light tackle in 10 to 20 feet — a solid backup when the fluke bite goes quiet.

Cupsogue Beach continues to be the most productive surf stretch in the zone, and the reason is bathymetric, not just seasonal — the sandbar troughs there hold bait against a moving current in a way the rest of the ocean beach doesn't right now, and that's been enough to draw both bass and blues within casting range at dawn and dusk. Anyone working the surf should focus on the cuts between bars rather than the open beach face.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward full, and that alone should sharpen these bite windows rather than blow them open. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving through the inlet channel and the west cut on each change, which should tighten up both the bass and fluke bite there even as the open bay stays soft. Watch for the first hints of the fall shift starting to nudge things — cooler nights are still a couple weeks off from meaningfully dropping bay temps, so this holding pattern likely persists through the week. If there's only one window to fish, it's the last two hours of the ebb at the inlet, working the deep edge where the cold water is still hiding.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: fluke scattered, bass sleeping, but the bunker are stacking up for fall
reports.subhead: Warm water has the flatties spread thin and the bass in a holding pattern, but the bait building along the beach says the turn is closer than the calendar suggests.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a mate leaning on the rail at the Captree docks Tuesday morning, coffee in hand, telling anyone who'd listen that he'd run six drifts off the west end of Robert Moses and boxed exactly one keeper fluke for his trouble. "They're out there," he said, "just not together anymore." That about sums up the week on this end of the South Shore, and it's not a mystery why.

Water's been sitting warm — 71 degrees plus out on the ocean side, and the bay's held that heat right through the back channels. Fluke don't love that. When the flats get warm and thin on oxygen, the fish stop schooling up tight and start spreading out looking for anything cooler, which is exactly what's happened from the Robert Moses bridges down through Nicoll Bay. The bite hasn't died, it's just gotten lazy and scattered — the fish that are biting are holding on channel edges and current-scoured structure where there's a cooler bottom layer to sit in, not out on the open flats where they were stacked in June and July.

That means the west channel around the Robert Moses bridge pilings, the deeper cuts off Democrat Point, and the drop-offs along the edges of the Fire Island Inlet channel are still worth your gas money. Boats working 25 to 35 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails or bouncing a Fluke Ball rig tipped with squid strips, have been picking through shorts to find keepers to five and six pounds. It's not a fast bite. It's a patient one — cover ground, find the seam where the current's still moving good water, and stick with it instead of running all over the bay chasing yesterday's report.

Striped bass are doing what late August stripers do around here — going quiet in the heat of the day and turning on after dark. Daytime action inside the bay and off the beach has been spotty at best, mostly cocktail-sized fish mixed with the bluefish on structure, but the real story is what's staging up off the beach. Bunker schools have been thickening up along the south shore beaches from Cedar Beach out toward Gilgo, and that's not nothing this time of year. We flagged this last week — said the pattern would sharpen as the moon swung toward full — and here we are, one day out from the full moon on the 28th, with those bunker schools tightening exactly like we said they would. Guys snagging bait off the beach and running it live through the inlet on the last of the incoming have connected with better fish, slot-class and a few overslots, working the seam where the inlet current meets the open bay just inside Democrat Point. That's your night program right now: livelined bunker, fished on circle hooks in 15 to 20 feet, right on that current edge as the tide turns.

Bluefish have been the one constant nobody's complaining about. Snapper blues are thick in the docks around Patchogue and Sayville — kids with bobbers and spearing are having a field day — while the adult cocktail blues are mixing into the fluke drifts and the structure bites out at the inlet, hammering diamond jigs and bucktails meant for something else entirely. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for a couple hours, that's still the move.

Here's the one to watch: the first scouting reports on false albacore are starting to trickle in from the inlet rips and the deeper cuts in the Great South Bay, right on schedule for the tail end of August. Rainfish and spearing are tightening up along the beach and in the bay rips, which is exactly the bait signature that pulls albies in tight to the structure. Nobody's called a real bite yet — it's a handful of boils and a few guys getting bit off — but with the moon building and the tides about to swing bigger, this is the week that pattern usually goes from rumor to real. Small Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs worked fast through the froth at Democrat Point or the east end rips off Smith Point would be the first thing I'd tie on if that bite shows itself.

Looking ahead, the moon goes full on the 28th, which means bigger water movement through the inlet and sharper, shorter bite windows everywhere from Robert Moses to Patchogue. Wind's holding out of the southwest in that 8 to 12 knot range, keeping the ocean manageable and the water clean. If you've only got one shot this week, make it the last two hours of the incoming at the inlet after dark for bass, or the outgoing at the bridge pilings for fluke — and keep an eye on the horizon for that first real albie blitz. The bait's building. The rest usually follows.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway Bridge after dark: the access point of the week as bunker stack up on the outgoing
reports.subhead: Full moon tides are squeezing bait toward the inlet, and the bridge lights are where the bass are cashing in.
reports.body_markdown:
If you've only got one shot this week, make it the Marine Parkway Bridge on the back half of the outgoing, after the sun's down. That's the access point paying off right now, and it's not close. You can walk right out under the span from the Rockaway side, get your bucktail or eel down into the current seam where the pilings break the flow, and let the tide do the work. Boat guys are doing the same thing from anchor upcurrent of the structure, letting bunker chunks or a live eel swing back into the shadow line. Either way you get there, that shadow line under the bridge lights is holding the most consistent bass in the bay this week.

Why there, why now — it's the bunker. Peanut and adult bunker schools have been building in the bay all month, and they're finally thick enough that the bass are organizing around them instead of just picking off stragglers. We flagged this a week ago, that the outer bay would start showing bait funneling toward the inlet as the season turned, and that's exactly what's happening — pods of bunker getting squeezed through the Rockaway Inlet and Beach Channel corridor on every tide change, with bass, and now a few bigger bluefish, riding the tide right along with them. The moon builds to full tomorrow, and we said that would tighten the current and concentrate the bait even more. It has. The swings at Marine Parkway and Cross Bay Bridge have been noticeably stronger the last few days, and that's pulling fish up onto structure that would otherwise be scattered out on the flats.

Daytime, this is still a summer pattern, not a fall one — water in the bay is sitting warm, mid-70s on the surface, and the bass know it. They're not chasing bait across open flats in the heat of the day; they're holding tight to bridge structure, channel edges, and anything with shade and current, and they're feeding hardest early, late, and after dark. Don't expect a repeat of a spring blitz on a sunny August afternoon. Expect a solid, honest bite in the right window if you fish the tide correctly.

Fluke are the clearest sign the bay hasn't turned yet. They've been soft and scattered for weeks now, spread thin across the warm flats from Grassy Bay to the JFK side, and the counts are down from where they were in June. The fish that are still producing are sitting on channel edges and deeper structure where there's a cooler bottom layer — the drop-offs along Beach Channel, the edges of the Cross Bay Bridge channel, and the deeper cuts inside Rockaway Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow right on bottom, are still drawing strikes, but you're working for keepers now, not culling through shorts. If fluke is your priority this week, fish the deep stuff on the moving tide and don't waste time on the shallow flats until the water cools.

Snapper blues are the one thing you can count on without much thinking. They're thick in every back bay channel and marina basin — Canarsie Pier, Motts Basin, the docks off Cross Bay Boulevard — and they'll hit small metal, Kastmasters, or a piece of spearing under a bobber pretty much any time of day. It's easy fishing, and it's a great way to get a kid or a first-timer bent up while the bigger stuff waits for better light. Mixed in with those snappers, especially on the evening tide near the inlet, cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound class are showing up on structure and around the bass, taking the same bunker chunks and swimming plugs.

Weakfish are around in their usual late-August rhythm — not a headline fishery, but a real one if you know where to look. Drifting bloodworms or small Gulp Sandworms on light jigs over the deeper mud in the main channel near Ruffle Bar, particularly on the tail of the outgoing, has been picking off a few keeper weakfish mixed in with the fluke drift. It's not a fish you're targeting exclusively, but it's worth having a lighter rig rigged up while you're working that channel edge.

For kayak access, Motts Basin and the marsh channels off Broad Channel are still the play — protected water, good current, and you can slip right up on bunker pods without spooking them the way a bigger boat will. Shore access at Breezy Point and along Rockaway Beach is quieter right now than it'll be in a month, but a few bass are working the surf line at night on swimmers and bucktails, especially around the jetties where there's a little structure to hold bait.

Looking ahead, the full moon tomorrow should keep pushing stronger tides through the weekend, and that's the thing to watch. If the bunker keep tightening up against the inlet the way they have been, the next step is the first real fall-style blitz — not this week, but the outer bay and Rockaway Inlet are exactly where it'll show first when it does. Fish the moving water, fish the structure, and keep an eye on the birds working the inlet mouth on the outgoing. That's your tell.

reports.headline: Forget the Fluke Grind — the Bunker Pods Off Short Beach Are Where the Smart Money's At
reports.subhead: While the bay crowd chases scattered fluke on warm mud, the real action is topwater on bait pods and a building tide that's about to get a lot stronger.
reports.body_markdown:
Every boat coming off the ramp this week wants to talk fluke, and every one of them is telling me the same thing — soft bite, fish scattered, marks all over the sounder but nobody biting with any conviction. I'm not surprised. That flat mud on the inside of the bay has been sitting in warm, thin water for two weeks straight, and fluke don't concentrate in that garbage — they spread out and sulk. If that's all you're fishing, you're fishing the wrong program right now.

Here's what I'd be doing instead: working the bunker pods stacking along Jones Beach and off Short Beach on the calm mornings, because that's where the next move is coming from. The bait's been thick off the beach for going on two weeks, rolling in tight, nervous balls right off the second bar, and where you've got bait like that stacked up in late August, you've got fish watching it — even in a stretch where the striper bite inside is supposed to be dead.

And let's be honest about that inside bite — it is a summer lull, not a fall run. The stripers sitting in Hempstead Bay and around the inlet structure right now are holding, not migrating, and they'll stay in that lazy pattern until the nights start cooling off for real, which is probably three weeks out yet. That means daytime bass fishing inside the bay is going to keep being tough sledding — small windows, mostly night-bite guys working the bridge lights and the channel edges after dark. But the ocean side, where that bait is stacked, is a different animal entirely, and that's the disconnect nobody's talking about.

We flagged this a few days back — said the moon building toward full would tighten up the tidal flow and sharpen the dawn and dusk windows at the inlet, and that's exactly what's setting up now with the full moon hitting the 28th. Tide swings are already noticeably stronger than they were a week ago, and that means more water moving through the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood — which is when the current edges off the jetty rocks and the deeper cuts in the main channel start holding fish tight instead of scattered.

The fluke that are biting are coming off the channel edges where that moving water keeps a cooler bottom layer alive — the drop along Sloop Channel and the deeper stretch off the West End are still worth a drift, especially on the last of the outgoing when the current is still hauling bait off the flats. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom, are outfishing bare bucktails and definitely outfishing bait sitters — the fish that are there want something moving, not something sitting dead in warm water. Depths of 15 to 25 feet along that channel edge have been the sweet spot; go shallower than that and you're back in the soft, spread-out bite everybody's complaining about.

Bluefish are still the one thing you can count on inside the bay right now. Snappers are thick around the Wantagh Bridge pilings and up into the Freeport creeks, and cocktail-class blues to three or four pounds are mixing right in with the fluke catches on the channel drifts — same bucktails, same depth, no extra work required. If you've got kids or you just want bent rods without overthinking it, that's your play.

Weakfish are the sleeper story this month, and the shop talk backs it up — a scattered but real showing of legal-sized weakfish coming out of the deeper holes in the bay on incoming water, mostly on soft plastics fished slow near bottom, sometimes on bait if you've got fresh peeler crab or bloodworms. It's not a sure thing, and it's not everywhere, but it's more consistent than it's been in a couple of seasons, and worth a look on the same tide stage that's been producing the fluke.

On the ocean side, the beach bite is going to be the story to watch over the next several days. With bunker still stacking off Short Beach and the stretch of Jones Beach toward the Coast Guard station, calm mornings before the wind builds are the window — topwater plugs and big soft-plastic swimbaits worked right through the edge of the bait balls have a shot at connecting with the bass and blues shadowing those pods, even in a lull month. It won't be every morning. Wind out of the southwest kills it fast once it builds past ten or twelve knots, which has been the pattern most afternoons.

Looking ahead, the full moon on the 28th should keep tightening those tide swings through the weekend, and that's good news for the inlet structure — expect the dawn and last-light windows at the jetty rocks and the main channel drop to keep sharpening as the extra water moves through. If you've only got one shot this week, take it on a moving tide at first light, work the bait if you see it stacked off the beach, and fall back to the channel edges with bucktails if the surface stays quiet. That's the honest read — not everything's biting, but there's enough here to make the trip worth planning around the tide, not just the calendar.

reports.headline: Off Chatham, a Sailfin Ghost Crashes the Bonito Party
reports.subhead: A sailfish showed up in a bonito school 200 yards off the beach — a sign of how warm and strange this water has gotten, and a preview of the albie run still building behind it.
reports.body_markdown:
Picture this: flat calm morning off Chatham, bonito busting bait on the surface the way they do when the water's right, and then a long, sickle-shaped dorsal knifes up through the middle of it that has no business being anywhere near 40 feet of water off Cape Cod. An Atlantic sailfish. , feeding, right in the thick of the bonito. I've fished this water my whole life and I can count on one hand the times anybody's logged a sailfish this close to shore up here — this might only be the second one on record. Doesn't mean much for your Tuesday afternoon trip, but it tells you everything about what's going on with the water temperature right now. It's warm, it's holding warm, and it's pulling fish up here that flat out shouldn't be here.

We flagged this zone for early bonito activity last week, and here it is — bonito are actively showing and getting caught from the Monomoy rips up through the mouth of the Sound. That warm push is exactly what does it. Regional readings off the Connecticut side of the Sound are sitting in the high 60s to low 70s, and inshore around the Cape and the islands the water's running that same range or better, which is squarely in bonito and soon-albie territory. The bonito bite has been the story so far this month — fish showing on bait pods over sand and gravel bottom around Monomoy, working the rip lines on the last two hours of the ebb when the current stacks bait against the shoal edge. Half-ounce Deadly Dicks and small epoxy jigs in olive/white have been the ticket, cast into the nervous water and worked with a fast, erratic retrieve. Some days it's stupid easy — three or four fish in twenty minutes if you find the right push of bait. Other days the wind kicks up out of the southwest, the surface goes choppy, and you can't find a single sign for an hour. That's been the pattern all month: good, not constant. Worth the run out, but bring patience and a full tank.

False albacore haven't shown in real numbers yet, and I'll be honest, I've been checking every day for two weeks now like a kid waiting for Christmas. Great Point on the ebb is where I'd expect the first real showing — that current line off the point concentrates bait hard when the tide's dropping, and albies love working that seam where clean water meets the roiled stuff coming off the rip. We're not there yet this week. I had one report of a scattered pod working briefly off Sankaty on a calm morning, gone in twenty minutes, no repeat. If the warm water signal holds — and that sailfish sighting says it's holding plenty warm — I'd expect albies to start showing in real numbers over the next two to three weeks. When they do, small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in bone or pink — worked fast on 20-pound fluoro leader will get it done. Until then, keep your eyes on the birds and don't waste gas chasing ghosts.

Striped bass are mixing in but not headlining right now. With the Sound running this warm, the bass have pulled back into that classic low-light pattern — strong at first light and again at dusk, quieter through the heat of the day. I've had decent luck working the edges of Horseshoe Shoal early, before the sun gets up, drifting live eels or bouncing a bucktail with a swimming mullet trailer along the sandy drop-offs where the current sweeps bait off the flat. Bluefish are showing consistently mixed into those same bait schools — nothing giant, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but they'll save a slow morning and they hit hard enough to keep things interesting on light tackle. Snapper blues are also thick in the back creeks and harbors around the island right now, which tells you the adult class fish should keep building behind them as we push toward September.

Fluke have been a mixed bag. Some boats working the edges of Nantucket Shoals with squid strips and Gulp on bucktails are finding keepers in 25 to 35 feet, but it's not a slam dunk — plenty of shorts mixed in, and you've got to move around to find the pockets holding size. I wouldn't call it the story of the week the way I might have hoped. It's there if you put the time in, but it's not carrying the report right now the way the bonito are.

Tide-wise, we're sliding off the recent push toward a weaker neap cycle heading into the first quarter moon, which should ease the current a bit over the next several days — good news if you've been getting pushed around out at the rips. Then we build back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that's when I'd expect current strength to really load back up around Great Point and Monomoy, which almost always kicks bait and predators into higher gear together. If the warm water pattern holds through that build — and there's no sign yet it's breaking — I'd bet on albies in numbers right around that window. That's where I'd put my money and my gas money this coming week: working the ebb at Great Point, checking the Monomoy rips for bonito each morning, and keeping half an eye out for anything with a fin that doesn't belong.

reports.headline: Race Point Rip on the Bunker: Bass Busting Topwater in Broad Daylight
reports.subhead: Humpbacks are marking the bait for us this week, and the stripers haven't needed the low light to feed.
reports.body_markdown:
Monday morning, half tide, I had the boat idling off Race Point waiting on a pot of coffee to cool when a humpback came up forty yards off the port rail and blew a breath you could smell. Didn't even flinch the guy in the bow seat — he'd already seen three whales working that same stretch of water since sunup. Where the whales are punching through bait balls, the bass are usually right underneath cleaning up what gets missed, and that's exactly what we found. Peanut bunker balled up thick over the deeper water off the Point, and forty yards inside them, stripers busting on top at ten in the morning like it was dusk. That's not normal for August in the Bay — usually this time of year the fish tuck into low light and you're grinding dawn patrol. But with bunker stacked this dense, the bass are overriding the sun and feeding whenever the bait's there for the taking.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the blitz would hold as long as the bunker schools stayed in the Bay, and here it is, still running strong into the third week of August. Race Point rip has been the epicenter. On the last two hours of the flood, we're drifting the edge in 30 to 50 feet, marking bait thick on the meter, and working live mackerel on a fish-finder rig or an umbrella rig with tubes when the fish are deeper in the column. When they come up and start showing on top, that's when you put the spinning rods down and pick up something you can throw — 9-inch Slug-Go in bone or albino, or a topwater popper like a Guppy or a Gibbs pencil, worked with some hesitation in the retrieve so it looks hurt. Fish have been running mostly schoolie to mid-20-inch class, but we've pulled a few over-slot fish, low 30s, out of the deeper edge of the rip where the current really rips through on that flood stage.

Peaked Hill Bars has been holding its own version of the same show. That stretch of shoal water gets skinny fast, and with the bunker pushing through, bass are pinning bait against the bar itself. Best window there has been the last of the outgoing into dead low, when the structure funnels everything moving through it into a tighter lane. Walking the edge with soft plastics on a light jighead, letting it swing with the current rather than horsing it back, has out-produced straight retrieves. Bluefish have been mixed into almost every one of these blitzes too — mostly 3 to 6 pounds, plenty of teeth marks on the plugs to prove it. If you're not okay losing a lure now and then, tie on wire or expect to re-rig.

Down toward Billingsgate, the shoals are holding structure-oriented bass and a heavier concentration of bluefish than we've seen up at the Point. That sunken island complex has always been a magnet for bait getting pushed around by tide, and this week's been no different — bunker stacking on the flats at the edges, blues working them hard on the last two hours of the flood. Live-lining a bunker on a stinger rig has been the most consistent producer there, though metal — a Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster in the 2-ounce range — will get bit just as fast when they're up top. Snapper blues, meanwhile, are thick in the back creeks and estuary mouths around Barnstable and Brewster, exactly the kind of building block we said to watch for a couple weeks back — small fish now, but that's usually a sign the adult class keeps filling in behind them as the month runs out.

Sandy Neck has been the better bet if you want a mixed bag without chasing blitzes. Fluke fishing on the flats there has been steady, not spectacular — working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails on the incoming has put keepers in the box, mostly 16 to 19 inches, with the occasional fish pushing 4 pounds. Striper activity along that beach has been more blitz-driven too, same bunker pattern showing up tight to the sand on calm mornings.

One oddity worth mentioning — there was a sailfish spotted just outside the Bay off Chatham this week, which tells you the water's running warmer and stranger than typical for mid-August. I wouldn't build a trip around chasing something like that, but it's worth keeping an eye out for anything unusual showing up in your spread or your chum slick.

Cod fishing has stayed quiet, and I'm not expecting that to change soon. The deeper structure off Billingsgate and out toward the Truro grounds needs the water to cool off before those fish move back onto it in numbers — that's typically a late-September into October pattern for us, and this year, with the water running warm the way it has, I'd guess it slides even later than usual.
