Tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should tighten up the current on both Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars and could sharpen the bite even further, assuming the bunker schools hold their ground. The one thing that would break this pattern fast is a hard wind shift pushing that bait off the beach and out of the Bay — worth watching the forecast before you commit to a full day on the water. If it holds calm through the weekend, I'd be back out on that flood tide off the Point with a scoop of mackerel and a topwater rod within reach.

reports.headline: Quick's Hole peanut bunker stacking up — bonito flashing, albies on the clock
reports.subhead: Warm water and building current have bonito showing early in the Sound, and the bait in the Elizabeth Islands rips says the albies aren't far behind.
reports.body_markdown:
Peanut bunker are balling up thick in the rip off Quick's Hole right now, tight little pods getting pushed and turned by the current like they know something's coming for them. I sat on that rip Tuesday afternoon on the last of the ebb and watched three separate bait balls get worked over from below — no visible fish, just that telltale nervous water, bait skittering sideways, then going quiet. That's not bluefish behavior. That's something faster underneath, testing the pack before it commits. I don't have a hookup to prove it yet, but I've fished that hole long enough to know what that looks like, and it looks like the first bonito are already in the neighborhood.

We flagged this a couple weeks back — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would push bait hard enough through the rips to bring bonito and albies into range around Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard, and that's exactly the pattern setting up now. The Sound's running warm, warmer than it has any business being in mid-August, and that Chatham sailfish sighting a few weeks back wasn't a fluke — the whole southern New England coast is sitting in an unusually warm pool of water that's dragging exotic fish north with it. Nantucket Sound already has anglers connecting on bonito. Buzzards Bay is next, and Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole are where I'd be parked waiting for it.

Here's the honest read: it's not blitz-on-top yet. I talked to two guys at the Cuttyhunk town dock who worked Canapitsit Channel and Robinson's Hole both tides Wednesday and came up with bluefish and one dropped bonito between them — no netted fish, but real signs of life. That's where we are right now: transitional, promising, not a sure thing. If you're heading out this week, fish the last two hours of the ebb through Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole, small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dick-style metals in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, worked fast on top of the peanut bunker schools. Don't overthink the retrieve — bonito want speed, and if albies are mixed in they'll want it even faster.

Striped bass are still in their late-summer holding pattern, and that's not changing until the water eases off in September. Daytime bass have gone quiet in the warm shallows — I'm not finding much inside Buzzards Bay proper between 10 and 4. But the Cape Cod Canal is a different animal entirely. The new moon tide dumped a serious surge of current through there, and slot and over-slot bass have been eating topwater plugs — Doc's or Guppy-style poppers — off the herring run current lines through the middle of the week. Fish that current seam hard on the last two hours of either tide, dawn or dusk, and you'll find fish stacked where the flow narrows near the railroad bridge.

Bluefish are thick and getting thicker. Snapper blues are packed into the back bays around Menemsha and up into the Cuttyhunk pond — that's the bait pipeline for everything else happening out there, and it's a strong tell that bigger adult blues will keep building through the rest of August into September. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod while you wait on the albies, drop small Kastmasters or bucktail teasers around the Menemsha jetty on the incoming and you won't wait long.

On the bottom, Mashnee flats are still the most consistent thing going in the bay for fluke — 3 to 5 pound fish coming on Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and bubblegum, 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow across 15 to 20 feet on the outgoing. The channel side of Mashnee has been better for scup and the occasional sea bass, small strips of squid on a two-hook bottom rig doing the damage in 25 to 30 feet. Structure east of Cleveland Ledge is worth a stop too — anglers running spot-lock trolling motors have quietly turned into the smartest guys on the water this month, holding dead-still over marks along Hog Island Channel and the Stony Point Dike drop-offs and jigging bucktails straight down without the hassle of anchoring twice a tide. If you've got the technology, use it — precision over structure is what's separating full coolers from empty ones right now.

Looking ahead, the tide is building back toward the August 28 full moon, and that's the thing I'm watching closest. More current through Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole means more bait getting pushed and compressed, which is exactly the recipe that turns a few nervous bait balls into a real blitz. If the warm pool holds its position — and there's no sign yet that it's breaking down — I'd bet on bonito showing in numbers around the Elizabeth Islands within the next week to ten days, with false albacore stacking in right behind them, same as they do every fall once the current gets some teeth in it. I wouldn't skip a trip to Robinson's Hole this weekend. Bring metals, bring patience, and watch that water — the bait's already telling you what's coming.

reports.headline: Stellwagen Basin in 110 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, whales pointing the way to bluefin
reports.subhead: Whale activity thick along the Edge this week is the tell — bait's piled up, and the bluefin are starting to work it.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ten feet on the sounder along the Stellwagen Edge Tuesday morning, and the bottom paint was so thick with marks I had to run the gain down twice. That's haddock water — soft mud basin, the kind of bottom that holds sand eels and worms this time of year — and the haddock have been sitting right on it, not migrating off it, not spooking off it. That's the pattern I want to see in mid-August.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefin activity around Stellwagen would keep building as bait stacked up on the bank, with whale activity on top a good tell for what's underneath. That's exactly what's playing out. The humpbacks have been thick along the Edge and working north toward Tillies Bank, and where the whales are lunge-feeding on sand eels, the bluefin aren't far behind. I had two boats radio me Thursday describing fish busting right through bait balls the whales had pushed to the surface — that's about as textbook as it gets for a Stellwagen tuna show. Doesn't mean every fish out there is eating a bar jig, but it means the forage base is doing exactly what it needs to do to hold fish on the bank instead of pushing them through.

Groundfish-wise, it's been a two-bottom program all week. Cod are still on the gravel — the harder patches along the Stellwagen Edge and out toward Tillies Bank where the bottom kicks up rougher, 90 to 130 feet depending on where you find the hard stuff on the plotter. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a chunk of clam has been out-producing bait-only rigs for me, mostly because the cod are eating aggressively right now — they want something moving, not just soaking. Fish have been running average-to-decent size, nothing to write home about in terms of giants, but a solid box of keepers if you work the edges where the gravel breaks up and put in the drift time.

Haddock are the more consistent story. Basin bottom — soft mud, 100 to 120 feet — has been holding fish tight, and a standard two-hook rig with clam bait or a small teaser jig has been getting bit steady on the drift. This is bread-and-butter Stellwagen haddock fishing, the kind that doesn't make headlines but fills coolers. Party boats working the deeper structure on the bank have leaned on this all week because it's dependable when the offshore stuff is more of a gamble.

And it is a bit of a gamble right now, if I'm honest. The bluefin activity is building, not established. I wouldn't tell a reader to burn a tank of fuel out to Carter Canyon or Cape Cod Tails chasing giants unless you've got eyes on breaking fish or a whale show worth following — those grounds are producing on temperature breaks, but the breaks have been moving day to day, and I've had guys find nothing where there was a blitz the day before. The smarter offshore money this week has been staying closer to the Stellwagen Edge itself, working the whale activity as it develops rather than running blind out to the canyon approaches on a hope.

Mackerel have been spotty as bait go-to's — some schools tight to the bank, some not, so if you're jigging your own bait before you set up on tuna, don't assume it'll be there. Check early, stock up, and don't burn daylight hunting mackerel once you've got fish showing topside.

Pollock have been mixed in with the cod on some of the harder structure, nothing to specifically target but a nice bonus fish on the jig when they show. Hake have been around the deeper mud edges of the basin in smaller numbers — not a program I'd build a trip around, but worth a drop if you're already anchored up on haddock and want variety in the box.

Moon's building toward the August 28 full, which should firm up the tide push over the next week and generally tighten up bait concentration on the bank — that's usually good news for both the groundfish and whatever's chasing the sand eels topside. If the whale activity keeps building the way it has, I'd expect the bluefin story to keep developing right along with it rather than fade. The wildcard is whether that offshore warm water holding position near the canyon approaches shifts — if it slides, the temperature break that's been organizing the tuna could move with it, and that changes where you want to be looking.

My plan for the coming week: mornings on the Basin mud for haddock while it's calm, working the gravel edges for cod on the back half of the tide, and keeping one eye on the horizon for whale activity every time we're running between spots. If you see the surface disturbed and birds working tight over it, that's worth a five-minute detour with a bar jig rigged and ready. It's not a guaranteed hookup, but it's the best tell we've got on this bank right now, and it's been paying off often enough to chase.

reports.headline: Plymouth Beach at Noon: Bass Crushing Pogies in Broad Daylight
reports.subhead: Boston Harbor stays a grind on the outgoing while Plymouth's daytime bunker blitzes make the drive south worth it.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip the harbor and run the truck down to Plymouth, and I don't regret it. When pogies stack tight to a beach and the bass decide feeding beats caution, you go where the bait is, not where the ledge is. That's the whole job some weeks — reading where the fish want to be, not where you wish they'd be.

What's happening off Plymouth Beach right now is the kind of thing you don't see every August. Full-sized pogie schools are holding tight against the sand, and stripers are blowing up on them at midday — not dawn, not dusk, noon, with the sun straight overhead. Hundreds to low thousands of fish working bait balls right off the beach, and hardly any boats or waders on them. We flagged this pattern building last week, said the dawn bite in the harbor would hold as long as bait stayed concentrated — this is the bigger version of that same story, just relocated south with more forage packed in tighter. When there's that much bunker in the water column, stripers stop caring about light levels. They just eat.

If you're running down there, don't overthink the presentation. A big topwater popper or a 6-inch soft-plastic swimbait chucked into the edge of the boil will get bit fast — the fish aren't picky, they're opportunistic. Same goes for a bunker-imitation glide bait worked just outside the melee; the bigger fish tend to sit under the school and eat the stragglers, not the ones getting worked in the middle. Keep the boat off the school itself and cast into it — running through it just scatters bait and shuts the window down early.

Back in the harbor, it's a different animal this week. Water's sitting warm — mid-70s inshore — and that's pushed the bass program back into the classic low-light pattern. Deer Island on the last two hours of the outgoing has been steady but not explosive: live mackerel drifted along the rip where the tide pulls off the flat, fish in the 26 to 32-inch range, mostly keepers with the occasional overslot mixed in. Spectacle Island's north side has been similar — eels fished slow along the drop into deeper water at first light before the sun gets high and pushes them down. Nothing blitz-worthy in the harbor proper, but a dependable pick if you're working structure correctly and hitting the tide change.

Nahant and the rocks up toward Gloucester have turned into bluefish country for now. Snapper blues are thick in the coves and river mouths — we called this building two weeks back, and it's playing out exactly like that, snappers everywhere setting up for the adult class fish that typically show as August turns to September. Right now it's mostly the smaller 1 to 3-pound blues hammering anything shiny — small Deadly Dick jigs, Kastmasters, silver spoons worked fast off the rocks at Bass Rocks and Brace Cove. A few 4 to 5-pound blues have mixed in on the outgoing, so keep a rod rigged heavier just in case. If the bunker schools that are lighting up Plymouth push north along the shore, expect that adult bluefish presence to build fast — that's the pattern to watch.

Cod and haddock offshore on Stellwagen have been a tough sell in this heat. Warm surface water has pushed whatever bottom activity there is deep, and the trips I've heard about have needed real depth — 180 feet plus — and even then it's been a slow pick, not a program. Not the priority right now with what's happening inshore.

Flounder's mostly an afterthought this time of year in the harbor — that bite really turns on again once the water starts cooling in September, so I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them right now.

Tide-wise, we're building back toward the August 28 full moon, and that means stronger current is coming both in the harbor and through the Cape Cod Canal corridor to the south. Stronger tides usually mean better current edges, which means better bait concentration, which is exactly what's driving the Plymouth pattern already. If that bunker stays tight to the beach through the weekend, I'd expect the blitz window to hold, maybe even sharpen up as the moon builds. The risk is weather — a stiff onshore blow or a push of cooler water could scatter that bait fast, and this kind of daylight event can shut off as quickly as it opened.

My plan for the coming week: mornings in the harbor working Deer Island and Spectacle Island on the last of the outgoing with live bait, then running south midday when conditions allow to check Plymouth Beach while that pogie show is still on. If the bait holds, that's where I'd put my time. If it slides offshore or gets pushed by wind, I'd shift back to the harbor rips and lean on the bluefish up around Nahant to fill the box while we wait for the next window.

reports.headline: 180 on the gravel, 210 on the mud: Jeffrey's split personality this week
reports.subhead: Cod are holding tight to the hard bottom while haddock work the mud basins, and the bluefin we flagged last week are starting to show.
reports.body_markdown:
180 feet on the north end of Jeffrey's Ledge, hard gravel and scattered boulder — that's been my first mark every trip out of Rye this week, and it's still holding cod. Not a slaughter, but steady. Three to six keeper cod a drift in that 170-190 foot band, mostly 8 to 15 pounds, a few pushing 20 on the bigger jigs. The pattern hasn't changed much from last month: find the hard edge where gravel meets a little rubble, drop a diamond jig or a chunk of clam on a high-low rig, and work it slow off the bottom. The cod are sitting right on that structure, not roaming, so precision on the drift matters more than speed.

Slide east and a little deeper — 200 to 220 feet where the bottom softens to mud and clay — and that's where the haddock have been stacking. This is the mud-bottom program I run every August, and it's been paying off. Haddock to 3 and 4 pounds on standard cod rigs tipped with clam, sometimes doubling up on the hi-lo when the school's thick under the boat. The sounder tells the story fast on these drifts — if you're marking that soft, spread-out return low to bottom, that's haddock water, and you fish it different than the gravel. Lighter jigs, slower lift, let the bait sit.

Platts Bank has been the wildcard. I made two trips out there this week and it split — one day loaded with pollock in the 90 to 110 foot range over structure, schoolie-sized but a few pushing 12 pounds, hitting jigs worked with a fast erratic retrieve up off bottom. The next day it was quiet, just hake scattered on the mud edges, which tells me the bait hadn't settled in yet. Pollock chase bait around more than cod or haddock do, so Platts is going to be hit or miss until whatever's pushing that bait through decides to hold still for a few tide cycles.

Tillies Bank and Scantum Basin I fished lighter this week, mostly scouting. Tillies still has cod on the gravel humps in the 150-170 foot range, similar story to the north end of Jeffrey's — small but steady numbers, nothing to write home about but enough to fill a cooler if you're patient and work the edges right. Scantum's been mostly hake and a few pollock over the softer bottom, nothing that changes my plan for the week.

Now the part everybody's been asking about at the dock — the bluefin. We flagged this coming a week ago, saying the bait was building on the ledge and the tuna trend would likely strengthen, and that's exactly what's playing out. I've had giants show on the meter working bait balls over the deeper flats off Jeffrey's, and I know of fish being hooked within sight of the ledge itself this week. It's not the daily circus you'll hear about further south or up in the Maine warm pockets — the water out here stays cooler at depth, typical for this stretch of the Gulf of Maine in mid-August, and that's kept the bite more occasional than reliable. But when the bait balls up tight over the humps, especially in that late-afternoon window when the tide starts to build, the giants are coming up on it. If you're rigging for tuna out here, keep a rod ready on the troll while you're working groundfish drifts — I've had guys hook up almost by accident chunking mackerel off the stern while waiting on a cod bite.

Mackerel themselves have been thick around Cape Ann and pushing out toward Thatcher Island, which is a good early tell — where the mackerel schools go, the bigger predators follow. I'd keep an eye on that corridor between Thatcher and the ledge over the next week as bait continues to concentrate.

Tide's been building toward the August 28 full moon, and that's going to matter more as we get into the back half of this week. Stronger tidal push means better current on the gravel edges — cod tend to feed harder when there's some water moving, so I'd expect the bite on the north end of Jeffrey's to sharpen up rather than fade as we approach the full moon. Haddock on the mud are less tide-dependent; they'll keep producing on the softer bottom regardless of how hard the current's running.

My read for the coming week: keep cod effort on the gravel structure at Jeffrey's in that 170-190 foot band, work haddock on the mud basins deeper, and treat Platts as a game-day decision based on what the morning marks show. If the bait stays put over the ledge humps, I'd expect the bluefin activity to keep building through the week rather than tail off — that's the single best offshore story going right now, even if it stays a bonus rather than the main event. Bring the jig rods for groundfish, but don't leave the trolling gear at the dock.

reports.headline: Monhegan mackerel and Boothbay bluefish: warm water pushes a southern fish north
reports.subhead: Snapper blues we flagged two weeks back are turning into keeper-class fish in the Damariscotta, while groundfish still hold deep in Penobscot Bay.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty years hauling traps off Monhegan and I can count on one hand the summers bluefish showed up thick enough in Boothbay Harbor to matter. This is one of them. I was running gear past The Cuckolds early last week, water slick and warm enough that it didn't sting my hands pulling wet warp, and there they were — a school of blues busting bait right off the mooring field, close enough that a fella on a Whaler was casting Kastmasters from his cockpit without even starting the engine. That's not normal water for this coast in mid-August, and it's not normal fish either. Old-timers in this harbor remember a handful of years like it, and they all说 the same thing — take advantage while it lasts, because Gulf of Maine warm pulses don't stick around.

We flagged this two weeks ago — said the snapper blues thick in the back bays and river mouths would keep building into adult-class fish through late August, and that's exactly what's happening in the Damariscotta and Sheepscot. The snappers that were finger-length in July are pushing 12 to 16 inches now, and mixed in are genuine 3- and 4-pound blues hitting topwater poppers and small metal off the mouth of the Damariscotta on the last two hours of the incoming tide. If you're throwing gear at them, keep it small — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or a 3-inch Slug-Go worked fast on top. They're not fussy, but they are moving fast through the current seams, so cover water instead of anchoring on one rip.

Striped bass are riding shotgun with that bait, same as they always do when mackerel and pogies stack up this thick. Eastern Egg Rock has been the most reliable striper water all week — the puffins are still working the surface bait balls out there, and where the birds are diving, there's usually a bass or two underneath cleaning up scraps. I've had the best luck working the western side of the rock on the last hour of the ebb, drifting live mackerel under a slip float, or working a white Deceiver through the froth when they're up on top. Fish have run mostly schoolies to 26 inches, with the occasional slot fish mixed in around dawn before the boat traffic picks up.

Mackerel themselves have been thick as I've seen them in a few seasons — Monhegan's ledges on the western side, in that 40 to 60 foot stretch off Manana, have been stacked with them most mornings on the last of the flood. A string of six mackerel jigs dropped straight down will load up fast, and that bait is exactly what's pulling the pollock up. Pollock have been breaking the surface at Monhegan in the evening light, working the edges where the current pinches around the ledges — cast a diamond jig or a 3-ounce Hopkins into the boil and let it flutter down through the school. Fish have run 3 to 8 pounds, with a couple pushing better than 10 taken on the troll working the drop-off east of the island.

Groundfish, meanwhile, are staying put right where they should be this time of year — deep, and out of the warm surface layer entirely. Cod and haddock are holding in the channels off Matinicus and in the deeper water east of Isle au Haut, 100 to 140 feet, and they want bait fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide. Jigging with a diamond jig tipped with squid, or drifting clam bait on a high-low rig, has produced steady if not spectacular numbers — a mix of legal haddock to 24 inches and cod that are mostly shakers with a few keepers mixed in. It's not the kind of fishing where you fill a cooler fast, but it's honest work if you're willing to run the extra miles out past Vinalhaven and fish the deep water seriously.

Stonington and Deer Isle have been quieter than Egg Rock or Monhegan this week, which surprised me some given how good the tide lines usually set up through that thoroughfare in August. Wind out of the southwest most days kept things a little sloppy on the outer ledges, and the bass that were there seemed to slide off with the chop. If you're fishing that stretch, I'd work the lee side structure around Crotch Island on the last of the ebb, when the current settles and bait gets pinned against the rocks.

Tides are building back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that's going to matter. Bigger water means stronger current lines at Egg Rock and Monhegan, which should tighten up the bass and pollock bite around the ledges and give the mackerel schools somewhere firm to hold instead of scattering with every tide change. If this warm pulse holds through the week — and there's no sign yet it's breaking — I'd expect the bluefish push into Boothbay and the Damariscotta to keep building right along with it, maybe far enough to see them working past the Cuckolds and into outer Muscongus Bay by month's end. That would be something worth writing about. For now, my money's on Egg Rock at first light and Monhegan on the last of the flood — that's where I'm putting my own time this week, and I'd have a jig rod rigged for pollock just in case the mackerel show up thick again.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Turns Bass, Blues Crash Higgins at First Light
reports.subhead: Warm water pushed the bait tight to the rocks this week, and for an hour on either side of the turn, Southern Maine looked like it meant business.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, half hour before the top of the incoming at the Pool, and a striper north of 30 inches about tore the rod out of my hands on a black Gibbs Danny worked slow across the current seam by the channel markers. Didn't see her coming — just felt the plug go from swimming to dead stop, then that heavy, stubborn pull toward the rocks that only a real bass gives you. She came in at 34 inches, fat, full of pogies, and went back to do it again to somebody else. That's the kind of take that reminds you why you stand in the dark waiting on a tide.

That's been the story all week — not everywhere, not all day, but at the Pool on the incoming, it's been the real thing. The water here jumped hard the last ten days, up out of the low 60s into the upper 60s and touching low 70s in the harbor mouths, and that's pulled bait tight against structure and kept it there longer than usual. Pogies and peanut bunker are stacked in the pool and along the flats toward Fletcher's Neck, and the bass are following them right up onto the sod banks on the push. Best window is the last two hours of the incoming through the top — after that the current goes slack, the bite goes quiet, and you're better off moving.

Higgins Beach has had its moments too, mostly at first light. Bluefish, not giants, mostly 2 to 4 pounds with a few pushing 6, have been slashing through pods of bait right in the wash, close enough that guys are hooking up on the first cast off the sand. Poppers and 1-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the foam have been drawing the strikes — don't finesse it, blues want commotion. By 8 or 9 with the sun up and the wind lying down, that bite shuts off hard. If you want a shot at Higgins, be there in the dark with coffee already gone cold.

Prouts Neck has been streaky, which is normal for this spot — it lives and dies on wind direction. We had a stretch of southwest wind mid-week that pushed bait right up against the ledges on the north side, and that turned on a decent bass bite for two mornings running, mostly schoolies with a few keepers mixed in on white Slug-Gos worked over the boulder fields. When the wind swings northeast or dies flat, Prouts goes quiet fast — the current there needs that push to concentrate anything.

We flagged last week that the striper-and-mackerel pattern would carry this zone through August, and that's exactly what's held. Mackerel have been thick off Pine Point pier and the jetty at Wells Harbor, schools rolling through on the tide changes and readily taking small Swedish Pimples and diamond jigs worked fast through the water column. Bring a few home for bait — a fresh mackerel strip fished on a fishfinder rig off the Pool rocks has out-produced everything else for the bigger bass holding deeper, especially on the dropping tide when the current pulls hard past the channel.

Flounder fishing has been steady, not spectacular, in Wells Harbor and up into the Kennebunk River mouth. Bloodworms and sandworms on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished slow on the bottom over mud and sand on the incoming, have been putting keeper flatties in coolers most mornings. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but it's a reliable box-filler when the surf bite goes soft midday.

Cod and pollock have held to the usual pattern off Cape Elizabeth — working the ledges and broken bottom in 40 to 60 feet with diamond jigs or tube-and-worm trolled slow has been producing a mixed bag, pollock outnumbering cod about three to one right now. Nothing huge, but enough action to make a slow surf morning worth turning into a boat afternoon.

We also called it on the bluefish — said the snapper blues packing the back bays and river mouths would build toward adult class as August wore on, and that's starting to show. The blues hitting Higgins and mixing into the mackerel schools off Pine Point are noticeably bigger than what we had three weeks ago. Expect that trend to keep building into September as the water holds warm.

Looking ahead: tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should sharpen up the current at the Pool and put more push behind that incoming bite — that's where I'd spend my time if I only had one morning. If the southwest wind cooperates again, Prouts Neck is worth a look too. Higgins stays a dawn-only proposition until the water cools some. And if the surf goes flat and quiet on you, there's no shame in running out to the ledges for cod and pollock — better than standing on dry rocks waiting on fish that aren't there yet.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 6:52: bass on bunker, bonito still a no-show off the Block
reports.subhead: Daylight blitzes are stacking bass on peanut bunker from the Ledge to Sandy Point, but the first bonito flip hasn't happened yet — here's why, and what's next.
reports.body_markdown:
SW Ledge slack hit at 6:52 this morning, and for about twenty minutes on either side of it we had bass stacked on the down-tide edge in 36 to 40 feet, working through a peanut bunker school like they had a schedule to keep. That's the tell right now — the fish aren't waiting for low light. There's so much bunker piled up between the Ledge and Sandy Point that the bass have stopped caring about the sun. We had three keepers and a dozen releases by 7:30, all on white bucktails in the 1.5-ounce range tipped with a 4-inch white Gulp, worked slow along the current seam where the ledge drops from 30 into the deeper water.

This is the same pattern that's been running from Narragansett Bay north — dense bait overriding the normal dawn/dusk rulebook. We're seeing it play out right in our own water. The rip line off Sandy Point has had the most consistent daylight activity all week, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the bunker get funneled tight against the beach and the bass pin them against the drop-off. If you're running out of Galilee, don't sleep past 8 a.m. thinking you missed it — some of the better blitzes we've seen have come at 10 and 11 in the morning, right in bright sun, with birds working tight over showering bait.

We flagged the bluefish angle a few days back — said the snapper blue explosion in the back channels was a sign adult-class fish would keep building through late August, and that's exactly what's happening. The blues mixing into these bunker blitzes now are pushing 3 to 6 pounds, not the little choppers we had in July, and they're plenty willing to eat the same bucktail the bass are hitting. If you want to separate the two, a wire leader ahead of a Deadly Dick or a bunker spoon will keep you in blues without shredding your bass gear every other cast.

Fluke fishing has been a grind-it-out proposition rather than a sure thing. We're finding keepers on the drift off SW Ledge and along the flats south of the island in 25 to 45 feet, but you're picking through a lot of shorts to find a 20-incher. Bigger baits are the move — a 5-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, fished slow and dragged rather than hopped, has been outproducing the smaller stuff. Best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, same as the bass, when the current tightens up the bait and the fluke stop being lazy. Black sea bass have filled in nicely on the same structure — the humps and rock piles southwest of the island are holding decent numbers on squid strips and clam, a dependable backup when the fluke bite is spotty, which it has been more often than not this week.

Now for the disappointment of the week — no bonito, no albies off the Block yet. I know the chatter out of Nantucket Sound and around the Cape has bonito showing and even a sailfish sighting off Chatham, which tells you the water up that way has gone unusually warm. We haven't seen that heat signature push into our rips yet. North Rip and the water off North Light and Clay Head are still fishing like mid-August striper and bluefish water, not albie water. My read is we're maybe two to three weeks out from the first bonito flip showing off Southeast Light, and that's contingent on this warm pattern holding and sliding our way rather than staying bottled up around the Cape. I wouldn't burn a trip specifically hunting bonito at the Block yet — but I'd keep a small metal rigged and ready in the boat, because when they show, they show fast.

Offshore, the tuna bite out toward Block Canyon and the East Canyons remains the more interesting long-range option for Galilee boats with the range to run. That warm eddy water pushing up from the canyons is still in position, and bluefin and some yellowfin opportunity is there for boats willing to make the trip — better than the dead water further south right now.

Tide-wise, we're five days off the new moon and building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should sharpen the current at every rip in this zone — SW Ledge, the Sandy Point rip, the water off North Light. If that bunker stays put through the build, expect these daylight blitzes to hold steady rather than fade, though the wind will have the final say — a stiff southwest blow will flatten the bite fast by pushing the bait off the structure. My plan for the coming week is early starts at the Ledge on the last of the ebb, then working east toward Sandy Point as the sun climbs, keeping one rod rigged with metal in case something with a longer tail shows up sooner than expected.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock Holds Bottom, Harpswell's Coves Run Thick With Snapper Blues
reports.subhead: A warm pulse pushing up from the south is stretching bluefish and bass activity further into the bay than August usually allows.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent an hour on the porch at Bailey Island last Tuesday evening with a cup of coffee and a pair of binoculars, watching a pod of peanut pogies get pushed tight against the rocks by something working them from below. Turned out to be a dozen or so bluefish, nothing over three pounds, but eager enough to send bait skittering across the surface in that nervous, silvery way that tells you exactly what's happening even before you see the fish roll. That's not an unusual sight for late August in the coves around Harpswell — what's unusual is how far it's crept up the bay this year, and how early in the month it started.

We flagged this two weeks back — said the snapper blues thick in the back bays and estuaries were a sign that adult-class fish would keep building through late August. That's exactly what's playing out. The coves off Bailey Island, the mouth of the New Meadows, and the back channels around Portland are holding good numbers of blues in the one-to-four-pound range, with a scattering of fish pushing five and six mixed in. Small poppers and quarter-ounce Kastmasters worked fast over the top are producing well on the last two hours of the incoming tide, when the bait gets pinned against structure and the blues stop being selective.

The warm water pushing north along the coast — the same pulse that's been driving daylight striper blitzes well south of us and stretching bluefin activity up toward the midcoast — is doing something similar here, just at a smaller scale. Casco Bay hasn't turned into Narragansett Bay, and it won't, but the striped bass have responded to the extra degree or two by staying active later into the morning than I'd expect for mid-August. Cape Small has been the most consistent spot for bass on the ledges — I've had good luck working the outgoing tide there with three-inch white paddletails on quarter-ounce jigheads, drifted along the rockweed edges in eight to fifteen feet of water. The fish are keying on sand eels and small pogies pushed out of the coves on the ebb, and the bite window has been running a solid hour past what I'd normally call quits.

Two Lights is fishing more like a classic dusk pattern — bass holding tight to the rocks, feeding hard in the last real light and again at first light, mostly on topwater. A black Gibbs pencil popper worked slow along the current seams there has taken fish to better than thirty inches this week, though the numbers have been modest — two or three keepers on a good outing, not a blitz by any stretch.

Out at Halfway Rock, the groundfish have held steady, which is really the story there most Augusts. Cod and the occasional haddock are still coming off the ledges in the forty-to-ninety-foot range, but you need to fish it on the slack — the current runs hard enough out there that anything but dead-low or dead-high water turns your jig into a kite. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or straight cut mackerel on a two-hook bottom rig, have been the go-to. It's not a fast bite, but it's a reliable one, and the fish have been decent size for this time of year — several cod in the six-to-nine-pound range reported by boats working the north side of the ledge.

Mackerel schools are still very much present around Peaks Island and along the Portland shipping channel edges, which matters both for the table and for bait. A string of mackerel jigs dropped through a school holding at twenty to thirty feet on the last of the incoming tide will fill a bucket fast, and that fresh mackerel is exactly what's been producing the better bass and groundfish catches elsewhere in the bay this week.

Worth watching closely over the next several days: if this warm pulse keeps pushing north the way it has, there's a real chance we start seeing some of the recreational bluefin activity currently concentrated up around York and Rockland work its way into range near Halfway Rock. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet — that's speculative, not something I've seen firsthand — but it's the single biggest variable I'm tracking right now, and I'll have a clearer read after this week.

The moon is building back toward the August 28 full, which should firm up the tidal swing across the bay and likely sharpen both the bass bite on the outer ledges and the bottom bite at Halfway Rock as current strength returns. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide at Cape Small early, then run out to the Rock and fish the slack around midday for cod. Not a guaranteed day, but the ingredients are lining up.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Has Blues Tight to the Rocks From Beavertail to Napatree
reports.subhead: Bass are mixed in on the blitzes at first light, scup and fluke are salvaging the slow tides, and the breachways are starting to whisper albie.
reports.body_markdown:
The peanut bunker showed up thick around Beavertail this week, balled up tight against the rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, and where there's bait like that stacked against structure, something's going to eat it. I watched three separate blow-ups off the Jamestown side Tuesday morning — bluefish mostly, three to five pounds, absolutely shredding through the pods, with a few slot bass mixed underneath picking off the scraps that drifted down. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch of rock: bunker pushed tight to the ledges, blues on top, bass working the bottom of the water column where the current pins the bait against the boulders.

Newport side has been the same story. Castle Hill and the rocks below Brenton Point have had bunker schools sitting in the wash on the last of the ebb, and if you're there at gray light with a white bucktail or a Deadly Dick, you can cast right into the melee. Problem is the window's short — once the sun gets up and that water warms another degree or two, the bunker scatter off the structure and slide into deeper water, and the bite goes quiet until the tide turns again. I've had my best luck fishing the hour before and the hour after low, working the seam where the current pulls off the ledge into the deeper wash.

We flagged the snapper blue push a few weeks back and said the adult class would build behind it — that's exactly what's happening. The three-to-four-pound blues chewing through those bunker schools are the fish that were snappers in the back bays a month ago. They've grown into real teeth now, and if you're fishing bunker chunks or working topwater at the breachways, expect them to show up in numbers before the bass do.

Speaking of the breachways — Charlestown, Quonochontaug, and Weekapaug are all worth a look right now, though it's more bluefish and schoolie bass than anything else at the moment. I fished the Charlestown breachway on a dropping tide last weekend and picked up bluefish steadily on a green machine trolled through the rip, with one bass around 26 inches that came off a white Slug-Go worked slow along the rock wall on the inside. No albies yet that I've seen or heard about, but the water's warm enough and the bait's right — this is usually the window where the first fish start testing the breachways before the real push shows up in September. I'd start checking Napatree and the mouth of the Pawcatuck in the next two weeks, especially on a calm morning when you can actually see fins.

Fluke have been a mixed bag. The deeper holes off Sakonnet Point — that 30 to 40 foot water off the rocks — have given up some decent fish on Gulp in white or pink glow, tipped with a strip of squid, drifted slow on the last of the outgoing. Nothing to brag about size-wise, mostly 16 to 19 inches, but enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the drift. Second Beach and the sandy stretches toward Sachuest have been slower — that warm surface water has fluke laying low, less willing to chase, so you need to bounce bottom right on their nose rather than working a fast retrieve.

Scup have been the honest bite all week. Anywhere there's structure — the rocks off Beavertail, the Jamestown Bridge pilings, the reef off Watch Hill — you can load a cooler with scup on squid strips and sandworms fished on high-low rigs in 15 to 25 feet. It's not glamorous but it's reliable, and on the days the bass and blues go quiet on you, that's where I've been filling out the trip.

Tog talk is starting around the docks even though the real bite is still weeks off. A few guys have been scouting the ledges off Watch Hill and around Napatree on green crabs during the slack tide, just checking which cracks are holding fish before the fall run gets serious. Too early to call it a pattern, but worth keeping in the back of your head as September approaches and that water starts to cool.

Looking ahead, the tide's been building toward the August 28 full moon, and that stronger flow should tighten the bunker schools even further against the rocks and sharpen up those dawn windows at Newport and Jamestown. If the wind stays cooperative — southwest and light, which is what we've had — I'd expect the blitz pattern to hold through the weekend. Watch for any shift to a hard onshore blow, though; that'll blow the bait off the ledges and scatter everything into deeper water fast. My plan for the next few days is early mornings on the Newport rocks for blues and mixed bass, then sliding down to the breachways midday to keep an eye out for that first sign of albies. It's close. Not there yet, but close.

reports.headline: East end pre-dawn ebb, 4-knot push: slot bass on top, squid stacking the lights
reports.subhead: New-moon current has the Canal doing what it does best — concentrating bait against structure and turning slot stripers into surface predators before the sun's even up.
reports.body_markdown:
0517, east end, ebb running somewhere around four knots off the Bourne side rocks — and the water in front of me exploded like someone dropped a manhole cover in it. That's the number I've been chasing all week. When that current hits its stride on the front half of the ebb, right around first light, the bass stop thinking and start eating.

Monday through Wednesday this week gave us the best window of the summer so far. New-moon minus tides pushed extra water through the ditch, and that extra flow does exactly what thirty years of watching this place has taught me it does — it pins bait against the rip line and structure until the bass can't help themselves. Slot fish and a fair number of over-slot stripers were blowing up on top within casting range of the rocks, mid-canal out to the east end, mostly in that last hour of darkness into the first hour of real light. Nobody had to work hard for it. A white or bone Super Strike Zig-Zag walked along the seam, or a 2-ounce Hab's Lure bucktail bounced just under the surface wash, both got hit before the retrieve even settled in.

We flagged this exact setup a week ago — said tidal flow was building toward its strongest point of the month and that it'd sharpen the bite on both bass and mixed bluefish inside 72 hours. That's precisely what happened. The bluefish have been in the mix too, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, slashing through the same bait pushes as the stripers, and they'll tear up a soft plastic fast so I've been running wire leader on the topwater rods just for the blitz windows.

The why here isn't complicated. Peanut bunker and pogies have been thick in the current seams, and when the ebb starts really moving — that four-, five-knot stretch through the mid-canal narrows — those baitfish get trapped against the rock walls with nowhere to go. Bass and blues don't need low light to feed when the buffet's pinned in place like that. That's the same pattern that's had fish blowing up in daylight from Narragansett clear up through Plymouth this month — bait density beating out the normal dusk-and-dawn caution. The Canal's just got the added kick of current doing the concentrating for free.

West end has been a different animal. Water temps in Buzzards Bay and around Wings Neck and Phinneys Harbor have been sitting warm enough that I'd bet on false albacore and maybe an early bonito showing before Labor Day — there's already word of bonito working Nantucket Sound and warmer water pushing exotics further up the Cape than usual this season. Nothing confirmed inside the Canal itself yet, but if that warm pulse holds, don't be shocked to see fin flashes off Mashnee Island or around Hog Island on a calm evening tide change. I'd keep a small epoxy jig or Deadly Dick rigged on a spare rod through Labor Day just in case.

Fluke have been a grind. West end drifts off Scusted Beach and down toward the Mashnee flats on the last of the ebb into dead slack have produced a few keepers, nothing to write home about — mostly shorts mixed with the occasional 18- to 19-incher on a Gulp Swimming Mullet in white, 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom where the current eases off. If fluke are your target, fish the slack itself, not the meat of the tide — too much current in the ditch and they just hunker down.

Night bite worth mentioning: squid have been stacking up thick around the light structure at both bridges, especially the Sagamore and Bourne pilings after dark. That's an extra forage layer sitting right under the bass, and it's probably part of why the topwater bite has stayed so consistent even outside the prime tide windows — there's always something for a hungry striper to eat down there right now.

Here's where I'd be careful. The moon's coming off its new-moon peak, so tidal push has already started easing slightly heading into the weekend. It's still strong enough to keep this topwater pattern alive through the next few days, but as we slide toward the weaker neap tides ahead of the August 28 full moon, expect the blitz windows to shorten and get pickier about timing. Instead of a 45-minute window of chaos, you might only get 15 good minutes right at the tide change. I'd fish tighter to the exact turn of the ebb — east end for stripers, west end structure for the outside chance at albies — rather than camping out for a long soak.

Looking ahead, tidal strength is going to build right back up as we approach that full moon at the end of the month, and that's when I'd expect this current-driven bite to sharpen again, maybe even outdo this week. If the warm water pattern holds in Buzzards Bay, the west end could turn into the more interesting story by early September, with albies and maybe a bonito mixing into the bass and blue game. For now, if you've only got one shot this week, take the pre-dawn ebb at the east end rocks. That's where the numbers — and the fish — have been lining up.

reports.headline: White Island Still Holding Cod While Hampton's Back Channels Fill With Snapper Blues
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty if you fish it like it's a hundred and thirty — the Shoals proved that again this week.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to write about. I've never understood that. Thirteen miles gets you the Piscataqua pushing out past Portsmouth Harbor, it gets you the Isles of Shoals sitting nine miles offshore in real groundfish water, and it gets you Hampton Harbor filling and draining twice a day with enough current to make a tide chart necessary reading. I trailer a twenty-foot Lund out of Rye Harbor most mornings and I fish this stretch like it's Jeffreys Ledge on a bad day and the Grand Banks on a good one. This week was more the former than the latter, but that's not the same as a bad week.

Cod are still stacked on the ledges around White Island and Duck Island, same pattern we've had since mid-July — nothing dramatic, just steady. I've been anchoring up on the northeast corner of White Island in 60 to 80 feet, letting the boat settle on the last of the ebb, and jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid straight down. Slack tide through the first hour of the flood has been the window — anything with real current running and the fish just aren't holding position the same way. Cod are running 3 to 6 pounds mostly, with the occasional fish pushing 8 that makes the trip worth the diesel. Haddock have been mixed in but thin — you'll pick off one or two on a good drift over the gravel patches southeast of Appledore, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. Water out there is still holding in that classic low-60s Gulf of Maine range, which keeps everything honest and slow-moving rather than blown out or bait-starved. We said a couple weeks back this zone would stay in its typical mid-August pattern rather than showing any of the warm-water excitement building to the south, and that's exactly what's held — no surprises, no wild card species, just the bottom program doing what it does this time of year.

Mackerel showed in good numbers around the Shoals early in the week, which is the real story if you're paying attention to bait rather than just species counts. Schools were working the surface around 6 a.m. off Star Island before the wind came up, and where you find mackerel that thick you generally find something interested in eating them. I picked up a few bluefish trolling small tinsel jigs behind the mackerel schools, nothing huge, 2 to 4 pounds, but scrappy and willing. The bigger blue fishing has been better closer to the harbors than out at the Shoals — Rye Harbor's outer breakwater and the mouth of the Piscataqua both had blues chasing bait on the last two hours of the incoming tide, and if you want steady action without the run offshore, that's where I'd put a rod.

Stripers are the interesting piece right now, and it's mostly a Hampton Harbor story. Snapper blues have been thick in the back channels behind Hampton Beach State Park for a couple weeks now, which is usually the tell that the bigger fish are close behind, and this week that started to bear out. I had reports of slot bass showing up on the flood tide pushing into the marsh creeks off Meadow Pond, feeding on mummichogs and small peanut bunker getting flushed out of the grass. Small white or chartreuse soft plastics on a light jighead, fished slow along the channel edges where the marsh drains into the main harbor, has been the go-to. Nothing blitzing, no top-water fireworks, but a real, catchable pattern on the last two hours of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing. Great Boars Head has produced a few fish from the surf too, mostly at first light on bucktails worked along the rock structure, but that bite has been more about timing than volume — you need to be there right as the tide turns, not an hour before or after.

Flounder are still around in the Piscataqua for the guys willing to anchor up and soak clam or sandworm on the bottom near the Route 1 bridge and down toward the Coast Guard station. It's not exciting fishing but it's honest fishing, and on a day when the wind's up and the Shoals run is a bad idea, it's a fine way to fill a cooler.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward the full on the 28th, which should push more water through Hampton Harbor and strengthen that striper pattern in the marsh creeks — bigger tides usually mean more bait getting flushed and more fish willing to chase it into the shallows. If the mackerel stay parked around the Shoals, I'd expect the bluefish bite there to hold steady through the week, maybe build a little as more forage stacks up. Offshore, if I've got a calm morning window, I'm still starting at White Island on the slack and working the tide change — that's produced every week this month and I don't see a reason to abandon it. Worth checking wind before you commit to the run out there; it's a different ocean nine miles off Rye than it is inside the breakwater.

reports.headline: 138 Feet on Barnegat Ridge: One Bluefin Bite for Every Twenty Trolls, But Sea Bass Won't Quit
reports.subhead: The warm edge we flagged two weeks back never left — it just moved the tuna bite inshore and left the sea bass biting steady on the reef structure.
reports.body_markdown:
138 feet. That's the number I keep coming back to this week — the depth at the northeast corner of Barnegat Ridge where the bottom breaks hard and the current stacks bait against the rise. I've fished that exact contour in Augusts going back a decade, and when the numbers line up the way they have lately, it tells me more than any single report can. This week it told me the tuna are still around, but they're not easy, and the sea bass are the sure thing.

Let's start with what's dependable. Shrewsbury Rocks in 45 to 65 feet has been holding jumbo sea bass all week, the kind that make you re-tie because the 20-pound fluoro leader looks thin all of a sudden. Squid strips over a double-hook bottom rig, six-ounce bank sinker to hold in the current, and don't be shy about adding a strip of clam to the top hook — the bigger fish on that structure have been picking at the clam scent first. Sea Girt Reef in a similar depth range, 50 to 70 feet, is producing the same story: good numbers, decent average size, but you have to work the wreck pieces tight. Sea bass this time of year sit right on the structure edge, not scattered over open sand, so if your drift isn't ticking bottom right on the pile, you're just burning bait. Axel Carlson Reef has been a little more hit or miss — some drifts stacked with keepers, others dead — which tells me the bait pods are moving around out there more than usual, probably pushed by the same warm-water intrusion that's been messing with the tuna grounds farther out. Triple Wrecks rounds it out as a solid backup when the others go quiet; smaller average fish there but more consistent action, good for filling a cooler on a day when you need numbers over size.

Now the tuna. I'll be straight with you — it's been a tough bite. We flagged two weeks ago that the warm-water edge sitting off our grounds showed no sign of retreating, and it hasn't. What that warm pool has done, though, is thin out the bite on the deeper lumps that usually carry bluefin this time of year, and pushed what action there is inshore onto structure like Barnegat Ridge and the Klondike humps. Boats working that 100- to 160-foot range on the Ridge and the Klondike this week are getting looks — spreader bars and cedar plugs pulling small to mid-size bluefin, with the occasional yellowfin mixed in on the temperature break — but the hookup rate has been low, something like one solid strike for every twenty trolling passes. That's not a bite you plan a whole day around. It's a bite you fish on your way to or from the reef structure, trolling the edges for twenty or thirty minutes before you commit to the sea bass grounds. If you connect, it's a bonus. If you don't, you haven't lost the day.

Mahi have been the pleasant surprise tucked into that same water. Anywhere you find a temperature seam or a scrap of floating structure near the Ridge or Klondike drop-offs, small pods of mahi have been sitting under it — schoolies mostly, two to four pounds, but eager. Small chunks of butterfish on a light spinning rod, no weight, just cast to the shadow line and let it flutter down, has been the move. Nothing that fills a fishbox on its own, but it turns a slow troll leg into a few extra fish in the cooler, and it's fun fishing on a day when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating.

On tog — nothing to report, because there's nothing to report legally. Ocean blackfish season is still closed here, so if you're marking fish on the wreck pieces at Shrewsbury Rocks or Triple Wrecks, write the number down and forget about it until October. That patience pays off; the fish that are sitting tight to structure right now, untouched, are the same ones that'll be biting hard the week the season opens.

The tide's been building back toward the August 28 full moon, and that's the number I'm watching hardest for the coming week. Stronger tidal push usually means better current over the reef structure, which tightens up the sea bass bite and gets more bait moving through the Ridge and Klondike corridor — which in turn is what it'll take to turn that one-in-twenty tuna strike rate into something better. If the warm pool holds its position rather than sliding east or west, I'd expect the inshore tuna pattern to stay roughly where it is — spotty, but present. If it shifts, the whole picture changes fast, and that boundary is the single thing worth checking before you commit fuel to a long troll leg versus a straight run to the reef structure.

My plan for the next few days: mornings on Sea Girt Reef and Shrewsbury Rocks for sea bass while the water's calm, a troll pass through the Ridge and Klondike on the way back in to test the tuna, and a rod rigged light for mahi under anything floating. That's a full day's fishing with a real shot at three species, and it doesn't depend on one bite carrying the whole trip.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke Crowd the Inlet While Snapper Blues Bulk Up at Tices Shoal
reports.subhead: The bay's gone thick and warm upstairs, so the good fish are pushing down toward the moving water — and the bait's telling on them.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-some Augusts ago I was still a kid mating on a Point Pleasant boat, and there was an old captain named Ernie who used to tell me the dog days turn fluke into a different animal. "They ain't hunting no more, Gus," he'd say, working a cigarette out of the corner of his mouth while we idled over a lump off the inlet. "They're laying in the current with their mouths open, waiting for something to fall on their head." I didn't get it then. I get it now, every single August, and this one is no exception.

The upper bay has gone flat and warm — I'd put it high 70s pushing 80 in the skinny water up around Toms River, and fish don't want to be in that stew if they don't have to. What's happened, same as every summer this stretch, is the fluke have pulled off the mud basins and pushed toward anywhere the tide keeps moving and the water stays a few degrees honest. That means Barnegat Inlet and Double Creek Channel right now are doing the heavy lifting for this whole zone.

I've had three trips through Double Creek this past week working the deeper bends on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the pattern's been consistent — not a banner bite, but a real one. Four-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pearl on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow along the channel edges in 12 to 16 feet, have been outproducing anything finesse-sized. Ernie was right — these fish are lazy right now, and a bigger profile gets bit when a small one gets ignored. Best fish of the week went 6 pounds off the elbow where Double Creek dumps toward the ICW, taken on the last of the outgoing with the current really ripping. Most days it's two to four keepers mixed with a pile of shorts, which for mid-August in this bay is honest work and I won't oversell it as more.

The inlet itself, right through the Coast Guard station and out toward the rocks at Barnegat Light, has been holding fluke tight to structure — the same story you're hearing up and down this whole stretch of shore right now. Bigger baits, slower presentations, fish sitting in the current seams waiting on the tide to bring dinner to them instead of chasing it down. If you're drifting the inlet, time it to the last of the incoming into the top of the tide — that's when the bait gets pushed hard against the rocks and the fluke stack up on the downcurrent side.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing in this bay for two solid months now, and I'll say it plain — we called this one. Back in the middle of the month the snapper blues in these back creeks and river mouths were still pencil-thin, and the read then was that they'd bulk up fast through late August. Well, here we are. I was up at Tices Shoal and around the mouth of Oyster Creek this week and those snappers have put on some size — plenty of them pushing 12 to 14 inches now, and mixed in with them are adult blues in the 3 to 5 pound class that weren't there two weeks ago. Small strips of bunker or a silver spoon behind a light wire leader is all you need. They're aggressive, they're everywhere in the back bay right now, and if you've got kids or a slow afternoon, this is your bite.

Striped bass are around but they're not making it easy. With the bay running warm the way it is, the bass have compressed hard into dawn and dusk, same as everywhere south of the Canal this summer. I've had my best luck working the rocks at Barnegat Light right at first light, and along the deeper edge of the Double Creek Channel right at last light, on bunker chunks fished on the bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current. Nothing to write home about in numbers, but the fish that are coming are decent — mostly slot-range, a few over. Don't expect much from the middle of the day. The water's too warm and they know it.

Blowfish and kingfish are both doing their usual late-summer thing in the sod bank creeks and the sandier stretches down toward Island Beach. Blowfish on small hooks with clam or squid strips in three to six feet of water off the marsh edges near Double Creek have been steady for anybody patient enough to sit on them. Kingfish are showing in the surf and inside the inlet on sandy bottom, bloodworms or Fishbites on a simple high-low rig doing the job. Weakfish, if you want the honest truth, are mostly a memory of May right now — I'm hearing the occasional one taken after dark around the lights at Barnegat Light, but that's a bonus fish, not a target this time of year.

We're building toward the full moon on the 28th, and that extra tidal push should sharpen up the current-driven spots — Double Creek, the inlet mouth, the rips off Barnegat Light — right when we need it, as the upper bay stays stuck in this warm holding pattern. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of the outgoing through Double Creek Channel for fluke, then slide out to the inlet rocks for the last light bass bite. That's where I'm putting my time, and where I'd tell any of you to start.

reports.headline: Holgate's Outer Bar Split In Two — Blues Inside, Fluke On The New Drop
reports.subhead: A summer swell carved a fresh slough off Holgate and the bite followed it — here's where to fish it and what's biting from the inlet to the Mullica.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning at dead low and something's different out there. The outer bar that's held its shape since June split into two distinct humps, with a new trough running maybe forty yards off the beach where there used to be one continuous shelf. You can see it from the dune line if the sun's low enough — darker water in the cut, lighter sand color on the inside bar. That kind of split usually means one thing: baitfish get funneled into that new trough and whatever's hunting them stacks up right on the edge of it. I fished the drop-off on the incoming Wednesday morning with a bone-colored darter and picked up three bluefish in the 3-4 pound class in maybe twenty minutes before the sun got too high and pushed them off the structure.

That's been the story on bluefish all summer and it hasn't slowed down — steady action, mostly 3 to 4 pounders with the occasional 6 to 8 pound fish mixed in, and it's holding both in the surf and inside. Snapper blues are thick right now in the back bay and river mouths — Graveling Point, the mouth of the Mullica, up into Great Bay proper. If you've got kids who want bent rods, small silver spoons or Kastmasters off the bulkheads at Beach Haven or the Causeway bridges will keep them busy for hours. We flagged a couple weeks back that the snapper density was a signal adult blues would keep building through late August into September, and that's exactly what's playing out — the adult fish mixing into those bunker pods along the beachfront are bigger on average than they were in July.

Fluke is the real story on LBI right now, though, and it's genuinely good. Boats running out of Barnegat Light and Beach Haven are posting 4, 5, even 7-keeper trips this week on structure — the reef sites, rock piles off the inlet, and the humps along the Barnegat Ridge. The pattern that's working is oversized baits fished tight to bottom: 6-inch chartreuse or pink Gulp grubs on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, tipped with a whole squid strip or a chunk of mackerel. If you're fishing structure and you're not occasionally ticking bottom, you're fishing too high — these fish are lazy in this warm water and they want the bait dropped right on their head, not swimming past twelve inches over them.

Bay-side, the pattern's shifted with the heat. The shallow flats in Great Bay and up toward Graveling Point are running warm — upper 70s pushing 80 in the skinny water — and that's pushed fluke out of the marsh edges and concentrated them right at the mouth of Little Egg Inlet, where the tidal exchange keeps water cooler and better oxygenated. Anchor up on the edge of the main channel there on the last two hours of the ebb and drift live spot or a Gulp Swimming Mullet on a light jighead through the current seam. That's where the keepers are sitting right now, not out on the open flats.

Striped bass are a tougher conversation. The warm water in the bay and along the beachfront has compressed the bite into tight dawn and dusk windows, same as everywhere south of the Canyon country right now. We called this exact pattern back on August 7 — said the bass bite would hold steady until temps ease off in September, and that building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen things up at current-driven structure. That's precisely what's happening. First light at Barnegat Light around the rocks, and again at the Holgate cuts on that new trough I mentioned, has been giving up slot fish mixed with the bluefish, mostly on darters and 5-inch soft plastic swimbaits worked slow along the bottom edge. By 7:30 or so the window's closed and it turns into a bluefish morning. Don't expect consistency — it's a couple fish in a tight hour, not a blitz.

Kingfish have been showing in the wash at Surf City and Ship Bottom early, before the beaches fill in — small stuff on bloodworm or Fishbites bounced along the sandy troughs close to shore, a nice light-tackle diversion if you're out there anyway for the bass window. Weakfish I'll be honest with you — scattered at best. A few fish showing on soft plastics in the evening up in the Mullica and around Graveling Point, but nothing you can plan a trip around right now. If you connect, it's a bonus, not a target.

Looking ahead, the moon's building back toward the August 28 full, and that added tidal push should sharpen the current at every cut and inlet mouth we've talked about here — Little Egg, Barnegat Inlet, that new Holgate trough. If the swell stays modest through the weekend I'd expect that structure to keep producing on the fluke side and the bass window to hold its shape at first light. Keep an eye on that Holgate cut, too — these things move fast in August, and by Labor Day it could look completely different again. The mullet run's still a few weeks out, but when the peanut bunker start showing thick in the wash off Holgate, that's usually the tell that the real fall pattern is about to switch on.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at Dawn: Blues on Top, Bass Ghosting the Runoff
reports.subhead: Two months of dependable bluefish carried the beat again this week while stripers stayed buried in dirty water and short daylight windows.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-fifteen, North Jetty at Manasquan, and there were already six rods stuck in the rocks before the sky turned from black to gray. That's normal for August. What's not normal is watching three of those guys hook up in the first fifteen minutes on nothing fancier than a bunker spoon dragged across the current seam where the inlet dumps into the ocean. Three-to-four pound blues, chopping through peanut bunker that have finally pushed tight to the beach after weeks of getting pushed around by runoff. I've been walking these rocks since before some of these guys had licenses, and I'll say it plain — the bluefish have been the one thing you could count on all summer, and this week didn't break that streak.

We flagged this two weeks back — said the blue bite would hold as long as the bunker stayed tight to the beach, and here we are, still doing it. Snapper blues are thick as gnats in Shark River and up in the back stretches near the Belmar bridge, which if you've fished this beat as long as I have, you know is the tell. Snappers this dense in mid-August mean the adult class fish keep showing through Labor Day and into the albie window. I had a kid next to me at Shark River Inlet on Tuesday morning slinging a Kastmaster into a snapper blitz so thick the water looked like it was boiling — no exaggeration needed, just a lot of one-pound fish eating everything that moved.

Bass have been the harder conversation. We've had close to eight inches of rain dump on this stretch over the last month, and that runoff has turned the nearshore water the color of chocolate milk from Sea Bright down through Avon. Stripers don't love feeding through dirty water in daylight, so what you're left with are tight windows — first light and last light, when the water's still cool enough and the light's low enough that a bass will commit. I worked the Sea Bright rocks Thursday at 5:30 with a black Danny swimmer and picked off one schoolie, maybe 22 inches, working the pocket on the north side where the jetty breaks the current on an incoming tide. That's one bass in ninety minutes of casting. Not the kind of morning you write home about, but it's honest, and it's what's out there right now. If you want a bass on this beat this week, fish the last hour of the incoming or the first hour of the outgoing, right at the jetty tips where the dirty water gets strained a little cleaner passing over the rocks, and don't expect volume.

Fluke have quietly been the better story for the guys working boats out of Belmar and Manasquan. Warm water this time of year makes fluke lazy, and lazy fluke want a bigger meal without much effort — that's why the oversized baits are outproducing the small stuff. Guys drifting the Manasquan Inlet channel on the last of the outgoing, working 4- to 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to the rock piles on either side of the inlet, have been putting three and four keepers in the cooler on a good drift — nothing like the LBI reports but respectable for water this warm. Depth's not deep in there, maybe 15 to 20 feet on the channel edges, but that's where the current concentrates the bait against structure, and fluke don't have to work hard to eat.

Blackfish and porgies are still off-season conversation for another few weeks, so I won't waste your time on them — but keep an eye on the calendar, because once the water starts to slide the other direction in September, the Sea Bright and Manasquan wrecks close in will start producing again and it always sneaks up on guys who weren't paying attention.

Here's what I'd do with the week ahead. The moon's building toward the full on the 28th, which means tide strength is going to pick up steadily through the weekend — good news for both the bass and the fluke, because stronger current means better bait concentration at the jetty tips and inlet mouths. If I had one morning to fish, I'd take the last hour of a strong outgoing at Manasquan's south jetty, right around first light, throwing a darter or a bigger swimmer through the white water where the rocks meet the sandbar. That's historically where the bigger bass show first once the tide gets some push behind it, especially if the runoff finally clears out with a stretch of dry weather. Blues will keep eating anything that moves regardless — that part of the program isn't changing anytime soon. Watch for false albacore too. It's a touch early yet for this stretch, but if the water temps ease off even a degree or two heading into September the way they usually do, Shark River Inlet and the Spring Lake jetties are where they'll show first, and when they do, small metal like a half-ounce Deadly Dick is the play.

Bottom line for this week: blues are the sure thing, fluke are the pleasant surprise if you've got a boat, and bass require patience, dirty-water patience, fished right at first light with low expectations and a willingness to walk more rocks than usual to find the one pocket that's holding fish.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: Bluefish Steady, Bay Fluke Tucked Tight, Drum Run a Distant Memory
reports.subhead: The rips are giving up honest bluefish on the tide change, the bay's holding weakfish and croaker in the channels, and if you're still hunting drum you're two months late.
reports.body_markdown:
Rips grade: fair. Not the kind of fair where I'm apologizing for it — fair like an honest B-minus. You work the tide right off Cape May Point, you eat. You show up whenever and drift wherever, you're chumming for nothing.

Here's why. The current through the Rips is still running hard on the ebb, especially that two-hour window before dead low when the outflow from the bay meets the ocean swell and everything gets churned up and confused — that's when the bait gets disoriented and the blues pile on it. I've been running bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs, 20 to 40 feet, right where that seam sets up between the Point and the shoal, and it's been a hook-up an hour, sometimes better. Size has been decent too — 3 to 4 pound blues mixed with a few pushing 6, not the snapper-class stuff you're pulling out of the back bays. Stripers on the ocean side? Forget it for now. That's a fall story. Anybody telling you different in mid-August is selling you something.

Hereford Inlet's been the more interesting story, honestly. Snapper blues are thick as fleas in there — Grassy Sound, the back channels behind Wildwood Crest, anywhere there's current pushing bait past a piling. We flagged a couple weeks back that those snappers were a sign the adult class would keep building through late August into September, and that's exactly the shape it's taking. Still mostly the small stuff right now, but I'm seeing more 2 and 3 pounders mixed in on the last of the outgoing than I was two weeks ago. Give it another couple weeks and that back bay bluefish bite is going to have some shoulders on it.

Fluke inside the inlet have been a mixed bag — plenty of shorts, a keeper here and there for guys working 4-inch Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to the bulkheads and the inlet's deeper holes on the last two hours of the outgoing. The water's warm enough now that these fish are lazy — they want the bait dragged slow right past their nose, not worked hard. Same story I told you two weeks ago and it's held: with the bay running warm on the surface, the bait's staying tight to structure, and that's exactly where the fluke and weakfish have parked themselves. We called that one and it's still playing out.

Speaking of the bay — if you're asking me about drum, I've got bad news. That run's done. Fortescue, the Cohansey mouth, the Ship John area — that whole show wrapped up back in May like it does every year, and there is nothing sniffing a clam down there right now worth your gas money. Anybody still hunting drum in August either doesn't fish the Delaware or is hoping I'll tell them something I can't. I won't sugarcoat that one.

What the bay's actually giving up right now is weakfish and croaker, and they're holding deep — the channels off Fortescue and down toward the mouth, 20 to 35 feet, not up on the flats where the water's baking into the mid-70s and climbing. Bloodworms and Fishbites on bottom rigs, or if you want to work for it, a bucktail tipped with squid strip dragged slow along the channel edges on the tail end of the flood. Kingfish and spot are showing on the lower bay flats too, which tells you the classic late-summer Delaware pattern is setting up right on schedule — that's your croaker season building, and it typically peaks over the next couple weeks as the water holds warm.
