The recent rain out of Jersey pushed a good slug of fresh water down through the upper bay, and that's staining things up around the Maurice River and upper Cohansey pretty good. If you fished up there this week and got nothing, that's why — the cleaner water and the fish that go with it have shifted down toward the lower bay and the ocean-side inlets. I'd stay south of Fortescue right now if you want water with some color to it instead of chocolate milk.

For keeper sea bass and better fluke, I'm sending guys offshore to the reef sites — the Del wrecks and Old Grounds have been the more consistent play while the bay itself goes soft and warm for anything with real teeth in it. Triggerfish have been mixed in around that same structure too, which is about right for this time of year — they like the warm water and they'll hang on the wrecks right alongside the sea bass.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change fast. The bay's going to keep running warm through the rest of August, which means weakfish and croaker stay deep in the channels and the fluke stay glued to structure rather than roaming the flats. If we get a stretch of northwest wind to knock that surface heat down a couple degrees, I'd expect the flats bite to open back up some. Until then, work the deep water, work the tide change at the Rips, and don't waste a trip looking for drum that left in the spring.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point noon blitz: bass busting peanuts in broad daylight
reports.subhead: Guys at Sabin Point are texting pictures of stripers exploding on bunker schools at lunchtime — the bay hasn't fished like this in years.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at Bold Point Tuesday morning grabbing coffee before I put the skiff in, and there's a guy leaning on his tailgate telling anybody who'll listen that he watched bass blow up on peanut bunker off Sabin Point at eleven in the morning — full sun, dead calm, birds screaming overhead. Normally I'd say the guy's exaggerating, but I've seen it myself twice this week off Nyatt Point, so I believe him. This bay is drowning in peanut bunker right now, little pogies stacked so thick they're darkening the water off Conimicut and pushing up into Greenwich Bay, and the bass have decided they don't care what time it is anymore. When the bait's that dense, the fish stop being nocturnal. That's exactly the pattern we flagged last week — said the blitz would hold as long as the bait stayed thick, and here it is, still going, right through the middle of the day.

The money move has been running the shoreline from Conimicut Point down past Nyatt and watching for diving terns and nervous water. When you find the peanuts balled up tight, cut the engine and drift a small white or pearl soft plastic — 3-inch paddletails on light jigheads, no weight if you can help it — right through the edge of the bait. Topwater walks a lot too; a small popper or a Zara Spook-style plug worked slow gets crushed the second it lands near a busting school. Most of what's coming over the rail is schoolie to mid-20-inch class, with the occasional slot fish mixed in when the blitz sets up over deeper water off Prudence Island's west side. It's not a guarantee — I burned an hour Wednesday afternoon running from Rocky Point to Warwick Neck with nothing showing, then found the whole thing happening off Nyatt twenty minutes later. You've got to keep moving and trust the birds.

Bluefish are riding shotgun in these same schools, and they're not shy about it — anything from a pound and a half up to four or five pounds is slashing through the bunker right alongside the bass. If you want bluefish specifically, a wire leader ahead of that same soft plastic keeps you from losing gear to their teeth. Down in the back coves and river mouths — Bullock's Cove, the mouth of the Providence River, up into the Barrington River — the snapper blues are absolutely thick, exactly the kind of building block we called for two weeks back when it comes to bigger blues later in the season. Kids on the dock with bobbers and bits of squid are having a field day with those, and it's a good sign for October if this keeps up.

Fluke have been the honest bite between the blitz windows. I've been working the channel edges off Nyatt Point and the drop-off along the west side of Prudence in 15 to 25 feet, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail tipped with a squid strip. It's not a banner year for size — most fish are 16 to 19 inches, plenty of shorts mixed in — but on a good outgoing tide you can put together a few keepers without much trouble. The mouth of Greenwich Bay has also been giving up a few better fish for guys drifting live killies on a fish-finder rig.

Scup are doing what scup do — stacking on every ledge and piece of hard bottom from Rocky Point down to Rose Island and Gould Island. Squid strips and clam on a simple hi-lo bottom rig, fished tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, will fill a bucket fast. Black sea bass are mixed in on the same structure, especially the rockier stretches around Prudence's north end — nothing huge, but steady action for anybody who wants a mess of fish for the table. At night, squid have started showing under the lights at the Henderson Bridge and around the docks in Bristol Harbor — small glow jigs or bare hooks under a light will connect if you're patient, and it's worth a look since that squid is part of what's holding the whole bait chain together right now.

Tide-wise we're building back out of the new moon slack toward the full moon on the 28th, and that extra push should tighten up the current lines and concentrate bait even more over the next week. Water's sitting warm through the upper and mid-bay, which is exactly why the fish are willing to feed on top in daylight instead of waiting for dawn and dusk. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd be running the stretch from Conimicut to Nyatt starting mid-morning, watching for birds, and I wouldn't leave the rod rigged with anything heavier than what it takes to work a peanut bunker imitation clean. Just don't expect every blitz to be a slam dunk — some pop for five minutes and vanish, others hold for an hour. The bay's giving you the window. You still have to be there when it opens.

reports.headline: Why Are the Sod Bank Fluke Suddenly Ignoring Your Bucktail?
reports.subhead: Warm water has made Absecon and Great Egg's fluke lazy and choosy — here's why bigger baits are outfishing the standard strip-and-bucktail rig this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I got the same question three times at the dock this week, so let's make it a lesson: why is a five-inch Gulp strip on a half-ounce bucktail — the rig that's caught fluke in these back bays for thirty summers — suddenly getting refused? The short answer is water temperature. The long answer is worth understanding if you want to keep filling the cooler through Labor Day.

All that rain we've taken over the last three-plus weeks — eight-plus inches of it — has pushed a lot of tannic, off-color water into the marsh creeks and stained the shallow flats behind Ocean City and Sea Isle. Fluke don't love hunting hard in dirty, warm water. What they'll do instead is park on a piece of structure — a bulkhead corner, a channel edge, a bridge piling — and wait for something to come to them. That's a fish conserving energy, not one chasing bait. So this week the program that's actually working is bigger, not flashier: whole squid strips, bluefish belly strips cut long, or a Gulp Swimming Mullet in white threaded onto a full ounce of lead, fished dead slow right on bottom in the deeper holes of the Absecon Channel and the sod bank drop-offs off Brigantine. Slow-rolled, almost stalled, tight to structure — that's the difference between three keepers and none this week. I had a mixed bag of fluke to 19 inches doing exactly this off the Rainbow Channel bend on the last two hours of the outgoing, when that cooler ocean water is still pushing through and the fish set up right on the seam.

Great Egg Inlet is fishing the same way — the fluke are there, they're just concentrated tight to the inlet mouth where tidal flow keeps the water a few degrees cooler than the stagnant flats up in the back. If you're marking bait on the meter around the Rt. 52 causeway rock piles, drop straight down with a heavier bucktail than you think you need. I wasted two hours last Tuesday guessing wrong on weight before I finally got bit.

Bluefish are the one thing in this bay you can set your watch by right now, and we called this a week ago — said the snapper blues packing the back bays would keep building toward adult class fish, and that's exactly what's happening. Absecon Inlet and the mouth of the Mullica have snappers thick enough to chum with sand, but mixed in now are real 3- to 4-pound choppers, with the occasional fish pushing 6 or 7. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — worked fast through the froth at first light is the play, before the sun gets high and pushes them down. If you're throwing bait, cut bunker chunks fished under a float in the rips at Great Egg on the outgoing will keep you busy without needing to cast a rod.

Striped bass, I'll be honest with you, are a tough sell right now. Bay water in the high 70s to 80 degrees shuts bass down to a narrow window — I'm talking the hour before and after first light, working current seams at the Absecon Inlet rock jetty or the Route 30 bridge pilings with a Storm 360GT Searchbait swimbait or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig. You might get two or three bites in that window and then it's dead until the sun drops again. Don't plan a whole trip around them yet — plan a trip that has bass as the bonus if you're out early for blues or fluke anyway.

Kingfish are quietly one of the better bets on this beat right now if you don't mind standing in the wash. Ocean City and Stone Harbor surf, first and second bar, bloodworms or Fishbites on a high-low bottom rig, has been steady for kingfish in the 8- to 11-inch range with the occasional bonus weakfish mixed in on the same rig — though I want to be straight with you, weakfish numbers are thin this year, a fish here and there working the deeper Great Egg channel edges on a dropping tide, nothing you should plan a trip around. Triggerfish have started showing on the rock piles inside Absecon Inlet, a genuine late-summer visitor when the water holds warm this long — small pieces of clam or shrimp fished tight to the rocks on light tackle will find them, and they're a fun change of pace even if they're not going in anyone's cooler.

Looking ahead, tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should push more water and more bait through these inlets and tighten up the fluke bite on structure even further — that's usually when the bigger doormats start showing on the same drop-offs that are holding shorts now. If the rain holds off and that stained water clears out of the back bays even a little, I'd expect the fluke to get more aggressive again and go back to eating a standard strip-and-bucktail. Until then, go bigger, go slower, and fish the seams where clean water meets dirty. That's the lesson this week, and it's one worth remembering every time we get a soaked August like this one.

reports.headline: Channel edges save the week: fluke stack the Chapel Hill drop while the upper bay stays stained
reports.subhead: With runoff still fouling the flats, I'm working current seams off the Hook and letting the back bay's snapper blues tell me where the bunker are hiding.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning before I even loaded the boat: skip the upper bay flats, go straight to the Chapel Hill Channel edge and work it on the last two hours of the outgoing. The reasoning's simple — we've had enough runoff the last couple weeks that the flats from Keyport down through Cliffwood are holding stained, warm water, and fluke don't want any part of that when there's a cleaner alternative twenty minutes away. The channel edges push tide, tide pushes bait, and bait is exactly where you want to be putting a bucktail in mid-August.

That decision paid off. We drifted the drop from the Chapel Hill Channel out past Flynn's Knoll on the last of the outgoing into the top of the incoming, and picked at fluke the whole way — nothing epic, but a steady trickle of keepers in the 18 to 21-inch range on 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom in 18 to 25 feet. The fish were sitting tight to the break where the mud gives way to sand and shell, which is textbook this time of year — warm water pushes fluke up shallow to feed, then they slide back down onto that harder bottom when the sun gets high. If you're marking bait on the meter right at that transition, slow down and work it twice.

Bass are still stuck in the same holding pattern we flagged a couple weeks back — said this zone typically doesn't turn over until the water starts cooling into September, and that's exactly what's playing out. Daytime striper fishing in the bay itself has been tough. The better window is first and last light, working bunker chunks or live bunker snagged fresh off the pods around Romer Shoal and Flynn's Knoll, then fished on a fishfinder rig right on the bottom as the tide starts to move. Nothing's blitzing on top in the bay — that peanut bunker topwater craziness everybody's talking about up in Rhode Island and the Cape isn't happening here, not with our water sitting warm and the bunker schools mostly holding tight and deep rather than getting corralled and pushed up. The Rip at the Hook has given up a few better fish on the last of the ebb when there's current stacking bait against the rocks, but you need to be there right at the turn — that window is short, maybe 45 minutes, and then it goes quiet again.

Snapper blues are exactly where we said they'd be — thick as fleas in the back bay, off the Keyport docks, up in the Navesink around the Highlands bridge, and along the bulkheads in Cliffwood. That's a good long-term sign. A summer full of snappers means adult bunker schools are staying close, which usually sets up a stronger adult bluefish push as things cool off. Right now the snappers themselves are good fun on ultralight gear — small silver spoons or a sliver of peanut bunker under a bobber, and kids on the dock are having a field day. The bigger blues, the 3 to 5 pound class, are showing sporadically wherever you find bunker pods getting worked from above, mostly early morning off Romer Shoal and out toward the mouth of the Shrewsbury.

Weakfish have been a disappointment, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Warm, stained water is exactly the wrong recipe for weakfish, and the reports back that up — scattered short fish here and there in the Navesink on the last of the incoming, nothing worth planning a trip around. If you're set on weakfish, fish the deeper holes in the river right at first light before the sun pushes the temperature up, using a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along bottom, but keep your expectations modest.

Porgies are around Romer Shoal and out toward the Ambrose Channel edge in decent numbers if you want steady, low-drama action — bottom rigs with clam or squid strips in 25 to 35 feet will keep a rod bent, and it's a good way to spend an afternoon with kids or when the fluke bite goes quiet on the tide change. Blackfish are still off-limits until the fall season opens, so no reason to be dropping crabs on the wrecks yet, but it's worth noting the structure out there — Romer Shoal and the rockpile off the Hook — will be worth marking once October rolls around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift through the coming week. The moon's building back toward the August 28 full, and that extra tidal push should sharpen the current-driven spots — the Rip, the Chapel Hill edge, the deeper cuts off Flynn's Knoll — even if the broader pattern stays the same until real cooling starts in September. If I had one day to fish, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide on the channel edge with bucktails for fluke, then swing over to Romer Shoal at last light and soak a bunker chunk for whatever bass are moving through. Keep it simple, follow the moving water, and don't waste time on the stagnant flats until the rain stops giving them a reason to be dirty.

reports.headline: Race Rock at 3.6 Knots: Bass Down Deep, Blues Stacked at the Thames
reports.subhead: Warm Sound water has the trophy bass hugging bottom on wire line, but the Thames mouth is loaded with snapper blues and the sea bass bite on Plum Gut structure is the week's steadiest paycheck.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-nine point four degrees at New London, seventy point nine at Kings Point — that gradient tells you everything about why the bass have gone quiet on top this week. Warm surface water like that pushes big stripers off the boils and down onto the bottom third of the water column, and that's exactly where I found them Tuesday working Valiant Rock on the last two hours of the ebb, wire line out 250 feet, tube-and-worm dragging bottom in 45 feet of water while the current ran a modest 3.6 knots over the rock. That's soft for The Race in August — we've seen it push 5 in a hard new-moon ebb — but soft current with warm water on top means the fish are stacked tight to structure instead of spread across the whole rip, and that made for a slower pick but a quality one: two fish over 30 pounds came off the wire in about ninety minutes of dragging, both right in the seam where the rock breaks the flow.

Slack at Valiant this week has been sliding into the late morning, drifting close to fifty minutes later each day as we come off the moon — that short window, maybe fifteen minutes either side of dead slack, is when I'll switch off the wire and throw bucktails. Four-ounce white and chartreuse, bounced slow along the bottom right as the current dies, has been picking up a few fish that the trollers miss because they're set up too shallow. Once the current builds back past 2 knots on the new flood, I'm back on wire, because that's when the bait gets pinned against the rock and the bass turn on.

Honest read: this isn't a blitz week. The daytime bite in the open Sound has that typical late-summer flatness to it — warm, calm, not much showing on top. If you want consistency right now, Plum Gut and the Sluiceway are where I'd send you. Black sea bass have been the steadiest thing going, stacked on the humps in 50 to 60 feet on the Gut side, taking squid strips and Gulp on half-ounce bucktails dropped straight down on the last of the ebb. Keeper-sized fish, good numbers, and it fills the box when the bass aren't cooperating. Fluke through the same water have been lazy — that warm layer on top does that to them — so I've had better luck fishing bigger baits, whole squid strips over a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged dead slow tight to the bottom contour rather than working it aggressively. Warm-water fluke want the bait to come to them.

We flagged the snapper blue pattern building two weeks back, and it's arrived right on schedule — the mouth of the Thames is stacked with them right now, along with a real showing of adult 3- to 5-pound blues mixing into the bait pushing through Race Rock at first light. Small metal, half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters, worked fast on the surface at dawn before the sun gets up, has been the move. Those adults are following the same peanut bunker schools that have been triggering the daylight blitzes further up the coast, and I'd expect that class of bluefish to keep building through the Race and into Plum Gut as more bait funnels through on the building tide cycle.

No albies yet, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. Nantucket Sound and the Cape are seeing early bonito activity and there's been enough warm water sitting off Chatham to push some exotic fish into range, which tells me the false albacore push toward eastern Long Island Sound is probably a couple weeks out rather than days. I'll be watching Little Gull Island and Great Gull Island closely once we get into the last week of August — that's historically where the first fall run of albies and bonito show up in this zone, working bait pinned against the rips on a hard current. Right now those spots are quiet, holding bluefish and the occasional straggler bass, nothing worth a special trip yet.

Looking ahead: tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, and that's the variable that matters most for the next ten days. As current speed climbs back toward 4-plus knots at Race Rock and Valiant, expect the bass to spread back out across the rip instead of holding tight to structure — that's when the wire-line trolling really opens up again, and it's also when I'd expect the first real push of bait and predator fish to move through the Gull Island rips. If the moon does what it usually does to this stretch of water, by the 25th or so we should see current strength and bait density both spike together, and that combination is what turns a grind-it-out week like this one into a proper Race bite. Until then, I'd fish the slack windows on bucktails, save the wire for the building current, and lean on Plum Gut sea bass to keep the day from being a skunk.

reports.headline: Wamphassuc Boulders Loaded With Peanuts, Scup Still the Sure Bet
reports.subhead: Bait is thick on the rocks from Ram Island to Watch Hill, but the albie run hasn't crossed into the Sound yet — here's where to spend your slack tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I poled the skiff off Wamphassuc Point Tuesday morning on the last of the ebb and the water over the boulders was nervous — not blitzing, just nervous. Peanut bunker balled up tight against the rock faces, maybe eight to twelve feet down, moving like they didn't trust the open water. That's the tell. When bait hugs structure that close instead of running the flats, something's pushing on it from below or it's just found the cool pocket and doesn't want to leave. Either way, it's exactly where you want to be poling a fly rod or flipping a small soft plastic.

Water's telling two different stories depending on which end of my beat you're fishing. Kings Point up toward the western Sound is reading close to 71, New London's holding around 69.4. That gradient matters here — Fishers Island Sound sits on the cool side of that line, and the bait knows it. It's why the boulder fields from Ram Island out to Wamphassuc and down to Esker Point have stayed loaded all month while water on the Connecticut side gets soft and lazy in the afternoon sun.

The porgy bite has been the one thing I could set a watch by. We flagged this over a week ago and it's held — scup fishing on the rock piles around Fishers Island and both Stonington breakwaters has been about as good as I've seen it in years. Small hooks, size 6 or 8, green crab or clam strip, just enough weight to hold bottom in the current — twelve to twenty feet on the east breakwater, a little deeper, twenty-five to thirty, on the rock pile off the Fishers side. Slack water and the first hour of either tide is when they really turn on. Fish to two pounds mixed in steady, and enough of them that a party of three can fill a cooler in a couple hours without much drama. It's not exciting fishing. It's dependable fishing, which this time of year is worth something.

Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure, deeper rock out past the breakwater mouth and around the edges of Fishers Island itself, twenty-five to thirty-five feet. Bucktail-and-Gulp combo or a simple high-low rig with squid strips gets it done. Nothing huge, but a mixed bag with the scup makes for a good morning without needing to run far.

Striped bass have been the trickier read. They're working the Race hard on the tide changes — that's the one spot in my zone where current does something violent enough to hold fish through the middle of the day, not just dawn and dusk. Live eels or a big paddle-tail swimbait worked through the rip on the start of the ebb has produced some quality fish, mid-20s to high-30s, but you need to hit the window right. Twenty minutes early or late and it's dead water. Inside the Sound proper, along the boulder fields where that peanut bunker is stacked, the bass bite has been more of a dawn-and-dusk affair — low light, small profile flies, sparse Deceivers or Clousers in olive over white, worked slow right off the rock edges at Ram Island and down toward Watch Hill. Daytime, with that bait pinned tight to structure and the sun high, the bass mostly sit under it and sip rather than blow up. You've got to go down and slow to get bit.

Now the question everyone at the dock keeps asking me — where are the albies? Truth is, they're not here yet, not in numbers I'd write home about. I had one report of a single fish chasing bait off the east end of Fishers Island midweek, and I believe it, because the peanut bunker blitz pattern running hard just to our east in Rhode Island water has been building all week on this current cycle. Tidal flow is strengthening again as we build toward the August 28 full moon, and that's usually the trigger that pushes albies and bonito west out of the Vineyard and Block Island corridor into our rips. It hasn't crossed the line into Fishers Island Sound proper yet. When it does, Watch Hill Reef and the outside edge of the breakwater will be the first places it shows, because that's where the bait funnels hardest on a dropping tide.

Fluke have been a disappointment if I'm honest. Little Narragansett Bay and the channel edges near the Mystic River mouth have given up mostly shorts, occasional keeper on a bigger bait — a whole squid strip or a 5-inch Gulp in white worked slow along the channel drop. Warm, stagnant water in the upper bay has them lazy rather than hunting, same pattern we're seeing region-wide. If you want fluke, fish the moving water near the inlet mouths, not the flats.

Looking ahead — if that current keeps building into the full moon, I expect the albie window to crack open here within the next week to ten days, probably starting at Watch Hill and the outer edge of Fishers Island before it ever shows inside the Sound. I'd have a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig ready on the console just in case, but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet. The scup and sea bass on the breakwaters are the sure thing right now, and the striper bite at the Race on the tide change is worth planning a whole morning around if you can hit the window.

reports.headline: Penfield's Ebb Tide Loads the Cows with Porgies While Bass Punch a Dawn-Only Clock
reports.subhead: Blackfish season's closed till September, but the reef structure from Cockenoe to the Cows is still paying off for anglers who fish the right tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Every Monday morning I sit down with the tide chart and ask myself the same question: which reef is going to hand me the best two-hour window before the boat traffic turns the water into a washing machine. This week the answer was easy. Penfield Reef, last two hours of the ebb, working the down-current side in 15 to 22 feet. That's where the bait piles up as the tide sluices off the reef complex toward Fairfield, and right now that's where the porgies are stacked thick enough to make it worth the run.

Water's sitting in the low 70s across the western basin — Kings Month reading close to 71, still warm enough to keep everything comfortable but not so warm it's shutting fish down like it can in a stagnant harbor. That's the difference this year between the open reef structure and the back-bay mud flats: the current keeps things moving, and moving water on a reef is money in the bank.

Porgies on the Cows off Stamford have been the most consistent thing I've fished all month. Small pieces of green crab or clam on a hi-lo rig, 2 to 3 ounces of lead depending on how hard the current's running, right on the humps in 12 to 20 feet around the top of the flood into the first hour of the ebb. Nothing fancy — just patience and staying anchored tight to the structure instead of drifting off it. Sea bass are filling in behind them on the same pieces, squid strips working better than clam once the sun gets up and the water clears a little. Fish are running mixed sizes, plenty of shorts mixed with keepers in the 14 to 16-inch class, so it's a sort-through-them kind of day, not a fill-the-cooler kind of day. Honest bite, not a spectacular one.

Blackfish are off the table right now — Connecticut's summer closure runs through the end of August, so don't waste bait on the rockpiles at Cockenoe or the Norwalk Islands hoping for tog. That structure's better spent on sea bass anyway this time of year. Cockenoe Reef has been firing better on the incoming than the ebb lately, current pushing across the rockpile and funneling bait into the channel edge on the northeast corner. That's a good spot to probe with a bucktail and Gulp swimming mullet for fluke too, though I'll be straight with you — most of what's coming over the rail in the Sound right now is short. We're getting keepers mixed in off the sandy edges near Sheffield Island on the last of the outgoing, working white bucktails tipped with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp in 18 to 25 feet, but you're culling through a lot of fish to find a dinner's worth.

Striped bass have been the toughest read of the week, and that's mostly a clock problem, not a fish problem. With the afternoons building into thunderstorm weather most days, the productive window has shrunk down to first light — I'm talking that first hour and a half before the sun really gets up and before the Saturday center consoles start running the flats off Greenwich Point. Peanut bunker are holding tight to the shoreline there, and bass are working them from the tip of the point out toward the Executive Club flats on the tail of the high tide, right before it turns. Small bucktails or a peanut bunker under a slip float have both worked, but once that sun climbs and the boat traffic picks up, those fish slide off the flat and go quiet. If you're fishing this weekend, get out before six or don't bother — the Cows and the reef structure around Norwalk get pounded by mid-morning and the bite shuts down accordingly.

We flagged this a couple weeks back — said the snapper blues stacking up in the back bays would be the tell that adult-class bluefish were building through late August, and that's exactly what's showing now. The mouth of the Norwalk River and the water off Cos Cob Harbor are throwing real 3 to 4-pound blues mixed in with the peanuts, snappers still thick enough in the coves that kids on the dock are catching them on bare hooks. That adult class should keep filling in as the month goes.

Looking ahead, tidal flow is building again toward the August 28 full moon, and that's usually when this whole system sharpens up — more push on the reefs, tighter bait concentrations, better current-driven windows at Penfield and Cockenoe both. If the afternoon storm pattern breaks even for a day or two, I'd put my money on an early morning troll off Penfield with fresh bunker chunks fished tight to the drop-off, targeting bigger bass working the current seam before the crowds. Until then, I'm sticking with the reef program — early tide, right structure, home before the boats show up.

reports.headline: Niantic fleet grinding porgies and sea bass — fluke need work, keepers are out there
reports.subhead: The drift boats are stacking porgy and black sea bass limits while fluke fishing turns into a numbers game from Twotree to Hole-in-the-Wall.
reports.body_markdown:
Stopped by the dock in Niantic Tuesday morning and one of the mates off the drift boat fleet was hosing down coolers full of porgies before the boat even finished tying up. That's the story right now on this end of the Sound — porgies and black sea bass are doing the heavy lifting while fluke make you earn every keeper.

Water's sitting around 69 to 70 degrees off New London, and that cooler water pushing through the Race and down through Twotree Island Channel is keeping this stretch a touch cleaner and more comfortable than what they're dealing with up in the western basin. That tidal flushing matters — it's why the bite out here has stayed more consistent through the middle of the day instead of shutting down hard like it does closer to the city.

Porgy fishing is the most dependable thing going. The rock piles off Black Point and the structure tight to Hole-in-the-Wall are holding good numbers, and the drift boats have been putting steady limits together on high-low rigs with sandworms and clam, fished right on bottom in 20 to 35 feet. Slack tide into the first hour of the new drift is when it turns on — porgies don't love ripping current, so the captains are timing their drops around the tide change and letting the boat settle before the first baits go down. Nothing fancy about it, just bottom rigs and patience, but it's meat in the cooler almost every trip.

Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure. McCook Point and the drop-offs around Black Point in 25 to 40 feet have been giving up a solid mixed bag — jigs tipped with squid strips or a chunk of green crab are getting bit, and the bigger fish are coming off bottom on the up-tide drift when the current's still got some push to it. It's not a wide-open bite, but it's a fill-your-bag kind of bite, and that's plenty this time of year.

Fluke is where things get honest. The Sound-wide pattern of mostly short fish has held true out here too — Twotree Island Channel and the flats off Niantic Bay are loaded with sub-legal fluke, and you're picking through a pile to find a keeper. The better move has been working Hole-in-the-Wall and the deeper edge near 40 feet where the water stays cooler and the bigger, lazier fish tend to sit tight to structure instead of chasing bait around. Bulked-up baits are the key — a whole squid strip over a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged dead slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Warm, stagnant water makes fluke sluggish, so a slower presentation with more scent is out-fishing anything zipped through fast.

Striped bass have been a dawn-and-dusk proposition. With Sound temps running into the high 60s and low 70s in the shallows, the bass have tightened their window — first light and the last hour before dark at the mouth of Niantic Bay and around Hole-in-the-Wall on the moving tide has been the play. Bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs are working for the guys anchoring the rip, and a few boats working eels after dark off Black Point have connected on slot fish in the 28 to 33-inch range. It's not the daylight blitz action they're seeing to the east right now, but it's real fish on a real pattern if you time the tide right.

Bluefish deserve a mention because we flagged this a few weeks back — said the snapper blues thick in the back bays would build into adult-class fish as August wore on, and that's exactly what's happening. The mouth of the Niantic River is loaded with snappers, and there's a growing mix of 3 to 5-pound blues showing up in that same water, cutting into the bass bite at times and giving light-tackle guys something to do when the stripers go quiet mid-day.

Blackfish are still just scouting mode — a few guys picking around the rockier stretches off Black Point with green crabs, nothing worth building a trip around yet, but worth remembering those spots for when the water starts to slide in September.

Looking ahead, tides are easing off toward the weaker cycle right now, but they'll start rebuilding as we push toward the full moon on the 28th. That stronger current should tighten up the bait around Twotree Channel and Hole-in-the-Wall and could be the trigger that gets fluke moving more aggressively instead of just sitting on structure. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide at Hole-in-the-Wall — fluke gear rigged and ready, but a bass rod loaded with an eel just in case the light goes right and something bigger shows up looking for an easy meal.

reports.headline: Goldenrod's Blooming, Snappers Are Thick — Stripers Wait for Last Light at the River Mouth
reports.subhead: The alewife run is a memory and the shad are long gone to sea, but the mouth still has a pulse if you fish the edges of the day.
reports.body_markdown:
Goldenrod's coming up along the causeway out to Great Island, and the marsh grass has that deep, tired green it gets in mid-August before it starts turning. That's always been my marker for where we are in the season down here — the alewives ran up through here back in April, the shad and hickories pushed through on their way to the falls in May, and now we're deep into the summer holding pattern that settles over this river every year about this time. No dogwood, no herring push, no river temp climbing out of the 50s. Just warm, slow-moving water and a river that's shifted its whole personality from spring urgency to summer patience.

The Sound's been running warm this month — Kings Point up near 71, New London holding just under 70 — and the river mouth off Saybrook Point and Great Island tracks right along with that, probably a touch warmer given how shallow and sun-baked those flats get by midafternoon. That warmth is exactly why the daytime bite on adult stripers has gone quiet. Big fish don't want to work hard in 78-degree water with the sun straight overhead. They're sliding into the deeper parts of the channel — the hole off Selden Neck, the drop just outside the Ferry Landing in Essex — and holding there through the heat of the day, then pushing back out toward the mouth as the light fails.

That dusk push is where the real action's been. I've had two solid evenings working the last of the outgoing tide off Great Island, throwing a white Bomber Long A along the edge of the flat where it drops into the channel — that seam holds peanut bunker thick as pepper right now, and the bass know it. Same story working the breakwater at Saybrook Point on the tail of the ebb: a half-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse trailer, dragged slow right along the rocks, has been picking up slot fish in that last hour of shooting light. It's not a blitz. It's two or three fish a trip if you put your time in at the right tide stage, which for me has meant fishing the last two hours of outgoing into the first hour of the new incoming, right around sunset.

What isn't subtle right now is the snapper blue bite. They're absolutely thick around the DEP Marina docks and stacked up off the Saybrook jetty, and any kid with a bobber and a piece of spearing is going to load the cooler. For anybody who wants a little more sport out of it, small Kastmasters or 1/8-ounce Deadly Dicks worked fast on light spinning gear will keep you bent all afternoon. We flagged a couple weeks back that this snapper push was a sign the adult class would keep building through late summer, and that's holding true — I've started seeing a few 3- and 4-pound blues mixed into the dusk striper bite off Great Island, chopping up the same peanut bunker schools. Give it another few weeks and those snappers will be respectable cocktail blues themselves.

White perch have been steady but you have to go find them — the deep hole below Selden Neck and the channel edge off the Essex waterfront, bloodworms or a chunk of nightcrawler on a simple bottom rig, fished right at first light before the boat traffic stirs everything up. Nothing dramatic, just a reliable dozen fish if you're patient and fish it quiet.

And if you've got kids or you just want an easy evening on the water, the blue crabbing in the marshes off Old Lyme — Lord Cove, Whalebone Creek — has been about as good as it gets this month. Chicken necks on a hand line off the DEP Marina dock or out of a canoe up in those back creeks, and you'll fill a bushel basket without much effort. That's the kind of low-stakes fishing this river does better than almost anywhere in the state right now.

Tide-wise, we're building back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that extra push should start moving more water and more bait through the mouth over the next week — I'd expect the dusk striper window to sharpen up a bit as that flow strengthens, since moving current is what's been concentrating fish at the edges of the flats all month. We called this pattern holding steady as long as the tidal flow keeps pushing bait downriver, and that's exactly what's happened — no real change, just the same reliable summer rhythm.

Looking ahead, I don't expect anything to change dramatically through the week. Daytime will stay slow and hot, dusk will keep producing modest but real numbers of slot bass off Great Island and the Saybrook breakwater, and the snapper blues will keep multiplying until some of them graduate into real fish. The bigger shift — when adult stripers start moving back into the river proper in numbers — is still a few weeks off, once that first real cool-down hits in September. Until then, fish the last light, fish the seams, and don't expect the river to hand you anything before sundown.

reports.headline: Scup Are the Sure Bet; Everything Else on the North Fork Wants Convincing
reports.subhead: Porgies are stacked over the rock piles from Mattituck to Orient while bass and fluke make you work mornings only.
reports.body_markdown:
There was a kid down at the inlet Tuesday morning, maybe twenty-two, twenty-three, throwing a topwater plug that cost more than my first outboard motor. Worked it beautiful too — walked it right along the current seam where the inlet dumps into the Sound, the kind of retrieve you'd teach in a video. Nothing touched it. I was twenty feet away soaking a clam belly on a simple hi-lo rig, not even paying attention, and I had two porgies and a blowfish before he'd finished his third cast. He looked over at me like I'd cheated somehow. I hadn't. I'd just been fishing this water since before his father was born, and some years the Sound doesn't care what your lure costs.

That's about the size of it out here right now. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod, it's porgy and scup — they've moved up onto the structure the way they always do in mid-August, and they're not shy about it. Rocky Point reef, the rock pile off Horton Point, the boulder fields tucked in around Orient — anywhere there's broken bottom in fifteen to thirty feet, drop a hi-lo rig with squid strips or clam belly and you'll be busy. Small hooks, size 6 or 8, because these fish have particular mouths and they'll strip a big hook clean without you ever feeling it. This has become the honest bite on my stretch of water. Not glamorous. Reliable.

Striped bass are a different conversation. The water's warmed up enough — Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound was reading close to 71, and even out toward New London it's holding around 69 — that the bass have gone and gotten sensible on us. Sensible meaning they feed early, before the sun really gets up on the water, and then they slide off into whatever deeper current edge they can find and sulk through the afternoon. I've had my best luck at first light off Horton Point, working the edge where the current sets against the point on the last of the outgoing, using bucktails in the half-ounce to three-quarter range, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of squid. By nine, nine-thirty, it shuts off like somebody threw a switch. That's not a complaint, that's just how August works on this shore. Plan around it or don't bother.

We said last week the bass would hold through this tide cycle as bait kept moving through on the current, and that's exactly what's happened — the fish are here, they're just disciplined about when they'll eat.

Bluefish are the story I'd watch closest going into the back half of the month. The creeks and coves from Mattituck down toward the Gut are thick with snapper blues right now, which anybody who's fished this coast a while knows is the tell — those snappers are next year's adults, but some years the bigger cousins show up fast on their heels, and I've started seeing exactly that. Had a report of slammers working bait pushed up against the rocks near Rocky Point earlier this week, chopping through peanut bunker with that nervous, boiling surface disturbance you can spot from fifty yards off. We flagged this — said the bluefish resurgence would spread east along the North Fork as bait redistributed with the tide, and here it is, right on schedule. If you find working birds anywhere between Rocky Point and the Plum Gut approach, don't overthink it — a metal jig or a bucktail thrown into the mess will get bit fast, before they push through and disappear.

Fluke, I'll be straight with you, have been mostly frustrating. Plenty of them around the deeper channel edges off Mattituck Inlet and drifting the flats east toward Horton Point, but the water's sitting in the mid-70s and that's put most of the keeper-sized fish into a lazy, uncooperative mood, while the sound stays full of shorts that'll steal your Gulp before a legal fish ever sees it. If you're set on fluke, fish the deeper water on the last of the ebb when there's still some cool water moving, white Gulp swimming mullet on a three-quarter ounce bucktail, dragged dead slow. You'll cull through some shorts to find a keeper, but they're there.

Weakfish have been scarce, which is nothing new for this stretch the last several seasons — a few showing mixed in with the porgy catches on clam, nothing to build a trip around. Blackfish season's not open yet on this end, but I've seen a couple of boats out scouting the structure around Plum Gut approach already, marking rock piles on the machine ahead of the fall push. Good habit. That water gets crowded once the season opens and you want your spots dialed in now.

Plum Gut itself has been running hard on the bigger tides, current ripping through there enough to make boat control the real challenge, more than finding fish. Bass and blues both use that current as a highway, and the edges where the rip meets slower water off Orient have been worth a drift if you can handle the boat traffic funneling through.

Looking ahead — we're building toward that full moon at the end of the month, and bigger tides usually mean more water moving and more bait getting stirred up along this whole stretch. If that holds, I'd expect the bluefish push to keep building east and maybe pull some bigger bass up onto the structure with it. I'd fish the early tide, watch for birds working anywhere from Rocky Point to the Gut, and not waste too much daylight chasing fluke that don't want to be caught. Bring patience and bring clams — the porgies, at least, won't let you down.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull rip still working the ebb, but you'll need first light to find willing bass
reports.subhead: Snapper blues have taken over the upper river while stripers slide into the low-light hours as the Thames warms into the high 60s.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a spot off Fort Trumbull where the current pinches between the point and the channel edge, and on a good outgoing tide you can watch the seam stand up like a fence line in the water — smooth on one side, nervous and boiling on the other. That seam has been the tell all week. Bass are still using it, but they're not holding in it the way they were three weeks ago when the water had more push and less heat. Now they're ghosting through on the tail end of the ebb, usually the last ninety minutes before dead low, and then dropping back down into deeper water once the sun gets up over the fort walls.

Water in the harbor and lower river has settled into the high 60s, which sounds cool for mid-August until you remember what this river was running back in July. It's enough heat that the bass have gone the way stripers always go when the thermometer creeps up on them — they've pushed their feeding into the dark hours and the gray hours, dawn and dusk, and gone quiet and lazy through the heat of the day. I fished the sub base pilings at 5:45 Tuesday morning on the last of the outgoing and had three fish in twenty minutes on a white 3/4-ounce bucktail bounced tight to the concrete, then nothing for the next hour once the sun cleared the trees. That's the window right now. Don't sleep through it.

Gold Star Bridge is still doing what it always does this time of year — holding fish in the shadow line on the downriver side of the pilings, especially on the bottom third of the tide when the current is still moving enough to keep bait pinned against the structure. Live eels have been the difference-maker there for anyone willing to fish them slow and let the current do the work instead of retrieving. Umbrella rigs and swimming plugs have taken a few too, but nothing you'd call consistent — this is more of a "put your time in and pick off two or three quality fish" bite than a blitz.

Upriver, it's a different story entirely, and a louder one. Snapper blues are thick from around the Poquonnock confluence right down through the flats above the bridge, chewing through schools of peanut bunker with the kind of reckless enthusiasm only a one-pound bluefish can manage. We flagged this building two weeks back, and it's held true — the juvenile blues haven't thinned out, they've thickened, and there's every reason to think some of these fish start pushing into adult class as we roll into September. If you've got kids or you just want steady bent-rod action, small silver spoons or Kastmasters on light spinning gear will keep you busy for hours up there. Down at the river mouth and along the harbor edge, the adult blues mixing with the stripers are running three to four pounds, occasionally bigger, and they'll hit the same bucktails and swim shads you're throwing for bass — which makes for some pleasant surprises and the occasional bitten-off leader.

Porgy fishing has been the most dependable thing going on the harbor structure and breakwaters — New London breakwater, the rocks off Pleasure Beach, anywhere there's a hard bottom edge in fifteen to twenty-five feet. Sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, fished on the bottom stages of the tide when the current slows enough to hold your bait in the strike zone, has been producing steady catches of porgies in the ten-to-twelve-inch range with enough larger fish mixed in to keep it interesting. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's the kind of thing you can count on when the bass get finicky.

Blackfish are still mostly a non-story right now — the summer stretch is typically quiet for them in this system, and I haven't heard of anyone targeting them seriously until the water starts cooling in September and pushes them back onto the rockier structure around Fort Trumbull and the breakwaters. That's a fall conversation, not an August one.

Tide-wise, we're coming off the strong new-moon push and easing into the softer first-quarter cycle, which explains some of the drop-off in aggression at spots like Fort Trumbull — less current means less concentrated bait, means less reason for a bass to commit in daylight. That'll start rebuilding again as we approach the August 28 full moon, and when it does, I'd expect the harbor and river mouth bite to sharpen back up, especially if any push of adult bunker works its way down from the Sound the way it has further east along the coast this month. If that bait shows up in the river mouth, it could trigger the kind of aggressive, more prolonged bass activity we're seeing from Narragansett up toward Plymouth right now — worth watching for.

For this week: fish the early and late tide stages, work Fort Trumbull and the sub base pilings on the last of the ebb, and don't discount the porgy grounds if the bass go quiet on you. If the moon builds the current back up like I expect, I'd start checking the river mouth for signs of bunker showing before the full moon hits.

reports.headline: New Haven Breakwall Porgies Keep the Rod Bent While Blues Sneak Back In
reports.subhead: Green crabs and hi-lo rigs are filling coolers on the rockpiles while sea bass hold deep and stripers slip into a dawn-only pattern.
reports.body_markdown:
Dropped a hi-lo rig baited with green crab off the outer breakwall Tuesday morning, right on the last hour of the flood, and had a double-header of porgies before my coffee went cold. That's the story of the season out here — you can set your watch by it. The scup are stacked on every rockpile from the New Haven Harbor breakwalls out to Charles Island, and they haven't cared one bit about the heat that's been sitting on top of this Sound for weeks.

The pattern right now is almost boringly reliable, which I say as a compliment. Anchor up tight to the breakwall rocks in 15 to 20 feet, or work the north side of Charles Island where the bar drops into deeper water, and a hi-lo with size 6 or 8 hooks tipped with green crab or squid strips is going to put porgies in the bucket on just about any tide stage. I like the last two hours of the flood into the top — current's still moving enough to keep bait scent working but it's not ripping you off the spot. Fish are running 8 to 12 inches with a scattering of chunky 13s mixed in, plenty big enough to fry up that night.

When you want a bigger tug, drop down to the deeper structure. Falkner Island's rockpiles and the edges of Stratford Shoal are holding black sea bass in 30 to 40 feet, and they've been the bonus fish all month — a nice change of pace from the porgy grind. Squid strips or a small piece of clam on the bottom hook of that same hi-lo rig works fine, but if you want to target sea bass specifically, jig a diamond jig or a bucktail tipped with Gulp right on bottom and hop it slow. They're not shy about eating right now, and a handful of keepers in the 14 to 16 inch range is a normal trip out there this week.

Fluke are the frustrating piece of the puzzle. Milford Gulf has been giving up drifts full of short fluke — plenty of bites, not much filling the cooler. That warm water sitting on top of the Sound has them lazy and undersized, the same story playing out across the whole basin right now. If you're set on a keeper, I'd fish the deeper edges of the Gulf on the outgoing where there's a little more current and cooler water pushing through, and stick with bigger baits — a whole strip of squid or a 5-inch Gulp swimming mullet on a bucktail — to weed out the dinks.

Stripers have gone quiet in the middle of the day, which isn't a surprise with the Sound running warm — we're talking mid-70s pushing toward 80 in the shallows. That compresses the bite into a tight window right at first light. I've been sliding out to the sandbar off Charles Island before sunrise, working a topwater popper or a soft-plastic swimbait along the drop where the bar falls into deeper water, and connecting with slot fish for about 45 minutes before the sun gets high and they slide off into deeper, cooler water. Same story off the Hammonasset flats — dawn is the whole show right now, and once that sun's up, you're better off switching to bottom fishing.

Here's the piece I'll flag because we called it a couple weeks back — said the bluefish resurgence would spread east from the Western Sound reef structure while porgy held as the anchor bite, and that's exactly what's playing out. Snapper blues have been thick in the harbor and around the breakwall pilings, snapping up small metals and Kastmasters, and I've started seeing a few adult-class blues, 3 to 4 pounds, mixing into the porgy spots off Charles Island. That's a good sign for late August — those adult blues tend to build right through Labor Day once the bait gets moving, and having them show up on structure alongside the porgies gives you a real one-two punch on a single anchor spot.

Worth mentioning: we've had that typical August pattern of afternoon thunderstorms rolling through, and I've had some of my best striper and bluefish action in that short window right after a front pushes through — the air pressure drops, the bait gets nervous, and fish that have been sulking in the heat turn on for twenty or thirty minutes. If you see those clouds building out toward Long Island in the afternoon, don't pack it in. Get your gear stowed, ride it out, and be ready to fish that first clearing.

Looking ahead, tidal flow is starting to build back up as we push toward the August 28 full moon, and that should sharpen everything — more current means more bait pinned against structure, which means better sea bass and porgy action and a real shot at extending that striper window past dawn. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd hit the Charles Island bar at first light for stripers, then slide over to the breakwall rockpiles once the sun's up and let the porgies do the rest of the work.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Tough Grind, Better Read: The 100-Fathom Edge Bailed Out a Slow Week South
reports.subhead: Four canyons, one warm pool that won't move — here's where it actually paid to run this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a C-plus week with a strong finish. Monday through Wednesday I burned diesel running between Spencer and Lindenkohl looking for the kind of green, clean water we had in July, and mostly what I found was empty ocean and a slick of bait that never held together long enough to matter. By Thursday the picture changed — not because the fish came back to the deep lumps everybody wants to run to, but because we finally figured out where they'd gone: shallower, onto the shelf itself, sitting the 100-fathom line instead of pushing all the way out to the thousand-fathom structure this fleet's been trained to chase since June.

That's the story of the whole southern stretch right now. The warm pool that's been parked over this water since early August hasn't moved much, but it's pushed the most productive edge up onto the shelf. You could see it in the results out of Ocean City — 334 boats fished six days of the White Marlin Open and the fleet only put three bigeyes on the dock. That's not a fleet that forgot how to fish. That's a fleet that ran to the same grounds that have produced for years and found them dead, because the water that usually sits over those lumps has slid inshore on them.

Here's how I worked it. Spencer first — I like Spencer early in any pattern shift because the canyon head sits close enough to the shelf edge that if the warm water's crawling shallow, Spencer feels it before Norfolk does. We worked the 100-fathom curve on the northeast wall Thursday, trolling a standard spread of ballyhoo behind cedar plugs with a couple green machines out the long riggers, hunting the temperature break instead of the bottom contour like we normally would. Marked scattered yellowfin on the troll that afternoon, mixed with a few gaffer mahi holding under a scrap of floating grass we ran into with actual bait under it. Nothing that filled a box in an hour, but enough bites to confirm the fish were there — just thin and moving, not stacked.

Lindenkohl was the disappointment of the week. Ran up there Tuesday expecting the same edge water that's carried us all summer and instead found a flat, dead push with almost no life past the drop-off on the meter. If you're planning a Lindenkohl trip this week, I'd hold off until somebody confirms that edge has re-formed. No sense burning the extra run for water that looked the way it did Tuesday.

Poor Man's is the canyon I keep coming back to because it's the shortest run and it's been the most forgiving when the bite gets choosy like this. We chunked butterfish over structure inside the canyon head Thursday night into Friday morning and picked at yellowfin in the 20-to-35-pound class, plus one respectable bigeye that came up in the chum slick around midnight. That's your night bite — with the warm pool sitting where it is, the bigeye pattern favors after-dark chunking over daytime trolling right now. Squid strips and butterfish chunks both drew fish, but butterfish held them in the slick longer.

Norfolk's the wild card because it's far enough south that it reads the warm pool differently than the other three, and this week that worked in our favor. One boat reported a wahoo on a high-speed spread — bird teaser up front, cedar plugs and a diving lure running planers around 14 knots along the shelf break south of the canyon. That's the first legitimate wahoo chatter I've had out of this zone all month, and it lines up with something we flagged a few days back — that the warm pool holding its position into mid-August would eventually start pulling wahoo up onto these edges. One fish doesn't make a run, but it's the kind of early signal worth watching if you're plotting your next trip south.

White marlin have been quiet across all four canyons — a couple of respectable bites on naked ballyhoo behind Sea Witches trolled over Poor Man's, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. Same story with bluefin. The water's simply too warm right now for them to hold anywhere but the deepest, coldest pockets, and those pockets have been hard to pin down this week.

If I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd run to Poor Man's for the night chunk bite and stage close enough to slide over to Spencer's shelf edge at first light if the overnight report comes back soft. The moon's building toward the August 28 full, which should tighten the tide and concentrate bait better than the slack water we've been fighting. If that warm pool holds its current position through the weekend, expect the shelf-edge pattern at Spencer and Norfolk to keep outproducing the deep water everybody's used to running. If it slides back offshore, the deep grounds could turn back on fast — that's the single biggest variable I'm watching heading into next week, and I'll be checking it every morning before I decide which canyon gets the first run.

reports.headline: Jumbo Blues Own the Rips at Shagwong While Montauk Waits on the Squid
reports.subhead: Slot bass and blues to double digits are stacked on the current edges, and the water's cooling just enough to make you believe the albies are close.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a specific week every August when the Point stops feeling like summer and starts feeling like Montauk again. This is that week. The tourist traffic on the Circle is still bumper to bumper, but out on the water the light's changing angle earlier in the evening, the bunker schools are getting nervous, and the fish know something the beach crowd doesn't. I've fished this transition my whole life and it never gets old — the sense that something bigger is loading up behind the curtain.

Right now the story at the Point is bluefish, and I mean real bluefish — not the summer snappers that have been thick in the harbor and up in Fort Pond Bay all month, but grown adult blues pushing eight, nine, ten pounds, chopping bait on top at Shagwong Reef and along the boulder field off the Lighthouse. We flagged this building back when the snappers first showed thick in the back bays — said the adult class would keep filling in through late August, and here they are, right on schedule. These fish are holding tight to the hard-running current edges, the visible boils where the rip pushes against the reef structure, and they're not subtle about it. If you see white water and diving gulls off the Lighthouse on the building tide, get a bucktail or a diamond jig in there fast, because that window can close in twenty minutes once the bait clears the seam.

The bass are mixed in with those blues, and the pattern that's working is almost identical for both species. Cast a 1.5-ounce bucktail — bare or dressed with a white or chartreuse tail — across the far edge of the rip, let it sink clean off the drop where the flat falls into the channel, then work it back with a slow, deliberate bottom hop. That's the North Bar program right now on the incoming, and it's producing slot fish consistently, with the occasional overslot mixed in for guys willing to grind through short fish to find them. Turtle Cove has been quieter for bass specifically but still worth a look on the last two hours of the outgoing, when bait gets flushed out of the cove mouth and stripers stage to ambush it in the deeper pockets along the rock line.

Water at the Point is sitting right around 69 degrees, which is a number I like this time of year — not so warm that the fish get lazy and scattered, cool enough that the bigger bass are comfortable holding shallow on the rocks instead of sulking in deep water during daylight. That's part of why the boulder field bite has stayed dependable even through the midday sun, which is unusual for August. I had a father-son team out earlier this week who worked the incoming at the Lighthouse rocks with bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs and iced two bass in the high twenties, plus enough blues to lose count, before nine in the morning.

South side surf and the fluke drifts have been more of a grind, and I want to be straight about that instead of dressing it up. The fluke bite off the ocean beaches has been mixed — plenty of shorts mixed with the occasional keeper to five or six pounds, and you're covering water to find the better fish rather than anchoring on one drift and waiting. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the sand-to-structure transitions, has been the most consistent producer. Porgies have been steadier and less glamorous — working the deeper structure off Fort Pond Bay with clam bait on standard porgy rigs will fill a cooler without much drama, which some days is exactly what you want.

Now, the question everyone's asking me at the dock is the albies. We called the arrival window around the August 12 new moon, and honestly, the timing hasn't quite lined up yet — I haven't had a confirmed albie or bonito push through the rips at the Point this week. But I'm not backing off that call, because the signs are building in exactly the direction you'd want. Squid have been pushing down hard off Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water cools, and historically when that squid line starts creeping toward the Race and into Block Island Sound, it's the trigger that supercharges our rip patterns here at Montauk — bait gets funneled through Shagwong and around the Point, and albies and bonito follow it in behind the blues. If that squid keeps sliding our way over the next week or two, I'd expect the first real showing right around the Point, probably working the rips on the last of the incoming when the current is still ripping hard enough to hold bait tight.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward the full on August 28, and that's usually when this whole pattern sharpens up — bigger tides, harder current, bait pushed with more authority through the rips. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd be at North Bar on the building incoming with bucktails, working the seam methodically, and I'd keep a bonito outfit rigged and ready in the rocket launcher just in case that squid line beats my prediction. Worth planning around, not worth betting the farm on just yet.

reports.headline: 71.2°F at the Bight Buoy: Hudson's Bigeye Chunk Slows, Yellowfin Hold the Edges
reports.subhead: A warm pool sitting right on the canyon wall has cooled the night bigeye bite — but the Claw and the Dip are still giving up daytime yellowfin and mahi for anyone working the edge instead of the deep water.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-one point two degrees at the Bight buoy, seas holding under four feet at five-second intervals. That's not a canyon read, but it tells me plenty about what's happening between the beach and the color change — the whole shelf is carrying more heat than it should for mid-August, and that warm water isn't stopping at the 60-fathom line. It's pushing right up onto the edge of Hudson Canyon, and that's the single biggest reason this week's bite looks different than it did two weeks ago.

Here's the honest version: the after-dark bigeye chunk bite that had guys buzzing near the edge earlier this month has gone soft. We flagged the warm water sticking around as a good sign for that pattern holding steady — and it did hold, for a stretch — but a warm pool sharing space with the canyon has a way of spreading bigeye out instead of concentrating them. I ran two trips out of Manasquan this week and put buckets down over 300 fathoms both nights with butterfish chunks and whole squid strips on 60-lb fluoro leader, and the count was thin. One bigeye each night, both around 150 pounds, both on the same slow incoming drift between midnight and 2 a.m. That's a fish worth the trip, but it's not the volume bite we were seeing when the water was tighter to the wall.

So this week I'm not committing a full tank of fuel to sit over water that's been quiet. The better play — and the one paying off for boats I've talked to at the dock — is working the shallower structure and the edges instead of pushing deep. That means the Claw and the Dip during daylight hours, trolling the 100-fathom line where the warm water is stacking bait against the break instead of just soaking through it. A standard spread of ballyhoo behind Green Machines, naked ballyhoo on 50-lb fluoro, and a couple of cedar plugs way back has been drawing yellowfin in the 25 to 40-pound class, mixed with schoolie mahi under any piece of floating structure — lobster gear, debris, weed clumps, anything holding shade. If you find a real weedline with color to it, slow down and work it with a spreader bar and a naked ballyhoo dropped back on a flat line. That's where the mahi show up in pairs and threes, not just the stray teenager everyone expects.

White marlin have been in the mix but scattered — I heard of two raised off the Dip on a dredge spread with a mix of squid chains and mullet, neither one converted, which tells you they're around but not committed yet. Wahoo have been quiet; if the water keeps holding this warm, I'd expect a few to show on high-speed spreads with cedar plugs and skirted Ilanders once the bait gets pushed tighter to structure, but I'm not seeing it yet and I won't pretend otherwise.

The number I'm actually watching this week isn't a temperature — it's the deep blue eddy water that's been pinwheeling in from the east and working toward the canyon complex. That kind of clean, blue, nutrient-poor water sounds like a bad thing, but when it collides with the warmer inshore water sitting on the wall, it can sharpen a temperature break fast and pull bait — and bigeye — right back onto the edge. I've seen this happen before: one good push of that eddy water onto the Hudson grounds and a soft pattern flips inside 48 hours. If it stalls out east of the canyon instead, expect the same mixed bag we're getting now — decent yellowfin and mahi on the troll, a long night for one or two bigeye on the chunk.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the August 28 full moon, and that stronger current should start sharpening bait concentrations along the 100-fathom break by the weekend. We called that current buildup a few weeks back, and it's arriving on schedule — the question is whether it lines up with that eddy water making its move at the same time. If both happen together, I'd expect the bigeye chunk to come back to life and the daytime troll to get more consistent instead of just good in flashes.

If I had one trip this week, I'd run to the Dip first thing, troll the edge through the morning with ballyhoo and a spreader bar looking for yellowfin and mahi under anything floating, then push out to deeper water only if I found bait stacked tight on the sounder by mid-afternoon. I wouldn't plan on a bigeye trip unless that eddy water shows real signs of pushing onto the grounds — right now the smarter money is on the shallower structure doing the producing, not the deep chunk. Keep an eye on that boundary between the warm shelf water and the clean blue pushing in from the east. That's the line that decides which version of this week's bite you get.

reports.headline: Bunker Push Bass Onto Southwest Ledge in Broad Daylight
reports.subhead: Building current toward the August 28 full moon is stacking bait against the Ledge and the North Rip — bluefish are the sure thing, bass and bonito are the maybe.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out past the breakwater Tuesday morning, flat calm, and the water off the Southwest Ledge had that green, oxygenated look it gets when the current's really moving — not the flat pewter shine of dead water, but that slight roll and shimmer that tells you bait is getting pushed. Ten minutes later the birds told the rest of the story. Terns working low and tight over a patch of nervous water, and under them, peanut bunker getting bulldozed by fish that clearly didn't care it was ten in the morning.

That's the thing about this run of bass we're in — they're not waiting for first light anymore. The bunker schools stacking up from Narragansett down through the Sound are thick enough that the stripers are blowing up on top in broad daylight, which tells you the bait density is winning out over their usual low-light caution. We're seeing pieces of that same pattern out here. Southwest Ledge in 25 to 40 feet has been holding fish that push up under bait pods on the last two hours of the incoming, and the North Rip did the same thing Wednesday evening — a hard boil that lasted maybe fifteen minutes before it went quiet again. I got one over 30 pounds out of that window on a white 2-ounce Deadly Dick fished bare, no teaser, just a straight retrieve through the wash. My mate missed two more on a chartreuse umbrella rig trolled slow along the edge where the ledge drops from 30 into 55.

I want to be straight about this bite because it's not a constant — it's a window bite. You catch the tide right, catch the bait pushed up against structure, and it can be twenty minutes of pure chaos. Miss it, and you're marking bait on the machine with nothing touching it. The building current into the August 28 full moon is the reason these windows are getting sharper. We flagged this a couple weeks back — said once tidal flow built after the new moon, Block Island Sound would turn on quickly once bait got pushed hard against structure, and that's exactly the mechanism driving these daylight blitzes now. Current does the work here more than anywhere else on this coast.

Bluefish have been the more dependable half of the equation, and honestly the more fun half some days. Adult class blues, 4 to 7 pounds, are mixing right into those same bunker schools around the wind farm structure and along the Ledge, and they'll hit anything that moves fast — Ava jigs, small pencil poppers, cut bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig if you want to sit still and let them come to you. We called the adult push building back on the 14th when snapper blues were still thick in the back bays and estuaries — well, here they are, grown into 4-pounders and running with the striper blitzes exactly like we thought they would. Great Salt Pond and Old Harbor are both loaded with snappers still, so the next wave behind these adults is already staged.

Fluke have been the disappointment of the week, if I'm being honest. Warm water on the sand between the Ledge and the island has made them lazy — you can mark fish on structure and still get nothing but soft, half-hearted bites. I fished four spots Thursday drifting 5-inch white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails and only boxed two keepers over 19 inches, both right on the edge of a rock pile where the current concentrates bait. If you're going after fluke this week, fish oversized baits tight to structure and be patient — this isn't the drift-and-cover-water pattern that works when they're aggressive. It's a finesse game right now.

Porgies are steady on the reefs southeast of the harbor, 20 to 35 feet, sandworms and green crab on a hi-lo rig, nothing dramatic but reliable if you want dinner. No real blackfish talk yet — too early, that'll build through September as water starts to ease.

The question everyone's asking me at the dock is bonito. We haven't seen them show at Block Island yet, but Nantucket Sound and the Cape Cod side are with them already, and there was a sailfish sighting off Chatham that tells you just how far this warm pattern has pushed things north. If that warm pocket holds and slides west the way these things sometimes do, I'd expect the first bonito sightings inside the Sound within the next week or two — probably around the can off Old Harbor or out past the breakwater where the water clears up fast. Worth keeping a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig rigged and ready even while you're bass fishing.

Offshore, there's bluefin building both to our west and out in the eastern canyons, and the honest answer is we haven't seen that push extend onto our own canyon-adjacent water yet. That's the single biggest variable I'm watching this week — if that warm edge shifts east even a little, Block Canyon could turn on fast. For now, my money stays inshore.

Looking ahead: if this current keeps building toward the full moon, I'd expect the bass blitzes at the Ledge and the North Rip to sharpen rather than fade — shorter windows, harder feeds. I'd fish the last two hours of the incoming at the Ledge and be ready to move fast if the birds tell you to. Bluefish should stay steady through the week regardless of tide. Fluke, keep your expectations modest and fish slow. And if you're out there and see fish busting bait on top with fins that don't look like stripers or blues — get a picture. I want to know before anybody else does.

reports.headline: A hundred-mile push to Atlantis, and the eddy that made it worth the diesel
reports.subhead: Yellowfin turned up on the east wall this week where the blue water finally pinwheeled in — the rest of the canyons stayed quiet.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, four hours out of Montauk, my mate leaned over the covering board and said the water looked like ink with a blue undertone — the kind of color you don't see enough of out here in August. We'd left the dock at 3:30, run the numbers to the east side of Atlantis, and by the time the sun cleared the horizon we had four lines in the water and no idea yet whether the color meant anything. By nine o'clock we knew. First fish came unglued at the leader — a yellowfin that shook a green machine on a short wind-on and left us staring at each other instead of at a fish in the box. Lost fish sting different offshore. You don't get a second cast forty miles from the beach. But we boated five more before noon, sixty to eighty pounds, clean fat fish that had clearly been eating well on whatever the eddy pushed in front of them.

That's the story of the week out here — an eddy of deep blue water pinwheeled in from the east and settled over the eastern and western sides of Atlantis, and the yellowfin followed it in like they were supposed to. We flagged this pattern building two weeks back and said the current behind it didn't look like it was breaking down anytime soon. It hasn't. If anything it's held tighter than I expected for mid-August, and that's the difference between a good trip and a burned tank of fuel with nothing to show for it.
