The program that worked for us, and for a few other boats working that same water, was straightforward: green and rainbow colors trolled through the warmest, cleanest part of the water column from mid-morning into early afternoon, then a swap to black and purple in that gray light right at sunrise and again as the sun dropped. Ballyhoo behind the smaller lures, a naked or lightly-skirted bird spread out front to draw the eye, and cedar plugs mixed in the pattern for the smaller yellowfin that wanted something subtler than a full daisy chain. Depth wasn't the story this week so much as water color — find where that blue eddy water pinched up against the greener inshore stuff, usually somewhere around the temperature break on the east wall, and that's where the reels started going off. A couple mahi came through the pattern too, nothing big, schoolies mostly, but a welcome bonus when you're grinding a long troll line waiting on a bite.

I want to be straight about the rest of the trip, because I don't sell hope out here — I sell what I saw. We ran a leg over toward Veatch on the way home hoping to find a piece of that same water holding over structure, and it was dead. Clean, but dead. No bait showing on the sounder, no birds working, nothing. Hydrographer and Oceanographer, from what I've heard secondhand from a couple of boats that pushed that far east this week, were quiet as well — same story, no bait stacked up, no temperature break worth working. That eddy water hasn't spread that far east yet, and until it does, or until something else pushes bait onto those grounds, I wouldn't burn the extra hour and a half of running time to find out. Atlantis is where the fish are right now, plain and simple, and that's not a knock on the other canyons — it's just where the water decided to go this week.

Bigeye and bluefin didn't factor into our week at Atlantis, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. There's giant activity happening well to our west that everyone at the dock has been talking about, boats stacked five miles wide on fish, but that's not my water and I didn't see it myself, so I'll leave that report to the guys running it. White marlin showed nothing for us either — no shots, no sightings, nothing worth mentioning. Wahoo the same. This was a yellowfin week, full stop, and a solid one if you were in the right piece of blue water.

On the fuel math, since that's the real cost of doing business out here: Atlantis is roughly a hundred miles from Montauk, more like a hundred-twenty if you're running out of Block Island or the Rhode Island ports. Call it five hours at a sane cruise, less if you're willing to burn the extra fuel to push it. That's a ten-hour round trip before you ever wet a line, so you'd better have a reason to believe the water's there before you leave the dock — and this week, for the first time in a couple weeks, I did.

Looking ahead, the moon's building back toward the August 28th full, and tidal push should firm up over the next several days. If that blue eddy holds its position over Atlantis — and there's no sign yet that it's sliding off — I'd expect the yellowfin bite to hold too, maybe improve as bait continues to stack on that edge. If it starts drifting east toward Veatch or Hydrographer, that's the one thing that would get me to shift my run, and I'll be watching the water color closely on the way out next trip to see if it's moved. Until then, Atlantis is getting my fuel, and I'd suggest it gets yours too if you're making the run from Montauk, Block, or the Bay this week.

reports.headline: Pulled Off the Deep Drops, Worked the Shelf Edge — Yellowfin and a Mahi to Show for It
reports.subhead: Bigeye chunking went quiet overnight, so we shifted daylight hours to the shelf break and found scattered but real action.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip our usual overnight anchor-up in the deep water and instead spend daylight hours working the shelf break on the troll. That's not how we've fished Wilmington most of this summer, but the numbers on the overnight chunk had gotten thin enough that burning fuel to sit still didn't make sense anymore. If the bigeye aren't cooperating after dark, I'd rather run bait spreads over structure I can actually see moving on the fish finder than hope a chunk slick pulls something up from a thousand feet of water that isn't there.

That decision paid off, modestly. We picked up three yellowfin in the 25 to 40 pound class trolling green machines and cedar plugs behind a spreader bar, worked tight along a temperature seam that's been sitting just east of the canyon's edge. The water out there has a warm pool parked on it that hasn't wanted to move, and that's the same warm pool that's been giving the whole area trouble all month — it's flattened out the color and temperature breaks that usually stack bait up over the deeper humps. What it has done is push some of the activity shallower, onto the shelf itself, which is exactly where we found our fish. One mahi, a stout bull pushing 20 pounds, came off a small grass patch holding some scattered floating debris — that's been the pattern for mahi lately, small isolated debris fields rather than big weed lines, so you've got to run visual and be ready to peel off the spread when you spot something.

Bigeye have been the frustrating story. We ran the chunk for four hours one night this week — butterflied bunker, a sabiki-caught bait or two mixed in, drifting a natural slick off the stern — and came up with one fish in the 120-pound range and a couple of short bites we never connected on. That's a long way from where this bite was running a few weeks back. The thermal boundary that's been sitting east of the canyon hasn't broken down, but it hasn't organized into anything productive either — it's just sitting there, flat and unhelpful, and until it either retreats or reshuffles, I'm not optimistic about the overnight numbers improving much. If you're set up to chunk, I'd still put in the time, because one or two quality bigeye is still a good trip for most boats. Just don't go in expecting a repeat of July.

White marlin have stayed a realistic bonus fish on the troll, not a target you can plan a trip around but one you'll see if you're pulling a naked ballyhoo spread with a couple of dredge teasers mixed in along any real temperature break. We had two bites in six days out, converted one, a fish right around 60 pounds that came unglued twice before finally sticking on a small ballyhoo skirted in pink and white. No wahoo this week for us, though I heard of one boat picking up a pair on high-speed lures worked over structure closer to the shelf edge — worth keeping a wahoo bomb rigged if you're already running that speed for marlin.

The honest read here is that Wilmington is fishing like a lot of the mid-Atlantic canyons right now — spotty, not dead, but nowhere close to lit-up. The traditional deep drops that usually load up this time of year have gone quiet, and from what I'm seeing and hearing, that's a widespread problem, not just a Wilmington issue. The fish that are around have moved up onto the shelf break, which tells me the warm pool sitting offshore of the canyon is squeezing the productive water into a narrower band than we're used to working. That's actually useful information — it means less running around guessing and more time working a specific stretch of water carefully.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason to change the plan much for the next several days. If that thermal boundary holds where it's sitting, I'd keep running daylight troll spreads along the shelf edge rather than committing full nights to the chunk — better use of fuel and time on the water for what's actually biting. If it breaks down or slides, and there's some chance of that given how long it's been parked there, I'd expect the deeper lumps to come back into play and the bigeye chunk bite to pick back up with it. That's the single biggest variable I'm watching this week — where that warm water sits three days from now will tell us whether we're back on the anchor after dark or staying on the troll through the shelf break. Bring dramamine either way; the ride out has been lumpy the last few trips and doesn't look like it's smoothing out soon.

reports.headline: August 17: Washington's Early Jump Has Run Its Course, and Now the Rest of the Fleet Caught Up
reports.subhead: Washington fired first this year like it always does, but the same warm pool that's stalling the southern canyons has finally caught up to us too.
reports.body_markdown:
Every August I do the same math. June is when Washington shows its hand — Gulf Stream positioning puts warm water on our edge weeks before the other canyons even think about waking up. July is when that head start turns into a real pattern, bigeye stacking on the temperature breaks while boats to our south are still waiting on their own water to sort itself out. August is the grind month, the one where the early jump either holds or gets erased. This year, by the middle of the month, I'm looking at erased.

Here's the honest version: Washington's not fishing bad, it's fishing average, and average in mid-August after the kind of June and July we had feels like a step backward even if it isn't one. The whole stretch of canyons is caught in the same squeeze right now — a warm pool sitting over the historically productive southern lumps that's pushed the bigeye bite into a real funk. I've talked to enough boats running our grounds this week to know it's not just us. The tournament fleet that worked this stretch a few weeks back struggled to find bigeye in any real numbers, and that tells you something when guys with good electronics and better instincts are coming back with thin fish counts.

What's working is what's always worked when the deep canyon proper goes soft — the 100-fathom line. Boats staying up on that edge instead of pushing into the deep water are outfishing the ones committing to the canyon interior. That's a positioning call, not a mystery. When the water in the canyon proper gets muddled by this kind of warm-pool intrusion, the bait and the predators that follow it tend to hold shallower, right on that shelf-adjacent structure rather than diving into the depths where the thermal layering gets confused. If you're running out this week, don't burn fuel and time pushing past that line hoping something better shows up deeper. It hasn't been there.

Wahoo and mahi are the more honest targets right now, and I mean that as a compliment to both species, not a knock on tuna. The weedlines and temperature breaks closer to the shelf have been holding real fish — wahoo coming on high-speed trolled rigged ballyhoo and deep-diving swimming plugs run at eight to ten knots along any hard color or temp change you can find, mahi stacked under whatever floating structure and weed mats you can spot working the same water. Bright skirted jigs and small poppers worked around the weed clumps have been drawing them up, and once you find one mahi under a mat there are usually five more with it — that part of the pattern hasn't changed all year. White marlin have been a legitimate bycatch on the troll spread out here too, though I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them right now — they've shown up enough on the temp breaks to keep the outriggers interesting, not enough to call it a target species this week.

Bluefin have been more of a rumor than a pattern out here lately — a few incidental fish on the troll, nothing consistent enough to build a trip plan around. If you're set on bigeye, I'd temper expectations hard right now. The deep canyon proper has been a low-percentage play for two weeks running, and burning a full tank to find out it's still soft isn't smart fishing, it's hope dressed up as a plan.

We flagged this coming — said back on the 7th to watch for that cooling signal pushing north and to expect steady conditions unless it did. It did, and here we are, the southern squeeze up on our own edge instead of staying somebody else's problem.

Looking ahead, the tide cycle is building back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that's usually when things get interesting again out here — stronger current means better bait concentration, and better bait concentration is usually what breaks a funk like this one. If the warm pool boundary slides back south in the next week, I'd expect the bigeye pattern to reactivate on the deeper structure fairly quick, Washington style — we tend to feel the good news early same as we feel the bad news early. If it holds where it's sitting, stick with the 100-fathom line, keep working the weedlines for wahoo and mahi, and don't force the deep water just because it's there. That's the call for right now, and I'll adjust it the minute the water tells me something different.

reports.headline: Peconic settles into August rhythm — porgies stacked at Shelter Island, snappers take over the docks
reports.subhead: Warm, glassy bay water has pushed the bite into tight dawn-and-dusk windows, but the bottom fishing around Shelter Island is as reliable as it gets this time of year.
reports.body_markdown:
By mid-August the Peconic has settled into that familiar late-summer groove — the water up top is soft and warm, the bays are glassy by ten in the morning, and everything that's biting is doing it on the edges of the day or down deep where the current keeps things honest. This is the bay I know best in this stretch of the calendar: not flashy, not a blitz, just steady work if you know where to put the boat.

Porgies remain the backbone of the report. Shelter Island continues to be the epicenter — Cedar Island light, the reef off Fleets Neck, and the rock piles running out from Jessup's Neck are all holding good numbers of scup in 15 to 25 feet. High-low rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, sandworms or clam strips, fished right on bottom on the last two hours of the incoming or the first hour of the outgoing, have been the ticket. These fish don't need much finesse this time of year — they're thick, they're hungry, and once you find the school over shell or rubble the action holds until the tide really starts to run hard. Anchor up tight, chum lightly with crushed clam, and you can fill a cooler without much drama.

Fluke are still modest, which is about what I expected. I said last week that the fluke pattern here would stay unspectacular through mid-August, and that's exactly how it's played out — the bay is holding fish, just not in the numbers or size that get anybody excited. The better drifts have been the channel edges: the cut off Jessup's Neck, the deeper stretch of Noyack Bay channel, and the flow lanes off Southold. Twenty to 35 feet, moving water, white Gulp swimming mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have been out-producing straight bait rigs. Most of what's coming over the rail is short to just-keeper, so it's a pick-through-them bite rather than a limit trip, but there are enough fluke in the mix to make an afternoon drift worthwhile if you're patient about it.

Weakfish are showing the way they usually do in August — intermittent, deep, and worth a look if you're already fishing the basins. Northwest Harbor and the mouth of Three Mile Harbor have both given up a few weakfish in the 25 to 40-foot holes on the slower stages of the tide, mostly on bucktails tipped with squid or on bottom rigs with a live killie. Nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around, but if you're porgy fishing nearby and want to drop a bait into the deeper water on the way in or out, it's not a bad side bet.

The real late-summer staple right now is snapper blues, and they're thick around the docks in Greenport, Sag Harbor, and up in Three Mile Harbor. This is the bite I flagged as building last week, and it's arrived right on schedule — small silver spoons, size 00 or 0 Kastmasters, or a bobber rig with a spearing chunk fished right off the pilings will keep kids and adults both busy for an hour at a time. It's a good sign for what's coming, too. When snapper numbers build like this through late August, the adult bluefish class tends to follow into September as the bay cools and the bigger fish push in behind the bait.

Striped bass haven't disappeared, they've just gone quiet in the middle of the day the way they always do when the surface water sits in the high 70s. The better window has been right at first light, working the rip off Jessup's Neck and the edges around Robins Island on bucktails or small swimming plugs before the sun gets up. There's also been some evening action working bunker chunks on the channel edges near Orient Point as the tide turns — nothing to write home about, but enough fish moving through to make dawn and dusk worth the alarm clock. The moon is still building back toward the full on the 28th, so tidal push has been on the weaker side this week; once that current strengthens up again it should sharpen the bass bite along those current seams and give the porgy and fluke fishing an extra gear too.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift in the next several days — the bay is going to keep doing its warm-water August thing, with porgies as the sure bet, fluke as a grinder's game, and bass and weakfish rewarding early risers and current watchers. If the wind stays out of the south and keeps things calm, I'd spend my time at Shelter Island in the mornings for porgies, then slide into the channels midday for a fluke drift while the tide's still moving. As we build toward that full moon and the tides strengthen, watch Orient Point and the mouth of the Gut — that's usually the first sign the fall transition is starting to stir, even if it's still a few weeks off.

reports.headline: The Bar East of the Jetty Moved Again — And the Bass Found the New Cut
reports.subhead: Junky ocean swell pushed bait and stripers into the throat of Moriches Inlet this week, with the real bite happening where the shifted sandbar meets the channel edge.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the east side of the inlet jetty at Cupsogue on Wednesday's low and the bottom read different than it did two weeks ago. The bar that usually sits tight against the rocks has slid east another fifteen, maybe twenty yards, and it's built up a shoulder where there used to be a smooth taper into the channel. That's not unusual for August — this inlet never sits still, it's been rebuilding itself since the '92 nor'easter reshaped the whole throat, and every blow since keeps nudging sand around the jetty tips. What matters for you is that the new shoulder creates a sharper drop-off, maybe six feet of relief in twenty yards, right where the ebb current funnels hardest. That's exactly the kind of edge stripers hold on, and this week they did.

The ocean's been running short and junky — the swell off the Bight has been sitting around four feet at five seconds, which is a mess for surfcasting the open beach but it's actually good news inside. That kind of chop keeps bait pushed off the outer bars and funneling into the inlet mouth, and the fish follow it. Cupsogue regulars who fished the last two hours of the ebb into dead low found bass holding right on that new drop, taking 1.5-ounce bucktails cast up-current and swung down across the seam, worked with a slow lift-and-drop on the bottom third of the retrieve. Nothing oversized — mostly 24 to 30 inches, a mix of school fish and a few solid slot bass — but consistent enough that guys were putting three or four in the box before the tide went dead. Same pattern held on the inside edge of the west jetty on the front of the flood, though that bite's shorter-lived, maybe 90 minutes before the current gets too soft to hold fish tight to structure.

Don't bother with the middle of the day right now. Bay water's been sitting warm through the afternoon — enough that the bite compresses hard into the first two hours of light and the last two before dark. I fished a noon tide Tuesday off Tuthill Point and never had a sniff; came back at 6 p.m. on the same tide stage two days later and it was a different bay. That's the pattern to plan around for the next week or two — mornings and evenings, skip the heat of the day unless you're specifically working deep holes.

Bluefish are the one thing that's been reliable no matter what the tide chart says. Snapper blues are thick in the back creeks off East Moriches and around the Forge River mouth — small, aggressive, and a great way to keep a kid busy on light spinning gear and a piece of spearing. We flagged this a couple weeks back, that the snapper class would build into real adult fish by late August, and that's exactly what's showing now. Out at the inlet itself, adult blues in the 3-5 pound range are mixing into the same current seams as the bass, and they'll hit the same bucktails, though a wire leader saves you some heartache. Topwater poppers thrown into visible boils off the jetty rocks on the last of the ebb have been drawing violent strikes — that bite doesn't last long once the current slacks, so you have to be ready when the boils show.

Fluke fishing inside the bay has been unremarkable — a lot of shorts, a scattered few keepers — and that tracks with what's happening in warmer, stagnant bay water across the whole South Shore this time of year. The better fish are holding tighter to the inlet channel itself, where tidal exchange keeps water a few degrees cooler than the flats up toward Mastic. Working the edges of the marked channel with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a Gulp swimming mullet, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent way to find a keeper in that 19-inch range. It's not a numbers game right now — plan on covering water.

Weakfish remain thin. I'm not going to pretend otherwise — the stock's been down for years and this August is no different. If you pick one up drifting a bucktail tipped with squid strip along the deeper holes off Pattersquash in low light, treat it as a bonus, not a target species. Porgies, on the other hand, have been steady and dependable on the bay bottom off Tuthill Point and around the East Moriches flats — sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig, 15 to 20 feet of water, good action for a slower afternoon when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Blackfish season's still weeks off, so leave the tautog gear in the garage for now.

Looking ahead, the tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, which should sharpen up that current edge at the new bar shoulder even more — stronger flow means a tighter, more defined seam for the bass to sit on. If the ocean swell backs off some, I'd also expect the surf bite at Cupsogue proper to pick back up, since calmer water lets fish work closer to the beach instead of holding deep in the inlet throat. Until then, work the tide stages tight, fish the edges the storms and swells keep redrawing, and don't waste daylight hours you don't have to.

reports.headline: The Ocean's Got a 4-Foot Chop — I'm Working the Rocks Inside Jones Inlet
reports.subhead: While everyone chases blitz reports from up the coast, the real, honest bite this week is in the current seams behind the jetty and the back bay creeks.
reports.body_markdown:
My phone's been buzzing all week with guys sending me screenshots of bunker blitzes up in Rhode Island and the Cape — fish exploding on top in broad daylight, no low-light window needed. Good for them. Down here, the ocean's carrying a 3-to-4-foot chop out of the south with a short, sloppy period, and there's no version of that where I'm walking the tip of the Jones Beach jetty to get pounded by whitewater for a maybe-fish. So while half the surf guys are standing out there getting salt in their eyes for nothing, I've been working the calm water behind the rocks and inside the inlet, where the current does the work instead of the swell.

That's the read this week — the ocean's too worked up to fish comfortably, and the bay and inlet mouth are holding the temperature break that's actually stacking bait. We've got water pushing low-to-mid 70s out front and even warmer in the shallow bay flats, which means the stripers aren't dumb enough to feed hard in the heat of the day. I said last week the morning schoolies would keep showing on the same current lines at first light, and that's exactly what's happening — dawn bite, current seam off the north side rocks near the Coast Guard station, small bunker and peanuts getting pushed through on the last of the outgoing. Schoolies to 26 inches, a few slot fish mixed in if you're working a swimming plug — I've been throwing a bone-colored Yo-Zuri Mag Popper and a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white Fin-S trailer, working it slow along the seam where the moving water meets the slack. Best 45 minutes of the day, every day, right around first light before the sun gets up over the dunes. After that it shuts down hard until the light drops again in the evening — that's the trade-off with water this warm, you get two tight windows and a whole lot of dead air in between.

Bluefish are the one thing that hasn't slowed a bit. Snapper blues are thick as fleas in the back bay creeks off Freeport and up around the Wantagh Bridge pilings, little guys 6 to 10 inches hammering anything shiny under a bobber — great way to get a kid hooked on this sport, literally. But the adult class is building behind them just like I figured it would. I'm seeing 3- to 4-pound blues mixed right in with the bunker schools inside the inlet mouth, and they're not shy about it — silver spoons, small metal, even bucktails get bit the second they hit bottom. If you're marking bait balls getting nervous on your sonar drifting past the Jones Inlet Coast Guard station, that's blues underneath, not stripers, more often than not this time of year.

Fluke's a mixed bag right now and I won't lie to you about it. The Sloop Channel drift has been giving up fish, but it's a lot of shorts for every keeper — the fish are bunching up near the inlet mouth where the tide keeps things cooler than the stagnant flats further up the bay, which is exactly the pattern you'd expect with the bay water sitting warm and lazy. I'm drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1-ounce bucktails, staying tight to the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, moving with the current instead of fighting it. Some days you'll put three or four keepers in the cooler over a few hours, other days you're culling through twenty shorts for one fish over 19 inches. If the wind lays down and gives you a clean drift on the last two hours of the incoming, that's your best shot — the fish get more aggressive when there's a little push of water carrying bait past them instead of them having to hunt for it.

Now here's the one I'm actually excited about — weakfish are showing again in South Oyster Bay, and I don't say that lightly because it's been a rough decade for that fishery around here. Guys working the flats off Short Beach after dark with bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, or soft plastics like a 4-inch pearl swimming shad, have been picking off weakfish in the 2- to 4-pound range on the deeper edges where the flat drops into the channel. It's not a stacked bite — you might get two or three bites in a night — but every one of those fish matters right now, because if this bay-side comeback is real, it's the best news this inlet's had in years. Handle them gentle if you're letting them go.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the full moon on the 28th, and that's going to push more water through this inlet than we've seen in weeks. That usually means the bunker get shoved through faster and the stripers and blues get more concentrated around the current breaks instead of spread out over the flats. I'd expect the dawn bite to hold steady through the week and probably sharpen up as the tides build — if I had to pick one morning to be standing on the rocks with a popper in my hand, I'd wait for a morning with a light northwest wind and fish the last two hours of the outgoing. That's when this inlet shows you what it's really got.

reports.headline: Ebb Tide Eels Are Putting Big Bass on the Rocks at Plum Gut
reports.subhead: Cooler water and hard current at the Race and the Gut are holding fish while the rest of the Sound cooks.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-fifteen in the morning, chest-deep on the Orient side of Plum Gut, and a 34-inch bass nearly ripped the rod out of my hands on the third cast of a slow-sinking eel. That's the report right there. The current was screaming — full ebb, maybe 4 knots — and that fish came off the edge of a rip that's been holding stripers all week. Landed two more before the tide went slack, both in the low 30s, one push over 38 inches that came off a Fin-S swimbait worked dead-slow along the seam where white water meets green.

The why is simple: the Race and the Gut flush hard enough to keep this end of the Sound running cooler and cleaner than everything west of Mount Sinai. New London's reading 69.4, Kings Point's up at 70.9 — that's a real gradient, and it's the difference between fish that feed all day here and fish that shut down to an hour at dawn in the western basin. We've got current-driven structure doing the work that warm, stagnant water can't undo. Bass are stacking on the downtide side of the reef at the Race in 25 to 40 feet, and they're doing it on the ebb specifically — that's when bait gets rolled off the flats at Fishers Island and swept into the rip where the stripers are waiting.

We flagged this pattern last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen the bite at current structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at both the Race and the Gut right now. Tube-and-worm trolled slow through the rip is still money, but the eel bite at night has been the standout — bucktail-and-eel combos, 1.5 to 2 ounces, cast across the seam and let it sink before you start the retrieve. Don't rush it. The fish are eating it on the fall, not the swim.

Bluefish are everywhere east of Mount Sinai right now, and this confirms something else we called — snapper blues have been thick in the back bays and creek mouths off Orient and Southold all summer, and now the adult class is showing up to back it up. Blues to 8 pounds are mixing right into the bass bite at the Race, hammering the same poppers and metal — Ava 27s, half-ounce Kastmasters — that you'd throw for stripers. If you're getting bit off constantly on wire leader, that's your answer. Bring some 40-pound fluorocarbon shock and just accept you're going to lose a plug or two a trip.

Fluke are a mixed bag. Inside the Gut and around the mouth of Orient Harbor you can find keeper-class fish holding on the tide-scoured bottom, but the ratio is running heavy on shorts — for every 19-incher I've boated off Fishers Island in 30 feet of water, I've thrown back six or seven teens. Squid strips over white Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow on the last two hours of the incoming, has been the most consistent combo. Don't waste time on the flats inside the harbors right now — the water's too warm and too still. Fish where the current is still moving cool water across structure.

Porgies are the one thing I'd call flat-out strong right now. The reefs and rockpiles off Orient Point and around Plum Island are stacked with humpies in the 20- to 35-foot range. Sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, light enough weight to feel the bottom but heavy enough to hold in the current — that's the program. Bring a five-gallon bucket, because you're going to fill it.

Blackfish are starting to show around the same structure — nothing to build a trip around yet, but I've picked up a few short togs jigging green crab on the drop near the rockpiles off Fishers Island. That'll sharpen up as the water starts to ease off in September. Not there yet.

Here's the one to watch: with warm water building to our east through Buzzards Bay and Nantucket Sound, there's a real chance false albacore or bonito push into Fishers Island Sound before Labor Day. I haven't seen it yet — no confirmed albie action in this zone as of today — but the setup is right, and I'll be running metal off the back of Fishers Island every morning this week just in case that bait shows up busting.

Look ahead: tidal flow is building toward the August 28 full moon, and that should only sharpen the bite at the Race and the Gut over the next week. If the wind stays out of the northwest and lets the current run clean, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut for bass, then slide over to the Orient reefs on the slack for porgies while you wait for the next stage. If a southwest blow kicks up and dirties the water, don't fight it — head into the back bays for snapper blues and keep your string tight until conditions reset.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Into the Harbors — Snapper Blues Riding Shotgun Behind Them
reports.subhead: The bait's telling the story before the boats do: pogies stacking in the back bays, adult bluefish trailing them west to east, and porgies still the sure thing on the reefs.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning at the mouth of a harbor I won't name — not because it's some secret, but because half the guys reading this already fish it — just watching. Not casting. Watching. There's a difference, and this time of year it pays off more than the first hour of blind chucking ever does. What I saw was peanut bunker, thick as smoke, pinned against a bulkhead by the tide, and snapper blues working them from underneath in short, nervous rushes. Terns were up over the mouth doing the twitchy little dips that tell you the bait's getting pushed, not just schooling for fun. That's late-August behavior right on schedule, and it's the same pattern I flagged a couple weeks back — snapper blues thick in the back bays as a tell that the adult class would keep building. Here it is, showing up right where we said it would.

The water's holding warm and stable across the Central Sound — Kings Point reading just under 71, New London a bit cooler at 69.4 — and that west-to-east gradient matters more than people give it credit for. It means the bait's tighter and more concentrated on the western half of my beat right now, and the bigger bluefish pushing in behind the peanut schools are following that warmth east at their own pace. I'd expect that adult bluefish presence to keep spreading toward Port Jeff and the Norwalk Islands over the next week or two as the gradient levels out, which lines up with what we called for the zone the other day — the bluefish resurgence spreading east from the Western Sound's reef structure. It's happening, just don't expect it to hit every spot on the same day.

Striper fishing has been the toughest piece of the puzzle, and I'll be straight about it — this warm, stable water has compressed the bite into a tight window. First light and last light, that's it. I worked the Stratford Shoal rip before sunrise Thursday on the last of the ebb and had two fish in the mid-20s on a white 1-ounce bucktail dressed with a chunk of pork rind, worked slow along the bottom where the current breaks over the shoal. By 6:30 the sun was up, the bite was over, and I didn't see another fish the rest of the morning. Same story at Middle Ground Light — a couple of guys anchored up there Friday told me they had fish on topwater poppers for maybe forty minutes right at gray light, then nothing. If you're chasing bass right now, set your alarm and plan your trip around the tide change at dawn, not around convenience.

Porgies and scup remain the honest bite on this beat, and honestly, they've been the honest bite all summer. Charles Island and the rockpiles off the Norwalk Islands are still stacked with them — hi-lo rigs, size 6 or 4 hooks, sandworm or clam belly, fished on the bottom in 15 to 30 feet on the last two hours of the incoming tide. It's not glamorous fishing but it's reliable, and with the afternoon thunderstorms we've been getting rolling through — typical for this pattern, they blow up fast off the heat and clear out just as quick — those brief post-front windows have actually produced some of the better porgy counts of the week. Fish seem to turn on for thirty or forty minutes right after the storm passes and the barometer starts climbing again.

Fluke are still mostly a disappointment inside the Sound proper — plenty of action, not much size. I've been picking through a dozen shorts for every keeper drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp off the drop-offs near Port Jefferson Harbor and the deeper water off Middle Ground. If you want a real shot at a keeper, work the edges where the bottom breaks hard, 25 to 35 feet, and fish it slow on the outgoing when the current pulls bait off the flats into the channel. That's where the bigger fish have been sitting, waiting rather than hunting — classic warm-water fluke behavior.

Blackfish aren't in the story yet. I checked a few of the rockier stretches off the Norwalk Islands out of curiosity and didn't get so much as a nibble worth mentioning. That's expected — tautog interest on structure usually doesn't build until we're closer to Labor Day, and we're not there. Worth filing away for three weeks from now, not this week.

Weakfish have been a ghost — I haven't had a credible report of one on this stretch of the Sound all month, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, the tides are rebuilding toward the August 28 full moon, and that extra push should sharpen up both the bass bite at dawn and the current-driven bait concentration everywhere from the Norwalk Islands to Stratford Shoal. If the bunker keep getting corralled into the harbor mouths the way they were this week, I'd bet on the adult bluefish class showing up in bigger numbers along the Connecticut shore by the time we get there. My plan for next week: first-light bass at the Shoal, then switch over to porgies on the rockpiles once the sun's up and the bass shut down. That's the rhythm this water's asking for right now — work the low light hard, then settle into the sure thing.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: the ocean's a mess, but the inlet's paying rent
reports.subhead: With a beat-up ocean pushing everything inside, bass and blues are stacking on current seams while bay fluke stay stubbornly short.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the fuel dock this morning asks me if it's worth running the beach at Democrat Point before work. I told him what I've been telling everybody all week — leave the waders in the truck and fish the inlet instead. There's a lumpy 4-footer rolling in off the bar right now, short-period junk, the kind of swell that makes standing on the sand feel like punishment more than fishing. Nobody's catching anything worth talking about out there. But run that same water fifteen minutes inside the rocks and it's a different world.

We flagged this a few weeks back — said the striper bite would stay the headline story through the middle of the month, and here we are. The bass haven't left, they've just gotten smart about where they sit. There's a real gap right now between what the open ocean's doing and what the bay and inlet are doing, and that gap is exactly why the fish are piling up on current structure instead of spreading out along the beach. Ocean water's sitting around 71 with that chop stacked on top of it, while the bay and back creeks are running noticeably warmer through the afternoons. Stripers don't love warm and they don't love junk water, so they're parking on the hard seams where moving current gives them relief from both — the rip off Democrat Point, the pilings under the Robert Moses bridges, the deeper cuts inside the inlet itself.

Best bite I've had this week has been the night tide at the inlet mouth, working the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to the rock line where the current stacks up, has been drawing bass from 24 up to 34 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in around the tide change. If you're bucktailing instead, stick with 1.5 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse, and let it swing down and through the seam rather than casting up-current — the fish are holding low and eating on the drop, not chasing anything across the top.

Bluefish have done exactly what we said they'd do back on the 14th. The snapper blues that were thick in the back bays a few weeks ago have grown into something with real shoulders. Patchogue River, the Swan River mouth, and the docks around Bellport are stuffed with fish in the one-to-three-pound class hammering small silver spoons and mini poppers off the bulkheads — a great, low-stakes evening with the kids if you've got them. Out at the inlet, adult blues in the three-to-five-pound range are mixing right into the bass schools on bunker chunks, and more than a few guys have had their bass rigs bit off clean by fish that size holding the same seam.

Fluke is the honest disappointment this week. The bay's full of short fish — Great South Bay flats off Sayville and Bay Shore are lousy with them, but you're picking through a dozen sublegal fish for every keeper. The better ones are stacking near the inlets themselves, where tidal flow keeps the water a few degrees cooler than the stagnant upper bay. Drifting 25 to 35 feet around the Robert Moses bridge pilings on the outgoing, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a 3/4-ounce bucktail have put a handful of 4-to-6-pound fish in the boat for me, but it's not fast fishing — more a game of covering ground and being patient with the drift speed than working one spot hard.

Weakfish are still around in small numbers, mostly a bonus fish rather than a target — a few keepers have come on soft plastics worked slow along the channel edges off Sayville right at last light, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. Porgies are steady if unglamorous on the south side of the bridges, bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 15 to 20 feet, good action if you want dinner without much drama.

Looking ahead, the tide's building back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that extra push should sharpen everything at the current-driven spots — the inlet rip, the bridge pilings, the deeper cuts by Democrat Point. If the ocean swell settles even a little, I'd expect the beach to open back up for surf guys working bunker chunks or big darters at dawn. Until then, my money stays inside the inlet on the incoming tide, and I'd rather work one current seam thoroughly than run all over the bay hoping to stumble into fish. That's been the difference this week between a slow trip and a good one.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Weakfish Working the Bridge Lights
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is pushing the real bite into the dark hours — here's where I'm putting my time before the full moon rebuilds the tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I made a call Tuesday night I've been making all month: skip the sunset crowd at the inlet and wait for the 11 p.m. slack to turn. Bay water's sitting warm right now, upper 70s pushing 80 on the flats by Tiana, and when it's like that the stripers don't want anything to do with daylight. They stack up in the deep hole on the ocean side of the jetty and wait for the outgoing to pull cooler water and bait past them. That's where I want to be — not at dusk when everybody else is casting into the pressure, but two hours into the ebb when the current's ripping and the boils start showing up tight against the rocks.

The pattern held again this week. Working the north jetty rocks on the outgoing, I've been getting slot bass and a few overslots on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, weight just heavy enough to hold bottom in that current — usually 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard the water's running. Eels work too if you want to cast and swim them through the seam where the deep hole meets the sandbar, but I've had better luck staying still and letting the chunk do the work. Best window has been that hour and a half after the tide really gets moving, before it goes slack again around 2 or 3 a.m. This is a stealth game — no lights on the deck, quiet with the anchor, and let the fish come to the smell, not the noise.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the other half of my nights. Weakfish are holding under the lights on the down-current side of the pilings, and they want it small and subtle — a bucktail, quarter to three-eighths ounce, tipped with a strip of squid or a small piece of bunker, hopped slow along bottom in 15 to 20 feet. The bite's been better on the last two hours of the outgoing than on the incoming lately, which tracks with how warm the bay's running — that current pulls cooler, cleaner water out from the back bay and the weakfish key on it. Sizes have been mixed, some short fish mixed with a few keepers in the 16 to 18 inch range, so it's not a bucket-fill night, but it's a real bite if you're patient and quiet about it.

Daytime fluke has been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about it — the bay's mostly throwing back shorts right now. Warm, stagnant flats away from current don't hold quality fish this time of year, so I've been running the drift tight to the inlet mouth and along the edge of the channel where the tide keeps things moving and a few degrees cooler. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted right along that channel edge in 12 to 20 feet on the last of the incoming, have put a few keeper-class fish in the box, but you're working for them. If you want numbers over size, the back bay flats off Tiana still hold plenty of shorts to keep rods bent while you wait on the tide to turn.

Bluefish have been the one thing you can count on without much thinking. Snapper blues are thick as ever up in the canal and around the back bay creeks off Hampton Bays — we flagged this building a couple weeks back, said the adult class would follow as the season pushed into late August, and that's exactly what's happening now. Bigger blues, 3 to 5 pounds with a few better, are mixing into the bait around the inlet on the outgoing, blowing up on the surface when the bunker get pinned against the rocks. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, half-ounce, worked fast — have been getting hit hard right at first light before the sun gets high, which lines up with that dawn window everyone's seeing region-wide right now.

Porgies are still around the reef structure inside the inlet and off Ponquogue in 15 to 25 feet, worm rigs with sandworm or squid strips doing the job on the bottom stages of the tide when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a ton of weight. Blackfish are still a few weeks off from being worth a dedicated trip, but I'd start scouting structure now for when that opens up.

Looking ahead, the tide's building toward the August 28 full moon, and that's going to sharpen everything at current-driven structure — the inlet jetty, the bridge pilings, the canal mouth. Bigger tidal swings mean stronger current, which means more bait getting pushed and more predictable feeding windows after dark. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd take the outgoing starting an hour before midnight at the inlet, work the deep hole quiet, and swing over to the bridge on the tail end of the tide for weakfish. That's the play until the moon gets fatter and the current really starts moving.

reports.headline: Snapper Blues Thick in the Back Bays, Just Like We Said — Now Watch the Adults
reports.subhead: Porgies are paying the bills on the Western Sound while fluke stay undersized and stripers keep banker's hours before the afternoon thunder rolls in.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop in City Island Monday morning was griping that he'd measured forty fluke off the Throgs Neck rocks Sunday and kept exactly none of them. I told him that's not bad luck, that's mid-August on the Western Sound — everything's running twelve to eighteen inches right now and you've got to kiss a lot of frogs before you find a prince. He wasn't thrilled, but that's the honest read on the flatfish this week and I'm not going to sell him a different story.

What I will tell him — and you — is that porgies have quietly become the best game going. Anywhere there's structure and current, from the rockpile off Hart Island down to the mussel beds inside Manhasset Bay, scup are stacked and biting like they know summer's got an expiration date. Small hooks, a strip of squid or a piece of clam, half-ounce sinker to hold bottom on the drift — that's the whole program. I've had guys limit out in ninety minutes working the drop-off east of Hart Island on the last two hours of the incoming, water still carrying that mid-70s warmth that's got everything with fins in a feeding mood.

Stripers are a different animal right now, and if you're not on the water by 6 AM you're chasing shadows. Kings Point is reading right around 71 degrees, New London's a good degree and a half cooler, and that west-to-east gradient is exactly why the Western Sound still holds fish tight to structure instead of scattering them thin. Execution Rocks on the tail of the outgoing has been good for schoolies and the occasional mid-20s fish on bunker chunks fished on the bottom, or a white bucktail worked slow along the edge where the rock drops into deeper water. Stepping Stones has been quieter than it was in the spring — that light isn't the highway it is in May — but I've still marked fish holding on the down-current side early, before the sun gets up and the boat traffic pushes them down.

By nine, nine-thirty, the thermometer and the humidity both start climbing and those afternoon thunderstorm cells build right on schedule most days this week. The bass go quiet, the bite shuts like someone flipped a switch, and you're better off running for porgies or blackfish than beating a dead horse on stripers past mid-morning. That's been the pattern for two weeks now and I don't see anything in the sky or the water changing it before we get some real relief in temperature.

Bluefish are scattered but present, mostly around Oyster Bay and off Matinecock Point where there's still enough bait moving to hold their interest. We flagged this a few days back — said the snapper blues thick in the back bays and estuaries were a sign the adult class would keep building, and that's holding up. I'm seeing more three- and four-pound blues mixed in with the schoolies off Matinecock than I was two weeks ago, and if that trend keeps climbing through late August into September like it usually does, we'll have a real fall run setting up early. Small metal — quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — worked fast on the surface has been the ticket when you find them working bait.

Weakfish have shown up in dribs and drabs around the mouth of Hempstead Harbor on the last of the outgoing, mostly smaller fish, nothing to write home about, but worth a cast or two with a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid if you're already out there for porgies.

One thing worth saying plainly: the upper harbors — Little Neck Bay, the inner reaches of Manhasset — have taken a hit from runoff after the recent rain, and the water in there is carrying more color and less oxygen than it should this time of year. If you fished a spot in there two weeks ago and it's been dead since, that's likely why. The fish know it too — they're pushing out toward cleaner, better-oxygenated water in the open Sound, which is part of why Execution Rocks and the Matinecock drop-off have stayed more consistent than the back bays.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the August 28 full moon, and that means tidal flow is going to sharpen up through the week. More current means better current edges, and better current edges mean the bass and blues both get pushed into tighter, more predictable feeding lanes — Execution Rocks, the Matinecock rip, the down-current side of Stepping Stones. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd want an outgoing tide starting an hour before first light off Execution Rocks, bunker chunk on the bottom to start, bucktail in hand for when the current gets moving. Get there early. Once those thunderheads start stacking up over the city, you've had your window.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier by kayak: fluke in the deep holes, snappers everywhere else
reports.subhead: With the flats baking under August sun, the bite has moved into the channels — and the bay's back-bay bluefish are building right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
I took the kayak out of Canarsie Pier again this week instead of running the boat, and it wasn't about saving gas — it's about where the fish actually are right now. Mid-August, the flats in this bay turn into a bathtub by ten in the morning. If you want fluke, you need to get into the deeper holes and channels where there's still some current moving and the water hasn't cooked all day, and a kayak lets me slide into spots along the edges of Duck Point Marsh and the channel drop-offs near Ruffle Bar that a boat can't sit on comfortably without swinging on the anchor all day.

That's exactly where the fluke have been. Nothing spectacular — this isn't a five-fish limit kind of week — but if you work the deeper bends where the channel drops from six feet down to twelve or fourteen, on the last two hours of the outgoing, you can put together a couple of keepers. I've been dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, bounced slow right on the bottom, and mixing in a strip of squid on the hook for scent. The takes have been soft — typical late-summer fluke behavior, lazy and picking rather than smashing — so I've been giving a beat before I set. Bay Streets and Head of Bay have both given up fish in that twelve-inch-to-just-shy-of-keeper range, with the occasional legal mixed in on the bigger drops.

The real story in the bay this week, though, is the bluefish, and I'm not going to pretend I didn't see this coming. We flagged it last week — said the snapper blues thick in the shallows were a sign the bigger class fish would keep building through late August — and that's exactly what's happening. If you've got kids or you just want steady, stupid-easy action, Canarsie Pier and the docks along Bergen Basin are lousy with snappers right now, one-inch to three-inch, hammering tiny silver spoons and bits of spearing under a bobber. But mixed in with them, especially in the last hour of light, I'm starting to see a few three- and four-pound blues showing up on light tackle — the kind of push that tells you the adult class fish are starting to filter in behind the peanut schools that have been building in the back creeks all month.

Striped bass are still around, but you have to work the tide right. Marine Parkway Bridge remains the most reliable spot in the whole zone, and it's still staging fish on the outgoing exactly like it always does — the current rips through those pilings and stacks bait against the structure, and bass sit in the eddies waiting for it to come to them. I fished the bridge on a Tuesday evening outgoing and picked up two schoolies and one just-shy-of-slot fish on a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white curly tail trailer, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the shadow line of the pilings. Bunker schools have kept moving through the bay on this tide cycle, which is the same thing we called last week, and as long as that bait keeps pushing through the inlet, the bass will keep using the bridge as a feeding station on the ebb. It's not a blitz — you're working for two or three fish a trip right now — but it's consistent enough to plan an evening around.

Weakfish are scattered, which is about what I expected for mid-August. I've heard of a few being picked up on the channel edges off Cross Bay Bridge on the last of the incoming, working bucktails tipped with a sliver of squid down near bottom in eight to ten feet. It's not a target-species kind of bite yet — more of a bonus if you're already fluke fishing that stretch — but worth a few casts if you're in the neighborhood.

Out at Breezy Point and along Rockaway Beach, the surf has been quiet for stripers in daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down this whole stretch of coast — warm water is pushing the bass bite into narrow windows right around dawn and dusk. If you want a shot at a beach bass right now, first light at Breezy with a swimming plug or a bucktail worked through the wash is still your best bet, but don't expect a long window. Porgies have been a nice consolation prize on the jetty rocks around the inlet — bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in fifteen to twenty feet has been steady enough to keep a rod bent while you wait for something bigger.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend. The tide cycle is easing toward the weaker phase before it rebuilds into the end-of-month full moon, so if anything, expect the bridge bite and the fluke pattern in the channels to hold steady rather than intensify. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the kayak back into the deeper holes on an outgoing morning tide before the sun gets high, then swing by Marine Parkway for the evening push. That combination has been paying off, and there's no reason to think it stops before Labor Day.

reports.headline: Deer Island bunker blitz holds on the new moon push, bluefish riding along for the ride
reports.subhead: I'm staying inside this week — the harbor's peanut bunker show is better than anything the North Shore rocks are giving up right now.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a decision to make Monday morning — run up to Gloucester and work the Cape Ann ledges on the dropping tide, or stay inside the harbor where the bunker's been thick since the weekend. I stayed inside. Wrong call maybe one day out of five, but the numbers said harbor, and the numbers were right.

We flagged this last week — said the dawn blitz pattern in the harbor would hold and that the building new moon current would likely intensify it, and that's exactly what's happened. President Roads and the water off Deer Island Light have had peanut bunker balled up tight against the channel edge every morning this week, with bass busting through them from first light until the sun gets up over the JFK Library. This is mid-August staging behavior — I don't usually see blitz activity this visible in the harbor until the bait starts pushing out in September, but the bunker schools have concentrated the fish hard against structure the whole way from Spectacle Island down through the President Roads channel, and the bass have followed.

Sizes have been mixed but real — plenty of 22 to 28-inch schoolies mixed with a better class of fish, 32 to 36 inches, holding a little deeper on the edges where the bigger bunker are stacked. Best producer's been a simple peanut bunker imitation — 3-inch Albie Snax in bunker color, or a white/chartreuse bucktail worked with a short hop-and-pause through the edge of the bait ball. When the blitz gets tight and visible, a topwater popper thrown right into the froth off Deer Island will draw violent strikes, but don't waste time popping open water — cast to the nervous bait, not the splashes behind it. Outgoing tide has been the best window, roughly two hours either side of the turn, when the current pulls the bunker off the flats and funnels them past the Deer Island rip.

Bluefish are riding shotgun in the same schools, and they're not small — I've seen 3 to 5-pound blues mixed right in with the stripers off Spectacle Island, which tells me the adult class fish are building the way they usually do this time of year behind a good peanut bunker push. If you're getting bit off and missing hookups on soft plastics, that's your blues — switch to a wire leader or a metal lure like a Kastmaster and you'll start connecting instead of losing gear.

Nahant's been a mixed bag. The rocks off East Point and the ledges running out toward Egg Rock are still holding bass, but it's been more of a north-shore grind than a blitz — one or two fish on a tide, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming when water pushes bait up against the structure. Live mackerel under a slip float has out-produced everything else out there this week, and mackerel themselves have been easy to jig up on Diamond jigs and Swedish Pimples in 20 to 30 feet right off the point, so bait's not the problem — it's just that the bass have their attention locked on the harbor's bunker right now and the North Shore rocks are getting the leftovers.

Gloucester and Cape Ann have been quieter on the striper front, but that's typical for mid-August — the better story up there right now is mackerel and the early groundfish grind. Cod and haddock are still around the deeper water off Cape Ann, but you're working 60 to 90 feet with jigs or clams on the bottom for a mixed bag rather than a sure thing, and I wouldn't plan a trip around it this week.

South of the city, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay are part of the same story running up the coast — bunker-driven bass activity has been showing from Narragansett clear up into Cape Cod Bay, and Plymouth's no exception. Duxbury Bay and the flats around Kingston Bay have flounder moving well on the low tide — small strips of clam or squid on a simple flounder rig in 8 to 12 feet of water over mud bottom has been steady, not spectacular, but a good option on a day when the bass bite's slow. Scituate's rocky shoreline has given up a few bass on the same live mackerel program that's working at Nahant, best fished on the last of the incoming right up against the ledges.

Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, which has kept the harbor calm enough to work the bunker schools without getting bounced around, and that's part of why the blitz has stayed so visible and workable. If that holds through the weekend and the bunker don't push out of the harbor, I'd keep working the Deer Island to Spectacle Island stretch on the outgoing tide — that's still the highest-percentage program in my zone. If the wind swings onshore and stirs things up, I'd shift south to Duxbury Bay and fish the flounder on the calmer water while waiting for the harbor to settle back down. Either way, keep an eye out to the south — there's real talk of the first false albacore or bonito of the season showing somewhere between here and Buzzards Bay in the next few days, and if that bait and warm water pattern keeps pushing north, Plymouth could be the first place in my zone to see one.

reports.headline: Great Point rip: doormats stacking the Shoals, still no albie in the boat
reports.subhead: Nantucket Sound is quietly running the best fluke bite in New England while every rip chaser east of Montauk waits on the first bonito.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a swirl behind the boat Tuesday morning off Great Point that stopped my coffee halfway to my mouth. Tight, fast, gone in a blink — the kind of boil that makes your hand go for the light spinning rod before your brain catches up. I fired a cast into the wash anyway. Bluefish, maybe four pounds, snapped off a peanut bunker imitation like it owed him money. Not what I wanted. But it's the kind of thing that's been happening all week out there — little flashes and false alarms that keep you leaning over the rail a beat too long, because everybody on this island knows the water's right for the real thing to show, and nobody's seen it yet.

Let's start with what IS happening, because it's been a genuinely good week if you know where to point the bow. Nantucket Sound and the Shoals are, right now, producing the best fluke ratio I've seen in years — not just around here, but compared to what I'm hearing out of the rest of New England. We're finding keepers and better drifting the sand-to-gravel transitions on the north side of the Shoals in 25 to 40 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. The back half of the ebb has been the money tide — enough push to keep the bait pinned and the bucktail ticking bottom without turning it into a boat anchor. We're seeing three, four keepers to every short, which for fluke fishing anywhere in New England this summer is a number worth writing down. A few fish have pushed past 4 pounds off the drop-offs south of Tuckernuck, and I heard secondhand of a doormat closer to 6 taken drifting bait — squid strip over a spearing — in that same stretch.

The bigger story region-wide is striped bass, and we're seeing our version of it here too. Peanut bunker have poured into Nantucket Sound and the bass have gone right after them, tight to structure around Horseshoe Shoal and along the current edges off Monomoy. This is a little unusual for mid-August — normally the bass have slid deeper and gone quiet on us by now, sulking through the warmest stretch of summer. Instead we've got visible blitzes, birds working low and fast over nervous water, bass punching bunker to the surface in short, violent windows. If you see the birds pile up, don't putt over — cut the engine well outside the school and let the boat drift in. Topwater plugs and 2-ounce metal have both worked once you're in range, but honestly a peanut bunker fly-lined on a fishfinder rig outfishes everything else when the fish are keyed that tight on real bait. Bluefish are riding shotgun in the same schools, which means wire or a heavy fluoro leader if you don't want to donate lures all afternoon.

We flagged a couple weeks back that building current into the new moon would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's played out — the Sound's channels have more push behind them now, and the bite at Horseshoe Shoal and the rips off Monomoy has firmed up right on schedule. Scup fishing has held up nicely too on the same structure, small hooks and squid strips over the rockier patches off Chatham keeping rods bent for anyone who wants a break from watching for bigger things.

And bigger things is where everybody's head really is. No confirmed albies or bonito yet anywhere from Montauk through Buzzards Bay, and that includes us. But the water's doing everything it's supposed to do to bring them in — it's warm, it's bait-thick, and we're past the new moon push from the 12th that usually kicks the migration corridor into gear. A hammerhead showed up in the surf down in Rhode Island this week, which tells you exactly how much warm, forage-heavy water is sitting out there right now. That's not albie confirmation, but it's the kind of secondary sign that makes a guy like me start rigging epoxy jigs a little earlier than I probably need to.

If I had one morning to burn this week chasing the first fish of the season, I'd be at Great Point on the last two hours of the ebb, working the rip where the current stacks bait against the shoal, watching for that tight, nervous surface disturbance that's different from a bluefish blowup — faster, more erratic, birds diving instead of hovering. I'd have a Deadly Dick or a small Albie Snax tied on and ready before I even left the dock. Sankaty's outer edge is worth a look too on the same tide stage, especially with any bait pushed up along the bluffs.

Best case, that first bonito or albie shows within the next few days and this report changes tone fast. If the pattern slides the way it sometimes does, we might be another week out yet. Either way the fluke bite on the Shoals is real and worth your time right now regardless of what shows up chasing bait behind it — I wouldn't skip a good doormat morning waiting on a fish that hasn't punched in yet.

reports.headline: Race Point on the push: bass crash peanut bunker as blitzes run up from the south
reports.subhead: Mid-August bunker blitzes have hit Cape Cod Bay early, with bass tearing up bait from Race Point to Sandy Neck while cod stay quiet on the deep stuff for now.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had the boat idling off Race Point, waiting on the tide to turn, and the water just erupted about two hundred yards off my bow. No warning, no gulls even — just white water and bass coming up under a pod of peanut bunker like someone flipped a switch. I've been drifting this Bay thirty years and you learn not to run at a blitz, you ease into it, let the boat drift down on the edge of the bait rather than plow through the middle and spook the whole show. Cut the engine, let her glide, and cast into the edge where the bunker are getting pushed against the current line. That's exactly what I did, and inside twenty minutes we had four bass in the 28 to 34 inch range in the box and released a handful more.

What's happening right now is a little out of the ordinary for the middle of August. Bunker-driven blitzes usually belong to September and October around here, the classic fall run signature, but this year the peanut bunker showed up early and stacked thick, and the bass followed them right up the coast — the same pattern that's been running from Narragansett Bay through Buzzards Bay is now showing at our doorstep. Whether that means an early fall staging pattern or just an early bait push, I can't say for certain, but the fish don't care what you call it. They're eating.

Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars have both been holding fish, but the pattern's been tide-dependent. The last two hours of the incoming, when the rip starts to build off the Race, has been the most reliable window — bait gets funneled and concentrated against the current seam and the bass sit underneath waiting for it to spill over. Slack water kills it dead out there; I've watched a blitz just evaporate the second the tide goes still, bass sounding down and bunker scattering. So if you're planning a trip, build it around that push, not around when you happen to be free.

Tactics have been simple because the fish are telling you what to do. Straight bunker imitations — 6-inch white or bunker-colored soft plastic swimbaits on a 1-ounce jighead, worked just under the surface through the edge of the commotion — have outfished everything else. When the fish get finicky and stop hitting the top-water stuff, dropping down to a bunker spoon or a diamond jig with a bit of bucktail tied on and working it through the water column has saved more than one slow stretch. Live-lining an actual peanut bunker on a small hook, if you can net a few off the school, is about as good as it gets when the bass get fussy, which they do once the blitz has been worked over by every boat in the harbor.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun in these same bunker schools, and they're not shy about it — choppers in the 3 to 6 pound class slashing through the bait right alongside the stripers. If you're throwing plugs and missing hookups on bass, there's a good chance a blue just cut your leader instead. Wire or heavy fluoro leader has been worth the extra rig time.

Fluke fishing stays what it's been all summer in this Bay — modest, honest work rather than a highlight reel. Billingsgate has been giving up a few keepers in that 18 to 22 inch class on Gulp in white or chartreuse dragged slow along the sand-mud transition in 15 to 25 feet, and the Barnstable flats off Sandy Neck have done similarly on the last of the outgoing when the water's still got some push to it. Nobody's filling a cooler on fluke right now, but a few for dinner is a realistic goal if you put in the drift time.

Mackerel have been around in decent numbers offshore of the Race, which is part of why the bass have been so willing — there's a layered bait buffet out there between the peanut bunker inshore and mackerel schools a bit further out. Jigging small diamond jigs or mackerel trees in 40 to 60 feet has been an easy way to fill the livewell if you want fresh bait for bigger bass, and it's also just a nice half hour of fishing on its own.

Cod remain the quiet story right now. The deeper structure out toward the edges of Stellwagen and the drop-offs beyond Peaked Hill hasn't turned on yet — water's still holding its summer warmth up top, and cod want that fall chill to push them back onto the humps and ledges in earnest. I wouldn't burn a trip targeting them this week. That bite's coming, just not yet.

Looking ahead, as long as those peanut bunker schools hold position in the Bay, I expect the blitz pattern to keep running, especially on that incoming push at Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars. If the wind stays out of the northeast and keeps that bait pinned against the outer beach, this could stretch on for another week or two before things settle into the more typical September pattern. I'd plan around the tide, not the calendar, and get out there while the bunker's still balled up tight.

reports.headline: Peanut bunker boiling off Cuttyhunk — the albies are close, but not here yet
reports.subhead: Stripers and blues are tearing through bait balls all week in the rips; the first false albacore of the season hasn't shown, but every signal says soon.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait told me everything I needed to know before I even got the boat wet Tuesday morning. Peanut bunker, thick as smoke, pushed up against the rocks at the mouth of Quick's Hole, and every few seconds the surface would dimple and burst — not albies, not yet, but stripers working from underneath like they were being paid by the fish. That's the story of Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard right now: bunker everywhere, predators stacked under them, and everybody standing around asking the same question. Where are the albies?

We flagged this last week — said the August 12 new moon would be the trigger, that building tidal current through the rips would push bait hard enough to pull bonito and false albacore into range at Robinson's Hole and Menemsha. Two days past that moon, the current is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. Vineyard Sound is ripping harder on the last two hours of the ebb than it has all month, and the bait is bunched into current seams instead of spread thin across the flats. That's the setup. What's missing is the confirmation — no albie, no bonito on the deck yet in this stretch of water, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. Close doesn't count on a fish scale.

What IS happening, and happening hard, is bass. The bunker-driven blitz pattern that's been running from Narragansett Bay clear up into Buzzards has our water fully in its grip. I had fish busting on the surface off the west end of Naushon early Wednesday, right at first light, working peanut bunker against the current line where the Elizabeth Islands chain funnels water between the Bay and the Sound. Twenty-six to thirty-four inches, mostly schoolies with a scattering of slot fish mixed in, and they wanted a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chunk of white pork rind more than anything with hooks on a swimming plug. When they got fussy on the plug bite, a 1-ounce Deadly Dick cast right into the boil and swept with the current out-produced everything else in the box two to one.

Cuttyhunk has been the most consistent piece of this puzzle. The rip off Canapitsit Channel, running on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide change, has held bass and bluefish shoulder to shoulder in the froth. Bluefish are riding this bunker wave just like the bass are — snapper blues thick in Menemsha Pond and Lake Tashmoo, adult class fish four to six pounds busting bait off Gay Head on the outgoing. If you want blues specifically, small metal — a half-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown into the surface chop and retrieved fast will get bit before your bucktail even sinks. They're not subtle right now.

Robinson's Hole is where I'm spending my mornings, because that's historically where the first bonito of the year shows, and the current structure there is textbook right now — hard rip on the ebb, bait pinned against the western edge near the Naushon shoreline, and enough depth change to hold fish through the tide swing. I fished it Thursday on the last two hours of the ebb into dead low and came up with bass to 30 inches and blues, no bonito, no albies. That doesn't mean they're not close. Water's warm, bait's dense, and there's a real chance somebody on this stretch of coast puts one in the box within the next few days — Montauk, Block Island, Fishers Island Sound, and this water are all lined up as the most likely first spots. I'd rather tell you honestly that it hasn't happened here yet than sell you a fish that isn't in the boat.

Fluke has been a quieter, steadier story. Working the drift off the north side of the Vineyard between Oak Bluffs and East Chop, in 20 to 30 feet on a moving tide, has produced keeper fish to 22 inches on a white Gulp Swimming Mullet paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom on the drift. It's not the Nantucket Shoals numbers you're hearing about further east, but it's honest fishing, and it's holding up better than it did in July.

Look — if I had one morning this coming week, I'd be back at Robinson's Hole on the ebb, or working Menemsha Bight where the current funnels bait past the jetty into open water. The tidal flow is building the way it should this many days past the new moon, the bait density is there, and the warm water pushing in from the south has every ingredient stacked for that first albie flash. I'd keep a rod rigged with a small Albie Snax or a Deadly Dick ready on deck at all times, because when it happens here, it happens fast and it's usually a blitz before you've even seen the fish. Until then, the stripers and blues are giving us plenty to do, and that's a good problem to have while we wait.

reports.headline: Stellwagen mid-60s on the gravel: bluefin pinning bait, cod still deep and stubborn
reports.subhead: Whales working the Basin, mackerel balled up thick, and the tuna bite we flagged a week ago is finally paying off boats that stuck with it.
reports.body_markdown:
128 feet on the gravel edge, water in the low-to-mid 60s at depth — that's the number that matters this week on Stellwagen. Surface is warmer, pushing summer temps, but drop a probe down through the thermocline and it's the same cold, green, nutrient-rich water mass we've had since the wind swung north-northeast a couple weeks back. That cold layer is why the bank's still fishing like the bank, even in the middle of August.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefin show would keep building as long as that cold water pattern held, and here it is. Whales are up and working the surface out over Stellwagen Basin most mornings, which is about the best tell you'll get that the bait's stacked underneath them. Mackerel schools are dense and tight, balled up defensively, and where you find the whales you're finding bluefin working the same bait from below. We've had boats jigging green machines and diamond jigs through the bait balls picking up school fish in the 60-to-100 pound class, and a few giants have shown up chasing the same pods along the Stellwagen Edge where the bank drops off into deeper water. It's not a fish-every-cast bite — you're reading birds, reading whales, and putting the boat in the right spot at the right time, but the ingredients are all there right now in a way they haven't been most of the summer.

Groundfish has been the tougher story, if I'm honest with you. Cod on the gravel patches out toward Tillies Bank have been there, but they're deep and they're not eager — we're marking fish on the sounder in that 100-to-130 foot range but you've got to put bait right on their nose. Clam and squid combo rigs on a standard cod rig, fished tight to bottom on the slower part of the tide, has been the difference between a couple keepers and a skunk.
