Jigging has been spotty; the fish are sitting heavy on structure and not chasing much this time of year, which tells me they're already keying in on the same bait the tuna are working, just staying low and lazy about it.

Haddock on the mud has been the more consistent of the two. Standard drift-and-jig over the softer bottom areas off the western side of the bank has produced decent numbers, fish running average size with a few chunky ones mixed in. Circle hooks and cut bait on a two-hook bottom rig, fished on the slower drift days, has out-produced straight jigging for us — haddock this time of year seem to want something sitting still more than something bouncing.

Carter Canyon has been more of a transition zone this week than a destination — we've marked bait moving through there but haven't had the kind of concentrated whale activity or consistent tuna sign that would pull me off the bank proper. Same with Cape Cod Tails — some scattered mackerel sign, nothing that's translated into a reliable bite yet. I wouldn't burn a day dedicated to either right now, but I'd keep half an eye on them as the bait shifts around over the next week or two, because that's usually how it goes out here — the bait moves, and a week later the fish follow.

Tide's been mixed this week, working through a post-new-moon cycle, and the stronger pushes have generally produced better drift speed for both the groundfish guys and the tuna guys running lines through bait schools. Slack water mornings have been quieter across the board — cod go tight to bottom, haddock stop moving, and the tuna scatter out until the current picks back up and reorganizes the bait. If you're planning a trip, I'd build it around the stronger half of the tide rather than fighting slack water hoping something happens.

Looking ahead, if that cold water mass holds — and there's no sign right now that it's breaking down — I'd expect the bluefin pattern on Stellwagen to keep building through the back half of August. Bait density is the whole story here, and right now it's about as good as we've seen it this summer. Cod's going to stay a grind on the gravel until we get some cooler nights working the water column, but haddock on the mud should stay steady if the tide cooperates. Best case, the whales keep working the Basin and the tuna sign holds through the week — worth putting a trip together around that if you can get the weather. If the wind shifts and knocks that cold layer around, I'd expect the tuna to scatter wider and get harder to pin down, so I wouldn't wait too long to get out there while it's holding together.

reports.headline: Mackerel Pull the String: Stripers Follow Into the River Mouths on the New Moon Tide
reports.subhead: Forty years watching this pattern and it never gets old — the bass show up right behind the mackerel, same as always, right on the new moon flood.
reports.body_markdown:
My uncle Eldon used to stand on the co-op dock with a mug of coffee going cold in his hand and tell anybody who'd listen that the mackerel come first, and the bass follow like they're tied to them with a string. I've watched that string get pulled every August of my life, and this week it happened right on cue at the mouth of the St. George River, where the tide runs hard past the ledges on the last two hours of the ebb.

We flagged this a week back — said the building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what showed up. The mackerel schools that had been scattered and thin through late July packed in tight against the breakwater at Boothbay Harbor and out around Ram Island, and the stripers moved in behind them like they'd gotten a phone call. Guys jigging small Swedish Pimples and diamond jigs in 15 to 20 feet off Ram Island are filling five-gallon buckets with mackerel inside twenty minutes some mornings, and that bait's not going to waste — the same water is holding bass in the 26 to 34-inch range working the current seams where the river spills into the bay.

St. George, Medomak, and Damariscotta river mouths have all been showing the same story on the last of the ebb into the new flood — bass stacked in eight to fifteen feet, hitting live mackerel drifted on a fish-finder rig or swimming a chunk under a slip float back into the seam. If you'd rather cast, a Rebel Jumpin' Minnow or a Doc's swimming mackerel plug worked across the moving water at first light has been drawing strikes, though the window's short — twenty, thirty minutes either side of the tide change and then it shuts down until the next stage. That's the honest truth of it this week. It's not a blitz. It's a grind you have to time right, and the guys putting fish in the boat are the ones who show up on the tide, not just whenever it's convenient.

Out around Monhegan the pattern's been steadier. The ledges on the southwest side are holding pollock working the surface on the early morning flood — schoolies mostly, but enough of them chasing bait balls that you can see the slicks from a half mile off. Under them, cod and a scattering of haddock are sitting in 100 to 140 feet, and jigging a diamond jig or bouncing a herring chunk on a two-hook bottom rig has been worth the trip out. It's not the haddock fishing of thirty years ago — nobody's pretending otherwise — but there's enough holding in that deeper water to make a respectable box if you work the ledges on the last two hours of the incoming.

Penobscot Bay itself has been quiet but honest. The deeper channels — Muscle Ridge, Two Bush — are still holding a mix of pollock and the occasional cod for guys running bottom rigs on the drift, and more than a few boats are coming back with a mess of lobster bycatch tangled in with the groundfish, which nobody's complaining about. Water's sitting in the low 60s across the bay, cold enough that we're not seeing any of the warm-water excitement working its way up the coast from southern New England. No albies showing here, no bluefish blitzes — this is Maine in August the way it's supposed to be, steady and a little slow to give it up.

Down around Eastern Egg Rock the puffins are still working but thinning out as the season turns, and the bass have been using the same bait-driven pattern — terns diving on mackerel schools pushed up against the ledges on the ebb, stripers underneath cleaning up what gets knocked loose. If you can find working birds out there in the last two hours of the tide, it's worth a few casts with a topwater popper before you move on.

Over toward Deer Isle and Stonington, the Eggemoggin Reach current has been the most consistent thing going — bass working the tide rips where the reach narrows, and pollock schooling on the surface at first light the same as at Monhegan. Isle au Haut's ledges are holding a few cod for the guys willing to run out that far, though it's a long haul for what's mostly a slow pick right now.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the week. The new moon tides are still building strength, and if that current keeps sharpening up at the river mouths and channel edges the way it has, the bass should keep following the mackerel right on schedule. Water temps aren't going anywhere fast in this zone — we're insulated from whatever's stirring up the coast to the south, and that's fine by me. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at the St. George river mouth on the last of the ebb with a bucket of fresh mackerel and enough patience to wait for the tide to do its work.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 205 feet: cod thin on the gravel, haddock steady over the mud
reports.subhead: Groundfish stayed textbook for mid-August while the first real bait pods showed up topside on the ledge — a preview of what October usually brings.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-oh-five feet on the sounder this morning, working the northeast corner of Jeffrey's Ledge where the gravel kicks up hard against the mud line. That transition is everything out here. Drop a jig six feet off bottom on the gravel side and you're fishing for cod. Drift twenty yards west onto the softer mud and you're suddenly in haddock country. Same tide, same boat, two different fisheries separated by a bottom change you can watch happen on the chart plotter.

Cod have been thin but honest this week — not a stacked bite, but a real one. We've been picking fish to 8 and 10 pounds on the gravel edges in 190 to 220 feet, jigging 12-ounce diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid on the drop. The key has been working the up-current side of the humps where the gravel piles into little ridges — cod sit tight to that structure and won't chase far, so short, sharp jig strokes right on bottom beat a big sweeping retrieve every time. Water at depth is still holding in the mid-60s, which is right where you want it for this fishery to stay honest through late summer. No complaints there, but no gangbusters day either — figure one keeper cod for every three or four you handle, with a lot of shorts mixed in that need to go back quick.

Haddock have actually been the more consistent player over the softer bottom toward Scantum Basin. Standard rig — a high-low with clam bellies or squid strips — fished right on the mud in 180 to 200 feet has been putting steady fish in the box, most running a pound and a half to three pounds, with the occasional slob pushing five. Haddock don't care much about current the way cod do; they sit and feed on that mud almost lazily, so a slow drift with light chum in the water has out-produced anything aggressive. If you're marking soft, rolling marks a few feet off bottom on the machine, that's your school — don't chase them, let the drift bring you back through.

Pollock have been mixed in on both bottoms, which is normal for this time of year, and we've picked a few nice hake off the mud edges on bigger, slower-worked jigs after dark on evening trips. Mackerel showed decent early in the week off Cape Ann on the way out, enough to load a bait tank without burning much time, though they've thinned some as the week's gone on — worth checking before you commit a whole trip to jigging bait, but don't count on it being a sure thing every morning.

The bigger story this week, honestly, is what's happening on top of the water rather than what's coming off the bottom. We've started seeing real bait pods building over Jeffrey's — tight balls of sand eels and pogies pushing up on the surface, gulls working hard, and a few boats reporting single bluefin showing on top without much commitment. That's the pattern I watch for every August. It's early yet — the real giant bluefin push on this ledge doesn't typically load in until October, when the bait gets dense and the fish start setting up to feed hard before they push offshore — but this kind of bait buildup in mid-August is exactly the setup that leads into it. Worth keeping an eye on if you're planning tuna trips later in the season; I wouldn't burn fuel chasing singles right now, but I'd note where the bait's concentrating, because that's usually where the giants show up in six to eight weeks.

We said last week to expect steady conditions with no major shifts through this stretch, and that's exactly how it played out — no fronts came through, no water temp swings, and the gravel-mud split held its pattern all week without disruption. That kind of predictability is actually good news for planning trips; when the pattern's steady, you can fish it with confidence instead of guessing.

Tide-wise, we're working through the cycle a few days past the new moon, and the stronger exchanges have kept bait moving and marks a little more spread than they'd be on a slack neap week. That's part of why the haddock bite on the mud has stayed more consistent than the cod bite on the gravel — haddock tolerate that current better and hold position, while cod get pickier about exactly where they'll sit when the water's really moving.

Looking ahead, if the bait pods keep building over the ledge and the mid-60s water holds at depth, I'd expect the groundfish pattern to stay right where it is — steady haddock on the mud, honest but not heavy cod on the gravel. Platts Bank and Tillies Bank are both worth a look if Jeffrey's gets crowded or the drift isn't setting up right; both have been holding similar mixed haddock and pollock action on their respective mud and gravel patches. I'd keep a longer look toward Cape Ann and Thatcher Island for weather windows, since the next stretch of the season is really about picking clean days to get out and watch that bait build — because when it finally tightens up in earnest, that's when this ledge turns into a different fishery altogether.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:40: Bass Are Pinning Bunker Against the Rock
reports.subhead: Two days off the new moon, the tide's running hard through SW Ledge and stripers are using it — bonito and albies are still a no-show, but the setup says soon.
reports.body_markdown:
6:40 AM. That's slack before the ebb at SW Ledge this week, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the top of the rock by 6:20, you've already missed the best fifteen minutes of the morning. I had the boat parked in 28 feet on the northwest corner Tuesday, right where the ledge drops from 18 down into the channel, and watched the sounder light up with peanut bunker getting pushed and pinched against the rock as the current built. Two minutes later the marks scattered and the rod bent. That's the whole game out there right now — read the bait, read the tide, be in position before the water starts moving.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at SW Ledge and down around Sandy Point. The spring tides off this moon are shoving more water through the rip than we've seen all summer, and it's dragging bunker schools right into the teeth of it. Stripers from 26 inches up to a genuine 35-pounder — landed Wednesday on a chunk of fresh bunker fished on a fish-finder rig in 40 feet on the down-current side — are using that current like a conveyor belt. If you're throwing artificials, a white or bone SP Minnow worked with a stall-and-twitch on the up-tide swing has been drawing the better fish, and bucktails in the 2-ounce range, white with a white curly tail, are cleaning up when you can get them down through the sweep without getting swept off the structure entirely.

The pattern holds at Sandy Point too, especially the last two hours of the incoming when bait gets funneled around the spit. I had a charter Sunday morning working the rip line off the point in 15 to 20 feet, and we picked at slot bass steadily on live bunker under a balloon, plus a couple of bluefish in the 6- to 8-pound class that showed up chopping bait on the surface — no surprise there, the blues are riding the same peanut bunker wave that's got stripers blitzing everywhere from Narragansett Bay up into Buzzards Bay this month. It's an unusual amount of visible bunker-driven activity for mid-August, honestly, more like an October pattern than what we usually see this time of year, and my read is it's early staging ahead of the fall push. Worth taking seriously if you're planning trips into September.

Here's the honest part: no bonito, no false albacore off Block Island yet. I've had my eyes on the water off North Light and out past Clay Head every trip this week, glassing for that telltale nervous water and diving terns, and it hasn't shown. The ingredients are all there — warm water pushing into the high 60s and low 70s across the region, bait stacked thick, and we're now two days past the new moon that typically kicks the current hard enough to bring albies and bonito ripping into the Block Island rips. Southeast Light and the rip off North Light are the first places they usually show when they do, so that's where I'd be running the spread of Deadly Dicks and small Albie Snax if you want to be the first one on them. My money says within the next week, once this tidal push settles into a rhythm, somebody's going to hook up off the island. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have the light tackle rigged and ready.

Fluke fishing has been fair, not great. We worked the drift off Sandy Point in 25 to 35 feet Thursday with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a fresh strip of squid, and put four keepers in the box against a lot of shorts. The bigger fish are still scattered — nothing like the doormat action other zones are seeing right now — so I'm treating fluke as a bonus fish this week rather than the target. Black sea bass, on the other hand, keep improving steadily on the reef structure south of the island in 60 to 80 feet. Green crab and squid combos on double bottom rigs are producing a solid mixed bag, and that trend should keep firming through the rest of August as water temps hold.

Looking ahead: I want to fish the SW Ledge slack again this weekend, ideally the Saturday evening tide when the moon's a little fuller and the current should run even harder through the rip. If the bunker stay stacked the way they have been, that's where the bigger bass will keep showing. And I'll be running out toward North Light and Southeast Light every trip looking for that first bonito flash — the water's right, the bait's right, it's just a matter of which morning it clicks. If I had one day to gamble on it, I'd pick a calm morning right around the next tide change and put the light spinning gear within casting range of that rip edge before the sun's even up.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock groundfish steady, mackerel schools pull bass to the ledges
reports.subhead: Two days off the new moon, the tide swing is doing exactly what a strong flood should do — stacking bait tight against structure from Peaks Island to Cape Small.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning drifting the eastern face of Halfway Rock with a spinning rod I have no business fishing off a boat, and it reminded me why I keep coming back to that piece of ledge every August. The rock sits where it always sits — six miles off Bailey Island, the same slab of granite it's been since before anyone I know was born — but what's happening around it changes by the week, and this week the change is worth writing down.

We're two days past the new moon, and the tidal flow it kicked up has done what building flow into a new moon usually does this time of year: sharpened the bite at the current-driven structure. I flagged that pattern building last week, and out at Halfway Rock it's arrived right on schedule. On the last two hours of the ebb, with the current really moving off the southeast corner, I marked pollock and cod stacked in that 60 to 90 foot depth where the ledge drops off into the channel. Diamond jigs — the heavier 4 to 6 ounce Norwegian-style jigs, worked with a short hop off bottom — took three keeper-class cod and a pile of pollock in about ninety minutes of fishing. Haddock have been scarcer out there than I'd like this month; I took one respectable fish and lost what felt like a bigger one on the way up, but the ratio of pollock to haddock this summer has been lopsided in pollock's favor. If you're going out for haddock specifically, fish the slack itself, right at the top of the tide, when the bait settles and they'll hold tighter to bottom rather than getting pushed off the structure by current.

The more interesting story this week, though, is what's happening in the upper water column. Mackerel schools have been thick and dependable through the bay all summer, and they haven't thinned yet — I've watched them roll on the surface off Spring Point, off the eastern side of Peaks Island, and in tight around the ledges off Cushing. That's the forage base holding this whole fishery together right now. Water's sitting in that classic Maine summer range, low 60s, which keeps mackerel comfortable and keeps striped bass working the edges where those schools get pinned against structure. Jigging small diamond jigs or Sabiki rigs off Peaks in 20 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming has been about as reliable as fishing gets in this bay — you can fill a five-gallon bucket in twenty minutes if the school is under the boat, and that bucket buys you the best live bait in Casco Bay for the bass.

Striped bass have been following that bait with the kind of patience I appreciate in a fish. River mouths — the Presumpscot, the mouth of the Royal, the Basin down toward Cape Small — have all been holding fish on the top of the tide and through the first two hours of the ebb, when baitfish get flushed out and bass set up to intercept them. Live mackerel under a slip float, fished right along the current seam where the river water meets the bay, has been the most consistent producer. For guys who'd rather cast than soak bait, a white or chartreuse bucktail worked slow along the bottom edge of those seams has taken slot fish as well, though I'd call that bite good, not great — you need to find the seam, not just the general area.

The ledge fishing for bass off Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small has been more of a dawn-and-dusk affair. I worked the ledges off Cape Small at first light Thursday with a topwater popper — a Yo-Zuri Sashimi, walked slow across the slick — and connected with two fish in the mid-20-inch range before the sun got high and the bite shut off. That's typical August ledge behavior here: the bass are there, but the window is short, tied tight to low light and moving water, and once the sun climbs and the tide slacks, they drop back into deeper water and go quiet. Two Lights has fished similarly — good for an hour around first light on a dropping tide, then it goes flat.

Bluefish remain the wildcard. There's a real push of bluefish moving up the coast right now, riding peanut bunker schools from the Sound clear up through Massachusetts Bay, and it wouldn't surprise me if some of that push works its way into outer Casco Bay before the month is out — we've had years where a late-August bluefish run shows up off Two Lights or out past Cushing almost overnight. I haven't seen it materialize inside the bay yet this week, and I'm not going to promise it's coming, but if you're rigging up for bass anyway, it costs nothing to keep a wire leader in the boat.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the broad pattern to shift much through the coming week. Water temperatures should hold steady in that low-60s range, mackerel should keep schooling reliably enough to bait up on, and the tidal flow — still building off this new moon cycle — should keep sharpening the bite at current-driven structure like Halfway Rock and the river mouths. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be back at Halfway Rock on the last two hours of an ebb tide with jigs in hand, and I'd have a bucket of fresh mackerel rigged for bass on the way home.

reports.headline: Bunker Push the Breachways: Bass Crushing Peanuts from Sakonnet to Napatree
reports.subhead: Rocks from Second Beach to Watch Hill are loaded with bait and blitzing stripers — the albies just haven't shown up to the party yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Peanut bunker are stacked so thick against the rocks at Second Beach this week you can see the wash go dark with them on a calm morning tide. That's the tell. When the bait pins itself tight to structure like that, something's pushing it, and right now it's stripers — not albies, not yet, but give it time.

We flagged this last week — said the building tide into the new moon would sharpen things up at the breachways and points, and that's exactly what's happened. The bass have been on the bunker hard from Sakonnet Point down through Jamestown's east side and into Newport's Ocean Drive rocks. I've been working peanut-imitating soft plastics — 5-inch white Slug-Go's and Hogy jr's, unweighted or on a light 3/8-ounce jighead — right through the froth where the bunker are getting pinned against ledge. Retrieve slow, let it sink between rock faces, twitch it out. Fish are running mostly schoolies to mid-20s, but there've been enough fatter ones mixed in — low 30s — that it's worth working a spot longer than you think you should.

Sakonnet Point has been the most consistent piece of structure all week. The bunker get squeezed into that funnel on the last two hours of the incoming, and the bass sit right on the edge of the rip off the point waiting for the current to disorganize the school. That's when you see the surface erupt — not a constant blitz, more like waves of it every 20 minutes as another push of bait gets shoved through. Second Beach has fished similarly on the outgoing, bait draining out past the rocks with the tide and stripers stacking up right where the wash meets the rip line.

Jamestown's rockier stretches — the ledges along the east passage — have been a slower, more technical bite. Less blitz, more picking. Guys drifting live bunker on a fishfinder rig tight to the rocks in 15 to 25 feet have done well on the slower tides, especially the last hour before the turn when the current eases and the fish can actually track a bait instead of getting blown past it.

Bluefish are riding right along with the bass in these same bunker schools, and they're not small — I've seen 3 and 4 pounders mixed into the blitzes at Sakonnet, plus snapper blues thick in the coves at Third Beach and up in the Sakonnet River proper. If you want steady bent-rod action without hunting for the exact right blitz window, tie on a metal — half-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — and just work the edges of the bait balls. You'll connect.

Now the albie question. Napatree and Watch Hill haven't seen the first fin yet, but the water's set up right for it — bait's dense, temps are warm, and Fishers Island Sound just to our west has all the right ingredients cooking too. Typically we don't see the first albies push into these breachways until late August or the first week of September, but with bait this thick this early, I wouldn't be shocked if they show ahead of schedule. When they do arrive, Napatree's the spot I check first — that sandbar drop where the rip forms on the outgoing tide funnels bait right past the point, and albies use it like a feeding lane. Watch Hill's east side and the Weekapaug breachway are close seconds. Keep an epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick tied on and just fish the bunker/blitz spots daily — the albies find these same bait concentrations, they just haven't crossed the sound yet.

Fluke have been modest, which tracks with what's happening most places in New England this year outside of Nantucket Sound. I've picked a few keepers drifting Gulp on bucktails in the sandy pockets off Second Beach and in the mouth of the Sakonnet River, but it's not a program I'd build a whole trip around right now. Scup, on the other hand, have been dependable filler — drop a piece of clam or squid strip down into any rocky pocket from Beavertail to Napatree and you'll have bait for the cooler in short order.

Tog are still tucked deep on the ledges — Beavertail, the rocks off Brenton Point, the humps outside Sakonnet — but this warm water has them uninterested. That bite doesn't really sharpen up until the water starts sliding down into the upper 60s, which puts us into September for real tog action. Not worth chasing hard yet.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the bunker schools wherever you find them stacked against structure — that's where the bass and blues are, and it's the same water the albies will use when they finally push in. Sakonnet Point on the incoming and Second Beach on the outgoing are my picks for this weekend if the wind stays reasonable. And I'd be checking Napatree every session, because when those first albies show, they don't stick around long before word gets out and the rocks get crowded.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool on the incoming still owns the night — bass to 28, mackerel stacked at Wells
reports.subhead: The new moon tide finally gave the current-driven spots some teeth, but this is still a river-mouth-and-rocks bite, not a blitz.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday night, low tide turning, I put a black Gibbs Danny across the mouth of the Pool and had a 28-inch bass on the third cast before my headlamp batteries were even warm. Missed two more blows in the dark that felt like real weight — the kind of headshake that makes you check your hooks twice before you cast again. That's the Pool doing what the Pool does on the incoming: current pours in over that sandbar, pushes mackerel and silversides ahead of it, and the bass stack up in the deeper channel edge waiting for the buffet to arrive. I've fished that push for the better part of thirty years and it still gets my hands shaking a little.

We flagged this last week — said the building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly the story right now. The moon's fresh off new, the tides are running big, and every spot in this zone that depends on moving water — the Pool, the mouth of the Saco, Wells Harbor, the back channel at Pine Point — is fishing better than it was two weeks ago when everything felt stuck in neutral.

Don't mistake that for a blitz, though. What's happening from Narragansett Bay up through Cape Cod Bay right now — bunker-driven, visible, surface-erupting bass — hasn't reached us and I wouldn't bet on it showing up here. Our water is still holding in that low-to-mid 60s range, cooler than the corridor to our south, and that keeps this a classic Maine pattern: fish working the tide against structure, not schools boiling on top in broad daylight. If you want the fireworks, you're looking at the wrong coastline this week. If you want a solid, honest bass in the dark on a plug, you're in the right place.

Pine Point has been quietly good on the last two hours of the incoming, working the channel edge off the jetty with a Northbar bottle darter or a bone-colored Super Strike — slow retrieve, let it wallow, because the bass there are eating mackerel that are getting pushed and disoriented by the current rip, not chasing anything fast. I had a mixed bag Thursday morning there — three bass between 24 and 27 inches, one that measured just a hair shy of slot, released clean.

Higgins Beach has had bluefish showing in shorter windows than I'd like — a solid half hour around the top of the tide where the sand fleas get stirred and the blues come through hot, hitting anything silver and fast. Small metal — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown into the wash and cranked hard has been the move. It's not an all-day bite. Miss the window and you're just casting at empty water, so time it to the tide charts, not to when you feel like showing up.

Prouts Neck has been a coin flip depending on wind. When it's blowing out of the southwest, which it has more days than not this stretch, the rocks fish well — bait gets pushed up against the ledges and the bass hold tight to structure, close enough that you're practically dropping the plug in your own shadow. A Danny or a Bottle Popper worked parallel to the rocks, right in that white water seam, has drawn strikes in the 26-to-30-inch range. When the wind swings northeast, forget it — that whole stretch turns into standing water and the fish scatter off the structure.

Mackerel have been thick enough at Wells Harbor and off Ogunquit's rocks that if you're not catching a few on a string of tinsel jigs dropped along the pilings, you're not really trying. They're the forage driving this whole pattern right now — striped bass pushing into the estuaries and river mouths are doing it because the mackerel are there, and that's held true from Kittery to Cape Elizabeth all month. Flounder fishing in Wells Harbor and the calmer stretches behind Biddeford Pool has stayed steady on the bottom — squid strips and sandworms on a simple flounder rig in eight to fifteen feet, best on the last of the incoming when the water's had a chance to warm and settle.

Cod haven't been a big story close to shore this time of year, which is normal — that's more a late fall and winter game for us once the water starts dropping. Pollock have been the better bonus fish around any hard structure — jetties, ledge piles, the rocks off Cape Elizabeth — hit with a diamond jig worked with a fast vertical jig-and-drop.

Looking ahead: the tides stay big for another few days off this new moon, so I'd keep leaning into the Pool on the incoming and Pine Point on that same push — those two spots have the most reliable current to work with right now. If the wind holds southwest into the weekend, Prouts Neck is worth the drive. What I'm watching for is any sign that bait starts thinning out of the estuaries as we roll toward September — that's usually the tell that the real fall run is close, and up here that's still the best fishing of the year once it gets going. For now, it's a solid, working-man's bite. Bring your headlamp, fish the tide, and don't expect the ocean to hand you anything for free.

reports.headline: Appledore Ledges Give Up Cod to 6 Pounds While the Piscataqua Runs Thick with Stripers
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know the bottom — groundfish holding tight to the Shoals structure while the river does the striper work.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of New Hampshire coast and figure there's nothing to write about. I've been running my 20-foot Lund out to the Shoals before sunup for going on fifteen years and I still haven't fished all of it. Thirteen miles on the chart doesn't mean thirteen miles of water — it means the Piscataqua pouring out past Portsmouth Harbor, Gosport Harbor tucked in behind Appledore and Star, and enough broken ledge and cobble bottom around the Shoals to keep a small boat guy busy every single trip. I fish it like it's a hundred and thirty miles. That's the whole secret.

This week the groundfish bite off Appledore held up better than the Hampton stuff, which tells you where I spent my mornings. Cod to six pounds came off the northeast side of the island in 60 to 80 feet, jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly on the slack before the tide turned, then switching to bait — whole clams and chunked mackerel on a two-hook bottom rig — once the current picked up and the jigs stopped hanging straight down. Haddock are around but they're not stacked the way they were in June. I marked pods on the sounder over some of the rockier patches south of Star Island and picked at them for maybe four or five keepers a trip, nothing you'd call a slam dunk. If you want haddock right now you need to be willing to move around and burn some gas checking marks instead of anchoring on one pile and hoping.

Water out at the Shoals is still running in that classic low-60s range at depth, which is exactly why the groundfish are behaving normally while everything south of the Merrimack is chasing peanut bunker blitzes in warm water. We don't get that show up here in mid-August and I wouldn't want it — cold, clean water holding cod and haddock on structure is the New Hampshire pattern, and it's held true again this week. We flagged this a week back — said this zone would trail the warmer water to the south and keep its own rhythm through the transition, and that's exactly what's playing out. No albies, no bonito, no blitzing bass chasing bunker schools on the surface. Just steady, honest groundfish and river stripers doing what they do this time of year.

Speaking of the river — the Piscataqua has been the better bet for stripers all week, and it's the current that makes it, not the moon phase alone. We came off the new moon on the 12th and the tidal flow built exactly like I expected, and the bite at current-driven structure sharpened right up with it. I've been working the seams below the Route 1 bridge and down around the General Sullivan area on the last two hours of the incoming, drifting live mackerel and eels on a three-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that push. Fish from 26 to 34 inches, a handful over the 28-to-31 slot going back, but enough keepers in that window to make it worth the trip. The back eddies on the Portsmouth side, right where the current breaks off the pilings, have been holding fish tucked up tight — a slow-trolled bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig through there on the last of the ebb has worked when the straight drift didn't.

Hampton Harbor has been more up and down. The inlet by Great Boars Head fishes well on the push of the incoming, especially the first two hours after dead low when bait gets funneled through the channel, but I've had mornings there with almost nothing showing and mornings with a dozen schoolies to 24 inches on soft plastics — five-inch white paddletails on a half-ounce jighead, worked slow along the bottom edge of the channel drop. Seabrook side of the harbor has snapper blues thick in the back creeks, which is normal for mid-August and a decent sign that adult blues will keep building through the fall as those fish grow into it. If you've got kids who want bent rods, that's your spot — small Kastmasters or Gotcha plugs off the docks near the bridge.

Mackerel are still around the Shoals in good numbers, which is half the reason the cod fishing has held — bait's there and the structure holds it. I jig for mackerel on light tackle first thing to fill the bait bucket, then switch over to the groundfish gear once I've got what I need. It's an efficient way to fish a small boat out there and it costs you nothing but twenty minutes.

Flounder have been an afterthought this year in the harbors — a few keepers on sandworms and clam bellies in Rye Harbor on calm mornings, but nothing to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the coming week. The tide's still building off that new moon push, so I'd keep working the Piscataqua current seams on the incoming for stripers and stick with the Appledore ledges for cod on the slack-into-building tide. If the wind stays out of the southwest and keeps things calm, I'll be back at the Shoals before most people's coffee is done brewing. That's still the way to fish this coast — early, small, and smart about the water you've got instead of wishing for more of it.

reports.headline: The 6:04 Ebb at the East End: Bass on the Bunker, Blues Riding Shotgun
reports.subhead: Two days off the new moon, the Canal's current is running hard and the bass are stacked tight to the bait — but you've got to hit the window.
reports.body_markdown:
6:04 this morning, east end, and the ebb was already ripping at better than four knots off the Railroad Bridge rip. That's the number I've been chasing all week. Two days past the new moon on the 12th, and the Canal is doing exactly what it does on a big spring tide — current stacking hard against the rip line, peanut bunker getting squeezed into that seam where the fast water meets the slower inside edge, and bass sitting right on the transition line waiting for the buffet to come to them. We flagged this a week ago — said the tidal flow building into the new moon would sharpen the bite on both ends, and that's exactly what's playing out right now.

The east end has been the story. From the Bourne Bridge down to the Railroad Bridge, bass are working peanut bunker schools that are getting funneled through on the back half of the ebb — best window's been about two hours before dead low through the first twenty minutes of the turn, when the current's still got some push but the bait starts bunching up instead of getting blown straight through. I've had good luck throwing 3-ounce Deadly Dicks and white/chartreuse Hogy epoxy jigs into the boils where you can see bunker getting nervous, letting it sink on a controlled drift with the current instead of fighting it, then working it back with the flow. Bluefish are mixed right into the same schools — some of them snappers, but plenty of adult class three and four pounders that'll about take the rod out of your hand on a Ballistic Missile popper worked across the top of the rip at first light.

West end's been a different animal, and that's normal for this time of year. Current seams off Mashnee Island and around Hog Island have been holding bass, but you have to work the stage of the tide more precisely — the bite there wants the last hour of the flood pushing into the top of the tide, when the water stacks up against Wings Neck and pushes bait into that flat calm pocket inside Phinneys Harbor. I had a solid forty minutes there Tuesday evening with schoolies to 28 inches on a soft plastic paddletail, white Al Gag Whip-It Fish rigged on a 3/4-ounce jighead, worked slow along the drop where the sand gives way to the deeper channel edge. Nothing huge, but steady, and enough to keep the rod bent.

Scusset Beach has been more hit or miss than the rip lines proper — the surf guys are getting into fish on the outgoing when bait gets pushed out past the jetty, but you're fishing into open water there and it's less current-structured than working the rip itself. If I only had one spot to send a reader with a rod and no boat, I'd still say the east end rocks below the Railroad Bridge on the last two hours of ebb. That's where thirty years of watching this ditch has taught me the bait gets concentrated hardest.

Honest talk on size: this isn't a slot-limit bonanza. Most of what's coming over the rail is schoolie to mid-20s, with the occasional slot fish mixed in on the harder tides. I haven't heard of anything over 34 inches out of the Canal proper this week, though the blitz activity building from Narragansett up through Buzzards Bay and into Cape Cod Bay tells me there are bigger fish staging somewhere close, probably following those same bunker schools that are pushing bass activity everywhere from Long Island Sound on up. Worth remembering this is peanut bunker season — small bait, and the bass chasing it right now are mostly built for speed, not size, until the bigger fish decide to show up behind them.

Slack water is still killing the bite dead, same as every August. When that current drops off — and on these bigger spring tides it can go from ripping to nearly flat in fifteen minutes — the bass scatter off the seams and go quiet. I've watched guys keep fishing through slack out of stubbornness and it just doesn't produce. Better to walk the bridge, grab a coffee at the bait shop, and be back rigged up when the current starts building again on the other stage.

No albies or bonito confirmed in the Canal yet, and I wouldn't expect them here specifically — this isn't their water even when they show up elsewhere on the Cape. But the water's warm enough and the bait's thick enough that if they do arrive in Buzzards Bay proper over the next few days, like the pattern building from Montauk on up suggests, don't be shocked if some push up toward the west end mouth chasing bait out of Phinneys Harbor.

Looking ahead: the moon's still working for us, tidal flow should stay strong through this week before easing back toward the quarter. If the pattern holds, I'd keep hitting that east end ebb window and working the west end top-of-flood push at Mashnee. Watch the wind — anything hard out of the southwest chops up the rip line and makes it tougher to read the boils, so pick your mornings.

reports.headline: 62 to 74 Feet: Sea Bass Steady on the Reef Line, Tuna Still Sitting Past the Ridge
reports.subhead: The nearshore wrecks are producing keeper sea bass on the drift, but the tuna bite stays out past Barnegat Ridge until that warm edge decides to come in.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-two feet on the inshore corner of Sea Girt Reef, current running maybe half a knot, and my sounder is stacked with sea bass marks sitting tight to the rubble on the up-current side. That's the number that told me where to make my first drop this week, and it's the number I keep coming back to — this time of August, the bass haven't pushed out to the deeper structure yet, they're still working the shallow reef edges where the bait's been holding.

Twenty years of writing depths and bottom composition in a soggy notebook teaches you that sea bass don't move much until the thermocline shoves them, and right now the thermocline hasn't shoved. Sea Girt Reef, Axel Carlson Reef, and Shrewsbury Rocks are all fishing the same way — decent numbers of keepers in the 13-15 inch class, a few pushing better, on Gulp Peach or white 5-inch swimming mullets threaded on a bucktail teaser above a standard sea bass rig, dropped straight down and worked with short lifts off bottom. Nothing that's going to fill a cooler in an hour, but a steady pick if you're willing to move the boat when the marks thin out. I fished Triple Wrecks Tuesday morning on the last of an outgoing tide and had a mixed bag — good sea bass activity early, then it went quiet as the current slacked off. That's been the pattern all week: strong for the first hour or two of a moving tide, then you're re-anchoring or hunting a new piece to keep the bite going.

I'll be straight with you — it's not a banner week out there. The sea bass fishing is honest work, not a sure thing. You need to be willing to run between pieces, check three or four spots on the reef network before you find the one holding fish that morning, and not get married to a single number in the book just because it produced last trip.

Further out, past Barnegat Ridge, the story is different and less settled. There's a warm-water edge that's been sitting out that way most of the month, and it's the kind of thing that can turn a slow day into a good one if you time it right. The tuna — yellowfin mostly, with bluefin mixed in on some of the deeper humps toward Klondike — have been working that break, but getting to them and finding the exact seam has been hit or miss depending on which day you go. I made the run out toward Klondike over the weekend chasing exactly that pattern and came up with one bluefin on the troll and a long quiet stretch after — the temperature edge had slid a little from where it had been sitting, and I was a mile or two off it most of the day. That's the game with these midrange grounds. You're not fishing a fixed spot, you're fishing where the water sets up that day, and sometimes you guess wrong.

Mahi have been scattered thin around any floating structure or temp break you find between the Ridge and Klondike — nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet, just fish showing up under the occasional weed line or piece of debris when you happen to run across it. If you're making that run, keep a spinning rod rigged with a small chartreuse jig or a strip bait ready, because those mahi won't wait around while you dig through a tackle bag.

Water's still warm enough to hold that edge out past the Ridge, and the wind's been cooperative — light out of the southwest most days, which keeps the ride out manageable and doesn't tear up the surface enough to blow the temp break apart. If that holds through the week, I'd expect the tuna bite to firm up rather than fade, especially on the troll-to-chunk transition in the evening hours when the sun drops and the bait gets nervous. But I wouldn't bank a trip on it without checking the latest position of that edge before you leave the dock — it's moved on me twice already this month.

For the guy who just wants fish in the box without burning four hours of fuel, I'd stay inshore this week. Work the reef network — Sea Girt, Axel Carlson, Shrewsbury Rocks, Triple Wrecks — on the moving tide, keep the boat mobile, and treat the sea bass bite as a morning program rather than an all-day soak. For the guy chasing tuna, understand you're gambling on where that warm pool sits the day you go, and Barnegat Ridge is your jumping-off point to find out — not necessarily where the fish will be.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and that offshore edge holds its ground, I expect the tuna pattern past the Ridge toward Klondike to keep improving into next week. The reef bite should hold too, though I'd expect the bass to start sliding toward the deeper pieces as the month wears on and the shallow water starts to lose its edge. I'll have my numbers ready either way.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at First Light: Blues Crash Bunker, Schoolies Ride the Edges
reports.subhead: Bunker pods pinned tight to the beach are turning the jetty country into a blitz alarm — the albies are still a no-show, but everything else about this week says they're close.
reports.body_markdown:
5:20 a.m., low tip of the Sea Bright rocks, and there were already four guys spread out over structure I usually have to myself this time of year. Nobody said much. You don't need to when the water in front of you is boiling with peanut bunker trying to climb out of the ocean. Bluefish underneath them doing what bluefish do — not subtle about it. One guy was throwing a bunker spoon on 40-pound braid, getting bit on almost every retrieve. Another had a wooden darter, worked slow through the froth, and came up with a bluefish that had a school bass practically riding shotgun behind it. That's the story right now up and down this stretch — the blues are the headline, but the stripers are working the margins of the same meal, and neither one is being shy about it.

This is the pattern we flagged last week — bunker pods pushed tight to the sand, and wherever they show, the tide change lights the fuse. It's playing out almost exactly like that at Sea Bright, at the north end of Monmouth Beach, and off the jetties below Long Branch. The bite windows are short and violent, usually the last hour of the outgoing and the first half hour of the new incoming, and then it shuts off like someone flipped a switch until the bait regroups. If you're fishing it, don't waste time on the slack. Get there for the tide change and be ready to move down the beach if the pod slides.

The swell's been an annoyance more than a dealbreaker. Ocean's been running close to four feet at five seconds out front, which makes the outside face of the Sea Bright rocks a good way to lose your footing and your rod in the same motion. I've been working the calmer pockets — the lee side of the jetties, the washes right at the base where the white water settles — rather than climbing all the way out to the tip. Bass have been sitting in that same wash, picking off stunned bunker, and you can cover it just fine with a Super Strike swimmer or a 3-ounce Ava jig without risking your neck on wet rock.

Down at Manasquan Inlet, the story shifts a little. Less blitz chaos, more steady grinding — which for August is honestly a fair trade. The jetty on the north side has been giving up bluefish to 4 pounds on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in about 10 to 12 feet at the mouth, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone slack. Fluke fishing inside the inlet has been steady rather than spectacular — 3-to-6 pound Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and pink shad, bounced along the channel edge in 15 to 20 feet on the drift from the Point down toward the Coast Guard station. Nothing to write home about size-wise most days, but there's real doormat potential in this corridor right now — the same trophy fluke pattern that's been showing up down toward Raritan Bay has fish in the high single digits turning up on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along bottom structure. Worth a few extra drifts before you give up on a spot.

Shark River Inlet has been the porgy story this week — bloodworms and clam on a bottom rig off the Belmar side jetty and the Route 35 bridge rocks, decent numbers of 10-to-12-inch fish stacked up in 8 to 15 feet on the last of the outgoing. Snapper blues are thick in the back of that inlet too, which is a good early sign — those fish grow up fast, and by mid-September the adult class behind them tends to show in force.

Blackfish are still weeks off — water's too warm and the season's not close — but I mention it because guys keep asking. Not yet. Patience.

As for false albacore — nothing. We said the new moon on the 12th would be the trigger to watch, and the tide's building the way it should through this current cycle, but nobody I've talked to on the rocks or at the bait shop has laid eyes on a single fin. The ingredients are all sitting there — warm water, bait stacked tight, sharper current — and that combination has a way of producing albies out of nowhere once it does. I'd keep a bag of Deadly Dicks and small metal in the truck for the next couple weeks regardless. Spring Lake jetties and the water off Belmar are typically where this stretch sees its first fish if they show at all, usually working the tide lines just off the rocks in the early morning glass.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend — bunker's still holding tight to the beach, blues are still going to crash it on the tide changes, and the bass will keep riding the edges of that chaos rather than driving it themselves. That's an early-season pattern more than a late-August one, honestly, and it's got me thinking this could be the leading edge of fish starting to stage for the fall run a little ahead of schedule. If the swell backs off even a foot, I'd get out to the tip of the Sea Bright rocks on the dawn outgoing and work a bunker spoon through the froth before the sun gets too high. That's where I'll be.

reports.headline: Double Creek doormats and snapper blues everywhere — the bay's running hot but the fluke are still there if you know the bends
reports.subhead: Water's pushing 78 in the shallows, but the channel edges are holding fish for anyone willing to fish the bottom of the tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember an August a long time back, mating on a Point Pleasant party boat, when the mate before me — old Charlie, gone now near twenty years — told me the bay in high summer is a lazy man's puzzle. Everything's still there, he said, it's just gone quiet and gone deep. You have to go find it instead of waiting for it to find you. I think about that every August, and this one's no different. The bay's pushing toward 78 degrees in the shallows this week, and that heat has pushed the bait and the fluke both down into the channel edges and the deeper holes where there's a little relief from the sun beating on the flats all day.

Double Creek Channel is doing what it always does for me in mid-August — producing on the bottom third of the ebb, when the current's still got enough push to pull bait off the shoulders and stack it in the bends. I've been running white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails down there, dragging them slow along bottom in 8 to 12 feet, and picking through a mess of shorts for every keeper. That ratio isn't great, but the keepers have been decent — 20 to 22 inches mostly, with one angler I talked to at the ramp in Waretown showing me a fish pushing 5 pounds he took on a killie under a bobber, drifted right along the edge where the channel drops off. Barnegat and Long Beach Island backbays have a reputation this summer for punching well above their weight on big fluke — somebody weighed a 12-pound-plus doormat over in Bayonne a couple weeks back, and I wouldn't be shocked if there's a fish that size sitting in one of these deep bends right now. If you're hunting a wall-hanger instead of dinner, fish live killies or mullet strips on a fish-finder rig right on the bottom where the channel narrows, and be patient. Doormats don't chase.

Oyster Creek's mouth is holding fish too, same story — last two hours of the outgoing, working the drop where the creek dumps into the bay. That's classic August pattern; the water's warm enough now that there's no thermal edge to exploit like you get in the cold months, so it's really about current concentrating bait, not temperature. Bucktail and Gulp combo, or a simple high-low rig with squid strips if the current's ripping too hard for plastics to sit right.

Snapper blues are thick as I've seen them in a few years — every dock, every marina basin from Toms River down to Forked River has snappers hammering silversides in the last hour of daylight. That's a genuinely good sign. Those fish grow fast, and by Labor Day some of them are pushing cocktail-blue size. If you've got a kid with a bamboo pole and a piece of bloody bunker on a small hook, that's your entertainment for the next month, and it's also a preview of the adult bluefish that'll be working through the inlet as September comes on.

Weakfish have thinned out from where they were back in May at the sedges — that bite's mostly a memory for this season, though I had a report of a couple of legal fish taken at dusk on the outgoing near the sedge banks off Tices Shoal, worked with a small swimming plug fished slow. Don't plan a trip around it, but if you're out there for something else and the light's going gold, it's worth a couple of casts.

Blowfish, on the other hand, are exactly where they should be — thick in the shallow, warm flats, especially around Tices Shoal and the skinny water off Cedar Creek. Small hooks, clam strips or squid, snelled two-hook rigs fished right on bottom in 3 to 6 feet. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about the most reliable thing going in the bay right now, and it's a great way to keep a kid or a first-timer bent over a rod all afternoon. Blue claw crabbing has been excellent in that same warm shallow water too — chicken necks on a hand line off any dock along the western shore will keep a pot full.

Striped bass in the bay proper have been scarce, and I'll be honest about that rather than dress it up. This time of year the resident fish push toward the inlet and the ocean side looking for cooler, moving water, and what I'm hearing from up the coast — Sound, Buzzards Bay, even up toward the Cape — is a genuine peanut-bunker-driven blitz pattern building early, which tells me the fall staging is starting to think about happening. It hasn't shown up here yet in any real way, but Barnegat Inlet on the last two hours of the incoming, right around the rocks and the Coast Guard station, is where I'd throw bucktails at dusk if I wanted a shot at a bass this week. Don't expect a blitz. Expect maybe one good fish if the tide and the light line up.

Looking ahead, we're a couple days off the new moon, and the tidal flow's been building nicely into it — that's exactly the kind of push that sharpens the bite at current-driven structure like Double Creek and the Oyster Creek mouth. I'd expect the fluke bite to hold steady to slightly improving through the coming week as that flow keeps concentrating bait in the bends, and I'd keep an eye on the inlet for the first real signs of bunker schools pushing through, because when they show, the blues and maybe a few bass won't be far behind.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Turns Keyport Flats and Flynn's Knoll Into a Feeding Lane
reports.subhead: A 12-pound-class doormat out of the back bays and bass stacking on bait tell you the same thing: the current lines are where you want to be this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning before I even hit the ramp: skip the open bay, go straight to the current edges. Flynn's Knoll, the Reach channel drop-off, the rip line off the Hook — anywhere the tide has to squeeze past structure. That's the program right now, and it's paying off.

We flagged this last week — said the building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly where it turned. Two days past the new moon and the swings are still stout, which means bait gets pushed hard against the edges instead of drifting loose through open water. Peanut bunker are stacking thick off Keyport and Union Beach, right up on the flats in three to six feet at first light, and every predator in the bay knows it.

Stripers are the headline. Not a blitz every day — I want to be straight with you, some mornings it's dead calm and you have to hunt — but when the bunker balls get pinned against the drop at Flynn's Knoll on the incoming, it lights up in patches. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or bunker-colored, worked with a slow lift-drop right off the edge where the flat falls into the channel, are drawing hits from schoolies up through mid-20-inch fish. A few bigger resident bass — mid-30s — have shown mixed in with what looks like an early trickle of fish staging ahead of the fall push south. That's not the full run yet, don't get it twisted, but the size class variety in the same drift tells you something's stirring early.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait, same spots, same tide stage. If you want nonstop action for an hour, run to where the bunker are getting pushed up against the rip at the Hook on the last two hours of the incoming — poppers or diamond jigs, wire leader unless you enjoy retying. Snapper blues are thick as fleas in the Navesink and Shrewsbury right now too. If you've got a kid who wants bent-rod action off a dock, small Kastmasters or spearing under a bobber in either river will keep them busy all afternoon.

Fluke is where I want to spend the rest of this report, because the story coming out of the back bays this month is real. A 12.3-pound doormat got weighed in at Bayonne, and fish that size don't show up as loners — there's usually a class of big females staging in the same general program before they slide out toward deeper water in September. I've been working the channel edges along the Reach and the drop-off south of the Flats on the tail end of the outgoing, into the turn, in 25 to 35 feet. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow, tipped with a strip of squid if the current's really moving. The ratio isn't fast — you're grinding through a lot of shorts to find the keeper — but the size potential is legit right now, and every serious fluke guy I've talked to at the dock this week has a fish in the high 20s or low 30s of inches to show for the effort. Romer Shoal's edges have also produced when the tide's running clean.

Porgies remain the reliable bread-and-butter play if you just want a bucket of fish for the table. The rubble and reef structure inside the bay — Romer Shoal's flanks, the humps off Keansburg — are holding solid numbers on bottom rigs with clam or squid strips. Nothing glamorous, but it's steady, and it's a good option on days the wind kills the current bite up top.

Conditions have been generally cooperative — warm, typical August water, current running strong with the fresh moon swings, and enough bait in the system to keep fish honest. Wind's been the wildcard some afternoons, kicking up a chop on the open bay that pushes me into the lee of the Hook or up into the rivers where it's protected.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the current-structure program through this week. The tides are still building off that new moon push, which should keep bait concentrated at the Knoll, the Reach, and the rip through the weekend. If the bass staging pattern I'm seeing continues to thicken — more mixed size classes showing in the same drifts — that's your early tell that the fall run conversation starts sooner rather than later this year. I wouldn't bet the house on a full-blown blitz just yet, but if you've got a weekday morning free, I'd fish the last two hours of the incoming at Flynn's Knoll first, then slide to the Reach channel edges for fluke once the tide turns. Have a backup spot in the rivers if the wind gets up — the Navesink's snapper blues never let you down when the open bay turns ugly.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: Bluefish Bail Out a Slow Bass Bite
reports.subhead: Stripers are ghosts at the Rips this week, but building tide off the new moon is turning on bluefish and fluke where it counts.
reports.body_markdown:
I'll give the Rips a C this week, and that's being generous. Bass are around, but they're not stacked up and they're not stupid. If you fished the Rips proper — the stretch running off Cape May Point out toward the tip where the ocean current collides with the outgoing bay water — you had to work for anything with stripes on it. August does this. The water's warm, the bait's scattered thin instead of balled up tight, and the bass that are here are more interested in holding deep and sulking than chasing anything on the surface. That's not me making excuses. That's just what mid-August looks like on this piece of water most years, and this year's no different.

What's saved the week has been bluefish, and they've saved it hard. Chopper blues, three to six pounds, have been riding the same bunker pods that are pushing bass activity up the coast from here to Rhode Island — we're just not getting the blitz version of it that they're seeing off Narragansett and Buzzards. What we're getting is a solid, dependable bite on the ebb, best in that first two hours when the tide starts pulling hard and the rip lines actually form up. Metal — Deadly Dick or a 2-ounce Hopkins — worked fast through the froth has been money, and if you want to slow down and work the edges, bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig sitting just off bottom in 30 to 40 feet has been picking off the bigger singles that don't want to chase. If you're bass hunting and getting blues instead, don't fight it. Keep a rod rigged for both and let the day tell you which one's biting.

We flagged this last week — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what happened. The two days since the new moon have brought noticeably harder current through the Rips and around Cape May Point, and that extra push is what's been concentrating the bait and giving the bluefish something to work with. It's also what's kept the fluke bite alive over at Hereford Inlet, which honestly has been the more consistent story this week if you're after something for the cooler.

Hereford's fluke bite has been fair to good on the channel drop-offs along the inlet, particularly where the deeper cuts fall off the sand flats near the jetty. The bay's run warm this summer, pushing into the mid-70s in the shallows, and that's shoved a lot of the bait — and the weakfish and croaker that were feeding on it — off the flats and into the cooler, current-scrubbed channel edges. Best fluke window has been the last two hours of the ebb, when that warm flat water empties out and drags bait with it right into the strike zone. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 12 to 18 feet, have out-produced bare bucktails two to one. Nothing giant — most fish 16 to 19 inches — but a few keepers mixed in most trips, which for mid-August is a fine trade.

Across in the Bay, the black drum run is long buttoned up — that's a May story and everybody who's called the shack this week asking about drum gets the same answer, come back in spring. What's left over there is a scattered weakfish bite, mostly at night or first light, working the deeper channel edges off Fortescue and down toward Brandywine Shoal. Same story as Hereford — the warm surface water has pushed the tide-sensitive fish down into 20 to 25 feet where the current keeps things moving and the water stays a few degrees cooler. Bucktails tipped with Fishbites or a chunk of squid, bounced slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, has been the play for the weakfish that are there. It's not a bite you build a whole trip around right now, but if you're already out drifting for something else, drop one down.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the Rips to turn into a bass blitz overnight — that's not really our pattern down here in August anyway, the way it can be further up the coast. What I do expect is the tide push to stay strong through the rest of this week as we build off the new moon, which should keep the bluefish honest and keep that fluke window at Hereford productive on the ebb. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at the Rips at first light working the early ebb with metal for blues, then sliding over to Hereford by mid-morning to hit that channel edge on the tail of the tide. Two different bites, two different baits, but both riding the same current that's finally doing some work for us again.

reports.headline: Barnegat Doormats on the Turn — Stripers Staging Offshore Ahead of the Run
reports.subhead: Trophy fluke are showing in the inlet current while early bass sign offshore hints the fall push is starting to load up.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the drone over the Holgate spit Monday morning before the wind came up, and the south end cut has moved again — not dramatically, but enough that the deep slough that's been running tight to the dune line for the past month has pushed about forty yards further offshore. That outer bar took a beating from the three-to-four foot swell we've had rolling through on a five-second period, and it's reshaping the whole south end. If you fished that inside trough last week and got nothing, don't blame the fish — the structure isn't where it was. I'd walk it at low light on the next low tide and re-map it before you commit a whole tide to it.

The real story this week isn't the surf, though — it's Barnegat Inlet. Fluke fishing through the inlet has stepped up in a real way, and I mean doormat-class fish mixed into the average catch, not just talk. Guys working the channel edges off the north side rocks and along the deeper cuts by the Coast Guard station are connecting on the moving tide — both stages, but the last two hours of the ebb into the bottom of the tide has been the window. Four- to six-inch Gulp swimming mullet in white or pink shad on three-quarter to one-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom where the current breaks over the humps, is the ticket. This mirrors what's been happening up in Raritan Bay all month — a genuine trophy fluke trend running down the Jersey coast, and a 12-plus pound doormat weighed at a shop up that way tells you the size class moving through right now is real. I've had two separate reports of fish over eight pounds out of the inlet in the last five days, which for mid-August is well above what we usually see this late in the season.

Back in the bay, the blowfish bite remains about as easy as fishing gets around here right now. Anchor up on the flats off Ship Bottom or in the deeper holes around Beach Haven, drop a piece of clam on a small hook under a sinker, and you'll have a bucket full inside an hour. It's not glamorous but it's a great way to get a kid or a first-timer hooked, and there's no shortage of them right now in Great Bay and up toward the Mullica flats.

Snapper blues have shown up thick in the back bay creeks — Graveling Point, the mouth of the Mullica, the marsh edges around Great Bay — and that's usually the tell that the adult bluefish class is close behind. I'm already seeing bigger blues mixed in on the ocean side, feeding on peanut bunker pushing along the beach on the outgoing. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks — worked fast through the wash at Holgate and the Ship Bottom jetties has been drawing strikes in the early morning hours before the sun gets high.

Now the piece I've been waiting on: striped bass. We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. I'm getting early sign of bass staging offshore of the island, holding on bait schools well outside the surf line, which is textbook pre-migration behavior. They're not in tight yet, and I wouldn't call it a bite you can plan a trip around from the beach, but boats working just outside Barnegat Light and off the north end are marking fish sitting under peanut bunker pods. This is exactly the kind of staging pattern that tends to build through the back half of August before it pushes bass tight to the beach for the fall run. If you're patient and willing to put in some scouting time, I'd be running the LRF or a slow-trolled bunker spoon outside the surf zone right now rather than pounding the beach — that's where the fish actually are.

Kingfish are still around on the ocean side sand — Beach Haven and the stretch south of Ship Bottom have been giving up a few on bloodworm or FishBites on a high-low rig fished tight to the wash, best on the incoming as the water warms through midday. Weakfish have gone quiet in the Mullica system, which tracks with the warmer water this time of year — I'd expect that bite to reawaken some in September as things cool.

Looking ahead: if this swell settles down by the weekend like the forecast suggests, I'd hit the reshaped Holgate cut on the dropping tide with a darter or a bucktail worked slow through that new trough — first crack at structure nobody's fished yet is worth the walk. The inlet fluke should keep producing as long as the tide keeps moving current over those channel humps, and I'd keep half an eye on the water outside the beach for signs those staging bass start tightening up. If the bait keeps pushing tight to the beach the way it has the last few days, don't be surprised if the first real surf blitz of the fall shows up sooner than the calendar says it should.

reports.headline: Rocky Point blows up: peanut bunker bring bass and blues topside on the new moon push
reports.subhead: The tide finally built like we said it would, and now there's white water off every point from Conimicut to Prudence.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning watching a guy load his cooler with peanut bunker off a cast net, and he looks up at me and says, "Vinny, there's fish crashing this stuff all the way out past Rocky Point." I didn't need him to tell me twice. I've been chasing peanut schools around this bay for twenty years and when the boys on the pier start talking about bait balls getting hammered in open water, you drop what you're doing.

We called this one. Said two weeks back that the building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and here we are — new moon was the 12th, and by the 13th the whole upper bay with peanut bunker getting pushed against the current lines off Nyatt Point and Conimicut. This isn't the herring run, that's long gone, we're way past Buckeye Brook season now. This is pure August peanut bunker, tight little schools stacking up in the rips, and stripers are using the bigger tide swings off this new moon to pin them against structure and just annihilate them.

Conimicut Light on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most reliable window. The current rips hard around that light on a big tide, and the bunker get funneled right into it. I've been throwing a 5-inch white Storm Shad or a bone-colored Super Strike Little Neck popper right into the edge of the boil and letting it sit for a second before I start working it — the fish are eating so aggressive right now that a slow twitch is plenty. Slot fish, mostly 26 to 32 inches, with the occasional overslot mixed in that'll make your reel scream. Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait, and they don't discriminate — I lost two bucktails to blues in one morning because I got lazy about checking my leader. Run 40-pound fluorocarbon minimum if you're throwing anything with a hook near those schools, because the blues are thick and hungry right now, snappers included if you're fishing close to the mouths of the coves.

Rocky Point itself has been the money spot for a shore guy with no boat. That rocky point structure holds current no matter what the tide's doing, and when the bunker get pushed up against it on an incoming tide, you get these visible boils right off the breakwater. I watched three guys hook up simultaneously Wednesday evening throwing everything from bucktails to topwater — didn't matter what was on the end of the line, the fish were eating anything that moved through the melee. That kind of chaos doesn't happen often mid-August, but the bait's been so dense this year the bass are staging early, probably getting a jump on the fall run before they'd normally show this kind of aggression.

Prudence Island's west side has been holding fish too, particularly around the ledges off the northern tip where the current squeezes between the island and the mainland. That's deeper water, 15 to 20 feet, and I've been dropping bucktails tipped with a chunk of bunker down into the seam on the last hour of the flood. Slower fishing than the blitzes up top, but more consistent — you're not relying on visible surface activity, you're just working the structure and letting the tide do the work.

Fluke are a secondary story right now but they're not absent. I've had a few decent ones, 18 to 20 inches, drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and pink off the flats south of Nyatt Point in about 12 to 15 feet, moving water on the outgoing. Nothing like the doormat numbers you're hearing about from the Jersey backbays, but there's enough fluke pushing into the bay behind the warmer water to make a drift worthwhile if the blitz isn't happening.

Scup fishing has been steady and honestly underappreciated with all this bass noise. The ledges off Rocky Point and the rockpiles around Nyatt continue to produce, small pieces of squid or sandworm on a high-low rig, bottom fished in 10 to 20 feet on either side of the tide change. Not glamorous, but it's meat in the cooler when the blitz fish won't cooperate on a particular tide. Black sea bass have shown up sporadically on the deeper humps out toward Prudence, nothing you'd plan a trip around specifically but worth a few drops if you're already out there. Weakfish have been quiet — I've heard of one or two caught incidentally in the upper bay on bucktails meant for bass, but I wouldn't target them specifically right now.

Looking ahead, this peanut bunker pattern should hold as long as the bait stays dense, and with the tides still building off this new moon, I don't see a reason for it to fall apart in the next several days. If the wind stays manageable, I'd be at Conimicut or Rocky Point on that last two hours of ebb, working the edges where the current squeezes the bait. If it gets sloppy topside, drop down to bucktails and fish the structure instead of chasing the surface show. Either way, keep your leader heavy — the blues aren't going anywhere, and neither is the aggression.

reports.headline: Why are the bluefish only biting before 7 a.m.? Read the bunker, not the clock
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker pinned to the surf line are running the whole show this week — from Brigantine blues to Absecon fluke to the first real weakfish of the summer.
reports.body_markdown:
I get some version of this question every August, usually from a reader standing on the Ocean City boardwalk at nine in the morning wondering why the blues that tore up the wash at six have vanished. The answer is always the same lesson: bluefish don't punch a clock, bait does. Peanut bunker have been pinned tight to the beachfront from Brigantine down through Sea Isle City, and those pods move with light and water temperature, not convenience. First light and the last hour of the outgoing tide is when the bunker get squeezed against the bar, and that's when the blues show themselves. By mid-morning the sun pushes the bait off the bar into deeper, cooler water, and the blitz you saw at sunrise just melts away. If you want consistency, you fish the tide, not the wristwatch.
