We flagged this pattern last week — said to watch for surface blitzes on scattered peanut schools in the early window — and that's exactly what's playing out along this stretch of beach. Absecon Inlet's north jetty and the Brigantine surf have both given up solid runs of cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound class on white bucktails and small Got-Cha plugs worked fast through the wash. If you're metal-fishing, don't overthink the retrieve — these fish are eating on reaction, and a jerky, erratic presentation outproduces a slow swim every time right now.

Striped bass are riding the same bait wave, though down here they're more of a supporting character than the headline they've become up in the Sound and Buzzards Bay. We're seeing them stage on the same peanut bunker pushes, particularly around the Great Egg Inlet rips and the deeper water off the Ocean City Music Pier, feeding hard on the last two hours of the outgoing when current stacks bait against the pilings. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped to the bottom and hopped slow through the current seam, have been drawing slot fish in the 26 to 30-inch range. It's not a blitz down here — it's a tide-window bite, twenty, thirty minutes of good activity around the turn, and then it shuts off until the next cycle. The new moon on the 12th put some extra push behind these tides, and that stronger flow has sharpened the bite exactly the way I expected it would — more current means more bait gets funneled into a tighter lane, and the bass know it.

Fluke remain the bread-and-butter story in the back bays, and the program hasn't changed much from what I've been teaching all summer. The sod banks off Absecon and the channel edges inside Great Egg continue to hold the better grade of keeper, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when bait gets pulled off the marsh and funneled through the deeper guts. I'm still running 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in white or pink shad, paired with a 1/2 to 3/4-ounce bucktail depending on how hard the water's moving, drifted slow along the drop from 8 feet down to 14. Townsends Inlet and the Stone Harbor side channels have also been kicking out keepers in that 18 to 20-inch range, with the occasional better fish mixed in — nothing like the 12-pound doormat that got weighed up in North Jersey this week, but a 5 or 6-pounder off the Sea Isle City bridge structure isn't out of the question if you're covering ground and staying on fresh bait.

Weakfish have started showing again in modest numbers, mostly incidental catches on the same fluke drifts along the channel edges in Absecon and Great Egg — nothing you'd plan a trip around yet, but worth noting because a few years back this time of season was when the pattern started to build. If you connect with one, it's usually on the same Gulp/bucktail combo, just a little higher in the water column than where the fluke are holding.

Surf fishing for kingfish has been a quiet, honest bite in the cooler morning hours before the sun gets up over the dunes — bloodworm and Fishbites on a high-low rig, fished right in the first trough off Ocean City and Sea Isle City beaches, has been steady enough to fill a bucket if you're patient and willing to be out there by 6 a.m. It's not exciting fishing, but it's reliable, and on a week where the bigger bite windows are short and tide-dependent, reliable counts for something.

Looking ahead, I don't expect this pattern to shift much through the weekend. The bait is staying pinned to the beach on the current tide cycle, and as long as that holds, the bluefish and striper windows should stay tight but productive around first light and the outgoing turn. If the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't stir things up too much, I'd put my time on the Great Egg rips for stripers on the last two hours of the outgoing, and the Absecon sod banks for fluke on that same water. Watch the moon phase easing off the new-moon push over the next week — as the tidal range narrows back down, expect these bite windows to stretch out a little longer, which is good news for anyone who can only get out for a couple hours at a time.

reports.headline: Bunker Balled Up Off Mattituck, and the Blues Finally Came Back to Eat Them
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker packed the inlet mouths all week, and for the first time since June the bluefish showed up to work them properly.
reports.body_markdown:
Ray Tuthill's been running charter out of Mattituck longer than I've had gray in this beard, and Tuesday morning he came by the bait shop with a look on him — not excited exactly, more like a man who'd just watched something he half-expected finally show up. Said he had bunker balled up so thick off the inlet mouth his depth finder looked like a bowl of stew. Told him that's no surprise to me. I've been watching the gulls work that same stretch for the better part of two weeks, and a gull tells the truth before the tackle shop chatter ever does.

We flagged this a week back — said the blues reappearing on the deep Western Sound reefs would push east along the North Fork as bait redistributed with the new moon tide, and that's exactly what's happened. The new moon came through on the 12th, tide's been building hard behind it, and that flow has done what it always does this time of year — pinned the peanut bunker tight against the beach from Mattituck clear out past Rocky Point. Where the bunker goes, the bass and blues follow, and this week they both showed up to the party.

Striper fishing off Horton Point has been the most honest work on my stretch. Guys working the rip on the last two hours of the ebb are doing well with bunker spoons and 1 to 2-ounce bucktails in white or chartreuse, bounced along bottom where the current stacks up against the rocks. Nothing enormous — most of what's coming over the rail is 24 to 30 inches, a mix of keepers and fish you're kissing goodbye — but it's steady, and on a slow retrieve through the seam you're getting bit more often than not on the right tide stage. Live-lining a snagged peanut bunker off a fish-finder rig has worked just as well for the guys who'd rather sit than cast, especially right at the Mattituck Inlet mouth where the bait funnels tight on the outgoing.

The bluefish are the real story of the week, though, and it's a welcome one. They'd been thin on this end of the Sound all July, but they've come back in numbers strong enough to matter, working the same bunker schools as the bass, sometimes right on top. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, anything that throws a wake — have been getting hit hard early and late, especially where you can see the bait getting nervous on the surface off Rocky Point. Snapper blues are thick in the coves too, which tells you the adult class fish coming through now are just the leading edge. Expect more of them as the month wears on.

Porgies remain the quiet, dependable worker on this beat — no drama, no blitzes, just steady action on the reefs and rockpiles off Orient and out toward the Plum Gut approach. Sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig in 15 to 25 feet is still doing the job. Nothing's changed there in weeks and I don't expect it to.

Blackfish season's still a ways off, but I've had three different fellows stop me at the launch this week asking about green crab supply and tying up double-hook Asian crab rigs, scouting the same rockpiles they'll fish come October. That's normal for mid-August — a man likes to know where his rocks are before the water cools and the tautog move onto them. Nothing to report yet but the intent, which is its own kind of sign.

Fluke have been modest but not absent — a few keepers coming off the deeper water outside Mattituck Inlet on white Gulp swimming mullets and small bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the incoming. Nothing to build a trip around, but worth a drift if you're already out there working bass water. Weakfish, I'll be honest with you, have been scarce on my end this week. A few reports of small ones taken incidentally on bucktails meant for something else, but nobody's targeting them with any confidence right now, and I wouldn't either.

The water's holding warm enough to keep this pattern rolling — readings from Kings Point down around 71 on the west end of the Sound, cooling off toward the high 60s as you work east toward New London, which is about what I'd expect for mid-August and puts my stretch squarely in the productive middle of that gradient. That kind of spread usually means bait keeps moving through on the tide rather than settling in one place, which is exactly what we've seen.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the last two hours of the ebb at Horton Point and the inlet mouths through this weekend — the tidal flow off this new moon should keep sharpening as it builds toward the next few days, and that's when the bass and blues tend to commit hardest to the rips. Keep an eye on the water out toward Plum Gut, too. There's warm water and bait moving through that corridor right now, and if the pattern holds the way it's been trending region-wide, this is about the time of year the first false albacore or bonito starts showing up in that current. Nobody's seen one on my end yet. But I've got a rod rigged for it just the same.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Packed Into the Boulders — Stripers Tight to the Rocks, Albies Still No-Shows
reports.subhead: The bait's pinned against the granite from Ram Island to Wamphassuc, the bass know it, and the first albie of the season still hasn't punched a card in Fishers Island Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
First light off Ram Island this week and the water over the boulder field was nervous — not boiling, just twitchy, the way it gets when peanut bunker are trying to disappear into rock they can't actually disappear into. I cut the engine forty yards out and poled the rest, the way my grandfather used to say you fish structure you can't afford to meet at speed. Sure enough, tucked into the pockets between the granite heads in six, seven feet of water, there were bass working the edges — not blitzing, just picking, the kind of quiet predation that tells you they've been there a while and aren't going anywhere.

That's been the story all week in the boulder country — Ram Island, Wamphassuc Point, the rock piles off Esker Point, out toward the edge of the Sound by North Dumpling. Peanut bunker and silversides have pushed hard against the structure, and the stripers are working them on the push of the tide, not the middle of it. I've had my best fly action on the last two hours of the incoming, when the current starts stacking bait against the up-current face of the rocks and the bass stop chasing and start ambushing. A 3-inch olive-over-white Clouser, weighted eyes, dead-drifted and then stripped short and fast right off a boulder edge, has been drawing the most committed takes. Light tackle guys are doing the same job with small white swim shads and soft-plastic peanut imitations worked slow over the same six-to-ten-foot water. Nothing enormous — mostly 22 to 28 inches, a scattering of overslot fish mixed in for those willing to grind it out through the slower stretches of tide.

Water's sitting in the upper 60s to low 70s through the central and eastern part of the Sound right now, warm enough that the bass aren't in any hurry, and that's part of why this bite has stayed steady rather than exploding — it's a slow, structure-anchored pattern, not a moving blitz. If you're used to blind-casting open water, this isn't that game. You need to read the rock, find where the current bends around a boulder and drops speed, and put the fly or the plug right in that seam. Miss the seam by six feet and you're fishing empty water in the middle of a productive tide.

Porgy fishing has been the quiet workhorse of the summer and it hasn't let up. Ram Island, the rock structure off Wicopesset, and the flats around North and South Dumpling are stacked with scup right now, and it's about as close to a sure thing as this fishery offers — sandworms or skimmer clam on a simple two-hook bottom rig, 15 to 25 feet of water, and you're bending rods. Black sea bass have been riding shotgun on the same structure, especially out toward the deeper rock closer to the Race, with squid strips producing keeper-class fish in the 30-to-40-foot range. Neither fishery is glamorous, but both have been dependable enough that I've sent more than a few slow-morning striper trips over to the porgy grounds just to save the day.

Fluke have been the tougher sell. Little Narragansett Bay's sand flats are holding some fish, but it's a grind — light bucktails tipped with Gulp in the 4-inch white or pink shad, drifted slow on the last of the outgoing, and you might scratch out two or three keepers over a full tide. I wouldn't build a trip around it right now. If someone in the boat wants fluke, fine, but I'm not planning mornings around that bite the way I am around the rocks.

Now — the question everyone's been asking me at the dock. No, I haven't seen an albie or a bonito yet, and nobody I trust has either, not here, not at Watch Hill Reef, not out toward Wicopesset Passage. We flagged the setup a week back — new moon on the 12th, building current, warm bait-rich water — and that part's held up exactly as expected. The tidal flow through the passages has been sharpening noticeably the last two days as the moon's pull builds, and there's real bait density out along the reef edges. A hammerhead sighting down in Rhode Island this week is the kind of signal that tells you the warm, forage-heavy water those fish like is sitting right off our doorstep. But the albies themselves haven't shown their hand in this corridor yet, and I'm not going to tell you they have.

If I had to bet, I'd put my money on the reef edges at Watch Hill and the rip lines off the east end of Fishers Island being the first place we hear about a hookup, likely within the coming week if this current keeps building the way it has. Until then, I'd keep the fly rod rigged for both jobs — small profile bunker flies for the bass in the boulders, and a bit of epoxy minnow pattern coiled up in the bag in case something with a sickle tail finally shows up on the reef. Worth checking those spots on your way out to the rock piles rather than making a special trip for a fish that hasn't arrived yet.

reports.headline: Cockenoe's Last Ebb: Porgies Stack Up While Bunker Blitzes Hit the Reefs
reports.subhead: With tog season still closed, I'm playing the last two hours of the ebb on Cockenoe and letting the bunker schools do the rest of the work.
reports.body_markdown:
Every week this time of year I have to make the same call: fish the reef for what's legal and biting, or waste a tide chasing what I wish was biting. Blackfish season's still closed here through the end of the month, so the tog gear stays in the garage. That decision made itself. The one that took more thought was which piece of structure to work off the last of the ebb — Cockenoe Reef, or run out to Penfield and fight the Fairfield boat traffic for a shot at sea bass. I picked Cockenoe, and I'd pick it again.

Here's the read. Kings Point is sitting around 71 degrees, New London's holding closer to 69 — that west-to-east gradient means the western end of the Sound is carrying more warmth and, more importantly, more bait than the water off New Haven. Everything from Greenwich Point through the Norwalk Islands to Sheffield has been thick with peanut bunker pushed tight to shore, and that's dragging schoolie bass and a good class of bluefish right up onto the structure with them. We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow off the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what showed up. The extra push on the ebb is stacking bait against the reef edges instead of letting it drift off into open water, and every predator in the western Sound knows it.

Cockenoe on the last two hours of the ebb into the first half hour of the new flood has been the most consistent window of the week. I'm anchoring on the outer bar in 15 to 20 feet, working sandworms and green crab on a standard high-low rig, and the porgies have been steady — not a blitz, but a bend-the-rod-every-drop kind of steady, with a mix of decent-sized scup and the occasional short-lived sea robin reminder that you're fishing structure, not sand. Sheffield Island's rockpiles on the north side are producing the same pattern in slightly shallower water, 12 to 15 feet, same rig, same tide window. If you're getting there after 9 a.m. on a Saturday, you're fighting for swing room with three other boats, so I've been sliding my start time up an hour and working the tide before the fleet shows.

The bluefish and schoolie bass story is happening in the guts between the Norwalk Islands and along the flats off Greenwich Point, and it's tide-dependent in a different way. As the ebb pulls bait out of the coves and marsh creeks, it funnels peanut bunker through the cuts, and that's where the blues have been cutting through in short, violent windows — sometimes ten minutes of surface chop and then it's over. I've had the best luck throwing 3/4-ounce chrome or bunker-pattern SP Minnows into the edges of those pushes, and bucktails in white or chartreuse, half-ounce, worked slow along bottom, have picked up schoolies in the same water when the surface action goes quiet. It's not the kind of bite you can plan a whole trip around — you need to be on the water and watching for the birds and the nervous water, then get there fast before it shuts down.

Penfield Reef and the Cows have been my play for sea bass, and that trend has been building gradually rather than exploding, which is honestly the more trustworthy kind of improvement. I'm working 25 to 35 feet of water on the ebb, squid strips and Gulp on bucktail jigs bounced tight to the rock piles, and the ratio of keepers to shorts has been ticking up week over week. It's not a fast bite — you're putting in time for a handful of quality fish — but it's real, and it should keep firming through the rest of August as that structure holds bait later into the season.

Fluke have been the quiet part of the week out here. A few keepers coming off the sandy stretches between Cockenoe and the Norwalk Islands on white Gulp swimming mullets and bucktail combos, but nothing like what the guys are seeing out toward Nantucket Sound right now. If fluke is your priority this week, I wouldn't build a trip around western Sound structure — treat it as a bonus while you're porgy fishing, not the target.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend unless the wind shifts hard out of the southwest and muddies up the shallow flats. The tide's still building off the new moon, which should keep sharpening the bite at current-heavy spots like Cockenoe's outer bar and the Penfield rockpiles. My plan is to keep working the early ebb before the weekend fleet arrives, and staying flexible enough to run to wherever the bunker schools push next — because on this stretch of the Gold Coast, the bait tells you where to fish, and this week it's been telling me to stay west.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Seam on the New-Moon Flood: Bass Holding Tight, Blues Chasing Peanuts
reports.subhead: Post-new-moon current has sharpened the rip at the mouth, and both stripers and bluefish are stacking on it.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the seawall at Fort Trumbull Tuesday evening and watched the rip line do something it hadn't done in about three weeks — hold its shape. Through most of late July that seam off the point was mushy, current pushing weak and diffuse, the kind of water that makes you squint and wonder if the tide's even moving. This week it's a clean, defined edge, current stacking against the old fort's granite base and peeling off into a visible crease you could set a watch to. That's the new moon doing its work. We flagged this last week — said the building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's showing at the mouth right now.

Water's sitting around 69.4 degrees down at the harbor mouth, which is on the cooler side for mid-August in this river, and I think that's part of why the fish are staying put instead of pushing further up toward the Bridge or holding shallow. Cooler water plus a stronger current seam equals fish that don't have to work as hard to eat — they just sit in the seam and let the bait come to them. Striped bass have been doing exactly that off Fort Trumbull on the last two hours of the ebb, holding in 15 to 20 feet right where the current breaks off the point. I've had the best luck there with bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, just enough weight to hold bottom in that push, and I'm not skimping on chunk size — half a bunker on a 6/0 circle hook has been outproducing smaller cuts. A few guys working eels after dark off the same stretch have connected too, though that bite's been more about timing than volume — you want to be there right as the tide turns, not an hour into it.

The bigger story this week, and one that matches what's happening from the Sound on down through Narragansett, is bait. Peanut bunker have flooded into the lower river and they're thick off Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach, rolling in tight pods right along the wash. Snapper blues have been all over them in the shallows — you can walk the beach at low light and see the surface nervous with them. That's produced some fun light-tackle action on small Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters for anyone who wants an easy afternoon with the kids, but it's also pulled adult bluefish up into the harbor to feed on the same bait, and those have been the better story. I had a solid half hour off the Pleasure Beach jetty Thursday morning working a white bucktail through a bunker school and connecting on blues in the 4 to 6 pound class, blitzing right on top for a stretch before it shut off as quick as it started. That's the pattern right now — short, violent windows tied directly to where the bait gets pushed by current, not sustained action you can count on lasting.

Porgies remain the steady, dependable piece of the puzzle. The riprap around the Gold Star Bridge pilings has been holding good numbers in 20 to 25 feet, and a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clam has been enough to keep a rod bent through most of a tide change. Nothing flashy, no size to write home about, but if you want fish in the cooler without chasing a blitz, that's the spot. Blackfish season's open here through the end of the month, and I've heard of a few decent tog coming off the rock piles near Fort Trumbull and the Pleasure Beach jetty on green crab, though it's early yet for that bite to really turn on — that's more of a September and October story once the water starts to slide the other direction.

What I haven't seen — and I want to be straight about this — is any sign of the bigger blitz activity that's apparently lighting up water from Narragansett Bay up through Buzzards Bay and into Cape Cod Bay right now. That's a bunker-driven push tied to early staging ahead of the fall run, and it's a real phenomenon worth watching, but the Thames hasn't gotten that memo yet. What we've got here is a tighter, more localized version of the same story — smaller bait pods, shorter feeding windows, fish that reward you for being in the right seam at the right tide stage rather than fish that are just everywhere.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working that Fort Trumbull rip on the ebb as long as this current pattern holds — the seam's only going to get more defined as we build toward the first quarter moon later this week, and that usually means a sharper, more predictable bite window rather than a bigger one. If the peanut bunker keep pushing into the harbor mouth the way they have been, I'd expect the bluefish blitzes off Pleasure Beach and Ocean Beach to keep popping in short bursts through the week, especially on the last of the outgoing when bait gets flushed out past the beach. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around chasing that blitz, though — treat it as a bonus if you're already out there working bass or porgies, and keep an eye on the gulls. They'll tell you where the bait's getting pushed before you ever see it yourself.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Riding Bunker Schools Into Twotree — Porgies Steady, Albie Watch Heats Up
reports.subhead: New moon current finally kicked the bass bite loose at the rips, but the fluke and the first false albacore are still make-you-wait propositions.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Captain Ray at the Niantic dock Tuesday morning loading coolers, and he didn't even let me get the question out before he said it — "Danny, the bunker are everywhere in the bay right now, and the bass finally found them." That's been the talk up and down the fleet all week. The peanut bunker showed up thick in Niantic Bay and pushed right up into the river mouth, and where there's bait like that stacked tight, the stripers don't stay quiet for long.

We flagged this last week — said the building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what happened. Twotree Island Channel has been the money spot on the last two hours of the outgoing, with schoolie-to-mid-30s bass working the bait against the current seam. Guys are doing well on 5-inch white Gulp swimming mullets rigged on half-ounce bucktails, cast up-current and swung through the seam so it swims naturally instead of dragging. A few of the drift boat regulars have also been dropping bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs right off the edge of the channel where it drops to 15-18 feet, and that's been picking off the bigger fish that are hanging back off the schoolies.

Hole-in-the-Wall has been more of a dawn-and-dusk deal — the current rips through there hard on a big tide and the bass use it to ambush bait getting funneled through. If you can time a trip for first light on the last of the incoming, that's when it's been happening. Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bunker pattern. Adult blues to maybe 4-5 pounds have been mixing in with the bass schools out toward Black Point, and inside the Niantic River the snapper blues are thick — good news for anybody trying to get a kid hooked on this sport, because those little guys will hit anything shiny on a light spinning rod.

Porgy fishing has been the steady, reliable story all week, no surprises, no excuses needed. Black Point and McCook Point rockpiles are still holding good numbers in that 20-25 foot range, and the party boats out of Niantic are putting anywhere from decent to real good bags together on sandworms and squid strips fished tight to bottom with a two-hook bottom rig. That bite doesn't care much about the tide stage — it's been productive on both the push and the drop, which makes it the easy call when the wind's blowing and you don't want to fight current for stripers.

Sea bass are doing what they do this time of year — improving gradually rather than exploding, which is honestly the pattern I'd expect heading toward fall. Guys scouting the deeper structure off Black Point and out toward the reef pieces are finding keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of shorts, so it's worth culling through but not a guaranteed limit trip yet. Squid strips and clam on a high-low rig has been the go-to, dropped right on the rock edges in 25-35 feet.

Fluke I've got to be straight with you — it's been a mixed bag at best in this end of the Sound. New London reading around 69 degrees, cooler than the western Sound, and that's kept the flatfish scattered rather than concentrated. A few boats drifting the sandy stretches off Niantic Bay and out toward the mouth of the river have scratched out keepers on Gulp swimming mullet and bucktail combos, but nobody's filling coolers. If fluke is your main target this week, I'd treat it as a bonus fish while you're really out there for bass or porgy, not the primary mission.

Now here's what's got the dock buzzing beyond the bass — there's real talk of bluefin pushing unusually far into the eastern Sound this month, which if it holds up would be a notable thing for this stretch of water. I haven't had it confirmed on my own beat yet, so I'm not going to oversell it, but it's the kind of development worth watching closely over the next week. Same with albies and bonito — the broader region between Montauk and Buzzards Bay is primed for a first sighting any day now given the warm water and bait density, and if that pattern extends into eastern Long Island Sound the way it sometimes does late in August, Twotree Channel and the rips off Black Point would be the first places I'd expect to hear about it.

Looking ahead, if this bunker pattern holds and the tide keeps building through the week, I'd keep working Twotree on the outgoing and Hole-in-the-Wall at first light — that's been the most consistent one-two punch for bass. Porgy guys, just keep doing what you're doing at Black Point and McCook, that bite isn't going anywhere. And keep half an eye on the horizon for anything busting bait on the surface — if the albies do show up in this corner of the Sound, it won't be subtle.

reports.headline: New Haven Breakwall on the Dying Ebb: Porgies Stacked, Sea Bass Sneaking In
reports.subhead: Bunker schools are pulling stripers and bluefish tight to Charles Island while the rockpiles keep grinding out porgies and blackfish.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, last two hours of the ebb, I'm working the outer arm of the New Haven breakwall with a high-low rig baited with green crab, and I've got a porgy pinning the rod tip down before the sinker even settles. Nine and a half inches, fat as a softball. Two drops later, another one just as good. That's the rhythm right now on the rockpiles — not fast, but honest, and the size class has crept up noticeably from where it sat back in July.

We flagged this last week — said the porgy bite would stay the most dependable structure fishing in this stretch while the bluefish push spread east from the Western Sound reefs, and that's exactly the shape of it right now. Porgies are thick on the breakwalls, the Merwin Point riprap, and the rockier stretches off Sandy Point, biting best on the last two hours of an outgoing tide when the current slows enough for them to leave the bottom clutter and feed in the open. Sandworm and green crab are both producing, though on calmer evenings I'll switch to squid strips because the porgies seem less picky about presentation when the water's laying down flat.

Sea bass are mixed in with the porgies on the same drops, which is the tell that the water's still carrying decent warmth — Kings Point read just under 71 the other day, and while I don't have a hard number off New Haven, the bite behavior says we're running close to that. Sea bass want a little more structure than porgies, so I've been picking through them tighter to the rock edges, dropping skimmer clam on a bucktail teaser above the hook. Nothing giant — mostly a foot to fourteen inches — but steady enough that if you're patient and willing to move a rod length here and there along the wall, you can put together a nice mixed bag without much trouble.

Blackfish are the wildcard. I made a few short drifts off Stratford Shoal and Falkner Island this week with green crabs on knocker rigs, and while I got a couple of teaser bites, the real tog bite hasn't kicked in yet — water's still a touch warm for them to commit the way they will once September cools things down. I wouldn't write the season off, but right now I'd call blackfish a bonus fish, not a target.

The bigger story, and the one every angler on this stretch is talking about at the dock, is the bunker. Peanut schools have been thick off Charles Island and along the bar that runs south off the point, and stripers are working them hard on the tide change — I watched three separate blitzes from the beach at Silver Sands over the weekend, gulls diving, bass busting bunker right up on the sandbar in three to six feet of water. That kind of visible mid-August surface activity is a little unusual for this time of year, and it lines up with what we called last week about the new moon tides sharpening the bite at current-driven structure. The stronger push around the August 12 moon has kept bait moving and concentrated tight to the bar, and the bass have been happy to follow it in.

The pattern that's worked for me: fish the last hour of the flood into the top of the high, casting bunker spoons and white paddle-tail swimbaits right into the edge of the bait balls off Charles Island. If the fish are busting on top, a topwater walk-the-dog bait will draw strikes, but once the blitz goes subsurface — which it usually does within twenty minutes — I switch to a bunker chunk fished on a fish-finder rig just off the sandbar drop where the water goes from three feet to twelve. Most of what's coming over the rail is slot-sized, twenty-four to thirty inches, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in chasing the same bait. Bluefish are riding shotgun in these same schools, and they're not shy — if you're using anything with hooks exposed, expect some leader damage. I've had good luck avoiding the worst of it with a short length of 40-pound fluorocarbon ahead of the lure.

Hammonasset and the Milford Gulf have been quieter by comparison — I made a pass through the Gulf on Thursday morning and found bait but not much committed feeding, which tells me the fish are still concentrating tighter around Charles Island and the harbor mouth rather than spreading evenly across the whole beat. Worth checking again if the bunker schools push east, but for now I'd put my time where the birds are working.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to break in the next week. The tide's still building strong off the new moon, bait's staying put, and the warm push through the Western and Central Sound isn't showing signs of backing off. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't kick up a chop on the bar, I'd fish the flood at Charles Island for bass and bluefish, then finish the day on the breakwall for porgies and sea bass as the tide drains out. That's the one-two I'm planning to run again this weekend, and it's about as reliable a combination as this stretch offers in mid-August.

reports.headline: Race at 3.6 Knots: Bass on Wire Line at Valiant, Slack Hits 15:42
reports.subhead: The bunker blitz corridor finally reached the Sound's hardest water, and the albies are close enough to smell — but they're not here yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Race Rock buoy was showing 3.6 knots of ebb at 1 PM Tuesday, and that's the number that told me to load the wire line instead of the topwater bag. Anything under four knots at the Rock and you can still hold bottom with 30 feet of 32-pound Monel and a white bucktail; push past four-and-a-half and you're just along for the ride. Slack at Valiant Rock came right on schedule at 15:42, and that eight-minute window before the current built back the other way produced the two best fish of my week — a 34-inch striper that ate a chartreuse bucktail with a white worm trailer stacked right on the down-current edge of the boulder field in about 42 feet, and a fat 29-incher that came off the same drift ten minutes later on a Ballistic Missile in bunker color.

That's the pattern right now: hunt the slack, not the roar. The Race and Plum Gut have both been running hard on this new moon cycle — we flagged it last week that the building tidal flow into August 12 would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened. The bass haven't left the rips, but they've gotten particular about when they'll eat in them. Full ebb or full flood, you can mark them stacked over the rockpile on the meter and still get refused. Cut the speed down to that four-knot window and they light up the rod tip instead of your sonar screen.

Water's still holding summer temps end to end — Kings Point up near 71, New London running about 69.4 — and that steep west-to-east gradient across the Sound is exactly why the bunker pods have been so thick pushing into the Gut. Peanut bunker schools have been getting pinned against the Plum Gut rip on the last two hours of the incoming, and where the bunker balls up, the blues show up fast and mean. I had a charter Thursday morning working diving birds off Great Gull Island — six- to eight-pound blues on wire, taking Hopkins No-Eql spoons and 2-ounce diamond jigs as fast as we could get them down. No wasted casts. That's the easiest money on the water this week if you don't mind losing a few hooks to the teeth.

Fluke and sea bass have been the quiet story out at the Sluiceway. It's not fast, but it's honest fishing — five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the 60- to 70-foot break where the bottom drops off toward Fishers Island Sound. Sea bass to 17 inches mixed in steady, especially on the last hour of the drift before the tide turned too hard to hold bottom. Nothing that'll fill a cooler by noon, but a solid, repeatable pattern if you're not chasing the blitz.

Now — the question everybody at the dock keeps asking is where the albies are. Short answer: not here yet, but the water's set up for it. We called this too — said the post-new-moon tidal push would be the trigger, and the ingredients are all sitting right in front of us. Bait's dense, the rip current is ripping the way albies like it, and Montauk and Block Island are both close enough that the first fish through either door could show up in Plum Gut or off Little Gull Island inside 72 hours. I've got epoxy jigs rigged and ready — half-ounce Deadly Dick and Albie Snax in bone white — but I haven't thrown one in earnest yet because I haven't seen the nervous water that tells me they're actually in the Gut. When they show, it usually happens fast and all at once, right on the tail of a strong outgoing at Plum Gut when the bait gets squeezed through that funnel.

What I'd tell anybody planning a trip this week: don't build the whole day around the albie hope. Build it around the bass and blues, which are legitimately good right now, and treat any bonito or albie sighting as the bonus. If you're running Valiant Rock or Race Rock, time your drift to hit slack water — check the tide tables for The Race specifically, not just New London harbor, because the timing differs by close to forty minutes and that gap is the difference between a stripe-on-every-drift day and a skunked one. Wire line still rules out there; braid with enough lead can work in the shallower stretches of the Gut, but at Race Rock's depth and current you want the wire down and staying down.

Looking ahead, if this bunker push holds and the tidal flow stays strong through the coming week, I expect the bass bite at Valiant and Race Rock to keep sharpening on those slack windows, and I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first confirmed albie report out of Plum Gut or Fishers Island Sound before the week's out. The water's right. We're just waiting on the fish to catch up to the conditions.

reports.headline: Nineteen Hours to Atlantis and Back — One Bigeye, One Broken Leader, and a Warm Edge Worth Chasing
reports.subhead: The canyon run out of Montauk cost us daylight and diesel, but the temp break at Atlantis is finally doing what it's supposed to do in mid-August.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at 4 a.m. Tuesday with 400 gallons in the tanks and a weather window that was supposed to hold until Thursday. It didn't quite hold — the swell built out of the southeast faster than forecast — but by the time it mattered we already had a fish in the box, so I won't complain about it.

Atlantis is a hundred-plus mile run from Montauk depending on where you jump off the shelf, and at eighteen knots that's the better part of six hours one way before you even wet a line. I run the numbers before every trip like it's church — forty gallons an hour cruising, more once you're trolling with the riggers full, and you don't leave the inlet without knowing exactly what a slow day costs you in diesel. This one cost us close to nine hundred dollars in fuel round trip. The bigeye we boxed at 2 a.m. paid for about half of it. That's the honest math of running this water — you don't do it for the fuel receipt, you do it because some weeks the canyon owes you and this felt like one of those weeks starting to turn.

We worked the east wall of Atlantis after dark, chunking butterfish over a temp break that was holding right around 70 to 72 degrees on the warm side — a clean, defined edge, not a smear, which is the kind of structure that actually holds fish instead of just holding bait. We had two runs on the bigeye rod before midnight, lost the first one on a chafed leader about ten minutes into the fight — my own fault, should've re-tied after the first bluefin scrape earlier in the day — and connected clean on the second. Eighty-some pounds, came up hard and stayed deep most of the fight, which is usually how the bigger ones behave out there. No yellowfin in the chunk slick that night, which surprised me a little given the bait we were marking, but the squid and butterfish balls were thick enough on the sounder that I expect that to change inside the week.

Daytime trolling on the way out and back gave us two yellowfin in the 25 to 35 pound class, both on a green-and-yellow bar pulled off the corner ahead of a naked ballyhoo, fish came from the edge of a whale-and-bird pile working bait about six miles short of the canyon proper. That's been the tell all season out here — find the whales, find the birds sitting low over nervous water, and you're usually within a mile or two of where the tuna are stacked underneath. We marked good bait balls the whole way out this trip, which is more than I can say for a lot of July runs, and it tells me the warm water that's been building east of the mid-Atlantic canyons is finally spreading into our zone the way we thought it would. We said as much last week — that the current pushing that warm pool east showed no sign of breaking down inside 72 hours — and here it is, sitting right on the edge at Atlantis exactly where we expected it.

Veatch has been the harder call this month. It's a longer haul out of the Rhode Island ports — Point Judith or Newport boats are looking at something closer to seven hours each way at a reasonable cruise, which means an overnighter is close to mandatory unless you've got a fast boat and a short attention span for sleep. The reports I'm hearing secondhand from guys running that direction have been mixed — some yellowfin on the troll during daylight, a few white marlin raised but not stuck, nothing that sounds like a sure thing yet. I wouldn't discourage anyone from making that run this week, but I'd go in with realistic expectations and a Plan B chunk bite lined up for after dark in case the trolling stays quiet.

Hydrographer and Oceanographer are still the longer commitment — you're talking a full day's run each way out of the RI ports or an even longer push from Montauk, and at that distance you're burning enough fuel that a slow trip really stings. I haven't been out there myself this week and I'm not going to pretend I know something I don't. What I can tell you is the same warm-water signature that's been building at Atlantis has been drifting east all month, and if that pattern holds, Hydrographer and Oceanographer should start firming up behind it inside the next week or two rather than ahead of it. That's usually how it plays out this time of year — the warm edge moves west to east through the canyon chain, and the bite follows it on a lag.

Wahoo and mahi have been incidental so far this trip — a couple of small mahi around a weed line on the way in, nothing worth planning a whole trip around yet, though that usually changes as August pushes toward September and the blue water settles in for good.

If I had one more trip in me this week, I'd run back to Atlantis rather than push further east. The temp break is defined, the bait is there, and the bigeye showed they're willing after dark. Veatch is worth the gamble if you've got the range and the patience for an overnight, but I'd treat Hydrographer and Oceanographer as next week's play, not this week's. Watch that warm edge — if it keeps sliding east the way it has all month, the whole chain lights up in sequence, and there's no sense burning the extra fuel before the water tells you it's ready.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Slow Monday, stacked Thursday: Norfolk yellowfin save a shaky week
reports.subhead: Poor Man's went dead flat early, but the warm edge held east of Norfolk and turned the back half of the week into real fishing.
reports.body_markdown:
Give this week a C-minus through Wednesday and a solid B by Saturday. That's the honest grade. We ran four different boats to three different canyons this week trying to find where the warm water actually sat, and for the first three days we were chasing our tail. Monday and Tuesday at Poor Man's were about as flat as canyon fishing gets — clean blue water, no real color change, no birds working, and a chunk line that just sat there untouched for four hours before we pulled the anchor and ran. That's the kind of day that makes you second-guess the whole trip, but it's also exactly why I don't commit one boat to one canyon and stay put all week. You've got to be willing to move.

Wednesday we made the call to run south to Norfolk instead of doubling down on Poor Man's, and that's where the week turned. The warm-water edge that's been sitting east of the canyons all month held its position, and where that blue water pushed up against the cooler green stuff along the drop, we found bait balled up tight and yellowfin working underneath it. We got bit almost as soon as the chunk hit the water — butterflied bunker on 60-pound fluoro leader, 6/0 circle hooks, fished with just enough weight to get down through the top twenty feet where the fish were holding. That bite ran steady through the afternoon in 250 to 300 feet of water right on the edge, fish mostly in the 25 to 45 pound class with a couple pushing bigger. Not a stacked-boat, gaff-every-five-minutes bite, but a real, consistent pick that kept rods bent most of the day.

Thursday and Friday we stayed in that same general area off Norfolk and found mahi scattered around anything holding structure — a mat of sargassum, a few pieces of debris, even a stray lobster trap buoy line. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range, but they came fast on bucktail-tipped Sabiki rigs once we found the first pod and worked it slow with chunks tossed to hold them up. If you find one mahi under a weed line, don't run off it — circle back, toss a few pieces of butterfished bait, and let the school show itself. We also had two white marlin flags Friday afternoon working a dredge and naked ballyhoo combo behind the spreader bars, raised one and got him to eat a hookless teaser but never converted it to a pitch bait in time. That's canyon marlin fishing in a nutshell some days — you get the shot, you don't always get the fish.

Saturday we pushed north to Spencer to see if the pattern was holding up the whole range, and it was mixed. Morning troll produced two bigeye mixed in with the yellowfin on the same spread — green-and-yellow Ilanders and small horse ballyhoo pulled at 6 to 7 knots along the 100-fathom break — but the afternoon chunk went quiet once the current slacked off. Bigeye showing up mixed into a yellowfin bite this time of year usually means the thermocline's still healthy and there's enough depth of warm water for those fish to sit deeper during the day and come up on the chunk in low light. We didn't stick around long enough Saturday to test that theory into the evening, which in hindsight might have been the move.

We never got to Lindenkohl this week — sea state kept building out of the southeast by Friday and it wasn't worth the extra run when Norfolk and Spencer were both producing. That's the tradeoff running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City always presents: you can't fish them all in one week, so you commit based on where the water's telling you to go, and this week that water was clearly sitting east of Norfolk and holding along the Spencer break.

On the wahoo front — nothing solid yet, but there's chatter building. A few boats working the high-speed troll with cedar plugs and small Ilanders behind planers off the deeper water past Norfolk have had a couple of gray ghosts show interest without committing, slashing bait off the line without eating hooks clean. That's usually the first sign before a real wahoo run gets going, and if this warm pool holds its position through the next week like it has the last ten days, I'd expect that bite to firm up. Worth running a dedicated wahoo spread — one or two lines with wire leader and a planer down deep — even while you're primarily fishing the tuna troll, because right now you genuinely don't know which fish is going to show up first.

Looking ahead, the call for next week is simple: stick with the warm edge as long as it holds east of the canyons. If it slides west or starts breaking apart, that yellowfin bite at Norfolk could get patchy fast, and I'd shift effort back toward Spencer where the bottom structure tends to hold fish even when the surface temperature break gets messy. Moon's past new and building toward the quarter, which should mean better current flow on the edges over the next few days — that's usually when the chunk bite tightens up and stays consistent through a full tide cycle instead of turning on and off. If you've got one shot this week, I'd take the early run to Norfolk, get bait in the water by first light, and be ready to move if the color change isn't where it was Wednesday. It moves. You've got to move with it.

reports.headline: Ran the long haul to Wilmington, trolled the break for six hours — three yellowfin, a mahi, and a bigeye after dark
reports.subhead: The warm eddy is still parked over the canyon, and running the extra fuel to fish it paid off — barely — this week.
reports.body_markdown:
The decision this week was simple math. I could've stayed closer, worked the inshore lumps, saved four hours of diesel — or I could run the extra distance out to Wilmington and fish a break that's actually holding structure instead of guessing at scattered bait. I ran the long way. Three trips out, and I'd do it again, though I won't pretend all three days paid the fuel bill the same.

The warm-water pool that's been sitting east of the canyon system all month hasn't moved much, and that's the whole story right now. It's been parked over the edge, feeding a clean break where the green inshore water gives way to that blue, current-streaked water everybody's chasing. When that edge holds still like this, it does the work for you — bait stacks up on it, tuna sit under it, and you're not burning half a day searching. When it wanders, you're back to running the ledge blind. This week it mostly held, which is why the fishing was decent instead of desperate.

We trolled the break early each morning — spreader bars with cedar plugs and Green Machines in the middle, naked ballyhoo and small Ilanders in blue-white and green-yellow out the long riggers, a bird teaser up top to draw eyes. First morning out, we picked off two yellowfin in the 25-30 pound class right on the color change, both on the short rigger ballyhoo, and had a mahi come up on the long bird and eat a naked bally — that fish went about 12 pounds, nothing to write home about but it filled the fish box while we reset. Second trip was slower — one yellowfin, a couple of chances that didn't stick, and a wahoo that came screaming through the pattern and cut a bird bar clean off the wire. That's the wahoo tax out here. You troll fast enough to interest tuna, you're going to feed one to a wahoo eventually and lose gear doing it.

White marlin showed exactly the way we figured they would this stretch — a bonus, not a target. We had one pop the long rigger ballyhoo on day one, pitched a naked bally back at him on spin gear, and he ate it and came unbuttoned boatside. That's about the going rate right now — a swipe or two a day if you're trolling the right water, not stacked fish. Anybody planning a trip around marlin numbers specifically is going to be disappointed; anybody treating it as a bonus while targeting yellowfin will be pleasantly surprised once or twice a trip.

The better story has been the overnight chunk bite. We anchored up on the edge of the canyon proper the second night, set a slow chunk line of butterflied bunker with circle hooks fished way back with no added weight, and let it soak through the dark hours. That's where the bigeye showed. One fish, but a good one — pushing 140 pounds, came up on the third or fourth chunk after midnight and took nearly forty minutes to get boatside on 50-wide gear. That's the trade-off with the overnight chunk approach: you're not going to load the boat, but when a bigeye finds the slick, it's a different class of fish than anything you're pulling off the troll. If you've got the crew and the patience to sit through a slow midnight drift with butterfish and bunker chunks going out steady, it's worth the time right now while that thermal edge is sitting where it is.

I'll be honest about the days that didn't work. The third trip out, the wind swung around and put a little chop on the edge, and the bite went quiet for almost four hours in the middle of the day — no marks, no birds working, nothing showing on the surface. We picked up one small mahi under a weed patch and called it. Not every run out there this week was a paycheck. The canyon's producing, but it's not stacked wall-to-wall the way it can be when everything lines up — moon, tide, bait, and edge position all at once.

Looking ahead, the read is straightforward: as long as that warm pool holds its position over the canyon edge, I'd expect the troll bite to stay steady on yellowfin and mahi, with wahoo as an occasional bycatch tax, and the overnight chunk to keep producing a bigeye shot for anybody willing to sit through the dark hours. If that thermal boundary starts sliding — east, west, doesn't matter which direction — the whole pattern resets and you're back to running around looking for where the bait went. I've seen that happen fast out here in mid-August before. For now, if I had one more trip to plan this week, I'd run out early, work the break hard through the morning hours while the water's calmest, and if the numbers are thin by early afternoon, I'd rather anchor up and let a chunk line soak into the evening than keep burning fuel trolling dead water.

reports.headline: 7-Degree Wall at 39°32'N Puts Yellowfin on the East Side of the Hudson
reports.subhead: The temp break has parked itself east of the canyon all week, and the boats willing to run the extra ten miles are finding tuna and mahi stacked on the color change.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-one point four on the inshore edge of the break, seventy-eight point six about eight miles east of it. That's a 7.2-degree jump in less than ten miles of longitude, and it's sitting almost exactly where I marked it a week ago — roughly 39°32'N, 72°05'W running down through 39°26'N, 72°18'W, which puts it draped right over the east wall of the Hudson and pushing out past the Dip. We flagged this last week — said the warm filament feeding the yellowfin bite would hold in place east of the canyon, and that's exactly what it's done. No retreat, no wobble. If you fished the color change this week, you were in the right spot.

The yellowfin have been sitting tight to that break in 600 to 900 feet of water, working bait pushed up against the thermal edge rather than roaming the whole canyon face. Green machines and cedar plugs in the shotgun and long rigger positions, ballyhoo naked or lightly skirted in blue/white and green/yellow on the shorts, trolled at 6 to 7 knots right along the seam where the blue water climbs over the green. That's not a random pattern — chlorophyll on the inshore side is still murky with upwelled canyon water, and the tuna are using the visual and thermal edge as a highway for bait. Once you find fish, drop the spread and switch to a slow chunk line with butterfish — several boats working the Claw and the water just east of it have done well soaking chunks on circle hooks once the sun gets low and the fish stop showing on top.

Mahi have been riding shotgun on that same break. Nothing giant — mostly schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range, with the occasional gaffer mixed in — but they're reliably stacked under any floating structure or weed line that's drifted into the warm side of the wall. If you're marking a temp jump and see any junk floating on the surface, slow down and pitch a bucktail or a spoon before you run past it. That's been the difference between a two-fish mahi day and a fifteen-fish mahi day this week.

Bigeye have shown up after dark on the chunk, mostly boats anchored or drifting slow right along the edge in that 900 to 1,100 foot range east of the canyon proper. It's not a wide-open bite — more a handful of quality fish for guys willing to soak butterfish chunks through the night and stay disciplined about scent trail and drift speed — but for mid-August that's a legitimate program, and it's the kind of thing that tends to build as the warm water sits in place longer.

What I haven't seen this week is a confirmed white marlin bite or a wahoo report worth putting in print, and I'm not going to invent one just because it's the season for it. The temp structure is right for both — that kind of clean thermal edge usually pulls a few billfish up shallow to sun themselves on baitfish schools — but nobody's called it in yet, so treat that as a possibility, not a promise. Same with swordfish. If you want to gamble on a daytime drop, the timing is classic mid-August: 1,200 to 1,600 feet along the edge of the canyon, squid strips or a dead squid rigged on an 18/0 circle hook under a light stick, fished on the slower moving side of the thermocline where the bottom temp holds cooler and steadier. Nobody's reported one landed this week, but the water column supports the pattern, and this is the stretch of the season where it usually starts producing.

Tide-wise, we're building current into the new moon, and that's sharpening things up rather than blowing them out — bait's getting concentrated instead of scattered, which tracks with what we expected heading into this window. Wind's been manageable, nothing that's kept the fleet off the edge, and the sea state out past the 100-fathom line has stayed fishable enough to work a full trolling pattern without getting beat up.

Looking ahead, the call is simple: as long as that warm pool holds its ground east of the canyon, the program stays the same — run the extra distance, find the 75-to-79-degree side of the break, and work the color change with a mixed troll-then-chunk approach. If the filament slides west toward the canyon face itself, which happens some years in late August, the fish should come with it and shorten the run for everybody. Watch the color change position day to day rather than trusting last week's numbers blindly — canyon breaks like this can slide five or ten miles in 48 hours if the current underneath shifts. Best case, it holds through the weekend and even sharpens with the building tide. Worst case, it slides east again and you're back to a longer run, but the fish themselves haven't shown any sign of pulling out. For now, if I had one day to fish this week, I'd run straight for 39°30'N, 72°10'W, idle down until I found the temp jump on the meter, and start pulling a spread right on that line before first light burns off.

reports.headline: Porgies thick around Shelter Island, bass sliding onto the bunker as the new moon tide builds
reports.subhead: The Peconic's holding its August heat, the porgy bite is as good as it gets, and stripers are starting to lean on the bait pushed into the bay.
reports.body_markdown:
By mid-August the Peconic has settled into the pattern it always finds this time of year — warmer than the Sound, warmer than the ocean side, and holding that heat like a bathtub that never quite drains. The bay warmed early back in April and it's been running its own clock ever since, and right now that clock says porgy time. If you've fished these waters more than a season or two, you know what that means: it's not a maybe, it's a certainty, and this week backed it up.

Shelter Island is doing what Shelter Island does in August. The porgies are stacked thick on the humps and drop-offs ringing the island — Cornelius Point, the flat off Jennys Creek, the drop along Ram Island Reef, and out toward Southold Shoal on the north side. Fifteen to twenty-five feet of water, sand and shell bottom, and it's about as close to guaranteed as bay fishing gets. High-low rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, sandworm or a chunk of clam, fished on the bottom on the last two hours of the incoming tide, and you can fill a cooler without much drama. These aren't giant porgies — mostly hand-sized, some pushing a pound and a half — but the numbers are there, and it's the kind of fishing you can bring a kid or a first-timer on and know they'll go home happy.

Fluke are the more honest story. I wouldn't call it hot — modest is the fairer word, same as it's been all August. The channels are still holding fish: the Noyack Bay channel edge, the drop off Jessup's Neck, and the cut along Robins Island where the current runs hardest on the ebb. Twenty to thirty-five feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid if the current's soft. You're picking through shorts to find keepers, and some drifts you strike out entirely — but a few boats out of Southold and Greenport have been putting three or four keeper fluke in the box on a good outgoing tide, which for mid-August in this protected water is about right. Don't expect doormats in here; that's an ocean-side story. This is meat-and-potatoes fluking, and right now it's meeting expectations, not exceeding them.

The bigger development is the striper pattern building on bait. We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12th new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened. Peanut bunker have been pushing into the estuary system in real numbers, and the schoolie bass are leaning on them hard. Cedar Beach on Shelter Island's north side, the rip off Jessup's Neck, and the mouth of Orient Harbor have all had stretches of visible surface activity — bunker getting pushed up, bass slashing through, gulls diving. Live-lined bunker on a fishfinder rig is the simplest way to connect, or if you'd rather cast, a bone or bunker-colored Bomber worked through the melee will draw strikes. Most of what's coming over the rail is schoolie-class, 18 to 24 inches, with the occasional slot fish mixed in — nothing to write home about size-wise, but consistent, and consistent counts for something in a summer where a lot of guys have been grinding for a handful of fish.

Plum Gut is starting to wake up too, though I'd call it early rather than arrived. The current there runs hard enough to hold bait even in summer, and with the new moon behind us and tidal flow building toward the next cycle, I've had reports of bass showing on the last of the ebb, working the rip lines where the Gut spits into Gardiners Bay. It's not the fall run yet — that's still weeks off — but it's the first hint of the staging that leads into it, and I'd keep an eye on that stretch of water heading into September.

Bluefish are riding the same bunker wave, and it's mostly a harbor story right now. Snapper blues are thick in Sag Harbor and Three Mile Harbor, which every bay rat knows is the tell that adult-class blues will keep building through the back half of August. If you've got kids with light spinning gear and a bag of small Gotcha plugs, the harbors are the place to burn an afternoon.

Weakfish remain the ghost in this report — scarce, as they've been for years now in the Peconic, though a few have turned up mixed in with the bass around Orient. If you catch one, handle it gently and let it go; that population needs every fish it can get.

Blackfish season's still off in the distance, but worth noting for planning purposes — the wrecks and rock piles around Plum Gut and off Orient will be where you want to be once that opens, and the porgy grounds we're fishing now are a good preview of what that structure holds.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the coming week. The bay's holding its warmth, tidal flow is still building off the new moon, and that combination should keep the porgy bite steady around Shelter Island and the bass leaning on bait wherever the current concentrates it. If I had one day to fish, I'd take the last two hours of an incoming tide at Cornelius Point for porgies in the morning, then swing over to Jessup's Neck or Cedar Beach on the evening ebb to see if the bass are pushing bait again. That's the Peconic in mid-August — reliable in some corners, still waiting to fully turn in others, and worth the trip either way.

reports.headline: August 14: Washington's Early Push Rolls Into Its Second Month
reports.subhead: The canyon that starts early is still holding its bigeye and mahi pattern while everybody else is just catching up.
reports.body_markdown:
I've said it for fifteen years and I'll say it again now that we're two weeks past the new moon in mid-August: Washington doesn't wait for the rest of the fleet. This canyon rides the Gulf Stream's inside edge earlier than Hudson, earlier than Wilmington, and by the time the calendar flips to August we're not starting a bite — we're managing one that's already a month old. That's the difference between fishing a canyon and knowing a canyon. Right now we're deep into the mature stretch of the season, past the frantic June scramble to find the first push of warm water, and into the steady grind where the fish know where the bait is and so do we.

The pattern this week has been consistent with what a mid-August Washington should look like. Bigeye have settled onto the deeper structure along the eastern wall, working the drop where the bottom falls from the 600-fathom curve down toward 900. Boats dropping squid and butterfish on the overnight drift are getting quality bites in that window between midnight and first light — not a stacked bite, but a repeatable one, two to four fish a trip if you put in the time and don't burn out your window chasing showier action elsewhere. Yellowfin have been more scattered, working the temperature breaks higher up in the water column, and the troll bite on green machines and small Ilanders behind the spreader bars has been decent but not explosive. You want to be working the seams where the cleaner blue water pushes against the green — that's where the bait's getting pinned and that's where the fish are sitting on it.

Mahi are doing exactly what mahi do this time of year — they're under anything that floats. Lobster pot warp, loose debris, even a stray patch of sargassum will hold a pod. I had a report of a good gaffer-class fish and a pile of schoolies come off a single piece of junk drifting on the edge, and that's the story right now: small debris fields scattered along the canyon, each one worth a few minutes of your time on the way out or the way back. Don't skip them to save fuel — that's free fish if you're paying attention.

Wahoo have been in the mix on the high-speed troll, particularly for boats running wire line and Braid rigged lures at 12 to 15 knots along the drop-off. It's not a dedicated wahoo bite yet — nobody's limiting out — but enough fish are showing up incidentally on the tuna spread that it's worth throwing one dedicated wahoo bomb deep in the pattern if you're already trolling that structure.

White marlin have been around the temperature breaks too, though the bite's been more of a tease than a program. A few pitch-bait opportunities on skipping ballyhoo for boats running dink baits behind the dredge, but I wouldn't plan a trip around marlin specifically right now — treat it as a bonus while you're really out there for the tuna.

Here's the thing about mid-August at Washington that a lot of boats forget: the crowd thins out. Everybody ran hard in July when the word got out that we were producing early, and now attention's shifted east toward the warm pool that's been sitting off Hudson and Wilmington. That's fine by me. Less traffic means less pressure on the same lumps and eddies, and the fish that are here haven't been pounded by six boats a day dropping the same squid rig on the same spot. If that warm-water pocket stays put east of the closer canyons over the next several days, I'd expect Washington to keep its share of the bigeye and yellowfin traffic rather than lose it to boats making the shorter run elsewhere. If it slides west, that's when things get interesting — and crowded.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this pattern to fall apart in the next week. The overnight bigeye bite along the eastern wall should hold as long as the thermal structure stays where it's been, and the debris-line mahi fishing should keep producing right through the end of the month — that bite typically doesn't fade at Washington until we're deep into September. Wahoo will likely stay a bycatch story rather than a dedicated target unless we get a real influx of bait pushing tighter to the drop. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd run straight for the eastern wall, set up the overnight drift on squid and butterfish, and troll the seam on the way home — that's the two-for-one that's been working, and there's no reason to think it stops now unless the water moves on us.

reports.headline: Bunker Schools Push the Point — and We're Two Days Into the Albie Watch
reports.subhead: Stripers and bluefish are stacked on peanut bunker from the Lighthouse to Shagwong, and the tide behind the new moon is setting up exactly what we said it would.
reports.body_markdown:
I've been standing on that boulder field below the Lighthouse since I was tall enough to see over the rocks, and there's a particular kind of August morning that tells you the season is about to turn. This is one of them. The bunker showed up thick this week — not the scattered pods we saw in July, but real, wide schools stacking off the north side and rolling around the Point on the tide change. Where the bunker go, everything else follows, and right now everything else means striped bass, jumbo bluefish, and a whole lot of nervous water.

The blitz activity has been visible from North Bar out past Shagwong Reef, and it's been consistent enough that I'm comfortable calling it the story of the week. Bass are busting bunker on top in that classic August pattern — slot fish mixed with a real number of overslot bass in the 30-to-40-inch class, working the edges of the bait balls where the current bends around structure. I had one morning on the incoming where three separate boils opened up within casting range of the boulder field, and every one of them produced. A 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 1-ounce bucktail got bit the second it hit bottom, but the better bite came on bunker spoons and topwater — a Hogy Pencil worked right through the froth pulled fish that never would've looked at a subtler presentation. If you want to go old school, a whole bunker on a fishfinder rig, fished dead-drift right on the edge of the boil, still puts big bass in the boat. Depths have been running 15 to 30 feet on the drops around the Point, tighter to the rocks on the building tide, then sliding out toward deeper water as the flow eases.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on this whole pattern, and I mean serious bluefish — not the snappers you're seeing in the harbors, but 8-to-12-pound choppers that'll shred a bucktail trailer in one pass. If you're fishing wire or heavier mono leader you're in business. If you're running straight braid to a soft plastic, budget for losses.

South side, the fluke bite has held up better than I expected for mid-August. The bigger tides this week pulled bait and moved fish, and I've heard of doormat-class fluke coming out of the deeper drifts off the ocean beaches — fish pushing past 6 pounds on white Gulp paired with a heavier bucktail, 3/4 to 1 ounce depending on how hard the current's running. The pattern's been the same all season: work the drift slow, keep bottom contact, and don't be afraid to switch to a bigger bait when the current picks up on the outgoing. It's not a five-fish limit every trip, but the quality has been there for anyone putting in the drift time.

Now to the story everybody at the dock has been talking about. We flagged this last week — said the albie and bonito push would trigger around the August 12 new moon as the tidal current built and started shoving bait harder through the rips. We're two days past that moon now, and the current is doing exactly what it needed to do. Squid have been building steadily to our east around Rhode Island and Nantucket, and that's the trigger that usually pulls the first wave of speedsters down into our rips. I haven't gotten a confirmed albie in hand yet myself, but the water's right — 69 degrees off the Point, clean, with good bait density — and every captain I've talked to at the dock this week is rigging Epoxy Jigs and small Deadly Dick lures just in case that first sighting comes off the east side near Frisco Grounds or out toward Shagwong. If you're heading out this weekend, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a 7/8-ounce metal ready to go alongside your bass gear. When it happens, it happens fast, and you don't want to be re-tying while the school's still up.

I want to be straight with you about one thing — this bunker bite, as good as it looks from a distance, has been patchy in practice. Some mornings the boils are everywhere and every cast connects. Other mornings the bunker have pushed off the structure entirely and you're running the shoreline burning gas looking for the next pod. The wind's played a role — a stiff southwest breeze the last few days has pushed some of that surface activity west of where I'd expect it this time of year, so don't assume the fish will be sitting in the same spot two days running. Cover water, watch the birds, and trust moving bait over a static spot.

Looking ahead, I expect this bass-and-blue bunker pattern to hold through the week as long as the bait stays put, and if the current keeps building the way it has, I'd put real money on Montauk producing the first confirmed albie or bonito of the season before this week is out. That's the moment everyone out here waits for — when the Point flips from summer pattern into that electric stretch that carries us into the fall run. It's close. I can feel it in the water.

reports.headline: Bunker Blew Through the Southwest Ledge — Bass Followed, Bonito's Next
reports.subhead: A week of bait-driven chaos around the island has stripers stacked tight to structure while everyone keeps one eye on the rips for the season's first bonito.
reports.body_markdown:
I knew something had shifted before I ever put the boat in the water Tuesday morning. There's a smell that comes off Block Island Sound when the bunker are thick — oily, almost sweet — and it was in the air at the dock before sunrise. Out past the breakwater the gulls were already working, wheeling low and dropping fast, and that's a tell you learn to trust after enough summers out here. When the birds are nervous like that at 5:30 in the morning, the bunker are already under siege.

They were. We ran out toward the Southwest Ledge and found peanut bunker balled up so tight against the structure they looked like a shadow on the bottom machine, and stripers were slashing through them from underneath — that classic push-up-and-explode pattern where the whole surface goes white for ten seconds and then goes quiet again. We sat off the edge in about 35 feet, let the current walk us across the top of the ledge, and worked white and chartreuse bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounces, right through the bait balls on the drift. Fish from 28 to 38 inches came off that structure all morning, with a couple that pushed past 20 pounds mixed in. Nothing that's going to make the cover of a magazine, but a strong, honest bite — the kind where you can put a dozen fish in the box in two hours if you're patient with your drifts and don't burn gas chasing every surface flurry you see.

The North Rip has been holding a similar pattern, though it's fishing better on the last two hours of the ebb than anywhere near the top of the tide. Current there does the work for you — bunker get funneled and squeezed through that rip line, and the bass sit underneath waiting for the current to disorganize the school. Live-lining bunker on a fish-finder rig with a 3/0 circle hook has been the most consistent producer, though guys throwing big topwater plugs — Doc's and Danny plugs mostly — have had some violent strikes right at first light. I pulled a 40-pounder out of that rip a couple weeks back and I keep going back because that fish is still down there somewhere, or one of his cousins is.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the tidal push into the new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened. Two days past the new moon now, the flow through the rips and around the Ledge has real authority to it, and that's precisely what's stacking bait and holding stripers tight to structure instead of scattering everywhere. This is peak current-window fishing, and it won't last in this exact form much longer.

Bluefish have been riding right alongside the bass in the same bait schools, and they're not shy about it — 4 to 8 pound blues chopping bunker chunks to pieces on wire leader, mostly showing up mixed into the same blitzes off the Ledge and along the north side of the island toward Old Harbor. If you're fishing bait for stripers and getting bit off constantly, that's your answer — the blues are in the mix, not stealing your show, just crashing the party.

Fluke fishing has stayed modest here through August, which tracks with most of the region right now — the real fluke story this month is up around Nantucket Sound, not Block Island. We're still picking away at keepers drifting Gulp and bucktail combos off the west side in 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming, but it's a fish-here, fish-there proposition, not anything to build a whole trip around. Porgies have been steady and reliable on the Southwest Ledge structure itself — bloodworms and squid strips on a simple hi-lo rig will keep a rod bent for anyone who wants a break from bucktailing bass, and it's a good option if the blitz shuts down mid-tide and you need something to do with your hands.

The story everyone's actually talking about at the dock, though, is the hammerhead a surfcaster hooked into over on the south shore this week. That fish doesn't show up in cold, empty water — it shows up when the water's warm and the bait is thick, which tells you everything about what's going on around this island right now.
