That's also exactly the kind of signal that has me and every other captain I've talked to watching the rips hard for the first bonito or false albacore of the season. Conditions are lined up about as well as they get — warm water, heavy bait, strong current off the new moon. It hasn't happened yet, but I'd be surprised if we get through the next week without someone hooking into the first one, somewhere between here and Buzzards Bay.

Looking ahead, I don't expect this bunker-driven blitz pattern to slow down much through the coming week — the bait's not going anywhere and the current's still working in our favor. If I had one day to fish, I'd be at the Southwest Ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, working the edge where the current spills off the structure, bucktails ready, and one rod rigged light in case something with a sickle tail decides to show up in the wash. Worth being ready for it even if it doesn't happen on your trip.

reports.headline: Bunker Blitz Turns Execution Rocks Into a Bluefish Highway
reports.subhead: The stripers here are running small and scattered while blues crash bunker pods from the Neck to Matinecock — here's where to find both.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island had his coffee going cold Tuesday morning, asking me the same thing three other guys had asked before him: "Where'd all these blues come from all of a sudden?" I told him what I've been telling everybody this week — they didn't come from anywhere. They've been sitting on that bunker the whole time. You just had to be looking in the right spot at the right tide to see it.

And the right spot, this week, has been the stretch from Throgs Neck out through Execution Rocks. I ran out Thursday morning on the tail of the outgoing and found bunker balled up so tight off Matinecock Point they were pushing rings on the surface, gulls working them from above, and blues underneath cutting them to pieces. Nothing subtle about it — you could see the slicks of oil on the surface from two hundred yards. Threw a Hopkins No-Eql off the transom into the edge of the bait and had a hook-up before it hit bottom. Blues running 4 to 8 pounds, a few bigger, and they didn't care what you threw at them — diamond jigs, bunker spoons, topwater poppers if you wanted to make it interesting. The water temp at Kings Point is reading right around 71 degrees, a couple degrees warmer than what they're seeing out past New London, and that gradient matters. Warm water on this end is holding the bait tight to the western structure — Exy Rocks, the Stepping Stones rockpiles, the Throgs Neck rip — instead of letting it spread out and thin. Concentrated bait, concentrated blues. Simple as that.

Now here's the honest part, because I'm not going to sell you a bill of goods. The bigger bass just aren't here in the numbers you'd want this time of August. The real cow action has been trailing east all summer — anything approaching slot size is mostly staying out past New Haven where the water's a shade cooler. What we've got in the Western Sound right now is schoolie bass, 18 to 24 inches mostly, mixed right in with those bluefish on the same structure. Execution Rocks on the outgoing is still doing what it's always done — current pulls bait off that rockpile and the bass sit right on the downcurrent side waiting for it. White bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how hard that tide is ripping, tipped with a strip of bunker belly, has been the most consistent producer. Don't overthink it out there. Drift the edge, keep contact with bottom, and let the current do the work.

We called this one last week — said the building tidal flow running into the new moon on the 12th would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened at Exy Rocks and the Throgs Neck rip. That extra push on the moon tides has the bait moving with more purpose, and the fish that are around are using it.

Fluke fishing has been modest — I want to be straight about that. It's not a bad bite, it's just not a banner one. Best results have come drifting the channel edge off Hempstead Harbor and the mouth of Manhasset Bay in 20 to 30 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the incoming tide pushing you along. You'll pick through some shorts to get a keeper, but the ones coming over the rail have been decent, 18 to 22 inches, a few better. Incoming has outfished outgoing on the fluke pretty consistently this week — cleaner water, and the bait gets pushed up onto those flats instead of pulled off them.

Weakfish, I'll be honest with you, are a shadow of what this Sound used to produce. I remember when you could load a cooler with tide-runner weaks off Hart Island in August and not think twice about it. These days you're lucky to pick off two or three keeper-class fish at dusk working the edge of Little Neck Bay on a bucktail tipped with a piece of squid or Fishbites. It's not nothing — but don't plan your whole trip around it. Treat it as a bonus if you're already out there for bass or blues at last light.

Porgies remain the one bottom bite you can count on without a lot of head-scratching. Stepping Stones and the reef structure around Hart Island have been holding fish all week — sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, anchor up tight to the rocks, and you'll keep bent rods most of the tide. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler, and on a week when the bigger bass are playing hard to get, that counts for something.

Blackfish are still off the table for most of you right now with the summer closure in effect through this stretch of the Sound — worth noting for the guys already asking, because that bite will matter again once the fall season opens and water starts cooling into October.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the bunker to leave Matinecock or Execution Rocks anytime soon — that thermal edge holding around Kings Point should keep bait stacked tight to structure through the week, and the blues will keep working it as long as it's there. If the nights start cooling off even a little heading into the back half of August, I'd expect some of those bigger bass currently staged east to start filtering back this direction on the tide changes — that's the pattern I've watched play out for thirty years on this water. Until then, fish the outgoing at Exy Rocks for schoolies and blues together, and don't be afraid to burn some gas checking Matinecock and the Neck rip on the way — that's where the bait is, and where the bait is, that's where you'll find fish worth bending a rod over.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Pours Through the Shoal — Bass and Blues Feed Below
reports.subhead: Bunker rafts are pushing hard through the Stratford Shoal narrows, and the bass and blues stacked underneath are the best story in the Central Sound right now.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning parked off the Shoal doing nothing but watching bait, and it was worth the gas. Peanut bunker are pouring through the Stratford Shoal narrows in tight, nervous rafts — not the loose scattered pods you see in July, but dense schools getting squeezed by the current the way this stretch of Sound always squeezes bait when it narrows between the Connecticut shore and Long Island. Terns were working them hard by 7 AM, diving in short, aggressive drops instead of the lazy circling you see when there's nothing pushing from below. That's the tell. When the birds go from circling to diving, something's under the bait, and Tuesday it was bass and blues both.

The blitz activity at the Shoal has been real, not a one-off. I've had reports of the same thing off Charles Island and along the western edge of the Norwalk Islands — bunker schools getting pinned against rock piles and current lines, stripers and blues working them from underneath in bursts that last twenty minutes then go quiet before firing again a quarter mile down current. This kind of visible surface blitzing in mid-August is a little unusual for this zone — usually by now the bait's thinned out and the fish have gone deep and lazy. What we're seeing instead looks like early staging behavior, fish grouping up on bait ahead of the fall push south, and the timing lines up with the tide.

We're two days off the new moon, and the tidal flow built into that cycle has been sharpening the bite at every piece of current-driven structure in the zone — we said that would happen back on the 7th, and the Shoal rip is proving it out. Bigger water movement means bait gets funneled harder through the pinch points — Stratford Shoal, the cut between the Norwalk Islands, the rip off Middle Ground Light — and the fish know exactly where to sit and wait. My best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when bait gets swept off the flats and concentrated right on the edge of the rip. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the frothy water, have been drawing bass in the 24 to 32-inch range with the occasional overslot mixed in. Blues in the 3 to 6-pound class are riding the same bait and will absolutely destroy a metal — a Deadly Dowsing or a Kastmaster thrown into the boil and ripped back fast is about as close to a guaranteed hookup as this sport gets right now.

We also called the bluefish resurgence spreading east from the Western Sound's reef structure, and that's exactly the pattern playing out — the blues have shown up in real numbers off the Norwalk Islands and are pushing east toward Charles Island and the Shoal. Porgy fishing has held up as the more dependable, less dramatic bite underneath all this — bloodworms and clam belly on high-low rigs in 20 to 30 feet of water over the reef structure off Port Jeff and the Norwalk rock piles are producing steady catches of decent-sized scup, the kind of bite you can set your watch to even on days the blitz doesn't show.

Fluke have been the quiet disappointment. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through the deeper cuts off Middle Ground and the mouth of Port Jeff Harbor has produced fish, but they've been mostly short, with only the occasional keeper in the 19 to 21-inch range mixed in. The water there is warm and stable — Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London's holding at 69.4, so there's a real west-to-east gradient across this stretch, and the fluke seem to be sitting in whatever cooler pockets they can find rather than feeding hard. I'd call fluke a secondary target this week, not a primary trip.

Weakfish have been a pleasant surprise mixed into the bass and blue action at dusk around the Shoal and off Charles Island — nothing like the numbers from twenty years ago, but legal fish in the 16 to 20-inch class have come on diamond jigs tipped with squid strips worked slow along the bottom edge of the rip on the last of the incoming.

Looking ahead, the tide keeps building through the week, and if the bait holds its position at the Shoal and around the Norwalk Islands, I'd expect the blitz pattern to continue, maybe intensify, especially on the outgoing around Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground. The risk is wind — if we get a stretch of southwest blow it'll scatter these bunker schools and spread the fish out, which would turn this from a targeted bite back into a search-and-hope situation. I haven't heard of any bonito or albie sightings pushing into the Central Sound yet, but with bait this dense and water this warm, I'll be watching the rips closely over the next week. If I had one trip to make, I'd be at the Shoal on the last two hours of the outgoing with a bucktail rod ready and a metal rod on deck, because right now that's where the bait is, and the bait is telling the whole story.

reports.headline: 38 Pounds on the Ebb — The Race Is Doing Work Again
reports.subhead: Bunker pods stacked from Plum Gut to Fishers Island have big bass feeding hard on the new moon current, while the albie watch heats up east of Orient.
reports.body_markdown:
Three a.m., chest-deep off the Orient rocks, and a 38-pound bass nearly ripped the rod out of my hands on the third cast of a bunker-colored Danny plug. That fish came off a rip line where the current was still ripping at close to five knots even on the tail of the ebb — the kind of push you only get a couple days after a new moon. I landed her, unhooked her in the wash, and by the time I got back to the truck my hands were shaking from more than the cold water. That's the eastern Sound in mid-August when it's right.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happening. The Race and Plum Gut are both running harder than they have in weeks, and the bass know it. Peanut bunker pods are getting squeezed against the rock piles and current seams, and every incoming tide is stacking predators on top of them. I've seen bass anywhere from 28 to 40 inches busting bunker on the surface at both ends of Plum Gut, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when everything funnels through that gut like water through a fire hose.

Water's holding a real gradient right now — Kings Point up around 70.9, New London sitting cooler at 69.4, Montauk close behind at 69.1. That west-to-east drop means the bait and the bass are staging tighter to structure out here than they are further up the Sound, which is exactly why The Race and the Gut are outfishing the open water. Bunker don't like getting pushed into cooler, faster water, so they bunch up hard against the rips — and that's a dinner bell for anything with teeth.

Tactics that are working: bunker spoons trolled just off the bottom through the heart of the Gut on the last of the incoming, umbrella rigs with hoses in bunker and chartreuse combos worked slow through The Race on the drift, and — if you can find surface activity — a big topwater or a 2-ounce bucktail with a white curl-tail trailer bombed right into the boil. I've had my best luck working the eddies on the Orient side of the Gut where the current backs off just enough to hold fish without blowing your line out straight. Depth there runs 15 to 25 feet on the shallow shoulders, dropping to 40-plus in the main channel — fish the shoulders on the up-current side first, then work deeper as the tide slacks.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bunker schools, and they're not small. Jumbo blues in the 8 to 12-pound class are tearing through bait balls off Fishers Island and along the rip lines east of Plum Gut, especially in that last hour of daylight when the light goes flat and everything gets aggressive. Wire leader is not optional right now — these fish are angry and they've got teeth to match the size.

Fluke fishing is holding steady but modest — nothing to write home about, but enough to keep the cooler from being empty. I've been picking up keepers to 4 pounds drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet off the Orient reef structure, working the last of the incoming when the drift slows down enough to keep bottom contact. Porgies are thick around the same structure if you want numbers over size — squid strips on a hi-lo rig, standard stuff, but it's a solid backup when the current's too hard for anything else.

Weakfish have been a no-show this year in this stretch, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you're specifically targeting weakfish out here, you're better off putting that time into the bass and blues that are actually showing up.

Here's the thing I'm watching hardest right now: the warm water and bait density building around Fishers Island Sound has all the ingredients for the first false albacore push of the season. I haven't seen one yet, and I'm not going to claim otherwise, but the setup is there — dense peanut bunker, clean current, and warm surface temps holding in the high 60s to low 70s. If you're fishing east of Orient this week, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig ready. When those albies show, they show fast and they don't stick around long.

Look-ahead: if this current pattern holds through the week, I'd keep hammering The Race and Plum Gut on the last two hours of the ebb — that's where the bait's getting squeezed hardest and where the biggest bass are showing. If the wind stays out of the southwest under 15 knots, the surface bite off Orient at first light should stay consistent. I'd also keep half an eye east toward Fishers Island Sound — if the albie run starts anywhere in this stretch of the Sound, that's where it breaks first, and you don't want to be the guy who heard about it two days late.

reports.headline: Push Past Midnight: Bass Fill the Deep Hole, Weakfish Ride the Bridge Lights
reports.subhead: Two days off the new moon, the outgoing tide is doing the heavy lifting at Shinnecock — if you're willing to fish it after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to skip the evening incoming and wait for the midnight ebb, and it was the right one. Two days past the new moon, the tidal push through Shinnecock Inlet is stacking up exactly the way I figured it would — current running harder, longer, and pulling bait through the cut in a way that daytime anglers just don't get to see. If you're only fishing the inlet on weekend mornings, you're missing the best window of the week.

Here's the thing about this inlet: the bass don't leave when the sun goes down, they show up. The deep hole on the inside of the east jetty, the one that drops off fast just past the rocks where the current from the bay meets the ocean draw, has been holding fish stacked from twenty to thirty feet down on the back half of the outgoing. I've been running a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig down into that hole starting about two hours before dead low, and it's produced slot bass steady, with a couple pushing past 34 inches mixed in. If you'd rather work artificials, a 2-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer, bounced slow along the bottom on the drift through the same stretch, has been just as effective and lets you cover more water.

The bunker are the whole story right now. Peanut schools have been getting pushed through the inlet on the ebb, and everything with fins is on them — bass, and jumbo bluefish that have shown up in real numbers over the past week, chopping bait right at the surface some mornings at first light near the jetty rocks. If you see the birds working tight over the water on the ocean side around sunrise, that's your signal — get a bucktail or a topwater plug in there fast, because those blitzes don't last.

Ponquogue Bridge has been quietly doing what it always does this time of year — holding weakfish tight to the pilings, but you have to fish it right. I've had my best luck starting about an hour into the outgoing, after dark, working the shadow lines where the bridge lights meet open water. Small white swim shads, three inches, on a light jighead, worked slow with just enough action to keep them ticking near bottom — that's been the ticket. Nothing huge, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but steady enough for a few keepers most nights, and it's a different kind of fishing than the bass game — quieter, more patient, more about reading the current against the pilings than covering ground.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest about that. The structure right at the inlet mouth — the rock piles and the drop-off where the channel meets the ocean — has been giving up better numbers than the open bay lately, which lines up with what I said last week about the new moon tide sharpening things up at current-driven spots. We called that one, and it's holding. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce bucktails, drifted slow along that structure on the outgoing, have put a few keepers in the cooler each trip, but you're working for them — I covered a lot of drift lanes off Tiana Beach and the bay side flats near Hampton Bays for a handful of fish each outing. It's not a bay full of doormats. It's a spot-specific bite, and you need to know where the bottom changes.

Porgies are still there for the taking on the inlet rocks, especially right on the tail end of the outgoing when the current slacks just enough to hold bottom with sandworms or clam on a simple two-hook rig. Not glamorous, but it's reliable, and it's a good way to fill an hour while you wait for the tide to turn back for the bass.

If you're thinking about running the canal through to the Peconic side, this is a reasonable week for it — just time it around the lock schedule and don't fight the current unnecessarily. I haven't heard much off the Peconic side worth chasing right now, so I'd stay put unless you've got a specific reason to make the run.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to break. The tide's still building strength coming off the new moon, the bunker schools show no sign of clearing out of the inlet, and the bass and blues are going to keep riding that bait as long as it's there. Water's still plenty warm for weakfish to hold tight to the bridge structure at night, and I'd keep working that program until it tells me otherwise. One thing worth watching — with warm water and bait this thick working up and down the south shore, there's a real chance something unexpected shows up around the inlet mouth before the month's out. Nothing confirmed yet, but I'll be out there after dark either way, so I'll let you know if the cast of characters changes.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier by Kayak: Snapper Blues Everywhere, Bass Still Playing Hard to Get
reports.subhead: I fished three access points this week and the story was the same everywhere — the bay's alive with bait, but the resident bass haven't caught up yet.
reports.body_markdown:
I put the kayak in at Canarsie Pier Tuesday morning, before the heat got stupid, because that's the one launch in this whole bay where I can paddle out, drift the flats, and be back at the truck before the sun turns the parking lot into a griddle. It's also the best seat in the house for watching what the bait's doing, and this week the bait's doing plenty — peanut bunker pushed thick against the pier pilings, snapper blues slashing through them from first light till the boat traffic picks up around eight.

We called this one last week — said the snappers were thick in the shallows and it was a sign the bigger bluefish push filtering through the Sound would eventually show up here too. Well, the snappers are still thick, maybe thicker. Little guys, four to seven inches, absolutely relentless on anything shiny. If you've got a kid who needs a fishing win, tie on a 1/8-ounce Kastmaster or a sliver of Gulp on a snapper rig and work the edges of the pier pilings on the last two hours of the incoming. You will not get skunked. What we haven't seen yet is those snappers translating into a real run of cocktail blues inside the bay itself — that piece is still a maybe, not a yes.

The bass story is more complicated, and I want to be straight with you about it instead of blowing smoke. We flagged back on the 7th that the resident stripers had mostly cleared out of the bay for cooler water elsewhere in the Bight, and that's held up. If you're paddling or wading the flats off Canarsie or up around the Cross Bay Bridge marsh edges expecting bass, you're going to be disappointed most days right now. Water's warm, bay's shallow, and bass don't love that combination in mid-August no matter how much bait is stacked up.

Where it's different is at the current-driven structure, and that's exactly what we said would happen once the tide built strength into the new moon on the 12th. I fished the outgoing at Marine Parkway Bridge Thursday evening and there's a real bite happening in that rip line under the span — schooner bass, mostly 20 to 26 inches, holding tight to the shadow lines on the pilings and picking off peanut bunker as the current rips them through. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, white or bunker-pattern — cast up-current and swung through the seam, is the move. So is a soft plastic, something like a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a light jig head, worked slow just off bottom in that 12 to 18 feet of water right off the fenders. Best window is the first two hours of the outgoing, right as the sun's dropping — that's when the bait gets pinched through the narrows and the bass stack up to ambush it. It's not a blitz. It's a real, workable bite if you're there at the right two hours and willing to grind a little.

Rockaway Beach has been more about bluefish and bunker pods running the wash than any real bass presence yet. I walked a stretch near the 90s Thursday morning and watched bunker schools nervous-water their way down the beach with birds working overhead — no visible blitz, but enough activity that I'd keep an eye on that corridor. If a real bass push does show up ahead of the fall run, that's usually where it announces itself first, with gulls diving on peanut bunker getting pushed against the sand.

Fluke fishing in the bay is holding at modest-but-honest. I worked the channel edge outside Rockaway Inlet on the last of an outgoing tide with a bucktail-and-Gulp combo — white bucktail, chartreuse Gulp trailer, dragged slow along the 15 to 22 foot channel drop — and picked at fish, nothing over three pounds but enough keepers mixed with shorts to call it a real pattern. If you're boat fishing, work the deeper cuts on the bay side of the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still moving bait but not screaming.

Porgies have been steady but unspectacular around the mussel beds off Ruffle Bar and the flats east of the Cross Bay Bridge — small stuff on bloodworms and clam, good for a chowder pot, not much else to report there. Blackfish are still weeks off; that bite doesn't turn on here till the water cools into fall. Weakfish have been incidental at best — a couple caught mixed in with the fluke bite near the inlet channel, nothing to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the bay's resident bass situation to change much until water temps start easing, which realistically means early-to-mid September around here. What I do expect to sharpen is that Marine Parkway Bridge bite, because the tidal flow is still building off this new moon and that rip under the span only gets better with more current behind it. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the bridge at the top of the outgoing with metal in hand. For everyone else, the kayak-and-snapper program at Canarsie is about as sure a thing as this bay offers right now — just don't expect those little blues to turn into anything bigger just yet.

reports.headline: Moriches Inlet's Ebb Cut Is Doing the Sorting Work For You
reports.subhead: Building tidal flow off the new moon has bass and blues stacking on the same current seams that fluke and porgies are using to feed — read the cut right and you can hit three species off one drift.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent an hour at the west jetty Tuesday just watching the water move before I made a cast, and what I saw told me more than any gauge could. The ebb was running hard off that new moon — two days past now — and the sand shoal off the west side is pushing the outflow into a tighter, faster lane than I've seen most of the summer. That's the storm-cut geometry doing what it does after a strong tidal cycle: the channel scours a little deeper, the current accelerates through the throat, and everything that swims gets funneled into a lane about sixty yards wide instead of spreading across the whole inlet mouth. Bait has no choice but to ride it. Predators know that.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon should sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's showing up now. The bass aren't blitzing on the surface like they are up in the Sound and further east, but they're stacked tight along that ebb seam on the drop, holding just off the bottom where the current breaks over the shoal edge. I've been running a 1.5-ounce bucktail, white or chartreuse, letting it sink all the way to the bottom on the upcurrent side and then working it back with the tide instead of against it — that's the mistake I see guys make here, fighting the flow instead of using it. Slot fish in the 28-32 inch range have been coming off that drift on the last two hours of the outgoing, with the occasional overslot mixed in for guys soaking bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig anchored just inside the jetty rocks.

Bluefish are the more reliable story right now. They're working both tide changes at the inlet, slashing through peanut bunker that's been pushed out of the bay on the ebb and pinned against the jetty rocks. Diamond jigs — half-ounce to one-ounce depending on how much current you're fighting — worked with a fast, erratic retrieve have been drawing steady strikes, and if you want to save your fingers, a wire leader in front of anything metal is not optional right now. These aren't the biggest blues of the year but they're consistent, and consistent is worth something when the ocean's been ugly.

Speaking of ugly — the open beach at Cupsogue has been a tough go this week. Swell's been running close to four feet with a short five-second period, which means it's steep, sloppy, and hard to read from the sand. That kind of wave energy churns the surf zone and pushes bait and predators off the outer bar into calmer, current-protected water. That's exactly why the inlet structure itself — the jetty rocks, the edges of the main channel, the flats behind Tuthill Point — has been outproducing the open beach. If you're set on surf fishing Cupsogue, I'd wait for a lull between swell trains or fish the last two hours of light when the wind typically backs off, but don't expect the classic sandbar bite you get on calmer weeks. The energy just isn't letting fish sit up on that bar right now.

Fluke fishing inside the bay is fair, not great — which is honestly about right for mid-August. The channel edges off Pattersquash and the deeper cuts near the Route 51 bridge are holding fish, but you're working through a lot of shorts to find a keeper. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the channel meets the flat, have been the most efficient way to sort through the population without burning through bait. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, work the deeper holes on the last of the incoming when bait gets pushed up onto the flats and fluke slide up to ambush it.

Bottom fishing has been the quiet bright spot. Sea bass and porgies on the inlet structure and the nearby rock piles are settling into that reliable late-summer pattern — small hooks, fresh clam or squid strips, and enough weight to hold bottom in the current has been putting a mixed bag in the cooler for anyone willing to grind through the short fish. It's not glamorous, but it's the most dependable meal you'll bring home off this stretch of water right now.

Weakfish have been quiet — I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish report out of the bay in weeks, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you're targeting them, you're burning time better spent on bass or blues.

Looking ahead, I expect that ebb-seam pattern at the inlet to hold or even sharpen over the next several days as the tidal range keeps building toward the next set of strong currents. If the swell backs off even a foot, I'd get back out to Cupsogue and work the bar on an early outgoing — that's when bait gets flushed out of the bay and stripers historically set up on the outer edge to intercept it. Inside the bay, I'd keep working those channel edges on fluke through the week, but don't expect the ratio of keepers to shorts to improve much until water temperatures ease off later in the month. And with bunker-driven bass activity blowing up everywhere from the Sound down through southern New England, I wouldn't be shocked if we start seeing more visible surface activity here too once that bait pushes further down the coast — worth keeping an eye on the inlet mouth at first light.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: bunker in the bay, bass leaning on the inlet current
reports.subhead: The ocean's been ugly all week, but Fire Island Inlet and the bay structure are holding up their end of the bargain.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a guy at the dock Tuesday morning, coffee in one hand, casting rod in the other, ask me if the bunker showing up off Democrat Point meant the blitz everybody's been posting about up in the Sound was finally coming our way. I told him what I've been telling everybody this week — we don't need the blitz. We've got our own thing going, and it's been quietly good if you fish it right.

The ocean's been a mess. Buoy readings out front have been running close to 4-foot seas on a short, choppy 5-second period, which is exactly the kind of sloppy, confused water that makes surfcasting off the ocean beaches a grind. Democrat Point looked like a washing machine most mornings this week, and I watched guys give up after an hour of getting hammered by whitewater with nothing to show for it. If you want to fish the surf right now, you're better off tucked in behind the point where the jetty breaks up the swell, or working the calmer stretches inside the inlet itself rather than the open beach.

That rough water out front has done something useful for us, though — it's pushed the bait and the bass activity inside, tight to structure, right where we like them. The inlet seam off Democrat Point has been holding stripers on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, right where that current rips past the rock pile. Guys live-lining peanut bunker on a simple fish-finder rig, 20-pound leader, circle hook, have been picking off slot fish in the 26 to 32-inch range along that seam, with a few better fish mixed in on the deeper edge where the channel drops off. If you don't have bunker, a bunker-colored Doc's Goofy Jig or a white bucktail with a chunk of pork rind gets it done fished right along bottom, slow, right through that hard current.

We flagged this a week ago — said the building tidal flow running into the August 12 new moon would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's played out. The moving water through the inlet and around the bridges has been stronger and more consistent than it was two weeks back, and the fish have responded by tightening up right on the seams instead of scattering through the open bay. That's the pattern I'd lean on through the rest of this week while the tides are still running big off that new moon.

Fluke have been a mixed bag — not hot, but not dead either. The Robert Moses bridges are still the go-to, working the west channel in 25 to 35 feet on the tail end of the outgoing when the current's still got some push to it. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, have been the ticket, with a few keepers to 22 inches coming out of there most days. It's been more of a "grind out your limit" fishery than a "load the cooler" one right now — expect to cover ground and cull through some shorts before you find your keepers.

Bluefish have shown up with some teeth behind them. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks around Patchogue and Sayville, which is a good early sign for the adult class fish that'll follow them in over the next few weeks. Out in the bay proper and around the inlet, we've had decent runs of cocktail blues to 3 pounds crashing bunker pods on the outgoing tide, and they'll hit anything shiny moving fast — a diamond jig or a Kastmaster worked through the melee will get bit in a hurry.

Weakfish have been a quiet story, which is about all you can say for weakfish these days. A few have turned up mixed in with the fluke drift off the bridges, mostly on the smaller side, and with the strict slot regulations still in place, most of what's coming over the rail is going right back over. Worth keeping a rod rigged with a light jig if you're already drifting that stretch, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

Porgies have been solid around the bridge structure and the deeper holes off Captree, working clam on a simple high-low rig in 15 to 25 feet. Nothing glamorous, but it's steady action if you want to fill an afternoon and bring home dinner.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the inlet current and the bridge structure while this bigger tidal swing holds through the week. If the ocean lays down even a little, Democrat Point surf could turn on fast once that swell drops below 3 feet — that's when the bass tend to slide back out toward the open beach to chase bait pushed around by the current. Until then, I'm fishing the seams, not the sand, and I'd tell you to do the same.

The bunker schools are still building in the bay, and where there's bunker, there's eventually bigger bass behind them. I wouldn't be shocked to see some real size show up on the inlet current in the next week or two if that bait holds. Worth checking in before you plan your next trip out — I know I'll be watching it close.

reports.headline: Forget the run to the canyons — Jones Inlet's rocks are stacked with bunker and blues
reports.subhead: While the fleet chases albies out east, the current lines inside Jones Inlet are doing all the work on bass, blues, and a fluke bite that won't quit.
reports.body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother's got their eyes on the offshore reports this week — bluefin talk, albie watches, canyon chatter. That's fine for guys with a 30-footer and gas money to burn. Me, I'm standing on the rocks at the inlet at 5:15 in the morning watching peanut bunker get pushed through the cut like they're running from something, because they are.

This is the pattern I wait all summer for. Mid-August, the bait gets thick along the south shore, and Jones Inlet turns into what it always turns into this time of year — a bunker highway with teeth on both ends. I flagged this a couple weeks back, said the building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happened. We had that new moon on the 12th, and the extra push on the tides has lit a fire under everything holding on the current lines — the jetty rocks, the mouth of Sloop Channel, the deep edge off Short Beach.

Striped bass are the headline, but don't go thinking it's blitz fishing every trip — it's not. What I'm seeing is first-light schoolies, mostly 20 to 26 inches, working the same rips where the bunker get squeezed through the inlet on the last of the outgoing. I've had my best luck casting bunker spoons and 2-ounce Ava jigs with a green tube right into the white water off the north jetty, letting it sink on the swing and ripping it back through the seam. You get a few fish, then it shuts off for twenty minutes, then it turns back on when the next wave of bait gets pushed. That's the rhythm right now — not a steady blitz, but reliable windows if you're willing to put in the time and read the current instead of just chucking and hoping.

Bluefish showed back up in real numbers this week, and they're not shy about it. Snappers are thick in the back bay creeks off Freeport and up around the Wantagh Bridge pilings — kids with bobbers and spearing are having a field day — but the adult class blues are the ones I care about, and they're hammering bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right in the main channel of the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb. Bring wire leader or you're donating hooks. These fish are riding the same bait wave that's been driving stripers from here up through the Sound, and if the bunker keep pouring off the beach the way they have, I expect the blues to keep building through the back half of August.

Fluke fishing has actually been the pleasant surprise. Guys have been sleeping on it because of all the bass talk, but the drift through Sloop Channel and the deeper holes off Short Beach has been putting keepers in the box on the outgoing tide, when the bait gets swept off the flats and funnels into the channel edges. I'm running 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in chartreuse, working 12 to 18 feet of water, bouncing bottom nice and slow. Nothing giant — most fish are running 17 to 19 inches — but it's a consistent pick if you're willing to make repeat drifts through the same stretch instead of running all over the bay burning gas.

Now here's something worth watching close — weakfish are trickling back into Hempstead Bay and South Oyster Bay, and I mean that as a real signal, not a fluke catch here and there. Guys working soft plastics on light jigheads around the deeper holes off the flats at dusk have been picking up weakies in the 16 to 20 inch range mixed in with the fluke. It's not a stampede yet, but after years of hearing guys complain about weakfish being a memory around here, seeing them show consistently enough to mention is a good sign for where this fishery's heading.

Water's still warm — mid 70s inshore, low 70s out at the edge of the bight — and that's kept things stable, not pushing fish out early. The ocean's been a little sloppy with some leftover swell rolling through, which is exactly why I'm not wasting time on the open beach right now. That energy is getting absorbed by the bar and the inlet mouth, and it's concentrating everything — bait, bass, blues — into the protected current seams instead of spreading it thin along miles of surf.

Looking ahead, if this tidal push holds and the bunker keep working down the beach, I'd expect the early-morning bass bite at the inlet to hold steady through this week, maybe build a little as we work toward the next tide cycle. The blues should keep riding shotgun on the same bait. Best case, we get one more good week of this before the fall push really starts stacking up. If the wind swings hard out of the southwest and messes with the water clarity inside, I'd shift over to the fluke drift in Sloop Channel until it settles back out. Either way, I'm not driving to the canyon for this. Everything I need is inside that inlet.

reports.headline: One-eighty on the sounder: haddock steady on the mud, cod thin on the gravel, bluefin working the Basin
reports.subhead: Warm water has the cod grounds quiet, but the mackerel schools pulling bluefin over Stellwagen Basin are the best sign we've had all month.
reports.body_markdown:
One-eighty feet on the sounder, mud from rail to rail, and the haddock have been sitting on it like they're bolted down. That's the number I keep coming back to this week — 180 to 210 feet on the Stellwagen mud, southeast of the Basin toward the edge of Tillies. Clean marks stacked two to four feet off bottom, and when the boat's holding right on the drift, guys are doubling up on haddock in the 3 to 5 pound class, some pushing 7. High-low rigs, size 6/0 hooks, fresh clam or a chunk of squid — nothing fancy needed. The haddock don't care about finesse this time of year, they care about you being on the mud and staying there.

Cod is the harder conversation. Warm water's pushed the surface layer down deep enough that the gravel edges — the classic 120 to 150 foot stuff off the northwest corner of the Bank and along the edge toward Carter Canyon — have gone quiet in the middle of the day. We're still picking cod, don't get me wrong, but it's a early-morning and evening game right now, and the fish have slid a little deeper and tighter to structure than they were in June. Diamond jigs and Norwegian-style jigs tipped with a strip of squid are outfishing bait on the drift — the jigging motion seems to wake fish up that are just sitting heavy on bottom in this warm-water stretch. If you're anchoring bait, go heavier on the sinker than you think you need; the current's been running harder than usual off the moon, and a slack presentation just sits there doing nothing.

Pollock have been a bonus fish more than a target — scattered marks up off bottom on the high spots around Stellwagen Edge and the northern end of Tillies, taking the same jigs meant for cod on the drop. Hake we're still finding at night on the deep mud in the Basin, 250 feet plus, for the guys willing to run out after dark with a chum bag and clam bait. Not glamorous fishing but it's steady if you know where the mud holds bait.

Now for the part of the report I actually want to talk about. The bluefin have shown up over Stellwagen Basin and along the edge toward Cape Cod Tails, and they're doing it the way they're supposed to in August — chasing mackerel balls that the whales are working right alongside them. If you see fin whales or humpbacks up on the surface out there this week, slow down and look around before you run past — nine times out of ten there's mackerel underneath them, and where there's mackerel stacked that thick, the bluefin aren't far. We've had fish show on top chopping bait, 50 to 80 pound class mostly, with a few bigger ones mixed in that nobody's landed yet. Live mackerel on a stinger rig has been the most consistent producer when you can jig a few up and keep them lively in the tank. Butterfly-style jigs worked fast through the school when the fish are down and not showing on top have also drawn strikes, but it's been a game of patience — you can sit on a good-looking whale push for twenty minutes and get nothing, then have it go off in a five-minute window.

Honest read on the tuna: it's not an every-day fish yet. Three trips out to the Basin and the Tails this week, we had shots on two of them, and only boated fish on one. That's not bad for early-to-mid August on the Bank, but it means you need to be willing to run around a little and read the birds and whales rather than parking on a number and hoping. The mackerel schools have been thick enough on the sounder — big red blobs from 30 to 60 feet down — that I don't think this bite is going anywhere for a while, but it moves around with the bait, and the bait moves around with the tide and wind.

Wind's been out of the southwest most afternoons, building a light chop by early afternoon that's made the morning bite the better window for everything — groundfish and tuna both. If you're planning a trip, I'd be leaving the dock in the dark and trying to be on the mud or working bait pushes by first light, because by 1 or 2 in the afternoon the wind picks up enough to make jigging sloppy and the tuna schools tend to scatter deeper.

Looking ahead, I expect the haddock bite on the mud to hold steady through the next week — that fishery doesn't care much about surface temperature, it's a bottom game and the bottom's been consistent. Cod should improve some as we get into cooler overnight temps and the water column starts to mix a little more, but I wouldn't call it a sure thing yet — I'd fish the early morning tide change on the gravel edges and not expect much midday. For the bluefin, if the mackerel stay stacked over the Basin and the whales keep working there, this could turn into the best stretch of the summer for shots at fish. If that bait pushes off the Bank the way it sometimes does late in August, I'd shift attention toward Tillies and the deeper edge toward the canyon approaches. Either way, keep an eye on the birds and the whales before you even wet a line — out here, they'll tell you where to fish before your fishfinder does.

reports.headline: Sankaty Rip: First Bonito Flash, Bass Still Playing It by Dark
reports.subhead: The first bonito showed on the south side this week — right on schedule — while stripers stay locked into low-light windows around Monomoy and the Shoals.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, working the Sankaty rip on the last of the ebb, I watched a school of something come up under a pod of bait and just erase it — no big splash, no birds working yet, just a boil that flattened out in about two seconds and left slick water where the bait had been. Too fast and too clean for bluefish. Too small a footprint for stripers. I made three casts with an epoxy jig before I even admitted to myself what I was hoping it was. Didn't connect that pass, but twenty minutes later a buddy running out of Monomoy texted me a photo of a bonito in the bottom of his boat, caught off the Vineyard side rips earlier that morning. First one I've had confirmed this year on our side of the Sound.

We said this was coming — flagged it a week back that the breachways and the Vineyard rips would see bonito within days, and here it is, right where we said it'd show first. It's not a push yet. It's scouts. One here, one there, working the edges where the current stacks bait against structure. Give it another week and I expect we'll start seeing them show consistently off Great Point and along the back side of Tuckernuck as water in the Sound proper catches up to what the open Atlantic side is already running. Right now the deep basin water is still a touch cool for a full-blown bonito show inside the Sound — the fish are hugging the warmer, current-scrubbed edges on the ocean side first. That's the pattern every year. Ocean rips first, Sound rips a week or two behind.

Stripers are still playing the summer game — tight to low light. Anything you catch during the heat of the day around here right now, you're catching almost by accident. The real window is that hour before full light and the hour after sunset, and Monomoy has been the most consistent piece of water for it. With the wind out of the southwest most mornings, the rips off the elbow and down toward the Powder Hole have been setting up clean — current pushing against the wind builds a nice standing wave and stacks bait right against the bar. I've had the best luck working a 2-ounce white or olive Deceiver on an intermediate line, swinging it through the seam where the white water meets the green, letting it sink on the drop before starting the strip. Fish have been mostly schoolies with the occasional 28- to 32-incher mixed in, nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady enough that two or three fish in that dawn window feels normal right now.

Chatham inlet and the back side of the Powder Hole have been doing similar work on the outgoing, especially with bunker starting to filter through — where you find the pods of bunker getting nervous, that's where the bigger fish are sitting, and that's also where the bluefish have been thickest. Cocktail blues, mostly two to four pounds, but a few chunkier ones mixed in chewing through wire leader like it's nothing. If you're throwing bucktails for bass and keep getting bit off, that's your answer — the blues have moved into the same bait as the stripers and they're not shy about it. Small wire leader or a heavier fluorocarbon bite tippet has saved me more lures than I'd like to admit this week.

Fluke have been the one truly dependable bite regardless of hour, and the full-moon tide swing this week sharpened it up nicely. Horseshoe Shoal edges and the deeper cuts off Monomoy Point have both been holding fish — nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper over 20, but good numbers on the drift with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the drop-offs where the sandy flats fall into 15 to 25 feet. The stronger current from the full moon has kept the bite compressed right around the tide changes — dead slack and you might as well be anchored for lunch, but the hour on either side of the change has been lighting up nicely with fish stacked on the current edges.

Albies are still a no-show around here, and I wouldn't expect them yet. Great Point usually doesn't see its first real wave until closer to the end of August into early September, once the bait gets pushed hard against the rip on the ebb and the water out at the tip cools a shade from the deeper Nantucket Shoals current mixing in. I'll be out there checking every few days regardless — that first blitz off the Point, with the terns wheeling and the surface exploding all along the rip, is the moment I wait for all summer, and I'll know it the second I see it.

For the coming week, I'd focus mornings on Monomoy for stripers before the sun gets up, keep an eye on the Sankaty and Great Point rips for any more bonito flashes on calm mornings, and lean on the fluke drift over Horseshoe Shoal around the tide changes if the bass window comes up empty. The southwest wind pattern looks like it'll hold, which keeps those Monomoy rips working in our favor — just watch the afternoon sea breeze building stronger by midweek if you're running a small boat out toward the Shoals.

reports.headline: Silversides Stack Robinson's Hole — First Bonito Flash Off Wasque
reports.subhead: The bait's finally thick enough to hold fish, and the season's first bonito scouts just showed on the Vineyard's south side.
reports.body_markdown:
Silversides are balling up tight in the rip at Robinson's Hole right now, thick enough that you can see the nervous water from fifty yards off before you ever see a bird. Squid are mixed in behind them, working the current seam on the Vineyard side of the hole, and that combination — squid and silversides stacked in a rip that's running hard on this full moon — is exactly what gets me up before the sun this time of year. It's the tell. Bait like that doesn't sit still long before something shows up to eat it.

And something did. First bonito scouts of the season flashed off Wasque this week, working the rip where the south shore current dumps into open water. Not a blitz, not consistent, just single fish and pairs showing on the surface for a few seconds at a time before disappearing back down. We flagged this corridor last week as sitting right on the edge of the turnover, with water warming into that low-to-mid-70s window and bait building — and here's the first confirmation. It's early. I want to be straight about that. One or two fish showing off Wasque is not a green light to run down there expecting a bonito blitz. But it's the signal I watch for every August, and it's right on schedule. I'd expect the next push to come through Menemsha and down into Robinson's Hole within the next week to ten days if this bait holds and the water doesn't get knocked back by a cold northeast blow.

Striped bass are locked into the low-light pattern you'd expect for mid-August — daytime fishing has been tough unless you're working current-swept structure or a river mouth that's holding a few degrees cooler than the open bay. Dawn and dusk around Woods Hole, working the rip off the draw pilings and down through the Eel Pond cut, has been the most dependable window. Bunker pods are scattered through the Elizabeth Islands side, and where you find them tight to structure — Quick's Hole, the lee side of Nashawena — bass are still showing under them at first light. I've had the best luck swimming a 3-ounce white bucktail with a white curly-tail trailer down through the deeper part of the rip on the last of the outgoing, letting it sink to the bottom third before working it back up through the water column slow. Nothing has been easy about it. You put in your dues at 5 a.m. or you don't connect.

Fluke have been the one thing I can send people to with real confidence. Doormats are holding on the channel edges and drop-offs where the bottom breaks from eight feet down into eighteen or twenty — the mouth of Quick's Hole, the edges of the Cuttyhunk channel, and the deeper cuts running out of Vineyard Sound toward Woods Hole. This full moon tide swing has been sharpening the drift bite right at the tide changes, which lines up with what I've been seeing on the water — slow periods, then a tight ten or fifteen minutes where three or four rods go down at once as the current eases through the turn. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along bottom, have been outfishing everything else I've thrown. Keep a squid strip on the hook if you can — the squid showing up in the rips right now tells you what these fish are already keyed on.

Bluefish are mixed. Snapper blues are thick in the back bays — Menemsha Pond, the shallows off Lambert's Cove — giving light-tackle guys steady, easy action on small metal and Kastmasters. The bigger cocktail blues haven't fully shown yet, but with peanut bunker starting to spread through the bay the way they are, I'd expect that to change fast. We called that pattern out a little over a week ago, and the bait's tracking right where we said it would. Give it another week and I think the cocktail blues push into the same rips holding the fluke and bass, especially around the Cuttyhunk side where the peanuts are thickest right now.

Scup remain the honest, boring-but-reliable fishery — Woods Hole structure, the Cuttyhunk breakwater, and the pilings around Menemsha basin are still stacked with them on squid strips and sandworms, bottom-fished on light tackle over rocky patches in ten to twenty feet. Good for a box of dinner fish while you wait on the tide to turn for something bigger.

Looking ahead, the moon coming off full should ease the current strength a touch by midweek, which usually settles the bite windows back into a more normal rhythm rather than the exaggerated swings we've had. I'll be watching Robinson's Hole and the Wasque rip closely — if that bait holds and water stays in the mid-70s, I expect the bonito reports to firm up fast, with albies not far behind. That's the pattern every year on this water. The first flash is never the run. But it's never wrong either.

reports.headline: Race Point on the last of the ebb: bass to 34 pounds on live mackerel
reports.subhead: The rip did the work this week — mackerel schools thick enough to snag, bass stacked underneath, and a Barnstable bluefish pattern building fast.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a father-son charter out of Provincetown, and I told them before we even cleared the breakwater — we're not running far, we're drifting Race Point on the last two hours of the ebb, and we're going to let the rip do the talking. That's how I've fished that water for thirty years and I'm not changing now. We snagged a few mackerel off the surface with a Diamond Jig rig maybe half a mile off the Point, hooked two live ones on 5/0 circle hooks under a fish-finder rig, and dropped them right into the seam where the color changes from that deep green to the churned-up white water. Twenty minutes in, the kid's rod buried and we came up with a 34-pound bass, fat and chrome, right off the structure at Peaked Hill Bars. That's the pattern right now and it's a good one — not easy, but good.

The rips off Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars have been holding bass all week, but you have to fish the stages right. Dead low and dead high, forget it — the water goes flat and the fish scatter off the structure. It's that last push of the ebb and the first hour of the flood where the current stacks bait against the sand bars and the bass move up to feed. Live mackerel is still the best bait out there, hands down, but I've had guys do well drifting umbrella rigs with tube teasers through the same water when the macks weren't cooperating. Depth's been 15 to 25 feet right on the bars, deeper — 30 to 40 — just off the edges where the drop-off meets the rip.

What I like about this time of year up here is that Cape Cod Bay doesn't shut down the way the water does south of the Cape. The Gulf of Maine keeps feeding cooler water in around the Race and along the backside, and that keeps the stripers willing to feed through the middle of the day, not just at first light. I've had good bites at noon on some of these drifts when guys down the coast are telling me their bass have gone nocturnal. Doesn't mean it's a free-for-all — you still want moving water and you still want to be on structure, not just anywhere in the Bay. But it's forgiving compared to what I hear from the Sound side.

Bluefish have been building in the harbors and creek mouths around Barnstable and Sandy Neck, and this is exactly the pattern I figured we'd see start to show — the peanut bunker have spread into those back-bay flats and the cocktail blues are tracking them in tight. Nothing giant, two to four pounds mostly, but steady, and fun on light spinning gear. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters, or a Deadly Dick if the current's got any push to it — worked on the drop of the tide through the channel edges off Sandy Neck has been putting fish in the boat pretty reliably in the last hour of daylight. If you're throwing topwater at dusk off the beach there, don't be surprised if you get bit on almost every cast for a stretch and then it just stops — that's the bait moving through, not the fish leaving.

Fluke fishing has been steady but not spectacular in the channels around Barnstable Harbor and out toward Sandy Neck flats. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the sandy bottom in 12 to 18 feet, been picking at keepers in the two-to-four-pound range. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but if you're patient and cover water on the drift you'll put a few in the cooler.

Cod's a different story right now. Billingsgate and the deeper structure out toward the Stellwagen edge haven't been holding much — this is typically a fall pattern for us up here, once the water starts to turn over and cool, and August just isn't the month. I wouldn't waste a trip on it yet. Give it another six weeks.

We're coming off a full moon this week, and that's put some real push into the tides — bigger swings, harder current on the rips, which has actually sharpened up the bite windows at Race Point rather than blowing them out. As that current eases over the next several days, I'd expect the bass to spread a little wider off the bars and the bite to soften up some, so if you've got a window this weekend, I'd take it. Best case, the mackerel schools hold tight off the Point and the bass stay stacked underneath them through the week. If the macks push off — and sometimes they do, chasing their own bait — I'd shift over to trolling tube-and-worm through the same rip structure rather than chasing bait around trying to snag it. Either way, fish the moving water, fish the structure, and don't be in a hurry. That's the whole game out here.

reports.headline: Deer Island Rip on the Outgoing: Live Mackerel Bass, Peanut Bunker Blues Inshore
reports.subhead: With the ocean running warm and slick, I stayed inside this week — and the harbor paid the bills better than the open rocks did.
reports.body_markdown:
I had three options Monday morning standing on the dock with coffee going cold: run north to the Cape Ann ledges, push south to Duxbury and the Plymouth flats, or stay put and work the harbor structure I know better than my own driveway. With the full moon pumping extra current through President Roads this week, I made the call to stay inside. That decision paid off.

Deer Island Light on the back half of the outgoing has been the most consistent thing I've fished all August. The rip that forms off the light as the tide pulls out of the inner harbor is stacking mackerel against the ledge, and the bass know it. I've been anchoring up-current of the seam and drifting live mackerel on a fish-finder rig with 3 feet of 40-pound fluoro leader, letting the bait swim naturally into the boil. Fish have been running 28 to 34 inches, with a few close to overslot mixed in on the last two hours of the drop. If you don't want to fuss with livies, a white 2-ounce bucktail with a chunk of pork rind worked slow along the bottom edge of the rip has produced too — just not with the same consistency.

Nahant's backside rocks are still holding fish, but that program has flipped hard to a low-light game. Midday out there right now is mostly dead water — the open ocean side has warmed enough that the bass have pulled off the exposed granite and tucked into the shade and current breaks until the sun drops. Dusk into the first hour of dark has been the window. Guys working topwater plugs off the rocks at Bailey's Hill and the Nahant causeway have had a few good bass, but it's a short window and you need to be there before the light actually fades, not after.

Spectacle Island and the flats off Long Island have turned into a bluefish program, and this is exactly what I flagged last week — the peanut bunker pushing into the harbor was going to pull cocktail blues right in behind it, and that's precisely what's happening now. Winthrop's shoreline and the mouth of the Chelsea Creek have snapper blues thick enough that a kid with a bobber and a piece of mackerel can load the cooler in an hour. The adult cocktail-sized blues, 2 to 4 pounds, are mixing into that bunker pod on the drop tide off Spectacle Island, and small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — thrown right into the nervous water has been money. No need to overthink it; match the peanut size and stay in the melee.

Gloucester and Cape Ann have been a mixed bag. The backside ledges off Eastern Point and Bass Rocks are still giving up bass on the change of tide, mostly at night now with live mackerel or eels drifted along the structure in 20 to 40 feet. Cod and haddock inshore are basically a non-event this time of year — that fishery belongs to spring and fall around here, and anyone telling you different this week is stretching it. If you want bottom fish right now you're better off running out to the deeper Gulf of Maine structure, and even then it's a grind, not a program.

South of the city, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay have been the flounder show. The flats inside Duxbury on the last of the incoming and the first hour of the ebb have been holding decent flounder in 6 to 10 feet — squid strips and sandworms on a simple spreader rig, fished slow right on bottom over the mud-sand transitions. It's not a fast bite, but it's a steady one, and it's a nice change of pace if the bass game has you frustrated. Bass in Duxbury Bay itself have been mostly a dawn deal, working the channel edges near the Powder Point Bridge on the first push of the incoming.

The pattern right now, north of the Cape, is that the Gulf of Maine's cooler water is keeping our estuaries and rivermouths more alive through the middle of the day than what's happening south of us — the harbor mouths and the Deer Island rip are fishing on a schedule closer to normal, while the open, sun-baked rock structure at Nahant and Cape Ann has shoved everything into the shoulders of the day. If the current stays strong behind this moon through the weekend, I'd keep working the Deer Island outgoing and the Winthrop bunker pods during the day, and save the exposed rock game for last light. If the wind stays light and the harbor keeps its color, I don't see a reason to change the program — but I'll be watching for that peanut bunker pod to push further up into the Mystic and Weymouth Back River, because when it does, the blues will follow it right up the ladder.

reports.headline: Sheepscot Stripers Hold the Day Shift While Monhegan Mackerel Thin Out
reports.subhead: Cool Gulf water keeps bass biting through the afternoon in the rivermouths, but the mackerel schools off Monhegan have gone quiet and the groundfish are sitting deep in the bay.
reports.body_markdown:
My father used to say the Sheepscot never lies to you, it just don't always tell you what you want to hear. I was maybe fourteen, standing on the ledge below the old boatyard with a bucktail jig and no clue what I was doing, when he told me that. Forty-some years later I still go back to that same stretch of river most August mornings, and this week it told me the truth again: the bass are here, they're eating, and they don't care what time of day it is — which, if you fish south of us, sounds like a small miracle right about now.

That's the story of this week in Midcoast waters. While the water south of the Cape has stripers pinned to a strict dawn-and-dusk pattern because of the heat, our end of the Gulf of Maine stays cold enough that the fish never fully shut down. I've been working the mouth of the Sheepscot and up into the Back River on the last two hours of the incoming, throwing a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse tube trailer, and connecting with schoolie bass from 20 to 26 inches steady through the middle of the day. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but it's honest fishing, and there's enough of them stacked on the current seams below Barter's Island that a slow afternoon can still put a dozen fish in the boat.

The Damariscotta's been similar — bigger fish showing on the flood around Glidden Ledge, taking live mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet, right where the river narrows and the tide really starts to push. If you've got a livewell full of mackerel, that's the play up there right now, not lures.

On the subject of mackerel — that's where I've got to be straight with you. Monhegan used to be a lock this time of year, jigging Diamond jigs or mack trees off the east side around the mooring field and filling a five-gallon bucket in twenty minutes. This week the schools have thinned considerably. I made the run out from Boothbay Tuesday expecting the usual and came back with maybe fifteen fish after two hours of hunting. They're around, but scattered and moving, not holding in the tight balls we saw in July. My guess is the bait's dispersed with the bigger tides we've had the past several days — heavier current tends to spread mackerel schools out rather than let them bunch up tight against structure. If you're headed to Monhegan for mackerel this week, don't plan your whole trip around it. Have a Plan B.

That Plan B, for me, has been bass and bluefish working the tide rip off Eastern Egg Rock. The puffins are still feeding chicks out there, and where there's bait for the birds there's usually bait for stripers underneath. I picked up several bluefish in the 3-to-5-pound class working topwater poppers along the western edge of the rock on the last of the ebb, along with a handful of keeper bass mixed in. Nothing explosive, but a solid hour of fish on nearly every cast when the tide's really moving.

Further out in Penobscot Bay, the groundfish have done what they always do this time of year — they've gone deep and stayed there. I fished the channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven last weekend, working the deeper cuts in 90 to 120 feet with diamond jigs and cod rigs baited with clam, and found a mix of small cod and a few decent pollock holding tight to the bottom structure. The pollock action was better up on top than down deep, actually — around Saddleback Ledge and off the west side of Isle au Haut, we had pollock busting bait right on the surface in the early morning, chasing what looked like young herring. Casting a 2-ounce diamond jig or a Slug-Go into the boils there produced fast action for an hour before the sun got up and pushed them back down.

Haddock have been harder to come by close to shore — you're better off running out toward Matinicus if you want a real crack at them, working the deeper water in 150 feet or better. I haven't made that run myself this week, but a few of the boats out of Stonington have reported decent numbers on the drift with clam-baited rigs, which tracks with where they usually sit this time of year once inshore water starts to warm up in the shallower parts of the bay.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically through the coming week. The tides will ease back some as we move off this stretch of bigger water, which should let the mackerel schools tighten back up — if that happens, Monhegan and the ledges off Boothbay Harbor should turn back on within a few days. The rivermouth bass bite should hold steady as long as the Gulf stays cool, which it will. If I had one day to fish, I'd take the last two hours of an incoming tide on the Sheepscot or Damariscotta, work the current seams with bucktails or live mackerel, and not worry about the clock. That's been the most dependable thing going all week.

reports.headline: The 5:52 ebb at the east end: bass on the rip, blues in the wash
reports.subhead: Full-moon current cranked the Canal to better than four knots this week — the bite followed the water, not the clock.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, 5:52, the ebb let go at the east end and by 6:15 the current meter in my head was reading better than four knots off the Herring Run. That's full-moon water for you — the kind of push that turns a lazy rip into a washing machine and pulls bass up off the bottom to feed instead of just holding station. I had two guys on stripers to 34 inches on that tide, both on 2-ounce Redfins worked right through the seam where the white water folds back on itself below the Sagamore side. That seam is everything right now. When the current's running this hard, the fish aren't spread out grazing — they're stacked tight on the edge of the fast water, using it like a conveyor belt, and if your lure isn't in that six-foot-wide window you're just casting at scenery.

This is peak-summer Canal fishing, and that means low light or nothing. I've said it for thirty years and it hasn't changed: once that water temp climbs through the 60s and pushes toward 70, the day bite mostly shuts off except right on the strongest stages of moving water. Dawn and dusk are carrying the whole show. The 5:52 ebb I mentioned was a dawn tide — that's not an accident, that's the pattern. Guys grinding it out at high noon on a weak tide are wasting gas. Give me the first hour of light on a hard-running ebb or the last hour before dark on a strong flood, every time, all summer.

The east end rip has been the more consistent producer this week, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current really combs bait through the Herring Run rip and down toward the Cribbon Point side. Bluefish have been mixed in thick there — 3 to 6 pounds, blitzing on top hard enough that you can hear it from the bike path. Poppers and small metal — half-ounce Kastmasters — will get bit fast when the blues are up, but if you want the bass underneath, drop a bucktail, half-ounce to an ounce depending on the stage, and let it swing dead in the current before you start working it. That's a lesson that's cost me fish over the years — start jigging too soon and you rip it right out of the strike zone.

West end has been slower to turn on, and that's typical for this time of year. The current seams there set up better on the flood, when water's pushing in past Mashnee Island and stacking against the flats off Hog Island. I had a report of a nice fish, mid-30s, taken right at the top of the flood in that current seam on a swimming plug worked slow — Bomber Long A, bone color, fished just outside the fast water where it eddies. That west end bite tends to lag the east end by a tide or two because the water has to travel the length of the ditch, and this week that lag has been obvious. If the east end's been hot on the ebb, give the west end another hour or two of that same tide stage before you commit.

Fluke have been a bright spot for guys willing to work the deeper cuts along the edges — 4-inch white Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow through the deeper holes off Mashnee and the Cribbon Point drop, has been picking up keeper-class fish in the 20 to 22 inch range on the slower stages of the tide, right around the last hour before slack when the current eases enough to hold bottom without a war going on.

Worth mentioning — we flagged this a week ago, that the bonito push would run RI breachways and Vineyard rips first, then Block and Montauk behind it. I'm hearing the first real scout reports now working up into the Buzzards Bay side near Wings Neck and Phinneys Harbor, which is exactly the doorstep for that Vineyard corridor pattern to spill into. Nothing inside the Canal itself yet — this ditch runs too much current and too much cold bottom water for bonito to hold — but if that pattern keeps building the way it's supposed to, don't be shocked if we start hearing about fish showing on the outside edges of Buzzards Bay proper within the next week or two.

Looking ahead, the moon's just tipped past full, which means the exaggerated current we've had all week — that four-knot-plus ebb, the hard flood stacking bait at the west end — is going to start easing back toward normal over the next several days. That's not bad news. Slightly less current usually means a slightly longer window to fish instead of one violent hour of peak flow. I'd focus the next week on the transition tides — the hour before max ebb and the hour after — when the current is strong enough to hold fish on the seams but not so brutal that you're fighting your own line the whole drift. Dawn at the east end, dusk at the west end, and don't be surprised if the bluefish crowd the bass out of the shallow water on the hardest pushes. That's the Canal in August — read the clock, read the current, and be standing in the right spot when the water decides to move.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock's Big Tide: Pollock Steady, Bass Working the Late Shade
reports.subhead: The full moon is stacking current at the Rock, and the bass have pushed into cooler water while the groundfish hold their ground.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Bailey Island Tuesday morning, drifting the ledge off the southern tip while the tide built toward the flood, and I noticed something I always look for this time of year: the herring gulls weren't diving, they were sitting. That tells you the bait's deep, not on top, and sure enough when I dropped a jig it found fish holding tight to the bottom in eighteen feet, right where the current pinches around the rockpile. That's been the story of the bay for the better part of two weeks now — the action is there, but you have to go get it rather than have it come to you.

We're riding a full moon this week, and anyone who's fished Halfway Rock long enough knows what that means: the current there gets serious, and the window to fish it well shrinks down to a tight slack period on either side of the tide change. I've had good luck timing my drifts to hit the last twenty minutes of the ebb and the first half hour of the new flood — that's when the pollock stack up predictably on the northeast corner of the Rock in twenty-five to forty feet, and a three-ounce diamond jig worked with a slow, steady lift will connect. Cod have been scarcer than I'd like to report — a few fish in the eight to twelve pound range came up mixed in with the pollock, but nothing like the numbers we'd see in October. Haddock, if you're hoping, forget it inshore this time of year; that's a fall and winter proposition out here.

Striped bass have given me the most to think about this week, and it comes down to water temperature. South of Cape Cod, the bass have gone nocturnal in the heat, but Casco Bay's Gulf of Maine water stays cool enough that our fish keep feeding through the middle of the day, especially around river mouths and current-swept points. I've been finding them at the mouth of the Presumpscot on the last two hours of the outgoing, working white and olive Deceivers along the current seam where the freshwater meets salt — that temperature break is doing exactly what it should, concentrating bait and pulling bass up onto it.
