Around Peaks Island, the backside drop-off has been producing schoolie bass to twenty-four inches on soft plastics — five-inch pearl white Slug-Go's on a quarter-ounce jighead, cast up-current and let it swing through the eddy. Nothing enormous, but steady enough that I've put fish in the boat four days out of five.

Cape Small and the outer Harpswell coves have been my most consistent bass water for size. I had a morning last week where three fish over thirty inches came off a ledge just inside Cape Small on topwater poppers at first light — that's the kind of window where the tide, the light, and the bait all line up for maybe ninety minutes before the sun gets too high and the fish slide back down into the depth. Once that happens, switching to a bucktail worked slow along bottom in fifteen to twenty feet has kept the bite going through midday, though the pace slows considerably.

Mackerel are the disappointment of the season so far. The big May runs that light up the whole bay have thinned out, and what's left is scattered and unpredictable — a school here off Jewell Island one day, gone the next. If you find them, small painted diamond jigs or a string of mackerel flies will still produce fast, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. They've become a bonus rather than a target, and that's worth knowing before you burn a morning looking.

Bluefish have shown up in modest numbers mixed with whatever bait schools are moving through the outer bay — nothing like the blitzes you'd hear about further south, but enough that a few boats working near Halfway Rock have picked up cocktail blues in the two to four pound range on small metal lures. It's not a dedicated fishery yet up here, more an incidental catch while you're jigging for pollock, but worth keeping a rod rigged with wire if you're seeing bait get nervous on the surface.

Looking ahead, the moon will start easing off its peak influence by the weekend, which should settle the tides back into a more workable rhythm — less of the aggressive slack-to-full-run swing we've had at the Rock, and more of a gradual build that gives you a longer fishing window rather than a short, sharp one. That's good news for anyone wanting to fish groundfish structure without watching the clock so closely. I'd expect the bass pattern to hold steady as long as we don't get a stretch of unusually warm, still weather that pushes surface temps up and pushes the fish deeper during daylight. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the early flood at Cape Small for bass, then run out to Halfway Rock on the tail of that same tide to work the pollock before the current builds too hard to hold bottom. Bring layers — the fog's been rolling in most mornings, and it doesn't burn off until well past nine most days out here.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool Incoming Still Wins: Bass to 28, Blues Crashing Peanut Bunker at Pine Point
reports.subhead: The Pool did what the Pool does at first light, and the bunker run finally dragged the blues into the back creeks like we said it would.
reports.body_markdown:
Six-fifteen Tuesday morning, incoming water just starting to push through the Pool channel, and I put a 9-inch black Danny Plug across the current seam off the eastern shore. Second cast, fish nearly ripped the rod out of my hand. Twenty-eight inches, fat, full of herring, came off the outer bar where the tide funnels bait past those rocks like a conveyor belt. That's the Pool for you — best hour in Maine striper fishing, and it doesn't care what the calendar says. Water's been running cooler up here than anywhere south of us, and that's exactly why this pattern holds through August when guys in Massachusetts are stuck fishing the dead of night.

That's the story of the whole zone right now. Gulf of Maine water stays honest — not warm-bath stuff like the Sound or the Vineyard — so our bass haven't gone nocturnal on us the way they do south of the Cape. You can still find them working daylight in the river mouths and around current-swept structure, especially the first two hours of an incoming tide when the bait gets pushed hard against the rocks. Biddeford Pool remains the textbook version of that pattern — fish staged on the flood, working the mouth where the river dumps into the Pool, then sliding back out as the tide slacks. I've had my best luck an hour before high, working topwater over the flats before the sun gets too high, then switching to a swimming plug worked slow along the channel edge once the light comes up.

Pine Point and the Scarborough marsh system have turned into the other story this week, and it's one we saw building. Peanut bunker have been thickening up in those back creeks for two weeks now, and the cocktail blues finally caught up to them — smaller fish, one to three pounds, but stacked tight and mean, blowing up on the surface right at the mouth of the marsh on the outgoing. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker would pull the blues into the back bays — and here it is, right on schedule. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, or a topwater popper if you want the show — thrown right into the boil gets bit instantly. Snapper blues are also thick right in Wells Harbor around the docks, which is good news if you've got a kid with a spinning rod and some worm chunks. Easy, steady action, nothing that'll bend a rod, but it keeps them interested.

Higgins Beach had one real blitz this week, Thursday evening, southwest wind pushing bait up against the beach and the blues came in hot for about forty minutes right at the base of the rocks toward the Cape Elizabeth end. Guys throwing poppers and Hopkins spoons got into fish in the three-to-five-pound range mixed with schoolie bass working the same push of bait. That window closed fast — by dark it was over, and Friday and Saturday it never repeated. That's the honest read on Higgins right now: when the wind sets up right and the bait's pinned against the beach, it can go off in a hurry, but it's not an every-evening thing. I'd check it at dusk on any day with a light southwest breeze and moving bait, but don't plan your whole week around it.

Prouts Neck has been fishing the way it always does on a southwest wind — the ledges on the ocean side load up with bait and bass tuck in behind the rocks working the current seams. I worked the outer ledges Sunday morning with a bucktail, three-quarter ounce with a white curly tail trailer, working it slow along bottom in eighteen to twenty-two feet, and picked up two schoolies and one 24-inch fish that ate right at the base of the rocks where the wash meets the calmer water. Nothing to write home about volume-wise, but quality water, and worth the walk out if the wind cooperates.

Mackerel schools are still thick along the whole stretch from Ogunquit down through Cape Elizabeth, and that's been the difference-maker for anyone fishing bait instead of plugs. Snag a few mackerel off the rocks with a Sabiki rig, then drift one live or cut fresh under a slip float around structure — that's produced some of the better bass this month, including a couple of overslot fish reported out of the Kennebunk River mouth on the tail of the outgoing.

Flounder fishing has been steady but unspectacular in Wells Harbor and up in the Kennebunk River — bloodworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished the last two hours of the outgoing where the current slows over the mud. Nothing huge, but a limit of dinner flounder isn't hard to come by if you're patient. Cod remain a boat game — the deeper ledges off Cape Elizabeth are still holding fish for guys jigging diamond jigs in sixty to eighty feet, though the bite's been more consistent early in the morning before the boat traffic picks up.

Tides have been running big all week off that moon, which sharpened the bite windows at the Pool and at Prouts but also made some of the beach fishing tougher — current ripping too hard through the middle two hours to hold bottom comfortably. That should ease up some over the next several days as we move off the peak lunar push, settling things into a more standard rhythm. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at Biddeford Pool on the incoming, first two hours of daylight, throwing a swimming plug along that channel edge. If the southwest wind holds through the weekend, Prouts Neck deserves a look too — that pattern rarely lets you down when the wind sets up right.

reports.headline: 180 feet of mud off the Ledge is stacked with haddock; the gravel's holding shorts
reports.subhead: Bluefin sign is building on the north end of Jeffrey's while the bottom bite settles into a steady, honest pattern.
reports.body_markdown:
One-eighty feet, soft mud, marks stacked eight to twelve feet off bottom on the sounder — that's the read on the west side of Jeffrey's Ledge right now, and it's been the most consistent thing I've run this month. Haddock don't care much about the calendar once they find a mud flat with sand eels working through it, and that's exactly what we've got between the 42°N line and the deeper basin edge north of Tillies. Clam bellies and squid strips on standard haddock rigs, two hooks, six ounces of lead to hold in the current, and you're not waiting long between bites. Average fish this week has been 20 to 24 inches, with enough 3- and 4-pound fish mixed in to make the bushel baskets heavy by noon.

The gravel is a different story, and it's the honest part of this report. Cod on the hard bottom — the classic humps and boulder edges on the east side of the Ledge, 130 to 160 feet — have been there, but they've been small. Plenty of 16 to 19 inch fish coming over the rail, a few keepers pushing 24, 25 inches mixed in, but nothing like the slow, heavy cod bite we want to see building into fall. I fished three trips out to the gravel this week and connected on legal cod every time, but it took working four or five different pieces of structure to put five keepers in the box. Jigs — the diamond jigs and the newer glow-tipped teasers — are outfishing bait on the gravel right now, probably because there's enough bait activity up in the water column that the fish aren't glued to the bottom the way they are in deep winter. If you're going after cod specifically, fish the up-current side of the humps on the drift, let the jig fall all the way to bottom, and work it up ten or fifteen feet before resetting. Don't waste time on a piece that doesn't show fish in the first two drifts — move.

Pollock have been a nice bonus on both bottom types, hitting jigs meant for cod up higher in the water column, sometimes 40 or 50 feet off bottom over structure. If you mark a school suspended mid-water on the sounder near the gravel edges, that's pollock, and they'll hit a bucktail or a diamond jig worked with a fast erratic retrieve better than anything worked slow.

Now the part I know everybody's asking about — the tuna. We're seeing bluefin sign build on the north end of Jeffrey's and up around the Stellwagen approaches, which is right on schedule for mid-August. Bait is the key here: mackerel schools have been thick on the surface in patches, and where you find the mackerel balled up and nervous, that's where the bluefin are working. I haven't seen the giant class fish yet — that's an October pattern once the herring and mackerel really concentrate along the ledge edge — but we're getting reports of school-size fish, 60 to 100 pounds, working bait on top early in the morning and again toward evening. Green stick and chunk baits both have accounted for fish this week, chunked mackerel drifted back on circle hooks in a slick, no weight, letting it settle naturally with the tide. If you're set up for it, keep the spread light and quiet — these fish have been touchy, showing on top for ten or fifteen minutes and then disappearing, which tells me they're moving through rather than holding tight to one piece of structure yet.

Hake have shown up in the deeper basin water, Scantum Basin especially, on the same mud that's holding haddock but usually a little deeper, 200 feet plus. If you're marking soft returns low to bottom and the haddock bite goes quiet for a stretch, drop a bait down and let it sit — hake will often save what would otherwise be a slow hour.

Wind's been manageable this week, nothing that's kept me off the Ledge, and the tide has been running with enough push on the mud to keep bait moving and haddock feeding through most of the day rather than just at the change. That's the kind of steady current pattern that makes the mud bite reliable rather than a two-hour window you have to hit exactly right.

Looking ahead, I expect the haddock bite on the mud to hold through the week — that pattern doesn't shift fast once it's established, and there's no reason to think the sand eels are clearing out anytime soon. The gravel cod should improve some as water starts to cool into September, but right now I'd plan a trip around the mud if numbers matter more to you than size. For the tuna, if the mackerel schools stay put on the north end through the weekend, that's where I'd spend a morning — but I'd have groundfish gear rigged as a backup, because that bluefin sign has been here-today-gone-tomorrow more than it's been a sure thing. Worth the run out if you can get an early start and the wind stays under 15.

reports.headline: Appledore Cod on the Slack, Stripers Working the Piscataqua All Day
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which fifteen feet of it holds fish.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and think there's nothing to say. I've got a 20-foot Lund and I fish this stretch like it's a hundred and thirty. The Shoals alone will eat a whole season if you let them, and this week they did exactly that for me — cod on the backside of Appledore before most folks had their coffee, stripers running the Piscataqua all day long because the Gulf of Maine hasn't caught the fever the water south of the Cape has.

That's the story right now. South of Cape Cod stripers have gone nocturnal, hugging bunker schools after dark because the water's too warm to move much in daylight. We don't have that problem up here. The Piscataqua stays cool enough, current-scrubbed enough, that stripers will feed right through the middle of the day if the tide's moving. I had fish Tuesday at 11am off the Memorial Bridge pilings, working the seam where the current split around the pier on a strong outgoing — big bucktails, 2-ounce white, bounced slow along bottom in 25 feet. Two fish over 30 inches, a handful of schoolies mixed in chasing the same current line. Dover Point does the same thing on the right tide — anchor up-current of the point, live mackerel or a chunk of pogy on a fish-finder rig, let it sit in the seam. The full moon this week has been running a stiffer tide than normal, and that stiffer current is exactly what wakes these fish up off the bottom structure.

Hampton Harbor's fishing more like a classic August pattern — stripers pushing through the inlet on the incoming, working the sandbars off Hampton Beach and the flats inside toward the marsh. Best window is the last two hours of the flood into the top, right as bait gets squeezed through the cut. Soft plastics, 4-inch white Slug-Go on a light jighead, or a popper at first light if you want to see it happen. There are cocktail bluefish mixed in there too now, chasing peanut bunker that's been thickening up in the back channels all month — small blues, a pound or two, but they'll hit anything that moves fast, and on a light spinning rod they're more fun than they get credit for. We said a couple weeks back that once the peanut bunker spread out, the back-bay blues would follow — that's exactly what's showing up in Hampton now.

Offshore, the Isles of Shoals are still producing cod, but you have to fish them right. Appledore's back ledges and the water off Duck Island are holding fish in 65 to 85 feet, and the bite window is tight — dead slack tide, either top or bottom, is when they'll come up off bottom and hit. I've been jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, working it just off the rocks where the structure drops. Missed the slack by twenty minutes on Thursday and the bite shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's the Shoals in August — precise, not generous.

Haddock have pushed further out than the Shoals proper. If you want haddock this time of year you're running to Jeffrey's Ledge, 180 to 220 feet, and that's a different kind of day — bigger boat, bait rigs or jigs worked slow off bottom, and you're looking at a full tide cycle out there to make it worth the run. Worth doing if the weather cooperates, but I wouldn't send a small trailer boat out there without a real weather window. Check the forecast twice.

Mackerel are thinning the way they always do once August water settles in warm. Rye Harbor mornings still produce — I had a dozen in twenty minutes on a mackerel tree off the harbor entrance at first light — but the schools are smaller and more scattered than June. If you want a bait bucket full for stripers or cod, get out there at dawn before the sun gets on the water.

Flounder are the one species I can't give you much on right now. Deep holes in the Piscataqua below the Route 4 bridge still hold a few blackbacks on bloodworms and sandworms, fished on the bottom on the slower stages of the tide, but this isn't peak flounder season and I wouldn't plan a trip around it.

Looking ahead, that full moon current should start easing off over the next few days, which usually settles the Shoals slack-tide bite back into a more predictable window rather than the compressed ten-minute pockets we've had. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light, I'd fish Appledore at first light on the morning slack and be back at the dock with a box of cod before the day boats even clear the harbor. If it swings onshore and kicks up the swell around the Shoals, I'd stay inside and work the Piscataqua current seams instead — that bite doesn't care much what the wind's doing offshore.

reports.headline: Peanut bunker pile into the breachways — blues on top, tog gone quiet on the ledges
reports.subhead: Full moon current is stacking bait at Charlestown and Weekapaug while the tog slide deep and the albies stay offshore for now.
reports.body_markdown:
Walked out on the rocks at Beavertail Tuesday morning and the bait told me everything I needed to know before I made a cast. Peanut bunker, thick as smoke, pushed up against the ledge on the last of the incoming, with silversides working the edges where the current split around the boulders. That's the tell this time of year — when the peanuts show that heavy along the rock, the blues aren't far behind, and sure enough I didn't have to wait long.

We flagged this a week back — said the peanut bunker spread would pull cocktail blues into the back bays and breachways inside two weeks, and here it is showing up right on schedule. Charlestown Breachway and the mouth at Weekapaug both had that nervous water Wednesday evening, bunker skipping on top, blues underneath cutting through them. Small Hopkins and half-ounce Deadly Dicks worked fine once you found the school, but honestly a bare bucktail with a strip of squid outfished the metal on the slower tide stages — these aren't the giant choppers yet, mostly 2 to 4 pound cocktails, but they hit like they mean it and they're consistent, which counts for something in August.

The full moon has the current running hard through all the breachways right now, and that's been the story for bass too, just not in daylight. Striped bass have gone strict low-light on me the last two weeks — nothing surprising given how warm it's sitting, but the pattern's been reliable if you're willing to fish the dark. Sakonnet River mouth on the last two hours of the outgoing has produced the better fish, stripers sitting on the current seam waiting on bunker and eels getting pushed out of the river. I've had my best luck there with a swimming plug worked slow just off the seam, right at the color change where the river water meets the Sound. Jamestown's breakwaters near the bridge have held fish too, but it's a short window — an hour either side of the tide change before the current gets unmanageable for anything but bait fishermen.

Tog have been tough, and I'll say that plain instead of dressing it up. This heat pushes them tight into the cracks and they don't want to move much off the bottom. I worked the ledges off Beavertail and out toward Brenton Reef on green crabs, fishing the slack right at the top of the tide when the current eases enough to hold bottom without dragging a ton of lead. Got a couple keeper-class fish out of maybe fifteen bites, most of which were just pickers stripping the crab clean off the hook. If you want tog this week, fish smaller pieces, half a crab instead of a whole one, and be patient — the good bite's still six weeks out when the water starts to slide the other direction.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing going, which tracks with how it's gone everywhere south of the Cape this summer. The channel edge at Charlestown Breachway on the dropping tide has been steady — 4 to 5 pound fish mixed with a lot of shorts, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper cut. Watch Hill Ledges and the water off Napatree Point have fished similarly on the outgoing, a little deeper, 25 to 30 feet, and worth the extra run if the breachway's crowded on a weekend tide.

Scup are about the one thing you can set a watch by right now. Newport Bridge pilings and the rocks off Jamestown have been thick with them all week, small hooks, squid strips or sandworms, any depth near structure. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the kind of steady action that keeps a rod bent while you're waiting on the tide to turn for something bigger.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't tell you otherwise. The bait's building the way it needs to — peanut bunker, bay anchovies starting to show along Second Beach and out toward Sakonnet Point — but the fish themselves haven't pushed into the breachways. Historically that first wave doesn't show at Napatree or Watch Hill until late in the month, sometimes not until the first week of September, and this year doesn't feel early. Worth watching the bait daily from here, because when the albies do show, it's usually fast — one morning nothing, the next morning boils all through the mouth of the breachway.

Looking ahead, the moon starts easing off full by the weekend, which should settle these breachway currents back into something a little more fishable for the tog crowd and take some of the sting out of the bass bite timing. If the wind stays light out of the south, I'd put my time into the Sakonnet mouth at first light and the Charlestown edge on the evening outgoing — that's where the bait's been heaviest and the fish have been the most honest about showing up.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:52: Bass Holding Deep, Bonito Knocking on Block Island's Door
reports.subhead: Full moon current is stacking bait on the Ledge and pushing the first bonito scouts toward Rhode Island water — here's where to be when they arrive.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack water at SW Ledge hit 6:52 this morning. I had the boat parked over 55 feet, right on the eastern edge where the ledge drops into the channel, and for about eighteen minutes the current went dead flat before the flood started building out of the south. That window is everything right now. With this full moon pushing exaggerated tidal current all week, the difference between fishing the Ledge at slack versus fishing it twenty minutes into the flood is the difference between marking bait and marking nothing.

Striped bass are still here, but they've gone strictly low-light on me, same as everywhere south of the Cape this time of year. The water up top is warm enough that daytime fishing over the Ledge is mostly a formality — I'm marking fish deep, hugging the structure, refusing to come up and chase anything until the sun drops or the current really starts ripping. My best bass this week came at last light and into full dark, working the down-current side of the Ledge with big Savage Gear sand eels and 2-ounce bucktails dressed with white pork rind, bounced slow along bottom in 45 to 60 feet as the tide turned to flood. Two fish over 30 pounds came off that drift Tuesday night, both in the same fifteen-minute stretch right as the current hit its peak push. That's the pattern — find the peak of the tide, not the beginning or the end, and be ready when it happens.

Now the bonito. We flagged this ten days ago — said the sequence would run RI breachways and the Vineyard rips first, then Block and Montauk behind that within the week. That's exactly how it's playing out. The Race and Fishers Island Sound are seeing real bonito now, and Vineyard boats are reporting fish on the south side. Nothing confirmed yet right off Sandy Point or North Light, but every year the pattern is the same — those fish work west and south along the warm edge until they hit the rip lines off the Block, and with surface temps holding in that favorable low-to-mid 70s band, I don't think we're more than a few days out. I've got small Deadly Dick and Deceiver patterns rigged and ready on 20-pound fluoro leader, because when they show at Sandy Point or the rip off North Light, it happens fast and it happens in a tight window on the tide change. I'll be running the east side of the island at first light starting this weekend, watching for diving terns and nervous water. If you're headed out there, don't wait for someone else to confirm it — the first wave always comes and goes before word gets around.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going, and the full moon swing is actually helping here rather than hurting. Doormats are sitting on the channel edges off Block Island — the drop-off south of the harbor entrance and the deeper water off Charlestown Breachway corridor — where the current stays cooler and keeps bait pinned against structure. I'm dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, on the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming when the drift speed is manageable. Landed a 7-pounder Wednesday in 38 feet drifting the edge of the Ledge itself, right where the sand gives way to rock — that transition line is holding fish all week.

Sea bass remain steady out on the reef structure south of the island, particularly the rockier stretches off Clay Head where the bottom breaks up hard. They're sitting right around the thermocline, same as they have all summer, so I'm fishing high-low rigs with squid strips and Gulp, working depths from 50 to 70 feet. Nothing spectacular, but a consistent fifteen-to-twenty keeper day if you put in the bottom time and move when the marks thin out.

Bluefish have been mostly a bait story. Snapper blues are thick in the Great Salt Pond and back in the Galilee channels, which is good news for anyone with a kid and a bobber rig. The adult blues are out there too but they're staying tight to bunker schools rather than spreading across open water — I've seen a few showers of bait get worked over off Sandy Point at dawn, gulls diving hard, blues slashing through peanut bunker for five or ten minutes before it shuts off just as fast as it started. If you see that happen, don't waste time — get a metal in there immediately.

Looking ahead, the moon's still working strong through the weekend before it eases off mid-week, so I'd fish the peak tide pushes at SW Ledge while that current stays exaggerated — it's concentrating both bait and bass right now. And I'd keep one eye on Sandy Point and the North Light rip every morning this week for those first bonito. Based on how fast they moved into the Race and the Vineyard, Block Island's turn feels close. Worth being out there when it happens rather than reading about it after.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point Holds the Scup, Bass Wait for the Lights to Go Out
reports.subhead: Snapper blues flood Greenwich Bay on peanut bunker, fluke stay steady on the flats, and the bass bite only shows up after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the piers Thursday morning watching a guy unload a five-gallon bucket of scup off a rowboat that had no business being that heavy, and he told me he never left Rocky Point. Didn't need to. That's the bay in August — you don't have to run anywhere. The porgies are stacked on the ledges from Nyatt Point down through Rocky Point in twenty-five to thirty-five feet, and they've been there for weeks. Squid strips and sandworms on a high-low rig, size 6 or 8 hooks, just enough sinker to hold bottom on the tide change. Slack water off the top of the flood is when they really pile on, but even on a hard-running current you can find a lee side of a ledge where they bunch up out of the flow.

The water's warm — upper bay's been running warmer than the lower bay all summer, same gradient you see everywhere from the Sound on down, cooler stuff hanging near the East Passage where the ocean influence pushes in, warmer up in the Providence River and Greenwich Bay. That split matters. It's why the scup bite stays honest on structure while the striper bite has gone strictly nocturnal.

Bass in the bay right now are a dawn-dark-and-midnight fish, full stop. I fished the Jamestown side of the Mount Hope Bridge two nights this week on the last of the outgoing and got into schoolies to about 26 inches on eels, drifted slow along the pilings where the current sets up a seam. Nothing during the day — I tried it, wasted two hours at noon throwing bucktails into water that felt like bathwater, not a sniff. That's the pattern everywhere south of the Cape this time of year: the fish pull back into low light and current-swept structure and sit tight until the sun's off the water. Buckeye Brook's herring are long gone — that run fed the spring push, not this one — so what's holding these bass now is whatever peanut bunker and small baitfish are working the bridge shadows after dark.

Speaking of peanut bunker — we flagged this a week ago, said the back-bay bluefish would track that bait push and the cocktail blues would spike inside two weeks. Well, here it is. Greenwich Bay is thick with snapper blues right now, and mixed into those schools off the mouth of the Providence River I'm seeing better-grade bluefish, two and three pounds, chopping bait on top in the last hour of daylight. Small metal — quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, or a Kastmaster if the wind's got a little chop on it — fished on light mono leader, not wire, because these fish aren't line-shy yet and you want the extra action out of the plug. If you've got kids who want bent rods, this is the trip. Fast, easy, and the blues don't care what time of day it is as long as there's bait in the water.

Fluke are doing what they always do in August around here — steady, not spectacular. Drifting the flats off Prudence Island and the channel edge below Conimicut Point, mostly in eighteen to twenty-eight feet, white and chartreuse Gulp on three-quarter-ounce bucktails. I'm seeing plenty of shorts, a keeper here and there, nothing that's going to make the wall. The better drifts have been on the tail of the outgoing when there's still enough push to keep the bait moving but the water's starting to slack — too much current up there and you're just plowing bottom, too little and the bait doesn't work right.

Weakfish are the interesting wrinkle. We said they'd follow the peanut bunker into the bays through August, and I've had two or three show up mixed into the fluke drifts off Nyatt Point this week — nothing big, mostly short, but they weren't there three weeks ago and now they are. Worth keeping an eye on if you fish light tackle on those flats; a soft plastic worked a touch slower than you would for fluke seems to be what's picking them up.

Looking ahead, the moon's just come off full, so the tides are still running strong through the weekend before they ease back to normal. That means the scup bite should stay locked in on the ledges — more current means more bait movement, more porgies feeding. For bass, I'd keep it simple: fish the last two hours of light into full dark around any bridge or point with current, eels or a swimming plug worked slow along the seam, and don't bother showing up at noon. If the wind stays out of the southwest and keeps this heat sitting on the bay, that low-light pattern isn't going anywhere for a couple more weeks. Best case, we get a cold front push through late in the week that knocks the surface temp down a couple degrees and pulls the bass back into a longer window. Until then, fish the dark, fish the structure, and bring enough squid for the porgies because that bite isn't slowing down.

reports.headline: Wreck 4108 at 140 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds, Mahi Working the Pot Lines
reports.subhead: The tide's ripping harder than it should for August, but the fish that matter are still exactly where twenty years of numbers say they'll be.
reports.body_markdown:
Wreck 4108 sits in 140 feet on the inside lip of the Mud Hole, and it's been holding sea bass to four pounds since the back half of July. That number's in my book from a dozen seasons of marking it, and it hasn't let me down this year either — but I'll tell you straight, the window to fish it clean has gotten narrow. We're coming off a full moon and the current on that wreck at peak tide is moving too fast to hold bottom with anything lighter than an 8-ounce bucktail. I've been running out there for the last of the morning slack, before the tide builds, dropping 6-ounce jigheads tipped with white Gulp Grubs and letting them settle right into the wreck's lee side. That's where the bigger fish are stacked, sitting just above the thermocline where the cooler water holds the bait tight to structure. Once the tide turns hard around mid-morning, I'm off it — no sense burning gas fighting a drift that's dragging your rig sideways across open sand.

Barnegat Ridge has been the more forgiving structure this week. Sixty to ninety feet of water, less current punch than the Mud Hole wrecks, and the sea bass there are smaller on average but steadier — a lot of 14 to 16-inch fish mixed with the occasional keeper pushing three pounds. Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are fishing the same way right now: clam-tipped bucktails or a Gulp swimming mullet on a 3/4-ounce jig, dropped tight to the reef balls on the drift. Shrewsbury Rocks has been quieter than I'd like for mid-August — more short fish than keepers — but it's still worth a stop on the way out if you're running past it anyway.

The story that's actually got my phone ringing this week is the mahi around the pot buoys. There's a real push of warm water sitting on the shelf right now — I was reading almost 79 degrees on the offshore buoy east of the Ridge, which lines up with what I'm seeing on the color change out past the twenty-fathom curve. That warm tongue has pot buoys and loose lobster gear loaded with bait, and where there's bait under a buoy in August, there's mahi cruising the shadow line underneath it. I've had guys casting small poppers and bucktails right up against the buoy and getting hit before the lure even settles. If you find one holding fish, work it slow and quiet — don't run the boat right over it, ease up current and drift down on it. Mahi in the 3 to 8-pound class have been the norm, with a few better fish mixed in for guys willing to put in the buoy-hopping time. It's not every buoy — you might check ten and find fish under two of them — but when you connect, it's worth the search.

Out toward the Klondike and the edge, the yellowfin sign has been real but spotty. The warm eddy positioning that's been feeding the mahi bite is also pulling some school-size yellowfin up onto the temp break, and a couple of the boats running that far have put together respectable days chunking butterfish on the color change, with small tuna spreads — Green Machines and cedar plugs — picking up fish trolling the edge between drops. But I want to be honest about this one: it's a run-and-gun proposition right now. You're covering extra miles to find where that break sits day to day, and not every trip out there connects. If the eddy holds its position through the week the way it has the last several days, that pattern should keep producing. If it slides, the fish move with it, and you're back to searching.

On bluefin, I'll give it to you straight — the Mud Hole lumps have quieted down from where they were a month ago. The bigger class of fish that was working those lumps in June and early July has largely pushed north, and what's left is school-size bluefin passing through early, usually right at first light on bait pods before the boat traffic pushes them down. If you want a shot, be on the water before sunrise with butterfish chunks ready to go the second you mark fish on bait. By eight o'clock, that window's usually closed.

Looking ahead, the moon's starting to ease off full, which should settle those wreck currents back into a more workable rhythm by midweek — good news for anyone planning to fish the deeper Mud Hole structure without fighting a firehose tide. Seas have been running modest, in the 2 to 3-foot range with a manageable period, which is fishable for the run to the Ridge or the edge, but keep an eye on the afternoon sea breeze — it's been building stronger by midweek lately and can turn a comfortable morning run into a sloppy afternoon comeback. If that warm water holds its position off the shelf, I'd keep working the pot lines for mahi and picking away at the wrecks for sea bass on the calmer tide windows. If it pushes further offshore, the yellowfin bite might improve as the break tightens up — worth checking before you commit to the long run.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: C-minus by day, B-plus at first light — bay weakfish picking up the slack
reports.subhead: Stripers are ghosting the rips in August heat, but bluefish, fluke, and a real weakfish bite on the bay side are keeping rods bent.
reports.body_markdown:
Rips get a C this week. Not a failing grade, but nothing to brag about at the dock either. Daytime striper action out at the Rips has been thin to nonexistent — water's warm, sun's high, and those fish know better than to sit in fast current in eighty-degree light. If you want a bass out there right now you're fishing the first hour of gray light or the last hour before dark, working the edge of the Rips where the outgoing current dumps off Cape May Point into deeper water. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped down and bounced slow on the bottom through the seam — that's still putting fish in the box, just not many, and not big. Call it two or three keepers a trip if you're grinding it out, more shorts than you'd like.

What's actually working the Rips right now is bluefish and fluke, and that's where I've been putting my charters. Fluke on the drift over the humps and the deeper stretch between the Rips and the Sub Base grounds, 30 to 45 feet, has been steady — not a doormat bite, but a keeper-a-drift kind of morning on 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the tide. Best window is the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the flood, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your line sideways. Bluefish have been the more consistent player — cocktail blues in the 2 to 4-pound class chopping bait right on the surface at the top of the tide near Hereford Inlet and off the Wildwood jetties. We flagged this a week back, said the peanut bunker moving through the back bays would pull the cocktail blues in tight, and that's exactly what's happening — anglers working the inlet mouth on incoming tide with small metal, half-ounce Kastmasters and Hopkins, are getting steady action, sometimes fish on every other cast when the peanuts get pushed up against the jetty rocks.

Bay side, the drum run is long done — that's a May story, and if you're still calling around Fortescue asking about black drum in August you're a couple months late. What's replaced it is a weakfish bite that's actually worth the drive. We also called this one — said the weakfish would track the peanut bunker into the bay through August, and that's showing up now on the deeper flats and channel edges from Fortescue down toward the mouth of the bay. Squid strips and bloodworms on a simple two-hook bottom rig, fished in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the falling tide and the first hour of the incoming, are producing weakfish in the 16 to 20-inch range, with a few better fish mixed in for guys anchoring tight to the channel drop near Brandywine Shoal. Croaker are riding along in the same spots, which tells you the water's holding that mid-70s warmth the bay likes for this pattern. It's not a fast bite — you're putting in bait time and waiting for the tide to turn things on — but it's real, and it's the most dependable thing going in the bay right now.

Triggerfish have shown up in ones and twos around the nearshore reef structure and wreck sites off the Cape, which happens most Augusts once the water settles into full summer mode. Small hooks, squid or clam, fished right on the structure — not a fishery to plan a whole trip around, but a nice bonus if you're anchored up there for sea bass or tog scraps.

Conditions-wise, we're riding a full moon this week, which means bigger tidal swings than normal — good news and bad news. Good news: it sharpens the bite windows at the Rips and at Hereford Inlet, concentrating bait and fish into tighter time frames right at the tide change. Bad news: if you're not on the water in that window, you're watching flat current and quiet rod tips. The ocean's been carrying a bit of a lump — nothing dangerous, two-to-three foot swell out of the south — but it's enough that I'd rather work the inlet and inside structure than grind it out on an exposed ocean drift this week.

Looking ahead, I expect the pattern to hold through the week — stripers staying nocturnal and picky at the Rips, fluke and bluefish carrying the daytime charters, and the bay weakfish bite building as more peanut bunker push down toward Fortescue and Egg Island. If the moon eases back off full by the weekend, tidal current should settle down a notch, which usually stretches the bite windows out a little longer instead of compressing them into that hard 45-minute slam around the turn. If I had one trip to plan this week, I'd fish the bay on the last two hours of the outgoing for weakfish, then swing over to Hereford Inlet on the incoming to chase the blues while the peanuts are still stacked against the rocks. Two different bites, two different bays — that's the game down here in August, and right now the bay's carrying more weight than the ocean side.

reports.headline: Where'd the Fluke Go? Down in the Guts at Great Egg, Not on the Flats
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker showed up in the back bays right on schedule, and the cocktail blues and weakfish followed them in.
reports.body_markdown:
Every August I get some version of the same question at the dock: "Coach, I'm marking fish all over my graph but I can't buy a bite — what am I missing?" This week it's fluke guys asking it, and the answer is a lesson in water temperature, not luck.

Surf temps have pushed into the high 70s from Brigantine down through Stone Harbor, and that's shoved the fluke off the open sand flats where they were sunning themselves in June and packed them into anything that holds cooler water — channel edges, drop-offs, the deep guts. If you're still drifting the shallow flats behind Ocean City hoping for a repeat of spring, you're fishing empty water. The fish are there, they're just three to five feet lower and tucked against structure where the current keeps things moving.

Great Egg has been my go-to teaching spot this week for exactly that reason. The channel guts running 18 to 25 feet off the Longport side are holding a mixed bag of keeper-class fluke and a stack of shorts, and the pattern only works right on the tide changes — the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low, when the current is still moving enough to keep a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullet ticking bottom without you having to add weight. Slow drifts, short hops, and don't be afraid to let it sit a beat longer than feels natural. The bite window is narrow but it's real — I put a 22-inch fish and two shorts in the cooler Tuesday morning working that exact stretch before the tide went dead and the bite shut off like someone flipped a switch.

Absecon Inlet is fishing the mirror image — better on the push of clean incoming water, not the outgoing. The sod bank edges along the Brigantine side in 12 to 18 feet are worth a look with live killies or spearing on a standard fluke rig, especially as that green ocean water floods in and pushes the murkier bay water back. It's not a red-hot bite. I'd call it honest — enough fish moving through on the tide to make the trip worthwhile, but you're covering water and culling through shorts to find your keepers, not limiting out on the first drift.

Striped bass are behaving exactly like you'd expect with water this warm — they've gone nocturnal on us. Daytime action around Absecon Inlet and the Brigantine jetty rocks has been thin to nonexistent outside a brief window right at first light. If you want bass, be on the water before the sun clears the horizon, working bunker chunks or a swimming plug along the current seams where the inlet rocks meet moving water. Once the sun gets up and that water starts to warm even more, the fish drop down and go quiet until dusk brings them back up.

Here's the part I've been waiting to write about. Two weeks ago I flagged that the peanut bunker moving into these back bays would pull the cocktail blues and weakfish in behind them — and that's exactly what's showing up now. Townsends Inlet has had genuine peanut bunker pods stacking up on the outgoing tide, and the bluefish chewing through them are running two to four pounds, a real step up from the snapper-class fish that have been the summer standard in the back bay channels behind Ocean City and Sea Isle. Small epoxy jigs and quarter-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the peanuts are doing the damage. Weakfish are riding the same bait wave — not a big showing yet, but legitimate keeper-class fish have turned up in the channels behind Stone Harbor and Sea Isle on bucktails tipped with a strip of fluke belly, fished slow along the bottom where the bunker schools are getting pushed by the current.

Kingfish are still working the surf wash at Ocean City and Stone Harbor beaches, same as they have been all summer, but the heat has them on a dawn-and-dusk clock too. Bloodworms or Fishbites on a high-low rig in the first wash line right after sunrise is still the most reliable read — once the beach gets crowded and the sun climbs, that bite fades fast.

We're coming off a full moon, and you can feel it in the current — the tides have been running stronger and the bite windows sharper than normal, which is exactly why timing the turn at these inlets has mattered more than usual this week. That extra push is what's been dragging the peanut bunker and the predators following them through the inlets on schedule. Expect that current strength to ease off gradually over the next several days as we move away from full, which should relax the bite windows back toward a more typical late-summer rhythm — less explosive, but more forgiving if you can't hit the exact tide change.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the inlet drop-offs and back bay channel edges on the tide changes rather than the open flats — that pattern isn't changing while surf temps sit in the high 70s. If the afternoon sea breeze builds like it typically does mid-August, expect some chop and discolored water on the open beach fronts by midweek, which would push me further into the protected inlet structure at Great Egg and Townsends rather than fighting it on the sand.

reports.headline: Holgate Rip Reshapes on the SW Swell — Fluke Hold the New Drop
reports.subhead: A slow, stubborn south swell rebuilt the bar off the third bowl, and the fluke found the new edge before the rods did.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate flat at dead low Tuesday, drone up, coffee going cold in the truck, and the cut that's fed us all summer wasn't sitting where I left it. We've been eating a soft SSW groundswell for close to two weeks now — nothing violent, 2 to 3 feet at six seconds, but steady enough to move sand every single tide cycle. It pushed a new bar up inside the old slough off the third bowl and cut a deeper trough on the ocean side of it than anything we had back in July. That's the kind of quiet reshuffle a lot of guys walk right past. The old spot looks the same from the dune line. It isn't the same underwater, and the fish already know it.

Fluke found that new drop first. I had three keepers and a mess of shorts off the edge of it Wednesday on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a 3/4-oz white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragging it slow off the lip where the trough meets the flat. Water on the ocean side is running warm — the open Atlantic buoy off the coast is reading near 79 degrees — so the fluke are doing exactly what they do this time of year: sitting on the coolest, most current-scrubbed structure they can find instead of baking on the flats. That new Holgate trough qualifies. So does the Little Egg Inlet channel edge on the Holgate side, where the bend narrows the current and doormats have been stacking on the last of the ebb — 5 and 6 pounders coming off there this week on Berkley Gulp in chartreuse, bounced right on bottom in 18 to 22 feet. Graveling Point's channel drop into the Mullica is fishing the same way — cooler, current-swept, holding fish while the surrounding bay flats sit warm and quiet.

Striped bass are a night fishery right now, full stop. Daytime heat has them locked down everywhere except river mouths and hard current seams, and LBI is no exception. The bite window is dawn, dusk, and full dark around bait schools, and Barnegat Light's north jetty has been the most consistent of those windows — bunker spooks and darters worked on the last two hours of the incoming, right where the light current pushes bait against the rocks. Nothing giant, mostly 24 to 30 inches with the occasional overslot mixed in, but it's a real bite if you're willing to fish it at 5 a.m. instead of 5 p.m. Little Egg Inlet mouth has produced the same pattern after dark, plugs worked along the current edge where the inlet dumps into the ocean.

Snapper blues are thick in Great Bay and up into the Mullica creeks, and that's not a surprise — we flagged two weeks back that peanut bunker would push a cocktail blue spike as that bait spread through the back bays, and that's exactly what's happening now. Kids on the docks in Beach Haven and Ship Bottom are having a field day on small Kastmasters and Gotcha plugs, and the adult blues are riding right alongside those bait schools at the inlet mouths — Little Egg and Barnegat Inlet both holding 3 to 5 pound cocktail blues chopping peanut bunker on the surface in the first hour of light. If you see the birds working tight over nervous water at the inlet, that's your invitation. Don't overthink the presentation — a straight metal retrieve through the school is all it takes.

Weakfish are doing the same math. We called this one too — peanut bunker pulling weakfish into the bay system through August — and Graveling Point and the mouth of the Mullica have both given up keeper weakfish this week on bunker chunks and soft plastics fished on the bottom during the last of the outgoing, when the current concentrates that bait against the channel edge. It's not a banner bite, a couple fish an outing if you put the time in, but it's real and it's better than it's been in a couple summers.

Kingfish are scattered through the surf troughs from Ship Bottom down to Holgate, small numbers on bloodworms and Fishbites in the wash, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus if you're already out there for fluke or bass. Black drum season on the bay flats has faded — that's a spring pattern and it's closed the book for the year. Tautog stays closed through the summer, as always, so don't waste a drift on the wrecks looking for them.

The moon just came off full, and that extra current strength sharpened the tide-change bites all week — you could feel it pulling harder than normal through the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb. That's going to ease back over the next several days as we move off the full moon, which usually settles the bite windows into a more predictable rhythm rather than the exaggerated push we just had. If I've got one day this week, I'm fishing that new Holgate trough on the outgoing with bucktails, then sliding to Barnegat Light at last light for bass around the bunker. Watch the swell — if it stays in this same soft SSW pattern, expect the sandbars to keep shifting week to week, and the guys who walk the beach and actually look at the cut before they cast are going to keep cashing in on structure nobody else has found yet.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke on the Drift, Weakfish Sliding Into the Sedges on the Peanut Run
reports.subhead: The shallows are pushing past 80 and shoving every fluke, weakfish, and blue claw crab into the channels — here's where to find them.
reports.body_markdown:
I was maybe fourteen the first August I mated on a Point Pleasant boat, and the skipper — old Sal Renna, God rest him — told me something I never forgot. He said, "Gus, in August the bay tells you where it's comfortable, and the fish just follow along." Forty years later I still think about that every time the mercury climbs and the shallows go from bath-warm to downright uncomfortable for anything with fins. That's exactly where we are right now, and it's why the last week of fishing has funneled itself into a handful of very specific places instead of spreading out across the whole bay the way it does in June.

The flats off Tices Shoal and the shallow sod banks up toward Berkeley are pushing near 80 degrees by midafternoon, and that's simply too warm for a self-respecting fluke or weakfish to sit in comfortably all day. What that's done is stack both species into the deeper, current-scrubbed structure — Double Creek Channel most of all. I've had three good drifts through there this week on the last two hours of the outgoing, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet along the drop where the channel falls from six feet down to twelve. Keeper fluke to five pounds have come off that edge, with the better fish holding right where the sandy slope meets the harder mud bottom — that's the spot where the bait gets funneled and pinned by the tide, and the doormats know it.

Weakfish have been the pleasant surprise. We flagged this trend back at the start of the month — figured the peanut bunker would push south and pull weakfish right into the bay with them through August — and that's exactly what's happening now. I've been finding schools of weakfish holding along the sedge banks south of Oyster Creek, particularly where the marsh grass gives way to a slightly deeper cut, on the last of the incoming tide. Small bucktails in pink or chartreuse, or a plain Kahle hook with a live killie under a slip float, worked slow along the edge of the grass has been the ticket. These aren't the 5-pound tiderunners we see in May off the same water, more 16 to 19 inches, but they're eating with some confidence in the low light of early morning and again right at dusk.

Speaking of low light — that's become the whole game for striped bass right now. Daytime bay temperatures have shut down the bite almost everywhere except right around the inlet structure and the cooler water pushing out of Oyster Creek's mouth on a strong ebb. Barnegat Inlet itself has been holding some bass around the rocks on the jetty side, particularly at first light when there's still a little chill in the air and bunker pods are working the surface. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, or a bunker chunk fished tight to the rocks on the bottom half of the outgoing, has produced fish in the 20-to-28-inch range with the occasional better one mixed in after dark. If you want a shot at a bigger bass, I'd rather be out there at 5 a.m. or after 9 p.m. than fighting the heat at noon — the fish simply aren't interested in daytime feeding right now, not in the bay, not with this water temperature.

Snapper blues are doing exactly what they do every August — thick as fleas in the shallows off Good Luck Point, up in the Toms River mouth, and along the docks in Forked River, chasing bay anchovies and rain bait in schools you can see dimpling the surface on a calm evening. Small Kastmasters, or a 1/16-ounce jig under a bobber for the kids, will get bit on nearly every cast. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the best thing going for teaching a kid to cast and catch something that fights back, and I'd argue it's the backbone of how most of us on this bay got started in the first place.

The adult bluefish have stayed mostly offshore and out toward the inlet edges, mixing into bait schools when the bunker push through — nothing like a blitz, but worth a look if you're running out past Barnegat Light on the right tide.

Blue claw crabbing has stayed strong right through this heat, which tells you something about how comfortable the crabs are with warm, slightly brackish water even when the fish are struggling with it. Bunker heads and chicken necks off any dock along the Metedeconk or up in Silver Bay have been producing full baskets most evenings.

The full moon this week has put some extra push into the tides, and I've noticed the bite windows at the channel edges — Double Creek especially — sharpening up right around the peak of the current rather than spreading out lazily like they do on a neap tide. If you're planning your week around one trip, I'd put myself on Double Creek an hour before the top of the outgoing, working that channel edge with bucktail and Gulp, then slide over to the Oyster Creek sedges as the tide bottoms out and starts to turn, right when the weakfish seem most willing to commit. As the moon works past full over the next few days, expect that exaggerated current to ease back to something more normal — which usually means the bite windows widen out again, even if they don't hit quite as hard in the moment. Keep an eye on the wind, too; a stiff afternoon southwesterly can turn the open bay chalky by midday, and that's when I'd rather be tucked into the channels anyway.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Bass on Bunker, Gone by Sunrise
reports.subhead: The stripers are a flashlight fishery right now — but the full moon tide is turning the fluke bite into the best reason to be out there.
reports.body_markdown:
Four-forty in the morning, low tide just starting to turn, and there were already two guys camped on the north jetty at Manasquan Inlet when I pulled up — headlamps off, standing dead still, watching a bunker pod nervous up against the rocks. That's the tell this time of year. You don't hear stripers in August, you feel the water change. One guy was working a Super Strike Little Neck popper, slow cadence, letting it sit dead in the wash between twitches. Took him maybe fifteen casts before something T-boned it right at the base of the jetty in maybe six feet of water. Fish went about 27 inches — good keeper, not a cow, but a real fish on a real cast, and by the time the sky started going gray he'd already put his rod down. That's the whole window right there. Fifteen, twenty minutes of gray light before the sun gets over the horizon, and then it's over. The water's too warm for these fish to keep working the rocks once there's light on it — they're pushed into a strict low-light pattern from Sea Bright down to Manasquan right now, and if you're not on the rocks casting before 5:15, you missed it.

Sea Bright's been the better bet for the dawn bass lately, honestly, because that stretch sits close enough to the Hook that it's catching the tail end of the bigger bunker schools working down from Raritan Bay. Guys throwing bunker-colored Danny plugs and darters off the rocks near the old fishing pier have had short windows of real violence — blitzy, five-minute flurries when a school gets pinned against structure — but it shuts off fast once the sun's up and the bait scatters. If you want a shot at that, fish the last hour of the outgoing on a falling tide when bunker get squeezed against the jetty face, and be ready to leave your rod rigged the second you see nervous water.

Once the sun's up, though, the real story on this beat is fluke, and it's been the more honest fishery all week. We're coming off the full moon and that extra tidal push has sharpened the drift bite noticeably at both inlets. Manasquan Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the better of the two — work the channel edge off the Route 71 bridge down toward the jetty tips, 18 to 28 feet, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets, slow enough that you feel bottom every third or fourth pump. Shark River Inlet's producing too, mostly on the incoming this week, same depth range along the north side channel near the Belmar side — a few keepers to 22 inches mixed with a lot of shorts, which tells you there's a strong year class coming through but the doormats are still scattered. Nobody's filling a cooler. Guys are grinding out two or three keepers on a good tide and going home satisfied, which for August fluke around here is about right. If the moon-driven current keeps the tide changes crisp through midweek, I'd expect that bite to hold — once it eases off toward the new moon, the drift slows and you'll need to work harder for the same fish.

Bluefish have been the more reliable action for anybody who just wants bent rods, and it's split into two distinct fisheries right now. Back in Shark River and up in the Manasquan back bay canals, snapper blues have gone thick — small, aggressive, snapping at anything shiny. Kids on the docks with a bobber and a sliver of bunker are having a field day, and there's a real run of slightly bigger cocktail blues mixed in behind them, which lines up with something we flagged last week — that the peanut bunker pushing into the back bays would pull the bigger blues in behind them inside of two weeks. That's exactly what's happening now, just a little ahead of schedule. Small wire leaders, quarter-ounce Kastmasters or a strip of bunker under a float, fish it on the last of the incoming when the bait gets pushed up into the creeks.

Out front, adult bluefish are still mixing into the bunker schools that show up at classic pinch points, and Sea Bright sits right at the bottom edge of that pattern coming down off Sandy Hook. If you catch a morning when the bunker get bunched tight against the rocks, don't be surprised if it's blues doing the damage instead of bass — they'll hit the same swimming plugs and poppers, just with more violence and less finesse.

No sign of albies yet, and it's early for them on this stretch — that's more a late-September story once the water starts to slide backward. Blackfish are closed this time of year regardless, so don't waste your bunker on the rock piles hoping for tog; that's an autumn program. Porgy trips out of Belmar and Manasquan have been steady but unspectacular, mostly a bottom-bouncing affair on the deeper structure for guys who just want dinner.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the early window for bass — dawn and the last light of dusk, structure-tight, bunker-driven, and gone the second the sun gets high. The fluke bite should stay sharp through the next couple of tide cycles while the moon's influence holds, then I'd expect it to soften a bit as we drift toward the new moon. If I only had one morning this week, I'd be on the Manasquan jetty at first light with a popper in hand, and I'd have a bucktail rigged in the truck for when the bass shut down and the fluke tide turns.

reports.headline: Race at 5.8 Knots: Bass Come Wire-Line, First Bonito Scouts at Valiant
reports.subhead: A brutal full-moon current is compressing every bite into a narrow slack window — but that window is producing quality fish, and the first bonito are finally showing at the Race.
reports.body_markdown:
Five point eight knots. That's what the max ebb ran through the Race on Tuesday's peak tide, forty-eight hours off the full moon, and it's the number that dictated everything I did on the water this week. When the Race is moving that hard, you don't fish it — you fish the ten or twelve minutes on either side of the turn, and you'd better know exactly when that turn is coming. At Valiant Rock this week that window has been running roughly six hours off the New London low, and it's been shrinking, not growing, as we push through this moon cycle. Miss it by fifteen minutes and you're not fishing anymore, you're just holding on.

Inside that window, though, the bass have been solid. Wire line has been the difference-maker — 30-foot drops of single-strand behind bunker spoons and small umbrella rigs, worked over the rockpile in 45 to 65 feet on the last hour of ebb sliding into slack. Once the current eases enough to hold bottom contact, I've been switching guys over to 2-ounce bucktails dressed with white pork rind, dropped tight to the rock and swept with the dying current rather than ripped against it. That subtlety matters right now — New London's reading 69.8 degrees, a solid five degrees cooler than the water sitting up around Kings Point, and that thermal edge is exactly why the bass are stacking on the eastern structure instead of spreading out through the open Sound. Cooler water, hard current, standing rock — that's the recipe, and Valiant and Race Rock have both been holding up their end.

The honest part of this report is that it's not an all-day bite. Outside that slack window, the current is simply too strong to present anything cleanly, and the fish know it — they tuck into the eddies behind the rock and wait it out just like we do. I've had trips where we boated four keeper bass in twenty minutes of slack and then spent the next three hours getting nothing but arm-tired from bucktails skipping off bottom in five knots of push. If you're planning a trip to the Race or Plum Gut this week, build your whole day around that turn. Everything else is just positioning.

Plum Gut itself has been the better bet for fluke over the bass grounds proper. The channel edges on the west side, where the bottom drops from 20 feet down into the 35-to-40-foot cut, have been holding doormats on the tide change — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow with the last of the current before it goes dead. The full-moon tide swing has sharpened that drift bite noticeably; bigger water movement means more bait getting swept off the flats and funneled through the Gut, and the fluke know exactly where to sit and wait for it.

Now for the fish everybody's been asking about. We flagged it last week — said bonito would show at the Race and the Fishers Island Sound corridor within days as temps closed in on that low-70s threshold, and here they are. Small scouting pods, nothing you'd call consistent yet, working bait pushed against the rip line off Little Gull and Great Gull Island. Epoxy jigs — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax in the smaller sizes — on 20-pound fluoro have drawn a handful of strikes on the edges of the current where it's calm enough to see the nervous water. This is not yet a fishery you plan a trip around. It's a fishery you keep gear rigged for while you're doing something else, because when it turns on in this corridor it turns on fast, and next week could be the week it does.

Black sea bass have stayed dependable and unglamorous, which is exactly what you want from them in August. The rockpile structure around Race Rock and the reef edges toward the Sluiceway are holding fish in that 50-to-70-foot range, right around where the thermocline sits this time of year. Diamond jigs tipped with squid, bounced tight to structure on the drift, have been steady without being spectacular — a good backup plan on days when the main current window doesn't cooperate or the wind kills your bonito scouting.

Bluefish have been mixed into the bass activity rather than running their own show — expect that to hold as bunker schools continue pushing through the Gut on their late-summer track. If you're wire-lining for bass and get bit off, don't be surprised if it's a blue instead; they're keying on the same bait right now.

Looking ahead, the moon's strength starts easing over the next several days, which should stretch those slack windows back out to something more forgiving — good news for anyone who's been getting squeezed by these five-plus-knot tides. I'd expect the bonito numbers at the Race and Fishers Island Sound to build through the back half of this week as the current calms and the water holds in that low-70s band. If I had one trip to make, I'd fish the Valiant Rock slack at first light for bass, then run out to the Gull Islands with epoxy jigs rigged and ready the moment the current lays down enough to see fish working.

reports.headline: Sandy Hook's Rip at First Light: Bass on Bunker, Fluke Sharpening on the Channel Edges
reports.subhead: The full moon is stacking current through the Hook this week, and that's the difference between a dead tide and a window worth setting an alarm for.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the call I made this week and I'm sticking with it: dawn at the Rip, then run the channel edges on the back half of the tide. That's the whole game plan right now, and if you try to do both at the wrong hour you'll end up with nothing in the box.

The bay's been sitting mid-to-upper 70s through the day, and that's enough to shut the bass down once the sun gets up. What's kept them honest is the bunker. Pods have been holding tight along the Hook's rips — that seam where the ocean water meets the bay current — and the stripers are using them the same way they do every August: hit hard at first light while there's still low light and a temperature break, then drop back down and go quiet once the heat sets in. I've had two mornings this week where the bunker balled up tight off the Hook right at the top of the tide change, birds working, and it turned into a real window — bass to 34 inches on live bunker under a balloon, and a few more on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right on bottom in 15 to 20 feet. Once the sun climbed, it shut off like someone flipped a switch. If you're going, be there before the light, not after.

The full moon is doing exactly what it should — pushing more water and more current through that rip than we've seen in weeks. That's a double-edged thing. More current means more bait gets pinned and stacked, which is good, but it also means the window is shorter and sharper. I'd rather fish 45 minutes of hard current with fish stacked than three hours of slack water with nothing showing.

Fluke are where I'd point anybody who wants a more dependable day. The channel edges around Flynn's Knoll and down toward Romer Shoal have been the most consistent producers, and that full-moon tide swing is sharpening the drift bite right at the turns. I've been dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets along the drop-offs in 25 to 35 feet, slow and right on bottom, and getting quality fish — nothing enormous, but a steady stream of keepers in the 18 to 21-inch range with the occasional better one mixed in. The edges hold up because the water there stays a few degrees cooler than the flats around them, and this time of year that's the whole story with fluke — they're not spread out anymore, they're pinned to structure where it's comfortable. Keyport Flats has some fluke on it too but it's spottier; I'd treat it as a second stop, not the main event.

Inside the bay, porgies and blowfish are doing the heavy lifting on the slower days, and there's no shame in that — it's meat in the cooler while you wait for the tide to set up for bass or fluke. Bloodworms and clam on high-low rigs over the structure off Old Orchard Shoal and around the bridge pilings near Ward's Point has been steady, nothing spectacular but reliable, which is more than I can say for some of the other stuff this week.

We flagged the peanut bunker push into the back bays a couple weeks back, and it's showing up now — cocktail blues have gotten thick in the Navesink and Shrewsbury, chasing those peanuts around the mouths of the creeks and under the bridges. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — worked fast on the retrieve is all you need. It's light-tackle fun and a good option for an evening trip when the main bay bite is dead flat from the heat.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you, haven't shown much in the bay proper this year. I keep hearing they should be tracking that same peanut bunker push, and maybe they will, but I haven't seen the numbers to back it up around here yet. If you're targeting them specifically, I wouldn't build a whole trip around it — treat any weakfish as a bonus while you're fishing for something else.

Looking ahead, the moon's still carrying extra push through the middle of this week, so I'd keep working the Hook at first light while that current stays strong — if the bunker schools hold their position out there instead of scattering, that early window should keep producing. Once we get a few days past full, the tide swings will settle back down and those bite windows will shrink back to normal length, so if you've got a morning free, I wouldn't wait on it. Keep an eye on the wind too — anything building out of the southwest midweek will put a chop on the Hook's outer edge and make that rip fishing miserable even if the bass are there. Inside the bay stays fishable in almost anything, which is exactly why the channel-edge fluke program is the safer bet if the weather turns.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull's Cool Seam Keeps Bass Honest While the Sound Cooks
reports.subhead: A three-degree edge at the river mouth and a full-moon current are buying daytime bites the open Sound can't offer right now.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the seawall at Fort Trumbull Tuesday morning watching the ebb pile against the point, and you could see the line where it happens — the darker, cooler water sliding out of the river meeting the flatter green stuff off the Ledge Light channel. That seam has been the difference-maker all week. New London's reading right around 70 degrees at the mouth, while Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound is pushing 72 and a half. Three degrees doesn't sound like much until you're the fish deciding whether to sit in the sun all day or duck into the river mouth where the current keeps things moving and the temperature stays civil. Right now the bass are voting with their tails, and they're voting for the Thames.

This time of year the open Sound goes quiet during daylight — the bass shut down and wait for low light, same as they do from Jersey up through the Cape. But river mouths and current-swept structure are the exception, and Fort Trumbull is about as good an exception as this coast has to offer. I've been working the rip on the back half of the ebb, anchoring up-current of the point and letting a 1-ounce bucktail with a white curl-tail trailer swing through the seam on a slow lift-and-drop. Twelve to eighteen feet of water, current still hauling, and the fish are stacked right where the flow bends around the old fort wall. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 30 inches — but a steady pick through the tide change, which is more than I can say for guys who tried the open harbor at noon and came back with nothing to show for it.

Gold Star Bridge has been holding up its end too. The pilings on the downriver side, especially the third and fourth from the Groton shore, are throwing enough current shadow that bass are tucking in tight and ambushing whatever peanut bunker gets swept through. I watched a guide boat working white paddletails on light jigheads — quarter-ounce, maybe three-eighths — right up against the concrete on the last two hours of the ebb, and they were getting bit often enough to keep at it for a solid hour before it went quiet on the slack. Timing matters here more than almost anywhere on the river. Miss the tide window at the bridge and you're just casting at empty concrete.

The full moon has sharpened everything this week — more water moving, harder current, tighter bite windows, but better ones. Dawn and dusk are still your best bets for the river mouth stripers, same pattern holding from here to Montauk. If you can only fish one tide, make it the last two hours of a night or early-morning ebb when the bunker and peanut bunker are getting flushed out past Fort Trumbull and the fish know it.

We flagged this a week back — said the peanut bunker spread would push cocktail blues into the back bays inside two weeks, and it's already showing. The coves off City Pier and up into the mouth of the harbor near the Thames Street docks are thick with snapper blues right now, and there's a noticeable uptick in bigger cocktail-class fish mixed in, 14 to 16 inches, chasing the same bait pods the snappers are working. Small gold Kastmasters and quarter-ounce poppers worked fast on the surface are money for both sizes. Kids on the dock with bobbers and spearing are cleaning up too — it's about as easy an action as this harbor offers all year, and it's a good one to bring a kid out for.

Porgies have settled onto the sandy patches inside the harbor and off Pleasure Beach, six to twelve feet of water, high-low rigs with sandworm or clam. Nothing spectacular in size but steady enough that if the wind's up and you don't want to fight the open Sound, it's a solid fallback. Blackfish are starting to show interest around the riprap at the bridge abutments and the deeper rock piles off Ocean Beach, though it's still early for that pattern to really turn on — I'd call it a bonus fish right now, not a target.

Ocean Beach itself has been quieter than the river — the surf's been mostly schoolies at first light on white soft-plastic swimbaits, nothing to write home about, and the exposed shoreline just isn't holding bait the way the river mouth structure is. If I had one morning this week, I'd spend it at Fort Trumbull on the back of the ebb, and I'd have the bridge pilings as my backup once the current started to lay down.

Looking ahead, the moon's still going to push hard current through the weekend before it starts easing off by midweek. That means the bite windows stay tight and predictable — work the tide changes at the river mouth and the bridge, don't waste tide fishing the middle of the day in open water, and keep an eye on the bunker schools working up past the sub base. If they hold in the river the way they have been, the blues and the bass ought to keep this pattern going through the week.
