If that bait pushes out toward the Race, I'd expect the action to thin out here and pick up out toward Fishers Island Sound instead.

reports.headline: Wamphassuc boulders at first light: bass hugging the rocks, first bonito scouts push into the Sound
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker are pouring through the boulder fields from Ram Island to Watch Hill, and the first bonito of the year showed right where we said they would.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait tells you everything if you slow down enough to watch it. This week off Wamphassuc Point I sat the skiff dead still on the pole for twenty minutes before I made a cast, just watching peanut bunker stack up in the current seam behind a boulder the size of a Buick. They were nervous, balling tight, then scattering, then balling again — the way bait moves when something bigger is working the rocks underneath them but hasn't committed yet. That's the tell. When bunker pin themselves against structure like that in Fishers Island Sound in August, there's a bass sitting in the shadow of that rock waiting for the tide to push the bait into its mouth instead of chasing it down.

Water's held a real gradient across the Sound this stretch — New London reading around 70, noticeably cooler than the western basin — and that cooler eastern water is exactly why the rock game has stayed a dawn-and-dusk proposition rather than an all-day bite. I've been on the water by 5:15, poling the skiff over the boulder fields between Ram Island and the Wamphassuc side before the sun gets hard on the water. Bass are there, but they're tucked tight to structure, not roaming open sand. Soft plastics — 5-inch white or bone Slug-Go rigged weightless, and 4-inch chartreuse-back paddle tails on 1/4-ounce jigheads — worked slow and bumped off the rock faces have out-produced anything with more hardware. You want the lure ticking the top of the boulder, not swimming three feet over it. Fish to 28 inches have come off that pattern, most on the last hour of the outgoing before dead slack, when the current stops shoving the bait around and the bass can finally pin it.

The breakwater at Stonington has fished the same way — a slack-tide, structure-hugging bite rather than a blitz. I had two guys out Wednesday morning working bucktails tipped with Gulp along the inside face of the breakwater on the last of the ebb, and we scratched out a handful of bass in that 24-30 inch window along with two shorts we put back. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but quality fish holding tight to rock, which is the honest read on this water right now — not a blitz, a grind, and you need to fish the rocks correctly to get bit.

Now the news that matters: bonito scouts showed in Fishers Island Sound this week, right in the corridor we flagged as imminent a few days back — the Race, this Sound, and the Vineyard rips were the sequence, and here they are, first fish confirmed exactly where we said they'd show. Watch Hill Reef is the classic early address for this, and I had a report of a small pod working bait on the surface off the reef on a calm morning mid-week. Nobody's sticking numbers yet — these are scouts, not a run — but if you want to be the guy who connects first, get a fly rod or a light spinning outfit rigged with a Deadly Dick or a 1-inch Albie Snax on 20-pound fluoro leader and start checking Watch Hill Reef and the eastern edge of the Sound toward Fishers Island on calm mornings. The water's in the right window for it, mid-to-high 70s inshore, and once these scouts feel comfortable they tend to build fast through the back half of August.

Fluke have been the more dependable player this week, and the full moon tide swing sharpened that bite noticeably. The stronger current through the passages and channel edges around Fishers Island Sound is exactly what doormat fluke want — they sit on the edge of the drop where the current sweeps bait past them, and this week's bigger tidal push concentrated them better than the slack water we had two weeks ago. Drifting the channel edges near Fishers Island with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has been putting keepers in the box, with a few pushing 4 pounds. Best drifts have come on the last two hours of the incoming, when the current's still got some shape to it but isn't ripping so hard you can't hold bottom.

Black sea bass are steady on the deeper structure off Fishers Island and around the rockier stretches near the reef — small strips of squid or clam on a double-hook bottom rig, standard stuff, but they're there in decent numbers if you want a mixed bag day.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the boulder fields at first light while this cooler eastern water keeps bass in a tight structure pattern — Wamphassuc, Esker Point, and the inside of the breakwater are where I'm putting my mornings. And I'd start checking Watch Hill Reef on calm days for those bonito scouts to build into something you can actually target with confidence. If the water keeps trending the way it has, the back half of August should turn this into a real run. Doesn't mean it happens on schedule — but that's where I'd be looking, rod in hand, watching the bait instead of the forecast.

reports.headline: Niantic Boats Grinding Fluke at 40 Feet — Black Point Sea Bass Won't Quit
reports.subhead: Full moon current has the drift bite sharp on the edges, and the first cocktail blues are sneaking into the river right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
Stopped by the dock in Niantic Tuesday morning and one of the mates off the drift boats was still hosing down the deck when he told me Monday's half-day put a dozen keeper fluke in the box, biggest one going better than seven pounds, out on the flat between Twotree Island Channel and the Bay. That's the kind of report that gets repeated at the bait shop by noon, and by the time I got over there myself, every rod holder on the wall had a story attached to it.

Here's what's actually happening out there. New London's holding around 69.8 degrees, which is a solid five, six degrees cooler than what they're dealing with over in the western Sound right now, and that's exactly why this end keeps producing while other zones get squirrely in the heat. The fluke don't want warm water any more than we want to fish in it, and the drop-offs off Black Point and the deeper cuts through Twotree Channel are holding that cooler layer right where the boats are drifting — 35 to 45 feet depending where you set up, current line running clean.

This full moon has put some real push into the tide, and that's sharpening up the bite windows at the changes. Boats that are timing their drifts to the last hour of the ebb and the first hour of the flood are the ones filling the cooler. Standard program: white or chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow right on bottom. When the current's really moving through Twotree, guys are bumping up to an ounce just to stay in contact. Nothing fancy about it — it's a bottom game, and the fish are sitting tight to structure where that current bends around the edges.

Black sea bass have been the steady Eddie all month and nothing's changed. Structure off Black Point and out toward Hole-in-the-Wall is holding fish stacked right around the thermocline, and that's typically 30 to 50 feet this time of year depending on where you're marking bait on the machine. Green crab and squid strips on a standard sea bass rig, two-hook bottom rig with enough weight to hold in the current — 4 to 6 ounces most days. Legal-size fish are mixing with plenty of shorts, so you're sorting through some, but limits aren't hard to come by if you're willing to move around and find the right piece of bottom.

Porgies are doing what porgies do — thick around the same structure, happy to eat whatever you drop, and a great option if you've got kids aboard or just want steady bend in the rod without overthinking it. Sandworms and clam on light tackle, anywhere there's rock or reef from McCook Point out toward the deeper water.

Striper action has gone strictly nocturnal with this heat. Daytime, forget the open Sound — those fish have shut down outside of a few current-swept pockets. But dawn and dusk around bunker schools, especially where the Niantic River empties out and any structure near Black Point that breaks up the current, guys are still connecting. Live-lining bunker or working bucktails through the low-light windows is the play. Don't expect much between 10 and 4 — that's naptime for these fish right now.

Now here's something worth flagging. We said a couple weeks back that as peanut bunker spread through the back bays, the cocktail blues would follow within two weeks — and that's exactly what's showing up in the Niantic River and the shallows around Twotree right now. Snapper-sized and up into cocktail-blue territory, chewing on small metal and epoxy jigs, giving light-tackle guys and kids with spinning rods some genuinely fun action in water that's easy to reach from shore or a small boat. It's not the big adult blues yet, but it's building, and if the bait keeps pushing this direction, don't be shocked if bigger fish show up behind them.

One more thing to keep an ear on — the guys running charters toward the Race have been talking bonito potential as that water holds in a favorable range. Nothing confirmed on my end yet for this zone specifically, but Fishers Island Sound and the Race corridor are exactly the kind of structure that lights up once those fish push through, and eastern Connecticut Sound anglers are close enough to make a run worth it if reports firm up.

Looking ahead, this moon's still got some juice left in it for another day or two, so I'd keep working those tide changes for fluke while the current's sharp. Once we get past full and things settle back to a more normal push, expect the bite windows to spread out a little rather than concentrate so hard at the changes — which usually means covering more water to find them. If the afternoon sea breeze builds like it's been forecasted, plan your drift boat trips or your own runs for the morning before it kicks up chop on the open Bay. Structure fishing stays money regardless — Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall aren't going anywhere, and neither is the sea bass.

reports.headline: August Heat Pushes Stripers to the River Mouth Seam, Cocktail Blues Show at Great Island
reports.subhead: With the Sound running warm and slack, the only relief on the Lower Connecticut is where fresh water meets salt — and that's where the fish are stacking.
reports.body_markdown:
Joe-pye weed is thick along the Old Lyme marsh banks this week, that dusty purple you get in the dog days, and the osprey chicks off Great Island are up on the wing now, testing those long legs over the flats before the whole family starts drifting south. That's always been my clock for where we are in the season — not the calendar, the birds and the weeds. And what they're telling me right now is that we're deep into the slow, heavy part of summer, when this river stops being a highway for migrating fish and starts being a refuge for the ones that already live here.

The shad are long gone — that run wrapped up back in May, and by the time the joe-pye blooms there isn't a roe shad or a hickory left worth chasing above Essex. What we've got now is the August pattern I've watched unfold on this river for fifty years running: stripers pulling off the open Sound and tucking into the cool seam right at the river mouth, where the outflow off Saybrook Point meets the saltier water pushing up on the flood. That thermal break is the whole game right now. The Sound itself is running warm — mid-70s out toward the mouth, pushing higher on the open water — and fish don't want to sit in that if they don't have to. The river mouth, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when all that cooler upstream flow is pouring out past the breakwater, gives them a lane of relief they can hold in without burning energy.

I've been working that seam hard on the outgoing, anchoring up just off the Saybrook Point breakwater rocks in 15 to 20 feet and drifting bunker chunks back into the current on fish-finder rigs, letting them settle right where the darker river water and the clearer Sound water are visibly grinding against each other. That current line is easy to spot on a calm morning — you'll see the color change and a little foam streak riding it. Stripers have been holding right on that edge, mostly schoolies and a few respectable mid-20-inch fish, and the bite's been tightest in that low-light window — first hour of light and again the last hour before dark. Midday, with this heat sitting on the water, it's been dead slow out there unless you can find deeper structure holding shade or a strong push of current. That's not me sugarcoating it — daytime action off the Point has been tough, and anybody telling you different this week probably hasn't been out there at noon.

Up around Essex and the DEP Marina, the white perch bite has stayed steady, which is the one thing you can almost always count on here in August. Small pieces of bloodworm or a sliver of nightcrawler on a light spinning rig, fished right off the marina docks and the deeper edges of the channel on the last of the incoming tide, has been putting perch in the 8 to 10-inch range in the boat pretty reliably. It's not glamorous fishing but it's honest fishing, and on a hot afternoon when the stripers have shut down, it's given plenty of folks something to show for their time.

Now here's the piece worth talking about — the cocktail blues. We said a week back that the peanut bunker were spreading through these back bays and that it'd start showing up in the bluefish within a couple weeks. It's early yet, but I'm already seeing the front edge of that pattern build. Snapper blues have been thick in the marsh creeks off Great Island, chopping bait on the surface in the skinny water at the edges of the flats, and I've had a couple reports of bigger cocktail blues — 14, 15 inches — mixing in with them on the last of the ebb where those creek mouths dump into the main river channel. Small Kastmasters or a bare bucktail jig worked fast through the froth has been the ticket for the snappers, and if you slow down and work the deeper cuts with a slightly heavier metal, you'll start separating out the bigger cocktail fish from the pack. Give it another week or two and I expect that pattern to really fill in as more peanut bunker push down from upriver.

Blue crabs, for what it's worth, are thick as I've seen them in years in the shallow coves around Great Island and up into the Lieutenant River — if you've got a couple of hand lines and some chicken necks, that's a fine way to spend a slow afternoon while you wait for the tide to turn.

Looking ahead, the moon's been full and the tides have had some real push to them, which has been sharpening up those dawn and dusk windows nicely at the river mouth. As we come off full moon over the next several days, that current strength eases back some, and I'd expect the bite windows to settle back into a more standard rhythm rather than the sharp, short spikes we've had. If we get a stretch of cooler nights — even a couple degrees off overnight lows — I'd look for that river mouth seam to get even more attractive to stripers, and I wouldn't be surprised to see slightly better daytime action follow. Until then, I'm planning my trips around first light and last light at Saybrook Point, and keeping an eye on Great Island for that cocktail blue pattern to keep building through the rest of August.

reports.headline: New Haven Rockpiles: Porgies by the Dozen, Sea Bass Riding Shotgun
reports.subhead: Full moon current sharpens the bottom bite on the breakwalls while stripers slide onto the Charles Island bar after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, top of the flood, I dropped a size 4 hi-lo rig dressed with squid strips off the New Haven Outer Breakwall and the sinker never got a chance to sit still. Porgies came up two at a time — 12 to 15 inches, fat as dinner plates, and mad about it. That's the kind of start that tells you the whole day's going to go right, and for once it actually did.

The breakwalls have been the story all week. Both the Outer and the West Wall are holding thick porgy numbers in 18 to 22 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing — basically anytime there's current moving but the wind hasn't kicked up a chop to push you off the spot. Clam is still king for bait, but I've been running a two-hook bottom rig with green crab on the top hook and squid on the bottom just to see which the porgies want more on a given tide, and honestly they don't care — they're eating everything down there right now. Mixed into that same structure are black sea bass, and not the dink humpbacks we were pulling in June. Guys working small strips of squid on 1/2-ounce jigheads, bounced right off the riprap, are finding keepers in the 14 to 17-inch range, some pushing 3 pounds. The sea bass want the deeper pockets between the rock piles, not the shallow lip, so if you're marking fish on the sounder but not connecting, slide out ten feet toward the channel side of the wall.

Falkner Island is fishing the same way but bigger. That reef structure off the island in 35 to 40 feet has been holding a better class of sea bass — diamond jigs tipped with squid strips, dropped straight down and worked with short hops off bottom, have been the ticket on the last hour of the ebb when the current lightens up enough to actually feel your jig. It's a run-and-gun spot; you might mark fish thick on one drift and get nothing the next, so I keep making short drifts and marking waypoints rather than anchoring up and hoping.

Blackfish are stacked on both the breakwalls and the Falkner rockpiles right now, which is a little bit of a tease since the season's closed for the summer stretch. Green crab drops on light tackle are producing plenty of catch-and-release action — 18 to 22-inch tog thumping the rod tip and peeling drag off spinning gear you'd normally use for porgies. It's fun, it's free, and it's a good preview of what October's going to look like once the season flips back open.

Stripers are a different animal entirely with the water running warm — Kings Point read 72.5 this week and the harbor itself has felt every bit that warm on the surface, so the bass have gone strictly low-light on us. Charles Island and that sandbar connecting it to Silver Sands are still the best bet, but you want to be there for last light into full dark on the building tide, not midday. Bunker chunks fished tight to the bar edge where the current sweeps around the point have been drawing strikes from schoolies up through 28-inch fish. A few guys working white paddletails on the drift over the bar right at dusk have connected too, but the chunk bite has been more consistent. Daytime, forget it — the fish are sitting deep and sulking until the sun drops.

Bluefish have been the pleasant surprise. We flagged the peanut bunker push a couple weeks back and said the cocktail blues would follow them into the back bays, and that's exactly what's showing up now — snapper-sized blues mixed with cocktail fish in the 2 to 4-pound range, working pods of peanuts right at the mouth of New Haven Harbor on the outgoing tide. Small metal, half-ounce Deadly Dicks or similar, cast into the boils has been about as simple as fishing gets this week.

Fluke are still around but you have to work for them. Milford Gulf and the channel edges off Welch's Point have given up a scattered pick of keepers — 18 to 22 inches — on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the deeper cuts on the last of the outgoing. It's not a banner fluke year in this stretch, and I won't pretend otherwise. You might make three drifts and get one fish, but that one fish has been a legitimate keeper more often than not, which counts for something.

This week's full moon has put some real muscle into the tides, and that's been the difference-maker on the bottom bite — more current means more bait getting pushed off the rocks, means more porgies and sea bass stacked up feeding on it. That current strength should hold through the weekend before easing back into a more standard push by midweek. If I had one trip to make, I'd hit the Outer Breakwall on the last two hours of an incoming tide for porgies and sea bass, then swing by Charles Island right at dusk with a bag of bunker chunks and see if the stripers want to cooperate. Bring both rigs — this time of year, the bite can flip on you fast depending on which way the light's going.

reports.headline: Porgies pay the bills while the bass wait for dark
reports.subhead: Daytime stripers are ghosts on the Sound this week, but scup on the reefs and fluke on the edges are keeping rods bent.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a fella pull up to the launch at Mattituck the other morning, still had the tags on his rod, asked me straight out where the bass were biting. I told him the truth, which nobody wants to hear in August: they're biting where the sun isn't. He looked at me like I'd told him to go fish on the moon. But that's the Sound in the second week of August — it doesn't care what you want, it cares what the water's doing, and right now the water's doing what warm water does. It sits on top, it gets soft, and the stripers go find somewhere with shade or current or both.

I've got numbers off the buoys that back up what I'm feeling with my hand off the transom. Kings Point down west is sitting around 72, 73 degrees. New London out east is closer to 70. That gradient runs right through my water, and it means the far end of my beat — Rocky Point on out to the Gut approach — stays a couple degrees cooler and a whole lot more comfortable for a striper that doesn't want to work too hard to breathe. So that's where I've been putting my time, and that's where the dawn bite has held up. Bunker are still moving through the Gut approach, not in the thick schools you get in October, but enough that the blues and the occasional bass are cutting through them at first light. Anchor up on the last of the ebb, live-line a bunker off a fish-finder rig, and don't be surprised if it's a bluefish that eats it — the adult blues have been running tighter to that bait than the stripers have, which tells you something about who's willing to feed in bright water and who isn't.

After sunup the bass go quiet and stay quiet till the light drops again. That's not me being cranky about it — that's just where we are. If you want a rod bent at nine in the morning, go sit on the reef off Rocky Point or work the rock piles out past Horton Point light with a bank sinker and half a green crab. Porgy fishing has been the most honest thing going on this beat all week — steady, dependable, no drama, fish stacked tight to structure regardless of how hot that surface water gets. I had a morning last week where the scup came two at a time on a high-low rig, size 6 hooks, clam strips working just as well as crab. Nothing glamorous about a porgy trip, but you go home with dinner, which counts for something.

Fluke have been the other honest fish. They've slid off the flats and settled into the deeper cuts and channel edges — Mattituck Inlet's outer channel, the drop past the jetty, anywhere the bottom breaks and holds a few degrees cooler water than the sand around it. Full moon's swinging the tides harder this week, and that extra push has sharpened the drift bite right at the turns. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, three-quarter ounce, dragged slow along the edge where the sand gives way to mussel bottom — that's produced keepers, nothing huge, but enough to make a trip worthwhile if you're patient with the drift and don't rush it.

Now — we said a couple weeks back that these August springs, the ones building through the 11th and into the 13th, would put some new life back in this whole stretch, and they're sitting right on the doorstep now. When that tide starts hauling harder through the Gut, I expect the bass that have been laying low to get pushed up onto the seams a little more, especially where that cooler water off Rocky Point meets the harder current. Worth being out there at first light on the building tide once those springs kick in — not because it's a sure thing, but because that's exactly the kind of current change that's put fish on the end of my line more Augusts than I can count.

Blackfish are still off the table — season's closed till fall, and truthfully the tog don't want much to do with this warm water anyway, they're tucked deep in the rock and staying there. Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't heard a real weakfish report worth passing along this month. A few years back you could count on them mixing with the porgies on the reef, but that's thinned out bad, and I'm not going to tell you they're around when I haven't seen it myself.

Look, this isn't a week to expect miracles. It's a week to fish smart — dawn and dusk for the bass and blues around bait, daytime for porgy and fluke on structure, and keep an eye on that moon tide building through midweek. If I had one morning to give you, I'd put you at the Gut approach an hour before first light with a live bunker out, and I'd have a bucktail rigged and ready in case the fluke bite turns on once the sun's up over the drop-off. Cover your bases. The Sound's not handing anything out for free right now, but it's not skunking anybody who shows up with a plan either.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the last of the ebb: porgies stacked, cocktail blues finally show
reports.subhead: The full moon current sharpened every window this week — fish the right two hours and the Western Sound still delivers.
reports.body_markdown:
Every Tuesday morning I sit with the tide chart and decide which piece of structure gets my first two hours of daylight, and this week the decision was Cockenoe over Penfield — not because Penfield's dead, but because the full moon push made current the deciding factor, and Cockenoe's rockpile holds bait tighter against hard-running water than Penfield's open reef does. That's the whole game out here. You're not picking a spot, you're picking a spot on a tide, and right now with the moon just off full and the current running harder than it has in a month, the reefs that concentrate bait in tight seams are outfishing the broader structure.

Cockenoe paid off. Porgies stacked on the northeast corner in 14 to 18 feet, thick enough that two guys anchored there Thursday afternoon on the last two hours of the ebb had their five-gallon bucket full of 12-to-14-inch scup before the tide went dead. Sandworm and clam on high-low rigs, size 6 or 8 hooks, just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — nothing fancy, porgies don't need fancy, they need you in the right depth on the right push. The Norwalk Islands rockpiles are doing the same thing right now, and honestly this is the mainstay fishery on the Western Sound in August. If porgies are your target, don't overthink it — find the hard bottom, fish the last two hours of either tide when the current's still moving but not ripping your line sideways, and stay off the top of the reef on the peak of the flood when the boat traffic parks right on top of the good water.

Fluke are still the more consistent grade-A fishery if you're willing to drift instead of anchor. The channel edge off Sheffield Island and the drop-off on the west side of the Norwalk Islands have both been giving up keeper fluke to 21 inches on white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 20 to 28 feet on the outgoing tide. Kings Point is reading 72.5 degrees, which is warm enough that the fluke are sliding toward the cooler edges where current sweeps the bottom clean — that's exactly where the drop-offs earn their keep. Incoming tide has been more hit-or-miss; I'd plan your fluke trips around the two hours either side of high water slack into the first hour of ebb.

Striped bass are in that classic mid-August low-light pattern — daytime is mostly dead water unless you're sitting on moving current, so I've shifted my bass trips to first light and last light around Greenwich Point and the lit pilings off the Cows. Live bunker on a fishfinder rig, fished tight to structure right at dusk, has produced schoolie-to-mid-20s bass consistently, with the occasional better fish mixed in on nights when the bunker schools are thick. Nothing blitz-worthy, and I want to be honest about that — this isn't June. You're working for individual fish in tight windows, not covering water hoping to run into a wolf pack. If you can only fish one window this week, make it the hour around sunset with bait actively moving on the tide.

We flagged the bluefish pattern last week — said the cocktail blues would follow the peanut bunker spread and show up within two weeks — and that's exactly what happened. Snapper blues have been thick in the back bays off Norwalk and Westport, and now we're seeing legitimate cocktail-class blues, 2 to 4 pounds, mixing into the bunker pods off Sheffield Island and around the outer Norwalk Islands on the last of the incoming tide. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — worked fast through the peanut schools has been the ticket. Nothing trophy-sized yet, but the size class is climbing week to week, which is the pattern you want to see this time of year.

Black sea bass are steady out on the Cows and the deeper structure off Penfield, holding in 25 to 35 feet where the water stays a few degrees cooler. Squid strips and Gulp on a two-hook bottom rig, fished right on the rockpile itself, not off to the side, has been the difference between a limit and a handful. I'll skip blackfish entirely this week — tautog season's closed through the summer here, and there's nothing to report until the fall opener puts them back on the table.

Boat traffic is the other half of this chess match right now. Weekends on Cockenoe and Penfield are a parking lot by 10 a.m., so I'm planning every trip around either the sunrise window or the last two hours of daylight, when the recreational fleet has cleared out and the reef gets quiet enough to actually fish it properly. Weekday mornings are still your best bet for uncrowded water on any of these pieces.

Looking ahead, the moon's sliding past full now, so expect the exaggerated current we've had this week to ease back toward a more standard push by the weekend — that usually softens the bite windows slightly but makes them more predictable, which I actually prefer for planning charters. If the afternoon sea breeze builds like it's been forecast, I'd get my fluke drifts done in the morning before the wind kicks the surface up over the shallower reef structure. Watch the tropics too — nothing on our doorstep yet, but late August is when a stray system can send swell up into the Sound and change everything for a few days.

reports.headline: Nine Hours to Atlantis, a Bigeye at 2 AM, and a Marlin We Didn't Expect
reports.subhead: Full moon current turned the east wall into a conveyor belt this week — yellowfin by day, bigeye by chunk, and the first real white marlin bite of the summer.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 4 AM Tuesday with the tank full and the fuel log started, because that's how you run to Atlantis — you don't leave anything to chance on a hundred-mile-plus round trip. Call it a hundred nautical miles each way from Montauk, nine hours of running time if the sea stays honest, and somewhere north of three hundred gallons burned by the time you tie back up. That math doesn't change whether the fishing is good or bad, so you plan for it before you ever look at a temp break.

What we found on the east wall was worth the diesel. The moon's full right now, which means the current on that ledge was running harder than it has in weeks, and a hard-running current on a canyon wall does what it always does — it pins bait against structure and makes everything downstream of it nervous. We trolled the 100-fathom curve down through the canyon head starting around first light, small tuna feathers and a naked bird spread at 6 to 7 knots, and had yellowfin all morning. Nothing giant — fifty to seventy pounds, the class fish we've been seeing all month — but they were there consistently enough that we never had to search hard. The color change was sharp, green water pinched right up against the blue, and every time we crossed it we got bit.

Around 10 AM we had a mahi come up under a mat of sargassum sitting off the edge, small school, nothing over ten pounds, but a nice distraction while we reset the spread. Then just after noon, on the long rigger, we hooked into something that took drag in that slow, deliberate way that isn't a yellowfin — a white marlin, and a good one, greyhounding twice before we got a leader touch and let her go. That's the first real marlin action I've had out there this season, and it lines up with what we'd been hearing — the numbers were supposed to start building by mid-August, and this week they did.

We fished the troll hard through the afternoon and then set up to chunk the night tide, and this is where the moon actually worked in our favor instead of against us. We'd talked last week about how a soft current trims the chunk bite down to almost nothing, and how the smarter play in that situation is to troll the break all day and save your chunking for the strongest tide of the night rather than commit to a full all-night drift hoping it turns on. This week the current was the opposite problem — too strong for most of the evening — but the same logic held. We waited for the tide to slack toward the second half of the night, around 1 AM, dropped butterfish chunks on 50-wide outfits with 6/0 circle hooks and no leader wire, just 60-pound fluoro, and connected on a bigeye a little after 2 AM. Not a giant — call it 180 pounds — but a bigeye off Atlantis on a August night bite is a fish you don't complain about, especially after running nine hours to get there.

Bluefin sign was scattered rather than concentrated — we marked fish on structure a few times on the sounder but never got a jumper or a real feeding frenzy to key on. That's consistent with what boats working Veatch and Hydrographer this week have described too — bluefin are around, they're just not schooled up tight enough yet to build a program around. If you're going to target them specifically right now, I'd fish structure edges early and late and not expect a blitz.

Water out at the canyons is holding warm — high 70s on the surface out toward the shelf break, warmer than the water right off Montauk Point, which is still in the mid-70s. That gradient is exactly what's pinning the warm-water species — yellowfin, mahi, marlin — up against the edge instead of letting them spread out over open water. As long as that edge holds its position, the bite should stay consistent enough to plan a trip around, though I wouldn't call it easy. We worked for every one of those yellowfin, and the marlin bite is still building, not blown wide open.

Looking ahead, the moon comes off full over the next few days and that should ease the current back toward something more normal, which usually settles bite windows into tighter, more predictable stretches rather than the all-day grind we had this week. If I had one more trip to plan before the pattern shifts, I'd run to Atlantis or Veatch, troll the wall hard from first light through early afternoon while the yellowfin are up and moving, and hold the chunk gear for the back half of the night tide rather than committing to it early. Keep an eye on the wider tropics too — nothing imminent that I've seen, but late August is when a stray system can push swell into these grounds fast, and a hundred miles offshore is not where you want to be guessing about that.

reports.headline: 78.8°F on the Bight Buoy — The Elbow Kink Paid Off Like We Called It
reports.subhead: A three-degree gap between shelf water and canyon blue held the yellowfin tight to the east elbow all week, but you had to find the seam to cash in.
reports.body_markdown:
Buoy 44025 out in the Bight read 78.8°F this week, wave heights running 2.6 feet at a six-second period out of the south-southwest — nothing that kept boats home, but enough chop to make you think twice about running the extra eight miles to the axis instead of working the wall. That 78.8 number matters because it's shelf water, not canyon water, and the gap between the two is where the whole story lived this week. On the canyon side, the break was running several degrees cooler and cleaner, and where that green-to-blue seam pinched hardest was right over the east elbow — 39°38'N, 72°32'W, give or take a half mile depending on the day. We flagged that corner last week as the one to watch if the post-front SST sharpened or kinked there, and that's exactly what happened. The eddy didn't spread thin across the shelf edge like it sometimes does in August — it pinched down tight against the 100-fathom line and held the bait, and the yellowfin, right on top of it.

That's the difference between a good trip and a long ride for nothing this week. Boats that ran straight to the classic Chicken Canyon numbers or spread out looking for color on the open bar had spotty results — a few knockdowns, a mahi or two, not much sustained action. The guys who worked the elbow, trolling green machines and Joe Shute bars with cedar plugs in the pattern, tight to where the water goes from a hazy green-blue to that gin-clear cobalt, found yellowfin stacked from 60 to 130 feet down, feeding hard on the temp break itself rather than scattered across it. Fish ran 25 to 45 pounds, mixed in with a few bigger ones that came unbuttoned before the gaff — August yellowfin on the Hudson tend to run a little leaner than the September fish, but there were enough of them to make the trolling spread worth the diesel. Skirted ballyhoo pulled slow and naked bally in the shotgun position both drew strikes, and once the fleet found the push, chunking bunker at anchor over the Dip after the trolling bite slowed turned into a steady pick through the afternoon into dusk.

Mahi were mixed in with the yellowfin along the same break, holding under any floating structure — lobster gear, weed clumps, the occasional stray pallet — and they didn't need much coaxing. A chunk of butterfish or a small spreader bar worked the edges pulled fish in the 8-to-15-pound range consistently, with a scattering of bigger bulls busting bait on the surface in clean patches of blue. If you saw birds working tight over a weed line inside that elbow zone, it was worth a stop even mid-troll.

White marlin numbers are building the way they should for mid-August, and this week bore that out — several boats reported multiple knockdowns on skirted ballyhoo pulled on the flat lines, with a few fish actually eating and coming tight. Nothing epic, but a legitimate uptick from three weeks ago, and if the pattern holds, the back half of August should see that number climb further as more fish push up the shelf edge behind the bait.

The night bite for swordfish stayed productive for the crews willing to put in the hours. Deep-dropping squid strips and whole squid on glow leads, working depths between 1,200 and 1,600 feet along the canyon's steeper contour lines off the Claw, kept a handful of boats in fish through the week. This isn't a volume bite — it's one or two quality fish a trip for guys who know how to read their sounder and hold position in current — but the swords are there, and the water column temperature profile out at that depth hasn't changed much despite the surface warming up top.

Bigeye sign showed up mixed in with the yellowfin on a couple of the deeper drops at last light, nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet, but worth keeping an eye on if you're already rigged for the night shift. Wahoo were incidental — a couple of fish came on high-speed trolled Ilanders and wine-glass style lures worked over structure near the Texas Tower grounds, but nobody's targeting them specifically right now with the tuna and mahi keeping rods bent.

Bluefin sign has been thin to nonexistent on the Hudson itself this week — the real bluefin action right now is sitting up on the New England grounds, Stellwagen and Jeffrey's Ledge, and that's not changing in the short term. If bluefin are your target, that's not our water this week.

The full moon has kept current running stronger than usual on the drift, which is worth factoring in if you're chunking — go up a size or two on your fluorocarbon leader weight and let more line out before locking up, because the extra current pulls baits shallower and faster than you'd expect. As the moon eases past full over the next few days, expect that current to relax back to a more typical Hudson push, which should tighten up the chunk bite even further.

Best case for the week ahead: the eddy holds its pinch over the east elbow and the yellowfin stay concentrated instead of spreading out as the moon settles. If it slides east the way these things sometimes do by mid-week, I'd shift attention toward the Dip and re-check the SST before committing to a long run. Either way, find the seam first — don't just run numbers, run the break.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Mixed bag early, Spencer sorts it out late: yellowfin on the chunk after we chased the break south
reports.subhead: A scrambled shelf edge cost us two days before Spencer's south wall came together on bait and warm water pushing 79 degrees.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the week: C-plus starting out, solid B by Thursday. That's the honest read. We had two days where the troll spread looked like it was fishing a parking lot, then Spencer's south corner turned into the kind of stop where you're re-rigging ballyhoo faster than the mate can pitch them.

Here's the why. That southerly blow that rolled through last week did exactly what we said it would — scrambled the surface layer and blurred the temp breaks for a good 48 hours. When we finally got back out past the 20-fathom line, the sharp edge we'd been running to north of Spencer was gone, mushy, no definition on the water color at all. But the warm tongue didn't disappear, it just slid — south and a little east, tucked in tighter around Spencer's southwest corner, working the 39-15/72-50 stretch instead of the usual push up toward Lindenkohl. We flagged that displacement before it happened, and that's exactly where the fish showed up once things settled.

Water out on the edge is running warm — mid-to-upper 70s on the surface, pushing 79 in spots — and that's a full-moon tide doing what full-moon tides do out here: ripping current across the break hard enough to stack bait against the wall. Yellowfin have been the backbone of the week. Best action came on the chunk, not the troll, once the sun got low — butterflied bunker on a 6/0 circle hook, no weight, just let it flutter down through the chum slick in 40 to 60 fathoms off Spencer's south edge. Fish in the 25 to 45 pound class, a few pushing 60. Morning troll bite was there but thinner than I'd like — naked ballyhoo behind Green Machines and small Ilanders, spreader bars out the back, still connecting but you had to cover more water to find the willing schools.

Mahi have been a bonus, not a target, riding under whatever weed lines we crossed running out — schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range under floating grass mats between the 100-fathom curve and Spencer proper. If you see the birds working a line, slow down, pitch a bare hook with a chunk of butterfish, and don't be shy about circling back.

Lindenkohl has been the disappointment of the four this week — same warm water signature should be there given how close it sits to Spencer, but the bait just hasn't set up the same way. We ran it twice, marked good structure on the machine, couldn't buy a bite either time. That's the kind of thing that happens when the edge relocates the way it did — Lindenkohl's contour doesn't hold the eddy the same way Spencer's southwest wall does, and this week that mattered.

Poor Man's has been quietly solid for the guys not wanting the long run. Closer to the beach, shallower water, and it's been giving up a mixed bag — smaller yellowfin, a scattered mahi or two, and enough white marlin activity on the troll to keep the outriggers snapping. Mid-August is right on schedule for white marlin building up along this stretch, and Poor Man's has had two or three raises most trips, sometimes more when the current's really moving on the push tide. Naked ballyhoo, small blue-white Sea Witches, run the spread a little tighter than you would for tuna — 20 to 30 feet back on the short riggers — and keep someone on the pitch rod with a dink ballyhoo ready the second you get a bill up.

Norfolk is the long haul out of Ocean City, and this week it rewarded patience. Bigeye have been showing on the night chunk in the deep water off the canyon's edge — 300 to 400 fathoms, drifting bunker chunks down deep with a glow stick on the leader, working the midnight-to-4-a.m. window when the current's slack enough to hold bottom without a ton of weight. Not a numbers game down there, one or two quality fish a trip, but they're big — 100-plus pound class. Wahoo have been mixed in on the high-speed troll running the edge at first light, deep-diving Yo-Zuris and Braid Marauders at 12 to 15 knots, single fish here and there rather than a pattern, which tracks — wahoo down that way tend to be a bycatch story in August, not a target.

Looking ahead, the moon's going to ease off full over the next few days and that should settle the current back into something more normal rather than the exaggerated push we've been fighting. If that happens the way it usually does, I'd expect the Spencer break to firm back up and possibly work its way back north toward Lindenkohl, which would put both canyons back in play together instead of one carrying the other. Best case, the warm eddy holds its current position through the weekend and Spencer keeps producing on the chunk after dark. If it slides again the way it did last week, we'll follow it — that's the whole job running this stretch, staying loose enough to chase the water instead of the spot on the chart. Worth keeping an eye on any tropical activity building out in the Atlantic too; a longer-period swell rolling in behind a storm system would be the next thing to reshuffle this deck, and we'd rather see it coming than get caught flat.

reports.headline: Skipped the chunk grounds, ran the sled to Wilmington's east wall — three yellowfin and a marlin release for eight hours of trolling
reports.subhead: The white marlin bite is building right on schedule, and the yellowfin are still holding tight to the same warm seam we've been fishing since July.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a decision to make at the dock, and it wasn't a hard one. Chunking had been solid on and off over the canyon's inshore lip, but the fuel burn to sit and soak butterflied bunker for eight hours only pays off if the fish are stacked and eating consistently — and the reports coming off that structure had been more "a few here and there" than a real pile. So I loaded the spread, topped off the tanks, and made the run out to Wilmington's east wall instead, working the 100-fathom break around 38°34' N, 73°58' W where the canyon starts to fall off hard into the deep. If I'm burning that much diesel, I want to be trolling water that's actually holding a temperature edge, not guessing.

And it was there. The warm-water eddy that's been sitting off the canyon corner all month is still in position, pinching the shelf edge and stacking a clean break where the bluer, warmer water — pushing into the high 70s on the surface — runs up against the cooler green shelf water. That seam is exactly where the bait wants to ride, and exactly where we found feathers of bird activity working the edge around midday. We pulled a mixed spread — green-and-yellow Ilanders over horse ballyhoo on the long riggers, a naked cedar plug in the shotgun, and a small spreader bar down the middle — and picked up three yellowfin in the 35-to-50-pound class right on that thermal line, plus a mahi that came up wild on a teaser and got the naked bait treatment before it ate. We also had a white marlin come tight to the long corner bait, jumped twice, and threw the hook before we could get a pitch bait in front of him — no shot at a release flag, but a good sign of what's building out there.

That's the pattern right now, and it's honestly right on the seasonal clock. We said a week back that the marlin numbers would keep building through August as the canyon warms and the bait tightens up on the edges, and that the yellowfin would stay steady rather than spectacular — holding the temperature break rather than blowing up in one spot. That's exactly what's playing out. Nobody's loading the box on tuna right now, but the fish are there consistently enough that a well-run troll day is putting meat in the fish box, and the marlin shots are becoming a real part of the day instead of a bonus.

Night action off Wilmington has also picked up for the deep-drop guys. A couple of boats working the true canyon depths — 700 to 900 fathoms off the drop past the 38°30' line — have been coming back with bigeye mixed into the tilefish catches on squid strips and glow-bead rigs, fished slow on electric reels after dark. That's not an everyday bite, but when the current's right and the moon isn't blowing out the drift too hard, it's worth the extra fuel to stay out past sundown rather than run home empty on the troll.

Wahoo have been a wildcard. We haven't targeted them hard, but two high-speed strikes on a black-and-purple Braid Marauder run at 12 knots down the wall suggest they're starting to show along the drop-off, which tracks with what we'd expect for mid-August as the water continues to warm and hold. If I had a day dedicated just to wahoo, I'd run that same wall at first light before the sun gets high, when they seem to be feeding closer to the surface.

Chunking is still viable, but I'd treat it as a Plan B rather than the primary play this week. If the troll bite goes quiet — which it can, especially through the heat of midday when the fish seem to sink — sliding into a drift over the canyon's inshore structure with butterflied bunker and a slow chunk line can still pull a yellowfin or two up, especially on the last two hours of daylight when the current eases. But right now, with the eddy holding position and the marlin starting to show consistently, trolling the edge is where I'm putting my time and fuel.

The moon just came off full, so the tidal push out here has been strong, which tends to sharpen the bite windows at dawn and again in the evening rather than spreading fish out evenly through the day. Over the next few days I'd expect that to ease back toward a more standard rhythm, which usually means a longer, steadier midday window rather than two short sharp ones. If the eddy holds its position through the weekend — and there's no strong sign yet that it's sliding — I'd keep running the same stretch of the east wall and expect the white marlin numbers to keep building as we get deeper into August. If it starts to slide east or the temperature break softens, I'd shift effort south toward the Baltimore Canyon corner and reassess from there. Either way, I wouldn't burn the fuel to sit and chunk blind this week — not with a bite this dependent on finding the right water first.

reports.headline: August 10, and Washington's White Marlin Are Running Two Weeks Ahead of Plan
reports.subhead: The volume yellowfin bite is holding on the eastern wall while billfish numbers build faster than the calendar says they should.
reports.body_markdown:
Every August I get the same question at the fuel dock: is Washington actually ahead of the pack, or do I just say that because it's my canyon? Here's the honest answer — this year it's not close. By the second week of August, Cape May boats are still hunting for consistency, Baltimore Canyon's still sorting out where the good water sits, and we've already had ten days of stacked yellowfin on the eastern wall with white marlin showing in numbers you'd expect closer to Labor Day. That's not luck. That's the Gulf Stream doing what it does off this stretch of the shelf — pinching warm filaments up against the canyon edge earlier than anywhere north of Hatteras, and this year it arrived right on schedule.

We flagged this back on the 3rd and again on the 6th — said the warm-water filaments would keep tuna concentrated on the break and that billfish numbers would build the way they should in early August. That's exactly what's happened. The yellowfin bite has been the bread-and-butter fishery all week, working the temperature break along the 50 to 60-fathom curve on the west and southwest walls, where the color change from canyon blue to green Mid-Atlantic water sets up a hard edge. Boats running spreader bars with cedar plugs up top and naked ballyhoo in the shotgun are getting bit consistently between 6:30 and 9 a.m., then again in the last two hours of daylight. Fifty to seventy pound class fish, mixed in with some smaller schoolies that'll test 20 to 30. Nothing giant, but steady — three to eight fish days for boats that stay on the troll and don't chase birds around all morning.

Mahi have been the bonus fish, and a good one. Anything holding structure — a lobster pot buoy, a mat of sargassum, a stray board — is holding fish. Small spinning outfits with quarter-ounce jigs, chartreuse or pink, worked around the pot lines have been putting dolphin in the box in the 8 to 15 pound range, with the occasional bull pushing 25. If you see one come up, stop the boat and pitch — they run in packs and the second and third fish are usually right behind the first.

White marlin is where Washington's really separating itself from the rest of the fleet right now. Numbers are building the way I'd expect for mid-August, but what's notable is how far along we already are — guys working dink ballyhoo and small circle hooks off the switch baits are getting into multiple releases per trip on good days, mostly along that same eastern wall where the water's held clean and blue in the mid-to-upper 70s. It's not a guaranteed six-bite day every trip — I had one boat radio in Thursday with just two bites all day after a slow start, then another crew twenty minutes away doubled up three times in an hour. That's canyon fishing in August — the fish are there, but you've got to find the exact seam where the temp break, the current line, and the bait are all lined up at once.

Wahoo have been a wildcard worth working for if you've got the gear. High-speed trolling with deep-diving lures — the heavy Braid or Ilander/Sea Witch combos rigged on wire — along the drop-off edges in 80 to 120 fathoms has produced a few nice fish in the 40 to 60 pound range for boats willing to run that speed spread alongside the slow-troll tuna gear. It's not a volume fishery right now, more a bonus if you're set up for it.

Bigeye have shown at night for the chunk-and-drift crews anchored up on the edge in 700 to 900 feet, working butterfish chunks on circle hooks with the lights down and patience up. Slow, but real — a couple of boats have iced fish over 150 pounds in the last week doing exactly that. Bluefin sign, for what it's worth, has been mostly a New England story this month — Stellwagen, Jeffrey's Ledge, even close to midcoast Maine — not really a Washington pattern in August, and I wouldn't burn fuel looking for them down here right now.

Conditions have cooperated. Surface temps on the wall have held in that mid-to-upper 70s range that keeps everything — yellowfin, mahi, white marlin — comfortable and feeding, and the moon's swinging past full this week, which has sharpened the dawn and dusk bite windows a little more than usual. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd run the eastern wall early, work the temp break hard on the troll until 9, then switch over to dink ballyhoo once the sun's up and the marlin start showing on the surface. Watch the afternoon sea breeze building through midweek — nothing that should shut down a canyon trip, but worth checking before you commit to a long run. Beyond that, keep an eye on the tropics; nothing's organized yet, but late August is when these systems start sending swell up the shelf, and Washington's the first canyon that feels it.

reports.headline: The Ledge Went Cold and Green Again — Bass Deep, Bonito Scouts Showing South
reports.subhead: Full moon current is stacking bait on the Southwest Ledge and North Rip while the season's first bonito nose into the corridors south of the island.
reports.body_markdown:
You feel the change before you see it out here. I was running out past the breakwater before first light Wednesday and the air over the water had that clean, mineral cold to it — the kind that tells you the upwelling is working before you ever drop a temp gauge. That's the Southwest Ledge doing what it does every August when the moon gets big and the current starts hauling. Cold, oxygen-rich water gets pulled up out of the depths and it stacks bait right on the edge of the structure. When that happens here, the striped bass don't wander far from it.

This week's full moon has put some real muscle into the tide, and that's exactly the kind of current that sharpens up the bite around the Ledge and the North Rip. Daytime action anywhere else on the East Coast right now is mostly dead — the peak-summer heat has bass everywhere from Jersey to the Cape pinned into a strict low-light pattern, holding tight in cooler water and only really feeding at dawn, dusk, and after dark. Block Island is a little different because we've got that natural refrigeration system built into the bottom. The Ledge and the Rip stay charged with cold, moving water around the clock, so we're getting bites through the day that boats working warmer inshore water simply aren't seeing.

Best fish this week came off the Southwest Ledge in 25 to 40 feet, working the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood — that current reversal is when the bass really come up off the bottom and start working the edge. Guys jigging 2- to 3-ounce diamond jigs tipped with a squid strip have been connecting, and a few boats trolling umbrella rigs and big parachutes through the deeper water off the Ledge have put 30-plus-pound fish in the box. I had a 40-pounder come off the North Rip Tuesday morning on a chunk of fresh bunker, fished on a fish-finder rig right on bottom in that fast water where the rip stands up — that fish never left the structure, just sat there waiting for the current to bring dinner to him. That's the whole story of this place. You're not searching for bass around Block Island in summer, you're finding the cold water and the bait, and the fish are already there.

Squid have been thick around the island this month, and that's been carrying a lot of this bite. Where you find squid concentrations on the sounder, especially around the Ledge and out toward the East Grounds, you'll usually find bass and blackfish working underneath them. Sea bass have stayed dependable on the reef structure off the south side — jigging bucktails tipped with squid strips in 40 to 60 feet has been steady, nothing spectacular, but a reliable box-filler if the bass bite is slow.

Bluefish have been mixed into the same water, chopping up the bunker schools that push through the rips on the tide changes. Nothing like the giant blitzes you get up at Montauk or Sandy Hook, but enough cocktail blues around to keep rods bent if you're throwing poppers or small metal off the back of the boat while you wait for the tide to turn. Fluke fishing has been the honest, dependable piece of the week — drifting the drop-offs and current-swept edges around the harbor and the south side with Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has produced a decent number of keepers, though you need to work the tide changes hard. The doormats are holding tight to the cooler water on the edges, same story as everywhere else this time of year.

Now here's the one I've been waiting to write. We flagged it last week — said the water on the south side was closing in on that bonito threshold and the first scouts wouldn't be far behind — and sure enough, there's early bonito showing at the classic corridors: the Race, Fishers Island Sound, and pushing into the Vineyard's south side. Nothing consistent yet around the island itself, but Montauk's holding water in the mid-70s and that warmth is working its way up the coast. If the pattern holds the way it usually does, we should start seeing real bonito and the first false albacore push into Block Island waters within the next couple weeks, especially once that warm water settles into the south-side rips.

Looking ahead, the moon will start easing off full over the next few days, which usually calms the exaggerated current we've had and settles the bite back into a more standard rhythm — still good, just less dramatic swings at the tide changes. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Southwest Ledge on the last of the ebb into the flood turn, right at first light, with a bucktail or a live eel worked slow along the bottom edge. That's where the cold water, the bait, and the big fish all come together right now. Keep an eye on the south side corridors too — once that bonito shows up in real numbers around the island, it's going to happen fast, and you don't want to be the last boat to hear about it.

reports.headline: The Bunker Are Home: Dawn Blitzes at the Point, Bass Pushing 30 Pounds
reports.subhead: Full moon tide has pinned the bait against the boulders — and the striper fishing at Montauk is doing what it's supposed to do in the second week of August.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a stretch of the calendar, usually the first two weeks of August, when Montauk stops being a fishery and becomes a machine. The bunker come home to the south side in numbers that blacken the water off the Lighthouse, the terns and gannets find them at first light, and everything that swims with a spine east of Shagwong knows exactly where breakfast is. We're in that window right now, and I'd argue we've been in it for about ten days straight.

I was out at 5:15 Tuesday morning, running the boat along the boulder field off the Point in maybe eighteen feet of water, and the whole south side was doing what it does when a big moon pulls a big tide — bait balled up tight against the rocks, refusing to leave, and stripers using the current to pin it there. This full moon has been generous. Water's holding around 76 degrees on the ocean side, which isn't classic bass water on paper, but the current is so strong right now that it's kept the fish feeding hard on the moving stages rather than sulking deep through the heat. That's the story of this whole week — strong tide, low light, bunker schools doing the work.

The pattern at North Bar has been the same three mornings running: bunker spoons and 2-ounce bucktails worked just under the surface on the last hour of the incoming, into the first hour of the outgoing, right where the rip stands up over that boulder structure. We've had bass to 28 and 30 pounds on topwater plugs — the big pencil poppers and Danny-style swimmers — when the fish are up and slashing, and switched to bucktails tipped with a strip of bunker belly when they slide down a few feet. Shagwong Reef has been holding fish too, though it's been more of a bluefish show there this week — jumbo blues in the 8 to 12 pound class mixed right into the bass schools, which means wire leaders or you're donating plugs to the bottom. Turtle Cove has fished better on the last two hours of daylight than at dawn, which tells me the bait's shifting position with the tide swing rather than sitting still — worth knowing if you're planning your morning around one spot.

Night fishing has held up too, and if you want a shot at something heavier than the daylight schoolies, that's still the play. Eels drifted slow along the boulder field on the building tide, fished tight to the rocks in the dark, have produced some of the better fish of the week — nothing I'd call a 50, but a handful in the 30s came off that pattern for guys willing to stay out past midnight. That low-light window matters more now than it did in June. Peak-summer heat pushes these fish into a strict schedule — dawn, dusk, full dark — and daytime action outside the current-swept structure has been thin. Don't waste a midday tide on flat, sunny water expecting a repeat of what happened at 5 a.m.

Fluke fishing has been the more dependable, less dramatic story. Lake Montauk's west basin has been giving up keeper fluke to 4 and 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails, drifted slow over the sand-and-eelgrass bottom on the outgoing as the lake drains through the inlet. The channel edge off Star Island jetty has done the same on that same ebb — deeper water, stronger current, bigger average fish, but you're fighting boat traffic through the harbor mouth. Porgies remain the honest man's fishery on Shagwong and the reef structure off the Point — small hooks, sandworms or clam, straight up-and-down in 25 to 40 feet, and you'll fill a bucket without much drama. That fishery doesn't get the ink the bass blitzes do, but it's about as close to a sure thing as this month offers.

What hasn't showed yet, and I get asked about it every single day at the dock, is albies and bonito. We flagged this water as the one to watch closest going into August, and the ocean-side temps have crept into that trigger range — but the switch hasn't flipped. Nobody I trust has iron in the boat yet off the Point or in the rips. That first wave typically shows in the final weeks of August, and with the surface temps sitting where they are, I don't think we're far off. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick in the rocket launcher when you're running bunker spoons — you don't want to be digging through a rod locker the morning they finally show up busting bait on the surface east of the Point.

Looking ahead, this moon's grip on the tide will start to ease over the next few days, and the bite windows should settle back into a more normal rhythm rather than the exaggerated dawn-and-dusk blitzes we've had. If the wind stays out of the west and the bunker schools hold their position along the south side, I'd keep working North Bar and the boulder field on the moving water — that's still the highest-percentage play on the Point right now. If the bunker push east toward Shagwong, follow them. They're driving this whole show, and they have been for two weeks straight.

reports.headline: The West Cut at Moriches Narrowed Again — and the Bass Are Using It Like a Funnel
reports.subhead: A skinnier gut off Cupsogue is concentrating current and bait right where the full-moon springs are about to load in more push than we've seen all summer.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the west end of Cupsogue on the last of Wednesday's ebb and the sandbar geometry has changed again — not dramatically, but enough to matter. The main gut through Moriches Inlet has pinched in maybe 15-20 yards from where it was running in June, pushing more volume through a tighter throat on the Fire Island side, off Smith Point. That's classic Moriches behavior — this inlet never sits still for long, and every time the channel narrows like this, the current through it accelerates and the bait gets squeezed into a tighter parade. Right now that parade is peanut bunker, and it's exactly what we flagged two weeks back — said to watch for peanuts showing in the back bay and to mark the August 11-13 springs as the window when hard current over new bar structure would sharpen things up. Here we are.

The full moon is doing its job. Tide swings are building through the weekend, and that extra push is exactly what a narrowed inlet channel needs to turn from a mediocre drift into a real one. Fluke fishing has been the backbone of the report all summer and it's holding that role — doormats stacking on the channel edges and drop-offs where the water stays a few degrees cooler than the surrounding flats. The stretch off Tuthill Point, where the bay channel drops from six feet to eleven along the edge of the marsh, has been giving up keeper fluke to white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Inside the inlet itself, the west side of the gut off Cupsogue — 18 to 22 feet — has been the better producer on the incoming, when clean ocean water floods back in and fluke slide up onto the edge to ambush bait getting pushed through that tighter throat.

Striped bass are behaving like every August striper south of the Cape right now — this heat has them locked into a strict low-light window. Daytime is mostly dead outside the cooler current-swept structure, but the inlet cut itself qualifies, and that's exactly why the narrowing matters. Dawn and dusk drifts through the new gut, working the current seam where the accelerated flow meets the flatter water on the bay side, have produced slot fish up to 30 inches on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, and on soft-plastic paddletails swung through the seam on the drop. If you're throwing bucktails, go heavier than you think you need — 1.5 ounces minimum to hold bottom in that squeezed current — and let it sink clean off the edge before starting a slow, rhythmic retrieve. That's a proven presentation for staged bass sitting tight to current breaks, and Moriches' new geometry is basically building you one.

Bluefish have split into two clear populations and you need to fish them differently. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks around East Moriches and Mastic — small, aggressive, chewing peanut bunker imitations and tiny Kastmasters off docks and bulkheads, good action for a kid with a light rod. The adult class is a different animal, holding tight to the bait schools at the inlet mouth and blitzing sporadically at dusk when bunker get pinched through the cut. If you see the surface nervous water and diving terns off Cupsogue in the last hour of light, that's your window — don't wait, that bite can close in fifteen minutes.

Weakfish are starting to show the pattern we expected — tracking the peanut bunker into the bay rather than sitting deep. A few keeper-class weakfish have come off the drop-offs near Pattersquash Island on bucktails tipped with strips of squid, fished slow along bottom on the last of the outgoing when the water's still got some push but the light is low. It's not a stacked bite yet, more a handful of quality fish mixed into the fluke drift, but it's worth working a few extra drifts through that zone if you're already out there.

Porgies remain steady, unglamorous, and reliable — clam-baited high-low rigs over the shell and sod-bank structure inside the bay, particularly around the deeper holes off Pattersquash, are filling coolers without much drama. Not much to overthink there.

Looking ahead: the springs build through Tuesday, and if the inlet keeps funneling current the way it's been funneling this week, I'd put my time on the dawn and dusk tides through that narrowed west cut off Cupsogue — that's where the bass and the bigger bluefish are going to stage while the extra push holds. Once the moon rounds off and the current eases back to normal, I'd expect the bite to spread out again and lose some of that concentrated edge, so if you've got a day this weekend, don't wait for it.

reports.headline: Porgies thick off Shelter Island, weakfish trail the peanut bunker into the bays
reports.subhead: Mid-August has the Peconic running its own clock — warm, calm, and stacked with porgies, fluke, and weaks working the tide changes.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic doesn't care what the ocean's doing. While the open beaches are getting hammered by a lumpy Atlantic and the Sound's fighting a steep west-to-east temperature split, our water sits protected behind the forks and just keeps doing its own thing — warm, mostly clean, and settled into that classic mid-August rhythm where porgies, fluke, and weakfish carry the load. I've said it before and I'll say it again: this bay warms first in spring and it holds its heat longest into fall, and right now, first week of August behind us, it's running full summer pattern with no complaints.

We flagged this last week — said a little cooled water behind that front would perk up the daytime porgy and fluke bite, and that's exactly what's happened. The scup around Shelter Island have been thick and cooperative, especially on the Route 114 bridge rips and out around Cedar Island and Coecles Harbor. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, half a sandworm or a piece of clam, fished in 15 to 25 feet on the last two hours of the incoming through the top of the tide — that's been the window. Guys anchoring up tight to the bridge pilings on a slack-to-moving tide are filling coolers with porgies from 12 to 15 inches, with a scattering of humpback jumbos mixed in for anyone soaking clam on bottom instead of jigging.

Fluke are doing what they always do in August — stacking up wherever the channels concentrate bait and current. Plum Gut is still the marquee spot but it's not for the faint of heart on a strong tide; if you can time a drift through there on the last of the ebb before it slacks, you're in business. Better bet for most boats has been the Orient Point channel edges and the deeper cuts in Noyack Bay off Jessups Neck, working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in chartreuse or pearl, dragged slow along the bottom in 20 to 30 feet. Keeper-size fluke, three to five pounds, have been coming steady on the outgoing, with the occasional doormat pushing six or seven pounds turning up on the deeper drop-offs where the water stays a few degrees cooler than the flats around it.

Weakfish are the story I've been watching closest, and they're tracking exactly the pattern we called — following the peanut bunker right into the protected coves. Hashamomuck on the north shore of the bay has had bunker balled up thick near the boat ramp, and weakfish have been slashing through them at dusk. Small bucktails, quarter-ounce, white or pink, cast into the edges of the bunker schools and worked with a slow twitch, have been drawing strikes from weakfish in the 16 to 20-inch range. Three Mile Harbor and Sag Harbor Cove are showing the same setup — bunker pushed into the shallows, weakfish and the occasional bass working the margins where the current funnels bait against the bank. If you're on the outgoing tide right at last light, that's your window, and it's been a real one, not a rumor.

Striped bass have been the tougher nut in this heat, same story as the rest of the coast — daytime bite is mostly shut down outside of current-swept structure, and the real action is happening dawn, dusk, and after dark around the bunker schools. Orient Point and the Plum Gut rip are still the go-to for that low-light bass bite — live bunker on a fish-finder rig, or bucktails worked deep along the rip edges as the tide starts to move, has been drawing slot fish and the occasional overslot in the dark hours. Nothing exploding, but consistent enough that it's worth setting the alarm early if bass are the target.

Bluefish-wise, the snapper blues have moved into the back bays in good numbers — Three Mile Harbor and the shallows off Sag Harbor have snappers chasing anything shiny, great light-tackle action for kids with small Kastmasters or Gotcha plugs off the dock. The bigger cocktail blues haven't shown in force yet, but with peanut bunker spreading through the bays the way it has, I wouldn't be surprised to see that change inside the next week or two as those blues start tracking the same bait the weakfish are on.

The full moon this week has put some real push into the tides, and that's sharpened up the bite right at the changes — fluke and porgies both have been snapping on when the current kicks in hard after a slack period, then going quiet again once it settles into a steady flow. Worth planning your trip around that first hour of moving water rather than fishing the whole tide blind.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the south-southwest like it's been, I'd expect this pattern to hold — porgies stacked at Shelter Island, fluke working the channel edges, weakfish riding the bunker into the coves at dusk. If we get a stretch of northerly wind that roughs up the open bay, I'd shift effort into the protected coves and harbors where the fishing barely notices the weather. Scallop season's still a ways off, so all the effort right now is squarely on these summer finfish, and there's enough happening to keep a rod bent most evenings if you put in the time on the tide.

reports.headline: Full Moon Outgoing: Bass Tuck Into the Deep Hole After Midnight
reports.subhead: With the ocean pushing 79 degrees, the real bite at Shinnecock is happening after the boats go home — in the dark, on the back half of the outgoing.
reports.body_markdown:
I stopped fighting the clock a long time ago. Every August, guys ask me why I'm rigging up at 10pm instead of hitting the inlet at first light, and the answer is simple — right now, first light is the worst time to be there. The ocean's sitting near 79 degrees off the beach, the sun's been baking the flats all afternoon, and every striper with a brain has slid into deep water and gone quiet until the heat breaks. So I wait. I fish the back half of the outgoing, starting a couple hours before the tide bottoms out, when that warm surface water finally starts draining off the flats and the current stacks bait against structure. That's when the inlet wakes up.

This week that meant the deep hole on the ocean side of the jetty, current ripping through by 11pm on a rising moon, and bass showing up right on schedule. Nothing enormous — mostly 26 to 32 inches, with a couple of fish pushing 34 mixed in — but they've been consistent for anyone willing to stand there in the dark and work it right. Livelined bunker under a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, has been the best producer. Guys throwing bucktails are doing fine too — 1.5-ounce white or bone bucktails, cast up-current and allowed to swing down through the hole before a slow, deliberate retrieve along bottom. The full moon this week has the tide moving with real authority, which sharpens that outgoing bite into a tighter window than usual — you get about ninety minutes of prime current before it goes soft, so don't waste the front end of it fumbling with rigs on the beach.

Inside the bay, fluke are still the most dependable fish going, and the canal remains the smart move if you want a shot without burning half a tank of gas running the ocean side. The lock-driven current at Shinnecock Canal County Park does the work for you — when those gates start opening, bait gets funneled and squeezed, and fluke stack up on that edge for the thirty to forty-five minutes the current's really moving.
