I've been doing well there with a half-ounce chartreuse bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet, bounced slow along the rubble bottom right where the current narrows. Bring extra rigs — that bottom eats hooks and jig heads, no way around it. Out in the open bay, the drift bite off Tiana and the flats south of the canal has been decent on the last two hours of the incoming, doormats mixing in with the shorts on white Gulp and squid strip combos in 15 to 20 feet, right along the edges where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper channel.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been a mixed bag — some nights the current lines up and you get a nice pull of fish holding tight to the pilings on the last of the outgoing, other nights it's dead quiet and you're better off targeting the blues that are sweeping through instead. When it's working, small pink or chartreuse jig heads with a soft plastic shad tail, fished slow and bounced right off the bottom structure near the bridge lights, have been the ticket after dark. The lights themselves matter — weakfish sit in that shadow line where the current brings bait past the pilings, and a well-placed cast into the dark edge beats blind casting into the lit water every time.

Bluefish have been the most reliable fish in the system the past two weeks, honestly — snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks off Tiana and Hampton Bays proper, giving kids and light-tackle guys steady action on small metal and Kastmasters. The adult blues are showing in sweeps through the inlet itself, usually pushing bait ahead of the tide change, and when they come through it's fast and violent for ten or fifteen minutes before they move on. Keep a rod rigged with a tin ready even when you're fishing for bass — those blues don't wait for you to switch gear.

Looking ahead, this moon-driven current isn't going to hold at this strength much longer. Once we're a few days past full, the tide swings will ease back to something more normal, and that means the bite windows at the inlet and the canal will widen back out a little rather than being crammed into that tight ninety-minute stretch. That's not necessarily bad news — it usually means a more forgiving bite for anyone who can't be out there at exactly the right minute. If the ocean holds in the high 70s like it has, I'd expect the bass to keep favoring the deep hole and current edges after dark rather than pushing onto the flats during the day, so plan around the night tide, not the sunrise. And if that peanut bunker keeps building in the back bay creeks the way it has, don't be surprised if the weakfish bite at the bridge firms up before the month's out — that's the pattern I'd be watching closest over the next couple weeks.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: night eels working, and the bay finally got its peanut bunker
reports.subhead: Rough ocean pushed the bite inside this week — the inlet and the back bays are where the real work's getting done.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a guy at the Captree fuel dock Wednesday morning ask me, half-joking, if the ocean forgot how to lay down. Fair question. We've had a lumpy Bight all week — 2.6-footers rolling in on a short six-second period, water out there pushing 79 degrees on the surface, which sounds nice until you realize that's bathwater for stripers and it's got the whole food chain either sulking deep or ducking inside where it's cooler. So that's where I sent him. That's where I've been sending everybody.

The thermal split right now is the whole story. Ocean's warm and sloppy, but Great South Bay and the inlet channels are running a few degrees under that, and any current seam that pulls cooler water past structure is going to hold fish. Fire Island Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the move — that's when the bay dumps its warmer surface water out through Democrat Point and the deeper, cooler stuff gets pulled up the channel edges. Bass are stacking there but they're not stupid about it. Daytime is basically a non-event unless you're right on that current break at first light. Real bite window is dusk into full dark, eels drifted or slow-trolled along the sod bank edges off Democrat Point and down toward the Robert Moses bridge pilings. Nothing heroic size-wise — mostly 26 to 32 inches, a few overslot fish mixed in for guys willing to sit out there past midnight — but it's a real bite if you're patient and quiet about it.

Fluke are still the most honest fish in the bay right now, and the full moon this week actually helped that fishery more than it hurt it. Bigger tidal swing means sharper current at the changes, and that's exactly when the doormats decide to feed. Best water's been the channel edges around the Robert Moses bridges, 25 to 35 feet, and the deeper cuts off Kismet and Oak Beach on the bay side. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, some guys tipping with a strip of squid for the scent trail, dragged slow right on the bottom through the last hour of the outgoing. We're seeing fish to five and six pounds mixed in with a lot of teen-and-under shorts, so it's a sort-through fishery, but the keeper ratio's been fair for August. If you're marking bait on the meter and not getting bit, move — the fluke are sitting tight to the drop, not spread across the flat.

Now here's something worth flagging — we said a couple weeks back that peanut bunker were pushing down from New England and would be in the bay inside of two weeks, and sure enough they showed up in the back creeks off Patchogue and around the Bellport flats this week. That bait push is exactly why the snapper blues and cocktail blues have gone from scattered to genuinely thick in the back bay. If you've got kids or you just want steady bend-in-the-rod action, small silver spoons or a bare hook with a sliver of bunker off any dock from Babylon to Sayville will keep you busy for an hour straight. The bigger adult blues are still tucked in tighter to the inlet and the ocean-side bars, ambushing those bunker schools on the move, so if you want a real fish on top instead of snappers, work the surf line at Democrat Point right at first light before the sun gets up and pushes everything down.

Weakfish have been a ghost story again this summer — I've heard of a couple caught incidentally on bucktails meant for fluke, nothing worth planning a trip around. Porgies are around the Fire Island reef structure and the bridge rubble in decent numbers on bloodworms and clam, but nobody's writing home about it either. Blackfish are still weeks off — don't waste bait on them yet.

One more thing worth knowing if you're a night owl: Heckscher State Park opened up Field 6 for night fishing this summer, first year ever, and it's legit — Friday, Saturday, Sunday, dusk to dawn, through Labor Day. You need a Night Sport Fishing Permit or the 4x4 permit on your dash, but if you've got it, that stretch of Great South Bay shoreline on the outgoing tide is worth a look for bass and blues working the channel edge in the dark, especially with the bay pushing that warmer water out past the marsh. It's a trial, so don't be the guy who ruins it for everybody — pack out your trash, follow the hours.

Looking ahead, the moon's coming off full and the tides will settle back to normal by the weekend, which should tighten up the bite windows again instead of spreading current out over a longer swing. If the ocean lays down even a little, I'd be watching the outer bars off Fire Island for the first sign of false albacore or bonito working bait balls — the surface temp's been sitting right in that window for a couple weeks now. Nothing confirmed yet, but that's exactly the kind of August surprise this beat throws at you when you're not looking.

reports.headline: Full Moon Torque Puts Bass Back on the Wire at The Race
reports.subhead: Current rebuilt like we said it would, and the stripers came back with it — plus the first real bonito signs are stacking up off Fishers Island.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, 3:40 a.m., east side of The Race. I'm up to my thighs on the rocks below the lighthouse throwing a jointed Gibbs Danny into water that's finally moving with authority again, and on the fourth cast something grabs it like it means business. Forty inches, maybe forty-one, hooked outside the mouth and buried into the current before I could get tight. Took me into the rip twice trying to spool me before I walked her up on the rocks. That's the fish that tells you the moon did its job.

We flagged this one — said the rips would rebuild toward the full moon and the striper and bluefish bite on bait pushed through them would sharpen up noticeably once current strengthened, and that's exactly what happened. The Race is running back in the 4-to-5 knot range on the big swings now, Plum Gut right behind it, and the bass that scattered and sulked during the neap lull are back on the current edges where they belong. This isn't subtle fishing. You're not picking through structure looking for stragglers — you're finding the seam where the moving water meets the slack, and the fish are stacked right on that line waiting for bait to get squeezed through.

The pattern that's working: fish the last two hours of the ebb and first hour of the flood at The Race, working bucktails — 2 to 3 ounces depending on how hard it's ripping — tipped with a white curl-tail or a chunk of fresh bunker, dropped off the edge of the reef structure on the west side and bounced down current. Let it sink clean, don't rush it, then work it back with a slow lift-drop through the seam. Bass have been running mostly mid-20s to low-30s inches with a handful of overslot fish mixed in on the dawn bite — nothing like the 40-plus I stuck Tuesday, but that's the kind of water that produces one big fish out of every dozen decent ones if you put your time in.

Bluefish are the other half of this story and they're not messing around. Jumbo blues, 8 to 12 pounds, are busting bunker pods hard in Fishers Island Sound and right through Plum Gut on the tide changes. Topwater poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Ava jigs in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range — are getting hit the second they land when the blues are up and slashing. If you see the birds working tight and nervous water, don't wait, get the boat on it, that window closes fast once the blues push the bait down.

Water's holding in a spot that's actually working in our favor out here. New London's reading right around 70 degrees, cooler than the western Sound, which is keeping the bass comfortable enough to stay active through more of the daylight hours than you'd expect for the second week of August — not an all-day bite, but the dawn and dusk windows are stretching a little longer than they were three weeks ago. Keep an eye on that gradient. If the eastern water holds steady in the high 60s to low 70s while the rest of the Sound keeps warming, this end stays the better play right through Labor Day.

Fluke are the dependable piece right now, and the Niantic fleet is proving the call we made last week — that fishery is basically neap-proof and it's carrying the zone through any current lull. Boats working 38 feet of water off Niantic Bay are still punching limits with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift over the mixed bottom there. A few doormats in the 6-to-7 pound class have come out of that stretch this week. If the rip bite goes quiet on you for a tide, that's where I'd put the boat.

Porgies are stacked up on the reef structure between Plum Gut and Fishers Island — bloodworms and clam on standard porgy rigs in 25 to 40 feet is still automatic if you're anchored up right on the rock piles. Not glamorous but it fills a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn back in your favor for bass.

Now the one I'm watching hardest — bonito. Water's sitting in that low-to-mid 70s window that historically gets this corridor moving first in the region, and The Race and Plum Gut are usually among the earliest spots to see them stack up when the temp's right. Nothing solid on the deck yet that I'd call confirmed, but the conditions are lining up. I'd have small Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax rigged and ready on a second rod this week just in case the first push shows on the surface — those things materialize fast and disappear just as quick.

Look-ahead: current stays strong through the weekend as we ride down off full moon, so I'd keep hammering the rip edges early and late. By midweek the swings ease back toward standard range — that's when I'd lean harder on Niantic for the sure thing and keep working dawn patrol at the Gut for whatever's still stacked on the seams.

reports.headline: Throgs Neck bunker pods pull bass and blues on the last of the dark
reports.subhead: The daytime bite's gone quiet with the heat, but the bunker schools stacking off City Island are turning on stripers and blues at first light.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island Avenue asked me Tuesday why his charter got skunked on bass at noon last week, working the same rockpile off Hart Island that put fish in the box back in June. I told him what I've been telling guys for thirty years in the dead of August — the sun's up too high, the water's too warm on top, and if you want stripers this time of year you fish the dark. Simple as that. He didn't love the answer, but it's the truth of the Western Sound in high summer.

Kings Point is reading 72.5 degrees, New London's sitting at 69.8, and that gradient tells you everything. The western end of the Sound holds the heat longer, and by two in the afternoon the top six feet off Matinecock or the flats inside Little Neck Bay is basically a warm bath. Bass don't want any part of that in daylight. What they want is the dark water down around Execution Rocks and the last hour of light through the Stepping Stones, when the current starts working and the temperature breaks a couple degrees on the drop.

The good news — and there's real good news this week — is the bunker. Big pods of peanut and adult bunker have parked off Throgs Neck and along the City Island flats, thick enough to color the water black in patches, and every predator in the Sound knows it. We flagged the bunker spread a week back as the thing to watch for cocktail blues, and here it is — snapper blues have thickened up in Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay, and the adult blues are riding those bunker schools right up against the bridge pilings at dawn. Guys throwing SP Minnows and small Deadly Dicks into the edges of those pods at first light are getting steady action, blues in the 3- to 5-pound range, some better.

Stripers are working the same bunker but on their own schedule — first thirty minutes of gray light and the last thirty of dusk, that's the window. Live-lining a bunker off a fish-finder rig, freespooled back into the pod, has produced the better fish — nothing enormous, mostly schoolies and a few keepers in the 26- to 30-inch range around the Execution Rocks rockpile on the last of the outgoing. If you're not there for that window, don't bother — I had two nights this week where the tide was right and the bass just weren't up, and one night where they hammered bunker so hard off the rocks it looked like rain hitting the surface. That's August for you. You put your time in on the tide, not the clock.

Fluke has been the more dependable player, and the moon's helping. We're coming off the full moon swing, and that extra push has sharpened the drift bite at the tide changes — I've had my best fluke drifts of the month working the channel edge off Matinecock Point and the deeper cuts inside Hempstead Harbor, 25 to 35 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. Doormats have been scattered but real — a 6-pounder came over the rail off Manhasset Bay on the last incoming Sunday, and I've heard of a couple better than that working the Throgs Neck side. The pattern's the same everywhere: fish it slow, right on the bottom, right through the moment the tide turns, because that's when the current-swept structure gives up its best window.

Porgies remain the honest man's fishery out here — you want a bent rod without overthinking it, anchor up on any of the rockpiles from Hart Island out to Execution Rocks, drop bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 30 feet, and you'll load the cooler. Nothing glamorous about it, but it's about as close to a guarantee as this Sound offers in August, and on a slow bass morning it's saved plenty of trips.

Weakfish have been quiet on my end — I know the bunker's supposed to pull them into the bays this month, and I've heard whispers of a few taken deep on bucktails around Manhasset, but I haven't put my hands on one myself, so I'm not going to oversell it. If you're targeting them, fish the same deep holes where the porgies and fluke are stacking and keep an open mind.

Blue claw crabbing, meanwhile, has been about the most reliable thing going — the back bays and marsh creeks off Little Neck and Manhasset are loaded, chicken necks on a hand line will keep a family busy for an afternoon while the men work the rod tips elsewhere.

Looking ahead, the moon's starting to ease off full, which should settle the current back into a more normal rhythm by midweek — shorter, gentler pushes at the bridge and reef rips instead of the exaggerated full-moon current we've had. That usually means the bite windows get a little more predictable, even if they don't get any longer. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd be at Execution Rocks forty minutes before first light on the outgoing, live bunker ready to go, and I'd have a bucktail rigged for fluke as backup once the sun gets up and the bass shut down. That's the two-fish plan that's been working for me all month, and I don't see any reason to change it yet.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Flood the Harbors — Blues Trail Close, Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: Watching the bait pile into Port Jeff and Oyster Bay this week told me more than any buoy could — here's what's chasing it.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning at the mouth of Port Jefferson Harbor just watching, not fishing, because the bait was doing something worth paying attention to. Peanut bunker — thick pods of them, maybe two to three inches, packed tight enough to shadow the bottom — were pouring out of the harbor mouth on the last of the ebb and scattering along the edge where the channel drops to 15 feet. Terns were working them hard, diving in tight little circles, and under that commotion I watched three separate blowups that weren't terns. That's blues, and they're right where the bait says they should be.

We flagged this two weeks back — said the bluefish would track the peanut bunker as it spread and that back-bay cocktail blues would spike within two weeks. Here it is. Northport Bay, Oyster Bay, and the Port Jeff inner harbor are all holding schoolie blues in the 12 to 16-inch range hammering that bait on the outgoing tide, and they're not hard to find once you spot the birds. Small Deadly Dick spoons, half-ounce Kastmasters, or three-inch Albie Snax in bunker patterns — fast retrieve, no finesse needed. Kids-on-the-dock fishing at its best, and it's a good early warning system for what's about to show up on the bigger structure.

Because where the peanut bunker concentrates, the bigger fish follow eventually, and the bass are already staging on it after dark. This time of year, with the Sound sitting warm — Kings Point read 72.5 the other day, a good four degrees ahead of what New London's showing to the east — the stripers just aren't interested in daytime work outside of moving current over structure. Stratford Shoal at night has been the play. Anchor up-current of the rip on the last two hours of the incoming, soak fresh bunker chunks or live peanuts on a fish-finder rig, 3/0 circle hook, and be patient. Guys working that shoal after 9 PM have been putting slot fish in the boat, along with the occasional 30-incher that decided to stick around instead of running the rip through to the Race. Middle Ground Light has fished similarly at dusk — bucktails, an ounce and a half, bounced slow along the drop just as the light fails, has drawn some quality fish off the rocks.

Daytime, honestly, the shoal bite has been a step slower than it was three weeks ago, and that tracks with what we expected — the neap tide early last week took the current down a gear and the daytime bite went with it. Full moon current is building back now, and I felt it Tuesday — more push through the rip than I'd seen in ten days. That should start sharpening the structure bite again by midweek, particularly at Stratford Shoal and around the Norwalk Islands where the porgies and sea bass have been holding steady through all of this regardless of tide strength. Sandworms and clam strips on a simple high-low rig, 20 to 35 feet around the rockpiles off Sheffield Island and the outer Norwalks, has been dependable — not exciting, but dependable, and that's worth something in August when a lot of other things are inconsistent.

Fluke have been the most honest fish in the zone. Channel edges and current-swept drop-offs are holding doormats where the water stays a few degrees cooler than the flats around them — the Port Jeff channel mouth, the drop just south of Charles Island, and the deeper cuts through the Norwalk Islands have all produced fish to five pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide, not against it. The full moon swing this week should sharpen those tide-change windows even more — the first hour after the turn has been when the bigger fish show.

Now, the thing I'm actually watching closest right now isn't in my zone yet, but it's close enough that I keep checking. Bonito season is right on schedule for a mid-August push, and the early word out of the Race and Fishers Island Sound is that reports are starting to firm up as water temps sit in that low-to-mid-70s sweet spot. That's the same water sitting off Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground right now. Every August I've fished this stretch, the bonito show up on bait first — small, tight, silver flashes chasing rain bait or tiny peanuts — days before anyone's marking them on a fishfinder. If you're out on the shoal and see something moving faster and more erratic than the blues, don't assume it's another cocktail blue. Have a small metal ready.

Looking at the week ahead: current strength is building back toward the full moon, which should put some snap back into the daytime shoal bite by Wednesday or Thursday if the wind cooperates. A stiff southwest blow would undo some of that, especially on the western end near Oyster Bay, but the central basin around Stratford Shoal tends to handle wind better than the western approaches do — it took the last blow in better shape than Huntington did. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Stratford Shoal rip on the building tide after dark, bunker chunks out, and keep a bucktail rigged for whatever shows up chasing that peanut bunker when the sun's still up.

reports.headline: Forget the noon fluke drift — the jetty bite doesn't start till the sun goes down
reports.subhead: With the ocean running warm and lumpy, Jones Inlet's best striper action is happening after dark against the rocks, not on the midday flats.
reports.body_markdown:
Every boat ramp conversation this week is the same: guys lining up at first light to hit the Sloop Channel drift for fluke, burning gas by 9 a.m., back at the dock with a cooler of shorts by lunch. I get it — the drift bite is real, and I'll get into it. But if you want to know where I've been putting my time, it's not out there in the noon sun. It's at the Jones Inlet jetty rocks, starting an hour before sunset and running into full dark, because that's when the stripers actually show up to eat.

Here's the thing nobody wants to admit in August: the ocean's running 78.8 degrees off the Bight buoy, which is bathwater. Stripers don't want anything to do with that kind of heat during the day. They tuck into the current-swept structure and cooler pockets and wait for the sun to drop before they'll commit to feeding. That's exactly the pattern I'm seeing at the inlet — dead quiet at 2 p.m., and then the last hour of light the bunker start getting nervous against the rocks and the bass show up underneath them like clockwork. I've been throwing bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3-ounce egg sinker, right into the wash where the jetty meets the channel, and hooking fish from the last hour of daylight through the first two hours of dark. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 30 inches, with the occasional keeper mixed in — but it's steady, and it's a lot better than standing out there at noon getting nothing.

If you want to fish it legit after hours, Field 1 East Bathhouse has the night access again this year — Friday, Saturday, Sunday, dusk to 6 a.m., and it's a good launch point for the eastern surf that runs current west toward the inlet. You need the Night Sport Fishing Permit and the DEC saltwater registry, no way around it, but it's worth the paperwork. That stretch holds sandbars better than the west end of the beach, and on the outgoing tide the current sweeps bait right along that structure.

Now, the fluke — I'm not going to pretend it's bad, because it's not. The drift through Sloop Channel and the deeper edges off the inlet is still the most dependable thing going in this zone right now. Guys are picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers in the 20 to 30 foot depths, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the channel drop-offs where the water stays a few degrees cooler than the flats. The full moon has the tide running harder than it has in weeks, and that stronger push is sharpening the bite right at the tide changes — first hour of the outgoing and the last hour of the incoming are when I'm hearing about the better fish, doormats up to 5 and 6 pounds mixed in with the boat-load of shorts. If you're going to fish it, go at the tide change, not the middle of the tide when everything's just laying there.

Bluefish are doing what bluefish do in August — riding shotgun on whatever bait's around. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks off Freeport and Wantagh, great for kids with a bobber and a piece of spearing, and there are cocktail blues mixing into the bunker schools at the inlet mouth during that same dusk window where I'm finding the bass. Don't be shocked if you hook a chopper blue on a bunker chunk meant for a striper — happens more nights than not right now.

Weakfish are still a bonus fish, not a target, but I'm hearing more legit reports out of South Oyster Bay than I have in a couple seasons — fish in the 16 to 20 inch range coming on soft plastics worked slow along the grass edges in the low-light hours. If the comeback's real, this is the kind of summer where it starts showing up in guys' coolers instead of just talk at the bait shop.

Porgies are exactly where you'd expect — jetty rock piles and the nearby bay structure, sandworms and clam on a hi-lo rig, and they'll keep you busy between bass bites if the action's slow.

We flagged a couple weeks back that the first peanut bunker scouts were showing up in southern New England and that the bay peanuts here were due inside two weeks — I haven't seen them stack up in the back creeks yet, but the timing lines up close, and when they do show, that back-bay food chain flips fast. Worth watching the marsh creek mouths on the outgoing tide over the next week or so.

As the moon slides past full, that exaggerated tidal push will ease back to normal, which usually settles the bite windows into something more predictable rather than the jacked-up current we've had. My plan doesn't change much — I'll keep working the jetty from last light into dark as long as the ocean stays warm, because that's where the fish want to be right now. If you're set on daytime fishing, hit the fluke drift right on the tide change and don't waste your morning fishing dead water in between.

reports.headline: Floyd Bennett kayak launch: fluke on the channel edges, blues thick off Canarsie Pier
reports.subhead: The bay's sitting near its ceiling and the ocean's a washing machine, so this week the smart money stayed inside — and it paid off on fluke, snappers, and one good bass at the bridge.
reports.body_markdown:
I launched the kayak out of Aviation Road at Floyd Bennett Field before sunrise Tuesday, and I picked that ramp on purpose. The ocean's been ugly all week — buoy data off the Bight had it running better than two and a half feet of chop with a short six-second period, the kind of slop that turns a nice ocean beach session into a workout for nothing. Inside the bay, though, it's flat and it's warm, and warm water with bait in it is exactly where I want to be paddling.

We flagged this last week — said the post-frontal stir off that Sunday blow would cool and re-oxygenate the bay right as the neap softened the current, and that's more or less what happened. Tuesday and Wednesday both had a cleaner, more comfortable feel to the water than the flat-out soup we had the week before. It didn't last long — by Thursday afternoon the bay had gone quiet again on that slack neap current, which tracks with what we expected. But that two-day window was worth being out there for.

Fluke were the play, and they've been the most honest fishery in the bay all summer. I worked the channel edge off Grass Hassock, 16 to 20 feet, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail nice and slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. Picked up four keepers in that stretch, biggest going about 22 inches, plus a handful of shorts that came off the hook or measured just under. The bite wasn't nonstop — I marked bait on the fish finder in three, maybe four tight pockets and had to hunt between them. If you're not marking bait, you're not marking fluke right now. Same story working the edge along the Cross Bay Bridge channel — a few boats anchored up there doing well on strip bait and squid combos fished right on bottom as the tide turned.

Canarsie Pier has been a snapper blue factory, and if you've got kids or you just want a bend in the rod every other cast, that's your spot. Small blues, 8 to 12 inches, are stacked in the shallows around the pier lights and along the bulkhead, eating tiny silver Kastmasters and 1/8-ounce Deadly Dick spoons fished fast on light spinning gear. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and it's about the only daytime bite that doesn't require you to think too hard about tide stage — those blues are on bait and they don't seem to care much about the clock.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Peak summer heat has them locked into a strict low-light pattern — this isn't the May run where you could find fish cruising the flats at noon. The daytime bite has gone quiet almost everywhere except the current-swept structure, and the Marine Parkway Bridge is exactly that kind of structure. I fished the pilings from the kayak on the last of Wednesday's outgoing, right at last light, and worked a bucktail with a white Fin-S trailer tight to the current seam on the down-current side. One fish, but it was a good one — mid-20s, thick, clearly staged up waiting on the tide to bring bait through. That's the pattern right now: bass holding at the bridge, at Breezy Point tip, wherever there's hard current and shade, and they're feeding hard for a short window around dusk and through the night rather than all day long.

If you want to fish that pattern from shore, Fort Tilden and Breezy Point are still your best bets, and both still require the NPS Fishing Access Pass at all times — the 193rd Street lot and the 222nd Street lot both take it, and yes, the annual passes are sold out for the year, so if you don't already have one, you're looking at day passes if they're available or fishing the free access at Canarsie Pier or Marine Park instead. Breezy Point's tip is the classic night bass spot for a reason — the rip where the bay meets the ocean concentrates bait hard on the outgoing, and that funnel effect only gets better as the moon builds.

And that's really the story for the coming week. We're heading into the new moon springs on the 11th through the 13th, and that's going to re-arm the current at the bridge and at the inlet in a way the neap just couldn't. Bigger tidal swings mean harder-running ebbs, which means more bait getting pushed through the pinch points, which means the bass that have been holding tight to structure should get a real reason to feed. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd want it under that new moon, working the outgoing at Marine Parkway Bridge or the Breezy Point tip with a bucktail or a swimming plug worked slow through the seam. Daytime, I'd stick with the fluke drift off Grass Hassock and the Cross Bay channel edges — that bite doesn't need a big tide to work, just bait, and there's been bait.

Worth noting the porgies have been mixing in around the bridge structure on bottom rigs with clam and squid, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus while you're anchored up waiting on the tide to turn. Blackfish season's still closed here, so that's one for the fall notebook. For now, work the moving water, fish the low light for bass, and don't expect the ocean side to fish clean until that swell backs off.

reports.headline: Terns Are Working Great Point Like They Know Something We Don't
reports.subhead: No green flashes on the Shoals yet, but the bird sign, the bait, and the water temps say bonito are close — meanwhile the stripers and blues are already paying rent in the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, first light, I'm sitting on the west side of the Great Point rip watching a mixed flock of terns work a nervous patch of water about eighty yards off the bar. They're diving hard, dropping and lifting, the way they do when there's something small and fast pushing bait up from underneath. I watched that spot for twenty minutes waiting for a green flash to break the surface — that first bonito of the year cutting through a peanut school — and it never came. What did come was a bluefish blowup, chunky three-to-five pound cocktail blues absolutely wrecking the same bait, which is its own kind of good news, just not the news I was hoping to write about this week.

Here's where we're at. The bonito aren't here yet on Nantucket Shoals, but I don't think it's a long wait. The signs pointing that direction out of Rhode Island breachways and the Vineyard rips earlier this week are exactly the kind of leading edge that tends to show up on our side of the Sound within days, not weeks — that's the sequence I've watched play out for going on fifteen years, RI and the Vineyard first, then Nantucket Shoals and Great Point catch the spillover. If that pattern holds, and there's no reason yet to think it won't with this stable weather sitting over us, I'd expect the first confirmed bonito over the Shoals sometime in the next week to ten days. Albies are behind that again — Great Point doesn't usually see its first real showing until deeper into August, so don't burn your legs off chasing false albacore just yet. Chase the terns instead and see what's actually under them.

What's real and biting right now is the striper work in the rips, and it's a nighttime and low-light game almost exclusively. Surface water in the Sound has settled into that classic mid-summer pattern — warm enough on top that the bigger fish have slid down onto structure and pushed their feeding into the dark hours and the tide changes. I've had my best luck working the drop on the north side of Old Man Shoal on the last two hours of the ebb, eels drifted just off bottom in eighteen to twenty-five feet, letting the current do the work instead of working the rod. Bass Rip has been doing the same thing — quiet at midday, then turning on hard about an hour before dark as the current builds and bait gets pinned against the shoal edge. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, weight enough to hold bottom in that current, have out-produced eels for some boats this week, especially on the tail end of the tide when the current slackens just enough for the chunks to sit still.

Fluke have pushed off the shallow flats entirely — too warm up top — and settled onto the deeper structure where the bottom stays workable. Monomoy Channel and the edges of Stone Horse Shoal have been the most consistent producers, twenty-two to thirty-two feet, drifting bucktail and Gulp combinations, four-inch white or chartreuse swimming mullets on three-quarter-ounce heads, dragged slow and heavy on the bottom of the drift. Nothing spectacular size-wise — most of what's coming over the rail is fifteen to eighteen inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but it's steady enough that a couple hours over that structure on a moving tide will put fish in the box.

The bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and that lines up with what we flagged a few days back about cocktail blues tracking the peanut bunker as it spreads through the back-bay and inlet zones — that's exactly what's happening off Monomoy and around the Chatham break right now, tighter schools of smaller blues chopping through bait pods in six to fifteen feet, easy pickings on top-water poppers or small metal if you can find the surface activity before it moves. The adult blues, the four-to-eight pound class, are running with bigger bunker schools out in open water off Great Point and Horseshoe Shoal, and those fish will hit bigger swimming plugs or bunker spoons trolled just outside the structure.

Tide and moon-wise, we're building out of the recent slack period toward fuller tides again, which should sharpen up the current-dependent spots — the Handkerchief, Bass Rip, the Monomoy rips on the outgoing — over the next several days. Stronger current means tighter bait concentrations, which means better odds on everything from the stripers to whatever shows up first when the bonito finally arrive.

Looking ahead, if the calm weather holds — and right now there's nothing on the radar to say it won't — I'd put my money on Nantucket Shoals and Great Point producing the first confirmed bonito of the season sometime in the next week to ten days, riding the same warm push that's already the Vineyard and RI side. Until then, work the low-light stripers on the shoal edges, hit the fluke grounds off Monomoy on a moving tide, and keep an eye on the birds. They usually know before we do.

reports.headline: 120 feet on the Stellwagen gravel: cod chewing, mackerel schools pulling bluefin up top
reports.subhead: Steady bottom bite on the Bank this week, and the first real tuna showing on the surface chasing mackerel — but you have to find the birds first.
reports.body_markdown:
128 feet of water on the northeast corner of Stellwagen, gravel bottom, and my sounder was stacked with marks sitting right on the bottom third — that's the read I've been getting all week and it's held up. Cod are there, they're just not stupid about it. You put a clam bait or a diamond jig with a teaser dropper down through that column and you'll know within the first ten feet off bottom whether they're eating.

We've been working the edge where the gravel transitions into softer bottom, that seam that runs along the northeast face toward Tillies. Cod to 15 pounds, most fish running 6 to 10, and they want bait moving — jigging a 12-ounce diamond jig with a red tube teaser well off bottom, or drifting whole clams on a high-low rig if the current's slack enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. When the tide's ripping over the Bank, which it has been on this cycle, you need 16 to 20 ounces just to feel the bottom, and that's when the bite can shut down fast — the fish don't want to chase in hard water. Best windows have been the last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of new tide, when things settle down enough for a clean drift.

Haddock have been more scattered than I'd like for early August, but where we've found them it's been good — soft mud pockets in 140 to 160 feet on the western side of the Bank, that classic mud-line country south of the Basin. These fish want a smaller hook, size 6 or 8, tipped with clam, fished right on bottom with minimal weight so the bait sits still instead of dragging. When you find a pod of haddock they're usually tight together, and you can load the box in twenty minutes and then it goes quiet — move the boat 200 yards and start over. That's been the pattern all week: find them, hammer them, they go quiet, you pick up and hunt again.

Now the fun part. Bluefin have shown up on the Bank chasing mackerel, and that's exactly what you want to see this time of year. Warm water's been pushing north and it's dragging bait with it — mackerel schools have been thick on the surface over the southwest corner and out toward Cape Cod Tails, and where you find the mac balls getting nervous, birds diving, whales working the same bait, that's where the bluefin have been showing. I had a morning last week where we ran up on a school of maybe forty fish busting mackerel on top, all in the 80 to 150 pound class from what we could see rolling — didn't stick one, but we had shots. Green machines and small poppers thrown right into the boil have drawn strikes, and if you can get a bait pinned or a spreader bar through the middle of a busting school, you've got a real shot.

The key with these fish is patience and not running the school over. They'll show, sound, and pop up again a quarter mile off — chase them and you'll blow the whole pod down. Better to set up ahead of where you think they're moving and let them come to you. Whale activity has been a good tell all week — humpbacks and finbacks working the same bait balls as the tuna, so if you see whale spouts and diving birds together, that's worth a long look through the glasses before you commit fuel to it.

Weather's been giving us a stable window — light southwest winds, seas laying down enough to fish comfortably out on the Bank and even push out toward Tillies without getting beat up. That's the kind of stretch you want to take advantage of before anything changes, because we're deep enough into hurricane season now that any tropical development needs watching. If the pattern holds through the weekend, I'd be splitting time — work the gravel early for cod while the tide allows a clean drift, then run out looking for mackerel schools and birds once the sun's up and the surface bite has a chance to show itself.

One thing I'll say plainly: the haddock bite isn't wide open right now. You have to hunt for it, and some drifts you'll mark fish and get nothing, other drifts you'll load up. That's just where we are in the season on the mud — it comes and goes in pockets rather than a blanket bite across the Bank. Cod on the gravel has been more consistent, which is a nice change from earlier in the summer when everything felt scattered.

Looking ahead, if this stable weather holds another few days I expect the mackerel schools to keep building on the Bank, which means more shots at bluefin showing on top. Keep an eye on the whale activity — where the big boys are working, the tuna usually aren't far off. I'd rather run out on a calm morning and spend an hour glassing for birds and spouts than blind-troll the whole Bank hoping to bump into fish. Bring the jigging rods regardless — even on a slow tuna morning, that gravel edge in 120 to 130 feet has been good enough to fill a cooler with cod while you wait for the surface to light up with bait.

reports.headline: The 5:52 ebb: bass stack the East End rip, blues ride behind
reports.subhead: Current's still soft off the neap, but the last two hours of every ebb are turning fish on both ends of the ditch.
reports.body_markdown:
5:52 this morning, East End, and the ebb hadn't even topped out yet when the first boil showed off the Bourne side riprap. That's the tell right now — you don't wait for max current on the Canal in early August, you fish the building stage, because the fish are already up on the seam before the flow ever gets to its strongest push. By 6:40, when the current was running a legitimate 3.5 to 4 knots east to west, there were three guys hooked up simultaneously off the Herring Run rocks, and that's about as good a sign as you'll get on a Friday morning in high summer.

We flagged this a few days back — said the bass bite here would stay tied to the strongest tidal exchange as the moon eased toward the next neap, and that's exactly the shape of things this week. Current's been on the soft side, nothing violent, which means the window of good fishing on each tide change is narrower than it was during the new moon push. You've got roughly ninety minutes on each end — the last hour and a half of the ebb, and the same on the flood — where the current has enough shoulder to push bait into the rip lines and hold fish in position. Miss that window and you're bouncing bucktails through slack water for nothing.

East End remains the better of the two right now. Fish it on the ebb from the power lines down toward the railroad bridge, working the seam where the fast water meets the eddy along the Sandwich side. Six-inch olive and white Slug-Go's on a light jighead, swung across the current and let to swim dead in the eddy line, have been drawing the better bass — nothing giant, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but a solid keeper-class fish mixed in most mornings. Bucktails in the 1.5-ounce range, bounced bottom on the drift-through, are picking up a few bigger fish holding deeper in the scour holes off the rocks. Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same tide, choppers up to eight or nine pounds hitting anything metal — Deadly Dicks and Hopkins in the 2-ounce range are getting hit the second they touch the rip.

West End is the trickier read this week. The current seams off the Mashnee side and down toward the Bourne Bridge abutment have been holding fish, but it's a shorter window — you want the last forty minutes of the flood specifically, when the water's pushing hard enough to stack bait against the rocks but before it goes full slack. I've had better luck there in the last hour of daylight than at dawn, which is a switch from earlier in the summer. Same l

reports.headline: Race Point at first light: bass on the mackerel, cod holding deep on Peaked Hill
reports.subhead: The big fish slid off the flats and into the rips this week — you just have to be there before the sun clears the dunes.
reports.body_markdown:
We were anchored up on the inside edge of the Race Point rip Tuesday morning, maybe 4:45, still dark enough that the loom of the light was doing more work than the sun. My sternman, a kid named Petey who's fished with me three summers now, dropped a live mackerel down on a fish-finder rig and didn't even get it to bottom before the rod buried. Thirty-four inch bass, fat as a football, came up thrashing in that gray light with the current just starting to run. That's been the story all week out there — you want to be on the water before the bay wakes up, because once the sun gets up over the dunes and that surface water warms into the mid-70s, the bigger fish drop off the structure and go quiet till dusk.

Thirty years drifting this bay and the pattern doesn't change much once we hit August — it just gets more particular about when. The bass haven't left, they've compressed. Race Point rip, the seam off Peaked Hill Bars, the drop-off on the northeast corner of Billingsgate — that's where the current concentrates the bait and the fish know it. We've been marking good pods of mackerel and sand eels stacking right on those rips at first light and again as the light fails in the evening, and the bass are using the moving water to pin bait against the structure rather than chasing it around open flats where it's too warm to bother.

Tide's been building back out of that soft neap stretch we had last week, and you can feel it — the rip off Race Point is starting to rip again instead of just nudging along. That's exactly what you want this time of year. A hard-running tide on a rip like that turns bait into confetti and gives the bass a reason to show themselves instead of holding deep and sulking. Best window has been the two hours either side of the top of the tide change, whether that's the last of the incoming building into slack or the first hour of the ebb pulling off Peaked Hill. Live mackerel on a three-way rig, fished just off bottom in eighteen to twenty-five feet, has been the ticket for the better fish. If you can't get mackerel, a big white or chartreuse tube-and-worm trolled slow through the same water has been drawing strikes too, though nothing beats a livie when they're up and feeding hard.

Bluefish have been mixed in with that same bait and honestly stealing a fair share of our mackerel before the bass get to them. We had a stretch Wednesday off the Race where the blues were slashing bait on the surface for a good twenty minutes — nothing giant, three to six pounds, but they hit like a freight train on anything shiny. Poppers and metal, Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks, worked fine when we could get in front of a surface show. We flagged a couple weeks back that peanut bunker moving into the shallows would pull cocktail blues into the back bay creeks, and that's exactly what's happening now — Barnstable Harbor and the marsh creeks behind Sandy Neck have snapper blues thick enough that kids on the docks are catching them on bare hooks. If you want light-tackle action with the family, that's your spot, incoming tide, small white bucktails or Kastmasters.

Fluke have mostly pushed off the shallow flats — too warm now on the inside of Barnstable Harbor and the flats around Sandy Neck during the day — and settled onto the deeper sand and gravel bottom out toward Billingsgate and the channel edges off Wellfleet. We've been picking at them drifting three-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails in twenty-two to thirty feet, tipping with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. Nothing huge, a few keepers to five pounds mixed with a lot of shorts, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you're patient and cover ground.

Cod are a slower conversation right now — it's early yet for the real push, that usually doesn't build until the water cools off in the fall — but we have been marking fish holding tight to the deeper structure on Peaked Hill Bars, the humps out past forty feet where the bottom breaks up. Jigging diamond jigs and running clams on high-low rigs has produced a few keeper cod mixed with dogfish, which tells you the bigger schools haven't fully staged yet, but the structure's starting to hold life again.

Looking ahead, if this tide keeps building the way it has the past few days, I'd expect the rip bite at Race Point and Peaked Hill to sharpen up through the weekend — moving water is the whole engine of this fishery, and right now it's turning back on. I'd be out there at first light with live mackerel if you can get them, working the slack-to-flood transition hard, then shifting to the flats or Billingsgate for fluke once the sun's up and the rip bite shuts down. Keep an eye on the bunker pushing into the harbors too — wherever those pods thicken up, the blues won't be far behind, and that's usually good for an hour of chaos right off the dock.

reports.headline: Silversides Stack the Rips at Robinson's Hole — Bonito Window Cracking Open
reports.subhead: Bait's balled up tight in every hole from Woods Hole to Menemsha, and the water's finally warm enough to make you believe the first bonito are close.
reports.body_markdown:
Silversides are stacking up thick in Robinson's Hole right now — I mean pinned against the rocks on the west side, flashing like a school of nervous dimes every time the current turns. That's the tell I wait for all summer. When the bait gets that nervous, tight, and silvery in the rip, something's coming to eat it, and this week it's mostly bluefish and the occasional big striper, but the water's finally sitting in that window where bonito show up without much warning.

We flagged this exact stretch a few days back — said the Vineyard rips would be in the first wave once RI breachways got going, ahead of Block and Montauk. I haven't had a confirmed bonito in the boat yet, and I'm not going to tell you I have when I haven't, but the ingredients are all sitting on the table. Squid showing in the deeper holes at Quick's and Robinson's, silversides balled in the current seams, and surface temps that finally feel right on the back of your hand instead of just warm-ish. If you fish this water every week like I do, you learn to trust that gut feeling before the first fish actually shows, and my gut says we're days away, not weeks.

In the meantime the striper bite has been honest work, not a gimme. Best fish have come off the west end of Cuttyhunk on the last two hours of the outgoing, working live eels and swimming plugs along the rockpile edges in 15 to 25 feet. Nothing giant — mostly 26 to 34 inches — but a steady pick if you're willing to drift it twice. Night tide has been better than day tide, which tracks with what everyone south of the Cape is seeing this time of year: fish sliding deep and feeding after dark while the surface stays warm through the afternoon. If you want a shot at something heavier, fish the last of the outgoing into the start of the flood at Woods Hole itself, right in the throat where the current squeezes — bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that whitewater. That's producing the occasional overslot fish for guys willing to sit through a lot of nothing.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and they're riding peanut bunker just like everybody predicted they would once that bait pushed further into the bay. Menemsha Basin and the rips off Lucas Shoal have both had these hard-charging pods of cocktail blues, 2 to 4 pounds, blowing up on top in short, violent windows — usually 20 minutes, then gone. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or a 3-inch Kastmaster — thrown right into the boil and ripped back fast is about as complicated as it needs to be. If you're marking bait suspended mid-column on the sounder around the Elizabeth Islands, don't overthink it, just cast into the commotion.

Fluke have quietly been the most consistent producer of the week, which always happens right before the albie run gets everyone's attention and nobody talks about the bottom fish anymore. Best drifts have been in 20 to 35 feet off the north side of Naushon and through the channel edges toward Quick's Hole, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the ebb. Keeper-sized fish, 18 to 22 inches, mixed with a lot of shorts you'll have to sort through. Scup have been thick around the Woods Hole drawbridge pilings and the rocks off Nonamesset — squid strips or clam on a light jig will keep a rod bent for the kids while you wait on the bigger stuff.

Tide-wise, we're coming off the last new moon push, and the currents through these holes have been running hard and clean, which is exactly what you want once the albies actually show — nothing kills an albie bite faster than slack, muddy water. Wind's been out of the southwest most afternoons, which stacks a little chop into Robinson's Hole by 2 PM, so mornings have fished cleaner across the board.

Looking ahead, if the pattern holds — stable high pressure, bait staying pinned in these rips, and surface temps easing another degree or two — I'd expect the first bonito to show at Robinson's Hole or off the Cuttyhunk side within the week, with false albacore trailing a few days to a week behind them like they always do. That's the sequence I've watched play out for fifteen seasons here, and nothing about this year looks different so far. My plan for the next few days is simple: first light at Robinson's Hole on the peanut-bunker/silverside pattern, small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks rigged and ready in case something with a torpedo body and a sickle tail shows up in that white water. Until then, work the stripers at night, keep the bluefish rod loaded with metal, and don't ignore the fluke bite just because everyone's staring at the horizon waiting on albies. That's how you miss a good week.

reports.headline: Deer Island Ledge on the Outgoing: Bass on Live Mackerel, Blues Torching the Winthrop Flats
reports.subhead: With Gulf of Maine water keeping this harbor cooler than everything south of the Cape, I'm staying inside the islands this week instead of running north to Gloucester.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday morning standing on the dock at Winthrop, coffee in hand, watching a bunker pod nervous up off Belle Isle Inlet: stay inside the islands this week. Not Gloucester, not the Dogbar Breakwater, not a run up to Halibut Point where the rock structure is gorgeous but the fish have been thin. The harbor's holding bait, the water's still comfortably cool thanks to that Gulf of Maine influence we get up here that Long Island Sound and the Cape just don't have this time of year, and that's the whole ballgame in early August.

Here's the read: while everything south of the Cape has pushed stripers into deep structure and nighttime-only feeding as surface temps sit in the mid-70s, our water stays a few degrees kinder. That means daylight bites. That means you can fish the Deer Island ledge at ten in the morning and still find fish willing to eat. I've had two solid mornings this week drifting live mackerel — snagged fresh off the Deer Island Light rocks on a sabiki, then downsized to a single hook and a small egg sinker — over that 30 to 40-foot drop on the outgoing tide. Bass to 34 inches, a handful of shorts, and one fish that made my rod tip disappear before I even had slack line out. Best window has been the first two hours of the ebb, when the current stacks bait against that ledge and the bass sit right on the edge of it.

Bluefish have been the loudest story in the harbor, and it's exactly the pattern we flagged coming — bunker schools thickening up and the blues riding shotgun on them. Winthrop's outer flats, Deer Island's north side, and the water off Nixes Mate have all had stretches of genuine topwater chaos this week, bunker getting bulldozed on the surface with birds diving into the mess. Poppers and 2-ounce Hopkins spoons thrown right into the boil have been getting bit on nearly every cast when it's happening — the trick is getting there before the school pushes off, because these blitzes move fast and don't sit still. I lost a popper to a blue that came clean out of the water off Long Island Head Tuesday evening, first cast, boat still drifting.

Night bite for bass has been the more reliable program if you want a sure thing over a blitz you have to chase. Tides have softened off the recent push, and just like we expected, that's compressed the bass into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure they can find — eels fished slow along the bottom at the Gut between the Brewster Islands and around the Fore River Bridge pilings have been steady after dark, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the current is still moving enough to keep the eel swimming naturally. Nothing giant, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but consistent, and that's what you want on a summer night trip.

Mackerel themselves have been thick enough off Gloucester's outer breakwater and around Cape Ann generally that bait has not been an issue for anybody — jig up a dozen in fifteen minutes most mornings and you're set for the day, whether you're feeding stripers or just want a mess for the pan. Pollock have been mixed in with them on the same structure, which is a nice bonus if you're jigging metal.

I'll be straight about the rest of the beat: flounder fishing is basically a non-event right now. That's a spring and fall program in this harbor, and August heat has them scattered and uninterested — I wouldn't plan a trip around them until the water starts cooling in September. Cod and haddock are still out there on the deeper humps toward Stellwagen, but between the summer regulations and warm surface water pushing what's biting deeper still, it's a long run for a modest return this time of year. If you want bottom fish, this isn't the month.

Looking ahead, I'm watching two things. First, whether that bunker pod off Winthrop holds through the weekend — if it does, the blue bite should keep producing topwater chaos on calm mornings, and I'd have a popper rod rigged and ready before I even leave the dock. Second, whether the tides keep softening into next week, because if they do, I expect the daytime bass bite off Deer Island to taper and the program to lean even harder into the night eel game at the Gut and around the bridges. That's the move I'd make if I only had one night to fish — sundown at the Fore River Bridge, eel on a fish-finder rig, patience through the first hour of dark before the current really gets moving. It won't be fast fishing, but it's been the most dependable thing on my water all week.

reports.headline: Monhegan Ledges: Pollock Up Top, Cod Down Deep, Bass Tucked in the Rivers
reports.subhead: Forty feet of clean water off Monhegan and a mackerel run that won't quit — but the stripers want the rivers this week, not the open bay.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a fella at the co-op Tuesday morning, hauling gear off a skiff he'd borrowed from his brother-in-law, tell me he'd fished the outer ledges at Monhegan for three hours and never touched bottom once because the pollock wouldn't let his jig get there. That's the kind of problem I like hearing about. Told him that's about right for early August — the bait balls up top, the pollock follow, and you can forget the cod jig till you've had your fun on the surface first.

That's been the story most of this week out around Monhegan. Anchor or drift the ledges on the south and east side — 40 to 60 feet of water, tide running — and you'll find pollock schooled up chasing mackerel and herring right in the top 15 feet. A white or chartreuse diamond jig, or even a bare Sabiki string if you want to load the cooler fast, will get bit as soon as it hits water. Once that surface bite settles, which it usually does an hour either side of the tide change, drop down to 70-90 feet on the deeper humps off the island's north end and you'll pick up cod, mostly school-size, some pushing 10-15 pounds, on a jig tipped with a strip of mackerel belly. Haddock have been scarce inshore — that's a deeper-water fish this time of year, and the ones I've heard of came from the basin between Matinicus and the Rockland dumping grounds, 150 feet or better, on the bottom.

Mackerel themselves have been thick right along the whole run from Boothbay out to Eastern Egg Rock. If you want bait or just want to bend a rod with a kid aboard, three or four gold hooks and a bit of chum off the Cuckolds or around The Hypocrites will keep you busy till your arm's tired. The birds tell the story out there too — terns and puffins working the surface off Egg Rock most mornings, which means the sand eels and mackerel are stacked shallow, and that's drawing bass in tight to feed as well.

Speaking of bass — that's been the tricky part of the week. Penobscot Bay proper has been quieter than I'd like for August. The stripers are around, but they're not holding on the open ledges and rockpiles the way they will later this month. Right now the better fish are tucked into the river mouths — the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, up around Wiscasset and the mouth of the Kennebec corridor — working the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets flushed out of the marsh creeks into cooler, cleaner water. A 4-inch olive or white soft-plastic swimbait on a 3/8-ounce jighead, worked slow along the current seams where the river water meets the salt, has been the most consistent producer. A few schoolies mixed with some solid 28-30 inch fish, nothing huge, but honest fish and steady enough to make an evening trip worthwhile.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect a stable, seasonal read across the zone — and that's exactly what's held. Nothing dramatic, no big temperature swing, no wind event to stir things up. Just Maine doing its steady August thing while the rest of the coast deals with warmer water pushing fish deeper or forcing a night bite. Up here we're still getting daylight action on bass because the Gulf of Maine keeps the whole system a few degrees cooler than folks are dealing with south of the Cape. That's worth remembering if you're used to fishing further down the coast — don't wait for dark up here, fish the tide instead.

Down around Deer Isle and Stonington, the groundfish pattern's holding too. The channel between Deer Isle and Isle au Haut, 80 to 120 feet depending where you drop, has been giving up pollock and the occasional keeper cod on jigs worked just off bottom during the last of the incoming tide. Bluefish have shown in small pods around the outer islands off Stonington, chopping bait on the surface in the afternoons — nothing like the blitzes you hear about further south, but enough 2-3 pound choppers to keep a spinning rod busy if you find the right slick of bait.

Vinalhaven and the deeper basin north of it toward North Haven remain a decent bet for anyone wanting a mixed bag — cod, pollock, and the odd haddock showing on the sounder in that 140-180 foot range. Slow-pitch jigging with a 6-8 ounce metal has been outproducing bait rigs down there this week, mostly because the current's been running harder than usual on the bigger tides, and the jig gets down and stays down better than bait on a hi-lo.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Winds have stayed manageable, no big blow forecast, and the bait's holding thick enough that both the bass and the groundfish have plenty to eat without having to move far. If you're planning a trip this week, I'd fish the rivers on the ebb for bass in the morning, then run out to Monhegan or the outer ledges midday when the tide's slack enough to fish comfortably, and clean up on pollock and mackerel while you're out there. By late August, once the bay starts cooling down at night, I expect the bass to spread back out onto the open structure — but for now, the rivers are where the smart money's fishing.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock Holds Its Groundfish While Bass Work the Island Edges
reports.subhead: Cooler bay water is keeping the bite honest through midday, even as the mackerel run thins and cod settle deeper on the ledges.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Peaks Island Tuesday morning, drifting the eastern edge where the current pulls hard around the ledge on the last of the ebb, and I noticed something I make a point of noticing every August: the gulls weren't working the surface the way they were in June. That's not a bad sign — it's a seasonal one. The mackerel schools that the bay in May and June have scattered and thinned, the way they always do once the water settles into its summer rhythm. What's left are smaller, tighter pods, and you have to hunt for them now rather than simply follow the birds.

I found one such pod off the Portland breakwater in about 40 feet, marked heavy on the sounder, and put two mackerel trees down on light spinning gear for maybe twenty minutes of steady action before they moved off. That's the pattern this week — good but not sustained, here and gone in a tide cycle. If you're after fresh bait for bass or bluefish, I'd treat any mackerel showing as a window, not a guarantee, and fish it hard the moment you find it.

The striped bass have been the more dependable story, and the reason is straightforward: Casco Bay's water hasn't overheated the way it has south of Cape Cod. Down there, stripers have gone nocturnal, pushed deep by water sitting in the mid-70s. Up here, the Gulf of Maine keeps feeding us cooler water through the tidal exchange, and the bass are still willing to work the flats and ledges well into the afternoon. I had good luck working the Bailey Island shoreline on the last two hours of the incoming, casting a 1-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse tail tight along the rockweed edge, letting it sink before a slow, methodical retrieve — the same approach that produces results on any current seam where bait gets pinned against structure. Fish in the mid-20-inch range, a few pushing 30, mixed with shorts that kept things interesting for anyone fishing with kids or students, which I still do more often than I probably should admit.

Harpswell's back channels and the mouth of the Basin have been holding fish too, particularly on the moving tide when bait gets funneled through the narrows. Live mackerel under a slip float, or a swimming plug worked slow through the current seam, has been the more consistent producer there than anything worked fast. Two Lights, characteristically, has been a dawn spot — surface activity for maybe forty minutes around first light before the fish drop back down, so if you're fishing that stretch, get there before the sun clears the horizon or don't bother.

Bluefish have started showing in numbers I'd call notable for early August — not blitzing yet, but present in the coves around Peaks and in the channel off Portland, chasing whatever bait concentrates near the surface. We flagged this pattern building a few weeks back, and it's holding — wherever the bait schools tighten up, the blues are finding them and feeding hard for short stretches. Snapper-sized fish are thick in the shallower coves for anyone wanting light-tackle action, and the adult fish have been mixed in with the mackerel schools, so don't be surprised if your mackerel jig comes back missing its tail.

Halfway Rock remains the most reliable groundfish structure in the bay, and this week reinforced why I keep sending people there rather than the closer, shallower ledges. Cod and haddock have settled into 70 to 90 feet on the northeast side, and the bite has been a slack-tide affair — you want that window when the current eases enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead, jigging diamond jigs or drifting clam baits along the structure. It's not a fast bite this time of year; midsummer groundfish fishing rarely is. But it's been steady enough that two or three fish per trip in the 3-to-6-pound range isn't unusual for anyone willing to work the ledge methodically rather than drift through it once and move on.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to shift dramatically. The bay's thermal structure has been stable, and as long as that stable weather window holds, I'd expect the same daytime striper activity along the island edges and the same slack-tide groundfish bite at Halfway Rock. If the wind stays out of the southwest and the tides keep building the way they have, I'd put my time on the incoming at Bailey Island for bass and slack water at Halfway Rock for bottom fish. Watch for the mackerel schools to keep contracting through August — by month's end, you may be relying more on jigs and metal than trees to raise them at all.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Still Pays: Bass to 28, Blues Crash Pine Point
reports.subhead: A rocky-shore stretch that's fishing better than it should this deep into a warm August, if you work the right hour of tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, forty minutes into the flood at Biddeford Pool, I watched a bass come up under a black Danny plug like it had somewhere to be. Twenty-eight inches, maybe six pounds heavier than that, and she hit the plug so hard the rod tip buried before I even felt the take. That's the Pool doing what it's supposed to do on the incoming — the current stacks bait against the rocks on the east side, the stripers slide in behind it, and for about ninety minutes you've got the best window of the day. I've fished that tide stage for going on twenty years and it still gets me every time. Miss that window and you're often just casting at empty water till the next cycle.

That's the honest headline for Southern Maine right now — good, not great, and very much tide-and-hour dependent. The water down south of the Cape has slid into that thick, warm mid-70s stuff that pushes bass off the surface and into deep structure at night. We don't have that problem up here. The Gulf of Maine keeps feeding cooler water along this stretch, and it's kept our fish willing to eat in daylight when the boys south of Boston are stuck fishing eels after dark. If you want a daytime striper right now, Kittery to Cape Elizabeth is the more honest bet on the whole coast.

Pine Point and the mouth of the Scarborough River system have been the story for bluefish. We flagged the peanut bunker push a couple weeks back and said it'd spike the back-bay blues within two weeks — that's exactly what showed up. Snapper blues are thick enough in the harbor channels that kids with bobbers and strips of mackerel are filling coolers, and the adult blues are working the edges where the river current meets the incoming salt, chopping through pods of peanuts hard enough to turn the surface white for a few minutes at a time before they push back out with the tide. Small metal — half-ounce to an ounce, Deadly Dicks and narrow Kastmasters — has been the right call there. Don't overthink it. Cast into the boil, let it sink two seconds, rip it back.

Higgins Beach has been more stop-and-start than blitz. I had one evening last week where the blues showed for maybe twenty minutes right at the change of light, chased a school of pogies right up into the wash, and then vanished like they'd never been there. Needlefish plugs and 3/4-ounce Hopkins worked when they were on, but I burned two hours of nothing before and after that window. If you're planning a Higgins trip, go at the tide change and don't expect a long bite — get in, get your shots, and don't be surprised if it shuts off fast.

Prouts Neck has been quietly solid on a southwest wind, which is the setup you want there. The wind lays the swell down along the front side of the point, cleans up the water, and pushes bait tight against the rocks where the bass sit and wait for it. I worked the outside edge on a falling tide with a Doc's swimmer in bone color and picked up two fish in the mid-20-inch range along with a couple of shorts that came unbuttoned before I could get a hand on them. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady enough that I'd go back on the next SW day without hesitating.

Mackerel are still thick off the ledges — Wood Island, the rocks off Cape Elizabeth, out past Prouts. Deadly Dicks or a mackerel tree jigged just under the surface will fill a bucket in twenty minutes most mornings, and if you want fresh bait for a night bass session at the Pool or off the Cape Elizabeth rocks, that's your move. A live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, drifted along a rock ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, has been quietly producing some of the better fish reports I've heard this month — nothing giant, but consistent 28-to-32-inch class bass.

Flounder are still around in Wells Harbor and the channel edges up in Ogunquit, though that bite has softened as the water's warmed — bloodworms and clam strips on the bottom, fished slow, still get a few keepers if you're patient. Cod are a non-story for the surf crowd this time of year; that's strictly a boat game well offshore of this beat, and not one I'm chasing from the rocks.

Looking ahead — if this southwest wind pattern holds through the weekend, I'd put my money on Prouts Neck again, same approach, outgoing tide, working the outside edge with swimmers. Biddeford Pool stays the highest-percentage spot in the zone as long as you respect the incoming window and don't waste time fishing it dead slack. And keep an eye on Pine Point — if that bunker keeps pushing in the way it has, the blue bite there could turn from good to genuinely wild before the month's out.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 210 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, cod tucked to the gravel edge
reports.subhead: A stable week out of Rye put solid groundfish in the box while the first real tuna sign showed up on the ledge's northeast corner.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-ten feet of soft green mud on the northeast flat of Jeffrey's, that's where I spent most of Tuesday, and it held haddock the way it's supposed to this time of year — not a blitz, but a steady pick, fish in the 3 to 5 pound range coming over the rail two and three at a time on diamond jigs tipped with clam. When the mud produces like that in early August, it usually means the water column above it hasn't scattered the bait yet, and that's exactly what we're seeing — sand eels holding tight, mackerel schools working the upper thirty feet, and the haddock parked right underneath where they don't have to work for a meal.

Cod is a different conversation, and it's a gravel conversation. I moved off the mud basin and ran west to the harder bottom in about 150 feet, the rocky transition zone where the ledge kicks up before it drops back into Scantum Basin. That gravel edge has been the more consistent cod producer than the deeper structure lately — fish in the 8 to 15 pound class, a few pushing 20, taking jigging spoons worked with a short hop off bottom, and skate-baited hooks on a high-low rig for the guys who'd rather sit still. The key this week has been staying tight to the break itself. Drift fifty yards off it onto flat mud and the cod disappear; hold the edge and they're there. That's been true on both the outgoing and incoming tide, though the bite windows have run a little longer on the ebb, probably because the current's pushing bait right along that gravel lip instead of lifting it off.

Platts Bank was quieter than I'd like this week. I checked it Thursday in about 195 feet and came away with pollock instead of the cod I was hoping for — decent fish, 6 to 10 pounds, hitting diamond jigs on the drop, but the cod bite there has been spotty enough that I'm not sending anyone out of their way for it right now. Tillies Bank I haven't fished since last week, and I'd rather tell you that plainly than guess at it. If you're running that far, call around the harbor first.

Now for the tuna, because this is the part of the report that's actually building the way I thought it would. We flagged last week that the bait holding on the ledge would drag the bluefin pattern along gradually through August, and that's what's happening — not a giant show yet, that's an October conversation off Jeffrey's, but school-class and mid-size bluefin have started working the approaches to Stellwagen and the southern stretch of the ledge where the mackerel schools have been thickest. I had two boats radio in feed sightings Wednesday afternoon, birds working hard over breaking bait about three miles off Thatcher Island, and one of them stuck a fish in the 150-pound class trolling a spreader bar through the melee. It's early, it's scattered, and you need to be willing to run and gun rather than anchor up and wait, but the ingredients are there. Mackerel jigged fresh off the rail and either live-lined or chunked out the back has been the better play than trolling alone when you find working birds — the fish seem to want something natural in the slick, not just something moving fast past them.
