Conditions have cooperated. We've had a stretch of light southwest wind and settled seas out of Rye, the kind of stable high-pressure window that lets you actually work the ledge methodically instead of getting bounced off it by afternoon chop. That stability is part of why the tuna sign has been building steadily rather than showing up in one big push — the bait's had time to set up and hold instead of getting scattered by wind-driven seas. Tide's been unremarkable, nothing extreme either way, which for groundfish purposes just means the bite windows have been tied more to time of day than tide stage — early morning and the last two hours of daylight have both produced better than midday on both the gravel and the mud.

Looking ahead, if this weather pattern holds through the weekend I'd keep working the same two zones — mud basin for haddock, gravel edge for cod — and I'd make at least one pass toward the Stellwagen approaches with jigs rigged and ready in case you run into working birds. The tuna pattern should keep building through the rest of August as long as the mackerel stay put, but it's still a find-the-feed operation right now, not a set-your-anchor one. If the wind swings onshore and kicks up the kind of chop that scatters bait off the surface, I'd expect the tuna sign to go quiet fast and I'd shift the whole day back to bottom fishing on the ledge, where the fish don't care what the wind's doing forty feet above their heads.

reports.headline: Appledore Ledges Hold on the Slack: Cod to 6 Pounds, Blues Crash the Piscataqua
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished it right — this week the Shoals gave up cod on the drop-off and the peanut bunker finally pulled blues into Hampton Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing here worth trailering a boat for. I've got a 20-foot Lund and I fish this water like it's a hundred and thirty. Between the Piscataqua current lines, the Hampton marsh, and six miles of open water out to the Shoals, there's more structure and more species turning over out here in a week than most guys see all season on a bigger stretch of coast. You just have to know where the bottom breaks and when the tide wants to hand it to you.

This week that meant being off White Island before 5 a.m., anchored up on the ledge in 70 feet with the tide just starting to slack. Cod have been mixed in with haddock out there most mornings, fish running 3 to 6 pounds with a couple pushing 8 coming over the rail on diamond jigs worked slow off bottom — nothing fancy, just a gentle lift-and-drop through the last hour of the ebb and the first hour of the new tide. Clam bait on a high-low rig still works if the jig bite goes quiet, especially once the sun gets up and the fish slide tighter to structure. I won't oversell it — it's been a mixed week, not a banner one. Some mornings the ledge produces a limit in an hour, other mornings you work three drifts for a handful of keepers and call it. That's high summer at the Shoals. The water up top has warmed enough that the fish are holding deeper and tighter to rock than they were in June, so if you're marking bait but not marking fish, drop another ten feet before you give up on a spot.

Mackerel have shown up in decent numbers around Appledore and Star Island, schools stacking on the sounder in 30 to 40 feet mid-morning. A three-hook Christmas tree rig with no weight needed will fill a bucket fast, and honestly that's been half the reason to run out there — fresh mackerel strips are outfishing frozen clam on the bigger cod when you can get them.

Closer to shore, the striper story has been the better one all week. Cooler Gulf of Maine water keeps these fish comfortable and feeding through more daylight hours than you'll find south of the Cape right now, and it's showing in the Piscataqua. The current seams below the Memorial Bridge and down through Portsmouth Harbor have been holding fish on both the last of the outgoing and the first push of the incoming — bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, worked across the seam and let it swing. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig has also been quietly productive for the bigger fish holding deeper in the channel near the Route 1 bridge pilings.

Hampton Harbor is where the week turned interesting. We flagged the peanut bunker pattern building a few weeks back, said it would spread and pull cocktail blues into the back bays — and that's exactly what happened. Peanuts have packed into the marsh creeks off Hampton and Seabrook, and bluefish have followed them in on the last two hours of the incoming, blowing up on the surface right at the mouth where the harbor narrows. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — thrown right into the boils has been the move, and there's enough size mixed in with the snappers now that it's worth the drive even if you're not running a boat. Stripers are working the same bait but sitting a little deeper and later, picking off peanuts on the dropping tide closer to the bridge.

Rye Harbor and Odiorne Point have been steadier than exciting — flounder still coming off the mud bottom on the incoming with worms fished tight to the bottom in 15 to 20 feet, nothing to write home about but a reliable meal if the Shoals run gets blown out. Great Boars Head has had a few solid mornings for surfcasters working the bar right at first light on the last of the outgoing, stripers sliding off the sand as bait gets pushed out with the tide — small swimmers or a live eel if you can find one has been the ticket.

Weather's held stable and that's kept this whole pattern intact — no big blow to scatter the bait, no dirty water pushing fish off the structure. If that high holds through the coming week I'd expect more of the same: groundfish mixed and honest at the Shoals, stripers working the Piscataqua tides, and those blues staying thick in Hampton Harbor as long as the peanut bunker keep holding in the marsh. If a system rolls through and stirs up the harbor, I'd shift effort back out to the Shoals ledges where depth buys you some insulation from a couple dirty days inshore. Either way, there's enough going on in these thirteen miles to keep a small boat busy every morning this week.

reports.headline: Beavertail bunker pods, blues on top, tog still asleep on the ledges
reports.subhead: Bait's stacked from Newport to Sakonnet but the bass have gone nocturnal — here's where the rocks are actually producing.
reports.body_markdown:
Peanut bunker are pouring off Beavertail right now, thick enough that you can see the ledge rock go dark under the surface at low light — a moving shadow instead of stone. That's the tell this week. Wherever that shadow shows, something's under it working the edges, and from Newport down through Sakonnet the bunker have pulled everything with teeth into the shallows.

Bluefish found them first, and they found them hard. Snapper blues are thick in every cove off Jamestown — Fort Wetherill, Mackerel Cove, the riprap below Fort Adams — light tackle guys are getting a fish every cast on 1/8-ounce Kastmasters and Gotcha plugs, no leader needed, just have fun with it. But it's the adult blues that made the week. We flagged this coming — said the cocktail blues would spike as the bunker spread, and that's exactly what showed up off Third Beach and around the Sakonnet Point rocks: 3- to 6-pound blues busting bait on top in the last hour of light, white water everywhere, gulls dropping on the pieces. Poppers and metal-lip swimmers thrown into the froth, don't overthink it. That bite's been the most reliable thing on the whole shore this week.

Bass are a different story, and it's the story we called last week too. With water sitting in the mid-70s off the ledges and tides softening out of the last push, the stripers have compressed into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest cracks they can find. Daytime bass fishing off the open rock has been quiet — a few follows, not much committing. Nighttime is where it's happening. Eels fished on the down-current side of the Jamestown Bridge pilings and the Newport Bridge structure have been picking up slot fish on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current stacks bait against the concrete and the bass sit tight to it. Sakonnet Point ledges are doing the same thing after dark — swim a 3-ounce bucktail with a big curl tail down along the rock face on the drop, slow, and let it bump bottom. That's producing better than anything thrown in daylight right now.

Fluke have done what they always do this time of year — they've abandoned the shallow flats for deeper structure where the bottom temp is more forgiving. The East Passage channel edges off Jamestown, and the deeper water at the mouth of the Sakonnet River, have both been giving up keeper fish to 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide. Nothing gangbusters, but steady enough that a few drifts will fill a limit if you're patient and stay on the bottom.

Scup are filling out the cooler without much effort — Fort Wetherill, the Newport breakwaters, and the rocks off Second Beach are stacked with them on squid strips and clam, 15 to 25 feet of water, bottom rig. Good action if you've got kids or guests aboard who just want bent rods.

Tog, I'll be honest, are quiet. This is the dead zone for blackfish season down here — a few are showing on green crabs worked into the deeper cracks at Beavertail and around the Sakonnet Point ledges on a good slack tide, but it's a fish here and there, not a program. That fishery wakes back up as the water starts cooling in September and October, when the tog push back onto the shallower structure to feed hard before winter. Right now I'd rather spend the tide on bass or blues than grind it out on tog.

Albies haven't shown yet on this stretch, but the pieces are lining up. Offshore water's holding in the mid-70s, bait's dense along the whole coast, and the pattern that usually starts at Montauk and Block Island before sliding into our breachways looks like it's building on schedule, maybe a touch early given how warm it's run. Watch Hill and Napatree are always first in this zone — the current through the breachway concentrates bait right at the mouth, and albies push in on the last of the incoming to run it down. Weekapaug fishes the same way a few tides later once the run establishes. Nothing confirmed yet this week, but if the stable weather holds and that warm-water push keeps spreading east like it's forecast to, I'd expect the first real showing in the next week or two rather than waiting for the usual September date.

One more thing worth knowing if you're bouncing between spots — the south-facing beaches, Second Beach, Matunuck, Charlestown, have been getting pushed around by a lingering ocean swell, running 3 to 4 feet with a short period, which has kept the surf stirred and made sight-fishing tough. The Sakonnet shore, facing more east and tucked behind the point, has stayed comparatively clean and has fished better for that reason alone — worth remembering when the buoys show any kind of leftover groundswell.

For the coming week: keep working the bridges and ledges at night for bass while the daytime bite stays lockjawed, ride the bluefish blitzes on bunker while they last, and keep one eye on the breachway mouths at Napatree and Watch Hill. If that albie push arrives on schedule, it'll show there first.

reports.headline: 75.9 on the Bight buoy: bluefin working the Mud Hole lumps, mahi stacked on the pot lines
reports.subhead: Warm water pushing into the inshore lumps has bluefin and mahi cooperating, but the sea bass numbers are the sure thing this week.
reports.body_markdown:
75.9. That's the reading off the Bight buoy this week, and it's the number that's had my phone going since Tuesday morning. Doesn't sound like much until you remember what that water was doing three weeks ago — mid-60s, gray, dead current. Now we've got a warm tongue pushing up against the edge of the Mud Hole and it's dragging bait and bluefin with it. Seas are running 3.6 feet at 6 seconds out of the south, which isn't glass but it's workable — anything 26 feet and up should have no trouble getting out and getting home dry.

The Mud Hole lumps have been the play. I'm marking bait stacked hard on the northeast lump in 110 to 130 feet, and we've had bluefin from schoolie size up to mid-40s class fish coming through on small blue-and-white spreader bars and cedar plugs run tight to the boat — 60 to 90 feet back, no farther. When the fish get finicky, which they have on the slower tide stages, we've switched to butterfish chunks drifted off the transom over the lump edge and that's when the better-grade fish show. It's not a wide-open bite — two out of my last three trips out there connected solid, one was a grind for three fish in six hours — but for early August that's a number I'll take. If the warm filament holds where it's sitting, I'd expect the Mud Hole to keep producing through the weekend. If it slides off to the east like these things do in a hurry, Klondike is the backup — same depth range, same lump structure, and we've had a few yellowfin mixed in out there on the edge where that warmer water is bleeding westward off the canyon breaks. Small purple-and-black Ilanders on the short rigger, green machines out back — nothing fancy, just get the spread in front of them.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the tuna bite would hold steady as long as this calm stretch stuck around, and that's exactly what's played out. The high pressure hasn't budged, the current's cooperating, and the fish are where the temperature says they should be. That won't last forever in August — watch the tropics — but for now it's the setup you want.

Mahi are the other story worth telling. We've been finding them stacked under the pot buoys working the stretch between Barnegat Ridge and the inshore edge, and under any weed line holding bait — you don't need much, a mat the size of a car hood will hold a pack. Small bailer-class fish mostly, two to five pounds, with the occasional three- or four-pounder that'll make you think you found a bigger school than you did. Sabiki-teased ballyhoo strips on light spinning gear has been the most fun way to work them, though a chunk line off butterfish will pull them up from under the structure if they're sulking deep. Best window has been late morning once the sun's had a chance to warm the surface layer — that's when they come up and show themselves.

Bottom fishing is still the most dependable thing going on this beat, and it's not close. Sea bass are holding heavy on the reef and wreck network — Axel Carlson Reef in 60 to 70 feet has been giving up good numbers of keepers, and there's a wreck sitting in 75 feet off the Ridge that's been holding some genuine jumbos, four-pound class fish, on bucktail-and-Gulp combos bounced right on the structure. Shrewsbury Rocks has been more of a numbers spot than a size spot lately — lots of 12- to 13-inch fish mixed with enough keepers to make it worth the anchor drop. Triple Wrecks, when we've had the current cooperating, has produced the best average size of anywhere I fished this month. Squid strips or clam on a double bottom rig, straight up and down, patience over structure — that's still the whole game. No surprises there, and that consistency is exactly why I keep coming back to those numbers year after year.

Blackfish season's closed through the summer so that box stays shut for now, and cod isn't a realistic target with water this warm — that's a late-fall conversation.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure stretch holds through the weekend the way it's been sitting, I'd keep working the Mud Hole lumps early and be ready to run to Klondike if the temp break shifts. Watch the wave state — if that southerly swell builds past four feet, the smaller boats should sit tight and let the bigger fleet work it. The sea bass grounds don't care what the weather's doing offshore, so that's your fallback on any day the ocean looks unfriendly past the three-mile line. I'll be out on the lumps again this week chasing that warm water while it's still sitting where we want it — worth the run if you can get out before it moves.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 6:52: bass down deep, first bonito flashes off Block's breachways
reports.subhead: Bunker still rules the rip after dark, but the real story this week is warm water pushing the first tuna-family fish into range off the island.
reports.body_markdown:
Six fifty-two this morning was the slack at SW Ledge, and I had the boat sitting right on the west edge of the drop in 55 feet, watching the current lay down before it turned to build east. That window — the fifteen minutes either side of slack — is when the bigger bass show themselves on the ledge in August. Once the current gets moving hard again, those fish drop off the structure and slide into the deeper cuts where the water stays cooler and the bait gets funneled tight. We marked stripers stacked from 60 to 75 feet on the second half of the outgoing, and they wanted eels — not bucktails, not tins, live eels dropped down on a three-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current.

That's the pattern right now south of the Judith and out toward the island: stripers have gone nocturnal and deep. Surface water is sitting in the mid-70s — Montauk read 74.5 this week, and the western Sound is pushing into the high 70s — which is warm enough that the better fish don't want to feed up top in daylight anymore. The night bite has been the more honest bite. We've had clients doing well drifting bunker chunks over SW Ledge and the humps off Sandy Point starting an hour before dark, running into the top of the flood. Fish to 35 pounds have come off that pattern in the last ten days, but it's not a blitz — you're working for two or three quality bites a trip, not a dozen. I'd call it a solid, honest bass bite right now, not a red-hot one.

Fluke have been the more reliable daytime fish, and that's typical for this stretch of summer. We're finding keepers on the drift south of Block in 35 to 50 feet, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid to give it some scent in current that's been running stronger than normal the last few days. The better drifts have been on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current slows enough to keep bottom contact without a two-ounce sinker dragging you sideways. Sizes have been decent — 18 to 22 inches with a few better fish mixed in — but you've got to move around to find them. We've burned through three or four drops before locking onto a stretch holding fish.

Sea bass are exactly where they should be this time of year — parked on structure and not going anywhere. The reef edges off Block and the rock piles inside SW Ledge have been giving up steady numbers on green and white Gulp jigs and standard sea bass rigs baited with squid, worked right on bottom in 40 to 60 feet. It's the most dependable box-filler in the zone right now. If a client wants a guaranteed dinner, that's where we go first.

Bluefish are running true to form, chasing bunker schools that have been thick off the Judith and around the mouth of the Harbor of Refuge. Adult blues in the 6 to 10 pound range have been busting bait on the surface some mornings, and when that happens it's a top-water program — poppers or metal-lipped swimmers thrown right into the froth. Inside the breachways, snapper blues are stacked up thick enough that it's been the easiest way to keep a kid on a rod bent all afternoon — small Kastmasters or Gotcha plugs under a bobber, nothing fancy required.

Now here's the part I've been watching closest. We flagged this last week — said the early albie-family activity would start showing off the island within days — and it's here, though it's early and it's thin. We've had two separate reports of small bonito flashing bait on the surface off Sandy Point and out past North Light, chasing what looked like silversides pushed tight against the beach. Nobody's boated one yet that I can confirm firsthand, but the water's right for it — squid have been building around the island and Nantucket Sound, and that's exactly the forage signature that pulls bonito in first, ahead of the false albacore. The one thing working against us right now is a leftover ocean swell — 3 to 4 feet at a short period off the outer buoys — which has kept the south side of Block a little sloppy and made it tougher to spot those surface flashes cleanly. If that swell lays down over the next few days like the forecast suggests, I expect confirmed bonito catches off the breachways and Clay Head within the week, with Block and the outer rips following close behind.

Looking ahead: if this warm, stable pattern holds, I'd keep the night program on SW Ledge and Sandy Point for bass, lean on fluke and sea bass for the guaranteed box, and start carrying a bonito rod rigged with small epoxy jigs or Deadly Dicks every trip out to the island — because when that bite tips over, it tips fast, and you don't want to be the guy who left the light stuff at the dock.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass sliding deep, snappers thick in Greenwich Bay
reports.subhead: Warm surface water has pushed the bay's striper bite into the shadows, but the bluefish and scup more than make up for it.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at Sabin Point around six the other morning, coffee in one hand, watching a guy from Warwick load a cooler with snapper blues he'd picked off the pilings in twenty minutes with a bucktail jig and a bobber. That's the tell right now — the small stuff is everywhere close to shore, and the big stuff has gone quiet during the day. Anybody who's fished this bay more than a summer knows what that means. The surface water's sitting in the mid-70s, the bass have wised up, and if you want the good ones you're fishing the edges of the light — first hour, last hour, or full dark.

Conimicut Point on the last of the ebb is still your best shot at a keeper striper in daylight, but I'm not going to lie to you — it's a grind right now. The fish that are there are holding tight to the channel drop where the current keeps things cooler, and they want it slow. Eels on a fish-finder rig, or a swimming plug worked dead slow along the rip line where the flat water meets the moving water. I had two fish there Tuesday morning on eels, both mid-20s, nothing to write home about but better than nothing on a summer morning in the upper bay.

Where the real bass are is Nyatt Point and the rocks off Rocky Point after the sun goes down. That stretch holds bait all summer — menhaden schools have been thick off the point for two weeks now, rolling up against the rocks on the incoming, and the bass are underneath them working the shadow line. Live-lined bunker on a 5/0 circle hook, no weight, just let it swim naturally into the current seam. Guys are also doing well soaking chunks — cut bunker on a fish-finder rig, 20-30 feet off the point, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the incoming tide. That's when the current pushes the bait tight against structure and the stripers stack up underneath it. It's a night bite now, plain and simple, and if you're not out there after 9pm you're missing the best of it.

The bluefish, though — that's where the bay's actually fun right now. Greenwich Bay is stuffed with peanut bunker, and both the snapper blues and the cocktail-size adults are all over them. We flagged this a few days back — said the peanut bunker spreading through the back coves would pull the cocktail blues in tight within a couple weeks, and it didn't even take that long. Anchor up off the Greenwich Bay Yacht Club moorings or drift the flats near Warwick Cove with a small Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick, and you'll get bit almost every cast on the smaller blues. Mix in a few bigger cocktail fish, two to three pounds, chasing the same bait — those are the ones worth keeping for the smoker. Light braid, small wire leader, and don't overthink it. The blues are doing the work for you.

Fluke have backed off the shallow flats with the warm water and pushed onto the deeper structure where the bottom stays cooler — that's classic August behavior in this bay. The channel edge off Prudence Island, particularly the drop near the north end toward Potter Cove, has been holding fish in 25 to 35 feet. Same story on Ohio Ledge — work a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, bounced slow along bottom on the drift, and you'll pick through some shorts to find keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range. The bite's better on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current thins out and you can actually feel the bottom.

Scup are the most honest fish in the bay right now — they're exactly where they're supposed to be. Rocky Point ledges and the rock piles off Nyatt Point are stacked with them in 15 to 25 feet. Squid strips or sandworms on a simple high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour if you find the right rock. It's not glamorous but it's about as sure a thing as this bay offers in August, and it's a good way to keep a kid interested while you wait for the tide to turn for bass.

Weakfish are still a rumor more than a pattern — a few scattered fish have shown up mixed in with the bluefish around the peanut bunker schools in the upper bay, which tracks with what we expected as that bait pushed in. Nothing to plan a trip around yet, but worth a cast or two if you're already working a bunker school with light tackle.

Looking ahead, this stable stretch of weather should hold through the week — light wind, steady tides, nothing to shake the pattern loose. That means more of the same: night bass on bunker at Nyatt and Rocky Point, steady blues in Greenwich Bay, and fluke holding on the deep edges around Prudence. If a front does roll through and stirs the upper bay, I'd expect the bass bite to actually improve for a day or two — a little turbulence gets them moving during daylight again. Until then, set your alarm for the dark hours if you want a real striper, and let the kids have fun with the blues in the meantime.

reports.headline: Rips Picky, Bay Weakfish Building, Blues the Only Sure Thing
reports.subhead: The Cape May Rips are grinding out short windows while Delaware Bay's weakfish pattern keeps filling in on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
Rips are a C-plus this week. Not a disaster, not a banner week either — just honest, tide-dependent fishing that rewards guys who show up on the right stage of the water and go home skunked if they don't. My father used to say the Rips don't owe you anything, and August is when that lesson gets taught the hardest. Ocean side surface temps are pushing into the mid-70s, the current lines off Cape May Point are still stacking bait, but the window where fish actually commit to feeding has gotten short and specific — first two hours of the ebb, full stop. Miss that and you're just trolling pretty water.

Here's the breakdown. Bluefish are the one thing I can put in the log with confidence. Bunker schools are thick from the Point out toward the Bunker Grounds, and the blues are riding them hard — 3 to 6 pounds, some better, busting bait on top in that classic August pattern where you see the slick before you see the fish. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, ounce to ounce-and-a-half, worked through the boils, or if you want to keep it simple, a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig soaking on the bottom in 25 to 40 feet right off the rip edge. That's producing all week, tide stages aside — blues don't care much about the clock like stripers do.

Stripers, though, have thinned out of the immediate rip structure the way they always do once the water gets into the mid-70s. What's left is holding deep on the reef structure and rubble near the mouth of the bay, and you need to fish it like a bottom fish now, not a run-and-gun surface bite. Jigging bucktails tipped with a strip of squid down in 35 to 50 feet on the last of the incoming has been the play for the boats still finding them, but I'll be straight — it's a grind. One or two fish a trip if you're patient, mostly schoolies with the occasional keeper mixed in. Not the kind of numbers that make for a good sea story yet.

Delaware Bay is actually the better story right now, and it's the one I flagged coming. We said the weakfish would track the peanut bunker into the bays through August and build into something real rather than a flash — and that's exactly what's showing up on the channel edges from Fortescue down toward Brandywine Shoal. Bay water is running warm, upper 70s in the shallows, which has pushed the weakfish and a good push of croaker onto structure where there's current relief — the edges of the shipping channel, the drop-offs near the Brandywine light, and the deeper holes off Fortescue. Evening tide is your window here, when the bay cools a couple degrees off its afternoon peak and the weakfish come up off bottom to feed. Bloodworms and Fishbites on a simple two-hook bottom rig, or a 3-inch chartreuse Gulp Shrimp on a light jighead if you want to work it more actively — both are taking fish in the 16 to 20 inch range, with croaker mixed in steady enough that nobody's complaining about the bycatch. This isn't the May drum run — that's long finished, and if you're still asking about black drum this time of year, you're a couple months late — but the weakfish pattern filling in behind it is legitimate and it's holding, which is more than I can say for some Augusts.

Fluke are still the most honest bite going if you want dinner. The party boats out of Cape May have shifted effort toward the Wilmington-adjacent grounds and the deeper reef structure offshore, mixing sea bass with a solid fluke count on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with a light bucktail, drifted along the bottom in 60 to 90 feet. That's a fish-a-drift kind of trip most days right now, better than what's happening close to the beach where the shallow flats have gotten too warm to hold quality fluke consistently.

Wind's been cooperative — light out of the southwest most days, seas manageable inside and out — which is the only reason the rip bite has stayed fishable at all through these short windows. If that holds into next week I'd keep working the bluefish on the bunker schools as your bread and butter, work the bay weakfish on the evening tide since that pattern shows no sign of backing off, and treat the rip stripers as a bonus rather than a target — deep structure, patient jigging, low expectations, occasional reward. If we get any wind shift out of the east that stacks up a groundswell, I'd pull off the ocean side entirely and just fish the bay — Fortescue will still be fishing regardless of what the Atlantic's doing. That's the two-bay game this time of year: one side grinds, the other side pays off, and knowing which is which on a given morning is half the job.

reports.headline: Holgate's inside cut is choking on peanut bunker — blues and weaks are stacked on the flood
reports.subhead: The bunker finally pushed south into the bay like we said it would, and now every cut from Beach Haven to Graveling Point has bait pinned against the marsh.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate cut Tuesday morning at low and the bottom told me everything I needed to know before I even wet a line. The inside bar that's been building all summer has finally pinched down into a real trough — maybe four feet deep at dead low, tight against the beach, and it was black with peanut bunker getting pushed up against the sand by something bigger working the deep side. That's the signature I look for this time of year. The outer bar's still soft and shifting from all the southerly wind swell we've had — buoy readings off the coast have been running 3 to 4 feet at short six-second intervals, which is just wind chop stacking on itself, not a real groundswell. It's kept the ocean side mediocre for plugging, but it's pushed all that bait tight to structure, and the back bay and inlet cuts are where the money's been.

We flagged this a few days back — said the bunker schools drifting down from the Manasquan corridor would spill into LBI's bays and light up the blues, and that's exactly what's happening. Snapper blues are thick from the Ship Bottom bulkheads down through Beach Haven, chopping bait on the surface most evenings on the last two hours of the outgoing. But it's not just snappers anymore — I'm seeing cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound class mixed in at Holgate and around the Causeway bridge pilings, hitting small metal-lipped swimmers and 1/4-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the peanut schools. If you want a family afternoon, that's your ticket — light spinning gear, no wire needed for the snappers, small hooks on bait or tiny poppers.

Weakfish are doing what weakfish do in August — they've slid in behind that same peanut bunker push, and the reports out of the deeper holes in Great Bay and along the Mullica channel edges have been better than I expected for this time of year. Nothing giant, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but they're eating. Best bite has been the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, drifting small Bass Assassins in pearl or bunker colors on 1/4-ounce jigheads through 8 to 12 feet of water off Graveling Point and the mouth of the Mullica. Slow retrieve, let it sink, twitch it back — weaks want it subtle, not ripped.

Fluke are still the most consistent bottom bite in the zone, but they've abandoned the shallow flats entirely with this heat. Barnegat Inlet's north and south edges are holding fish in 15 to 25 feet on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current really rips and stacks bait against the rocks. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, tipped with a fresh spearing strip if you've got it — that combo's been putting keepers in the box, mostly 17 to 20 inches with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in. Little Egg Inlet's channel edges are fishing the same way on the outgoing, especially the drop-off just inside the rocks where the sand gives way to that harder bottom.

Striper fishing has settled into the summer pattern we all know and don't love — it's a night game now. Surface water's sitting warm enough that the bass have gone deep and nocturnal, holding around the bridge structure at the Causeway and the deeper holes off Beach Haven, feeding hard on bunker after dark. If you're serious about a keeper bass right now, that means bunker chunks or live bunker under the lights on the bridge, fished on the bottom during the tide change, or working a swimming plug slow through the pilings at 10 or 11 at night when the current's moving. Daytime bass are mostly a wishful-thinking proposition through the heat.

Kingfish are still showing on the ocean side sandbars, particularly the troughs off Ship Bottom and Surf City where that inside cut structure I mentioned holds up. Bloodworm and Fishbites on a high-low rig, cast into the trough on the incoming, has been steady if unspectacular — good action for kids and a nice change of pace between fluke drifts.

As for the bonito watch — the ocean's sitting right at 75.9 degrees off the coast, which is exactly the number that usually tips the first false albacore or bonito sightings on LBI's outer bars. Nothing confirmed yet, but with that kind of surface temp and bait already staging in the cuts, I wouldn't be shocked to hear reports out of the Barnegat Light rips within the next week or two. Worth keeping a small metal in the plug bag just in case.

Looking ahead, if this southerly wind pattern holds and keeps stacking short-period swell on the outer bar, I'd keep my effort inside — the inlets and back bay cuts are where the bait is and where the fish are eating. If the wind backs off and the ocean lays down flat for a stretch, that's when I'd run the beach at first light looking for albie signs on the bar breaks. Either way, watch that tide — everything worth catching this week wants moving water.

reports.headline: Where did the fluke go? Try the sod bank guts, not the flats
reports.subhead: The shallow bays got too warm for comfort, so the fluke and weakfish slid into the channel edges — and the peanut bunker call from two weeks ago just landed.
reports.body_markdown:
I get this question every August, almost word for word: "Mr. Freeman, we fished the same sod bank we've been killing it on since June and got nothing — where'd they go?" Fair question. Class is in session.

The shallow flats behind Brigantine and up in the Absecon meadows have been sitting in the mid-70s for weeks now, and fluke don't love that. They're not gone, they just moved — off the skinny mud and into the deeper guts, the channel edges, and the drop-offs where moving water keeps the bottom a few degrees cooler and the oxygen fresh. I've had my best luck lately working the deeper bends off Absecon Inlet in 15 to 22 feet, and the cuts along the Intracoastal near Graveling Point in Great Egg Harbor Bay in similar depths. Drop a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, work it slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, and you're in business. I had four keepers to 19 inches out there Tuesday on that exact combo, mixed with a handful of shorts that needed to go back and grow up.

The better bite has actually been on the structure — the Route 30 causeway bridge pilings in Absecon Bay, and the rock piles along Great Egg's channel markers. Fluke are stacking tight to that cover during the day, ambushing bait as it sweeps by on the tide. Chartreuse bucktails with a Berkley Gulp swimming mullet trailer, cast up-current and bounced back with the sweep, has been the difference-maker. Don't be afraid to go heavier than you think you need — 1 ounce if the current's really running — because staying on bottom is everything right now.

Now here's the one I want to flag, because we called this a few weeks back: the peanut bunker pushing into the back bays was going to pull the weakfish with it, and that's exactly what's happening. I've had reports of legal weakfish — 14 to 17 inches, a few better — coming out of the deeper holes in Absecon Bay and around the Route 52 causeway in Great Egg on light jigs and small swimming plugs worked over peanut schools at dusk. If you find the bunker balled up nervous on the surface, get a Storm Shad or a 3-inch Gulp swimming shad down under them on a light jighead. That pattern should only get stronger through the rest of August as more peanuts filter into the estuary.

Bluefish are the easy button right now if you've got kids or first-timers in the boat. Snapper blues are thick in nearly every back bay creek from Brigantine down through Sea Isle — small spoons, Kastmasters, anything shiny thrown on light spinning gear will keep a rod bent all afternoon. The adult blues are still doing their dawn-and-dusk thing along the beachfront, chasing bunker schools that are getting pushed tight to the sand at Ocean City, Sea Isle City, and down around Townsends Inlet. If you see the gulls diving and the water nervous just off the second bar, that's your window — it doesn't last long once the sun gets up and the bait scatters back offshore.

Striped bass have settled into the pattern you'd expect for early August — they want the dark and they want structure. Nighttime bunker chunking around the Absecon Inlet rocks and the Great Egg Inlet jetty has been the more consistent approach than daytime casting. Fresh bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, tight to the rocks on the last of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, has produced a few keeper-class fish in the 28 to 32-inch range for guys willing to put in the late hours. Daytime striper fishing in the surf has been mostly a non-event — the water's too warm and too bright for them to want to commit in the wash.

Surf guys working bait rigs at Ocean City and Stone Harbor Point have kingfish and mullet thick in the wash right now, which is exactly where they should be this time of year. Bloodworm or Fishbites on a high-low bait rig, fished in the first thirty yards of surf on the incoming, has been steady if unspectacular — good action for a family outing, not a trophy hunt. I'd also keep an eye on the jetty rocks at Townsends and the wreck structure off Great Egg for triggerfish — they show up sporadically this time of year around anything hard on the bottom, and small pieces of clam or squid on a light jig will find them if they're home.

Looking ahead, the tide cycle is building stronger through the week, which should sharpen up that fluke bite on the channel edges — more current means more bait movement, and more bait movement means more fish committing to feed rather than just holding. If the weather stays settled, I'd spend my time on the last two hours of the outgoing at either inlet, working structure with bucktails, and save the chunk bait for after dark at the rocks. That's where I'd put my own boat this weekend, and I'd have the light jigs rigged and ready in case that weakfish bite keeps building the way I think it will.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks, First Light: Blues Chew Bunker While the Bass Play Hooky
reports.subhead: The jetty rats are getting their arms worked over by cocktail blues while the stripers sit this one out until dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six this morning I'm out on the north jetty at Sea Bright, coffee going cold in the rod holder, and there's already three guys ahead of me picking their way out over the wet rocks with headlamps still on. Nobody's talking. That's how you know something's happening — jetty rats go quiet when the birds are already working before the sun's even up.

And they were working. A bunker school the size of a football field was getting worked from underneath, and every few minutes the whole thing would erupt — blues busting through, gulls dropping on the scraps, that unmistakable sound of water getting slapped by something angry. Guys were throwing bunker spoons and topwater poppers into the edges of it, not even into the thick of it, because you don't need to. The blues were following the bait right up against the rocks. Cocktails mostly, a few pushing three and four pounds, and enough of them that by seven o'clock everybody out there had bent a rod more than once.

We flagged this one a few days back — said the bunker schools would keep spreading with this stable high-pressure stretch and that cocktail blues in the back bays and along the beachfront would spike because of it. Well, here it is. Sea Bright's had it two mornings running now, and word from Belmar is the same thing's setting up off the Ninth Avenue jetty and down toward Spring Lake. If you see gulls sitting low and nervous over a patch of water at dawn, don't wait around — paddle out or walk fast, because these schools don't sit still long once the sun climbs.

Here's the honest part, though. The bass have mostly checked out on us. Ocean temps are sitting in the mid-70s out past the bar — 75.9 at the buoy off the Bight — and that's summer-pattern water, which means stripers are doing what they do this time of year: going nocturnal and hugging deeper, cooler structure. I picked at a few schoolies working the Manasquan Inlet rocks two nights ago on the last of the outgoing, throwing a black Gibbs pencil popper along the north jetty face in that skinny water where the current pinches through, but it was one here, one there, nothing you'd call a pattern. If you want a crack at a bass right now, fish it dark — an hour before first light through sunrise, working the jetty rocks at Manasquan or the Shark River Inlet on the last two hours of the ebb, when bait gets flushed out through the gut and stripers stack up to ambush it. Swimming plugs and darters worked slow along the rocks, not bucktails — the water's too warm for them to chase hard, so you want something they can eat without working for it.

Fluke are still the more dependable daytime play. The Shark River channel and the deeper holes inside Manasquan Inlet have been giving up keeper fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming and the top of the outgoing when the current's got some push but hasn't gone slack. Depths of 15 to 25 feet inside the inlet channels have been the sweet spot — deep enough to hold cooler water, structured enough to hold bait. Nothing spectacular, but a couple keepers for a morning's work is a fair trade this time of year.

Porgies are thick on the nearshore structure off Belmar and Manasquan — the usual reefs and rockpiles in 30 to 50 feet — and they'll keep any kid or first-timer busy while the adults chase the blues. Bloodworms or clam on a high-low rig, nothing fancy needed. And the back bays behind Shark River and the Manasquan River are stuffed with snapper blues right now, which is good news if you've got a young angler who wants nonstop action on tiny gold spoons or spearing under a bobber off the docks.

What I'm watching for the next week is whether that bunker push holds. This high-pressure stretch we've had — light winds, settled seas, the surf running maybe three to four feet at a longer period — is exactly the kind of pattern that keeps bunker schools moving steady along this stretch instead of scattering. If it holds, I'd expect the blitz action to keep sliding both directions from Sea Bright, hitting Asbury Park and down through Belmar and Spring Lake over the coming days. Worth checking the jetties at first light regardless of where you live on this stretch — the birds will tell you before anything else does.

As for albies — too early to promise anything, but with this much bait sitting inshore and water temps where they are, I wouldn't be shocked if the first false albacore showed up scouting the Manasquan Inlet rips by the end of the month, a couple weeks ahead of the usual calendar. I'll be watching the birds and the boils same as always. For now, if you want a bent rod at dawn, the blues are your best bet — and they're not shy about it.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke to Four Pounds, Snapper Blues Thick in the Sedges Behind Tices
reports.subhead: Forty summers on this bay taught me August is a shallow-water game before nine and a deep-channel game after — this week proved it again.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember an August like this one back in the early nineties, running the skiff out of Forked River before first light because my old mate Sonny told me the bay would cook by ten and we'd be wasting bait after that. He was right then and he's right now, forty summers later — this bay doesn't change its clock just because the tackle's better and the boats are faster. When the surface water sits in the mid-to-upper 70s like it has all week, everything that swims in here gets smart about when it feeds, and if you're not on the water by six you're fishing the leftovers.

That's exactly the pattern I've been working the past several days, and it's paid off, though not without some early frustration. The shallow flats and grass beds — Tices Shoal, the marsh edges behind Good Luck Point, the guts running into Oyster Creek — have been loaded with snapper blues since the bunker started pushing peanut-sized pods into the back bay. We flagged this coming a couple weeks back, that the cocktail blues would follow the peanut bunker in as it spread through the system, and that's exactly what's happened. Small blues, mostly cocktail-sized this week with a few pushing bigger, are hammering anything shiny worked fast through the grass on the early flood and the first two hours of the outgoing. Half-ounce Kastmasters, chrome or gold, and small Got-Cha plugs worked on light spinning gear will get bit as fast as you can cast, but only in that window before the sun really climbs. By nine-thirty the blues drop off the flats into deeper water and the bite goes dead until the evening tide starts moving again.

Weakfish are mixed in with that bunker push too, which is a little unusual for August — I mostly associate the tiderunners with May around the sedge banks, but the peanut bunker have drawn some weakies into the bay this month, holding tight to the deeper edges of the grass flats where the current keeps things a few degrees cooler. Nothing huge, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the fourteen to eighteen inch range, but they're there on the last of the incoming, working the drop-offs along the Route 37 bridge flats and the deeper cuts near Tices. Small bucktails tipped with a Fishbites strip or a sliver of squid, bounced slow along bottom, has been the ticket.

Fluke fishing is where the real consistency has been, and it's holding up because those fish have done what fluke always do in the dog days — they've abandoned the baking shallow flats for the deeper structure where the current keeps bottom temps workable. Double Creek Channel has been my go-to this week, drifting the deeper bends in twelve to eighteen feet on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming, when the current's still got some push to it but isn't ripping. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance, have produced keepers to four pounds, with a good number of shorts mixed in that you'll have to sort through. The inlet-adjacent water off Barnegat Light channel edges has also been holding fish, though that bite's been spottier — some days you load the box, other days you work three hours for two keepers. I wouldn't call it lights-out fluking, but it's steady enough to plan a trip around if you're willing to move around and find where the current's working for you.

Striped bass have gone quiet by day, which tracks with what I'd expect this time of year — with the bay running warm, those fish that are around have shifted to a nighttime pattern, holding on deeper structure and feeding after dark when the water cools a touch. I haven't put much effort into bass this week because the daytime bay isn't the place for them right now, but if you want to chase them, fish the channel edges near the inlet after sundown with bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, and be patient.

Blowfish and kingfish have been a nice bonus on the bottom for anyone soaking bait in the deeper holes — Oyster Creek's warm outflow area has had a few blowfish mixed in on small hooks with squid strips, and kingfish have shown along the channel edges on sandworms fished on light spinning tackle. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but a welcome diversion between fluke drifts.

Looking ahead, if this stable weather pattern holds — light winds, no fronts pushing through — I expect the bunker-driven action to keep rolling through the coming week, with the same early-and-late rhythm holding true. The snapper blues and weakfish should stay tucked into the grass flats as long as that peanut bunker keeps working through the system, so I'd keep working Tices and the Oyster Creek flats at first light. For fluke, Double Creek Channel remains my pick, especially on that last hour of outgoing when the current's still moving but manageable. If you're only getting one trip in, I'd make it a dawn start — the bay rewards the early boat this time of year, same as it always has.

reports.headline: The Race at 4.3 Knots: Wire-Line Bass Still Holding on Valiant Rock
reports.subhead: Currents are rebuilding out of the neap, the bass are deep and current-locked, and the first bonito are still a county away.
reports.body_markdown:
Four-point-three knots. That's what the max ebb was running through the Race on Wednesday afternoon, timed off Valiant Rock, and it's the first real number I've clocked all month that tells me the current's rebuilding out of that neap slump we limped through in late July. That extra push matters more than any water-temp reading I could give you, because in this rip, current speed is the tide. When it's running under three knots, the Race fishes soft and scattered. Above four, the boils stack up off Valiant and Race Rock proper, bait gets pinned against structure, and the bass show up to eat.

New London's reading 77.4 at the surface this week — warm, no question, and warmer than Kings Point at the west end of the Sound, which tells you the whole eastern basin has been soaking under this stretch of light air. But surface temp doesn't run the Race. What runs the Race is the cold water the current rips up off the bottom, and on that Wednesday max ebb I had 30 feet of wire out over 55 feet of water off the northeast corner of Valiant, and the transducer thermometer showed a good eight degrees colder than what New London was reporting at the surface. That's the whole game out here in August — find the cold seam the rip is pulling up, park a bunker spoon or a black bucktail with a pork rind trailer right in it, and let the wire do the work getting it down through the churn.

Slack came at 1:42 that afternoon, and I mean slack — not the loose, sloppy version you get on a weak tide, but a real stand-still where you could feel the boat go quiet under your feet. We worked five minutes either side of it with bucktails, straight vertical over the rockpile, and connected on two bass in the low 30s and lost a better fish that came unbuttoned right at the boat. That's honest work for this time of year — the Race in August isn't a numbers game, it's a timing game, and if you're not within that fifteen-minute window around the turn, you're fishing empty water no matter how good your gear is.

Plum Gut has been the more consistent producer the last several days, mostly because the bunker have pushed hard into the Gut's western edge, right off Orient Point, and the bluefish have followed them in thick. We flagged this coming two weeks back — said the peanut bunker push would spread cocktail blues into the back bays within the window, and that's exactly what's happening now along the inshore flats behind the Gut. Snapper-sized blues are stacked in the shallows, and the adult bunker schools pushing through the main current are getting hammered by bigger blues on top, blitzes lasting ten, fifteen minutes at a stretch on the last two hours of the ebb. Epoxy jigs in bone or chrome, cast right into the froth, get bit almost every drop. No albies or bonito in the mix yet, but that's the next shoe to drop.

On the bonito front — we called the sequence on this one too. Rhode Island breachways and the Vineyard rips first, Block Island and Montauk behind that within the week, east-end Long Island inlets coming in last. Montauk's sitting at 74.5 right now and climbing, which puts it right at the edge of that threshold. I haven't marked a single bonito or albie in the Gut yet, and I wouldn't send anyone out here specifically hunting them this week — but with water this warm pushing east and the bait already staged, I'd expect the first fish to show around the Gut, Little Gull, and Great Gull within seven to ten days, not weeks. When they do, it'll be epoxy jigs and small metal worked fast through the rip on the last of the ebb, same as every year.

Bottom fishing has quietly been the most dependable thing out here. Black sea bass are thick on the reef structure around the Sluiceway and Bartlett Reef, holding in 50 to 65 feet, and they're not picky — chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips are getting bit steadily on every drift, keeper fish mixed with a lot of shorts you'll have to sort through. Fluke have been spottier, mostly smaller fish off the edges of the reef where the current softens up, and I'd call that bite mixed at best right now — worth a stop on the way out or in, not worth building a whole trip around.

Offshore, the seas have had a little lump to them — 3.6 feet at a six-second period out past the open water, out of the south, which isn't dangerous but it's been enough to make the ride past Race Rock uncomfortable on an outgoing tide when wind and current oppose each other. Pick your window on the back half of the ebb when it flattens, or wait for the morning glass before the sea breeze fills in.

Look ahead: with the current rebuilding and no tropical trouble on the radar yet, I expect the Race and the Gut to keep sharpening through the week. The slack windows are going to keep shifting later each day as we move through the cycle, so check your tide chart before you leave the dock — five minutes late to the turn out here and you've missed the whole show. I'd bet on the bass holding to the same pattern, deep and current-locked, and I'd keep half an eye toward Little Gull for the first bonito showing. If the buildup keeps going the way it has been, I don't think we're far off.

reports.headline: Ram Island boulders holding bunker and bass — fluke slide deep, albies still a rumor
reports.subhead: The rock piles from Wamphassuc to Fishers Island are stacked with peanut bunker and school bass, but the first false albacore haven't shown — yet.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a pod of peanut bunker working the boulder field off Wamphassuc Point right now that I've been watching for four days straight, and it tells you everything about where this week sits. They come off the rocks on the last of the ebb, pinned tight against the granite where the current breaks, and every evening around dusk something big pushes through and scatters them into the air. That's your bass. Not blitzing, not showing on top for long, but they're there, working the same six or seven boulders like they're punching a clock.

This is the pattern now — deep structure, low light, bunker-driven. Water's sitting warm, high 70s across the Sound, and with that kind of heat the stripers want the shade and the cooler water down around the rocks, not up on the surface chasing bait in daylight. I've been poling the skiff over the Ram Island boulder field at first light and again right at dark, working the edges where the rock drops into eight to twelve feet, and that's where the fish are holding tight. Live-lined bunker on a 5/0 circle hook, no weight, just enough current to walk it back into the structure, has been the most consistent producer. If you want to go artificial, a 2-ounce bucktail with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer, worked slow along the rock seams on the last two hours of the outgoing, will find fish that the boat traffic hasn't already pushed off. Most of what's coming over the rail is schoolie to mid-20s, but there are better fish mixed in — I had one push 34 inches off the north side of Fishers Island working the tide change at Wicopesset Passage, right where the current stacks up against the rock pile on the ebb.

Fluke have done exactly what they do this time of year — they've abandoned the shallow flats and slid onto deeper structure where the bottom stays workable. Fishers Island Sound is holding up its end, and honestly it's one of the better fluke stretches in the whole Sound system right now. I'm finding them on the channel edges and humps between the mainland and the island, 25 to 35 feet, drifting bucktail-and-Gulp combos — white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a ¾-ounce bucktail — nice and slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone slack. Keeper-sized fish, some pushing 4 and 5 pounds, mixed in with a lot of short fish you'll have to sort through. Patience pays here more than speed.

Sea bass are still doing their reliable summer thing on the harder structure — the reef pockets off Watch Hill and the rock piles tight to Fishers Island's south shore are holding fish all day, not just on the tide change. Jigs tipped with squid strips, dropped right to the bottom and worked in short hops, keep them coming. It's not exciting fishing, but it's dependable, and on a slow bass evening it's saved more than one charter for me this summer.

The boulder fields themselves are quiet on the tautog front right now — that's a fall game for me, and these same rocks off Ram Island and Esker Point that I'll be picking apart with green crabs in October are just holding bass and bait at the moment. No sense forcing a bite that isn't ready.

As for albies — nothing yet. I've been watching the temperature breaks closely because this stretch of water, sitting right at the boundary between the warmer western Sound and the cooler open water off Fishers Island, is exactly the kind of edge that pulls the first scouting fish in. The gradient right now is steep — warmer readings toward New London, cooler out toward the open Sound — and that kind of contrast is what stacks bait and draws albies up the coast. I haven't seen a fin yet off the breakwater or around Ram Island, but I've got my 9-weight rigged and sitting in the rack, because when they show here it's usually fast and it's usually right on the temperature seam.

Tide's coming out of a soft neap stretch, and you could feel it on the water — less push, softer breaks around the boulders, bait sitting looser than it should. That's about to change. We're building back into stronger tidal flow over the next several days, and in a place like Fishers Island Sound, where the whole game is current breaking against rock, that matters more than almost anything else. Expect the bite at Wicopesset Passage, the Stonington Breakwater, and the north side of Fishers Island to sharpen up as that flow rebuilds. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide at Wamphassuc Point with a bunker chunk soaked tight to the rocks, and I'd have the fly rod ready in case something silver and fast shows up chasing the same bait. Nothing confirmed on that front yet — but the water's got the right feel to it, and that's usually how it starts.

reports.headline: The Rip at the Hook holds blues under bunker while channel-edge fluke keep paying at Keyport
reports.subhead: First light on Sandy Hook's rip, midday on the channel edges, evening on the Navesink for weakfish — this week's bay is a three-tide puzzle.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday night sitting on my tailgate at the Amboy launch ramp: mornings this week are for the Hook, not the flats. Here's why. Bunker schools have been stacking hard against the rip at Sandy Hook on the tail of the outgoing, and where the bunker pile up that thick, you don't leave them to go poke around Keyport in the dark. You fish the meatball first, then you go find your fluke once the sun's up and the bait scatters.

And that's exactly how the week has gone. First light Tuesday, we ran out past Horseshoe Cove and found bunker balled up so tight along the rip line you could see them nervous on the surface before the birds even committed. Blues came up under them in typical August fashion — 3 to 6 pounds, ravenous, cutting bunker in half on top. We didn't even need lures at times, just drifted a chunk of fresh bunker on a fish-finder rig, 2 ounces of lead, right into the edge of the boil, and let it sink eight to ten feet. Hookups came fast. Mixed in were a few schoolie stripers, 22 to 26 inches, sliding along the bottom of the bait ball rather than up top — that's the pattern right now, bass staying low and working the scraps while the blues do the violence up top. If you want a bass specifically, don't fish the surface chaos. Drop a bucktail — white or chartreuse, ¾ ounce — down through the bait and let it flutter on the bottom before you start working it back. That's where the stripers are eating.

We flagged this pattern a few days back — said the bunker pushing into the bay on tide and wind would keep the blitz intensifying, and that's held true. The bait hasn't thinned out, and as long as it stays parked on that rip through the week, the blues and the low-riding bass will keep using it as a buffet.

By 9 or 10 a.m., though, that bite goes quiet — sun gets high, boat traffic picks up out of the Hook, and the bait pushes off. That's when I point the boat back into the bay and go to work the channel edges off Keyport and Flynn's Knoll. This has been the more consistent, less flashy program all summer, and it hasn't slowed a bit. Fluke are sitting tight to the drop where the flats fall off into 18 to 25 feet, right where the current sweeps bait off the shallows and dumps it into deeper water. Standard drift with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a bucktail, or bounced bare bucktail tipped with squid strips, has been the ticket. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts, but we're seeing enough 19- to 22-inch fish mixed in that a limit isn't a stretch if you put in the drift time. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, when the current is still moving enough to keep your bait working but hasn't gone slack yet.

Water's sitting in that mid-70s range through the bay right now, which is exactly the kind of warmth that pushes weakfish and peanut bunker into the back rivers. We caught wind of this building a week ago, and it's playing out now on the Navesink and up into the Shrewsbury — weakfish showing on the flats near the Highlands bridge and up past Red Bank, chasing peanut bunker that have moved into the skinny water. Light jigheads, ¼ ounce, tipped with a 3-inch pearl or chartreuse paddletail, worked slow along the channel edges on the last of the ebb, has been drawing strikes from weakfish in the 16- to 20-inch range. It's not a numbers game yet — two or three fish an evening if you work it right — but the pattern is building, not fading, and I expect that to keep filling in as more peanuts get squeezed into that skinnier water through the rest of August.

Porgies are still a solid backup at Romer Shoal if the wind kicks up and you don't want to fight the open bay. Anchor up on the shoal in 15 to 20 feet, clam or sandworm on a high-low rig, and you can put together a respectable mess of porgies without burning a lot of gas or nerve.

Wind's been the swing factor. When it lays down out of the southwest in the early morning, the rip at the Hook fishes clean and the bunker stay concentrated. Push any harder and that bait scatters before you even get the lines wet, so I'd plan around the calm windows rather than fighting a stiff breeze out there. Inside the bay, the channel-edge fluke bite doesn't care much about wind — it's tide-driven, not surface-driven — so that's your fallback no matter what the morning throws at you.

Looking at the week ahead, if this bunker stays parked on the Hook rip and the wind cooperates at first light, I'd keep hammering that pattern hard before it inevitably breaks up and scatters into the bay proper. Once that happens, expect the blitz energy to spread thinner across Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal rather than concentrate in one spot — good for coverage, tougher for consistency. Either way, the fluke on the channel edges aren't going anywhere soon, and the weakfish push into the rivers is just getting started.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull's ebb line is running deep — and the blues found the bunker
reports.subhead: Seventy-seven degree water pushed the Thames stripers nocturnal, but bunker schools off Ocean Beach are keeping the blues honest all day long.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the Fort Trumbull wall Tuesday evening watching the ebb line pull away from the point, and it's narrower than it was two weeks ago — tighter, faster, folding back on itself right where the old submarine net used to hang. That seam is doing exactly what it does this time of year: concentrating everything that's moving with the tide into a rope of current about forty feet wide. New London's surface water is sitting at 77.4°F right now, which is warm enough that the stripers in this river have gone full nocturnal. If you're fishing that seam at two in the afternoon, you're probably fishing an empty house. Fish it an hour before dark into the first two hours of the ebb, and it's a different story.

The bass pattern right now is classic mid-summer Thames: fish holding deep and tight to structure during daylight, sliding up onto the current edges to feed once the light drops. Gold Star Bridge pilings have been the most consistent producer — I've had reports of fish in the 28-34 inch range coming off the downriver side of the pilings on the incoming tide, 30 to 35 feet down, eels worked slow along the concrete and bunker chunks fished on the bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current. Nothing explosive, but steady if you're willing to fish the dark hours. Fort Trumbull itself has been better on the back half of the ebb, working swim shads and bucktails through that deep hole off the point — 25 to 40 feet — letting the jig sink all the way to bottom before starting the retrieve. That's where the bigger fish have been sitting, using the depth to escape the heat the same way they would in December, just for the opposite reason.

We flagged this pattern two weeks back — said the outgoing tide would keep producing the most consistent bite as long as the weather stayed stable, and that's exactly how it's played out. The stable high pressure sitting over the Sound hasn't given us much current variation, so the tide change itself has become the trigger. No tide change, no bite. Simple as that this time of year.

Where things have actually picked up is the bluefish. Bunker schools have moved into the outer harbor and along Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach in real numbers, and the blues found them hard. We called this one too — said the blues would track the bunker distribution and the back-bay action would spike, and that's exactly what's happening. Adult blues in the 3-6 pound class are working those bunker schools in open water off Ocean Beach, and when they push a pod up against the surface you'll see the whole thing erupt — bunker skying, blues slashing through, gulls dropping on the scraps. If you can get out there when it happens, a big topwater popper or a bucktail with a strip of pork rind thrown right into the boil will get bit fast. It doesn't last long — five, ten minutes sometimes — so keep the boat ready and don't waste time changing lures once you're on fish.

Inside the harbor and up into the river mouth, snapper blues are thick — good news if you've got kids or grandkids who just want bent rods. Small Kastmasters or a piece of spearing on a bare hook off any dock from Pleasure Beach up toward the Coast Guard Academy will keep them busy for hours.

Porgies have been solid out at Bartlett Reef and around Black Point, fishing the high tide with sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig. Nothing huge — mostly 9 to 12 inch fish — but they're biting consistently enough to fill a cooler if that's what you're after, and it's a good way to spend a slow afternoon between striper sessions.

Blackfish are still a minor story right now. A few anglers picking at small ones around the rock piles near the bridge on green crab, but the real blackfish bite in this river doesn't turn on until the water starts cooling in September and October. I wouldn't make a special trip for them yet — file that one away for six weeks from now.

Looking ahead, the tide is rebuilding out of the recent neap phase, which should sharpen up the current-dependent spots — Fort Trumbull's rip especially, and I'd expect the Gold Star pilings bite to get a little more aggressive as the flow strengthens. If the stable pattern holds through the weekend, I'd plan around the tide change no matter what you're targeting — fish the last two hours of daylight into dark on the ebb for bass, and keep an eye on the bunker schools off Ocean Beach for blues any time of day. The one thing worth watching is the calendar — we're deep into hurricane season, and this kind of calm stretch tends not to last forever. If something starts spinning up in the Atlantic, I'd get my Thames trips in early in the week rather than betting on the weekend.

reports.headline: Niantic fleet says it plain: fluke deep, sea bass steady, bass biting after dark
reports.subhead: Soft neap currents kept things quiet through Black Point and Twotree, but the tide's about to get its legs back.
reports.body_markdown:
I was leaning on the counter at the tackle shop Tuesday morning listening to one of the Niantic drift boat mates gripe about the current, and he said something that stuck with me: "Water's warm enough to swim in, current's dead enough to nap in." That's about the most honest summary of the last week I've heard. The neap tide phase really did flatten things out through Black Point and Twotree Island Channel, and the fleet felt it — not a bad week, just a soft one, and soft weeks make you work for every fish.

Water's running warm out here. New London's reading 77.4°F, which is a good five degrees above where Western Sound sits right now, and that gradient matters. It's pushed the fluke off the shallow flats in Niantic Bay and onto deeper structure where the bottom stays workable — 30 to 40 feet in Twotree Island Channel and along the edges of the Black Point reef complex. The drift boats that adjusted depth early in the week did fine; the ones that kept working the shallower drifts inside the bay got picked apart by shorts. Bucktail and Gulp combos are still the ticket — white 5-inch Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's light like it's been. Keeper fluke to 22 inches have come off those deeper channel drifts on the last two hours of the outgoing, when there's at least a little push to work with.

Sea bass and porgies have been the honest fallback all week, and I mean that as a compliment, not a knock. Hole-in-the-Wall and the rock piles off Black Point are holding fish tight to structure, and with the current soft, that's exactly where you want to be — sea bass don't need a screaming tide, they need bait sitting still enough for them to find it. Green crab and squid strips on standard sea bass rigs, 4 to 6 ounces of lead depending on drift speed, straight down into the structure. Porgies have been mixed in on the same spots, plenty of them in the 10 to 12 inch range, keeping rods bent even on the slow days. We flagged this exact pattern a few days back — said to expect steady bottom fishing through this transitional stretch with just light adjustments to presentation, and that's precisely what's played out. Nothing flashy, just dependable.

Striper fishing has gone almost entirely nocturnal, which tracks with what you'd expect once surface water sits in the mid-to-upper 70s. Daytime trips around McCook Point and the mouth of the Niantic River have been mostly quiet, but guys working bunker schools after dark — snag-and-drop rigs or just live-lining a bunker off the structure near the river mouth and along Black Point — have connected with some real fish, mid-20s to low 30-inch range, holding deep and feeding hard once the light drops. If you've got the patience for a late trip, that's where I'd be putting my time right now, not grinding it out at noon in flat calm water with the sun beating down on a slack tide.

Bluefish have been riding those same bunker pods, and the back-bay stretch of the Niantic River has snapper blues thick enough to keep a kid entertained for an afternoon — small silver spoons or tiny bucktails under a bobber, easy action, good way to get someone hooked on this sport who isn't ready for an all-nighter chasing linesiders. Adult blues have been chopping bunker schools out toward Twotree and off Black Point in short, violent windows — nothing sustained, but when you find the birds working, it's worth a few casts of a topwater popper before they move on.

Blackfish are still off the table this month with the summer closure in effect, so don't waste drift time looking for them around Hole-in-the-Wall — that bite picks back up once the season reopens in the fall, and I'll have plenty to say about it then.

Looking ahead, the tides are about to get some muscle back. We're building toward the full moon, and that means the soft, sleepy current we've dealt with all week through Black Point and Twotree should sharpen up over the next several days. When that current strengthens, the fluke bite in the deeper channel stretches typically gets more consistent — bait gets pushed harder against structure, and the fish stack up instead of scattering. If the wind stays cooperative, I'd plan a fluke trip for later this week over an early one, timing it to hit the building tide rather than the tail end of the neap. For stripers, keep the flashlight handy and fish the dark side of the tide change around the river mouth and Black Point — that pattern isn't going anywhere as long as the bunker schools hold position and the water stays warm. Sea bass and porgies will keep producing regardless of what the current does, which makes Hole-in-the-Wall about as close to a sure thing as this beat offers right now.

reports.headline: Silversides Pour Off the Marsh — Bluefish and School Bass Crowd the River Mouth
reports.subhead: August's dog-day warmth has pushed the baitfish out of Great Island's guts, and everything with teeth is waiting at the door.
reports.body_markdown:
By the first week of August the marsh grass at Great Island has gone from that bright new-green of June to the deep, almost blue-green color it holds through Labor Day, and that's always told me more than any thermometer. When the spartina thickens up like that, the silversides and peanut bunker that have been hiding in the guts and pannes all summer start pushing out on every dropping tide, and the predators know it before we do. I've watched this pattern come and go for fifty summers on this river, and it never fails — warm water pushes bait toward the mouth, and the fish follow right behind it. We said as much a few days back, that the warm river flow would keep shoving bait and predators down toward Saybrook Point through this stable stretch of weather, and that's exactly what's unfolding right now.

The river itself is running warm and a little sleepy on the surface — nothing like the ripping cold flow you'd see in April with the shad pushing through. Out in the Sound the gradient is steep, Kings Point sitting around 75 and New London pushing past 77, and the river mouth is splitting the difference, warm on top with a cooler push of fresher water underneath on the last of the ebb. That thermal layering is exactly where I want to be fishing — Saybrook Point breakwater, the flats off Great Island, and the deeper cuts around the DEP Marina where that cooler bottom water holds through the heat of the day.

Snapper blues are thick right now in the shallows off Old Lyme and up into the coves around Great Island — small, aggressive, and about the most fun a kid with a spinning rod can have on this river. Half-ounce gold Kastmasters and tiny Deadly Dicks worked fast on the surface are doing the damage, best on the first two hours of the incoming when the warmer marsh water starts sliding back over the flats. Mixed in with them, and this is the part worth paying attention to, are bigger adult blues — three and four pounds, sometimes better — that have been riding the peanut bunker schools right up to the mouth. I had a report of fish busting bunker hard off the Point on a calm evening tide, the kind of surface commotion you can see from the breakwater rocks.
