Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, or a bucktail with a strip of pork rind trailing it, worked along the current seam where the river water meets the Sound — that's been the ticket.

Striped bass are still here, but I'll be straight with you, they're not stacked up the way they were in May. What we've got now are holdover school fish and a scattering of better ones working the tide changes, particularly the last hour of the ebb when bait gets flushed hard out of the marsh creeks into the main river channel off Great Island. White bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter, tipped with a strip of squid, bounced along that channel edge in eight to fifteen feet, has been the most consistent producer. Don't waste your time fishing the slack — these fish want moving water pushing bait past them, and on this river that means fishing the tide, not the clock. Essex has been quieter than I'd like this week, but the deeper holes below the town dock have given up a few better bass after dark, fish that seem to be holding on that cooler bottom layer through the heat of the day and only committing to feed once the sun's off the water.

White perch fishing has actually been the most dependable thing going, if you're willing to slow down for it. The shaded deep holes above Essex and along the Lyme side channels are holding good numbers, and small grass shrimp or a piece of bloodworm on a simple two-hook bottom rig, fished right on the bottom in eight to twelve feet, will keep you busy. It's not glamorous fishing, but on a river that's otherwise running warm and a little quiet in the daylight hours, it's the kind of steady action that keeps you sharp for when the tide turns and the blues start showing again.

Looking ahead, the tide is starting to build back out of the neap phase we've been sitting in, and that extra push should sharpen up the bite everywhere current matters — the breakwater, the river mouth flats, the deeper bends around Essex. If the bunker schools stay put and this stable, calm weather holds through the week, I'd expect the blitz activity at the mouth to keep building rather than fade, especially on evening tides when the light goes flat and the bait gets nervous. If a front does push through and stirs up the river, I'd shift my time to the perch holes and wait it out — that pattern doesn't care much about wind. Either way, this is a week to fish the moving water and let the tide tell you where to be, same as it's always been on this river.

reports.headline: Neap Tide Slack Turns the New Haven Breakwalls Into a Porgy Clinic
reports.subhead: Light current off the outer wall stacked scup three deep on the same drop, with sea bass mixed in and blackfish starting to test the rocks.
reports.body_markdown:
Thursday morning, outer New Haven breakwall, and I'm standing there with a spinning rod that's basically a toy — 10-pound braid, a size 4 hook, half a green crab pinched on — and I'm hooked up before the anchor's even settled. That's not exaggeration, that's just what a slack current does to a rockpile full of porgies. Three fish deep on the same drop, biggest one nudging 13 inches, and I hadn't even finished my coffee.

We flagged this a few days back — said the neap tide coming in around the 5th and 6th would ease the current on structure and make the bottom bite sharper, and that's exactly what showed up. Less push means your bait sits still instead of getting dragged sideways off the rocks, and for porgies and sea bass that's the difference between a nibble you can't convert and a fish in the cooler. The current's starting to build again now as we move away from neap, but for the first half of this week it was about as clean as bottom fishing gets on this stretch.

The scup bite has been the headline all week — outer breakwall, Charles Island rockpile, and the humps off Falkner Island are all holding fish in the 8-to-15-foot range depending on tide stage. High-low rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, squid strips or clam belly, fished tight to the rock edges on the last of the incoming through the top of the tide. That's when the current lays down enough to actually feel the bite instead of just feeling your sinker bounce.

Sea bass are mixed right in with the porgies on the same drops, which is the pattern you want in August — steady water in the mid-70s keeps them locked onto structure instead of wandering, and they're not picky. Squid strips, clam, even a chunk of porgy from the last fish work fine. I had a stretch off Falkner Island where every third drop was a keeper sea bass, 14 to 16 inches, nothing huge but a nice mixed bag with the scup filling out the rest of the cooler.

Blackfish are the wildcard right now. I'm marking them on the rockpiles — Charles Island, the Gulf rocks off Milford, a few spots along the New Haven wall — but they're not fully committing yet. Green crabs on a jig head, dropped right into the pockets between boulders, got me two teasing bites and one fish that came unbuttoned at the surface. Water's still on the warm side for them to go full aggressive. I'd expect that to sharpen up as we get into September and the temps ease off a touch, but if you want to scout now, half crabs on light tackle in the 10-to-20-foot zone around the rockier structure is the move — just don't expect a banner day yet.

Stripers are the tougher conversation. The Charles Island sandbar has been giving up fish, but it's a nighttime and dawn program right now — daytime action off that bar has gone quiet with the warm water sitting up top. I fished the bar on an outgoing tide right before first light with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig and picked off two schoolies in the 22-to-25-inch range before the sun got high and shut it down. If you want a shot at something better, Stratford Shoal at night on bucktails or swimming a live eel along the edge where the current breaks is still your best bet for a bigger fish — that structure holds bass that don't want to fight bright sun and warm surface water.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — snapper blues thick in the harbor and around Hammonasset, adult blues showing occasionally where bait pods bunch up off the breakwalls. Nothing like a sustained blitz yet, but with peanut bunker starting to spread through the harbor mouths, I wouldn't be shocked if that cocktail blue bite in the back coves sharpens up over the next week or two as those bait schools thicken. Worth keeping a bucktail or a small popper rigged and ready if you're bottom fishing and see bait get nervous on the surface.

Fluke have been the quiet, dependable piece of the puzzle. Drifting the sandy edges off Charles Island and the deeper channel water toward Stratford Shoal with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has been picking off keeper-class fish in the 18-to-20-inch range, mixed with plenty of shorts you'll have to sort through. Nothing spectacular, but steady enough to fill out a dinner if the tide's right.

Looking ahead — current's rebuilding now off that neap low, which usually means the bottom bite gets a little more technical again. You'll want to fish it smarter: slower drifts, heavier sinkers to hold bottom, and picking the tide stages where the push eases even briefly. If the stable weather holds, I'd put my money on the porgy and sea bass action staying strong through the weekend, with blackfish starting to show real commitment as we roll toward Labor Day. For stripers, I'd keep it a dawn-and-dusk game at Charles Island and save the serious effort for Stratford Shoal after dark.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Soft Ebb: Fluke to 5 Pounds While Bunker Blues Bust Off Greenwich Point
reports.subhead: With the current gone slack under this neap moon, I pulled off Penfield's rockpile and let Cockenoe's deeper edges do the work — and the fluke followed.
reports.body_markdown:
Every week this time of year I have to make the same call — Penfield or Cockenoe — and this week Cockenoe won, easy. Here's the thinking. We're sitting in a neap tide right now, the current soft and lazy on both ends of the swing, and Penfield Reef needs some push to work right. That reef fires when the ebb is ripping hard enough to pin bait against the rockpile and give blackfish and porgies something to fight against. Soft water off Penfield just means fish sitting tight to structure, not feeding aggressively, and boat traffic drifting through with no drift to speak of. Cockenoe, on the other hand, has enough depth variation — that 20 to 35 foot break running off the northeast corner — that fluke will still slide and feed even when the current's barely moving. So that's where I put my time, and it paid.

Fished the last two hours of the ebb Tuesday and again Thursday morning, working 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along that break where the reef drops into the channel. Boated four keeper fluke both trips, biggest going just over 5 pounds Thursday, plus a pile of shorts that needed measuring twice. The bite wasn't a blitz — you had to cover water and hit the drop repeatedly — but it was steady enough that I never doubted the spot. With the current this soft, downsizing the jig head mattered. A full ounce just sat there; the 3/4 let the plastic breathe on bottom without plowing.

The real story this week, though, is the bunker. We flagged this coming — said the peanut pods would spread and the cocktail blues would follow — and that's exactly what's happening off Greenwich Point and around the Cows. Kings Point is reading 74.8 degrees, a good three degrees cooler than what's showing up toward New London, and that west-to-east gradient is keeping the bunker schools stacked tight on our end of the Sound instead of scattering east. I watched adult bunker balled up off the Point Wednesday evening with blues underneath punishing them — surface explosions, birds diving, the whole show. If you can get out there in that last hour of light, a topwater popper or a bunker spoon thrown right into the boil will get bit almost every cast. Just don't idle through the school on the way in — that's the fastest way to shut it down for the next boat.

Sea bass and porgies are holding true to form on the Cows and around Sheffield Island structure, 25 to 40 feet, high-low rigs with squid strips and clam. Nothing spectacular, but it's dependable — the kind of bite you build a half-day trip around when the fluke aren't cooperating or the wind's wrong for the reef. Sea bass are running mixed sizes, plenty of shorts mixed with keepers, so bring the ruler and don't assume every bend of the rod is a fish worth the cooler.

Striper fishing has gone fully nocturnal, which is normal for early August with surface temps sitting in the mid-70s across most of the western Sound. Daytime, they're down deep on structure — the drop-off edges around Sheffield Island and the rock piles off Greenwich Point — and not real interested in much. After dark is a different animal. Anglers working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs off the Norwalk Islands are picking up stripers in the 28 to 34 inch range on the last two hours of the incoming, right as bait gets pushed up against the island edges. If you're going to make the trip, that tide window is worth building the whole night around — showing up two hours too early just means sitting on dead water.

Blackfish is technically fair game but I'm not putting real effort in yet — that bite doesn't turn on with any consistency until the water starts cooling in September and the current builds back up. A few guys are picking at them opportunistically on the reef structure, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it this week.

Boat traffic on the weekends has been what you'd expect for early August — thick around the Norwalk Islands mooring fields and stacked up on Cockenoe by midday Saturday. My move has been getting out before 7 AM to fish the tail of the overnight tide before the parade starts, then switching to the Cows or deeper Sheffield Island water in the afternoon where the pleasure boats don't bother anchoring.

Looking ahead, this neap phase should start building back toward the new moon around the 12th, and once that current firms up, I expect Penfield to come back into play — that reef wants push, and it'll get it. If the bunker stay thick off the Point through the weekend and the weather holds calm, I'd keep chasing those blues in low light. The fluke bite on Cockenoe should hold steady regardless of tide strength given the depth variety out there, but I'd watch for the bite to sharpen noticeably once real current returns midweek.

reports.headline: A 2 A.M. Bigeye at Atlantis, and What the East Wall Taught Me About Waiting
reports.subhead: Ninety-eight miles down and back out of Montauk for one good bite window — here's why the run still pencils out this week.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at 4 a.m. Tuesday, and by the time we cleared Frisbee's the sky was still doing that gray thing it does before it commits to daylight. Ninety-eight miles to the Atlantis wall, 39°49'N, 71°28'W, running the edge where the bottom falls from 600 fathoms into black water. At 21 knots on the 46, that's about four and a half hours each way, and at roughly 16 gallons an hour cruise you're already 300-plus gallons into the day before you've wet a hook. That's the arithmetic of fishing out here. You don't run to Atlantis, Veatch, Hydrographer, or Oceanographer on a whim — you run because the numbers on the chart and the numbers in the tank both say it's worth it.

We got there mid-afternoon, trolled the break through the warm part of the day like we said we would, and it paid off — a pair of yellowfin in the 45-to-60-pound class came off a spread of Green Machines and a naked ballyhoo run long on the shotgun, right along the thermal seam where the water goes from a milky green to that dark cobalt you only see out past the hundred-fathom curve. One mahi, a stray, maybe 15 pounds, grabbed a bird/dredge combination we had set inside the pattern — no real school under it, just a loner riding the edge current. We marked a school of bait stacked tight on the meter around 180 feet and worked it twice, but the yellowfin had already fed and gone quiet by early evening.

That's when we set up to chunk. We'd said last week that soft neap current would trim the peak off the chunk bite, and that's exactly what we found — the tide went slack for almost two hours right at dusk, and the slick just sat there doing nothing. We held off on committing bait until the current started building again around 10 p.m., and that's when it turned on. Butterfish chunks, no weight, freespooled off the stern in the dark, and around 1:45 in the morning we hooked a bigeye that took forty minutes to get boatside — 190 pounds, thick shoulders, the kind of fish that reminds you why you burned the fuel to get out here in the first place. We lost a second one at the leader when it made one more run under the transom and popped the hook. That's the lesson about the east wall: the fish are there on a soft tide, but they make you wait for the current to give you a reason to believe.

Bluefin are mixed into this pattern too, more so than you'd expect for early August. The shelf water north of the canyons is running cooler than the filaments pushing up from the south, and that cooler edge is exactly where boats working the troll are picking up bluefin in the 80-to-150-pound range alongside the yellowfin, particularly up around the Hydrographer and Oceanographer approaches where the temperature break sits tighter to the edge. If you're running out of Block Island or a Rhode Island port, that shortens your leg — Hydrographer is a more reasonable run from Point Judith than it is from Montauk, and worth factoring into where you point the bow depending on which port you're leaving from.

Wahoo showed once, on a high-speed lure pulled at 14 knots on the way back in through Veatch, a fish that hit and came unbuttoned before we ever saw color — no complaints, that's how wahoo go most days out here, one shot and gone. Mahi have been scattered rather than schooled, mostly stray fish under floating structure rather than the kind of concentrated push you'd find under a well-defined weed line. White marlin are starting to show some interest — we raised one behind the spread at Atlantis on Tuesday afternoon, didn't get a bite, but that's usually the first sign before the real activity builds as the tides rebuild through the week.

The way I read it, the pattern we called a few days back is holding: troll the break through the day for yellowfin and whatever marlin activity is building, then commit to the chunk on the strongest push of current rather than sitting on a dead tide hoping it turns. That's what worked this week and it's what I'd do again. If the current keeps rebuilding out of this neap phase the way it usually does, expect the bigeye bite to sharpen up on the night tides through the weekend, and the daytime troll bite for yellowfin should hold as long as the water stays stacked with bait along that 100-to-600-fathom transition.

Worth saying plainly — this isn't easy fishing and it isn't cheap fishing. You're committing a full tank and a full day of running before you know what the current's going to do. But if you've got the range and you pick your window right, the fish are out there rewarding patience over volume right now. I'd rather make one clean run to Atlantis and get one good bigeye at 2 a.m. than burn half the fuel chasing five different pieces of structure hoping one of them lights up. Plan your fuel, watch the tide build, and don't leave the dock unless you're ready to wait the slack water out.

reports.headline: Plum Gut sharpened up right on schedule — bass tucked tight on the seam
reports.subhead: Porgies are steady, the first blackfish are peeking out, and the bass have gone back to feeding after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
There was a kid down at the Mattituck Inlet dock Tuesday morning, maybe ten years old, working a bucktail rod half his size, hauling in snapper blues one after another off the bulkhead while his father stood there with a coffee doing nothing useful at all. I watched that for a good twenty minutes before I even rigged up. Told the father his kid was going to outfish him by noon. He didn't argue. That's the kind of morning it's been out here — the little stuff snapping fast and easy, the big stuff making you work for every bite.

Water's been sitting warm the length of the beat, mid-to-upper 70s depending where you dip a thermometer, warmer the further east you go toward the Gut than it is up around the inlet. That's backwards from how it usually lays out this time of year, but the wind's had a say in it. We had that southerly blow blow through a few days back, and I said at the time it would push cleaner, cooler water against the warm side and sharpen up the thermal seam out at Plum Gut. That's exactly what happened. Bass have been stacking tight against that line on the last two hours of the ebb, holding right where the cold water and the warm water shake hands. Trolled bunker spoons and wire-line umbrella rigs have been doing the damage for the boats that know how to hold a drift through that current — it's not forgiving water, the Gut, never has been, and if you don't respect what it does to a hull you'll learn the hard way.

Shore side, the bass have gone nocturnal on me, same as they do every August when the days get sticky. Daytime, they're down deep and sulking. After dark, they come up onto the rock structure — Horton Point, the boulder field off Rocky Point, the riprap out toward Orient — and they'll feed hard for a couple hours around the tide change. I've had decent nights on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, sinker just heavy enough to hold bottom in the current, and on black or dark-green soft plastics swum slow along the rocks. Nothing enormous — most going 26 to 32 inches — but enough of them, and enough consistency, that I'd call it a real bite, not a rumor. Bring a headlamp and patience. The blitz boys chasing bunker schools out in open water during the day are catching bigger fish, but that's a different game than what I fish.

Bluefish are thick wherever the bunker are thick, which right now is most everywhere along the beat. Snapper blues have taken over every cove and marina basin from Mattituck to Orient — fun for the kids, useless for the freezer, but they'll keep a rod bent. The adult blues are out with the bass working the bunker schools, and when those schools get pinned against the shore near Rocky Point you'll see the whole surface come apart for a few minutes. Doesn't last. Get there or don't, that's the blitz game.

Porgy fishing's been the most honest thing going. Sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, fished on the rock piles and the reef structure off Rocky Point and out toward the Gut approach, and you can fill a bucket without much fuss. Scup don't care about the heat the way stripers do — they've been steady all summer and they're steady now. If you want a fish dinner without a lot of drama, that's your play.

First blackfish of the year started showing up on the same structure this week, which always gets my attention. Green crab on a jig head, worked slow around the boulders. Most of what's coming over the rail right now is undersized, and I've been putting them all back without much thought about it — early sign more than a real bite yet. But it tells you the water's doing what it's supposed to do heading into fall, and it's worth remembering where you found them for when the season and the size catch up to each other.

Fluke are out on the deeper structure now, off the flats and onto the channel edges and reef humps where the bottom stays cooler. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, have taken a few decent fish, nothing spectacular but a fair fish or two most trips if you keep moving and keep your bait fresh. Weakfish have been scarce — a few show up mixed in with the porgy catches on the same structure, nothing you can plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward those springs around the 11th through the 13th, and that's going to re-arm the whole zone — stronger current through the Gut, sharper tide changes along the beach, fish pushed to feed harder on a shorter clock. Until then I'd fish precisely rather than long. Pick your structure, pick your tide window, and don't waste daylight hours on the bass — save that energy for after dark and let the porgy and fluke carry the boat during the day. If the wind stays out of the south a while longer, that seam out at the Gut is worth another look before the bigger tides scramble it back into something new.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday, roaring Thursday: Spencer's break reformed right where we said it would
reports.subhead: A southerly blow scrambled the edge for two days, then Spencer and Norfolk both turned on yellowfin as the water sorted itself out.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the week: B-plus, and it earned every bit of that grade the hard way. Monday was a throwaway — that southerly blow pushed 3 to 4 foot seas out of the south, mean direction dead out of 178, and it took the clean edge we'd been running to Spencer and turned it to mush. We said it would happen before it did — flagged that the breaks would blur for a day or two and likely reform south or seaward of where they'd been sitting. That's exactly the play. By Wednesday the water sorted itself back out, and Thursday we found yellowfin stacked on a filament that had slid a good eight to ten miles southeast of where we'd marked it the week before.

Here's how the week actually ran, canyon by canyon, because that's the only way to talk about this stretch of bottom.

Spencer was the story. We ran out of Cape May working the 100-fathom curve on the northeast wall, roughly 39°08'N 72°38'W, and once that break reformed it reformed clean — sharp color change, birds working bait pushed right up against the edge. Yellowfin from 35 to 60 pounds came on the troll early, green machines and small Ilanders pulled at 6 to 7 knots over water we marked in the mid-70s on the surface, and once we found the push we shut down and chunked butterfish over it. That's when the bigger fish showed — a couple bigeye in the 100-pound class came up from depth on a straight butterfish drift with no weight, baits sinking naturally off the stern in that oily slick. Stable high pressure the last several days made it an easy canyon to fish two, three days running — no weather bailouts, no wasted fuel.

Lindenkohl, just south of Spencer around 38°58'N 72°46'W, was more of a mixed bag. We picked at mahi under a weedline on the way out — schoolies to 8 pounds, small stuff but fun on light spinning gear with skirted ballyhoo — and a couple white marlin showed on the troll but wouldn't commit past a bite-off. If you're running Lindenkohl right now I'd have naked ballyhoo and a spread of dink baits ready for those whites rather than counting on the bigger meat spread alone. It's there, but it's not stacked the way Spencer was.

Poor Man's — the closer run, inshore of the 100-fathom line around 38°37'N 73°10'W — fished more like a bait-and-troll day than a chunk day. Good for boats that can't commit to the full run. We marked wahoo signs on the fishfinder screaming through bait balls near the edge and picked off two nice ones, 40 and 55 pounds, on high-speed trolled Yo-Zuri Bonito lures pulled at 12 knots. That canyon's the sleeper for guys who want a shorter ride and still want a shot at real fish, but the tuna bite there was slower than Spencer — a couple stray yellowfin, nothing like the numbers up north.

Norfolk was the surprise. That's the long run for us out of Ocean City, but the reports coming back from boats working the 200-fathom break down there had bigeye and yellowfin both showing on the same push of warm water that's been feeding Spencer. If the filament that reformed after Monday's blow keeps sliding south the way it has, Norfolk could be the better bet by the weekend — it's already getting the leftovers of the same temperature break, just a few days behind.

Across the board, the stable weather is doing the heavy lifting right now. No wind, no seas to fight, and boats that can commit two or three days in a row are cashing in on it. That's the read Hooper and I have both been circling for weeks — mid-August, warm Gulf Stream filaments pinned against the shelf edge, bait and tuna both holding tight to the breaks. It's about as textbook as this fishery gets, but textbook doesn't mean automatic. We still had to find the reformed edge, and it took a day of running around with the temp gauge before Spencer paid off.

Looking ahead — tides are softening back toward first quarter, and that shift usually means less current-driven chaos on the drift and better conditions for the troll and the daytime deep-drop. If you've got swordfish gear rigged, this is the window. Softer current makes it easier to hold bottom at 1,200 to 1,600 feet without fighting the boat all day, and Norfolk in particular has a track record for daytime swords once things calm down like this. I'd split my time — troll Spencer early morning while the temp break is freshest, then either chunk it through midday or make the run south to check Norfolk before committing the boat to a full sword drop. Keep an eye on anything spinning up in the tropics, because this calm stretch won't last forever, and when it breaks it usually breaks the pattern along with it.

reports.headline: 75.9°F at the Bight Buoy — the Filament Finally Kissed the Canyon Wall
reports.subhead: A three-degree jump on the shelf pushed warm water onto the edge, and the yellowfin followed it right to the Dip.
reports.body_markdown:
Buoy 44025 out in the Bight is reading 75.9°F this morning, running a solid three-plus degrees warmer than what we were seeing two weeks back. That number matters more than it looks. Shelf water in the high 70s means the filament that's been teasing us off the canyon edge finally pushed inshore enough to override the cooler upwelling that had the yellowfin scattered and deep. Wave state is nothing to write home about — 3.6 feet at a 6-second period, mean direction out of the south — a little sloppy on the ride out but nothing that shuts down a spread once you're on the grounds.

I ran 68 nautical miles out of Manasquan Tuesday to the Dip, roughly the 39°32'N, 72°32'W stretch, and the water column told the story before we even wet a line. Color went from a dirty green shelf water to a clean cobalt blue right at the 100-fathom curl, and the temp gauge on the troll spread jumped almost two degrees in under a mile. That's the kind of kink we flagged last week — said if the SST break sharpened or bent over the canyon's east elbow, that corner would be the spot — and that's exactly where we found bait balled up and birds working tight circles.

Yellowfin were on the warm side of that break, mostly 20 to 40 pounds, with a couple pushing 50. We picked them up trolling a mixed spread — green machines and small ballyhoo skirted in blue/white on the short riggers, a spreader bar with squid chains down the center, cedar plugs way back. The fish wanted the smaller offerings once the sun got up high; naked ballyhoo behind a small green/yellow bird outfished the bigger bar two to one by midday. Bigeye showed up on the overnight drift — we chunked butterfish over the edge between the Claw and the Dip starting around 9 p.m., dropped glow-stick rigged baits to 150 feet, and connected on two bigeye in the 80-100 pound class before 2 a.m. That bite dies fast once the current lays down, so timing the drift to the building tide matters more than people give it credit for.

Mahi were scattered but not absent — found a decent weed line drifting northeast off the temp break holding gaffer-sized fish, 8 to 15 pounds, plus a pile of schoolies that came up on chunks the second we slowed the boat. If you find floating structure — a pallet, a bucket, anything — stop and pitch a bucktail or a small ballyhoo before you troll past it. Wahoo have been an incidental catch on the high-speed gear, one solid 45-pounder taken on a black/purple Braid Marauder run at 14 knots along the break, but nobody's targeting them specifically yet — the water hasn't held long enough at that clean blue color to build a real pattern.

White marlin are around but thin. We raised two off the Claw on the troll — both came unbuttoned before the pitch bait connected — and heard of one release out near Texas Tower on the way home. Not enough volume yet to call it a pattern, more a bonus if you're already tuna trolling and keep dredge teasers in the water.

Bluefin haven't materialized at the canyon itself this stretch — that fish is showing further north and east right now, more a Block Island and Stellwagen story as warm water pushes bait that direction. If bluefin are the target, I'd look elsewhere this week rather than burn fuel hunting them at Hudson.

Swordfish scouting during the day has been quiet but not dead — we marked bait stacked tight to bottom in 1,400 feet off the southwest edge of the canyon on the sounder, the kind of structure that usually holds a daytime drift. Haven't had the right window to put a squid-and-light rig down there yet, but that's on the list for next trip if the sea state cooperates.

Tides are softening out of the recent push, easing toward the next neap phase, and that's exactly the setup where trolling starts gaining share over the chunk — less current means baits track cleaner and fish have an easier time committing to a moving target instead of holding tight to a chunk slick. We called that shift last week and it's playing out — troll numbers this week beat the chunk numbers for the first time in a month.

Looking ahead, if that filament holds its position and the break stays sharp over the east elbow, I'd run the same coordinates again before I'd chase anything new — the Dip through the Claw, working the blue-water side of the 100-fathom line. If a front pushes through and knocks that warm tongue back offshore, the bite likely follows it out past the canyon proper, and you'd be running an extra 15-20 miles to find the same water. Watch the color change on the way out before you commit to a spot — it's telling you more right now than any single number on a gauge.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Running Cold and Green — Bass Gone Deep, Bonito Knocking
reports.subhead: The water off the island shifted color this week, and that shift is telling me more than any forecast could.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge before first light Tuesday and the air had that clean, mineral smell it gets when the deep water starts pushing up over the structure — a little cooler on the skin, a little heavier in the lungs. By the time there was enough light to read the surface, I could see why. The water had gone from that flat summer blue to a deep bottle green, streaked with foam lines where the current was working against the rock. That's oxygenated water climbing the ledge, and every August it means the same thing: the biggest bass on this whole stretch of coast have quit chasing bait up top and gone down to live where it's cold and clean.

That's exactly the pattern right now. Surface temps south of the island are sitting in the mid-70s, plenty warm enough to shut the daytime bite down on the flats, but the bass haven't left — they've just gone vertical. I'm finding them in 40 to 60 feet on the Southwest Ledge and out toward the North Rip, holding tight to structure through the day and only really committing to feed on the tide changes, especially the last two hours of a building ebb when the current really starts ripping bait off the edges. Night fishing has been the better call all week. Live eels drifted slow along the rock piles on the Ledge, and bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off the North Rip on the change of tide, have both been producing — not a blitz, but quality fish, the kind that make you check your drag before you set the hook. If you want numbers, fish daytime and expect to work for it. If you want size, fish the dark hours around the tide change and be patient.

Bluefish have been the more reliable daytime story. Bunker schools have been thick off the west side, and wherever those pods bunch up tight against the current, the blues have been putting on a show — real topwater violence, the kind where you can hear it before you see it. We flagged this pattern a few days back, that as long as the high pressure held and the bunker stayed concentrated, you'd get exactly this kind of surface explosion, and that's precisely what's been happening on calm mornings off Grace's Cove and out past Cow Cove. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — thrown right into the boil have been getting hit on nearly every cast when you find the right pod. The trick is timing: get there before the boats pile on and scatter the school.

Fluke have pushed off the shallow flats and settled into deeper water, which is the normal August move. I've had the best luck drifting the channel edges off Great Salt Pond and the drop-offs on the west side in 25 to 35 feet, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, slow and steady along the bottom. It's not been wide open — you're covering water to find the fish holding on structure rather than picking them up everywhere — but the quality has been good, several fish pushing 4 to 5 pounds mixed in with the shorts. Squid strips on a bucktail have also been worth having rigged as a second option; there's a lot of squid around the island right now and the fluke know it.

Scup fishing has been about as good as it gets — an easy, reliable pick if you want dinner without much drama. Anchoring up on the hard bottom off Old Harbor and around the Ledge with squid strips or sandworms on a simple two-hook bottom rig has been filling coolers fast. It's not glamorous fishing, but on a day when the wind's up and the bass bite is tough, it's the play that keeps a trip from being a skunk.

Now, the one everyone's been asking about at the dock — bonito. They're not here yet, not confirmed, but everything about this week says they're close. Surface temps are pushing into that low-to-mid-70s window where they usually show, squid and scup are thick around the island giving them forage to follow in on, and the pattern we've watched build all summer has been marching steadily up the coast — RI breachways and the Vineyard rips first, Block and Montauk right behind. I haven't hooked one yet myself, and I won't tell you I have, but I'd be very surprised if the first fish weren't showing on the south side within the next several days, especially if this stable weather holds. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with Deadly Dicks or small epoxy jigs ready on the boat — you don't want to be digging through a tackle box when the first school shows up busting bait on the surface.

Looking ahead, the tide's rebuilding out of the recent neap phase, which should sharpen up the bite windows across the board — better current on the Ledge and the Rip means a more predictable feed for the bass, and better current generally means tighter, more concentrated bluefish blitzes. If the calm, high-pressure pattern holds through the week, I'd fish the tide changes hard for bass, work the bunker pods early for blues, and keep half an eye on the horizon for that first bonito wake. If a system starts brewing out in the Atlantic, that changes everything fast — this is peak hurricane season, and the island doesn't give you much warning when the weather turns.

reports.headline: August 7 and Washington's Already Past Its Prime Window — Time to Adjust
reports.subhead: The wall is still paying off but the pattern's shifting from chunk to troll as tides go soft into next week.
reports.body_markdown:
I've been running this canyon long enough to know the calendar lies to you if you let it. Every other captain on the VHF is talking like mid-August just started the season — for Hudson, for Wilmington, sure. Not here. Washington runs on its own clock because of where it sits relative to the stream, and by the first week of August we're already past the opening act and deep into the second. If you're planning your first trip of the year out here this week thinking you caught the front end of it, you didn't. You caught the middle, which honestly might be the better seat.

We flagged this last week — said the yellowfin would carry the volume on the temperature breaks along the wall, that the billfish presence would build the way it does in early August, and that boats grading their weeks honestly would call it a B-plus: fish in the box every trip, the only knock being consistency trip to trip. That's exactly what's playing out. Nobody's getting skunked out here right now, but nobody's calling their outfitter to brag about a 20-for-20 morning either.

The warm filament that's been sitting on the edge since late July hasn't moved much, which is the whole story. It's held bait and held fish along that break where the canyon wall drops from the 100-fathom curve down toward the 1000, roughly working the stretch from 39°08'N, 72°33'W south through 39°02'N, 72°28'W. That's still the address. Surface temps on the warm side of that break are pushing mid-to-upper 70s, cooling off fast once you slide back over the edge into green water — and that seam is where the yellowfin are stacking up to feed, mixed in with scattered bigeye that are showing better after dark than during the day.

Trolling a standard spread — Green Machines and Zukers in the shotgun, naked ballyhoo and a few skirted horse ballyhoo down the middle — has been the more consistent producer through the daylight hours, and that's going to matter more as we roll into next week. Tides have been softening out of the recent stretch and they're going to keep going that direction, which historically shifts the percentages here away from chunking and toward the troll. If you've been a chunk-and-wait guy on the wall all summer, this is the week to start moving the boat again instead of anchoring up on the drift and hoping the current brings them to you.

That said, chunking bunker and butterfish over the deeper structure — the humps and the drop just north of the main canyon axis — is still putting yellowfin in the box for the boats willing to sit on it, especially in that dawn window before the sun gets high. It's just not the layup it was two weeks ago when the current was still ripping and the bait was pinned tight against the edge.

White marlin have been the pleasant surprise. Numbers aren't huge, but they're building the way they should for this point in the season, and we're seeing them come up on dredge teasers and small blue-and-white islanders worked just off the temperature break rather than deep in the canyon proper. If you've got a pitch bait ready and someone on the bridge with sharp eyes on the temp gauge, you're in decent shape to get a shot or two per trip. Mahi are scattered under whatever weed lines are holding — nothing to write home about in size, mostly schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range, but they'll fill a cooler slot while you're working bigger fish on the troll. Wahoo have shown up on the high-speed gear worked right on the color change itself, not sitting off it — that's an important distinction this time of year, the wahoo want the edge tighter than the yellowfin do.

We also called the frontal timing right — said the passage would churn things inshore but that the southern canyons, Washington included, take southerly wind better than the New York bight boats do, and that by midweek the window would open back up settled. That's held true. The blow pushed through, kicked up a short-lived chop on the grounds, and by Wednesday it laid back down into the kind of glass we've had most of this week.

Looking ahead, I'd treat this coming week as a transition trip more than a repeat of what worked in July. With the tide continuing to soften, I'd lean harder into the troll pattern early and save the chunk bags for late afternoon into dusk when the current picks back up enough to hold a slick. If that warm filament holds its position along the wall — and there's no strong signal yet that it's sliding — the yellowfin should keep grading out as a B-plus fishery: dependable, not spectacular, worth the run. If it starts sliding east the way these things sometimes do into September, I'd expect the bite to follow it, and boats will need to shift their coordinates east of that 72°28'W line to stay on the fish. For now, that's where I'd put my spread.

reports.headline: Trolled the Elbow at sunrise, anchored on the break after dark — yellowfin, a bigeye, and one green-lit wahoo to show for it
reports.subhead: Stable weather let us run deep and stay out; the fish rewarded patience more than horsepower this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night looking at the fuel burn and the forecast: run the 82 miles to Wilmington, troll the edge from first light until the sun got high, then sit on anchor and chunk through the evening bite instead of running home. With gas the way it is, you don't burn diesel twice in a day chasing a maybe. Calm seas and light out of the southwest meant we could commit to the long day without worrying about getting bounced around on the way back, so we took it.

We picked up the warm filament coming off the Stream right where it always seems to set up this time of year — pushing up over the canyon edge around the Elbow, 38°45' north, 72°28' west, with the color change and a hard temp break where the water jumped a couple degrees inside a half mile. That's the kind of seam that stacks bait, and it did. Flying fish everywhere, a few scattered patches of weed holding small mahi, and enough surface activity that we started with a spread instead of committing straight to the chunk.

The troll produced better than I expected for early August — three yellowfin in the 30 to 45 pound class came off a mixed spread of naked ballyhoo and small green-and-yellow Ilanders run off the shotgun and long riggers, plus a nice wahoo, low 40s, that grabbed a deep-diving lure run off a planer down the middle. Wahoo bites have been sporadic all summer out here, so getting one clean strike in daylight felt like a bonus rather than something to bank on. We lost a second wahoo bite to a bite-off on straight mono — should've had wire on that position from the jump, and that's on me. Lesson relearned: if the water's got that oily, warm look to it, wahoo are working the same seam as everything else, so rig for them even if you're targeting tuna.

White marlin showed too, and this is right on the clock for where we expected them. We flagged last week that the marlin bite would build through August rather than peak and fade, and that's exactly what we're seeing — three bites on dink ballyhoo behind small blue/white Sea Witches, two hookups, one release at the boat on a fish that came unglued at the last second on a circle hook that hadn't fully rotated. Nothing to complain about there. The marlin are following the same temperature edge as the tuna, working the current seam where the bait gets pinned against the drop.

Once the sun got up high and the troll bite went quiet — which it does out here by mid-morning once the light flattens the water — we shut down and set up to chunk over the drop past the 100-fathom curve, working the edge where it falls into 300, 400 fathom water off the southwest corner, what some of the Cape May boats call the Sled. Butterflied bunker chunks on straight 50s, no weight, letting it drift naturally down the current, put a bigeye in the box a little after dark — right around 90 pounds, came up slow and heavy on the second hook down, which is usually how they show themselves out here. Yellowfin kept picking at the chunk line through the night, nothing huge, mostly 25 to 35 pounders, but steady enough that we never really had a dead stretch. That matches what I said last week too — the yellowfin bite is steady rather than spectacular right now, holding right on that edge where the bait's riding the seam, not exploding in big pushes but reliable if you're patient and stay on the temp break instead of running around chasing birds.

Water on the inside of the break was running warmer than the open canyon water, which is typical for this time of year as the Stream throws off these filaments — you'll see it on the temp gauge before you see it on the surface, a jump of two, sometimes three degrees inside a quarter mile. That's the whole game out here in August: find where that warm tongue is laying against the canyon wall, and sit on it rather than running all over the numbers hoping for a bigger push.

What I'd do differently next trip: rig at least two positions with wire from the start given how active the wahoo have been on that seam, and I'd bring more bait for the chunk — we went through bunker faster than expected once the yellowfin got working under the boat after dark.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure stretch holds like it's supposed to, I'd run the same play — troll the Elbow early, chunk the drop after dark — and I'd expect the white marlin numbers to keep building as we get deeper into August. The risk is the calendar: peak hurricane season is right around the corner, and one storm system spinning off the Stream can rearrange these filaments overnight. Until that happens, this is the pattern I'd fish, and the pattern I'd tell any of the other Indian River or Cape May boats to run too.

reports.headline: Bunker on the Reef, Bass in the Dark: Montauk's August Turn
reports.subhead: The Point's gone quiet on top and loud underneath — bunker pods thick off the Lighthouse, blues crashing them in daylight, bass working the boulders after the sun drops.
reports.body_markdown:
This is the stretch of the season where Montauk asks you to be patient, and if you've fished the Point long enough you know that patience here always gets paid back with interest come September. Right now we're sitting in that in-between water — surface temps off the Lighthouse holding around 74, 75 degrees, warm enough to push the big resident bass off the top and into their summer pattern: deep, tight to structure, and mostly nocturnal. That's not a knock on the fishing. That's just what forty years on this rock has taught me happens every August, and this year is following the script.

The boulder field off the Lighthouse is still the epicenter, but you've got to fish it different than you did in June. I've been working the incoming tide starting about two hours before the top, easing bunker chunks and whole eels down into the pockets between the rocks, letting the current do the work. Rich guys will tell you they're catching bass in broad daylight off the rocks right now — I'd be careful trusting that unless it's overcast and the tide is really honking. My best fish this past week, a mid-30s bass that took a live eel fished on a fish-finder rig in maybe 15 feet of water, came at 11 p.m. on the building tide, right in that seam where North Bar's current wraps around and meets the deeper water off the Point. That's the program right now — go after dark, fish the current edges, and don't expect it to be fast. Two, three quality bites a tide is a good night this time of year.

What's not subtle at all is the bluefish. Bunker pods have been thick off Shagwong Reef and out past the Point, and the blues have been all over them in full daylight — the kind of surface chop and diving gulls that'll pull every boat within five miles off its anchor. Bucktails, poppers, anything chrome thrown into the melee will get bit, and these aren't snappers — we're talking three, four, five-pound cocktail blues with some genuine slammers mixed in. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the peanut bunker would keep spreading and that back-bay blues would spike as a result — and that's exactly what's playing out now. Fort Pond Bay has peanut bunker stacked at the east end creek mouth, and the cocktail blues have followed them in on the incoming tide. Small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster — worked fast through the froth is all you need there, and it's a great spot to bring a kid or a first-timer because the action is nonstop even when the Point bite goes quiet.

Weakfish are trickling into that same bunker pattern. Lake Montauk, particularly around the Star Island jetty on the outgoing tide when the harbor drains hard through the inlet channel, has been giving up weakfish in the two-to-four-pound class to guys drifting bucktails tipped with a strip of squid along the current seam. It's not a blitz — one or two fish an outgoing tide if you put in the time — but weakfish in Montauk waters always feel like a bonus, and with bunker thick in the bay right now I expect that bite to hold through the rest of the month.

Fluke have slid off the shallow flats and settled onto the deeper structure, which is normal for August. I've had the most consistent action drifting the drop-offs around Frisco Rock and the deeper edges off Shagwong in 35 to 50 feet, 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, working the drift slow and staying in contact with bottom. Fish aren't huge — most going 16 to 19 inches — but there are keepers mixed in, and porgies have been riding shotgun on the same drifts. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod, anchor up on the reef structure off the harbor mouth and soak sandworms or clam on the bottom for porgies — that bite has been steady and reliable all week, no drama, just consistent pulls.

Now here's what I'm watching closest heading into next week. Water's sitting right at that threshold temperature where false albacore and bonito start showing around the rips — we're not there yet with confirmed fish, but the ingredients are lining up: warm water pushing out of the Sound, bait getting pressured into tight balls off the Point, and that first cool night or two of building current that usually flips the switch. I've seen this pattern plenty of Augusts — the water creeps into the mid-70s, everybody starts talking about it at the dock, and then one morning somebody's hooked up to something that peels drag like nothing else in the striper zone. If I had to bet, I'd say the first confirmed albie or bonito shows up east of the Point or out toward Shagwong within the next week to ten days, especially if this stable weather holds. Until then, my time's going into the night bass bite at the boulders and the reliable daytime action on blues and porgies — proven fish over speculative ones, every time, until the calendar tells me otherwise.

reports.headline: Peconic settles into the mid-70s — porgies stacked at Shelter Island, weakfish riding the bunker into the coves
reports.subhead: A cooling southerly knocked the edge off the heat and woke up the bottom bite exactly like the bay usually does this time of year.
reports.body_markdown:
By the first week of August the Peconic has settled into its deep-summer rhythm, and if you've fished these waters as long as I have you can practically set your watch by it. Water temps are sitting in the mid-70s across the bay proper, warmer in the shallow coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor, a touch cooler out toward the Race where Gardiners Bay starts feeling the pull of Plum Gut current. That front that pushed through midweek brought a stiff southerly and roughed up the surface for a day, but behind it the water dropped a degree or two — and just like I figured it would, that knocked the porgies and fluke into gear again. We flagged that exact pattern a few days back, and it played out almost to the letter: the Peconic takes a southerly a lot better than the ocean beaches do, and the bay bounced right back with a stronger daytime bite than we'd had the week before.

Shelter Island is doing what Shelter Island does in August — porgies thick around the reef structure off Cornelius Point, the rips under the Route 114 bridge, and the drop-offs outside Coecles Harbor. Anchor up in 15 to 25 feet, get a chum pot of ground clam or mussel going, and fish small hooks with squid strips or sandworm on a high-low rig. These porgy have been running a good average size this month, plenty in the 12 to 14 inch class with a few chunkier fish mixed in on the slower tides. Best window is the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high — the current slows enough that the chum holds together and the fish stack up instead of scattering.

Fluke are exactly where they should be for this point in the season — off the shallow flats and into the channels where the bottom stays workable. The North Race, the edge of the Jessup's Neck channel, and the deeper cuts around Robins Island have all been giving up keeper fish on the drift. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, worked slow along bottom in 20 to 30 feet, are getting it done, and a few boats have done well tipping bucktails with a strip of squid for extra scent when the current's light. Outgoing tide has been the better call — it pulls bait out of the shallows and concentrates the fluke along the channel edges where they're waiting.

Weakfish are the story worth watching right now. We said back at the start of the month that they'd track the peanut bunker into the bays through August, and that's precisely what's happening — schools of peanuts are pushing into Noyack Bay and the mouth of Sag Harbor Cove, and the weakfish are right behind them, holding in the deeper holes, 15 to 20 feet, working the tide changes morning and evening. Small bucktails or bunker-imitation soft plastics, fished slow near bottom, have been picking off fish in the 3 to 5 pound range. They're not schooled up thick everywhere, so it pays to move around and find where the peanuts are balled — the birds working the surface will usually tell you before your fishfinder does.

Bluefish are riding that same bunker distribution, and the cocktail blues have started showing in the back bays right on schedule — Three Mile Harbor and the creeks off Northwest have both had pods of snapper-to-cocktail blues chopping at peanut bunker on the surface in the early morning. Light tackle, small metals or a Gulp shad on a jighead, and you can have steady action for an hour before the sun gets too high and they slide off.

Striped bass have gone the way stripers always go once the bay settles into the mid-70s — they've pulled off the flats and into deeper, cooler structure, and the best action now is a nighttime game. Channel edges around Orient Point and the deeper holes toward Plum Gut are holding fish that are feeding hard after dark on bunker chunks and eels fished on the bottom. Daytime, your best shot is right around the tide change when moving water pulls bait past the deeper rips — I've had better luck working the last hour of the ebb into the turn than blind-casting the flats at noon.

Looking ahead, if this stable, southerly-leaning pattern holds, I'd expect the porgy and fluke bite to stay solid through the coming week, with the weakfish continuing to build as more peanut bunker pushes into the coves. Keep an eye on Gardiners Bay and the water off Orient as we move deeper into August — the current through Plum Gut is starting to carry more bait, and that's usually the first sign the fall transition is loading up, even if it's still weeks away. For now, work the tides, keep your baits small and natural, and don't sleep on that early-morning window before the sun climbs — that's where the bay's showing its best cards right now.

reports.headline: The East Bar at Cupsogue Built Out 20 Yards — And the Fluke Followed the New Edge
reports.subhead: Rough ocean and a shifting inlet geometry pushed the bite inside — here's where the channel structure is holding fish this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the jetty rocks at Cupsogue on a low tide Tuesday and watched a hump of sand break the swell that wasn't there three weeks ago. That's the east bar, and it's built out a solid twenty yards since the last blow pushed through in July. This inlet never sits still — every summer it reshapes itself under steady southwest wind and moderate surf, and this year's no different. What matters for us is what that new bar geometry does to the current: it's tightening the ebb flow through the main channel, speeding it up on the last two hours of outgoing, and that's exactly where the fluke have set up shop.

Offshore, the ocean's been a mess — NY Bight buoy readings had seas around 3.6 feet at a short six-second period most of this week, which is choppy enough to keep the surf fishing at Cupsogue's ocean side inconsistent and push bait and predators into the more protected inlet channel and back bay. Water out there is sitting around 76 degrees, plenty warm, but that short-period slop doesn't give bass or bluefish a clean feeding lane along the open beach. So the fish have moved to where the structure does the work for them — current edges, channel drop-offs, the deeper cuts behind the bars.

Fluke have been the most dependable read all week. The best fish are coming off the channel edge on the bay side of the inlet, right where that new bar drops into eight to twelve feet of water. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, have been picking up keepers to five pounds. A few guys working the deeper hole off Pattersquash Island with squid strips tipped on bucktails have done even better — that hole holds current on both stages of the tide and it's been quietly one of the better producers in the whole system this month. Don't sleep on it just because it doesn't get talked about as much as the inlet itself.

Bluefish have been the more reliable action for anyone who just wants bent rods. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks off East Moriches and Mastic — small metal and Kastmasters worked fast under diving terns will get you all the light-tackle action you want for an evening. The adult blues are stacking closer to the inlet mouth, chasing bunker schools that have been pushing through on the last of the incoming. If you can find the school — and this week they've been showing up off Tuthill Point in the last hour of the flood — bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig or a bunker spoon trolled slow through the pod will get you into eight- to twelve-pound blues without much trouble.

Weakfish have been mixed in on those same deeper holes, but they're not thick. A few decent fish, two to four pounds, have come off the channel structure near the Coast Guard station on soft plastics fished slow along bottom during the tide change — that dead window right at the top or bottom when current goes still for twenty minutes is when they've shown best. It's not a bite you can plan a whole trip around yet, but worth a few casts if you're already out there working fluke.

We flagged this two weeks back — said to watch for the first peanut bunker showing up in the back bay, and marked the Aug 11-13 springs as the window that current over the new bar geometry should turn into the best bass stretch of the month. The peanuts have started showing along the grass edges off the East Moriches flats this week, small and scattered but there. That's the signal. Bluefish will track that bait expansion fast — expect the cocktail blue action in the back bay creeks to spike hard over the next ten days as those peanut schools grow and spread toward the inlet mouth.

Striped bass have been the quiet story so far — mostly a nighttime bite, working the deeper cuts on the outgoing with bunker chunks or eels, and mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 24- to 28-inch range around the inlet structure. That's typical for early August with surface water sitting in the mid-70s; the bigger fish are holding deep and feeding after dark. But if that peanut bunker keeps building toward the new moon springs on the 11th through 13th, the hard current running over that reshaped bar should concentrate bait right where the bass want to feed — and that's the window I'd circle if I only had one shot at a decent striper this month.

Porgies have been a steady, unglamorous producer for anyone anchoring up on the hard bottom inside the inlet — clam or squid on a hi-lo rig, nothing fancy, and you'll fill a cooler in an afternoon. Blackfish are still a few weeks off from their real season but a handful have come off the rock piles near the jetty on green crab for patient anglers fishing slack tide.

If I had one day this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the Pattersquash hole for fluke, then swing over to Tuthill Point on the last hour of the flood to intercept those bunker-chasing blues. And I'd keep an eye on that bar off Cupsogue — inlets like this one don't hold still, and the next good blow could move that structure again before the springs even get here.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Weakfish Own the Bridge Lights
reports.subhead: With the ocean pushing mid-70s water, the real action at Shinnecock starts when the sun goes down and the tide starts pulling.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a decision to make Tuesday night: fish the inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing, or head over to Ponquogue and work the bridge lights on the tail of the incoming. I picked the inlet. Reason was simple — the ocean's sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s out past the jetties, and that kind of water pushes the better bass to feed after dark when the surface layer cools a touch and the bait gets nervous. Daytime fishing out there right now is mostly blues and short fluke. The grown-up bass show up when the light's gone.

So I set up on the north side of the inlet, tight to the deep hole where the channel scours out against the rocks, and waited for the tide to really start pulling — that back half of the outgoing when the whole bay is draining past you. Livelined bunker on a fish-finder rig, no weight beyond what it takes to hold bottom in that current, and I let it swing naturally into the seam where the fast water meets the slower eddy behind the jetty rocks. Two bass in the mid-30-inch range came out of that spot in about ninety minutes, both fat, both clearly feeding on the bunker pods that have been holding just outside the inlet mouth all week. Nothing giant, but real fish, and they came on the same stretch of tide both nights I fished it. If you're going to gamble one night this week, that back-half outgoing at the inlet is where I'd put my money — just watch your footing on those rocks in the dark and carry a light you trust.

Ponquogue Bridge is still doing exactly what it does in August, and I mean that as a compliment. Weakfish are stacked around the pilings, feeding on the peanut bunker that's flooded into the bay over the last couple weeks. We flagged this pattern a while back — said the weakfish would track the peanut bunker into the bays through August, and that's precisely what's unfolding under those bridge lights right now. Half-ounce jig heads in pink or chartreuse, tipped with a Bass Assassin or a 3-inch Gulp minnow, worked slow along the current seams where the light meets the shadow line. Best window is the last hour of the incoming into the top of the tide, when the peanuts get pushed up against the structure and the weaks stack underneath them. I've had three- and four-pound weakfish come off there on consecutive nights, along with a fair number of cocktail blues mixed in chasing the same bait. It's not a guaranteed fish every cast, but it's consistent enough right now that I'd call it the most reliable bite in the whole system.

Fluke have slid off the shallow bay flats as that water's warmed up, and they're holding deeper now — the channel edges off Tiana and the deeper drifts toward the inlet mouth, 15 to 25 feet, where the bottom stays cooler and the current keeps things moving. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, still the standard. It's been a mixed bag out there — plenty of shorts, a keeper here and there, nothing to write home about. If you want a legitimate limit trip you need to cover water and not get married to one drift.

Bluefish are scattered but present — snapper blues thick in the back bay off Tiana and around the canal mouth, adult blues chasing bunker schools just outside the inlet on the ocean side. Nothing blitz-worthy yet, but the bunker are there in numbers, and given how fast that peanut bait has moved into the system, I wouldn't be shocked to see the cocktail blue action spike hard in the bay within the next week or two.

The canal's fishing the way it always does this time of year — current-driven, and you need to time the locks. Best window is right as the locks start opening, that 30-45 minute stretch when everything gets concentrated and moving, and again about ninety minutes before they close for the night. Bucktails tipped with squid strip or Gulp minnows on simple one-hook rigs, because that rubble bottom will eat anything fancy. If you're planning a night session there, remember you need the Suffolk County Night Fishing Permit for the 10pm-6am window — daytime access is free and open, but after dark they check.

Looking ahead, the tide swings are building back up out of the recent slack stretch, which should sharpen the bite everywhere current concentrates bait — the inlet hole, the bridge pilings, the canal locks. If that holds through the weekend, I'd stay on the same script: inlet after midnight on the outgoing for bass, Ponquogue on the incoming for weaks. Watch the bunker schools outside the inlet too — if the blues commit to them the way they have the last few summers, that could turn into the best surface action of the month.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: ocean's a washing machine, so we're fishing the inlet seam
reports.subhead: With 3-4 foot swell rolling outside, the fluke, bass, and blues have crowded into Fire Island Inlet and the bay's deep channels — and that's exactly where I've been.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a guy at the dock this morning, tackle still shrink-wrapped, asking if he should run his 21-footer out past the inlet for some deep-water action. I looked at him, looked at the swell breaking white over the outer bar, and said, "Buddy, you'll spend more time bailing than fishing." That's been the story all week — 3 to 4 feet of leftover ocean swell stacked up on a short period, the kind that turns a nice morning into a chore if you're not set up for it. So I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen: leave the open water alone this week and fish the seams. The inlet and the bay are holding fish, and honestly, they're holding better fish than the beach front is right now.

Here's the why. Offshore, the Bight is sitting around 76 degrees on the surface with that swell rolling through — not dangerous, but sloppy enough that bait and predators alike are ducking for cover. That pushes everything toward structure, and there's no better structure on this whole stretch of coast than Fire Island Inlet and the channels running off it. Fluke have piled onto the deeper water around the Robert Moses bridges — I'm talking 30 to 45 feet, right along the pilings and the current break where the sand drops off into the channel. Outgoing tide has been the move, dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails nice and slow along bottom, letting the current do the work instead of ripping it. Picked up a mixed bag Tuesday morning — a few shorts, one heavy 5-pounder that came off the west side of the second bridge on a chartreuse bucktail tipped with squid strip. Nothing to write home about in numbers, but the quality's there if you're patient and you're willing to drift it three or four times before committing to a spot.

Striped bass are doing what they do in August — going nocturnal and staying close to bait. Bunker schools are still working the beach and pushing into the inlet on the tide changes, and the bass are shadowing them, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when everything funnels out of the bay through Fire Island Inlet. Live-lined bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to the rip line off Democrat Point at first light or after dark, has been the ticket. I had two solid fish — one just over 30 inches — off the point Wednesday at sunrise, both on bunker chunks fished on the bottom in maybe 15 feet of water where the rip pushes out past the jetty rocks.

Worth mentioning for anybody who hasn't heard: Heckscher State Park opened up night fishing on a trial basis this summer, Field 6 only, Friday through Sunday, dusk to dawn, through Labor Day. You need the Night Sport Fishing Permit or the 4x4 permit on your dash, but if you've got it, that stretch of Great South Bay shoreline is worth a look on an outgoing tide — the bay's dumping warm water and bait right past there, and it's the kind of quiet structure edge that summer bass like to work after dark. I haven't fished it myself yet this trial run, but I've got it circled for next week if the wind cooperates.

Bluefish have been the most reliable fun on calm mornings — and we've had a few of those between swell events. Bunker pods are getting worked over right off the beach from Kismet down past Cherry Grove, and when the blues get under them it's blitz fishing, plain and simple. Poppers, metal, doesn't matter much — get near the commotion and cast into it. Just watch your leader, these aren't snapper-sized, some of these cocktail blues are pushing 3 to 4 pounds and they'll chew through light mono without blinking.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been thin. A few reports of fish coming out of the deeper holes off Patchogue and around the West Sayville flats on bucktails at dusk, but it's not a pattern yet, more like scattered luck. What I am watching closely is peanut bunker — we flagged a couple weeks back that they'd be pushing into Great South Bay behind the New England run, and I'm starting to see small pods of them stacking in the back creeks off Bellport and Patchogue on the last of the ebb. If that holds, the weakfish and the cocktail blues both should tighten up behind them over the next week or two — peanuts draw everything in this bay once they show.

Looking ahead, if this swell backs off like the pattern suggests, I'd keep an eye on the outer sandbars off Robert Moses and Democrat Point late in the week. Surface temps pushing past 70 out there means it's not crazy to think the first false albacore or bonito of the season could show up chasing bait balls along the beach — it's happened before around this calendar mark. I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but I'll have a small metal rod rigged and ready just in case, because that's the kind of surprise you don't want to miss because you left the right lure at home.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Into the Norwalk Islands — Blues Are Waiting at the Door
reports.subhead: The bait told the story before the bite did — and the neap slowdown we flagged last week showed up right on schedule at Stratford Shoal.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching. Not fishing — watching. There's a difference, and this time of year it matters. Off the mouth of Oyster Bay Harbor and again inside the Norwalk Islands, I found peanut bunker balled up so tight the surface looked dimpled, like rain falling on flat water. Terns were working them in short, nervous dives, not the big diving blitzes you get later in the month, but enough to tell me the peanuts have arrived in numbers worth paying attention to. That's the tell. When the bait shows up in the back bays like this in early August, the blues are never far behind, and this week they weren't.

We flagged this exact move last week — said the peanut bunker distribution would expand and back-bay cocktail blues would spike within two weeks. Didn't even take that long. Port Jeff Harbor, Northport Bay, and the pockets behind the Norwalk Islands are all holding schoolie-to-cocktail blues in the 1-3 pound range, hammering anything silver and small. Half-ounce Kastmasters and small Deadly Dicks worked on the top on the last two hours of the incoming have been the move, especially at first light before the boat traffic pushes the bait down.

The bigger story this week was the current, or the lack of it. We also called that the August 5-6 neap would take a full gear off the daytime shoal bite by Wednesday, and Stratford Shoal proved it out. I fished the rip there Wednesday afternoon on a tide that should have been ripping and instead just sort of shuffled through. Marks were there on the machine but they weren't feeding — stacked tight to bottom in 35 to 45 feet, not chasing anything. That's neap water for you on that shoal; without the push, the bait doesn't get pinned against the rocks and the bass and blues have no reason to commit. If you fished the shoal midweek and came home disappointed, it wasn't you.

The SW blow that rolled through mid-week hit the western approaches harder than it hit us here. Oyster Bay and the water off Larchmont and Hempstead Harbor churned up with some chop and a little discoloration, but the central basin — Stratford Shoal, Middle Ground Light, the deeper water off Charles Island — took it in stride. Cleaner water behind the front actually nudged the daytime bite back up briefly Thursday, right where we thought it would. If you had to pick one piece of water to fish through unsettled weather this week, the central basin was it.

Night fishing has been the more consistent bass program with surface temps sitting in the mid-70s — Kings Point read 74.8°F, and it's noticeably warmer working east, with New London pushing 77.4°F. That west-to-east gradient matters: the fish on our side of the Sound are a touch more comfortable than what the eastern boys are dealing with, but they're still daytime-shy. I've had my best luck anchoring up-current of the Stratford Shoal rip an hour before the tide turns, soaking chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig in 30 to 40 feet, letting the scent work while the tide builds. Eels drifted along the rocky edge at Charles Island after dark have also produced, mostly fish in the 24 to 32 inch range, with the occasional better one mixed in on the peak of the flood.

Fluke fishing has been the one truly dependable piece of this week's puzzle, and it's staying that way as the shallow flats warm past comfortable. The channel edges off Middle Ground Light and the deeper drop-off on the north side of Stratford Shoal, 45 to 60 feet, have been holding fish that will make a dinner. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide pushing you along, have out-produced everything else I've thrown. Doubles up to 4 pounds have come over the rail more than once this week, though you have to grind through a lot of shorts to find them — it's not a fast bite, it's a patient one.

Porgies are scattered but present on the rockier structure around the Norwalk Islands and the reef pockets off Charles Island, small hooks and sandworms still the simplest way to load a cooler if that's your speed. Blackfish season's still off in the distance, but a few incidental catches on the fluke grounds tell me the fish are already staged on structure, which is normal for this point in summer.

Haven't seen the first bonito of the season yet, and I've been looking — every bait school I glass gets a second look for that quick, torpedo-shaped shadow cutting through the peanuts. Not there yet. Given the water we're sitting in and the bait now stacked from Oyster Bay to the Norwalk Islands, I wouldn't be shocked if that shows up before the month is out, but this week it's still blues and bass doing the work.

Looking ahead, the current is building back out of this neap, and if that holds, I'd expect the Stratford Shoal daytime bite to firm back up by the weekend — that's usually how it goes once the tide gets its legs back under it. If you're picking a day, I'd fish the shoal on the building flood Saturday morning and have a bucktail rigged for fluke as a backup if the bass don't cooperate right away.

reports.headline: Riis Landing Bay Side: Snappers, Fluke, and a Waiting Game for the Bridge
reports.subhead: With the ocean still churned up from last week's blow, I launched off the bay side and let the tide do the sorting — here's what showed up.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip the ocean beach entirely and put the kayak in at Riis Landing, on the bay side of Fort Tilden. That's the move when the surf's still got a leftover shoulder on it and the wind hasn't fully settled — you get protected water, you can actually see what you're doing, and honestly this time of year the bay side wakes up earlier in the day anyway before the sun cooks the flats. I've fished that stretch enough summers to know it rewards patience more than horsepower, and this week that patience paid off in bits and pieces rather than one big score.

We flagged this last week — said the post-frontal stir after that SSW blow would cool the water and clean it up right as the neap softened the current, and that's more or less what happened. Tuesday through Thursday gave me a noticeably better window than the days right after the front came through.
