The water off Riis Landing had that clean, slightly green color instead of the churned-up brown it had over the weekend, and the fish responded to it — not a blitz, but a real bite window in the two hours around the last of the outgoing.

Snapper blues are thick in the channels right now, and I mean thick — anywhere the current runs past a break in the marsh grass or funnels past a culvert, you'll find pods of them chasing whatever's small and silver. If you've got a kid or a buddy who just wants bent rods, small silver spoons or a sliver of spearing on a snap swivel under a bobber is all you need, fished right off Canarsie Pier or the Ave U bridge up in Gerritsen Creek. No permit hassle at either spot, which matters this year with the Gateway passes sold out — Canarsie Pier and the creek mouth at Marine Park are your no-fuss options if you didn't get in on that March sale.

Fluke are still around but they've pushed off the shallow flats and settled onto the deeper channel edges and drop-offs where the bottom stays a touch cooler under all this August sun. I picked up two keepers and a handful of shorts drifting the edge of the channel off Riis Landing in 12 to 15 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, working it slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. That's been the pattern all week — the fluke bite dies fast once the tide goes dead, so you've got a window and you need to be in position for it, not driving around looking for it.

Stripers are the harder story right now. Daytime bay fishing for bass in August is mostly a bust — they know better than to sit in shallow warm water with the sun beating down, so if you want them you're fishing the dark hours, and the spot everybody with a brain points to is the Marine Parkway Bridge on the outgoing. The current sluicing through those pilings at night pulls bait past the structure and stages fish right in the seam. I had one short bass and lost what felt like a better one to a piling on 20-pound braid fishing a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig off the rocks there Wednesday night, incoming tide bleeding into the first hour of the outgoing. It's not a numbers game right now — one or two fish a tide if you put your time in, which is honestly about right for early August in the bay.

Porgies have been a reliable backup when the rest of it's slow. Working bloodworm or clam on a hi-lo rig around the Cross Bay Bridge structure and the deeper holes off Floyd Bennett Field will put fish in the cooler even on the days everything else goes quiet. Weakfish reports have been thin and scattered — a couple of guys mentioned marking them on the flats near Motts Basin but I haven't put one in the boat myself this week, so take that as a maybe, not a target.

Here's the thing about this stretch — we're sitting in that in-between spot on the moon. The neap that softened everything out on the 5th made for slack, lazy tides, which is exactly why the daytime bite got a little better even as the nighttime bass bite stayed sluggish; less push means less urgency for a fish that wants current to work. That changes fast. The new moon springs building for August 11-13 are going to re-arm those bridge ebbs with real current, and that's when I expect the Marine Parkway pattern to sharpen back up — bigger tide swings mean more bait getting pushed and pulled past that structure, and bass respond to that the way they always have. If I've got one night to fish next week, that's the window I'm circling — first big push of moving water on the outgoing, right at the bridge, bunker chunks or a swimming plug worked along the current seam.

For access, if you're bay-side and don't want to fight for a Gateway permit spot, Riis Landing and Canarsie Pier are your friends this month. If you want the ocean structure and don't mind the walk, Fort Tilden's 193rd Street lot still has the Fishing Access Pass system running and the groins there hold bass on the outgoing once the surf settles down from this latest blow. I'd give the ocean side another few days to lay down before I commit a whole trip to it — the bay's been the more honest bet this week, even if it's not blowing anybody's doors off.

reports.headline: Neap tide sulk, then the Gut wakes back up
reports.subhead: The Race ran soft and quiet for three days straight — then last night's current found its legs, and the stripers found the wire.
reports.body_markdown:
4:12 a.m., Plum Gut, standing on the rocks at the Orient side with a needlefish in the current seam. Three casts, nothing. Then the fourth swings through the eddy behind the boulder and a striper stops it cold — mid-30s, not a giant, but it came off the bottom hard on a current that finally had some shoulder to it. That fish told me everything I needed to know about this week: the rips are waking back up.

We flagged this last week — said The Race would go soft and the bass would spread out and sulk through the neap, and that's exactly what happened. For three, four days the current at The Race and Plum Gut was running weak, maybe 1.5 to 2 knots on the max instead of the 4-plus we like, and the bite went from violent to lazy. Bass scattered off the hard structure, blues stopped showing on top, and anybody fishing those rips like it was July got humbled. But tides are rebuilding fast toward the coming full moon, and last night at The Race I watched the surface texture change in real time on the last two hours of the ebb — current stacking up again off Valiant Rock, birds working the disturbed water, and bass showing under them for the first time in days.

Water's warm right now — New London reading up around 77, Kings Point closer to 75 — which pushes this fishery into that classic late-summer pattern south of the Cape: bass go deep and nocturnal, feeding hardest on the dark side of the tide. That's exactly why the 3 a.m. program at Plum Gut and the rocks off Orient Point is producing better than anything you'll find at noon right now. If you're fishing days, fish deep structure — the drop-offs on the west side of The Race in 40 to 60 feet, working bucktails and diamond jigs tight to bottom on the strongest stage of the tide you can find. If you're fishing nights, work the current seams and eddies with big swimming plugs and needlefish, cast across the seam and let it swing dead through the slack pocket behind the rock — that's where that 30-plus fish ate.

Bluefish are riding the bunker pattern hard right now, same as everywhere else in the Sound. Adult blues are chopping bunker schools in open water off Fishers Island and out toward the Race, and when you find working birds over a bunker pod, that's your green light — snap jigs or bunker spoons trolled fast through the melee will connect. Snapper blues are thick in the back creeks around Orient and up into the Mystic and Niantic river systems, giving light-tackle guys easy, steady action on small Kastmasters and Gotcha plugs. We called the peanut bunker push two weeks out for cocktail blues in the back bays, and with bait already showing thick in those same creek mouths, that timeline's tracking right on schedule.

Fluke is the fishery carrying this zone through the current lull, and it hasn't missed a beat. Niantic's fluke boats have been punching limits consistently in 38 feet, and that pattern's held exactly like I expected — the bottom fishery doesn't care whether the rip is running hard or soft, it just wants clean structure and moving bait. Same story working the edges of The Race itself and through Fishers Island Sound — drift bucktail/Gulp combinations, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of squid, along the drop-offs where the sandy bottom meets rock and gravel. Depths from 25 to 45 feet have been the sweet spot, best drift speed around a knot to a knot and a half. Slow that drift down too much in the soft current and you lose bottom contact; too fast and you skip right over the fish. When the tide was weak this week, guys who adjusted lead weight down and slowed their retrieve kept catching. That's the fluke game in a nutshell — it's neap-proof if you're willing to adapt.

Porgies are stacked on the reef structure around Fishers Island, especially the rock piles off the north side — small hooks, sandworms or clam, right on bottom, and you can fill a bucket in an hour if you find the school. Good option for a slower tide day when the rips aren't worth the trip.

Looking ahead: as the moon builds toward full, expect The Race and Plum Gut current to keep sharpening through the weekend, and that should tighten up both the bass and bluefish bite considerably. If the current comes back the way it should, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut before first light — that's historically where the bigger fish show. Keep an eye on bait movement in the back creeks too; if peanut bunker keep pushing the way they have, the cocktail blue bite in the estuaries should turn from steady to genuinely good within the next week or two. Bring a rain jacket regardless — this is still hurricane season, and any tropical system spinning up out there could scramble this whole pattern fast.

reports.headline: Skip the Fluke Boats — The Real Meat's at the Rocks After Dark
reports.subhead: While the center console crowd drifts Sloop Channel at 9 a.m., the bass are stacking bunker schools on the outgoing tide once the sun's down.
reports.body_markdown:
Every morning this week I watch the same parade leave the ramps at Cedar Creek and Norman J. Levy — twenty boats running west to drift Sloop Channel for fluke before the heat gets bad. Good for them. I'm not knocking a fluke dinner. But if that's all you're doing in August, you're leaving the best fish of the week on the table, and it's not even close.

The bass have gone nocturnal on us, same as they do every summer once the surface water sits in the mid-70s. Buoy readings off the Bight are showing 75.9 degrees with some leftover swell — 3-4 footers still rolling in behind that southerly blow we caught over the weekend. I told you that blow was going to leave the beach ugly for a day or two, and it did — Field 2 and Field 4 stayed a washing machine through Tuesday. But the water's cleaning up now, and that matters because the bass don't want the surf loaded with sand and foam. They want it flat and dark, with bait pinned against structure.

That's exactly what's setting up at Jones Inlet right now. I've been working the jetty rocks off Short Beach and the east end of Jones Beach on the last two hours of the outgoing, right into the start of the low. Bunker schools are stacking in the deeper cuts along the inlet edge, and where you've got bunker in August, you've got bass working them from underneath after dark. Nothing complicated about the presentation — a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the rocks, or if you want to work it, a 2-ounce bucktail with a white teaser dropped down the current seam where the jetty meets the channel. I had three fish to 28 inches Thursday night doing exactly that, one over the slot that went back, and lost something bigger that just leaned into the current and didn't budge — probably wrapped me around the base of the rocks.

Field 1 is worth mentioning here because the state finally got the night fishing window right this year — dusk to 6 a.m., Friday through Sunday, all the way through November. If you've got your Night Sport Fishing Permit and your DEC registry squared away, that east end stretch is money right now because the current runs hard west into the inlet mouth and stacks bait against that first sandbar cut. I'd rather fish that three nights a week than fight the boat traffic on Sloop Channel any day.

Now — we called the peanut bunker move last week, and it's starting to show. I've had reports of small pods pushing into the back bay creeks off Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge flats, nothing thick yet, but enough that the snapper blues have found them. If you've got kids or you just want steady light-tackle action, small Kastmasters or Deadly Dicks off the bridge on the last of the incoming are getting hit every third or fourth cast. Give it another week to ten days and I expect those peanuts to spread through the whole bay system, and when that happens the cocktail blues and the bass both flip a switch. That's when the real back-bay blitz shows up — bunker pushed into the shallows, birds working, everything happening at once. Not there yet. Close.

Fluke are still around if you want them, but the pattern's shifted with the heat — they've slid off the shallow flats onto the deeper channel edges, 18 to 25 feet, in Sloop Channel and the West Channel drop-offs near the inlet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing, are still the ticket, and there are keepers in that mix, but you're working for them now instead of them being everywhere like June. Porgies are holding steady on the ocean-side reefs and the rock piles off Point Lookout — bring sandworms and clam, fish it on the bottom, and you'll eat.

Weakfish talk keeps coming up at the dock, and I'll say this — I've seen more short weakfish mixed in with the fluke catches in the bay than I have in years. Nothing keeper-sized that I've heard of, but the fact they're showing at all in numbers is worth paying attention to. If that trend holds another season or two, we might actually have a real weakfish fishery back in this bay, not just a memory guys tell stories about.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my night gear rigged and ready. If the ocean stays calm behind this pattern the way it looks now, I expect the bunker schools to hold tight to the inlet structure through the week, and the bass bite should stay steady on that outgoing tide — best window right around the last two hours before low, into the first hour of the new flood. If the peanuts flood the bay like I think they will inside ten days, that's when this whole thing gets loud. Until then, I'm at the rocks after dark, and I'm not apologizing for skipping the fluke drift to do it.

reports.headline: Neap Tide Squeezed the Rips — Execution Rocks Still Gave Up Bass After Dark
reports.subhead: A soft moon killed the daytime current, but fluke on the reefs and bunker-chasing blues kept rods bent from Throgs Neck to Matinecock.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop in City Island this week wanted to know why his Tuesday afternoon drift past Hart Island produced nothing but a single dogfish and a snapped leader. I didn't need to look at a tide chart to answer him — I could feel it in my knees walking the dock. That current just wasn't moving. We're three days off the first-quarter neap, and I said it last week and I'll say it again: this moon is softening every current-driven bite in the Sound. The bridge rips, the reef edges, Execution Rocks, Stepping Stones — they're all running on borrowed current right now, and the windows are shorter and weaker than they were two weeks ago. That's not bad luck. That's physics. Time it right and you can still eat. Show up at the wrong hour and you're the guy complaining at the bait shop.

Here's where the timing actually paid off. Execution Rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing, right around dusk, has been the most consistent thing I've fished all week. Water's warm — Kings Point is reading high 74s — so the stripers aren't exactly aggressive in bright sun, but once that light drops and the tide starts pulling hard off the rockpile, bass in the 26 to 34-inch class have been stacking on the down-current side. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig, or if you can find them, live mackerel, fished right on bottom in that 30 to 40-foot depression off the rocks. Bucktails work too if you're willing to work for it — 1.5-ounce white with a chunk of pork rind, cast up-current and let it swing dead on bottom through the sweet spot before you start cranking.

Stepping Stones has been quieter than a normal August, and I'll be straight with you — that's the neap talking. The light usually turns that stretch into a highway on the spring tides. Right now it's more like a back road. I still marked fish there on both tides Wednesday, but they weren't feeding hard until the tide really got moving in the last ninety minutes before the top. If you fish it, fish the clock, not the calendar.

Fluke are the one thing that hasn't cared one bit about the neap, and that's the best news I've got this week. The reef structure off Matinecock Point and the mixed bottom running out toward Hart Island have been holding steady numbers of keeper fluke in 25 to 35 feet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the drift, have out-produced everything else I've tried. A few guys are still doing well on bigger fish — one came across the scale in Port Washington at just under 7 pounds, taken on a bucktail-and-Gulp combo tipped with a squid strip, fished in that deeper channel water off the Manhasset Bay entrance.

Bluefish are doing exactly what you'd expect with bunker schools spread the way they are. Adult blues are working the peanut and adult bunker pushing through the mouth of Manhasset Bay and off Matinecock, and once you find the school getting worked from above by gulls, it's not subtle — cast a metal-lip swimmer or a diamond jig into the boil and hang on. Snapper blues, meanwhile, have completely taken over Little Neck Bay and the inner reaches of Manhasset. If you've got a kid who wants nonstop action, small silver spoons or Kastmasters off the dock in the last two hours of daylight will keep a rod bent all evening. We flagged the bunker distribution spreading a couple weeks back and said the cocktail blues in the back bays would follow — and here they are, right on schedule, chewing through anything shiny in three feet of water.

Weakfish are the sleeper story right now. They've been trickling into the same bays holding the peanut bunker — Manhasset, Little Neck, the shallower flats off Whitestone. Nothing to build a whole trip around yet, a fish here and there mixed in with the fluke on light jigs and 4-inch swimbaits, but it's the kind of pattern that tends to build through the back half of August as more bunker push into those bays. Worth keeping a rod rigged light if you're working that water anyway.

Looking ahead, the moon starts building back toward full over the next week, and that means the current is only going to get stronger. If the pattern holds the way it usually does off a neap, expect the Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones bite to sharpen up fast by the weekend — more current means more bait getting pushed off the structure and more predictable feeding windows, instead of the short, moody ones we've had. I'd plan around the last two hours of the outgoing at Execution Rocks and the top of the incoming at Stepping Stones, and I'd keep fluke gear rigged regardless, because that bite hasn't needed the moon's permission to stay good. Watch the wind too — if we stay light out of the southwest the water should stay clean enough to keep sight-fishing those bluefish blitzes when they show.

reports.headline: Double Creek fluke bite holds steady as bunker blitzes light up Barnegat Inlet
reports.subhead: Weakfish have gone deep and quiet for August, but fluke on the channel edges and bluefish at the inlet are keeping rods bent.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a kid on the boat this week, maybe nine years old, asking me why we were running the edge of Double Creek Channel instead of anchoring up on the flat where his dad said the fluke were thick back in June. I told him what I've been telling people for forty years — the bay doesn't sit still just because the calendar says summer. Come the first week of August, with the flats baking under afternoon sun and water temps up where nothing wants to be shallow past ten in the morning, the fish slide off into the channels and hold there until the tide or the hour drags the bait back up. That kid caught his first keeper fluke twenty minutes later in eleven feet of water on the drop-off past the "S" turn, and I got to feel like I knew something again.

That's about the size of it out there right now. The bay is carrying its full August heat load — warm on top, a little cooler down where the current scours the channel bottom — and that thermal split is doing most of the work for us. Double Creek Channel has been the most consistent thing I've fished all week, drifting the deeper bend in twelve to sixteen feet on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when the current's still got some shape to it but isn't ripping. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a sliver of squid, dragged slow along bottom — that's been the winning combination. Keepers to five pounds, a lot of just-short fish mixed in, which tells me there's a decent class of fluke coming up behind this year's crop. Slack water kills it dead, so time your drift around the moving water, not the clock.

Weakfish I have to be honest about — they've gone quiet the way they always do once the water gets properly warm. The May run at the sedge banks feels like a different season entirely. What few weakfish anyone's finding now are holding deep, off the mouth of Oyster Creek and down along the channel edges toward Waretown, and they're coming on bait — bloodworms or a live killie under a slip sinker — fished right on bottom in the cooler pockets. It's not a bite worth planning a whole trip around this week. If you connect, treat it as a bonus, not the plan.

Bluefish are where the real energy's been. Bunker schools have piled up thick in the bay this month, and every tide change at Barnegat Inlet has been producing surface blitzes — birds working, blues busting bait right up against the rocks on the north side. I flagged this pattern last week, said the building tidal push toward the new moon would sharpen up the current-driven spots, and that's exactly what's happened at the inlet. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in the one-to-two ounce range — thrown right into the froth on the outgoing has been about as easy as bluefishing gets. Bring wire leader or you'll donate more lures than you keep. These blitzes have been short-lived, ten, fifteen minutes at a crack, so when you see the birds start dropping, don't dawdle getting over there.

Blowfish and kingfish are doing their quiet August thing, which for those two species means steady rather than spectacular. Blowfish are stacked up in the deeper holes off Barnegat Light and around the channel markers near Tices Shoal, biting on small pieces of clam or squid fished on a simple two-hook rig right on the bottom. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler for a shore dinner, and it's about the most reliable thing going for kids and grandkids who want steady action without a lot of technique. Kingfish have been working the sandy stretches just inside the inlet and along the edges of Island Beach, small strips of bloodworm or squid on a high-low rig in eight to fifteen feet of water. Nothing big, but a plate of kingfish fillets never disappointed anybody.

We had a run of those typical early-August thunderstorm afternoons this week too — the kind that shut the surface bite down cold for two or three hours and then hand it right back on the evening tide. That's held true again this year, same as it does most Augusts, and it's worth building your day around. Mornings and evenings have simply outfished the middle of the day, storms or no storms.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th is going to push more water through this bay than we've seen in a couple of weeks, and that stronger tidal flow should sharpen up everything current-related — the inlet blitzes, the channel-edge fluke bite, even the blowfish holes where a little extra push moves bait past them. If I had one day to fish this coming week, I'd want the two hours around the inlet tide change with metal ready for blues, then slide back into Double Creek on the tail of that same tide for fluke before the sun gets too high. It won't be a banner week for weakfish no matter what you do, but the rest of the program is holding up fine for the middle of August.

reports.headline: The Water Went Green on the Ledge — and Something's Coming Behind It
reports.subhead: Stripers are still stacked on the Southwest Ledge, but the sharks are working them hard, and the first bonito are knocking on the door from Watch Hill.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge Tuesday morning before first light, flat calm, and the water had that cold, green weight to it that tells you the current's about to start pulling hard. You get a feel for that out here after enough years — the air changes, the swell tightens up, and you know the tide's building toward something. With the new moon coming August 12, that's exactly what's happening. The current through the rips is starting to load up, and everything that's been sitting loose and lazy all July is about to get pushed around with a purpose.

The bass are still here, and they haven't gone anywhere — that's the one constant on this island in August. I've been marking good concentrations of stripers from 40 to 60 feet on the northwest corner of the Ledge, right where the structure drops off into that mixing water. Live eels on the drift, slow-trolled just off bottom on the last two hours of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer. I pulled a 34-pounder off there Wednesday on an eel fished behind a three-way rig with just enough lead to keep it ticking bottom without snagging up. The North Rip has been holding fish too, mostly on the west side where the current stacks bait against the drop — tube and worm still works there if you want to cover water, but the eel bite at night has been better than anything in daylight.

Here's the part I need every one of you to hear, because it matters more this year than it has in a long time. We're seeing heavy brown shark activity working the same structure the bass are holding on, and the mortality rate on released fish that get worked by sharks after the fight is brutal — we're talking somewhere near 90 percent of those fish don't make it. If you're fighting a good bass on the Ledge or around the North Rip this week, get it to the boat fast. Don't play it out on light drag just to enjoy the fight. Use heavier gear than you think you need, get the fish up, and if you see shadows working under the boat, consider just not fighting that next one at all. This isn't a scare tactic — it's what's actually happening out there right now, and it's specific to this stretch of water. I'd rather you catch fewer bass and know they swam away clean than land three and lose two to sharks before they ever get a hook out.

On the bonito front — we flagged this last week, said the new moon current would be the trigger, and it's already happening. Watch Hill and the Sakonnet stretch have had a legitimate bonito push moving through, and that leading edge is close enough now that I expect the first committed sightings inside Block Island Sound any day. Nothing confirmed on our own water yet as of this morning, but the signs are all there — the water temperature's holding in that comfortable summer range, bait's getting pushed hard through the rips as the tidal range builds toward the 12th, and that's precisely the recipe that flips this fishery on fast once it starts. If you want to be ready, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a Deadly Dick or a small Albie Snax on standby anytime you're out around the Southeast Light structure or drifting bait through the mouth of the Great Salt Pond. When they show, they show suddenly, and you want to already have a rod in your hand.

Bluefish have been a mixed bag — some real gators mixed in with the bass on the Ledge, taking the same eels, but the consistent chopper action has been off the East Grounds on diamond jigs, 2 to 3 ounces, worked with a fast retrieve through the bait schools. Fluke fishing off the island has been steady but unspectacular — the usual mix of shorts with the occasional keeper in the 20-foot range off the breakwater and around Cormorant Cove, white Gulp swimming mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage on the drift. Nothing to write home about, but a fun way to fill a cooler while you wait for something bigger. Porgies remain thick around the docks and the shallower rock piles inside the Sound — bloodworms and squid strips on high-low rigs, easy family fishing if you've got kids aboard who want steady action. Blackfish season's still closed here, so leave the crabs at the shop for now.

Looking ahead, I'd put my money on the next five days being about watching, not just fishing. The tidal range is going to keep building into Wednesday's new moon, and that's when I expect this whole thing to sharpen up — bass bite tightening on the structure, and a real shot at that first bonito or albie showing up inside the Sound. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd want it to be Tuesday or Wednesday on a strong outgoing tide at the Ledge, working eels early and keeping a bonito rod rigged the whole time just in case. Handle your bass fast, keep the fight short, and watch the water — it's about to start telling you something different than it has all summer.

reports.headline: Deer Island's Dawn Blitz: Blues and Bass Crash Bait Before the Ferries Run
reports.subhead: The harbor islands are lighting up at first light while the North Shore ledges hold their pattern into the new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
I made my call for this week Monday night looking at the tide chart: I'm staying inside the islands before sunrise, then running the boat up to Cape Ann in the evenings. That's where the action's been, and that's where I think it stays through the weekend.

Outside Deer Island, from about 4:30 to 8am, the harbor's been doing something I look forward to every summer — bait pods getting squeezed against the light and the edge of President Roads by the outgoing current, and blues and bass piling on top of them in full view. I've had mornings this week where I idled out of the marina in the dark, cut the engine off the Deer Island light, and watched the surface go white before I even had a lure tied on. Poppers and stickbaits worked over the boils — a Doc-style walker in bone or chartreuse, worked with a hard walk-the-dog cadence — and you don't need to be subtle about it. The blues are running 3 to 6 pounds and hitting like they're mad about something, and mixed in are schoolie-to-mid-20s bass that will occasionally give you a legitimate teeth-rattling take on a topwater plug. If you want the bigger bass specifically, switch over to a live mackerel under a balloon or slow-trolled on a stinger rig — that's been the ticket for the fish pushing 30-plus inches that are sitting a little deeper under the blitz, letting the blues do the dirty work up top.

This window is tide-dependent and it's tight. You want the last two hours of the outgoing pushing bait off the flats around Deer Island and Winthrop, and once the tide goes dead slack around mid-morning, the whole thing shuts off like someone flipped a switch. I've fished the same water at 11am with nothing to show for it. Get there early or don't bother.

Spectacle Island's north drop-off has been holding fish too, though it's a different program — this is a structure bite, not a blitz. I've been drifting live mackerel and chunked pogies along the 25 to 35-foot break on the last of the ebb, and picking up bass in the mid-20s to low 30s pretty consistently, along with a few bigger fish that came unglued before I could get a good look at them. The Graves, out past the outer islands, is worth a shot on a strong tide if you're comfortable running exposed water — that ledge has produced some of the better bass of the summer for guys fishing bucktails tipped with mackerel strips, worked slow along the bottom on the drift.

Nahant and Egg Rock have been steady on the North Shore side. Nothing explosive, but a reliable evening bite — eels and live mackerel fished tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, right at dusk. Cape Ann is the same story: Eastern Point and Bass Rocks are holding bass through the rock structure, and the pattern hasn't changed much since July. We said last week this holding pattern would carry through until water temps ease off in September, and that's exactly what's happening — no big shift, just steady work if you fish the tide right. What has changed is the tidal push building into the August 12 new moon, and I can already feel it sharpening the bite around current-driven spots like the Graves and the mouth of the harbor. Bigger swings mean more water moving, more bait getting displaced, and more fish committing to structure instead of scattering.

Flounder guys, don't sleep on Duxbury Bay and Kingston Bay right now. The flats are holding decent numbers on the last of the ebb tide, sandworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished slow along the mud-to-sand transitions. Plymouth Harbor's been quieter but not dead — a few keeper flounder came off the flats on calm mornings before the wind picked up.

Cod and haddock guys are going to want to keep an eye offshore. There's real bluefin interest building out toward Stellwagen Bank right now on green water and bait concentrations — we flagged that trend last week and it's holding. It's not squarely my inshore program, but if you're running a bigger boat out of Gloucester and have the range, that's worth knowing about before you commit a whole day to bottom fishing.

Looking ahead, I expect the harbor blitz to hold through the weekend as long as bait stays stacked against Deer Island — and with the new moon building, I think it actually gets better before it tapers. The North Shore rock bite should stay steady through the ledges at Nahant and Cape Ann, no reason to expect a shift there yet. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be off Deer Island at 4:30, poppers rigged, watching the light for the first boil. If the harbor's dead by the time you get there, Spectacle Island's drop-off is my backup, and it rarely lets me down on a clean outgoing tide.

reports.headline: Peanuts Pour Through Robinson's Hole — First Bonito Flashing on the Ebb
reports.subhead: Buzzards Bay's bait is stacking in the rips right on schedule, and the first bonito of the season are cutting through it four days ahead of the new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
The peanut bunker showed up in Robinson's Hole on Tuesday's outgoing tide like someone flipped a switch — dense, nervous pods getting pushed through the gut between Naushon and Pasque, and by Wednesday morning there were bonito underneath them. Not a blitz. Not yet. But real fish, cutting sideways through the bait with that unmistakable flash, and enough of them that three different boats working the hole on the last two hours of ebb connected on doubleheaders. That's the tell I wait for every August, and this week it arrived.

We flagged this exact window nine days ago — said Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard were sitting in the classic staging corridor and that the building new moon current would be the trigger. The new moon hits August 12, and the bonito that pushed through Rhode Island's Watch Hill and Sakonnet corridor over the past week have crossed the line into the bay right on that timetable. What we're seeing now is the leading edge — a handful of fish per tide, not a wall of them — but the direction is right and the timing lines up too cleanly to be coincidence.

Quick's Hole is running the same script, maybe a tide behind Robinson's. Silversides are balling up on the Elizabeth Islands side on the last of the flood, and there were reports of bonito showing there Thursday afternoon, chasing bait right up against the rocks on the Pasque side. If you're picking a spot this weekend, I'd still lean Robinson's first — it's been the more consistent producer the last three seasons on the opening push, and the current there sets up cleaner for a long drift with a Deadly Dick or a half-ounce Albie Snax worked fast through the froth. Keep your retrieve honest — these early-run bonito are eating small and fast, and a slow presentation gets ignored.

False albacore are close behind, per usual, but nobody's put one in the boat yet that I've heard confirmed. Historically they trail the bonito into the bay by a week to ten days once the bait gets thick enough to hold them, so I wouldn't be shocked to see the first albies working the rip off Menemsha by the back half of next week if this bait stays put through the new moon.

Striped bass haven't gone anywhere, and that's worth saying plainly because everybody's attention is about to shift entirely to the albie run. There's a steady pick of schoolies and a few keepers working the rip current off Cuttyhunk on the last two hours of the outgoing, especially where the tide rips past the western end of the island into deeper water. Live eels fished on the drift, or a bucktail bounced slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet, has been the play. Nothing gigantic — most fish are in the 24 to 32 inch range — but it's a dependable bite while you're waiting on the bonito to thicken up, and it should hold through the new moon since building current tends to sharpen this pattern rather than shut it down.

Bluefish are mixed in with that bass bite in the same rips, chopping bait on top some mornings around Cuttyhunk and off the Elizabeth Islands. Nothing like the gator run some of the western waters are seeing, but a few solid 4 to 6 pound blues have been chewing through wire leaders meant for stripers, which tells you the bait density out there is real.

Fluke fishing is the honest disappointment of the week. Drifting the deeper holes off Woods Hole and around Cuttyhunk with Gulp on light bucktails has produced fish, but they're mostly short — a lot of 15 and 16 inchers getting released for every keeper. The warm surface water this time of year pushes the better fluke down into the deeper cuts, and you need to be fishing bottom hard on the last of the ebb to find the bigger ones. If fluke is your priority this week, I'd fish early, before the boat traffic and the sun get the shallower flats churned up.

Scup are everywhere they always are in August — Oak Bluffs pier, the Woods Hole channel, anywhere there's structure and current. Squid strips or sandworms on a simple hi-lo rig will keep a rod bent all afternoon if the bonito bite goes quiet on you, and it's a good way to keep kids or first-timers busy while the adults work the rips.

Looking ahead: the tidal range keeps building through Wednesday's new moon, and that's exactly the mechanism that should pull more bait — and more bonito — through Robinson's and Quick's Hole over the next several days. If the pattern holds the way it did last August, expect the bonito numbers to build noticeably by the weekend of the 15th, with the first legitimate albie showing up somewhere in that same window. I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Robinson's Hole through midweek, watch the bait balls close, and have a light spinning rod rigged with something small and fast ready to go the second you see that first nervous water. Worth getting out there before the crowds figure out it's started.

reports.headline: Race Point on the Ebb: Bass Mixed with Bluefish Ahead of the New Moon Push
reports.subhead: The rip's holding fish but you have to work the tide stages right — here's what's biting from Race Point to Barnstable this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had the boat idling off Race Point about forty minutes before the top of the tide, watching the rip line start to build against a light southwest breeze. There's a moment out there, right when the current starts pulling hard against the shoal, where the water goes from flat to nervous — little boils, terns dropping, and then that first swirl behind the boat that tells you the bass have found the same seam you did. That's the whole game this time of year. You don't chase the fish around the Bay in August, you let the rip bring them to you.

We've been drifting Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, and the pattern's been consistent even if the numbers haven't been huge. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 30 feet of water, right on the edge where the sand drops into the deeper cut, has been the most reliable way to connect. We're also dropping big soft plastic eels — 9-inch, weighted, slow-jigged near bottom — when the mackerel aren't cooperating, and that's picked up a few better fish in the 30-pound class. Nothing epic, but a legit keeper-and-up mix, with enough overslot fish mixed in that you want a good release plan and a net that can handle them.

Bluefish have been more of a wildcard. Some mornings you'll find a school of choppers working bait right on the surface off Peaked Hill, and for twenty minutes it's as fast as anything in the Bay — poppers, or just bare bucktails ripped through the froth, get bit every cast. Other days they've vanished off that same piece of water entirely. That's typical August blues — they're following bait, not structure, so if you find working birds, get on them fast, because they don't stick around.

Fluke fishing has been the honest disappointment of the week. Billingsgate and the flats off Sandy Neck have decent bottom and warm, clean water, but we've been grinding for keepers — lots of shorts on Gulp and squid strips, not much size to show for it. I think the warm surface layer has pushed some of the better fish down into slightly deeper water than we've been fishing, so if you're on the flats and it's slow, don't be afraid to work out toward 25 to 30 feet before you give up on the drift.

Cod have gone quiet, which isn't a surprise for August. The deeper structure off Billingsgate and out toward the edge of Stellwagen holds some fish, but the water up top is too warm to pull them shallow, and without a strong reason to grind bottom in 100-plus feet of water in mid-summer, most of the fleet's left them alone. If you want a cod, this isn't the month to force it — wait for the water to turn over in the fall.

Mackerel have been steady bait, which matters more than the mackerel fishing itself. We've had schools stack up inside Provincetown Harbor and along the back side of the Race, and that's been our live-bait source most mornings — a few Diamond jigs or Swedish Pimples dropped over a marked school fills the well in ten minutes, and that bait's been the single best producer for bass all week.

The tide's been the deciding factor more than anything. We flagged this pattern last week — said the building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon should sharpen the bite at current-driven structure — and that's exactly what's been happening at the rips. The bigger the swing, the harder that water rips through the bars, and the harder it rips, the more bait gets pinned and the more the bass show up to eat it. Slack water has been dead almost everywhere we've fished, which tells you all you need to know about working the stages instead of just showing up and drifting blind.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the next few days to build on this as the new moon tightens up the tidal range. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it's been, I'd fish Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars on the last two hours of the ebb through the first hour of flood, live mackerel or eels near bottom, and keep an eye out for surface activity from the blues — they'll tell you where the bait's pushed. Fluke guys, I'd push a little deeper than usual off Sandy Neck and Barnstable until that top layer cools off. And if you're set on cod, I'd hold off — that bite doesn't turn on until the Bay starts losing its summer heat, and we're not there yet.

reports.headline: The 5:52 ebb: bass stacked on the East End rip, bluefish crashing through, bonito on the doorstep
reports.subhead: Four days out from the new moon, the Canal's current is loading up and the bite is sharpening right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
5:52 this morning, East End, and the current was already running better than three and a half knots off the Bourne bridge rip. That's early for this kind of push — we're not even at the new moon yet, four days out from the 12th, and the Canal's already tightening its belt. I stood on the rocks below the Railroad Bridge and watched the rip stand up hard against the light east breeze, and inside of twenty minutes I had two bass in the 28-30 inch range come off a white Savage Gear sand eel, fished on the swing and let it stall right where the seam folds back on itself.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon should sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. The Canal doesn't care what the calendar says about summer doldrums. It cares about how much water is moving, and right now there's more water moving through that ditch than there's been in three weeks. Every stage of the tide is running harder, which means the transition windows — the hour before and after max ebb or max flood — are producing more consistent hits instead of the stop-and-start pecking we had through late July.

East End remains the show for bass. The rip off the Bourne side, especially on the back half of the ebb when the current's still hauling but starting to organize into a cleaner standing wave, is where the fish are holding tightest. Eels — live ones if you can get them, otherwise the soft-plastic imitations — worked on a slow drop-back through the foam line have been the most consistent producer. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or olive, dragged bottom on the last hour of ebb before the slack, have also been picking off fish that are sitting deeper in the trough. Bluefish are mixed in and aggressive, mostly in the 3 to 6 pound class, and they'll murder a topwater plug worked through the rip on the last of the flood before the water goes flat. If you're throwing metal for bass and keep getting your leader shredded, that's your bluefish answer right there — don't fight it, just switch over for twenty minutes and have some fun with them.

West End is a different animal right now, and it's worth paying attention to why. Mashnee Island and the seam off Hog Island have been holding a scattered but real fluke bite — nothing to write home about, three or four keepers in a good session on Gulp swimming mullets bounced along the bottom on the last of the incoming, but enough to make the drift worthwhile if bass aren't cooperating. The real story at the west end this week is what's not here yet but is close. Buzzards Bay is seeing the first real bonito push cross over from the Rhode Island side, and Phinneys Harbor and the water off Wings Neck are exactly the kind of current-seam structure that lights up when those fish decide to run the Canal's mouth chasing bait. I haven't had a confirmed bonito in hand yet out of the west end this week, and I'm not going to tell you they're stacked up because they're not — but the conditions are lining up. Building tidal flow, warming inshore water, bait getting pushed hard through the seams — that's the recipe, and it's the same recipe that's already put bonito into the Watch Hill-to-Sakonnet corridor and pushed them into the Bay itself. If I had one morning to gamble on it this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb off Mashnee with a small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or similar — and I'd be ready to change my whole game plan if I saw fish busting bait on the surface.

Slack water, both ends, has been mostly dead the last ten days, and that hasn't changed. If you're canal fishing and you show up at true slack expecting action, you're going to stand there with a rod in your hand and nothing on the end of it. That's always been the rule here — the fish feed on current, not on stillness — but with the tidal range building toward the new moon, the dead slack windows are getting shorter and the transition into moving water is getting sharper. That's good news if you're the kind of angler who can read a tide chart and show up twenty minutes before the turn instead of twenty minutes after.

Looking at the next several days, I expect this pattern to keep sharpening right into the 12th. Bigger tidal range means faster current, faster current means the rips stand up harder and hold bait tighter, and that should mean more consistent bass and bluefish action at both ends through the weekend. Scusset side has had a quieter week for me — some short bass mixed with schoolie bluefish on small metal in the surf off the beach, nothing worth planning a trip around specifically, but worth a stop if you're already out there working the east end and want to check the surf on your way in. The bonito watch is the thing I'll be paying closest attention to over the next 72 hours — if that Buzzards Bay push keeps advancing the way it's been advancing, the west end could get interesting fast, and I'd rather be standing there with a bag of small metal in hand when it happens than reading about it after the fact.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips picky but fishable: blues on top, shorts underneath, drum long gone
reports.subhead: Warm water and building new-moon tide are sharpening the bite at structure — but you've got to work for it right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Rips grade: picky but fishable. That's the honest read this week, and I'm not going to dress it up for you. We're getting bluefish — good ones, 4 to 8 pounds — chopping bunker on top when the tide's right, and we're getting stripers, but they're mostly schoolies and the occasional low-slot fish, not the kind of numbers that make you forget what month it is. August on the Rips is what it is: warm water, scattered bait, and a bite that depends entirely on you being in the right seam at the right stage of tide.

Here's the why. Delaware Bay water dumping out past Cape May Point is running mid-to-upper 70s right now, and that warm water doesn't hold bait the way a cooler push does — it scatters it. So instead of finding one big wad of peanuts and working it all afternoon, you're hunting pockets. The best window I've had all week has been the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the flood, right where the bay current collides with the ocean side over the shoal structure. That collision line is where the bait gets pinned and the blues and bass show up to work it. Miss that window and you're just marking bait on the sounder with nothing underneath it.

Tactically, I've been throwing 1.5 to 2-ounce bucktails in white and chartreuse, working them with a slow lift-and-drop right through the seam, and when that's not drawing strikes I've gone to live bunker on a fishfinder rig, freelined back into the current. That's put bluefish in the box consistently and picked up a keeper bass here and there, but I want to be straight with you — it's not a slam dunk. Some drifts you get bit twice, some you get bit zero times. You need the tide stage right or you're wasting gas.

Now, if you're asking about black drum — that ship sailed in May, and it sailed a while ago. Nobody's finding drum in Delaware Bay in August, and if someone tells you different they're either lying or confused about the calendar. That run is done until next spring, full stop.

What is producing steady, honest numbers is weakfish in the bay channels. They're sitting deep — 18 to 25 feet — off Fortescue and down around Brandywine Shoal, and they want bloodworms or shedder crab on a high-low rig fished right on bottom, slow and patient. This isn't a fast bite, but it's a real one. Guys working those channels on the last two hours of the ebb are putting together decent counts of weakfish mixed with kingfish and croaker as bycatch, which tells you the bait's stacking in the deeper water as the shallows heat up past what those fish want to tolerate.

Fluke are the other bright spot, and honestly the most reliable thing I've got for you this week. The mouth of the bay and the back-bay drop-offs off Hereford Inlet are holding fish, and the pattern's simple — drift 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along the edges where the deeper channel breaks up into the flats, and time it for the last two hours of the outgoing when bait gets flushed off the shallows into that deeper water. I've had fish to 22 inches doing exactly that, nothing spectacular, but a legitimate keeper mixed into the shorts most drifts.

Offshore of the inlet, on the nearshore reef structure, sea bass and porgy have been steady — not fast, but dependable — on clam and squid fished tight to bottom. Triggerfish are mixed in on those same pieces too, which is normal for this time of year once the water's held warm this long. If you want a bend-the-rod afternoon without burning a tank of fuel chasing bait pockets, that's your play.

We flagged this last week — said the tides would build toward the August 12 new moon and sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's happening. The rip current is running harder every day as we approach the new moon, and that extra push is concentrating bait tighter against the shoal edges than it was seven days ago. I expect that trend to keep building right through the weekend and into early next week.

So here's my read going forward: if I've got one shot at the Rips this week, I'm fishing the two hours before the moon and the two hours after, betting the stronger current does what stronger current usually does — pins bait hard against structure and turns picky fish into willing ones. If that doesn't materialize, I've got Plan B sitting right there in the bay — the weakfish and fluke patterns aren't glamorous, but they're honest, and honest beats hopeful every time out here.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds its groundfish on the slack while bass work the river mouths
reports.subhead: Cold Gulf of Maine water keeps the bite predictable this week — steady if you fish the structure right, quiet everywhere else.
reports.body_markdown:
I anchored off Halfway Rock Tuesday morning, right at the top of the tide, and watched the current go from a whisper to nothing at all — that dead slack window when the whole bay seems to hold its breath. A gull working bait fifty yards off the ledge told me everything I needed to know before I ever dropped a line. Mackerel, tight to the surface, getting pushed by something below. That's the tell this time of year: find the birds, find the bait, and the groundfish are usually stacked underneath waiting for the current to give them an excuse to feed.

That's been the story of Casco Bay this week — patient, structured, a little slow if you're not fishing the right piece of bottom. The water's held cold and clean, no warm-water push showing up anywhere in the bay, which keeps this whole system leaning northern. Pollock, cod, and the occasional haddock are exactly where they should be in early August: down on the hard bottom around Halfway Rock, Jewell Island's eastern ledge, and the rockpile off Eagle Island, sitting in 60 to 90 feet. Diamond jigs — the 4- and 6-ounce chrome ones — worked on a slow lift-drop through the last hour of the ebb and the first hour of the flood have been the most consistent producer. I took two keeper haddock and a pollock over 8 pounds off Halfway Rock doing exactly that on Wednesday, right as the tide started to build again after the slack. Cod have been scattered but present — nothing to write home about in numbers, but a few nice fish in the 6- to 10-pound range coming up on cut mackerel bounced right on bottom.

Striped bass have settled into their August pattern, which means they've mostly abandoned open water for the river mouths and the structure that holds bait against current. The Presumpscot mouth, the Royal River off Yarmouth, and the Harraseeket up in Freeport have all been giving up fish on the last two hours of the incoming, when the tide pushes bait up against the pilings and the grass edges. Live mackerel under a slip bobber, or a chunk of the same fished on a fish-finder rig, has out-produced everything else I've tried. Down toward Cape Small and around the ledges off Bailey Island, the bass bite has been more about structure than tide stage — soft plastics, an 8-inch white paddle tail on a 3/4-ounce jighead, worked slow along the rock faces at half-tide, has taken some respectable fish in the 28- to 34-inch range. Nothing enormous, but a solid, honest bite if you're willing to cover water.

Mackerel themselves are still around, just not in the tightly packed schools you'd have seen back in May. Bailey Island's Mackerel Cove and the backside of Peaks Island have both had pockets of fish moving through on the tide changes — small jigs, the classic mackerel tree with no bait needed, will still load a bucket in twenty minutes if you find the right push of current. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them right now, but they're a fine way to fill a cooler with fresh bait for the bass and groundfish while you're out there anyway.

Bluefish have been a non-event this week, and I want to be straight about that rather than pretend otherwise. With the bay running cold and no warm intrusion showing up on the thermal side, there's just no reason for them to push this far north in numbers yet. If that changes — and it can change quickly if a warm eddy slides up the coast — I'll be the first to say so. For now, don't plan a trip around bluefish in Casco Bay.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the holding pattern would persist until the new moon tides built enough current to sharpen things up at structure, and that's exactly what's happening as we run into the August 12 new moon. The tidal range is noticeably increasing day over day, and I felt it firsthand at Halfway Rock — the drift picked up speed through the week, and the groundfish bite got more decisive with it. That's not a coincidence. Bigger tides mean harder current through the ledges and river mouths, which means bait gets pinned against structure more aggressively, which means the fish feed with more conviction instead of picking at things.

Looking ahead, I expect that trend to keep building right through the new moon. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of the ebb at Halfway Rock for groundfish, then run into the Harraseeket or Royal River on the building flood for bass — that tide sequence lines up nicely on most days right now. Two Lights is worth a look too if you're fishing from shore; the current runs hard enough there on a big tide to hold bait, and a few schoolie bass have been taken casting bucktails off the rocks at the base of the light on the incoming. The pattern's stable, the water's cold and clean, and the fishing rewards anyone willing to read the tide chart before they read the water.

reports.headline: Falkner Island Porgies Won't Quit, Blues Sneaking Back Into the Gulf
reports.subhead: The rockpiles are stacked with porgies and keeper sea bass while the first real bluefish push in weeks starts nosing into Milford Gulf and the New Haven breakwalls.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, second drift off the outer New Haven breakwall, my nephew Nico's ultralight nearly went swimming before I got the net under it — a fat porgy, thick through the shoulders, that hit a piece of green crab like it hadn't eaten in a week. That's been the story on the rockpiles all week: porgies stacked deep, feeding hard, and not particularly picky about how you present it to them.

I've been running the same milk run I run every August — Falkner Island's south side rockpile, the Charles Island bar, and the riprap along both breakwalls at New Haven Harbor — and the porgy bite has been the one constant while everything else sorts itself out. Anchor up in 15 to 25 feet on the down-current side of the structure, two-hook bottom rigs, size 4 or 2 hooks, green crab or sandworm, just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. On the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming at Falkner, we've been putting eight, ten fish in the cooler an hour without much effort — mixed in with keeper sea bass to 16 inches that clearly haven't gotten the memo that summer's supposed to be slow for them.

Sea bass have actually been the pleasant surprise this week. Stratford Shoal, on the western edge where the rockpile drops into 30-35 feet, has been holding fish that don't feel like they've been picked over yet — probably because most of the boat traffic out there is running past toward the bass grounds and not stopping to jig. Bucktail teasers tipped with squid strips, dropped right to bottom and worked with short hops, have been the ticket. Bring green crab too — on the slower bites, a live crab on a plain hook out-produces the jig two to one.

Blackfish are still finding their legs. Season's open and I'm seeing a few caught almost by accident by guys targeting porgy and sea bass on the same rockpiles — crushed green crab worked slow along the base of the structure at Charles Island has turned a couple of decent tog in the 16-18 inch range. It's not a dedicated bite yet, more of a bonus, but as the water starts easing off its summer high I expect that to sharpen up through September.

Striped bass are the harder conversation right now. Surface water's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s across the Central Sound, which is pushing most of the real feeding activity down onto structure and current lines rather than up top where you can see it. The Charles Island sandbar has still been giving up fish on the tide change — not a blitz, but a legitimate bite — working live-lined bunker or a bucktail with a chunk of pork rind or Gulp trailer, right where the bar drops off into the channel on the last two hours of the flood. We flagged this pattern last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon should sharpen things up at current-driven structure — and that's exactly what's playing out. The moon's set for the 12th, and I've noticed the current already running harder through the Charles Island rip and around the Milford Gulf breakwater than it was ten days ago. That extra push is going to matter.

Bluefish are the story I've been waiting to write. After a genuinely quiet July out here, there's a real resurgence building from the western end of the Sound and it's starting to nose into our water. I had a report of a mixed bag off the Milford Gulf breakwall Thursday evening — a couple of two- and three-pound blues mixed in with the porgies, hitting small metal jigs meant for something else entirely. That's usually the tell. When blues start showing as bycatch on bottom rigs, it means the schools are pushing bait up shallow and it's only a matter of days before they're actively working the surface. I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a half-ounce Kastmaster or a small diamond jig on deck at the New Haven breakwalls and Hammonasset this week, just in case that surface bite flips on. Worth noting — if you're fighting stripers anywhere near structure loaded with bluefish activity, don't dawdle on the release. No shark issue out here like they've got out east, but a longer fight in warm water does the fish no favors either way.

Fluke have been the disappointment of the summer, honestly. I'm not going to sell you a story that isn't there — the sand flats off Hammonasset and the mouth of the Housatonic near Milford Gulf have been giving up mostly short fish, a keeper here and there on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid, drifted slow on the last of the ebb. If fluke's your priority this week, I'd treat it as a bonus while you're anchored up working the rockpiles for porgy, not a dedicated mission.

Looking ahead: if that tidal push keeps building into the 12th like it's been building the last few days, I expect the Charles Island bar to turn on harder for stripers on the flood, and I wouldn't be shocked if the bluefish push solidifies into something you can plan a trip around by this weekend. Best case, we get a real surface bite at the breakwalls before the week's out. If the blues stall out west of us, I'd just keep doing what's working — porgies and sea bass on the rockpiles, blackfish as the bonus, and a rod rigged for blues just in case.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Pile Up at the Shoal — Blues Follow the Squeeze
reports.subhead: Bait funneling through the Stratford Shoal narrows is dragging bluefish east and holding stripers deep until the new moon flips the tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching before I made a cast. That's the job half the time out here — you don't fish the fleet, you fish the bait, and right now the bait is telling a clear story around the Shoal. Peanut bunker are pouring through the Stratford Shoal narrows in tight, nervous pods, pushed by current and squeezed by the way the Sound pinches down through the middle. Mixed in with them are bay anchovies flickering silver on the surface at first light off Charles Island, and I'm seeing silversides stacked thick along the Norwalk Islands flats on the last of the outgoing. When bait gets funneled like this — physically compressed by the geography instead of just schooled up on its own — it draws attention fast. That's exactly what's happening.

Kings Point is reading warm, 70.9°F, and New London on the eastern end is a touch cooler at 69.4. That gradient matters. It means the Central Sound right now — Stratford Shoal on down through the Norwalks — is holding the warmest, most stable water in the zone, and it's acting like a lid that keeps bait and gamefish concentrated rather than spread thin. Bluefish have been rebuilding out of the deeper reef structure to our west — Middle Ground, 11B, 28C — and that push is exactly what I've been watching move east through the week. I had a solid run of blues to 6 and 7 pounds working bunker pods over the Middle Ground Light rip on the last two hours of the outgoing, casting Hopkins jigs and metal-lip poppers into the surface wash where the bait was getting pinned against the current. If you see birds working tight and low instead of high and scattered, that's usually blues underneath, not just gulls picking scraps.

Striped bass are still playing the deep and dark game we called out last week — said the deep/night pattern would hold until the new moon tides started stirring things up, and that's still exactly where we are. Daytime bites have been sluggish and short-lived, mostly at first light and last light, with the better fish coming off the bottom in 30 to 45 feet along the Stratford Shoal rip and the drop-offs east of the Norwalk Islands. Plastic eels — 9-inch black or dark purple — fished slow on a 3-way rig with 2 to 3 ounces of lead, dragged right along bottom on the last of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer. A few boats working bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have connected after dark drifting the Charles Island flats, picking up fish in the mid-20s to low-30s, nothing gigantic but steady enough to make the trip worthwhile if you're willing to fish the clock instead of the calendar.

Porgies remain the one bite you can set a watch by. Structure around the Norwalk Islands and the rockier stretches off Charles Island are stacked with them — bloodworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without a half-pound of lead. Nothing flashy, but it's the bite that never lets you down out here in August.

Fluke have been the frustrating one. Small fish dominating the counts in the western half of my zone — lots of 14 to 16 inchers around Oyster Bay and the Huntington-side flats — with only occasional keepers mixed in. I haven't heard of anyone tearing it up on the drift with bucktails and Gulp this week; it's more a game of covering ground and culling through shorts than locking onto a pattern. If you're set on fluke, I'd fish the sandier bottom east of Port Jefferson Harbor on the outgoing, working white and chartreuse 4-inch Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and tight to bottom.

Weakfish have shown up only as incidental catches — a couple mentioned taken at dusk on soft plastics fished for bass — nothing you could call a pattern yet, more a reminder they're still out there than a reason to target them specifically.

Looking ahead, the tidal range is building hard into the August 12 new moon, and that's the piece I'm watching closest. Bigger swings mean stronger current at every rip and edge in this zone — the Shoal, the Norwalk reefs, the Middle Ground — and stronger current usually means the deep/night bass pattern finally cracks open into something more aggressive on the moving tides. If the bluefish push continues sliding east the way it has all week, I'd expect blues showing more consistently around the Norwalk Islands and even pushing toward the Connecticut shoreline by the weekend. And with bonito already working their way west out of Rhode Island waters, it's worth keeping half an eye on the eastern end of my beat — Charles Island and beyond — for the first sign of them showing up as the current sharpens and the bait keeps getting squeezed through this narrow stretch of Sound. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have a small metal or an epoxy jig rigged just in case.

reports.headline: The Race at 4.1 Knots: Bass Holding the Bottom on Valiant, Bonito Still a Rumor at Plum Gut
reports.subhead: Building current into the new moon has stripers locked to structure on wire line while the Gut waits on its first albie of the season.
reports.body_markdown:
4.1 knots. That's what The Race was running on the back half of Thursday's ebb, and that number tells you almost everything you need to know about this week. When the current's cranking that hard through Race Rock, stripers don't chase — they park. They tuck behind the boulders and let the tide do the work, and that means wire line and bucktails bounced tight to structure, not swimming plugs worked through open water.

We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure — and that's exactly what's happening at Valiant Rock right now. The rock itself sits in 35 to 50 feet depending on where you set up on it, and the fish have been holding on the down-current side, right where the rip folds over the structure and drops into the eddy. I've been running wire trolled bunker spoons through there on the last hour of ebb, then switching to 3- and 4-ounce bucktails — white with a chartreuse tube, or plain bone-white when the water's clean — for the slack itself. This week's slack window at Valiant has been running late morning, roughly ten to twelve workable minutes before the rip fires back up going the other way. Miss that window and you're fighting the current instead of fishing it.

The fish themselves are a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about that. Some drifts through Race Rock we're picking at schoolies in the low twenties, other passes we're connecting on fish pushing into the upper thirties, occasionally better. It's not a slam-dunk trip — I had one charter last Tuesday where we worked the rock for ninety minutes and only had two fish to show for it, then Wednesday morning the same spot gave up six keepers in forty minutes on the identical tide stage. That's the nature of fishing a rip this strong — the bite window is narrow and you need to be sitting on the spot when the current speed and the bait line up, not just anywhere near it.

Water's reading 69.4°F down at the east end of the Sound, and that's clean, cool water compared to what's sitting up in the Western Sound near 71. That gradient matters — the bass holding on Valiant and Race Rock are sitting in water that hasn't been beat up by the same heat stress you're seeing further west, and it's part of why this stretch keeps producing quality fish through the dog days while other parts of the Sound go quiet on the bass.

Plum Gut and the Sluiceway have been a different story this week — and a slower one. The current through the Gut has been ripping just as hard as The Race, 3 to 4 knots on the bigger tides, but I haven't had a single confirmed albie or bonito report out of there yet. The push everyone's watching is still working its way out of the Rhode Island corridor and into Buzzards Bay — it hasn't crossed the Sound to us. Given how fast that building tidal range through the August 12 new moon usually pulls bait and predators west, I'd bet on the first bonito or albie showing in the Gut or off Montauk within the next week, but it's not here yet, and I'm not going to tell you to run out and burn gas on epoxy jigs before the fish arrive. Have your Deadly Dick and half-ounce epoxy jigs rigged and ready, because when that push does show, it shows fast and it's usually gone just as quick if you're not on it.

Sea bass have been the reliable play while we wait on the bonito. Little Gull Island and Great Gull Island both have humps and rockpiles holding fish in 40 to 60 feet, and jigging bucktails tipped with squid strips has been steady — not a blowup bite, but a consistent one, fish in the 14 to 17 inch range with the occasional bigger knothead mixed in. If you want a sure thing this week, that's closer to it than the bass rips.

Bluefish have been building back in on the western reefs of the Sound, and if that pattern keeps sliding east the way it usually does in mid-August, I expect we'll start seeing gator blues showing up on the same structure we're fishing for bass — Race Rock, Valiant, the edges of the Gut. Worth having a wire leader rigged behind the bucktail just in case, because a bluefish will cut you off on a plain mono leader before you even feel the strike.

One more thing worth passing along if you're running east toward Block Island — there's a real shark predation problem on released stripers over there right now, mortality on released fish running uncomfortably high. It hasn't been an issue on our side of the Sound, but if you're making that run, keep your fight times short and get fish back in the water fast.

Looking ahead: the tidal range is only going to keep building into the August 12 new moon, which should sharpen the bass bite further at Race Rock and Valiant — bigger swings mean harder current, and harder current on this structure has been good to us all week. My money's on the bonito push finally crossing into Plum Gut and the eastern Sound sometime in the next seven to ten days behind that stronger tide. Until then, I'd spend my time on wire and bucktails over the rocks and keep the epoxy jigs in the bag, rigged and waiting.

reports.headline: Fourteen Hours Round-Trip to the Canyon Edge, and the Reel Never Stopped Singing
reports.subhead: A long run to a distant temperature break paid off in yellowfin and a lost bigeye, with tidal range building toward the new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at 3:40 in the morning, and I told the mate we'd be back by six that night if the fish cooperated. They didn't entirely, but close enough. The grounds we ran to are a hundred-plus miles from Montauk depending on where you jump off the shelf, and at eighteen to twenty knots that's five hours out, five back, and whatever's left in the middle is your fishing day. Do that math before you leave the dock, not after. We burned through about three-quarters of our fuel just getting there and getting home, which left us maybe four hours on the grounds — enough to find them, not enough to feel greedy about it.

We found warm, clean water pushing along a wall in close to the 1500-fathom curve, a hard color change you could see from the tower before you could see it on the plotter. Ballyhoo on the surface, some small blackfin scattered under birds, and the kind of nervous water that tells you something's working bait underneath. We pulled a standard spread — Ilanders and ballyhoo down the middle, green machines and a spreader bar out back — and it didn't take long. First fish up was a yellowfin that ran the reel down to backing before we turned him boatside, better than sixty pounds, clean fat fish that had clearly been eating well. Twenty minutes later something bigger got into the pattern, took a short rigger bait and just kept going straight down instead of running off. We fought that one for the better part of forty minutes before the hook pulled. Bigeye behavior, that dive — we'll never know for sure, but that's what it felt like on the other end of the rod.

We can't speak to how other boats are doing on other pieces of structure right now — we only fished the one spot, and that's the only water we can vouch for. What we can say is that the temperature break we found was sharp and well-defined, and the bait activity on it was steady the whole time we were on the grounds. Anyone making a long run out should expect that kind of setup to hold for at least a few days if the water stays put, but we'd rather report what we saw firsthand than pass along secondhand claims about grounds we didn't fish ourselves.

If you've got the fuel budget for a run like this and the patience to work a temperature break once you find it, that's the play right now — cover the distance, find the color change, and let the spread do the rest.

reports.headline: Twotree fluke steady, Black Point sea bass thick — the dock's watching for the first albie
reports.subhead: Niantic and Waterford boats are grinding out solid mixed bags while the whole fleet keeps one eye on the Race for the season's first false albacore.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the dock at the Niantic launch Tuesday morning watching the *Blackhawk* unload, and I swear every other sentence out of the mate's mouth was "albies." Not because anybody's caught one yet — nobody has, not here — but because the chatter's been building since last week when I told you this zone, sitting right off the Race with all that current running past Twotree and Black Point, was worth watching as the new moon loaded up. We're three days out from that August 12 new moon now, tidal range building every day, and the fleet's primed. Nothing's shown up on the tuna sticks yet. But give it a few more days of stronger current pulling that Rhode Island warm water through Watch Hill and into the eastern Sound, and I wouldn't be shocked if the first one gets stuck somewhere between Hole-in-the-Wall and the Twotree can.

In the meantime, the bread and butter is still paying the bills. Fluke fishing out of Niantic has been steady, not spectacular — the kind of week where you keep moving and you keep a few fish, but you're not filling a cooler by 9 a.m. Twotree Island Channel has been the most consistent stop, 28 to 35 feet, working the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the flood when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a half-pound of lead. Guys are doing well with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, or a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in pearl white on a light jig head, dragged nice and slow along the channel edge where the sand meets the mussel bottom. Hole-in-the-Wall has produced a scattered better grade — a few fish pushing 4 and 5 pounds mixed in with the shorts — but you're picking through a lot of fish under 16 inches to find them.
