Water's sitting around 69 to 70 degrees off New London, a touch cooler than the western Sound, and that's kept the fluke comfortable and spread out rather than balled up tight, which is part of why it's a pick, not a slaughter.

Black sea bass have been the more reliable rail-filler. Black Point's rock piles and the reef structure off McCook Point are holding good numbers in 25 to 40 feet, and on the right drift — light current, not screaming — the party boats have been putting decent bags together with squid strips and Berkley Gulp on standard sea bass rigs. Legal fish are running 14 to 17 inches with enough shorts mixed in to keep it interesting for the kids on board. Best window has been the top of the tide into the first hour of the drop, before the current gets too ripping to hold bottom cleanly.

Porgies are doing exactly what porgies do in August — keeping the rail busy and the little ones smiling. Niantic Bay's breakwaters and the shallower structure around the river mouth have been thick with scup in the 10 to 12 inch range, occasional jumbo mixed in. Small hooks, half a sandworm or a chunk of clam, bottom rig, nothing fancy. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the most dependable thing going on my beat right now, and it's a good call if you've got a slow afternoon and want guaranteed bend in the rod.

Striped bass have been the frustrating one. There are fish around the Race and working the rips off Black Point on the bigger tides, but the bite's been on-again, off-again — you need to be there right as the tide turns, and if you miss that window by twenty minutes you're fishing empty water. A few boats have connected on bunker schools pushing through Twotree Channel, live-lining or snap-jigging bunker spoons, with fish in the 20 to 30 pound class coming over the rail on the better days. But it's not an every-trip thing right now. I'd call it a tide-dependent bite, not a bite you can plan a whole day around.

Bluefish are the one thing actually trending up, and that tracks with what's been building west of us — the resurgence that started on the deep reefs in the western Sound has been sliding east all week. We've had a couple of legitimate blitzes reported off Hole-in-the-Wall in the last few days, gulls working bait right on the surface, and boats running metal — Kastmasters and half-ounce Ava jigs — into the middle of it have had no trouble getting bent. If you're bunker chunking for stripers and the blues show up and steal your bait, don't fight it, just switch over. They've been running 3 to 6 pounds with a few bigger ones mixed in.

Blackfish season's still a ways off here, but I'll tell you the dock talk has already turned to scouting. A few guys have been quietly checking the rock piles off Black Point and around McCook, not fishing them hard, just marking bottom and confirming structure holds fish before the fall run gets going.

Looking ahead: that new moon on the 12th is going to stretch the tidal range out and sharpen up every current-driven spot on this beat — the Race, Twotree, the rips off Black Point. If the warm water corridor keeps pushing west like it has been, I'd start swinging a small metal jig or an epoxy pattern off the stern when you're running between drops, just in case something with a torpedo body and no patience shows up early. That's the move I'd make this week — fish the fluke and sea bass like normal, but keep a rod rigged light and ready, because if the albies do show, they won't announce it.

reports.headline: 3 A.M. at the Gut: One Cast, One 34-Pound Bass, and a Sound Building Toward Something
reports.subhead: The current's loading up for the new moon and the first signs of albie water are creeping toward The Race — here's what's actually biting right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-fifteen Wednesday morning, standing on the rocks at Plum Gut with the tide just turning to ebb, I put a Gibbs Danny plug on the seam where the fast water meets the slick behind the boulder pile. Third cast, the plug got walloped so hard I thought I'd hung a mooring. Thirty-four pounds of striper, hooked in six feet of white water, released in under ninety seconds because I wasn't about to stretch that fight in current that strong. That's the kind of bite the Gut gives up right now — not volume, but quality, and only if you're willing to fish it in the dark on the moving water.

That's the pattern across the eastern end right now: deep, current-driven, mostly nocturnal. We flagged this two weeks back — said the deep/night bass pattern would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon stirred the pot, and that's exactly what's happening. New London's reading 69.4 degrees, which is soft compared to the mid-70s piling up in the western Sound, and that gradient is exactly why the biggest fish out here are still holding deep on structure and current edges instead of chasing bait up on the flats during daylight. The Race is fishing the same way — big bass stacking in the eddies off the lighthouse rock pile on the last two hours of the ebb, plastic eels and 2-ounce bucktails bounced tight to bottom in 25 to 40 feet, and you want to be there before first light because once the sun's up over Fishers Island, the bite shuts like a door.

Bluefish are the better daytime story right now. That resurgence that's been building through the western Sound over deep reef structure has pushed east — I had a solid pick of 4- to 8-pound blues off Fishers Island Wednesday afternoon, working bunker chunks and diamond jigs in 30 feet off the north side, current still running hard enough that you needed a jig heavy enough to hold bottom without babysitting it. Nothing gator-sized yet out here, but the size is trending up week over week, and if the pattern that hit Sandy Hook keeps marching this direction, don't be shocked if we see real teeth on the beach by Labor Day.

Porgies are the bread and butter right now and they're not messing around. Structure fishing off Orient Point and the rock piles around Plum Gut is stacking porgies to 2 pounds on sea worms and squid strips, high-low rigs, size 4 hooks, fished right on the bottom on the slower stages of the tide when the current lets you actually hold in one spot. This has been the most consistent bite in the zone for three weeks running — not glamorous, but if you want fish in the cooler, this is where you get them without burning gas or sleep.

Blackfish scouting is underway too, early but real. I've been marking fish on the sonar around the rock piles off Fishers Island and the reef structure south of Plum Gut, green crab drops producing a few undersized tog already. Too early to target them seriously — season's not open and the bite's not dialed in yet — but the presence is there, and that's worth banking for when the fall pattern kicks in.

Here's the part that matters most for the next 72 hours: the new moon on the 12th is loading the tidal range fast, and that's the same mechanism that's been pushing bonito out of Rhode Island through Watch Hill and Sakonnet toward Buzzards Bay. We called this zone as an early beneficiary of that push back on August 3rd, said the eastern Sound sits close enough to open water off The Race to catch spillover if albies or bonito start showing before the new moon peak — and the corridor's still building in that direction. Nothing confirmed yet inside The Race or Plum Gut itself, but the warm current extension is real and this is exactly the kind of setup — building tide, warming edge water, bait pushed tight to structure — that flips the switch fast once it starts.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at the Gut before sunrise for bass, then slide over to the Fishers Island rock piles midday for blues and porgy, and I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig in the rocket launcher just in case something with a forked tail shows up chasing bait on the surface. That's not a guarantee — it's a bet based on where the water's heading. The tide's building, the temperature gradient is sharpening the bass bite into a tight window, and the corridor that feeds albies into this end of the Sound is getting more current and warmer water by the day. Worth being out there when it flips.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: the ocean's a washing machine, so everything's stacking in the inlet
reports.subhead: Rough surf and a warm ocean layer are pushing bass, fluke, and blues into Fire Island Inlet's current seams ahead of the August 12 new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls his boat up next to mine at the Captree fuel dock Thursday morning, looks out past the barrier beach where the swell's still humping up green and white, and says, "You going out there today?" I told him no chance — not with 44025 reading almost four feet at five seconds and a mean direction dead out of the south. That kind of washing-machine water off the beach doesn't drown the fishing, though. It just moves it. And this week it moved everything into the inlet.

That's the story right now on the South Shore: the open ocean is a mess, running warm on the surface — low 70s out past the bar — but rough enough that bait and predators alike are ducking into the protected current seams instead of sitting exposed on the beachfront. Fire Island Inlet has been the address. Democrat Point on the outgoing has been holding stripers tight to the rip where the incoming tide from the ocean side collides with the bay water pouring out — that seam is doing exactly what it always does when the surf's up and dirty: it concentrates everything that wants to eat.

I worked that rip three mornings this week on the last two hours of the ebb, anchoring up-current and drifting bunker chunks back on fish-finder rigs, 3 ounces of egg sinker to hold bottom in maybe 12 to 18 feet. Picked up stripers to 32 inches, a couple of shorts mixed in, nothing that's going to make the cover of a magazine but a real, honest bite — three keepers one morning, a skunk the next when the wind swung and killed the current push. That's the truth of inlet fishing this time of year: when the tide's moving right, it's good. When it goes slack or the wind fights the current, it shuts off fast. I'd rather be honest about that than tell you it's a sure thing every trip.

Bluefish have made a real comeback the last week or so after a quiet July, and they're doing it right alongside the bass in that same inlet water. Snapper-sized fish have been thick off the docks in Patchogue and Bayshore for weeks, but now we're seeing real cocktail blues, 3 to 5 pounds, blitzing bunker schools that got pushed tight against the beach by the swell. If you see the birds working off Democrat Point or along the ocean side of the barrier near the Fire Island Lighthouse rip, throw a diamond jig with a green tube, or a bunker spoon if you've got the metal — you don't need finesse, they're eating anything that flashes.

Fluke are a mixed bag right now, and I'll level with you — the bite at the Robert Moses bridges has slowed from where it was in June. Water's warm, current's still solid on the outgoing under the spans, and we're still picking fish, just fewer of them and more shorts in the mix. Best drift has been on the south side of the Captree side channel in 25 to 30 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the tide, tipped with a strip of squid. A couple of guys have had four-pound-plus fish doing that same drift right at the base of the pilings on the last hour of the ebb, but you're earning those, not stumbling into them.

Weakfish have shown flashes in the bay — a few reports of fish in the 18 to 20 inch range around the deeper holes off Nicoll Bay and near the Sayville flats on soft plastics fished slow on bucktails at dusk — but it's spotty enough that I wouldn't plan a trip around them specifically. Consider it a bonus if you're already out there working bass or fluke.

Porgies are doing what porgies do in August — they're everywhere in the bay, and they're an easy box-filler if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Sandworms or clam on a high-low rig over the mussel beds off Sexton Island or in the channel edges near West Sayville, 15 to 20 feet, and you'll load up in twenty minutes. Good for a kid's first trip or when you just want to feel something pulling back.

We flagged this last week — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure — and that's exactly what's playing out at the inlet right now. The rip at Democrat Point has gotten meaner and more productive every day as the tidal range builds, and that trend's got another two, three days to run before it peaks.

Looking ahead: if the swell holds through the weekend, I'd stay off the exposed beachfront and keep working the inlet seams and bay structure — that's where the fish are concentrated and that's where they'll stay as long as the ocean's kicking up. If the surf lays down by midweek and that south wind backs off, I'd expect some of that bass and blue activity to spread back out along the Fire Island beaches on the early morning tide, which is when I'll be walking the sand at first light with a bucktail rather than running the boat. Either way, watch that new moon tide on the 12th — bigger water movement usually means a better bite at the bridges and the inlet, provided the wind doesn't turn it into another washing machine.

reports.headline: Boulder fields holding peanuts, stripers going deep — Watch Hill corridor is the one to watch
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking on the rock piles from Ram Island to Wamphassuc, but the albies haven't crossed the line yet — the new moon on the 12th is the trigger everybody's circling.
reports.body_markdown:
First light off Ram Island Wednesday, and the water over the boulder field was nervous before I even cut the engine. Peanut bunker, balled tight, pushed up against the granite in maybe six feet of water, flickering like a school of minnows trying to disappear into the rock itself. That's the tell this time of year — when the bait starts hugging structure instead of running open water, something's pushing it. I poled the skiff along the edge, quiet, watching for the boil that didn't come. Not yet. But the bait knows something's coming before we do, and right now it's balling up tight against every rock pile from Ram Island down through the Wicopesset Passage.

The striper pattern out here hasn't changed much from what I was seeing a week ago, and that's not surprising — I said then that this holding pattern would run until the tide started building into the new moon, and that's exactly where we are. Fish are deep, they're feeding at night and on the edges of light, and they're not showing themselves on top the way they will once that current really starts moving. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, New London's a little cooler at 69.4, and that gradient matters — the eastern Sound stays a touch behind the western Sound all summer, which is part of why our albie window always opens a beat later than Long Island's. Right now that cooler water is holding stripers down on the structure rather than pushing them up to chase.

Best bass action has come off Wamphassuc Point and the boulder field east of Esker Point, fished on the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low, working eels and jointed swimmers — Red Fins and Bombers in the darker colors — slow and deep along the rock edges. A few fish to 30 inches came off Wamphassuc on live eels fished at night, drifted with just enough weight to keep them ticking the bottom without hanging up in the boulders, which out here is its own skill. You lose gear on this bottom if you're not paying attention to the drift speed. I've buried more bucktails in Fishers Island Sound rock than I care to count, and I still do it.

The Stonington breakwater has been steadier than the open rock piles, especially on the slack tide change, which is when the current stops fighting you and you can actually work a jig down into the rocks without snagging every other cast. Fluke have been mixed in there too, along the sand pockets between the rip-rap, mostly on white Gulp swimming mullets tipped with squid strips, fished tight to the base of the breakwater on the last of the flood. Nothing huge — most going 16 to 19 inches — but enough keepers mixed in to make the stops worthwhile if you're patient with the drift.

Black sea bass are still cooperating on the deeper structure out toward Fishers Island — the rock piles and scattered boulder fields off the north side hold them well into August, and small pieces of clam or squid on a simple two-hook bottom rig will produce steadily in 20 to 35 feet. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler while you wait on the bigger story developing to our east.

And that story is the bonito and albie push working through the Watch Hill corridor. I've had my eye on that warm current line for two weeks now, the way it runs off Watch Hill and pushes bait through the rips toward Sandy Point and into Little Narragansett Bay. We flagged this pattern last week — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would be the trigger that sharpens the current-driven bite and likely brings the first albies and bonito into range at Montauk, Block Island, and the eastern Sound. Nothing confirmed yet on this side of the line — no hookups, no boils reported off Napatree or the Watch Hill reef — but the ingredients are all there. Bait's staging, the current is about to load up harder with the new moon four days out, and that corridor runs straight into our water.

If I had one day this week, I'd spend the early morning working the boulder fields with the fly rod — small Deceivers and Clouser minnows worked slow along structure edges for stripers while the light's low — and I'd keep a rod rigged with a small metal, a half-ounce epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick, ready to go the second I see a nervous patch of water or a bird working tight over bait near Sandy Point or the Wicopesset rips. That's how the albie bite starts out here — not with a blitz, but with one bird, one boil, and if you're not already rigged you miss it.

By this weekend, with the tide building harder into the 12th, I expect the striper bite to sharpen on the structure — moving current always wakes up the boulder fields — and I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first albie report cross the line from Watch Hill into our water by early next week. Worth checking the rips daily starting now. Just don't expect fireworks yet. Right now it's still bait and patience, watching the rocks, waiting for the water to tell you it's time.

reports.headline: 71.2°F on the Bight Buoy, and the Warm Filament Still Sits East of the Wall
reports.subhead: The temp break that's been feeding the yellowfin bite hasn't moved — which means the run gets longer before it gets easier.
reports.body_markdown:
71.2°F. That's the read off the buoy sitting out in the Bight this week, and while that number is inshore of where we actually fish, it tells me something useful: the shelf water pushing offshore hasn't cooled down, and whatever's feeding the warm filament east of the Hudson wall is still getting resupplied. I've said it for two weeks running now — the core of warm water that's been driving the yellowfin bite is parked east of the canyon, not directly over it. That hasn't changed, and it's the single biggest factor in how your day goes out there right now.

Run time from Manasquan to the top of the canyon is a little over 90 miles, call it four hours at a comfortable 22 knots, and once you're standing on the 100-fathom line the story is consistent with what I told you last weekend: the real concentration of bait and fish is still off to the east, sitting on the temperature breaks rather than parked on Hudson structure itself. We flagged this on the 4th — said the warm filament feeding the yellowfin bite all week was still in place east of here and the program would stay the same east-wall, temp-break game. It has. Boats willing to run the extra 8 to 12 miles off the edge and work the 66-to-70-degree color changes are finding the better grade of fish. Boats stopping right on the wall are getting a mixed bag — some marks, some quiet stretches, nothing you'd call consistent.

What's actually working: trolling a mixed spread of small green machines and blue/white Ilanders pulled behind bird teasers at 6 to 6.5 knots wherever the water color shifts from that green-gray inshore water to the deeper cobalt blue. Naked ballyhoo rigged on 50-wide setups off the long riggers has been drawing strikes when the trolled plastic gets ignored — August yellowfin in the 25-to-45-pound class can be particular about that. When you mark bait balls on the sounder, especially anywhere the temp break tightens up, shutting down and chunking butterfish has paid off better than staying on the troll. Small pink-and-white jigs worked around any floating weed lines are worth a few casts too — mahi have been scattered under the grass mats this month, nothing like a June school-fish blitz, but enough to fill a fish box if you're patient and willing to idle and look.

For the bottom guys, the swordfish game hasn't changed much either — daytime drops in 1,400 to 1,800 feet along the drop-offs adjacent to the canyon proper, squid strip and glow combos on the deep drop rigs, drifting with the current rather than fighting it. That part of the fishery doesn't care much where the warm filament sits on the surface; the deep scattering layer and the bottom temperature structure down there are far more stable week to week than what's happening up top.

I want to be straight with you on the overall grade of the bite: it's good, not great, and it's location-dependent in a way that punishes guys who won't run the extra distance. I talked to a couple of captains at the dock this week who worked the immediate canyon structure and came home with two or three fish for the trip — not bad, but not what they were hoping for given the time of year. The boats that pushed east onto the sharper temperature breaks did noticeably better, with some solid multi-fish days on yellowfin and a mahi or two mixed in under the weed. White marlin have been quiet on our side of the canyon this week — I haven't had a confirmed release to report, and with the bulk of pelagic activity sitting east, that's not surprising. If billfish are the priority, that's another reason to make the longer run rather than working the immediate Hudson structure.

Sea state has been manageable — nothing brutal, moderate swell, the kind of day you can work a spread comfortably without beating up the crew. Wind's been cooperative too, which matters more than people give it credit for when you're running 90-plus miles each way.

Looking ahead: the new moon lands August 12, and tidal current is already building toward that peak range. We called this too — said building tidal current into the new moon should sharpen bait concentrations along whatever edge holds the warm water, and that's exactly the mechanism to watch this week. Stronger current usually means tighter bait balls and cleaner marks on the temp breaks, which should make the east-wall program even more productive if the filament holds its position. The variable that matters most right now is whether that warm core drifts west toward the canyon itself over the next several days — if it does, the bite comes back to Hudson proper and cuts your run time down. If it stays put, keep planning on the longer push east. I'd plan for the second scenario until the water tells me otherwise, but I'll be watching the break position daily and adjusting the run accordingly. Either way, get your baits in the water early — the morning bite window on the temp breaks has been outproducing the afternoon two trips out of three this month.

reports.headline: Kayak Over Surf This Week: Fluke and Weakfish on the Bay's Deep Edges
reports.subhead: With bass scarce and the ocean chopped up, the smart play in Jamaica Bay this week was staying inside and working the channels.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to leave the surf rods in the truck and put the kayak in off the Motorless Boat launch instead. The swell rolling into Rockaway and Breezy Point has been messy all week — nothing dangerous, but enough push and period to turn the beach into a washing machine and make Marine Parkway Bridge's usual outgoing bass show a non-event. When the ocean's stirred up like that, the bay is where the fish and the fun are, and paddling lets me sneak into the channel edges and holes that the bigger boats can't work as tight.

We flagged this a few days back and it's held up: striped bass have mostly cleared out of Jamaica Bay for cooler water elsewhere in the Bight, and there's just not much resident action here right now. I worked the usual staging water off the bridge on two different outgoing tides this week and came up with nothing but a couple of small blues for my trouble. If you're set on bass, you're better off waiting for that first real cool pulse in September than beating this water right now — it's warm, it's shallow, and it tracks the air temperature closely, exactly the pattern we expected to hold through this stretch of summer.

What IS working is fluke, and it's been a legitimate bright spot. I've had my best drifts in Grassy Bay and along the edge of Duck Point Meadow, working 8 to 14 feet of water on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still moving bait off the flats but hasn't gone fully slack. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along bottom, have been the ticket — most fish in the 15 to 18 inch range with a scattering of keepers pushing 20. The channel edge off Ruffle Bar has produced too, though it's spottier — you need to hit it right on that tide change or you're wasting drifts.

Weakfish are still around in decent numbers, but you have to fish the last hour of daylight into dusk to connect consistently. I've been anchoring up on the channel edges near Silver Hole and working a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, letting it settle and just twitching it along bottom. Nothing huge — mostly 16 to 20 inches — but it's a real fishery right now if you're willing to fish the light-fading window instead of the middle of the day.

Snapper blues are absolutely thick in the shallows off Canarsie Pier, Hamilton Beach, and along the bulkheads by Motorless — this is prime kid-fishing right now, small Kastmasters or spearing under a bobber, and it's a good early read on the broader bluefish comeback we've been watching build. The bigger blues haven't fully pushed into the bay yet, but I've heard of some heavier fish showing on bunker schools right at Rockaway Inlet, which tells me there's real bait moving through and it's only a matter of time before that filters back into the bay proper.

Porgies are holding on the humps and channel edges near Yellow Bar — sandworms or clam on a simple bottom rig, 10 to 14 feet of water, and they've been steady if unspectacular. Blackfish are still off-limits until the fall season opens, so leave those spots alone for now and save them for October.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the new moon on the 12th, and the extra push in current strength should sharpen up the bite at every current-driven spot in the bay — Cross Bay Bridge, the mouth of Grassy Bay, the deeper cuts by Ruffle Bar. That's usually when the fluke and weakfish bite gets a little more aggressive and a little more predictable, because the moving water concentrates bait right where the fish are already sitting.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the kayak or a shallow-draft boat through the channels rather than fighting the surf until that swell settles down. If you want bass, patience is the better strategy than effort right now — wait for the first real cool nights and watch the bridge current again once that water starts to turn. For everything else, this coming week with the building new-moon tide should be some of the better fluke and weakfish fishing we've had all summer, provided you're willing to work the tide changes and not just show up whenever. The Rockaway blitz everyone's already asking about is still weeks off — but bunker showing at the inlet and blues building underneath them is exactly the kind of early signal that gets me excited for what October's going to look like.

reports.headline: Forget the Fluke Boats — The Rock Pile at Jones Inlet Is Where the Real Work's Getting Done
reports.subhead: While the fleet grinds out short fluke in Sloop Channel, the night bite on bass at the inlet jetty is quietly the best thing going this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Every boat I know is stacked up in Sloop Channel right now working the fluke drift like it's the last week of summer that matters. I get it — it's easy fishing, chartreuse bucktail and a strip of squid, drift the drop-off, wait for the thump. But I've been telling guys at the bait shop the same thing for two weeks: that bite is steady, not special. Small fish, a keeper here and there, nothing to write home about. If that's your speed, fine, but I've been putting my hours in somewhere else — the rock pile on the east side of Jones Inlet, after the sun goes down, working the current seams where the real bass have been holding.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear: the ocean's been ugly. Close-period chop, three-plus feet of slop rolling in off the bar, not the kind of water that makes for good beach fishing off Jones Beach right now. So the fish that would normally be working the wash have pulled inside — into the inlet channel, along the rocks, up into the deeper current cuts where the water stays clean and the bait gets funneled through on the tide. That's exactly where I've been finding bass. Not giant numbers, but quality — 28 to 34 inches, a few pushing better than that, holding tight to the jetty rocks on the last two hours of the outgoing and right through the bottom of the tide into the first push of the flood.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep, current-driven bite would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon tide stirred things up. Well, the new moon's two days out now, and I'm already feeling the difference in the swing. Tuesday night's drift through the inlet channel moved noticeably harder than it did a week ago, and the bass responded — three fish in the slot in about ninety minutes on a bucktail-and-eel combo, 3/4-ounce bucktail with a 6-inch white worm trailer, worked slow along the base of the rocks where the current breaks. If you're fishing bait, fresh bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, tossed into the seam where the jetty meets the main channel, has been getting hit consistently right around the tide change — that dead-slack window when everything settles and the fish move up to feed before the current builds back the other way.

Bluefish are the other piece I've had my eye on. We called this too — said the bluefish wave building down in Jersey and around Sandy Hook could push north and reinforce the bite here, and I think that's starting to happen. I had a mixed bag Wednesday morning working bunker schools just inside the inlet mouth — mostly bass, but two bluefish in the 4 to 6-pound class mixed in, hit on a Hopkins jig worked fast through the school. Nothing like a blitz yet, but the bait's there and the blues are starting to show up behind it. If that northward push keeps building the way it did in Jersey, don't be surprised if the next week or two turns into real bluefish weather at the inlet — keep a wire leader in the bag just in case.

Weakfish are still the sleeper story in Hempstead Bay this summer, and I don't think enough guys are paying attention to it. South Oyster Bay, especially the deeper holes off Freeport and up toward the Wantagh Bridge, has been holding weakfish that'll actually pull drag — nothing gigantic, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but that's a real comeback for a fish that's been an afterthought around here for a decade. Grass shrimp under a float, fished slow along the channel edges at dusk, or a small bucktail tipped with squid worked right along bottom near the bridge pilings on the last of the incoming — that's been the ticket. Fish it quiet, fish it slow, and don't horse them — weakfish have paper mouths and you'll lose half of what you hook if you're not patient.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th is going to swing the tides hard, and that's usually when this inlet turns on. Bigger current means more bait getting pushed through the cut, which means the bass and blues stack up tighter on the structure instead of spreading out across the flats. If I had to pick one window for the next week, I'd take the two nights around the new moon, fishing the rocks from an hour before the tide turns through the first hour of the flood. The fluke in Sloop Channel will still be there if you want an easy afternoon, but if you want to feel a real fish bend a rod, the jetty's earning its name again. Bring a headlamp, bring patience, and don't be the guy still parked in the fluke drift when the real bite's happening twenty minutes away in the dark.

reports.headline: Holgate's new cut is holding blues on the outgoing — fluke locked to the bridge shadows
reports.subhead: Building tidal range ahead of the Aug. 12 new moon is starting to sharpen the bite at every piece of structure on the island.
reports.body_markdown:
Walked the south end at Holgate Tuesday at first light and the beach had changed shape on me again. That three-to-four foot swell that rolled through off the Bight over the weekend chewed a new cut about 150 yards north of the old one — deeper, narrower, with a hard drop-off on the south shoulder where the trough dumps into the bar. I could see the color change from the dune line, that dark green gut cutting against the lighter sand flat. Spots like that don't stay secret long once the bait finds them, and by Wednesday morning there were peanut bunker getting pushed around in the wash and small stripers — mostly 18 to 24 inches — slashing through them on the last of the outgoing.

That's been the pattern up and down the island all week: small, scattered striper action working bait pods in the surf, mostly a dawn-and-dusk deal, nothing you can set your watch to but enough to keep a plug bag interesting. I've been doing best with a darter or a needlefish, something slim that reads as a peanut and not a full-grown menhaden, worked through the trough on the last hour of the outgoing and first hour of dead low. Ship Bottom and Beach Haven beaches have both been giving up a few, same story — small fish, tight to the wash, gone once the sun gets up over the dunes.

The better, more consistent story right now is inside. Fluke have settled onto the channel edges and bridge structure where there's current and a shot of cooler bottom water, and that's exactly where I've been finding them. The Beach Haven and Ship Bottom bridges are both holding fish in that 8 to 12 foot zone on the pilings' shadow line — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the slack right at the tide change, has been the money presentation. Don't work it fast. These fish are sitting tight to structure in warm, shallow back-bay water and they want it crawled past their nose, not ripped through. Legal fish have been mixed with a lot of shorts, so it's a pick, but a 4- to 5-pound fluke off the Ship Bottom span on Sunday's high slack tells me the bigger fish are still around if you're patient and fishing the right three feet of water.

Weakfish have been spotty — that's the honest read. A few fish showing on the channel edges up around Graveling Point and into the Mullica system on the incoming, taken on small swim shads and bucktails tipped with Fishbites, but it's nowhere near a sure thing. If I had to put money on it I'd fish the deeper bend just off Graveling Point on the front half of the incoming, when that cooler Mullica water is still pushing out and meeting the flood — that seam has produced for me the last two Augusts running.

Bluefish are the piece that's actually improved. Barnegat Inlet has been showing more consistent blues on the tide change, both ebb and flood, fish in the 3- to 6-pound range busting bunker pods right in the rips off the north jetty rocks. Metal — Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks in the 1- to 2-ounce range — worked through the white water on the outgoing has been getting hit hard for short windows, then it shuts off until the next push of current. I think these are fish getting squeezed south out of the bluefish build that's been developing up toward Sandy Hook and the western Sound — bait's tight to structure right now and the blues are following it down the beach.

Kingfish have shown in small numbers on the outer bars at Holgate and down toward the inlet on bloodworm-tipped high-low rigs in that 3- to 5-foot sandy wash — nothing to write home about yet, but worth a rod in the sand spike if you're already surfcasting for stripers.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep, current-driven bite would hold and sharpen once the tide range started building into the new moon, and that's exactly what's happening. The moon's five days out from new on the 12th, tidal range is stacking day over day, and every piece of structure on this island — the bridges, the inlet rips, the Holgate cuts — is starting to fish harder on the swings. That's not an accident. More water moving means more current pinning bait against structure, and that's when these fish stop scattering and start feeding on a schedule.

Looking ahead, I'd focus the next few days on the moving tides at Barnegat Inlet for blues, the bridge shadow lines on the slack for fluke, and I'd keep half an eye on the surf for anything unusual working bait — this time of year, with warm current pushing down from the Bight, an early bonito or albie showing up off the beach wouldn't shock me, though I haven't seen or heard of one yet on this stretch. If the tidal range keeps building clean through the weekend without a big blow messing up the water, I'd bet the fluke bite on the bridges gets better before it gets worse, and Holgate's new cut is worth another look once this next round of swell settles down and lets you read it properly.

reports.headline: Rose mallow blooms on Great Island — stripers hold deep water while the marsh runs the show
reports.subhead: Dog days on the lower Connecticut mean the fish go where the current is, and this week that's the river mouth and not much else.
reports.body_markdown:
The swamp rose mallow is up along Great Island, that big pink hibiscus that only shows itself for about three weeks a year in the high marsh off Old Lyme, and every August I use it the way some men use a calendar. When that bloom opens, I know the river's done giving. The shad are long gone — they ran up past Hartford back in April and May, spawned, and the survivors slipped back out to sea weeks ago. What's left down here at the mouth in August is a different kind of fishing, quieter, hotter, and it asks you to go find cool water instead of waiting for fish to come to you.

I've watched fifty Augusts do this to the lower river, and it never changes much. The flats warm up fast under a high sun, the marsh creeks go nearly bath-water by afternoon, and anything with fins that isn't a mummichog or a killifish pushes down toward where the river dumps into the Sound and the water actually moves. Right now that means Saybrook Point, the mouth itself off Fenwick, the deep cut by the railroad bridge, and the current seams off the DEP Marina. That's where I'm finding stripers, and that's about it — I want to be straight with you, this isn't a week where you can fish anywhere on this river and do well. You have to go to the moving, cooler water or you're wasting bait.

The bass are there, though, and they're not small fish for the most part — schoolies mixed with a decent number of mid-20-inch fish holding on the bottom edge of the deep water off the breakwater, 15 to 22 feet, right where the outgoing tide funnels past the rocks. I've had the best luck starting an hour before the top of the tide and fishing through the first two hours of the ebb, drifting live eels or chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig, letting it sit right on bottom in that current seam where the river water meets the incoming salt. If you'd rather cast, a white or chartreuse 5-inch soft plastic swimming mullet on a 3/4-ounce jighead, worked slow along that same bottom contour, has been drawing strikes from the fish that are actively feeding rather than just holding. Nighttime has been better than daylight this week — the water's cooler, the bass move up shallower to feed, and there's less boat traffic pushing them off the structure.

Great Island and the flats around Lord Cove are holding the summer's other story — snapper blues, thick in the coves where the peanut bunker and silversides have been schooling up in the calmer water off the marsh edges. Small profile lures are the whole game here: half-ounce Deadly Dicks, small Kastmasters, or a bare gold hook with a sliver of bunker under a bobber if you've got kids along, which is really who this bite is for. It's not a trophy fishery, but it's steady, it's fun, and it's happening on the last two hours of the incoming when the bait gets pushed up into those shallow flats.

White perch have gone quiet on me the last couple weeks, which is normal — they've retreated to the deeper holes in the tidal creeks like Selden and Chester Creek and they're feeding mostly at dusk on small nightcrawler pieces or a tiny chartreuse jig worked slow along bottom. If you want white perch in August you fish the last hour of light and the first hour of dark, not midday.

What's really carrying this river right now, if I'm honest, is the blue crabbing. It's about as good as I've seen it in years, especially back in the marsh creeks off Old Lyme and around Lord Cove — chicken necks on a handline, or traps set in three to five feet of water on a falling tide, and you're pulling doubles and triples of legal crabs without much effort. If the fishing's slow some afternoon, that's where I'd send you instead.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the holding pattern at the river mouth would continue and that building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now. The moon's going new on the 12th, and the tidal range through Saybrook Point and the mouth is already noticeably stronger than it was ten days ago. More water moving through that cut means more bait getting pushed and pulled past the bass holding there, and historically that's when this bite gets from good to very good for about four or five days around the new moon. If I had one window to fish this week, I'd take the outgoing tide the evening of the 11th or the morning of the 12th, right at the breakwater, with eels or bunker chunks on bottom and a bucktail rigged as backup for when the current really starts ripping. Bring bug spray for the greenheads — they're as thick in that marsh grass as I've seen them, and they don't care what the moon's doing.

reports.headline: Stellwagen gravel in 110: cod stacked tight, bluefin working the mackerel schools topside
reports.subhead: Cold, green water holding on the Bank has the groundfish steady on bottom and giant bluefin pinning bait on the surface — a two-fer week out of Gloucester.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ten feet on the meter, gravel edge on the southwest corner of Stellwagen Bank, current running slack to the first hour of the flood — that's where we found the cod Tuesday morning, and they were sitting right where they should be this time of August. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, working them off bottom in six-foot lifts, and getting solid thumps from fish in the 8-to-15-pound class, a few better mixed in. Nothing epic, but steady. You drop, you get bit, you move a quarter mile when it goes quiet, you get bit again. That's how gravel fishing works out here — it's not a pile, it's a pattern, and this week the pattern held.

Haddock have been on the mud, like always, but I'll be honest — it's been a mixed bag in the deeper basin area of the Bank. We worked the transition zone where the gravel rolls off into softer bottom, around 130 to 150 feet, and found pockets of decent-sized haddock, 3 to 6 pounds, mixed with a fair number of shorts we had to cull through. Clam bait on a standard haddock rig, small hooks, fishing tight to bottom on the anchor. Some drifts produced, some didn't. If you're headed out for haddock specifically, I'd fish two or three spots in that basin transition before committing — don't burn the whole tide in one hole hoping it turns on.

Now the real story this week is topside. The water on the Bank has stayed cold and green through this whole stretch — no warm intrusion pushing in from the south, no signal of that changing — and that cold, nutrient-rich water has kept the bait thick. Mackerel schools have been balled up hard over the deeper structure off the drop-off, and the bluefin have been right on them. We flagged this building pattern last week, said the bluefin show would keep growing as long as that cold water pattern held, and that's exactly what's happened — more fish showing daily, more consistent surface activity, birds working the same real estate as the tuna.

We've had multiple hookups on the troll running spreader bars and green machines just off that drop-off in the 150-to-200-foot range where the bottom starts to fall away, mackerel balled up thick on the sounder in that mid-water column. When we mark a school getting worked from below, that's when we've been pitching stickbaits and pencil poppers into the commotion — topwater eats on giant bluefin never get old, and we've had a few blow up right at the boat that'll keep you up at night replaying it. Not every school stays up long enough to get a bait to it, and not every pass produces, but the fish are there in numbers we haven't seen yet this summer, and that's worth noting heading into the back half of August.

Beyond this immediate area, we don't have any confirmed reports to pass along this week — nothing solid enough to put a number or a location behind. When something firms up, it'll be in the column.

The moon's building toward new on the 12th, and that means tidal range is about to sharpen up across the whole Bank. For groundfish, that usually means shorter, more defined bite windows — the fish feed hard on the push and shut down on the slack, so timing your drift to the tide change matters more than it did during the slower neap water we just came off. For the bluefin, more current usually means better bait concentration along the drop-off, pinning those mackerel schools tighter against structure instead of letting them spread out over open water.

reports.headline: Monhegan ledges on the ebb: pollock topside, cod deep, bass stacking the rivers
reports.subhead: Cold water's holding the bay quiet, but the river mouths and Monhegan's ledges are still giving up fish for those who know where to look.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-one years hauling gear and chasing fish out of this harbor, and I can tell you the second week of August has a rhythm that doesn't change much, even when everything else does. I was out hauling off Two Bush Island Tuesday morning when Dave Alley came over the radio griping that Eastern Egg Rock was thick with mackerel and not a tern working them. That told me more than any thermometer could. When the bait's that dense and the birds aren't diving, it means the mackerel are holding deep and steady, not getting pushed around by anything chasing them hard. That's been the story of this whole stretch of water for weeks now — steady, cold, and unbothered.

We called this one last week — said Midcoast Maine would stay the calmest, coldest zone on the chart, and here we are. Nothing's shifted. The Gulf of Maine water sitting on Penobscot Bay hasn't warmed a lick, and that cold cushion is keeping the southern fish — the bluefish especially — mostly out of the picture this far north. I've had exactly one report of a bluefish this month, a single fish off Ram Island, and I wouldn't build a trip around them right now. If you want blues, you're better off waiting till Labor Day, if they show at all.

What's working is what always works when the bay stays cold: striped bass holding tight to the river mouths where the water warms up and the bait concentrates. The Damariscotta River mouth, down around the Gut and the flats off Fort Island, has been giving up bass to 30 inches on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Sea worms fished on a simple slip rig, or chunked mackerel drifted along the current seam where the river water meets the salt, has been the ticket. The Medomak River mouth off Waldoboro has been similar — smaller fish mostly, schoolies in the 18 to 24 inch range, but they're stacked thick enough on the outgoing that a bucktail or a swimming plug worked slow along bottom will connect more often than not. The Back River up behind Southport has had a few slot fish too, taken on topwater at first light before the sun gets on the water — Zara Spooks and pencil poppers worked over the mussel flats on the last of the flood.

Monhegan's been the bright spot for anybody willing to make the run. Pollock have been busting bait on the surface off White Head and around the ledges to the northeast of the harbor, especially in the last hour of the ebb when the current pulls hard around the island and pushes bait up against the rock. Diamond jigs, 2 to 4 ounces depending on the drift, worked with a fast retrieve through the boils — that's been about as reliable a bite as we've had all summer. Fish are running 3 to 6 pounds, with the occasional bigger one mixed in. If you see the surface nervous with bait and gulls dropping in, that's your window, and it doesn't stay open long — twenty, thirty minutes before the current slacks and the fish drop back down.

Groundfish are still where they've been all season — deep, and patient anglers are still finding them. Cod are holding in the channels around Isle au Haut Bay and off the eastern side of Vinalhaven, 140 to 180 feet, on the last of the ebb when the current's still moving enough to keep bait suspended off bottom. Haddock have been scarcer this far into the bay — you'll do better running out toward Matinicus if haddock specifically is the target, but a few have come up mixed in with the cod on jigs worked right off the bottom, three or four cranks up and let it settle again. Nothing's been fast, but it's been steady, and for August in a bay this cold, steady is about what you can ask for.

The moon's building toward new on the 12th, and that's the one thing I'd watch closest over the next several days. More tidal range means more current, and more current at spots like the Muscle Ridge Channel, the mouth of the Damariscotta, and around Monhegan's ledges usually sharpens things up rather than shutting them down. If the extra push gets the bait moving more aggressively, I'd expect the pollock bite at Monhegan to hold or improve, and I'd expect the river-mouth bass to feed a little harder on that stronger outgoing water. I wouldn't count on the bluefish showing just because the tide's building — that's a water temperature problem, not a current problem, and nothing in the pattern suggests that's changing soon. My money this week is on the same three spots that have been paying off: the Damariscotta mouth on the outgoing, Monhegan's ledges on the last of the ebb, and the deep channels around Isle au Haut for anybody patient enough to soak a jig.

reports.headline: Five Days to the New Moon, and the Point Is Coiling
reports.subhead: Bass are holding tight to the boulders, jumbo blues are working the rips, and the first albie of the season is closer than it's been all summer.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a specific feeling at the Point in early August, and if you've fished it as many years as I have, you know it the second you step onto the rocks before first light. The water's still warm — 69 degrees off the Lighthouse, holding steady — but the air's got that first hint of change in it, and the current feels like it's loading up for something. Five days out from the August 12 new moon, and Montauk is coiling. I don't mean that lightly. Every year around this window, the tidal range starts building, the rips sharpen, and the whole east end shifts gears. This year's no different, except maybe a little more obvious than usual.

The striper bite has been a holding pattern for weeks now, and that's not a complaint — it's just where we are in the calendar. Fish are still here, they're just doing what August bass do: sitting deep on structure during the day and working the current edges hard at night. The boulder field off the Point, that stretch between the Lighthouse and North Bar, has been giving up quality fish on the top of the incoming, right at first light. I had a guy sight-cast an eel into the white water last Thursday and connect on a 38-inch fish that buried itself in the rocks for a solid five minutes before we turned it. That's the kind of fish this stretch produces when the tide's right — not numbers, but the real deal. Bucktails in the 2- to 3-ounce range, white or olive, worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been the more consistent daytime play. Don't overwork it. Let the current do the work and just keep contact.

Shagwong Reef has been holding bluefish, and I mean real bluefish — 12, 14 pounds, the kind that used to be a Montauk given and lately have felt more like an event. They're sitting on bunker schools that have been pushing through Block Island Sound, and when those schools tighten up over the reef on a building tide, it gets loud fast — birds diving, bait skying, the whole show. Chunked bunker on wire leader has been the ticket for anchoring on them, but if you want to cast, a bomber or a big popper worked through the surface chaos will get bit just as hard. Turtle Cove's had some smaller blues mixed with schoolie bass working bait pushed into the corner on the last of the outgoing — good action if you've got kids in the boat and want bent rods without a long run.

Fluke's been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest about that. The drift off the south side beaches has produced some quality fish — four- and five-pounders on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 30 to 40 feet — but you're working for them. Plenty of shorts mixed in, and some drifts you'll go twenty minutes without a knock. The better bite's been happening on the humps and drop-offs south of the Point where the bottom breaks up and holds bait, rather than the flat sand. If fluke's your priority this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping you off the structure.

Now here's the part everybody's been asking about at the docks. We flagged this pattern building last week, and it's still lining up — squid have been pushing hard into Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound as that water climbs into the high 50s and low 60s, and that's the exact signal that precedes Montauk's rips turning on for false albacore and bonito. It hasn't happened yet. I want to be straight about that — nobody's boated an albie off the Point as of this week, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. But the pieces are lining up almost textbook: warming current corridor, squid staging to the east, and a new moon five days out that's going to put some real muscle into these tides. If there's a year the switch flips right on schedule, this feels like it.

Offshore, the boats running out toward West Atlantis have been into yellowfin over 100 pounds, with white marlin showing and the occasional blue marlin in the spread — a strong summer bite holding steady on the warm water anchored out there. Bluefin eight to sixteen miles out have grown into better-class fish too, and the guys have shifted off the troll and onto jig and chunk now that those fish are sitting on bait rather than running it down. That's a good sign for everything closer to shore — when the bait's thick enough to hold bluefin that tight to the beach, it tends to trickle down into everything else feeding behind it.

Looking ahead, I'd focus the next few days on the current-driven spots — North Bar on the building tide, the boulder field at dawn, Shagwong when the bunker's thick — because that's where the bite's been most honest lately. And I'd keep one rod rigged light and ready for albies starting Monday. If the tidal range does what it usually does heading into a new moon, the rips around the Point are going to sharpen fast, and when that first fish shows, it's not going to give you much warning.

reports.headline: The West Bar Rebuilt Itself Again — Fish the New Seam, Not Last Month's Spot
reports.subhead: Moriches Inlet's bottom shifted under the July swell, and the bass and blues found the new edge before most anglers did.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the skiff through the cut Tuesday morning on a dropping tide and the depth finder told me something the charts won't show you for another year: the west bar off Cupsogue has built back in, maybe two feet shallower than it was in June, and the main channel has squeezed itself against the Westhampton side. That's not unusual for August — the inlet does this every summer as the longshore drift piles sand off the jetty stub and the current finds the path of least resistance — but it matters this week because the fish have already relocated to the new seam, and a lot of guys are still working water that isn't holding structure anymore.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the real story here wouldn't be this weekend, it'd be what shows up once the tidal range builds into the August 12 new moon. That's exactly what's happening. The moon is pulling harder water through the cut every day now, and that increased flow is doing what it always does at Moriches: sharpening the edges, concentrating bait, and giving the bass a reason to stack instead of scatter.

Right now the best window is the last two hours of the outgoing on the ocean side of the inlet, right where that new west bar drops into the channel. I'm marking bait — peanut bunker and rainfish — getting pinned against that edge as the water pulls out, and the bass are using the deeper cut like a funnel. Bucktails in the 1.5-ounce range, white or olive, cast up-current and allowed to swing down along the drop, are outproducing everything else I've tried. Let it hit bottom once, then keep it just ticking the sand on a slow retrieve — the takes are coming right where the seam meets the flat, not out in the open water. Sizes have been mixed, mostly high-twenties to low-30-inch fish, with the occasional slot pushing 34. Nothing epic, but honest fish on a consistent pattern, and that's worth more to me than a one-day blitz.

Cupsogue itself has been decent from the beach for the same reason — that outgoing water dumping bait past the swimming beach and around the point gives surfcasters a real shot if they're willing to walk. I talked to a guy Thursday who worked the stretch between the second and third parking field with a Danny swimmer at first light and had three fish to 30 inches before the sun got high. That's the kind of report I trust — not a blitz, just a guy who understood the tide stage and put himself in front of moving water.

Bluefish have been the wildcard. Some mornings the birds are working bunker schools right off the inlet mouth and you'll see gators in the 8-to-12-pound class ripping through, other mornings it's dead calm and you'd swear there isn't a blue in the bay. My read is they're following the same bunker pods pushing tight to the beach that we're seeing region-wide right now, and they're not committing to Moriches specifically — they're just passing through when the bait funnels past. If you see working birds off Tuthill Point or the inlet mouth, don't wait, get on it, because that window closes fast.

Fluke fishing inside the bay has been steady but unspectacular — the kind of bite where you need to move to find quality. The channel edges off Pattersquash and the deeper holes toward Tuthill Point have given up keepers to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the outgoing when the water's still got some push to it. Slack tide has been dead there — no current, no drift, no bites, which tells you the fluke in this bay are still ambush feeders working current lines rather than roaming the flats in this warm water.

Weakfish have been scattered and honestly disappointing — a few reports of fish in the 2-to-3-pound range around the deeper holes near the Moriches Inlet bridge on soft plastics fished slow along bottom, but nothing you could call a pattern yet. Porgies are more reliable if you want steady action — anchoring up on the deeper structure inside the bay near the Inlet with sandworms or clam has been producing good numbers of scup in the 10-to-12-inch range, a solid bend-your-rod option on a day when the current-driven bite isn't cooperating.

Looking ahead, the building tidal range through the August 12 new moon should keep sharpening that cut bite at the inlet — more water moving means more bait getting pinned, more bass committing to the seam instead of holding loose. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't blow the inlet dirty, I'd fish that new west bar drop on the last two hours of the outgoing through the weekend and into early next week. If a blow does come through and reshapes that bar again, don't assume the spot — go find where the new cut is before you start casting. This inlet rewards anglers who read the bottom, not the memory of where the fish were last month.

reports.headline: Great Point Rip Holds Its Breath — Bonito Close, Bass Never Left
reports.subhead: The Sound's still stacked with stripers on the structure while every rip chaser on the island keeps one eye east for that first bonito flash.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, half-tide, I'm sitting on the north side of Great Point watching a tern wheel and drop twice, then just... quit. No follow-up birds, no nervous water, nothing. That's been the story of my bonito watch for two weeks now — little false alarms, single birds working bait that never turns into the real show. I've had my 7-weight rigged and ready in the rocket launcher so long the cork's starting to fade. Still no bonito in hand off the Point. But I'll tell you what — I don't think it's far off, and I'm not the only one holding my breath.

Here's why. The bonito push that's been working up through Rhode Island — Watch Hill, Sakonnet, that corridor — has already crossed into Buzzards Bay. That's the leading edge of the run, and it's pointed right at us. We flagged this last week, said the August 12 new moon would be the trigger that builds enough tidal current to push bait hard through the rips and finally bring bonito and albies into range out here, and that's exactly the mechanism setting up now. The moon's still building, current through Muskeget and the Broad Sound side of the Shoals is getting stronger every tide, and that's the kind of flow that concentrates sand eels and silversides right where the predators want them. If I had to bet on when the first bonito gets weighed at a Nantucket dock, I'd put my money on the back half of this week into the weekend, once that new moon current really starts ripping through Great Point and around Monomoy's elbow.

Until then, the bass have been doing all the work, and honestly, they've been worth the trip on their own. Nantucket Sound itself — Horseshoe Shoal, the edges around Wasque, the rips off the south side of the Shoals proper — has a solid keeper-and-short mix right now, and it's not subtle. These fish are sitting tight to structure, current-protected water, not out in the open exposed stuff. That's the tell. Bait's concentrating where there's current break and bottom relief, not out on the flat, featureless middle of the Shoals, and the bass know it. I've been running umbrella rigs and bunker spoons over Horseshoe on the last two hours of the ebb, marking fish stacked on the edges of the drop where the current stacks bait against the shoulder. Bucktails — the 2-ounce white ones I always default to out here — worked slow along bottom on the up-current side have been just as effective, especially for the shorts mixed in tight to the sandy humps.

What's not working right now is fluke on the open Nantucket Shoals grounds. I made the run out there twice this week hoping for a repeat of some of the better days we've had, and it's just underwhelming — a few undersized fish, nothing worth staying on. The contrast with the Sound couldn't be clearer. Out on the open Shoals there's no current protection, no structure to hold bait tight, so everything's spread thin and moving. Inside the Sound, on the other hand, structure and current do the concentrating for you. If you want fluke this week, don't waste the fuel running to the open Shoals — work the edges of the channels around Monomoy, the drop-offs near Chatham inlet, drifting Gulp on light bucktails, chartreuse and white both producing. Slower drifts on the last of the outgoing have been better than fighting a hard tide.

Scup fishing has quietly been solid too, and it's an easy one to overlook when everybody's chasing albies and bass. Anywhere there's hard structure in the Sound — rock piles, old wreckage, the rubble edges around Monomoy Point — you can anchor up, drop squid strips or clam on a simple two-hook bottom rig, and load a cooler in an hour if the tide's moving right. It's not glamorous but it's about as sure a thing as this Sound offers right now, and it's a good fallback for anybody who spent the morning watching empty water for bonito that never showed.

Wind's been the other factor worth mentioning — we've had a mostly manageable pattern this week, nothing that's blown the rips out, which has helped keep the Great Point and Monomoy current lines fishable on both the ebb and the early flood. If that holds through the weekend and the new moon keeps building tidal strength like it should, I think the pieces are close to lining up. Warmer water pushing up from the south, current strengthening through the rips, bait getting squeezed into tight seams — that's the recipe. It's not here yet. But every rip chaser I've talked to at the dock this week has the same look on his face: watching, waiting, rod rigged.

My plan for the coming days is simple. I'll keep working Great Point and the Monomoy rips on the moving tides, especially around the new moon push on the 11th and 12th, because if the bonito show up anywhere first, it's going to be in that kind of current. In the meantime, the bass on Horseshoe Shoal and the scup on the structure are paying the bills. If you're headed out this week, don't skip the sure thing chasing the maybe — but keep that light tackle rigged, because I don't think we're watching empty water much longer.

reports.headline: Conimicut goes quiet at noon, loud at midnight — scup stacked, bass gone nocturnal
reports.subhead: Fluke are finally pushing into the bay proper as the new moon tide builds and the bass slide deep to beat the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning watching a guy in a Carhartt jacket — in August, mind you — pull scup after scup off the bottom on a high-low rig, and he says to me, "Vinny, this is the easiest twenty minutes of fishing I've had all summer." That's about right for where the bay's at right now. The scup bite is the one thing you can set a watch to. Everything else takes a little more thought.

Buckeye Brook ran dry on herring weeks ago — that whole spring parade that pulls the first big bass into the upper bay is long over, and the fish that came in on it have scattered into their summer pattern. That means less schoolie chaos around the herring ladders and more of that deep, sulking, nighttime bite that Narragansett Bay gets every August when the surface water goes flat warm and the stripers drop into the holes to sweat it out. I've been marking fish in 25 to 35 feet off Nyatt Point and along the Prudence Island shoreline where the bottom drops fast, and they're not up chasing bait in daylight — they're down there waiting for dark.

If you want those fish, you're fishing the last two hours of daylight into full dark, working the outgoing tide when the current pulls bait off the flats and funnels it past the points. Eels are still the closer for me — a foot-long live eel on a 3-way rig, just enough weight to hold bottom in that current off Conimicut, fished slow and patient. Guys doing well at night are also dragging umbrella rigs slow along the edges of the channel off Prudence, picking up fish in the mid-20s to low 30s, nothing giant, but real bass, not schoolies. Daytime, your best shot is early — first light — before the sun gets up on the water and pushes everything down. After that it's a scup and fluke game until dusk.

And the fluke — that's the story I like this week. They've been pushing harder into the bay proper than they have all summer, showing up in Greenwich Bay and along the flats off Conimicut Point in 15 to 20 feet. Nothing wall-hanger size, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a few keepers mixed in, but there's enough of them now that a slow drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid, will put fish in the box. Best water's been the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, when there's still current moving bait but the water hasn't gone dead slack. Once it goes slack off Greenwich Bay the bite just shuts off — I've sat through it enough times to know not to fight it, I just pick up and run to the scup grounds instead.

Speaking of which — the scup are thick right now on every rocky ledge in the bay that holds current. Nyatt Point, the rip off Conimicut, the rocks along Rocky Point, the Prudence Island shoreline — anywhere there's structure and moving water, there's scup stacked on it. Squid strips or sandworms on a two-hook bottom rig, small hooks, light enough line that you can feel the tap-tap before they steal your bait. This is the easiest meal in the bay right now and it's basically foolproof — kids, first-timers, guys who don't know a herring from a hardtail can all catch a limit of scup off these ledges this week.

Black sea bass are riding shotgun with the scup on the same structure, a bonus fish more than a target, but I've heard of a few decent ones — 15, 16 inches — coming off the rockier stretches around Prudence on the same rigs. Weakfish are still a ghost story in this bay. I hear the occasional report out of Greenwich Bay on a soft plastic worked slow near dusk, but it's not something I'd plan a trip around — more like something you stumble into.

We flagged this last week — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's starting to happen. The tidal range is stretching out day by day, and you can feel it standing on the rocks at Conimicut — more push, more current, more bait getting moved around on the points. That's good news for the ledge bite and it should tighten up the night bass pattern too, since more current means more bait getting swept past those deep holes where the stripers are holding.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the same program through the weekend — scup and fluke by day, bass by night — but I'd pay close attention once we get inside 48 hours of the new moon. If that tidal range keeps building the way it's shaping up, the points and rips are going to get more aggressive, and that's usually when the bass push up out of the deep holes to feed a little earlier in the evening instead of waiting for full dark. I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first reports of bluefish showing up mixed into those bait schools either — they've been building steam out toward the Sound, and this bay doesn't usually miss out for long once that starts. Worth keeping a wire leader in the box just in case.

reports.headline: White Island Rockpile on the Slack: Cod and Haddock Mixed, Stripers Working the Piscataqua Seam
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't mean thirteen miles of options — it means you'd better know every rock, and this week the Shoals paid for that knowledge.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure I'm running out of places to fish by Wednesday. I've got more water inside that thirteen miles than most guys work in a season. The Shoals alone are nine islands and about as many distinct pieces of bottom, and I fish it like it's a hundred and thirty miles of Gulf of Maine, because structurally that's what it is. This week that mindset paid rent.

I was off White Island before 5 AM Tuesday, tide bottoming out around 5:40, and I sat on the rockpile on the northeast corner in about 70 feet waiting for the slack to set up clean. That first twenty minutes of dead water is when the cod come off the structure and feed loose instead of holding tight in the current — and it showed. Jigging diamond jigs, the 4-ounce chrome ones, tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, and I had cod to 8 pounds and a couple of haddock in the mix, which is the part worth mentioning. Haddock have been thin around the Shoals all summer — this was the first day in a few weeks I saw more than one or two. Whether that's a real push of fish or just a good morning on a good piece of bottom, I can't say yet. One trip isn't a pattern. But if I had to bet where I'd put my next haddock trip, it's back on that same rock on the next slack tide, not blind-drifting somewhere new.

Gosport Harbor and the back side of Appledore have been quieter than I'd like for cod — water's cold and green out there the way it usually runs in August, which is normally good news for groundfish, but the fish have been scattered rather than stacked. I marked bait on the sounder in 55 feet off Duck Island Wednesday and never got more than a bump. Sometimes the mackerel schools pull the cod's attention off the bottom entirely, and that's what I think happened — the macks have been thick enough around the Shoals this week that jigging a bare Swedish Pimple with three or four hooks, no bait needed, filled a bucket in fifteen minutes some mornings. Good news if you want table fare and a break from bottom fishing. Bad news if you were counting on those cod being predictable.

Inshore, the story's at the river mouths, same as it always is this time of year. The Piscataqua is running strong current through Portsmouth Harbor with the building tide range — we flagged this last week, said the sharpening current into the new moon would turn on the structure-oriented bite, and that's exactly what's happening at Henderson Point and off the end of Pierces Island. Stripers are stacked on the seam where the river current meets the harbor eddy, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets pushed out of the back channels. I've been throwing swimming plugs — a Slug-Go rigged weightless, white, worked slow through the seam — and picking up schoolies to about 26 inches with the occasional better fish mixed in. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, drifted right down the current line off Fort Point, has been the better bet for the bigger bass, but you need to be anchored right, not just close.

Hampton Harbor is doing its usual August thing on the incoming tide — bass and blues pushing up through the inlet on the flood chasing bait out of the marsh, then dropping back out on the ebb. I've had decent luck working the channel edge off Great Boars Head with a bucktail, half-ounce white, bounced slow along bottom as the tide starts to push in. Bluefish have been the wildcard — quiet most of July, and now starting to show again in the harbor mouth and off Odiorne Point, chopping up schools of peanut bunker close to the rocks. Nothing gator-sized, mostly 2 to 4 pounds, but they hit hard enough on topwater poppers to wake you up at 6 AM. If that bluefish comeback keeps building the way it has the last few days south of here, I'd expect more of that action at the river mouths through the rest of August.

Flounder have been steady but unspectacular in the Piscataqua's mud channels and the back of Hampton Harbor — small hooks, sandworms or clam bellies, fished right on bottom on the slower part of the tide. Not a trip to plan a whole day around, but a solid backup if the wind kills the Shoals run.

Looking ahead: the new moon on the 12th is going to push tidal range up noticeably, and that should sharpen every current-driven spot I've mentioned — the Piscataqua seam, the Hampton inlet, the rockpiles at the Shoals where slack water timing matters. If the wind stays reasonable out of the west, I'd run out to White Island again on the next good slack and see if that haddock bump was real or a fluke. If it blows, I'm working the river mouths on the bigger tides and letting the current do the work for me. Either way, thirteen miles is plenty if you know which rocks to sit on.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 210 feet: haddock holding the mud, cod thin on the gravel edge
reports.subhead: Steady green water and building bait have the ledge fishing true to form for early August, but the cod bite still needs work to find keepers.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-ten on the sounder this morning, soft mud color coming back on the eastern flat of Jeffrey's Ledge, and that's exactly the water I wanted to see. Haddock like that bottom — soft, gray-green, a little give to it — and this week they were sitting right where the chart says they should be, holding tight to the transition where the mud flattens out east of the main ledge before it drops toward Scantum Basin.

We've had four trips out this week, three of them solid, one a grind. The pattern's been consistent: haddock from 190 to 230 feet on the mud, working a slow drift with clam bait on standard two-hook rigs, 6-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom in the current. Fish ran 18 to 24 inches, a few pushing bigger, and when we found a patch of them the bite came in flurries — five, six fish in ten minutes, then dead again until the drift carried us back over the same stretch. That's typical August haddock behavior out here. They're not spread evenly across the mud, they're bunched in pockets, and you earn your limit by working the GPS track back and forth until you find where the pocket sits this particular tide.

Cod have been the tougher story, and I'll be straight about it — the gravel bite on the western edge of the ledge, the classic 120 to 160 foot structure where you'd normally expect keeper cod stacked up on the hard bottom, has been thin. We picked at a few fish jigging diamond jigs and 8-ounce Norwegian jigs tipped with squid strips, but for every keeper we saw two or three shorts come over the rail. Water's still cold and green down there, which is the right color, but the cod just haven't packed onto the gravel in numbers yet this year. I talked to a couple other boats out of Rye and they're seeing the same thing — scattered, not stacked. If you're going after cod specifically right now, I'd treat it as a bonus fish while you're haddocking rather than build the whole trip around it.
