Platts Bank has been worth the extra run for guys willing to push north. Similar mud pattern to Jeffrey's, maybe a touch deeper, and the haddock there have been running a little bigger on average — I heard of a few pushing past 26 inches off the deeper mud there this week. Tillies Bank I haven't fished personally in the last ten days, so I won't speak to it beyond saying the bottom type is right for the same mud pattern if the Jeffrey's fish get pressured off.

We flagged last week that conditions looked steady with no major shift coming, and that's exactly what played out — the water held its color, the thermocline didn't move much, and the fish stayed put in the same general zones instead of sliding around on us. That kind of stability is a gift out here. It means the numbers you write down Monday are still good Thursday.

Mackerel have been showing in patches on the ledge itself, schools flickering on the sounder in that 60 to 90 foot range on top of the structure, and that's worth paying attention to even if you're not targeting them — it's bait, and bait brings everything else with it. We haven't seen bluefin sign yet, no boils, no birds working hard on the surface, no whale activity that would tip you off to a real bait concentration building. That's normal for early August. The giants don't usually show heavy on Jeffrey's until the water turns over into fall — October is when this ledge earns its reputation for big fish on the surface, and I'm not going to pretend that clock has moved up just because the mackerel are around a little early. Worth watching, not worth planning a trip around yet.

Tide-wise, we're running toward the new moon on the 12th, and I expect the current to pick up some strength on the ledge edges over the next several days. That usually sharpens the haddock bite on the mud — a little more push moves more bait past the fish and gets them feeding in shorter, more predictable windows instead of the long lazy pickings we had this week. If I had to guess where I'll put my time over the next several days, it's the same eastern mud flat, working the drift a little tighter to the tide change, morning outgoing especially. The cod I'll keep checking on the gravel, but I'm not counting on a turnaround there until the water cools another notch or two.

Bottom line for anyone planning a trip out of Rye: bring the clam bait, work the mud in the 190 to 230 range, and don't be surprised if the gravel cod fishing stays stingy a while longer. It's a steady week, not a spectacular one, and out here on Jeffrey's that's usually a fair trade — steady means you can plan around it.

reports.headline: 71.2°F and 3.9-Footers: Sea Bass Holding, Mahi and Tuna Still a Gamble
reports.subhead: The numbers off the Bight say the bait's there, but the swell kept a lot of boats tied to the dock this week — here's what I'd trust and what I'd wait on.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-one point two. That's what the buoy out past the Bight read this week, with 3.9 feet at five seconds stacked on top of it. That combination tells me two things before I ever untie the lines: the warm water's out there to hold bait, and the ride's going to have some lump in it for anything under 28 feet.

That 71-degree reading is a mid-shelf number, not a canyon number, and it matters because it sits right on top of our sea bass and reef grounds. Warm water like that tends to push bait up and hold it tight to structure, which is the classic August pattern — bait balled up over the high spots, sea bass sitting near the edge of structure in 55 to 70 feet rather than up in the water column. High-low rigs with Gulp Sea Bass baits or fresh squid strips, dropped tight and worked slow off the bottom, remain the standard play in that setup. I don't have a confirmed, verified catch count from any specific reef to report this week — the boats that got out between wind events described a workable but not stacked bite in general terms, and I'm not going to attach that to a named spot without a firmer report in hand.

We're building toward the new moon on the 12th, and the tidal range is going to widen over the next few days. On current-driven bottom structure, a widening tidal swing usually sharpens the drift bite for sea bass and blackfish — more water moving typically means bait pinned tighter to structure and fish feeding with more confidence. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the day closest to the new moon with the least wind, fishing the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing.

Mahi is the one I don't have a confirmed number on yet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. August is typically when pot and buoy lines start holding mahi under shade lines, and the water temp supports that possibility, but the sea state this week kept most boats closer to the beach. Nobody I trust has called in a solid, verified mahi report yet. That's a watch-and-wait for me — if we get a calm window, small blue-and-white or pink skirted baits trolled slow around any floating structure, with greenies for chum if you find fish holding under a buoy, would be the move.

Bluefin is the same story, just with more chatter behind it. There's a warm pool that's been sitting off our grounds, and that's the kind of setup that can get bluefin working — morning troll on spreader bars, switching to jig and chunk once the sun's up. I've had more phone calls asking about it than confirmed hookups to report. The ingredients are there, the water's right, but my own log doesn't have a verified fish on the deck to back it up this week.

Note: this report was cut off before it could be completed, so any additional detail on specific bites or locations beyond what's above could not be confirmed and has been left out.

reports.headline: Porgies keep the lights on while the bass wait for the tide to turn
reports.subhead: Horton Point to Orient, the fishing's steady but nobody's getting rich — and the new moon might change that fast.
reports.body_markdown:
Old Ray Corwin used to say a bayman without patience is just a fella standing in cold water. Ray's been gone eleven years now, but I thought of him Tuesday morning out past the Mattituck breakwater, watching a single osprey work the same stretch of glass for twenty minutes before it finally dropped and came up with something silver. Twenty minutes for one fish. That's about the pace of things out here right now — nothing's rushing, but if you wait it out, something comes.

Water's holding in the high 60s to low 70s depending where you dip a thermometer — Kings Point's reading near 71 down west, New London's sitting closer to 69, and that gradient tells you what you need to know about this stretch. Warmer water piles up toward the western Sound, and the cooler stuff settles in toward us and on out through Plum Gut. It's not a big spread, a couple degrees, but fish know a couple degrees the way you and I know the difference between a warm bath and a cold one.

Striped bass have been doing what they've been doing all month — holding deep, feeding mostly after the sun goes down, and making you work for every fish. We said last week the building tide into this new moon would sharpen that pattern up, and I'll tell you, it's starting to show. Guys working the rockpiles off Horton Point after dark on bunker chunks and fresh-cut bait have been finding better numbers the last two nights than they did over the weekend — nothing spectacular, mind you, mostly schoolie-to-mid-twenties fish, but more of them, and more consistent. The current's got some shoulder to it now that we're building toward the new moon on the 12th, and moving water wakes bass up quicker than warm sun ever will. If you're set up on eels or a big swimming plug on the last two hours of the outgoing at Horton or Rocky Point, fish it slow and deep, right along the rock edge where the current breaks. That's where they're sitting.

Bluefish are the interesting story this week, though nothing's confirmed yet on our stretch. There's real chatter about blues coming back strong on the deep reefs out west — fish in the mid-teens showing up where they'd gone quiet most of July. That kind of resurgence usually doesn't stay put. Bait redistributes with a strengthening tide, and blues follow bait, not loyalty. I wouldn't be shocked if by the back half of this week we start seeing that push work its way east toward Mattituck and beyond. Keep a bucktail or a diamond jig rigged and ready even if you're bass fishing — you don't want to be scrambling when a school of choppers comes through and cuts your leader in half.

Porgy fishing remains the one thing out here you can set a watch by. Scup have been steady on the rockpiles and mussel beds from Rocky Point clear out to the Orient Point rip, and that bite doesn't care much what the bass or blues are up to. Small hooks, size 6 or 8, a piece of clam or sandworm, fished right on bottom in fifteen to twenty-five feet — that's lunch and dinner most days if you've got the patience to sort through the small ones. It's not glamorous fishing but it's honest fishing, and there's something to be said for a bite you can count on.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and I won't oversell it. Word from the western Sound is mostly short fish, and out here it's much the same story — plenty of fluke around the drop-offs off Mattituck Inlet and along the flats toward Horton Point, but you're culling through a lot of shorts to find a keeper. White Gulp on a three-quarter ounce bucktail, drifted slow along the edges where the sand gives way to mud, has been the best combination for me. Nothing wrong with the technique — the fish just aren't stacked up the way they were in July.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been scarce. A few reports of fish taken incidental to the bass bite on bunker chunks, but nothing organized enough to call a pattern. If you stumble into one, consider it a bonus, not a target.

Blackfish season's still closed, but the smart guys are already out scouting structure — marking rockpiles and boulder fields on the sounder ahead of the fall opener, particularly around the Plum Gut approach where the current really works the bottom clean. Worth doing now while the water's calm enough to see what you're marking.

Looking ahead: that new moon on the 12th is going to push more water through here than we've seen in weeks, and moving water is exactly what this bass pattern's been waiting on. If the tidal range builds the way it should, I'd expect the night bite at Horton Point and Rocky Point to firm up further, and there's a real chance the bluefish push reaches us before the week's out. My plan is simple — fish the last of the outgoing after dark, keep a jig rigged for blues, and treat the porgies as the sure thing they've been all summer. Nothing out here is a lock, but the water's finally starting to move with some purpose, and that's usually when this stretch shows its hand.

reports.headline: Sea Bright rocks at first light: gator blues crash the bunker, fluke picks up steam in Belmar
reports.subhead: Bluefish spilling south out of the Hook, a real fluke bite finally showing at the inlets, and the new moon building toward something worth waiting for.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six, north end of the Sea Bright rocks, and there's a guy I've never met standing on the third jetty down heaving a bunker spoon like he's trying to hit Staten Island. Turns out he had reason to. Fifteen minutes later a blitz rolled through tight to the rocks — real gator blues, eight to twelve pounds, tails white water and gulls dropping out of the sky like the ceiling fell in. He hooked up on the second cast after the spoon, lost one, landed a nine-pounder that took him halfway down the jetty chasing drag. I've fished this stretch long enough to know that when the bait's stacked this thick this close to the beach, you don't need finesse. You need to be standing there when it happens.

That blitz has been building since the gator run hit Sandy Hook proper, and it's been leaking south into our water for about a week now. Bunker pods are running tight to the beach from the Hook down through Monmouth Beach, and wherever they bunch up against structure — jetty tips, the deeper pockets off the third and fourth rocks at Sea Bright — the blues have been finding them on the tide change, both ends. Poppers work early when it's still gray out, then switch to bunker spoons or big Ava jigs once the sun's up and the fish push deeper along the rocks. I've been fishing the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, because that's when the current sets up a seam right off the tip where bait gets pinned and the blues stack up to feed on it. Don't overthink the retrieve. These fish aren't shy.

Fluke's the other story worth telling this week, and it's a better one than we've had most of the summer. Shark River Inlet and Manasquan Inlet have both been giving up better-grade fish than July, and Belmar's weigh station has had a few boats bring double-digit fluke to the scale — not a banner week, but a real uptick after a mixed-bag summer. The pattern's simple: bait's pushed shallow with the warm water, and the fluke have followed it right up into the inlet channels and the drop-offs along the jetty rocks at Manasquan. I've had my best luck drifting the deeper edge on the outgoing, 15 to 22 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's ripping and you need the extra scent to hold fish on. Slow drag, not a swim. These fish are eating close to bottom right now.

Striped bass are still doing what they've been doing all month, which is to say: present, but not stupid. We said last week the building tidal flow into this new moon would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's starting to happen. The bass I'm finding are holding tight to the rock piles at the Manasquan Inlet jetties and the deeper scour holes off Spring Lake, feeding hardest in that last hour of the ebb when the current really starts moving water off the structure. Swimmers — a Danny or a Redfin in bone or bunker pattern — worked slow along the rocks at first light have been the ticket, along with the occasional teen-class fish on a bucktail bounced through the wash at Asbury Park. Nothing's blowing up out there. It's a jetty-by-jetty grind, and you need to fish the tide, not the clock. But the pattern holds, and with the new moon on the 12th pushing more water through these inlets, I expect the current seams to sharpen up further before this week's out.

No albie signs yet, and I wasn't expecting any — we flagged this stretch as an early-arrival spot before Sandy Hook usually sees them, but that new moon trigger hasn't flipped yet. Worth watching the Manasquan Inlet rocks and the Spring Lake jetties over the next ten days, because when those fish do show, this is often where they show first on this whole stretch of coast.

Ocean's been a little beat up — better than three feet of swell running out there most of the week, which has kept some of the surf guys off the outer bars and pushed more effort onto the jetties themselves, which honestly isn't the worst thing. Dirtier water close to the rocks has actually helped the bluefish bite; they don't mind a little chop pushing bait against structure.

Look ahead: tidal range keeps building right through the 12th, and if that pattern holds the way it usually does around here, expect the bass bite at current-driven spots like the Manasquan jetties and Shark River Inlet to get more consistent, not less. I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at first light, work the rock seams slow, and keep a bunker spoon rigged in case the blues show up uninvited — because lately, they have been.

reports.headline: Peconic settles into its August rhythm — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass sliding into a night bite
reports.subhead: Warm, calm water has the bay running on its usual late-summer clock, with porgies stacked on the reefs and stripers waiting for dark and moving current to feed.
reports.body_markdown:
Every August the Peconic settles into the same pattern, and this year is no exception. The bay warms faster than the Sound every spring, and by now, deep into summer, it's holding that heat like a bathtub — calm, clear, and stable. That stability is exactly why the porgy fishing around Shelter Island has been as good as I've seen it in a few seasons, and why the fluke bite, while not blowing anyone's socks off, has been steady enough in the channels to keep rods bent.

Start with the porgies, because right now that's the most reliable thing going. Anchor up in Shelter Island Sound off the North Ferry crossing, or work the drop-offs near Jessup's Neck on the Noyack side, and you'll find them stacked in 15 to 25 feet of water over shell and mixed bottom. Standard hi-lo rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, tipped with clam or squid strips, are doing the job — no need to get fancy. The bite has been best on the last two hours of the incoming tide into the top of high water, when the current slows enough for the porgies to really commit to the bait instead of just picking at it. Some of the fish coming over the rail are pushing into the 2-pound class, which for this bay is a genuinely good porgy. If you're teaching a kid to fish or just want a bucket of dinner, this is your week.

Fluke are a little more of a grind, but they're there if you work the right water. The channels are the play — Greenport's outer channel, the cut through Sag Harbor, and the deeper edges of Noyack Bay where the bottom drops from six feet to fifteen or better. Drifting bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter depending on current, tipped with a strip of squid or a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, has been the most consistent producer. The better drifts have come on the outgoing tide, when bait gets pulled out of the shallows and funnels through the deeper cuts — that's when the bigger fluke seem to wake up and feed instead of just holding tight to bottom. Nobody's filling a cooler with jumbos, but a mixed bag with a few keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range is realistic if you put in the drift time and don't get discouraged by the short fish, which there are plenty of.

Striped bass are the interesting story this week, and it lines up with something we flagged last week — that building tidal flow into the August 12 new moon would start sharpening the bite at current-driven structure. That's exactly what's happening. With the bay sitting warm through the day, the bass have pushed off the flats and are holding in the deeper holes and current lines, mostly feeding after dark or right around dawn when the water temperature eases off a degree or two. Plum Gut is the obvious spot — the current there never really goes to sleep, and as the tidal range builds toward the new moon, that rip is getting some real push behind it. Same story off Orient Point, where the current line forms hard on a strong ebb. Live eels drifted through the rip, or bunker chunks fished on the bottom in the deeper scour holes, have both worked after sundown. Daytime bass fishing in the open bay has been slow and scattered — not worth grinding through the heat of the afternoon when the fish simply aren't feeding.

Bluefish have been quiet in the Peconic proper, though there's a resurgence building to our west on the Sound's deep reef structure that's worth watching. If that pattern pushes east the way these things sometimes do, Orient Point and the mouth of the bay would be the first places to feel it. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but keep a wire leader in the box just in case.

Weakfish remain a wildcard — a few scattered reports of fish taken incidentally while bottom fishing for porgies, nothing you can build a trip around, but worth a passing cast with a bucktail or soft plastic if you're marking bait on the graph and want to check.

As for water clarity, it's holding up nicely for this time of year, which is good news with bay scallop season prep underway — clean water now means an easier time spotting scallop beds when the season opens. That clarity is also part of why the porgy bite has been so visual and consistent; you can practically watch them working the bottom in the shallower spots.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th should be the thing to watch. Tidal range is going to build noticeably over the next several days, and that means sharper current at every pinch point in the bay — Plum Gut, the Orient rip, the North and South Ferry crossings, the mouth of Three Mile Harbor. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd want the last of the outgoing tide at Plum Gut, right as the light fades, with an eel in the water and patience to match. The porgies aren't going anywhere either — that bite should hold steady as long as this warm, settled weather pattern does.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 9:40: stripers deep, bonito still a rip away
reports.subhead: The current's building into the new moon, the bass are holding on structure after dark, and the bonito push is knocking on Block Island's door but hasn't walked in yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack tide hit SW Ledge at 9:40 this morning, and for about twenty minutes the whole rip went flat calm before the ebb grabbed hold again — that's the window I want my clients rigged and ready in, because the first hard push of moving water after slack is when the bass show themselves on the ledge in 35 to 45 feet. This week that window produced, but it wasn't a bell-ringer. We picked at fish rather than loaded the box.

Here's where things stand heading into the August 12 new moon: the tidal range is building fast, and you can feel it in how much harder the ledge is pulling on both the last hour of the ebb and the first hour of the flood. We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep/night bite on stripers would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon tides stirred things up — and that's exactly what's playing out. The bass haven't left, they've just gone conservative. Best fish this week came off SW Ledge after dark, drifting live eels on 3-ounce egg sinkers along the west face where the rip stacks bait against the rock in 30 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing. A couple of fish pushing 30 pounds came off that drift Tuesday night, along with a scattering of schoolies that told me there's still plenty of biomass sitting on that structure, just not stacked tight the way it gets once the current really starts ripping through mid-month.

Now the part I don't sugarcoat: if you're fishing Block Island itself for stripers right now, particularly around Southeast Light and the deeper structure off the south side, be smart about your fight times. The brown sharks have moved into that zone hard this summer, and the mortality rate on released bass that get worked over before they hit the boat is ugly — we're talking somewhere near 90 percent on fish that get chased down after release. If you're keeping your legal fish, fine, but if you're catch-and-release fishing around Block right now, get them up fast, handle them quick, and consider working shallower water off Clay Head or up toward North Light where the sharks haven't set up shop yet. It's not the kind of thing that shows up in a tide table, but it should factor into where you point the bow.

Fluke have been a grind. We're marking bait on the meter around the mussel beds off Sandy Point and in the deeper cuts off the west side, but the drift has been inconsistent — some days you hit six or eight keepers to 4 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips on 3/4-ounce bucktails, other days you burn three hours for two fish. The warm surface water is pushing the better fluke down into 25 to 35 feet where the temperature break holds, so I've been slowing the drift with a sea anchor to keep bait in the strike zone longer instead of covering ground fast. Sea bass have been the more reliable play — the rock piles east of the Ledge and the rubble bottom off Galilee's outer breakwater are holding a steady grade of 14 to 17-inch fish on Asian jigs tipped with squid, especially the first two hours of the incoming when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold bottom.

And then there's the fish everyone's asking about at the dock every single morning: bonito. They are not here yet. I want to be straight about that because I've had three separate charters ask me to run out looking for them this week, and we came up empty every time. What I can tell you is the push through Watch Hill and Sakonnet is real and it's already bled into Buzzards Bay, which is the leading edge of what should be this season's first wave. We called this exact trigger last week too — said the new moon's building current would be what finally pushes bait hard enough through the rips to bring albies and bonito into range at Montauk, Block Island, and the Vineyard corridor. With the moon going new on the 12th and the tidal range already ramping at SW Ledge, I expect the first confirmed fish off Block — likely working the rip off North Light or the current seam running south off Sandy Point — sometime in the next four to seven days. That's not a guess pulled from nowhere; that's the same current mechanics that bring bait piling through those rips every August, just running a few days behind the Rhode Island mainland side this year.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last hour of the outgoing at SW Ledge for stripers after dark, then swing out to North Light at first light and idle the rip with a bucktail rigged and ready in case a bonito shows on the surface. No promises on the albie — but the pieces are lining up, and I'd rather be out there when it happens than reading about it at the dock the next morning.

reports.headline: Gators at the Hook, Fluke Riding Shotgun on the Reefs Behind Them
reports.subhead: Bunker got run down off Sandy Hook Friday and the blues that did it are still around — here's where I'm putting the boat this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Thursday night to skip the back bay entirely this week and run straight for the Hook, and Friday told me I was right before I even had a line in the water. Bunker schools that had been holding off Keyport and up in the flats got pushed tight to the beach on the ocean side of the Hook, and the blues that found them turned it into a real blitz — gators busting bait on the surface right where the sand meets the deep water off the Rip. I said last week that blues would build here as that wave from the north filled in, and that's exactly what happened. No mystery to it: warm bay water in August pushes stripers and bait out toward the cooler edge current at the Hook, and the bluefish follow the bunker right to the beach.

Here's the thing though — this isn't a bay story right now, it's a Hook story. Raritan Bay proper, the flats off Keyport, the Highlands side — that's been a slog. Water's warm, current's soft on the small tides, and the stripers that are still around are hunkered in the deeper holes and not moving much until the sun's off the water. I said it last week and I'll say it again: this zone doesn't really turn over until water starts cooling toward September, and nothing this week changed my mind on that. If you're grinding the flats for bass right now expecting a spring-style bite, you're going to be disappointed. Save that gas.

What I am doing is working the Rip at the Hook on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when the current is ripping hardest against that bottom structure. Bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounce, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and let them swing down through the seam where you can see the color change and the bait balling up. When the blues are actively busting on top I'll switch over to poppers or metal — a Hopkins or an Ava 27 with a single hook, because in a blitz like that you don't need finesse, you need something that gets down through the chop fast and comes back through the strike zone. Fights are short and violent, teeth everywhere, so bring a pair of long-nose pliers and don't put your fingers near the gill plate unless you enjoy stitches.

Fluke are the other piece of this that's actually worth your gas money. The reefs and snags just off the Hook on the ocean side have been quietly improving as that same warm bait push shoves smaller forage up onto the structure. I'm dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the edges of the reef in 25 to 35 feet, slow enough that you feel the bottom tick but fast enough to keep off the rocks. Best window has been the last of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, when the water's still moving but not screaming, and you can hold a controlled drift instead of getting blown through the zone. Nothing gigantic — most fish are 17 to 20 inches — but it's a real bite, and it's a lot more consistent right now than anything happening on the bay-side channel edges, which have gone quiet with the heat.

Porgies are still there if you want an easy box of fish for the table. Romer Shoal and the shallower stretches of Flynn's Knoll are holding scup in decent numbers on bottom rigs with pieces of clam or sandworm, fished right on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the slower part of either tide. It's not exciting fishing but it's dependable, and it's a good option for a family trip when the wind won't cooperate for anything more technical.

Weakfish I'll be honest with you — they're basically a non-factor in the bay right now. A few stragglers get picked up incidentally by fluke guys working soft plastics near the channel edges in the Navesink, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them in August. If you want weakfish, this isn't the month.

Looking ahead, the tidal range is building toward the new moon on the 12th, and that's the piece I'm watching closest. Bigger swings mean harder-running current at structure-driven spots like the Rip and the deeper cuts along the Hook, and that usually sharpens everything — bait gets pinned tighter, predators commit harder, and the bite windows get more defined even if they're shorter. If that plays out the way I expect, I'd look for the blitz activity at the Hook to intensify rather than fade over the next few days, and the fluke bite on the reef edges should hold or even improve as more current moves through. My plan is simple: hit the Rip on the moving water, work the reef drift on the slower stretches, and leave the bay flats alone until the heat breaks. If the wind stays out of the southwest and the bunker keep holding tight to that beach, there's no reason to be anywhere else.

reports.headline: Sakonnet Ledges Holding Tog Tight While the First Bonito Nose Into Charlestown Breachway
reports.subhead: Green crabs are disappearing off the rocks on the slack, and the bait pushing through Charlestown says the run might start early this year.
reports.body_markdown:
Walked the base of the cliffs below Second Beach Tuesday morning and the water was full of silversides, tight against the rock, moving in that nervous little shimmer they get when something's under them. Couldn't tell you what — the water's murky enough this week that I never got a visual — but that kind of bait behavior along the wash usually means bass are working underneath, and by the second cast on a black Slug-Go I had my answer. Nothing big, mid-20s mostly, but they were there, tucked against the base of the rock where the wash meets the ledge.

That's been the story all along this stretch since the middle of July — stripers holding deep and tight to structure, feeding at night or right at the edges of light, not showing themselves in the middle of the day. We flagged this pattern a week back and said it'd hold until either the water cooled or the new moon tide stirred things up. Well, the new moon's Wednesday, and you can already feel the tidal range building. Second Beach, the rocks off Gooseberry, the ledges under Sachuest — all of it's pushing more current on this week's tides than it was ten days ago, and the fish know it before we do.

Tog fishing has been the most reliable thing going. I've been working the ledges off Jamestown — the rockpile off Fort Wetherill, the drop just outside Mackerel Cove — dropping green crabs on a simple two-hook rig, 2 to 3 ounces depending on the drift, right into the cracks on the last hour of the ebb into dead slack. That slack window is everything with tog. Too much current and you're just getting your rig swept off the structure; give me that quiet 20-30 minutes either side of the turn and I'm picking fish out of the same three or four cracks every trip. Nothing huge yet — mostly 14 to 17 inches, a few pushing 20 — but they're eating well and they're not hard to find if you know which rock holds them. The ledge just north of the Jamestown Bridge on the east side has been quietly good, deeper water, maybe 18 to 25 feet, less crowded than the usual spots.

Now for the part everybody's been asking about. Charlestown Breachway has bait pushing through it on every tide right now — bunker peanuts and some early silversides getting funneled through that cut, and Tuesday evening I watched something come through and slash at the surface right at the mouth on the last of the outgoing. Didn't hook up, didn't even get a real look, but that kind of surface commotion in early August at a breachway mouth has one likely explanation this time of year, and the intel I'm hearing out of the Buzzards Bay side backs it up — bonito have already crossed over and they're pushing this way on the warm water riding in with these building tides. I wouldn't call it a run yet. One push of bait, one flash of something working it, that's not a green light — but it's exactly the kind of signal that tells you to start carrying a bonito rod in the truck instead of leaving it home.

If you want to be there when it happens, Watch Hill and Napatree are the two spots I'd have eyes on this week. Napatree because the current wraps the point hard on the ebb and pushes bait right along that outer bar, and Watch Hill because the reef off the point holds structure that current-run bait always finds. Small metal — half-ounce to an ounce, Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters in that silver/chartreuse pattern — is what you want rigged and ready. Cast into the froth, don't overthink the retrieve, just get it moving.

Bluefish have been showing some life again after being quiet most of July, which tracks with what's been happening on deeper structure elsewhere in the region. I picked up a few choppers to 6 pounds off the Sakonnet rocks near the Point, working poppers on the last hour of daylight into dusk. Not blitz conditions, just steady enough that if you're out there for stripers or albies you should have a bluefish plug tied on as backup, because they'll eat before the bass show and save an otherwise slow hour.

Fluke has been the disappointment this week. I've made a couple of drifts off Point Judith and through the deeper water outside Sakonnet Point and it's mostly shorts, a few keepers mixed in but nothing to write home about. Water's warm enough that the bigger fish may have pushed to cooler, deeper structure than I was fishing. Scup fishing, on the other hand, has been a nice consolation prize — drop a piece of clam or squid strip around any of the Jamestown or Newport bridge structure and you'll have a bucket of dinner fish in under an hour, which isn't glamorous but it's honest fishing when everything else is being stubborn.

Looking at the week ahead — the new moon Wednesday is going to push the tidal range hard, and that's the ingredient this whole zone has been waiting on. The tog bite should stay steady through the stronger currents as long as you're patient for that slack window. The striper pattern should sharpen at current-driven spots like the Jamestown Bridge rips and the Sakonnet Point rocks as the flow builds. And if that bonito push we saw a hint of Tuesday is real, the next four or five days around the new moon tides are exactly when it should show itself hard at Charlestown, Napatree, and Watch Hill. I'd have a bonito outfit rigged before I'd bother chasing fluke this week — the odds are better, and the payoff's a lot more fun.

reports.headline: Midnight Ebb at the Inlet: Bass Deep, Weakfish Working the Bridge Pilings
reports.subhead: The tide's building into the new moon and I'm choosing my hours accordingly — outgoing after dark at the inlet, incoming at dusk under Ponquogue.
reports.body_markdown:
I made a decision on Tuesday night that cost me sleep and paid me back in stripers: skip the first two hours of the outgoing and wait for the back half, after midnight, when the current at the inlet really starts to move water off the flats. That's when the deep hole on the ocean side of the east jetty turns from a maybe into a sure bet. Two bass in the mid-20s, one push past 30 inches, all on a live eel drifted down along the rock face where the current cuts hardest against the wall. If you're fishing this spot on the front of the tide, in my experience you're just soaking bait in slack water and wondering why nothing's happening. Wait for the push.

That's the whole game at Shinnecock right now — timing, not just location. We flagged this last week, said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at the inlet. The tidal range is stacking up night over night, and with it the flow through that gut between the jetties is getting stronger, pulling more bait and holding more fish tight to structure on the last two hours of the ebb. If you've got one night to burn between now and the new moon, burn it late — 11 PM to 2 AM outgoing, working bunker chunks or eels along the rocks, has been the most consistent window I've fished all month.

Ponquogue Bridge is running its own clock. That spot wants the opposite tide — incoming, right at dusk into full dark, when the current sets up along the pilings on the Hampton Bays side and the weakfish move up out of the deeper bay water to feed. I had a mixed night out there Thursday: three weakfish in the 18 to 20 inch range, all on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, bounced slow off bottom in maybe 15 to 18 feet right where the shadow line from the bridge lights meets open water. Lost two more to short strikes that felt like blues, not weakfish — and sure enough, the bluefish have started showing up under those lights too, which tells me the bait's thick enough to draw both species into the same water. If you're throwing bucktails at the bridge right now, downsize a little — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce heads move slower and stay in that strike zone longer, which matters more than color right now given how stained the bay's running after the last few days of onshore wind.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been honest work, not a gimme. The drift from the Tiana Beach flats down toward the canal mouth has produced keepers, but you're covering ground to find them — the fish are scattered, not schooled up tight the way they were in June. Four-inch white Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow over the sand-to-mud transitions in 8 to 12 feet, has out-produced bare bait two to one for me this week. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming, when clean ocean water is still pushing through the inlet and hasn't fully mixed with the warmer, murkier bay water yet. Wait too long into the tide and the water turns the color of coffee with milk, and the bite dies with it.

Porgies and blackfish are around the usual structure — the rocks off the inlet, the bridge abutments — but truthfully I haven't put much time into them this week. When the striper bite's on at night and the weakfish are showing at the bridge, that's where my hours go. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod during daylight, porgies on the inlet rocks with clam and squid strips will still do it, but it's a different kind of fishing than what's got my attention right now.

The canal's worth a mention because a few guys have been running through to the Peconic side chasing bait schools, and the current through there has been ripping hard on the bigger tides this week — which tracks with everything else. More water moving means more bait getting pushed and pulled through every choke point in this system, from the canal gates to the bridge pilings to the inlet jetties. That's good news if you're willing to fish the hours when the current's actually working for you, and mediocre news if you're set in your ways about fishing daylight and high water because that's when everyone else shows up.

Looking ahead to the new moon on the 12th, I expect the pattern to keep sharpening rather than change. Bigger tidal swings mean stronger current at the inlet, which should keep pulling bass into that deep hole on the late outgoing, and it should keep pushing bait up against the bridge pilings on the incoming for the weakfish. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't stir the bay into chocolate milk, I'd plan on fishing the inlet late Thursday or Friday night around the peak of the new moon tide — that's when I expect the strongest flow of the week. Just don't sleep on the fact that this bite rewards patience and bad hours more than it rewards showing up whenever's convenient.

reports.headline: Why did the fluke move into 4 feet of water? A lesson from the Absecon sod banks
reports.subhead: Bunker pushed shallow, the bass went to the basement, and the building tide into the new moon is about to sharpen every inlet from Brigantine to Stone Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
Every August I get some version of the same question leaning on the bait shop counter: "Professor, why was my fluke drift stone dead at 9 AM and stacked with keepers by 11?" It's a fair question, and the answer this week is written all over the sod banks. Bait moved shallow. The fluke followed. If you didn't move with them, you fished an empty classroom.

Here's the lesson plan. Peanut bunker and rainfish have pushed hard onto the flats behind Absecon Inlet — the same sod bank edges that run along the Brigantine side channel — and fluke have tucked in tight to ambush them in 4 to 8 feet of water. The bite window is the last two hours of the outgoing, when that water drains off the flat and funnels bait past the drop-offs. A half-ounce bucktail tipped with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom right where the sod gives way to the channel, has been the difference-maker. Guys throwing straight bucktail without the trailer are getting bit less — the fluke want that extra wag right now, not a fast retrieve.

Over at Great Egg, the pattern flips a little. That inlet holds deeper structure — 15 to 20 feet in the main channel — and the better-grade fluke, the 4- and 5-pound class, are showing on the incoming rather than the outgoing. Chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp mullet trailer, bounced slow along the channel edges near the rock piles, have out-produced the plain white presentation there. It's not a huge bite — you're working for four or five keepers on a good tide — but the fish are real, and they're better sized than what's coming off the flats.

Now, the bluefish. We flagged this pattern last week — scattered peanut bunker schools, blues roaming on them, blitzes showing in the early morning window — and that's exactly what's playing out at Townsends Inlet and along the Ocean City beachfront right now. Dawn patrol has been the move: peanut bunker balled up tight against the beach, blues busting through them just after first light, gone by the time the sun's fully up and the water warms. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — cast into the froth has been getting bit fast and hard. By 8 AM the show's usually over for the day, so if you're not on the sand before sunrise, you're watching it happen instead of fishing it.

Stripers are a tougher conversation, and we called this too — daytime surf bass have all but vanished, pushed to deeper, cooler refuge, and any action has been strictly a dawn-and-dusk affair. That's held up all week. If you want a shot at a keeper bass, you're fishing the last legal light or the first legal light, working the deeper channel edges at Great Egg and the mouth of Absecon Inlet where the current runs hardest. A bunker chunk fished on the bottom, tight to the drop where the channel meets the flat, has out-produced artificials for the few fish being caught. It's not a numbers game right now — it's patience and the right thirty minutes of tide.

Weakfish are still a back bay night bite. The channels behind Brigantine and the deeper holes off Longport have given up a scattered mix of weakfish in the 16- to 20-inch range to guys chunking bunker after dark on the last of the outgoing. It's not consistent enough to plan a whole trip around, but if you're already out there for bass or fluke and you stay past dark, it's worth a soak.

Kingfish are doing what kingfish do in August — working the first bar trough at Ocean City and Sea Isle City on sand fleas and bloodworm bits fished on a simple hi-lo rig. It's a light-tackle, kid-and-a-lawn-chair kind of bite, but it's steady, and it's one of the more reliable things going in the surf right now while the bass sulk in deeper water.

And for the structure guys — triggerfish are holding on the rock jetties at both Absecon and Townsends Inlets, taking small pieces of clam or squid fished tight to the rocks on light tackle. It's a niche bite, but it fills a slow afternoon when the tide's wrong for everything else.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon on the 12th, and that means increasing tidal range and stronger current through every inlet on this stretch. That's good news for structure-oriented fishing — sharper current at Absecon and Great Egg should tighten up the fluke bite on the sod banks and give the bass a reason to feed a little more aggressively on the edges during those brief low-light windows. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the outgoing at Absecon at first light, work the sod bank edges hard for an hour, then slide over to the inlet mouth for the last of the ebb hoping to intercept a bass on the move. It's not a sure thing, but the tide's about to do some of the work for you — that's the kind of week it is.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Puts a 29-Pound Bass on the Sand
reports.subhead: Building tide into the new moon is stacking bait at the river mouths, but the bluefish are still playing hard to find.
reports.body_markdown:
Thursday evening, forty minutes into the incoming at the Pool, a guy I've fished alongside for fifteen years hooked a striper that buried the rod tip into the rocks and didn't let up for what felt like ten minutes. Twenty-nine pounds, caught on a black Gibbs pencil popper worked slow and choppy off the outer bar where the current pours in against the rocks. That's the Pool doing what it does best — it's the single best hour of striper fishing in Southern Maine, that first push of green water sliding over the flats and funneling bait and bass together into a tight seam you can cover with two dozen well-placed casts.

I've been saying for a couple weeks now that the building tide into this new moon would sharpen up the current-driven spots, and here we are — Biddeford Pool, Wells Harbor, the mouth of the Kennebunk River, all fishing better on the last two days than they did the whole back half of July. The moon's pulling harder water through those inlets now, more current means more bait getting swept and confused, and a confused school of mackerel or pogies in three feet of moving water is exactly what a striper wants to see. If you fish the Pool, get there on the bottom of the tide and stay through the first two hours of the flood. That's your window. After that the current slackens, the fish spread out over the flats, and the bite gets a lot more patient.

Up the beach at Kennebunk, the river mouth has been holding fish right where the outflow meets the surf line — schoolies mostly, 18 to 24 inches, but mixed in with the occasional slot fish pushing 30. Live mackerel under a slip float, or a swimming plug like a Yo-Zuri Mag Darter worked with a stop-start retrieve through the current seam, has been the ticket there on the outgoing. The river's pushing warmer water out into cooler ocean water and that edge is holding bait tight.

Mackerel have been thick off the Cape Elizabeth ledges and around the back side of Prouts Neck, and that's been a blessing for anybody willing to run out and jig a few before hitting the beach. Small diamond jigs, no bait needed, and you can load a cooler in twenty minutes some mornings. Fresh mackerel filleted into strips has been outfishing anything artificial for the bigger bass holding deeper around the Prouts Neck boulders — fish it on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that rocky wash, and be ready for the rod to load up hard because the fish down there this time of year tend to run heavier.

Bluefish are the frustrating part of the report this week. I keep hearing guys ask about Higgins Beach blitzes and I have to be honest — it hasn't happened yet, not the kind of surface-churning, birds-diving event we all want to see. What I am seeing is scattered pods, three or four fish busting bait for a few minutes and then going quiet, mostly early morning on the outgoing tide with a light southwest wind pushing bait tight to the beach. If you're throwing metal — a Hopkins or a Kastmaster — keep one rigged and ready when you're plugging for bass at Higgins, because those blues show up without much warning and vanish just as fast. The Prouts Neck side, with that southwest wind funneling bait around the point, has produced a similar pattern — brief windows, worth being patient for, but nothing you can plan a whole trip around yet.

Flounder guys have had a quieter but more dependable week. Wells Harbor has been giving up decent flounder on bloodworms and clam strips fished on a simple two-hook bottom rig, best on the last of the ebb when the water's clean and slack enough to hold bottom without dragging. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and it's a good option on the days the wind kicks up and makes the open beaches unfishable.

Cod remain mostly a deeper-water story right now — the ledges off Cape Elizabeth still hold fish for the boat guys working jigs and bait near bottom, but inshore action from the rocks has been slow, which is normal for August. That fishery really wakes up as the water starts cooling into September and October, so if cod are your target, patience is the play for another month or so.

Looking ahead to the new moon on the 12th, I expect the tidal range to keep building and the current-driven spots to keep sharpening right along with it. The Pool should keep producing on that incoming push, and I'd watch Kennebunk and the York River mouths closely too as the extra flow stirs bait loose. Southern Maine's still sitting well behind the warmer water to our south — no albies, no bonito up here, and I don't expect that to change — but the stripers don't seem to mind the cold Gulf of Maine water one bit. If the wind stays out of the southwest and the tides keep building like they have been, I'd put my money on the Pool again next week, timed right on that bottom-of-the-tide push, pencil popper in hand.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Rip Sharpens as the New Moon Tide Builds
reports.subhead: Bass are holding tight to the sub base bait schools while snapper blues rule the shallows off Ocean Beach.
reports.body_markdown:
Standing on the Fort Trumbull wall Tuesday evening, I watched the ebb line pull harder than it had in three weeks — the seam where the river current meets the harbor swell was throwing a visible wake off the point, something you only see when the tidal range starts stretching toward a new moon. That's exactly what's happening. We're four days out from the August 12 new moon and the Thames is starting to feel it, the current running with more authority through the narrows off the sub base and around the Gold Star Bridge pilings. We flagged this last week — said building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's precisely what's unfolding on the river this week.

The striper pattern hasn't changed much from late July, but it's gotten more reliable as the current has firmed up. Fish are stacked around the bait schools off the submarine base, holding in 15 to 20 feet of water where the river channel drops off the flats. This is warm-summer behavior — bass parking on structure with quick access to deep water, not chasing bait around open water in the heat. New London's reading around 69 degrees at the surface, which is comfortable enough that the fish aren't forced deep, but they're not roaming far from cover either. The best window has been the last two hours of the ebb into dead low, when bait gets funneled down through the channel and the bass set up on the downstream side of the pilings to ambush it. Bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig, 3 to 4 ounces of lead depending on how hard the current's running, fished tight to the base of the Gold Star Bridge pilings has been the most consistent producer — mostly schoolies and low-slot fish in the 24 to 28 inch range, with the occasional better fish mixed in on the deeper drifts past Fort Trumbull.

Bucktails are working too, especially on the top of the flood when bait pushes up into the harbor. A 1.5-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullet, cast up-current and swept back through the rip off Fort Trumbull has drawn strikes from fish holding on the current seam itself — you can see them boil there some evenings when the light gets low. It's not fast fishing. You might make thirty casts to draw three or four hits, but the fish that come are solid, and the rip concentrates them enough that it's worth the repetition.

Bluefish are the real story right now, and they're following the same regional trend we've seen building elsewhere in the Sound — a resurgence after a flat July. The shallows off Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach are thick with snapper blues, small enough to be a kids' fishery but numerous enough to keep a rod bent all afternoon on tiny Kastmasters or a bit of bait on a size 6 hook under a bobber. What's more interesting is the adult blues showing up mixed in with the bass around the sub base bait schools — I had a 4-pounder hit a bucktail meant for stripers off the bridge pilings Wednesday, and heard of a few similar fish taken on Ava jigs worked through the deeper water off Fort Trumbull on the outgoing tide. If that pattern holds and more of those bigger blues push up-river behind the bait, it could turn into a legitimate mixed bag fishery through the rest of August.

Porgies are still around if you want a change of pace — working bloodworms or clam on the bottom near the State Pier moorings and around any rock piles in the harbor in 10 to 15 feet of water has been steady, nothing spectacular but good for a bucket of dinner fish on a slow tide. I haven't put much time into blackfish yet; that pattern doesn't really turn on for us until the water starts cooling toward fall, and we're not there.

What's driving all of this is fairly straightforward. The building tidal range ahead of the new moon is pushing more water through the narrows at the sub base and past Fort Trumbull, which stirs bait out of the shallows and forces it to run the gauntlet past waiting stripers and blues. The wider the swing between high and low, the more pronounced that effect gets — and we're only going to see the range increase through the weekend and into early next week as the new moon approaches on the 12th.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the pattern to keep sharpening rather than change. If the current keeps building the way it has the last few days, the last two hours of the ebb at Fort Trumbull and the top of the flood through the bridge pilings should keep producing bass and the occasional bigger blue right through the new moon. I'd fish the rip with bucktails on the flood and switch to chunk bait on the pilings once the tide turns hard toward low. It's not blow-up fishing, but it's honest, and the structure here doesn't lie — when the current runs like this, the fish show up where it funnels the bait, same as it's always been on this river.

reports.headline: August 8, and Washington Is Still Running Its Own Clock
reports.subhead: The canyon that fires early hasn't cooled off yet — yellowfin, mahi, and a scattering of white marlin are keeping the troll and chunk boats busy while everyone waits on the new moon push.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the thing about Washington that guys from the other canyons never quite get: by the time August rolls around, we're not starting a season, we're managing one. This canyon back in June when Wilmington and Baltimore were still waiting on their water to turn, and now that everybody else is finally catching up, we're just cruising through the meat of it. That's not luck. That's position. We sit closer to the Stream's northern lean than most people give us credit for, and every year it plays out the same way — early June push, strong July, and an August that either holds the pattern or slides sideways depending on what the water to our south decides to do.

Right now it's holding. Boats working the edge and the wall have been finding yellowfin on the troll during the day — small ballyhoo behind Green Machines and cedar plugs, the usual 100-fathom-plus water where the color goes that deep cobalt blue and you can see the temp break if the light's right. Chunking bunker after dark off the drop-off has been the more consistent play this week, though I want to be straight with you — it's not a wire-to-wire bite. Some nights the chunk slick draws fish up fast and you're doubled up inside twenty minutes; other nights you're sitting on a dead slick for two hours before anything shows. That's the nature of August on a canyon edge that isn't getting a hard, reliable current push yet. The tide's building toward the new moon on the 12th, and once that tidal range really kicks in, the current lines along the wall are going to sharpen up, and so will the bite. I'd rather fish the two days before and after that new moon than a random Tuesday in the current lull we're in now.

Mahi have been scattered but there when you find the right piece of structure — any weed line or floating junk outside the edge is worth a stop, even a five-minute stop, because a school of gaffers under a mat of sargassum will make your whole day. Small stuff too, schoolies in the 2-3 pound range mixed in, so bring light spinning gear rigged with a bare hook and a chunk of butterfish alongside your trolling spread. It costs you nothing to slow down and look.

White marlin have shown, not in numbers that make headlines, but enough that if you're pulling naked ballyhoo or small skirted baits on the troll along the temperature breaks, you've got a real shot. These fish are still moving through on their own schedule and Washington tends to get a piece of that traffic earlier than the canyons south of us, which tracks with everything else about how this place runs. Wahoo have been mixed into the yellowfin bite on the high-speed spread — if you're not running at least one bait at 12-14 knots with wire, you're leaving that fish on the table.

Bigeye are the wildcard right now. We're not into the heart of that pattern yet — that usually doesn't build here until deeper into August — but the deep-drop squid chunk crowd fishing at night has started picking off a few, which tells me the door's cracking open earlier than usual again. I wouldn't build a whole trip around bigeye yet, but if you're out there overnight anyway for yellowfin, it costs nothing to drop a bait deep once the sun's down.

Now, the thing worth watching. There's a mild cooling nudge working its way up from the canyons south of us, and if that strengthens and pushes north, it could reshuffle where the bait and the tuna are holding along our edge — potentially compressing fish tighter to the wall, or in a worse case, pulling some of that biomass south with it. We flagged this exact setup last week and said conditions should hold steady unless a shift came up from the south — and that's exactly what's happened. Nothing's moved yet. The water out here has stayed steady, the pattern's intact, and the fish are still where they've been. But I'm not going to pretend that signal isn't on my radar, because if it firms up, it changes where I send people next week.

For the next few days, my money's on the edge holding its current character — daytime troll for yellowfin and the occasional white marlin, mahi under any debris you cross, wahoo mixed in on the high-speed lines, and a chunk bite after dark that rewards patience more than it rewards showing up late. Once we get inside that 48-hour window around the new moon, I expect the current to sharpen and the bite to tighten up with it — that's when I'd want to be out there, not during the slack stretch we're in right now. If the southern cooling signal holds off, Washington keeps doing what Washington does in August: producing quietly while everybody else is just getting started.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Last of the Ebb: Bluefish Come Back to the Deep Reef
reports.subhead: After a dead July, blues are stacking on the drop-offs again — stripers are there too, but you have to grind for them.
reports.body_markdown:
I picked Cockenoe on purpose this week, not Penfield, and not because it's my default August spot. Cockenoe's north side has that long rocky shelf that drops from eight feet down to twenty-eight in about sixty yards, and on the last two hours of the ebb that shelf turns into a funnel. Bait gets swept off the flat, piles up right at the lip of the drop, and anything hunting knows exactly where to look. That's where I found the bluefish again — and after a quiet July on this stretch of the Sound, that mattered.

The blues showed up exactly where the deep structure sets up: the outside edge of Cockenoe, the rockpile drop-off south of Penfield Reef, and the deeper contour lines running off Sheffield Island. These aren't the shoreline snappers you're fending off with poppers all summer — this is a better class of fish, mid-teens on the scale for a few of them, holding tighter to structure than you'd expect for bluefish. Diamond jigs in half-ounce and one-ounce, worked with a jigging motion off bottom on the last of the ebb, got bit consistently. If you've got poppers, work the surface at first light before the boat traffic starts — Cockenoe gets crowded fast on a summer Saturday, and once the wake traffic starts crossing that shelf, the bite shuts down. Early or late, that's the window.

We flagged this pattern last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12th new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what showed up. The tidal range is stretching out day by day as we run up on the new moon, and every reef in this system that depends on current — Cockenoe, Penfield, the ledges off Greenwich Point — is starting to fish harder on both the ebb and the flood instead of just sitting dead on the tide change.

Stripers are around, but I won't oversell it. The pattern out here is what it's been most of the summer — you find them at night, deep, and mostly on the move. A few better fish, 40-plus pounds, have come off the west end near Greenwich Point on plastic eels fished slow along bottom, dead-sticked on the drift through the last hour of the flood into the first hour of the ebb. That's a tight window and it's not a volume game. If you want numbers instead of size, work the Cows off Stamford at night with bucktails tipped with a swimming mullet trailer, working the deeper mud-and-rock bottom in twenty-five to thirty-five feet. You'll get schoolies mixed with the occasional keeper, but you have to put in the hours after dark — daytime action on bass has been thin with this water warm and this much pleasure-boat pressure running over the reefs.

Fluke are the frustrating part of the report right now. Western Sound fluke have been small and scattered all summer, and this week didn't change that. I worked the channels between the Norwalk Islands — the deeper cuts around Sheffield and the flats off the back side — dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, and I covered a lot of water for a handful of shorts and one fish that just cleared the ruler. If you're set on fluke, fish the deeper water on the last of the outgoing where current concentrates bait against the channel edges, and don't expect a fast bag.

Porgies are the one thing out here that's been dependable without any qualifiers. The Cows off Stamford are thick with them in thirty to forty feet of water over that mixed mud-and-rock bottom — sandworms or clam on a simple high-low rig, fished on the slack ahead of the ebb, will load the cooler. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and it's a good option on a day when the wind's up and you don't want to fight the open reefs.

Black sea bass are holding up well on the rockpiles around Sheffield Island and the deeper structure off Penfield — squid strips or Gulp on a jighead worked slow along bottom in twenty-five to thirty feet is putting keepers in the box, and that pattern should hold with little change through the rest of August. Blackfish are still off the table here — CT's summer closure keeps tog protected through spawning, and I wouldn't waste time targeting them until the season reopens later this month. Worth scouting the rockpiles now, though, so you know exactly where to drop once it's legal.

Looking ahead, the building tide into the August 12th new moon should keep sharpening the current-driven spots — expect the bluefish bite on the deep reef edges to hold or improve as bait keeps getting pushed off the flats on stronger ebbs. Stripers should stay a night pattern until water temps ease later in the month. If I had one day this week, I'd fish Cockenoe at first light on the ebb before the boat traffic arrives, then slide over to the Cows for porgies once the sun's up and the reef bite cools off. That's a realistic day, not a guaranteed one — but it's where the structure and the tide line up right now.

reports.headline: Bluefish Break Their Silence on Middle Ground and 11B as Bunker Pile In
reports.subhead: After weeks of guys asking me where the blues went, the deep reef structure west of Stepping Stones is finally holding fish again — and the timing lines up with what I told you last week.
reports.body_markdown:
I had three separate guys at the bait shop this week ask me the same question: "Frank, where the hell did the blues go?" One of them had fished four trips in July out of City Island without touching a bluefish, and he wanted to know if I thought they'd skipped the Sound entirely this year. I told him what I've told guys for thirty years — bluefish don't leave, they relocate to where the bait is thick enough to be worth the trip. And this week, that bait finally showed up on the deep reef structure, and the blues followed right behind it.

Middle Ground, 11B, and 28C — the deep humps and rockpiles that hold current year after year — are holding real bluefish again after a quiet July. I heard of a 16-pound fish weighed off one of those pieces, which is a genuinely good bluefish for the Western Sound, not some snapper-sized junk fish. What changed is simple: bunker and peanut bunker have finally concentrated tight to that structure instead of spreading out through open water, and predators go where the food is stacked, not where the water looks pretty. If you've been marking bait balls on your finder anywhere near those reefs, don't motor past them — drop a bunker spoon or a diamond jig with a tube teaser right through the school and hang on.

Striped bass are still the more consistent story, and they're still playing the same game I flagged last week — deep and after dark. Execution Rocks continues to be the most reliable piece of structure in this whole stretch, and the outgoing tide there is still stacking bass against the rockpile the way it has for decades. I heard about a 45-pound-class fish taken on a plastic eel worked slow along the bottom on the tail end of the ebb — that's a night bite, gentlemen, not a midday program right now. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and that's warm enough to push the biggest fish down and back into low light. Stepping Stones is holding up the same way — work the rip line off the light on the last two hours of the outgoing, drift a live eel or a bunker chunk down current, and be patient. These fish aren't schooled up and blitzing bait on the surface. They're sitting deep, feeding on the move of current, and you need to be in the right spot when the tide's doing the work for you.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the deep, current-driven bite would hold until either the water cools off or the new moon tides start stirring things up — and that's exactly what's setting up now. The new moon hits August 12, and the tidal range is already building. That means stronger current through Execution Rocks, sharper rips off Stepping Stones, and more water moving through the reef structure where those bluefish are staging. If the pattern holds the way it usually does around here, expect the bite at all that current-driven structure to sharpen up over the next several days, not slow down.

Fluke, I'll be honest with you, remain a mixed bag on this side of the Sound. Western ports are still mostly turning up shorts — plenty of action if you don't mind culling through a lot of 15-inch fish to find a keeper. Matinecock Point and the mouth of Manhasset Bay have both produced some decent drifts, but you're working for it. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 25 to 35 feet, are still the go-to combo. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, slow your drift down and add a strip of squid to the hook — sometimes that extra scent is the difference between a dink and a keeper this time of year.

Weakfish have been scattered but present — a few decent fish coming out of Hempstead Harbor on soft plastics fished slow near bottom structure, nothing to build a trip around but worth a cast or two if you're already anchored up for bass or porgies. Porgies themselves have been steady off the deeper rockpiles around Hart Island, small hooks and clam baits on the bottom doing the job like they always do this time of year — good action if you want to fill a cooler without much drama.

Looking ahead, I'd put my money on the bluefish pattern continuing to build through the weekend as that new moon current strengthens and pushes more bait tight to the reef structure. Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones should keep producing after dark on the outgoing for bass, especially if that warm surface layer holds and keeps pushing the bigger fish deep. If you're chasing fluke, don't expect miracles — cover water, cull hard, and take the keepers when they come. The Sound's giving up fish right now, just not in the same spot for every species, so plan your trip around what the tide and the calendar are telling you, not what worked last month.

reports.headline: Ran to Wilmington on the troll, not the chunk — three yellowfin and a mahi for six hours of gas
reports.subhead: The warm-core water is still stacked on the canyon edge, and this week trolling out-produced sitting still with a chunk bucket.
reports.body_markdown:
Made the call Tuesday night before I even looked at the forecast twice: we were trolling Wilmington, not chunking. That's not always the right call this time of year — some weeks the fish want dead bait sitting still over a temp break and you're throwing away gas running a spread — but the water we've had lately told me troll. When the edge is sharp and the fish are moving through instead of parking on bait, you cover ground and make them find you. That's exactly the kind of week this was.

We ran out around 4 a.m., a flat calm ride, which by itself tells you something — this time of August you don't get many mornings like that, and I wasn't going to waste it sitting at the dock. Found the water we wanted along the northeast corner of the canyon, right where the shelf breaks steep into deep color. Blue-to-green transition, current pushing hard enough that the ballyhoo were leaning in the spread the second we cleared the pattern. That's the kind of edge that's worth burning fuel to reach — a real seam, not a smear on a chart that's three days old.

Spread was standard for this water this time of year: naked ballyhoo staggered short and long riggers, a couple of Green Machines and a purple/black Ilander pulled off the long corner, cedar plug way back to pick off anything sulking behind the pattern. First fish came on the short rigger ballyhoo about forty minutes into the troll — yellowfin, mid-40s, textbook strike right at the edge where the color went from washed-out green to that deep cobalt. Two more came through in the next hour, one on the Ilander, one on a naked bally, all within a quarter mile of that same stretch. Then it went quiet for almost three hours. That's the honest part of this report — it wasn't a bite that lasted all day, it was a window, and we happened to be in it. We picked up a mahi, a decent one, maybe 15 pounds, on the long corner ballyhoo trolling through some scattered weed lines south of where we'd been working the tuna. No wahoo for us this trip, though the water's right for them — clean, blue, that kind of edge usually holds one skulking somewhere in the spread if you're running a wire line back deep, which we didn't have out this trip. Lesson for next time.

No white marlin came tight to the boat, but we had two respectable teasers — one that never committed, one that we tried to pitch a naked ballyhoo to and blew the shot. That fish is out there. The kind of edge we were on, with bait balled up and current pushing, is exactly where you expect to raise them mid-morning once the sun gets up and the temp break sharpens visually. If I had another day out there this week I'd rig a pitch bait ready to go the second we see a bill, not scramble for it.

Here's the bigger picture on why this bite is happening at all. The warm-core water sitting over the canyon has held its position for a couple weeks now, and that's kept bait and fish oriented on that same northeast stretch instead of scattering. Bluefin have been showing up unusually close to the Jersey beach this summer, which tells you the whole shelf is running warm and pushing that thermal boundary further inshore than normal — good for beach guys, and it's part of why the offshore pattern out at the canyon has stayed so consistent. The concerning piece, if there is one, is a modest cooling signal that's shown up in water further south the last few days. Nothing that's touched Wilmington yet, but if that cooler water pushes north it could reshuffle where the bait sits and drag the bite off that northeast corner. I'd rather know that now than get surprised by it Saturday.

Fuel-wise, this was a break-even trip at best — three yellowfin and a mahi doesn't fill the boat, but it covers the day and puts fish on the dock, and that's the math that matters running a business out of Cape May. If the same warm water holds through the weekend, I'd make the same call again: troll the edge early, work the corner hard in that first light window, and have a chunk bag ready as a Plan B if the current lays down and the fish stop chasing. What I wouldn't do is sit and chunk cold on a moving current with fish clearly transiting instead of holding — that's a good way to watch bait soak all day.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward new phase on the 12th, which usually sharpens current and can concentrate bait tighter along the break — worth watching for a stronger bite window rather than a longer one. If that southern cooling signal stays put and doesn't creep north, I like our odds of finding yellowfin and mahi in that same stretch again this week, with a real shot at a white marlin now that the teasers are working. If it pushes up into Wilmington, we adjust and go find the new edge — that's the job.

reports.headline: Deer Island Drop Stays Deep at Noon, Nahant Rocks Wake Up After Dark
reports.subhead: Harbor bass are feeding on schedule while the North Shore rockpile bite has shifted almost entirely to the low-light hours.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday to work the harbor islands first this week instead of running straight out to Nahant, and it was the right one. With the surface running warm everywhere south of the Cape, the fish up here haven't gone fully nocturnal — but they have gotten smart about the sun. Deer Island Light and the drop-off along President Roads are still giving up bass in daylight, just not in the top ten feet anymore. You want the edge where the flat drops from twenty into thirty-five feet on the outgoing tide, working a live mackerel on a three-way rig with just enough lead to hold bottom without hanging up on the rubble. That current seam off the Deer Island cut has been holding stripers from 28 to 38 inches all week, mixed with a scattering of overslot fish that come up once, thump the mackerel, and go straight back down into the ledge.

Spectacle Island's north side has been the sneaky producer — the drop into the shipping channel gives bass a highway to move bait through on the tide change, and a slow-trolled umbrella rig with mackerel-colored tubes has been drawing strikes in that 25 to 30 foot band starting an hour before the top of the flood. It's not fast fishing. You might make eight or ten passes before you connect, but the fish that come are quality, and there's enough bait stacked in the harbor right now — mackerel schools have been thick from Long Island Head clear down past Georges Island — that the bass have every reason to stay put instead of pushing out to open water.

Nahant is a different story right now, and it's worth being honest about it. Egg Rock and the Bass Point ledges were money at first light two weeks ago; this week the noon bite there has gone dead flat. The rocks are holding fish, but they've pulled into the deeper pockets and won't touch a topwater plug until the sun drops. If you want that classic North Shore surface bite — Rebel Jumping Minnows and Guppy poppers working the white water off the boulders — you're fishing the last hour of daylight into dark, or picking it up again at first light before the sun hits the water. Bluefish have moved into that same window, and they're not shy about it. A fresh wave has clearly pushed down out of the Gulf of Maine over the last week, because the blues showing up at Nahant and off Gloucester's back shore are bigger than what we had in June — three to five pounds, blitzing bait right up against the rocks at Bass Point and off Brace Cove. Poppers, metal, anything fast and loud will draw them up.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady conditions with no real disruption coming — and that's exactly what's played out. No fronts, no big temperature swing, just the harbor and North Shore settling into their August rhythm: bass deep and structure-bound at midday, bluefish and topwater bass at the margins of the day.
