Up around Cape Ann, Halibut Point and the ledges off Rockport are holding the same mackerel-and-bass pattern as Nahant, just a few degrees cooler, which is buying an extra hour or two of daylight activity on the outer ledges. If you've got a boat that can handle the run out past the Dry Salvages, there are still schoolie-to-mid-30s bass working the edges where the bottom breaks from 40 to 60 feet, though you're better off jigging a diamond jig tipped with a strip of mackerel belly than trying to troll through that rocky bottom.

South of the harbor, Duxbury Bay and the Plymouth flats are running their own program entirely — flounder fishing has actually picked up nicely on the last two hours of the incoming tide. Sandworms and skimmer clams fished on a simple spreader rig off the bottom in eight to twelve feet inside Duxbury Bay have been steady, nothing huge, but a solid box of flounder for anyone willing to sit on the anchor through a tide change. Striper action in Duxbury and Kingston Bay has been quieter, mostly small fish working bait pods on the last of the ebb near the channel markers.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the new moon, and that's going to matter. Stronger current through the Deer Island cut and around President Roads should tighten up that drop-off bite and might finally push some of those Nahant rock fish back into a daytime pattern if the extra push stirs the bait. If I had one trip to make this coming week, I'd take the last two hours of an outgoing tide at Spectacle Island with live mackerel, then swing over to Bass Point right at last light with a popper rod rigged and ready. Watch the sky — any real cooling snap would only help, resetting some of that midday lockjaw we're seeing on the rocks. Until then, fish the tide changes and don't waste daylight where the fish have already told you they won't show.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole Bait Balls Tighten Up — Albies Still One Tide Behind
reports.subhead: Silversides and peanut bunker are stacking in the rips between the Elizabeths and the Vineyard, and every sign says the first false albacore push is close, but nobody's boated one yet.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the rocks at Robinson's Hole Thursday evening on the last hour of the ebb and watched a bait ball the size of a Volkswagen get pushed through the gut between Pasque and Nashawena, terns working it from above, a bluefish or two slashing underneath. That's the tell. That's the exact bait signature — small silversides mixed with peanut bunker — that shows up right before the albies find it. It's just not albie season yet, not officially, even though the water's telling me it wants to be.

We flagged this corridor last week — said Menemsha, Gay Head, and the Elizabeth Island rips were the prime staging ground for the false albacore and bonito push, and that the building tide cycle into the new moon would be the trigger. Here we are, bait stacking up in all the right spots, and I'll be honest with you: I haven't heard a confirmed albie or bonito hookup out of this zone yet. Scout fish, maybe — a few guys running out of Menemsha have had quick, unconfirmed flashes on the surface off Squibnocket that could've been bonito working bait and gone before a cast got out. That's how it starts. That's exactly how it starts every year. The new moon lands August 12, and the tide is already building toward it — bigger swings, harder current through Quick's Hole and Robinson's Hole, which is the fuel this whole run needs. If I had to bet, the first real hookups come in the next seven to ten days, right around that new moon and the few days after when the rips are ripping hardest.

While we wait on that, the bread-and-butter bite has been the scup, and it's been dependable. Fishing squid strips and sandworm chunks on standard high-low rigs off the Woods Hole pilings and around the Vineyard Haven harbor structure, guys are filling coolers with foot-long scup on the last two hours of the incoming. Nothing glamorous, but it's a sure thing when the flashier stuff is still a question mark.

Striped bass have gone quiet in the daytime, and that's not a surprise given how warm the surface layer has gotten — we're seeing that pattern hold right across southern New England, fish sliding deep and turning nocturnal rather than working the surface in the heat. Buzzards Bay side, the better bass have been coming off the deeper edges around Naushon and the Middle Ground on eels and bunker chunks fished after dark, outgoing tide, working the deeper holes in 25 to 35 feet where the water stays a few degrees cooler. If you're set up to fish the tide change at 10 or 11 at night off Woods Hole, that's been worth the lost sleep. Daytime bass fishing has been tough sledding — I won't sugarcoat it. A lot of casts for not a lot of fish unless you're specifically working that night window.

Fluke have been the most consistent producer in daylight hours, and that hasn't changed. Drifting the sand between Naushon and the Buzzards Bay mainland, and again off the Vineyard side toward Oak Bluffs, 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullets have been picking up keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — steady rather than a blitz, which is about what you'd expect for early August with water this warm and stable. Depths of 20 to 35 feet on the last two hours of the ebb have been the sweet spot, when the current slows just enough to work the jig properly without getting swept off the structure.

Bluefish are the one species that's been unambiguously good, and that tracks with what's happening up and down the coast right now — warm surface water has these fish fired up everywhere. Off the Cuttyhunk rip and the Sow and Pigs reef, diamond jigs and topwater poppers worked through the白 boils on the outgoing tide have produced non-stop action, three- to six-pound blues mixed with the occasional bigger fish. If you want guaranteed bent rods this week, that's where I'd point the boat.

Looking ahead: the tide keeps building toward the 12th, and that's the window I'm circling on the calendar. Menemsha Bight and Devil's Bridge off Gay Head are the first places I'll be checking every morning starting midweek — small profile baits, Albie Snax in bone or pink-white, half-ounce Deadly Dicks, ready to go the second I see fish working bait on the surface instead of just birds working bait underneath. Until then, work the scup and fluke bite in daylight, hunt the bass at night in the deeper holes, and keep an eye on that bait. When the silversides start getting nervous and the terns start diving harder than normal, that's your signal — not a forecast, not a guess, just fish telling you what's coming.

reports.headline: Race Point slack tide, a bent rod, and a 38-pound bass that wouldn't quit
reports.subhead: While the water south of the Cape pushes bass into deep, nocturnal patterns, the Bay stays cool enough to keep the bite honest in daylight — and this week proved it again.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, dead slack at Race Point, and I had a guy from Worcester in the stern who'd never felt a striper pull like that before. We'd drifted the rip three times with nothing but a couple of short bluefish to show for it, and I was about to pull the mackerel and try Peaked Hill Bars instead. Then the current started to build again off the last of the ebb, that first hint of push you feel in your palms before you see it in the water, and his rod loaded up like someone hung a truck tire on it. Thirty-eight pounds, fat as a football, came up out of that green water with a mackerel still hanging out the corner of her jaw. That's the rip doing what it's supposed to do — you just have to be patient enough to let the tide tell you when.

That's been the story of the Bay all week. While the fish south of us — down through the Sound, off Jersey, along most of the coast — have gone deep and noctural on account of that low-to-mid-70s surface water, we're not dealing with that problem up here. The Bay holds its temperature better than open coastline, and that's kept our bass willing to feed in daylight on the rips instead of sulking until dark. I've been telling guys at the co-op the same thing for two weeks now — the water stays cooler north of the Cape, and it shows. We flagged this pattern last week, said conditions would stay steady through stable water, and that's exactly what played out. No surprises, just consistent work if you put the time in.

Race Point remains the money spot on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood — that window where the rip stands up and the mackerel schools get pushed and squeezed against the structure. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20-pound fluoro leader, just enough weight to keep bottom contact without killing the natural swim — that's been the ticket for the better fish, 28 to 40 pounds. If you can't get mackerel, bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 40 to 60 feet will still draw strikes, just don't expect the same class of fish.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more of a bluefish show this week, and a good one — three- to six-pound choppers thick on the surface during the last hour of daylight, chewing through peanut bunker pushed up against the bar. Poppers and Deadly Dicks worked fast across the top get hit hard. There's bass mixed in underneath that blitz too, but you have to slow down and get a bucktail or a swimming plug down through the chaos to connect with them — the blues will eat first if you let them.

Billingsgate has quieted some for the cod compared to earlier in the summer, but it hasn't shut off. I marked scattered fish on the deeper edges, 65 to 80 feet, drifting clam baits and diamond jigs tipped with squid strips on the last of the incoming tide when the current slows enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead. Nothing to write home about — a few fish in the 8 to 12 pound range for guys who put in a full tide's worth of drifting — but it's honest work if cod is what you're after and you're not expecting a pile.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing going off Sandy Neck and down toward Barnstable Harbor, holding on the sandy flats in 15 to 25 feet where the tide runs clean over clam and mussel bottom. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the outgoing, have been putting keepers in the box mixed with plenty of shorts — steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for early August. If you want a numbers day with a shot at a few dinner fish, that's where I'd send you.

The moon's building toward new phase over the next several days, and that means stronger tides pushing through both rips by the weekend. If that current comes in clean and doesn't get blown out by any weather moving through, I'd expect Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars to fish better than they have all week — bigger pushes of water usually mean bigger pushes of bait, and bigger bait means bigger bass showing up to eat it. That's the pattern I've watched play out for thirty years on this water, and I don't see a reason it breaks now. Worth planning a morning around the building flood at Race Point if the wind cooperates. I'll have mackerel rigs ready either way.

reports.headline: Great Point rip full of birds, but it's blues under them, not bonito — yet
reports.subhead: Two weeks of watching the horizon for the first scout bonito, and Nantucket Sound keeps handing me chopper blues instead — for now.
reports.body_markdown:
I had my hopes up Tuesday morning. Terns stacked three deep over the rip off Great Point, working a nervous push of bait right where the shoal drops from four feet to twenty on the last of the ebb, and for about ten seconds I let myself believe. Then the first fish came up and it was a chopper blue the size of a Duraflame log, not a torpedo-shaped bonito, and about forty of his buddies came with him. That's been the story of the last week and a half out here — the rips are loaded, the birds are working, and it's blues, blues, blues.

Not that I'm complaining, because the bluefish bite right now off Nantucket is about as good as it gets. Great Point rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been holding fish from five to twelve pounds, and they're eating anything that moves fast — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Hopkins in the chrome finish worked through the white water where the current stacks against the shoal. Sankaty's outer bar has been doing the same thing on the incoming, birds working the edge where the deeper green water meets the sandy shallows. If you want steady bend in the rod and don't mind losing a few lures to the teeth, this is the two-week window to be out there.

Striped bass are around, but they've gone quiet in the way stripers do when the surface water sits in the low-to-mid 70s the way it has been. I'm seeing very little daytime action on the Sound side — Horseshoe Shoal has been dead calm during the day, no birds, no boils, nothing worth a cast. The fish haven't left, they've just gone deep and nocturnal on us. My best intel this week has come from guys running the Monomoy rips after dark on the building tide, working big paddletails and bunker-colored plugs slow along the bottom edges where Monomoy Point drops into the channel. That's producing better-than-average fish, some pushing 30 inches, but you're fishing midnight to 3 a.m. to get it. During the day, don't waste your tide on the flats expecting a bass blitz — go find the blues instead and save the bass game for the dark.

Fluke have been the honest bread-and-butter fish all week, and honestly the most reliable thing I can point you to right now. The bite on Nantucket Shoals structure — the humps and edges south and west of the Great Point rip in 25 to 40 feet — has been steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for early August. Keepers mixed with plenty of shorts on white and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide pushing you across the structure. Monomoy's flats on the harbor side have also been kicking out fluke on the last of the outgoing, working the channel edges where the sand drops off into deeper water. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but it's fish in the box on a day when the albie/bonito grounds are giving you nothing.

And that brings me to the fish everybody's actually asking about. Two weeks ago I said the bonito potential was building here right alongside what's happening in Buzzards Bay and around the Vineyard, tracking the same warm push. That's still exactly where we sit — building, not arrived. I haven't had a confirmed bonito crossed off the list yet off Nantucket, and neither has anybody I trust at the dock. But the ingredients are lining up. Water's been holding warm enough long enough, the tides are starting to load up as we work toward the new moon on the 12th, and that's historically the trigger that gets the first real wave of bonito and albies pushing up over the Shoals and into the rips at Great Point and off Monomoy. I'd bet on the week bracketing that new moon being when we start seeing real scout fish, not just birds and blues.

So here's what I'd do with my time this week. Mornings and evenings, work the Great Point and Sankaty rips on the moving water for blues — it's active, it's fun, and it's a guaranteed bend in the rod. Midday, if the sun's high and the rips go quiet, shift to the Shoals structure for fluke on bucktails and Gulp, slow and patient on the drift. If you're willing to burn a night, the Monomoy rips after dark on eels or big plugs are worth the lost sleep for a shot at a real striper. And keep one rod rigged light and ready — an Albie Snax or a small Deadly Dick on 20-pound fluoro — because when that first bonito shows up on the edge of the Great Point rip, and I think it's coming inside the next ten days, you won't get a second cast to make it count.

reports.headline: Stellwagen's 128-foot edge: haddock on the mud, cod tight to the gravel, tuna working the top
reports.subhead: Bait's stacked from the Bank to Tillies and the bluefin haven't left — steady groundfish and a building tuna bite make for a full-day trip right now.
reports.body_markdown:
128 feet on the sounder, gravel-to-mud transition on the western edge of Stellwagen, and the bottom's showing that broken, patchy return that tells you cod are sitting right on the structure change. That's been my number all week. Not one number for the whole Bank — every drift is its own decision — but that 120-to-135 range on the edge, where the hard gravel gives way to softer mud, has been the most consistent depth for keeper cod since Sunday. Clam bellies and clam/squid combos on a standard cod rig, dropped straight down and worked slow off bottom, six inches at a time. Nothing fancy. The fish are there, they're just not stupid — you jig too aggressive in this clear, settled water and they'll follow the bait up and refuse it.

Haddock have been the better bite, honestly, and they're sitting deeper and softer than the cod — 140 to 165 feet on the mud patches inside Stellwagen Basin and on the flats north of the Basin toward Tillies. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or the two-hook haddock rigs with small hooks and a bit of bait, have been putting good numbers of 20-to-24 inch fish in the box. The mud there is holding worms and small crustaceans and the haddock are working it in loose schools — you mark them on the machine as a low, dense cloud six to ten feet off bottom, and that's when you slow the boat and let people drop. Some boats are limiting on haddock in under two hours of actual fishing when they find the right patch. Other days it's a slower pick, twenty or thirty fish for a full boat over four hours. It's mud fishing — you have to move to find where they're feeding that day, and the areas that produced Tuesday were quiet by Thursday.

Pollock have been mixed in on the deeper gravel edges, especially the drop-offs on the northeast corner of the Bank toward Tillies, 150 to 190 feet. These fish are aggressive — jig fast and vertical with a diamond jig or a heavier jighead and they'll crush it on the drop. Nice fish too, several in the 15-to-20 pound class reported this week, which is a good sign for later in the fall when the bigger pollock stack up on those same edges.

Hake are a night fishery mostly, but for boats willing to make the run and fish after dark, the deep mud in Stellwagen Basin — 200-plus feet — has been holding good numbers. Squid strips or whole small squid on a simple rig, right on bottom, and you can load a cooler with hake in a hurry once the sun's down and they come up off the bottom to feed.

Now the tuna. We flagged this last week — said the bluefin bite would hold as long as bait stayed concentrated on the Bank, and that's exactly what's happened. Mackerel schools are thick over the gravel on the western and southern edges, and the whales are working right through them, which is your best visual marker out there right now. Where you see whale activity and diving birds, push the boat that direction and start looking for surface fish or marking bait balls on the sounder in the upper 40 to 60 feet of water over 100-to-150-foot bottom. Green machines and small green/yellow spreader bars trolled around the edges of the bait have been drawing strikes, and the jig-and-troll guys working butterfly jigs on the fish that show under the birds have had some of the better fish of the season — several bluefin in the 200-to-300 pound class reported off the southwest corner of the Bank and down toward Cape Cod Tails this week. It's not a sure thing every trip — some days the fish are up chasing and eating anything, other days they're finicky under the bait and you need to slow-troll or switch to a smaller profile to get bit. But the ingredients are all there: bait's holding, whales are working it, and water's been clean and settled, not blown out.

Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, laying down by midday, which has made for comfortable running to Tillies and back without beating anybody up. That stability is a big part of why the bait's staying put instead of scattering — no big blow to push it off the Bank. If that holds into next week, I'd expect the same general pattern: cod tight to the gravel edges in the 120-135 range, haddock working the mud patches deeper, and the bluefin staying on the bait wherever it concentrates, which right now is mostly the western and southern flanks of Stellwagen.

What I'd watch for is any real wind event out of the east or northeast — that's the kind of blow that can scatter bait fast and push the tuna and the mackerel schools off the Bank structure entirely. Short of that, this is about as reliable a stretch of offshore fishing as we get in early August. If you've got one day to give it, I'd fish the tide change on the gravel for groundfish first thing, then spend the afternoon running the edges looking for whale activity and bait before the light gets flat. That's the program I'd run myself this week.

reports.headline: Napatree Peanut Bunker Ball Up, Tog Reopens on Crab, Albies Still a Tease
reports.subhead: The breachways are loaded with bait and bluefish are hammering it in daylight — but the stripers and the first albie run are waiting on darkness and the new moon tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Napatree Point Tuesday evening and watched a peanut bunker school get squeezed against the breachway wall so tight the water looked like it was boiling from underneath — except it wasn't bass doing the boiling, it was blues. That's been the story on this whole stretch of shore the last ten days. The bait is here, it's thick, and it's daytime bluefish cashing in on it while the stripers wait for the sun to go down.

Water along the ocean-facing beaches has been sitting in that low-to-mid-70s range, which is warm enough that the bass have pulled off the immediate structure during daylight and gone nocturnal. I'm not fighting that pattern anymore, I'm fishing it. Best bass action I've had has been after dark off the ledges at Sakonnet Point and the rock piles below the Jamestown bridge — eels on a slow drift, or bunker chunks fished dead-still in the current seams where the rock drops into deeper water. Nothing huge, mostly mid-20s to low-30s inch fish, but they're eating with confidence once the light's gone and the water cools a couple degrees off the surface heat.

Daytime belongs to the blues right now, and they've been aggressive. Second Beach and the beach break off Sakonnet have had bluefish blitzes chasing the same peanut bunker and silversides that are drawing everything else in. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, half-ounce and up — worked fast across the surface will get bit almost every cast when the birds are diving. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these blues have teeth and they're not shy about using them on 20-pound mono.

Fluke have been the honest bite of the summer and nothing's changed there. Drifting the sandy edges off the Weekapaug reefs and inside the Charlestown breachway on the last of the outgoing tide has been steady — not a blitz, but steady, which is exactly what I expected out of this bite a week ago and exactly what's playing out. Keeper fish mixed with a lot of shorts, four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet. If you're patient and keep moving the drift to find the cleaner sand pockets between the rock piles, you'll put a few in the cooler.

Big one for this time of year — tautog season reopened August 1st, and I've already had two solid outings on green crabs around the humps off Jamestown and the ledge structure outside Newport harbor. Slack tide is when you want to be anchored up tight to the rock, because once the current starts running these fish tuck into the cracks and won't come out for anything. I've been finding fish in 15 to 30 feet, dropping straight down on a jig head tipped with a whole green crab, and letting it sit right on the structure rather than working it. First week back after a closure they're usually a little easier — haven't been pestered in months — so if you've got a tog rod that's been sitting in the garage, now's the window before the crowds figure it out.

Now for the albies — everybody's asking, nobody's seeing them yet. Not at Napatree, not in the Watch Hill breachway, not off Sakonnet. The bait's right, the timing is right, but I haven't had a confirmed sighting of a fin or a tail push through any of the breachways on this stretch. What I will say is the tide is building toward the new moon, and that's exactly the kind of current strength that tends to trigger the first push of albies into structure like Napatree and Watch Hill. I've seen this pattern enough Augusts in a row to trust it — stronger tides mean more bait getting funneled through the breachway mouths, and albies follow bait through a funnel better than almost any other fish we get down here. If I had one morning to burn this week, I'd be standing on the Napatree rocks at first light with an Albie Snax or a small epoxy jig tied on, just in case the first wave shows early.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much change in the next 24 hours — warm surface water, bluefish dominating the daylight hours, bass staying nocturnal along the rocky structure. Where it gets interesting is 48 to 72 hours out, when that new moon tide really starts to load up. That's the window I'd watch closest for the first real albie sign in the breachways, and it's also when I'd expect the striper bite to get a little more aggressive after dark as the stronger current stirs up more bait along the ledges. No reason to change what's working until then — eels and chunks after dark for bass, poppers and metal for blues in the daylight, green crabs on the humps for tog, and Gulp on bucktails for the fluke. Keep an eye on that tide table and don't be surprised if the breachways go from quiet to busy in a hurry once the current really starts to run.

reports.headline: 5:40 Max Ebb, East End: Eels Find Bass in the Dark, Blues Mixed Through
reports.subhead: The current's still building toward the August 12 new moon, and every strong stage is turning fish on somewhere between Scusset and Mashnee.
reports.body_markdown:
5:40 this morning, max ebb, east end — 4.1 knots ripping past the Herring Run and I had two guys on eels before the sky even started to gray up. That's the number I care about right now. Not the air temp, not what the charter boats are posting on social media. The current speed on that ebb tide, because that's what's turning these fish on and off like a switch, and right now the switch is flipping harder every day as we build toward the new moon on the 12th.

Here's where we are. Surface water in the Canal is sitting warm — same story as the rest of the coast, low-to-mid 70s on top — and that's pushed the striper bite into a deep, nocturnal pattern almost everywhere except right here. The Canal stays cooler down in that channel, current keeps it turning over and mixing, so we're still getting some daytime activity, but the best fish are absolutely coming after dark on the stronger stages. I had a client Thursday night on the west end doing a slow swim with a 9-inch Gibbs pencil through the seam off Mashnee, right where that current pinches down along Hog Island, and he connected on a 34-incher on the second cast of the max flood. That's the pattern — you want to be fishing the two hours around max current, doesn't matter which end, and you want to be doing it in the dark or in that gray light right before sun-up or right after sundown.

East end has been the more consistent water this week. The rip off the herring run and down toward the Sandwich side keeps stacking bait against that current seam on the ebb, and the eel guys are cleaning up — I'm talking 10- to 12-inch live eels, slow-drifted right along the seam where the moving water meets the slower water, letting it sink and swing naturally instead of ripping it through. Fish from 28 inches up to a 38 I heard about Tuesday night, though that one came off boatside before the net found it. Bluefish are mixed in on both ends of the Canal right now, choppers up to 8 pounds hammering topwater and swimming plugs during daylight max current, which is honestly some of the more fun action going because you don't need darkness for them like you do the bass. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the building full-moon push would sharpen the current and improve the feeding windows, and that's exactly what's played out. The blues never left, they just got more aggressive as that tide built.

West end, Mashnee and Wings Neck side, the current seams have been holding fish consistently on the last two hours of the flood specifically — that's when the water really starts ripping past the rocks and bass tuck into the eddies waiting for bait to get swept through. Swimming plugs — Sebile Magic Swimmers, black-back/silver-belly pattern — have been the ticket there after dark, worked with a slow, steady retrieve right along the current break. Don't rip it. Let the current do the work and just keep tension on the line.

Fluke have been a modest but honest bite for anyone working the sandy stretches down in Phinneys Harbor and along the flats off Mashnee on the slower stages of tide, when the current backs off enough to fish bucktails and Gulp without getting swept sideways. Nothing blitz-level — this is a steady pick, keepers mixed with shorts, three or four fish an outing if you're covering ground, mostly on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom. That's held stable and I don't expect it to change much this week — no reason for it to, the water's calm and stable through that stretch.

Now the one everyone's asking about — albies and bonito. Nothing showing inside the Canal itself yet, but the word from the Buzzards Bay mouth and around the Elizabeth Islands is scout fish starting to show, and that lines up with what I'd expect this time of year as the tide builds toward the new moon. If that pattern holds the way it usually does, we should start seeing the first real push into the west end current around the 8th to 10th, right as those tides really start ripping. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet, but if you're already out there working the west end for bass on the evening flood, keep a rod rigged with a small metal or an epoxy jig within reach. You don't want to be scrambling when they show.

Look-ahead: expect this same pattern to hold and intensify through the week. Current speeds are only going to build as we approach the 12th, which should sharpen every bite window on both ends — bass and blues on the strong stages, day or night, with the night bite staying the more reliable bet for the bigger bass. If a front comes through and knocks the surface temp down even a couple degrees, don't be surprised if the bass shift back toward more daytime activity across the whole system. Until then, watch the clock, fish the current, not the calendar.

reports.headline: Monhegan and Eastern Egg on the ebb: bass holding, pollock working the top
reports.subhead: Groundfish still down deep in the bay channels, mackerel thick enough to jig your own bait, and the stripers want structure, not open water.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-some years back, an old lobsterman named Cyrus Pratt told me something I never forgot: "The tide don't care what time your alarm went off." I was twenty-two, running my own skiff for the first time out past the Cuckolds, and I'd shown up two hours late on a dead slack thinking fish would wait for me. They didn't. Cyrus laughed about it for a decade. I think about that lesson every August when the water gets bright and lazy and guys want to fish whenever's convenient instead of when the tide says go.

This week's been a Cyrus week. The bite's here, but it's tide-dependent and it doesn't forgive a late start.

Stripers are holding tight to structure rather than roaming open water, which is normal for early August but still catches people off guard. Best fish have come off the last two hours of the ebb around the mouth of the Damariscotta River and along the ledges off Boothbay Harbor — 24 to 32 inches, a few pushing 34, taken on live mackerel and pogies fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 25 feet. If you're throwing hardware, a white Zoom Fluke on a 3/8-ounce jighead worked slow along the drop-offs near the Thread of Life has been drawing strikes right at first light, before the sun climbs high enough to push fish deeper. North of Cape Cod we still get the daytime bite the southern guys have lost to warm water — that's the one advantage of fishing cold. Don't waste it sleeping in.

Mackerel are running thick enough that you can fill a bait bucket in fifteen minutes off Ocean Point or around Monhegan's harbor mouth. Mackerel trees, no weight needed most mornings, schools right on the surface chasing bait. That's been the real engine behind the striper and bluefish action — plenty of fresh mac around means the bigger predators don't have to work hard, and neither do you if you use it right.

Bluefish have shown up in scattered pods around Eastern Egg Rock, mixed in with the puffins working the same bait balls. Nothing like the Jersey shore blitz you hear about from farther south, but enough 3- to 6-pound choppers on cut mackerel or a fast-retrieved Hopkins spoon to make a morning worthwhile. They're moving with the bait, not holding, so if you find birds diving, get there quick — that window can close in twenty minutes.

Pollock are the fish surprising people right now. Big schools working the surface off Monhegan's western ledges and around Eastern Egg Rock on the incoming tide, sometimes visible from a quarter mile off by the slick, nervous water. Sight-cast a chartreuse Slug-Go or a topwater popper into a boil and hold on — these aren't the harbor pollock you catch off the dock, some going 8 to 12 pounds. Best window's been an hour either side of the tide change, before the current gets ripping and pushes the bait too deep to chase on top.

Groundfish are still where they should be for this time of year — cod and haddock holding in the deeper channels of Penobscot Bay, particularly the water between Vinalhaven and Isle au Haut and out toward Matinicus, 100 to 160 feet, on structure you'd recognize if you've ever hauled a trawl through there. Diamond jigs tipped with a clam strip, worked on the bottom third of the water column on a strong ebb, have been the ticket. It's not the September run yet, but it's steady enough that a half-day trip out of Stonington or Rockland is worth the fuel if you're patient and willing to move around until you mark fish.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold stable through the first days of August, and that's exactly what's played out. No thermal surprises, no big shift in where the bait's sitting. The Gulf of Maine stays cold enough that these fish don't need to run for deep water like the stripers south of the Cape do; they just settle into their usual seasonal addresses and wait for the tide to bring the groceries.

I won't pretend it's been easy fishing. Plenty of boats went out this week and came back with less than they hoped, especially midday when the sun's high and the water goes slick and dead. The fish that are biting are biting hard on the moving water and shutting off almost completely on the slack. That's worth knowing before you plan your day around lunch instead of the tide chart.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward new phase over the next week and a half, which should tighten up the currents around Monhegan and the Thorofare and sharpen the bite windows even further — shorter, more violent, more predictable if you're there for them. If I had one morning to fish this coming week, I'd be anchored off Monhegan's western side on the top of the incoming, mackerel jig in one hand and a bass rod rigged with live bait in the other, waiting for the birds to tell me where to look.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds its cod, and the bass never left the ledges
reports.subhead: Casco Bay's cool water keeps the daytime bite honest while points south go nocturnal — mackerel, bass, and groundfish all working on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Jewell Island Tuesday morning, engine idling, watching a mackerel school dimple the surface off the eastern side of the ledge — hundreds of them, tight and nervous, with a dozen terns working the edge of the bait like they were grading papers. That's the kind of thing thirty years on this water teaches you to read before you even wet a line. When the mackerel bunch up that tight, something's pushing them, and it's usually bass or bluefish working from underneath.

Sure enough, ten minutes later, three keeper-class stripers came off the same ledge on small white bucktails bounced through the bait ball. Nothing heroic — twenty-eight, thirty, thirty-one inches — but steady, and taken in broad daylight at ten in the morning, which is worth noting. South of Cape Cod, in the warmer water, the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal this time of year, feeding under cover of dark because the surface temps in the low-to-mid seventies make daytime feeding thermally uncomfortable for them. Up here, Casco Bay is running cooler — mid-to-upper sixties on most days near the ledges — and that keeps our fish willing to work in daylight the way they always have. It's one of the real advantages of fishing this bay in August: you don't have to set your alarm for 3 a.m. to find them.

The ledge structure around Jewell, Cliff Island, and the back side of Great Chebeague has been holding bass consistently on the last two hours of the ebb into the turn — moving water pulls bait off the rocks and the stripers sit below, picking off what tumbles down. Small tins — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked on a slow retrieve through the current seam have been the most efficient producers, though live mackerel, when you can get one to stay on the hook long enough to fish it, still can't be beat as a livelining bait off these same drop-offs.

Halfway Rock continues to be the most dependable piece of structure in the bay for groundfish, and that hasn't changed from what I told you last week — I said then to expect little shift through the coming days, and that's exactly what's held. Cod and a few haddock are still coming off the deeper water on the northeast side of the Rock, in that eighty-to-hundred-and-ten-foot range, best worked on the slack around the turn of the tide when you can actually hold bottom without your jig sweeping sideways into the rocks. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly have been the go-to, dropped straight down and worked with a short, sharp lift-and-drop. It's not been a banner week — I'll be honest, some drifts produced nothing but a few cunner and a lot of patience — but on the days the tide cooperated, we put three or four keeper cod in the boat along with a haddock or two, which for early August groundfishing in this bay is a fair result.

Mackerel remain the most reliable fish in Casco Bay right now, and if you've got kids or a client who just wants bent rods, that's still the play. Schools are thick around Halfway Rock, off the southern tip of Peaks Island, and scattered through the mouth of the bay toward Two Lights. A string of small tinsel jigs, no bait required, dropped into a breaking school will load up fast — I watched a father-son team off Peaks fill a five-gallon bucket in under twenty minutes on Sunday. Use them fresh for bass bait that same day and you've closed the loop nicely.

Bluefish have been thinner up here than what's being reported to our south — the Jersey shore and the Sound are seeing a real push of blues right now, but Casco Bay hasn't seen much more than the occasional straggler mixed in with the bass off the outer islands. That's fairly typical for this water; the bulk of the bluefish push tends to stall out well south of us most years, and there's no strong signal yet that this year's different.

Down at Cape Small and off Bailey Island, the rips have been fishing best on the building tide — an hour either side of the flood seems to concentrate the bait against the ledges there, and bass have been sitting in the wash on the down-current side. Casting soft-plastic swimbaits, four to five inches, into the white water and letting them sink before starting a slow retrieve has worked better than burning them through — the fish there seem to want it presented like something struggling, not fleeing.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon over the next several days, and that means stronger tidal push through the bay's channels and around the ledges. I'd expect the groundfish bite at Halfway Rock to sharpen as the current strengthens and pushes more bait tight to structure — that's usually how it plays out here. If the wind stays reasonable, I'd put my time on the morning ebb at Jewell or Cliff Island for bass, and save the slack water windows for a drift over Halfway Rock's deeper structure. Patience pays on this bay in August. It always has.

reports.headline: A 34-Inch Bass Off the Pool, and Blues Chewing Through Higgins Beach
reports.subhead: The incoming tide at Biddeford Pool is still the best hour in this state, and the bluefish have finally shown up in numbers worth chasing.
reports.body_markdown:
Half past five Tuesday morning, I'm standing on the rocks at the mouth of Biddeford Pool watching a guy from Saco fight a bass that had no business eating a pencil popper in six feet of water. Thirty-four inches, fat as a football, came off a white Gibbs Pencil Popper worked with short jerks right through the seam where the incoming current bends around the ledge. That fish had been sitting in the deeper hole waiting for the tide to push bait through the gut, and when it turned, he ate. That's the Pool in a nutshell — you wait for the water to start climbing, you work that current seam where it funnels past the rocks into the inner basin, and if there's bait around, something eats. Best hour of the day on this whole stretch of coast, and it hasn't changed in thirty years.

The good news this week is the bluefish finally showed some teeth. Higgins Beach has had blues working the outer bar on the last two hours of the incoming, chopping through pogies and sand eels hard enough that you can see the slicks from the parking lot. I had one morning where the water just turned nervous — bait skipping, gulls dropping — and I put a Deadly Dick tin through the middle of it and came tight before it hit bottom. Three fish, biggest maybe six pounds, in about fifteen minutes, then it shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's blues for you. They don't linger and they don't apologize. If you're throwing metal at Higgins, go with something that casts far and sinks fast — a 2-ounce Hopkins or a Kastmaster in silver — because these fish are chasing bait on top and you need to get in the water column before they move off the bar.

Striper fishing overall has been honest work, not a gift. The water up here is still running cool enough that the bass haven't gone full nocturnal like they have from the Cape south — that's the one advantage of fishing above Portland right now, the fish are still willing to feed in daylight instead of only after dark. But you're not walking up and slaying them on every tide. Prouts Neck has been the most consistent spot when the wind sits out of the southwest, which it did most of last week — that wind pushes bait tight against the rocks on the ocean side and the bass follow it in. I've done well there on a black Danny plug worked slow along the edge of the structure, right at the last two hours of the ebb when the water's draining off the rockweed and everything gets funneled into the pockets. Cape Elizabeth's ledges have given up a few fish too, mostly at first light on Sluggos rigged weightless, drifted through the washes.

Mackerel are still schooled up off the Wells Harbor breakwater and around the Ogunquit rocks, and that's worth your time even if it's not glamorous — a string of Sabiki jigs or a small diamond jig dropped through a school will fill a cooler in twenty minutes, and fresh mackerel strip is about the best bass bait you can hang on a hook if you want to fish bait instead of iron. Flounder are showing in the usual soft-bottom spots at the mouths of the Kennebunk and the Saco, especially on the last of the incoming when the water's warmed a touch and they slide up onto the flats — bloodworms or clam on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished slow and patient.

Cod are still there if you want to make the run — the deeper ledges off Cape Elizabeth in 60 to 90 feet have kept producing on diamond jigs and bait, though it's a smaller-boat game this time of year with the pleasure traffic thick on weekends.

We're building toward the new moon, and that means the tides are getting some shoulders to them — stronger push, stronger drain. That's usually good news for the Pool and for any current-fed spot on this stretch, because more water moving means more bait getting displaced and more reason for bass to sit on the seams and wait. If the southwest wind holds into the weekend, I'd be at Prouts Neck on the dropping tide and at Biddeford Pool right as the water starts to climb — that first hour of push has been the most dependable window all summer. Higgins is worth a scouting run too, but don't build a whole trip around the blues; they're moving targets right now, here one tide and gone the next. Bring the metal, bring the plugs, and don't be surprised if you have to cover some rock to find where they're stacked up today.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:42: Fluke Steady, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Bonito Scouts Off the Block
reports.subhead: The Ledge tide windows are still paying off in daylight — but the real bite has moved to the dark, and the bonito are starting to show their cards.
reports.body_markdown:
Six-forty-two this morning, SW Ledge went dead slack. I had the boat parked over twenty-eight to thirty-four feet with marks stacked tight to the bottom before the current even hinted at swinging the other way. That five, six-minute window right at the turn is when you get one clean drift before the rip starts working again, and this week that's exactly when the fluke wanted to eat.

Let me be straight about what's happening out there right now, because I don't like selling a slow week as a hot one. The fluke bite off the Ledge and down toward the Harbor of Refuge rocks is steady, not explosive. We're picking through a mix of shorts and keepers on almost every drift — four, five keepers to a trip in that 19 to 22-inch range, with the occasional four-pounder mixed in. Nothing blitz-level, but it's dependable, and dependable is worth something in August. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails have been the ticket in that 28-34 foot band, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. Once the tide builds past mid-stage, I've had better luck dropping to a 1-ounce head just to hold bottom and keep contact with the structure. We flagged a couple weeks back that this fluke pattern would stay steady rather than turn into a blitz, and that's exactly how it's playing out — keeper-size fish mixed with shorts on almost every structure drift, nothing dramatic, just consistent work if you put in the drifts.

Striped bass have gone quiet in the daylight, and there's a reason for it. Surface temps have been sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range across the Sound and out toward the Block, which is right at the edge of what stripers tolerate comfortably during the day. They're not gone — they've just gone down and gone nocturnal. My best bass action this week has come after dark, working the SW Ledge rip on the last two hours of the outgoing with eels and bunker chunks fished tight to bottom in that same 25-35 foot zone. We've also had success drifting off North Light after 9 PM on the incoming, working big soft plastics slow along the bottom where the current pinches around the rocks. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 30-inch fish with the occasional better one mixed in — but they're eating with confidence once the sun's down and the water cools a couple degrees. If you're set up to fish nights, this is the pattern right now. Daytime bass fishing at the Ledge has been mostly dead unless you're right on the turn of the tide when the cooler water briefly gets pushed up from below.

Now the part everybody's been asking about at the dock — bonito. We're seeing scout fish. Not a push yet, but scouts, which is exactly what you'd expect three weeks out from the new moon. I had two flash through a spread of Point Jude glass minnows off Sandy Point on Sunday, and a charter working the rip off Clay Head reported the same thing — quick, aggressive, gone in seconds. That's the tell. We called this pattern building last week, saying to expect more scout reports as the seasonal bait and temperature triggers lined up, and here they are right on schedule. The building tides toward the August 12th new moon are the trigger everybody in this corridor is watching. Once that tidal push strengthens, Block Island Sound is usually one of the first mainland-adjacent zones to see albies and bonito commit for real, and the squid and bait building around the island right now suggest we're close.

Bluefish have been the reliable bonus fish all week, and a good one — 3 to 6-pound blues mixed right into the fluke drifts off the Ledge, plus a stronger showing of bigger fish, 8 to 10 pounds, working the surface off Sandy Point in the early morning on peanut bunker imitations and small metal. If you want non-stop action for a few hours, that's your play — small Deadly Dicks or 1-ounce Kastmasters worked fast on the surface.

Black sea bass remain the honest bycatch on any bottom drift around the Ledge structure or the reef pockets off the southeast corner of the island — 14 to 17 inches mostly, biting squid strips and small jigs fished right on the bottom.

Looking ahead: if the tidal build continues clean into the new moon window, I expect the bonito scouts to turn into a real showing sometime in the next week to ten days, most likely first around Sandy Point and Clay Head where the rips concentrate bait hardest. The bass pattern should stay nocturnal until we get either a real cooling trend or that new moon current stirs the water column enough to push cooler bottom water up during the day. If a front comes through and knocks temps down even a couple degrees, watch for stripers to shift back to a more traditional daytime rip bite at the Ledge — that's the wildcard worth watching this week.

reports.headline: Appledore Ledges Give Up Cod to 8, Stripers Push the Piscataqua on the Flood
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished all of it — this week the shoals paid, the river paid, and the beach was the one that made you work.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of New Hampshire coastline and figure there's nothing to write home about. I've been running my Lund out to the Shoals for going on fifteen years and I'll tell you what — those thirteen miles fish like a hundred and thirty if you know where the bottom breaks. Appledore, the backside of Star, the humps off White Island, Broad Cove, the Piscataqua's whole tidal length up to Dover Point — that's not a short list. It's just a list nobody bothers to make because they're staring at a map instead of a fathometer.

This week the Shoals did the heavy lifting. Cod fishing off Appledore's northeast ledge has been the best of the summer so far — 60 to 85 feet of water, slack tide into the first hour of the ebb, jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly. Boated three keepers Tuesday morning, biggest one going 8 pounds, with a handful of shorts thrown back for good measure. Pollock are mixed in on the same drift, hitting the same jigs a little higher in the water column, which tells you the bait's stacked mid-depth right now. The mackerel are thick around Appledore and Star — jig a Sabiki rig for five minutes before you even think about groundfish and you'll have all the fresh bait you need. That's the whole trick out there. Fresh mackerel beats anything frozen you're carrying in the cooler, and the cod know the difference.

Water's held cooler here than just about anywhere south of us, and that's the reason this bite has stayed a daytime pattern instead of turning nocturnal like what's happening down in the Sound and off Jersey. Stripers south of the Cape have gone deep and gone dark, feeding mostly at night because the surface is running warm enough to shut them down during daylight. North of Cape Ann we're insulated from that — the Gulf of Maine keeps its cool, and that's kept our bass willing to feed in daylight, especially on the moving tide.

Speaking of bass — the Piscataqua has been the sleeper this week. Current there does more work than any lure you tie on, and with the tides building toward the new moon, that current's got some teeth to it now. I fished the flood off Henderson's Point and again up near Dover Point, working a white 3/4-ounce bucktail with a curl-tail trailer, bounced right along the bottom where the current seam sets up against the pilings. Picked up stripers to 28 inches doing exactly that, with a couple better fish that came unbuttoned before I could get a look at them — one of those days where the strikes felt heavier than what came to the boat. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to structure on the last two hours of the flood, has also been putting fish in the boat for the guys anchoring up near the Memorial Bridge pilings. If you're bait fishing, don't sit and wait — reposition every twenty minutes to stay on the seam as the tide builds, because that seam moves.

Hampton Harbor's been more stop-and-go. The inlet on the incoming tide is still the play — stripers pushing bait up through the cut on the last two hours of the flood, same as every August — but it's not the volume bite it can be. I worked the channel edge off Great Boars Head with a chartreuse soft-plastic swim shad and managed two schoolies in an hour of fishing that should've produced more. The bait's there — you can see the peanut bunker balling up along the edges of the marsh — but the bass haven't committed to it the way they will once that new moon tide really starts ripping. Give it another week.

Flounder guys have had a quieter time of it, but Little Harbor and the flats inside Rye Harbor are still worth a drift with bloodworms or a piece of clam on a simple spreader rig, especially on the last of the outgoing when the water's clean. Nothing to brag about — a dinner's worth if you put in the time, not a fish story.

Bluefish are the wildcard. There's a fresh push working its way up the coast from south of the Cape, and if that continues the way it's been trending, don't be surprised if you start marking blues off Odiorne Point or even out toward the Shoals in the next week or two. I haven't seen them yet up here myself, but the signs point that direction, and when they show, they usually show fast — a slick, diving birds, and suddenly every rod on the boat is doubled over.

Looking ahead: the building tides toward the new moon should sharpen up both the Piscataqua bass bite and the Hampton Harbor push — stronger current means tighter feeding windows but better ones. At the Shoals, if the mackerel stay stacked the way they are, I'd keep running out to Appledore early, working the slack into the first hour of tide movement before the current gets too hard to hold bottom. That's been the window all week, and I don't see a reason for it to change unless the wind swings hard out of the southeast and roughs up that ledge water. Watch the forecast, but if it's clean, I'll be out there before most people's coffee's done brewing.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 175 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, cod thin on the gravel edge
reports.subhead: A steady groundfish week on the Ledge, with the first real bluefin sign showing on Tillies as the water starts to soften south side.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran the numbers on Jeffrey's three times this week and they told the same story each trip: 175 to 190 feet on the west side of the Ledge, hard mud bottom, marks stacked three and four feet off bottom on the sounder — haddock, and plenty of them. That's the pattern for early August out here. The mud holds the worms and the small crab, the haddock sit right on it, and once you find the depth that's holding fish, it doesn't move much day to day. We've been anchoring up in that 180-foot band north of the Bank, running clam bellies and herring chunks on standard cod rigs with 6-ounce bank sinkers, and it's been about as reliable as this fishery gets — limits of haddock, 20 to 24 inches average, a few pushing 28, in three to four hour drops.

The gravel edge is a different animal right now, and I want to be straight about it: cod have been thin. We're marking them on the transitions where the mud breaks into cobble and gravel, usually in that 140 to 160-foot range on the eastern flank of the Ledge, but the numbers are down from where I'd want them this time of year. A boat working that edge might put three or four keeper cod in the box over a full day of jigging diamond jigs and 6-inch Gulp Grubs on bucktails. That's not a skunk, but it's not the gravel bite we had in June either. My read is the cod have slid deeper and scattered with the water holding steady and warm on top — they're there, but you're earning every one right now, not filling a box on autopilot.

Platts Bank has been worth the extra run for guys willing to make it. Similar story — mud holds haddock in the 170 to 200-foot range, and we've had a few pollock mixed in on the drift, chunky fish in the 8 to 12 pound class that'll hit a diamond jig worked with a hard sweep off bottom. Tillies Bank has been quieter for groundfish this week, but that's where the interesting sign showed up — more on that below. Scantum Basin I'd skip for now; deeper, colder water down there and the marks just haven't been worth the run given what's producing closer to home.

Hake have been a solid consolation prize on the slow tides. We've picked up whiting-sized hake and a few nicer ones over 5 pounds on the mud in that same 175 to 190-foot zone as the haddock, usually right at the tide change when everything else goes quiet. If you're fishing bait anyway, leave a rod down — they'll show.

Now the part I've been watching closest. We flagged last week that this would be a stable, typical late-summer Gulf of Maine pattern, and that's exactly what's played out — steady groundfish, no big disruption. But stable doesn't mean static, and the first real bluefin sign of the season showed up on the south end of Tillies this week as warmer water has started working up against the Ledge's southern edge. Nothing giant yet — a few boats marking fish and getting shots on the troll with spreader bars and green machines in that softer, bluer water — but it's early. Historically the real giant bluefin push on Jeffrey's doesn't load up until late September into October, when the mackerel and herring get pushed up tight to the structure and the big fish come up onto the Ledge itself. What we're seeing now is scout fish, the first wave riding that warm edge north. Worth having a rod rigged if you're already out there for groundfish, but I wouldn't plan a dedicated tuna trip around it yet.

Mackerel have been spotty but present around Cape Ann and off Thatcher Island — enough to jig up bait for the trip out, not enough to call it a mackerel bite in its own right. If you need fresh bait for haddock or want livies for a tuna shot, work the top 30 feet with a string of mackerel jigs near the Island on the way out; it's hit or miss but costs you fifteen minutes.

Looking ahead: tides are building toward the new moon, and on this Ledge that usually means better current on the mud and a haddock bite that tightens up even more predictably around the slack windows. I'd expect the mud pattern to hold steady through the week — 175 to 190 feet, clam and herring, haddock and hake. The gravel cod bite needs a cooling trend or a bait push to really turn back on; until then I'm treating it as a bonus, not the plan. And I'll be watching that south Tillies water closely — if the warm push holds and strengthens instead of fading, we could see bluefin numbers build faster than the calendar usually allows. That's the trip I'd want to be ready to pivot into on short notice.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: C-Minus for Stripers, A for Blues, Weakfish Doing Their Job at Dusk
reports.subhead: Warm water has pushed the bass deep and nocturnal, but a fresh wave of bluefish and a reliable dusk weakfish bite are carrying the two-bay game this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Rips grade this week: C-minus on stripers, straight A on blues, B-plus on fluke if you know where to look, and an incomplete on drum because that ship sailed back in May. That's the honest read, and I'm not going to dress it up.

Here's why. Water off Cape May Point and through the rips has been sitting warm — mid-70s and holding — and that's shoved the bass down and put them on a nighttime clock. I've had two charters this week work the outgoing tide through the rips at first light, working 20 to 40 feet with white bucktails tipped with a strip of Gulp, and we picked at fish, nothing you'd write home about. Two shorts, one 29-incher that went back, and a lot of quiet rod holders. That's what warm water does to a striper — they'll feed, but they do it after the sun goes down or right at first light when the thermal layer's thinnest. If you want bass right now, fish the last hour of dark into sunrise on the outgoing, bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig soaking bottom in that 25 to 35 foot band off the Point. Anything past 8 a.m. and you're mostly wasting bait.

What's not slow is the bluefish. There's a fresh wave pushing down the coast right now, and it's showing up hard in the rips and right at the mouth of Hereford Inlet. These aren't dink blues either — mixed sizes with some genuine choppers in the 4 to 6 pound class hitting bunker spoons and diamond jigs worked fast through the current seams. If you're marking bait getting worked over on the sounder near the Inlet jetty on a moving tide, don't overthink it — toss a Hopkins or a Kastmaster and hang on. This has been the most consistent action of the week, hands down.

Fluke are holding up their end, and we flagged this last week — said the bite would stay steady rather than blitz-level, with keepers mixed in among the shorts on structure-oriented drifts, and that's exactly what's playing out. Hereford Inlet channel edges near the Coast Guard station, 15 to 25 feet, drifting on the last of the flood into the top of the ebb, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail is putting keepers in the cooler along with plenty of shorts you're throwing back. We also called the reef bite softening as the shallow bay water climbed — that's held true too. The inshore reef sites right off the Cape aren't producing like they were three weeks ago; the fluke have slid to deeper structure and toward the mouth of the bay where there's more exchange and cooler bottom water. If you're running out to the reef, fish it deep and don't waste time on the shallow edges — that pattern's played out for now. Triggerfish are showing up as a nice surprise on those same deeper wrecks, hitting small chunks of clam on a simple bottom rig. Nothing to target specifically, but a fun bonus when the fluke bite is slow between drifts.

Over on the Delaware Bay side, the drum run wrapped up back in May like it always does — if you're asking about black drum in August, I'll save you the trip, they're gone until next spring. But weakfish have been doing quiet, honest work, and this is the other call we made last week that's holding: the bay bite has stayed a low-light, current-driven program, with weakfish and flounder showing best on moving tide at dawn and dusk. Fortescue and the mouth of the bay have been the sweet spots — 12 to 18 feet, Gulp shrimp on a light jighead or a bucktail tipped with a shedder crab strip, fished right on the bottom as the tide starts to move. Midday, when the sun's high and the water's dead calm, forget it — I've had charters sit on marked fish for two hours at noon and get nothing, then watch the rods bend the second the tide broke at 6 p.m. That's the pattern right now, and it's not changing until the water cools.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon and the tides are going to get some teeth back in the next few days. Stronger current usually means a better shot at the rips holding fish through more of the tide cycle instead of just the dawn window, so if I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd take the pre-dawn outgoing at the Point and stay through the first hour of light, then run over to Hereford for fluke on the back half of the flood. Keep an eye on the sky too — any afternoon thunderstorms rolling off the mainland can muddy up the bay fast and shut the weakfish sight-bite down for a tide or two. If that happens, give it a day to clear before you make the run to Fortescue. Otherwise, this pattern's stable enough to plan around — just don't expect the bass to cooperate until nights get longer or a real cold front finally shows up.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at Dawn: Blues Run the Jetties, Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: The bluefish showed up right on schedule and haven't left — but if you want a real striper, you're fishing this by moonlight, not sunrise.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-fifteen Tuesday morning, north jetty at Manasquan Inlet, and there were already four guys standing on the rocks I usually have to myself. Word travels fast when the blues are running — one of them had a bluefish still flapping on the rocks before I'd even climbed over the first boulder. That's the story of the last two weeks on this stretch, and it hasn't slowed down.

The Miss Belmar has been stacking limits of bluefish since the end of July, and I've watched the same pattern play out from the rocks — smaller fish first, then bigger ones mixing in day by day. That's not the same tired resident school getting worked over morning after morning. That's fresh fish pushing down from the north, stacking on top of what's already here. We flagged this exact move last week — said watch for bigger fish signaling a new wave, and here it is, cocktail blues giving way to three- and four-pound choppers on the same drift.

For shore guys, the pattern is simple and it's been reliable, which after twenty-five years out here I don't take for granted. First light, before the sun gets high enough to push the bait down, the blues are up on top at the Manasquan north and south jetties, at the Shark River Inlet rocks, and along the Spring Lake jetties. White and chrome metal — Ava 27s and 17s — worked with a fast retrieve gets bit the second it hits the water when there's a blitz going. Once the sun's up and the surface action dies, switch to poppers, a Gibbs or a Yo-Zuri stickbait, and work them slower along the edges where the current sets up against the rocks on the incoming tide. That current seam is where the bait gets pinned, and where the blues sit waiting for it.

Fluke have been the honest bread-and-butter fish all week, and I mean honest — not a blitz, not a giveaway, but steady if you put in the drift time. The Manasquan Inlet channel on the outgoing tide, 20 to 25 feet, has been giving up keepers mixed with a lot of shorts on 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch chartreuse Gulp swimming mullets, dragged slow along bottom. Shark River's a little different animal — that one fishes better on the incoming, working the sod banks and channel edges in 15 to 20 feet with the same bucktail-and-Gulp combo, sometimes swapped to smoke or pink when the water's got a little color to it after a blow. Sea bass are riding along on the same drifts wherever there's structure — rock piles off the Shark River reef and the edges around the inlet rocks themselves — and a squid strip on the bucktail hook takes care of both species without changing your rig.

Now the part nobody wants to hear but everybody already knows: the striper bite on the rocks at dawn has been mostly dead. Water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s on the surface, and bass don't love that kind of warm water in daylight — they've slid deep and gone nocturnal, same as they do every summer when it gets like this. I've stood on the Sea Bright rocks at first light three mornings this week and had exactly one fish to show for it, a schoolie that clearly didn't get the memo. If you want a real striper right now, you're not fishing sunrise — you're fishing two hours either side of midnight. Eels drifted off the jetty tips at Manasquan Inlet on the outgoing, working the drop-off where 8 feet falls to 12, have produced better than anything I've thrown in daylight. Same goes for swimming a big Danny plug or a Gibbs pencil popper along the Sea Bright rocks after dark — slow, methodical, working the wash where the white water meets the rock face. It's not fast fishing. It's one good fish for a lot of casts, which is about what you'd expect when the whole population's decided daylight isn't worth the trouble.

Porgies have been a nice consolation prize for anybody who wants steady action without the late-night commitment — bloodworms or clam on a high-low rig off the Shark River rocks or the base of the Manasquan jetties has been filling coolers with decent-sized scup, especially on the bottom half of the incoming when the current slacks enough to keep bait down without getting swept.

Looking ahead, the tides are building toward the new moon, and that extra push of current usually does one of two things around here — either it stirs the bass out of their nighttime funk a little early, or it does nothing until the water actually cools off. I'd bet on the latter unless we get a real break in the heat. The bluefish, though, I don't see any reason to slow down as long as that bait stays thick along the beach — if the size keeps climbing the way it has, there's probably another wave stacking up somewhere north of us right now. Worth getting up early for. Just don't expect the stripers to cooperate until the sun's been down a while.

reports.headline: Wreck 2586 in 130 feet: sea bass to 4 pounds, yellowfin working the 200-foot break
reports.subhead: Bluefin still showing on the Mud Hole lumps at first light, mahi stacking the lobster gear, and bonito starting to stage off Sea Girt ahead of the August 12 new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
Wreck 2586 sits in 130 feet on the inside edge of the Mud Hole, and it's been in my book since 2011 as a sea bass wreck that never quits in early August. This week it proved it again — four- and five-man limits of black sea bass to 4 pounds, most of them coming off the up-current side of the structure on the last two hours of the incoming tide. Green crab and Gulp Grubs on 6-ounce sputniks got it done when the current was running hard; once it slacked off, guys switched to plain bucktails tipped with squid strips and kept picking at the bigger fish holding tight to the wreck's high spots. If you're running out of Manasquan or Belmar and want a sure thing before you commit to the long ride, this is where I'd start the day.

The bluefin have been more of a first-light proposition on the Mud Hole lumps — the 20-fathom humps on the east side, roughly 128 to 140 feet, where the bait's been holding tight since mid-July. Trolling spreads of small cedar plugs and green machines behind the boat at 6 to 7 knots have been drawing strikes right at gray light, and by 8 a.m. the window's usually closed. A few boats have had better luck switching to jigging — vertical work with 6-ounce Shimano Butterflies once they mark fish on the sounder holding 40 to 60 feet down over the lump. This isn't a stack-'em-up bite. It's two or three fish for the boats that put in the time and don't overrun the school with a second pass.

Farther out, the yellowfin bite is exactly what we called last week — the warm filament riding the canyon edges has tuna working temperature breaks and current seams in 200-plus feet of water, and the boats connecting are the ones running bait balls and working birds rather than blind-trolling. I had a report of yellowfin to 45 pounds coming off the edge inside the Triple Wrecks corridor, taken on a mix of trolled spreader bars and a chunk line once the boat found the right piece of structure holding bait under the birds. That thermocline everyone's been watching — bait and fish stacked in the 60- to 90-foot band under a hard temperature break — has held steady through this stretch of warm, settled weather, and there's no sign of it breaking down yet.

Mahi are doing what mahi do in August — they're on the pots. Lobster gear and high-flyers scattered across the Barnegat Ridge and out toward the deeper structure past the Klondike have been holding schoolies in the 2- to 4-pound range, with an occasional gaffer mixed in. The play is simple: idle up on the buoy, pitch a small chunk or a sabiki-caught bait off the stern, and let the school follow the boat before you commit lines. Don't blast in with the motor running — you'll spook the whole pod before you get a bait wet.

Bonito are still in a staging pattern rather than a full push, which tracks with what I'd expect this early in August. I've had a couple of scattered scout fish reported off Sea Girt Reef and along the edge of Shrewsbury Rocks, working bait pushed up against the reef structure in 60 to 70 feet, but it's not consistent enough yet to plan a trip around. The building tides heading into the August 12 new moon are the thing to watch — stronger current on that reef structure usually pulls the bonito and false albacore in tighter, and that's typically when the pattern goes from a curiosity to a real fishery. I'd keep half an eye on the Sea Girt and Shrewsbury numbers over the next ten days.

Blackfish and cod are off the table right now — both species want cooler water and tighter structure work that doesn't line up with an August pattern in this zone. I've got my tog spots marked and my rigs tied for the fall reopener, but there's no sense burning gas on Axel Carlson or the deeper wrecks for blackfish this week. Save that trip.

Wind's been the manageable kind — building sea breeze most afternoons out of the southwest, nothing that's shut down the fleet but enough that I've had guys moving their sea bass trips to the morning and saving the tuna run for when the breeze lays down closer to sunset. Worth building your day around if you're making the run past the 20-fathom line.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd expect the sea bass wrecks to keep producing at the same pace — that pattern's been remarkably stable through the warm stretch, and Wreck 2586 along with a couple of the numbers I've got marked near the Klondike edge should keep paying off on the same tide-and-bait combination. The tuna bite is the one I'm watching closest. If that canyon-adjacent filament holds its position through the week, the yellowfin bite over 200 feet should stay consistent for boats willing to run and work the birds. If it slides south or the thermocline breaks down under a cold front, I'd expect the fish to scatter and the Mud Hole lumps to become the more reliable bluefin bet again. Either way, I'd have my numbers ready for both scenarios before I leave the dock.

reports.headline: Holgate's south cut reformed overnight — fluke steady, bass gone nocturnal
reports.subhead: A fresh cut off the Holgate refuge line is reshaping the drift, while daytime heat pushes stripers into the dark and fluke keep grinding on the sod banks.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the south end at Holgate Tuesday morning on the low and the beach told me something changed. There's a new cut about 200 yards north of the last refuge marker, cutting through what used to be a solid bar. Last week's onshore blow and the building tides into the full moon reshaped that whole stretch — we said the tides would sharpen things up going into the full moon, and here's the proof, a fresh trough scoured out with a hard rip line running off the point on the outgoing. That kind of structure change is exactly what you want to find before everyone else does. I marked it on the phone, walked it at low again this morning to see how it held, and it's still there. Depth in the trough is running four to six feet over sand, dropping to eight where it meets the channel edge. That's a bass spot after dark and a fluke spot on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up onto the flat.

Speaking of fluke — that bite hasn't skipped a beat. Bucktail and fluke-belly combos are still doing work in the Barnegat Inlet rips, same pattern we flagged last week, and it's translated well into Little Egg too. I've been running a half-ounce white bucktail with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet in white or pink shad behind it, dragged slow along the channel edges off Graveling Point in 12 to 18 feet on the last of the outgoing. Keepers are mixing with shorts pretty consistently — not a blitz, but steady enough that a couple hours on the drift usually puts two or three fish over 18 inches in the cooler. The sod banks in Great Bay proper, particularly around the mouth of the Mullica where it dumps into the bay, are holding fish too on live killies fished on a simple three-way rig, 10 to 12 feet of water, moving with the tide instead of anchoring dead still.

Striped bass have gone underground, literally and behaviorally. Surface temps in the low-to-mid 70s across the back bay and inlet have shoved them off the daytime program — I'm not seeing much worth chasing in the surf between sunup and sundown right now. The better play has been bunker chunks fished after dark around the rocks at Barnegat Light and along the bridge structure at the Causeway, where current breaks up against the pilings and creates a cooler seam even in August heat. Guys working that pattern from 9 PM to 1 AM on the outgoing have been finding slot fish, occasionally something bigger, holding tight to structure where the current slows just enough for an ambush. That new cut at Holgate I mentioned — I'd bet money it starts holding bass on the outgoing once the water cools a touch more overnight, especially once we get past this full moon push and into slightly calmer nights.

Bluefish are the one species that doesn't care about the heat, and they've been the most reliable daytime action on the beat. Choppers mixed with smaller cocktail blues are working the inlet rips at Barnegat Light and along the surf line from Ship Bottom down to Beach Haven, especially on the first two hours of the incoming when bait gets funneled through the inlet mouth. Metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins, anything in the one to two ounce range — worked fast through the wash has been drawing strikes, and if you want to save your leaders, wire or heavy fluoro is not optional right now. There's a real wave of blues pushing down the coast and it's showing here the same way it's showing everywhere else on the Jersey side.
