Weakfish have been thin but not absent — a few legal fish coming out of the deeper holes in Great Bay on live mullet and killies, mostly incidental catches while fluke fishing rather than a targeted bite worth planning a trip around. Kingfish are still showing in the surf wash at Ship Bottom and Beach Haven on bloodworms and Fishbites, small but consistent, a good option if you've got kids on the beach and want steady rod-bending action without much fuss.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a major shift over the next several days unless we get a wind shift or a cold front that breaks up this warm surface layer. The fluke bite should hold on the sod banks and inlet structure as long as the water stays stable, and I'd keep working that new Holgate cut on the outgoing tide to see how it develops — cuts like that either fill back in within a couple weeks or become a real feature for the rest of the season. Building tides toward the new moon will add current strength, which should sharpen both the inlet fluke bite and give the bluefish more current to work with in the rips. For bass, night trips with bunker chunks around structure remain the higher-odds play until something cools this water down. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be at that new cut two hours before dark with a bucktail in hand, watching to see if the bass find it before the fluke crowd does.

reports.headline: Conimicut on the ebb: stripers go dark, fluke and scup carry the bay
reports.subhead: The bass slid into the channel and started feeding after sundown, but scup on the ledges and a steady fluke drift are keeping rods bent through the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the Fields Point ramp Tuesday morning, hosing off a cooler that had more ice in it than fish, and he says to me, "Vinny, where'd all the bass go?" I told him the same thing I've been telling everybody who'll stand still long enough to listen — they didn't go anywhere, they just got smart. Buckeye Brook herring run fed those fish back in April and May, pushed a fresh wave of stripers up through the Providence River and into the upper bay. Now it's August, the surface water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s from Conimicut down past Nyatt Point, and those same bass have dropped into the channel edges and gone nocturnal on us. That's not a mystery, that's just how it works when the top of the water gets too warm for a fish that likes to work.

If you want stripers right now, you're fishing after the sun goes down, and you're fishing deep structure — the Conimicut Point drop-off on the last two hours of the ebb, the channel edge off Nayatt Point, or down around the Bullock's Point Light rip where the current stacks bait against the rocks. Live scup on a fish-finder rig, or a chunk of fresh bunker soaking on the bottom in 20 to 25 feet, has been the trick. A couple guys working the Mount Hope Bridge piers after dark on eels have done alright too, nothing overslot, mostly schoolies to mid-20s, but enough to keep you out there past midnight. Daytime, forget the open flats — those fish just aren't up there feeding when it's 75 degrees on top. Work the shade lines under the bridges, the Jamestown-Verrazzano included, on the front of the incoming.

Fluke are the fish keeping this bay honest right now, and honestly we called this — said last week the fluke bite would stay steady rather than blitz-level, and that's exactly the shape of it. Drifting Greenwich Bay off Warwick Neck and down along the edges of the Bay Channel toward Prudence Island, guys are picking through a lot of shorts to find their keepers, but the keepers are there. Four-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the bottom through 15 to 25 feet — that combo has been putting fish in the box on the last of the flood into the top of the ebb, when the current's got enough push to keep your bait moving but not so much you're bouncing bottom like a jackhammer. Sabin Point and the flats off Colt State Park have both been giving up two- and three-pound fish mixed with the occasional four, nothing to write home about size-wise but a legit, repeatable bite if you put in the drift time.

Scup are stacking hard on the rocky ledges right now, which is exactly where you'd expect them this time of year — Rocky Point, the Ohio Ledge off Prudence, and the rock piles around Fox Island are all holding good numbers. Sea worms or squid strips on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinker just enough to hold bottom in that current — that's a fish-a-drop deal some afternoons, and it's the kind of action that's perfect if you've got kids in the boat or you just want to fill a cooler without overthinking it. Black sea bass are mixing in on some of those same rocky spots, especially the deeper structure off Prudence and down toward the East Passage, and they're a nice bonus on squid strips fished tight to the rocks.

Bluefish are working the warmer flats same as everywhere else along the coast right now — that warm surface mass has them fired up, and the bay's no exception. Greenwich Bay and the flats off Rocky Point have had bluefish blitzing bait on the surface some mornings, and if you see the birds working and the water nervous, throw a Kastmaster or a Hopkins and don't overthink your retrieve, just get it moving. Sizes have been mixed, a lot of cocktail fish in the 2- to 4-pound range with the occasional bigger one mixed in, similar to what's being seen up and down the coast right now as a fresh push works south.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you, have been quiet. A few reports of fish taken incidentally while fluke fishing down around Prudence, nothing consistent enough to call a pattern. If you're specifically hunting weakfish this week, I wouldn't build a trip around it.

Looking ahead, the tides are starting to build toward the new moon, and that extra current should help both the fluke drift and the night bass bite — more water movement means more bait getting pushed around structure, and that usually wakes fish up on the change. If we get a stretch of cooler nights or a front comes through and knocks that surface temp down even a couple degrees, don't be surprised if the bass start showing daytime activity again around the bridges. Until then, I'd fish the ebb at Conimicut after dark for bass, hit Greenwich Bay on the tide change for fluke, and swing by the ledges at Rocky Point for a guaranteed bent rod on scup. That's a full day, and it's the kind of week where the bay rewards patience over hope.

reports.headline: Bass go nocturnal off Flynn's Knoll — fluke keep it honest in the channels
reports.subhead: With bay water pushing into the mid-70s, I moved my whole program to last light and let the fluke bite carry the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to stop fishing the flats until the sun's off the water, and that decision's paying the bills right now. Keyport Flats and the mouth of the Navesink are sitting warm — I'm talking bathwater by 2pm — and the bass know it. They've slid off the shallow structure and dropped onto the channel edges and humps out toward Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal, and they're not coming up to feed until the light backs off. So that's where I'm putting my evenings: anchored or drifting slow right on the lip of the channel drop, soaking chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig, 3/0 circle hook, just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. Last two trips out, the bite didn't start until almost dark, but once it went, it went — 28 to 34-inch fish, a few overslot mixed in, all in that last hour of light through the first couple hours of full dark on the incoming.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker-driven activity would hold through the start of August, and it has. The bunker schools are still balled up thick off Keyport and pushing down toward the Highlands, and as long as that bait stays, the bass will keep working it after dark instead of chasing it in the heat of the day. The tell to watch for is if those bunker pods start thinning out or scattering — that's usually the first sign the whole pattern's about to flip and you'll need to hunt instead of just showing up where the bait is.

During daylight I'm not wasting time trying to force stripers that don't want to eat — I'm running the channel edges for fluke instead, and that bite has been the most honest thing going in the bay all summer. Structure edges along the Reach — the drop where the sand meets the channel mud off Middle Ground and down through the Chapel Hill Channel — are holding keeper-size fish mixed with plenty of shorts, which is exactly the steady, grind-it-out pattern we called last week, not a blitz, but dependable. White and chartreuse 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow on the drift, tipped with a strip of squid if the current's really moving. Depth's been 18 to 28 feet, best on the last two hours of the outgoing when the water's still got some push to it but isn't ripping. I had a stretch Sunday morning where three keepers came in twenty minutes off one short drift, then it went quiet for an hour — that's fluke fishing in August, you put your time in and take what the tide gives you.

Bluefish are the loudest thing happening right now, and they're building fast. That warm surface push that's been stacking blues up and down the Jersey coast is spilling right into the Bight and through the Hook, and I'm seeing bigger fish mixing in with the schoolies at the Rip. If you're out there on the last of the incoming, throw a diamond jig with a tube teaser or a bunker spoon right through the rip line where the current stacks bait against the edge of the shoal — you'll know it's happening when the birds start working tight and the water starts boiling. It's not a subtle bite. I lost a whole bucktail leader to a bluefish that had no business being that thick this early in August, so if you're targeting fluke in the same water, bring extra leader material or you'll be retying all afternoon.

Porgies are stacked up on the reef structure around Romer Shoal and holding tight to the rock piles — small hooks, sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, bottom bounced right on the structure. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady meat in the cooler if that's what you're after, and it's a good option on a day when the wind's got the open bay chopped up and you want to stay tucked closer to the Hook.

Weakfish have been a ghost this summer — a few incidental fish coming up mixed in with the fluke drift, nothing you can target with confidence, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, the tides are starting to build again as we push toward the new moon, and that extra current should sharpen up both bites — the bass program at last light and the fluke drift during the day. If the bunker stay put off Keyport, I'd keep working the same evening pattern through the weekend: get to the channel edge by Flynn's Knoll with an hour of daylight left, soak chunks through dark on the incoming, and don't be in a hurry to leave once it gets good. Daytime, stick with the fluke on the channel structure and treat any bluefish blitz at the Hook as a bonus, not a distraction — but watch your leaders. If a front pushes through and knocks the surface temp down even a couple degrees, I'd expect the bass to come back up shallower and feed earlier, and that's the day I'll be back on the flats instead of the channel edge.

reports.headline: Double Creek fluke keep coming steady — weakfish deep, snappers everywhere in between
reports.subhead: Warm, stable water has settled into a real August pattern on the bay, with the best fish coming off moving current and the last hour of light.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember an August back in the late '80s, running a charter out of Forked River with two brothers from Pennsylvania who'd never seen a snapper blue in their lives. We anchored up near the mouth of Oyster Creek on the last of the incoming, dropped tiny bucktails tipped with spearing, and those boys couldn't reel fast enough. That's the thing about this bay in high summer — it doesn't need to be complicated. The water's warm, the bait's thick, and if you fish the moving tide instead of the dead slack, something's usually willing.

That's exactly the pattern I'm seeing right now, and it's the same one we called last week — stable, warm, southwest-wind conditions keeping the bite concentrated on the moving water rather than spread out all day. It's held. Mornings have been quiet on the slack, then the tide turns and the rods start bending.

Fluke are still the most dependable thing going. Double Creek Channel has been the play — that stretch where the sand humps up between the deeper cuts. Drift it on the last two hours of the ebb with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp trailer, bounced right on bottom in 12 to 18 feet. I've had keepers to 5 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts — call it one keeper for every four or five fish over the rail, which is honest summer math, not a blitz. Squid strips on the hook of the bucktail have been outproducing plain Gulp when the current's really moving, probably because the scent holds up better against the push.

Weakfish haven't disappeared, but they're not the shallow sedge-bank fish you find in May. Right now they're sitting deep — the channel edges off Tices Shoal and the deeper bend below Barnegat Light have given up a few 16- to 18-inch weakfish on the last of the outgoing, mostly to guys drifting bucktails tipped with a sliver of fresh spearing or working the bottom slow with a Fin-S rigged on a light jighead. It's not a numbers game right now. It's a bonus fish while you're fluking, and I'd treat it that way.

Snapper blues are the story for anybody with a kid on the boat or a light spinning rod they want to bend. They're everywhere in the back bay right now — off the docks in Toms River, along the bulkheads near Forked River, up into the mouth of Oyster Creek where the water still runs a touch warmer than the open bay even in summer. Tiny gold spoons, small Kastmasters, or a strip of bunker on a snapper rig under a bobber will get bit within minutes on the top of the tide. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the kind that keeps people coming back to this bay for forty years, same as it did for me.

Bigger bluefish are a different animal, and there's real reason for optimism there. The word up and down the Jersey coast has been a fresh wave of blues pushing south, and I expect that to start showing at Barnegat Inlet and along the Island Beach surf line any day now — bigger fish mixed into what's already a strong resident population. If you're throwing metal off the beach at Island Beach State Park, work it right at first light before the sun gets high, because these August blues feed hard early and then go quiet once the water starts to heat up on the surface.

Striped bass are where things get honest. With surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s through the bay, the bass have gone deep and mostly nocturnal — this isn't unique to us, it's the whole coast right now. Daytime bass fishing in the bay in August is mostly a waste of gas unless you're working the deepest holes with something big and slow. Your better bet is the night bite: anchor on a channel edge near Oyster Creek or the deeper water off Double Creek after dark, soak a bunker chunk or a live eel on the bottom, and be patient. It's not the May run, but a 28- to 34-inch bass at 10 p.m. on a calm night is a real thing right now for guys willing to sit still.

Blowfish are thick on the sod banks along the west side of the bay — clam on a small hook, light sinker, drop it right along the bank edges on the last of the falling tide, and you can fill a bucket in an hour if you've got the patience for it. Kingfish have been scattered but present on the ocean side, mostly in the surf troughs at Island Beach on bloodworm or Fishbites, better on the smaller incoming tides than the bigger pushes.

Watch the afternoons — this is peak thunderstorm season, and I've had more than one trip get cut short by a wall of black cloud rolling in off the Pine Barrens around 3 or 4 p.m. When that happens, the bite shuts down hard for a couple hours and then usually comes back strong on the evening tide once things settle. Plan around it rather than fighting it.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and I expect the current to get a little more authority behind it over the next several days — that usually sharpens up the fluke bite on the channel drifts and can trigger a better push of bass activity if a front comes through and knocks the surface temps down even a couple degrees. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of an evening ebb on Double Creek for fluke, then sit on Oyster Creek after dark for bass. That's where I'd put my money.

reports.headline: Why Won't the Bass Touch Anything After Sunrise? Absecon's Nighttime Answer
reports.subhead: Fluke keep the sod banks honest while stripers go strictly nocturnal in the warm water — here's the class lesson for the week.
reports.body_markdown:
I got the same question three times this week, from three different guys standing at three different rail bridges — Absecon, the Route 30 causeway, and one fella texting me from Longport. All three wanted to know the same thing: why are the stripers only hitting for that first gray half hour at dawn, and then nothing?

Here's the lesson. Surface temps along this stretch have settled into the low-to-mid 70s, and that's simply above the comfort range for daytime striper activity. These fish aren't gone — they're just smart. They've pulled off the flats and pushed into deeper, cooler refuge during the day and shifted to a mostly nocturnal feeding pattern. You want a shot at them right now, you fish the edges of the light — that first hour of gray at Brigantine inlet, or the last hour before full dark working the deeper holes off the Route 30 bridge pilings on a dropping tide. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, 3/4 to 1 ounce, worked slow along bottom. Daytime, forget it — you're better off putting that rod down and picking up the other one.

Because the other rod, the fluke rod, is where the real schoolwork is happening. The sod banks in Absecon and up through Great Egg Inlet continue to be the most dependable classroom on this beat. I had three trips this week working the drift along the edges of the Great Egg channel, 8 to 14 feet of water, moving bait — 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with a 3/4-ounce bucktail — and it's a steady bite. Not a blitz, not a bend-the-rod-every-drift kind of week, but steady. Keepers mixed in with plenty of shorts, exactly the pattern I told you to expect. We flagged this last week — said the fluke bite would stay steady rather than blitz-level, with keepers mixed among the shorts on structure drifts — and that's precisely what's showing up on the sod banks day after day. The water's warm and stable, which keeps this bite dependable, but it also means you're culling through a lot of 15-inch fish to find your dinner. Best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when the bait gets funneled off those grass edges and the fluke stack up tight to the drop.

Inside the back bays proper — the channels behind Ocean City and up around Sea Isle — I'm hearing about a few weakfish mixed in with the fluke catches, mostly at first light on bull minnow fished on a simple fishfinder rig, bounced slow along the deeper holes near the ICW channel edges. Nothing to build a trip around, but if you're already out there working fluke structure, don't be shocked if a weakfish grabs your bait instead. Keep a net handy and handle them gently — they don't forgive rough treatment.

On the beachfront, the kingfish have been solid citizens all summer and this week is no different — small strips of bloodworm or Fishbites on a high-low rig, fished in the wash right off Ocean City and Stone Harbor, 2 to 4 feet of water, first couple hours after sunup. Reliable, unglamorous, good for a bucket and a kid who wants to feel something pull.

Now, the bluefish. There's a wave of them working down the Jersey coast right now, building off a strong push that started further north and has been gaining size as it comes south — I'd expect that pattern to keep extending into this stretch over the coming days. I haven't seen the blitz hit Absecon or Townsends yet in any consistent way, but the ingredients are there: warm surface water, bait pushed tight to the beach, and a hungry migratory class of blues working their way down. Keep an eye on the birds working tight over the surf line at dawn between Brigantine and Ocean City — that's usually the tell before the blues show in force. Metal — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — will out-produce plastic once they're in close and slashing.

On the triggerfish front, quiet for now — that's more of a late-summer, structure-and-warm-water pattern that tends to develop around Townsends and the reef edges once the water holds steady into late August. Worth checking again in a couple weeks, not this one.

Looking ahead: we're building toward the new moon, and tidal strength is going to pick up noticeably over the next several days. Stronger current on the sod banks should tighten up the fluke bite and concentrate bait along the drop-offs — that's good news for the drift program. If a cooling front pushes through behind that building tide, and there's some chance of that this week, it could reset the striper pattern back toward something closer to normal daytime feeding. I wouldn't plan a trip around that possibility yet, but if the wind swings out of the northwest and temps drop even a couple degrees, I'd be back on the bridge at first light instead of last light. Until then, class stays in session on the sod banks — that's where I'd spend my time.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Last of the Ebb: Fluke Steady, Bass Now a Night-Shift Game
reports.subhead: With Kings Point pushing past 70 and the reefs stable, the day bite belongs to fluke, bluefish and porgies while the stripers wait for dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Saturday morning I had a decision to make before the sun even cleared Sheffield Island: fish the flood on the inside of the Norwalk Islands where the moorings fill up by 9, or slide out to Cockenoe Reef and work the last two hours of the outgoing before the weekend armada showed up. I took Cockenoe. On the ebb, the bait gets pulled off that reef edge and funnels down into the sand seam on the east side, 18 to 22 feet, where the fluke stack up waiting for it. That's the chess move this time of year — fish the tide that moves bait away from structure, not the one that pins boats on top of you.

It paid off. Fluke to 5 pounds came off that seam on 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets threaded on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with just enough lift to keep ticking bottom. Mixed in were plenty of shorts — same story we flagged last week, keeper-size fish scattered through a lot of undersized company, a steady grind rather than a blitz. That's exactly the pattern right now on every sand patch adjacent to structure from Cockenoe down to the flats off Penfield. If you're covering ground with the bucktail and getting hit but coming up short, don't leave — just slow the drift and let it sit a beat longer before the hop.

Bluefish are the other bright spot, and they're not subtle about it. Anywhere bait gets pushed against structure — the north side of the Norwalk Islands, the rip off Greenwich Point, the edge of the Cows — you'll see the surface go nervous mid-morning as the blues work through. Straight bucktail or a diamond jig with a tube worked fast through the wash will get bit instantly. Bigger fish have been mixing in with the smaller choppers, which tracks with a fresh wave pushing down the Sound. Wire leader isn't optional right now unless you enjoy losing tackle.

Porgies on the Cows are about as reliable as this zone gets in early August. Anchor up on the rockpile in 15 to 25 feet, soak sandworms or clam on a simple high-low rig with size 6 or 8 hooks, and you'll have a bucket of dinner fish inside an hour on the right stage of tide — I like the two hours either side of dead low, when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without a two-ounce sinker fighting you the whole drift. Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure, showing up as a welcome bonus on the reef edges around Cockenoe and Penfield when you're jigging for the porgies or working a bucktail for fluke.

Stripers are the one piece of this puzzle that's changed gears. With Kings Point reading just under 71 degrees and holding, that's warm enough on the surface to push the bass down into the deeper basin water and onto a mostly nocturnal clock — this is the same pattern showing up west of us through the whole Sound. Daytime, they're not up chasing bait on the reef tops the way they were in June. At night, though, resident bunker schools are holding in the deeper water between the Norwalk Islands and Sheffield, and off Greenwich Point in that 30-to-40-foot basin, and that's where the bass are working them after dark. Live-lining a bunker under a balloon or working a bunker-imitation swimbait slow through that depth after 9 PM has been the move — quieter water, less pressure, and fish that are actually willing to feed instead of just holding deep and sulking through the heat of the day.

One thing I'm not doing right now is chasing blackfish. It's too early — that's an October-into-November program on the rockpiles at Penfield and Greenwich Point once the water starts sliding back down through the 50s. Anybody telling you different this week is either guessing or fishing a spot I haven't seen produce yet.

Boat traffic is the other variable you have to play around all August. Sheffield Island and the inner Norwalk Islands turn into a parking lot by mid-morning on weekends, so if you're working structure there, get it done on the early stages of the tide before 9 AM or wait until the dinner crowd clears out around 5. Cockenoe and Penfield see traffic too but there's more room to spread out and still find clean water on the drift.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a big shift in the next several days. The thermal gradient across the Sound — warmer here in the west, cooler as you move toward New London — should hold, which means the fluke and porgy bite stays steady and the bass stay nocturnal unless we get a real cooling push or a wind event that mixes the water column. Tides are building slightly as we work toward the next new moon, and if that current gets some teeth to it, I'd expect the night bass bite off Greenwich Point and in the Cockenoe basin to sharpen up. That's where I'll be putting my time this week — bucktails and Gulp through the fluke window at first light, then back out after dark for the bass once the current really starts moving.

reports.headline: Valiant Rock at 4.1 knots: bass still biting daylight while the rest of the Sound goes nocturnal
reports.subhead: Hard current keeps The Race and Plum Gut cool and honest even as Kings Point pushes past 70 — plus the first real bonito chatter building toward the Aug 12 new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
4.1 knots. That's what the ebb was doing off Valiant Rock on Tuesday afternoon, and it's the number that tells you everything about why this rip is still fishing during the day while the rest of the Sound has gone to bed. Slack this week is running roughly twenty minutes either side of the tide charts for New London — call it a ten-minute true window if you want clean bottom contact with wire. Miss it by much and you're bouncing bucktail off rock at an angle that'll cost you gear and fish both.

Here's the thing everybody west of us is dealing with right now: Kings Point is reading 70.9, and stripers in that kind of water go deep and nocturnal because daytime surface temps in the low-to-mid 70s just aren't comfortable for them to feed up top. Back in the bays and harbors, guys are switching to night trips because that's the only way to connect. We don't have that problem the same way out here, and it's not luck — it's mechanics. The Race and Plum Gut are running 4, sometimes 5 knots through a rock garden that drops to 100-plus feet in places. That kind of current doesn't let the water column sit still long enough to stratify. New London proper is reading 69.4, a degree and a half cooler than Kings Point, and down in the guts of the rip itself, on the bottom where the wire line lives, it's colder still. The turbulence is basically doing the bass a favor — keeping the whole column mixed and feedable around the clock, which is exactly why daytime bass fishing on wire and bucktails still works here when it's shutting down everywhere else in the Sound.

We're running 20 to 28-ounce wire drops off Valiant Rock and Race Rock on the last two hours of the ebb, bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1.5 to 2 ounces, tipped with a sassy shad or a strip of squid when the current's really honking. Depth is 40 to 70 feet depending on where you sit relative to the rockpile, and you want to feel that jig ticking bottom, not swinging free — if it's swinging free you're too shallow in the water column for this current speed and you'll skip right over the fish. Sizes have been solid, most fish 28 to 36 inches, with a few better ones mixed in on the shift from ebb to slack when bait gets pinned against the rock. Bluefish are riding shotgun on almost every drift right now — there's a real wave of them pushing down from the north this year, and Plum Gut and the Sluiceway have both been getting worked over pretty good on top when the tide's ripping. If you want to save your bucktails, throw a heavier metal — something like a diamond jig or a Deadly Dick — into the boils and let the blues have that instead.

Fluke have been the honest bite this week — not a blitz, just steady. We flagged this pattern already: keepers mixed with shorts on structure drifts, and that's exactly what Valiant Rock and the sandy edges off Great Gull Island have been giving up. Four-inch Gulp in pink shad or white on a half-ounce to one-ounce bucktail, dragged slow across 25 to 35 feet of sand adjacent to the rock, has been putting keeper fluke in the boat at a rate of maybe one in four or five fish. Not a limit trip, but a dependable one if you're willing to grind through the shorts. Sea bass are the bonus fish on the same drifts — drop a Gulp or a squid strip tight to the structure itself, right on the drop-off where rock meets sand, and you'll pick off a few 15 to 17-inch fish without even trying.

Now the one everybody's been asking about: bonito. We said last week that the water at Montauk, Block Island, and the Vineyard corridor had already crossed the seasonal threshold and it was just a matter of the tides building enough current to trigger the first real push. That's exactly the setup we're in now — Montauk's holding at 69.1, and with the new moon on August 12 stacking the tides day by day, current strength through Plum Gut and the Race approaches is only going to increase between now and then. I haven't had a rod bend on bonito yet this week, but the bait's showing on the meter around Little Gull and Great Gull in tighter, nervier schools than we saw two weeks ago, and that's usually the tell. I'd have an epoxy jig rig ready — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce, fished on light fluoro, worked fast on a rip or slack edge — and I'd be checking the Gut every session from here through the new moon.

Look-ahead: if the tides build the way they should into next week, expect the current through The Race and Plum Gut to strengthen noticeably, which should tighten up the slack windows even further — plan your bass trips around ten-minute pockets, not twenty. The bass and blue bite should hold steady on wire and bucktails as long as that mixing keeps the rip cooler than the rest of the Sound. And if the bonito or albies are going to show anywhere first, my money's on the Gut and the water around Great Gull sometime in the next seven to ten days, as that building current finally gives them a reason to commit.

reports.headline: Niantic boats grinding fluke at 40 feet — Black Point sea bass steady, stripers gone nocturnal
reports.subhead: The eastern Sound is running a few degrees cooler than the rest of the water and it's holding the bite together while everyone else deals with dead-warm surface temps.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the mates off the Waterford fleet at the bait shop Thursday morning loading up on squid and spearing, and he told me straight up: "We're not setting the world , but we're not getting skunked either." That's about the most honest summary of this week you're gonna get, and it tracks with everything I'm seeing and hearing up and down this stretch.

The drift boats out of Niantic have settled into a groove on fluke in about 38 to 42 feet off the bay mouth and out toward Twotree Island Channel. It's not a bang-bang bite — more like work for your fish, mixed shorts with enough keepers in the 19 to 22 inch range to make the trip worth it. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails are still the go-to, tipped with a strip of squid for scent, dragged slow on the tail end of the drift where the current's easing off. Guys who are marking bait on the sounder and slowing the drift down with a sea anchor are doing noticeably better than the ones bombing through the same water at full drift speed. Fluke this time of year get lazy in the heat — you gotta bring the bait to them, not make them chase.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable thing going. Black Point and the rock piles off Hole-in-the-Wall are stacked with them, and they're mixing right into the fluke drifts as a bonus that's honestly outproducing the target species some days. Double-hook bottom rigs with Asian squid strips or clam, dropped right on the reef edges on the last two hours of the incoming, that's the play. Fish are running a good average size too — plenty of 14 to 16 inchers, some pushing 17. Porgies are thick in Niantic Bay proper, especially around the mooring fields and out toward McCook Point, and if you've got kids or you just want a bucket of dinner fish, sandworms or clam on a high-low rig in 15 to 20 feet will keep the rod bouncing all afternoon.

Now here's the thing that's shaping everything right now — the thermal gradient across the Sound. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, New London's sitting around 69.4. That two-degree difference doesn't sound like much, but it matters. The western and central Sound is running warm enough that stripers out there have gone almost entirely nocturnal, pushed deep and feeding mostly after dark. Out here, we're cooler, and that's kept a little more daytime activity going, though it's far from the wide-open bite you'd want. I'm still telling guys the best striper play right now is first light and last light, working eels or fresh bunker chunks on the drop-offs around Black Point and the deeper cuts in Twotree Channel. Daytime, if you want a shot, go deep — 25 to 35 feet, slow-trolled bunker spoons or umbrella rigs, right on the current seams. It's a grind, not a guarantee, but the fish are there if you put the time in on the right stage of tide.

Bluefish have been the one bright spot that doesn't require finesse. Schools have been running through Hole-in-the-Wall and pushing up into the mouth of the Niantic River chasing bunker, and when they show up top it's an easy game — diamond jigs, or if you want the fun version, poppers and Kastmasters worked fast across the surface. Sizes have been solid, a lot of 3 to 5 pounders with some bigger choppers mixed in, which lines up with what's been happening for the fleets to our west — there's a fresh wave of blues pushing down the coast and this stretch of the Sound is getting its share.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the new moon, and that's worth paying attention to over the next week or two. Stronger current means better current edges, better bait concentration, and it's exactly the kind of setup that can trigger the first false albacore push into this end of the Sound. I flagged this a couple weeks back — said this zone was worth watching given how close we sit to the Race and the Fishers Island corridor — and while nobody's connected on an albie here yet, the ingredients are lining up. Squid are building around the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound side, current's about to get stronger with the building tides, and that's the recipe that usually brings the first fall speedster sightings into Fishers Island Sound and eventually our way. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but if you're out there anyway working blues or bass, keep a rod rigged with a small metal or an epoxy jig, just in case something silver and fast rips through the bait.

Look-ahead for the week: I'd stick with the fluke/sea bass combo drifts on the calmer tide stages, work stripers on the edges at dawn and dusk rather than midday, and keep an eye on Hole-in-the-Wall for bluefish blitzes when the bunker pods show. If the wind stays out of the south and the water holds steady, this pattern should carry through the coming week pretty much as-is. A cold front or a stretch of northerly wind could stir the deeper bass out of their nighttime funk and back into a more normal daytime pattern — that's the wildcard I'd watch for.

reports.headline: Wamphassuc Rocks at First Light: Bass Sliding Deep, Sea Bass Holding the Day Shift
reports.subhead: The boulder fields are still producing, but the stripers have gone nocturnal and the albie watch is just starting to get interesting.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a window right at first light, before the sun gets up over Fishers Island, when the boulder fields off Wamphassuc Point go quiet in a way that tells you something. No nervous water, no terns working — just the low hum of current moving through the rocks. I poled the skiff through there Tuesday morning and watched a school of peanut bunker pour off the ledge in a tight silver rope, no predators pushing them, just moving with the tide. That's the tell right now. The bait's here. The bass aren't up chasing it in daylight anymore.

Water's been sitting in that low-to-mid 70s band across the western Sound — Kings Point up near 71, New London running a touch cooler at 69.4 — and that gradient matters more than people think. The cooler water east of us is why Fishers Island Sound still fishes better in daylight than the water off New Haven or the Norwalk Islands, but even here the stripers have pushed down into the deep holes around Ram Island and gone to feeding mostly after dark or in that gray hour before sunrise. We called this coming — said last week the striper bite here was tied directly to tide strength coming out of neap, and sure enough, as the current's built back up this week, the fish have gotten more predictable, just not necessarily more visible. You want them, you're fishing the breakwater rocks and the Ram Island boulder field on the last two hours of the outgoing, at night, swimming a 3-inch olive-over-white Deceiver or a soft-bodied eel through the current seams where the rock drops into deeper water. Light tackle guys doing well with 1-ounce bucktails, white or chartreuse, bounced slow off the bottom on the drift — not ripped, just walked down along the ledges where the boulders stack up eight to fifteen feet.

Daytime, the more honest bite right now is fluke and sea bass, and that's been steady rather than spectacular — which is fine, that's what August gives you here. Sandy pockets between the boulder patches off Ram Island and the flats inside Little Narragansett Bay have been holding keeper fluke mixed with plenty of shorts, standard Sound pattern this time of year. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent combo — you're covering ground over that mixed bottom, letting the jig tick the sand and pop up over the rock edges. Depths between 15 and 25 feet off the eastern side of Fishers Island have given up the better-grade fish, four and five pounds mixed in with the dinks.

Sea bass and porgy are the dependable structure bite right now, and I mean dependable — every trip out to the reef pile off Wamphassuc or the rocks tight to Ram Island, squid strips on a high-low rig, and you're into fish inside the first ten minutes. Nothing glamorous, but it's honest fishing, and it fills a cooler when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Blackfish season's closed through this stretch, so I'm scouting those same rocks for the fall reopener rather than fishing them — and there's plenty of tog sign around the breakwater boulders and out toward Wicopesset, which is good news for October.

Now the part everybody's actually asking me about at the dock — albies and bonito. Nothing yet. I want to be straight about that. We're watching Watch Hill Reef, Napatree Point, and the rip off East Point every morning for that first nervous water, the diving terns, the small dark backs breaking the surface — and it isn't there. The water's warm enough, temps at Montauk and Block Island have crossed the threshold that usually kicks this off, but the tidal push hasn't built enough yet to concentrate bait the way it needs to. The new moon on the 12th is the date I've got circled. Building current into that moon, especially on the outgoing at Napatree and around the tip of Fishers, is when I'd expect the first scout fish to show — small pods, here one tide and gone the next, before the real run fills in. If I had to bet, I'd say we're seven to ten days out from the first real sign, not longer.

What I'd do this week: fish the rocks at night for bass if you want a shot at a real fish, keep it honest with fluke and sea bass in daylight because that bite's not going anywhere, and start checking the reef edges at Watch Hill and Napatree every dawn from here on out with a bag of epoxy jigs and a 7-weight rigged and ready. When the albies show, they don't give you much notice, and around here the guys who catch the first wave are the ones who were already looking.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Ebb: Stripers Down Deep, Bluefish Own the Top
reports.subhead: The Thames has stratified hard this week — cool water underneath, warm slick on top, and the bite has split right along that line.
reports.body_markdown:
You can see the seam now without even dropping a thermometer. Stand on the Fort Trumbull point around the top of the ebb and watch the surface — it's gone glassy, almost oily, that flat warm sheen you get in early August once the sun's had all July to work on it. But drop a bucktail down eight, ten feet along that rip line off the point and it's a different river down there. Cooler, tighter, more current push. That's where the stripers have gone, and they're staying there through most of the daylight hours.

New London's reading around 69 degrees at the surface, which sounds modest until you remember how that number sits on top of a harbor that doesn't flush fast. The Thames holds heat in its upper few feet and lets the current do the work underneath, and right now that stratification is dictating everything. Bass are down in the green water hugging the channel edges — off the sub base pier faces, along the Gold Star Bridge pilings, and in that deep hole below Fort Trumbull where the river narrows and the current really cranks on the ebb. They're feeding, but they've gone mostly nocturnal and low-light. Best window I've had this week was forty minutes either side of last light, drifting live eels and chunked bunker on fish-finder rigs right along the base of the bridge pilings, letting the current sweep the bait into the seam instead of anchoring dead on it. Twenty-six to thirty-two inch fish, a handful of shorts mixed in, nothing over the slot but steady if you're patient and you're fishing the tide change correctly — start that drift on the last hour of the ebb when the current's still got some shoulder to it.

Daytime, if you want stripers, you have to go get them in the shade — under the bridge structure itself, tight to the pilings where the sun never quite reaches bottom, jigging bucktails and soft plastic paddletails straight down on 3/4 to 1-ounce heads. Slow lift-and-drop right against the concrete. That's producing better than anything worked out in open water in the middle of the day.

Bluefish, on the other hand, want the warm top layer and they're not shy about it. This is the pattern we flagged last week — said the porgy and bluefish bite around the sub base and river mouth would hold steady while bass activity built with the tide, and that's exactly how it's playing out. Blues are running the surface from the harbor mouth out past Pleasure Beach, blowing up on peanut bunker and small mullet in a foot of white water early in the morning. Diamond jigs, half-ounce to an ounce, worked with a fast erratic retrieve, or metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — cast right into the slicks. Nothing subtle needed. These aren't the biggest blues of the year but there's real numbers of them, two to four pounds, and they'll keep you busy for an hour at first light before they slide off with the bait.

Porgies remain the honest bread-and-butter right now, and if you want a bend in the rod without overthinking tide charts, this is it. Anchor up on the hard bottom off the sub base, or drift the flats outside Fort Trumbull in 15 to 25 feet, sandworms and clam on a hi-lo rig, small hooks, light sinkers. They're stacked and cooperative regardless of tide stage, which makes them the fallback when the stripers are being difficult about their schedule. Ocean Beach side has had decent porgy scratching too, a little shallower, 12 to 18 feet, same rig.

What's driving all of this is pretty simple current mechanics layered on top of a warm surface mass that doesn't want to mix. The Thames is a working river — current through the Gold Star Bridge and around Fort Trumbull is strong enough on a good ebb to keep bottom water turning over even while the top three or four feet just sits there and cooks in the sun. That's your two-tier fishery right now: blues and porgies up top and in the mid-column, bass down deep and mostly after dark.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and that means the tides are going to get some real muscle back into them over the next several days. Stronger current through the Fort Trumbull rips and around the bridge pilings should push more bait through those seams and could be enough to pull some stripers up onto a more traditional dawn and dusk pattern instead of strictly after dark — I've seen that shift happen before when the tidal push builds enough to break up the surface layer a little. It's not a guarantee the bass go shallow again, but if I had one evening to fish this week, I'd take the building tide on the ebb at Fort Trumbull, eels drifted deep, and stay out through last light into full dark. That's where the better fish have been, and stronger current only helps that pattern hold.

reports.headline: August Heat Sends Saybrook Stripers into the Dark Hours
reports.subhead: With the shad run six weeks gone and river water pushing into the mid-70s, the bass have gone nocturnal while bluefish and snappers own the daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
The silversides are running thick along the Great Island flats now — you can see them balling up against the marsh banks at low light, little flashes of nervous water that tell you everything about where the predators are staying. That's the real calendar down here in August. Forget the tide chart for a minute. When the silversides bunch up tight like that, with terns working them from above and something pushing from below, you know the river's settled into its dog-days rhythm. I've watched this happen every August for fifty years and it never gets old, even when the fishing itself gets stubborn.

And it has gotten stubborn, if I'm honest with you. The shad are long gone — pushed out to sea back in May, the hickories right behind them — and what we're left with for the next six weeks is a striped bass fishery that's decided daylight isn't worth the trouble. Water temps in the lower river and out toward the Sound have been sitting in that mid-to-upper 60s to low 70s range, warm enough that the bass have shifted hard nocturnal. I talked to a guy at the DEP Marina ramp last Tuesday morning who'd fished the outgoing tide from 4 AM to sunrise off Saybrook Point and had three fish in the mid-20s to keep him honest, all on live eels drifted along the breakwater rocks. By 7 AM, with the sun up and the water flat calm, it was over. Nothing. That's the pattern right now — a tight window either side of first light and last light, and dead water in between.

If you want stripers, plan around that clock. The river mouth itself — that stretch from the outer breakwater at Saybrook Point up through the mouth channel — is holding fish around the bunker schools that have pushed in with the warm water. Chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished tight to bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, has been the most consistent producer after dark. If you're throwing plugs, work the eddies off the rock jetties at Saybrook Point right at first light with a black Danny-style swimmer or a bone SP Minnow — slow, twitchy retrieve, right in that seam where the current breaks off the rocks. North Cove in Old Lyme has given up a few fish the same way, right at dawn before the powerboat traffic stirs the cove up.

Bluefish are the ones actually earning their keep in daylight right now, and that tracks with what's happening up and down the whole Sound this summer — warm surface water, bait pushed shallow, and blues more than happy to feed hard in conditions that put stripers off. Snapper blues have moved into the marina basins and along the Essex town dock in good numbers, which is a nice thing to hand a kid with a bobber and a strip of squid — they're maybe 6 to 9 inches now, aggressive, and they'll keep a rod bent all afternoon if you're patient. The adult bluefish, 3 to 6 pounds, have been working the Great Island flats and the mouth of the Lieutenant River on incoming water, chopping up the same silverside schools the terns are keying on. Small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — cast into the surface action and retrieved fast has been the ticket. Don't overthink the blues right now. They're not subtle.

White perch, if you're looking for something to fill a slower afternoon, are still holding in the deeper holes up around Essex and above — 12 to 18 feet, soft mud bottom, right where the river narrows a bit. Small jigs tipped with bloodworm or a sliver of bunker, fished slow near bottom on a dropping tide, will still take a limit of perch in the 8 to 10 inch range most days. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as sure a thing as this river offers in August, and it gets you out on the water when the striper bite has shut down for the day.

We're building toward a new moon over the next several days, and that's going to put more push into these tides than we've had — worth watching, because a stronger current through the mouth and along Great Island usually pulls more bait through and can extend that dawn window a little longer than usual. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at Saybrook Point breakwater working the last hour of dark into first light on the building tide, eel or plug, and I'd have bunker chunks rigged as backup once the sun came up in case the bass had already slid off. It won't be easy fishing. It rarely is in the first week of August on this river. But the bones of a good bite are there if you're willing to keep banker's hours in reverse.

reports.headline: Bass gone nocturnal, bluefish picking up the slack — Mattituck to the Gut
reports.subhead: Warm water's pushed the stripers into the dark hours, but the bluefish, fluke, and porgy never got the memo.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a fella pull his skiff up alongside mine off Rocky Point Sunday, must've been eleven in the morning, sun already high and mean. He'd been trolling bunker spoons since seven with nothing to show but a sunburn and a bad attitude. Asked me where the bass were. I told him the truth — they're home. Sleeping it off. Come back at nine tonight and fish the same water and you'll think somebody flipped a switch. He didn't believe me. Most guys that age don't, not till they've fished the Sound sixty summers like I have and watched this exact thing happen every August since Nixon was in office.

Water's sitting in the low seventies right along our stretch — Kings Point's reading just under 71, New London's holding around 69 and a half, which tells you the whole Sound west to east is one long warm bathtub right now with barely a degree of relief anywhere. That's not fish-killing warm, but it's warm enough that a striped bass with any sense at all isn't going to burn calories chasing bait in broad daylight when the water's comfortable and slow-moving all night long. We flagged this pattern last week — said the mid-70s temps would keep bass a low-light player here, and that's exactly the hand we've been dealt. Daytime, they're down deep off the drop-offs by Horton Point and Rocky Point, sulking in whatever cooler water they can find, maybe forty, fifty feet down. Come dusk, they slide up onto the structure and start working the current edges, and that's your window.

Best bass action I've heard of or had myself has come after dark off Horton Point, drifting bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs right along the rock pile where the bottom breaks from hard to soft. Eels fished slow on a slight drift have taken a few keepers too, nothing spectacular, mostly high twenties to low thirties inches, a slot fish here and there mixed with fish you've got to let swim. Plum Gut approach has been holding some better-grade stripers on the tail of the ebb when that current really starts ripping — that's a spot where I tell people bring your heaviest bucktail, three-quarter to full ounce, and let it get down into the rip before you start working it. Current there doesn't forgive a light head. But even at the Gut, it's mostly a dawn-and-dusk game right now, not a two-in-the-afternoon game.

What's making up for the bass going quiet is the bluefish, and they have been dependable in a way the stripers haven't. There's a push of them coming down out of the western Sound right now, and it's spilling into our water — fish mixed in size, a lot of two and three pounders but enough five- and six-pound choppers mixed in to keep your arm sore. They've been thick off Mattituck Inlet on the outgoing, blitzing bunker pods right at the mouth, and a few boats have found them stacked up off Rocky Point too. Nothing fancy needed — a diamond jig or a topwater popper thrown into a working school will get bit fast. Just watch your fingers around the release, these are fresh, aggressive fish, not the lazy resident blues we sometimes get late season.

Fluke's been the steady eddy in all this, same as we said it would be. Sandy patches adjacent to the reef structure off Mattituck and out toward Rocky Point have been giving up a consistent mix of keepers and shorts on the drift — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, sometimes tipped with a strip of squid if the current's really moving. Nobody's filling a cooler in an hour, but if you work three or four drifts over the right bottom you'll put a few keeper fluke in the boat, four to six pounds on the better ones. It's a patient man's bite, not a blitz, and that's fine by me — I never trusted the blitz bite anyway, it never lasts.

Porgy fishing continues to be what it always is out here — unglamorous, reliable, and a good way to keep the kids interested while you wait for the sun to drop and the real bass window to open. Anywhere there's structure between Mattituck and Orient, a bit of clam on a hi-lo rig will get you bites all afternoon. Blackfish season's still closed in our waters till fall, so leave the tog gear home for now.

Looking ahead, the tide's building toward stronger pushes over the next several days, and that extra current should sharpen up both the Plum Gut bass bite and the bluefish blitzes at the inlets — moving water concentrates the bait, and concentrated bait is what turns a so-so evening into a good one. I wouldn't expect any albie or bonito showing this far up the Sound yet — that push tends to hit Montauk and the Race first and take its time working west to us, if it comes at all this early. If I only had one evening to fish this week, I'd be at Horton Point an hour before dark with bunker chunks and eels both rigged and ready, and I'd stay till the tide turned.

reports.headline: Falkner Island Porgies Stack Up, Bluefish Crash the Charles Island Bar
reports.subhead: Warm water has stripers sulking after dark, but the rockpiles are stacked with porgies and sea bass for anyone willing to soak worms on the bottom.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a kid two rods down from me on the Falkner Island rockpile double up on porgies before I'd even gotten my second sinker to the bottom — 30 feet of water, half-flood tide, and those things were coming over the rail two at a time on hi-lo rigs with green worms. That's the kind of morning that makes you forget you spent half of July getting skunked on stripers in the daylight.

Let's talk about why. Kings Point is reading 70.9, New London's sitting at 69.4, and everything in between — which is us, Central Sound — is running warm and stable. That's murder on daytime striper activity but it's rocket fuel for porgies, sea bass, and bluefish, and that's exactly the split we're seeing right now. We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions would hold steady with no major shift, and keeper fluke mixed with shorts on structure drifts — and that's precisely what's playing out on the bottom.

Falkner Island remains the money spot. I'm anchoring up on the northeast side in 25 to 35 feet, and the porgy bite is best from half-tide through the top of the flood — current isn't ripping so hard that you're chasing your sinker across the reef, but there's enough push to keep the scent trail working. Green worms and squid strips on size 8 hooks, standard two-hook bottom rigs, 2- to 3-ounce sinkers depending on how much tide is running. Sea bass are mixed in as a bonus, and a few of them are pushing 15, 16 inches — good enough to keep the pan happy. I'm seeing more shorts than keepers most drifts, but if you cover three or four spots on the reef you'll fill a cooler.

The New Haven Harbor breakwalls — both the outer wall and the stretch off Sandy Point — have been quietly good for porgies too, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing. Less crowded than Falkner, shorter run if you're trailering out of Morningside or City Point, and the structure holds fish tight to the rocks. Same rig, same bait, just fish it tighter to the wall than you think you need to — porgies are hugging the rockpile itself, not sitting off it in open sand.

Now the fun one. Bluefish showed up hard around Charles Island this week, working bait pods right off the sandbar on the outgoing tide. I had three fish over six pounds Thursday evening casting 3/4-ounce Kastmasters and Hopkins spoons into the wash where the current rips off the bar — light spinning gear, 20-pound braid, and it felt like every cast got bit. This tracks with what's been happening the length of the Sound this summer; that warm surface layer everyone's complaining about for stripers has been an absolute gift to the blues. If you want a fight on light tackle right now, the bar off Charles Island at last light is the play.

Stripers are the frustrating part of the week. With surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, the bass have gone deep and mostly nocturnal — I'm hearing about fish being picked off Stratford Shoal after dark on live eels drifted along the deeper edges, 25 to 40 feet, slack tide into the first hour of the ebb. Daytime, forget the sandbar entirely unless you're there at first light before the sun gets on the water. I made two dawn trips to Charles Island this week and only touched one fish, a schoolie, on a white Slug-Go worked slow along the drop-off. That's the honest report — the bass are around, but they're not playing during banker's hours right now.

Blackfish are starting to show a little life on the deeper rockpiles off Milford Gulf, 30 to 40 feet, but it's early and spotty — a fish here and there on green crab, nothing to plan a trip around yet. That'll get better as water starts to cool into September.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon and the tides are going to strengthen through the week, which should tighten up the bite windows on the reefs — expect the porgy and sea bass action to compress into shorter, more defined tide stages rather than the all-day grazing we've had. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't stir up New Haven Harbor, I'd fish Falkner or the outer breakwall on the building flood and be done by early afternoon. For bass, my money's still on dusk-into-dark at the Charles Island bar or a night run out to Stratford Shoal — that's where the size is right now, even if the numbers aren't blitz-level. Bring patience and eels, not confidence and daylight.

reports.headline: 5.8-Degree Break at 39°20'N Holding Yellowfin on the Canyon's East Wall
reports.subhead: The warm filament we flagged last week never slid off — it's still parked over the Hudson, and the tuna know exactly where the edge is.
reports.body_markdown:
5.8 degrees. That's the spread I marked yesterday running the SST overlay before first light — 79.4°F on the blue water side of the filament, down to 73.6°F where it meets the canyon's cooler upwelling near the 100-fathom curve. That's about as clean a break as you'll find on the Hudson all season, and it's sitting almost exactly where I said it would last week when the winds stayed offshore and stable. We flagged that the pattern would hold as long as the edge water didn't cool off — and it hasn't. The filament's still parked over the canyon, running roughly east-northeast from 39°22'N, 72°48'W down through 39°10'N, 72°28'W, which puts the hottest push of water right over the Dip and spilling out toward the Claw.

That break is doing exactly what it's supposed to do — pushing bait up out of 900 to 1,400 feet of water and stacking it against the thermal wall where the yellowfin are working. Boats running out of Manasquan and Shark River have been putting spreads out starting around the 100-fathom line, working east along the color change — you can see it if you're paying attention, a hard line between green-blue chlorophyll-rich water inshore and that gin-clear cobalt on the canyon side, chlorophyll readings dropping under 0.3 mg/m³ once you cross it. Ballyhoo skirted in pink/white and green machine combos, run 30 to 40 feet back off the shotgun and riggers, have been drawing strikes consistently once boats hit that edge. Cedar plugs and small Zucchi-style trolling lures in the pattern have also been picking off fish in the 40 to 60-pound range on the troll, especially in that 8 AM to 11 AM window before the wind fills in.

Bigeye have been showing on the meter holding deep during daylight, sitting tight to bottom structure in the 900 to 1,100-foot range along the canyon wall near the Claw — no surprise there, that's textbook daytime behavior for them, hugging the thermocline where the water's stable and dark. Guys running deep drops with squid strips and glow beads on 200-pound fluorocarbon leaders have connected after dark on drift, working the same real estate the daytime bigeye vacate once the sun goes down and they come up to feed in that 400 to 600-foot band.

Mahi have been mixed in wherever there's floating structure — pushed-up weed lines were showing thicker than I've seen in a couple weeks, probably a byproduct of that same warm filament dragging Sargasso mats up from the south. Most of what we're seeing is schoolie-sized, 3 to 8 pounds, but there've been a few gaffer-class fish in the 12 to 15-pound range holding under the bigger mats out past the Dip. Small chartreuse and pink squid daisy chains worked slow past the weed edges have been the ticket, and it's worth a few minutes with lightweight spinning gear and a chunk of butterfish once you spot color under the mat — that's usually where the bigger ones are hanging.

White marlin sightings have picked up too, though it's been more teaser strikes than actual releases — a handful of boats out of Brielle and Point Pleasant have had multiple shots on dink ballyhoo and green machine teaser combos worked off the outriggers, but conversion's been spotty. That's typical for early August before the fish really commit — the water's right, the bait's right, but they're still testing the spread more than eating it. If you're marlin-focused, I'd stack more dink baits and less hardware, and keep someone on the pitch rod at all times.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story more than a target — a couple fish in the 30 to 45-pound range came off high-speed spreads run just inside the break itself, where the current shear tends to hold them. If you're not specifically rigged for wahoo with wire leader in the mix, don't be shocked if you get bit off — worth running at least one or two wire-leadered lures if you're covering that edge water seriously.

Honest read on the week: it's been good, not great. Three trips I know of personally connected on all three, but fish counts were modest — four to seven yellowfin per boat, one or two bigeye on the overnight drift, mahi filling in the gaps. This isn't a wide-open bite where you just point the boat and troll — you need to find that exact break, and it's moved a few miles east since Monday as the eddy shifts. Bring patience and a good chart.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward new phase over the next several days, which should tighten up current on the canyon edge and could sharpen the bite window in the early morning hours. If the filament holds its current position — and there's no sign in the chlorophyll or SST data of it sliding off yet — I'd expect the pattern to stay consistent through the weekend. The one thing to watch is any cooling trend on the edge water; if that break narrows below 4 degrees, that's your signal the warm water's starting to lose its grip on the canyon, and you'll need to run farther east to stay on fish. For now, I'd set up on that 39°20'N line and work the color change methodically — that's where I'm putting my program this week.

reports.headline: The Ledge Went Quiet at Noon and Loud at Midnight — First Bonito Scouts Showing
reports.subhead: Bass have slid deep and nocturnal off the island's structure, but the tide is building toward the new moon and the first albie-and-bonito scouts are already testing the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it — stepped out on the porch at Payne's dock around five in the morning and the air had that flat, heavy stillness that usually means the water underneath is doing something different than the surface lets on. No wind to speak of, glassy out past the breakwater, and the gulls weren't working. That's the tell on this island. When the birds go quiet at first light in August, the bait's not up top — it's down deep, and the bass are down there with it.

That's exactly the pattern we've been in for the better part of two weeks now. Surface temps around the island are sitting in that upper-60s to low-70s range, warm enough that the stripers don't want any part of the shallow reef tops during daylight. They've pulled off the crown of the Southwest Ledge and down into the 40- to 60-foot water along the edges, and mostly they're not feeding hard until the sun's well down. I've had my best luck the last few nights working the Ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, drifting live eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard it's running. Same story out at the North Rip. Daytime it's dead quiet up top, but drop a bunker chunk down into 50 feet on the drop-off after dark and you'll know pretty quick if there's a 30-pounder sitting on that structure. Pulled a 38-pound fish off there Tuesday night on a whole fresh bunker, and the guy fishing next to me on the charter boat had one push 40 an hour later. They're there. You just have to fish the clock, not the calendar.

Bluefish are the daylight consolation prize right now, and they're not shy about it. Bait pushes have been moving through off the southwest corner and around Southeast Light, and when you find the birds working — which, unlike the bass pattern, they will do for blues — you can load the boat fast. Deep-diving stainless spoons in chrome or chartreuse trolled through the melee, or if you want to have some fun with it, cast poppers right into the boil. Fish are running 4 to 8 pounds, plenty of teeth, and they'll keep kids and visiting anglers happy while the bass sulk through the heat.

Fluke fishing has stayed the most dependable thing on the island, which isn't flashy but it's honest work and it's putting dinner on the table. The sandy stretches off the Coast Guard Channel and the drop near the Great Salt Pond entrance have been giving up a steady mix of keepers and shorts on the drift — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along bottom on the last of the incoming. We said last week the fluke bite would stay steady rather than blow up into anything blitz-like, and that's held true — no explosion, just solid, repeatable numbers if you cover the right bottom.

Now for the part I've had my eye on since late July — the albie and bonito watch. We flagged Block Island as one of the top zones on the coastwide radar for the season's first real push, and this week the scouts started showing. Nothing you'd call an arrival yet, but a few boats working bait around the rips off the southwest corner have had single fish crash bait and vanish just as fast — the classic scout pattern before the school shows up in force. The new moon builds through August 12, and that's the trigger everybody on this dock is watching for. Bigger tides mean harder current through the Ledge and the North Rip, which stacks bait tighter against the structure and usually is what flips the switch on these fish. If you're rigging up for it, keep a light spinning outfit ready with small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax in bone or pink — because when they show, the window can close in twenty minutes.

Porgies have been a nice quiet bite for anyone wanting an easy afternoon — Point Judith and the drop-offs along Narragansett Bay's outer edge have been thick with scup on squid strips and sandworms over mixed bottom, small hooks, light tackle, kids' rods. Nothing glamorous, but it's fun fishing and the freezer appreciates it.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the bass pattern to shift much in the next few days — the water needs either a real cooling trend or a stronger blow to push surface temps down enough to get these fish moving in daylight again, and I don't see that in the forecast yet. So if you're chasing stripers, plan around the tide, not the sun — first hour of dusk through the top of the flood has been the sweet spot on the Ledge all week. But keep one rod rigged light and ready for a run to the rips if word comes across the radio that something's busting on top. That first real bonito school of the year can show up with almost no warning once the moon starts pulling harder, and out here, being ten minutes late usually means you missed it.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Slow Monday, loaded Thursday: Norfolk yellowfin and the first real white marlin flurry of August
reports.subhead: A rough start off Poor Man's turned into a three-canyon run that finally put marlin flags up at Norfolk.
reports.body_markdown:
Monday was a grind and Thursday made up for it — that's the report card for this week, and if you fish four canyons out of two inlets like I do, you learn to live with that split. We started the week at Poor Man's, around 38°32'N, 73°57'W, chasing leftover push from weekend wind, and the water there was still working through a green-to-blue transition on the edge. Marked bait, marked structure, couldn't buy a strike before 10 a.m. By Tuesday I'd had enough of that and ran north to the Spencer/Lindenkohl string instead, and that's where the week turned.

The warm filament off the Gulf Stream has been sitting stubborn against the wall between Spencer (38°44'N, 73°58'W) and Lindenkohl (38°50'N, 73°50'W) for going on two weeks now, and it hasn't moved much. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the warm push would hold the canyon wall and the tuna and mahi bite would keep producing while white marlin activity built underneath it. That's exactly what showed up. Wednesday morning we set up a chunk line on the 600-fathom break at Lindenkohl, butterfish and bunker chunks fished on 6/0 circle hooks, and had a steady pick of yellowfin in the 25-40 pound class from first light until the sun got high and the fish slid deeper. Nothing frantic, but a real bite — six boats working that same stretch of edge all morning and everybody I talked to on the radio was getting bit.

Thursday is where it got interesting. We ran south to Norfolk, out past 37°44'N, 74°30'W, on intel that the temp break down there had tightened up and cleaned out overnight. Trolled a mixed spread — Ilander/ballyhoo combos in the shotgun, a spreader bar down the middle, naked ballyhoo skipping off the flat lines — and inside of two hours we had our first white marlin flag of the season up, then a second an hour later. Neither fish came tight, we went 0-for-2 on the release, but two legit bites in a morning after a season of scattered singles tells you the marlin are starting to stage the way they're supposed to this time of August. Bigeye showed up that same night on the drop-back, one fish right around 140 pounds taken on a deep chunk after dark, six hours into a soak with lights down and butterfish strips fished off a fluorocarbon leader in 700 feet of water.

Mahi have been the wildcard piece all week. Anywhere we crossed a weed line or a piece of floating structure — pallets, a lobster ball, a stray car tire once, don't ask — there were schoolies stacked underneath, 3 to 8 pounds, and a couple of gaffers pushing 15 mixed in on the better pieces. Small skirted jigs and a handful of Sabiki-caught bait tossed live off the stern will keep a school fired up around the boat for twenty minutes if you work it right, and that's free fish while you're running between canyon edges anyway.

Wahoo have been quieter than I'd like for early August. We picked up two on high-speed gear — Braid Marauders and a black/purple Ilander combo run at 16-18 knots off the wire line — both at Norfolk on the same stretch of clean blue water where the marlin showed. That's usually the tell: when the wahoo start showing on the same water as the white marlin, the whole southern string is getting into its rhythm for the month.

What didn't work: sitting still and hoping. Poor Man's stayed off most of the week, still working through some leftover chop and discolored water from the weekend blow, and I wouldn't burn fuel there again until it cleans up. If you've only got one day and you're deciding between canyons, I'd lean toward Spencer or Lindenkohl right now for the more consistent yellowfin chunk bite, with a look south toward Norfolk if you've got the range and want a shot at that building white marlin and bigeye combo after dark.

Looking ahead, if that warm filament holds its position on the wall — and there's no sign yet that it's sliding — I expect the yellowfin chunk bite at Spencer and Lindenkohl to stay steady through the coming week, the mahi to keep stacking under any structure you cross, and the white marlin numbers at Norfolk to keep building rather than fade, which is the normal pattern for this point in August. The one thing I'm watching is whether that edge tightens up enough to concentrate the bigeye bite into a shorter window after dark — if it does, that's where the bigger fish are going to come from. I'd have the chunk gear and the deep-drop rig both rigged and ready before you leave the dock, because right now you genuinely don't know which one you're going to need.

reports.headline: Ran the extra eight miles to Wilmington's inshore corner — three for five on yellowfin, one bigeye after dark
reports.subhead: Skipped the crowded Washington grounds for a cleaner break off the Wilmington wall, and the fuel bill paid for itself.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a decision to make at the fuel dock — run the usual line out to Washington Canyon where four other boats were already talking on the radio, or push the extra eight miles northeast to Wilmington's inshore corner where the satellite shots showed a tighter, cleaner temperature break. I made the call to burn the extra fuel. That corner, up around 38°42'N/74°00'W where the wall drops from the 100-fathom curve into the 300s, has been holding an eddy edge that's tucked in nice and stable since late July, and I wanted first crack at it before the fleet figured out the same thing.

Glad I did. We had the spread out by 0630 — naked ballyhoo behind Mold Craft wide-range lures on the long riggers, a green machine bar down the middle, and a pair of Ilanders skirted in pink/white running the shorts. First knockdown came inside twenty minutes on the edge itself, where the water goes from a hazy green-blue to that dark cobalt in about a quarter mile. That's the tell — you can see the break with your eyes before you ever look at a number, and the birds know it too. We had frigates working bait balls right on the line all morning.

Ended up three for five on yellowfin, fish in the 35 to 55-pound class, all right on that seam where the temp jumps. Lost two at the boat on short bites and one just came unbuttoned on a green machine — happens when the fish are eating aggressively but not committing fully, which tells me the bait underneath wasn't as thick as it looked on the surface. Mixed in with the yellowfin we picked up two mahi, a stray dolphin pair sitting under a clump of sargassum about a half mile off the main break, nothing huge, schoolies in the 8 to 12-pound range, but they came easy on the same spread without any adjustment.

No wahoo Tuesday, which surprised me a little given how clean that water looked. Wednesday we ran the high-speed gear — Ilanders and Ling lures rigged behind planers, pulled fast at 12 to 14 knots along the same wall — and picked up two wahoo in the 30s working the structure where the canyon bends toward the northeast, roughly 38°45'N/73°57'W. That bite window was short, maybe forty minutes right at first light before the sun got up on the water, but it was clean and repeatable both mornings we tried it.

White marlin have been the frustrating part of the week. We had two bites on the troll — one pulled the hook on a naked ballyhoo before we could drop back, the other came unglued on a circle hook rigged bait we'd switched to specifically for that shot.
