Marlin numbers feel like they're there in scattered pairs and singles along the same break, not stacked up the way they can be in a good August, but present enough that if you're covering the right water you'll get a look. I'd call it a look-and-lose week more than a hookup week for billfish specifically.

The better decision, honestly, was staying out after the troll bite died midafternoon and setting up to chunk overnight rather than running back in. We anchored on a temperature lump just inside the 100-fathom line, cut butterflied bunker on circle hooks, no weight, just let it drift back naturally in the chunk slick with glow sticks taped to the leader once it got dark. Bigeye showed up around 2200 — one fish just under 200 pounds that took forty-five minutes to get to the boat on 80-pound fluoro leader. That's the kind of fish that makes the whole overnight worth it, but I want to be straight with you — that was one bite in about five hours of soaking baits. We had bluefin show interest twice, boat-side swirls, no takers. The bigeye bite out here right now is real but it's a grind, not a program you can count on producing every trip.

Water's holding warm and stable through this stretch, which is the main reason I'm not seeing any reason to change the pattern yet. The eddy that's set up off Wilmington's northeast corner doesn't look like it's sliding anywhere fast, and as long as it holds its position relative to the 100-fathom curve, that's where I'm putting my time rather than running further out to the deeper water off Baltimore. Tides are building toward the new moon, which should tighten up current on the break and could sharpen the bite window rather than spread it out — that's usually a good sign for concentrated action rather than fish scattered across five miles of water.

If I had one day this week, I'd troll that same northeast corner early, switch over to high-speed gear for an hour right at first light for a wahoo shot, then make the call by 1400 whether the day justifies staying out to chunk after dark. The bigeye are there for the boats willing to put in the overnight hours, but it's not a guaranteed program — it's earned one bite at a time. Watch for any cold front sneaking down from the north later this week; that's the kind of thing that can push this eddy around and reset the whole pattern in a day.

reports.headline: August 3: Washington's Already Fishing Like Mid-Month
reports.subhead: The canyon's running two weeks ahead of the calendar again, and the yellowfin/mahi combo we called last week is exactly what showed up on the color change.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the thing about Washington that guys running out of the other canyons still haven't figured out after all these years — we don't wait for August to fish like August. By the first week of the month, this canyon's usually already running the pattern the Norfolk and Baltimore boys won't see until the 15th or later, and this year's no different. Gulf Stream's been tight to our edge since late June, and that head start compounds. June was slow feeling, July built fast, and now on August 3rd we're sitting in what I'd call a full mid-August bite three weeks early. I don't say that to brag. I say it because it changes how you should fish this week versus how your buddy fishing Poor Man's Canyon is fishing his.

The west wall — that stretch running down from around 38°48'N, 74°42'W where the 100-fathom line breaks hard into the canyon proper — has held the most consistent water all week. You're dropping off that ledge from 600 feet down into 1,400, 1,800 feet fast, and that kind of vertical relief is exactly what stacks bait against structure when there's any current push at all. We've had a modest eddy sitting off the northeast corner of the canyon, spinning slow but steady, and it's been pulling a nice color change right across the top third of the wall — that green-to-blue seam is where I've spent most of my trolling hours this week, and it's paid.

Yellowfin have been the backbone of it, 50 to 75 pounds, coming on the troll early and then switching over to the chunk once the sun gets up and the fish go soft. Ballyhoo behind Sea Witches in dark colors — black/purple, green machine — worked the troll along that seam in the morning, then butterflied bunker on a slow chunk once we anchored up on the color break itself. Mahi have been riding right on top of that same edge, some nice ones in the 12 to 20 pound range mixed with the usual schoolies under any bit of floating grass. We flagged this exact combination last week — said boats working the color change would see a mix of yellowfin and mahi — and that's precisely what's been in the box.

White marlin have started showing on the temp break itself, which usually runs somewhere in the 76 to 78 degree range this time of year along that eddy edge. Nothing stacked up yet, but we've pulled two or three a day dredging naked ballyhoo and small green machines behind spreader bars, mostly right where that warm tongue pinches against the cooler canyon water. If you're rigged for it, don't ignore the marlin bite just because the tuna are easier — those fish are here and they'll be here more as that eddy tightens up, which I expect it will over the next week or so as the moon builds toward new.

Wahoo have been a bonus, not a target — a couple caught high-speed trolling right along the lip of the wall in that 600 to 800 foot zone, planers down deep pulling Ilanders in blue/white. If you want a wahoo specifically, work that ledge itself rather than the open color change; they're holding tighter to structure than the tuna are right now.

Bigeye have shown at night on the chunk for boats willing to sit out there past dark, mostly southeast of the main eddy in the deeper water past 1,500 feet. Nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet — one or two a trip for guys putting in the hours — but that's normal for early August here. That fishery tends to build through the month as the water settles and the deep scattering layer gets more predictable.

I won't oversell the week. It's been good, not great — a solid tuna and mahi bite with marlin and wahoo mixed in, but you still have to find the right piece of the color change and sit on it. I had one trip where we worked three miles of edge before we found fish holding tight, and another where they were right where we expected them inside twenty minutes. That's the difference between reading the eddy correctly and just running to numbers you fished last month.

Looking ahead, if that eddy keeps tightening the way it's been the last few days, I'd expect the marlin bite to firm up first — they like a cleaner, sharper break than the tuna do. Wind's been cooperative, nothing over 15 knots out of the southwest, and if that holds through the weekend I'd put my money on the west wall color change again, working the troll early and settling into the chunk once the sun's high. If a front pushes through and knocks that eddy apart, I'd shift east toward the deeper structure and fish it as a scattered bite rather than a concentrated one. Either way, Washington's still running ahead of the pack — that's not going to change just because the calendar says early August.

reports.headline: A Bigeye Came Off the Gaff at Atlantis — Here's What We Did About It
reports.subhead: The warm water we flagged last week finally pushed onto the canyon wall, and the tuna bite at Atlantis is worth the fuel — if you can stomach the run.
reports.body_markdown:
We hooked a bigeye at first light on the east wall of Atlantis Tuesday morning, fought him boat-side for twenty-five minutes, and lost him at the leader when the mate's first gaff shot skipped off his shoulder. Second shot missed clean. He sounded, the hook pulled somewhere around two hundred feet down, and that was that. Nobody said much. You run ninety-some miles to that piece of bottom, you don't get to be precious about one fish. We picked up the trolling lines, reset the spread, and by ten o'clock we'd boxed two yellowfin in the 60-pound class off the same stretch of temperature break. That's the canyons for you — long way out, short memory required.

The run from Montauk to Atlantis is right around 100 nautical miles depending where you jump off the shelf, call it five and a half hours at an 18-knot cruise, and at today's diesel that's not a trip you make on a whim. From Block Island or the Rhode Island ports it's a bit longer to Atlantis but shorter to Veatch, which sits closer to home water around 40°00'N, 69°15'W. We've been splitting our weeks between the two, and this week Atlantis was clearly the better piece of real estate.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the warm eddy pushing toward the shelf break would get tuna and marlin activity building, with mahi showing on any floating structure, and that's exactly what showed up. The break itself has firmed up nicely along the 100-fathom curve on the east side of Atlantis, and the color change there is sharp enough to see from the bridge — green water inside, that blue-green offshore water outside the line. Yellowfin have been sitting right on that seam, mixed with a fair number of small bigeye that are showing up on the troll during daylight, which isn't typical — usually you need to soak baits after dark for the bigeye. We ran a standard spread for the yellowfin bite: Green Machines and small Islander lures in the shotgun and long riggers, ballyhoo behind Sea Witches in the shorts, running 6 to 7 knots. When the yellowfin got finicky mid-morning, dropping the speed half a knot and switching the flat lines to naked ballyhoo turned it back on.

Wahoo have been mixed into that same water, and we took two on high-speed gear — cedar plugs and Braid Marauders in black-and-purple, run at 14 to 16 knots off a separate set of rods rigged with wind-on leaders and heavy mono top shots. Wahoo don't show every trip out there, but when the water's this stacked with bait, it's worth burning fifteen minutes running the high-speed pattern through the canyon before you settle into the tuna troll.

Mahi have been scattered but not absent — we picked off a half dozen fish, 4 to 10 pounds, around a weed line that had built up on the eastern edge of the canyon, holding sargassum and enough small baitfish that the mahi were stacked underneath it. Small skirted ballyhoo and bare hooks with a chunk of butterfish did the work once we slowed the boat and pitched baits instead of trolling through.

White marlin showed twice on the temp break in the afternoon, both times on the long rigger ballyhoo, both times a missed bite rather than a hookup — that fish is notoriously light on the take, and if you're not watching the line the whole time you'll never know he was there. We didn't convert either one, which is honest reporting: the marlin are around, but they're not stacked up thick enough yet that you can count on one.

Hydrographer and Oceanographer have been quieter by comparison — a few boats working Hydrographer reported a slower pick, mostly smaller yellowfin and no bigeye activity to speak of, and Oceanographer is enough of a run from any of our home ports that nobody's bothered making the trip this week to check it firsthand. That's the eastern canyon math — you commit fuel and a full day to find out, and right now the intel says Atlantis is holding the better water.

Night fishing for bigeye at Atlantis has been a mixed bag. We drifted baits over the edge two nights this week — squid strips and butterfish chunks fished on balloons at various depths down to 150 feet — and connected once, lost the fish I mentioned up top, and had one more bite we never converted. That's not a bad ratio for bigeye, which are never an easy fish, but it's not a guaranteed box either.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward new, which typically strengthens current on the canyon edges and can either concentrate bait right on the break or scatter it depending on which way the eddy moves. If that warm water holds its position through the weekend, I'd keep running Atlantis — the yellowfin bite there has been the most consistent thing going, and the wahoo and mahi are a bonus on top of it. If the eddy slides east like these things sometimes do, Veatch becomes the shorter, smarter run out of Block Island or Point Judith. Either way, check the fuel tanks twice before you leave the dock — out here, that's the only guarantee you get.

reports.headline: Point Bass Have Gone to Bed With the Sun — Eels After Dark Are the Play
reports.subhead: Daytime's quiet at the Lighthouse, but the night shift is loaded, and the albie clock is ticking toward the August 12 new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a rhythm to August out here that never changes, not in fifty years of watching this water. The Point goes to sleep in the daylight and wakes up hard after dark, and that's exactly what's happening right now. Montauk's holding at 69.1 degrees, which by East End standards is cool and clean for this time of year — but it's still enough to push that warm surface layer down over the reef, and the bass have responded the way they always do: they've gone deep, they've gone nocturnal, and if you're fishing the Lighthouse rip at high noon expecting daytime blitzes, you're going to go home disappointed.

I've been running the boulder field off the North Bar at first light and again at last light for two weeks now, and the pattern's holding. On the building tide — that two-hour window before and after the turn — the bass are stacking up tight to the rocks in 15 to 25 feet, and they want an eel. Not a swim shad, not a bucktail in daylight — a live eel, snelled on a 7/0 short-shank hook, drifted right along the boulder seams where the current breaks. We've had fish to 38 pounds off that stretch this week, mostly between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m., and every one of them came on the incoming when the rip was really running. During the day, if you want a shot, go subsurface with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig and fish it deep and slow off the Elbow — you'll pick at fish, but it's not the show it'll be after the sun drops.

Bluefish are the daylight consolation prize, and they're not shy about it. Shagwong Reef has been holding good numbers of choppers in the 8-to-12-pound class, working bait schools in 30 to 40 feet on the last of the outgoing. Umbrella rigs and diamond jigs both work, but if you want to have some fun with them, throw topwater poppers into the boils — they're feeding aggressively enough right now that you don't need finesse, you need presence. This is the tail end of that northern push everybody's been talking about all month, and it's still paying off out here even as it winds down elsewhere.

Fluke fishing has been the honest, dependable piece of the puzzle. It's not blitz-level — I want to be straight with you about that — but it's steady, and steady is a good word in August. We flagged this exact pattern last week: keepers mixed with shorts on the structure-oriented drifts, and that's precisely what Turtle Cove and the sandy stretches off the south side beaches have given up. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet, have been the ticket, with a few nicer fish — four and five pounds — coming off the drop-offs adjacent to structure on the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're grinding for dinner fish, this is where I'd put my time during daylight hours while we wait on the bass to wake back up.

Offshore, the bottom fishing has been genuinely excellent — porgies thick on the structure in 50 to 60 feet with squid strips and clam, and sea bass mixed in on the same drops for anyone willing to run out past the Point and soak bait on the rockpiles. It's not glamorous, but it's meat in the cooler on days when the surf isn't cooperating, and right now it's about as sure a thing as this beat has to offer.

Now, the piece everybody's really asking about at the dock: albies and bonito. We called this one — said the building tide cycle off the July 29 full moon, stacked against the calendar, put us in a 10-to-14-day arrival window, and that window is very much open right now. I haven't had a confirmed albie in the boat yet, but the signs are lining up the way they always do right before Montauk lights the fuse — bait's getting nervous around the rips, there's bunched-up peanut bunker showing off the south side, and the water's holding that clean, cool edge that albies and bonito like to run right along. This place is usually first in the region to turn it on once the fish commit, and with the new moon building on August 12, I'd have my epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks rigged and ready by this weekend, not next week.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift in the next 48 hours — the bass will keep doing their deep, nocturnal thing, the blues will keep working Shagwong on the outgoing, and fluke will keep paying steady dividends on the south side drifts. But by the 72-hour mark, as that new moon tide starts building real strength, I'd be watching the surface off the Point and North Bar closely for the first albie showings. If a front doesn't come through and mix things up, this is the window. My money's on the boulder field after dark for bass this week, and my eyes are on the horizon for the first fin cutting through bait on the surface — because when Montauk turns that corner, it doesn't ease into it. It happens fast, and you want to already be rigged when it does.

reports.headline: Peconic settles into high summer — porgies deep and steady, bass gone nocturnal
reports.subhead: The bay's warmed past the point where stripers want daylight, but porgies, fluke, and weakfish are keeping rods bent from Shelter Island to Sag Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
By the first week of August the Peconic has settled into that thick, warm rhythm it gets every summer once the surface climbs into the mid-to-upper 70s. This bay always runs a few degrees ahead of the Sound and the ocean beaches, and that head start cuts both ways this time of year — it got the bass biting weeks before everyone else back in April, and now it's pushing them into the same deep, nocturnal pattern the rest of the coast is only just starting to see. I've fished this water long enough to expect it. Doesn't mean I like it, but I know how to work around it.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern here would stay quiet and stable with no real disruption on the horizon — and that's exactly how it's played out. No fronts, no big temperature swings, just steady warm water and a bite that rewards anglers willing to fish the right structure at the right stage of the tide rather than expecting a blitz to show up on its own.

Stripers are still around, but they've pushed off the flats and into deeper holes and channel edges, feeding mostly after dark or in that gray window right at first light. Robins Island's west side, the drop-off outside Jessup Neck, and the deeper bend of Noyack Bay have all given up fish in the 26 to 34-inch range to guys drifting live eels or bunker chunks on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're set on daytime bass, your best shot is working the current seams around the Shelter Island ferry docks or the rips off Cedar Island Point where the moving water keeps things cooler and the bait stacks up. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom on the down-current side, have taken a few keeper-class fish for me this week — not a pile, but enough to make the stops worthwhile.

Porgies are the story right now, and they haven't slowed a step. The deeper holes around Shelter Island — the classic spots off Hay Beach, the drop just outside Coecles Harbor, and the flats-to-channel transition near Big Ram Island — are holding thick schools in 18 to 25 feet of water. Standard hi-lo rigs with size 4 or 6 hooks, tipped with squid strips or sandworms, are producing steady doubles on the last two hours of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. These aren't just the usual 9 and 10-inch pan-sized fish either — I've had several better than 12 inches over the rail this week, which tells me there's a good class of porgies moving through ahead of what should be an excellent fall run.

Fluke fishing has stayed exactly what it's been most of the summer — dependable, not spectacular. The channels running between Nassau Point and Robins Island, along with the deeper cuts off Southold and the mouth of Sag Harbor Cove, are holding keepers mixed with plenty of shorts on drifts through 15 to 25 feet. White or pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the drift rather than worked hard, have been out-fishing bait rigs for me the last two weeks. The bite's better on the moving stages of the tide — either direction — and dead slack tends to shut it down completely, so plan your drifts around the push rather than fighting through the lulls.

Weakfish are still showing in modest numbers, mostly at dusk and into the early dark around the deeper holes in Three Mile Harbor and the flats off Northwest Creek. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but if you're already out there for bass at last light, a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along bottom has picked up a few nice ones in the 4 to 6-pound class. Bluefish, meanwhile, are enjoying this warm stretch as much as anything in the bay — good numbers of choppers in the 3 to 6-pound range are running the surface around Orient Point and along the edges of the main channel, especially on bunker pods that have been thick this week. Wire leaders or heavy fluorocarbon are a must if you're throwing poppers or metal at them, because they'll bite through anything lighter without slowing down.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break in the next several days. Water's stable, tides are building slightly as we work toward the next new moon, and that added current strength should sharpen up the porgy and fluke bites on the stronger stages of the tide even more. If a cold front or heavy rain moves through and knocks the surface temperature down even a couple degrees, watch for the stripers to shift back toward a daytime pattern — that's when I'd expect the flats around Shelter Island and Robins Island to come back alive during normal daylight hours. Until then, fish the moving water, fish the depth, and don't expect the bass to cooperate until the sun goes down. There's also quiet talk starting up at the docks about bay scallop season prep — a little early yet, but it's a sure sign everyone around here already has one eye on fall.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Stacked at Stratford Shoal — Bass Feeding Underneath, Not On Top
reports.subhead: The bait's telling you where the bass are, but you won't see them until the sun goes down.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning idling the edge of Stratford Shoal with the sun still low, and what I saw told me more than any temp gauge could. Big bunker pods — thick, dark rafts of them — pushed up tight against the rip, moving with the tide instead of against it, gulls working the edges but not diving hard. That's the tell. When the birds are hovering instead of crashing, the bunker aren't getting pressured from below. Not yet, anyway. Not in daylight.

That's been the story of the last week across Central Sound. The bait is here — bunker stacked at the Shoal, peanut bunker showing thick in the back coves off Oyster Bay and Cold Spring Harbor, silversides working the shallows around the Norwalk Islands on the last of the incoming. But the bass underneath them have gone quiet during the day, and the water tells you why. Kings Point is reading 70.9 on the west end, New London's still a touch cooler at 69.4 on the east end of my beat, and that gradient matters. The bass have pulled off the surface and dropped onto the deep structure — the drop at Middle Ground Light, the rockpile edges at Stratford Shoal, the deeper cuts between the Norwalk Islands — and they're waiting for dark.

We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the striper bite would stay a low-light player as long as surface temps sat in the mid-70s, and that's precisely what's playing out. If you're fishing this zone right now and you're not on the water for the last hour of light through the first couple hours of dark, you're fishing the wrong window.

The guys doing well on bass are working bunker schools at last light with big paddle-tail swimbaits — 9-inch white or bunker-colored — worked slow just under the school, or switching to live bunker on a fish-finder rig once it's properly dark, drifted along the Stratford Shoal rip on the last two hours of the ebb. That current edge concentrates everything — bait gets pushed and pinned, and the bass slide up out of the depths to work it without burning energy in warm surface water. Eels fished the same way off Middle Ground Light have also been producing after 9 PM, mostly mid-20s to low-30s fish, with the occasional better one mixed in.

Bluefish are the ones cashing in on the daylight hours the bass are giving up. Choppers are hammering those same bunker pods from mid-morning through early afternoon at Stratford Shoal and off Charles Island — if you see the surface actually erupt, that's blues, not bass. Bucktails and diamond jigs worked fast through the melee will connect, and there's enough size mixed in now — 3 to 6 pounds, some better — that it's worth carrying wire leader if you're throwing hardware into a busting school.

Fluke have been the most dependable part of the report, and nothing about that has changed. Structure-oriented drifts off the Norwalk Islands, the sod banks inside Oyster Bay, and the sandy stretches adjacent to the Port Jeff reef are still giving up a steady mix of keepers and shorts. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the drift, continue to be the go-to. It's not a blitz bite — we said that last week too, and it's held — but it's a bite you can plan a trip around. Two to four keepers a trip if you cover water and stay on structure, mixed with plenty of teasers.

Porgies are thick on the Stratford Shoal rockpile and around Middle Ground, and if you want a stress-free afternoon with a cooler full of fish for the table, that's still the easy button right now — small hooks, sandworms or clam, anchored up tight to structure on the tide change. Blackfish season's a ways off yet, but a few incidental catches on the porgy rigs suggest they're already staging on that hard bottom.

Here's what I'm watching heading into next week. The moon's building toward new, and the tides are going to get stronger through the weekend into early next week — more current means more push on that Stratford Shoal rip, more current means bait gets displaced and concentrated harder against structure. That's usually the trigger that either wakes the bass up earlier in the evening or, if a front comes through and knocks the surface temp down even a couple degrees, could shift them back toward a more traditional daytime pattern. I'd keep an eye on any cooling trend this week — even a modest one could put fish back on top during normal hours instead of forcing everyone into the night shift.

And for those of you who know what I'm watching for this time of year — no bonito signs yet in Central Sound. It's early. The exposed edges toward Montauk and the Race tend to see them first, and once that push starts working west along the bait, the Norwalk Islands and Charles Island stretch are usually next in line. I'll be watching the bait, not the fleet, and I'll let you know the minute it shows.

reports.headline: 3 A.M. at The Race: One Cast, One Bass, and a Whole Different Bite
reports.subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers nocturnal — the Race and Plum Gut are still delivering, but only if you're willing to fish in the dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Third cast, 3:20 a.m., current screaming through The Race at what felt like every bit of five knots — a 9-inch black Gibbs pencil popper got hammered so hard I thought I'd hooked the bottom of the boat. Thirty-eight inches, girthy, came up out of the eddy behind Valiant Rock like she'd been sitting there waiting on the tide to turn. That fish told me everything I needed to know about this week: the daytime bite is dead, and the night bite is the whole program right now.

Water's warm across the board — New London's reading 69.4°F, and that's colder than the western Sound, which is pushing low-to-mid 70s. That gradient matters. Stripers don't like feeding hard in surface water that warm during daylight, so they've gone deep and nocturnal, exactly like I've seen every August when the thermocline sets up shallow and stable. The fish aren't gone. They're just smarter than the guys still soaking bunker chunks at noon.

The Race and Plum Gut are the two spots in this entire zone that stay productive through this pattern, and it's because the current keeps things churned and oxygenated even when the rest of the Sound goes flat and warm on top. I'm fishing the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, working the rip lines off Valiant Rock and the north side of Plum Gut with 2-ounce bucktails tipped with a chunk of pork rind, dropped into the seam and bounced along bottom in 25 to 40 feet. Eels still work if you can find them — a 10-inch live eel, slow-trolled or drifted through the same rip, has been my most consistent producer for the overslot class fish. Everything's coming on the dark side of the tide change, an hour before and after the current goes slack. Don't waste your time in the middle of a hard ebb — the fish are staged in the eddies, not fighting the main flow.

Bluefish are the other story right now, and they're not shy about daylight. Warm water is bluefish water, and Orient Point and the rip off Fishers Island have had jumbo blues mixed right in with slot bass on the same current edges, same boils, same structure. I've been running topwater — Super Strike poppers and 1-ounce metal — right into the surface commotion off the East End of Fishers, and it's producing double-digit blues in a morning along with the occasional bass that muscles its way into the feed. If you see birds working tight over a rip near Race Rock or the Fishers Island breakwater, don't overthink it — throw straight into the boil, not past it.

Fluke fishing has stayed exactly what we called it last week — steady, not spectacular. I've been drifting the sod banks and structure edges around Plum Gut and Orient Point Reef in 20 to 35 feet, and it's a mixed bag of shorts with enough keepers in the 18-to-22-inch range to make it worth the drift. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the incoming — that's been the combo. It's not a blitz bite. It's a grind-it-out bite, and that's fine by me in August.

Porgies and blackfish are still the reliable daytime program if you want something that doesn't require a 3 a.m. alarm. The reef structure off Fishers Island and the rock piles around Race Rock have been holding good numbers of porgies in 30 to 50 feet on sandworms and clam, and blackfish are starting to show on the deeper structure as the water stays stable — small green crabs on a jig head, worked tight to the rocks on slack tide, will get you into fish without much drama.

What's got me paying attention heading into next week is the moon. We're building toward the mid-August new moon, and that means tidal strength is ramping fast through The Race and Plum Gut. Historically this is exactly when the first false albacore and bonito show up on the edges of this corridor, pushed by the same current strength that's already stacking bait against the rocks at Fishers Island. I haven't seen albies yet this season in this zone, but the ingredients are lining up — squid pushing down from the Rhode Island side, stronger current, and warm stable water everywhere except right in the rips. If I had to bet, I'd say the first real showing happens within the next 7 to 10 days, and Fishers Island's east end will be the first place it happens.

If you've got one trip in you this week, fish it in the dark. Hit the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut with a bucktail or a live eel, work the eddies behind the rocks, and be patient — the bite window is short, maybe 45 minutes around the tide change, but it's real. Daytime, shift your focus to blues on the rip edges and fluke on the sod banks. That's the honest split right now: night for bass, day for everything else.

reports.headline: The Cut Off Cupsogue Is Pinching Down — And the Bait Is Stacking In the Throat
reports.subhead: Moriches Inlet's main channel has tightened against the west jetty, concentrating bunker, fluke, and blitzing blues into a narrower, more predictable lane.
reports.body_markdown:
I've been watching the throat of Moriches Inlet narrow for about three weeks now, and this week it's obvious even from the beach at Cupsogue. The main channel that used to run fairly centered between the jetties has pinched against the west rocks — probably 20, 25 yards of lateral shift since the last real blow pushed sand off the ebb shoal. What that does mechanically is simple: same volume of water, tighter cross-section, faster current. On a strong outgoing you can stand on the west jetty now and watch the seam boil where it used to just swirl. That seam is where everything is happening.

Bunker have been pouring through that cut on the last two hours of the ebb, especially around first light, and the bluefish are riding shotgun on them right into the surf line at Cupsogue and down toward Pikes Beach. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker push would keep the inlet and beachfront blitzing on low light while fluke stayed steady inside on the channel edges — and that's exactly how it's playing out. Blues from two to six pounds are crashing bunker schools hard enough to throw spray visible from the parking lot at Cupsogue around 5:30 to 6:15 AM. Bucktails and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything that matches the 4-5 inch bunker profile — thrown into the froth get bit almost every cast when it's happening. It doesn't last long, 20 minutes to half an hour before the blitz slides west with the tide, so you have to be positioned before it starts, not chasing it.

Inside the bay, the fluke bite is the more dependable story, which tracks with what deeper, cooler channel structure should be doing with surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s. The sod banks along the Pattersquash Island channel and the drop-off edges around Senix Creek are holding keeper fluke in 8 to 14 feet, with the better fish coming right where the channel bottom breaks from hard sand into that softer mud edge. Standard drift with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, or a spearing/squid strip combo, worked slow along that seam on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. It's not a blitz — it's a steady pick, one or two keepers mixed with a handful of shorts most drifts, which is honest summer fluking, not a highlight reel. The East Moriches flats off Senix and around Tuthill Point are producing the same way, slightly shallower, 6 to 9 feet, better on the first two hours of the incoming before the sun gets high.

Striped bass are where the thermal story really shows up. Surface water in the bay and off the beach is warm enough that daytime bass activity is close to shut down — that low-70s surface layer pushes them deep and nocturnal, same pattern showing up from here through the Sound. If you want bass right now, you're fishing the inlet itself after dark, working the scour hole that's deepened on the inside edge of that shifted channel — I'm reading it at 18 to 20 feet now where it used to be closer to 14. Bunker chunks or a whole eel drifted through that hole on the last two hours of the ebb, right where the current dumps out of the narrowed throat, has been the most consistent way to connect. Slot fish mostly, with the occasional overslot mixed in on the darkest part of the tide around the new moon, which is building now and should add real push to the current by the weekend.

Weakfish have shown up sporadically on the same channel edges as the fluke — nothing you can plan a trip around, but a few keeper-class weakfish have come off Senix Creek on light jigs fished right on bottom during slack water transitions. Worth a cast or two if you're already out there for fluke, not worth a dedicated trip yet.

Porgies are stacked on the inlet rock piles and the jetty structure itself, which makes sense given how current has concentrated bait right along that new pinch point. Sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig dropped tight to the rocks on either jetty, incoming tide, is about as close to guaranteed action as this zone offers right now — good for a bucket of dinner fish even on a slow bass or fluke day.

Looking ahead, the building tides into the new moon should sharpen this whole pattern rather than break it. Stronger current means a harder-defined seam at the inlet throat, which should concentrate both the bunker-driven bluefish blitzes and the bass that are working that scour hole after dark. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't stack up ocean swell into the cut, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at first light for blues, then slide into the bay on the incoming for fluke. If a cold front does slide through in the next few days and knocks surface temps down even two or three degrees, don't be surprised if bass start showing some daytime willingness again right on that same current seam — that's the one thing that could change this pattern fast, and it's worth watching the sky for.

reports.headline: Everybody's Drifting Fluke at Noon — The Real Bass Are Working the Rocks at Midnight
reports.subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers off the daytime pattern, but the jetty bite after dark is the best-kept secret at Jones right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Every boat ramp conversation this week starts the same way — guys asking where the fluke are biting, like that's the only game in town. Meanwhile I'm loading eels into a cooler at 9pm and heading for the west jetty rocks at the inlet, and nobody's asking me a thing. That's fine by me. Less company on the rocks.

Here's what nobody wants to admit: the ocean's sitting around 71 degrees off the beach right now, with some junky 4-foot swell riding in at short 5-second intervals — sloppy, uncomfortable, not the kind of water that gets stripers cruising the surf in daylight chasing bunker schools like they were in June. That surface warmth pushes bass deep and nocturnal. They don't shut off, they just clock out for the day shift and punch in after the sun goes down. I've fished this inlet long enough to know that pattern cold, and this week it held up exactly like I expected. We flagged this last week — said the night bass bite would be the better play for trophy-class fish while the daytime bite stayed fluke-and-blue driven — and that's exactly how it's playing out.

So here's where I've been: the rocks on the west side of Jones Inlet, fishing the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, dead low around 1am this week with the tides we're running. Eels on a fish-finder rig, or bunker chunks fished on the bottom if the current's not ripping too hard. The current sweeps bait right off the tip of that jetty into the deep water, and that's where the bigger fish are sitting, waiting for it to come to them instead of chasing it down in the wash like they do in October. Landed a 34-inch fish Tuesday night on a chunk soaked in that deep slot off the rocks, and lost something bigger that just about ripped the rod out of the sand spike. That's the kind of fish that's around right now if you're willing to lose sleep for it.

During the day, the fluke bite is exactly what it's been all summer — steady, not spectacular. Sloop Channel and the drop-offs along the edges of the Jones Inlet channel are holding keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, which is about what I told you to expect last week too. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the sand-to-mud transitions in 15 to 25 feet, outgoing tide gives you the cleanest drift. I'm not seeing blitz-level fluke action anywhere in the bay, but if you cover ground and work the structure right, you'll put a few keepers to 4 pounds in the cooler. Don't expect miracles — this is a grinder's bite right now, not a walk-up-and-load-the-boat bite.

Bluefish are the one thing actually picking up steam. There's a wave of blues pushing down out of the Sound and along the Jersey coast right now, and I think it's starting to spill into our rips. I had three separate mornings this week working diamond jigs — half-ounce to one-ounce, no bucktail, just bare metal — through the rip line off the inlet on the last of the incoming, and connected on choppers to 6 pounds each time. Nothing giant, but steady, and getting more consistent by the day. If that northern push keeps rolling the way it has for the Jersey boats, I expect this bluefish bite at the inlet to get stronger before it gets weaker.

Now here's something worth paying attention to — the weakfish. They've been quietly building back into this bay for a couple seasons, and this week I finally started hearing about legit numbers again out of the deeper holes in South Oyster Bay, particularly around the channel bends off Freeport. Guys working small soft plastics — 3-inch chartreuse or pink shad-tail bodies on light jigheads, fished slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing — are picking off weakfish in the 18 to 22-inch range in the evening. It's not a fleet-wide pattern yet, and I wouldn't build a whole trip around it, but if you're in that area at dusk it's worth ten casts.

Porgies are still holding tight to structure around the jetty rocks and the pilings under Wantagh Bridge — nothing fancy needed there, sandworms or clam on a hi-lo rig, small hooks, and you'll fill a bucket in an hour if you find the right piece of rock.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon and the tides are only going to get stronger through the weekend, which should sharpen up both the bass bite at the rocks and get that bluefish push moving harder through the rip. If a front comes through and knocks that surface warmth down even a couple degrees, don't be surprised if the bass start showing up earlier in the evening instead of waiting for full dark — that's the tell I'd watch for. Until then, I'm sleeping in and fishing at night, and I'd suggest you do the same.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier at First Light: Snapper Blues, Short Fluke, and a Sneaky Keeper or Two
reports.subhead: The bay's stuck in its August groove — light tackle up top, big bass hiding deep and feeding after dark, until the tide starts building toward the new moon.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to launch the kayak out of the Motts Basin ramp instead of running the boat down to the inlet, and it was the right one. When the bay's this warm and this still, you want to be somewhere you can slide into skinny water quiet — no engine noise, no wake — and work the marsh edges before the sun gets high and pushes everything down. That's been my thinking all week: pick the access point that matches what the water's actually doing, not what I feel like fishing.

And what the water's doing right now is running warm, stable, and a little sleepy in the middle of the day — classic August bay. We said last week this was a pattern that needed a tide change or a front to really turn over, and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing's blown up, nothing's crashed. It's just steady, workmanlike fishing if you're willing to adjust your hours and your targets.

From the kayak, working the flats off Ruler's Bar and the channel edges near Big Egg Marsh on the last of the incoming, I've been finding short fluke almost everywhere — sandy pockets in 8 to 12 feet, drifting a 3-inch white Gulp swimming mullet on a 1/4-ounce jighead, just enough weight to feel bottom without plowing it. Mixed into those shorts, maybe one in six or seven fish, is a keeper. Nothing spectacular, but honest work if you cover water and don't marry one drift too long.

Canarsie Pier has been the money spot for anybody fishing from shore with kids or without a boat at all, because the snapper blues showed up hard the last ten days and they haven't left. Small hooks, strips of spearing or a sliver of bunker under a bobber, fished right off the pier pilings on any stage of tide — that's been steady fun, and every so often a bigger cocktail blue muscles in and surprises somebody using gear that's way too light for it. If you want a slightly bigger grade of bluefish, work the Cross Bay Bridge rocks on the outgoing with a small metal — quarter-ounce Deadly Dick or similar — cast up-current and let it swing.

The bigger bass are exactly where the warm water says they should be: deep, and mostly nocturnal. Marine Parkway Bridge is still the spot, but you need to shift your clock. I fished the outgoing there two nights ago starting around 10 p.m., working bucktails — 1-ounce white with a white Gulp trailer — tight to the pilings and letting the current sweep them down along the structure. Two fish in the mid-20s, one push to 30, all on the same drift pattern, all in that first hour of hard outgoing water when the current stacks bait against the concrete. Daytime at that same spot has been dead for stripers. If you show up at noon expecting the same bite, you're wasting a tide.

Breezy Point surf has been quieter than I'd like for early August. A few schoolies mixed with bluefish on bucktails and swimming plugs right around first light, but nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet. That water's still waiting on real current and a break in this heat to wake up the way it can in September.

Weakfish have been the wildcard — not a target you can plan on, but real if you're fishing the channel edges through a tide change with the right presentation. I picked up two nice ones, one close to four pounds, working a small chartreuse twister tail on a light jighead along the drop-off near the Cross Bay Bridge on the tail end of the outgoing, right where the deeper channel meets the flat. That's a small window, maybe 20 minutes around the tide change, but it's real if you're there for it.

Porgies and blackfish are still mostly a September-October conversation in this bay — too warm right now, and the blackfish especially want that first real cool-down before they commit to structure. I wouldn't spend a trip chasing them yet.

Looking ahead, the tides start building toward the new moon over the next couple of days, and that's the thing that could actually change this pattern instead of just repeating it. Stronger current means more oxygen turning over in the bay, better bait movement, and — if we get any front activity mixed in, even a modest one — a real chance the bass shift back toward a daytime bite instead of hiding until dark. I wouldn't bank a whole trip on that shift happening by the weekend, but if I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the early morning outgoing at Marine Parkway and have a backup plan to slide into the bay for fluke if the bass don't show. That's the honest play right now — steady light tackle up top, patient nighttime work for the bigger fish, and an eye on the building tide for the first real sign this thing turns over.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: bass gone to the night shift, fluke still paying the bills
reports.subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers deep and nocturnal, but the inlet's still handing out keeper fluke and the blues never left.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the scale Tuesday morning with a cooler half-empty and a face like he lost a bet. "Mari, where'd all the bass go? I fished the Robert Moses bridge for two hours on the last of the ebb, nothing but blowfish and a couple rat blues." I didn't even have to look at the thermometer to answer him — I already knew. Water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the beach and inside the bay, and when it gets that warm on top, the bass do what they always do this time of year: they go down and they go dark. Literally. Daytime bite on stripers right now is a coin flip at best. Nighttime, working bunker chunks or eels around the deeper holes off Democrat Point and the west end of the inlet, that's where the real fish are living.

We called this one a few days back — said the surf pattern would hold through stable weather but a pop-up thunderstorm could knock it sideways for a day before it reset. That's basically what happened. We had one squally afternoon roll through midweek, turned the surf off Fire Island a little sloppy and stained for about six hours, and the blues scattered off the beach front. By the next morning it had cleaned back up and the bunker schools were right back where they started, just off the bar at Kismet and working east toward Lonelyville.

Speaking of the blues — they are absolutely the story of the week, and I mean that in the best way. Cocktail blues, two to four pounds, some genuine choppers mixing in up to six or seven, and they're hammering everything from the beach out to a half mile. If you're surfcasting Fire Island at first light, white or bunker-colored Hopkins spoons and Ava jigs with a strip of pork rind are getting hit on nearly every retrieve when you find the bait balls. From the boat, same story off Democrat Point and along the outside of the inlet bar — troll a small spoon or cast poppers into the surface commotion when the birds start diving, and you'll load the box fast. This is the wave Mother Nature owed us after a slow June, and it's holding as long as that warm surface layer stays put.

Fluke are still the steady paycheck, and honestly this bite hasn't changed much in three weeks, which is a good thing. We flagged this pattern last week too — keepers mixed with shorts, steady rather than a blitz, and that's exactly what's showing up on the drift. The Robert Moses bridges, both the east and west spans, are producing fluke to five and six pounds in 25 to 35 feet of water on the tail end of the outgoing tide, when the current is still moving enough to keep your bucktail ticking bottom but hasn't gone full slack. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of fluke belly or squid, dragged slow along the channel edges — that's the program. Inside the bay, the flats off Nicoll Bay and around the Sexton Island cuts near Sayville are holding shorts mostly, but there are enough 19- and 20-inch fish mixed in to make it worth a few drifts before you run out to the bridges for the bigger stuff.

Great South Bay itself has been quiet on the striper front during daylight — too warm, too much boat traffic, too much sun on the flats. But work the deeper holes off Patchogue and the channel edges near Fire Island Inlet after dark, live eels or fresh bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, and there are still real bass in there, some pushing into the high 20s and low 30s. The tide matters here more than almost anything else this time of year — I want the first two hours of the incoming after sunset, when the cooler bay water starts pushing back in against that warm outgoing layer and creates just enough of a temperature edge to get the bigger fish moving and feeding.

Porgies and blackfish are still mostly a summer afterthought right now — there's a decent porgy bite on the reefs and rock piles off Fire Island Inlet on green crab and clam, but nobody's targeting them seriously with the blues and fluke this active. Weakfish have been scarce; a few reports of incidental fish mixed in with the fluke catch on the bay flats, but nothing like a dedicated bite worth chasing yet.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and that means stronger tides are coming by the weekend. Bigger swings usually stir the water column and can jolt the bass out of that strict nocturnal pattern, especially if we get any overnight cooling. If the wind stays out of the south and southwest and the surface holds warm, I'd keep playing the same hand — blues and fluke during the day, bass after dark. But if we catch a cold front behind one of these afternoon storms, don't be surprised if the daytime bass bite wakes back up at the inlet seam on the first hour of the incoming. That's the window I'll be watching closest, and where I'd have my rod rigged and ready if I only had one trip this week.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Weakfish Still Working the Bridge
reports.subhead: With the surface water running warm, the real bite at Shinnecock happens after the sun's been down for hours — not right at dusk.
reports.body_markdown:
I skipped the 9 p.m. slack this week and made myself wait. That's the mistake most guys make out here in August — they show up right at dark, fish the tail end of the incoming, and wonder why the inlet feels dead. It's not dead. It's just not ready yet. With the water running warm the way it has been, the bass at Shinnecock have gone almost fully nocturnal, and they don't really turn on until the tide's been ripping out for an hour or two and the deep hole below the Coast Guard station has had time to load up with bait getting flushed out of the bay.

So that's where I put my time this week — 1 a.m. to about 4 a.m., fishing the last two-thirds of the outgoing on the ocean side of the jetty. Eels drifted along the rock edge on a fish-finder rig, and bunker chunks fished dead-still on the bottom in that 18 to 22 foot hole, produced the best fish — a few in the mid-30s, mixed with a lot of schoolies that wouldn't leave the bait alone. Nothing epic, but consistent enough that I stuck with it three nights running. If you're a plug guy, a black Danny or a bone-colored Gibbs pencil worked across the current seam where the outgoing water meets the ocean swell will draw strikes, but you need to be quiet getting into position — no white deck lights, no slamming hatches. These fish in the hole are educated and they spook off a hull shadow same as they spook off a bright flashlight.

Ponquogue Bridge is still doing what it does in early August, which is weakfish after dark on the outgoing, though I'll be honest — it's a thinner bite than it was three weeks ago. The fish that are there are quality, mostly 18 to 22 inches, holding tight to the pilings on the bay side where the current breaks around the concrete. Bucktails in the 3/4-ounce range tipped with a strip of squid, bounced right along bottom in that 12 to 15 foot depth, are still the most reliable presentation. A few guys are doing well on small ribbonfish-imitation soft plastics too — something with flash and a subtle wobble seems to matter more than color right now. Bring a headlamp with a red lens if you're going to be handling fish or retying — full white light over that bridge rail and you'll watch the whole school slide off into the dark.

During the day, the fluke bite has stayed the most dependable thing going on in the bay, and honestly we called this one — figured the drift out here would stay steady rather than blitz-style, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats working the sod banks off Tiana Beach and the channel edges near the Canal mouth are picking up a mix of keepers and shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails, 12 to 18 feet of water, moving bait just fast enough to keep it ticking bottom on the last of the incoming into the start of the outgoing. Nothing that fills a cooler in an hour, but steady enough that a patient drift puts two or three keepers in the box most trips. Porgies are mixed in on the same structure if you switch over to sandworms on a hi-lo rig — good action for kids or anyone who just wants bent rods without overthinking it.

Bluefish have shown up stronger than they have in a few weeks, which tracks with the warm surface water pushing down the coast right now. I've seen decent-sized blues — some pushing 5 and 6 pounds — chopping bait on the surface just outside the inlet in the early morning gray light, right before the sun gets high enough to shut them down. Diamond jigs or wire leader with a Hopkins if you want to avoid getting bit off. They're not sticking around long once the light comes up, so that's a dawn-only window, not an all-day thing.

As for the Canal and the run through to the Peconic — bait's been moving through there steadily on the tide changes, and that matters more than people think. When you see peanut bunker and spearing pushing hard through the Canal on an outgoing, it's usually a signal that the same forage is about to show up on the Montauk side within a few days. Worth keeping an eye on if you're planning a trip east later this week.

Looking ahead, the tides are building toward the new moon, and that stronger current should sharpen up both the inlet bass bite and the bridge weakfish, at least for a few nights. If a front comes through and knocks the surface temp down even a couple degrees, I'd expect the bass to loosen up and feed a little earlier in the evening instead of making us wait until 1 a.m. Until that happens, though, I'm staying on the night shift.

reports.headline: Stripers Gone to Ground — Execution Rocks Now a Night Shift
reports.subhead: Bluefish and fluke are carrying the daylight hours while the bass wait for dark and deep water on the Western Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop on City Island asked me straight out Thursday: "Frank, where'd all the bass go? I fished Stepping Stones three mornings this week and got skunked." I told him the same thing I've been telling everybody who'll listen since the temps climbed into the low 70s — the bass didn't go anywhere. They just stopped punching the clock during business hours.

Kings Point is reading 70.9 this week, and that's warm enough to shut down a lot of the daytime feeding you'd expect around Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones light. I've fished this stretch since before anybody had a chartplotter, and I've seen this pattern plenty of Augusts — when the surface layer gets soft and stable like this, the stripers slide down into the deeper basin water off Hart Island and along the Execution Rocks channel edge, and they wait for dark. New London's still sitting a touch cooler at 69.4, which tells you the whole Sound is holding this same soft, settled character right now, not just our end.

So that's where I've been putting my time — last two hours of light into full dark, and again right before first light, working live bunker and fresh mackerel chunks on fish-finder rigs in 25 to 40 feet off the northeast face of Execution Rocks on the outgoing tide. Had a solid mixed bag of slot fish Tuesday night, one pushing 34 inches that ate a whole bunker practically on the drop. The current there on the ebb pulls bait right off the rockpile and funnels it along that edge — it's been a producer for three decades and it isn't quitting on me now, it's just moved its hours. Stepping Stones is doing the same thing after dark — eels fished on a slow drift over the rubble bottom near the light have been worth the trip for anybody willing to stay out past ten.

Daytime, if you want steady action instead of a long wait for dark, the bluefish are doing the heavy lifting. Fresh fish have been pushing down into the Sound and they're stacked up around the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings and out toward Hart Island on the last two hours of the incoming. Diamond jigs and topwater poppers worked over visible surface activity — you'll see the birds working and the blues busting bunker on top — and it's about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. Bigger fish are mixing in with the smaller choppers, which tells me there's a fresh wave still filtering down from the east.

Fluke have been the most dependable read of the whole week, and honestly it's playing out about the way I figured it would. We said last week the keeper bite would stay mixed in with shorts rather than turn into anything explosive, and that's exactly what's happening on the drifts off Matinecock Point and through the Manhasset Bay channel. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, along the sandy edges in 20 to 30 feet on the tail end of the outgoing. You'll pick through a lot of 15-inch fish, but there's a keeper mixed in most drifts — nothing to write home about, but steady enough to fill a cooler if you put in the time and don't get frustrated culling shorts.

Weakfish have shown up in small numbers in the deeper holes off Hempstead Harbor, mostly at dusk on bucktails tipped with squid strips fished slow along bottom. Nothing like the old days when you could count on them stacking up there in August, but a few nice ones in the 4-to-5-pound class have come over the rail for guys who know to fish that last hour of light. Porgies remain about the most reliable thing going for anybody who just wants bent rods without overthinking it — sandworms on the bottom around Execution Rocks and the rockpiles off Matinecock will keep a rod busy all afternoon.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and that stronger tidal push over the next few days should stir the water column enough to get a few more stripers moving on the edges during daylight, especially on the front half of the outgoing when there's real current running. I wouldn't bank on a full return to the old daytime pattern just yet — it'll take either a real push of current from the bigger tides or a cold front to break up this warm, settled layer and reset things. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the outgoing at Execution Rocks starting an hour before sunset and stay through the first hour of dark, bunker chunks soaking on the bottom, bucktail rod rigged and ready in case the blues show up first. That's the way to cover both bases without wasting the tide.

reports.headline: 168 feet off the west side: haddock stacked on the mud, bluefin working the top of the Bank
reports.subhead: Stable high pressure held like we said it would, and Stellwagen rewarded anyone willing to run the gravel and watch the birds.
reports.body_markdown:
168 feet, mud bottom, west side of Stellwagen off the Basin edge — that's where I found the best marks all week. Haddock were stacked two and three deep on the sounder, tight to bottom in that soft gray mud that runs along the 160-to-220 line between the SW Corner and the Basin. Jigged them on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, and on the slower drifts we did just as well on a standard high-low rig with clam. Fish ran 18 to 24 inches, a few pushing better than that, and it didn't take long to fill a cooler once we found the right patch of bottom. The mud doesn't move much this time of year — it's the same real estate it's been for decades — but you still have to hunt for where the bait's sitting on any given tide.

Cod are a different story, and I'll be straight with you: recreational cod on Stellwagen right now means mostly catch-and-release, with the federal closures doing what they do in August. We picked up a handful of nice fish — 8 to 12 pounds — jigging the gravel patches up on the northern flank near the Fingers, 90 to 110 feet, but they went back over the side. If you want a cod dinner this month you're better off putting your energy into the haddock and letting the cod swim. That's just where the regs sit right now, and fighting it doesn't change anything.

The story everybody's asking about at the dock is the tuna, and I'll tell you what we're actually seeing rather than what people wish we were seeing. Bluefin are scouting — that's the right word for it. Mackerel schools have been thick on top of the Bank, 60 to 90 feet of water in spots along the eastern edge near Tillies, and we've had days where the birds are diving, the whales are working right through the same bait, and somewhere underneath all that commotion there are tuna cutting through. Marks on the sounder showing 40 to 60 feet down over 100 to 130 feet of water — that's your giant class fish pushing up on the bait balls. Some boats connected trolling green machines and spreader bars through the froth; others got shut out entirely on the same piece of water two hours later. That's the nature of scouting fish. They're here, they're not settled yet, and the bite windows are short and unpredictable day to day. If you're rigging for bluefin right now, I'd have a chunking spread ready to deploy the second you see the surface activity — don't wait, because it can shut off just as fast as it .

We flagged stable conditions holding through this stretch last week, and that's exactly what played out — light winds, clean water, no big fronts pushing through to stir up the Bank. That steadiness is a big part of why the haddock bite on the mud stayed so consistent; when the water's not getting kicked around, those fish sit predictably and you can work a drift methodically instead of chasing marks all over the chart. Same reason the mackerel schools have had time to build up on top of the Bank instead of getting scattered by a blow.

Pollock have been a nice bonus around the wreck structure on the northern end and along some of the steeper drop-offs into the Basin — 15 to 20 feet of jigging line off bottom in 100 to 130 feet, using the same diamond jigs we're running for haddock. They school up tight and when you find them you can load the box fast, though they don't hold like the haddock do — one pass and they scatter.

Whale watching boats have been running right alongside the same bait schools we're targeting for tuna, which tells you everything about where the forage is sitting this week. Humpbacks working the surface on mackerel, sometimes right on top of Tillies, sometimes drifting closer to the Basin edge depending on where the bait's pushed to. If you see whale-watch boats parked somewhere unusual, that's worth a look — they're following the same signal we are.

Hake have shown up mixed in with the haddock catches on the mud, nothing to target specifically but a welcome bycatch on the same rigs. Nothing unusual there for early August.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this pattern to break hard in the next few days. The high pressure's been steady, the water's clean, and the bait's holding position on top of the Bank rather than getting pushed off by weather. If that holds, I'd keep working the mud for haddock as your bread and butter — it's the most reliable thing going right now — and treat the tuna as a bonus you chase when you see the birds and whales working. I wouldn't run offshore specifically banking on bluefin connections yet; the scouting pattern needs another week or two to solidify into something you can plan a whole trip around. What I would do is keep gear rigged for both on the same trip, because right now you genuinely don't know which one's going to show up first when the marks light up on the screen. Watch for any wind shift out of the southwest building through the weekend — that's the kind of thing that could stir the mud line and scatter the haddock, so if you've got a window before it, I'd take it.

reports.headline: Great Point Rip on the Ebb: Bluefish Crash the Bait, Bonito Still a Ghost
reports.subhead: Two weeks of watching that green flash and it still hasn't shown — but the bunker pushing into the Sound are pulling blues and bass right behind them.
reports.body_markdown:
I was sitting off Great Point Monday morning, engine just idling, watching terns stack up over the rip on the last of the ebb — that tight, nervous hover they do right before they fold and drop. Bait was getting hammered underneath, water boiling white in patches maybe fifty yards wide. I ran up on it expecting to see that quick, chopping green flash that means bonito, or the harder, more surgical explosion that means albies. Instead it was bluefish — good ones, three to six pounds, just wrecking a pod of peanut bunker that had pushed in tight against the rip line. Not what I was hoping for, but I wasn't complaining once I got a Deadly Dick into the middle of it.

That's been the story for two weeks now. I keep expecting the first bonito of the season to show at Great Point or off Sankaty Head, and every morning I go out half-convinced this is the day. It isn't yet. But the pieces are there — the water's carrying real warmth, the bait is thick and getting pushed into tight seams by every tide change, and the temperature breaks that usually tip things off are starting to firm up out toward the Shoals. I've heard the same scouting talk out of Buzzards Bay and around the Vineyard — nothing confirmed, just guys seeing shapes they can't quite call yet. When it flips, it tends to flip fast. I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first real report out of this zone inside the next week to ten days, especially if this stable weather holds and the water keeps climbing in the low 70s inshore.

What we called correctly last week is playing out almost exactly as expected — this bluefish run is entirely about the bait. Wherever the bunker pods reform after getting pushed around by tide and wind, the blues show up within hours. Right now that's meaning the north side rips off Monomoy and the edge of Horseshoe Shoal, where bunker have been getting squeezed by current and picked apart. Bucktails and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything that throws flash — have been the ticket, worked fast through the froth. No need to overthink presentation right now; the blues aren't fussy, they're just violent.

Striped bass have settled into the pattern you'd expect for early August — they're not up chasing bait in the heat of the day, they're holding deep on structure and waiting for the light to change. Best fish have come off the Monomoy rips and around the deeper edges of Chatham inlet on the front half of the incoming, fished right at first light with eels or bunker chunks worked slow along bottom. A few guys have done well live-lining bunker over the deeper humps on Horseshoe Shoal at dusk, letting the current carry the bait naturally into the strike zone rather than working it hard. We're heading into the neap around the 5th and 6th, and that's going to soften current everywhere from the Point down to Monomoy — when that happens, the bass tend to compress onto the strongest remaining current hours and the deepest, coolest water they can find. That's the window I'd fish hardest this weekend, particularly the early morning push before the sun gets high.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing out here right now, honestly. Drifting the edges of Horseshoe Shoal and the flats off Monomoy Point in 15 to 25 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails have been putting keeper fluke in the boat consistently, with a scattering of shorts mixed in on every drift. The water's warm and stable enough that they're feeding actively through most of the tide, not just the peak of the moving water, which makes for a more forgiving day if you're short on time. If you want a bend in the rod without chasing shadows on the rips, that's where I'd start.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift in the next few days — the high pressure's holding, the bait's staying put, and the bluefish should keep working those same seams off Monomoy and Horseshoe Shoal as long as the bunker don't scatter. The bass game gets a little trickier as the neap sets in and current goes quiet; lighter jigs and slower presentations will matter more than they did last week. And I'll keep making the run out to Great Point and Sankaty every morning with my eyes locked on the water color, because sooner or later that first bonito is going to show, and when it does I want to be the one who sees the flash before anyone else does.

reports.headline: Peanuts Ball Up at Robinson's Hole — The Albies Aren't Far Behind
reports.subhead: Bait's stacking in the rips from Quick's Hole to Menemsha, the water's finally right, and the first false albacore of the season could show any tide now.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Robinson's Hole Thursday evening and watched peanut bunker ball up so tight against the current line you'd have thought someone poured a bucket of mercury into the water. Terns were diving on them, a couple of bluefish were slashing through from underneath, and out past the second rip line I saw a nervous flicker of bait get pushed sideways hard enough to make my stomach drop — that quick, violent push that isn't a bluefish. Couldn't confirm it. Didn't see the fish itself. But that's exactly the kind of push that means something toothy and fast just came through underneath.

We flagged this zone two weeks back as one of the better bets in New England for the season's first albies and bonito, and everything happening in the water right now backs that call up. The temperature breaks are set up textbook — warm water pooling in Vineyard Sound, colder push still coming through Quick's Hole and Robinson's Hole on the bigger tides, and bait getting squeezed right into the seam where those two temperatures collide. That seam is where I'm putting my time over the next week and a half. Nobody's boated a confirmed false albacore in our waters yet this year — I want to be straight about that, no albies in the box, no bonito on the leader — but the bait behavior, the birds, and the water temp gradient are all lining up the way they do right before the first scout fish show. Historically that's late here, but this feels early-normal, not late.

While we wait on that, the fishing that's actually happening has been solid, if you know where to put the anchor. Striped bass have gone exactly where you'd expect with surface temps sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s — down deep on structure through the daylight hours, then sliding up to feed hard in the low-light windows. Sow and Pigs Reef off Cuttyhunk has been giving up bass to guys jigging bucktails and diamond jigs tight to the rocks on the last two hours of the ebb, fish mostly in the 26 to 32-inch range with a few better ones mixed in after dark. The Woods Hole ledges are holding fish too — that's a night bite almost exclusively now, eels drifted on the current seams by the Coast Guard station producing better than anything thrown in daylight. If you want a day fish, you're going deep — 25 to 40 feet over structure, heavier bucktails, slow bounces, patience.

Fluke are having their best stretch of the summer right now and I'd be fishing them hard if the albie itch weren't so strong. Menemsha Bight has been quietly excellent — 4 to 6-pound fish coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow through 18 to 25 feet of water on the last of the incoming tide. The Woods Hole channel edges near the drawbridge have produced too, though you're fighting current there that can rip through at 3-plus knots on a big tide — light tackle guys, bring heavier jig heads than you think you need or you'll never feel bottom. Scup fishing has been the easy money all week — structure around Tarpaulin Cove and the rocks off Naushon are stacked with them, squid strips or sandworms on a simple high-low rig putting a fast dozen in the cooler for anybody who wants dinner without much drama.

Bluefish have been scattered but present wherever bait's been thick — a few blitzes reported off Oak Bluffs on schools of peanut bunker pushed close to the beach, topwater plugs and tins getting bit hard for short windows before the fish disappear as fast as they showed. That's a bait-driven fishery completely — find the bunker, find the blues, and when the bunker move off the blues go with them within hours.

Tide-wise, we're sliding into the neap around August 5th and 6th, and that's going to soften the current through the rips noticeably — Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole both run harder on the bigger tides, so expect the water to lay down some mid-week before building back up toward the next new moon push. Softer current means lighter jigs, slower drifts, and honestly it's not the worst thing for albie scouting — those fish will sit and pick at bait in a gentler rip just as happily as a screaming one, sometimes more comfortably.

If I had one day this week I'd fish the last two hours of daylight at Robinson's Hole on the building tide after the neap, watching for that nervous bait push and a fin that isn't a bluefish. Bring both an albie rod rigged with a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig and your bass gear, because right now you genuinely don't know which one's going to show first. That uncertainty is the whole fun of the first two weeks of August out here — everybody's watching the same rips, waiting for the same one boil that changes the whole conversation for the rest of the fall.

reports.headline: Race Point Mackerel Balls Draw Bass Up — Cod Still Sulking Deep
reports.subhead: A softening tide and thick mackerel schools set up a strong dawn bite off the Race, while Billingsgate fluke keep the afternoons honest.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, first light, I had the boat idling on the north side of Race Point, watching the meter light up like a Christmas tree. Mackerel — thick, ball after ball of them, holding right on the edge where the rip meets the deeper water. I dropped a Sabiki down through the middle of one of those balls, came up with three at once, and before I even had them in the well I saw the reason those macks were bunched so tight. A big swirl, then another, right under the bait. Bass. We hooked a live mackerel through the collar on a 5/0 circle, freelined it back into the melee, and it didn't get twenty feet before the rod bent in half. That fish went thirty-eight inches. We had two more in the low thirties before the tide slacked off and the whole show shut down like someone flipped a switch.

That's been the pattern all week off Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars — mackerel stacking on the rip lines at first light and again toward dusk, and the bass riding up underneath them for a short, violent window before they drop back down. Surface water in the bay is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s now, which is warm enough that the bigger fish don't want to sit up in it all day. They're doing what they always do this time of year — holding deep on the structure through the heat of the day, then coming up to hammer bait in the low-light hours. If you're out there at noon casting into empty water, that's not bad luck, that's just where the fish are supposed to be. Best move during the day is dropping bucktails or jigs down onto the humps along the Bars, working them slow off bottom, rather than beating the surface.

Sandy Neck has been a different game — quieter water, less current, but the stripers there have been sliding up onto the flats after dark chasing sand eels and small bait pushed in by the tide. Guys drifting live eels along the edges of the deeper guts off Sandy Neck after sundown have done well, nothing giant but a steady pick of schoolies and a few keepers mixed in. Bluefish have been in and out — when the bait schools hold together you'll get a short window of chopper blues busting bait on top, but it's not the sustained blitz you sometimes get here in August.
