It's bait-driven entirely. Wherever the mackerel or peanut bunker bunch up tight, the blues show within the hour. When the bait scatters, so do they.

Billingsgate has been the more dependable afternoon play. The fluke bite over that shoal has been solid — not a doormat bonanza, but a steady pick of fish in the 18 to 22 inch range, with a few pushing toward five and six pounds mixed in. We've been drifting the sand edges on the moving tide with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, working them slow along bottom, and switching over to squid strips when the current really starts moving. The fluke are feeding hardest on the last two hours of the incoming, when the water's pushing bait up off the flats and onto the drop.

Cod, I'll be honest with you, have been scarce. This is typical for early August — the deeper structure off Provincetown, the humps out past eighty, ninety feet, just aren't holding fish the way they will once the water starts cooling in September and October. A couple of boats have picked at a few fish jigging diamond jigs tipped with squid strips over the deeper structure, but it's been slow, inconsistent work, more of a bonus than a target species right now. If cod are what you're after, I'd wait another month before putting serious time into it. Right now your time is better spent on the bass and fluke.

We're heading into a neap tide over the next few days, and that's going to soften the current across the whole bay — the rips off Race Point and Peaked Hill won't run as hard, which usually means the bait doesn't get pushed and concentrated the same way. When that happens, the bass bite tends to compress into shorter windows right around the strongest push of current, and the presentations need to slow down to match it. I'd expect the early morning bite off the Race to still produce, but I wouldn't be surprised if it's a tighter window than what we saw this week — maybe forty-five minutes instead of two hours. Lighter jigs, slower retrieves, and patience on the drift will matter more than usual the next few days.

Looking ahead, keep an eye on those mackerel schools. As long as they're stacking on the rips at Race Point and Peaked Hill, the bass will keep showing up to feed on them in the low light. If the macks scatter or move off the structure, the bass pattern will shift with them — probably deeper, probably tighter to Billingsgate and the deeper edges off Barnstable. That's where I'd start looking if the Race goes quiet. For now, if you can get out for that first hour of daylight, it's worth the trip. Just don't expect it to last all morning.

reports.headline: Deer Island Ledge on the Last Ebb: Bass on Live Mackerel, Flounder Working the Flats
reports.subhead: Mid-summer has the harbor's bass locked to structure by day and feeding hard at first and last light — here's where I'm putting the boat this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Every morning this week I've had the same argument with myself at the dock: harbor islands, North Shore rocks, or run south to Plymouth. This week the harbor wins, and it's not close. The bait's stacked on the Deer Island ledge, the current's still got some teeth in it before the neap softens things up, and the bass have settled into the pattern I expect out of early August — deep on structure through the heat of the day, up on the pogies and mackerel at first light, last light, and after dark.

I've been starting at the Deer Island Light drop-off, working the edge where the channel falls from 15 feet to 30 on the last two hours of the ebb into dead low. Live mackerel and pogies on a fish-finder rig, 20-pound fluorocarbon leader, just enough weight to hold bottom without killing the bait's action. That drop is a highway for forage getting pushed out of President Roads, and the bass are sitting right on the lip waiting for it to spill over. Nothing enormous — mostly 26 to 34 inches, with a couple of overslot fish that came unbuttoned before I got a hand on them — but it's been a consistent bite, not a fluke morning. Same program works Spectacle Island's north ledge on the push of the flood, though I've had better luck there with a swimming plug worked slow over the rocks at first light than with bait.

If you'd rather stay shallow and light-tackle, Nahant is fishing the way it should in August. The rockpile pockets between the causeway and East Point are holding bass that slide up into two and three feet of water after dark chasing pogies pinned against the boulders. A black Sluggo on a 3/8-ounce weighted hook, or a Redfin swimming just under the surface, worked slow through the wash — that's the ticket. I had three fish over 30 inches out there Tuesday night in under an hour, then it went dead quiet for the rest of the tide. That's the nature of the rocks right now: short, sharp windows tied to the tide change, and if you're not there for it, you're just casting at empty water.

Gloucester and Cape Ann are holding mackerel schools thick enough that you can find them by the birds working before you ever mark them on the sounder, and the bass are shadowing those schools around the outer ledges off Rockport and Straitsmouth. Jig the mackerel on small diamond jigs for bait or bring a few home for the pan, then switch to a bucktail or umbrella rig and work the same water — the bass have been mixed right in, sitting under the bait balls in 25 to 40 feet. It's not a blitz, it's a working pattern, and the fish have been there for anyone willing to make the run out past the harbor mouth.

South of the city, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay have flounder fishing that's been steady and underrated all summer. Sandworms and clam strips on a simple spreader rig, fished on the flats at the top of the warm afternoon tide, are still putting fish in the bucket — nothing that'll win a tournament, but a solid meal and an easy day for anyone who wants to get off the rocks for a stretch. Scituate's had bluefish showing wherever peanut bunker have pushed up into the harbor mouth, and when those blues find the bait it turns into fast, violent topwater fishing for twenty minutes at a time — small Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast across the surface, no leader needed to be subtle about it, just keep your fingers away from their teeth when you unhook them.

We flagged last week that conditions in this zone would hold stable with no big thermal shift coming, and that's exactly how it's played — no cold-water surprises, no sudden bait crash, just the same warm, settled mid-summer read carrying through. That stability is why the pattern's been so readable: bass down deep on the ledges by day, up shallow on the rocks and drop-offs during the low-light windows, bluefish trailing whatever bait concentrates.

The tide range is narrowing into the neap over the next couple days, and that's going to change how I fish the harbor by the weekend. Softer current means less push over structure, which means I'll be going lighter — smaller jigs, slower retrieves, more patience letting the bait sit instead of relying on the current to do the work. The bridges and channel edges around Deer Island and the Chelsea River mouth tend to hold the strongest remaining current through a neap cycle, and that's where I'd put my time after dark this weekend if the bite up top goes quiet. Cod and haddock chances remain a deeper-water game right now — Stellwagen's edge and the offshore ledges off Cape Ann are the play if you want bottom fish, working jigs and diamond jigs tight to structure in 100-plus feet where the water stays cool enough to hold them through the summer.

If I had one trip to make this week, it's the Deer Island ledge on the last two hours of the ebb, live mackerel down deep, switching to a bucktail on the drift once the tide goes slack. The bait's there, the structure's there, and the fish have been showing up on schedule. Just don't expect it to stay easy if that neap tide takes the current out of it — that's when this bite gets fussy, and you'll need to slow everything down to keep drawing strikes.

reports.headline: West End on the 6:14 Flood: Bass Hold the Seam, Blues Crash Late
reports.subhead: With the tide range shrinking into the weekend neap, the Canal's bite is compressing into shorter, sharper windows — and you'd better be standing there when they open.
reports.body_markdown:
6:14 flood, west end, Tuesday morning — I had a rod bent inside four minutes of the current turning at the Mashnee cut, a school bass maybe 26 inches coming off the seam where the flood pushes hard against that rock pile off Hog Island. That's the tell right now. The water's mid-to-upper 70s, thick and warm on top, and these fish don't want to work for a meal in that kind of heat. They want the current to bring it to them, and they want it fast, in the first hour of a strong stage, before the seam gets sloppy and spreads out.

That's the whole story of the Canal this week — it's a current clock, and the window's getting shorter by the day. We're sliding into the neap around the 5th and 6th, which means peak flow at both ends is easing off, and anybody who's fished this ditch for more than a season knows what that does. The rips get lazier, the seams get mushier, and the fish that were willing to sit right in the teeth of a 4-knot flood start backing off into deeper water where it's cooler and less work. We flagged this pattern last week — said the softening current would push the better fish onto the deepest, coolest structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now. Night eels at the Bourne and Sagamore Bridge pilings, and down at the Route 6 Gut where the water stacks up against the abutments, are turning into the more consistent play after dark than daylight jigging anywhere along the ditch.

Daytime, if you want a bass, you're fishing deep and you're fishing the drop-off edges. West end guys working 2-3 ounce diamond jigs and white/chartreuse Ava-style jigs tight to the bottom off the Mashnee flats and along the Hog Island channel edge have been picking at fish in that mid-20s to low-30-inch range, nothing giant, but real, and enough to make a morning worthwhile if you're willing to grind bottom on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got enough push to hold bait against structure.

East end's been the bluefish end of the equation. Bunker pods have been rolling through on the last of the night tides and again around first light, and where they concentrate — off Scusset Beach and out toward the rip line at the canal mouth — the blues have been all over them, blowing up on top hard enough to hear from the beach. This is a bait fishery straight through, no mystery to it: wherever those bunker schools reform after getting pushed around by boat traffic and current, the blues show up behind them within the hour. Topwater poppers and 3-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the melee have been drawing quick, violent strikes, sometimes two and three fish before the school scatters again. If you're marking bunker balling up tight on your sounder near the east end jetty, don't wait — that window closes as fast as it opens.

Fluke have been a nice side story for the guys willing to work the flats around Mashnee Island and the channel edges by Hog Island on the moving tide. Nothing giant, but keeper-class fish in the 18 to 20-inch range have come on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow across the sand-to-mud transitions on the last two hours of either tide when the current's still got some shape to it but isn't ripping so hard you can't feel bottom.

Now here's what's got my attention for the coming week, and it's not something I can promise you yet — bonito and albies. We haven't had a confirmed fish inside the Canal proper, but Buzzards Bay on the west side has been warming fast, and Wings Neck and the mouth of Phinneys Harbor are exactly the kind of temperature-break water that tends to produce the season's first scouting fish. If those temp breaks hold and squid keep pushing into the Bay the way they've been doing regionally, I wouldn't be shocked to hear about a bonito or two showing at the west end rip in the next week to ten days. Worth having a small epoxy jig or Deadly Dick rigged and ready if you're already out there for bass.

My plan for the week: fish the strongest hour of current on either end at first and last light, don't waste effort on the slack, and if the neap softens things up as much as I expect by the weekend, I'm sliding my best hours to full dark at the bridges with eels. That's where this bite is heading, and it's where I'll be standing.

reports.headline: Monhegan Ledges on the Ebb: Bass Push the Structure While Pollock Work the Top
reports.subhead: Mackerel are thick enough to feed the whole bay, and that's dragging stripers and groundfish both into range this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I was hauling gear off the backside of Monhegan Tuesday morning, southwest ledge, and had to stop the boat twice because the mackerel were showering so thick they looked like rain hitting the water sideways. Forty years I've watched that happen out there, and it never fails to mean something. Where the mackerel pile up this time of year, the bigger fish aren't far behind, and this week they weren't.

Striped bass have settled into the pattern I'd expect for the first week of August — holding tight to structure through the heat of the day and coming up on the mackerel schools at first light and again toward dusk. The river mouths are the place to start. Damariscotta, Medomak, and the St. George have all been giving up fish on the last of the incoming and the first hour of the ebb, when the current pulls bait out of the marsh grass and stacks it against the ledge rock. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a big white or chartreuse bucktail worked slow along bottom in twelve to twenty feet, has been the ticket. Nothing fancy. The bass don't need convincing when the bait's this thick — they need you in the right spot at the right minute of tide, and that's the whole game up here.

Eastern Egg Rock has fished the way it usually does in early August — a little bit of everything if you're willing to work for it. Bass around the edges of the rock on the push tide, mackerel stacked over the deeper water to the south and west of it thick enough that you can jig a rod bent double in under a minute, and the puffins doing their business overhead like they always do this time of year. If you want mackerel for bait or the pan, that's your spot. Diamond jigs, no bait needed, straight up and down in fifteen to thirty feet.

Groundfish are where the real story is for anybody running out past the islands. Penobscot Bay's deeper channels — the water off Two Bush, the drop-offs east of Vinalhaven, the ledges running down toward Isle au Haut — have been holding cod and haddock in the classic pattern, working the bottom in a hundred to a hundred-eighty feet where the water stays cool no matter what the surface is doing. Jigging has outfished bait this week, diamond jigs and heavier soft-plastic tails worked with a short hop off bottom. Pollock, meanwhile, have been coming up on top over structure around Matinicus and the outer ledges off Stonington, chasing the same mackerel that are drawing everything else in. If you see birds working and pollock rolling on the surface, that's your cue to put down the bottom rig and throw something shiny on top — a Deadly Dick or a light diamond jig worked fast through the melee will get bit fast.

We flagged conditions holding steady through this stretch last week, and that's exactly what's played out — stable high pressure, clean water, bait thick enough to organize the whole food chain from mackerel up through bass and groundfish. That kind of stability is a gift this time of year, and it's why the fishing's been dependable rather than spectacular. Nobody's filling a cooler in an hour, but a patient boat working the right tide stage has been finding fish pretty consistently.

Bluefish remain the exception up here — a few showing around the outer islands and in Boothbay's outer harbor when the water's warmed enough, but this isn't Jersey or the Sound. If you connect on a blue up this way in early August, treat it as a bonus, not a target species.

Looking ahead, the moon's sliding toward neap around the fifth and sixth, and that's going to soften the current everywhere from the Muscle Ridge Channel out to Monhegan. When that current lays down, the bass tend to spread off the hard structure and settle into the deeper eddies where the bait pools up rather than getting pushed past — that's a pattern I've watched play out plenty of Augusts. It doesn't mean the fish disappear, it means you slow down and fish the troughs and the back sides of ledges instead of the fast water. Groundfish trips should hold up fine regardless, since the deep channels don't care much what the tide's doing on the surface, but the pollock topwater bite will likely go quieter for a few days until the current builds back.

If I had one day this week, I'd run out to Monhegan on the last two hours of the ebb, work the southwest ledge with bucktails first, then switch to jigs on the pollock if I see them showing. Bring mackerel gear regardless — you'll want bait either way, and right now there's no shortage of it out there.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock on the slack: cod holding deep, bass riding the mackerel push at Bailey
reports.subhead: The bay's structure is doing what August structure does — cod tucked in the cold water, stripers and blues stacked wherever the mackerel decide to show.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning drifting off the back side of Peaks Island watching a raft of herring gulls work a bait ball no bigger than a rowboat, and it told me most of what I needed to know about this week. The mackerel are still here, but they're not the solid, mile-long schools we had in late May and June — they've broken into pockets, and you have to go find them rather than have them find you. That's a normal August transition, not a red flag, but it changes how you fish the bay.

Halfway Rock remains the anchor point for anyone serious about groundfish this week. I marked cod in 90 to 130 feet on the northwest side of the ledge, holding tight to bottom where the water stays coldest, and the pattern held true to what I'd expect for early August — you need the slack, or close to it, to get a clean vertical presentation down to them without your jig sailing off into the current. Diamond jigs in the 4- to 6-ounce range, tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked better than bare metal this week. Haddock were mixed in but scattered — I took two keeper-sized fish over three trips out there, which tells you this isn't a bang-bang bite right now. It's a patience bite. You put your time in on the slack, you cover the ledge methodically, and you take what the tide gives you.

The moon is sliding toward neap around August 5-6, and you can already feel the current softening at the Rock and out around Jewell Island. That's worth planning around. Weaker tidal push means groundfish spread out more over the structure instead of holding tight to the hardest current seams, so I'd widen my drift pattern rather than working the same six-foot lane over and over. It also means the window for a clean vertical jig stretches a little longer on either side of the actual slack, which is a small mercy if you're working the ledges solo.

Striped bass are doing exactly what I expected them to do this time of year — holding deep on structure through the warmest part of the day and coming up to feed hard at first light and again at dusk. I've had good reports of bass working the ledges off Cape Small and around the mouth of the New Meadows, chasing pogies and the scattered mackerel pods right at daybreak. Live-lined mackerel on a fish-finder rig is about as simple and effective as it gets out there, but if you don't want to run bait, a white bucktail with a chartreuse curl-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom on the last hour of the incoming, has been drawing strikes off Bailey Island near Mackerel Cove — appropriately enough. Daytime action has been tougher, mostly limited to guys jigging deep over structure at Ram Island Ledge and getting the occasional fish willing to commit in 40-plus feet of water.

Bluefish are the wild card this week. When they show, they show hard — I heard from a Harpswell captain who ran into a genuine blitz off Elm Island for about twenty minutes before it shut off as fast as it started. That's the nature of the bluefish right now: they're following bait, not holding structure, so you need to be mobile and ready to run when you see the birds working or the water start to nervous up. Metal lures — anything in the Hopkins or Kastmaster family — cast into the edge of a breaking school will get bit immediately if the fish are actually there.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions in the bay would hold steady through the week — and that's roughly what's happened. Nothing exploded, nothing collapsed. The bay is doing its normal early-August work: bait scattering, fish settling into low-light routines, groundfish tucking into the cold water on the ledges. It's an honest week, not a spectacular one.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the neap tide to soften current enough that Halfway Rock and Old Anthony's Ledge fish a little slower and a little wider through the weekend — lighter jigs, longer drifts, more patience required. For stripers, I'd focus my time on the dawn window at Cape Small and the Bailey Island ledges where mackerel have been showing, since that's where the bass are actually committing to feed. If the bluefish show again off Harpswell, treat it as a bonus, not a plan — they're moving too much right now to count on. Watch the wind through midweek; if it stays out of the southwest and light, the surface stays clean enough to sight-fish bait balls, which is half the game out here this time of year.

reports.headline: Wood Island Ledge Gave Up a 28-Pound Bass on the Incoming — Then Went Quiet
reports.subhead: Biddeford Pool's morning flood is still the best hour in Southern Maine, but you've got to be there for it — the rest of the tide is a coin flip.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, half-tide incoming, fog still sitting on the water off Wood Island. I put a black Danny plug on the outside edge of the ledge where the current starts to stack against the rock, and on the third cast something hit it like it meant to end my week. Twenty-eight pounds, fat as a football, full of mackerel. That's the Pool doing what it does best — bass staging on the bar waiting for the tide to shove bait over the top, and for about ninety minutes it was as good as this beat gets all summer. Then the tide filled in, the current went soft, and it was over. That's the honest version. One great hour, and I worked the rest of the morning for a follower and nothing else.

That's basically the story of the whole zone right now — short, sharp windows, and a lot of dead water in between. We're sliding toward the neap around the 5th and 6th, and you can feel the current losing its shoulders already. Less push means less bait getting flushed out of the marshes and over the structure, which means bass aren't being forced to feed — they're doing it on their own schedule, and that schedule is dawn, dusk, and full dark. We flagged this coming — said the fish would tighten up onto the hardest current hours and the deepest structure once the tides went slack, and that's exactly what's happening at the Pool channel and around Wood Island Harbor. If you're fishing the middle of the day right now, you're fishing for company, not fish.

Mackerel are still thick off the Cape Elizabeth ledges and out past Prouts Neck, which is good news because that's the bait pushing bass up tight to the rocks. Snag a few on a mackerel tree, drop one back on a fishfinder rig into the deeper cuts off Prouts on a falling tide, and you'll find fish holding right on the bottom in fifteen to twenty-five feet, especially when there's a little southwest wind blowing bait against that shoreline. That wind direction is the one to watch down there — it piles water and forage right into the rocks at Prouts Neck and makes the whole stretch from the Neck down toward Bald Head fishable with big swimmers and pencil poppers worked slow along the edges.

Higgins Beach had a real moment of it Thursday evening — pogies got pushed up tight to the sandbar by a body of bluefish that came through like a chainsaw. Birds diving, blues busting bait on top, the whole show for maybe forty minutes right at last light. Anybody throwing a silver Kastmaster or a Hopkins through the melee got bit, some fish pushing six, seven pounds with teeth that'll take a chunk out of a soft plastic if you're not paying attention. That's a bait-driven bite, pure and simple — wherever those pogy schools reform after getting scattered, the blues show up within hours. If the bunker stay put off Higgins, that pattern should run again this week, but bluefish blitzes up here come and go with the bait schools, and I wouldn't plan a whole trip around one location without a backup.

Pine Point's been quieter for stripers but solid for flounder — the channel edges off the Nonesuch and Scarborough River mouths are holding fish on the bottom, bloodworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig, fished right on the last of the outgoing when the current's carrying the flats water out through the cut. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady action if you want dinner and don't mind soaking bait for a couple hours.

Night fishing is where the real bass are right now. Cape Elizabeth's rocky points, the mouth of the Pool, and the deeper water around Wood Island Harbor are all holding bigger fish that are laying up on structure through the heat of the day and coming up to feed after dark. An eel on a slow swim past the ledges, or a big darter worked just under the surface in that first hour of full dark, has been the move for anyone willing to put in the hours. It's not fast fishing. It's a couple of good bites a trip if you're in the right spot on the right stage of tide, but the fish that come are usually the better ones.

Offshore, if you've got a boat that'll run out into the cooler Gulf of Maine water, cod and pollock have stayed steady on the deeper structure — nothing dramatic, just consistent, which this time of year I'll take.

Looking ahead: with the tides softening into the neap, I'd expect the bite to keep compressing into those tight windows — dawn and dusk at Higgins if the bait holds, the incoming hour at the Pool for anyone who can time it right, and night eels for the ledge-huggers at Wood Island and Prouts Neck. If the southwest wind holds through the weekend, Prouts Neck is where I'd put my time. If it swings around and kicks up a lot of chop, I'd rather work the calmer water inside the Pool and let the tide do the sorting for me.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 210 feet: haddock thick on the mud, cod thin on the gravel edge
reports.subhead: Bait's stacking on the ledge, the haddock are holding tight to structure, and the first bluefin scouts showed up behind the boat this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Two hundred ten feet, straight mud, northeast corner of Jeffrey's Ledge — that's where I found the best marks of the week, a tight red smear sitting six to ten feet off bottom that turned into haddock as soon as the jigs hit it. That basin mud between Jeffrey's and the edge of Scantum holds haddock this time of year the way a magnet holds shavings, and this week it delivered. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, worked in a slow lift-drop right on the meter mark, put good numbers of 18 to 22 inch haddock in the box on three of four trips out. No need to horse the retrieve — these fish are eating on the fall, and if you're ripping the jig too fast you're pulling it right past their nose.

Cod is the harder story right now. I worked the gravel edge on the western side of Jeffrey's — the transition where the mud gives way to hard bottom in about 165 to 185 feet — and found cod, but scattered, not stacked. A few fish in the 8 to 12 pound class came up on jigs, a couple better ones in the mid-teens on bait, but you had to grind for them. I made three separate drifts across the same stretch of gravel Tuesday before I found a pod worth stopping the boat for. That's typical August pattern on this ledge — the cod aren't gone, they're just spread thin and holding tighter to the harder structure than they were in June. If you're going after them, fish the up-current edge of the gravel where it breaks toward the mud, drop a cod rig with clam or herring belly, and be patient. Don't waste time on soft bottom expecting cod — that's haddock water, different fish, different address.

Pollock have been the wildcard and honestly some of the most fun fishing of the week. Mid-water marks over the deeper basins — 40 to 60 feet off bottom in 200-plus feet of water — turned into pollock blitzes on a few drifts, six and eight pound fish hitting jigs on the drop before they even got near bottom. If you see that kind of mid-water sign on the meter, don't bother sending the jig all the way down. Work it through that band and you'll save yourself the grind.

Mackerel showed up in numbers around Platts Bank and along the inshore edge of Jeffrey's this week, which is exactly the kind of bait signal that gets my attention this time of year. The Gulf of Maine water out here is running noticeably cooler than what they're dealing with south of the Cape, and that temperature difference is exactly why bait wants to be here — herring and mackerel pushing onto the ledge, stacking up where the cooler water holds. We flagged this a couple weeks back, said conditions looked set up to stay favorable for offshore runs, and that's held true — steady weather windows all week let us get out and cover ground instead of sitting at the dock watching a forecast fall apart.

And where there's bait building like this, the bluefin start paying attention. We had two separate sightings this week — one behind the boat off the southeast corner of Jeffrey's, one further out toward Tillies Bank — fish showing on the surface, working a bait ball, gone before anyone got a bait in the water. That's scouting behavior, not committed feeding, and I want to be straight with you about that. Nobody I've talked to at the dock has hooked up yet. But this is exactly how the pattern starts every year — bait concentrates on the cooler water of the ledge through late July into August, tuna show up to check it out, and by the back half of the month they're committing hard enough to troll or chunk consistently. If you want to get ahead of it, I'd run a spread of green machines and a couple of ballyhoo behind the boat while you're groundfishing the ledge anyway — costs you nothing, and if those scouts turn into feeders you want to already be dragging something through the water.

Tide-wise, we're sliding toward the neap around the 5th and 6th, which means current on the ledge edges will soften up some heading into next week. That's worth knowing for the gravel bite specifically — cod tend to key on current pushing bait across those hard edges, so with the tide easing off, I'd expect the gravel fishing to get a touch tougher before it gets better again on the next building tide. Haddock on the mud don't seem to care much either way; that bite's been steady regardless of tide stage, which tells me it's more about the bait holding in that basin than current strength.

Looking ahead, if the weather holds the way it's been holding, I'd put my time on the mud for numbers of haddock, work the gravel patiently for a mixed bag of cod, and keep a trolling spread out on every trip regardless of target — the tuna scouting isn't a guarantee of a bite yet, but the ingredients are lining up the way they do most years right before the real bluefin fishing turns on. I wouldn't book a dedicated tuna trip just yet. I would keep gear rigged and ready, because when these fish commit on Jeffrey's, it tends to happen fast.

reports.headline: Shoals Cod Hold Deep, Bass Sneak Into Hampton on the Flood
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't mean thirteen miles of fishing — the Isles of Shoals still stack fish nobody bothers to find.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure that's the whole story for New Hampshire. It's not. Run out past White Island, work the backside of Appledore, drop a line off Duck Island Ledge in a hundred and fifty feet — you're fishing water that behaves like it's off Chatham or Monhegan, not tucked between two states that barely claim a coastline at all. I trailer a 20-foot Lund out of Rye Harbor most mornings before the sun's up good, and by the time the tourist boats are loading up for their nine o'clock run to the Shoals, I've already got a box going.

This week the pattern out there has been steady if you respect it. Cod are still down on the deep structure off the Shoals — 130 to 180 feet, sometimes deeper on the humps southeast of Duck Island. Diamond jigs, the heavier ones, 8 to 12 ounces depending on drift speed, worked with a short hop off bottom, have been the most consistent producer. A couple boats out of Rye have done well soaking clam bellies on a simple two-hook bottom rig in the same water when the current's light enough to hold bottom without a ton of weight. Fish have run mostly in the 5 to 10 pound class, with the occasional double-digit fish coming up when someone finds a pocket that hasn't been worked over. Haddock have been spottier — you'll mark them on the sounder in loose clusters rather than the tight schools you want, and it's taking more moves to put a limit together than it did back in June. If you're haddock-specific right now, plan on burning gas checking three or four spots rather than parking on one.

The tide's about to soften up on us. We're sliding into a neap around the 5th and 6th, and that's going to knock the current down noticeably out at the Shoals and in the Piscataqua both. When that happens, drop jig weight and slow the retrieve — the fish don't move as far to feed when the water's barely moving, so you need to put the jig right on their nose rather than count on drift to cover ground. I've seen this exact stretch before in early August: current goes soft, cod tighten up right on the structure instead of spreading over it, and the guys who keep fishing like it's still ripping end up working way too fast over fish that would've eaten a slower presentation.

Stripers have been the more interesting story this week, honestly. Mackerel schools are working the coast in good numbers right now, and wherever those pods bunch up near structure, bass and blues are showing up to hammer them. Rye Harbor breakwater and the water off Great Boars Head have both given up bluefish blitzes in the last week — nothing you need a boat for, casting metal, Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters, into visible surface activity has been enough. The stripers have settled into that classic mid-summer rhythm: they're holding deep on structure through the heat of the day and coming up hard at first light, at dusk, and after dark. If you're fishing daylight hours, you're jigging deep or live-lining a mackerel over structure and waiting. If you can fish the edges of the day, that's when the real bite happens.

Hampton Harbor keeps doing what it's known for — bass sliding in on the incoming tide to work the bait pushed up into the back channels, then dropping back out with the ebb. I've had my best luck there fishing the last two hours of the flood, right as the current starts to slow near the top, with a live mackerel or a chunk of fresh bunker fished on a fish-finder rig tight to the deeper channel edges near the inlet. After dark, that same stretch has been worth an eel swim for anyone willing to stay out past the tourist traffic. Seabrook side of the same system has produced similarly — the bait doesn't care which side of the channel it's on, and neither do the bass.

Flounder have been quiet, which isn't a surprise for early August — that's a spring and fall fishery here more than a summer one, and the deeper holes in the Piscataqua near Portsmouth Harbor are about the only place worth a drift right now if you're set on flatfish. I wouldn't build a trip around it this week.

Looking ahead: expect the softening tide to keep pushing cod tighter to structure through the weekend, which actually makes them easier to find once you commit to slowing down. Bass and blues should keep riding the mackerel schools along the open coast as long as that bait stays put, and Hampton's harbor mouth should keep producing on the flood as long as the bait keeps funneling through. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd run the Shoals early on a light-current morning for cod, then swing back toward Rye Harbor in the evening to see if the blues are still working the breakwater. Small water, but it never runs out of things to show you if you're willing to look.

reports.headline: Beavertail bunker push blues onto the ledges, doormats stack the East Passage
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker are pouring off the rocks from Brenton Point to Sakonnet, and everything with teeth is following them in.
reports.body_markdown:
Walked out onto the ledges below Beavertail Tuesday morning and the water was nervous before I even made a cast — peanut bunker stacked three deep against the rocks, silversides skittering on top of them, and something big pushing from underneath. That's the tell this time of year. When the bait gets that jumpy right against structure, you don't need a fish finder, you need a rod in your hand and your feet already wet.

That bunker push has been the whole story along the south shore this week, from Brenton Point down through the Dumplings and into the mouth of the Sakonnet. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bluefish bite was entirely bait-driven, that wherever the bunker re-formed after a blow, the blues would show within hours — and that's exactly what's playing out. Second Beach had a solid blitz Thursday evening, gulls working tight over busting bait, blues in the 3-6 pound range crushing everything from Hopkins jigs to topwater poppers. Sakonnet Point has had the same show on and off, best right at first light before the boat traffic pushes through. If you see the bunker balled up tight against a ledge, don't wait — that window can close in twenty minutes once the blues move through and scatter them.

Striped bass are playing the game they always play in early August — deep and quiet on structure through the day, up and hunting in the low light. The rocks off Beavertail and around the Dumplings are holding fish 25 to 40 feet down, and daytime action there means dropping bucktails or diamond jigs and working them slow off the bottom. But dawn and dusk change everything. I've had my best action swimming a 3-ounce bucktail with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer right along the base of the ledges at Sakonnet Point on the last two hours of the incoming, right as the light starts to go flat. Night eelers working the Sakonnet River bridges and the pilings around Jamestown have been doing well too — nothing giant, mostly 26 to 34 inches, but steady enough to make the late shift worth it.

Fluke are about as good as they get right now, which lines up with what the whole region is seeing this time of year. The East Passage rip off the Newport Bridge has been holding doormat-class fish in 30 to 45 feet, and drifting the edge of that channel with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail has produced fish to 6 pounds for me twice this week. Sakonnet River mouth is fishing the same way — work the channel edges on the dropping tide, keep the boat moving slow, and don't be afraid to bounce bottom hard. The warm, stable water has these fish feeding aggressively on the move, and that pattern should hold as long as this settled weather sticks around.

Tog are a mixed bag right now, and I'll be honest about it — midsummer isn't when this fishery shines. The deep ledges off Beavertail and the rockpiles around Gould Island are holding fish, but they're tucked into the cracks and cooler pockets in 35 to 50 feet, and you're working for every bite. Green crabs on a jig head, dropped right into the crevices on the slack tide, have picked at a few keepers, but it's slow, patient fishing more than a bite you can count on. I'd treat it as scouting for the fall run rather than a primary target right now. Scup, on the other hand, are an easy, reliable pick off almost any rocky point from Newport to Napatree — bloodworms or squid strips on a high-low rig in 15 to 25 feet will keep a rod bent all afternoon if that's the kind of day you're after.

Albies haven't shown yet, and I want to be straight about that rather than tease something that isn't here. Every year guys start asking about Napatree and Watch Hill the first week of August, and every year I tell them the same thing — it's early. That first push into the breachways usually doesn't happen until temperature breaks start stacking up in September, though with squid starting to show around the region and the water holding steady, this is worth watching closer than usual. I'll be checking the rock at the tip of Napatree and the mouth of the Weekapaug breachway on my evening walks, looking for that nervous water and diving birds that tell you they've arrived early.

Looking ahead, the tides are sliding toward neap around the 5th and 6th, which means current everywhere from the East Passage to the Sakonnet River is going to soften up. That calls for lighter jigs and slower retrieves on the fluke grounds, and it usually means the bass tuck tighter to structure and feed in shorter windows. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of daylight at Sakonnet Point on the incoming — bunker still pushing, bass and blues both still working that structure, and enough light left to see the water turn.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 9:40 — Bass Down Deep, Doormats Up Top, Bonito Still a Ghost
reports.subhead: The current window is shrinking into the neap, the fluke bite is peaking on the rips, and the first albies of the year are close but not here yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge hit right around 9:40 this morning, and I had exactly eleven minutes before the new push started stacking bait against the rock. That's the game out there right now — short windows, hard current, and you either time it or you waste a tank of gas marking fish you can't get bucktails down to. We're running into the neap on August 5-6, and you can already feel the ledge softening a half-hour earlier than it was two weeks ago. That matters more than people think, because SW Ledge doesn't fish on a clock, it fishes on how much water is actually moving across that 35-to-55-foot structure. Less push means less bait getting pinned, means the bass get lazier about showing themselves in daylight.

And that's exactly the pattern I've been telling clients to expect. We flagged this a few days back — said that as the tides softened, the bass would compress into the strongest current hours and pull onto the deepest, coolest structure, with night eels at the Gut and the bridges becoming the move. That's precisely what's happening. Daytime trips at the Ledge are producing, but you're working for it — jigging diamond jigs and 2-ounce bucktails tight to bottom, mixing in the occasional live scup when we can net one off the rockpile. The fish are there, holding on the down-current side of the boulders in 40 to 50 feet, but they want it presented slow and dragged, not ripped. Once the sun drops and that current builds back through the evening tide, the same fish move up onto the flat and you can work bunker chunks or eels on a light three-way rig without needing to be a surgeon about depth control. That's been our best two hours of the week, hands down — 7:30 to 9:30 in the evening, stripers to 34 inches, a couple pushing 20 pounds, all on fresh-cut bunker fished just off bottom.

Sandy Point at the south end of the island is still the most consistent bass water we've got after dark. The rip there doesn't care about neap tides the way the Ledge does — it's got its own current signature off the tip, and it's been holding fish tight to the drop where the sand gives way to deeper water. Eels drifted through that seam on the last two hours of the outgoing have been steady, nothing giant, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but consistent enough that I'd call it the safer bet if you only get one shot at a night trip this week.

Daytime, fluke's been the better story, honestly. We're sitting right in the middle of the peak window for doormat-class fish, and Block Island's channel edges and rip lines are holding up their end. Best fish of the week came off the edge of the rip running north of North Light — a six-and-a-half-pound flattie on a white Gulp Swimming Mullet paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, worked slow on the drift in about 28 feet. The pattern's simple: find where the sand meets structure, drift it with the tide instead of the wind, and keep contact with bottom without dragging bucktail through the rocks. We've had multiple keeper drifts a day out there, mixed with a healthy number of shorts you've got to sort through, which is normal for this time of year but does slow you down some.

Sea bass have stayed dependable on the same structure — the wrecks and rock piles off Point Judith and the deeper reef pockets south of the island keep coughing up 14-to-17-inch fish on squid strips and Gulp on high-low rigs. Nothing spectacular, but it's the kind of bite you can lean on when the bass window doesn't line up with your trip.

Now, the question everyone's asking at the dock: where are the bonito? Not here yet, not in any real numbers. I've had a couple of quick, unconfirmed flashes off Clay Head chasing bait on the surface, gone before anyone could get a cast in, and that's about it. The water's warming into the right range for it — surface temps pushing into the mid-70s regionally, and that's exactly the kind of break that usually kicks the first scout fish loose off Block Island. Given how things have lined up the last few seasons, I'd expect the real scattered reports to start within the next week to ten days, likely showing first off the southeast corner near Clay Head or out around the East Grounds where the current stacks bait against the drop. If you're itching to get ahead of it, keep small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks rigged and ready, because when they show, they show fast and don't stick around long enough for you to re-tackle.

Looking ahead, I'd play the neap the way it wants to be played — lean on the low-light bass bite at Sandy Point and the Ledge rather than fighting slack water in daylight, keep the fluke gear rigged for the rip lines while that bite is still hot, and start checking the surface off Clay Head every trip out, because that first bonito of the season doesn't announce itself with a phone call.

reports.headline: Sea Girt Reef, 65 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds While the Mud Hole Waits on Bluefin
reports.subhead: Canyon tuna keep building at Hudson, Wilmington and Washington, but the inshore lumps haven't turned on yet — here's where the book paid off this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Sea Girt Reef, 65 feet, four miles off the inlet — that number has been in my book since 2007 and it hasn't stopped paying rent. This week the tugboat wrecks on the north end of the reef held sea bass stacked two and three deep on the fish finder, and we boated fish to 4 pounds on double-hook rigs tipped with clam and squid strips, bounced tight to the structure on the last two hours of the incoming. That's the pattern right now up and down this stretch — Axel Carlson Reef running the same depth range is doing the same thing, and Shrewsbury Rocks in the shallower 40 to 50 foot water is holding smaller fish but plenty of them. The sea bass bite has been the one thing I could set a watch by all summer, and August hasn't changed that. Bring 6-ounce bank sinkers if you're fishing the reef on a moving tide — current's been stout enough to require it, especially around the new moon push.

Now here's the honest part of the report. The Mud Hole lumps — the ones I mark bluefin on most Augusts once the bait piles up over that broken bottom in 60 to 90 feet — haven't shown me a thing yet this week. I ran out three times looking for the diving birds and the nervous water that usually tips off a bluefin push onto the structure, and what I found instead was clean, quiet water and bait sitting deep, not balled up tight the way it needs to be for those fish to commit. The Klondike was the same story — good sea bass down deep on the rockpile stretches, but no sign of tuna working the lumps. I'm not going to sell you a bite that isn't there. If the bluefin are around, they're still holding out past the 20-fathom curve, which lines up with what the canyon boats have been marking.

And that's where the real story has been. Hudson, Wilmington and Washington canyons have had one of the better stretches of yellowfin trolling I've seen in a few Julys, and that pattern carried straight into this week. We called this three weeks back — said the stable high pressure was quietly building one of the better July tuna setups in recent memory, with yellowfin and some bigeye activity improving at those three canyons, all within range of a Manasquan run — and that's exactly the pattern that's held. Boats working spreads of green machines and cedar plugs off the temp breaks on the edges of those canyons are still connecting, with bluefin mixed in on the troll and some chunking success once the sun gets high and the fish go quiet on the surface baits. The tide range is narrowing into the coming neap around August 5-6, and when current softens like that, trolling tends to outproduce chunking — the bait doesn't stack as hard on structure, and a moving spread covers more water than a static chunk slick can. If you've got the range for a canyon run this week, that's where I'd put my gas money before I'd burn it hunting bluefin on the inshore lumps.

Mahi have started showing the way they always do this time of year — not on the reef structure, but out past Barnegat Ridge and the Klondike on the pot buoys and any bit of floating junk you can find drifting the warm filaments pushing in off the Gulf Stream edge. We picked up a mixed bag of schoolie mahi, a couple pushing 6 pounds, working small bucktails and strips of squid around lobster pot warps in maybe 25 to 30 fathoms east of the ridge. That's textbook August timing for this fishery — the pots concentrate bait, the mahi sit under them, and if you're patient enough to work every buoy you pass instead of running past them, you'll put a few in the box. Water out there was reading warm and clean, close to 76 degrees on the surface, with a moderate three-foot swell out of the southeast that made for a comfortable ride but did put a little push on the drift — light jig heads worked better than straight bucktails to keep baits down in the strike zone.

Bonito haven't shown yet on our reefs, and with the swell and warm surface water sitting the way it is, I wouldn't expect them for another week or two — that's more of a late-August, early-September pattern for us once the bait pods tighten up over structure like Sea Girt and Shrewsbury Rocks. Tog and cod are off the table this time of year in these depths, so I won't pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, I'd keep sea bass trips locked into the reef and wreck network — that bite has been the most reliable thing on my numbers all season and nothing about the conditions suggests it's slowing. For tuna, I'd still favor the canyon run over the inshore lumps until I see bait ball up tight and birds working the Mud Hole again — if that changes with the softening tide this week, I'll be the first one out there checking it. Keep an eye on the pot lines past the ridge for mahi through the rest of August; that pattern usually holds as long as the warm water keeps pushing inshore.

reports.headline: Rocky Point on the ebb: blues chew bunker, scup stack the ledges, fluke slide up the bay
reports.subhead: The bunker schools are thick from Conimicut to Prudence and the blues found them — the harder question this week is where the bass are hiding in the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the Fields Point pier Thursday night watching three guys work bunker snags off the seawall, and every one of them had the same complaint — too much bait, not enough room to swing a rod. That's the story of the bay right now. Pogies are stacked from the Providence River clear down past Nyatt Point, and where you find them thick, the blues are on them like they've got a grudge. I watched a school get worked over off Rocky Point Wednesday evening, birds diving, water boiling white for maybe ninety seconds, then it moved off toward Prudence and went quiet again. That's the pattern — find the bait, get there fast, because it doesn't sit still.

We flagged this a week back — said the bluefish are a bait-driven fishery, plain and simple, and wherever the bunker re-form after a blow, the blues show up within hours. That's exactly what's playing out. No mystery to it. Snag a bunker on a treble weighted rig off the Conimicut breakwater or drift a chunk under a float off Nyatt, and if there's bait around, you're in business. Topwater poppers work when they're actively busting — a big pencil popper or a Hogy walking bait thrown right into the froth off Rocky Point has been drawing violent strikes, mostly bluefish in the 3-6 pound class with the occasional bigger one mixed in.

Bass are trickier, and I won't pretend otherwise. Surface water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s through the bay, warm enough that the stripers are doing what they do this time of year — holding deep on structure through the daylight hours and only really committing to feed at first light, last light, and after dark. Daytime, guys jigging bucktails over the drop-offs at Conimicut Point and along the edge of the Providence River channel are picking at fish, but it's slow, technical work — bounce a half-ounce white bucktail with a curly tail trailer right on bottom in 20 to 25 feet, and you might get two or three bites in an hour where you'd have gotten ten a month ago. The real bass are coming after dark, eels and big swim shads worked slow around the bridge pilings and the rip lines off Nyatt and Rocky Point on the last two hours of the outgoing.

Here's the piece worth paying attention to heading into this weekend — the tide range is narrowing fast into the neap around August 5th and 6th. That current's going to go soft in a lot of spots that depend on hard water movement to load bait against structure. We called this one too — said last week that as the tides soften, the bass compress into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's precisely what I'd expect through the weekend. When the flow's weak, don't waste your time on the flats — go to the bridges and the channel edges where whatever current there is still concentrates. Slow your presentation down to match it. A bucktail that worked on a strong moon tide two weeks back needs to be fished twice as slow right now, or you're just pulling it past fish that can't be bothered to chase.

Fluke are the bright spot, and they're doing what fluke do in August — pushing up into the bay behind the bait. Greenwich Bay has been holding fish along the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, and the Providence River itself has produced some surprising keepers off the deeper holes near the bridges. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, three-quarter ounce, dragged slow on the drift with the outgoing water — that's been the ticket. Nothing giant, mostly fish in the 18 to 20 inch range with a few better ones mixed in, but it's a dependable bite when the bass and blues are making you work for it.

Scup are exactly where you'd expect them — thick on the rocky ledges from Rocky Point down through Conimicut and out around the edges of Prudence. Sea worms or squid strips on a high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide stage — I like the last of the incoming through the top of the tide when the current's still moving bait past the rocks but hasn't gone full send yet. Black sea bass are mixed in on the same structure around Prudence, though the bigger ones want you fishing tight to the rock piles rather than the open sand.

Weakfish have been scarce — I haven't heard a solid report on one all month, and I'm not going to pretend they're around when they're not.

Looking ahead, I don't see a big thermal shift coming — the pattern's been stable and I'd expect it to hold through the coming week, warm water, thick bait, bass playing hard to get in daylight. If I had one evening to fish, I'd be at Rocky Point right on the tide change into dark, throwing bucktails first, then switching to eels once the light's gone. That's where the current still does something even on a softening tide, and that's where the bass are going to be.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: B-Minus Bass, Solid Fluke, Drum Long Gone
reports.subhead: The rips are fishable on the right water but you're working for every bass — fluke are the honest bite right now.
reports.body_markdown:
I'll grade the Rips a B-minus this week, and that's being generous to the bass. Fluke earn the only A on my card. If you want the truth instead of a sales pitch: the striper bite out front has gone the way it always does first week of August — fish holding deep on structure through the day, only showing themselves in a tight window at first light and again after the sun's off the water. Anybody telling you different either hasn't been out or is selling you a charter.

Water out at the buoy off the Bight is sitting around 75-76 degrees with a low swell running, nothing that's shutting things down but enough lump that I'm picking my days on the outer rips carefully. Inside, where the bay water dumps out through Cape May Inlet and around the Point, temps are pushing into the mid-to-upper 70s — that's warm enough that the stripers want no part of open water at noon. They're stacked on the deep edges of the Rips itself, the humps off the Point, and the pilings under the Cape May-Lewes Ferry terminal, sitting tight to structure and current seams. My best fish this week — a 34-incher — came at 5:40 in the morning on a live eel, slow-trolled along the north edge of the Rips on the last hour of the incoming, right where the sand gives way to the rock pile in about 25 feet. After that window closed, it was quiet until dusk.

Here's the thing about the tide right now — we're sliding into a neap cycle over the next couple days, and that's going to soften the current through the Rips noticeably. Less water moving means the bait doesn't get pinned as hard against structure, and the bass get lazier about chasing it. If you fish the Rips this weekend, don't expect the kind of rip you saw during the new or full moon push — plan on lighter leadheads, slower presentations, and patience. I'd rather fish the two hours around the tide change than blind-cast through a slack, weak-moving tide with nothing showing on the surface.

Fluke, though — fluke are doing exactly what they're supposed to be doing in the first week of August, and this is where I'd point anybody who wants a fish box instead of a story. We're drifting 30 to 50 feet on the outer edge of the Rips and along the Hereford Inlet channel, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets, chartreuse and white both working depending on the light. Doormat-class fish are showing — we had a 6-pounder off Hereford on Tuesday's outgoing, and shorts have been thick enough that you're culling through a dozen fish to find your keepers. The bite's been best on the back half of the ebb, when the bait gets pulled out of the inlet and pinned against the channel edge in that 20-30 foot stretch. If fluke is your priority this week, that's your spot and that's your tide.

Bluefish are following the bunker pattern everybody up the coast is seeing — pods pushing into the mouth of Hereford Inlet and stacking up along the jetty rocks on the Wildwood side. Nothing blitz-scale down here yet, but enough fish that a bucktail or a Kastmaster thrown into a bait ball at first light will get you bit fast. Small to mid-size blues mostly, 3 to 5 pounds, but they'll wreck your leader and your morning in the best way.

Now for the honest part nobody wants to hear in August: the Delaware Bay drum run is done. That's not a slow week, that's just the calendar — black drum is a May fishery down here, Fortescue and the Cohansey mouth were producing fish up to 40 pounds back in the spring on fresh clam and now that window's closed until next year. Anybody asking me about drum this week, I'm telling them the same thing my father told guys who asked him in August thirty years ago — wrong season, come back in the spring.

What the bay is holding onto is weakfish, and that's a pattern worth chasing if you've got a bay boat. The back channels up toward Fortescue and into the grass-lined creeks are holding weakfish tight to the edges on the tide change, with warm bay water in the mid-70s keeping them actively feeding rather than sulking. Bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the channel drop, have been the ticket — nothing giant, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but a legitimate bite worth running for if the ocean's blown out.

Looking at the week ahead — we flagged this coming, and here it is: with tides softening into the neap through the 5th and 6th, expect the bass to compress even harder into the deepest, coolest structure and the strongest current hours. That means night eeling at the Rips and around the ferry terminal pilings becomes the play, not daytime jigging. I'd also keep an eye on the wreck and rock-pile structure off the Point — triggerfish have a habit of building through August as the water peaks, and the pieces close to shore are worth a bucktail drop if you're already out there for sea bass. No promises on numbers yet, but the pattern's right for it. My plan this week is simple: fluke in the mornings on the moving tide, bass at first and last light on structure, and I'm not wasting a trip on the Rips during a dead slack neap tide when I could be filling a cooler with doormats instead.

reports.headline: Where'd the bass go at noon? Ask the neap tide and the bridge lights
reports.subhead: Daytime stripers have gone underground with the mid-70s water, but the fluke are peaking and the triggerfish are finally showing on the wrecks.
reports.body_markdown:
I get this question every August, and I got it three times at the ramp this week: "I fished Absecon Inlet at one in the afternoon and never had a sniff — what happened to the bass?" Class, this is the easiest lesson on the syllabus. Water's sitting in the mid-70s off the beachfront, low 70s in the back bay channels, and a striper's metabolism doesn't love that. They're not gone. They're down deep on structure — the Route 30 bridge pilings, the rock piles at the base of Absecon Inlet, the Ocean City bridge abutments — sitting tight to shade and current until the sun drops. Come dusk, dark, and the early flood, they climb up and feed. That's the whole pattern right now, and it's not going to change until the water cools.

We flagged this shift last week, and it's playing out exactly as expected — as the tides soften into this weekend's neap (bottoming out around August 5-6), the current at the inlets gets lazier, and that pushes bass into the strongest hours of moving water and the deepest, coolest structure they can find. Night eels — the classic 6- to 9-inch rigged eel, or a black/purple Slug-Go on a jighead — fished slow along the bridge lights at Absecon and the Ninth Street bridge in Ocean City has been the play after 9 p.m., outgoing tide especially. Daytime, if you insist on trying, drop bucktails or jig a soft plastic tight to the Great Egg rock jetty on the bottom third of the tide. Don't expect much before last light.

Now the fluke — this is where I'd spend my daylight hours, because the program is as good as it's been all season. Doormat-class fish are showing on ocean-side structure and inlet rips from Absecon down through Great Egg, and the back bay sod banks are holding steady numbers too. My best fish this week came off the edge of the Great Egg reef in 22 to 28 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails with the outgoing tide pulling hard — a 5-pounder and two keepers in the 19- to 21-inch range in about ninety minutes. In the back bay, the Rainbow Channel edges and the sod banks off Bader Field are still stacking shorts with enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the gas, minnow-and-Gulp combo on a light egg sinker, fished slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets flushed off the flats. Townsends Inlet and the Sea Isle side channels are producing the same way — nothing easy, but steady if you keep the boat moving and cover water.

Bluefish are the wild card. The bunker-driven blitz that's been tearing up the beachfront from Belmar south hasn't fully arrived here yet, but I wouldn't sleep on it — bunker schools have been pushing south along the coast, and this fishery is entirely bait-driven. Wherever those pods settle, blues show up within hours. Keep an eye on the surf off Ocean City and Brigantine for diving birds and nervous water; if the bunker set up tight to the beach, bring a metal-lipped swimmer or a diamond jig and don't wait around, because these blitzes come and go fast.

Here's a bright spot that's new for the season: triggerfish. We noted a couple weeks back that the first ones were showing on the inshore pieces, and sure enough they're building now on the wrecks and rock piles off Absecon and Great Egg as the water's peaked into the high 70s nearshore. Small pieces of clam or squid on a light fluke rig, fished right on the structure, has been drawing strikes from anglers who know to look for them — most are still on the smaller side, but a few keeper-class fish are mixed in. If you've got a wreck number in that 40- to 60-foot range off the reef sites, it's worth a stop on your way out or back.

Surf-wise, kingfish are still working the wash from Ocean City down to Stone Harbor on bloodworm and Fishbites rigs, small stuff but a fun way to fill a bucket on a calm morning tide. And offshore, the settled high-pressure pattern has kept the mako and thresher fleet busy running out of Absecon Inlet — not my program, but it tells you the ocean's been flat and cooperative, which is exactly why the inshore bite has been so structure-dependent this week. No wind to stir up bait, no current to push fish around — they're sitting right where the temperature and tide put them.

Looking ahead: as this neap tide bottoms out this weekend, expect the bass bite to compress even further into that narrow night window at the bridges and inlets — lighter jigs, slower retrieves, patience over volume. Fluke should hold strong through the coming week since the water's stable and the bait's still moving on the tide. And if that bunker pod finally slides south past Long Beach Island, watch for the blitz to show on the Ocean City and Brigantine beachfront within a few days of it arriving — that's a fast-developing pattern, so if you hear about it, don't wait for the weekend.

reports.headline: Holgate's South Bowl Cut Deepens — Bass Feeding the Trough After Dark
reports.subhead: The bunker push we flagged last week finally hit Barnegat Light, while fluke keep grinding on the inlet edges through the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
Flew the drone over the south bowl at Holgate before the sun was even up Sunday, and the cut's changed shape again. That inside trough that's been running parallel to the beach for the last three weeks has pushed another fifteen, twenty yards south and dug deeper — I'd guess four to five feet on the low now where it was barely three. The 3-foot swell out of the southeast that's been rolling through at a 7-second period isn't big, but it's steady enough to keep working that sandbar, and steady swell at low period like that reshapes structure faster than people think. That trough is holding bait right now — you can see the nervous water in the drone footage, peanut bunker and mullet stacked tight against the drop.

That's exactly where the bass are living, but only after the sun goes down. Daytime water on the ocean side is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s — 75.7 out at the buoy off the Bight — and stripers in that kind of warm water go nocturnal and structure-bound. During the day they're deep on the Barnegat Light rocks and under the Ship Bottom and Beach Haven bridge pilings, not eating much of anything worth chasing. Come dusk they slide up onto the bars and into cuts like that Holgate trough to hunt. I fished it two nights this week on the last two hours of the outgoing, swimming a black Bomber Long A slow through the trough, and connected on three fish, biggest going 29 inches. Eels fished on a fishfinder rig tight to the Barnegat Light north jetty rocks after dark have been the more consistent producer for the guys putting in the hours — that's the play right now, and it's about to matter more. We're sliding into a neap tide the next couple days, currents softening up through the 5th and 6th, which means less water movement to trigger a bite. When that happens the bass compress into the strongest current windows and the deepest structure they can find — the Little Egg Inlet gut and the bridge pilings become the spots worth your night hours over the next week.

The bluefish news is the one I called last week and it's playing out almost exactly on schedule. Bunker pods pushing south out of the Belmar corridor have reached Barnegat Inlet and are starting to funnel past Beach Haven on the tide changes, and the blitzes are following them in. Guys working the outside of the Barnegat jetty on the last of the incoming this week found surface chaos — bunker getting bulldozed, blues in the 3 to 6 pound range crushing everything, best on wide swimming plugs and 2-ounce Kastmasters worked fast through the froth. It's not an all-day thing yet — the pods are still moving, not settled — but if they hold like they did in past years, Beach Haven Inlet and the water off Holgate's north end should get their turn within the next tide cycle or two.

Fluke are still the most dependable meal ticket on this stretch, and this is peak season for it. Doormat-class fish are showing on the ocean structure off Beach Haven — the reef pieces in 25 to 35 feet — and in the rip line right off Little Egg Inlet where the outgoing current dumps bay water into the ocean and stacks bait against the shoal edge. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift through that rip, have been putting keepers in the box, with a few fish pushing 5 and 6 pounds mixed into a lot of shorts that need throwing back. Inside, the channel edges through Great Bay and up toward Graveling Point are producing too, though smaller — spearing and Gulp combos on light jig heads, working the deeper bends where the current sweeps bait off the flats on the outgoing.

Weakfish are a bonus right now, not a target — scattered fish showing in the Manahawkin channels and the deeper cuts of Barnegat Bay, mostly picked up by guys fluking who happen to hook one on a Gulp shrimp worked slow near bottom on the last hour of the tide. Nothing like the Delaware Bay run, but worth a cast or two if you're already back there. Kingfish are still working the ocean wash from Ship Bottom down through Holgate on bloodworm and Fishbites rigs fished tight to the beach on a slow incoming — small fish, good for a chowder, not much more. Black drum are basically done for the year up in the Mullica and Graveling Point flats — that spring window closed weeks ago and they've pushed back out to deeper water.

Looking ahead, the neap tide through midweek is going to soften everything up — less current means the bass window narrows to the peak of the tide swing and the deepest structure, so plan night trips around the strongest hour of movement rather than fishing the whole cycle. If the bunker keep pushing south the way they have been, I'd expect the blitz activity at Barnegat and Beach Haven inlets to build through the week rather than fade — that's the one to watch closely on the tide changes. Fluke should hold steady on the ocean structure as long as this water stays warm and stable, though the bite's been more grind-it-out than easy — expect to cull through a lot of shorts for your keepers right now.

reports.headline: Bunker Round the Hook: Blues Blow Up on Top, Bass Slide Under at First Light
reports.subhead: The bunker we said were coming from Belmar showed up right on schedule — now it's about picking your window before the neap softens everything.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Sunday morning before I even had coffee in me: run to Flynn's Knoll first, not Romer Shoal, because the bunker pods I'd been watching stack off Keyport all week were finally thick enough to hold fish through a full tide change instead of scattering on the turn. That's the difference this time of year — August bunker schools are nervous, they get pushed around by every boat and every blitz, and if you're not sitting on the ones that are settled, you're just burning gas watching birds work water you already left.

We flagged this two weeks back — said the bunker pushing north out of the Belmar blitz zone would round the Hook and pull blues and bass in behind them within a day or two — and that's exactly what happened. Raritan Bay has bunker stacked from the Chapel Hill Channel all the way up into the Reach, and the bluefish found them fast. This is as good a topwater bluefish stretch as I've seen in this bay in a few years. Poppers and bunker spoons worked over breaking pods at Flynn's Knoll and along the edge of Romer Shoal are getting hit on nearly every cast when the blitz is up — 3 to 6 pound blues mostly, with some better ones mixed in that'll strip drag if you're using anything lighter than 20-pound braid. Best window has been first light through about 8 AM, before the boat traffic scatters the pods and pushes them down. By midday the bunker sound deep and the surface action shuts off — that's when guys switch to jigging bucktails or diamond jigs down 15 to 25 feet where the pods are holding tight to bottom structure off the Knoll.

Striped bass are in the mix, but they're playing it smart the way they always do once the water sits in the mid-to-upper 70s like it is now. You're not going to find keeper bass chasing bunker on the surface at noon — they're down deep on structure, holding along the Ambrose Channel edges and the deeper humps off Romer Shoal through the day, and coming up to feed under the bunker schools right at dawn and again as the light fails in the evening. I had my best bass action last week live-lining bunker under a balloon rig, drifting the edge where the Knoll drops into the channel, right on the tail of the incoming tide — three fish between 28 and 34 inches in about forty minutes before the sun got too high and they dropped back down. After that window closes, if you want bass, you go to bucktails and eels worked slow along the bottom near the bridge pilings in the Highlands or right in the Navesink River mouth after dark. That's been the more reliable bass program lately — not exciting, but it produces.

Fluke are having their moment too, and honestly this might be the best all-around week of the summer to fish the bay because you can bounce between blitz action and a solid doormat bite without changing zip codes. Keyport Flats has been holding fish in 12 to 18 feet, but the better-grade fluke — I had one go just over 5 pounds Thursday — are coming off the channel edges where the flat drops into deeper water, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. The Chapel Hill Channel edge and the drop just off Ideal Beach have both been productive on that same pattern. Porgies are still around the reef structure off the Hook for anyone who wants a change of pace and dinner that doesn't require a fight.

Here's the thing to watch this week: we're sliding into a neap tide around August 5-6, and that means less water movement, softer current everywhere in the bay. That's usually bad news for current-dependent bites, but it can actually concentrate bunker pods that would otherwise get pushed around by a stronger tide — so don't be surprised if the blitz stays tight and predictable rather than spreading out. The tradeoff is the fluke bite may go a little quieter on those slack tide stretches, since less current means less bait movement off the channel edges. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the calmer morning, hit Flynn's Knoll right at first light for blues and any bass riding under the pods, then slide over to the Chapel Hill Channel edge for the last of the outgoing to hunt fluke before the tide goes dead. Keep an eye on the bunker — as long as they stay thick in the bay, this pattern holds. If a blow scatters them out toward the ocean side of the Hook, the whole program resets and we're back to hunting.

reports.headline: Double Creek doormats and bunker-fed blues — the bay's mid-summer rhythm sets in
reports.subhead: Fluke are stacking the channel edges, bluefish are chewing through bunker at the Inlet, and the stripers have gone nocturnal — here's where to put your time this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a August like this one back in the early eighties — flat calm mornings, bunker so thick off the Route 9 bridge you could walk on them, and my old skipper, Nick the Greek — no relation, just what everybody called him — telling me, "Gus, when the bait's this thick, you don't go looking for fish. You go stand where the bait is and wait for them to find you." Forty-some years later that's still the whole game on this bay in August, and this week it's playing out exactly the way he taught me.

The bay's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s right now, which is warm enough that the big fish have gone smart on us. Striped bass are doing what they do every summer once the water gets like bathwater — they're holding tight to deep structure through the day and only really turning on in that low-light window, dawn, dusk, and after dark. We flagged this coming a week back — said as the tides softened toward the neap the bass would compress onto the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure — and that's exactly what I'm seeing now. Barnegat Inlet itself, the rocks along the north side, and the pilings under the Route 37 and Mathis bridges are holding fish that come alive on the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or bunker chunks bounced right along bottom in 15 to 20 feet, are the ticket after dark. Daytime, if you want a shot, you're jigging deep — bucktail or a heavy soft plastic worked slow along the channel drop by the Coast Guard station.

Fluke, though — fluke are the bright spot right now, and Double Creek Channel is doing what it's supposed to do this time of year.
