The drop-offs on the edges, where the channel falls from six feet down into twelve to fifteen, are stacking bait against the thermocline and the fluke are sitting right on that seam. Drifting the edges on the last of the incoming with a half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce bucktail tipped with a four-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet has been putting keepers in the box, with a few pushing four and five pounds mixed into the shorts. Same story working the drop from the ICW channel down toward Tices Shoal — anywhere that current sweeps bait off a flat into deeper water, set up a drift and cover it slow. Squid strips on a bucktail teaser rig are still worth having tied on too, especially when the bite's finicky on an outgoing that's running light with this narrowing tide range.

That bunker business is the real story of the week, though, and it's spreading down from up north the way I figured it would when I saw the schools thickening a couple weeks back — if the bunker keep re-forming after these afternoon thunderstorm blowouts, the blues show up within hours, and that's been happening right on schedule. Big pods of adult bunker are working the bay from the mouth of Oyster Creek down through the Inlet itself, and wherever they bunch up tight against a current line the bluefish are hammering them on top — the kind of surface explosion you can see from the causeway. If you can get out early, before the wind fills in, run up on a nervous bunker school inside the Inlet or along the edge of the Double Creek channel and throw a metal-lip swimmer or a bucktail with a pork rind trailer right into the boil. It's not subtle fishing. It doesn't need to be.

Weakfish have mostly slid off the sedges now — that classic May pattern along the marsh banks north of Good Luck Point has wound down, and what's left are a few holdover fish working deeper water at night, mostly incidental to the fluke and bass bite rather than something you'd target on purpose. If you're set up for stripers after dark on bunker chunk near the Inlet rocks, don't be shocked if a weakfish grabs it instead — I had that happen twice last week.

Blowfish are exactly where they should be for early August — sandy, grassy bottom around Tices Shoal and the flats off Island Beach, small pieces of clam or squid on a snapper rig with a small hook, fished on a light outgoing. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and it's the kind of thing that keeps a kid entertained on the boat while you wait for the tide to turn for the real stuff. Kingfish are showing in ones and twos on bloodworm rigs fished on clean sand bottom near Barnegat Light and along the ocean side troughs off Island Beach — nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth a rod in the sand spike if you're already surfcasting for something else.

Looking ahead, this stable high-pressure stretch should hold the bunker where they are for a few more days, which means the blue bite stays lit off the Inlet and the bass keep their pattern tight to structure after dark. The tide range keeps narrowing into the weekend neap, so current-dependent spots like the Inlet rocks and the bridge pilings will fish a touch softer — lighter jigs, slower presentations, patience on the drift. If I had one evening this week, I'd be anchored on bunker chunk along the north jetty an hour before dark, with a fluke rod rigged and ready for the ride out through Double Creek.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues Ripping Bunker, Bass Sliding in Behind
reports.subhead: The bunker blitz we flagged two weeks back has spread the length of the beat — but you still need to be standing in the right spot when it happens.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-forty this morning, north jetty at Manasquan Inlet, and there's already three guys spread out on the rocks before the sky's done anything more than turn gray. One kid I didn't recognize was throwing a pencil popper like his arm was . An old-timer next to him — wire leader, bunker spoon, the whole rig looking like it hasn't changed since Nixon — wasn't saying a word, just working it slow and steady through the current seam off the tip. Neither one had a fish in the box yet, but neither one looked worried, and about ten minutes later I found out why. A pod of bunker came pushing out of the inlet on the last of the ebb, maybe forty yards off the rocks, and the water underneath them just came apart. Blues, and plenty of them, blowing up the surface like someone dropped a case of dynamite in the wash. The kid's popper got hit on the second cast after that. The old-timer's spoon got bit on the drop.

That's the story of this whole stretch right now, and it's been the story for a couple weeks — bunker schools holding thick from Belmar down through Manasquan, blues stacked underneath them and blowing up any time the bait gets pinned against structure. We said back on the 20th that this pattern would keep spreading north toward Sandy Hook and south toward LBI as long as the high pressure held, and that's exactly what's happened. I fished Sea Bright rocks Tuesday morning and the same thing was going on up there — bunker balled up tight against the third jetty down from the fishing pier, blues crashing them on the last hour of the incoming. It's a simple equation this time of year: find the bunker, find the blues. They're not hiding from each other.

Stripers are in on this too, but they're playing a different game. During the day, with surface temps sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s, the bass are down deep on structure — the rock piles off Spring Lake, the deeper pockets at Shark River Inlet, tucked under the blitz rather than in it. Dawn and dusk is when they come up to feed on the same bunker the blues are hammering, and that's your window. I've been picking off schoolies and a few keepers on white bucktails, an ounce and a half, worked slow along the bottom of the inlet channel at Manasquan on the last two hours of the outgoing — 15 to 20 feet of water, right where the current funnels past the rock pile. After dark, eels have been the better call for the bigger fish. Threw eels off the Belmar jetties two nights ago on the incoming and connected with a 34-incher that never showed itself until it was halfway up the rocks. That fish wasn't up chasing bunker on top — it was sitting deep, letting the current bring the meal to it.

Worth mentioning: the tide range is narrowing into the neap around the 5th and 6th, and when that current softens up, the bass tend to tighten into the strongest remaining flow and the deepest, coolest structure they can find. That means the bridges — Route 35, the Shark River span, the Manasquan River bridge pilings — start producing better than the open beach on eels and bucktails fished tight to the structure after dark. If the surf bite goes quiet next week, that's where I'm headed before I write it off as a bad week.

Fluke fishing has been the most reliable part of the report, honestly, and the least dramatic. This is peak season for them and it shows — doormat-class fish coming off the channel edges inside Manasquan Inlet and Shark River Inlet, plus the humps and rip lines just outside both. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift in 20 to 30 feet, have been putting fish in the box, including one four-pounder I watched come over the rail of a boat working the Manasquan Inlet channel Wednesday on the last of the incoming. If you're fishing from the jetties for fluke, work the deeper pockets right off the rocks on the tail end of the outgoing — bait gets funneled out and the fluke sit right there waiting on it.

Here's the honest part: it's not been easy money every single dawn. I put in three mornings this week for two that were worth talking about. The blitz windows are real but they're short — twenty minutes, sometimes less, before the bunker push through and the blues go with them. You need to be standing in the right spot when the school comes by, which means showing up before first light and being willing to walk the jetty rocks in the dark to find where the bait's holding that particular tide. Guys who show up at seven and fish one spot for three hours are the ones telling me it was slow.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the pattern to change much through the weekend — stable high pressure, warm stable water, bunker schools still thick enough to keep the blues committed. If the bait continues sliding south the way it has, don't be surprised if the hot zone drifts down toward Bay Head and beyond by the weekend. And once we're into that neap water midweek, start thinking bridges and deep structure after dark for the stripers, because the current's not going to be doing the work for them the way it has been. Bring eels. Bring patience. Watch the birds before you watch anything else.

reports.headline: The Race at 3.8 Knots: Neap Squeeze Sends Bass to the Wire at Valiant Rock
reports.subhead: As the tide range collapses into Wednesday's neap, the daytime bite goes deep and slow — and the real action shifts to the dark hours at Plum Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
3.8 knots. That's what Race Rock was running on the last big ebb I fished, down from the 5-plus knot walls we were bucking three weeks ago on the full moon. That number tells you everything about this week — we're sliding into the neap on August 5-6, and every rip from Valiant Rock to the Sluiceway is going to feel it. Softer current means the bass stop stacking tight on the up-current edge of structure and start spreading out, which means you have to work harder and think slower to find them.

Valiant Rock has been the honest spot all week. Slack at the Rock ran right around 10:20 in the morning and 4:45 in the afternoon on my last two trips out there, and that window — fifteen, twenty minutes either side of dead slack — is when I've been marking the biggest concentrations of bass sitting tight to the rockpile in 55 to 70 feet. Wire line with a 2 1/2-ounce bucktail dressed in white bucktail hair and a strip of pork rind, trolled at a slow walk right through that transition from ebb to slack, has been the difference-maker. Three fish over 30 pounds came off that program for me this week, all on the last twenty minutes of the ebb before the water went dead. Once the current builds back the other way past a knot and a half, the bite shuts off fast — the fish drop off the structure and scatter into the deeper holes on either side of the Rock, and you're better off picking up the sea bass rods.

We flagged this pattern last week — said as the tides softened, bass would compress into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure, and that night eels at the Gut and the bridges would become the play. That's exactly what's happening. Plum Gut after dark has been quietly better than the daytime bite at the Race this week. Live eels, 10 to 14 inches, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 35 to 45 feet on the last two hours of the incoming — that's producing the better class of fish, 34 to 40 inches, with almost no daylight shorts mixed in. Water temp at New London is sitting at 69.6, which is on the cool side for early August, and that's keeping bass comfortable enough to feed a little later into the morning than you'd expect this time of year. Kings Point to the west is running 72.9, so there's a real gradient building across the Sound, and that cooler water on our end of things is a gift right now.

Fluke fishing has been the most consistent thing going, and it's not close. Doormat-class fish are showing on the edges of the Sluiceway and along the channel drop on the west side of Plum Gut, 40 to 60 feet, drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails with a spearing teaser six inches up the leader. I had a stretch Tuesday where four drifts produced four fish over 5 pounds, along with a steady pick of shorts that kept the rods bent even when the big ones weren't showing. This bite doesn't care much about the neap — fluke are still locked onto the moving water regardless of speed, and with the season at its peak right now, I'd put this as the most reliable meat-in-the-cooler play on the whole beat.

Bluefish have been around but patchy — a few schools of choppers busting bait off Great Gull Island in the early morning, gone by 8 o'clock. This fishery is entirely bait-driven right now; wherever the bunker pods hold, the blues show up within hours and then move on when the bait shifts. I haven't found a concentration worth building a whole trip around this week, but if you're out there anyway working the rips, keep a metal jig rigged and ready.

Black sea bass remain the fallback everybody can count on. Little Gull Island's rockpile and the structure around Valiant Rock are both holding fish in the 15 to 20 inch range on squid strips and Gulp on a high-low rig, 50 to 65 feet, any stage of the tide. It's not glamorous but it fills a cooler when the rip goes quiet on you between slacks.

No albies or bonito yet — I want to be straight about that, because I know guys are already asking. The ingredients are close. Temperature breaks are building at Montauk and Block Island right now, and that's exactly the setup that usually tips the first scattered fish into the Gut and around the Sluiceway. I'd put good odds on the first confirmed reports coming out of this stretch of the Sound within the next week to ten days, especially if this softer current pattern holds and lets warmer water pool up around the islands. I'll have epoxy jigs rigged and ready every trip starting now — no sense being unprepared when they show.

Looking ahead: expect the neap to keep squeezing current speeds through midweek, which means lighter jigs, slower trolling speeds, and tighter attention to the actual slack window rather than the tide chart's general guess. If you've only got one trip in you, I'd fish the evening slack at Valiant Rock into the start of the new ebb, then run the eels at Plum Gut after dark. That's where the fish are, and that's where I'll be.

reports.headline: Ram Island Rocks Go Quiet by Day, Loud After Dark — Fluke Steady, Albies Still a Rumor
reports.subhead: The current's easing toward the neap and the bass have followed it down into the rockpiles, where the real work now happens after the sun drops.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a window at Wamphassuc Point right at first light where the peanut bunker come off the boulders in a nervous sheet, and if you're not already positioned when that happens you've missed the best twenty minutes of your day. I was out there Tuesday before 5:30, poling the skiff along the edge where the granite drops from three feet to eleven, and watched three separate bunker showers get worked over from below before the light was even good enough to see my leader knot. That's the tell right now — the bait's holding tight to the rock, and the bass are coming up to get it in the low light, then sliding back down into the structure once the sun's on the water.

We flagged this a couple weeks back — said the softening tide heading into the neap would widen the window and favor slower presentations, and that's exactly what's playing out. The moon's pulling toward neap around August 5-6, and you can feel it in the rips already. Fishers Island Sound isn't ripping the way it was three weeks ago. The Race current still moves plenty of water, but through the Sound itself — Ram Island, the gut off Wicopesset, the flow around Wamphassuc — it's softened enough that I've gone from 2-ounce bucktails to 1-ounce and 3/4-ounce without losing bottom contact. A white bucktail with a chunk of sea worm or a 4-inch white Slug-Go trailer, dead-drifted right along the boulder seams on the last hour of the outgoing, has been the money presentation. Slower water means the bass have more time to look at what you're throwing, so I've slowed my retrieve to almost nothing — just enough hop to keep it off the rocks.

Daytime, the bigger fish have gone deep and sullen, which is typical for early August with water in the upper 60s to low 70s out here. New London's reading around 69.6, and that's cool enough to keep fish comfortable holding tight to structure through the heat of the day rather than roaming. I'm finding stripers stacked on the deeper edges around Ram Island and the outer breakwater rubble in 15 to 20 feet, mostly uninterested until the tide starts moving again. Come evening, though, they push up onto the shallower boulder fields — 4 to 8 feet of water — and that's when eels fished on a light fishfinder rig, drifted right through the wash off the breakwater at dusk and after dark, have been putting slot fish and a few overslots in the net. Nothing giant, mostly 28 to 34 inches, but consistent if you're willing to fish the dark.

Fluke fishing has stayed the most dependable thing going. The channel edges through the Sound — between Fishers Island and the mainland, and the deeper cuts off Ram Island — are holding fish through the peak of the season the way they're supposed to. Drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, over 20 to 30 feet of water on the moving tide has produced steady keepers, with a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds mixed into the shorts. Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same drifts wherever there's any rock or shell mixed into the bottom — no secret to it, just find hard bottom on the fish finder and drop.

What I haven't seen yet, and what everybody keeps asking me about at the dock, is albies. Nothing. Not a fin, not a nervous bait ball getting hammered from below, not a single confirmed sighting from anyone I trust out past Watch Hill Reef or along the outer rips. That's not unusual for the first days of August — the pattern up and down this coast has warming temperature breaks starting to show at places like Block Island and the Vineyard, and that's the kind of signal that typically precedes the first scout fish showing up here by a week to ten days. I'd expect the first real sighting somewhere out around Watch Hill Reef or the rips off the eastern end of Fishers Island before the middle of the month, not before. If you're itching to start throwing epoxy jigs and Albie Snax, I wouldn't blame you, but I'd save the gas money for another week.

Tog are holding on the same rockpiles as always — Ram Island, the breakwater rubble, the boulder fields off Esker Point — but I'm leaving them alone this time of year and so should you; there's no reason to stress fish sitting tight to structure in warm water when there's nothing to gain from it.

Looking ahead, if the current keeps softening into the neap like it's doing, I'd expect the low-light bite on the rocks to stay the most reliable window through the weekend — eels after dark at the breakwater and Ram Island, bucktails on the last of the outgoing at Wamphassuc. Fluke should hold steady on the channel edges regardless of tide strength. And I'd keep one eye east toward Watch Hill and Fishers Island Sound's outer edge for that first bait-nervous water that tells you the albies have finally found the temperature break they're looking for.

reports.headline: August Low Water Pins Bass and Blues to the Saybrook Rocks
reports.subhead: With the river running warm and thin, the striper and bluefish game has shrunk down to the mouth, the dawn hours, and the breakwater riprap.
reports.body_markdown:
By the first week of August the river tells you where to fish just by how it looks. The milfoil and water chestnut have choked out half the coves from Selden Creek down through Lord Cove, the ospreys off Great Island are flying young birds that dive-bomb the flats now instead of just the adults, and the current itself has gone soft and warm, the color of steeped tea from three weeks without real rain. This is the deep-summer river, and it fishes nothing like the river I was writing about in April. The shad are long gone up past Holyoke. What's left is a mouth-focused game, and it's been that way for two weeks running.

Here's the pattern I've watched play out for decades on this stretch, and it's holding true again this year: once the upper river warms into the high 70s and the weed growth locks up the coves, the striped bass and the bluefish both get pushed down to the one place that still has cold seams and moving water — the river mouth itself, from the Saybrook Breakwater out past the outer bar toward the Sound. The Sound side data backs up what I'm seeing on the water — Kings Point reading near 73 degrees, New London closer to 70 — and the river mouth sits right in that same range, warm enough that the fish don't want to sit in open water all day. They're holding tight to structure — the breakwater riprap, the rocks around the Nutmeg tower, the drop along Calves Island bar — and they're only really willing to feed hard in the low-light hours.

That's exactly the pattern we flagged a couple weeks back for this stretch of river — activity concentrating around dawn, dusk, and the tide changes — and it's still the whole ballgame. I had two mornings this week where the first hour of light, right on the last of the outgoing tide, produced striped bass to 28 inches on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right off the breakwater rocks, and then by 7:30 it was over. Dead. Sun gets up, water clears, fish drop back down into the deeper current seams and won't touch anything until the tide turns again or the light goes down. If you're used to all-day action from the spring run, this isn't that. This is get-there-before-sunrise fishing or plan on fishing after dark.

Bluefish have followed the bunker pods right into the mouth, same as they've been doing up and down the whole coast this summer with bait schools driving the bite everywhere from here to Raritan Bay. I watched a pod of peanut bunker get raided right off Great Island at first light Tuesday — birds working, blues blowing up on top, the kind of five-minute window where every cast on a small white Deceiver or a Kastmaster gets bit and then it's over as fast as it started. If you see the gulls diving off the flats or along the outer bar, don't wait — that bait won't sit still for long with blues under it.

At night, the bigger bass show up. I've had better luck the last ten days working eels — plain old live eels, no rig tricks needed — around the breakwater light and the rocks off the Lynde Point side, fished slow on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some shoulder to it. That's where the better fish are, the 30-inch-plus class, and they want it slow and close to the bottom, not swimming fast through the water column. Bucktails still work if you don't want to mess with eels — white or chartreuse, an ounce and a half, bounced along the Calves Island bar edge on the same stage of tide.

The white perch bite has actually been the more dependable thing this week for anyone who wants a full bucket rather than a trophy. Whalebone Creek and the deeper holes up around the DEP Marina are holding decent numbers, and they'll eat grass shrimp or small bloodworm-tipped jigs after dark when the tide's moving, regardless of how brutal the daytime heat has been. It's not glamorous but it's honest fishing, and it's about the only thing in this river right now that isn't shut off by the sun.

Worth saying plainly — this has not been an easy week. Daytime fishing anywhere in the lower river has been mostly dead water, and I've had mornings where the window was so short I only got two fish to the boat before it shut off entirely. The Sound's heading into a neap tide around the 5th and 6th, which means the current through the mouth is going to soften up even more over the next several days. That's going to shrink the productive windows further, not widen them — expect the tide changes to matter more than ever, and I'd lean toward lighter bucktails and slower eel presentations to match the weaker flow. If I only had one shot this week, I'd take the last hour of the outgoing at first light off the breakwater, eel in hand, and I'd be packing up and gone before the sun cleared the trees at Old Lyme.

reports.headline: Thames goes slack toward the neap — bass tuck into the pilings, blues hold at the river mouth
reports.subhead: As the tide range narrows this week, the bite window gets shorter and the fish get pickier about where they sit.
reports.body_markdown:
You can feel the current losing its grip before you ever look at a tide table. I was under the Gold Star Bridge Thursday evening on the last of the ebb, and the seam that usually rips hard enough to hold your jig at an angle was barely nudging my line. That's the neap talking — we're sliding into the softer tides around August 5-6, and anybody who's fished this river long enough knows what that means. The bass stop roaming and they go find the one piece of structure that still moves water reliably, and they sit on it.

Right now that's the bridge pilings and the deep pocket off Fort Trumbull where the river narrows and the current gets squeezed even when the rest of the harbor goes quiet. We flagged this pattern last week — said that as the tides softened, bass would compress into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. Daytime fishing has gotten tougher. Surface temps in the harbor are pushing toward 70, a touch cooler than what they're seeing down toward Kings Point, and that gradient matters — our end of the Sound stays a few degrees behind the western basin all summer, which is part of why this river holds fish deep into the heat that shut down other spots. But even here, midday sun on slack water puts the bass down on the bottom, hugging the pilings and the rock at Fort Trumbull, and they're not moving much until the light changes.

The move has been eels after dark, fished slow and heavy right against the pilings on whatever current there is — a 3/4-ounce egg sinker ahead of a swivel, six-foot fluorocarbon leader, letting the eel settle and just twitching it back through the seam. I had two fish over 30 inches that way Wednesday night working the downstream side of the bridge on the tail of the outgoing, and lost a third that felt bigger when it wrapped me around a piling. That's the game right now — fewer opportunities, but the fish that are there are quality, and they're not leaving structure to chase you around.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player this week, and it's a straight bait story. Bunker are holding thick right at the river mouth off Ocean Beach and pushing up as far as the Pleasure Beach line on a good push of tide, and wherever that bait balls up, the blues show up within the day. I watched three separate blitzes off Ocean Beach on Tuesday morning — nothing coastwide-blitz size, but enough fish crashing bait on top that a metal-lipped swimmer or a 2-ounce Kastmaster thrown right into the boil got hit on the first few casts every time. That bunker-driven pattern is the same thing playing out from Raritan Bay on down — bluefish go where the bait is, full stop, and right now the bait is sitting at our doorstep instead of pushing further up the river the way it does in a stronger tide. If you're on the beach at first light with bait visible on the surface, don't wait — those windows have been closing fast once the sun gets up and the bunker sound.

Porgies have quietly been the most dependable fish in the harbor all week, and I mean that as a compliment — nobody's out here talking about scup, but if you want bent rods for the kids or a guaranteed dinner, anchoring up on the mud-and-shell patches inside New London Harbor, especially the flats off the Fort Trumbull side in 15 to 20 feet, has been steady on high-low rigs with squid strips or clam. Small hooks, light sinkers, drop it to bottom and wait — that bite hasn't cared one bit about the softening tide, because those fish aren't current-dependent the way the stripers are.

Blackfish are mostly an afterthought this time of year — the water's too warm and they're tucked tight to structure not feeding heavy, and most of us are saving that game for the fall reopening anyway. I wouldn't spend a tide targeting them right now; better to put that time into the bridge or the beach.

Looking at the week ahead, the neap keeps tightening through the weekend, which means shorter, more defined bite windows rather than all-day grazing. If I've only got one evening, I'm fishing the last two hours of the outgoing at the Gold Star Bridge with eels, right on the pilings, and I'm there before the light's gone because that transition period — dusk into full dark — has been when the bigger fish commit. For bluefish, keep an eye on the river mouth and Ocean Beach at first light; if the bunker stay put through this stretch of stable weather, that topwater window should keep producing, but if the bait redistributes with the softer current, the blues will follow it and you may need to run down toward Pleasure Beach to find them again. Either way, this isn't a week to expect fish to come find you. Go to the structure, go to the bait, and fish the tide change like it's the only thirty minutes you're going to get — because right now, it often is.

reports.headline: New Haven Break Gives Up Jumbo Porgies While Charles Island Bar Holds Bass After Dark
reports.subhead: Bottom fishing is peaking on the rockpiles as the tide eases toward neap — but the stripers want you out there when the sun's down.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, outer New Haven breakwall, high skimmer rig loaded with sandworm, and a porgy comes up that makes the guy next to me put his rod down just to look at it. Better than a pound and a half, flank flashing gold in the sun, and he's grinning like he just found money in an old coat. That's the breakwall in early August for you — you never know when the next drop is going to be the fish of the trip.

This is peak season on the rockpiles right now and it's not subtle. Porgies are stacked on the New Haven Harbor breakwalls in 15 to 20 feet, thickest on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high water, when the current slacks enough that a light skimmer rig with squid strips or sandworm actually sits still on the bottom instead of getting dragged sideways. I've been running 1/2-ounce sinkers on 12-pound braid, small hooks, size 4 or 6 — bigger porgies are surprisingly leader-shy this time of year and a bulky rig gets you fewer bites. Sea bass are mixed right in with them, especially out toward the tip of the outer wall where the rock drops into deeper water. Squid and clam belly are still the ticket, and the keepers have been running 14 to 16 inches with enough shorts in the mix that you're working for your limit, not filling a bucket in twenty minutes.

Falkner Island has been the more consistent sea bass spot the last two weeks — the rockpile structure off the northeast side in 25 to 30 feet is holding fish that don't seem to care much what the tide's doing, though the bite sharpens noticeably on the last of the ebb when bait gets pulled off the structure and the bass bunch up to intercept it. Bring bucktails with a squid teaser trailer if you want to cover ground instead of just soaking bait — you'll pick off the more aggressive fish that way and save your clams for the pickier ones.

Stratford Shoal is fishing the way Stratford Shoal always fishes in high summer — good porgy and sea bass numbers on the rockier stretches, but the current there is honest and unforgiving, and this week it's actually working in our favor. We're sliding into a neap tide around August 5th and 6th, and the softer swing means less sinker weight, cleaner drifts, and a lot more precision when you're trying to hold a bait tight against a specific piece of structure instead of getting swept off it every fifteen minutes. If you've been frustrated fishing the Shoal on a big tide, this is your window — go lighter, feel the bottom better, and you'll catch more fish for the same effort.

As for tog — we're still in the summer closure, so if you're marking fish tight to the rock piles at Falkner or the Charles Island reef, admire them and move on. That fishery comes back in a few weeks and it'll be worth the wait.

Now the striper story is a different animal entirely, and it's exactly the story we flagged last week — that as the tides soften into the neap, bass would stop roaming and compress onto the deepest, coolest structure, feeding hardest in the tightest current windows. That's precisely what's setting up on the sandbar off Charles Island right now. Water's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s on the surface, which means daytime bass are holding deep, tucked against the drop-off on the north side of the bar, mostly uninterested in anything you throw at them until the sun starts to go down. But from last light through the first couple hours of dark, on the last of the outgoing when bait gets pulled off the flat and funnels along that sandbar edge, the bass come up and they come up hungry. Live eels have been the most consistent producer — slow-troll them along the drop or drift them back on a fish-finder rig — with bucktails in white or chartreuse picking up fish on the retrieve when there's current to work with. Nothing enormous yet, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but a few overslot fish have shown in the mix for guys willing to fish the full dark hours instead of packing it in at dusk.

Bluefish remain entirely a bait story this month. Wherever bunker pods have been holding — and they've been moving around off Hammonasset and occasionally pushing up toward the Milford Gulf — the blues show up within hours and it turns into topwater chaos for as long as the bait stays put. It's not a spot you can circle on a chart and count on; it's a spot you find by watching the birds and the surface nervous water that morning. Bring wire leader and something loud — a Hopkins jig or a bunker spoon — because when they're on the bait they're not fussy.

Fluke have been the quiet steady performer over sand pockets around the Milford Gulf and off Hammonasset in 15 to 25 feet, working the moving water with 4-inch white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom. Nothing gigantic, but a legal fish or two most drifts if you're patient about covering ground.

Looking ahead: with the neap easing current everywhere, I'd spend the next several days on the rockpiles — porgies and sea bass should stay strong and the lighter tide makes for more comfortable, more precise fishing. For stripers, plan around the last two hours of light and the first couple hours of dark at Charles Island; that's where the fish are concentrating and where the effort actually pays off right now.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Punching Fluke Limits at 38 Feet While the Race Goes Quiet on the Neap
reports.subhead: Captain Terry's boat put six keeper doormats in the box Tuesday and the mate told me the sea bass bite off Black Point hasn't missed a day in two weeks.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the mates off the Niantic fleet at the tackle shop Wednesday morning buying squid strips, and he had that look guys get when the boat's been putting fish in the box. Told me Tuesday's half-day trip limited out on fluke in under four hours, mostly in that 36- to 40-foot stretch between Twotree Island Channel and the mouth of Niantic Bay. Biggest fish went six and a half pounds on a white Gulp Swimming Mullet teased behind a bucktail, drifted slow on the last two hours of the incoming. That's been the program all week — nothing fancy, just gulp and squid strips on a spreader rig, working the sand-to-mud transitions where the current pushes bait up against the channel edge.

The water's cooler out here than it is west of the river — New London's reading around 69.6, which is a good ten degrees behind what Kings Point's showing down toward the western Sound. That gap matters. It's kept our fluke and sea bass biting steady instead of shutting down the way warmer water can do to bottom fish in August. Guys grumble about it being "only" high 60s, but that's exactly why the doormats are still cooperating out here while other zones start slowing down on the fluke.

Black sea bass have been the more dependable of the two, honestly. Hole-in-the-Wall and the rock piles off Black Point are holding fish stacked tight to structure — 20 to 35 feet, and you want to be right on top of the rocks, not drifting past them. Green crab and squid combo on a high-low rig, bounced bottom on the anchor, has been the ticket. Party boat scuttlebutt says limits of keeper sea bass most trips this week, with a few 3-pound-plus fish mixed in when they hit the deeper edges of the reef structure. If you're going after them yourself, fish the slower part of the tide — dead low or right around the turn — because when that current really rips through there it's near impossible to hold bottom without snapping off in the rocks.

We flagged this last week — said the coming neap would soften current speed through here — and that's exactly what's happening now heading into this weekend's first-quarter neap. Twotree Channel and the Race have both gone noticeably slower on the last couple drifts I've heard about, which is actually good news for fluke guys because it lets you fish lighter bucktails, down to 3/4-ounce, and keep better bottom contact without getting dragged off the structure. If you're used to fighting 2-ounce jigs through there on a big tide, back off — you'll actually present better with less lead right now.

Striper action has settled into the pattern you'd expect for early August — fish are down deep on structure during the day and coming up to feed at the edges of light. Guys working the Niantic River mouth and around the bridges after dark with eels have been picking off decent fish, mostly mid-20s to low-30s inches, nothing spectacular but steady enough to be worth the late nights. Daytime, if you want a shot at a bigger fish, it's live-lining or jigging deep over structure — McCook Point and the rock piles off Black Point in 25 to 40 feet have given up a few better bass to guys working bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along bottom. Nothing blitzing, nothing you'd call easy, but consistent if you put the time in during that dawn and dusk window.

Bluefish have been scattered rather than schooled up out here — nothing like the bunker-driven chaos happening to our west. When you do find them, it's usually because a pod of peanut bunker got pushed into the bay, and the blues show up within a tide or two of that bait arriving. Keep an eye on the surface around Niantic Bay and the outer edge of the channel — diving terns are still your best early warning system. Topwater poppers or a simple diamond jig will get bit fast once you find the pod, but it's not the kind of thing you can plan a trip around right now; it's opportunistic.

Porgies have been a nice bonus fish mixed in with the sea bass around Black Point and the reef structure off Hole-in-the-Wall — bloodworms or squid on a simple two-hook rig will keep the rod bending between bigger bites.

Looking ahead, this softer neap tide should hold through the weekend into early next week, which means lighter presentations and more patience on the drift, but also more comfortable fishing for anyone bringing kids or newer anglers out. I'd focus effort on the fluke grounds in that 35- to 40-foot band off Twotree and Niantic Bay while the current's manageable, and keep working sea bass around Black Point on the slower tide stages. Water temps out east aren't likely to jump much given how the Sound's laid out right now, so I don't expect a dramatic shift in what's biting — just a continuation of what's already working. If a squid push does show up along the eastern edges the way it's been building toward Rhode Island, that could sweeten things further for the reef fishing, so I'll be watching that closely and reporting back.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Last Ebb: Fluke to 6 Pounds, Porgies Stacked on the Cows
reports.subhead: Warm water has the reef program running on low-light windows and softening tide — here's where I'm putting my anchor this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I made a call Saturday morning I don't make often — I skipped Penfield entirely and ran straight to Cockenoe. Not because Penfield's dead, but because it was 9 a.m. on a bluebird weekend and the mooring field off Southport was already staging six center consoles and a charter boat for the same piece of rock. Cockenoe's reef edge, on the other hand, drops off clean into 15-18 feet of water on the southwest corner, and it doesn't get the same foot traffic because half the fleet doesn't know the drift line. That's the kind of math I do every weekend now — where's the structure that fires on my tide window and doesn't have three boats parked on top of it.

The fluke bite off that Cockenoe edge has been the most consistent thing in my zone all week. Last two hours of the ebb into the top of the tide change, the current sweeps bait off the reef crown and stacks fluke right on the drop where 8 feet turns into 18. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow, right on bottom, letting the boat do the work on the drift. Took a 6-pound doormat Tuesday on that exact program, and we had four keepers in about ninety minutes before the tide went slack and the bite just shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's fluke fishing right now — tight windows, not all-day grinding.

Kings Point is reading 72.9 degrees, and that warmth is exactly why the daytime bass bite has gone quiet on top. Stripers are doing what they do in early August — holding deep on the hard structure through the sun hours and only coming up to feed at the edges of the day. Sheffield Island's channel, that 15-to-20-foot cut on the north side, has been the spot for that. I've had two solid sessions there right at last light, live-lining peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig with just enough weight to keep it down in the current, and both nights the fish showed in the last 45 minutes before full dark. Nothing huge — mid-20s to low-30-inchers — but consistent enough that I'd plan around it again this week.

We flagged this pattern last week — said that as the tides softened, bass would compress into the tightest current windows and hold on the deepest, coolest structure. That's exactly what's playing out at Sheffield and off Greenwich Point right now. The bite isn't spread out anymore. It's a 45-minute window on the ebb or right at dusk, and if you're not there for it, you're just trolling around in empty water.

The porgy bite on the Cows has been the bright spot for anyone who wants steady action without needing a perfect tide. That shallow structure off Stamford floods hard on the incoming, and porgies pile onto the mussel beds once there's three or four feet of water covering the rocks. Hi-lo rigs with sandworm or squid strips, small hooks, light enough weight to feel the bottom without snagging — we've been loading the cooler with porgies in the 10-to-13-inch class on the flood, best two hours before and after high water. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the most reliable thing going in the western Sound right now, and it's a great option when the weekend boat traffic makes the reef proper unworkable.

Black sea bass have been holding true to form on the rockier structure — Penfield's deeper flanks, 20-25 feet, and the rubble off Greenwich Point. Squid strips or Gulp saltwater shrimp on a knocker rig, bounced right on bottom. It's a grind-it-out fishery this time of year, nothing spectacular, but if you're patient you'll pick through shorts to find enough keepers for dinner. I'd fish it on a slower stage of the tide, not dead high or dead low, because that's when the fish seem to actually feed instead of just sitting tight to the rocks.

Bluefish have been following the bunker pods, and where those pods concentrate off Greenwich Point and the outer Norwalk Islands, the blues show up fast and don't stick around long. It's bait-driven entirely — no bunker, no blues. When I've found working birds over a pod near the Cows, a top-water popper or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig has produced quick, violent action for twenty minutes before the school moves. Worth having a rod rigged and ready, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it — plan around structure and let the blues be a bonus.

We're heading into the neap around August 5-6, and that's going to soften current across the board — Cockenoe, Penfield, the cut at Sheffield, all of it. When that happens I'll be dropping jig weights and slowing presentations, because a weak push means bait doesn't get swept off structure as hard, and fish get lazier about chasing it. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the last two hours of the ebb at Cockenoe for fluke, then swing to Sheffield right at dusk for a shot at bass on bunker. Keep an eye on boat traffic on the weekend — the reefs that get pounded by 10 a.m. Saturday are dead water by noon, and the smart move is either getting there at first light or finding the piece of structure nobody else bothered to learn.

reports.headline: Water's split down the middle at Plum Gut — and the bass know it
reports.subhead: Warm water pushing from the west, cold water holding the Gut — the fish are stacking right where the two meet.
reports.body_markdown:
Fella pulled up to the ramp at Mattituck Inlet Tuesday morning, boat still had the dealer sticker on the windshield, asked me where the bass were biting. I told him the same thing I've told every man who's asked me that question in sixty years on this water — depends which bass you mean, and depends what time of day you're willing to go looking for them. He didn't much care for that answer. Went out anyway, ran the shoreline at noon with topwater plugs, came back skunked and a little sunburned. That's not bad luck. That's just August.

Here's what's actually going on out there. The Sound's got a real temperature seam running through it right now — Kings Point way west is sitting near 73, and by the time you get out to New London it's dropped to under 70. That gradient doesn't stop at some invisible line on a chart, it drags right along our stretch, and the fish feel it before we do. Water this warm on the surface pushes the bass down and back, holding tight to structure through the daylight hours, and they don't come up to feed proper until the light goes soft. I've watched this pattern my whole life and it never changes with the calendar, only with the thermometer.

So the bass bite here has become a dusk-and-dark proposition, same as it always does this time of year. Best water's been the rip off Orient Point and the push into Plum Gut itself, where the current keeps things stirred and a few degrees cooler than the flat water either side of it. Guys eeling there after sundown are doing right by themselves — a whole or half snake eel, weighted just enough to hold near bottom on the drift, worked slow through the seam where the Gut current meets the slower Sound water. We said last week the tides would soften up heading toward this neap and that it'd push the bass onto the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure — night eels at the Gut and working the bridge-adjacent rock — and that's exactly the program now. Nothing mysterious about it, the fish just go where the water's comfortable and the bait's easy.

Daytime, if you want bass, you're jigging deep over structure — the rock piles off Horton Point, the drop past Rocky Point — bouncing a bucktail or a diamond jig right on the bottom where they're holding tucked out of the sun. It's not fast fishing. You might work a spot forty-five minutes for two fish. But two keeper stripers off structure in the middle of the day beats an empty box, and it's honest work for honest fish.

Porgy's your bread and butter right now, no argument. Scup fishing on the reef structure off Horton Point and out toward Plum Gut is about as good as it gets all year — small hooks, squid strips or clam, bounced right on bottom, and you'll fill a bucket without much fuss. This is the fishery I send the kids and the first-timers to when the bass are being difficult, because it just about always produces.

Fluke's holding up nicely too. The channel edges and current-swept flats between Mattituck and Rocky Point have been giving up decent-sized fish on the last two hours of the outgoing — 3-inch white Gulp on a bucktail, or a strip of squid trailing a spearing, dragged slow along bottom where the current's cutting a seam. Nothing I'd call a doormat bite, but a few fish in the 20-to-24-inch range most trips out, which is plenty for a summer dinner.

Bluefish are around but scattered, and they're chasing bait, not tide charts. Wherever the bunker pods bunch up tight along the shoreline you'll get a flurry — poppers and metal will get hit hard for twenty minutes and then it goes quiet as the bunker move off. That's the whole story with blues this year. Find the bait, find the fish, and don't expect them to stay put.

Weakfish I've got nothing good to tell you. A few reports of small ones taken incidentally on bass gear near the inlet, nothing worth planning a trip around. That fishery's been thin for years out here and this week's no different.

Tide's easing toward the neap around the 5th and 6th, which means the Gut and the Race will run slower than they have — lighter jigs, slower retrieves, less brute force needed to hold bottom. That's not a bad thing. Slower current can actually concentrate bait in the seams rather than blow it through, and some of my better Plum Gut nights have come on the softer tides, not the hard ones.

Worth keeping an eye on the temperature break right at the Gut approach over the next week or two — that's historically where the first false albacore or bonito show up scouting through, once the water settles into that mid-to-upper 60s range on the cooler side of the seam. Too early to call it, but I'd rather tell you to watch for it now than have you surprised when someone hooks one off Orient and nobody believed the leader that came back.

reports.headline: Ran the Wilmington Northeast Corner on Fuel-Math Alone — Three Yellowfin and a White Marlin Bite to Show for the Diesel
reports.subhead: A stable high and a softening tide made the call easy this week: troll early, chunk if the bite stalls, and don't burn extra miles chasing a break that hasn't moved much.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning before we ever left the dock: troll first, chunk as backup, and don't run past the northeast corner looking for something better. That's not a glamorous decision, but it's the right one when fuel's pushing $4.60 at the marina and the trip's got to pay for itself. We'd flagged last week that the midweek blow was going to nudge the eddy edge some, and it did — but the northeast corner of Wilmington held as the high-percentage starting point, same as it's been for going on three weeks now. We just had to verify the break on the way out instead of assuming it, and that fifteen minutes of running the temp gauge saved us from wasting gas on the wrong water.

The run out of Indian River put us on the canyon around 38°49'N, 73°57'W, working the 50 to 100-fathom transition where the bottom falls off the shelf and the Gulf Stream filament has been laying a warm tongue against the cooler shelf water. That seam was sitting right around 75-76°F on the warm side, dropping to the low 70s on the inside edge — sharp enough to see bait balling up and birds working it from a mile out. We trolled a standard spread — naked and skirted ballyhoo, a couple of Ilanders in blue/white and green machine off the shotgun — starting around 7 AM and working the color change north to south along the break for about four hours before we connected. Three yellowfin, all in the 35-50 pound class, came off that same stretch of water within about ninety minutes of each other, which tells me the school was sitting on that edge rather than roaming. We also had a white marlin come up on the long bait and eat it half-heartedly — no hookup, but it's the first marlin interest I've had in two weeks, so worth mentioning if you're a troller with mixed-bag intentions.

Bluefin were mixed in but scattered — we marked fish on the sounder in that 60-80 foot range on the temp break but never got a dedicated bite going on them. That's consistent with what I'm hearing up and down the canyon string this week: bluefin are around, but they're not stacked tight enough yet to target specifically. If you want bluefin, you're more likely to pick them up incidentally while working the yellowfin spread than by hunting them directly right now.

No wahoo for us this trip, though we had the high-speed line out most of the day. Water clarity out there was decent, not gin-clear, and the wahoo bite tends to want that cobalt, ripping-clean water — we didn't quite have it Tuesday. If I run again this week I'd add a second high-speed rig with a bigger lead and fish it closer to the color change itself rather than the open blue, since that's where we've picked up wahoo in past Augusts.

Mahi were a bonus, not a target — we picked up two schoolies, maybe 6-8 pounds, off a mat of sargassum drifting right on the break. If you've got light spinning tackle rigged, keep it ready; those weed lines are holding fish and a quick pitch bait can save an otherwise slow stretch between trolling passes.

As for chunking — we didn't need to switch over Tuesday because the troll bite held, but I want to flag the timing here because it matters for anyone planning a trip this week. The tide range is narrowing into the coming neap around August 5-6, and that's going to soften the current out on the canyon edge. Softer current means your chunk slick holds shape longer and drifts slower, which is exactly the setup you want for a night bigeye bite on butterfish chunks. If the troll bite stalls out there in the next few days, that neap tide is your cue to switch tactics rather than keep burning fuel running the spread. I'd anchor up or drift-chunk right on that same northeast corner break, butterfish chunks with a few whole ones skipped out as teasers, starting a couple hours before dark and working through the first part of the night tide.

Conditions on the ride out were manageable — three-foot swell, seven-second period, nothing that beat up the boat, and that's held steady enough that I don't expect weather to be the limiting factor this week. The bigger variable is whether that eddy edge holds its position or slides again. Best case, it stays put through the weekend and the yellowfin keep sitting right on that same stretch of the break — in that scenario I'd run the same numbers again without hesitation. If it slides east like these filaments tend to do when the Stream pulses, I'd shift my starting point a few miles that direction rather than assume the fish moved with it exactly.

Bottom line for anybody planning a trip: the yellowfin bite on Wilmington's northeast corner is real but it's not a lock — three fish in six hours of trolling is a decent day, not a slaughter, and you earned every one of them working the break properly. If I had one day this week I'd go early, troll the temp change hard through the morning, and have chunk gear rigged as a fallback once that neap tide starts softening the current. That's the trip I'd book, and it's the one that makes sense on the fuel gauge.

reports.headline: Nine Hours to the East Wall — Bigeye at 2 A.M. and a Marlin We Never Boated
reports.subhead: The run to Atlantis cost us a full tank and a night's sleep, but the temp break paid the diesel bill and then some.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 9 PM Thursday with 340 gallons in the tanks, and I told the mate we'd be lucky to see the rail bend before midnight. That's the math on this run — Atlantis Canyon sits about 100 nautical miles south-southeast of the Point, and at a 24-knot cruise that's four-plus hours just to reach the color change, another hour or two working the edge before you commit to a drift, and then the same four hours home with whatever's in the box. You don't run to the east canyons on a whim. You run because the report, the water temp, and your gut all say the same thing, and this week they did.

We set up on the east wall around 39°49'N, 71°43'W, working a break where the water went from a dirty green-blue into that cobalt you only see when the shelf water's pushed in clean. Trolled a spread of Green Machines and a naked ballyhoo down the middle through the afternoon — one yellowfin in the 40s, lost a wahoo strike that shredded a lure but never came tight, and a white marlin that came up on the long rigger, danced twice, and let go before the mate could get a hand on the leader. That's the canyon for you. It gives you a look and takes it back.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the slot bluefin were holding steady, bigeye showing at the edge, and a marlin raised right where the shelf turns from green-blue to cobalt would confirm what's been building all month. That's exactly what happened out there Thursday night. Once the sun dropped we shut down the trolling gear, drifted the edge, and started chunking butterfish over a slick. Bigeye showed on the sounder around 11 PM, sitting deep — 200, 250 feet — and we picked at them steady through the night on 60-pound fluoro leaders and circle hooks, three fish to the boat before the tide turned against us around 4 AM and the bite went quiet. Not a stacked night, but three bigeye and a keeper yellowfin off one drift is a good return on the fuel burn, and it's the kind of consistency we've been seeing build since mid-July.

The bluefin have been the reliable piece of this puzzle all season — recreational-slot fish scattered along the temperature breaks from Veatch down through Atlantis, mixed in with the yellowfin on the troll during daylight and showing up again on the chunk after dark. Nothing's been a slaughter, but boats working the edges consistently are putting two, three, sometimes four keeper-class bluefin in the box alongside the yellowfin, and that's real money against the diesel bill.

Here's what's changing the calculus for next week: the tide range is narrowing into the coming neap around August 5-6, and that softer current is going to favor the troll over the chunk in the rip-dependent spots. Less current means less bait getting pushed hard against the edges, which means less reason for tuna to hold tight on a slick — they'll be roaming more, and a moving spread covers water a static chunk bait can't. If you're planning a trip this week, I'd lean troll-heavy early, then switch to chunk gear only if you mark fish holding on the sounder rather than just passing through.

Mahi have been a bonus, not a target — a few short bursts of gaffer-class fish under scattered weed lines and the occasional lobster gear float working the flat water between Atlantis and Veatch, taking small chartreuse feathers meant for something bigger. Wahoo remain a low-percentage, high-reward proposition; we've heard of a couple caught on high-speed rigs — Ilanders over cigar minnows run at 12-14 knots — but nobody's targeting them exclusively out here yet. The water hasn't gotten hot enough at depth to concentrate them the way it will later this month.

For boats running out of Block Island or the Rhode Island ports toward Hydrographer and Oceanographer, the extra 20-30 miles of run compared to an Atlantis trip changes the trip planning more than the fishing itself — you're looking at closer to five hours each way at a fuel-conscious cruise, which means committing to an overnight if you want any real time on the grounds. Worth it if the SST breaks are set up right; not worth it if you're just going to poke around. I'd call ahead to whoever's been out there in the last 48 hours before you commit that kind of fuel.

Looking ahead, the stable high pressure that's held all week isn't showing signs of breaking yet, and that's the single biggest reason this bite has stayed consistent instead of going lockjaw. If it holds through the weekend, I'd expect the yellowfin and bluefin pattern to continue on the troll during daylight with the bigeye picking up again after dark on the chunk, especially once the neap current settles in and slows things down enough for a slick to actually hold. Watch for the white marlin to start showing more consistently too — one raised fish is a tease, but the water color and the bait we're seeing say more are coming. If the wind stays out of it, that's where I'd put my next trip.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Solid B+ Week: Spencer Yellowfin Steady, Norfolk Wahoo Crash the Spread
reports.subhead: Warm water pinned against the canyon edges kept the trolling bite honest all week, with Norfolk's wahoo run stealing the show.
reports.body_markdown:
If I'm grading this week, I'm giving it a solid B+. Not the A we had back in mid-July when everything from Spencer to Norfolk was stacked with yellowfin, but a week where every boat I talked to at the Cape May Canyon dock had fish in the box and a story about the one that got off. The knock is consistency — some days you had to run the whole 60 miles to find the right water, other days it was right there waiting on the edge.

Here's the why. The Bight's holding warm, clean water — 75.7°F out at the edge buoy, seas a manageable 3 feet at a long 7-second period, which means it's rollable but fishable, no white-knuckle rides. That warm push has been leaning into the canyon walls at Spencer and Lindenkohl for about ten days now, and it's dragging bait with it. When that happens, the yellowfin quit roaming and start setting up shop on the humps and the 100-fathom curve, which is exactly where we found them.

Spencer's been my go-to this week. Working the north wall around the 100 to 250-fathom transition, trolling a mixed spread — green machines and cedar plugs down the middle, ballyhoo and mullet chains off the riggers — put yellowfin in the 30 to 55-pound range in the box most mornings. Best window was that first hour of light before the wind filled in, water color running that deep cobalt blue right where it meets the green edge. A few boats switched to chunking butterfish once the sun got high and the trolling bite went quiet — that's the move if you're patient, anchor up on the temp break, let the slick build, and wait for that first tuna to show color under the transom.

Lindenkohl was more of a mixed bag. Good bluefin mixed in with the yellowfin trolling the same 100-fathom stretch, but you had to grind for it some afternoons — long stretches of nothing, then a triple hookup out of nowhere. That's canyon fishing in August, though. The fish are there, they're just not dumb about showing themselves in the heat of the day.

Norfolk is where the week got interesting. Wahoo showed up hard on the high-speed gear — planers and wire line pulling Ilanders and cedar plugs at 12 to 15 knots along the drop, and guys were connecting on fish in the 40 to 60-pound class working the edge where Norfolk's wall falls off fast into deep water. That warm water influence Hooper — sorry, that warm water everybody's been talking about — is exactly the kind of setup that pulls wahoo up onto these canyon edges, and Norfolk sits far enough south that it gets the benefit first. If you're chasing wahoo specifically, that's your canyon right now, not Spencer, not Lindenkohl.

Poor Man's stayed quieter, which tracks — it's the shallowest and closest-in of the four, and without a strong bait push it doesn't hold fish the way the deeper canyons do. A couple of mahi came off weed lines drifting rigged ballyhoo and small chunks of butterfish under the color changes, but nobody I talked to made a special trip out there this week. I'd keep it in the back pocket for a quick run if the wind's up and you can't make the longer haul.

Bigeye have been showing at night on the chunk, mostly reported out of Spencer and Lindenkohl both — that's your classic pattern, sun goes down, the bigeye come up off the bottom structure to feed, and a well-soaked chunk bait on circle hooks, lightly weighted, fished way back in the slick will get bit. White marlin have been scattered through all four canyons but nothing consistent enough to call a run yet — a few pulled ballyhoo skirted with blue/white or pink/white got looks, one or two hookups, but I wouldn't build a trip around it just yet.

We flagged this last week — said the softer tides heading toward the coming neap would shift the emphasis toward trolling and the daytime deep-drop, and that's exactly what's playing out. The tide range is narrowing into that August 5-6 neap, current's going slack in the canyon breaks, and that softer water is favoring the troll over the drift-chunk in a lot of spots. If you're rigging for swords, this is the window — daytime deep-drop tactics work better when you're not fighting a hard current to keep your bait down near bottom structure.

Looking ahead, the high pressure's holding, seas stay manageable, and that warm water isn't going anywhere fast. I'd lean Spencer and Lindenkohl for yellowfin and bigeye, and if wahoo's the target, make the longer run to Norfolk while that warm edge is sitting right on the wall. Poor Man's is your backup plan, not your primary. Watch the tide easing into the neap — that's your cue to lean harder on the troll and less on the anchor-up chunk for the next several days.

reports.headline: 75.7°F at the Buoy, a Harder Break Sits at the 100-Fathom Curve
reports.subhead: Yellowfin and bluefin are splitting a tightening thermal edge on the Hudson's northern wall, and a softening tide is starting to hand the edge back to the trollers.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-five point seven degrees at the surface off the Bight, three-foot swell running at seven seconds — that's a transit report, not a fishing report, and it told me what I'd find seventy-some miles out before I ever cleared the inlet. Surface water that warm sitting on top of a three-second gap between wave period readings means there's stratification happening below it, a layer of cooler water still sitting on the bottom of the mixed zone. That's exactly the setup you want going into the canyon in early August — warm cap, cooler subsurface, and a hard edge where the two meet along the shelf break.

I found that edge running along the 100-fathom curve near 39°48' N, 72°35' W, right off the northern wall where the canyon starts to open up before it drops toward the Dip. Color change was sharp — green, chlorophyll-heavy water pushing out from the coast on the inside, clean blue 74–76°F water sitting on the canyon side. That's the kind of break that holds bait, and it held bait again this week. Squid and small mahi-sized weed clumps were scattered right on the seam, with a few respectable windrows of sargassum drifting south of the Dip that had mahi stacked underneath — mostly schoolie-sized, eight to fifteen pounds, with a couple better fish pushing twenty coming off small yellow-and-green feather rigs pulled tight to the grass.

The yellowfin bite has been a two-part story this week, and I want to be straight about it because it wasn't a wire-to-wire green light. Trolling in the morning on the color change produced steady but not stacked action — green machines and small Ilanders in the 40–50 range, ballyhoo naked and skirted mixed through a nine-line spread, picking up yellowfin in the 25–45 pound class working the temp seam between 39°45' and 39°50' N. By midday, with the sun high and the surface glassy under that stable high pressure, the troll bite went quiet for stretches. The better numbers came after dark, chunking butterfish at anchor over 100 to 130 fathoms near the Dip and along the eastern edge of the Claw — that's where the bulk of the bigger yellowfin, some pushing 50-plus, came aboard on 30 to 50-pound fluoro leader, small circle hooks, and a slow, thinned-out chunk line to keep them working the boat instead of the current.

We flagged this a week ago — said the softening tide into the coming neap would start shifting the advantage back toward trolling, and that's exactly what's playing out. With the range narrowing into the August 5–6 neap, current on the canyon edge has eased noticeably compared to two weeks back, and the troll bite in the early morning window has picked up relative to the chunk bite, which had been carrying the week before. If that trend holds, I'd expect the balance to keep tipping toward trolling through the weekend, especially on that 100-fathom seam where the bait's been sitting tight.

Bluefin have been mixed into both patterns, mostly smaller class fish in the 40–70 pound range, taking the same trolled spread as the yellowfin rather than showing as a separate push. Nothing large-class showing consistently inside the canyon proper this week — the bigger bluefin action has stayed north, out toward the Gulf of Maine grounds, and what we're seeing here reads more like scouts working the same bait balls as the yellowfin rather than a dedicated bluefin push. Worth setting one flat line a little heavier — 50-pound mono instead of straight fluoro — if you want to hang onto one of the better ones without getting worked over on standard yellowfin gear.

White marlin reports have started to spread out from what was a tight cluster two weeks ago, and this week that pattern continued — scattered raises along the temp break south of the Dip, mostly on naked ballyhoo behind Sea Witches in the top slots of the spread, with a couple of confirmed releases in the 39°40' N corridor. It's not a stacked bite yet, more a scattered one, but the direction is right — more boats reporting fish each week rather than fewer, which is what you want to see heading into the heart of August.

Wahoo have been a bycatch story so far — a couple taken on high-speed gear run early, before the troll spread went out, working the drop-off edge in 90 to 110 fathoms where the bottom breaks hard. Nothing to build a dedicated trip around yet, but worth a couple of lines in the water if you're running out before first light.

Looking at the week ahead: the high-pressure pattern shows no sign of breaking, which keeps the surface calm and the canyon fishable, but it also means that afternoon glass-off that's been killing the midday troll bite is likely to repeat. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd run out early, work the 100-fathom seam near 39°48' N on the troll through mid-morning, then either push into the Dip to anchor and chunk after the bite slows, or stay mobile and hunt weed lines south for mahi if the troll goes cold. The neap tide should keep softening current through midweek, which favors the troll pattern holding its recent gains — but I'd still have the chunk gear rigged and ready once the sun gets high.

reports.headline: August 3 and Washington's North Wall Is Still Doing the Heavy Lifting
reports.subhead: Two months into the season the chunk bite is fading with the tides, but the troll is picking up the slack right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
By the first week of August I've usually got a pretty good read on how the season's going to shake out, and this year Washington did exactly what it always does — showed up early and settled into a rhythm before the other canyons even got their spreads wet. We were seeing yellowfin on the temperature breaks back in June when boats running out of the other inlets were still soaking bait for bluefin off the beach. That head start matters. It means by early August, when everybody else is just figuring out where the fish are, we've already got three patterns dialed in and we're watching for the fourth.

Right now that fourth pattern is the shift from chunk to troll, and it's happening on schedule. We flagged this last week — said the overnight chunk bite would peak Wednesday through Friday inside the 100-fathom curve on the north wall, and that's exactly how it played out. Guys anchored up there Thursday night into Friday morning had some of the better yellowfin counts of the month, mixed with a few bigeye showing up on the bite windows around 2 and 4 a.m. The moon was still working for us then. Now we're sliding into the neap — tide range narrowing through the 5th and 6th — and that current isn't pushing bait against the wall with the same authority. When the drift softens, the tuna spread out, and chunking loses its edge. That's when the troll starts carrying the weight, and I'd bet on that trend holding through the weekend.

The bite itself has been honest work, not a gimme. We're not lighting up six-packs of yellowfin in an afternoon — this is a fifty-fifty proposition most days, four or five fish in the boat if you found the right piece of structure and the color change lined up. The stable high pressure that's been sitting over the whole mid-Atlantic has kept run conditions about as good as they get — flat enough to troll a nine-line spread comfortably, seas running two to three feet with a long period out at the edge of the shelf, nothing that's going to beat up a canyon run. But calm water and light current also mean the bait isn't getting pinned the way it does when there's some push behind it, so you're covering ground to find pockets instead of parking on one spot and letting it come to you.

Mahi have been the bright spot for the trollers working the color edges and any floating structure — a few nice pods in the 8 to 15 pound class coming off small green machines and skirted ballyhoo pulled just off the paddocks of grass lines. If you see even a single mat of sargassum out there this week, slow down and work it — those fish have been holding tight to any bit of cover they can find. White marlin sightings have been spreading week over week just like we expected, mostly on naked ballyhoo and small blue/white Islanders run flat lines, and a couple boats have gotten multiple bites in a day without necessarily converting all of them — typical August white marlin behavior, they'll play with a bait longer than they commit to it.

Wahoo have been a bonus fish more than a target — a few high-speed trollers pulling cedar plugs and small Ilanders at 12-15 knots along the drop-off have picked off one or two on days when the water clarity out past the 100-fathom line has gone that deep cobalt blue that tells you you're sitting in real Gulf Stream water, not just warm coastal runoff. That blue water pushing up against the canyon edge is the whole reason Washington runs ahead of schedule every year — we're closer to that current than Hudson or the canyons north of us, and it shows in how early the tropical species show up and how long they stick around into the fall.

Bluefin have been mixed in but not the headline story here the way they've been up north on Stellwagen and Jeffrey's Ledge, where the cooler Gulf of Maine water is holding bigger concentrations. Down here they're incidental — a fish or two crashing the chunk slick at first light, usually smaller schoolies mixed with the yellowfin, nothing you'd plan a whole trip around.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd play the neap tide the way I always do out here — lean harder into the troll through midweek while current is soft, working the eddy edge and any temperature break you can find on the meter, then swing back toward the chunk as the tide starts building again into the weekend. If the eddy holds its position off the north wall like it has all month, that's still the high-percentage water. If the post-blow satellite shots this week show it sliding east — and there's some chatter that it might drift with this stretch of settled weather — I'd shift effort toward the canyon's eastern flank and give up a little bit of the wall advantage for fresher water. Either way, the fish are here and the conditions are cooperative. You still have to find the color change and put a bait in the right piece of water, but that's always been true out here, early season or late.

reports.headline: Peconic Pushes Into the Upper 70s — Porgies Pile Up at Shelter Island While Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: The bay's running its full August pattern now — thick scup on the bottom, fluke scattered but real in the channels, and stripers only showing themselves after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic runs on its own clock, and every August it hits the same stride — full heat, slack afternoons, and a bottom bite that doesn't care what the sun's doing. This bay warms faster than the Sound every spring, and by the first week of August it's paying that heat back with interest. We're deep into the upper 70s in the coves and flats now, warmer in the skinny water off Hashamomuck and Cornelius Point, and that heat has pushed the whole system into its classic midsummer rhythm — porgies thick on structure, fluke working the channels on the moving tide, and the resident stripers sliding down onto deep structure to sit out the daylight hours.

Shelter Island is doing exactly what it does this time of year. I fished the Route 114 bridge rip on the last of an outgoing tide Wednesday morning and it was about as textbook a porgy session as you'll get — 15 to 20 feet of water, high-low rigs with size 4 hooks, sandworm and skimmer clam, and fish stacked so thick you'd mark bait balls on the bottom before the anchor even set. Cornelius Point and the Fleet's Neck side are holding the same class of fish — mostly 12 to 14 inches with enough 15s mixed in to make it worth culling. Coecles Harbor has been quietly good too if you want to get away from boat traffic. Crushed clam chum off the stern turns a decent bite into a steady one — the scup follow that scent trail up in the water column and you'll start picking off fish mid-column instead of dead bottom.

Fluke are a different story this week — present, but scattered, and you have to work for them. The North Race off Robins Island and the channel edges between Nassau Point and the island have been the most consistent, 25 to 35 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and dragging bottom on the outgoing. I'm getting keepers in that spread — nothing over 22 inches, but a few solid teens mixed with shorts most drifts. Jessup Neck has been softer, more shorts than keepers, which tells me the bigger fish have pushed into deeper water as the surface temps climbed. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, try slowing the drift down even further — with the water this warm, fluke aren't chasing anything fast.

Stripers have settled into the pattern we called out a couple weeks back — as the tides softened toward the neap, bass would compress into the strongest current windows and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at Plum Gut and Orient Point right now. Daytime, forget it unless you're jigging deep on structure — the fish are down on the bottom of the Gut in that hard current, uninterested in anything but a vertical presentation right on their nose. But after dark, eels fished on the last of the ebb around the Gut and under the bridges at Shelter Island have been producing solid fish in the high 20s to low 30s. First light is the other window — bucktails worked along the rip edges at Orient Point before the sun gets up high enough to push the fish back down.
