Bluefish are following the bunker, plain and simple, and right now those schools are moving through Gardiners Bay unevenly — some mornings you find blitzing fish off Gull Pond and near Orient, other mornings the bay's dead calm with nothing showing. When you find the bunker, it's fast and violent — poppers and 2-ounce metal at first light, don't overthink it. When you don't find bunker, don't waste your morning searching blind — check the birds first.

Weakfish are still a bonus fish rather than a target, but they're around. Hashamomuck's protected cove has given up a few solid weakfish on the outgoing tide working bucktail tipped with a strip of squid along the sand/shell bottom, and South Jamesport Beach on the north fork side has been holding the same mixed bag — weakfish, porgy, and the occasional keeper fluke working the beach on that same outgoing push. Both are good family spots if you want an evening on the sand instead of a boat day — just mind Hashamomuck's day-use hours if you're planning an early start.

We're heading into the neap around August 5-6, and that's going to soften current through the Gut and the connecting cuts even further over the next few days. That's typically the window where I slow everything down — lighter bucktails, longer pauses, more patience on the drift — and it tends to produce a few bonus fluke that the faster tides pushed off the structure. I'd focus the next week on early and late sessions: porgies at first light off Shelter Island while the water's still cool enough to have them shallow, then fluke on the slower afternoon drifts through the channels, and save the last hour of daylight and the first couple hours of dark for stripers at the Gut. If the bunker schools hold in Gardiners Bay, check them daily — that bite can turn on and off within the same tide.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Goes Quiet at Noon, Comes Alive After Dark — Bonito Window Cracking Open
reports.subhead: Bass have pushed deep into the structure through the heat of the day, and the first temperature break that could carry albies or bonito is finally showing on the meter.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it Tuesday morning — that flat, oily calm off the Southwest Ledge with no wind pushing against the tide, the kind of stillness that usually means the water's about to tip over into something. Sure enough, when I ran the thermometer probe off the transom around the Ledge, I got a reading that told me what my gut already suspected: we're sitting right on the edge of a temperature break that could carry the first hardtails of the season. We flagged this a week ago — said a half-degree bump plus spring-tide mixing and late-July sun would push us into bonito water inside 7 to 10 days. Today's Day 7. I'm not going to tell you there's a bonito in the boat yet, but the water feels right, and I'd be scouting the Ledge and the rip off the north end with small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in olive — any time you've got calm glass and moving current.

The bigger story this week is what the bass are doing, and it's textbook August. Daytime, they've gone down and gotten quiet — sulking on structure in 40 to 60 feet around the Southwest Ledge and holding tight to the boulder fields off the North Rip, not up chasing anything you can see. I marked good bodies of fish on the meter around midday Wednesday sitting right on bottom, refusing to come up for anything, which is exactly what you'd expect with surface temps pushing into the mid-70s. The bite doesn't die, it just moves to the edges of the day. First light and last light, those same fish slide up onto the structure to feed, and that's when live eels fished on a fish-finder rig, or bunker chunks drifted back with the current, start putting bass in the boat — a mixed bag of schoolies with enough overslot fish mixed in to keep it interesting. Night has been the better play overall. Anchoring up-current of the Ledge and soaking eels after dark has produced some genuinely heavy fish this week, the kind that make you check your drag before you even make the cast.

Tides are the piece that's about to change things. We're sliding into a neap around August 5th and 6th, and I already noticed the current softening at the North Rip on Wednesday's ebb — nowhere near the strength it was running two weeks ago. We talked about this exact shift last week, that as the tides go soft the bass compress onto the strongest remaining current and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's precisely what I'm seeing set up. Over the next several days I'd expect the day bite to get even more stingy and the night bite at the Gut-style structure — deep water adjacent to hard current — to become the more reliable play. Lighter jigs, slower drifts, patience. Don't force a bass to bite in slack water at noon when you can wait three hours and get a real window at dusk.

Fluke are the one bright spot that hasn't needed any translation this week — this is peak season for them and the fish are cooperating. Drifting the sandy stretches and channel edges around the Southwest Ledge and out toward Block Island's south side, we've had good numbers of keepers, some pushing into doormat range, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance. The bite's been best on the back half of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping so hard you can't hold bottom. Porgies have been thick around the same structure — anybody who wants a guaranteed bend in the rod with sandworms or clam on a high-low rig off the Ledge or around Point Judith's rock piles isn't going home empty-handed, even on the days the bass make you work.

Bluefish have been more of a rumor than a pattern out here so far. There's bait moving through — pods of bunker showing up in Rhode Island Sound waters — but I haven't seen the sustained blitzes here that they're getting to our west along the Jersey and Long Island beaches. That fishery lives and dies with where the bunker sit, and right now the biggest schools are holding closer to shore on the mainland side. If bunker push out toward the island in any real number, the blues will be on them within hours — that's just how it works — but for now it's scattered fish mixed in with the bass rather than its own dedicated bite.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the next few days around the low-light windows for bass, keep the eel bucket full for after dark at the North Rip and the Ledge, lean on fluke during the day because that bite's dependable, and keep one rod rigged light and ready for anything that looks like a hardtail cutting through bait on the surface. If the temperature break holds and the water stays clean, I wouldn't be surprised if the first confirmed bonito or albie report out of Block Island comes before next week's column.

reports.headline: The Point Goes Quiet at Noon, Then Erupts: Bass Deep in the Boulders, Bunker Everywhere You Look
reports.subhead: Dog-day stripers are holding tight to structure through the heat, but the bunker schools and a softening tide are setting up the next move.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a rhythm to the Point in early August that anybody who's fished it for more than a season learns to respect. The big bass don't disappear this time of year — they just go underground, tucking into the boulder fields off the Lighthouse and North Bar where the water stays cool and the current never stops moving. You have to go find them, and you have to fish the clock, not the calendar. That's exactly what's happening right now, and it's about as honest a read as I can give you.

Water at the Point has settled around 70 degrees, which sounds cool until you remember what the surface has been doing on a flat, sunny afternoon — pushing warmer than that skin-deep, enough to shove the bass down onto structure during daylight and hold them there until the light starts to fail. I've had the best luck jigging bucktails and diamond jigs — 4 to 6 ounces depending on the drift — down into 50 to 80 feet along the boulder field between the Light and North Bar, working them slow and vertical right on bottom where the rock breaks the current. Get the jig moving too fast and you're just tiring your arm out. Let it fall, twitch it, let it fall again. That's when the thump comes.

Dawn and dusk are still the money windows, and this week they've been worth setting an alarm for. Bunker schools have been thick off Shagwong and drifting past Turtle Cove, and where you find the bunker balled up and nervous, the bass and blues are usually working underneath or right through them. I watched a school get bulldozed off the Elbow at first light Tuesday — birds diving, bunker skying, then that unmistakable boil of bass coming up through the middle of it. Poppers and big Danny-style swimmers worked the edges of the bait got hit hard, and a few guys snapping bucktails through the chaos on 60-pound fluoro leader put nice fish in the boat, mostly 20 to low-30-inch fish with a couple of overslots mixed in.

The bluefish have been the more reliable of the two right now, and it's exactly the pattern we flagged last week — this is a bait-driven fishery, plain and simple, and wherever the bunker have re-formed after getting pushed around, the blues show up within hours. Poppers and darters off Turtle Cove and along the south side rips have been getting hit hard enough to test your drag, some fish pushing into the 8 to 10-pound class. If you want a workout with topwater gear, this is your week.

Fluke fishing has been the steadiest thing going, and honestly the least dramatic to write about because it's just been solid, day in and day out. Drifting the Lake Montauk basin and the harbor entrance near Star Island on the outgoing tide, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails tipped with squid strips have been putting keeper fish in the cooler consistently, with a few doormats pushing 6 pounds coming off the deeper edges of the channel near the jetty. On the ocean side, the structure off the south side beaches has been holding fish too — smaller boats working the sod banks and rock piles in 20 to 35 feet have found good numbers, though you have to cull through some shorts to get there.

The bottom bite hasn't skipped a beat, and that's no surprise — we said the porgy and sea bass fishery out here is weatherproof, and it's picked up exactly where it left off. Shagwong Reef and the humps off Frisbie's have been giving up porgies all the way to 2 pounds on top-and-bottom rigs with clam and squid, plus a mix of sea bass for anybody dropping bucktails or diamond jigs tipped with squid down into 40 to 60 feet. It's not glamorous, but it's the kind of fishing you can set your watch by out here, and right now it's about the most dependable thing on the chart.

Offshore, the bluefin bite has stayed alive on the recreational slot fishery since the trophy closure, with boats working the grounds south and east of the Point under a stable weather pattern. That's a long run from the harbor, but the reports have been consistent enough that it's worth the gas if you've got the boat and the weather window.

Here's what I'm watching hardest this week: the tide is easing toward neap around August 5th and 6th, and when that current softens up, the bass at the Point and around Shagwong tend to compress into the strongest remaining current hours and slide into the deepest, coolest structure they can find. That means the daytime jigging window gets tighter, and the play becomes night eels — live eels drifted slow through the rip at the Gut and around the bridges after dark, when the bass climb up to feed under cover. If you can only fish one tide this week, fish the last two hours of the outgoing at night.

The other thing I keep half an eye on every August is the first albie or bonito scout, and the ingredients are lining up — squid pushing into Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound waters, temperature breaks sharpening along the south side rips. Nothing confirmed yet out here, but if you're fishing the rips off the Point and you see nervous water and small, fast slashes instead of the big rolling boils of a bass blitz, don't assume it's just bluefish. Keep a small epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick tied on just in case. That first fish of the season always shows up when you least expect it, and out here, it's usually right around now.

reports.headline: Slack Water Lies: Why I Wait Past Midnight for the Inlet to Turn
reports.subhead: The outgoing after 1 a.m. is holding bass in the deep hole, weakfish are stacking under the bridge lights, and the canal locks are still the best-kept secret in the bay.
reports.body_markdown:
I don't leave the dock until the boat traffic dies and the running lights thin out. That's the whole trick to this time of year — the inlet by day is a highway of head boats and jet skis, and the bass that live in that deep hole on the west side just shut down and sulk on the bottom until the noise stops. So I wait. I want the tide to be at least two hours into the outgoing before I drop anchor, and I want it dark enough that the only light on the water is what's bouncing off the Ponquogue Bridge pilings a mile up the bay.

That patience has been paying off. Water's sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s inshore, and with days like we've had this week, the bass have gone strictly nocturnal. Daytime, they're pinned to structure in the deep water, not interested in much of anything. But once that sun drops and the current starts ripping out through the inlet, they climb up out of that hole and start working the current seams where the bait gets squeezed through the rocks. I've been live-lining bunker on a fish-finder rig, 3 to 4 feet of leader, right along the north jetty where the outgoing current sets up a hard seam against the rock. Eels have worked just as well — snag one on a plain hook, no weight, let it swim naturally in that current, and don't set the hook until you feel the fish load up the rod, not just a tap. Slot fish mostly, a few pushing past 32 inches, nothing enormous yet, but steady enough that two or three rods in the water for two hours after the turn will put fish in the boat most nights this week.

We flagged this pattern last week before it showed up — said that as the tides softened heading into the neap, bass would compress into the strongest current windows and push deeper onto structure, and that's exactly what's happening. The tide range is narrowing hard into the August 5-6 neap, and I've noticed the current at the inlet just isn't ripping the way it was two weeks ago. That means shorter bite windows, but more concentrated ones. If you're fishing the inlet this week, don't spread yourself over four hours of tide — pick the strongest hour of the ebb, usually right around max current about two hours after the turn, and fish it hard. Everything else is filler.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the most reliable thing I've fished all month, honestly. Weakfish are holding tight to the shadow lines under the bridge lights, and they want a slow presentation — half-ounce jig heads with pink or chartreuse Bass Assassins, dropped right into the seam where the light meets the dark water, then just a slow lift-and-drop through the water column. Best window is an hour before the tide turns to outgoing through about an hour into it, when the current is moving enough to hold the bait but not so hard that you're bouncing bottom the whole time. I had four keeper weakfish two nights ago working that exact window, mixed in with a bunch of blues that came through chasing the same bait — small ones mostly, cocktail-size, but they'll hit those same jigs and cut you off if you're not paying attention to your leader.

Daytime, the bay's been about fluke. Nothing spectacular, but honest fishing — drifting the channel edges off Tiana Beach in 12 to 18 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. The doormat bite everyone's talking about on the ocean side hasn't really translated into the bay yet — what I'm seeing inside is mostly fish in the 16 to 19 inch range, keepers but not the big pool-winning class fish showing up on the open coast. If you want a shot at a real doormat, you need to run out through the inlet on the calmer mornings and work the rips just outside, but with the ocean running a little sloppy this week — three-foot swell out there — that's not a trip for every boat.

The canal's been quiet but not dead. If you time it to the lock openings, that 30 to 45 minute window when the gates start moving water, fluke and the occasional weakfish stack up on the Peconic side waiting for bait to get pushed through. I fished it twice this week and it's the same story both times — dead water, then twenty minutes of real activity right as the current picks up, then it shuts back down. Worth the drive if you're already in Hampton Bays and want a change of scenery, but I wouldn't make a special trip for it right now.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning into the dark hours at the inlet through this neap tide — shorter, sharper windows, deep structure, live bait over lures. If the ocean lays down by the weekend I'd take a run out to the rips for fluke before the crowds get out there. And keep an eye on the bunker schools working the beach — if they push into the inlet mouth, the bluefish will find them fast, and that's a daytime show worth chasing with a bucktail or a diamond jig when it happens. Nothing's blitzing yet, but the bait's around, and that's usually all it takes.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: the day bite went deep, but nights are lighting up the inlet
reports.subhead: Bunker in the bay, bass pinned to structure till dark, and fluke still stacking the bridge rips — here's where I'd spend my hours this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls up next to me at the Captree fuel dock Thursday morning, tells me he drifted bucktails over the reef for three hours and had nothing but a couple of short blues to show for it. I asked him what time he started. Nine a.m. That's your problem right there, I told him — this time of year, with the ocean sitting warm and the sun already up hard by eight, the bass have already punched out and gone down to the cool side of the structure. You want them, you've got to be on the water before the gulls are.

That's the read right now on the South Shore, and it's about as textbook mid-August as it gets. Water off the beach is running warm — the buoy out in the Bight was showing water temp near 76 degrees with a 3-foot swell riding a 7-second period, which tells you the ocean's got some push to it but nothing that should keep a good boat off the structure. Inside the inlet and up in the bay it's running warmer still, and that heat is exactly why the striper pattern has flipped to what it always does in high summer: fish holding deep and tight to structure through the daylight hours, then sliding up to feed hard at dawn, dusk, and after dark.

Democrat Point and the rock pile off the Fire Island Inlet jetty have been the most consistent producer for that low-light window. First light, guys drifting bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs off the rocks on the outgoing have been connecting with slot bass and the occasional overslot, and there have been real bunker schools pushing through the inlet on that same tide, which is dragging bluefish and stripers up onto the surface in flashes you can see from the beach — bait exploding, birds diving, the whole show. When you catch one of those, a topwater popper or a bucktail with a bright teaser above it thrown right into the boil will get bit fast, but the window doesn't last, so if you see it, don't wait to re-position — throw.

We flagged this exact shift last week — said that as the tides softened heading into the neap, bass would compress into the strongest current hours and the deepest, coolest structure, and that's precisely what's playing out. The tide range is narrowing hard toward the neap around August 5th and 6th, and with less water moving, the current windows at spots like the Robert Moses bridges and the deeper cuts of the inlet are shrinking. That means less time to work them but more concentrated fish when you hit it right. Night eeling around the bridge pilings on the strong half of the tide has been the move — a 9-inch live eel or a swim-bait rigged slow along bottom, worked right through the pilings on the last two hours of the ebb. That's where I'd be putting my time after dark this week if bass are the target.

Fluke are having their best stretch of the summer, and that part hasn't changed a bit. Doormat-class fish are showing on the ocean-side structure and the bridge rips at Robert Moses, plus the usual channel edges out toward the Democrat Point flats. Thirty feet of water, moving tide — doesn't much matter which direction as long as it's actually moving — with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, teased with a strip of squid, dragged slow along bottom. I had a 6-pounder come off a drift right along the north side of the bridge on the last outgoing Tuesday, and there were three or four other keepers in the box that same trip. This bite should hold through the next couple weeks before the fall shuffle starts pulling fish toward the deeper water.

Porgies remain the most dependable thing going in this bay, and they don't care what the moon or the tide chart says nearly as much as bass do. Structure spots around Captree and the reefs off Fire Island Inlet are still giving up steady counts on bloodworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, bottom in 20 to 35 feet. If a client's day gets blown out by wind or a slow bass bite, that's always my fallback, and it hasn't let anyone down yet this summer.

One thing worth passing along for the surf guys without a boat — Heckscher State Park opened up night access at Field 6 this year on a trial basis, Friday through Sunday nights from dusk to dawn, running through Labor Day. You need a Night Sport Fishing Permit or a 4x4 permit on the dash, but if you've got one, that bay shoreline puts you right on the outgoing water pouring out of Great South Bay, which is exactly the kind of current edge that stacks bait and pulls bass shallow after dark. Worth checking out if you're bay-bound and want a legit night option without running a boat.

Looking ahead, expect the softening tides to keep squeezing that bite window tighter through the weekend — less water moving means you've got to be precise about when you fish, not just where. I'd focus effort on the two hours around the strongest current at the bridges and the inlet after dark, and keep working the bunker schools for blues and bass wherever they show on the surface. It's also about that time of year I start watching the temperature breaks out toward Democrat Point and the ocean beaches for the first false albacore scouts — Fire Island's usually one of the earlier landfalls on the Island when they show. Nothing yet, but I'll be watching the water color and the bait pattern close over the next couple weeks.

reports.headline: Cupsogue Bar Held Its New Shape — And the Fluke Found It
reports.subhead: The sand that piled up after last month's blow is still there, still funneling bait, and this week it started paying off on the flood.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the drift line off Cupsogue three times this week with a handheld and a piece of chalk in my head, tracing the edge that formed when that late-July blow pushed sand east into the throat of the inlet. Last week I told you that edge was worth working on the building flood. It held. The bar hasn't moved more than a few yards since, which for this inlet is practically frozen in place — Moriches likes to rearrange itself every time you turn your back, but this particular cut has stabilized into a real piece of structure, with a six-to-nine foot trough running parallel to the new shoal and a hard current seam right where the two depths meet.

That's where the fluke have been sitting. Not stacked, not a slaughter, but a real, repeatable bite on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and pink shad, 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with squid strips, right along that seam in 7 to 10 feet of water. I had four keepers to 21 inches Tuesday morning working that exact stretch, and I watched two other boats do the same thing without anyone saying a word to each other — everybody's found the same seam because the bottom is telling everybody the same story right now. The mistake guys are making is drifting too fast on a hard flood. Slow the boat, use enough weight to feel bottom every third or fourth crank, and hold that bucktail right on the transition rather than letting the current sweep you off it into the flat sand where there's nothing.

Bass are a different animal right now, and the ocean side has a lot to do with it. Offshore buoy readings put the open Atlantic in the mid-70s with a leftover three-foot swell still running out of the southeast — enough chop that the ocean bar at Cupsogue has been unproductive for daytime casting, too roiled for the bass to hold comfortably against the beach in daylight. So they're doing what they do every August: sliding into the inlet's deeper cuts and the bay-side structure during the day, and coming up on the ebb after dark to work the bait that gets flushed out of the marsh creeks. I fished the night ebb Thursday off the rock jetty at the west end of the inlet with a black darter and a bone SP Minnow, and connected with three fish in the 26-to-29 inch range in under two hours, all on the second half of the drain when the current really gets moving through the throat. That's the pattern I'd lean on again this week — Tuthill Point's channel edge and the bridge structure up toward Westhampton are holding fish for the same reason, current compression plus low light. Bucktails with a curly-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom, have out-produced anything fished fast.

Bluefish have been the wildcard, exactly like I flagged. No sustained blitz yet inside the bay, but there's been bait around — bunker pods reforming tight to the beach in scattered pockets between Cupsogue and Smith Point, and when one of those pods gets pinned against the bar you get five minutes of total chaos and then it's over. I had one of those mornings this week, ran into breaking blues off the ocean side for about ten minutes on a topwater popper before they vanished back into deeper water. If you're going to chase that, keep a rod rigged with a heavier wire leader ready at all times and don't waste time on long casts — get tight to the boil.

Weakfish are still scattered rather than concentrated, mostly picked up as bycatch on the fluke drift over the channel edges inside the bay near Tuthill Point, a few keeper-sized fish mixed in with a lot of shorts. Porgies are steady but unglamorous over the hard bottom patches east of the Inlet — small pieces of clam on a hi-lo rig will keep a rod bent if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating, good option for a slow morning. Blackfish season's still off for most of you, but I'm seeing fish stacking on the deeper rock piles already, worth remembering for when the season opens.

Heading into next week, the tides are sliding toward the neap around August 5-6, and that changes the equation. Weaker current means the fluke bite on that Cupsogue edge will need a longer window — fish the peak of the flood rather than the whole cycle, because there won't be enough push to hold bait on the seam outside of that peak hour or two. For the bass, softer current usually means they tuck even tighter to the deepest, coolest structure — the Gut-adjacent holes and the bridge pilings become the most reliable bet, and I'd lighten up bucktails to 3/4 ounce so you can work them slower without losing bottom feel. If the ocean lays down at all behind this swell, the bar at Cupsogue is worth a dawn look for bass and blues working bait tight to the beach — that's always been this inlet's best-kept surprise, and it takes zero warning to happen.

reports.headline: One Eel, One Take — A Gut Bass Over 35 at 2 A.M.
reports.subhead: The current's bleeding toward neap, and the eastern Sound's bass are compressing into the last hard water hours of the tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-fifteen Monday morning, chest-deep on the rocks below Orient Point, I put a 12-inch snake eel on the swing into Plum Gut current that was already softer than it should've been for this stage of the tide. One cast. One thump on the drop. Thirty seconds later I've got a bass pushing 36 inches thrashing in the wash, gill plates flaring in the headlamp. That fish told me everything I needed to know about this week.

We flagged this exact move last week — said as the tides softened toward the coming neap, bass would pull off the scattered pattern and compress into the strongest current hours, with night eels at the Gut and the bridges becoming the play. That's exactly what's happening. The Race and Plum Gut are both easing off as we drift toward the neap around August 5-6, and instead of five-knot water blasting through on every stage of the tide, you're getting maybe two solid hours of hard current bracketing the peak of the ebb or flood. Outside those windows, it's soft, it's slow, and the fish know it.

During the day, forget the top of the water column. Bass are holding deep on structure — Valiant Rock, the reef off Fishers Island, the drop-offs along the Gut's western edge — sitting in 30 to 50 feet and refusing to commit until the light drops. I've had one solid afternoon this week jigging a 3-ounce diamond jig tipped with a strip of squid down into 40 feet off Race Rock, and it took patience — long enough that I second-guessed the spot twice before a 28-incher finally kissed the bottom bounce and stayed hooked. That's the story right now: the bite is real, but it's not falling in your lap during banker's hours. Dawn, dusk, and full dark are where the current concentration and low light line up, and that's where the size shows.

Bluefish are riding shotgun with the bass wherever bunker pods are stacking, and there are real pods moving through the Gut and off Orient Point right now. When they collide with current edges, it gets violent fast — I watched a blitz break loose off the Orient Point rip Tuesday evening, blues in the 8-to-12-pound class shredding bunker on the surface for maybe twenty minutes before it shut off as quick as it started. Poppers and metal-lip swimmers thrown into the froth will draw strikes, but you need to be there when it happens. These aren't blitzes that hold — they're moving targets tied to bait, not schedule.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going. Drifting the edges of Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip in 20 to 35 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing has produced consistent action — 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, dragged slow along bottom, working the current seams where sand meets rock. Nothing giant this week, mostly 16-to-19-inch fish with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in off the deeper stretch near Fishers Island Sound, but the ratio of keepers to shorts has been solid enough that it's worth a full tide if you've got the boat for it.

Porgies and blackfish are exactly where you'd expect them — stacked on structure. Bartlett Reef and the rockpiles around Fishers Island are loaded with porgies right now, and sandworms or pieces of clam on a simple high-low rig will keep a rod bent all afternoon if you don't mind the smaller fish mixed in. Blackfish season's open through the end of August, and green crab worked slow on the same structure has been picking off tautog in the 3-to-6-pound range for guys willing to anchor up and be patient instead of drifting through.

Weakfish have shown up sparingly — a few scattered fish taken on bucktails near the mouths of the tidal creeks off Orient, nothing you'd plan a trip around, but worth a cast or two if you're already working that water for bass.

Water's still holding a real gradient across the zone — New London reading in the high 60s, cooler than the western Sound, which keeps this end of the beat fishing more like early summer than the bathwater conditions further west. That cooler water is exactly why the bass here are still aggressive and why the structure bite has stayed strong instead of collapsing into a dawn-only pattern like you're seeing closer to the city.

Looking ahead: as the tide range keeps narrowing into the neap, expect the pattern to sharpen rather than fade — shorter windows of hard current, but the fish jammed into them tighter. If I've got one night this weekend, I'm back on the rocks at the Gut fishing the last two hours of the ebb into slack, eel on a fish-finder rig, no split shot, letting it swing naturally into the seam. Daytime, I'd rather jig structure at Race Rock or Valiant Rock than blind-cast open water — the fish are down there, they're just not coming up until the light and the current both cooperate. Keep an eye on the temperature breaks off Fishers Island and Orient over the next couple weeks too; that's typically when this zone gets its first look at fall speedsters, though nothing's shown yet and I'm not chasing ghosts until I see actual sign.

reports.headline: Bunker Get Squeezed Through Stratford Shoal — Bass and Blues Riding the Pinch
reports.subhead: As the Sound narrows and the tide eases toward neap, the bait has nowhere to hide — and neither do the fish underneath it.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning drifting off the Shoal doing nothing but watching birds, and it told me more than any temp gauge could. Terns were working tight little knots over peanut bunker balled up right where the Sound necks down between the Long Island side and the Connecticut shoreline — that classic Stratford Shoal squeeze where the whole water column gets funneled through a skinnier lane. The bait wasn't spread out cruising, it was stacked and nervous, diving for the bottom every time a shadow passed under it. That's not weather behavior. That's predator behavior.

Kings Point is reading 72.9 degrees, New London's sitting at 69.6, and that gradient matters more than people give it credit for. The warmer water on the western end is holding bait comfortably, but as you push east toward the Shoal and beyond, that bunker starts bunching up against the cooler push instead of just drifting through it. That's exactly the kind of choke point that turns a wandering bait school into a fixed target — and fixed targets get found fast by bass and blues that don't want to work any harder than they have to in August heat.

The striper bite has settled into the pattern you'd expect for this time of year — fish holding deep on structure through the bright hours, then sliding up to feed hard at first light, last light, and after dark. Middle Ground Light and the deeper edges around the Shoal have been holding fish during the day on bucktails worked slow along bottom, but the real quality has come after the sun drops. Guys running eels at the bridges over on the Norwalk side — the causeway spans and the cuts around the Islands — have been doing well on the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, snake-style presentations right along the pilings where the current squeezes past the structure. We flagged this pattern last week, saying that as tides softened toward the coming neap, bass would compress onto the strongest current hours and the deepest structure — that's precisely what's playing out now, and the eel bite at the bridges has been the clearest proof of it.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going right now, and it's living up to the seasonal peak everyone talks about in late July into early August. Boats drifting the channel edges off Port Jeff Harbor and working the deeper flats around Middle Ground Light have been putting doormat-class fish in the box — nothing giant every drop, but a steady grind of fish in the 3 to 6 pound range mixed with enough shorts to keep you busy. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow across the sandy-mud bottom on the tail end of the outgoing tide, has been the go-to. The bite isn't uniform everywhere — I had one drift off Charles Island last week that produced nothing but shorts for two hours before we found the right depth change and started connecting on keepers — so it pays to keep moving until the sounder shows that subtle break where sand gives way to structure.

Bluefish are riding shotgun with the bunker wherever it concentrates, and that's been most consistent right in that Shoal corridor and along the edges of the bait pods pushing past the Norwalk Islands. When the blues show up under a bunker school, it's not subtle — the water goes white and the birds go crazy — but those windows have been short-lived this week, ten or fifteen minutes of chaos before the whole show moves fifty yards and you're chasing it again.

Porgies remain the most reliable fish in the zone right now. Every reef from Bridgeport out to New Haven has been giving up steady counts on the incoming tide, small pieces of clam or squid on a simple high-low rig doing the job without much finesse required. We called this building trend a week ago and it's held — if you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for the kids or for dinner, this is still the play.

Blackfish are still off the table with the season closed, but I'd be lying if I said I wasn't already circling a few rock piles off Norwalk for October. Weakfish have shown up here and there in the marsh creeks around Oyster Bay and the back sides of the Islands, but sporadic enough that I wouldn't build a trip around them yet.

As for the bonito — nothing confirmed in my water yet, but I'm watching. The thermal gradient east of here needs to clean up and the bait needs to keep pushing in tighter pods before that first push shows on this side of the Sound. Looking ahead, that neap tide settling in around the 5th and 6th should keep softening the current through the Shoal and the Gut-adjacent structure, which means lighter jig heads and slower retrieves are the right call for the next several days. If the bait stays squeezed the way it is right now, the bass and blues underneath it aren't going anywhere — they're just going to keep getting easier to find.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway Bridge After Dark: Bass Working the Shadow Lines on the Last Ebb
reports.subhead: Bay bass have gone nocturnal and structure-bound — fluke and weakfish are picking up the daytime slack in the channels.
reports.body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Aviation Road at Floyd Bennett Field before six on Thursday, mostly because I wanted to beat the heat and the boat traffic, and partly because that ramp puts you right into the mouth of the bay without fighting a current the whole way out. Paddled the edge toward the Marine Parkway Bridge and let the last of the incoming push me along the channel drop-off. That's the play in August — pick your access point to match the tide, not the other way around. Kayak in the morning while it's calm and cool, truck to the bridge or the surf at night when the real bite happens.

Because right now, the bass have checked out of the shallow bay during the day. Water up top is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s across most of the flats, and stripers don't want any part of that with the sun up. They've slid out to the cooler structure — the bridge pilings, the deep channel bends, the inlet edges — and they're only really feeding hard at dawn, dusk, and full dark. We flagged this exact shift last week, said to fish the last hour of the ebb into dark and the first couple hours of the new outgoing after midnight, and that's precisely what's been producing. I fished the bridge Tuesday night on the tail of the ebb, eeling live snakes under a fish-finder rig, 2-ounce egg sinker, right down in the current seam off the pilings on the Rockaway side. Two fish to 30 inches, one right at the slot line that went back, both on that last hour before the tide went dead slack. Guys drifting bucktails — bone white, 1-ounce — through the same seam on the change back to outgoing picked up a couple more just after midnight.

During the day, though, it's fluke and weakfish carrying the bay. This is peak fluke season and the bay's holding up its end — channel edges off Cross Bay Bridge, the deeper holes inside Grassy Bay, and the flats off Canarsie Pier have all been giving up keepers. Nothing gigantic, mostly 17 to 20 inches, but steady if you work the drift right. Half-and-half white/chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the outgoing, has been the most consistent combo. Bring some Berkley Gulp Swimming Mullet in pink shad too — a few of the better fish this week came on that when the plain white wasn't drawing strikes.

Weakfish have been mixed in with the fluke on those same channel edges, especially early morning before the boat traffic picks up. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but a few keeper-class fish in the 16 to 18 inch range came off the bottom near the Marine Parkway Bridge rip on bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're marking bait balls on the sounder near the bridge, slow down and jig it — that's where they're holding.

Canarsie Pier this week has been snapper central. If you've got a kid or you just want steady light-tackle action without driving out to the ocean beaches, small silver spoons or tiny bucktails under a bobber off the pier are producing non-stop juvenile bluefish in the afternoon. It's not glamorous but it's fun, and it's free — no permit needed there, unlike most of the NPS lots right now which are sold out for the season.

Surf side, Fort Tilden and Breezy Point are still the after-dark bass program if you've got your Fishing Access Pass. The 193rd Street lot and 222nd Street lot both require it around the clock this time of year, so don't roll up without one. I fished the groins off 193rd Street Tuesday on the outgoing — same story as the bridge, quiet until the last hour of the ebb, then a couple bass in the mid-20s came through chasing something in the wash. Swim shads and darters worked better than bucktails there; the water's clean enough right now that a subtler presentation gets more looks.

We're heading into a neap tide around the 5th and 6th, which is going to soften the current everywhere — the bridge rip, the inlet, Grassy Bay. When that happens I'd downsize presentations across the board: lighter bucktails, slower retrieves, smaller profile eels. Weaker current means the fish don't have to commit as hard, so give them more time to find your bait.

One more thing I'm watching closely — it's early August, and this is exactly the window where the first false albacore or bonito scouts start showing at the inlet mouth if the water stays clean and the bait stays thick. Nothing confirmed yet in the bay, but I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with small metal — Deadly Dicks, epoxy jigs — in the truck just in case something silver and fast starts busting bait off the Marine Parkway rocks. It hasn't happened yet, but the calendar's right for it.

Next week, if this stable weather holds, I'd keep splitting time the same way: fluke and weakfish on the channel edges during the day, bass at the bridge and the surf on the last of the ebb into full dark. If a front pushes through and stirs up the bay, the bite could get moodier fast — but as of now, the pattern's holding.

reports.headline: Kings Point reads 73 degrees and the bass have gone nocturnal at the bridges
reports.subhead: Warm, slack-tide Sound water has pushed the bass into a night bite while fluke and porgies carry the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shack on City Island asked me Tuesday why nobody's soaking bunker chunks off the bridge at noon anymore. Told him the same thing I've told every man who's asked me that question in thirty years on this water: because the fish aren't there at noon. Kings Point buoy's reading 72.9 this week, and when the western Sound gets that warm on top, the bass do what they've always done — they slide down onto structure and sulk through the daylight, then come up to hunt once the sun drops and the water cools a half a degree. This isn't news to anybody who's fished Execution Rocks longer than a season, but every August somebody forgets it, and every August I remind them.

So here's where the intel from the dock lines up with what I've seen with my own eyes off Hart Island and the Rocks the last ten days. The night bite at Throgs Neck Bridge has been the most reliable thing going. Eels — plain old live eels, snelled to a 1/0 or 2/0 circle hook, no weight or just enough to get them down into that current — fished tight to the pilings on the last two hours of the ebb. That's when the bait gets squeezed through the pilings and the bass are sitting right on the seam waiting for it. I had two nights this week where the first hour after dark was dead and then it turned on hard for about ninety minutes right around the bottom third of the tide. Fish in the 28 to 34 inch range, mixed slot and just-over, nothing monstrous but steady enough that three or four rods working the bridge on a weeknight put fish in the boat.

Execution Rocks is still doing its thing on the outgoing, same as it's done every summer I can remember, but you've got to work it at the right hour now. Forget the mid-afternoon troll — that's a bait-soaking exercise in August heat. Dusk into full dark, drifting bunker chunks or a whole live bunker on a fish-finder rig along the north side of the rockpile where the current rips hardest, that's your window. The bunker schools I flagged off Matinecock back in June haven't gone anywhere — if anything they've thickened up, and the blues have been all over them in open water off the point, blitzing on top some mornings before the sun's fully up. If you want bluefish, that's still the play — bunker spoons or wire leader with a bucktail teaser, fish where the birds are working, and don't wait around, because those pods move.

Now the good news, and it's genuinely good — fluke and porgy fishing is about as strong as it gets all year right now, and it doesn't care one bit about the bass going nocturnal. Stepping Stones and the reef structure off Matinecock Point have been holding porgies stacked up in 20 to 35 feet, and they're eating clam and squid strips on standard high-low rigs without much finesse required. Kids' trip, grandfather's trip, doesn't matter — that bite's been consistent right through the warm stretch. Fluke have been coming off the channel edges around Hempstead Harbor and the deeper drop-offs near Execution Rocks, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push to it but isn't ripping. Nothing giant — most fish 16 to 20 inches, a few keepers mixed in over 20 — but a satisfying pick if you're willing to drift a few different depths to find where they're stacked that day.

We flagged this last week — said the softer tides heading into the first quarter moon on August 5th would push the bass toward the strongest current hours and the deepest structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at the bridges right now. As that moon comes to first quarter this week, the tidal range is going to keep shrinking, which means less water movement, which means the bite windows get shorter and more concentrated. I'd rather fish a big tide any day, but a softer tide isn't a death sentence — it just means you've got to be precise about timing. Don't show up to Throgs Neck two hours before the tide change expecting fireworks. Show up right as the ebb hits its strongest push and fish through the last two hours of it. That's been the difference between a two-fish night and a skunk this week.

Weakfish have been a mixed bag — a few citations coming out of the deeper holes around Little Neck Bay on bucktails tipped with squid strips fished slow along bottom, but it's not a consistent pattern yet, more a bonus fish than something to plan a trip around. Blackfish season's still closed in most of these waters through the summer, so that's a fall conversation, though I'll tell you the rockpiles off Hart Island are going to be loaded once that opens back up.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break unless we get a real weather shift. High pressure's been stable, water's staying warm, and that means the night-bite-for-bass, day-bite-for-fluke-and-porgy split is going to hold through most of August. If I had one night this week to fish, I'd be at Execution Rocks on the outgoing starting an hour before sunset, working live bunker deep along the rock edge, and I'd have eels rigged as backup once it goes fully dark. Daytime, I'd be drifting bucktails off Matinecock for fluke while the porgies keep the rods bent between drifts. It's not a blitz-every-cast kind of week, but it's honest fishing, and if you respect the tide clock, you'll come home with something worth cleaning.

reports.headline: Everybody's Drifting Sloop Channel for Fluke — I'm Working the Inlet Rip at Dusk
reports.subhead: The doormats are there for the boat guys, but the real money right now is on the moving current and the after-dark bass sliding into the rocks.
reports.body_markdown:
Every guy I talked to at the ramp this week wanted to tell me about the fluke bite in the bay — Sloop Channel, the flats off Short Beach, everybody drifting Gulp and bucktails like it's the only game in town. And look, I get it, the fluke are there and they're feeding good on the moving tide. But I'm not a bay guy in August. I'm an inlet guy, and right now the inlet is where the real story is, especially once the sun starts dropping.

Here's the thing nobody wants to talk about in July and August — the ocean side of Jones Beach has been rough, sloppy, three-foot swell rolling in on a short period, and that junk water pushes everything with fins into the channels and the structure where it's calm. That's exactly what's happening at Jones Inlet right now. Water on the ocean side is sitting warm, mid-70s, maybe pushing higher on the surface, and that heat combined with the chop has the bass doing what they do every summer — holding deep on structure all day, then coming up hard at first light and again at dusk and through the night to hit bait.

I've been working the rocks at the inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing and into the start of the incoming, right at last light. That current edge where the deep water meets the shallow flat on the west side of the inlet — that's holding bass in the 26 to 34 inch range, mixed slot fish with a few overslots mixed in, and they're eating eels. Not artificial eels, live eels, snap them on a fishfinder rig or just a plain hook through the lips and let the current do the work. Bunker chunks are working too if you can't get eels, fished on the bottom in that same seam. The bite window is tight — maybe 45 minutes on either side of last light, then again a couple hours before dawn if you've got the stomach for it.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the current would stay strong into early August and that's the window to fish hard water before the tides go soft, and that's exactly what's playing out. The moon's sliding toward that first-quarter neap around the 5th and 6th, and once that hits, the current through the inlet is going to lose some teeth. Right now though, we've still got good push on the tide, and that's pulling bait through the rip and stacking bass right behind it. I wouldn't waste this week's strong water — once the neap sets in, you're going to need to fish the absolute peak of the current to get bit, probably down at the Wantagh Bridge pilings or deeper holes where the current concentrates even when the range is small.

Bluefish are doing their thing just outside the inlet mouth, and this is where the boat guys have an edge on us jetty rats — bunker pods are holding tight to the beach on the ocean side after getting pushed around by the swell, and wherever those pods sit, the blues find them fast. If you see birds working tight over the water just off Jones Beach, that's your signal, run there and throw poppers or just troll umbrella rigs through the edge of the bait. From the beach, if a pod pushes in close to the bar, you can connect with bucktails and metal, but you need to be in the right spot at the right time — it's not a sure thing casting blind.

Fluke, fine, I'll give the bay its due. Sloop Channel and the flats around Short Beach are holding decent numbers on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, fish in the 18 to 22 inch class on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4 ounce bucktails, working depths of 12 to 20 feet where the channel bends. If you want a doormat, drift the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth itself where the current really rips — that's where the bigger fish sit waiting on bait getting swept through. But I'm telling you, once that sun gets low, I'm reeling in the fluke rod and picking up the eel outfit.

Weakfish are still a bonus fish more than a target right now, but I've heard of a few being picked up in the bay on light jigs during the same tide stages as the fluke — worth a look if you're already out there, don't build a whole trip around it yet.

Looking ahead, the next few days should still fish well on the inlet structure while we've got strong tidal push, but that neap coming in around the 5th and 6th is going to soften things up fast. When that happens, I'd shift my effort to the deepest, coolest water I can find at the peak of whatever current is left — the Wantagh Bridge at night, the deepest bends in the inlet channel, anywhere the water still moves with authority. If the bunker stay tight to the ocean beach like they have been, keep an eye on the birds — that blitz can fire off with almost no warning, and when it does, you want to already be rigged and ready, not scrambling for tackle in the truck.

reports.headline: Race Point on the ebb: mackerel schools pull bass up, cod holding tight off Billingsgate
reports.subhead: A calm week on the Bay — bass and blues stacked on bait at Race Point, cod still there if you find the right piece of bottom off Billingsgate.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, an hour before the top of the ebb off Race Point, the sounder with a school of mackerel sitting at 35 feet, tight and nervous, the way they get when something's underneath them. I dropped a rod with a live mack down through the school on a fish-finder rig, no weight to speak of, just let the current do the work. Didn't take thirty seconds before the rod bent hard and stayed bent. Twenty-six pound bass, fat and bright, came up thrashing in that green rip water where the outgoing tide runs against the shoal. That's been the story all week out there — find the mackerel, and the bass aren't far behind.

The rip off Race Point has been holding up the way it does this time of year, best from the last two hours of the ebb into the slack, working the seam where the deeper water — 30 to 45 feet — meets the shallower bar. We've been drifting live mackerel and whole squid on fish-finder rigs, letting the boat set the pace rather than working the reel. Bass have run 20 to 30 pounds mixed with a good number of schoolies, and there's enough of a push of bigger fish in there that a few boats have had 30-plus pound bass on umbrella rigs trolled slow along the edge where the rip flattens out. Peaked Hill Bars, just south, has had bluefish mixed into the same water — sand eels showing on top, birds working, blues in the 4 to 8 pound class hitting metal, Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters worked fast through the froth.

We called this one last week — said stable conditions would hold through the week, and they have. Light southwest wind, no real chop to speak of, and that's kept the rip fishing consistent rather than the boom-and-bust you get when a blow stirs up the bottom. Cape Cod Bay is still running cooler than the Sound and Buzzards Bay right now, and that's the whole ballgame up here — while stripers down south are getting pushed deep and nocturnal by warm surface water, our bass are still willing to feed in daylight on structure because the Gulf of Maine keeps this water in a range they like. It won't last forever, but for now, it's working in our favor.

Cod have been a different story — there, but you have to earn it. Billingsgate shoals, out in 55 to 70 feet on the drop-offs east of the flats, has given up a handful of decent cod, 8 to 15 pounds, on diamond jigs tipped with squid strips, worked right on the bottom during the slack water when the drift slows enough to keep the jig down where it belongs. It's not the kind of bite where you fill a cooler — some drifts we marked fish and never got a bite, others we boated three keepers in twenty minutes. The cod are there, holding tight to specific humps and ledges rather than spread out, and if you're not sitting right on the structure with your sounder, you're just burning gas. I'd rather make five short, precise drifts over the right piece of bottom than one long drift over nothing.

Fluke fishing has been the more dependable program if you want a full box without the guesswork. Barnstable Harbor's channel edges and the flats off Sandy Neck have been giving up keeper fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range, mixed with plenty of shorts, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing as warm water drains out of the marsh creeks. That warm water pouring off the flats pushes bait — and the fluke — right to the channel edges, and a slow drag along that seam has been more productive than working the open flat itself. Brewster's flats, on the low side of the tide, have had a few stray fluke too, though that bite's thinner than Barnstable.

The moon's building back toward the new moon on the 12th, and the tides are starting to swing a little harder than the dead-flat neaps we had midweek. That's going to sharpen up the rip at Race Point — more current means a tighter, more defined edge for the bass and bluefish to work, and I expect the mackerel schools to hold there rather than scatter. If the pattern holds the way it has, I'd fish the two hours either side of the ebb at Race Point for bass and blues, and save the middle of the day for a run out to Billingsgate to work the cod on the slack. Keep an eye on the wind — if it swings around to the east and builds any real sea, the rip gets ugly fast and the drift turns into a chore instead of a pleasure. Barring that, this is a solid week to be out there, not a blowout, but honest fishing on a Bay that's still fishing the way it's supposed to in high summer.

reports.headline: Great Point Rip: Blues Crashing, Terns Working, Albies Still a No-Show
reports.subhead: Two weeks of watching the Point for the first bonito and all I've got so far is chopper blues and a lot of hope.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, half-light, I'm idling off Great Point with the ebb just starting to run, and the terns go from lazy circles to a full stoop in about four seconds flat. Bait balls up tight against the rip line, gets pushed and pinned by the current seam, and something underneath starts working it from below. I'm easing the boat in thinking this is it, this is the morning — and it's blues. Good blues, mind you, four to eight pounds, absolutely stacked on peanut bunker getting squeezed against that rip. But blues all the same. No green backs, no torpedo shapes knifing through the bait. Not yet.

I've been watching for bonito and albies for two weeks now, same as every August. The water's right for it — Nantucket Sound is holding real heat this year, pushing into the mid-70s in the shallows and even brushing up near 80 in some of the back pockets off Monomoy on a sunny afternoon slack tide. That's warmer than the stripers want, and it shows. We flagged this a week back — said the bass would keep sliding deep and staying nocturnal as long as this warm, stable stretch held, and that's exactly the program right now. Daytime, the bass have all but vanished off the visible structure. Come dusk and through the night, they're stacking on bunker chunks and eels around the elbow at Chatham Inlet and along the Monomoy bar, working 20 to 30 feet of water where the bottom stays cool even when the surface is soup-warm. If you're on Monomoy after dark, fresh bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that current, and patience — that's the program. Not fast fishing, but real fish, mostly mid-30s to low 40-inch class.

Fluke have been the most honest fish in the Sound. Steady, not spectacular, but you can set your watch by it. Horseshoe Shoal and the edges around Muskeget Channel are holding fish in 25 to 35 feet, and the drift over the sandy cuts off Tuckernuck has been kicking out keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the current rather than against it. Scup are riding shotgun on the same drifts, which tells you the bottom's still cool enough down there to hold bait, even with the surface running warm.

Now, about the albies and bonito — here's where I have to be straight with you. Nothing confirmed in the Sound yet. Not off Great Point, not off Sankaty, not around Monomoy. But the signs are stacking up the way they do right before the switch flips. Squid have been showing in real numbers pushing into the Sound and around the Vineyard side, which is usually the tell — bonito track squid and silversides, and when the bait shows, the fish aren't far behind. We called this the week before last, saying the thermal setup at Montauk, Block Island, and the Buzzards Bay corridor had crossed the seasonal threshold and just needed the tide cycle to trigger the first real push. The tide's building back now toward the August 12 new moon, current's getting stronger through the rips every day, and that's usually the ingredient that's been missing. If I had to bet, I'd say the first scout showing in this zone comes off the Sankaty rip or the tip of Great Point on a strong ebb sometime in the next week to ten days — small, single fish first, testing the rip, before it turns into anything you'd call a blitz.

Wind's been the easy part of this whole stretch — stable out of the southwest, nothing over 15 knots most days, which means the rips have been fishable top to bottom instead of getting blown out and turned to washing machine chop. That's kept the blue run consistent at the Point. If you want the most reliable fish in the Sound this week, that's it — work the rip on the first two hours of the ebb, cast a Hogy or a Deadly Dick past the seam and let it swing through, and expect blues in the 5 to 8 pound range with the occasional bigger chopper mixed in. It's not subtle fishing. They hit like a freight train and you'll go through a few leaders.

Look, I'd love to tell you the albies showed up this week. They didn't. But every piece of this puzzle — the squid, the building tide, the thermal edge sitting right off the Vineyard and pushing toward us — says the window's close. I'll be out there every clean morning with the SW wind, watching that rip off Great Point for the first torpedo shape under the terns. If the tide keeps building the way it should into next week, and a scout or two starts showing at Block Island or Montauk like the pattern usually goes, don't be surprised if the first Nantucket albie report breaks within the next several days. Until then, work the blues, work the fluke, and fish the bass at night. That's the honest state of the Sound right now.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole loaded with peanuts, bass and blues eating good — albies still a no-show
reports.subhead: The bait is exactly where it should be and the water's crossed the mark, but the first albie of the season hasn't shown its tail yet in Buzzards Bay or the Vineyard rips.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Robinson's Hole Tuesday evening watching peanut bunker ball up so tight against the current seam they looked like a shadow moving under the surface. Silversides doing the same thing over at Quick's Hole, pinned against the west side current line on the last two hours of the ebb. That's the tell. That's the bait signature we watch for every single year right before the first albie shows, and right now it's checking every box except the one that matters — I haven't had a confirmed albie or bonito report cross my desk yet out of this corridor. Close. Not there.

We flagged this corridor as one of the hottest early-arrival zones on the coastwide watch last week, and the setup hasn't backed off one bit. Water's pushed well past the seasonal threshold everywhere from Woods Hole down through the Elizabeths, the tide is still carrying push from the full moon, and it's building again toward the August 12 new moon. That's the exact recipe — warm water, hard current, bait getting squeezed through the rips. It's a matter of days, not weeks, but I'm not going to tell you the fish are here when they're not. Anyone telling you they boated an albie in Buzzards Bay this week ahead of me is either mistaken or fishing a different ocean.

What IS biting, and biting well, is the interim program that always carries us into the albie window. Striped bass are stacked on the west side of Cuttyhunk and along the backside of Nashawena, working the rips on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming — that current-change window is money right now. Bass in the mid-20s to low 30-inch class, some better fish mixed in after dark, eating swimming plugs and 1.5-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse tails bounced right off the rip edge where the sand gives way to cobble. Bluefish are thick through the same water, chopping bait on top hard enough that you can hear it from the boat before you see it — poppers and single-hook Deadly Dicks worked fast across the slicks have been producing non-stop action, though these blues will fray you off if you're running mono leader, so step up to 40-pound fluoro minimum.

Fluke are holding to the script too — steady rather than spectacular, which is exactly how I'd describe it to a buddy who asked me straight. Drifting the drop-off outside Tarpaulin Cove and the deeper edges around Quick's Hole in 25 to 35 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with squid strips, dragged slow on the moving tide. Keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — you're working for your five fish, not filling a cooler in an hour, but the quality fish are there if you cover water and stay on structure edges rather than open sand.

Scup fishing has been the easy win all week, and honestly it's a good way to keep the rod bent while you're waiting on bigger things to show. Squid strips and sandworms on double-hook bottom rigs around the Woods Hole draw bridge pilings and the rocky structure off Nonamesset are producing steady action, good eating-size fish, no drama, just consistent bites on the bottom during the tide change.

Here's how I'm reading the next stretch. The bait's doing exactly what it should — balling tight in the rips, getting pinned by current, sitting right where albies and bonito want to find it when they push through. Water temps have crossed the mark across the whole regional watch, from Montauk up through here, and the tide's building back toward that mid-August new moon push. If I had to put money on a spot for the first fish, I'd watch Robinson's Hole and Menemsha basin hardest — both have deep, fast current lines right against structure, which is exactly the setup albies use to pin bait when they arrive. Gay Head's rip is the other one I'd keep an eye on; when the tide runs hard there on a clean afternoon with light wind, that's historically been ground zero for the first scout fish of the season.

My plan for the coming week is simple — keep the light spinning gear rigged with small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks in the rocket launcher, fish the bass and blues on the rip changes like I have been, and check the bait balls at first light and last light every single day. That's when the first albie tail usually shows, a quick slash through a bait pod that's gone before you can even get a cast off. If a stretch of calm, sunny days holds through the weekend and that tide keeps building, I would not be surprised to hear the first credible report out of this water within the next week to ten days. Until then, the bass and blues are worth the trip on their own, and the fluke and scup will keep you occupied between rip changes. Just don't put the epoxy jigs away yet.

reports.headline: Deer Island's Ebb Gives Up Bass on Live Mackerel, Bluefish Chop Up the Flats
reports.subhead: With the harbor pushing 74 degrees, I'm fishing structure at first light and last light and letting the bluefish have the middle of the day.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night sitting at the wheel with a chart light and a cup of coffee: this week I'm staying inside the harbor early and pushing out to Nahant and the Cape Ann ledges when the sun climbs. The reasoning's simple. Surface water in the inner harbor is sitting in the mid-70s, which is above where a striped bass wants to work hard during daylight. That doesn't mean the fish left — it means they've gone vertical, they've gone nocturnal, and they've gone to the coldest, deepest structure they can find within range of the bait. Deer Island Light and the flats off Spectacle Island have both of those things: a hard channel edge, current that rips on the ebb, and enough depth to hold cooler water underneath the warm skin on top.

We flagged this pattern last week — called for steady, unspectacular conditions to hold through the stretch, and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing dramatic, but consistent enough that the guys putting in the pre-dawn hours are eating well.

The program at Deer Island has been live mackerel on a three-way rig, 20 to 30 feet down, fished tight to the edge where the flat drops into the main channel. Start that drift right as the tide turns to outgoing — you want the first hour and a half of ebb, when bait gets swept off the flat and stacked against the drop. I've had schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass show up consistently in that window, with the better fish coming right at first light before the sun gets up over the Boston skyline. Eels work too if you can't get mackerel — same depth, same drift, slower retrieve.

Flounder are still cooperating on the same flats once the tide goes fully slack — small hooks, sandworms or clam bellies, right on bottom in 15 to 20 feet off the Deer Island side. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady enough for a bucket of dinner if you're patient and fishing light.

Bluefish are the other half of this story, and they're the fish benefiting most from this warm surface layer. They don't care that it's 74 degrees — they thrive in it. I've had them chopping bait on top off Winthrop Flats and along the Deer Island shoreline in the middle of the day, which is exactly when the bass go quiet. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks — thrown into visible surface commotion have been producing fast, aggressive strikes. If you see gulls working tight and nervous water, that's your window; it doesn't last long before the school moves.

Out on the North Shore, Nahant's rocky points — Bass Rocks side and the ledges off East Point — are still the better bet for evening bass. I fished the last two hours of light there Thursday on an incoming tide and connected on three fish to 28 inches working a white/chartreuse bucktail along the boulder edges, letting it fall into the pockets between rocks and hopping it slow. Cooler Gulf of Maine water keeps that shoreline more honest through daylight than the harbor, so it's worth the run if you want a shot before dark instead of after.

Up toward Gloucester and Cape Ann, the structure fishing has been steadier than flashy. Halfway Rock and the ledges off Salt Island are holding mackerel in decent numbers on diamond jigs worked 30 to 50 feet down — good bonus action while you're scouting for bass activity on top. Cod and haddock reports off the deeper Cape Ann ledges have been thin this time of year, which tracks — that fishery wants cooler water and more current push than we're getting on this easing tide cycle. I wouldn't make a dedicated trip for groundfish right now; treat it as a bycatch bonus while jigging mackerel.

South toward Plymouth and Duxbury Bay, the pattern mirrors the harbor — warm surface water pushing better bass activity into dawn, dusk, and full dark. Duxbury Bay's flats have given up some solid schoolies on soft plastics worked slow along the channel edges as the tide starts moving, but daytime action has been spotty at best. If you're fishing that water, plan around the tide change, not around convenience.

Tides are easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which should soften current speed a touch — expect slightly less violent rips at spots like Deer Island and the Nahant ledges, but also less concentrated bait, so don't be surprised if the bite windows shrink a little in length even as they stay just as reliable in timing. Wind's been stable out of the southwest, no fronts on the immediate horizon, so I don't expect a hard reset to this pattern. If I had one day this week, I'd take the early ebb at Deer Island with live mackerel, then run up to Nahant for last light on bucktails. That's where the structure, the current, and the temperature break all line up in my favor right now.

reports.headline: 120 feet on the Stellwagen edge: bluefin on the bait balls, cod still tight to the gravel
reports.subhead: Whales, mackerel, and tuna are stacked on the northern edge while the groundfish stay honest on the bottom.
reports.body_markdown:
Ninety-five to one-twenty feet, that's where I've had the marks stacked up along the northern edge of Stellwagen all week, right where the gravel humps roll down into the basin. That's the number I keep coming back to. Below the thermocline, water's still cool enough to hold groundfish tight, and up top the surface has stayed warm enough to keep bait pinned in tight balls that the whales and the tuna are both working over.



We flagged this last week — said the bait and whale activity on the Bank would keep building and pull bluefin with it — and that's exactly how it's played out. Mackerel showed up thick on the edge starting Tuesday, packed into balls the size of a truck, and every time we found one there were finbacks or humpbacks slashing through it with birds working the surface. Where you've got that combination, the bluefin aren't far behind. We've had fish from 60 to well over 200 pounds coming up on greenstick and on bait, working the drift along the edge in 100 to 130 feet, mostly on the northeast corner where the current runs harder against the structure. Trolling spreads with green machines and small bird rigs have been drawing strikes, but the better fish came on chunked mackerel fished on a slow drift once we found the ball and shut the engine down. Jigging Shimano Butterflies through the bait itself has worked for the smaller schoolies mixed in underneath.



That's the reliable program right now, and I'd call it one of the more consistent things going on the whole coast this week — not lights-out every set, but steady enough that if you find the bait, you'll get a shot. Two out of three trips out there this week we connected, and the miss was more about sea state than fish; we had a stiff southwest breeze push in Thursday afternoon and it broke up the ball we'd been working before we could get gear in the water.



Down on bottom, the cod bite has been more of a grind, which is normal for late July. The fish are there, but they're sitting tight to the gravel patches in that 100 to 140 foot range on the western side of the Bank, and you need to work them with jigs rather than expect them to come up and chase. Diamond jigs tipped with a piece of squid, worked slow off bottom with short hops, have been the ticket — the fish aren't aggressive in this warm-water stretch, so a subtle presentation beats ripping it hard. We've had keeper cod to 15 pounds doing that, but you'll mark fish and have to work through some short ones before you connect with a slot fish.



Haddock have been the better bet for a full cooler. They're sitting on the mud patches in Stellwagen Basin, 130 to 160 feet, and they've been much more willing than the cod to come up for a bait. Standard high-low rigs with clam or squid strips, fished right on bottom, have been steady — not a banner week, but consistent enough that if you're patient and stay on the mud rather than chasing structure, you'll fill out a limit without too much trouble. Pollock have shown up mixed in on some of the deeper gravel edges near Tillies Bank, and those fish have actually been more aggressive than the cod, hitting diamond jigs worked with more speed and a longer sweep.



Hake have been scattered through the same deep basin water as the haddock, mostly picked up incidentally on bottom rigs rather than targeted, though a few boats working after dark near Stellwagen Basin have done well specifically on hake using cut bait fished right on bottom.



The wind's been the wildcard more than the water this week. We've had a run of light to moderate southwest breeze most days, which keeps the surface warm and bait balled up nicely for the tuna game, but it also means afternoon seas build enough on the Bank that you want to be planning your groundfish drops for the morning and shifting to the tuna hunt once the sun's higher and the wind fills in. Tide's swinging through the back side of the recent moon, current's still got some push to it, and that's helping keep bait concentrated rather than scattered — which is exactly why the whale and tuna activity has held together as well as it has.



Looking ahead, if the bait stays balled up on that northern edge and the whales keep working it, I'd expect the bluefin pattern to hold through the coming week — that's been the single most dependable program out there right now. Worth being at the dock early and idling out to the edge before the wind fills in, because the calmer the morning, the easier it is to spot the birds and the whale blows from a distance and get on the ball before it scatters. For groundfish, I'd stick with the plan that's been working: mud for haddock, gravel for cod, and don't expect the cod to be easy — work them slow and be patient. If a front pushes through midweek like these August systems tend to do, expect a day or two of chop that'll shuffle the bait balls around; when that happens, give it a day to resettle before you go looking for the tuna again.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push: Blues Crash Second Beach While Bass Go Nocturnal on the Ledges
reports.subhead: Warm water has stripers hunting after dark off the rocks from Newport to Sakonnet, while bluefish tear up bait schools along the open beaches and the breachways wait on their first albie.
reports.body_markdown:
Peanut bunker are stacked so thick against the rocks at Second Beach right now you can see the water nervous from fifty yards out — that flickering, silver shiver that tells you something's underneath pushing them.
