Same story along the wash at Matunuck and down at East Beach in Charlestown. That bait's been getting worked hard for about ten days, and it's the bluefish doing the damage, not the bass, which tells you a lot about where this water's sitting right now.

Surface temps have been running warm — mid-70s to pushing 80 in the shallow coves — and that's outside the comfort window stripers like. So the bass haven't left, they've just gone underground. I've been hopping the ledges below Fort Adams and out around Beavertail in Jamestown at first light and getting nothing but small stuff and a few short bass mixed with scup, but the same water at 9 PM with an eel or a chunk of bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the rock face has been a different animal. Two nights last week I had fish to 34 inches off the ledges below Castle Hill, both on the last two hours of the outgoing with the current still moving good. Sakonnet Point's fishing the same way — daytime is quiet, but work the rip off the point after dark on a big bunker head or a whole eel drifted through the seam where the current splits around the rocks, and there are bass willing to eat. This is a warm-water pattern through and through: bass feeding on the tide changes and in the dark, holding deep and tight to structure through the heat of the day. Nothing wrong with the fish being there, you just have to fish the clock instead of the sun.

Bluefish are the ones cashing in on this warm stretch, and they're not shy about it. Second Beach has had gulls working bait pods just off the sandbar most mornings this week, and if you can get a Hopkins or a diamond jig out past the breakers before the blues push the bunker into the whitewash, it's a fish a cast for a stretch. Same read at Weekapaug and along the beach toward Napatree — peanut bunker and small mullet getting hammered right at the surf line, blues running 3 to 6 pounds with the occasional bigger one mixed in. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these fish are cutting people off left and right on straight mono.

Fluke have been the honest, dependable part of the week. Nothing explosive, but a steady bottom bite off Jamestown along the Dumplings and out toward Whale Rock, drifting 4-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet of water on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. Keepers mixed with a good number of shorts — I'd call it a two-keeper, six-fish kind of drift most days, which is fine for August. Sakonnet River channel edges near the Tap's have produced similarly, best on slack-adjacent water when the drift slows enough to keep the bait down.

Tog talk is quiet right now, and that's expected — this warm a stretch of water, they're tucked deep in the cracks and not feeding hard. I've marked good numbers of fish on the sounder around the rockpiles off Newport and out at Whale Rock, which tells me the population's there and waiting. That's a September conversation, not an August one. Worth remembering those spots now while the water's warm and easy to read, because when the first cold nights knock the temperature down, that's when the green crabs go back in the bucket and those same rocks turn on.

As for albies — we flagged the breachways as the spot to watch heading into this stretch, and the ingredients are still lining up but the fish haven't shown yet. Squid are building in numbers around the RI shoreline according to what's been reported to our east, which is exactly the kind of forage shift that pulls albies and bonito tight to structure once the water temperature and current pattern lock in. Napatree and the Watch Hill side of the breachway are where I'd keep half an eye out starting this week — small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks ready in the bag — but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet. It's a scouting mission right now, not a sure thing.

Look at the week ahead and I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Warm, stable water, no major weather disruption in sight, tide building back toward the mid-August new moon — that keeps bass on the night program, blues chewing the beaches during daylight, and fluke steady on the structure drifts. If I had one trip to make, I'd fish last light into full dark off the Jamestown or Sakonnet ledges on bunker or eel, and I'd carry a light spinning rod rigged for albies just in case that breachway bait gets nervous while I'm standing there. Won't cost you anything to be ready.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Still Pays: Bass to 28, Bluefish Crashing Higgins
reports.subhead: Cooler Gulf of Maine water keeps stripers shallow and structure-bound while mackerel schools stack Pine Point and Wells Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, first light, I'm standing on the ledge at the Pool watching that incoming current stack up against the rocks the way it's done for me a thousand mornings, and a 28-inch bass comes up under a black Danny plug like she's got a train to catch. That's the hour. Right there. Water pushing in past the bar, bait getting pinned against structure, and stripers stacking up to feed before the tide tops out and everything goes quiet. I've said it before and I'll say it till they bury me — the first hour of the incoming at Biddeford Pool is the best hour of striper fishing this state has to offer, and this week it proved it again.

Here's the thing about Southern Maine right now, and it's the reason we're still catching fish in daylight while guys south of the Cape are cursing warm water and fishing at midnight: our water hasn't cooked off the way theirs has. Down in the Sound and off Jersey they're pushing 70-plus degrees and shoving bass onto deep wrecks, fishing bunker chunks after dark just to get a bite. Up here the Gulf of Maine is still running cool enough that stripers are comfortable working structure in daylight — ledges, river mouths, current seams — on a normal, unhurried summer program. We flagged this pattern holding as long as the weather stayed stable and mild, and it has. That's exactly what's kept the Pool, the Saco River mouth, and the rocks off Cape Elizabeth fishing the way they should this time of year.

The bass themselves have been a mixed bag — plenty of schoolies in the 18 to 24-inch range mixed with better fish pushing 28 to 32 inches, and I heard of one over 34 taken on a live mackerel off Wood Island on the last of the outgoing. Nothing epic, nothing you'd call a slaughter, but steady enough that if you put in the time on the right stage of tide you're going home with something to show for it. Pencil poppers and Danny-style swimmers have been the ticket at first and last light around the Pool and the mouth of the Saco. Once the sun's up and the bite goes quiet, switch to bucktails — half-ounce to one-ounce white or chartreuse — worked slow along the bottom in the deeper cuts off Wood Island Harbor. That's where the bigger fish have been holding through the heat of the day, sulking on structure and waiting for the tide to turn again.

Bluefish are the other story this week, and it's a good one. Higgins Beach has had a couple of honest blitzes — peanut bunker and small mackerel getting pushed right up onto the sand on the last two hours of the incoming, blues busting through them like they're mad about something. I watched one Saturday evening that had guys reeling up half-bitten pogies for twenty straight minutes. Metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, anything silver you can chuck far and retrieve fast — has been the play. Don't overthink it. When they're up and crashing, match the retrieve speed to the panic in the bait and you'll get bit. Pine Point has seen the same bait pushing through on calmer mornings, though the blitzes there have been shorter and more scattered — more of a here-and-gone than a sustained run.

Prouts Neck has been a story of wind direction, same as it always is. A southwest breeze pushes bait and current right into that stretch of rock, and when it's blowing 10 to 15 out of the southwest, the outside ledges have been worth a soak with topwater at dawn. When the wind swings onshore or dies flat, the bite there dies with it — I fished it Thursday in a dead calm and managed one fish in three hours. Not every day's a winner out there, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Mackerel have been thick off Wells Harbor and Ogunquit, schools rolling through on the tide changes, and if you want bait for eels or live-lining, that's your spot — small Swedish spoons or a mackerel tree will fill a bucket in twenty minutes most mornings. Flounder fishing off Wells has been steady but unspectacular — bloodworms and clam bellies on the bottom in the channel edges near the harbor, mostly keeper-sized fish, nothing to write home about but a nice change of pace on a slow tide.

We're coming off the full moon tides and easing toward neap over the next several days, which usually softens the current push a little — expect the bite windows to shrink slightly and get more particular about exact tide stage. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be back at the Pool on the first hour of an early incoming, throwing a pencil popper into the white water off the ledge and betting on that same push of current that's fed me for years. As we build back toward the August 12 new moon, look for that tide energy to return and the bait to reconcentrate — that's usually when Prouts Neck and the river mouths turn from decent to genuinely good.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack Runs 6:40 AM — Bass Are Deep, Bonito Are Still a Rumor
reports.subhead: The rip is stacked with bait and bottom-hugging stripers, but the albie/bonito window everyone's watching hasn't cracked open yet.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge hit 6:40 this morning, and for about twenty minutes the whole rip went glassy before the current turned and started stacking again. That's the window I want — the last of the ebb pulling bait off the ledge, bass sitting in 55 to 65 feet waiting for it to spill over. We marked fish stacked tight to bottom on the west edge, right where the ledge drops off into the channel, and it took a 2-ounce bucktail dressed with a chunk of fresh bunker to get down to them fast enough before the current picked back up. That's the story of this whole week out here — you've got a short window to work with, and if you're not precise about the tide stage you're fishing empty water.

Water's warm, and that's pushing the bass into a pattern that's more nocturnal and more structure-locked than I'd like for the end of July. Surface temps out toward the Ledge and down around North Light have been sitting in the mid-to-high 70s, well above that 68-to-72 window stripers actually want to live in. So the good fish — and we're still finding fish in the 28 to 35 pound class — are holding deep during the day and only really committing to feed on the tide change, at first light, or after dark. Eel-and-bunker chunk combos fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the flood at SW Ledge have been the most consistent producer for us this week, but consistent doesn't mean easy. We're putting in the hours to get two or three quality fish a trip, not filling a cooler.

Fluke have been the more dependable program, and if you want a fish that'll actually cooperate right now, that's your play. Drifting the drop-off between Sandy Point and the rip line in 25 to 35 feet, we're picking up keepers mixed with a lot of shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the sand-to-mud transition. The better fish — a few pushing 6 pounds — are coming off the harder structure closer to Clay Head, where the bottom breaks up and current sweeps bait past the rock piles. Black sea bass and tautog are backing up that pattern nicely on the same structure; if you're marking bait and current is moving, drop a green crab or a squid strip on a jig head and you'll usually connect within a few drifts.

Now, the question everyone at the dock keeps asking: where are the bonito? Honest answer — not here yet, not in numbers anyone should build a trip around. We flagged this a few days back, said the water temperature at Block Island and Montauk had crossed the threshold where bonito typically show, and that building tide into the next new moon on August 12th would be the trigger. That call still holds, but I'm not going to tell you they're stacked off North Light when they're not. What I will say is the bait is right — we're seeing good pods of sand eels and small bunker working the surface off Sandy Point and around the Ledge itself, and that's exactly the kind of forage that pulls albies and bonito in fast once the temperature break lines up. If you're itching to scout, I'd be doing exactly that — running light spinning gear with small Deadly Dicks or epoxy jigs, working the surface around North Light and Cormorant Rock on the calmer mornings, just in case you stumble into the first wave. But I wouldn't plan a whole charter around it yet.

Bluefish, on the other hand, are exactly where you'd expect them with water this warm — they don't mind the heat the way stripers do, and they're the ones actually blitzing right now. We've had good runs of choppers in the 4 to 8 pound class working peanut bunker schools along the beach south of the breachway and out toward the Ledge on the tide change, and they'll hit just about anything with flash — Kastmasters, poppers, doesn't matter much when they're fired up like that.

For boats able to make the run, the offshore edges are still holding tuna on the warm-water lines, and that piece of the puzzle hasn't changed much — worth the trip if you've got the range and the weather window, but that's a long day from Galilee and not something I'd send a half-day charter after.

Looking at the week ahead: the tide's building back toward that August 12th new moon, which should start reconcentrating bait around the rip lines and structure instead of letting it spread out in this slack summer current. If a temperature break sets up on that warm-water edge in the next several days — and the signs are pointing that direction — this is the window where I'd expect the first credible bonito or albie report to break loose off the Block. Until then, I'm fishing SW Ledge on the tide changes for bass, working the fluke drift off Sandy Point during the day, and keeping a rod rigged light just in case something fast shows up on the surface when I'm not looking for it.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds the mackerel; bass working the ledges on the last of the ebb
reports.subhead: Steady groundfish and a patient bass bite reward anglers who read the tide right around Casco Bay's structure this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I anchored up on the northeast corner of Halfway Rock Tuesday morning, about an hour before dead low, and watched something I've seen a hundred times but never tire of: terns working a bait ball so tight to the granite you'd think they were going to fly into it. Mackerel, thick as I've seen them this season, holding right on the rock's edge where the current compresses against the ledge. That's the tell. When the birds are stacked that low and that close to structure, the mackerel are pinned against something, and where mackerel get pinned, bass and groundfish aren't far behind.

This is exactly the kind of week I expected when I said conditions would hold steady and typical for mid-summer Maine — and they have. The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is doing us a favor right now. While the water south of Cape Cod is pushing into the mid-70s and shoving striped bass onto deeper wrecks and night patterns, Casco Bay is still comfortably in that 66 to 70 degree window bass actually prefer. That keeps our fish on a more conventional daytime structure program — not explosive, but dependable, which for late July is about all you can ask.

The mackerel jigging at Halfway Rock has been the most consistent thing going. Small diamond jigs, quarter-ounce to half-ounce, no bait needed, dropped right to the edge of the ledge in 20 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the ebb. I had a father-son team out of South Portland tell me they filled a cooler in forty minutes Wednesday afternoon doing exactly that. Where you find those mackerel balled up, work a bucktail or a soft plastic — I like a 3-inch white shad body on a half-ounce jighead — just under the school. Bass have been intercepting stragglers on the drop, particularly on the last hour of the ebb into the first of the flood, when the current slackens enough for fish to hold position and feed without burning energy.

Striped bass around Peaks Island and the back side of Cushing have been a patience game this week rather than a numbers game. I'm marking fish on the sounder over the mussel beds off the eastern side of Peaks in 15 to 25 feet, but getting them to commit has meant slowing way down — a 1/2-ounce bucktail dressed with a chartreuse curl-tail, dragged dead slow on the bottom through the last of the outgoing. Harpswell's been similar. The ledges off Bailey Island — particularly that stretch running south toward the Punkin Nubble — have given up schoolie-to-mid-30-inch fish to guys drifting live mackerel under a slip float on the early flood, right as the tide starts to push bait back up onto the flats.

Cape Small has quieted some compared to two weeks ago, but it's still worth a stop if you're running that far south anyway. The rip that forms off the point on a moderate ebb has been holding fish, mostly in that mid-20s to low-30s range, taking topwater plugs at first light before the sun gets high enough to push them down.

Groundfish remain the backbone of the deeper water program, and that hasn't changed. Cod and haddock are still coming steady off the deeper structure around Halfway Rock — 80 to 110 feet on the northwest side where the bottom breaks hard — and off the ledges south of Bailey Island in similar depths. Jigging diamond jigs or bouncing a teaser-and-bait combo on the bottom during slack or the first hour of a tide change has been the most productive window; once the current really starts ripping through there, you spend more time re-rigging than fishing. Haddock have been running a bit smaller than I'd like this month, plenty of shorts mixed in, so bring a scale and know your minimums before you fill the cooler.

Bluefish remain scarce this far into the Gulf of Maine — the warm-water blitz pattern that's been tearing up the Jersey and Long Island beaches on peanut bunker simply hasn't pushed this far north, and with our water staying cool, I wouldn't expect it to. If you want bluefish, that's a trip south, not a Casco Bay trip.

Tide-wise, we're coming off the big pulls of the full moon and easing toward a neap cycle over the next several days, with the bay building back toward the August 12 new moon after that. That means somewhat gentler currents through the middle of next week — good news for anyone fishing bucktails on the bottom around Bailey Island or Cape Small, since the drift speed will be more manageable. It also means the mackerel schools may loosen up and spread rather than balling tight against structure, so if you're planning a Halfway Rock trip, I'd get there sooner rather than later in the week while the bait's still concentrated.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to shift dramatically. Barring a passing thunderstorm — and early August around here usually throws at least one at us — expect the groundfish bite to stay steady on the deeper ledges, bass to keep working the shallower structure on the tide changes, and the mackerel to remain the reliable backbone of the week. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be back on that northeast corner of Halfway Rock an hour before low, watching for the birds.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 180: haddock stacked on the mud, cod holding the gravel edge, first bluefin breaking on Stellwagen's approach
reports.subhead: A steady week of numbers fishing on the Ledge, with early bluefin scouting the bait balls off the southern end.
reports.body_markdown:
One-eighty feet on the sounder, soft mud from the transducer down to the bottom, and the haddock marks stacked up like a layer cake eight to twelve feet off bottom. That's been my number all week on the flats north of the Ledge proper, working the mud basin between Jeffrey's and the edge of Scantum. Haddock this time of year want that soft bottom and they want it in depth — anywhere from 165 to 195 feet has been holding fish, and the good marks come up thick right around the top of the tide when the current slacks enough to hold a straight drift.

The rig hasn't changed and it doesn't need to: high-low bottom rigs, size 3/0 circle hooks, clam bellies or squid strips, six to ten ounces of lead depending on drift speed. When the current's really moving — and with the tide building back toward the August 12th new moon it has been moving — I've had to go to twelve ounces just to hold bottom on some drifts. Haddock have run a clean 20 to 26 inches, with enough shorts mixed in that you're culling through fish, which is a good sign for the fall. Limits haven't been automatic but a determined boat working the mud has had no trouble putting a solid box together in three or four hours.

Cod is a different conversation, and it's a gravel conversation. The edge where the mud gives way to hard bottom and boulder — that transition zone running along the western flank of the Ledge in 90 to 140 feet — is where the cod have been sitting tight to structure. This is jig water more than bait water right now. Six and eight-ounce diamond jigs, tipped with a strip of squid, worked with a short hard snap off bottom, has been outproducing static bait rigs two or three to one when the fish are actively feeding. When they're not, a whole clam on a circle hook soaking right on the gravel will still pick off a few keepers. Sizes have been mixed — a lot of 24 to 30 inch fish with the occasional 15-pounder mixed in, usually right on the steepest part of the drop where the gravel rolls into deeper water.

Pollock have been riding shotgun on both bites, which is typical for this time of year — they sit up off the bottom over the same structure holding cod and haddock, and they'll jump all over a diamond jig worked on the fall rather than the bottom bounce. If you're marking fish suspended 20 to 40 feet up off a gravel pile, that's pollock water, and a faster retrieve with the jig will separate them from the cod underneath.

Hake fishing has quieted some compared to June, but the basin still produces after dark. Scantum's deep water — 250 feet plus — has had a few boats working chum bags and diamond jigs tipped with squid at night with decent results, though it's not the numbers game it was a few weeks back. If you want hake specifically, plan a late-evening trip and be patient; it's a slower bite but the fish run good size when they show.

Now the part everyone's been asking about at the dock — bluefin. We flagged this last week, said the pattern would hold through the week, and it has. The warm surface push that's been running unusually far north for late July has kept a mackerel and pogy show working the approaches to Stellwagen, and where there's bait stacked under whale activity, there's tuna working underneath it. I've had reports of school and medium bluefin breaking on bait balls south of the Ledge, working the same warm edge that's been feeding the canyon bite further south. This isn't the giant push yet — that's an October program on the Ledge proper, when the mackerel schools get dense and the big fish move in tight to feed hard before the water turns. Right now it's scouting fish, singles and small pods, working the surface in the morning glass and disappearing once the wind builds a chop. Trolling small spreads of green machines and bird rigs around visible bait and diving birds has connected with a few, but it's not a program you can set your watch to yet.

Mackerel themselves have been reliable bait fish, schooling up in that 30 to 60 foot range on structure edges, and a Sabiki rig dropped through a school will fill a livewell in ten minutes most mornings. That's been the ticket for guys wanting live bait insurance if a bluefin shows itself.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the next several days. The tide keeps building toward the new moon, which should sharpen up the drifts on both the mud and the gravel and probably push haddock a little tighter to the bottom during the strongest push. If the bait holds on the southern approaches to Stellwagen, I'd expect the bluefin scouting reports to keep trickling in, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them yet — plan it around the mud and the gravel, where the numbers have been dependable, and treat any tuna sign as a bonus.

reports.headline: White Island Ledge on the Slack: Haddock to 7 Pounds, Stripers Working the Piscataqua Seams
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've fished all of it — this week the shoals paid, the harbor stripers made you work, and the mackerel showed up right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and think New Hampshire's an afterthought between two states with real fishing. I've never seen it that way. Thirteen miles gets you the Piscataqua's cobble bottom and iron current, it gets you Hampton Harbor's sandbars sliding under a boat at half tide, and it gets you six miles out to the Isles of Shoals where the bottom drops into real groundfish structure — ledges, boulder fields, and gullies that fish the same as anything you'd find running two hours from a bigger port. I trailer a 20-foot Lund and I fish this stretch like it's a hundred and thirty miles of coast, because if you know where the rock piles are, it is.

This week that meant mornings at Appledore and White Island before most people had their coffee going. The Gulf of Maine's still running cool enough to keep this a daytime, structure-based program — not the deep, nocturnal grind you're hearing about from the bass south of the Cape where the surface water's pushing into the high 70s and shoving stripers onto wrecks after dark. We flagged that pattern holding steady last week, and up here it has — cooler water, normal tide-and-structure fishing, no need to wait for full dark. Haddock have been the better story on the ledges around White Island and the Appledore backside in 70 to 90 feet, taking clam bellies and diamond jigs tipped with squid strips on the last hour of the ebb into dead slack. Fish to 7 pounds came over the rail Tuesday morning, mixed with pollock and a few keeper cod that wanted the bottom third of the water column, not up in the jig column where the pollock were sitting. If you're marking bait stacked tight to the rock on the sounder, that's your window — the slack, before the current builds back and scatters everything off the structure.

Mackerel showed up in numbers around the Shoals this week too, right on schedule for late July. Diamond jigs and small Swedish Pimples, no bait needed, in 40 to 60 feet over sand pockets between the ledges. They're not just a bonus catch — fresh mackerel strip is about the best haddock bait you can cut yourself, so a lot of guys are jigging a dozen fish first thing and using the rest for bottom rigs the rest of the morning. Simple, cheap, and it works.

Inshore, the striper program has been honest work rather than easy work. Hampton Harbor's been giving up fish on the push tide through the inlet — that first hour and a half of incoming when bait gets funneled past the jetty rocks and stripers stack up to ambush it. Live mackerel and bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig near the rock pile on the north side have produced slot fish to 34 inches, but you need to be there right as the tide turns, because once it's running hard the bite window closes fast and doesn't reopen until the next stage. Rye Harbor's been a flounder spot more than a bass spot this week — small hooks, sandworms, fishing the mud pockets just outside the harbor mouth on the last of the outgoing, nothing huge but steady action for anyone who wants dinner without burning gas.

The Piscataqua's been the most reliable bass water on the beat, which isn't surprising given how much current that river moves. Stripers are holding on the current seams below the Memorial Bridge and around the pilings up toward Portsmouth Harbor, feeding on the tide change rather than blind-casting the whole cycle. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, cast up-current and swung through the seam has been the most consistent presentation — you're imitating a baitfish getting swept out of the eddy, and that's exactly the moment stripers commit. A few bluefish have started mixing in around Odiorne Point and off Great Boars Head, chopping up bait pods close to the rocks in the last two hours of daylight. Nothing like the blitz conditions you're hearing about down on the Jersey and Long Island beaches where warm water's got blues thriving while it pushes bass deep — our water's still too cool for that kind of sustained chaos — but there's enough bluefish showing now that I'd carry a wire leader rig alongside your bass gear if you're working the Boars Head rocks in the evening.

Tide's easing off the last full moon and sliding toward neap over the next several days, which typically softens current speed at the Shoals and on the Piscataqua both. That usually means slightly longer slack windows at the ledges — good news for the haddock and cod program, since a longer slack gives you more time to work a piece of structure before the current builds back. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd plan on hitting White Island or Appledore early, working the slack hard, then coming back inside to catch the tail of the incoming at Hampton Harbor in the afternoon. If a front pushes through midweek like these August systems tend to do, I'd shift days rather than fight a chopped-up ocean six miles out — the groundfish will still be there when it clears.

reports.headline: Monhegan Ledges Hold Pollock on Top, Mackerel Thick Off Eastern Egg Rock
reports.subhead: Groundfish still working the deep channels of Penobscot Bay while stripers stick to structure through the warm stretch — a steady week, nothing wild.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty years ago my father took me out past Monhegan on a morning just like this one — flat calm, gulls working close to the rocks, and he told me the mackerel would tell you everything you needed to know about the rest of the season. If they're thick and staying thick into August, the pollock and the bass will follow them right up to the surface. I thought of him this week hauling gear off Allen Island, because the mackerel are exactly where he'd have expected them — schooled up tight off Eastern Egg Rock, puffins diving through them at first light, and the pollock stacked right underneath doing the same thing we've watched them do every summer since Reagan was in office.

We flagged this last week — said the traditional midsummer Maine program would hold through the week — and that's about the size of it. Nothing dramatic, nothing collapsing, just the Gulf of Maine doing what cool water does when the rest of the coast south of Cape Cod is running warm and pushing everything deep. Our water hasn't budged much past the mid-60s in the open bay, which means the bass and the groundfish are still willing to work a daytime tide instead of hiding until dark like they're doing from Boothbay south to the Sound. That's the one advantage we've got right now, and it's worth using while it lasts.

Monhegan's ledges have been the most consistent piece of water all week. Fishing the ebb off the southwest side in 40 to 60 feet, jigging diamond jigs and 6-inch soft-plastic shads for pollock that are running 3 to 6 pounds, with a few better fish pushing 8 mixed in deeper on the drop. Same spot's been holding stripers up on the shallower rock piles — schoolies mostly, 24 to 30 inches, taking topwater poppers at first light before the sun gets high and pushes them down onto the structure. By 8 or 9 in the morning you're better off switching to a bucktail and working it slow along the bottom edge where the ledge drops into deeper water.

Eastern Egg Rock itself has been a mackerel show more than anything, and that's fine — those schools are pulling everything else in behind them. Bass have been working the edges of the bait, and we've had a few bluefish mixed in too, which isn't typical for us this far north but isn't unheard of either when there's this much forage stacked up. Small metal jigs, Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks, worked fast through the school will take mackerel by the bucket, and if you slow down and let a swimming plug sink through the middle of the bait you'll draw the bass and blues up out of it.

Penobscot Bay's been the quieter half of the report, but quiet doesn't mean empty. The deeper channels between Vinalhaven and Isle au Haut are still holding cod and haddock — not the numbers we had twenty years ago, nowhere close, but lobstermen are pulling the occasional cod as gear bycatch in 80 to 100 feet off the western side of the Fox Islands Thorofare, and a few charter boats working jigs and bait rigs down in that same water have put together decent mixed bags of cod and haddock, most fish in the 3 to 8 pound range. If you're headed out there, fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still moving enough to keep bait pinned against the bottom structure, then hold through the slack before the flood picks back up.

Stonington's been a mackerel and pollock town this week too — the same pattern repeating itself up and down the coast wherever there's a ledge and moving water. The bite off the outer islands there has been best on the last of the incoming, fish stacked tight to structure in 30 to 50 feet, and a few stripers showing up on the flood tide working bait pushed up against the rocks near the harbor entrance.

Tides have been strong coming off the full moon, easing now toward the middle of the cycle, and that's actually helped — enough push to keep bait moving without blowing the whole bay out. Wind's been light out of the southwest most afternoons, which keeps the surface calm enough for topwater work early and jigging later without fighting a chop.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this to change through the first week of August. The water south of us stays warm and keeps pushing quality bass and bait north along the coast, which should keep feeding our pattern rather than disrupting it. If a frontal system pushes through midweek like they tend to this time of year, expect a day or two of dirty water and slower fishing right behind it, then a quick return to normal once it clears. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the early ebb at Monhegan before the boats crowd the ledge, work the topwater bite for an hour, then switch to jigs and stay on the pollock through the tide change. That's about as sure a bet as this coast offers in late July.

reports.headline: East end on the 4:52 ebb: bass on the eel bite, blues run the bait through daylight
reports.subhead: The full-moon push did exactly what we said it would — now the tide's easing toward neap and the program shifts to full dark.
reports.body_markdown:
4:52 AM. That's when the ebb really got moving at the Sandwich side this week, and if you weren't rigged and drifting an eel past the Bourne Bridge piling seam by 4:30, you missed the best twenty minutes of your night. I've fished this ditch long enough to know the current doesn't care what time your alarm says — it cares what the moon says, and right now we're still riding the tail of the full moon push, with tide stages running strong and current speeds up around 4 to 4.5 knots on the peak ebb at the east end. That's canal-standard big-water speed, the kind that pins bait against the rip line off Scusset and makes big bass stop thinking and start eating.

We flagged this coming last week — said the building full-moon tide would sharpen the current push and open up the feeding windows, and that's exactly what's played out. The bite hasn't been all-day easy, but the tide-change windows have been money. East end, working the last hour of the ebb into the top of the slack, guys throwing 9-inch swimming plugs — Gags, Beachmasters, the darker patterns — through the seam where the rip meets the flat water off Scusset Beach have connected on bass in the 28 to 36-inch range after dark. Daytime, that same stretch is bluefish water. Blues are thriving in this warm surface layer that's pushing bass down and out — mid-70s water at the surface, maybe kissing 80 in the shallows on a hot afternoon, and that's blue heaven. Diamond jigs and Ava 27s worked through the froth when the bait schools push through on the tide have been good for quick limits, fish mostly in the 3 to 6 pound class, some bigger mixed in when a bunker school gets pinned against the rocks.

West end tells a different story right now. The current seams off Mashnee Island and up into the mouth by Hog Island are holding fish, but you have to work the stages right — the top third of the flood, before the current really builds, has been the window. Bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how much water's moving, bounced along bottom through the seam where the deeper channel water meets the shallower flat off Mashnee, have picked at fluke — nothing spectacular, mostly 15 to 18 inches with a keeper mixed in here and there, but steady enough to make it worth a drift if bass aren't cooperating. Phinneys Harbor has stayed quieter than I'd like this week — warm, still water in there, and without a hard tide push flushing bait through, it's been mostly small blues and the occasional schoolie bass chasing silversides at first light.

Here's the truth on the bass right now: the big fish are still here, but they've gone strictly nocturnal on us. That warm surface water — I'm talking mid-70s to near 80 from the Bay side clear through Buzzards Bay — has pushed the quality fish off the shallow structure during daylight and onto the current-swept holes and the deeper edges, where they'll only really commit to feeding on the strongest tide stages, dawn, dusk, or full dark. That's why the 4:52 ebb mattered this week, and why the corresponding evening ebb — running close to 5:15 PM by my watch — has been the other reliable window. Eels fished dead-drift on a fish-finder rig, or live-lined and let to swim naturally through the rip, have out-produced everything else after dark. If you're bucktailing in daylight expecting the same results you got in June, you're going to be disappointed — the fish simply aren't up shallow chasing plastic at 2 in the afternoon anymore.

Now, the tide's about to ease. We're coming off the full-moon peak and sliding toward neap over the next several days, current speeds dropping a bit on both ends. That usually means the bite windows get shorter and pickier — the fish won't be forced to feed as hard, so you need to be exactly where the bait is exactly when the current turns. I'd focus the next week on the last two hours of the night ebb at the east end and the top of the flood at the west end, because those are the stages that'll still be moving enough water to concentrate bait even as the overall push softens.

One more thing worth watching: with squid starting to show around the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound edges and inshore temps holding in a range that's finally right for it, I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first bonito or false albacore scout report out of the Buzzards Bay corridor within the next week or two — that's a Woods Hole and Wings Neck story more than a straight canal story, but it's close enough to our water that I'll be watching for it. For now, though, the canal's still a bass-and-blues program, tide-driven like always, and that's not changing anytime soon. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd take the late ebb at Scusset with a black eel and patience, and I'd have a bucktail rigged as backup for when the blues show up and ruin the eel supply.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass go deep and nocturnal while scup keep the rods bent
reports.subhead: The upper bay's running warm and quiet on top, but the ledges and the night bite are carrying the week.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Dom down at the Sabin Point ramp Tuesday morning, hauling his skiff out with two schoolie bass in the cooler and that look guys get when the fishing's fine but not what it was in May. "Where's everybody at," he said, not really asking. I didn't have to tell him. The herring run through Buckeye Brook wrapped up back in April, and every bass that rode that run north through the Providence River has scattered out and gone smart on us. That's the story of the whole upper bay right now — not bad fishing, just bass that know better than to sit around in warm water during daylight.

The upper bay's been running warm on the surface for weeks now, pushing into the mid-70s off the piers and holding there under this stretch of sun and light southwest wind. That's above the comfort window for a big striper, and it's shoved the better fish off the flats and down onto structure — the Nyatt Point ledge, the drop along Conimicut Light, the deep water off Poppasquash Point, and the east side rip along Prudence Island where the bottom falls to 30, 35 feet. Those are night spots now. I've had my best luck the last two weeks on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, working live eels or chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig right on the bottom in that 25-to-35-foot band off Nyatt. Full dark, dead low light, that's when the bigger fish show. Daytime, you're mostly working schoolies in the 20-to-26-inch range on top of the same structure, and they'll eat a white bucktail dragged slow off the ledge, but the slot fish and up have gone strictly nocturnal. That's exactly the pattern we flagged holding steady this week, and the bay hasn't given us a reason to argue with it.

Fluke are the better daylight bet right now, and they're pushing well up into the bay chasing the same warm water that's got the bass hiding. Greenwich Bay has been quietly productive — the channel edges off Warwick Neck and the drop-off outside the cove in 18 to 25 feet are holding keeper fish mixed with a lot of shorts, which is honest summer fluke fishing, not a blitz. Same story working the Providence River shipping channel off Fields Point and down toward Conimicut Point, where the bottom drops from the flats into 25 to 30 feet of water. Drift that edge on the last of the incoming into the top of the high, dragging a chartreuse bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, or a 4-inch white Gulp on a light jighead if the current's soft. You'll pick through a bunch of small fish for every keeper, but the keepers have been decent — fish to 22, 23 inches coming out of Greenwich Bay this week.

Scup are the one thing in this bay that hasn't complicated itself at all. Rocky Point, the rock pile off Nyatt, the ledges around Prudence Island — anywhere there's structure in 15 to 25 feet, scup are stacked and eating without much fuss. Sandworms or a piece of clam belly on a high-low rig, light spinning gear, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide. This is the fishery I send beginners to right now because it's the most dependable thing going in the bay — no drama, just bent rods, best around the tide change when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without a two-ounce sinker.

Bluefish have started showing with a little more purpose the last week, working peanut bunker schools at the mouth of the Providence River and off Conimicut Point, especially in that hour around dusk when the bait balls up tight against the current line. That tracks with what's been happening the length of the coast — blues thriving in this warm water while the bass duck it — and the bay's version of it has been smaller, snapper-to-cocktail-size fish mostly, but there's been enough two-to-four-pound fish mixed in off Rocky Point to make a small metal or a Deadly Dick worth throwing if you see the surface nervous.

Weakfish and black sea bass are around but not what I'd call a target right now — a few weakfish showing up as bycatch on the fluke drifts in Greenwich Bay, and sea bass holding tight to the rockier structure off Prudence, but neither is worth a dedicated trip with everything else going on.

Looking ahead, the tide's easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which should settle the current down and make that Nyatt/Conimicut night program even more workable — softer water means you can hold bottom with less lead and fish that eel more naturally. If the sun keeps cooking the surface like it has, expect the bass to stay locked into that dawn, dusk, and full-dark pattern right through the week, with the daytime action belonging to fluke and scup. Keep an eye on the river mouth for bluefish activity building as we push toward the second week of August — if that bait keeps concentrating the way it has, the blitz windows at dusk could get a lot more interesting before the new moon on the 12th resets everything.

reports.headline: Rips Report Card: Blues A-, Bass D, Weakfish Finally Cashing the Check
reports.subhead: The rip line off the Point is still moving water, but it's bluefish and weakfish paying the bills while bass have gone into hiding until dark.
reports.body_markdown:
If I had to grade this week on the water, here's the card: bluefish get an A-minus, weakfish are climbing toward a B, fluke is a C that needed a location change to pass, striped bass is a flat D during daylight, and black drum — that class is over, kid, go home. That's where we're at heading into August.

The rips off Cape May Point are still doing their job current-wise. That color line between the Delaware Bay outflow and the green ocean water is showing up sharp on the back half of the ebb, and the bait is there — peanut bunker getting pushed and balled up right on the seam. But the bass that used to camp under that bait all day have wised up to the warm water. Surface temps sitting in the upper 70s pushed them off the shallow structure and out to the reef sites — Cape May Reef, Wildwood Reef, the edges out toward the Old Grounds — where they've gone almost strictly nocturnal. If you want a bass right now, you're fishing the last two hours of dark into first light, live-lining bunker or working an eel slow along bottom on the turn of the tide. Daytime trolling through the rips for bass has been mostly a bluefish tax this week — you'll get bit, just not by what you're targeting.

And that bluefish tax isn't a bad consolation prize. Blues have been the one species actually thriving in this warm water mass, and the rips have had a steady pull of 2- to 5-pound choppers on diamond jigs and green-tube Ava 27s, worked through the rip on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's really cranking against the shoal. Bunker spoons trolled at 3 to 4 knots through the same water have been just as productive if you don't want to jig. It's not a blitz every trip, but it's a dependable bend in the rod, and worth the gas if bass aren't cooperating.

Fluke's been the tell of the summer. We flagged this last week — said the bay bite would soften as the shallows warmed and the better play would shift to deeper reef structure and the mouth of the bay, and that's exactly how it's played out. Inside the back bays and up around Hereford Inlet, the fluke bite has gone quiet and picky, mostly shorts. Move out to Wildwood Reef or Cape May Reef in 40 to 55 feet, though, and there's still a real bite going — 5-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the moving tide, mixing keepers with the shorts. It's not a beach-bum program anymore; you need to run out to structure to find fish willing to eat.

Weakfish are the other call that's playing out — we said last week to expect that bite to keep climbing as the water held steady, and it has. Delaware Bay's channel edges near Miah Maull Shoal and around Brandywine Shoal Light have been holding weakfish in 20 to 30 feet, and the last two hours of the incoming tide has been the window. Pink or chartreuse soft-plastic shad bodies on light jig heads, or straight bloodworms on a simple bottom rig, have both been drawing bites. Nothing like the old-timer weakfish runs my father used to talk about, but for the current state of that fishery, a mixed bag of keeper-class fish two or three days a week is a genuinely good sign.

As for black drum — that ship sailed in May and it's not coming back this year. Fortescue's quiet on that front, just the odd straggler getting picked up incidentally by guys soaking clam for something else. If you're still asking about drum, you missed the window; start planning for next May instead.

One more thing worth a mention if you're bottom fishing the reef sites: triggerfish have been showing up as a bonus on clam baits fished tight to structure on Cape May Reef. Not a target species most guys plan a trip around, but a fun surprise when the fluke bite goes cold on the drift.

Looking ahead, the tides are easing off the post-full-moon push and sliding toward neap over the next several days, which usually means a little less current speed through the rips and a slightly calmer bite window overall. That's fine for weakfish and fluke, who don't need violent water to feed, but it typically softens the bluefish blitz pattern some as bait disperses with the slacker current. By the back half of next week, we'll be building tide again toward the August 12 new moon, and that's when I'd expect the rips to sharpen back up and bass activity — even at night — to get a little more aggressive around the bait balls. If the warm surface layer holds like it has, don't expect striped bass to come back to a daytime program anytime soon. Plan your trips around dark, fish the reef structure for fluke, and work the bay's channel edges for weakfish on the incoming. That's the honest version of this week, no sugarcoating it.

reports.headline: Barnegat Inlet rip still paying on fluke while the beachfront turns into a bluefish game
reports.subhead: A new cut cut into the Holgate flat this week, and it's telling you everything about where the bait — and the blues — are stacking up.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning at first light, low tide bottoming out, and there's a new cut carved into the outer bar that wasn't there two weeks ago. Leftover groundswell — we've had 3 to 4 foot stuff rolling through on a short 5-second period most of last week — has been chewing on that flat, and it finally broke through in a spot about 200 yards south of the last parking access. That's a real feature now: deeper water pinched between two humps, current funneling through it hard on the ebb. I marked it on my phone, because that's exactly the kind of structure that holds bait when everything else on this beach is getting hammered flat and featureless by swell.

And bait is the whole story right now. Water's sitting in the mid-70s to pushing 80 in the shallows, which is above where striped bass want to be, but bluefish love it, and they've got it. We flagged this a week ago — said the bunker-bluefish blitz working up from South Jersey would spread into our stretch, and it has. Beach Haven north through Ship Bottom has had legitimate blitz mornings, bunker pods getting pinned against the bar and blues busting on top hard enough to see the spray from the dune line. Bring metal — Deadly Dick or a 1.5-ounce Ava jig in chrome — and don't overthink it, just get it in front of the school before they slide down-beach. Some bigger blues have mixed in since late last week, mid-teens mixed with the choppers, so if you're throwing bucktails for something else and get bit off, that's why.

Fluke are still the more dependable program, and Barnegat Inlet keeps paying like we said it would. The rips off the north jetty and the reef structure on the ocean side are holding keeper-class fish on bucktail and fluke-belly combos — 3/4-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail, six-inch strip of fluke belly or a swimming mullet trailer, worked slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. Depth's the key: 15 to 25 feet where the current's ripping over structure, not the flat sand in the middle of the channel. The full moon tides we've been riding have been building nicely into that window, sharpening up the dawn push through the inlet, and that's when I've heard of the better counts — multiple keepers to 22 inches, mixed with plenty of shorts you'll cull through.

Inside the bay, it's a quieter game but not a dead one. Channel edges off Ship Bottom and the bridge structure at Manahawkin have fluke sitting tight where there's a slight thermal break from the current, and a Gulp swimming mullet on a light jighead, three-eighths ounce, dragged slow through those seams on the last of the incoming has been worth the trip for a few guys I talked to at the shop. Weakfish are showing incidentally in the deeper holes on the bayside — Graveling Point and up into the lower Mullica have produced a few in the 18 to 20 inch class for guys soaking bloodworms or a small Gulp shrimp on bottom around dusk. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up for stripers or drum.

Speaking of stripers — that bite has gone almost entirely nocturnal, and that's not going to change until the water backs off. With surface temps sitting where they are, the resident bass around Barnegat Inlet and the nearby wrecks are holding deep during daylight and only really coming up on bunker schools after dark or right at the tide change. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, soak a whole bunker on a fish-finder rig, 2 to 3 ounce sinker depending on the drift, tight to the inlet rocks or the wreck structure just outside on the last two hours of the ebb into the top of the flood. That's been the play, and it's a slow, patient one — a handful of quality fish a night rather than a blitz.

Black drum season's essentially closed the book on itself for this stretch — that window was April into May around the inlet and Little Egg, and those fish have long since pushed north and offshore. Tautog's closed for the summer too, so if you're structure fishing the reef sites, know you're targeting fluke and bass only right now, nothing to keep off the bottom otherwise.

Out in the surf, kingfish have been showing on the outer bars in decent numbers — small but steady, biting bloodworm or Fishbites on a high-low rig in that 2 to 4 foot zone right where the wash meets the bar. Good action for kids or anyone who wants a rod bent between the bigger blitz windows.

Looking ahead: tides are easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next few days, which should calm the current enough that bunker schools spread out a little and the blitz activity gets patchier rather than pinned in one spot — cover water instead of camping. If an afternoon thunderstorm rolls through, which is typical this time of year, expect a short pause in the bite followed by a reset. The next real trigger is the build back toward the August 12 new moon, when I'd expect bait and predators to reconcentrate hard around the inlet and that new Holgate cut. I'll be watching that cut closely — it's early, but it's the kind of structure that turns into a real producer once the current really carves it out.

reports.headline: Where'd the Blues Go? Chasing the Bunker Schools from Ocean City to Townsends
reports.subhead: The blitz we flagged last week finally rolled into South Jersey water — but the real lesson this week is in the tide charts, not the boils.
reports.body_markdown:
How many of you called me this week asking the same question: "Darnell, is it worth driving to the beach before work, or should I wait for the evening tide?" Fair question, and it's the right one to be asking right now, because the answer changes by the hour with this bait migration we're in the middle of.

Let's start with the receipts. We told you last week that the bluefish blitz working down from North Jersey would keep pushing south as the bunker schools tracked the beach, and that's exactly what happened. By Wednesday there were peanut bunker balls getting pinned against the Ocean City boardwalk beaches and down through Sea Isle City on the incoming tide, with blues from cocktail size up to six and seven pounds crashing through them in the wash. Same story off Townsends Inlet — the bait comes down the beachfront on the push, gets squeezed against the jetty rocks, and the blues pile in for twenty, thirty minutes at a stretch before it goes quiet and moves on. If you're fishing it, don't waste time on big topwater plugs when the water's boiling — a simple 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Gotcha plug fished on wire leader will get bit as fast as anything, and you don't lose your whole tackle box to bluefish teeth.

Here's the classroom part. Surf and inlet water is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s right now, and that's well outside where striped bass want to be — their comfort zone runs 68 to 72 degrees. So while the blues are thriving in this warm water, the bass have gone the other direction: deep, structure-oriented, and mostly nocturnal. If you want a striper this week, your best window is full dark to first light, working bunker chunks or eels on the bottom at Absecon Inlet along the rock pile on the outgoing, or drifting the deeper rip off Great Egg Inlet where the current digs a trench close to 25 feet. I had a report of a mid-20-inch fish and one better one pushing 30 inches coming off cut bunker fished tight to bottom on the last two hours of the ebb at Absecon — that's your program until the water cools.

Fluke are the dependable lesson plan this time of year, and they haven't disappointed. The sod banks off Brigantine are still holding fish in that 8 to 15 foot depth range, and the pattern hasn't changed all summer — drift with the outgoing tide as it pulls bait out of the marsh creeks, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a strip of squid. You're going to catch plenty of shorts doing this, but the keepers are mixed in, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when everything funnels out of the back bay channels. Absecon Inlet's channel edges, 20 to 30 feet on the drop-offs, have been holding better average size — fish to 5 pounds reported this week on the same bucktail-and-Gulp combo, though you'll need enough lead to hold bottom against that inlet current, so bump up to an ounce or an ounce and a quarter on a strong tide.

Weakfish have been a quiet bright spot for the guys fishing at night. If you're working the back bay channels under the lights at the Route 52 causeway or the bridges through Ocean City, small soft plastics like a 4-inch Storm Shad on a light jig head have been picking up weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch class mixed in with the white perch and small stripers. It's not a numbers game, but it's a nice change of pace after a day of bluefish teeth and short fluke.

Surf regulars working the troughs at Ocean City and down toward Stone Harbor have kept kingfish coming steady on bloodworms and Fishbites fished on a high-low rig, best around the morning high tide when the wash is calm enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. And for the guys who like to fish the jetty rocks at Absecon Inlet, this is prime time for triggerfish — small ones mostly, but they'll hammer a piece of clam or sand flea fished tight to the rocks in that 4 to 8 foot zone, and they're a fun distraction between bluefish runs.

Looking ahead, the tide is still running strong off that recent full moon, but it'll start easing toward neap by midweek, which usually means the bait disperses a little and those tight, explosive blitz windows spread out and get harder to predict. I'd expect the bluefish pattern to hold through the weekend if the southwest wind stays put and the water stays warm, but don't be surprised if the boils get shorter and more scattered by Tuesday or Wednesday. If a cold front does slide through later in the week like some are expecting, watch for it to shuffle the deck — a quick drop in surface temp could push bait tight to structure again and give the striped bass a reason to feed a little earlier than 11 p.m. That's the kind of shift worth adjusting your whole evening around, so keep an eye on the sky before you plan your tide.

reports.headline: Sea Girt Reef in 68 feet: sea bass to 4 pounds, bluefin working the Mud Hole thermocline
reports.subhead: The bottom bite is steady money right now — the tuna bite is real but you have to find the temperature seam, and it's moving.
reports.body_markdown:
Sea Girt Reef, 68 feet of water, four and a half miles off the inlet. That's the number I gave three different boats this week and all three came back with sea bass in the box — some pushing four pounds, most a solid fourteen to sixteen inches, which tells me the population out there is mature and it's not thinning out the way it usually does by late July. I've fished that reef for going on fifteen years and the pattern holds: pile of clam shells and tire structure on the south end, current running enough to keep bait tight to bottom, and the fish stack up in the breaks between the high spots. Squid strips on a two-hook bottom rig, or a Gulp Grub in white on a 4-ounce jig if the tide's really moving — either one works when you're right on top of the structure. Axel Carlson and Shrewsbury Rocks are producing the same way, slightly shallower water, slightly smaller average fish, but you won't go home skunked.

That's the dependable half of the week. The other half — the tuna — is where you earn it.

We flagged this last week: surface temps offshore running into the upper 70s with a well-defined thermocline holding bait in that 60 to 90 foot band, and that's exactly what's setting up the bite on the Mud Hole lumps right now. I had a report Tuesday of bluefin working bait balls on the northeast corner of the Hole, birds diving, fish coming up on the troll in that same depth window — spreads with green machines and cedar plugs out at 100 to 120 feet on the wire, small green-and-white or naked ballyhoo up top. Not a wide-open bite. More like windows — an hour of activity when the bait gets pushed up against the thermocline edge, then it goes quiet until the current shifts again. That's typical for this time of year on the Hole. You want to be on the water early, working the edges where the warm surface layer meets that cooler subsurface push, and you want your eyes on the birds more than your eyes on the sounder.

Farther out, yellowfin are working the canyon-adjacent structure from Hudson south through the Washington and Wilmington drops, riding a warm-water filament that's pushed further north than you'd expect for the end of July. That's outside true midrange range for most of the Manasquan/Belmar fleet unless you're running a boat that can cover sixty-plus miles comfortably, but for the guys who make that run, the reports have been solid — yellowfin in the 30 to 50 pound class on trolled ballyhoo and small spreader bars, and some jigging success once they're marked holding under the birds. If that filament holds its position — and there's no sign yet that it's sliding — I'd expect that yellowfin bite to stay consistent into next week. The risk is always the same out there: these warm tongues move, and a boat that found fish Tuesday can find nothing Thursday if the edge shifted twenty miles overnight.

Mahi are just starting to show around the pot buoys and any floating structure inshore of the Klondike — weed lines, lobster gear, the occasional piece of debris. It's early. I wouldn't call it a pattern yet, more like a handful of scattered fish, small ones mixed with a few keepers in the 4 to 6 pound range, taken on small spreader bars and split-tail mullet skirts pulled slow past the pots. August is when that fishery typically turns on around here as the warm water builds and holds, so if you're planning a trip specifically for mahi, I'd give it another week or two before betting the whole day on it. Right now it's a bonus fish while you're running out to the tuna grounds, not a destination.

Bonito and false albacore haven't shown in this zone yet, and I'm not going to pretend they have. The thermal setup up in Montauk and Block Island has crossed the threshold where those fish typically arrive, and if that pattern pushes south the way it usually does, we could see early scouts working the surf line and inlet edges off Sea Girt or Manasquan within the next couple weeks. Worth keeping a light spinning rod rigged with small metal on the boat just in case you run into a nervous bait pod on the way out — but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

Sea conditions have been workable but not flat — running 3 to 4 feet at a short period out on the reef line, which is fine for bottom fishing but makes the ride out to the Mud Hole and beyond a bit of a washing machine in an afternoon sea breeze. If you're running out there, I'd leave early, fish the tuna window in the calmer morning hours, and be ready to duck inshore to the reef structure if it kicks up.

Looking ahead: if this warm-water pattern holds through the week the way it has the last several days, I expect the sea bass bite to stay steady on Sea Girt, Axel Carlson, and the Barnegat Ridge wrecks, and the bluefin window on the Mud Hole to keep opening in short bursts tied to bait movement rather than any all-day blitz. The yellowfin bite south should hold as long as that filament stays put — that's the piece I'd watch closest, because when it slides, the whole game moves with it. Mahi should build through August as usual. Bonito, keep an ear out — this is the window where the first real report could break.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues Chop the Surface, Bass Have Gone to Ground
reports.subhead: Six straight days of bluefish limits off Belmar and blitzing surf from Sea Bright to Manasquan — but the stripers want nothing to do with daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six, north side of the Manasquan jetty, and I'm standing next to a kid throwing a Yo-Zuri popper into what looks like a pot of boiling water. Peanut bunker are getting shredded thirty yards off the tip, blues coming up under them like they're being fired out of a cannon, and this kid's grinning like it's his first day on earth. It's not blitz season yet where I need to remind anybody how to act — it's the kind of morning where you just point and cast and something eats.

We flagged this pattern coming — said back on the 24th this was the leading edge of a coastwide blitz, and by the 27th we were calling the bunker-bluefish run the story of the month. Here it is, still running. The boat out of Belmar has strung together six days straight of limit bags, and word from the dock is bigger fish started mixing into those bags around the 27th — proper 6, 7 pound blues, not just the choppers. That's a fresh wave pushing down from the north, and it's been feeding the surf same as it's been feeding the rail.

Water's sitting warm — mid-70s pushing toward 80 in the shallows off the beach — and that's the whole story right there. Blues love it. Bass hate it. Stripers want that 68-to-72 window, and right now the only way to find water that cold on this stretch is to go deep or go dark. I've had two decent nights on the rocks at Sea Bright this week — nothing that'll make the wall at the tackle shop, but a few fish in the 28 to 32 inch range on live eels drifted off the north jetty on the last two hours of the outgoing, into the start of the incoming. That tide change is when the current slows enough for an eel to swim natural instead of getting swept sideways into the rocks. Fished it around 11pm and again just before first light — dead water in between, which tells you these fish are strictly a dark-hours program right now. Bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig, fished tight to the base of the rocks at Manasquan Inlet's south jetty, have taken a couple more after midnight, but you're working for every bite. Anybody telling you the bass bite is easy this week is selling you something.

During the day, forget the stripers and go where the blues are, because that part of the program is honestly fun fishing. Spring Lake and Belmar jetties are holding pods of peanut bunker getting worked over on both tides — I watched three separate blitzes Tuesday morning between 6 and 8am, one right off the Belmar fishing pier, bait getting pushed right up against the rocks and blues crashing through it in full daylight, no subtlety required. Poppers and darters — the old standby Gibbs Polaris, a Super Strike popper if the water's got any chop on it — thrown right into the froth. You don't need finesse. You need to get a lure in the water before the school moves fifty yards down the beach, which they will, over and over, all morning.

Fluke's been the quiet, honest bite while everything else makes noise. We said last week the inlet structure and the nearshore reef sites would carry the fluke program through the full moon tide build, and that's exactly what's happened — steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for this time of year. Manasquan Inlet channel, 20 to 28 feet on the drift, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, working the deeper cuts on the last of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but you're not getting swept into the rocks. Shark River Inlet's been giving up a similar grade of fish — mostly keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, nothing over 4 pounds that I've seen or heard about, but a limit's very doable if you're willing to make three or four drifts through the same stretch. Sea bass are filling out the box on the days the fluke bite is slow to start — same structure, same drift, they just eat first thing before the fluke get moving with the sun higher.

Tide's still carrying some push from the full moon, and that extra flow has helped keep the bait pinned and moving, which is half of why the blitz windows have been so reliable. That's going to ease over the next several days as we drift toward neap, and when it does I'd expect the blitzes to spread out a little — bait less concentrated means the blues have to work harder to find it, and you'll have to work harder to find them. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to in early August, it'll scatter things for a tide or two before it resets.

My plan for the coming week: dawn and last light on the rocks with eels and bunker chunks for stripers, accepting it's a grind; daylight hours chasing the blitz wherever the gulls tell me to go, from Sea Bright down through Spring Lake; and a couple of fluke drifts at Manasquan and Shark River on the tide changes to round out the box. Keep an eye out for the first false albacore scouting reports — too early yet on this stretch, but if that warm-water edge holds and pushes a temperature break up the coast, they won't be far behind the blues.

reports.headline: Barnegat Bay fluke slide deep as the shallows hit 80 — bluefish keep kids busy, weakfish thin out
reports.subhead: Heat's got the flounder hugging channel edges and bridge structure while snapper blues save the trip for everybody else.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a summer back in the late '80s, right around this same stretch of July, when my old skipper on the Point Pleasant boats told me something I never forgot: "Gus, when the mud flats start steaming, the fluke go looking for the basement." We were anchored off Tices Shoal that morning, watching heat shimmer come up off the sedge at low tide, and sure enough the flounder we'd been picking off the flats all June had vanished. We found them that afternoon stacked in eighteen feet of water on the edge of Double Creek Channel, and I've chased that same pattern every scorching July since.

That's exactly where we are right now. The shallows in the back bay — up around Toms River, the flats off Good Luck Point, the skinny water inside Oyster Creek — are pushing close to 80 degrees under this stretch of sun and southwest wind, and the fluke have done what they always do when it gets like this: they've packed up and moved into the deeper channels and bridge structure where the water stays a few degrees more livable. Double Creek Channel has been the most consistent address, 15 to 22 feet on the drift, and the Route 37 bridge pilings on the Seaside side are holding fish tight to the current seams. Standard program — 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a chunk of squid or a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some shoulder to it. We're getting a mix of keepers and shorts, nothing blitz-style, but a patient drift will put two or three fish over 18 inches in the box for anybody willing to work the structure instead of just soaking bait in open water.

Weakfish have been the disappointment of the week, if I'm honest. Back in May those sedge banks down toward Barnegat Light were holding solid pods of tiderunners, but the heat's scattered them — I'm hearing about isolated pockets on the drop-offs near the Inlet channel edges, mostly at first light or the last hour of dusk when the water's cooled a touch, and they're not schooled up tight enough to call it a pattern yet. If you want a shot, work a 1/4-ounce chartreuse or pink jighead tipped with a strip of squid right on the lip where the channel drops from six feet to twelve, and be ready for it to be one or two fish and done.

What's actually saving trips right now is the bluefish. Snapper blues and small cocktail fish are thick throughout the bay — off the docks in Forked River, along the bulkheads at Barnegat Light, out at Tices Shoal — and they'll hit just about anything that flashes. Small Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, or a piece of bunker on a snapper rig under a bobber is about as easy as fishing gets, and it's the best thing going for anybody with kids aboard who just want bent rods. We flagged this pattern last week and said stable, hot conditions would keep it running steady through the weekend — that's held up exactly as expected, and there's no reason to think it breaks unless the wind shifts hard out of the northeast.

Striped bass are around but they've gone the way they always do this time of year — deep and nocturnal. The water's simply too warm during daylight for them to feed comfortably, so the better fish are holding on structure in the deeper stretches near Barnegat Inlet and feeding mainly after dark or right on the tide change at dawn. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom near the Coast Guard station channel, or a live eel drifted through the inlet rips on the tail of the outgoing, have accounted for a few decent fish in the 28 to 34-inch range for guys willing to fish the graveyard shift. It's not a numbers game right now — it's one good bite a trip if you put in the time.

Blowfish are still there for anybody who wants a relaxed afternoon — sandy bottom pockets inside Barnegat Light and along the ICW near Waretown are holding good numbers on small pieces of clam or bloodworm fished on a two-hook bottom rig. Kingfish are mixing in on the same bottom, especially where there's a little sand and shell mix, so it pays to keep a rod rigged light while you're anchored up for blowfish.

Tides are easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which usually softens the current just enough to spread bait out rather than concentrate it — expect the fluke bite to stay steady rather than explosive, and the bluefish to keep doing what they're doing regardless. What this bay really needs is a passing front to knock a few degrees off those shallow flats; if we get one, even a glancing shot of rain and cooler air midweek, I'd expect the flounder to push back up onto Tices Shoal and the flats off Good Luck Point, and the weakfish bite to tighten back up on the drop-offs. Until then, fish the channels, fish the structure, and don't waste tide chasing fish that packed up and left the shallows for a reason.

reports.headline: Bunker Push the Bay Full of Blues, Bass Slide Deep and Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: With Raritan Bay running warm and bunker schools thick from Keyport to the Hook, blues own the daylight and stripers only show once the sun's down.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the call I made Tuesday morning standing on the bulkhead in Perth Amboy watching bunker pods roll past thick as a carpet: mornings on the flats for fluke, evenings working the bunker schools for blues, and save the bass program for full dark. That's the split right now, and if you try to force stripers during the day in this water temp, you're wasting bait.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker-bluefish push coming up from the south would hit this zone hard by the weekend, and it did. The bay's holding bunker in numbers I haven't seen stacked this heavy since early June, rolling thick off Keyport, working up past Flynn's Knoll, and pushing into the mouth of the Raritan. Where the bunker go, the blues follow, and right now they're everywhere in that school — snapping at the edges, blowing up on top mid-morning off Romer Shoal, and again in the last hour of daylight along the Hook side of the channel. Nothing subtle about it. If you see gulls diving and mullet-colored water churning white, put the boat on it and throw metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks, Ava jigs with a green tube, anything that flashes through that ball fast. You don't need finesse for these blues, you need to get a bait in the strike zone before the school moves off, because they're covering ground fast chasing bunker pushed by the tide.

Stripers are a different animal right now and this is the part guys keep getting wrong. Bay surface temps have been sitting in that mid-70s range, pushing toward 80 in the shallower flats by afternoon, and that's above where bass want to be. They're not gone — they're just smart. They're sitting deep, either suspended under the bunker schools or holed up on structure — the wrecks off Romer Shoal, the deeper cuts through the Chapel Hill Channel, the drop along the edge of Flynn's Knoll where the bottom falls from eight feet to eighteen. During the day those fish are basically shut down. Wait for the last hour of light and through the night and it flips completely. I've had my best bass action this week drifting bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 2-3 ounces of lead depending on current, right on the bottom edge of that Flynn's Knoll drop starting an hour before dark and running through the first part of the incoming tide. Fresh bunker beats frozen right now — cut a fresh one you snagged out of the school an hour earlier and it's a different bite entirely. Eels fished the same way, slow-trolled or drifted along the Highlands side of the channel after dark, have also been putting bigger fish in the boat — nothing huge, mostly mid-20s to low 30-inch fish, but they're there if you commit to the night program.

Fluke are the honest, dependable piece of this whole puzzle and they haven't cared one bit about the warm surface water because they're living on the bottom where it's cooler.
