The Keyport Flats have been steady — not blitz numbers, but a solid keeper mixed in with shorts on almost every drift if you're covering the channel edges right. I've been working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, drifting the drop-offs where the flats fall into the channel in 12 to 20 feet. The Chapel Hill Channel edge and the deeper water off Great Beds Light have both given up keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range on the outgoing tide, when current pulls bait off the flats and concentrates it right on that edge. Slow drift, bounce bottom, don't overwork it — these fish are eating, they're just not chasing far.

The Navesink hasn't been anything special this week — warm, slow-moving water, and I'd rather burn gas running to the Hook side than waste a tide up there right now. If you want a change of pace, weakfish have shown in small numbers mixed with the bluefish schools on bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished slow near bottom on the edges of the bunker pods — nothing to build a trip around, but a nice surprise if one grabs.

Looking ahead, I don't expect this pattern to break unless we get a real shift in weather. The tides are easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which should slow the current a touch and might let those bunker schools spread out rather than staying balled tight — if that happens, the blitz-style blue fishing could thin out even as individual blues stay around. Bass will stay married to the night program as long as this warm stretch holds; the only thing that changes that is a real cool-down or a string of northeast wind stirring the bottom. If I had one evening this week, I'd be on the bunker schools off Flynn's Knoll right at last light, working blues on top until the sun's down, then switching to chunk bait on bottom for an hour of dark before calling it. That's where the bay's telling me to be right now.

reports.headline: Valiant Rock Slack at 11:42: Bass Holding on Wire in 55 Feet
reports.subhead: The Race is easing toward neap but the bass never left Valiant — you just have to hit the window right.
reports.body_markdown:
Four-point-one knots. That's what I clocked on the last max ebb through The Race on Wednesday, GPS-tracked drifting off Valiant Rock with 400 feet of wire out the transom. A week ago that same tide was running closer to five — we're sliding off the full moon push toward neap as the tide cycle winds down before it builds back up for the August 12 new moon. Less water moving through the gut means the bite windows stretch a little longer, which is good news if you've ever tried to get a bucktail down through five knots of white water and felt like you were fishing a fire hose.

Here's what that means on the water: slack at Valiant this week is running close to 11:40 in the late morning and shifting into the early evening around 6:15, give or take ten minutes day to day — check your local corrected tide before you commit, because a five-minute miss on either side of true slack there is the difference between a controlled drift and getting your wire line swept sideways into the rocks. I've been starting my drifts about twenty minutes before predicted slack, working from the 55-foot trough on the northeast side of the rock down into the 70-foot hole, wire line straight down with a 2-ounce bucktail tipped with a chunk of fresh bunker. Bass are there — not stacked, but present, mostly mid-20s to low 30s with a few pushing 20 pounds mixed in when I hit the tide change right on the nose. Anything after slack, once the current starts building again, the fish drop tight to the bottom of the rock pile and you need the wire just to hold depth against the drift.

Race Rock itself has been quieter than Valiant — I think the bait's thinner there right now, and with the Sound running warmer than the fish like (Kings Point read 70.9 this week, New London closer to 69.4), the stripers are picking their structure carefully, holding wherever the current stacks bait against hard bottom rather than spreading out over open rock. That thermal split between the western Sound and out here at the eastern end matters. New London's cooler water is exactly why we're still seeing quality fish on structure instead of pushed strictly nocturnal like they are further west and down the Jersey shore, where Hooper's crew and everybody else is reporting bass going deep and dark because the surface is pushing near 80.

Plum Gut has been the more consistent read the last several days. Current there tops out lower than The Race — I saw 3.6 knots on the last good ebb — but it concentrates bait hard against the east side drop-off toward Great Gull Island. Bluefish have moved in thick on that structure, choppers in the 8-to-12-pound class hammering diamond jigs and bucktails fished just off bottom in 35 to 50 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're throwing wire for bass and getting your leader bit off every other drift, that's your answer — the blues are mixed right in with the stripers right now, and honestly some days they're outnumbering them two to one. Not a bad problem to have if you just want bent rods, but if you're targeting bass specifically I'd fish bunker-tipped bucktails on the bottom third of the water column and let the smaller profile jigs stay up top for the blues.

Fluke have been steady rather than spectacular on the sand pockets flanking the Gut and along the edges of the Sluiceway, drifting Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails through 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming. Keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — a decent box fish if you cover water, not a limit-in-an-hour bite. Sea bass remain the most dependable thing going right now. The wrecks and reef structure north of Plum Gut and around Little Gull are holding fish all day regardless of tide stage, and that's been the honest bread-and-butter program while the bigger species sort themselves out.

On the albie and bonito front — nothing confirmed yet in the Gut or off Valiant, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. We flagged two weeks back that water temps at Montauk and Block Island were crossing the threshold and that building current should trigger the first real showing, and Montauk's still sitting right at 69.1, which is squarely in that window. I've had my eyes on the rips off Great Gull and the Sluiceway edge every trip, epoxy jig rigged and ready, and I haven't seen a scout yet. That could change fast — these fish show up on a good temperature break with almost no warning, and the building tide cycle heading toward mid-August is exactly the kind of setup that's produced early runs in past years.

For the coming week: with tides easing toward neap, expect longer, more fishable slack windows at Valiant and the Gut, which favors the wire-line program over covering water fast. If you've got one trip in you, I'd fish the evening slack at Valiant Rock and work the drop into darkness — that's where the bigger fish have been showing. Keep a bucktail rigged light in the box just in case something with a torpedo body and no patience for a slow retrieve finally shows up in the Gut.

reports.headline: Ram Island bait balls hold tight, but the albies haven't found Stonington yet
reports.subhead: Bass are stacking on structure as the tide rebuilds out of neap — the false albacore push is close, just not here.
reports.body_markdown:
I poled the skiff over the boulder field off Wamphassuc Point on the last hour of Wednesday's ebb and watched a school of peanut bunker come apart against a rock the size of a Buick — scattering in every direction, some of them skipping clear of the water. That's the tell. Something was under them, working the seam where the current pinches between two granite heads about four feet down. I couldn't get a fly through it before the school reformed and slid off toward deeper water, but I didn't need to see the fish to know what that was. Bass do that to bait around here. Bluefish don't bother with the subtlety.

That's been the story most of this week — bait getting nervous around structure, current doing the work, fish showing up when the tide gives them a reason to. We flagged this last week — said the Sound's current had gone soft on the neap cycle and the bite would come back as the tide rebuilt — and that's exactly what's happening. New London is reading 69.4 degrees, which is comfortable water for stripers to sit tight to rock instead of running deep and nocturnal like they're doing out west where Kings Point is pushing near 71. That few degrees of difference matters. It's why Fishers Island Sound is still a daylight program right now while other parts of the coast have gone to bunker-and-eel-after-dark mode.

The stripers I'm finding are on the classic spots — the boulder chain running off Ram Island, the rock pile east of Wilcox Reef, and the drop just outside the Stonington breakwater where the bottom goes from six feet to eighteen in about thirty yards. Slack water and the first hour of the flood have been the window. I'm throwing a 3/8-ounce bucktail dressed with white curly-tail, working it slow along the bottom contour so it ticks off the rock without hanging. On the fly side, a olive-and-white Deceiver on an intermediate line, cast tight to the boulders and stripped erratic, has drawn some of the better fish — nothing huge, mostly 22 to 28 inches, with the occasional fish pushing 34 that made the leader hum for a few seconds before it wedged me into the rocks and I lost it. That's the tax you pay fishing this water. You lose gear here. It's part of the deal.

Fluke have been steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for this time of year. The mouth of the Mystic River and the flats off Enders Island are holding fish on the last of the outgoing, staging on the sand pockets between the mussel beds. Four-inch white Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow, has been out-producing bigger baits — the fish down there are picking, not aggressive, and a subtle presentation gets more bites than a big splashy one. Keepers have been mixed with plenty of shorts, so it's a sort-through-them program, not a fill-the-cooler one. Black sea bass are doing what they always do out toward the Watch Hill Reef and around East Point — reliable, unglamorous, biting green crab and squid strips on the bottom in eighteen to twenty-five feet. If you want dinner and don't need a story to go with it, that's still the surest bet in this whole stretch of water.

Now, the albies. Everybody's asking, and I don't have them yet. The setup is close — the temperature threshold that gets albies moving has already been crossed out at Montauk, Block Island, and up into the Buzzards Bay corridor, and this section of the Sound is usually one of the earlier stops once that push starts working west, given how close we sit to those eastern approaches. But close isn't here. I ran Wicopesset Passage and along the edge of Fishers Island at first light three mornings this week looking for that nervous, scattered bait pattern that means albies are working underneath it, and what I found was gulls sitting quiet on the water and bait moving in slow, undisturbed pods. That's not an albie sign. That's just bait doing its thing.

What I'd watch for over the next week: the tide is building back out of neap toward the August 12 new moon, which means more current strength through Fishers Island Sound and Little Narragansett Bay, and that's exactly the kind of push that tends to bring the first scouting albies and bonito in behind the bait they're chasing. If I had one morning to spend chasing them, I'd be at the Watch Hill rip or working the rock line off Napatree Point on an outgoing tide with a small epoxy jig rigged and ready, because that's usually the first place this water shows sign — even a single blitz that lasts ten minutes and then vanishes. Until then, the stripers on structure are the honest play. Fish the rock, fish it slow, and respect that this ground doesn't give anything away for free. It never has, going back to when my grandfather was running boats out of the Portuguese fleet — you learn where the rocks are, or you pay for not knowing.

reports.headline: Dog Days on the River — Bass Go Deep, Snappers Take Over the Coves
reports.subhead: With the shad long gone upriver and the water pushing into the mid-70s, the lower Connecticut settles into its slow, warm-water summer rhythm.
reports.body_markdown:
The greenheads are thick in the marsh grass off Old Lyme this week, which tells you everything you need to know about where we are in the season. Shad are a memory now — those big roe fish that packed the river back in April, working up past Essex toward the Enfield rapids, they're long gone, scattered somewhere between here and the headwaters of Massachusetts and Vermont, doing what shad do this time of year, which is nothing anyone on this river gets to see. That run feels like a lifetime ago by the time you're standing on the rocks at Saybrook Point in July with sweat running into your eyes and the marsh smelling like low tide and cut grass.

This is the slow season on the lower river, and I mean that in the way an old-timer means it — not dead, just patient. The river's running low and warm, the current soft on the ebb, and with Long Island Sound holding in the low 70s off Kings Point and high 60s off New London, our water at the mouth here isn't far behind. I'd put the flow off Saybrook Point in the mid-70s most afternoons, and that number matters, because striped bass don't love water that warm. They tolerate it. Above 72 or so they start looking for relief — deeper water, moving current, shade under a dock, anything that isn't direct sun on shallow flats.

What that means on the water is simple: the good bass fishing has shrunk down to a window. Dawn, dusk, and full dark. I've had better luck the last two weeks working the channel edge off the Baldwin Bridge and the deep bend below Essex right at first light, before the sun gets up over the trees and starts cooking the flats. Live eels drifted on the current seams, or bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig tight to the bottom where the channel drops off — that's been the program. Nothing explosive, but a couple of solid fish in the 28 to 34-inch range have come off that stretch on the outgoing tide, right as the current starts really moving water out past Great Island.

Speaking of Great Island — that's still the nursery it's always been, and right now it's snapper blue water, plain and simple. Those young bluefish are thick in the coves and guts behind the island, chasing whatever's small and silver in three and four feet of water. If you've got a kid who wants steady action, small silver spoons or a piece of squid on a bare hook under a bobber back in those channels will keep a rod bent all afternoon. It's not glamorous fishing but it's honest fishing, and it's about the best bet going in the heat of the day when the bigger stuff has gone quiet.

White perch are doing what they always do in late summer — working the marsh creeks and the slower water up around the DEP Marina in Old Lyme, taking small jigs and worms fished slow along the bottom. Nothing trophy-sized, but a mixed bag of perch and the occasional small bass in that same stretch has been enough to make an evening worthwhile, especially with the bugs backing off once the sun drops.

The bigger bluefish — the choppers — have shown up sporadically at the outer bar off the river mouth when there's bait around, usually bunker pushed in tight by the tide. I heard of a run of them working the rip off Saybrook Point for about twenty minutes on an outgoing tide last week, enough to turn a slow morning into a good one for whoever happened to be positioned right with a metal jig in hand. That's the nature of it this time of year — short, sharp windows, not sustained action. You need to be in position when the tide and the bait line up, and then you need a little luck.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions would hold stable and that the warm-water bass pattern would persist as long as the weather stayed put — and that's exactly the week we got. No fronts, no big wind shift, just steady heat and a river settling into its summer groove. I don't expect much to change over the next several days either. The moon's building back toward the new moon on August 12th, which means tides will start pushing a little harder as we get into next week, and that extra current could help stir things up at the mouth and around Great Island. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at the Baldwin Bridge current seam an hour before first light with an eel in my hand, working the last of the dark before the sun starts pushing that water temperature back up. After that, I'd be looking for shade, a cold drink, and waiting for the tide to turn again after dark.

reports.headline: Plum Gut Stayed Quiet — Rocky Point's Porgies Never Missed a Beat
reports.subhead: Warm water is keeping the bass honest after dark, but the scup bite on the reefs is the one thing you can plan a whole day around.
reports.body_markdown:
Kid pulled up to the Mattituck ramp Tuesday morning, maybe twenty-five years old, rod already rigged with a topwater plug, asking me if the bass were "going off" out front. I told him what I tell everybody who asks me that this time of year — go home, come back at nine o'clock tonight. He looked at me like I'd told him to go fish the parking lot. Didn't listen, of course. Fished two hours in bright sun, caught nothing but a sunburn, and I saw him back at the ramp at dusk rigging up a bunker chunk like he'd had the idea himself all along. That's how it goes out here in late July. Nobody believes the water temperature until it costs them a morning.

And the water is warm — Kings Point's reading just under 71, New London's sitting at 69 and change, and out my way in between, it's about the same story. That's above where a striped bass wants to live comfortably, and they know it better than we do. We said last week the mid-70s water would keep the bass a low-light game on this stretch, and that's exactly the hand we've been dealt. Daytime, they're down deep on the rock piles off Horton Point and Rocky Point, sulking, not feeding much. Come dark, they come up onto the current edges to work.

Best bass action right now is right at the mouth of the Gut and around Orient Point, fished on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, full dark or close to it. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or a whole eel drifted back through the rip if you've got the current for it — that's what's putting fish in the boat. Nothing huge, mostly schoolies and a few solid teens, but a couple guys have found slot fish working the seam where the Gut current meets the flat water off Orient. Don't waste your time bombing casts out into open water — these fish are sitting tight to the edges and the boils, feeding on the push, not chasing bait across open sound. Feather your cast right into the seam and let it sink.

Now the porgies — that's the bite I'd send a stranger to right now with confidence, and I don't say that about much this year. Rocky Point reef and the rock piles off Horton Point are stacked with scup, and they haven't slowed a step in this warm water, unlike the bass. Hi-lo rigs, size 4 or 6 hooks, clam or squid strips, right on the bottom in twenty to thirty-five feet. You'll go through shorts, but there are enough eight-and-nine-inch fish mixed in to make a nice pan of them. This is the bite you take a kid or a first-timer to. Steady, no drama, but it fills a cooler.

Blackfish are still mostly a memory for now — water's too warm for them to be doing much of anything, and I wouldn't waste bait on them till the water starts to slip back down in September. Fluke are around but scattered — I've heard of decent drifts along the channel edge at the Mattituck Inlet mouth, white Gulp swimming mullets on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing. You'll pick at shorts most of the drift and then find a stretch where two or three keepers come over the rail in twenty minutes. That's fluke fishing out here right now — not a blitz, just patience rewarded in patches.

Bluefish are the ones taking full advantage of this warm water nobody else wants. They don't care that it's pushing 71 degrees — if anything they like it. Peanut bunker schools have been getting worked over off Rocky Point and out toward Orient in the last light of the evening, blues busting bait on the surface hard enough to hear it from shore. Poppers or a diamond jig with a bit of surgical tubing will get hit fast if you can find the school, though they don't sit still long. If you see the birds working, don't wait — that window closes in ten minutes sometimes.

Weakfish I'll be honest with you — thin. A few reports of small fish mixed in with the bass at night around the Gut approach, nothing worth planning a trip around.

As for what's coming up on the Gut — I've had my eye out for the first albie scouting reports the way I mentioned last week, water's certainly warm enough for them to be curious, but nothing's showed yet that I'd call real. Full moon's put some extra push in the tides this week, which has helped stir bait around the structure, and if that current stays lively into next week while the surface holds warm, I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first albie or bonito rumor out of the Gut before the middle of August. Until then, I'd plan my week around the porgies for the guaranteed fun and save my night hours for the bass at Orient and the Gut mouth. If the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it's been, that pattern should hold — but keep an eye on any thunderstorm blowing through midweek, because a hard rain will dirty up the inlet mouth fast and shut the bite down for a tide or two until it clears.

reports.headline: Penfield's Ebb Window Pays Off in Blackfish While Bunker Keep Blues Stacked on the Cows
reports.subhead: The reef clock is running on schedule right now — fish the last two hours of ebb and you're in business; miss it and you're just burning gas.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday I had a decision to make at 5 a.m. sitting in the driveway with the truck running: Penfield Reef on the tail of the ebb, or run out to the Cows and chase the bunker schools that had been getting worked by blues all weekend. I picked Penfield. Here's why — that reef doesn't fish on just any tide. You want the last ninety minutes to two hours of the ebb, right as the rockpile starts to show its teeth and the current is still moving hard enough to sweep crabs and worms off the structure into the current break on the down-tide side. Too early and the water's still too deep over the reef to concentrate anything. Too late and it's dead slack with no current to push bait. That window is narrow, and this week it lined up with first light, which meant I had the reef mostly to myself before the weekend warriors even had coffee going.

It paid off. Blackfish to five pounds on green crab, fished on a knocker rig right up against the rock face in 12 to 18 feet, with a couple of porgies mixed in on the same drift using clam on a simple high-low. That's the read right now on Penfield — the porgies are thick enough that if you're not getting bit within a few minutes of anchoring up, you're in the wrong spot, not the wrong day. Same story out at the Cows off Stamford, where the porgy and black sea bass bite has been steady on the moving tide, either side of the change, working bloodworm or squid strips over the rockpile in 20 to 25 feet. Sea bass have been running a little better than average size for late July — 14 to 16 inches isn't rare out there right now, which tells me the warmer water sitting around 71 degrees on the western end of the Sound is keeping them comfortable and feeding instead of shutting down like they sometimes do this deep into summer.

The bluefish, though — that's been the story of the week, and it's not really a surprise. We flagged this pattern last week, that the blitz conditions would hold as long as the warm water stayed put, and that's exactly what's happened. Peanut bunker schools have been getting run over by blues from the Norwalk Islands down through Sheffield Island and out toward the Cows, mostly a mid-morning to early afternoon program once the sun's up and the bait pushes to the surface. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — worked right through the surface commotion has been about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. If you see the water nervous and gulls working low, don't overthink it, just get a lure in there before the boat traffic scatters the school, because on a Saturday that window can close in twenty minutes once six center consoles converge on the same slick.

Striped bass have been the tougher assignment, and I won't dress it up. With Kings Point reading 70.9 and the whole western basin running warm, the bass are doing what they do this time of year — sliding off the shallow structure during daylight and setting up on deeper current edges and holes, feeding mainly at first light, last light, and through the night on bunker and eels. I've had better luck working eels along the channel edge off Greenwich Point on the last of the incoming, right at dusk, than I have anywhere on the open reef structure during the day. If you want a daytime shot at a slot fish, the drop-off on the northeast side of Cockenoe Reef during the first hour of the ebb has produced a few, but it's a needle-in-a-haystack proposition right now compared to the reliability of the bottom bite.

Fluke are the honest middle-of-the-road fish this week — not a blitz, not a bust. Channel edges around the Norwalk Islands and the drop-off on the west side of Sheffield Island have been giving up keepers mixed with plenty of shorts on white Gulp swimming mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift during the outgoing. Nothing that'll fill a cooler fast, but steady enough that if you're patient and willing to cull through shorts, dinner's not a problem.

Tides are easing down off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which usually means current speeds soften a touch on these reefs — worth noting because some of these structure bites, especially Penfield and the Cows, actually get a little more forgiving on timing when the tide isn't screaming. I'd expect the porgy and blackfish program to hold steady through the week, the bluefish blitz to keep showing up wherever the bunker schools settle, and the stripers to stay locked into that dawn-dusk-dark pattern until we get a real cool-down. If I had one morning to burn this week, I'd still take Penfield on the ebb — but I'd have the popper rod rigged and ready in case the gulls tip me off to something better on the way out.

reports.headline: Twotree Fluke Bite Rebuilds as Tide Fills In — Black Point Stacked With Sea Bass
reports.subhead: The neap slack finally broke, and from Niantic Bay to Hole-in-the-Wall the drift boats are putting keepers in the box again.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic fleet mates filling the bait tank Tuesday morning and he didn't even let me finish my coffee before he started talking fluke. Said the last three days out of the bay have been the best stretch since the Fourth — fish stacked up on the edges of Twotree Island Channel in 35 to 45 feet, and for the first time in a couple weeks the current actually had some shoulder to it. We flagged this exact thing last week — said the softened neap current was holding this zone back and it'd come around as the tide cycle rebuilt, and that's precisely what happened. Once that current started moving real water again, the fluke that had been sitting on their hands started sliding up onto the drop-offs to feed.

The program right now is textbook Twotree: white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow along the channel edge on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the high. Keepers are mixing with a lot of shorts, so it's not a five-minute limit trip, but guys are grinding out three, four, five keeper fluke a rod in a half day when they hit the tide right. Black Point has been the same story in slightly shallower water, 28 to 35 feet, with the better fish coming off the sandy pockets between the rock piles rather than sitting tight to structure. If you're bouncing bucktails there, don't be afraid to let it hop bottom on the drift — the bigger fish have been eating on the pause, not the retrieve.

Sea bass are the sure thing right now, and I mean that in the honest sense — not blowing smoke, just telling you what's biting. Black Point reef and the rock piles off Hole-in-the-Wall are loaded with them in 30 to 50 feet. Jigging Spro bucktails tipped with squid or fresh clam is putting good numbers of 14 to 17-inch fish in coolers, with a scattering of shorts you'll be tossing back all day. Bring extra clam — they'll strip a hook clean in ten feet of current if you're slow to reset. Porgies are riding shotgun on the same drifts, chewing sandworms and clam on high-low rigs anywhere there's shell or rock, and they've been a nice bonus for anybody who wants a mixed bag rather than a species-specific trip.

Striped bass are the interesting piece this week, because Eastern Sound water is actually running a touch cooler than the rest of the Sound — New London's reading around 69.4 degrees, versus the low-to-mid 70s you're seeing farther west toward the city. That's still inside the window where bass will feed with some confidence during the day, not just at first and last light. It's showing on the water — guys working bunker schools off McCook Point and the mouth of the Niantic River at dawn are still connecting on slot fish up to 30-something inches, working white bucktails and small bunker spoons through the edges of the pods. But once the sun gets up and that shallow water warms, the bite shuts down fast and the better fish slide off into deeper, current-swept water and don't show again until dusk. If you want a real shot at a bigger bass, fish live eels or chunked bunker on the outgoing at Hole-in-the-Wall after dark — that's been the more consistent producer for size the last two weeks, even if the numbers are lower than the dawn bunker bite.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with those bunker schools, and when they show up they show up hard — cocktail blues to slammers blitzing bait right on the surface off Black Point and the outer bay in the early morning. Poppers and metal like a Kastmaster or a Hopkins will get bit fast when they're up, but it's a short window before the school moves or sounds.

Now here's the piece everybody at the dock has started whispering about. We put this zone on early bonito and albie watch a few days back given how close we sit to the Race and Fishers Island corridor, and there's chatter starting to circulate about bait behavior out that way that's consistent with the first scouts showing up. Nothing confirmed yet, no verified fish on the beach, but the water's setting up the way it usually does right before those first false albacore show — warm stable water, good bait concentrations, current lines sharpening up as the tide rebuilds toward the August 12 new moon. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet, but if you're out around the Race or working the rips off Fishers, keep a light spinning rod rigged with an epoxy jig or a small Deadly Dick within reach. That's the kind of thing that shows up with zero warning.

Looking ahead, the tide's only getting stronger as we build back toward the new moon, which should keep concentrating bait and fish around structure at Twotree and Black Point. If we get a passing thunderstorm or two this week — pretty typical for early August — expect a day or two of disrupted current and dirty water before it settles back into rhythm. My plan for the next few days is simple: fluke and sea bass on the day tide, bunker schools at first light for stripers, and an eye on the horizon for that first albie sign.

reports.headline: Breakwall Porgies Stack Up While Charles Island Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: Sea bass and porgies keep the rockpiles honest in daylight, but the stripers have punched the night shift card at Charles Island and the Shoal.
reports.body_markdown:
Friday morning, half tide coming in, I dropped a double-hook rig tipped with green crab off the outer breakwall at New Haven Harbor and had a doubleheader of porgies before my buddy Ray even got his second rod rigged. Eight-inchers, some pushing nine, coming two at a time off the rocks on the east side where the current sweeps hardest. That's the story of my week — the structure stuff hasn't blinked, even while everything pelagic in this Sound has gone squirrely with the heat.

Water's sitting in the low 70s across the western basin — Kings Point read 70.9 the other day, and that warmth has pushed clean into our zone. New London out east is still a couple degrees cooler at 69.4, and that gradient matters more than people think. It means the porgies and black sea bass, which don't mind warm water one bit, are locked in and feeding hard on the reef structure — Charles Island bar, the rockpiles off Milford Gulf, both jetties at the harbor mouth. But it also means the stripers, which like it more like 68 to 72, have gone deep and gone dark. If you're bass fishing at noon right now off Charles Island, you're wasting bait.

Sea bass have been the real bright spot. I've had good drifts in 25 to 35 feet off Falkner Island on the last two hours of the incoming, squid strips and clam belly on a two-hook bottom rig with 3-ounce sinkers to hold in that current. Fish to 17 inches, a few shorts mixed in that go back, but enough keepers that three of us walked off with a dozen good ones Sunday. The bite window there is tight — it dies the second the tide goes slack, so time your trip around the moving water, not the clock.

Blackfish are still a touch early for the real conversation, but I've been picking up a few incidental fish jigging green crab around the rockpiles at Stratford Shoal, which tells me the tautog are starting to stage even if the dedicated bite is a few weeks off yet.

Stripers are the frustrating part of the week, and I'll be straight about it — daytime action off Charles Island bar has been dead slow. I made three trips out there between 10 and 2 and managed one 24-inch fish on a white bucktail worked slow along the sandbar drop-off. That's it. What's actually happening is the fish have slid off that structure into deeper, cooler water and gone strictly nocturnal — dawn, dusk, full dark, working bunker schools on the tide changes. If you want stripers right now, fish the bottom of the ebb into the top of the flood starting an hour before sunset, working eels or bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet off the north side of the island, or drift live bait over the deeper edges of Stratford Shoal after dark. That's where the quality fish are sitting out the heat.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the neap tide had softened the current and it'd rebuild over the next few days, and sure enough the moving water off Falkner and the harbor mouth has come back with some real push behind it this week. That stronger current is exactly why the porgy and sea bass bite has stayed consistent — moving water stacks the bait against structure, and these fish don't need convincing.

Bluefish have been showing in pulses off Hammonasset and along the beach at Charles Island, chopping through peanut bunker schools mid-morning. Nothing like the sustained blitz pattern they're seeing down the Jersey shore right now, but if you see birds working close to the beach, a silver spoon or a Hopkins jig thrown into the fray will get bit fast — just watch your fingers on the release, these have teeth.

Fluke have been a quiet, steady presence in the deeper basin off Milford Gulf, 25 to 40 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on bucktails tipped with squid strips. Nothing huge — most going 16 to 18 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but it's a dependable program if the bottom bite is what you're after and you want a break from the structure grind.

Looking ahead, I don't see much changing in the next few days. Wind's been light and stable, water's holding warm, and that combination should keep the porgy and sea bass program rolling on the rockpiles same as it has been. The building tide cycle heading toward the mid-August new moon should start concentrating bait tighter around the structure, which is usually when the blackfish start showing up in real numbers on purpose instead of by accident. For stripers, I'd keep playing the night program at Charles Island and the Shoal until this warm stretch breaks — if we get a good northeast blow or a cold front pushes through, watch for those fish to slide back up onto the bar during daylight again. Until then, set your alarm for last light, not first.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Rip Still Working the Ebb — Bass Deep, Blues Owning the Surface
reports.subhead: New London's water is running a shade cooler than the rest of the Sound, and that half-degree is buying the Thames a better bass bite than most river systems get in late July.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a spot off Fort Trumbull where the current pinches between the old fort wall and the river channel, and on a hard ebb it throws a standing seam you can read from fifty yards out — a line of nervous water where the smooth flow off the flats collides with the deeper channel push. That seam has been holding fish all week, and it's the first place I point the bow when the tide turns.

New London is reading 69.4 degrees right now, which doesn't sound like much until you put it next to what the western Sound is carrying — Kings Point up near 71. That degree and a half matters more than people think. It's kept our stripers from getting pushed into the strict nocturnal program that's shutting down daytime bites from the Housatonic on west. We're not seeing blitz-quality daytime fishing, but the bass haven't abandoned structure during daylight either — they're just holding deeper in it, and you have to go get them instead of waiting for them to show.

The Gold Star Bridge pilings are still the most reliable structure in the system. On the last two hours of the ebb, I've been working the downstream faces of the center pilings with 1-ounce bucktails dressed with a strip of pork rind or a 4-inch white paddle tail, dropping to the bottom and working it back up in short hops. Fish are sitting tight to the concrete in 18 to 22 feet, and most of what's coming over the rail is 24 to 30 inches — a few better ones mixed in after dark. If you can fish it blind on the incoming tide too, don't skip it; the pilings hold fish on both stages, they just sit in different spots depending on which way the water's pushing.

We flagged this last week — said the bass activity would pick up as the tide cycle built, and that's exactly what's happened. The current strength off the sub base and down through the river mouth has been noticeably stronger the past several days, and the fish have responded by stacking tighter to the defined current lines instead of spreading out over open bottom.

Bluefish are the story nobody should be surprised by. They love this warm surface layer that's been shoving bass deep everywhere from here to Jersey, and the river mouth has had them working peanut bunker schools most mornings this week, right off the mouth where the Thames dumps into the harbor near Pleasure Beach. Cast small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters — into the surface nervousness and you'll get bit fast. Some fish pushing 4 to 6 pounds mixed into the smaller choppers, and if you're throwing topwater, a Yo-Zuri Mag Popper worked in short, aggressive strokes has been drawing the bigger blues up off the bottom of the school.

Porgies are still the honest bread-and-butter bite around the sub base and the deeper holes off Fort Trumbull. Bottom rigs with size 6 or 4 hooks, sandworm or clam strips, fished in 20 to 35 feet on the slower stages of the tide — this hasn't changed in weeks and it isn't going to. It's not exciting fishing but it's steady, and if you're taking someone out who wants bent rods without a lot of technical demand, this is still your play. I had a father-son trip out of the harbor Tuesday morning that put twenty-some keeper porgies in the cooler in about two hours of soak time, nothing fancy about it.

Blackfish are still closed water this time of year in Connecticut, so if you're seeing them stacked up on the rockpiles off Ocean Beach — and I have been, on the sounder — leave them be and make a mental note for the fall reopener. They'll still be there.

What I'd watch going into next week: the tide cycle is building back toward the August 12 new moon, and that usually means stronger current through the Thames corridor, which is good news for the bass pattern holding at the bridge and the fort. If we get a passing thunderstorm or a wind shift out of the southwest — which wouldn't be unusual for early August — expect a day or two of dirty water off the river mouth that'll shut down the sight-fishing for bluefish, though the bottom bite for porgies should hold up fine since that's not dependent on clarity. If the current stays strong and the water holds in the high 60s, I don't see any reason the Fort Trumbull rip and the bridge pilings don't keep producing through the coming week. Fish the tide changes, work the seams instead of the open water, and don't be afraid to go slow and deep for the bass — that's where they're living right now.

reports.headline: Eleven Hours to Veatch, One Bigeye in the Box, and a Blue That Wouldn't Come Tight
reports.subhead: Warm water finally pushed up onto the shelf break this week — the run got shorter, the bite got real, but you still have to earn it.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the Montauk inlet at 4:15 Tuesday morning, dark enough that the outer buoy light was the only thing worth looking at, and didn't see the east wall of Veatch until almost nine. That's the math out here — you don't fish these canyons, you commute to them. Call it 108 nautical miles from the inlet to the drop at 39°56'N, 69°42'W, and at a cruise of 20 knots that's five and a half hours one way, burning somewhere around 16 gallons an hour on the mains. Add the troll time, add the run home, and you've spent eleven hours of engine time to buy four hours of actual fishing. I don't complain about it. I just make sure the fuel log adds up before I leave the dock, because there's no gas station out past the 100-fathom curve.

What we found when we got there made the number worth it, mostly. The warm filament that's been pushing north off the Stream all month has finally set up tight against the canyon wall — we marked a clean break from 71 up into the mid-70s right along the edge, which is about two weeks early for water that warm to be sitting this far north in late July. We flagged this pattern building last week, and here it is holding: yellowfin stacked on that break, working bait right up against the thermocline in 900 to 1,100 feet of water. First fish came on a naked ballyhoo off the shotgun position around 8:40, and from there it was a solid two hours of yellowfin in the 40 to 60 pound class, six for eleven on a spread of Green Machines, a couple of Ilander/ballyhoo combos in dark colors, and one Joe Shute rigged bare that outfished everything else for reasons I still can't explain.

The bigeye came later, and it came hard. We'd shut the engines down around noon to drift and jig a temp break where the sounder showed bait stacked from 200 down to 400 feet, and on the second drop with a butterfish-tipped Nomad jig, something ate it at 280 feet and didn't come up easy. Twenty-five minutes on 50-pound braid, and we got a 165-pound bigeye to color before he made one more run we almost didn't stop. That's the fish that makes the fuel bill make sense.

We had a white marlin come up on the long rigger teaser around 1:30, ate a ballyhoo, and threw the hook on the second jump. That's how it's gone for marlin all month out here — plenty of shots, not a lot of fish actually stuck. If you're running for billfish specifically right now, I'd fish smaller circle hooks and slow your drop-back, because these fish are eating and not committing the way they will once that water settles in through August.

Hydrographer fished similarly when a buddy of mine ran out of Point Judith Wednesday — he's closer to that piece than we are from Montauk, maybe 95 nautical miles from the breakwater to 39°57'N, 69°00'W, and he had a clean yellowfin bite early with a couple of mahi mixed in around a weed line he found drifting south of the canyon. Mahi have been the bonus fish all month — anytime you cross a good weed line or a piece of floating junk out there, stop and pitch a bucktail or a small popper, because there's almost always a school sitting under it, even if it's just schoolies in the 5 to 10 pound range.

Oceanographer is the one I haven't gotten a good read on this week — it's the longest run from our ports, and with the wind holding out of the southwest and light, most of the RI and Block Island boats have been shading toward Veatch and Hydrographer where the fuel math is more forgiving. I'd expect Oceanographer to be fishing similarly given the same warm push, but I can't vouch for it firsthand yet, and I'm not going to sell you water I haven't run to.

Bluefin have been scattered on the inshore edges closer to the Sound side and up toward Stellwagen tied to whale and bait-ball activity, but that's not really our program out here — the canyon bluefin bite has been quieter than the yellowfin, mostly incidental fish mixed in with the tuna schools rather than a targeted push. Wahoo showed up as a couple of incidental fish on the high-speed lines rigged with Ilanders in blue/white, nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth having a rod rigged for if you're already trolling that spread.

Looking ahead, the warm filament shows no sign of sliding back south, and if it holds through the week I'd expect the yellowfin bite to stay steady on both Veatch and Hydrographer, with mahi as a reliable bonus around any structure you cross offshore. The marlin bite should firm up once this water sits in place a little longer — right now the fish are there but green, eating and not always sticking. If I had one day to burn fuel this week, I'd run for that east wall at Veatch on the first light of a calm morning and fish the temp break hard before the wind builds in the afternoon, because that's where the bait's holding and that's where the tuna are working it.

reports.headline: 7.4°F Split at 39°34' — Yellowfin Camped on the Warm Side of the Dip
reports.subhead: A Gulf Stream filament pushed further north than it should for late July, and the canyon edge is holding fish because of it.
reports.body_markdown:
Seven point four degrees. That's the spread I logged running the edge Tuesday between the shelf water sitting at 71.2 and the warm filament pushing into the Dip at just under 79. That's not a normal late-July number for this canyon — usually by now the whole shelf's evened out and you're hunting for a break instead of tripping over one. This year the Stream kicked a tongue of warm water north of where it usually sits, and it's been parked on the 100-fathom line for the better part of two weeks. That's the whole story right now. Find the color change where that warm water meets the green shelf water, and you find the fish.

I ran out of Manasquan Thursday, put the spread in at the Dip around 39°33'N/72°45'W, right where the canyon wall starts to break steep on the chart. Water there was reading high 70s on the surface, clean blue, with a hard rip line visible from a half mile out — you could see the foam and the weed collecting on it before you even got the lines wet. That's your visual cue. Birds were working it too, terns diving on bait pushed up against the seam. We picked up yellowfin in the 25-40 pound class on that edge, mostly on the troll — green machines and Joe Shute bars in the middle of the spread, naked ballyhoo with a chartreuse Sea Witch off the shotgun. Nothing giant, but a consistent pick, four fish in about ninety minutes of working that one temp break before it slid on us mid-afternoon.

The Claw was slower. I had a report of a bigeye taken there overnight on the chunk — butterfish soaked out on a fluorocarbon leader, no weight, dead-sticked back about sixty feet on the drift in 900 feet of water — but that's one fish, one boat, one night. Don't read that as the Claw lighting up wholesale. The warm water hasn't fully committed to that piece of structure yet; it's been more of a Dip and 100-fathom-line story this week, with the Claw riding the edge of the filament rather than sitting inside it.

Mahi have been the bonus fish, and an honest one — scattered, not stacked. We picked up a dozen keeper-class mahi in the 5-8 pound range working floating weed lines out past the Dip, mostly on small pink and white feather jigs cast ahead of the boat once we spotted the mat. That's a run-and-gun fishery right now, not a set-and-troll one. You need eyes on the water, not just rods in the spread. Some boats are finding bigger fish, 15-20 pounds, holding under isolated debris rather than the big weed mats — worth a look if you're marking floating junk on the way out.

Wahoo have shown up incidentally, a couple of cutoffs and one fish boated trolling a high-speed spread with a black/purple Braid Marauder at 14 knots along the edge of the warm water, which tells me there's a thermocline down there worth checking with the temp probe if you're rigged for it. White marlin have been quiet on my end this week — a couple of raises reported working ballyhoo dink baits south toward Wilmington, but nothing consistent enough on the Hudson itself to call it a pattern yet.

We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as the weather pattern held, and that's exactly what's played out. Stable winds out of the southwest, light seas, and that warm filament refusing to slide off the canyon wall. The mahi call held too — scattered but consistent is precisely what we got, not a blitz, but reliable enough to fill a fish box if you put in the time on the weed lines.

Here's my read going into next week. As long as that 79-degree water holds its position on the Dip and doesn't retreat south, I'd keep working that same stretch — 39°32' to 39°36'N along the canyon wall, working the color change on the troll early, then switching to chunk and drift once you find bait stacked on the sounder. If you see the edge water start cooling back toward 74-75, that's your signal the filament is sliding off the canyon and you'll want to run further east toward Block or south toward the Elephant Trunk to find it again. Moon's building back toward the August 12 new moon, tides picking up incrementally through the week, which should help concentrate bait tighter to the structure rather than spreading it thin across open water. I wouldn't call this the best week of the summer, but it's a real bite on a real temp break, and right now that's more than a lot of boats can say. Watch the water, not the calendar.

reports.headline: July 31 and Washington Still Hasn't Given Up Its Head Start
reports.subhead: A Gulf Stream filament pushing farther north than it should this late in July is keeping yellowfin, some bigeye, and scattered mahi stacked on the break while the other canyons play catch-up.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock: why does Washington fish two, three weeks ahead of Wilmington and Baltimore when they're barely thirty miles apart on the chart? The answer's the same every year too — geometry. Washington sits where the shelf break kinks just right to catch Gulf Stream filaments before they wrap north, and this July that filament came in early and it's still sitting there, stubborn, like it doesn't know the calendar says August is two days away.

I've had the boat on the color change most of this past week, working the edge that's set up loosely between 38°08'N and 38°14'N, 73°58'W to 74°03'W — call it the northeast corner of the canyon proper, where the 100-fathom curve starts to roll over into the real drop. Surface temp on the blue side of that break has been running warm, low-to-mid 70s, with a hard edge you can see in the water color even before the machine confirms it. That's the kind of break that holds fish, and it's held them for going on three weeks now without sliding on us. We flagged this pattern holding back on the 24th — said stable weather would keep the action steady — and here we are at the end of the month with the same filament still parked in the same water.

Yellowfin have been the bread and butter, mostly 25 to 45 pounds, coming on the troll along that break in the mid-morning and again in the last two hours of light. Green machines and small cedar plugs in the pattern, run tight to the boat, have been drawing the first strikes, and once you find the school a naked ballyhoo behind a Sea Witch will keep them interested longer than the hard plastics will. Depth's not really the story here — these are surface-oriented fish riding the temperature break, not fish you're marking on structure at 900 feet. The break itself is the structure.

Bigeye have shown, but it's a night program, and it's been hit or miss. Boats willing to sit on the edge after dark and chunk butterfish over a chum slick in 700 to 1,100 feet of water have taken a few in the 60-to-90-pound class, mostly on the second or third drift once the slick's had time to build. I wouldn't call it consistent — for every boat that connected this week, I heard from two that sat all night and never got a real bite window. That's bigeye fishing in late July on this canyon; you're buying a lottery ticket with better odds than most, not a sure thing.

Mahi have been scattered rather than schooled up — the kind of bite where you're picking off a pair here, a single there, off any bit of floating structure or weed line that's held together in this wind. Small stuff, mostly schoolies in the 5-to-12-pound range, though I did hear of a mixed pod pushing 20 pounds working bait balls a little south of the main break, closer to 38°02'N. Bailer-style with a spinning rod and a small skirted ballyhoo or a bubblegum-pink jig has been the fastest way to pick through them once you stop the boat.

White marlin have been around the edges of that same temp break, and we've had a handful of bites on the dredge — naked ballyhoo behind a squid chain, dropped back soft, has drawn the eats. Nothing to write home about in numbers, two or three raises on a good day, but the fish are there and they're eating when you get the presentation right. Wahoo have been more of a bonus than a target — a couple boats high-speed trolling the drop with Ilanders and wire leader picked off singles in the 30-to-50-pound range working the same stretch of break where the yellowfin have been holding. That tells you something: when the temperature line is this well defined, everything from mahi to wahoo to tuna is stacking on it rather than spreading out across the whole canyon.

I want to be straight with you about the week: it hasn't been a banner bite. It's been a good, honest, working-man's bite — you find the break, you work it methodically, and you get rewarded, but it's not the kind of week where every trolling rod goes off at once. The fish are concentrated on a narrow seam, and if you're not sitting on that seam you're not getting bit. Boats running blind lines north or south of that 38°08' to 38°14' stretch came home with a lot less to show for their fuel.

Looking into next week, the pattern I'd bet on holding is the filament itself — there's nothing in the wind or pressure setup that suggests it's sliding out anytime soon, and with the tide cycle easing toward neap before building back toward the August 12 new moon, I expect bait and predators to stay fairly concentrated rather than spread thin. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to in early August, it might knock a day off the calendar, but it shouldn't move that break more than a few miles. My plan is to keep working that northeast corner early and give the night bigeye program one more shot before the moon starts building — if the filament holds position like it has all month, I don't see a reason to look elsewhere yet.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Turned Green and Cold Overnight — Bass Sliding Deep, Bonito Watch Stays Hot
reports.subhead: A temperature break off the Ledge has the bass program shifting nocturnal while the island keeps one eye on the horizon for the season's first false albacore.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Southwest Ledge Tuesday morning before first light and the air had that different weight to it — heavier, cooler, the kind of morning that tells you the water underneath has shifted even if the surface looks the same. Sure enough, when I dropped the temp gauge over the side, we'd dropped a couple degrees from where we sat a week ago. That's the whole story right there. The warm surface mass that's been sitting on the Sound and pushing up from the Jersey coast has finally started interacting with the cold, clean upwelling that makes this island what it is, and the bass know it before we do.

Here's the thing about Block Island in late July — when the surface water gets into the mid-70s and pushes toward 80 like it has the last two weeks, the bass don't leave, they just go down and go quiet during the day. I've fished this pattern every summer for twenty-some years and it never fails. The fish stack on the deeper structure — the Ledge itself, the drop-off on the north side of the North Rip, the humps off Coast Guard Channel — and they wait for the tide change or full dark to feed. We caught bass to 34 pounds this week, but every single one of them came between 9pm and 3am, on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, over 35 to 55 feet of water on the Ledge. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 3-ounce egg sinker, 40-pound fluorocarbon leader, is still the most reliable way to connect after dark. If you want to go artificial, a 9-inch black or dark green Slug-Go worked slow along the bottom on the drift has been drawing strikes too — the darker profile shows up better against a night sky than anything bright.

Daytime striper fishing has been tougher, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. We worked the North Rip hard on Thursday afternoon during a strong tide change and only picked at fish — three keepers in four hours of drifting live eels through the rip, which on a good July day should produce a lot more than that. The water up top is just too warm for them to commit during daylight right now. If you're set on a day trip, fish the last hour of daylight into dusk on the west side of the island off Grace's Cove, where the bottom holds cooler water longer, or hit the rips right at the tide change and don't waste time on slack water — the bass simply aren't using the structure when the current stops moving.

Bluefish have been the daytime save. They don't care about the warm water the way stripers do, and we've had steady action on choppers from 4 to 9 pounds working peanut bunker schools off the south side of the island, particularly around Black Rock and down toward Southeast Light. Bucktails in white or chartreuse, half-ounce to an ounce depending on how deep the bait's holding, fished on a fast retrieve through the bait balls, will get bit almost every cast when the birds are working. It's not subtle fishing but it's produced when the bass wouldn't.

Fluke have been the most dependable meat-in-the-cooler fish this week. Drifting the sand and gravel patches off Charlestown Beach and the entrance to Great Salt Pond, 20 to 35 feet, we've had keepers to 6 pounds on the outgoing tide using a classic Fluke Killer rig — a white bucktail teaser ahead of a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce jig head, dragged just off bottom. It's a steady program, not a blitz, but you'll put dinner in the boat most days if you keep the boat moving with the current and stay on the drift lines where the bottom transitions from sand to broken shell.

Porgies have been thick around any structure holding bait — the rockpiles off New Harbor and the drop-offs near the Coast Guard station have been loaded, and if you've got kids aboard or just want steady bend in the rod, sandworms on a simple high-low rig will keep everyone busy between the bigger fish efforts.

Now, the question everyone's been asking me at the dock — where are the bonito and albies? We flagged this water as one of the top zones on the coastwide watch list, and I stand by that read. The temperature break I felt this week is exactly the kind of setup that pulls albies and bonito up onto the rips once the bait gets pushed and concentrated by the building current. We're not there yet — nobody's boated one off the island as of this week, and I don't want to tell you different. But the ingredients are on the table: warm water offshore, a cold edge developing right where we fish, and the tide building back toward the August new moon. If I were rigging up for it, I'd have a 7-weight or a light spin rod with small Deadly Dicks and Epoxy Jigs ready to go, and I'd be watching the North Rip and the water off Southeast Light closely on calm mornings — that's usually where the first scout shows up around here.

Looking ahead, expect the bass to stay locked into that dawn, dusk, and full-dark program as long as the surface stays warm, so plan your trips around the tide changes rather than the clock. Bluefish should keep providing the daytime entertainment on bait schools, fluke will stay steady on the drift, and I'd keep that light tackle rigged in the rocket launcher just in case that first bonito shows up on the temperature break we're all watching for.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Mixed Bag Monday, Money Wednesday: Spencer Chunk Bite Carries the Week
reports.subhead: A warm filament off the Stream kept yellowfin honest at Spencer while Norfolk's white marlin bite finally showed some teeth.
reports.body_markdown:
Grading this week a solid B. Monday and Tuesday were a grind — six-hour runs to Spencer with only a few marks on the meter and a couple of teaser bites that never turned into hookups. Wednesday changed everything. That's the day I want to talk about, because it tells you where to point the bow the next few days.

Here's the setup: we've got a Gulf Stream filament pushing warm water unusually far north for the end of July, and it's sitting right up against the canyon wall from Hudson down through Wilmington and into our water — Spencer, Lindenkohl, and on into Norfolk. High pressure's been parked over the mid-Atlantic for the better part of ten days now, winds out of the southwest and light, seas mostly 2 to 3 feet with the occasional 4-footer riding through on a longer period. That's a fishable ocean, and it's held the warm edge in place instead of letting it slide out or get chewed up by a front. We flagged this pattern last week — said the southern canyon grounds would keep producing tuna and mahi with white marlin building as the season point demands — and that's exactly the arc we're on.

Spencer's been our go-to. We're working the 100-fathom curve on the northeast side, roughly the color change where you go from that olive-green inshore water to clean blue, somewhere around 38°45'N by 73°50'W depending on the day the edge sets up. Wednesday we anchored up on a good temp break — you could see it in the water color and feel it in the chunk slick pulling bait — and put down butterfish chunks on 50-pound fluoro leader, 7/0 circle hooks, no weight, just let it flutter down naturally in the current. Yellowfin from 25 to 45 pounds, steady through the morning bite window and again for about ninety minutes right at last light. Nothing spectacular in size, but consistent — six to nine fish in the box most days this week when the chunk bite connected. A couple of bigger models pushing 60 came off the troll on green machine spreader bars pulled early morning before we set up to anchor.

Lindenkohl's been quieter, and I think it's simply positioning — the warm filament hasn't wrapped as tight around that canyon as it has Spencer, so the bait hasn't stacked up the same way. We ran up there Thursday, marked some scattered fish on the meter around 300 to 400 feet, but couldn't buy a solid chunk bite. If you're going to fish Lindenkohl right now, I'd troll it rather than anchor — ballyhoo and small Ilanders in blue/white and green/yellow combos, working the drop-off edges rather than sitting still.

Poor Man's has been the mahi spot all week, and that's typical for a canyon that close in — it doesn't need the same deep-water temp break to produce, it just needs floating structure. We found two decent weed lines Tuesday holding gaffer-class mahi, 8 to 15 pounds, and worked them with small skirted jigs and bucktails cast right into the shade line. If you're running a shorter day out of Ocean City and don't want to burn fuel to Spencer, Poor Man's with a mahi program is the smart call right now — quick bite, good eating fish, and you're back at the dock by early afternoon.

Norfolk is the story to watch. That's our southernmost run, and it's where the white marlin activity has actually started building the way we expected for this point in the season. We had two white marlin bites Wednesday trolling ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, converted one, and heard from another boat working the same edge who went two-for-three. That's not a red-hot bite, but it's a real uptick from where we were two weeks ago, and it lines up with the warm water continuing to push and hold along that canyon wall. There's bigeye potential down there too on the night chunk — we haven't connected yet, but the water column temps and bait presence say it's worth a soak after dark if you've got the fuel range and the patience.

Bottom line for the week ahead: as long as this high pressure holds and that warm filament stays pinned against the canyon structure — and both of those look stable through the next several days — I'd keep Spencer as the primary target for the chunk bite, run Poor Man's for a quicker mahi trip, and start committing more time to Norfolk if you're chasing white marlin or want a crack at bigeye after dark. The one thing that could change this fast is a frontal passage — early August tends to throw a quick thunderstorm system through, and if that happens the bait can scatter and you'll need a day to relocate the edge again. Watch the color change before you committing to an anchor spot, and don't be afraid to burn an extra twenty minutes running the edge before you set up. That's what separated our Wednesday from our Monday.

reports.headline: Ran the Wilmington Elbow on a hunch — three yellowfin, one bigeye bite that got away
reports.subhead: A warm Gulf Stream filament pushed further north than it should this late in July, and it's stacking bait right where we wanted it.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a choice to make at the fuel dock: run straight out to the 28-fathom hump and chunk, or burn the extra diesel to the Elbow and troll the edge where I'd marked a hard break the week before. Chunking's cheaper and it's a sure bait draw, but with the boat full and a long ride ahead, I wanted moving baits in the water the second we hit color. We ran the troll. That decision paid for the fuel and then some.

The break was sitting right where I left it, holding around 38°34'N, 74°08'W on the northeast corner, with the temp gauge jumping from the mid-70s into the upper 70s in about a quarter mile — that's the kind of shelf water tuna use as a highway marker. This is the warm filament that's been the talk of every canyon from here down through Washington — it's pushed further north than you'd expect for the tail end of July, and it's dragging Gulf Stream water right up onto the edge instead of staying pinned south like it usually does this time of year. We flagged this exact pattern holding steady last week, and here it is, still doing its thing three days later.

We pulled a standard war spectrum — ballyhoo skirted in blue/white and green machine off the riggers, naked ballyhoo down the shotgun, spreader bar down the center — through the 100-fathom curve and out to about 250 fathoms where the bottom really falls off the shelf. Marked bait balls stacked up tight on the meter right on the thermocline around 90 feet, and it didn't take long. First yellowfin came on the long rigger around 9:15, a chunky 45-pounder that ate the naked ballyhoo clean. Two more came through mid-morning working the same stretch, both in the 35-50 pound class. Not a stacked bite by any stretch — we worked that edge for six hours and those three fish were it for hookups, though we had two more knockdowns we never connected on, one of which pulled drag hard enough and deep enough that I'd put money on bigeye. That's canyon fishing in late July: you get shots, you don't always close them.

Mahi were scattered but present wherever we found floating structure — a mat of sargassum about a mile off the break gave up two schoolies in the 8-10 pound range on small green machine spreader bars we dropped back after the tuna bite slowed. If you're running the edge and see any weed line or debris, even a five-gallon bucket or a pallet, it's worth the five-minute detour. Mahi are opportunistic right now, riding whatever shade they can find, and they don't need much of an excuse to show up in your spread.

White marlin gave us one legitimate look — a fish came up on the long teaser late morning, wouldn't commit to the pitch bait, and disappeared. That's been the pattern boats are reporting up and down this stretch: shots are there, conversions are spotty. If you're serious about marlin right now, I'd rig a dedicated pitch rod with a select ballyhoo and keep someone on it full-time rather than trying to run a mixed spread and react. The fish are eating slow and cautious in this warm, clean water — they're not crashing baits, they're inspecting them.

Wahoo have been quiet on our end this week, though we heard of one boat working the Baltimore Canyon side picking off a couple on high-speed lures worked deep along the drop. If wahoo are on your target list, I'd rig a couple of deep divers behind planers on the outside lines and let them ride below the main spread rather than dedicating the whole troll to them — they're a bonus fish right now, not a primary target.

The moon's coming off full and tides are easing toward neap over the next several days, which usually softens current on the edge a touch — that's not a bad thing for trolling since a moderate current keeps bait from getting blown off the break entirely. Wind's been light out of the southwest, seas comfortable, and that stable high-pressure pattern is exactly what's kept this warm filament pinned in place instead of sliding back south like it typically would this late in the month.

Looking at the next few days, I'd expect the status quo to hold through Saturday — steady yellowfin on the temp breaks, mahi wherever there's floating cover, and marlin shots for anyone willing to dedicate a rod to it. The bigger question is early next week, when the typical early-August frontal disturbance could roll through and stir things up for a day or two before the pattern re-establishes. If that happens, I wouldn't panic — these warm-water filaments have been resilient all month, and the bait's not going anywhere fast. My plan is to keep working the Elbow and adjust east or west a few miles based on where the sharpest color change sits that morning. If you're headed out, mark your break the day before if you can, because it's shifted a mile or two most days this week, and finding it early saves you fuel and gets baits in front of fish before the bite windows tighten up midday.

reports.headline: Peconic Pushing Past 76 — Porgies Piled Up at Shelter Island, Bass Gone to Nightshift
reports.subhead: The bay's run warm enough now that the stripers want the dark and the porgies don't care what time it is.
reports.body_markdown:
By the end of July the Peconic has usually settled into its summer rhythm, and this year's no different — the bay warmed early back in May like it always does, and now in the last week of the month it's sitting well up into the mid-70s across most of the open water, pushing 78 in the shallow coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor by mid-afternoon. That's above the comfort window stripers like, and it shows in how they're behaving. We flagged this ten days back — said stable, warm weather would keep pushing the pattern deeper and more nocturnal, and that's exactly what's playing out across the whole bay complex right now.

Daytime bass fishing has gone quiet almost everywhere except right around dawn. The better action is happening after dark and in that gray hour before first light, with fish working the deep water off Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip on the tide changes. Guys drifting bunker chunks or live eels along the north side of the Gut on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood have been finding slot fish in 25 to 40 feet, right where the current stacks up against the drop. During the day those same fish slide back into the deeper holes in Gardiners Bay — the flat off Cartwright Shoal, the hole east of Gardiners Island — and mostly sulk until the sun drops. If you want bass right now, fish the edges of the day, not the middle of it.

The good news is the porgy fishing hasn't slowed one bit, and honestly this is the time of year Shelter Island earns its reputation. Coecles Harbor, the flats off Cedar Island, and the drop-off outside Dering Harbor are absolutely stuffed with porgies right now, 12 to 15 inches with plenty of jumbos mixed in over 14. Small hooks, half a clam or a piece of squid, fished on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the incoming through the top of the tide — that's been the money window all week. No need to overthink it. Chum helps but isn't required when they're schooled up this tight.

Fluke are stacked in the channels the way they always are once the water settles into summer pattern. The Sag Harbor channel, the deeper cuts off Jessups Neck, and the drop along the Greenport side of the bay have all been giving up keeper fish mixed with plenty of shorts. Four-inch white or pink Gulp on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom on the outgoing tide, has been the most consistent producer — a couple boats working the channel edge off North Haven have put together limits of keepers to five pounds doing exactly that, working the drift right where the channel breaks up onto the flat. Bounce a strip of squid on the bucktail hook if the bite's finicky; it's made the difference more than once this week when the plain Gulp wasn't drawing strikes.

Weakfish are showing incidentally in those same deep holes where the bass are holed up during the day — nothing to plan a trip around, but if you're working bait on bottom in Gardiners Bay or the deeper stretches off Southold and you hook something that doesn't feel like a fluke, don't be shocked if it's a weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch range. Bluefish have been mixing into the bay too, chasing peanut bunker schools that have pushed in from the Sound side — nothing like the blitz action happening out on the ocean beaches this week, but enough activity around Orient and the mouth of the bay that a few boats working topwater plugs at first light have found choppers in the 3 to 5 pound class busting bait on the surface.

Tide-wise we're easing off the full moon push and heading toward neap, which usually softens the current enough that the fluke bite slows a touch on the slower stages but the porgy and bass fishing barely notices — those species care more about temperature and light than raw current speed this time of year. Wind's been light out of the southwest most days, which keeps the bay flat and comfortable but also lets that surface layer keep building heat, so don't expect the bass pattern to change much until we get a real blow to mix things up.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the status quo to hold through the first few days of August — porgies thick around Shelter Island, fluke steady in the channels, bass locked into their dawn-dusk-and-dark program. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to this time of year, it could stir the water enough to trigger a short daytime bass window right after it passes — worth having a rod rigged and ready if you see one building. Otherwise, fish the tide changes at Plum Gut for bass, work the Shelter Island flats for porgies, and drag bucktails through the channels for fluke. That's been the program, and there's no reason to think it breaks before the tide starts building back toward the August 12 new moon.

reports.headline: Bass Gone Deep, Blues Up Top, and the Albie Window Cracks Open
reports.subhead: The Point is doing its late-July shuffle — quality stripers holed up on structure, bluefish running the surface, and the first credible albie window closing in fast.
reports.body_markdown:
I've stood on that boulder field below the Lighthouse enough Julys to know what this water looks like when it's holding its breath. Surface temp at the Point is sitting around 69 degrees, which sounds cool until you remember what the rest of the coast is doing — mid-70s to near 80 from Jersey up through the Cape. That gap is the whole story right now. Montauk stays the last cold-water refuge on this stretch of coast, and that's exactly why the quality fish are still here instead of pushed north into the Gulf of Maine like everywhere else.

But cold-water refuge doesn't mean easy fishing. The bass have gone deep and they've gone smart. I'm finding them stacked on the humps off Shagwong Reef and down in the deeper guts of the boulder field on the ocean side, but they're not up feeding in the middle of the day like they will come October. Right now it's a tide-change and after-dark program. The building tide off the July 29 full moon has been running hard through the rip, and that's when the bigger fish slide up onto the structure to work bunker schools that have been holding just off the drop. I had a 38-pounder come off the North Bar at 5 AM last Tuesday on a fresh bunker chunk, fished on a fish-finder rig with 60-pound fluoro leader, right as the tide turned from ebb to flood. That window — the hour around the turn, both day and night — is where the real fish are living this week. Daylight hours in between have been mostly quiet for anything over slot size, though you'll pick at schoolies working bait pods scattered through Turtle Cove on the last of the outgoing.

Bluefish are the ones benefiting from all this warm water everybody else is complaining about. They don't care about the thermal squeeze the way bass do, and they're all over the rip lines and bait balls from the Point out to Shagwong in good numbers through the middle of the day.
