Diamond jigs, poppers, anything chrome thrown into a working boil will get bit right now — jumbo blues in the 8 to 12 pound class, teeth like a bandsaw, exactly the kind of daytime action that's been missing from the bass bite. If you want steady rod-bending without waiting for the tide change, this is your play.

Fluke fishing has stayed dependable, which is more than I can say for some Julys. Drifting the edges off Frisco Ridge and out along the deeper flats south of the Point, we're seeing keepers mixed with plenty of shorts — nothing blitz-level, just steady structure fishing on 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the drift slow so the jig ticks bottom without dragging through the mussel bottom too hard. Offshore, the sea bass and porgy fishing on the humps and wrecks has been about as good as it gets all season — heavy bags, good average size, and it's given a lot of boats a reason to run wide when the inshore bite gets stingy.

Now, the thing everybody's actually asking me about at the dock: the albies. We flagged this setup two weeks running — said the water temp sitting right in that 68-to-72 degree band, combined with tides building back out of neap toward the August 12 new moon, was the classic recipe for the season's first false albacore and bonito. That water temperature is still exactly where it needs to be. The current strength is building. What I don't have yet is a confirmed fish in anybody's hands — no albie has crossed my gaff or anyone else's that I trust as of this week. But every piece of the puzzle Skinner and the boys down the beach are seeing — squid pushing into the Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound water, the temperature break setting up along the south side — points to this being the window. If I had one morning to burn looking for the first scout school, I'd be running the temp break off the south side beaches at first light with a Deadly Dick or a small Got-Cha plug rigged and ready, working from the Lighthouse east toward Shagwong, watching for diving terns and nervous water rather than committing blind.

Looking at the week ahead — tides are easing back off the full-moon peak toward neap, which historically slows the bass bite even further during daylight and pushes it harder into full dark. I'd fish bunker chunks and eels on the turn, work the rip during the bluefish window for guaranteed action, and keep one eye on the horizon for that first small, fast-moving school that doesn't look like anything else out there. That's usually how it starts — not a blitz, just three or four fish busting bait for thirty seconds before they vanish. When that happens, everything changes fast, and I intend to be on the water when it does.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Hugging Inlet Bottom While Blues Own the Surface
reports.subhead: With the bay running warm, the real bass bite has moved to full dark on the last of the ebb — and the first scout reports for albies are starting to circle.
reports.body_markdown:
I made a call this week that cost me a sunset session but paid off twice as hard at midnight. Instead of hitting the inlet at last light like the day boats, I waited for the outgoing to really get moving — an hour past the turn, current stacking hard against the jetty rocks — and fished straight through to 2 a.m. That's where the bass have been all month, and with this bay running warm the way it has, that's where they're staying.

Here's the read: surface temps out front have been sitting up in the mid-70s, which is above where a striper wants to work hard in daylight. So the fish that are here — and there are fish here — have pushed down into the deep hole on the east side of the inlet, the scour just inside the rock pile, and they're only really turning on to feed when the sun's been gone a few hours and the current's got some shoulder to it. I've been anchoring up on the last two hours of the outgoing, eeling live snake eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that 20-25 foot hole, and letting the current do the work. No retrieve, just patience. Landed a stretch of bass from 26 to a fat 34 inches over three nights this week, none of it fast, but steady enough that I kept rebaiting. Bunker chunks on a 5/0 circle hook worked the same water when the eels ran short — bluefish showed up on those too, which tells you the blues are pushing right into the same current seam as the stripers after dark, not just chopping bait on top like they do at noon.
8
The daytime picture out front is a different animal entirely, and this is where the warm water is doing exactly what it's supposed to — favoring the bluefish over the bass. If you want a bent rod in daylight, work the beach off Tiana on peanut bunker schools with a stainless popper or a Ava jig on wire, retrieved fast through the surface commotion. That fishery has been consistent, not spectacular, but reliable enough to fill an afternoon while you wait for dark. Just don't expect quality stripers mixed in there right now — they've gone nocturnal and they're not coming back to the surface in 78-degree water to prove a point.

Ponquogue Bridge has been my other stop, and the weakfish have cooperated better than I expected given how warm the bay's gotten. Incoming tide, an hour before and after the top, working the shadow lines under the span with a 1/4-ounce bucktail dressed in white bucktail hair, tipped with a strip of squid or a sandworm. The weakfish sit right on the current edge where the bridge lights meet the dark water, and they'll hit that jig on the drop more than the retrieve. Fish have run 16 to 20 inches, a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, which is about the honest state of that fishery this summer — worth the trip, not a guarantee.

Fluke in the bay have been the most dependable thing going, if you're willing to move around and find the right piece of bottom. The channel edges off Tiana and the drop-offs on the west side of the canal mouth have both been holding fish — drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of fluke belly for scent, and cover ground slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets pulled off the flats into the channel. Keepers mixed with plenty of shorts, nothing blitz-level, but a few solid fish in the 20-22 inch range came out of that program this week. The canal itself has had some traffic too — a handful of guys working the current there into the Peconic side have picked up stray weakfish and fluke moving through on the tide swap, which tells me there's still exchange happening between the two systems even with the water warm on both ends.

We flagged this zone last week as one to watch for the season's first albie or bonito scout, and there's been some bait movement worth noting — small sand eels and rain bait pushing through the inlet rips on the last of the ebb, exactly the kind of forage that pulls false albacore in tight to structure once the temperature threshold gets crossed. Nothing confirmed yet, no hookups, but the ingredients are lining up faster than they usually do this early in August, and this stretch of beach has a habit of showing signs before Montauk does.

Looking ahead, the tide cycle is easing down toward neap over the next few days before it starts rebuilding toward the August 12 new moon, and I expect that softer current to push the bass even deeper and more strictly nocturnal for a stretch — less water movement means less reason for them to commit outside of full dark. If the warm, stable pattern holds like it has, I'd keep working the inlet hole late and let the bridge and bay structure fill in the daylight hours. If a cold front or a squall line comes through and knocks the surface temp down even two degrees, watch for the bass to show a little more willingness at dusk instead of waiting for 1 a.m. — that's the kind of shift that changes my whole schedule for a week. Until then, I'll be out there after most of the town's gone to bed, eel bucket in the boat, waiting on the tide.

reports.headline: The Cut at Moriches Narrowed Again — And the Bass Know Exactly Where It Went
reports.subhead: A summer shoal is choking the inlet down to one hard lane, and everything from bunker to bass is funneling through it on the last two hours of the ebb.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the depth finder through the inlet Tuesday on a dropping tide and the number that jumped out wasn't the depth — it was how fast it changed. Eighteen feet off the Cupsogue side, then eleven, then six inside of eighty yards. That's the shoal off the east jetty building out again, the same one that reformed after the spring nor'easters, and it's doing what it always does in high summer: squeezing the whole outgoing flow into one narrow, hard-running lane along the Westhampton side of the channel. If you fished this inlet last month and the drift felt different, that's why. The bottom moved.

That narrowed lane is exactly where the bait is getting stacked and exactly where the bluefish are working it over. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker-driven blitzes at the inlet and beachfront would hold with the tide building, and that's precisely what's happening. Peanut bunker are getting pinched through that cut on the last two hours of the ebb, and the blues are waiting on the seam where the fast water meets the eddy behind the jetty rocks. Cast a 1-ounce Deadly Dick or a chrome Kastmaster into the boil, let it swing, and you're tight in two or three cranks. These aren't cocktail blues either — plenty of three and four pounders mixed with the smaller stuff, enough to make you re-tie leaders every third fish.

Striped bass are in that same current but they're not playing the same hours. Surface water out front is sitting in the high 70s, well above where bass want to be, so the good fish are holding low — right on the bottom of that new cut, in eight to twelve feet, and they're only really committing during the last hour of dark and the first gray light before the sun gets on the water. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, weight just heavy enough to hold bottom in that current, is the simple and effective program. I had a client stick a 34-incher off the Cupsogue side at 5:15 a.m. Thursday, right as the tide was going still — that dead-slack window before the flood is when the bigger fish seem to commit, probably because the current stops shoving bait through and lets them feed instead of just holding position.

Inside the bay, the fluke bite has been the most dependable thing going, and it's holding to the pattern we called — solid fish on the channel edges, not the flats. Work the drop-off along the edge of the channel off Tuthill Point, and the deeper cuts running past Smith Point where the current sweeps bay water out toward the inlet. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow with the drift, not ripped — that channel edge bottom is soft enough that an aggressive hop just buries the hook in mud. Keeper fish in the 18 to 20-inch range are mixing with plenty of shorts, so it's not a five-minute limit, but a couple hours of patient drifting will put two or three keepers in the cooler most days right now. Bigger fish seem to want the deeper edge — 14 to 18 feet — where the bottom stays cooler under that warm surface layer.

Porgies are stacked tight to structure right at the inlet rocks and around the Cupsogue jetty base, and that bite hasn't slowed a bit. Small hooks, half a sandworm or a piece of clam, right on bottom in that rocky scour. It's not glamorous but it's about as sure a thing as this bay offers in late July, and it's a good way to fill a bucket while you're waiting for the light to drop enough to switch over to bass gear.

Weakfish are around but thin — a few keeper-class fish showing up as bycatch on the bass chunk baits after dark, nothing you'd plan a whole trip around. If that inshore squid push that's been building up around Rhode Island keeps sliding this way over the next couple weeks, I'd expect the weakfish bite to firm up some, but that's a September conversation more than an August one.

Wind's been out of the southwest and stable, which is part of why this pattern has held together as long as it has — no chop pushing sediment through the inlet, no dirty water breaking up that current seam. The tides are easing off the full-moon push toward neap over the next several days, which should slacken the inlet flow just enough that the bluefish blitzes may spread out a bit rather than staying pinned to that one narrow lane. I wouldn't call that a bad thing — it just means covering more water at Cupsogue and along the Westhampton beachfront rather than parking on one spot.

Looking ahead, I expect the bass to stay locked into that dawn-and-dark program as long as this surface warmth holds, and the fluke to keep producing off those same channel edges regardless of what the tide cycle does — that bite's more about structure than moon phase. The one thing worth watching is any afternoon thunderstorm rolling through, which happens fast and often in early August; a hard downpour can dirty the bay side quickly and shut the fluke bite down for a tide or two. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet, right at that new cut, working bunker on bottom into first light. That's where the current, the bait, and the bass are all lining up right now.

reports.headline: Eel bite cracks open at the Gut — 40 inches on the first drift
reports.subhead: Current came back to the Race and Plum Gut this week, and the bass that vanished on the neap showed up hungry after dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-eighteen in the morning, tide dead ebb at Plum Gut, and my buddy Sal's rod loads up like someone hooked a mooring ball. Forty inches, maybe 26 pounds, came off a snag-proof eel drifted right off the tip of Plum Island where the current pours into the deep water. That fish ate on the second cast after we hit the seam — not the middle of the rip, the edge of it, where the fast water folds against the slow. That's the tell right now. These bass aren't roaming. They're pinned to current edges because the water on top is too warm to sit in all day.

We called this exact turn last week — said the neap tide had gutted the current in the Race and Plum Gut and the bite would come back as the flow rebuilt. It rebuilt. Kings Point's reading 70.9, New London's sitting at 69.4, and that's warm enough to shove quality bass off the flats and into the current-scrubbed depths where the water stays a few degrees cooler and the oxygen's better. Dawn, dusk, full dark — that's the program now. Daytime bass fishing in the Gut and the Race is mostly dead water unless you're marking fish deep and dropping bucktails on them, and even then it's a grind.

Plum Gut itself is fishing best on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, working the west side drop where it goes from 20 feet to better than 50 in a hurry. Snag-proof eels and 3-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse tails, dead-drifted and bounced along bottom, are outproducing everything else. If you're on a boat, drift the edge — don't anchor in it, you'll get bounced around and lose the presentation. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig off the bottom will pick up stragglers too, especially right at the turn of the tide when the current slacks enough to hold bottom.

The Race is a different animal — bigger water, harder current, and it wants effort. Wire line trolling bunker spoons and umbrella rigs through the pinnacle structure west of the lighthouse is still putting bigger fish on the deck, mostly in that 15- to 25-foot band where the reef breaks up the flow. I had one push 35 pounds come off a spoon on the last of the incoming two nights ago, right where the surface goes from smooth to boiling in about ten feet. That boil is the whole game out there — cast or troll right along the edge of it, not into the white water itself.

Bluefish are the story nobody's complaining about. They love this warm surface layer that's pushing the bass down, and Orient Point and the rips off Fishers Island have had peanut bunker getting hammered on the surface most mornings this week. Poppers and 2-ounce metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — worked fast through the froth are getting hit on nearly every cast when the birds are working. This blitz pattern is the same one that's been running the length of the Jersey and Long Island beaches for a week straight, and there's no reason to think it stops here. If anything it keeps spreading east as bait pushes toward the Gut. Worth running out early before the wind builds and the surface glass goes choppy — that window is short, usually gone by 9 a.m.

Fluke fishing is steady, not spectacular. Structure drifts off Orient Point and along the edges of Plum Island in 25 to 40 feet are giving up keepers mixed with a lot of shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktails, worked slow on the drift with the current, not against it. Nothing blitz-level, but if you cover ground and stay on structure you'll put dinner in the cooler.

Porgies are about the most reliable thing going right now on the reefs around Fishers Island — bloodworms and clam on high-low rigs in 20 to 35 feet, pretty much any stage of the tide. Good action if you want a bend in the rod between bass runs, and a solid backup plan on a slow morning.

Looking ahead, tides are building again toward the August 12 new moon, which should keep rebuilding current strength through the Gut and the Race over the next week — good news for the eel and bucktail program. Watch for the first scouting reports of false albacore starting to show around Fishers Island and the Race as bait concentrations tighten up; the water's in the right range for it and it usually starts as a rumor before it's real. If a August thunderstorm rolls through and muddies things up for a day, don't panic — this pattern's been consistent enough that it should snap right back once the water clears. I'll be on the rocks at 3 a.m. either way.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway Bridge After Dark: Bass Grinding Bunker While the Bay Runs Warm
reports.subhead: With the bay pushing near 80 degrees, the bass have gone nocturnal and the blues have taken over the daylight shift on Rockaway's beachfront.
reports.body_markdown:
I took the kayak out under Marine Parkway Bridge at 4:45 Tuesday morning, before the sun even thought about coming up, and I'll tell you why — this bay is running warm enough right now that daytime bass fishing inside Jamaica Bay is mostly a waste of gas or paddle strokes. When the surface temps push into the mid-70s and flirt with 80 in the shallows, stripers want no part of it during daylight. They slide down onto the current-scoured bottom under the bridge, in that deeper cut where the tide rips through on the outgoing, and they wait for dark to come up and feed. So that's where I went, and that's where you should be going too if you want a shot at a real fish right now.

It paid off. Fished bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3-ounce sinker to hold bottom against that current, right off the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Picked up two bass in the 26 to 30-inch range and missed a third that felt heavier before it pulled off. Nothing that's going to make the cover of a magazine, but solid, honest fish, and exactly the pattern I expected given how hot this bay has gotten. The bunker schools pushing through the bay right now are the whole story — where you find pods of peanut bunker stacked up near the bridge or along the Cross Bay Bridge pilings, there's usually a bass or two shadowing them after dark. Eels work too if you want to cover more water — a live eel drifted slow along the bridge fenders on the incoming has been my second option when the chunk bite goes quiet.

During the day, the action has flipped almost entirely to bluefish, and that's not a surprise — warm water is bluefish water, and they're the ones cashing in while the bass hide out deep. We flagged this pattern last week, that the blitz running the Jersey and Long Island beachfront would keep spreading north toward the Sandy Hook and Raritan Bay side, and sure enough it's pushed right up into our stretch. Rockaway Beach has had legitimate blitz mornings this week — peanut bunker and small mullet getting run up onto the sand from Beach 90th down toward Beach 116th, with blues busting bait right in the wash. If you're fishing the surf, get there at first light before the joggers and the sun push the bait back out. Metal — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick — cast right into the froth will get bit almost every cast when it's happening. Poppers work too if you want the visual, but honestly the blues aren't picky when they're plowing through bait like that.

Fluke fishing has been steady, not spectacular, which is about right for the end of July. The channel edges off Cross Bay Bridge and the deeper cuts around Grassy Bay and Ruffle Bar are holding fish, but you've got to work for keepers. I've been drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, along the drop-offs where the mud flats fall into the channel — anywhere from 15 to 25 feet. Getting a lot of shorts mixed in with the occasional keeper, so it's a numbers game more than a guaranteed box of fish. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming, when clean water is pushing back into the bay off the ocean side and the fluke seem to key up on it before the flat slack kills the bite.

Weakfish have been a footnote — a few scattered reports of small ones coming up near the bridge structure at night mixed in with the bass bite, nothing worth planning a trip around. Porgies are around Canarsie Pier if you want an easy family outing — bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig off the pier at half-tide will keep the rods bent for the kids even if nothing else is happening. Blackfish are still a month or so off from being worth chasing here.

We're coming off the full moon and those tides are still running strong, which is part of why the outgoing current under the bridge has been pushing so hard and holding the bass tight to structure rather than spreading them out. As we ease toward the neap tide over the next several days, expect the current to slacken a bit, which could actually spread the bunker schools out more and make the bass bite a little less predictable — I'd fish the bigger tide swings while they last if your schedule allows it.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a major shift unless we get a real thunderstorm system roll through, which is typical for early August and could knock the surface temps down a degree or two and briefly scatter the bait. If that happens, watch the bay right after — a cooling rain can actually trigger a short window of daytime bass activity before things settle back into the nocturnal pattern. Otherwise, my plan for the coming week is the same as this one: dawn and dusk on the bridges for bass, first light on the Rockaway sand for blues, and channel drifts for fluke in the middle of the day when nothing else is biting anyway.

reports.headline: Everybody's Blitzing Blues at Sunrise — I'm on the Rocks After Dark for Bass
reports.subhead: Warm ocean water has the bass shut down all day, but the inlet rocks at night are holding up their end of the deal.
reports.body_markdown:
Half the guys I talk to at the bait shop this week are up at 5 a.m. chasing the blitz on the beach, and I get why — peanut bunker and mullet getting hammered right off the sand is a hell of a sight. But I'm not fighting that crowd. I'm out at the jetty rocks off Short Beach two hours after sundown with a bunker chunk soaking on the bottom, and that's where the real fish have been.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear in July: the ocean's too warm for stripers to play the daytime game right now. We're sitting up around 71, 72 degrees off the beachfront, and that's above the comfort zone for a big bass. So they're doing what they always do when the water gets like this — they go nocturnal, they slide onto the harder structure, and they wait for the tide change to push bait through the inlet before they commit to feeding. I've said it before and I'll say it again — this pattern isn't going anywhere as long as this weather stays put, and this week proved it out again. Same story, three nights running.

The program at the rocks has been simple. I fish the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, right at the mouth of Jones Inlet where the current sweeps bait past the jetty tip. Fresh bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of weight to hold bottom against that current, cast up-current and let it swing down into the pocket behind the rocks. Landed a 34-incher Tuesday night and lost something bigger that just leaned on the drag and took me into the rocks — that's the kind of fish that's around right now, you just have to fish the dark hours to find it. Eels work too if you can get your hands on live ones, snap-cast them out and let them swim naturally on a slow retrieve past the tip.

During the day, the bass program basically shuts off at the inlet mouth, but that's fine, because bluefish don't care one bit about warm water — matter of fact they love it. We flagged this pattern last week and it's still running exactly the same: bluefish are the beneficiary of this whole warm-water setup, and the blitz action along the beachfront has kept spreading, not slowing down. Jones Beach surf, Field 6 through Field 10, incoming tide has had choppers in the 3 to 6 pound range crashing bait right in the wash. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins jigs — thrown into the melee has been about as close to a sure thing as this sport gets right now. If you want a slower, more controlled bite, work the rip off the inlet itself on the same incoming water with bucktails or poppers; the current edge there stacks blues tight enough that you can pick through them for the bigger models instead of just grabbing whatever hits first.

Fluke has been the steady, unspectacular money-maker all month, and this week didn't change that. Sloop Channel is still doing it — drift the drop-offs on the edges where the channel falls off from 8 feet down into 18, 20 feet, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a squid strip if the current's really moving. Keepers mixed with plenty of shorts, nothing to write home about but enough to keep a rod bent on most drifts. The bridge structure at Wantagh has been holding some too, right along the pilings on the last of the outgoing when the current slackens enough to fish a lighter jig head.

Now the fish I actually get excited to talk about — weakfish are legitimately showing back up in the bay, and I don't say that lightly because for years I wouldn't even bother mentioning them. Guys working South Oyster Bay on soft plastics, 4-inch pearl or bunker-colored paddle tails on light jig heads, have been picking up weakfish in that 18 to 22-inch class working the deeper holes off the marsh edges on the last two hours of the outgoing. It's not a blitz, it's a handful of fish here and there, but five years ago you wouldn't catch a single one, so I'll take it as a sign this fishery's finally coming back to life in this system.

Blackfish and porgies are basically an afterthought this time of year — water's too warm and the tog won't turn on again until the fall push, though you can still scratch out porgies around the Freeport bridge pilings on sandworms if you're bored on a slow tide.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend. Tides are easing off the full moon toward neap, which should actually help the night bass bite settle into a more predictable rhythm around the tide changes instead of the harder push we've had. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they usually do in early August, it might stir things up for a day, but the underlying pattern — blues up top in daylight, bass down deep after dark — should hold right through the build toward the mid-August new moon. That's when I expect the bait to really stack up tight in the inlet again, and that's when this thing gets interesting.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks bass go quiet at noon, wide open after dark on bunker chunks
reports.subhead: Warm water has flipped the switch on the Sound — stripers are night-shift only while bluefish run the daylight bunker schools from Matinecock to the Throgs Neck.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a guy at the bait shop this week swear up and down that the bass have left Execution Rocks. Told him the fish didn't go anywhere — they just changed their hours. That's been the story on the western Sound for two weeks now, and it's not changing anytime soon with this water staying warm through the day.

Kings Point is reading 70.9 this week, and that's on the surface — out at Execution Rocks and around the Stepping Stones, that top layer's been sitting in the high 60s to low 70s straight through the afternoon. Compare that to New London out east at 69.4 and you can see the gradient — the western end of this Sound is running warmer than it has any business being at the end of July, and stripers don't love it. They're doing exactly what thirty years of watching this water tells me they'll do: sliding down onto structure during the day and only really showing themselves on the tide changes, at first light, and after the sun goes down.

Execution Rocks has still been good — better than good, honestly — but you need to be there for the right window. The last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, right around dusk, has been the money stretch. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 2 to 3 ounces of weight depending on how hard that current's ripping, dropped right along the rockpile edge where it drops from 15 feet down into the 30s. I've had guys anchor up there at 7pm with a chum slick going and not touch a rod until it's full dark, then it's bent rods for an hour straight — fish from 26 inches up to a couple that pushed 40. Live eels drifted on the same structure after 9pm have been the ticket for the bigger models. Daytime, forget it — I've fished that rock at noon three times this month and gotten nothing but sunburned.

Stepping Stones is running the same program. That light has been a spring highway for decades, but right now it's strictly a tide-change and night bite too. The current there is still the draw — bass are using it as a highway between Execution Rocks and the bridge, they're just moving through on their own schedule now instead of ours.

What's filling the daylight void is bluefish, and they are absolutely making the most of this warm water. We flagged this pattern last week and said it would hold as long as the weather stayed stable — and it has. Matinecock Point has had bunker stacked up thick since June, and the blues have been shredding through those schools all week, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the bait gets pushed up tight against the point. Bucktails with a strip of pork rind, or just a bare metal like a Hopkins or an Ava jig worked through the melee, will get bit almost every cast when the birds are working. Snap swivel above the leader unless you enjoy losing gear — these blues have teeth and no patience.

Fluke fishing has been the steady hand through all this. Hart Island and the channel edge running off it have been holding keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — standard summer ratio, nothing to write home about but enough to put dinner in the cooler. Drifting with 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in the 4-inch size, working the drop from 20 feet down into the channel at 35, outgoing tide. The bite's better on the last two hours before dead low when the current's still got some push to it but isn't ripping your bucktail sideways.

Porgies remain the honest man's fish around City Island right now — anchor up on any of the reefs off the north shore, clam or bloodworm on a high-low rig, and you'll load the cooler without much drama. It's not glamorous but it's about as sure a thing as this Sound offers in late July.

Weakfish have been scattered — a few reports out of Little Neck Bay and up in Manhasset, nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around, but worth a drift if you're already out there working bucktails for fluke.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend — the tides are easing off the full moon push toward neap, which usually means a little less current strength and a little more patience required, but the warm surface layer isn't going anywhere with this weather pattern locked in. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to in early August, it might mix the water enough to knock the bass off their spots for a tide or two, but I'd expect the night bite at Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones to bounce right back. My money this week is on fishing dusk into dark for the bass and hitting the bunker schools off Matinecock in the middle of the day for blues — that's where the action actually is right now, and no sense fighting the thermometer.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: blues are stupid, bass went to bed, and everybody's asking the wrong question
reports.subhead: The peanut bunker blitz we called last week is still running the beach — but if you want stripers, you're fishing in the dark now.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the fuel dock yesterday morning, cooler full of ice, no bait, and asks me straight up: "Where are the bass?" I told him what I've been telling everybody all week — you're not going to find them where you found them in June. He looked at me like I'd told him Santa wasn't real.

Here's the truth of it. The water's warm — buoy readings off the beach are sitting around 71, 72 degrees, and that's pushed the stripers clean out of their comfort zone. Bass like it closer to 68-70. When the ocean runs hot like this, those fish don't leave, they just go down and go nocturnal. I'm talking Fire Island Inlet structure, the rockpile off Democrat Point, the deeper cuts along the barrier beach — all producing, but only in that window from last light through the dark hours, and best right around the tide change. Eels and bunker chunks fished tight to structure on the last of the outgoing has been my go-to. Daytime, forget it — you're wasting bait.

Now the bluefish — that's a different conversation entirely, and it's the one I actually want to have with you. We flagged this exact pattern last week, said the blitz would keep running as long as the bunker stayed on the beach and the weather held stable, and here we are — it's still going. Peanut bunker schools are getting pushed right up against the sand from about Cedar Beach down through Kismet and Corneille Estates, and the blues are hammering them in that classic surface-boil, birds-diving, water-turning-white way that makes your heart rate jump even after twenty years of seeing it. I had a customer's kid catch eight blues in twenty minutes off the beach two mornings ago on nothing fancy — a 3/4-ounce Kastmaster in chrome, long cast, fast retrieve right through the froth. Poppers work too if you want the visual, and honestly there's nothing better than watching a blue crash a topwater at first light with the sun coming up over the inlet.

The bigger blues have been mixing in more since around the 27th — not just the schoolies anymore, some real choppers in that 8-10 pound class showing up in the mix. If you're throwing bucktails for bass and getting bit off, that's your answer — it's blues, and they don't care what you had planned.

Fluke's been the steady hand all month, and it still is. Nothing explosive, but dependable, which honestly is what fluke fishing should be. Robert Moses bridges — both spans — are holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot range on the drift, and the pattern hasn't changed: chartreuse bucktail with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer, dragged slow along the bottom, working the current seams where the pilings break the flow. Best window is the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, when the bait gets funneled through and the fluke stack up to intercept it. I'm seeing a mix of shorts and keepers, maybe one keeper for every four or five fish in the box — nothing to write home about, but enough to keep rods bent and put dinner on the table if you're patient and keep moving. The channel edges off Captree and out toward the inlet mouth have been holding fish too, especially on that harder-bottom transition where the sand gives way to shell.

Weakfish are around in the bay but it's spotty — a few nice fish coming out of Great South Bay on bucktails and soft plastics fished slow near the bottom, mostly in that deeper water off Sayville and out toward the Fire Island lighthouse flats. Nothing to build a trip around, but worth a drift or two if you're already out there for fluke. Blackfish season's closed right now so we're not chasing tog — that conversation picks back up in the fall.

Tide-wise, we're coming off that full moon push, so the current's still running hard, and we're easing toward neap over the next several days. That's actually good news for the bay bite — less current means the fluke drifts slow down to a manageable pace instead of you having to add extra weight just to feel bottom. Wind's been out of the southwest and stable, which is exactly the kind of pattern that keeps a beach blitz alive — no wind chop pushing the bait off the sand, no dirty water rolling in.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the blues to keep running the beach as long as this weather holds — and this time of year, that's usually until a thunderstorm or a cold front rolls through and scatters everything for a day or two before it resets. Early August tends to bring one of those disruptions, so if you've got a window this week, take it. For bass, I'd keep the program the same — dark hours, structure, patience — and don't be surprised if the first albie or bonito scout reports start trickling in from further east as we push toward the next new moon. That's usually the tell that the season's starting to turn, even if the calendar still says summer down here at Captree.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Balling Tight on Stratford Shoal — Blues on Top, Bass Gone Deep and Dark
reports.subhead: The bait's telling the story of a Sound split in two: warm surface water pushing stripers into basements while blues and porgies feast up top.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning off Middle Ground Light with the binoculars up before the rod ever came out of the holder, and what I saw explained the whole week. Peanut bunker — dime to half-dollar size — balled up tight against the rip current, nervous, pushed shallow, with terns working them from above and something bigger working them from below. That something turned out to be bluefish, not bass, and that's the tell right now. When the birds are diving and the water's boiling but you're not marking stripers under it, you know the thermal layer's doing exactly what it's been doing all month.

Kings Point is reading 70.9 degrees, New London's sitting at 69.4, and that gradient across the Sound is real — it's warmer the further west and shallower you go, cooler as you swing east toward the Race. We flagged this pattern last week: striped bass are a low-light player only as long as surface temps hold in the mid-70s, and that's held true to the letter. The bass haven't left, they've just gone to the basement. I'm marking good concentrations of them 30 to 45 feet down on the meter around Stratford Shoal and the deeper drop just north of Charles Island, but they're not interested in anything during daylight hours unless it's dead-drifted right on their nose.

The program that's actually working is the one I've been running for two weeks now: bunker chunks or a whole fresh eel on a fish-finder rig, fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the outgoing tide and into the top of the incoming, right at first light or after dark. I had two fish over 30 inches Thursday night drifting eels off the east side of Stratford Shoal in about 38 feet, current still moving decent even on this softening tide cycle. That's the other piece of this — we're coming off the neap and the current through the deeper channels has been sluggish, which concentrates bait less aggressively than it should this time of year. As the moon builds back toward the August 12 new moon, expect that current to sharpen up again, and when it does, the bass should tighten up on the structure edges instead of spreading out.

Daytime, if you want steady action instead of the grind-it-out night program, the blues are your play. They don't care about the warm water — they love it — and they're stacked on the same bait schools the bass are avoiding. Norwalk Islands has been the most consistent water for this: run the channels between Sheffield and Cockenoe, look for the diving birds, and throw poppers or Hopkins tins into the melee. Fish are running two to five pounds, occasional bigger ones mixed in, and it doesn't take finesse — just get something shiny in front of them on the retrieve and hang on.

Fluke are the honest, dependable piece of this puzzle right now. Not exciting, but real. I've had good drifts off Port Jeff Harbor mouth and along the edge of the Middle Ground flats in 25 to 35 feet, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. The keepers are mixing with plenty of shorts — for every legal fish you're probably culling three or four undersized, so it's a numbers game, but the structure-and-drift pattern is holding steady the way it usually does in late July. Slow the drift down as much as you can stand; the water's warm enough that these fish aren't chasing anything fast.

Porgies have been the quiet standout. Anchor up on any rocky patch — the reef structure off the Norwalk Islands, the rockpile edges around Charles Island, even inside Port Jeff Harbor near the breakwater — and small hooks with sandworm or clam belly will load the cooler fast. This is about as easy as Sound fishing gets right now, and it's a good call if you've got kids or guests aboard who just want bent rods.

What's got my attention heading into next week isn't any of that — it's what I haven't seen yet but expect to any day. The bait's been building all month, the water's warm enough, and this is exactly the calendar window where bonito start showing on the western edges of the Sound, usually first as scattered reports around the Race and working their way toward Stratford Shoal by mid-August. I haven't marked any yet, but I'll be watching the bait balls closer than usual this week — when bonito show, they show fast and they show subtle, a different kind of nervous water than blues make. If a cold front pushes through in the next few days and knocks the surface temp down even a degree or two, that could be the trigger. Until then, I'd fish the tide changes hard for bass, hit the birds for blues, and keep one eye on anything that looks like small, fast fish slashing through the peanut bunker instead of just crashing them.

reports.headline: No albies yet at Great Point — but the bluefish are pinning bait against every rip on the Shoals
reports.subhead: Terns are diving, blues are blitzing, bass have gone to the dark hours — and the first bonito push is still a few tide cycles away.
reports.body_markdown:
I sat off the tip of Great Point Wednesday morning with the engine idling, watching a mixed flock of terns and a couple gulls working a nervous patch of water maybe eighty yards off the rip line. Bait was getting pushed up tight — sand eels, some peanut bunker mixed in — and every few seconds something would explode underneath it, white water and all. I'll be honest, my first thought was albie. Second look, watching the boils roll instead of blow straight up, told me different. Bluefish. Good ones, three to six pounds, just wrecking that bait ball on the last of the ebb.

That's been the story all week from Great Point down through Sankaty and out onto the Shoals — bluefish are the show right now, and they're not shy about it. The water's sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s in the shallows on a calm afternoon, and that heat has pushed the striped bass into their summer pattern — deep, structure-oriented, mostly nocturnal. Bluefish don't care. They're riding the same bait schools that have been pouring through the Sound for weeks, and they'll hit it in bright sun same as dusk.

Best tactic right now is metal — half-ounce to two-ounce diamond jigs snapped hard on the retrieve, or a bomber-style popper walked across the top when they're up busting bait visibly. Great Point rip on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most reliable window, but I've had similar action off Monomoy Rip and along the edge of Horseshoe Shoal where the current stacks bait against the drop. Don't overthink the retrieve — blues want speed and flash, not finesse. A few guys working topwater poppers off Sankaty at first light have had some of the better blitz sessions of the summer, fish crashing the surface so hard you can hear it from fifty yards.

Striped bass are around, just not where you'll find them at noon. The pattern's been consistent — fish holding deep on the current seams and ledges through the day, then sliding up onto structure after dark to feed. Chatham's inlet structure and the deeper cuts around Monomoy have been producing after-dark bass on chunked bunker and live eels, fished on the bottom or drifted just off it where the current runs hardest. If you want a shot at a real fish, that's the window — an hour before to an hour after the tide turns, dark water, patience. Daytime bass bites have been the exception, not the rule, and I wouldn't plan a whole trip around one.

Fluke have softened up in the shallower stuff as the heat's pushed them toward deeper water. The better fish have been coming from the channel edges and rip-adjacent structure around Monomoy and the deeper cuts off the Sound side of Nantucket — 25 to 40 feet, moving water, white or chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom. It's not a numbers game right now, more a quality-over-quantity deal, but there are keepers mixed in if you're willing to work the drift instead of anchoring up and waiting.

Now — the question everyone's been asking me at the dock for two weeks straight. No, I have not seen a confirmed bonito or albie on Nantucket Shoals yet. I've been watching Great Point and the rips off Sankaty every day this week for that telltale sign — smaller, tighter boils, fish that come up and vanish instead of thrashing on top — and it just hasn't shown. Water off Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard has already crossed the temperature threshold that usually kicks this fishery off, and the moon's building toward full in early August, which means current through these rips is only going to get stronger over the next several days. Nantucket typically lags that Vineyard/Buzzards push by a week or two most years, and I don't see any reason this season breaks that pattern. If I had to guess, I'd say we're close — close enough that I'll have my epoxy jigs and Albie Snax rigged and ready every time I leave the dock.

We said last week this zone would hold steady with no major shifts coming, and that's exactly what's played out — the bluefish blitz has kept rolling, the bass have stayed nocturnal, and nothing's changed in a hurry. That stability actually works in our favor here, because it means when the current does build enough to pull bonito and albies up over the Shoals, the bait and the structure will be sitting exactly where we expect them.

For the coming week, I'd focus mornings and evenings on Great Point and Monomoy Rip for bluefish on metal and poppers, keep a bunker chunk or eel rig ready after dark around Chatham and Monomoue's deeper structure for bass, and check the Great Point rip line every single day for that first small, tight boil that doesn't look like a bluefish. If the building current does its job over the next few tide cycles, that's when this whole report changes.

reports.headline: Deer Island Rip Still Owns the Night — Mackerel Working, Cape Ann Holds the Day Bite
reports.subhead: Boston Harbor's stripers have gone deep and nocturnal like everywhere else, but the Gulf of Maine's cooler hand keeps Cape Ann fishing in daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a choice to make Monday morning — run the boat up to Cape Ann and fish the ledges in daylight, or stay in the harbor and work Deer Island on the night tide. I split the difference, and it told me everything I need to know about this water right now.

The harbor itself has gone quiet in the sun. Surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off Deer Island and Spectacle Island have pushed the bass down and back, and they're not interested in showing themselves at noon. I fished the Deer Island Light drop-off on the last two hours of the outgoing Tuesday evening — that ledge falls from 15 feet down to better than 40 fast, and it's always held fish, but this week they wanted it after dark. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20 feet down, drifted right off the rip where the current pinches past the light, produced three bass in the mid-20s to low 30s inches between 9 and 11 p.m. Nothing before dark. That's the pattern coastwide right now and Boston Harbor isn't exempt — daytime fish holding tight to structure and current seams, only committing after the sun's off the water.

Spectacle Island's channel edge gave up bluefish in the same window, chopping through peanut bunker pushed up against the rocks on the last of the ebb. Small metal — half-ounce Kastmasters, silver — worked better than anything with a bait smell to it once the blues got locked onto the peanuts. If you see the surface nervous off Spectacle in that last hour of outgoing, don't overthink it, just get metal in the water fast.

We flagged this last week — said to expect steady, unspectacular conditions to hold through the week — and that's exactly what the harbor gave us. Nothing blew up, nothing died. Bass are there, bluefish are chasing bait, but you're working for it and you're working after dark.

Cape Ann is a different animal, and that's why I ran up there Thursday. The Gulf of Maine keeps that water a few degrees cooler than the harbor, and it shows — Halibut Point and the Rockport breakwater side gave me stripers in daylight, which the harbor flat-out wouldn't. Fished eels along the rocks on the incoming, working the current seams where the ledge drops off into 20-plus feet, and picked up fish through the late morning that I simply wasn't getting in Boston proper. Egg Rock off Nahant is holding the same pattern — daytime bass on structure, better on the last two hours of the flood when bait gets pushed up against the granite. If you want a shot at bass with the sun up this week, point the bow north, not south.

Mackerel are still stacked around The Graves and President Roads, and that's worth knowing even if you're not targeting them directly — those schools are exactly what's pulling bass and blues up onto the harbor's outer ledges after dark. I jigged a limit in twenty minutes off The Graves Tuesday morning on small diamond jigs, mostly for bait, and used half of them live that same evening at Deer Island. If you're running a night program, don't buy bait — catch it on the way out.

South of the harbor, Plymouth and Duxbury Bay are quietly doing their thing. Flounder on the flats inside Duxbury on sandworms and pieces of clam, fished on the bottom on the last of the incoming when the water's warmed the mud flats a touch — nothing dramatic, but steady enough that a couple hours there beats sitting on your hands waiting for the harbor bite to turn on in daylight. Scituate's ledges are holding a few bass as well, mostly a dusk pattern similar to what the harbor's doing, eels and chunk bunker along the rocky stretch north of the harbor mouth.

Moon's building toward full in early August, and that current is going to get stronger through the current-dependent spots — Deer Island Light, The Graves, the Nahant ledges. Stronger current usually sharpens these bites rather than killing them, so if the pattern holds, I'd expect the night program in the harbor to get a little more consistent over the next week, and Cape Ann's daytime bite to stay steady as long as that Gulf of Maine water keeps things a few degrees under what Boston's running.

My plan for the coming week: harbor after dark, North Shore before noon. If I only had one trip, I'd fish the Deer Island rip on a Tuesday-or-Wednesday evening outgoing with live mackerel, and I'd have eels rigged as backup for when the tide slacks. No blitzes to report, no fireworks — just solid, structure-based fishing if you're willing to work the tide and the clock instead of the calendar.

reports.headline: Race Point slack tide: 38-pound bass on live mackerel, and the mackerel are stacked deep
reports.subhead: The Bay's staying cooler than the Sound this week, and that's exactly why the bass are still eating during daylight out here.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, six-fifteen, we're anchored up on the west side of Race Point in about 55 feet, right where the rip folds over that hard sand edge, and the fishfinder lights up with mackerel from the surface clear down to the bottom. Thick as I've seen them all summer. We dropped a couple down on light jigs just to confirm what we were looking at, and inside of ten minutes we had a livewell full and lines out on balloon rigs, drifting them back into the seam where the moving water meets the slower stuff off the bar. Slack tide was maybe forty minutes off, current easing up, and that's when the rod in the stern corner just loaded over and stayed down. Twenty minutes later we had a 38-pound bass in the net, fat, full of mackerel, exactly where she should've been.

That's the story of the Bay right now, and it's a different story than what's happening south of us. We said last week this stretch would hold up better than Nantucket Sound as the season pushed into the warm stretch, and that's exactly what's playing out. The Sound and the ocean beaches down toward the Vineyard are running warm enough that the bass have gone mostly nocturnal — daytime fish sulking deep, only really turning on after dark. Cape Cod Bay hasn't crossed that threshold. The water out here is still cool enough, especially on the north side around Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars, that we're getting a legitimate daytime bite, and it's built entirely around these mackerel schools stacking on the rips.

The pattern all week has been the same. Find the mackerel — and this year they've been sitting tight to structure, not spread out over open sand — then work the edges on the last hour of the ebb into slack. Peaked Hill Bars has been just as good as Race Point some mornings, maybe better on the smaller tides, because that structure holds bait even when the current's not ripping hard. Live mackerel under a balloon, freelined back with just enough weight to get it down eight or ten feet, has out-produced everything else. A couple of guys have done well slow-trolling umbrella rigs with mackerel-colored tubes through the same zones on the last of the incoming, but nothing's beaten a live bait doing what a live bait does when a big bass is sitting downcurrent with its mouth open.

Bluefish have been riding right alongside that bait, and they've been the more reliable fish this week if you just want steady action instead of waiting on one big bite. Sandy Neck has had bluefish blitzes most mornings on the outgoing tide, bunker and mackerel getting pushed up against the beach, birds working tight, blues in the eight-to-twelve-pound range hammering anything silver you throw at them — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, don't overthink it. That blitz pattern has been building all month and there's no sign of it backing off. If anything I'd expect it to keep spreading down toward Barnstable Harbor as more bait works its way along the beach.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, honestly, and I won't dress that up. The flats off Barnstable and around Sandy Neck channel have given up some nice fish to four and five pounds on white Gulp swimming mullets and bucktails, but you're working for them — long drifts, lots of empty stretches, then a flurry near a channel bend or a mussel bed where the current squeezes. Billingsgate has been quieter than I'd like for this time of year. The shoal itself is holding bait, but the fluke bite there has been more shorts than keepers. I think the water's still a touch cool on that structure for them to really set up in numbers — give it another couple weeks.

Cod are still mostly a story for later in the season out here, but we've started marking decent fish on the deeper humps north of Billingsgate, 90 to 110 feet, on the sonar during a couple of afternoon runs. Nothing worth targeting hard yet — one or two fish on diamond jigs when we dropped down out of curiosity — but that's usually how it starts. By late August, early September, that structure fills in and becomes a real fishery. Worth keeping in your back pocket if you're out there anyway working the bass.

Moon's building toward full in the first days of August, and that's going to matter. Current through these rips has been soft to moderate most of this week, which is part of why the bite windows have been short — twenty, thirty minutes around the slack when the mackerel bunch up and the bass move in to feed. As the tides build with the moon, I expect that window to widen and the current on Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars to sharpen up the whole pattern. If the mackerel stay put — and there's no reason to think they won't with water this cool holding steady — the next week should set up as well as anything we've had this summer. I'd be out there working the last of the ebb into slack, live mackerel rigged light, watching the birds and the meter before I ever drop a line.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole Loading Up With Bait — The Albies Just Haven't Shown Yet
reports.subhead: Sand eels and silversides are stacking in the rips between Pasque and Nashawena, water's crossed the threshold, but the first false albacore of the season still hasn't punched a card.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the rocks at Robinson's Hole Tuesday evening with the tide just starting to run and watched a ball of silversides get pushed into a tight knot against the Pasque side, nervous, flashing, doing that thing they do right before something eats them. Nothing hit. I watched it for twenty minutes. That's where we are right now — the table's set, the bait's here, and the guest of honor hasn't walked in yet.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the water had crossed the seasonal threshold and the building current off the full moon should be enough to trigger the first albie or bonito scouting reports within a few days. The current part is right on schedule. Tides through Robinson's and Quick's Hole are running noticeably harder than they were two weeks back, that classic mid-summer rip starting to snap on the last two hours of the ebb. But as of this week I haven't had a confirmed albie or bonito in hand or heard one from a boat I trust. Close, not there. If you're itching to be first, I get it — I am too — but don't burn a Saturday convinced they're already stacked up. They're not, not yet.

What IS happening, and happening well, is the striped bass game, just not in the way you'd want at noon. These fish have gone nocturnal on us with the inshore water sitting warm — I'm seeing surface temps in the low-to-mid 70s from Quick's Hole down through the Cuttyhunk side, and that pushes stripers deep onto structure during daylight and up onto bait only after dark. The move right now is eels and bunker chunks fished on the down-current side of the rips at Cuttyhunk and around the backside of Nashawena after sundown, into the first couple hours of the incoming. Guys working the west end of Cuttyhunk with a whole bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, have been finding slot fish and the occasional overslot in that 15-25 foot depth range where the rip dumps into deeper water. Daytime, if you want a shot, fish the thermocline — deep bucktails, 2 to 3 ounces, dropped down along the drop-offs on the Woods Hole side where the current keeps things cooler, worked slow on the bottom third of the water column.

Bluefish have been the reliable show for anyone who wants action without waiting for dark. They're riding the same bait schools pushing through Woods Hole and along the backside of the Vineyard toward Oak Bluffs, and when they find bunker pinned against structure it turns into a proper blitz — poppers and single-hook Hopkins get bit the second they land. This matches what's been building the whole coast — the bunker-driven blitz pattern that's been marching north, and Buzzards Bay is squarely in that lane right now. If you see gulls working tight and diving hard off the Elizabeth Islands, don't wait, that window closes fast.

Fluke have softened up some in the shallower stretches of the bay as the heat's pushed them toward deeper structure — I'm hearing better numbers out of the deeper bends off Robinson's Hole and the channel edges around Quick's Hole than off the open sand flats that were producing in June. White Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been the ticket, with the better fish coming right at the current edge where it dumps into deeper water.

The bright spot with zero complications is bottom fishing. Scup and black sea bass have been about as steady as this zone gets — the classic structure around Middle Ground, the ledges off Menemsha, and the rock piles between Cuttyhunk and Nashawena are stacked with keeper-class sea bass and scup thick enough that a bucket limit isn't a stretch on a good drift. Squid strips or clam on a double-hook bottom rig, 2-3 ounces of lead depending on current, right on the structure. This is your Plan B while we wait on the albies — reliable, fast, and it keeps the rod bent while you scout for the real deal.

Looking ahead: the moon goes full in the next few days and that current is only going to build from here. If the pattern holds the way it usually does, I'd expect the first legitimate albie or bonito sighting somewhere in this zone within the week — Robinson's Hole and the mouth of Quick's Hole are where I'd have my eyes first, followed by the rip off Menemsha once the bait gets pushed that direction. I'll be out there checking the bait balls every evening tide change, and the second something eats one, you'll hear about it here first. Until then, fish the dark for stripers, chase the gulls for blues, and hit the bottom structure for a guaranteed bend in the rod while the real show finishes loading.

reports.headline: 138 feet of gravel on the Stellwagen edge: cod scratchy, mud haddock steady, bluefin on the meatballs
reports.subhead: Whales and mackerel are stacked on the same water off the northwest corner, and the tuna are starting to notice.
reports.body_markdown:
138 feet, gravel bottom, northwest corner of the Bank — that's where I had the anchor down Tuesday morning with two charters aboard and a sounder full of marks that turned out to be mostly dogfish. That's the honest start to this report. Cod have been a grind out there this week, not a bust, but you're earning every fish.

We worked that gravel patch off the northwest corner for two hours on the last of the ebb, jigging diamond jigs and teasers tipped with clam, and came away with six keeper cod in the 6 to 12 pound range, mixed in with a pile of shorts we had to shake off quick. The water on the surface up there was pushing into the mid-60s, which is about right for late July, and the fish were sitting tight to the hard bottom where the current breaks over the ledge. If you're chasing cod on the Bank right now, don't waste time on the flats — go find the gravel edges and fish them slow and vertical. The bite windows are short, usually tied to the tide change, and once the current slacks the fish seem to shut down for an hour before picking back up.

Haddock have been the more dependable play, and that's typical for this time of year. We ran out to the Stellwagen Basin, 190 to 210 feet on the mud, and found solid marks holding just off bottom. Standard haddock rigs — high-low with a pink or chartreuse tube fly and squid strips — have been putting fish in the box steady, nothing giant but a good grade of 2 to 4 pound haddock with enough 5-pounders mixed in to keep it interesting. That mud bottom out there stays productive right through the summer because the water column holds cooler and more stable than up on the crown of the Bank, and the haddock like it that way.



Now for the fun part. The bluefin have shown up chasing mackerel, and it's been enough to get boats excited without being a sure thing yet. We've had mackerel schools breezing the surface off the eastern edge of Stellwagen most mornings this week, right around the same water where the whales have been working — humpbacks and finbacks plowing through bait balls, which is about the best sign you can ask for that there's forage stacked up. Where you find the whales tearing into the mackerel, the bluefin aren't far behind, usually sitting a little deeper and picking off stragglers.

We flagged this last week — said the bluefin interest would keep building around the bait concentrations on the Bank, and that's exactly what's playing out. Since the July 3rd trophy fish closure, the recreational slot fishery has stayed a steady, workable pace rather than anything explosive, and that's held true here too. We've seen fish in the 50 to 70 inch class come tight to a green machine trolled behind a spreader bar, and a couple boats working chunk lines off drifting mackerel schools have connected on live bait rigs — a single mackerel on a 6/0 circle hook, no weight, just fed back into the chum slick. It's not a bite where you're going to load the boat, but if you put in the time around active bait and working whales, you've got a real shot.

Tillies Bank has been quieter for us this week — less bait sign, less whale activity, and the couple times we ran out there the water felt slack, no real current push. I'd stick closer to home on Stellwagen proper until that changes.

Moon's waxing toward full in the first week of August, and that should start sharpening the tide swings on the Bank, which is good news for both the groundfish and the tuna. Stronger current means better current breaks on the gravel for cod, more defined edges on the mud for haddock to stage against, and tighter bait concentrations for the bluefin and whales to work. If that current builds the way it usually does heading into a full moon, I'd expect the haddock bite on the mud to stay the most reliable meat-in-the-box option, with cod picking up on the gravel as the tide starts moving harder again.

For the tuna, the pattern to watch is simple — go where the mackerel and the whales are, not where they were yesterday. That bait has been moving around the eastern and northeastern edges of the Bank day to day, and the bluefin are following it, not holding a fixed piece of structure. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd run out early, find the whale activity, and work the edges of that bait with a mackerel rig before committing to a groundfish plan. Worth the run if the weather holds — and right now it looks like it will.

reports.headline: Second Beach Blues Run Hot, Beavertail Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: Bunker blitzes are hitting the ocean beaches on schedule while the rocky shore's bass have gone strictly nocturnal — here's where to fish both.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Beavertail Tuesday morning with the sun barely up and watched a school of peanut bunker get pushed right up against the ledge, so thick the water looked like it was boiling from underneath. That's the tell this time of year — when the bait starts pinning itself against structure at first light, something's pushing it, and out here in late July that something is almost always bluefish. Sure enough, ten minutes later the blues came through and it was game on for about twenty minutes before they pushed off toward the point.

That's been the pattern all week from Newport down through Sakonnet. We said the bunker-driven blitz would keep marching up the coast, and it has — Second Beach and the stretch off Sakonnet Point have both had daytime blitz windows this week, usually on the front half of the outgoing when bait gets squeezed against the beach or pinned on a rip. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, half-ounce Deadly Dicks — are getting bit the second they land if you're in the right spot at the right tide. The trick is timing. These blitzes don't linger. I've had fifteen-minute windows produce a dozen blues to eight pounds, then nothing but empty water for two hours. If you see birds working tight over bait near the rocks, don't wait — get a cast in before the whole thing slides down the beach.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Inshore surface temps are sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range, and that's put the bass on a strict nighttime schedule. Daytime, they're down deep on structure — the ledges off Beavertail, the rips under the Newport Bridge, the east passage current seams off Jamestown — just holding tight and not doing much. Wait for dark and they wake up. Eels drifted on the current seams off Beavertail and Fort Wetherill from an hour before high through the top of the tide have been the most consistent producer I've heard about, with a few schoolies mixed with some better fish pushing 30 inches. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in the Sakonnet River channel after dark are doing the same job for guys who don't want to fuss with live eels. Daytime bass fishing on the south shore right now is mostly a waste of gas unless you're working deep water with jigs right on bottom.

Fluke have softened up in the shallow spots the way they usually do once the water gets this warm — the open flats inside the Sakonnet and off Second Beach have gone quiet. The better fish are sliding into the deeper current, Charlestown Breachway and the channel out front of Watch Hill Reef, where the water keeps moving and stays a few degrees cooler. Four-inch white Gulp on quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb through Charlestown, has been picking at keepers mixed with a lot of shorts. Not a banner week for fluke, but honest work if you put in the drift time.

Scup are everywhere on the ledges right now and they're the easy button if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating — squid strips or sandworms on a hi-lo rig right on the rocks at Beavertail or the Jamestown bridge pilings will fill a cooler fast, and there's nothing wrong with that on a hot afternoon.

Tog guys, I know you're itching — I've had three separate conversations this week about which cracks are holding fish. Season's closed until August 1st here, so for now it's scouting only. I've been easing crabs down into a few spots off Beavertail and the Jamestown side just to confirm what's home, and there's fish there. When the season flips open next week, start on the slack around the new moon tides — dead low or dead high, whichever gives you the cleanest drift-free window — and work green crabs tight to the base of the ledges in 15 to 25 feet. I'll have specifics once I've had a proper crack at it.

On the albie front — nothing yet, and I want to be straight about that instead of hyping something that isn't here. It's still a touch early for the south shore breachways; that push usually doesn't show at Napatree, Watch Hill, or Weekapaug until the back half of August into September when the bay anchovies and silversides really thicken up in the current. I have been seeing more silversides pushing through Napatree on the outgoing this week than I did two weeks ago, which is the kind of early signal I look for. Worth keeping a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig in the bag if you're out there working bluefish, but I wouldn't plan a trip around albies just yet.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August and that ought to sharpen up current in the breachways and around Beavertail, which should help both the night bass bite and eventually tip off the albie arrival. If the wind stays out of the south and the ocean holds the moderate chop it's had — a few feet at five seconds, nothing dangerous but enough to keep the surf stirred — I'd stick with the early-morning and dusk blitz windows on the beaches, save the bulk of my bass effort for after dark on the ledges, and start easing into the breachways with the light albie gear as August gets closer.

reports.headline: East End on the 6:04 Ebb: Bass Hold the Rip, Blues Crash the Seam
reports.subhead: The moon's building toward full, current's coming back with authority, and the west end is one warm push from its first bonito of the year.
reports.body_markdown:
Six-oh-four this morning. That's when the ebb hit max push off the Railroad Bridge, and I had a rod bent inside of ninety seconds. Thirty years I've watched that clock, and it still gets me every time — the current builds, the bait gets pinned against the seam, and for about ninety minutes on either side of max flow, the east end turns into the best piece of moving water on the Cape. Right now, in the thick of late July, that window is everything. Miss it and you're fishing dead water. Hit it and you're in business.

We flagged this pattern last week and said it'd hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around — and here we are. The Canal is running its classic mid-summer script: stripers stacked on the current seams, feeding hard on the strong tide stages, and going quiet in between. The difference this week is the moon. We're building toward full in early August, which means the tidal push through the ditch is getting stronger every day. Bigger swings mean harder current, and harder current means the rips are setting up sharper and the bite windows are getting more violent, if shorter.

East end first. The rip line off the Railroad Bridge and down toward Scusset has been the most consistent piece of structure all week, but only on the meat of the tide. Dawn ebb has been my money window — that 5:30 to 7:00 stretch when the sun's just up and the current's ripping hard enough to hold bait against the rocks. Bass to 34 inches have come on swimming plugs — a Redfin or a Danny-style glide, fished with the current, not against it, letting the plug swim naturally through the seam rather than burning it back. After dark it's a different game entirely. Water temp's sitting where it sits every late July — warm enough that the bass have gone mostly nocturnal, same as everywhere south of here. Daytime fish are holding deep in the thermocline seams and only really committing after the sun's down, so if you want quality, you fish the dark side of the strong tides. Eels on the drift, bunker chunks anchored up tight to the rock pile below Scusset — that's where the bigger fish are coming from, 15 to 25 pounds, mostly after 9 PM on the building ebb.

Bluefish are mixed right into those same lanes, and honestly some nights they've been thicker than the bass. Choppers to 8 pounds are hitting the same plugs, same current seams, same tide stages — no real separation between the two species right now, which means if you're targeting one you're going to catch the other. Keep a pair of pliers handy and expect some leader damage if you're running mono.

West end tells a slightly different story. Mashnee Island and the flats around Hog Island have been holding fluke — not a blitz, but a real fishery if you work the channel bends where the current keeps things cool and moving. That matches what's happening everywhere south of us: the shallow open flats have gone soft as the water's warmed, but anywhere with structure and current still holding fluke consistently. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through the deeper bends off Mashnee on the last two hours of the ebb, has put keeper fluke in the boat — nothing huge, mostly 16 to 19 inches, but steady.

Here's the one I'm watching hardest right now: Buzzards Bay water has crossed the threshold where bonito and albies start showing, and the west end of the Canal is basically the front door to that water. Wings Neck and Phinneys Harbor sit right in the funnel. I haven't had a confirmed bonito report out of the west end yet, but with the current building the way it is and bait getting concentrated tighter against the seams, I'd bet money we see the first one inside the next week to ten days. If you're itching to be the guy who gets the first report, I'd be working the outgoing tide off Wings Neck with small metal — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster — worked fast through any nervous water or diving terns.

Slack water's been the tell-all this week. When the current goes flat — and up top it can go dead calm for a solid twenty minutes at both ends — the bite shuts off like someone hit a switch. I've watched guys keep grinding through slack out of stubbornness and it never pays. Better to walk the bank, watch the birds, and be rigged and ready the second that water starts moving again.

Look ahead: with the moon still filling out, expect the current to keep strengthening through the week, which should sharpen those bite windows even more — shorter, harder, more violent. I'd focus effort on the dawn and dusk pushes at the east end for bass and blues, and keep half an eye on the west end for that first bonito sign. If the pattern holds, and there's no reason yet to think it won't, this stays a tide-clock fishery through the first week of August. Know the push, be there when it turns, and don't waste your time in between.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 5:52: Bass Buried Deep, Blues on Top, Bonito Still a Question Mark
reports.subhead: The ledge is fishing on a ten-minute window right now — everything else is happening after dark or up top on bait.
reports.body_markdown:
5:52 AM. That's when the tide goes slack at SW Ledge this week, and if you want a real shot at a daytime striper off that structure, that ten-minute window around the turn is your play. I ran out there Tuesday morning, watched the sonar light up on the down-current face at 52 feet right as the current died, worked a bucktail through it for maybe eight minutes — one fish, a schoolie that came unbuttoned at the boat — and then the tide swung and every mark on the screen dropped back into the rocks like someone pulled a curtain. That's the ledge right now. It's not dead, it's disciplined.

Here's the why. Surface water on both sides of the Block — Montauk's reading 69.1, and I'd put SW Ledge and the west side of the island in that same neighborhood, maybe a degree warmer in the afternoon sun. That's warm enough that the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding tight to structure and current seams — the down-tide face of the ledge, the humps off Southwest, the deeper cuts around Sandy Point — and they're not interested in chasing much until the sun's off the water. After dark is a different story.
