Guys working bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs off the ledge in 45 to 60 feet, and guys swimming eels along the rock piles at Sandy Point and off North Light, are still connecting with real fish — some pushing 30 pounds, a few better. If you want a daytime bite right now, the slack window is genuinely your best shot; if you want numbers, you're fishing at night.

Fluke have done exactly what fluke do when the shallow water gets warm and sleepy — they've pushed off the flats and into the deeper channel bends where there's still moving, cooler water. The Harbor of Refuge drop and the deeper stretch along the West Wall have been the most consistent producers, along with the edge off Whale Rock where the bottom breaks toward 30-35 feet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the last two hours of the ebb — that's been the combination putting keepers in the box, mixed in with a lot of throwbacks. It's not a wide-open bite. You're covering ground to find the pockets, but there are fish there if you're willing to move.

apBluefish are the one thing that's been unambiguous. Bunker schools have been running thick along the beachfront from the Galilee breakwater down toward Sandy Point, and where that bait gets pinned against structure on a moving tide, the blues have been blitzing hard — birds working, fish busting bait right on the surface. I had a charter into that Wednesday off Sandy Point on the last of the incoming, popping topwater plugs and Deadly Dicks into the melee, and we lost count of fish in under an hour. If you see the birds diving and the water nervous, don't overthink it — get a metal in there fast before the school moves.

Black sea bass have quietly been the most dependable bite in the whole zone. The reef structure around SW Ledge and the rockier bottom off Block's southwest corner, working 80 to 100 feet, has been holding solid numbers of keeper sea bass on squid strips and clam bellies fished on a standard two-hook bottom rig. It's not glamorous, but it's about as close to a sure thing as this zone offers right now, and it's a good fallback plan on a day when the top-water bite is slow.

Now, the one everybody's asking me about at the dock — bonito. Not yet. Water temps on both sides of the Block have crossed the threshold where they typically show, and we flagged that arrival window a few days back expecting it to come due about now. It hasn't happened yet in this zone, at least not that I've confirmed with my own eyes or a rod bent over it. What I can tell you is the moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means the current through the rips — SW Ledge, the rip off North Light, the water off Clay Head — is about to build noticeably. That's exactly the mechanism that concentrates bait and triggers that first bonito showing. If I had to bet, I'd watch the surface around North Light and off Southeast Light on a building tide over the next week, small Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs rigged and ready in the console. But I'm not going to tell you they're here when they're not.

Looking ahead: I'd fish the slack windows at SW Ledge for daytime bass, shift to eels and chunks after dark for the better fish, keep working the deeper fluke edges on the ebb, and stay ready for that first bonito flash the moment the current sharpens up toward the full moon. It's a working week, not a gimme — but there's enough happening across the board to make the run out of Galilee worth it if you pick your tide and stick to the plan.

reports.headline: Monhegan pollock on the boil, stripers hugging the cool water at the river mouths
reports.subhead: Groundfish still hold in the Bay's deep water while the bass push into every spring-fed mouth from the Kennebec to the Medomak.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a fellow stop me at the Co-op dock Tuesday morning, hauling gear off the *Sea Hag*, and he says to me, "Rusty, water's warm enough to swim in off Ocean Point." I told him that's exactly the problem. Forty years watching this coast and I can tell you the surface heat does two things every July — it pushes the stripers into the mouths where the rivers keep dumping cold water, and it makes the groundfish sulk deeper in the Bay than most sport boats bother to go. Neither one is news to anybody who's fished here longer than a season, but it bears repeating because half the boats I see anchored up on open water this week are fishing water that's ten degrees too warm for what they're after.

The bass have been thick and predictable where the fresh water hits the salt. Kennebec mouth off Popham, the Sheepscot around the Cross River ledges, and the Damariscotta down by Fort Island — all three have been holding fish on the last of the ebb and the first two hours of the flood, when the current stacks bait against the ledge rock and the cooler outflow keeps the water livable through the heat of the day. Live mackerel under a slip float has been the best producer, but guys drifting chunk mackerel on fish-finder rigs in 15 to 25 feet are doing just as well without the hassle of keeping bait alive. After dark, eels on the swim have taken some good fish off the Damariscotta ledges — nothing enormous, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but steady, and that's the pattern we flagged last week when we said this warm, stable stretch would keep the bass locked into that river-mouth program. It has, right down to the tide stage.

Monhegan's been the bright spot for anybody willing to make the run. Pollock have been busting bait right on the surface off White Head and around the backside ledges at first light — schoolie-sized mostly, two to five pounds, but they'll hit anything silver thrown fast, and it's a fine way to fill an hour before the bigger fish wake up. There have been bass working those same ledges on the tail of the tide, sliding up onto the rock as the current slackens, and a few boats have picked off stripers to 34 inches on topwater plugs worked right in the wash. Eastern Egg Rock has been similar — the puffins are still working the bait balls out there, and where the puffins are diving you'll usually find bass or mackerel underneath doing the same thing from below. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid have been drawing mackerel by the bucketful around the Rock, which is as good a livewell fill-up as you'll find this time of year.

Out in Penobscot Bay proper, the groundfish story hasn't changed and isn't likely to. Cod and haddock are holding in the deep water — the channel east of Vinalhaven, the deep hole off Isle au Haut, and the drop-off between Matinicus and the Bay islands are all still stacking fish in 150 to 220 feet. You need to jig it heavy, and you need to fish it on the slower stages of the tide, because that current runs hard enough through those channels to sweep a light jig sideways before it ever touches bottom. Herring strips or a diamond jig tipped with squid, dropped straight down and worked with short hops off the bottom, has been the ticket. It's not a numbers game — three or four keepers for a morning's work is a solid trip right now — but the fish are there if you're willing to fish deep and slow instead of chasing surface activity that isn't happening in that colder water.

Bluefish are still mostly a rumor up here, though I'd keep half an eye open. The bunker-driven blitzes that have been tearing up beaches to the south have been pushing steadily northward all month, and there's been enough warm water sitting in the outer bay that I wouldn't be shocked to see scattered blues show up around Boothbay or Pemaquid before August gets old. Nothing confirmed yet — just something to watch if you're fishing the open water outside the river mouths.

The moon's building toward full over the next week, which should sharpen the current through the Bay's channels and the Thorofares, and that's good news for the groundfish game — stronger tide means better drift speed for the jig and more predictable bite windows around the turns. For the stripers, as long as this warm, settled weather holds, I'd expect the same program to keep running: fish the cool water at the river mouths on the moving tide, save the ledges at Monhegan and Egg Rock for early and late light, and don't waste a morning fishing open bay water for bass that have already moved somewhere colder. If a front comes through and mixes things up, that could change fast — but for now, this is a coast that's telling you plainly where to be, if you're willing to listen to the water instead of the calendar.

reports.headline: Shoals Ledges Give Up Cod to 8 Pounds While the Piscataqua Keeps Its Bass Honest
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline sounds thin until you've fished the drops off Appledore and the seam at Henderson's Point on the right tide.
reports.body_markdown:
People see thirteen miles of coastline on a map and figure there's nothing here worth trailering a boat for. I've been running my 20-foot Lund out to the Shoals before sunrise for going on fifteen years, and I can tell you those thirteen miles fish like a hundred and thirty if you know where the bottom breaks. This week proved it again — cod, haddock, mackerel, stripers, and bluefish, all inside a morning's run from Rye Harbor.

Start with the Shoals, because that's where the week's best fish came from. White Island and the ledges south of Appledore have been holding cod in the 60 to 90 foot range, and I mean holding — not just passing through. We had a stretch on Saturday's slack tide where three of us put five keeper cod in the boat, biggest going right around eight pounds, on skimmer clams fished tight to bottom with just enough weight to feel the structure. Haddock have been mixed in but smaller, mostly shorts, with a few keepers coming off the rockier stretch between Star and Duck Island on diamond jigs worked with a short hop. The pattern's been the same all month — you want the last hour of the ebb into the first hour of slack, when the current lays down enough to hold bottom without a boat anchor's worth of lead. Fish the moving water hard and you're pulling gear instead of catching.

Mackerel have been thick around the Shoals ledges too, schooling tight enough that you can jig a few dozen in fifteen minutes on a string of small crappie jigs or a mackerel tree, then use the fresh ones for bait or just take a cooler home for the smoker. That mackerel show is also feeding the bigger picture — bluefish have followed the bait right up onto the ledges and into the mouth of the Piscataqua, and they've been willing daytime, which isn't always the case once July gets hot. Blues to four and five pounds have been busting on top around Odiorne Point and off Frost Point, chewing through anything metal — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, anything with flash worked fast on top.

The striper story is a little more nuanced, and it's worth being straight about it. Down south the bass have gone nocturnal with surface water sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and that pattern's creeping into our southern stretch too — Hampton and Seabrook have had their slow stretches midday. But the Gulf of Maine water up here stays cooler than the Sound, and that's kept some daytime activity going around the river mouths and ledges where southern New England guys are stuck waiting for dark. The Piscataqua's been the most consistent piece of that puzzle. Henderson's Point and the seam below the General Sullivan Bridge have both been giving up stripers to 30 inches on the last two hours of the incoming, fish holding in the current break waiting for bait to get swept through. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the bottom edge of the seam, have outfished everything else I've thrown. A few guys working live mackerel under the Memorial Bridge on the same tide stage have done even better after dark, which tracks with what's happening everywhere else on the coast right now — the bigger fish are playing it cautious once the sun's up.

Hampton Harbor has been a mixed bag. The inlet's producing schoolie bass and the occasional slot fish pushing in on the tide, especially the last of the incoming when bait gets funneled through the channel by Great Boars Head. Peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig, or a soft plastic swimbait worked slow along the channel edge, has been the play. But it's been spotty — some days the harbor's stacked with bait and fish, other days it's dead water for two hours before anything shows. If you're fishing Hampton right now, don't burn your whole trip on one spot. Move with the bait.

We called this stretch of stable weather last week, and it's held — no major thermal shift, no blown-out surf, no sudden cold-water push off the Shoals to scatter the groundfish. That stability is exactly why the cod bite has stayed consistent instead of turning on and off with every weather system, and why the bluefish have kept riding that mackerel bait right through the harbor mouths instead of pushing offshore.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which means current is going to sharpen up fast over the next week. That's good news for the Shoals — stronger current concentrates bait tighter against the ledges and usually tightens up the cod bite around the slack windows even more. It's a mixed bag for the harbor bass, though — stronger tides mean shorter, more violent bite windows at Henderson's Point and the Hampton inlet, so timing matters more than it has the last few weeks. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the early slack at White Island for cod, then run back in to hit the Piscataqua seam on the tail of the incoming before the current gets ahead of the presentation. That's the play I'm making, anyway — box first, coffee after.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 150 feet: cod holding the gravel edge, haddock buried in the mud at Platts
reports.subhead: A steady week of structure fishing on the Ledge — nothing explosive, but the depths are sorting fish exactly where they should be in late July.
reports.body_markdown:
One-fifty feet, hard gravel, the edge where Jeffrey's Ledge falls off toward the basin — that's been my starting mark all week, and it's still the most consistent water I've got. Cod don't sit on flat gravel, they sit on the transition, right where the rock breaks up and rolls into softer bottom. Mark that seam on the sounder, drop a diamond jig or a high-low rig baited with clam, and you're in business. Fish have been running 24 to 30 inches, a few pushing better than that, with the biggest one I weighed this week going 14 pounds off a boat out of Rye running the same stretch I fish north of the Ledge tower.

Haddock's a different story and a different bottom entirely. I've been working Platts Bank in 220 to 250 feet of soft mud, and that's where the haddock want to be this time of year — head down in the current, feeding on whatever's drifting through on the tide. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or clam belly have been the ticket, worked with a short lift-drop right off bottom. Don't work it too hard. Haddock feed close to the mud, and if you're ripping the jig two and three feet off bottom you're fishing over their heads. Fish have been coming up in that 20 to 24 inch class, clean and fat, with decent numbers — not a slam dunk trip, but if you find the right drift and hold the boat on it, you can put a good box together.

Pollock have scattered up in the water column over structure between Jeffrey's and Tillies Bank, 80 to 110 feet down over bottom that reads 130 to 160. These fish are chasing bait higher than they were a month ago — I've marked them suspended, not glued to bottom, which tells me the mackerel and herring pushed them up. Jigging a bucktail or a Norwegian-style jig through that mid-water column has been the move, and it's been a nice change of pace from bottom fishing — pollock hit hard and don't quit pulling. Hake are still down in the mud holes of Scantum Basin, best worked at first light or the last hour of daylight, and that's been more of a night-bite pattern lately as the water's stayed warm on top.

Mackerel have been thick on the surface out on the Ledge — not a fishery in themselves for most of my guys, but they matter. Where the mackerel are balled up, that's where everything else is staged underneath, and it's also bait for the tuna gear if you're carrying a spread. Whales have been working the same bait pockets between Jeffrey's and the Stellwagen approaches, which is as good a sign as any that the forage base out there is healthy right now.

On the bluefin — it's early yet. The real giant fishery on the Ledge doesn't usually turn on until October, when the bait balls up tight and the big fish push in behind it. What we've had this week is scattered sign: a few boats marking singles rolling on bait between Jeffrey's and the Stellwagen line, likely early scouts riding a warm filament that's pushed up from the south. I wouldn't build a trip around it yet. If you're out there groundfishing and you see fish up, it's worth a look, but the real window is still two months out.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, if unspectacular, structure fishing through the stretch, and that's exactly what's played out. Nobody's filling the box in twenty minutes, but if you know your bottom and fish the right depth for the right species, you're coming home with fish. That's the Ledge in late July — it rewards patience and precision, not luck.

Tide's been building as the moon works toward full in early August, and that's actually helped. Stronger current means the haddock on Platts hold tighter to structure and the cod on the gravel edge feed more aggressively during the peak of the push. I'd plan around the bigger tide swings this coming week rather than fighting slack water — get out to the Ledge or Platts on the front half of the flood or the back half of the ebb, when the current's really moving, and you'll see better marks and better hookup ratios.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change in the next few days. Cod will keep holding the gravel edges around Jeffrey's, haddock will stay buried in the mud out at Platts and up into the Basin, and pollock will keep suspending over structure wherever the bait sits. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, it'll keep laying flat enough to run out comfortable from Rye, and that's really all you need this time of year — clean water, the right depth, and the patience to fish it properly. I'd keep an eye on the mackerel schools too. When they thin out or move, that usually tells you the bigger fish underneath are about to shift with them.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds cod on the slack while the ledges keep bass honest after dark and before dawn
reports.subhead: Casco Bay's cooler water is buying stripers daylight hours the rest of the coast doesn't have — but you still have to find the tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past the Rock Monday morning, engine idling, watching the current lines braid together the way they do about forty minutes before dead slack, and I thought about how little this bay changes from year to year even as everything around it does. Halfway Rock doesn't care what the surface water is doing off Montauk or Sandy Hook. It cares about tide, structure, and bait, in that order, and this week it delivered on two of the three.

Groundfish first, since that's where the discipline pays off. I fished the northeast side of the Rock in 70 to 90 feet on the last hour of the ebb into slack, diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, and connected on cod in the 4 to 8 pound range, with one better fish that pulled hard enough to make me second-guess my drag setting before I got a look at him — call it 12 pounds, released clean. Haddock have been scattered rather than schooled; I marked a few pods on the sounder holding tight to bottom but they weren't feeding hard, which tells me the bait — likely herring fry and small pollock — hasn't concentrated yet the way it will once the tide swings build back toward full moon. That's worth watching over the next week. The slack window at Halfway Rock is short, maybe twenty minutes on either side of the change, so if you're marking fish and not getting bit, don't burn line waiting them out — reposition and try the drop on the western ledge instead.

Bass have been the more interesting story, and here's where Casco Bay is doing something different than the rest of the coast right now. Farther south, from New Jersey through southern New England, stripers have gone essentially nocturnal — surface water's sitting in the low-to-mid seventies and the fish are holding deep on structure until dark. We don't have that problem yet. Our water's still cool enough — I'm reading mid-to-upper sixties around the mouth of the Presumpscot and off Peaks Island — that bass are willing to work the ledges in daylight, provided you're fishing the right stage of tide. Bailey Island's back side, the ledges off Mackerel Cove, has been giving up slot fish on the incoming, an hour either side of the tide change, on 3/4-ounce chartreuse bucktails worked slow along bottom, occasionally on live mackerel when we could get them to stay on the hook. Cape Small's river mouth — where the New Meadows dumps warmer, baitfish-rich water into cooler bay water — has produced some of the better numbers this week, fish up to 30 inches on topwater at first light before the sun gets high and pushes them down onto the drop-off. Harpswell's ledges have been quieter, more of a one-or-two-fish morning, but the quality's been decent when they show.

Mackerel are thinning out, which is normal for this point in the season — the big May and June runs have mostly pushed offshore or dispersed, but there are still pockets working the Portland breakwater and the backside of Peaks Island in the early morning, small jigs on a Sabiki rig, fish running 10 to 12 inches. If you need bait for the bass or the cod trip, that's still your best bet, just don't expect the density we had two months ago.

The surprise this week — and it's a small one, worth mentioning because it's unusual for this bay — has been a few bluefish showing up around the mouth of Casco Bay proper, inside of Two Lights. Warm year, warmer than most, and it's pulled a few blues north of their usual range. Nothing like the blitzes you'd see from bunker schools farther south, just occasional fish in the 3 to 5 pound class mixed in with the bass on topwater plugs. I wouldn't plan a trip around them, but if you're working the ledges off Two Lights on a moving tide, don't be shocked if something with a sharper set of teeth than a striper hits your plug.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, typical mid-summer Maine conditions through the stretch, and that's exactly what's held. Warm, stable air, water temperatures cool enough to keep the bass working daylight tides, groundfish holding tight to structure at Halfway Rock. No surprises, which in this business is its own kind of good news.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full in the first week of August, which should sharpen current through the bay's rips and channels — Halfway Rock, the mouth of the New Meadows, the gut between Peaks and House Island. Stronger current usually means better bait concentration, and better bait concentration usually means the haddock I've been marking but not hooking start feeding in earnest. If I had one morning to fish next week, I'd take the last of the ebb at the Rock for groundfish, then run into Cape Small on the incoming for bass before the sun climbs too high. Watch the wind — if it swings southwest and holds, the bay can get a light chop that makes the ledge work sloppy, and I'd rather fish a clean tide than fight a messy one.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool Incoming Coughs Up a 34, But the Real Bite's Waiting for Dark
reports.subhead: Bass have gone nocturnal on the warm surface water, bluefish are running Higgins in daylight, and the mackerel are still stacked on the Cape Elizabeth ledges.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday night, an hour into the incoming at the Pool, a guy I've fished next to for fifteen years — never says much, doesn't need to — hooked into something on a black Gibbs Danny that bent his 9-footer into a horseshoe and didn't quit for ten minutes. Thirty-four inches, thick through the shoulders, came off the outer bar where the channel dumps into the basin. That's the fish that tells you the story right now: they're in there, they're eating, but you're going to work for it and you're going to do most of that work after the sun goes down.

Surface water along this stretch has been sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, which for Kittery to Cape Elizabeth is warm enough to shut the daytime bite down but not so warm it's chasing the bass out of the system entirely. That's the trade we've got right now compared to everything south of us — Massachusetts and Rhode Island are dealing with stripers that won't touch anything before midnight, full stop. Up here the river mouths and the cooler ledge water still give you a shot in daylight, but it's thinner than it was in June, and the real windows are opening at dusk, at dawn, and through the dead of night.

Biddeford Pool is still the best hour in Maine surf fishing and it hasn't lost that title. The incoming tide pushes bait — mackerel, pogies, the odd school of peanut bunker — through the cut and into the basin, and the bass stack up on that current edge waiting for it. Right now the pattern that's working is fishing the last two hours of dark into first light, working the outer bar and the drop just inside it with big swimming plugs — Danny-style plugs in black or dark green, and needlefish for guys who want to cover more water with less splash. Slow retrieve, feel for the current seam, and don't be afraid to let the plug sit and swim on a semi-slack presentation right where the channel bends. Daytime, you're mostly getting shorts and the occasional keeper on the bottom of the tide when there's some cloud cover, so if you can only fish daylight, pick an overcast morning and don't expect a repeat of that 34.

Higgins Beach has been the bluefish show all week, and it's a legitimate one. Bunker schools are riding the beachfront in daylight, tight to the surf line, and the blues have been on them hard on the push of the tide — mid-morning into early afternoon has been the window two days running. These aren't snappers. Guys are into 3- to 6-pound blues on Kastmasters, pencil poppers, and darter-style swimmers worked fast across the surface. When the bunker get pinned against the bar and the water goes nervous with bait skipping, that's your signal — cast into the boil, not past it, and keep the retrieve moving. It won't last all day. Once the tide turns and the bait scatters, the blues follow it back out and the window closes until the next push.

Pine Point and Prouts Neck have been more of a grind. With the wind sitting out of the southwest most days this week, Prouts has actually fished better than you'd expect — that wind pushes bait tight against the rocks on the south side and gives the stripers a current edge to work without beating up the surf too bad. Best window there has been the last of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, fishing bucktails and soft-plastic jerkbaits tight to the ledge rock in 10 to 15 feet. It's not a blitz. It's two or three fish for a couple hours of casting, which for late July around Prouts is honest work, not a bad night.

Mackerel are still holding on the open ledges off Cape Elizabeth and out toward the Wells and Ogunquit rockpiles, and that's not nothing — it's bait for the guys chunking at night, and it's also a solid hour of its own fun if you want to load a cooler on Sabiki rigs before the sun's fully up. Cod have been quiet, which is normal for this water and this month — nothing worth chasing specifically right now.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the warm, stable stretch would keep pushing the bass toward nocturnal feeding, and that's exactly what's playing out from the Pool to Prouts.

Moon's building toward full over the next several nights, which means more current push through places like the Pool cut and around Prouts Neck's ledges — that's going to sharpen the bite in current-dependent spots and probably extend the good window at Biddeford by another twenty or thirty minutes on either side of the tide change. If the southwest wind holds into the weekend, I'd fish Prouts on the last of the outgoing and be at Biddeford Pool for the two hours around the incoming after dark — that's where I'm putting my time. Higgins in daylight if the bunker are still stacked, because that bite's been reliable enough to build a morning around. Bring dark plugs, bring patience, and don't expect the daytime bass bite to hand you anything easy until this heat breaks.

reports.headline: Wreck 3402 in 82 feet: sea bass to 4 pounds, bluefin still working the Mud Hole edges
reports.subhead: The bottom bite never blinked this week while the tuna scattered wide on the temperature breaks — here's where the numbers paid off.
reports.body_markdown:
Wreck 3402, 82 feet of water, about nine miles off the inlet on a heading I've run since before some of you had a boat license. That number's been good to me for twenty years and it didn't let me down this week — sea bass stacked on the up-current side, biggest one going just over four pounds, and enough 14-to-16-inch keepers coming over the rail that we had our limit inside ninety minutes on a Tuesday morning. That's the story of the summer out here: the bottom bite is the one thing you can write down in pen.

Sea bass have been holding tight to structure on Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef too, both running 60 to 80 feet depending where you drop, and the pattern's been the same all month — squid strips on a two-hook rig with 6-ounce bank sinkers, or a Gulp Grub in white/chartreuse on a jighead if the current's light enough to work it vertically. The fish are eating hard on the first hour of a moving tide and shutting down fast once it slacks, so timing your drop to the tide table matters more right now than which wreck you pick. Triple Wrecks, sitting deeper at 105 to 120 feet, has been kicking a few cod mixed in with the sea bass on the bigger pieces — not a fishery you plan a trip around this time of year, but a nice surprise on a bait pickup when you're marking fish stacked tight to the wreckage on the sounder.

The Mud Hole lumps have been the tuna story, though it's been a scattered one. We're a few weeks past the July 3rd trophy closure now, and the recreational slot bluefin bite has settled into the pattern I expect this time of year — fish spread wide across the temperature breaks rather than balled up on one lump. I flagged this exact thing last week, said the tuna bite would hold steady as long as the weather cooperated, and that's exactly what's played out. High pressure's held, the water's stayed clean, and the bluefin keep showing on the same edges — 60 to 90 feet of water on the western lumps, chunking butterfish over a slow-sinking spread once you find bait on the meter. Nothing's been a slam dunk. Three trips out to the lumps this week, we connected on two, and both times it took working the drift, not sitting still, to put the boat over active fish. That's a good ratio for late July, but you still need to find the life — birds working, bait balled tight, maybe a whale surfacing — before you put a bait in the water.

Yellowfin have been the deeper-water target, holding off the canyon edges where that warmer offshore water's been pushing filaments up onto the grounds — we're talking 78 to 80 degree readings out where the Gulf Stream edge meets the shelf, well past what the inshore buoys are reading closer to the beach (NY Bight's been sitting around 71 degrees with a light 4-foot swell out of the south, manageable but enough to make the ride out a little sloppy). Troll-and-chunk spreads have stayed productive out there under this settled weather — green machines and small skirted ballyhoo on the troll, then switching to butterfish chunks once you raise fish or mark bait. That's a longer run than most of my Mud Hole trips, but the consistency's been worth the fuel for guys willing to make the push.

Mahi haven't stacked up yet — not surprised, we're usually two, three weeks out from that pattern setting up hard on the floating structure and weed lines. I've seen a handful of stray fish come up under debris on the way out to the canyon grounds, nothing you'd call a pattern, more a preview of what August usually brings once the pots and pallets start collecting real weed. Worth keeping a spinning rod rigged with a small skirted jig ready on the ride out just in case you cross a piece of structure, but I wouldn't build a trip around it yet.

Bonito are the one I'm watching closest heading into next week. Water's crossed the threshold where they typically show, and the moon's building toward full, which should tighten up the current through Shrewsbury Rocks and the inshore structure where they usually announce themselves first around here. Nothing confirmed in my zone yet, but the ingredients are there — I'd keep a light spinning outfit with a small metal or epoxy jig rigged and ready if you're running past that stretch on the way out to the reef grounds.

Looking ahead: if this high pressure holds through the weekend, I'd expect the sea bass bite to stay the most reliable thing on the schedule, the Mud Hole tuna to keep producing for boats willing to work the drift rather than anchor up and wait, and the canyon yellowfin bite to hold as long as that warm filament stays put on the edge. Watch the moon — full phase midweek should sharpen the current everywhere, which could be the trigger that finally brings the first bonito into the log.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at First Light: Blues on the Bunker, Bass Gone to Ground
reports.subhead: The bluefish blitz we flagged last week finally rolled north into Sea Bright — the stripers, meanwhile, want nothing to do with daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-forty a.m., low tide plus an hour at the Sea Bright rocks, and I'm standing next to a kid I've never met who's got a Super Strike Zig Zag tied on and no idea what he's about to see. A bunker pod the size of a tennis court comes boiling down the beach, and it erupts — blues, blues, blues, tails slapping white water into the gray light. He hooks up on his third cast. So do I, on a chartreuse Danny swimmer worked half-speed across the seam off the third jetty down from the lighthouse. Ten-, eleven-pound blues, mean as hell, cutting leaders if you let them get bulldog on you. This is the bunker blitz we said last week would push north out of Raritan Bay and show itself along this stretch within a couple days — and here it is, right on schedule, right on the rocks at Sea Bright.

That's the daytime story right now, and it's a good one if you don't mind losing a few plugs to bluefish teeth. The blitz windows have been running on both the last hour of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming — bait gets pinned against the jetty faces at Sea Bright and up through Monmouth Beach, and the blues come through in waves, not a steady grind but real windows, twenty, thirty minutes of chaos and then quiet for an hour. Bring wire or heavy fluoro if you want to keep your plug inventory intact. Poppers on top when they're up, bucktails with a stinger hook worked through the wash when they've sounded.

Stripers are a different animal entirely this week, and if you're only fishing daylight hours you're going to think they left the building. They haven't — they've gone nocturnal, plain and simple. Surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the beach have pushed the bass down onto structure and current seams during the day, and they're not interested in showing themselves again until the sun's well down and the water cools a degree or two. I worked the Manasquan Inlet jetties three nights running this week — the north side rocks on the last two hours of the incoming, fishing whole bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig in about 15 feet of water tight to the rock pile. Two keepers Tuesday night, one Thursday, nothing spectacular but real fish, 28 to 33 inches, and every one of them came after 10 p.m. Eels are doing work too — a rigged green eel drifted slow along the Shark River Inlet south jetty on the dropping tide picked up a fish just short of 30 inches for a guy I know from Belmar who's fished that same fifteen feet of rock for longer than I've been walking this beach.

Fluke have softened up in the shallow stuff, same story as everywhere else on this coast right now — the flats have gone quiet and the fish have slid into the deeper, moving water where it stays cooler. Manasquan Inlet channel, particularly the bend just inside the rock jetties where the current squeezes through, has been the most consistent producer. I've been dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet right along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, and it's been good for a fish or two a drift — nothing over 20 inches, mostly 16 to 18, so you're culling through shorts to find keepers, but they're there. Shark River Inlet is fishing the same way — work the deeper edge on the channel side of the railroad bridge, outgoing water, and don't be afraid to slow the drift down with a little extra lead. The fish holding there right now aren't chasing anything fast.

Porgies have been a reliable, unglamorous bite around the Manasquan Inlet rock piles and the Spring Lake jetties — sandworms or clam on a high-low rig, bottom in 10 to 15 feet, any stage of tide really, though I like it best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Good for a bucket of dinner fish if the blitz and the bass game leave you wanting a slower afternoon. Blackfish season's closed up here through the summer, so that's a fall conversation — I'll get back to the tautog talk once October rolls around.

Wind's been the wildcard the last few days, and it's worth watching — a stiff onshore breeze can shut down the rock fishing at Sea Bright fast by chopping up the water and pushing the bait off the beach entirely, so if you see white water building and no bunker showing, don't waste your morning, go straight to the inlets instead. The moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means building current through both Manasquan and Shark River inlets over the next week — that should sharpen up the fluke bite in the channels and probably tighten the window on the nighttime bass bite too, concentrating them harder on the current seams instead of spread out over open structure.

My read for the coming week: the blitz should keep working its way along this stretch as long as the bunker keep moving north, so I'd be at Sea Bright or Monmouth Beach at first light watching for birds and nervous water before you do anything else. For bass, forget the sunrise patrol — set your alarm for 9 or 10 p.m. instead and fish the inlet jetties on bunker chunks or eels through the incoming. And for fluke, the deeper inlet bends are outproducing the open flats right now, so that's where I'd put my drift time if I only had one tide to fish.

reports.headline: Holgate's New Cut Found the Bluefish First — Fluke Sliding Into the Inlet Rips
reports.subhead: A storm-carved slough at Holgate turned into a bait trap this week, and the bunker blitz we flagged last week showed up right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning at first light and the beach looked different than it did two weeks ago — that happens fast down there. A modest south swell over the weekend cut a new slough about 200 yards north of the refuge fence, carved a trough maybe four feet deep at low tide with a sandbar humped up on the seaward side. That kind of structure doesn't sit empty for long on LBI in late July. By Wednesday there was bunker stacked in that trough thick enough to color the water bronze, and the bluefish found it before I did — I heard the pop of a blitz from the parking lot before I even had my waders on.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bunker-driven blitz working up from South Jersey would find LBI and intensify inside 48 to 72 hours, and that's exactly what's happened. The bait pods are riding the warm surface layer right along the beachfront from Holgate up through Beach Haven and into Ship Bottom, and the bluefish are pinning them against the new cuts and bars on the moving tide. Best windows have been the first hour of light and the last hour before dark, which lines up with when the light drops enough that the blues stop spooking off the pods and start slashing through them. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins, anything in the 1.5 to 2 ounce range that you can bomb into the melee — have been the move. If you can match the bunker size with a bigger paddletail swimbait, even better; the blues aren't picky when the bait's balled up that tight.

Fluke have gone the other direction, and it's a pattern I see every summer once the flats hit the mid-70s. The open bay drifts inside Manahawkin and Little Egg Harbor have gone quiet — too warm, too slow-moving — and the fish have slid into the current seams where the water actually moves and stays a few degrees cooler. Barnegat Inlet and Beach Haven Inlet are carrying the load right now. I've had my best luck working the deeper bends on the channel side of Beach Haven Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet right along the bottom where the current stacks bait against the drop-off. Nothing huge — most fish are running 17 to 20 inches — but there's enough of them stacked in that seam to make a short drift worth repeating six or eight times in a tide. Little Egg Inlet is fishing similarly on the ebb, especially the deeper hole just inside the rock jetty, though you're fighting boat traffic there on weekends.

Striped bass are basically nocturnal at this point, and that's not going to change until the water cools off in September. Surface temps along the beachfront and in the back bays are sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, which pushes bass deep and shuts down any real daytime activity except on the edges of structure where there's a thermocline to hide in. The play after dark has been bridge structure — the Route 72 causeway pilings and the Manahawkin Bay Bridge abutments — working bucktail eels and fresh bunker chunks tight to the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. A few guys working the Barnegat Light rocks after midnight with darter-style plugs have connected on schoolie-to-mid-20s fish working the current seam off the jetty tip, but you need to be out there at 11 p.m. or later, and even then it's a few fish a trip, not a blitz. That's the honest state of it right now — the bass are there, they're just not stupid in this heat.

Black drum season wrapped up back in June — that Mullica and Graveling Point bite on the incoming tide is done for the year, don't waste a trip on it. What's interesting is the weakfish. I've had a couple reports of weakfish showing after dark in the deeper holes off Graveling Point and up into the Mullica proper, fish in the 16 to 19 inch range hitting bucktails tipped with squid strips on the bottom of the outgoing. It's not a fishery yet, more a handful of fish here and there, but it's worth a look if you're already out there chasing bass at night — bring an extra rod rigged light.

Kingfish are the one bright spot for the sand-spike crowd. Bloodworms and Fishbites on high-low rigs have been picking at kingfish in the 8 to 10 inch class along the Beach Haven and Ship Bottom fronts, best on the bottom two hours of the incoming when the surf is calm enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. Nothing to write home about size-wise but it's steady action for anyone dragging kids to the beach with a rod.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which should sharpen current everywhere from the inlets to the bridge structure — that usually tightens up both the fluke bite in the rips and the after-dark bass bite around structure. If the bunker keep holding along the beachfront the way they have this week, I'd expect the blitz windows to keep firing through the weekend, especially with calm winds forecast. If I only had one trip, I'd fish Holgate or Beach Haven Inlet at first light for blues, then circle back after dark to the Route 72 bridge for bass on the outgoing. Watch the wind — anything out of the east chops up those beachfront blitzes fast.

reports.headline: Where'd my fluke go at 2 o'clock? Ask the thermocline, not the tide chart
reports.subhead: Shallow bay fluke have punched out for the season — the program now lives in the inlet channels, while bunker push a bluefish blitz toward Absecon.
reports.body_markdown:
I got the same question three times this week, from three different guys at three different counters, so let's make it a lesson. "Darnell, I drifted the flats off Rainbow Channel all morning, marked bait, marked fish on the graph, and couldn't buy a bite after one o'clock. What happened?" What happened is the sun did its job. Those shallow sod bank flats — the ones that were stacked with keeper fluke back in June — are running warm enough now that the fish have simply left the classroom. When surface water in four and five feet of back bay sits in the high 70s all afternoon, summer flounder go looking for the nearest air conditioning, and around here that means the deeper bends and the inlet mouths where moving water keeps things cooler and oxygenated.

So here's where I've been putting my clients and myself the last two weeks, and where I'd keep sending you. Absecon Inlet, the stretch right along the Coast Guard station down to the Route 30 bridge, holding 18 to 25 feet on the channel edges — that's been the most dependable drift in my zone. Fish it on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current is still strong enough to hold your bucktail down but has thinned the boat traffic. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a fresh spearing strip, dragged slow along the drop where the sand gives way to mud — that combination has been outproducing bare bucktails two or three to one for me. Great Egg Inlet is running the same story. The deep bend by the Rainbow Channel range markers and the hole off Broad Thorofare, both holding fluke to 19 inches, some to 21, on the last of the outgoing into dead low. If you're marking bait balls of spearing or rain bait stacked on the ledge, slow your drift down — a fluke that's already got a belly full of forage isn't chasing a fast retrieve in July heat.

Now the bigger story this week, and one we saw building — the bluefish blitz that's been working its way down from the North Jersey beaches has arrived at our doorstep. We flagged this pattern last week, that stable southwest wind and warm water would keep pushing those bunker schools south, and that's exactly what's happening. Ocean City's beachfront, from the 34th Street jetty down past Corson's Inlet, has had bluefish blowing up on bunker pods right in the wash on the incoming tide, usually in that first hour after the tide turns when the bait gets pinned against the sandbar. Bring a metal — a 2-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — and don't overthink it, just get it past the boil and rip it back through. Sea Isle City's had the same show off the Promenade, and I expect it to keep marching toward Longport and the Absecon Inlet jetties over the next few days if this weather pattern holds. Watch the birds — when the gulls start working tight and diving instead of gliding, that's your signal to close the distance fast, because these blitzes don't sit still for long.

Stripers are a nighttime assignment now, full stop. Daytime surface temps have pushed the bass down onto structure and current seams where they're comfortable, and they're not coming up to feed until the sun's been off the water a while. My best producer has been the rock piles at the Absecon Inlet jetty, fished after dark on the incoming, bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig soaking bottom in 15 to 20 feet. A few guys working live eels along the Great Egg Inlet range structure have connected too, mostly on the top of the tide when current slackens enough for the eel to swim naturally instead of getting swept sideways. Don't expect numbers — this is a one or two fish a night proposition right now, but the fish that are coming have been quality, mid-20s to high-20-inch class with a few overslot mixed in.

Weakfish have shown some encouraging signs in the back channels — Risley Channel and the deeper cuts through Broad Thorofare have given up a few keeper-class weakfish on the evening incoming, mostly to guys drifting Bass Assassins in pink shad or a simple bucktail-and-bait combo along the mud bottom. It's not a program yet, more a signal worth watching, and if it holds through the next couple weeks it could turn into something real by late August.

Kingfish are still a solid bread-and-butter option if you want a bend in the rod without much fuss — Ocean City and Sea Isle beachfront, early morning before the crowds set up, bloodworms or Fishbites on a high-low rig in the third slough. And if you like a challenge, the triggerfish have been holding tight to the rock jetties at Absecon Inlet, taking small pieces of clam fished right against the structure on light tackle — frustrating, technical, but a fun change of pace on a slow tide.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which should sharpen up that inlet current and make the fluke drifts even more productive on the stronger stages of the tide. If the southwest wind pattern holds through the weekend, I'd expect that bluefish blitz to keep pushing south past Ocean City toward Longport and possibly right up against the Absecon Inlet beachfront. Best case, we get a run of consecutive good mornings on the bunker schools before they slide further down toward Cape May. Worst case, a wind shift scatters the bait and you're back to hunting — either way, I'd have a bucktail rod and a metal rod both rigged before you leave the dock.

reports.headline: Double Creek Holds the Fluke, Weakfish Sneak In on the Dawn Tide
reports.subhead: The bay's gone thick and warm, but the channel bends and the sedge banks are still paying off if you fish the right hour.
reports.body_markdown:
Back when I was mating on the Point Pleasant party boats, there was an old-timer named Sal who used to say the bay in late July was like an old friend who'd stopped answering the phone — still there, still cares about you, just doesn't feel like talking during the day. I've thought about that line every summer since, and this week it's dead on. Barnegat Bay has slid into that heavy, syrupy stretch of the calendar where the shallows sit in the mid-70s by afternoon and the fish that made May and June so good have gone quiet, or gone deep, or gone nocturnal. Doesn't mean the bay's done with you. It just means you have to fish it on its terms now, not yours.

Fluke are the clearest example. A month ago you could drift the open flats off Tices Shoal and pick at keepers all morning. That bite has softened hard as the shallow water warmed past what these fish want to sit in during daylight. What's holding up is Double Creek Channel — the bends where the current stays honest and the bottom drops into that deeper, cooler stretch. I've been working the outside of the turns on the last two hours of the incoming, dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, and picking up keepers to five pounds along with plenty of shorts that make you work for your fish. Same story at the Barnegat Inlet-adjacent stretches — anywhere the current keeps moving is holding fish, and anywhere it goes slack and shallow has gone dead as a doornail by ten in the morning. If you're going to fluke this week, get out early, hit the channel structure, and don't waste your tide on the open flats.

Weakfish are the pleasant surprise. The back-channel bite that's been building statewide has found its way into our sedge banks, and I mean specifically the stretches south of Oyster Creek where the marsh drops off into deeper cuts. First light, before the sun's had a chance to punch through, has been the window — soft plastics, 4-inch chartreuse or pink Bass Assassins on a light jighead, worked slow along the channel edges. Nothing frantic about the retrieve. Let it sink, twitch it twice, let it sink again. These fish aren't chasing anything down right now, they're eating what drifts past them, so match that pace. I had two anglers out of Forked River last Tuesday morning who boated four weakfish in that 16-to-19-inch range before seven a.m., then nothing the rest of the day. That's the pattern — tight window, good fish, then it shuts like someone flipped a switch.

Bluefish are still the most reliable thing going, and if you want visible, aggressive action, that's your fish this week. Bunker pods are pushing in and out of the inlet with the tide, and the blues are riding right on top of them. I've watched them push bait against the Barnegat Light bulkheads and off the north end of Island Beach on the outgoing, and when that happens it doesn't matter what you throw — a Hopkins jig, a bunker spoon, a topwater popper — they'll eat it. We flagged this pattern last week, said the bluefish push would keep spreading along the coast as the bunker moved, and that's exactly what's playing out here, with fresh schools showing at the inlet mouth on nearly every tide change. Just watch your leader — 20-pound fluorocarbon minimum, because these fish are runing bigger than the usual summer cocktail blues and they'll cut you off on wire-light gear.

Striped bass are where the honesty has to come in. They've gone essentially nocturnal on us, same as the rest of the coast from here through southern New England. Daytime, they're holding deep on the channel structure and current seams around the inlet, refusing to show themselves except as the occasional sonar mark you can't tempt. We called this one too — said the pattern would hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around, and it has, day after day of calm and heat with nothing to break the thermal stack. If you want bass, you're fishing after dark now — eels drifted on the current seams inside the inlet, or bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the deeper bends of Double Creek. I put a client on two schoolies and one 27-incher last Thursday night working chunk bait off the rocks near the inlet on the last of the ebb. Slow fishing, but real fishing, and the kind of thing that rewards patience over volume.

Crabbing, for what it's worth, is about the easiest thing going right now — the heat that's shutting down the daytime bite is exactly what the blue claws want, and the back creeks are thick with them. If the fishing's slow, that's not a bad way to spend an afternoon with the kids.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break unless we get some wind and a real tide-flushing event to knock the shallow water down a few degrees. If the calm holds through the weekend, I'd keep doing what's working — early mornings on the weakfish at the sedges, fluke worked deep in Double Creek on the moving tide, bluefish whenever you see bait get pushed around the inlet, and stripers strictly after dark. If we get a blow out of the northeast that stirs things up, watch for the fluke bite to wake back up on the flats for a day or two after — that's happened before, and it's worth checking Tices Shoal again if the weather turns.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: eels working slot bass while scup pile the Rocky Point ledges
reports.subhead: The Providence River's gone quiet on daytime bass, but the night bite and the bottom bite are carrying the bay through the heat.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a guy who ties off at the Fields Point pier most mornings, retired dockworker, fishes for an hour before the heat gets stupid, and he's been telling me the same thing for two weeks straight: 'Nothing's moving till the sun's gone.' He's not wrong. That's the whole story of the upper bay right now.

Back in May and June, Buckeye Brook was doing what it does — herring stacking up in that run, bass following the smell of them right up into the Warwick coves, and for about six weeks it was as easy as this fishery gets. That window's closed. The herring are long gone, the water in the upper bay has crept into the mid-70s on the surface, and the bass that were slashing bait in broad daylight off Conimicut in June have gone nocturnal on us. It's not that they left. It's that they got smart.

I've been fishing Nyatt Point and the flats off Rocky Point starting an hour before sundown through the first couple hours of dark, and that's where the slot fish are showing. Live eels on a 3/0 circle hook, no weight if the current allows it, drifted right along the drop where the rocky bottom falls into deeper water on the outgoing tide. Had a couple of fish push 30 inches doing exactly that last Tuesday, both right at the top of the ebb when the current was still moving hard enough to keep the eel swimming natural instead of just sitting there. If you're set up for chunking, fresh bunker chunks fished on the bottom in that same stretch after full dark has been drawing bluefish and the occasional bigger bass mixed in — bring more chunk than you think you need, because the blues will pick a chunk bait apart in about four casts once they find it.

Daytime, honestly, the upper bay bass bite has been tough. I won't sugarcoat it. If you're out there at noon working topwater over the flats like it's May, you're going to get skunked and you're going to be miserable doing it in this heat. Save your gas and fish the tide change at dusk instead.

Fluke are the one that's actually moved on us, and not in the direction guys want to hear. The shallow stuff — the flats off Warwick, the inside edges of Greenwich Bay — has gone soft. Too warm, not enough current exchange to keep it fresh. The fish that are still biting have pushed down toward the deeper channel edges around Prudence Island and the drop-offs on the west side of the bay where the water's still moving and holding a couple degrees cooler. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel break in 25 to 35 feet, on the last two hours of the incoming — that's produced the better fish, a few keepers to 21 inches mixed into a lot of short fish you've got to sort through. It's not a banner fluke summer in the bay right now, but it's fishable if you go where the current still runs.

What's carrying the daytime action, no question, is the bottom bite. Scup have piled onto every rocky ledge from Rocky Point down through the east passage, and that fishery hasn't slowed a bit with the heat — if anything it's gotten better as the scup pack tighter around structure to escape the warm surface layer. Simple rig: two hooks, size 6 or 8, squid strips or sandworm, small enough sinker to feel bottom without dragging, anchored right up on the rock piles. You can limit out in an hour some mornings if you find the right ledge and the tide's got some push to it — I like the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, before it goes dead slack and the bite shuts off for a while. Black sea bass are mixed in on the same structure a little deeper, and they've been a reliable bonus fish all month on the same rigs, just fished a touch heavier to hold bottom in the current seams.

Bluefish are around, riding whatever bait pods are getting pushed up the bay on the tide, and they'll show up wherever the bunker are thick — I had a stretch off Conimicut two weeks back where they blew up a school right at the surface for about fifteen minutes and then vanished like they were never there. That's the pattern with them right now: not a sustained blitz, more of a hit-and-run. Keep a rod rigged with a wire leader and a Kastmaster or a metal-lip swimmer ready, because when they show, you've got a short window before they push off again chasing the bait.

We flagged it last week and it's held — stable, hot, calm pattern, and that's exactly what's kept the bass on the night shift and the bunker-chasing blues moving around unpredictably instead of settling into a real blitz. I don't see that changing in the next few days unless we get a real wind event to mix the water column and knock the surface temp down. Until then, my plan stays the same: eels at dusk off Nyatt and Rocky Point, scup rigs on the ledges in the morning before it gets brutal, and fluke gear pointed at the deeper edges around Prudence where the current's still doing some work. If a front comes through and drops the surface temp a few degrees, watch for the bass to come back up shallow during the day — that's the tell I'd be looking for heading into August.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips Grade Out C-Plus: Stripers Go Nocturnal, Weakfish Finally Show Some Teeth
reports.subhead: The ocean side is a daytime chore with a nighttime payoff, while Delaware Bay's back channels are quietly turning into the better bet this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Grading the Rips this week, I'd call it a C-plus. Fishable, not easy, and you're paying for every fish with a strong back and a willingness to fish the clock instead of the calendar. Daytime water on the ocean side is sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range that pushes stripers off the top and down onto structure, and once that happens in late July, they don't come back up until the sun does. I ran the Rips proper Tuesday morning on the tail of the outgoing — 18 to 35 feet, working bucktails tight to bottom over the humps — and picked at fish, nothing you'd brag about at the dock. The real work has shifted to last light and after dark. Eels drifted on three-way rigs along the current seams off Cape May Point, and bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 25 to 40 feet through the new dark hours, are where the keeper-class fish are coming from. That's not me sugarcoating it — that's just where the fish are living right now, and it lines up with what the whole coast is doing this time of year. If you want stripers in the Rips in July, you fish the night tide, full stop.

Fluke has softened up in the same way. The open sand inside Hereford Inlet that was holding fish in June has gone quiet as that shallow water heats up faster than the fish want to tolerate. What's still working is the harder structure — the mouth of Hereford, the deeper bends along the inlet channel, and out toward the reef sites where you've got current moving and cooler water underneath it. Four- and five-inch white and chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow through 25 to 45 feet on the last of the incoming, is still putting keeper fluke in the box, just not in the numbers we had a month back. If you're used to drifting the flats, adjust — go find the edges.

Now for the story I actually want to tell you about. We flagged this last week — said weakfish activity in Delaware Bay would keep climbing as the water held steady — and that's exactly what's happening. The back channels from Fortescue up toward Brandywine Shoal have pushed into the mid-70s, and instead of killing the bite like it does with fluke, it's concentrated the weakfish into the deeper channel bends where the tide keeps oxygen moving. First light and dusk are the windows — I had two solid mornings this week working soft plastics, four-inch paddletails in pearl and chartreuse on light jigheads, bounced slow along the channel drop-offs in 15 to 22 feet on the front half of the incoming. Weakfish to 20 inches, mixed with a few shorts, and enough consistency that I'm calling this a real pattern, not a one-day fluke. Bucktails tipped with a strip of squid worked the same water just as well on the dusk bite. If this keeps building through the first week of August the way it's trending, Fortescue's going to be the better half of my two-bay game for a while.

Black drum, if you're wondering — done. That run wrapped up back in May like it always does, and anybody still soaking bunker chunks off Fortescue looking for drum in July is fishing a calendar that already closed. I get the question every week this time of year and the answer's always the same: come back to me in April.

Kingfish and croaker are steady, unglamorous, and exactly what they should be for late July — bloodworms and Fishbites fished on the bottom off the Wildwood bulkheads and the ocean beaches on the incoming tide keep putting fish in coolers for the families who don't want to run offshore. It's not a headline bite but it's a reliable one, and reliable counts for something in a summer where the bigger fish are making you work nights and edges for everything.

Bluefish are trickling through on bunker pods along the beachfront and into Hereford, giving surfcasters intermittent windows rather than sustained blitzes. When the bunker balls get pinned against the jetty rocks on a moving tide, you'll see the blow-ups, but they're short and scattered rather than the kind of sustained chop we sometimes get in August. Worth having a metal lure rigged and ready, not worth planning your whole morning around.

Moon's building toward full in the first days of August, which should sharpen the current through the Rips and Hereford both — more push on the tide usually means a tighter bite window but a better one when it hits. My plan for the coming week is simple: keep the daytime hours on fluke around the harder structure, shift to the night tide for stripers in the Rips, and lean into the weakfish pattern in the bay while it's building instead of waiting for someone else to confirm it first. If the bay water holds where it's at and doesn't spike further, I'd expect weakfish to keep climbing into next week. If a cold push or a big blow rearranges things, that's a different conversation — but right now, that's where I'd put my time.

reports.headline: Bunker Push Finally Hits the Hook — Blues Blitzing, Bass Gone to Nights
reports.subhead: The bait we've been tracking up the Jersey beach all month is stacking on Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal, and the bluefish found it first.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the call I made this week: mornings on the Flats and the Reach for fluke, evenings at the Rip, and I'm keeping one eye on Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal all day because that's where the bunker are finally piling up. We flagged this a few days back — said the blitz pushing north out of the central Jersey shore was going to land here by the weekend, and it did. Wednesday morning off Flynn's Knoll I watched three separate bluefish blow-ups inside twenty minutes, bunker getting pushed into balls so tight the surface looked like it was boiling from underneath. That's not a metaphor, that's what six-pound blues do to peanut and adult bunker schools when they corner them against the Knoll on a dropping tide.

If you want blues right now, don't overthink it. Run out to Flynn's Knoll or Romer Shoal on the last two hours of the ebb, find the diving gulls and the nervous water, and throw poppers or big Ava jigs with a topwater teaser trailing behind. You don't need finesse — these fish are eating anything that moves fast and looks panicked. I've had guys tell me they got bit on bare bunker spoons just skipped across the top. Slot-sized blues, four to seven pounds, some bigger mixed in, and they're not shy about it. The bite windows are short — twenty, thirty minutes of pure chaos then it shuts off as the school moves — so stay mobile. I've been running from the Knoll to Romer Shoal to the mouth of the Raritan chasing the same bait ball basically all week.

Stripers are a different story right now, and if you're expecting daytime bass the way we had them in April and May, that's not what late July gives you. The bay's sitting warm — shallow water on the Keyport Flats and up in the Navesink has been running into the mid-70s by afternoon, and that pushes bass off the flats and down into deeper holds where they go nocturnal. I'm not chasing bass in daylight right now. I'm fishing the Rip at the Hook after dark, working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs down near bottom in twenty-five to thirty-five feet, right where the current runs hard against the tip. Two nights out of three I've put keeper bass in the box this week — nothing huge, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but steady enough that it's worth losing the sleep. The other trick that's working: live eels drifted through the same stretch on the last of the incoming, right as the tide starts to slacken around the Hook structure. That's when the bigger fish seem to show.

The fluke program has softened up some, which I want to be straight about. The open Flats bite that was so reliable in June has gone quiet in the shallow stuff — too warm, too much bait pressure from the blitz probably scattering things. What's still working is the channel edges out toward the Reach and along the drop-off on the Keyport side, twenty-five to thirty feet of water where there's still some cooler water moving. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the lip where the sand drops into the channel — that's where I've been finding keeper fluke, four fish for me on Tuesday, two of them over 20 inches. It's not the wide-open drift bite from a month ago. You've got to work the structure now, not just cover water.

Porgies remain the honest bonus fish in this bay and they haven't slowed a bit. Anywhere there's a wreck or rockpile near Romer Shoal or off the Highlands, bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig will keep you busy between bluefish runs. It's not glamorous but it's a guaranteed bend in the rod while you're waiting on the next blitz to show up on the surface.

Weakfish have been a whisper more than a pattern this month — a few fish reported out of the Navesink on soft plastics fished slow along the deeper bends, nothing I'd call a fishery yet. Worth a cast or two if you're already in the river working the last of the ebb, but I wouldn't build a trip around it.

Tide-wise, we're coming off a stretch of building current as the moon works toward full in early August, and that's going to matter. Stronger current means the bait gets pinned harder against structure — good news for the bluefish blitz continuing to intensify around the Knoll and Shoal, and good news for the Rip at night because more current means more bass willing to feed against it. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I expect the blitz to hold here through the weekend before it either burns out or pushes further north toward the Sound. My money's on it lingering — the bunker schools I've seen the last two days are thick, not thinning out.

What I'd do this week: mornings and evenings at Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal chasing surface blitzes on poppers, fluke midday on the channel edges off the Reach with bucktail-Gulp combos, and bass after dark at the Rip on chunks or eels. It's a three-shift day right now if you want to hit everything, but that's late July on this bay — the fish are around, you just have to fish the right water at the right hour.

reports.headline: Cockenoe After Dark: Stripers Slide Into the Rocks While Blues Run the Daylight
reports.subhead: With the Sound sitting warm from Greenwich to Bridgeport, the reef game splits in two — bass at night, everything else on the moving tide.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to skip the daytime drift over Cockenoe and instead set up on the east end drop-off two hours before dark — the last of the ebb sliding into the bottom of the flood, right where the reef falls from eight feet into eighteen. That's the kind of decision you have to make right now. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and by mid-afternoon the shallows off Greenwich Point and the flats around Sheffield Island are running warmer than that. Bass don't like it. They've gone underground during daylight — holding deep on the structure, sitting on current seams, refusing to commit until the sun's off the water. You can beat your head against that with a bucktail at noon, or you can fish around it. I fish around it.

That means bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3/0 circle hook, fished tight to the rockpile on the drop at Cockenoe's east end, or drifted eels through the Sheffield Island channel on the last two hours of outgoing into the top of the flood. Greenwich Point's rocks are doing the same thing after dark — current pushing bait against structure, stripers sliding up out of the deeper holes to work it. Nothing has been easy about this pattern. You're putting in dock-to-dark hours for a handful of fish in that mid-20s-inch range with the occasional better one mixed in, but that's the trade you make in late July heat. Daytime drifting on the flats is close to dead right now for bass — don't waste the tide on it.

Where the daylight bite is actually productive is bluefish, and that's been the story all month. We flagged this pattern last week — said the blitz would hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around — and it has. Bunker pods are still getting worked over off Greenwich Point and up and down the Norwalk Islands string, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the tide pins the bait against the rocks. Topwater poppers and 2-ounce Deadly Dicks worked fast through the froth are doing the damage. Get there early — by 8 or 9 a.m. the weekend boat traffic through that stretch turns the blitzes into a demolition derby, and the fish scatter the second three center consoles converge on the same slick.

Fluke has softened up the way it always does once the shallow water gets uncomfortable. The open-flat drift off the Norwalk Islands that produced all June has gone quiet — those fish have pushed into the channel edges and deeper cuts around Sheffield Island, 25 to 35 feet, where there's still cooler water moving. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift through the channel bend, are still turning fish, but you're covering more water for fewer bites than you were a month ago. Structure-oriented fluke fishing now, not flat-water fluke fishing.

Black sea bass are holding up as the most dependable bottom bite on the beat. Cockenoe Reef and the outer rockpile at Penfield Reef, 20 to 30 feet, squid strips or clam belly on a bucktail teaser rig, bounced right on the structure — that fishery hasn't slowed a bit through the heat. Porgies are thick on the Cows off Stamford, 20 to 35 feet on those humps, sandworms and clam on a high-low rig. That's about as close to a sure thing as this beat has right now — light tackle, steady action, good for a kid's first trip or a slow afternoon when the bass game isn't worth the gas.

One thing I'll say plainly: don't bother with blackfish right now. The Cows and Penfield hold good tog structure, but this is the dead zone for that fishery — they're scattered and uninterested until the water starts to turn in October. Save the crab and green crab money for fall.

Boat traffic is the other variable I'm playing chess with every trip. Weekends through the Norwalk Islands are a circus by mid-morning — wake after wake rolling through the cuts, pushing bait and fish off the structure. If you can only fish Saturday or Sunday, be on the water at first light and off by 9, or wait for the evening tide when the marina crowd thins out. Weekday mornings are still clean.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, which should sharpen up the current through Sheffield Island channel and around Cockenoe's east end — stronger tide, tighter bite windows, but better odds when you hit it right. If the warm, stable pattern holds like it has, I expect the bluefish blitzes to keep pushing along the beachfront and the bass to stay locked into their after-dark rhythm. I wouldn't change my program: reef structure at night for stripers, moving tide for everything else, and an early alarm clock on the weekends.

reports.headline: Fishers Island Sound Boulders Wake Up: Sea Bass Thick, Stripers Gone to the Dark
reports.subhead: Current's building back out of the neap, sand eels are pinned against the rocks, and the albie clock is ticking louder every tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Poled the skiff over the boulder field off Ram Island Tuesday morning, low light, and the sand eels were doing what they do this time of year — balled up tight against the rock faces, nervous, getting pushed around by something underneath them I couldn't see yet. That's the tell. When bait sits that tight to structure and won't leave it, there's usually a reason, and out here in late July the reason is almost always sea bass working the crevices or stripers staging deeper in the current seam waiting on dark.

We said last week the current had gone soft on this neap cycle and the bite in current-dependent water would taper until it rebuilt — and that's exactly what's happened. The tide's coming back now as the moon works toward full in early August, and you can feel it in the rip off Wamphassuc Point and through the gut between Ram Island and the mainland. Water's moving with purpose again on the last two hours of the ebb, which is when I want to be there. Slack water in this sound is a dead zone for anything that eats — the fish here live and die by current, and for three or four days they didn't have much to work with.

Black sea bass have been the most honest fish out there. Structure from the Fishers Island Sound boulder fields down through the rock piles off Esker Point is holding them thick — 14 to 18 inches, some pushing better than that, stacked tight to vertical rock faces in 15 to 25 feet. I'm dropping small green crabs and Gulp Peach Swimming Mullets on light jigheads, quarter to three-eighths ounce depending on how hard the current's running, and letting it bounce right down into the cracks. You feel the take different on these rocks than you do on sand — it's a thump right at the bottom, and if you don't set fast they're back in the crevice with your jig before you know it. This has been the most consistent thing in the Sound for three weeks running and it hasn't slowed a bit.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Surface temps at the western end near New London are sitting in the high 60s, and once you get up into Little Narragansett Bay and the Mystic River mouth on a sunny afternoon it's pushing low 70s. That's warm enough to shut the daytime bite down almost completely. I haven't had a keeper bass on a rod in daylight in over a week — not for lack of trying. What's working is fishing the last two hours of light into full dark, eels drifted through the current seams off the Stonington breakwater, and bunker chunks fished on the bottom in the deeper holes around Fishers Island Sound where the water stays cooler. Slot fish have come from both spots, along with a couple of bigger models pushing past 34 inches off the breakwater rocks on the outgoing tide around 9 and 10 pm. If you want stripers here right now, you're a night owl or you're not catching much.

Fluke have softened up in the shallow spots the way they always do once it gets hot — the open sand flats inside the bay aren't holding much. But the edges are still good.
