I've had decent drifts along the channel bend off Watch Hill and through the deeper cuts between the Fishers Island boulder fields, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom where the moving water stays cool even when the flats around it don't. Nothing huge — mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but steady enough on a good tide stage to be worth the trip if fluke's what you're after.

Now the one everybody's asking me about at the dock — albies and bonito. Nothing confirmed yet in this stretch of water, and I'm not going to tell you different just because it's the last week of July and everybody wants to hear it. But the pieces are lining up. Water temps at the mouth of the Sound have crossed the line where these fish start showing in a normal year, and the current's rebuilding fast now that we're out of the neap. Bonito tend to show first in the rougher water off Watch Hill and the outer edge of Fishers Island before they push into the calmer Sound water, so that's where I'd be looking first — small epoxy jigs and Deceiver flies worked fast through any nervous water or diving terns. If the pattern holds the way it usually does, I'd expect the first real signs within the next week to ten days, and once they show in this Sound they tend to stay through September.

Looking ahead — I'd fish the sea bass hard while the current's building, it's the surest thing going right now. For stripers, commit to the dark hours around the breakwater and the Mystic River current lines rather than burning daylight for nothing. And keep a rod rigged light with epoxy jigs in the boat from here on out, because when the albies do show in Fishers Island Sound, they don't give you much warning — and I don't want to be the guy still tying on a bucktail when the water starts boiling.

reports.headline: The Race Runs Hot at 3.6 Knots: Bass Go Deep, Plum Gut Sits on Albie Watch
reports.subhead: Trophy stripers have shoved off into the nighttime program while the Gut waits on the first real push of false albacore.
reports.body_markdown:
Race Rock was reading 3.6 knots on the last big ebb I ran through there, and that number tells you almost everything you need to know about this week. That's strong water for late July — not maximum-spring strong, but strong enough to hold bait hard against the rock and strong enough to keep the bass from showing themselves in daylight. When The Race is running like that with surface temps sitting in the high 60s to low 70s, the fish don't fight the current in the open — they tuck down on the structure and wait for dark.

Kings Point is up at 70.9, New London's holding at 69.4, and that gradient matters. The western Sound is warmer and more mature right now, but out here at the eastern gates, the water's still cool enough on the bottom third of the column to keep big bass comfortable through the day. Problem is, comfortable doesn't mean visible. I've had three trips this week where the sounder showed good marks stacked on the downcurrent side of Valiant Rock in 35 to 50 feet, and daytime presentations — wire line, big bucktails, jigged slow off the bottom — got looked at more than they got hit. Two fish boated Tuesday afternoon, both in the low 30-inch range, both came right at the top of the ebb before the current built past 2 knots. That's the window. Once Race Rock gets past 3 knots at midday, I'm not wasting bucktails on it — I'm coming back at night.

After dark is where this fishery is actually happening right now. Eels drifted on wire through the Race and Plum Gut, bunker chunks soaked on the up-current edge of the Sluiceway on slack tide — that's producing the real fish, 20 to 40 pounds, holding tight to the bottom structure where the thermocline gives them cover from the warm surface layer. If you're going to fish this pattern, know your slack to the minute. Race Rock's slack this week is running roughly 20 to 25 minutes ahead of the printed time at New London — the rock chokes the flow and the water keeps moving after the tide technically turns. Valiant Rock slacks a touch later than Race Rock itself, usually 10 to 15 minutes behind. Miss that window by half an hour in either direction and you're fishing 2-plus knots of water that'll bury your wire line before it ever gets to the fish.

Plum Gut is the one everybody's asking me about, and I'll be straight with you — no confirmed albies or bonito through the Gut yet. We flagged the early scouting window last week, and the water's finally sitting right for it: temps have crossed the threshold at Montauk (69.1) and along the approaches, and the moon's building toward full in early August, which means current through the Gut is only going to get stronger and more concentrated over bait in the next week to ten days. That's exactly the setup that triggers the first real showing. I've got the epoxy jigs rigged and ready — half-ounce and three-quarter-ounce, unpainted and green mackerel pattern — but right now the Gut is still mostly bluefish, and they're not shy about it. Blitzes on bunker schools pushing through on the last two hours of the ebb, cocktail blues to 6 pounds tearing up peanut-sized bait right on the surface off Great Gull Island. If you want fast rod-bending action while we wait on the albies, that's your play — small metal, Deadly Dicks and half-ounce Kastmasters, cast into the froth and retrieved fast.

Fluke have thinned out on the open flats the way they always do once the shallow water heats up, but the inlet-adjacent structure is still working. Drifting the deeper bends off Plum Gut and the edges of the Sluiceway in 25 to 40 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails has been steady if not spectacular — a few keepers to 5 pounds mixed with a lot of shorts, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the moving water pulls bait off the structure. Black sea bass are the one bottom fishery that hasn't skipped a beat all summer — the reef structure around Little Gull and the rock piles off Race Rock are holding good numbers on squid and clam belly in 40 to 60 feet, and that bite doesn't care what the surface temp is doing.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full over the next week and that's going to push current speeds up through the Race, Plum Gut, and Fishers Island Sound — bigger max flows, but also cleaner, more predictable slack windows once you learn where they shift to. If the pattern holds, I'd expect the nighttime bass bite to stay the most reliable program through early August, and I'd keep a rod rigged for albies every single trip through the Gut from here on — the water's ready, we just need the fish to commit. Best case, they show within the next week while current's building and bait's getting pinned in the rips. If they slide past us into August without showing here, Block Island and the Race approaches would be my next stop to check.

reports.headline: Joe-Pye Weed's Up, Bass Have Gone to Night Shift Below Essex
reports.subhead: With the shad run a distant memory and the river running warm, the bass have slid into the dark hours — but the bluefish are still willing to show themselves in daylight off Great Island.
reports.body_markdown:
The joe-pye weed is chest-high along the Great Island marsh edges now, that dusty pink bloom that tells you summer's settled in for good, and the young ospreys off Griswold Point are flying their own hunts, no longer waiting on mom to drop a bunker in the nest. That's where we are on this river — deep summer, the kind where the shad run feels like something you read about rather than something that happened four months ago. The alewives and the hickories are long gone upstream and out, and what's left in the current now is a different fishery altogether.

Water in the shallow flats off Great Island and up into North Cove has been running warm — into the mid-to-upper 70s on a sunny afternoon, no different from what the Sound stations are reading down at Kings Point and New London, roughly 69 to 71 out in open water. That's warm enough that the striped bass in this river have done what they do every July: gone nocturnal. I've said it before and I'll keep saying it because it holds up year after year — when the surface sits in the low-to-mid 70s, the bass you find rod-in-hand at two in the afternoon are the exception, not the rule. We flagged this pattern building last week and it's held exactly as expected — the daytime river has gone quiet, but after dark it wakes up.

If you want bass right now, you fish the dark hours off Saybrook Point — the breakwater and the outer bar where the river current collides with incoming Sound water. That collision is the whole game this time of year. On the outgoing tide, the river pushes out cooler, tannic water that rides up over the denser salt water from the Sound, and it creates a thermal seam right at the mouth that bass use like a highway. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, slow-walked along that seam from an hour before high tide through the first few hours of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer I've heard of — fish in the 24 to 32-inch range, with the occasional better fish pushing 36. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 12 to 18 feet off the Point, same tide stage, have also been drawing bites, mostly after 9 or 10 at night once boat traffic clears out.

During daylight, the bass that are around are holding deep and tight to structure — the drop-off at Ferry Point, the pilings and scour holes around the Baldwin Bridge, and the deeper bends up toward Essex where the channel drops to 20-plus feet. A bucktail dragged slow along the bottom through those areas on the last two hours of the ebb has picked at a few fish, but it's been a grind — more blanks than bites, and I won't pretend otherwise. If you're only fishing daylight hours right now, set your expectations accordingly and treat any bass as a bonus.

Bluefish have been the more honest daytime player. They're following bunker schools that have pushed up into the lower river and along the flats off Great Island, and unlike the bass they haven't gone shy about showing themselves — you can see the nervous water and the occasional slash on the surface mid-morning and again in the last hour of daylight. Working topwater plugs or diamond jigs through those bunker pods on a moving tide has been good for choppers in the 3 to 6-pound range, with the odd bigger fish mixed in. That bluefish push matches what's been building up and down the coast this month — bunker-driven blitzes spreading both south and north — and the lower river's version of it has been reliable enough that I'd call it the surer bet for anyone who wants action they can see rather than fish blind for after dark.

For those who'd rather skip the night shift altogether, white perch have been steady in the deeper coves — North Cove, the water off DEP Marina, and the bends up past Essex. Small jigs tipped with bloodworms, fished slow along bottom in 8 to 15 feet on the last of the incoming, have been filling out a lot of quieter mornings. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's honest, and the perch have been cooperative all month.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means stronger tidal current building through the river mouth over the next week or two. That should sharpen both patterns — a harder-running outgoing tide will pull more bait and more bass through that thermal seam off Saybrook Point after dark, and stronger current should keep the bunker schools moving and the bluefish on them through the daylight hours off Great Island. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the outer bar an hour before high, eel in hand, waiting on that seam to load up as the ebb takes hold. Bring bug spray. The no-see-ums out on that flat this time of year are as reliable as anything else on this river.

reports.headline: Bass gone to the night shift — porgies picking up the slack out front
reports.subhead: Daytime stripers have quit the reefs, but scup, bluefish, and a few night-tide bass are keeping rods bent from Mattituck to the Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
Kid pulled up to the ramp at Mattituck Inlet Tuesday morning, maybe six-thirty, and he had that look — the one where a fella's spent three hours working a rip he caught fish in back in June and got nothing for it but a sunburn. He asked me straight out, "Pat, where'd the bass go?" I told him the same thing I've been telling fellas at that ramp for sixty summers when the water gets like this. They didn't go anywhere. They just quit working days.

That's the truth of it right now. Sound surface is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s — Kings Point's reading just under 71, New London's holding around 69 and change, and that's enough heat to push the stripers down onto structure and current seams where it's cooler, and to shut their daytime feeding off almost entirely. I've seen this pattern more summers than I care to count. When the water gets up into that range, the bass don't disappear, they just go nocturnal on you. Come dusk they climb back up onto the rock piles off Horton Point and Rocky Point and they'll eat — eels fished slow along bottom, bunker chunks soaking on a fish-finder rig in the current seams where the reef drops into deeper water. Last few nights the guys fishing the two hours either side of the tide change off Horton have done best, mostly schoolies with a few better fish mixed in, nothing to write home about size-wise but a real bite if you're willing to be out there when it's dark and the mosquitoes are working you over.

Daytime, if you want bass, you're fishing deep and slow over structure and hoping. I wouldn't build a trip around it. What I would build a trip around right now is porgies, because that bite hasn't missed a beat all month. The scup are thick around the rock structure and reef edges from Mattituck straight through to the Orient side, and they don't care one bit that the surface water's warm — they're down on bottom where it's cooler and the current keeps bait moving past them. Hi-lo rig, two hooks, squid strips or a piece of clam, small enough hooks that you're not feeding them a mouthful they can't handle. Anchor up tight to the rock piles, not right on top, and let the current bring the smell to them. Some real dinner-plate fish coming over the rail this week, not just the pan-size stuff.

Fluke have softened up some in the shallower water, same story as everywhere else on the Sound this time of year — they've slid off the open flats and into the deeper channel bends and the mouths where there's still cool water moving. Mattituck Inlet itself has been the more consistent producer, working the channel edges on the last of the ebb with a bucktail and a Gulp strip, white or chartreuse, dragged slow along bottom. Plum Gut approach has given up a few better fish too for the boats willing to work the deeper edges where the current cuts hard, but you need to time it right — that current there doesn't forgive a sloppy drift.

Bluefish are still the most reliable thing to actually see happening on the water. Bunker pods have been pushing through past Rocky Point and around the inlet mouth at first light, and when the blues get under them it's the real thing — surface busting up, gulls working it over, blues in the three-to-six-pound range hitting anything shiny you throw at them. Poppers, metal, doesn't much matter, just get it in front of them before the school moves off, because they don't sit still long. Weakfish have been mixed in here and there on the same tides the bass are working at night, nothing you can plan a trip around, but a nice surprise on a bunker chunk if one finds your bait.

Moon's building toward full in the first days of August, and that means the current through the Gut and the Race is going to sharpen up as we go. That's worth watching close. Every year about this time, once that current gets some real push behind it, bait starts stacking against the structure out there and you get your first hints of something different showing up — I'm not going to promise anything's arrived yet because nothing has, but Plum Gut and Orient Point are exactly where I'd be keeping one eye open over the next week or two as that tide builds. In the meantime, fish the porgies with confidence, work the bass after dark if you've got the patience for it, and don't waste your good daylight hours pounding water that's already told you it's not going to give up a striper before the sun goes down.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Stacking Sea Bass at Twotree While Bass Go Nocturnal on Black Point
reports.subhead: The party boats are grinding out limits of black sea bass on the reef structure, but if you want a striper you better be fishing after the sun goes down.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic charter guys at the bait shop Tuesday morning loading coolers with squid and green crabs, and he told me flat out — "the sea bass are the story right now, everything else you gotta work for." That's about as honest a read as you're gonna get from a guy who's on the water five days a week, and after checking around with the rest of the fleet, he's not wrong.

Black sea bass have been the most dependable thing going in this zone. The drift boats working out of Niantic have been putting anglers on solid catches at Hole-in-the-Wall and out along Twotree Island Channel, working the rock piles and rubble bottom in 40 to 60 feet. Squid strips and Gulp Sea Bass Bites on a double-hook bottom rig are getting it done, and there's enough porgies mixed in on the same drops — sandworms and clam bits on a high-low rig — that nobody's coming back with an empty cooler even on the days when the bigger sea bass aren't cooperating. This has been the one bite in this zone you can set a plan around, tide stage doesn't seem to matter as much as just finding the right piece of structure and staying anchored tight to it.

Fluke is a different conversation, and it's the mixed bag kind of week where you gotta be honest about it. The open flats inside Niantic Bay have gone quiet as that water sits in the high 60s to low 70s — New London's reading around 69.4°F, which isn't brutal, but it's enough to push the fluke out of the shallow sand and into the deeper channel bends where the water keeps moving. Twotree Channel and the mouth of the Niantic River, right where the current squeezes through, have been the more consistent producers — drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet on the last of the outgoing has put keepers in the boat, but you're covering water to find them, not just parking and waiting. If you're used to easy summer flatty fishing inside the bay, adjust your expectations and follow the deeper structure.

Stripers are the toughest read right now, and it's not because they're not around — they are — it's because the daytime bite has essentially shut off. With surface temps sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range, the bass have gone nocturnal, holding deep on current seams and structure through the day and only committing after dark. Black Point and the rocks off McCook Point have been the spots where the guys willing to fish the night tide are connecting — bunker chunks fished on fishfinder rigs along the current edges, or eels swum slow through the rip at Hole-in-the-Wall on the incoming, starting an hour before dark and working through the change. We flagged this pattern last week and said it would hold as long as the warm, stable weather stuck around — it has, and the fish are behaving exactly the way that forecast said they would. If you're a daylight fisherman right now, striped bass is going to frustrate you. If you can fish dusk into the night tide, you've got a real shot.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with whatever bait shows up in the bay. When bunker push into Niantic Bay on a moving tide, the blues show up right behind them, and there's been a couple of legitimate blitz windows this past week right off the river mouth and along the beach toward McCook Point — poppers and metal, anything shiny thrown into the melee, gets bit. It's not a sure thing day to day since it depends entirely on where the bait sets up, but when it happens it happens fast and it's worth having a bag of Deadly Dicks in the truck just in case.

Blackfish are off the table right now with Connecticut's summer closure in effect, so don't waste bunker crab bait on tog until the fall season opens back up — save that gear for October.

As for what's coming, the moon's building toward full in early August and that means current should be rebuilding through this whole stretch, the Race, Fishers Island Sound, right on down into Twotree Channel. Stronger flow is going to sharpen up every current-dependent bite in this zone — the sea bass fishing at Hole-in-the-Wall should stay steady or even improve as the water starts moving with more authority, and the fluke bite in the channel bends should tighten up too as the current does more of the work pulling bait past the structure. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take an evening tide at Black Point for stripers and follow it with a morning drift at Twotree for sea bass and porgies — that's about as complete a day as this zone offers right now. Just don't expect the stripers to cooperate before the sun goes down.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Rips Go Quiet at Noon, Loud at Midnight — Stripers Sliding Deep, Blues Still Chasing Bunker
reports.subhead: New London's holding a cooler read than the rest of the Sound, but the fish still know it's late July — daylight belongs to the porgies, dark belongs to the eels.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the seawall below Fort Trumbull Tuesday evening watching the ebb build against the fort's old stone footing, and you could see the seam sharpen right on schedule — that clean line where the river current peels off the rock and meets the harbor swing. Twenty years watching that seam and it still tells you everything. Right now it's telling me the stripers have gone underground during the day and only show themselves once the light's off the water.

New London's reading 69.4 degrees at the surface, which is actually the cool corner of the Sound this week — Kings Point to the west is pushing near 71. That gradient matters more than people think. It means the Thames and the harbor mouth are holding onto a little more oxygen and a little more comfort for bass than the water to our west, but make no mistake, we're still deep into that mid-summer stretch where daytime stripers want nothing to do with the surface. I've been finding them stacked on the down-current side of the Gold Star Bridge pilings, 18 to 25 feet, sitting tight to the concrete where the tide breaks and slows just enough for them to hold without burning fuel. During the day that's a bottom bite or nothing — eels on a fish-finder rig, bunker chunks anchored with 3 ounces of lead to hold in that current, fished dead slow on the last two hours of the ebb. After dark, though, those same fish slide up onto the flats off Fort Trumbull and the river mouth proper, and that's when eels swum slow on a plain 3/8-ounce jighead start producing better fish — nothing giant, mostly schoolies and low-20s, but a couple of guys have put mid-30-inch bass on the beach fishing the Fort Trumbull rip an hour either side of the tide change, working the current seam where the fresh river water folds into the salt.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the warm, stable weather would keep stripers locked into this nocturnal script, and that's exactly what's playing out. Nothing dramatic, nothing that's going to fill a cooler by 10 a.m., but if you're willing to fish the dark hours and work structure instead of open water, there are fish to be had.

Bluefish are the ones putting on the show right now, and they don't care what time it is. Bunker pods have been running the harbor from Pleasure Beach up toward Ocean Beach, and when the tide's moving — doesn't matter ebb or flood, just moving — you'll see the water erupt where the blues pin a school against the beach or against the riprap. Poppers and metal — the classic 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown right into the froth is about as simple as fishing gets right now, and it's been paying off with blues in the 3 to 6-pound class, plenty of them, enough to keep rods bent even on days when the striper bite is a grind. If you see gulls working tight and diving hard off Ocean Beach, don't wait — that bait won't hold in one spot long, and the blues push it fast.

Porgies have been the steady, unglamorous producer all month, and they're still there. Fort Trumbull's rock pile and the rip lines around the sub base pilings are holding good numbers on bloodworms and skimmer clam, fished on a simple high-low rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current — 2 to 3 ounces depending on the stage of tide. Best window is that hour before and after the tide change when the current eases and the porgies stack up to feed instead of fighting the flow. Nothing trophy-sized, mostly hand-sized fish in the 10 to 12-inch range, but it's a reliable way to bend a rod with kids or when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Blackfish are still shut down for the summer closure and won't be back in play until the fall opener, so if you're itching for tog, that wait continues.

Hickory shad have thinned out from where they were earlier in the season — a few stragglers still show on light jigs and small Kastmasters up in the river above the bridge on the last of the incoming, but that window's closing fast as the water holds in the high 60s to low 70s. Don't plan a trip around them at this point; treat any shad as a bonus while you're working the same stretch for stripers or blues.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, and that means current through the Race and up into Fishers Island Sound is going to strengthen over the next week, which should sharpen every seam in the Thames system — Fort Trumbull, the bridge pilings, the river mouth flats. If that holds, I'd expect the nighttime striper bite to get a little more consistent and the bass to push a bit shallower on the stronger tides as bait gets squeezed harder against structure. My plan for the next few outings is simple: eels after dark on the Fort Trumbull rip on the building current, bunker chunks off the bridge pilings on the slower stretches of the ebb, and metal in hand any time I see birds working off Ocean Beach. It's not a blowup bite on any one species, but between the blues on top and the bass willing to show after sundown, there's enough going on to make the trip worth planning around the tide chart rather than the clock.

reports.headline: Falkner's Rockpile Porgies Feast While the Current Finds Its Legs
reports.subhead: Sea bass hold tight to structure from the Gulf to Stratford Shoal, stripers go nocturnal, and the neap tide's grip is finally breaking.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a guy on the outer breakwall Tuesday morning hook into a porgy that buried his rod tip so hard I thought he'd snagged a keg. Turned out to be a fat 13-inch scup, mouth full of green crab, and he had four more just like it in the bucket before the tide even turned. That's the kind of week it's been out here — not flashy, but if you know where the rocks sit and you're willing to fish the bottom instead of the surface, there's real reward waiting.

Porgies are thick right now on every piece of structure from the New Haven breakwalls out to Falkner Island. I've been running hi-lo rigs with size 4 hooks, sandworm on one, a chunk of green crab on the other, 2 ounces of lead to hold bottom in 20 to 30 feet. Falkner's outer rockpile has been the standout — anchor up-current on the last two hours of the incoming and let the chum bag do its work. The bite there has been steady enough that I'm not exaggerating when I say limits by 9 a.m. aren't unusual if you're anchored right and the current's moving.

And that current matters more than usual this week. We were dealing with a soft neap cycle that left a lot of these spots barely moving — you'd drop anchor at Stratford Shoal and watch your line hang straight down with no push at all, which is death for porgy and sea bass fishing. We called that one last week, said it'd rebuild as the moon worked back toward full, and sure enough the last few days the flow's come back with some authority. Tuesday's ebb at the Gulf was ripping enough that I had to bump up to 3 ounces just to hold bottom. That's a good problem to have.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on every rockpile in the zone. Milford Gulf has been quietly excellent — squid strips on a bucktail teaser rig, dropped tight to the rocks in 25 to 35 feet, outgoing tide. I had a stretch last Thursday where every other drop produced a keeper sea bass in the 14 to 16 inch range, mixed with enough shorts that you had to sort through a few before filling out. Stratford Shoal is holding fish too, but it's deeper and current-dependent — you want the tide moving, not slack, or you're just marking fish on the sounder and watching them ignore you.

Blackfish are off the table for now — CT's summer closure has us locked out until fall, so don't waste bait on tautog jigs out at Charles Island's rockier stretches. Save that program for October.

Stripers are the trickiest piece of the puzzle right now, and that's mostly a water temperature story. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, and New Haven Harbor's been sitting in that same low-70s range — warm enough that the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding deep on the edges of the Charles Island sandbar or tucked into the current seams off Stratford Shoal, not doing much. But work that same water after dark on the last two hours of the incoming, drift eels or fish a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig off the bar, and you'll find them willing. Had a report of a mid-20-pound fish taken off the southwest corner of Charles Island around midnight last week on a chunk — that's the program right now, and it should hold as long as this warm, stable stretch of weather doesn't break.

Bluefish are the daytime consolation prize. Bunker pods have been moving along Hammonasset and the flats off Falkner, and when the blues get under them it's a fast, sloppy affair — bucktails, poppers, whatever you've got, just get it in the water before the school moves off. It doesn't last long in any one spot, but it's been reliable enough this week to be worth a look if you're passing through anyway.

Fluke have thinned out on the open flats the way they always do once things heat up — I haven't bothered drifting the shallow stuff off Hammonasset in a couple weeks. Better luck's been in the deeper bends, particularly the channel edges near the Housatonic mouth and the deeper cuts around the Gulf. White Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been picking through a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts.

Looking ahead, I like where this is headed. The current's rebuilding as we push toward the full moon in early August, which should sharpen up both the porgy/sea bass bite on the rockpiles and give the striper fishing at night a little more push to work with. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd put my Saturday morning at Falkner's outer pile chasing porgies and sea bass, then swing back for a midnight run at Charles Island if the tide lines up. Watch that moon — bigger swings mean better structure fishing, and that's where this zone earns its keep.

reports.headline: Trolled the Wall Till It Died, Anchored Up, Chunked Our Way to Six Yellowfin
reports.subhead: A warm filament pinned to the northeast wall kept the troll bite alive till 10 a.m. — after that, the chunk bag did the work.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to run Wilmington instead of pushing further south to Baltimore, and it came down to fuel math and one look at the imagery. The eddy that's been spinning off the Stream all month is still parked right where I want it, pushing a filament of 78-79°F water up onto the 100-fathom curve on the northeast wall, somewhere around 38°48' N, 74°10' W. That's a 20-mile run I can afford to burn twice if I have to. Baltimore's break looked softer and further offshore — more fuel, less certainty. So Wilmington it was, and I'd make that call again.

We left the dock at 4 a.m. and had lines in by first light, running a standard spread — naked ballyhoo on the long riggers, a green/yellow Ilander-ballyhoo combo down the shotgun, small Joe Shutes on the short corners. The troll bite was real but it wasn't a bonanza — three yellowfin in the 35-50 pound class by 9:30, all right on that temperature seam where the water goes from a milky green to that clean cobalt blue. You could see the color change from the helm, no instruments needed. Once the sun got up high and that seam went slack around 10, the bite died flat. Trolled another ninety minutes for nothing and made the switch.

That's when we ran up-current about a mile, killed the engine over 900 feet of water, and started chunking butterflied bunker off the stern. Took maybe twenty minutes of soaking chunks and a slick before the first fish showed under the boat — and once one showed, they stacked up fast. We put three more yellowfin in the box on the chunk over the next two hours, all on 50-pound fluoro leader, 3/0 circle hooks buried in a bunker chunk, freelined with just enough weight to get it down through the first 30 feet. One bigeye, close to 150 pounds, came up out of nowhere on a bait we'd let sink deeper than the rest — that's the fish that makes the whole day's fuel bill worth it. Six yellowfin and a bigeye for six hours of trolling and three hours at anchor. Not a blowup day, but a solid one, and the kind of numbers that pencil out fine against a 40-mile round trip.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the yellowfin bite would hold steady as long as the high pressure sat over the canyon grounds, and that's exactly how it's played out. The stability up top is keeping that Gulf Stream filament pinned in place instead of sliding off, which means the same stretch of the wall that produced Tuesday should still be productive through the weekend if the weather holds, which right now it looks like it will.

Bluefin are still around but scattered wide — since the July 3rd trophy closure most of what we're seeing are slot fish, 27 to 47 inches, mixed in with the yellowfin on the same temp break. A couple of boats working the canyon this week picked up bluefin on smaller cedar plugs and green machine spreader bars fished tight to the boat, inside 100 feet of wake. Nothing to build a whole trip around, but a welcome bonus if you're already spread out for yellowfin.

Mahi are the wildcard right now — genuinely scattered, not concentrated. We found one decent weedline drifting northeast around 38°42' N, 74°12' W with a scrap of debris holding maybe a dozen fish, 8 to 15 pounds, that jumped all over small skirted ballyhoo and a couple of bubblegum-pink chuggers we threw at them once we spotted the color change. But that's the only real pod we saw all week — most boats are picking off a fish or two incidental to the tuna troll rather than targeting them specifically. If you find floating structure — a pallet, a bucket, anything — it's worth a five-minute stop with a spinning rod and a small bucktail before you move on.

Wahoo showed once, briefly — one fish on a high-speed pass at 38°45' N, 74°08' W, taken on a black-and-purple Ilander with a planer, first thing at dawn before the sun got up. That's a low-percentage play unless you're specifically rigged for it, but worth a mention because it tells you the water column has some real structure to it out there.

White marlin gave us one release Wednesday, a fish that came up on a naked ballyhoo skipping off the left flat line, hooked on a circle and released clean in about four minutes. Scattered reports of one or two more releases elsewhere on the grounds — not a stacked bite, but they're present.

Looking ahead, I'd plan on the same play for the next few days: troll the wall early while that temperature seam is sharp and visible, then be ready to shut down and chunk once the sun kills the surface definition, usually mid-morning. The moon's waxing toward full in early August, which should tighten up current on the grounds and could sharpen the bite further — worth watching for a stronger push of bait onto that eddy edge. If the high pressure breaks down or that filament slides south the way eddies sometimes do, I'd shift attention toward Baltimore before committing another full tank to Wilmington. For now, though, the wall's producing, the fuel math works, and that's the trip I'll keep running until something changes.

reports.headline: A 7-Degree Wall at the 100-Fathom Line — Yellowfin Sitting on the Warm Side
reports.subhead: A Gulf Stream filament pushing 78°F water onto the canyon edge has drawn a hard line in the chart, and the tuna know exactly where it is.
reports.body_markdown:
Seven degrees. That's the break I pulled off this week's SST composite, and it's the number that's been running the whole show out at Hudson. Shelf water sitting at 71.2°F — that's straight off the NY Bight buoy, and it lines up with what Montauk's reading at 69.1°F and what Kings Point's showing at 70.9°F closer to the beach — versus a filament of Gulf Stream water pushing 78 to 80°F onto the eastern wall of the canyon. When you get a spread that wide sitting right on top of the 100-fathom line, you don't need a forum post to tell you where the fish are. You need a chart and a compass.

I ran out of Manasquan Tuesday, 39°51'N, 72°40'W over the canyon head, then worked the wall down toward 39°38'N, 72°08'W — the Claw — where the warm filament was pinched up hard against the drop. That's where we found color change you could see from the tower, green shelf water bleeding into a cobalt blue tongue, and it's exactly where the yellowfin were sitting. Trolled a mixed spread — green machines and Joe Shute bars on the short riggers, a spreader bar with naked ballyhoo down the middle, cedar plugs way back — and picked at yellowfin in the 25 to 45 pound class through the morning. Nothing explosive, but steady enough that by 11 AM we had five in the box and moved into chunking mode on the drift once the sun got high and the trolling bite went quiet, which it always does once that filament water starts to heat up on top.

Chunked butterfish and bunker on the drift right on the break at the Claw, and that's where the bigger fish showed — a 68-pound yellowfin came up on a plain hook, no weight, drifted back 60 feet into the chum slick around 1 PM. The bluefin slot fishery is still doing exactly what it's been doing since the July 3rd trophy closure pushed everybody into that 27-to-73-inch window — scattered but consistent, mostly on the temp breaks rather than concentrated schools. We picked up two in the slot on cedar plugs pulled at trolling speed just inside the warm tongue, both around 60 pounds, and I heard similar counts from boats working the Dip a little to the south, 39°33'N, 72°16'W. If you're targeting bluefin specifically, I'd fish smaller profile baits — 6-inch cedar plugs, small Ilanders — over the bigger canyon spreads, because right now the slot fish are eating smaller forage than the yellowfin are.

Mahi were a mixed bag. We found one respectable weed line drifting on the warm side of the break, maybe half a mile of scattered sargassum with two lobster pot floats tangled into it, and pulled six dolphin off it in the 6-to-12 pound range on naked ballyhoo and small green-and-yellow Ilanders. That's about what I'd call a normal late-July mahi day out there right now — not a bailing frenzy, but worth a stop if you spot the structure. Wahoo were quieter this week. We had one hit-and-miss strike on a high-speed cedar plug at first light near the Claw, no hookup, and that's been the pattern — a few boats scoring one or two on the dawn troll right on the edge of the break, nothing consistent enough to build a whole trip around yet. White marlin showed twice on the long teasers but wouldn't commit to the pitch bait either time, which tells me they're around but not concentrated — probably still working bait pockets scattered along the shelf rather than sitting tight on the wall like the tuna are.

Sea state was workable all week — 3.9 feet at a 5-second period out of the south off the bight buoy, which means it's a little sloppy on top but nothing that should keep a canyon-capable boat home. High pressure has held the whole pattern together, and that's exactly what we flagged last week — said the bite would hold steady as long as the weather stayed put, and it has. No fronts pushing through to mix that filament out or scatter the break, which is the best thing that can happen for consistency out here.

For swordfish guys: daytime drops on the slope south of the Dip, 1,200 to 1,800 feet, have been producing — squid strips and glow gear, standard deep-drop rig, best window still first light through mid-morning before the sun gets high enough to push fish deeper on the thermocline.

Looking at the next several days, the moon's waxing toward full in early August, which should tighten current through the canyon and could sharpen up the vertical jig bite for bluefin as bait gets pushed harder against the wall. If that filament holds its position — and there's no reason in this pattern to think it won't move much in 72 hours — I'd keep working the Claw and the stretch just north of the Dip on the warm side of that break. If it slides east the way these tongues sometimes do late in the week, I'd follow it out past 72°W rather than keep grinding water that's gone cold on the chart. Either way, that 7-degree line is the only number that matters right now.

reports.headline: The Point Holds Its Breath: Bass Go Dark, Albies Sit on the Threshold
reports.subhead: Water at the Lighthouse is sitting right on the number that starts the fall run early — but nobody's iron has found it yet.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a specific feeling that settles over the Point in the last week of July, and if you've fished this rock long enough you learn to recognize it. The bass have gone quiet in the daylight. The bait's staging instead of running. And everybody who's serious about this game starts checking the water like it owes them money, because somewhere out past Turtle Cove or off the Lighthouse, the first albie of the year is going to show up, and nobody wants to be the guy who missed the first day.

We're not there yet. I'll say that plainly, because I said last week this was the window to watch, and I stand by it — the water off the Point has been sitting right at 69 degrees, which is exactly the number that's historically kicked off the scout schools of false albacore and the first bonito push. But sitting at the threshold and crossing it are two different things, and as of this week I haven't had a confirmed report of either fish, not at the Point rip, not at the Elbow, not at Shagwong. What I have seen is nervous water and a few unexplained boils off Camp Hero that could've been albies, could've been blues working peanut bunker, and I'm not going to tell you it was one or the other just because I want it to be. Keep glass on the horizon this week. The moon's building toward full in early August, and that current strength is exactly what stacks bait against the rips and finally tips this thing over. If I had to bet, I'd say we're inside a week, not two.

While we wait on that, the bread-and-butter fishery at the Point hasn't skipped a beat, it's just moved its hours. With surface temps sitting where they are, the striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding deep on the boulder field structure off North Bar and along the current seams east of the Lighthouse, and they're not interested in much. After dark is when this fishery earns its reputation. I've had my best nights working the incoming tide through the boulder field, working a 9-inch black eel slow along bottom, letting the current do the work instead of ripping it back. The takes come subtle at first — a little extra weight, then the rod loads up — and the fish have been mixed slot-to-overslot class, with a few pushing into the 30s reported out of the surf crowd working North Bar on bunker chunks fished on fish-finder rigs with 6 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that rip current. If you're fishing after dark, fish the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide — that's when the current's pushing bait up onto the structure and the bigger fish commit.

Bluefish have been the daytime show, and a good one. Bunker schools are still thick off the south side and around the Point itself, and when the blues get under them it's the kind of surface chaos you can see from the Lighthouse parking lot — diving gulls, popping water, the whole show. These aren't snapper blues either — 8 to 12 pounds has been common, some bigger, and they're murdering everything from bunker spoons to topwater poppers worked fast across the melee. If you find the birds, get there quick, because these blitzes have been short-lived, twenty minutes and gone, the school pushing off with the tide.

Fluke have softened up some in the traditional drift zones as the shallow water's warmed, which tracks with what's happening everywhere else on the Island this time of year — the fish are sliding toward deeper, moving water. Best results have come off the Elbow and along the deeper edges of Frisbee Rock, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet, tipped with a squid strip. It's not been a bent-rod fishery, but a few keepers to 6 pounds have come out of there each trip, and the quality's been decent even where the quantity hasn't.

Porgies remain the honest fishery out here right now — Shagwong Reef and the structure off Cartwright Shoal have been holding good numbers on clam and squid baits fished on standard high-low rigs, and that's a fishery that doesn't care what the water temperature's doing upstairs. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod with the kids, that's your play this week while the rest of us stare at the horizon waiting for something with a sickle tail to show up.

Looking ahead, I think the next 72 hours are the ones that matter most for the season. The current's building into the full moon, the water's already crossed the line it needs to cross, and historically that combination is what turns "maybe" into "confirmed" out here. My money says the first real albie report comes off the Point rip on a falling tide, likely worked with small epoxy jigs or a Deadly Dick cast into nervous water. Until then, fish the bass at night, chase the blues when the birds tell you to, and keep a rod rigged light just in case the water tips over while you're out there.

reports.headline: Two Bluefin, One Broken Outrigger, and the Case for Atlantis Over Veatch This Week
reports.subhead: The chunk bite held on the west wall while the troll spread paid for the fuel — here's how the run shook out and where I'd point the bow next.
reports.body_markdown:
We cleared the Point at 0330 Tuesday with 180 gallons in the tanks — enough to make Atlantis and back with a weather margin, not enough to go chasing a rumor another forty miles east to Veatch. That's the arithmetic you live with out here. Every mile past the canyon edge is a mile you're paying for twice, once going and once coming back with less fuel than you'd like if the wind decides to have an opinion on the way home. I made the call for Atlantis before we left the dock, and I'd make it again.

First light put us on the west wall in about 800 fathoms, trolling a spread of green machines and a naked ballyhoo off the shotgun, and we didn't have to wait long. A pair of bluefin, both mid-70s to low-80s, came up on the short rigger inside of twenty minutes of each other — textbook slot fish, exactly the size class that's been holding steady out here since the July 3rd trophy closure pushed everybody's attention down into that range. We iced both, then the troll bite went quiet the way it does once the sun climbs and the fish slide down off the warm skin water.

That's when we set up to chunk on the east wall, working butterflied bunker down a slow chum slick over a temperature break we found running right along the 100-fathom curve — water pushing 79 degrees on the warm side of the seam, dropping into the mid-70s on the cold side. Yellowfin have been sitting right on that kind of edge all month, and Tuesday was no different. We had three bites in about ninety minutes on circle hooks buried in bunker chunks, freespooled back with the reel in strike, and boated two — a 45-pounder and one closer to 60. Lost the third at boatside, hook pulled clean, which happens enough on chunk fish that I don't lose sleep over it anymore.

What I do lose sleep over is the wahoo that hit the long bar rigger at first light and cut us off before we ever saw color. That's the tax you pay running high-speed spreads through canyon water this time of year — you're going to donate a lure or two to something with teeth. We didn't see another wahoo sign the rest of the day, but the one bite told me they're around, which is worth knowing if you're setting up a dawn troll pattern on the drop-offs.

Mahi were scattered rather than schooled — a few teenagers came up under a mat of sargassum weed inside the canyon proper, and we picked off four on bucktail-and-ballyhoo combos flipped right into the shade line before they wised up and scattered. Nothing like the gaffer-class mahi push you sometimes get when a real weed line sets up, but enough to make it worth keeping a rod rigged and ready any time you cross floating structure. White marlin showed twice on the long teaser, both times refusing to commit to the pitch bait, which tracks with what I've seen most of the summer — plenty of interest, not much conversion. If you're marlin-focused, keep the naked ballyhoo dredge in the water and be patient with the pitch rod; they'll eventually make a mistake, but it won't be often.

We flagged this pattern last week and it's held — steady bluefin pace, yellowfin working the warm filaments, nothing dramatic changing day to day under this settled high-pressure setup. That stability is the whole story right now. No fronts pushing through, no hard temperature swings, just a canyon system doing what it does in late July when the Gulf Stream keeps feeding warm water onto the edges and the fish stay put on it instead of running.

For the boats coming out of Block Island and the RI ports, Hydrographer and Oceanographer are the longer commitment — figure another twenty-plus miles past what a Montauk boat burns to reach Atlantis, and that's before you factor current and sea state on the way home. If you're making that run, I'd want a flat forecast both ways and a full tank with margin, not a tank that gets you there and leaves you praying on the return leg. Worth it if the temperature break is sharp and the reports are fresh, not worth it on spec.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full in early August, and that means more current pushing through these canyon systems over the next week. Stronger current sharpens temperature breaks and usually tightens up where the bait — and the tuna behind it — decide to sit. I'd expect the chunk bite to stay productive on whichever wall is holding the sharpest edge, and I wouldn't be surprised to see the bluefin bite hold its pace as long as this weather window stays open. If it breaks down into wind and sea, the smart play is running less distance for more certainty — Atlantis over Veatch, the west wall over a Hail Mary sixty miles east. Fish the water you can get home from.

reports.headline: Peconic settles into deep summer — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass gone to the night shift
reports.subhead: The bay's locked into its July rhythm: daytime belongs to porgies and fluke in the channels, nighttime belongs to stripers working the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic runs on its own clock, and by late July that clock says: warm water up top, cooler water down deep, and fish sorting themselves accordingly. This bay always warms ahead of the Sound and the ocean beaches — it's shallow, it's protected, and the sun's had all spring and half the summer to work on it. Right now it's sitting warm and glassy on most mornings, especially up in Noyack Bay and the upper reaches of Three Mile Harbor, and that heat is doing exactly what it does this time of year: pushing the day-biters into structure and sending the stripers to work the night shift.

We flagged this pattern last week — said conditions would hold stable through the stretch, no major disruption — and that's precisely what's played out. No storms, no cold fronts, no big wind events to stir things up. Just steady heat and a bay settling into its mid-summer groove.

Start with the good news, because there's real good news: porgy fishing around Shelter Island is as good as it gets anywhere on the East Coast right now. The west side drop-offs off Cedar Island and the deeper water outside Coecles Harbor are holding heavy, hungry schools in that 15- to 25-foot range. Standard hi-lo rig, size 6 or 4 hooks, sandworm or skimmer clam, dropped right to bottom on the last of the incoming or the first hour of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone slack. You don't need to finesse these fish — they're stacked and they're eating. The trick this week has been sizing up your bait a little, because the small stuff gets picked clean by the shorts before a keeper-class porgy even gets a shot. Bigger clam chunks are weeding out some of that nuisance bite and putting bigger fish in the cooler.

Fluke have done what fluke do in a warm July — they've pulled off the open flats and tucked into the channels where the water keeps moving and stays a few degrees cooler. The bend in the Noyack Bay channel and the deeper cuts near the Three Mile Harbor entrance have both been holding fish, though I won't call it easy. It's been a numbers game more than a slam-dunk — you're covering water, working bucktail-and-Gulp combinations (white or chartreuse, 3/4-ounce head, 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer) on a slow drift through 20 to 35 feet, and you're culling through a fair number of shorts to find the keepers. Best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current is still moving enough to keep that Gulp trailer working but hasn't gone dead calm and lifeless. A couple of guys have done well switching to bigger, fresh-cut squid strips on the same rig when the current slows — bigger profile seems to trigger fewer but better-quality bites in that stagnant water.

Weakfish are still around if you know where to look, and the deeper holes in Gardiners Bay have been the most consistent producer — that's a dusk-into-dark bite, working bucktails tipped with squid or drifting a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig right along the bottom where the deeper, cooler water holds. It's not a numbers fishery the way it was a generation ago, but the ones that come over the rail have been quality fish, and the evening bite has been the reliable window.

Striped bass have gone quiet during daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down the whole coast this time of year — surface water in the low-to-mid 70s pushes them down onto structure and current edges, and they mostly stay there until dark. The move is fishing the rips at night: Plum Gut, the drop-offs off Orient Point, and the current seams along the edges of Shelter Island's east side. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig or bunker chunks soaked on the bottom have been the producers, and the bite windows are tight — usually tied right to the tide change, whether that's the top of the flood or the start of the outgoing. The moon's building toward full over the next week or so, and that means the current through Plum Gut and the Race is going to sharpen up considerably. That's worth watching closely, because a stronger push through that gut usually means a better window for bigger bass working the rip edges after dark.

Bluefish have been showing in that classic sporadic, opportunistic way — chasing bait right into the inlets and creek mouths, especially around Sag Harbor and the mouth of Three Mile Harbor. Nothing sustained, but when a school of bait gets pinned up against structure on a moving tide, the blues show up fast and leave just as quick. Worth keeping a metal or a popper rigged and ready if you're working those areas, because you won't get much warning.

One thing worth watching as we roll into August: with the heat this settled and the wind this calm, the shallow, mud-bottom stretches of the upper bay — parts of Noyack, the back ends of the harbors — can start to run low on oxygen if nothing stirs the water for stretches at a time. I haven't seen distress yet, but it's the kind of thing that sneaks up on a bay like this. If you're fishing those upper reaches, the early morning and late evening hours are going to fish better than midday, both for comfort and because that's when the water's freshest.

Bay scallop prep is underway too — a few boats have been out checking grass beds ahead of the fall opener, and the early read is encouraging, though it's early. If the current pattern holds — stable heat, building moon current, porgies stacked at Shelter Island — I'd expect more of the same through early August: good daytime action on porgies and fluke, a quality-over-quantity weakfish bite at dusk, and stripers staying loyal to the night shift until something finally breaks the heat.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday, redemption Thursday: Norfolk pays off, Spencer stays stingy
reports.subhead: A week of route-hopping between four canyons taught me the yellowfin moved south before the fleet did.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the week: C-plus overall, but that's an average of a D and an A, and knowing which canyon earned which grade is the whole ballgame right now.

Monday and Tuesday I ran Spencer and Lindenkohl off Cape May, and honestly, I wasted diesel. Water on the edge at Spencer — I'm talking the 39°20' N, 72°30' W stretch where the 100-fathom curve kinks — was still holding decent color, but the temp break had gone soft. No hard edge, no birds working it, and the meter showed bait scattered thin instead of balled up tight the way you want it before you pull spreader bars. We trolled green machines and cedar plugs off the shotgun for six hours and put two gaffer dolphin in the box and not much else. That's not a disaster, that's just a canyon that hasn't lit its filament yet this cycle.

Wednesday I made the call to run further south, and that's where the week turned. Poor Man's has been the sleeper all month, and Norfolk finally paid rent. Down around 37°10' N, 74°40' W, the Gulf Stream is throwing a legitimate warm tongue up onto the edge — we were marking 79 to 80 degree water right on the break, which is exactly the number that gets yellowfin to commit instead of just window-shopping. We chunked butterfish over a hard current line in about 850 fathoms starting at first light, and it was steady — not stack-em-up crazy, but a fish every twenty to thirty minutes for four hours, mostly 25 to 45 pound yellowfin, a couple pushing 60. Naked ballyhoo and small skirted ballyhoo on the flat lines did the damage once the chunk got them fired up and looking for the next thing that swam by.

We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as the high pressure stuck around, and that's exactly what happened. The stable weather kept the canyon edges clean and let that warm filament stay put instead of getting torn up and pushed around by wind-driven current. That's the whole story of this week in one sentence: patience with the pattern paid off more than horsepower did.

Bluefin have been the quiet reliable player since the trophy fish closure hit July 3rd. We're seeing slot-class fish, mid-40s to bumping 70 inches, scattered across the same temperature breaks the yellowfin are using — Norfolk and Poor Man's both produced bluefin this week on smaller cedar plugs and green-and-yellow machines pulled fast, 7 to 9 knots, right along the color change. Nobody's boating a truckload of them in one trip, but if you're grinding a canyon edge for yellowfin, don't be surprised when a bluefin jumps the chunk line at dusk instead.

Mahi have been exactly what we called last week too — scattered but honest. You're not going to find a mile of grass loaded with gaffers, but any bit of floating structure — a lobster pot warp, a mat of sargassum, even a stray piece of dunnage — is holding fish. We picked off a dozen keeper-class dolphin this week just by running the edges between Poor Man's and Norfolk with a spotter up top and a couple of pitch rods rigged with small skirted ballyhoo ready to fire the second we saw color or debris.

White marlin activity is building the way it's supposed to for late July, and Norfolk's edge is where I'd point the bow if that's your target. We had two bites and one release on dink ballyhoo behind small Sea Witches, both fish coming up on the long riggers in that same 78-80 degree water. It's not a full-blown bite yet, but the trend line is right — more fish showing every week as that Gulf Stream water keeps pushing warmer filaments up onto the shelf edge.

Lindenkohl and the northern half of Spencer are the ones I'd put on the back burner for now. Until that edge sharpens back up and the bait balls tighten, you're burning fuel for a mixed bag at best. If you've only got one day and you're launching out of Cape May or Ocean City, the run to Poor Man's or Norfolk is longer, but this week it was the difference between a photo of two mahi and a fish box that actually needed ice.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if the high pressure holds — and right now there's nothing in the tropics forcing a change, though that's worth watching as we roll into August. If that filament stays parked on Norfolk and Poor Man's, I'd expect the yellowfin bite to hold steady to build through early next week, with the white marlin count ticking up as more fish push north along the edge. If a system spins up and stirs the stream, that warm tongue could shift on us fast, and I'd be back to scouting Spencer and Lindenkohl for the reset. For now, my plan is simple: run south, chunk the break, and keep ballyhoo in the water till something eats.

reports.headline: North Rip Gone Quiet by Day, Loud After Dark — And the Current's Building for Bonito
reports.subhead: Bass have slid off the daylight bite and into the dark, bluefish are still hammering bunker on the rips, and the first false albacore window is closing fast.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it — Tuesday night, running the Southwest Ledge around ten, the water had that heavier, slicker feel under the hull, the kind of surface tension you get when the current's really loading up against the moon. We're pushing toward full moon in early August, and you can already feel the tide building a day ahead of schedule. That's the kind of signal that matters more out here than any number on a screen.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal on us, and that's been the story for two weeks now, not just this one. Daytime surface temps sitting in the low-to-mid 70s have pushed the fish down onto structure — the edges of the Ledge, the drop-offs along the North Rip, anywhere there's a thermocline to hide under. I've been marking fish stacked 35 to 50 feet down on the meter in the middle of the afternoon, completely uninterested in anything, and then watching that same water come alive two hours after sunset. The pattern's been consistent enough that I'll say what I said last week and stand by it — as long as this warm, stable weather holds, the bass are going to keep playing this game. Eels drifted on the down-current side of the Ledge after dark have been the most dependable producer, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current, usually 3 to 5 ounces depending on the stage of the tide. Bunker chunks fished the same way off the North Rip have worked too, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when bait gets pinned against that structure. I pulled a 34-pounder off the Ledge Sunday night on an eel, and a buddy fishing bunker chunks off the Rip iced a 40 the same night — both after 11 PM, both on slack-to-building current. Daytime trolling with umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm out past the Ledge has still produced the occasional fish, but it's a fraction of what you'll get after dark right now.

Bluefish have been the daylight show, and a good one. Bunker schools are still thick around the island — you can see them from a half mile off when the birds start working — and the blues have been pinning them against the rips on both the north and south ends. Southwest Ledge in the morning has been holding some real gorilla blues, 8 to 12 pounds, busting bait on the surface enough that you can run and gun with poppers or big soft plastics and connect quickly. I've had good luck with 3-ounce metal — Hopkins and Kastmasters — cast right into the boil and retrieved fast. This bunker-driven blitz pattern has been building for weeks now and it isn't slowing down; if anything it's spreading, and I wouldn't be surprised to hear it's still pushing hard into the bays to our west and north over the next few days.

Fluke have softened up some in the shallower stuff, which tracks with what's happening everywhere south of us — the flat, sun-warmed water isn't holding fish like it did in June. But the deeper structure has kept producing. The channel edges outside the Great Salt Pond entrance, and the deeper water off the southeast corner of the island, have both been giving up keeper fluke in the 20 to 40 foot range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, dragged slow on 3/4-ounce bucktails. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but quality fish mixed in — a few over 5 pounds this past week.

Now the one everybody's asking me about at the dock: bonito and albies. I'll be straight with you — nothing confirmed yet out here. Water's crossed the threshold where we'd expect to see the first fish, and the current is building the way it needs to with this moon cycle, which is exactly the setup that usually triggers it. But building current alone doesn't put fish in the boat — you need the bait to actually get pinned and worked, and I haven't seen that happen yet around the rips or off the Ledge. If I had to bet, I'd say we're closer than we were a week ago, and the next stretch of building tide into the full moon is the window I'd watch hardest. If you're itching to be the first one to connect, I'd be working the rip lines at first light with small metal and epoxy jigs, watching for diving terns and any nervous water — that's usually the tip-off before anyone gets a rod bent.

Offshore, the bluefin slot fishery has stayed steady on the grounds south of the island, which is worth a mention if you've got a bigger boat and don't mind the run — that bite hasn't skipped a beat since the trophy closure kicked in July 3rd.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the weekend unless the wind shifts. Keep the bass game nocturnal, keep working the bunker schools for blues in daylight, and keep one eye on the rips for that first bonito showing — this is the week I'd expect it, if it's coming at all.

reports.headline: July 27: Washington's Still Running Its Usual Head Start
reports.subhead: The eastern wall is holding warm water and yellowfin while boats up north are still waiting on their break to show.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock — why is Washington already dialed in when guys running out of Manasquan or Montauk are still hunting for their break? Simple answer: geography. We sit far enough south and close enough to where the Gulf Stream likes to throw its filaments that we get first crack at 78-80°F water most seasons, sometimes by two to three weeks. This year's no different. By the third week of June we had a clean edge setting up along the 100-fathom curve on the eastern wall, and it's held there, more or less, ever since. Late July is when Washington should be cooking, and it is — not lights-out, but honest, consistent, the kind of canyon fishing you can plan a trip around.

The read this week: warm water is still pushing onto the edge, holding a temperature break right around the eastern wall between 38°37'N and 38°42'N, 72°48'W to 72°52'W. That's been the address all month. South of there, past the 250 line, the water goes soft and green — not worth the fuel. North, up toward the Washington/Wilmington saddle, it's mixed and unsettled. Stay on that eastern wall where the blue meets the green and you're in business.

Yellowfin have been the backbone of the trip report this week, and they're doing exactly what a stable high-pressure pattern says they should. Troll-and-chunk spreads working the color change in 900 to 1,300 feet have put fish in the box on most trips — nothing gangbuster, but a hard pull of ballyhoo and small Green Machines skirted behind the spreader bars has drawn strikes in that 78°F push, then once the trolling bite goes quiet around mid-morning, butterfish chunks on 20 to 30-pound fluoro leader, drifted back in the chum slick, have kept rods bent through the heat of the day. Fish have run 20 to 45 pounds, nothing giant, but they're eating.

Mahi have been the pleasant surprise, and honestly, we flagged this pattern last week — said the scattered-but-steady mahi bite would hold as long as the offshore high held, and that's exactly what's happened. Weed lines and any floating junk along that eastern wall edge have been holding fish in the 3 to 12-pound class, occasional bull in the teens mixed in. Small hookless teasers with naked ballyhoo dropped back to any surface-feeding pod has worked better than blind trolling — these fish are visual right now, and if you're not scanning for weed lines and high flyers you're leaving fish on the table.

Bigeye have been a night bite, like always this time of year, and the northeast wall in 1,000 to 1,400 feet has been the spot. Deep drops on squid and butterfish, glow sticks on the leader, dropped down after dark on the slower tide stages — that's produced the better-grade fish, 80 to 150 pounds, though it's not an every-trip thing. You need to commit to the overnight and you need calm water to fish it right, which we've had.

Wahoo have shown but they're not thick yet — a fish here, a fish there on high-speed gear, planers and Ilanders in the 62 to 66-fathom stretch along the wall. That's a August pattern that's arriving a touch early, which fits the whole seasonal theme around here. White marlin sign has been scattered — a few tags, a few raised and not converted, mostly on ballyhoo strings behind the dredge in that same warm push. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth having the pitch bait rigged.

Bluefin have stayed mostly a Block Island and Stellwagen story since the July 3rd trophy closure shifted effort north, but we're still seeing slot-class fish mixed in on the canyon grounds, particularly where bait's been thick on the temperature break. Nothing that changes the game plan — yellowfin and mahi remain the money species out here right now.

Looking at the next week, I don't see a reason for this to change much. The high-pressure pattern that's kept the water settled and the edge clean isn't going anywhere fast, and that eastern wall break has been remarkably stable for going on six weeks now — longer than I'd have bet on back in June. If I had a trip to plan, I'd run straight to that 38°40'N, 72°50'W stretch, start trolling the color change early, and be ready to switch to chunk once the sun gets high. Keep an eye on the weed lines for the mahi, and if you've got the crew and the fuel for an overnight, the northeast wall bigeye drop is worth the extra hours. August around here usually means the wahoo numbers build and the white marlin bite sharpens up — if that early-arrival pattern holds true to form again this year, don't be shocked if Washington gets there before everybody else does, same as always.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Pinned on Charles Island — Blues Crash, Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: The bait's telling the story of a Sound that's warm on top and hungry underneath, with the first bonito clock ticking toward August.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning parked off Charles Island doing more watching than fishing, and it was worth it. There's a bunker school — proper peanut size, maybe two to three inches — that's been holding tight against the rocks on the west side since the weekend, and it's not moving much even on the tide change. That's the tell. When bait balls up and refuses to run, something's pushing it from below. Sure enough, terns were working the edges all morning, and every third or fourth dive triggered a boil underneath — bluefish, mostly cocktail size but with some better fish mixed in, six and seven pounds, slashing up through the peanuts and leaving slicks of oil on the surface.

That's been the pattern across the middle Sound all week. Bunker schools are stacked from Charles Island down through the Norwalk Islands and out toward Stratford Shoal, and the blues are riding them hard during daylight. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod right now, find the birds, idle up quiet, and cast small bunker spoons or a 2-ounce Hopkins past the edge of the bait. You don't need to hit the middle of the school — the blues are working the perimeter where the peanuts get stripped off and disoriented.

Stripers are a different conversation entirely, and it comes down to temperature. Kings Point is reading right around 71 degrees, New London's a touch cooler at 69.4, and that gradient matters — the western and central Sound is holding warmer water on top, which means the bass have gone essentially nocturnal. I marked good numbers of fish on the sounder over the rockpile structure off the Norwalk Islands and along the Stratford Shoal drop-off in the afternoon, sitting deep, 25 to 35 feet down, refusing to commit during the heat of the day. Come back after dark and it's a different fishery. I fished the flat off Middle Ground Light Thursday night on the incoming, anchored up, chunked fresh bunker on fish-finder rigs, and picked off three fish in the 28 to 33-inch range in about two hours of soak time. Eels fished slow-drifted over the same structure are producing too — if you've got the patience to work them.

Fluke have followed the same logic as the bass, just without the wait for darkness. The open, shallow flats have gone quiet — too warm, not enough moving water — and the better fish have slid into the channel edges and the deeper structure where current keeps things stirred. The break off Stratford Shoal, where it drops from around 20 feet down into the 50s and 60s, has been the most consistent producer, along with the rip that builds around Middle Ground Light on a strong tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, have out-produced bare bait rigs for me two trips running. Nothing huge — most fish in the 16 to 19-inch range with a few keepers mixed in — but steady enough to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're willing to work the deeper water instead of drifting the flats out of habit.

Porgies, for what it's worth, are about the easiest thing going right now. The reef structure around the Norwalk Islands is thick with them, and anchoring up with clam or worm on a simple high-low rig will keep a rod bent all afternoon. It's not glamorous, but it's a good way to fill a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn toward a better bass or fluke window.

One thing worth flagging — we said last week that the neap tide cycle had softened current flow through the deeper Sound channels, and that's exactly what played out. The moving water through Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk gaps has been noticeably weaker the last several days, which is part of why the fluke bite went soft on the flats and why the fish that are biting have needed structure to hold current against. That should start correcting itself. The moon's building back toward full in the first days of August, and as that current rebuilds through the narrows, I'd expect the bite to sharpen — especially at Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground rip, where a stronger tide concentrates bait instead of just letting it drift.

The other thing I'm watching closely, because it's the beat I know best, is bonito. It's not time yet — water's there, current isn't quite built up enough to pin bait the way these fish like — but the Norwalk Islands are usually the first place in my zone to show signs, typically in the first half of August once the tide really starts running again. I'll be watching the bunker schools for that telltale tightening, when peanuts start getting worked over by something faster and more violent than a bluefish. If the rebuild happens the way it should over the next week, I wouldn't be surprised to hear the first confirmed report out of the Norwalk chain by early August. Until then, work the bait, fish the structure, and save your night trips for the bass — that's where the real, consistent action is right now.

reports.headline: Skip the Slop — the Real Bite's Inside Jones Inlet After Dark
reports.subhead: While the fleet fights a beat-up ocean front for bluefish, the jetty rocks and channel edges are quietly producing bass, fluke, and a weakfish comeback nobody's talking about.
reports.body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is parked on the ocean beach at first light this week, watching bunker schools get bulldozed by blues in three feet of whitewater, getting their teeth rattled by a 3.9-foot swell that never lays down long enough to fish it right. I get it — a bluefish blitz is a hell of a thing to watch. But I've been running the other way. Dead low tide, I'm walking out on the west jetty at Jones Inlet with a bag of eels and a bucket of bunker chunks, and I'm not fighting anybody for water.

Here's the thing about that ocean front right now — 71-degree water stacked up against a short, choppy period like that isn't fishable water, it's washing-machine water. The bass know it. They've gone almost completely nocturnal on us, same as they have from here down through Jersey, and that's not new — we flagged that pattern last week and it's held right through the heat. During the day these fish are sitting deep on structure, tucked into current seams off the rocks or holding on the edge of the channel where the water's a couple degrees cooler than the flats around it. You want them, you come back after the sun drops.

My program right now is simple. I fish the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, right at the Jones Inlet jetty where the current rips past the rocks. Whole bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 4/0 circle hook, just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — 3 to 4 ounces depending on how hard it's ripping.
