reports.subhead: The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is buying us daytime bass while the rest of the coast fishes the dark — take advantage while it lasts.
reports.body_markdown:
I took the outer route past Peaks and out toward Halfway Rock on Tuesday morning, and what struck me wasn't the fish so much as the water itself — that dark green-blue color holding steady, none of the murky freshwater push you sometimes get after a heavy rain week. Casco Bay is running clean and cool for late July, and that single fact is doing more work for us right now than any tide table.

Here's the thing worth understanding, and I say this having watched the coast from a professor's remove for thirty summers now: south of us, from Jersey up through Long Island Sound, the striper fishery has gone nocturnal. Surface temps down there are pushing into the mid-70s, forcing bass onto thermoclines and deep structure, feeding only at the edges of daylight or in full dark. We don't have that problem here. The Gulf of Maine keeps its foot on the brake, and Casco Bay's water — even inshore around the coves — hasn't hit that threshold. So our bass are still willing to work shallow ledges and estuary mouths in daylight, particularly on the push of the tide. That's a real advantage this time of year, and it's worth planning around rather than assuming it'll last forever.

Mackerel are the backbone of the week. Schools have been thick off Halfway Rock and along the drop north of Jewell Island, showing up as nervous water and diving terns any time from mid-morning through early afternoon. Small chrome Swedish Pimples and mackerel jigs strung three or four to a line, dropped to 20-30 feet and worked with a short snap, are filling coolers fast. If you're marking bait but not connecting, drop deeper — I've had mornings where the mackerel sat tight to bottom in 40 feet even with birds working the surface, chasing something smaller we couldn't see.

Those mackerel schools are exactly why the striper bite has held up on the ledges around Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small. Bass are shadowing the bait, and I've taken fish to 30 inches working live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished right on the last two hours of the incoming near the ledges off Ragged Island. The take is subtle — a slow pull-down rather than a hit — so keep your drag light and let the fish load up before you set. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, worked slow along bottom on the slack before the ebb, have also been productive around the mouth of the New Meadows River and the ledges off Cundy's Harbor. Nothing explosive, but steady — three or four keeper-class fish on a good tide, which for mid-summer bay fishing is a fair result.

Groundfish remain a Halfway Rock story, as they generally are this time of year. Cod and a scattering of haddock are holding on the structure in 60 to 90 feet, and the pattern hasn't changed much from what I described last week — the slack water either side of the tide change is when you want your bait down. Clam and herring chunks on a standard cod rig, fished tight to the rock's northern face where the bottom breaks up into boulder and gravel, have produced fish in the 6 to 10 pound range. It's not fast fishing. You're putting in time for quality over quantity, and that's been true of this rock for as long as I've fished it. Two Lights hasn't been as productive for groundfish this month — too much boat traffic and not enough structure relief close in — but it remains a reliable spot for mackerel and the occasional bluefish push when the bait runs thick along that stretch of coast.

Bluefish have made a modest appearance in the bay's outer reaches, nothing like the blitz conditions unfolding to our south where blues are tearing through bunker schools from Jersey to western Long Island Sound. Here we're seeing occasional cutoffs on mackerel rigs and the odd blue mixed in with striper catches off Jewell and Cliff Island, nothing organized enough to target specifically yet. Worth keeping a wire leader in the tackle box regardless.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady action on the tide changes through this stable weather stretch — and that's held true. The bay hasn't given us anything dramatic, but it's given us dependable fishing, which this time of year is worth more than a hot week that burns out fast.

Looking ahead, the moon is working toward the next quarter, which means tidal swings will be moderate rather than extreme — good news for anyone fishing the ledges, since you won't be fighting the kind of hard current that makes bottom fishing at Halfway Rock miserable. If the weather holds calm through the weekend, I'd focus effort on the first two hours of the incoming at the Cape Small ledges for bass, and shift to Halfway Rock's slack water windows for cod and haddock. If a front comes through and stirs up the surface, expect the mackerel to push deeper and the bass bite to compress into narrower windows around first light. Either way, this cooler water is a gift right now — the rest of the coast would trade for it. Fish it while you've got it.

reports.headline: Monhegan pollock on top, mackerel holding the bay together
reports.subhead: Groundfish still down in the channels, bass working the river mouths at first light, and the mackerel schools are doing more work than they get credit for.
reports.body_markdown:
Back in the late 80s I had a sternman, Dale, who used to say the bay didn't care what the calendar said — it fished the way it fished, and your job was to figure out which day you'd gotten. Forty years later that's still the only forecasting system I trust. This week the bay gave us a pretty fair hand, provided you were willing to run early and fish the tide instead of the clock.

Starting with what's easy: mackerel are thick from Ram Island out past The Cuckolds, and they've been thick for two weeks now, which is exactly what's kept the striper program alive in the tidal rivers. You don't hear much fuss made over mackerel, but they're the reason there's bait to hold bass in the Sheepscot and up around Wiscasset on the last of the ebb. I had a customer Tuesday morning jigging a small chrome Diamond jig off the Sheepscot bridge pilings at first light, and inside forty minutes he'd boated eight mackerel and had two decent stripers — one a hair under 30 inches — follow a school right up into the current seam and swat at his jig on the retrieve. Switched him to a 6-inch olive Slug-Go, weightless, and let it swing dead-drift through that seam, and that's when the bass started eating for real. Nothing huge, mostly 24 to 28 inches, but a solid dozen fish over two hours on the dropping tide before the sun got up over the trees and shut it down.

That's the pattern right now, and it's the same one we called last week — conditions here have stayed stable, water's held in that comfortable mid-to-high 50s range close to shore, cooler out in the bay proper, and that's kept our stripers shallower and more willing to feed in daylight than what you're seeing from the Cape Cod Canal on south, where the heat's pushed everything down to a dawn-dusk program. We're the lucky zone this time of year. I don't say that often.

Offshore and down around Monhegan, the story's been groundfish, and it's been a genuinely good week for it. Pollock are up on the surface around the ledges off the eastern side of the island — Norton Ledge and out toward Smutty Nose — chasing pogies and sand eels in that nervous, boiling way pollock do when they're really into bait. I had a report from a captain I trust who ran out there Saturday on the last two hours of the incoming and found pollock busting the surface for a good twenty minutes straight, took fish to 8 pounds on white bucktails and swimming plugs cast right into the melee. That's a fun fish to catch on top, and it doesn't last — usually blows out once the tide turns and the bait scatters, so you've got a window, not an all-day bite.

Down deeper, in that 90 to 130 foot water off Monhegan's western side and out toward the deeper channels between the island and Matinicus, cod are still holding where they always hold this time of year — hard bottom, ledge edges, structure that breaks up the current. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, working them slow off bottom, has been the most consistent producer. Sizes have been modest — most fish 3 to 6 pounds, a few pushing 10 — but for late July that's about what you'd expect and about what we've been getting for years now out there. Haddock have been scarcer, a few mixed in on the same drifts but nothing to build a trip around specifically.

Eastern Egg Rock continues to hold its bass in that scrappy, opportunistic way it does all summer — stripers working the edges where the current runs past the rock, feeding on whatever the tide pushes past, sand eels mostly. Light tackle, small soft plastics, nothing fancy. Not a numbers fishery but a reliable one if you're passing by on the way out to Monhegan and want to make a stop.

Penobscot Bay itself has been quieter than I'd like to report. The deeper channels off Vinalhaven and down toward Isle au Haut still hold some groundfish — pollock mostly, a scattering of cod on the drop-offs — but it's spotty work, and I heard from two different boats this week that put in three, four hours and had to work hard for a handful of keepers. If you're going to fish the bay proper right now, fish the tide change hard, right at the top or bottom, and don't waste time on slack water. That's when what fish are there tend to feed.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Water temps in close have stayed steady, mackerel show no sign of thinning out, and as long as that bait stays put the striper bite in the rivers and around the bay mouths should keep holding through the week. Monhegan's groundfish should stay put too — that's deep, cool water and it doesn't turn on a dime. If I had one day to fish this week I'd run out to Monhegan on a rising tide, hit the ledges for pollock on top first light, then work down to cod once the surface bite dies, and finish the day back in close chasing bass off the river mouths on the evening ebb. Long day, but that's about as complete a Midcoast trip as you're going to string together right now.

reports.headline: 180 feet on Jeffrey's: haddock thick on the mud, cod holding tight to the gravel edge
reports.subhead: The bottom's doing exactly what it should this time of July — you just have to fish the right five feet of it.
reports.body_markdown:
Two hundred and ten feet of water on the west side of Jeffrey's, mud bottom, and the sounder with that fuzzy grey haze eight feet off the bottom that means haddock are stacked and feeding. That's been the story most of this week — you find the soft stuff, the mud basins between the humps, and you find fish. Move fifty yards onto the gravel and hard rubble on the ledge's spine, up around 130 to 160 feet, and the picture changes completely. Marks get sparser, tighter to bottom, less spread — that's your cod water, and you've got to fish it different.

I've had my best mornings this week working that exact transition zone, where the mud gives way to broken gravel on the northeast corner of the ledge, inside of Cape Ann but still well out past Thatcher. Anchoring up on the gravel edge with clam and squid combo rigs, cod have been running a solid mixed bag — plenty in the 24 to 30 inch class, a few pushing better than that, though nothing that's going to make the scale groan this week. Jigging with 8 to 12 ounce diamond jigs, teaser dropper above, has worked when the current's moving right — slack tide kills it, so I've been timing my drifts around the two hours either side of max flow.

Haddock have been the more consistent producer, and honestly the better eating too. Working the mud basins in 180 to 220 feet with standard haddock rigs — two hooks, bait up with squid strips or clam belly, small bit of green or chartreuse tube for attraction — and letting it sit just off bottom rather than dragging it. These fish want it presented clean, not bounced around. Limits haven't been automatic but a well-fished drift has been putting a dozen keepers in the box most trips, mixed in with a few pollock that come through in that mid-water column when the tide's really humming.

Platts Bank has been fishing similar to Jeffrey's — same mud-versus-gravel read applies, and I had a trip out there Tuesday that mirrored what we've seen closer to home, haddock thick on the softer bottom west side, cod scattered but present on the eastern rubble. Tillies has been quieter for me this week, water's a touch warmer out that way and the bite's been softer, more of a pick than a program. I'd put my time closer to home right now if you're choosing between the two.

The bluefin piece of this puzzle is starting to develop the way it does every summer before it really turns on in the fall. We're seeing whale activity pushing bait up onto Stellwagen's approaches and along the edge of Jeffrey's itself — sand eel and herring balls getting worked hard by humpbacks and fin whales, and where the whales are, the tuna show up to clean up behind them. I had one client hook and lose a fish trolling a spreader bar over a bait ball on the southern end of the ledge last week, decent fish, probably 200-plus, gone after a short fight on light drag. That's the pattern right now — scattered giants working bait balls opportunistically, not the concentrated push we'll see once the mackerel and herring really stack up in September and October. If you're rigging for bluefin now, I'd keep gear ready but not build a whole trip around it yet. Better odds are still a month or two out.

Regionally the recreational slot fishery down toward Block Island and the canyons has been grinding steady since the trophy closure came through July 3rd, and that pattern holding stable is a decent sign for what's coming our way once the giants really commit to the ledge later this season. Worth watching.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, if unspectacular, structure fishing through the next few days — and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing explosive, but reliable numbers if you fish the right bottom type for the right species and don't waste time working gravel for haddock or mud for cod.

Wind's been cooperative, nothing over 15 knots most days, and that's let us hold position properly on both the gravel and the mud without a lot of drift-and-reset headaches. If that holds through the weekend I'd expect the same read to continue — haddock steady on the mud in that 180 to 220 range, cod a more disciplined pick on the gravel edges where you need patience and a well-placed bait rather than covering water.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on any building southwest wind later in the week — that can push a chop onto the ledge that makes precision anchoring tougher, especially working that gravel-mud transition where five feet of position matters. If it stays clean, my plan is the same one that's worked all week: hit the mud early for haddock while the bite's fresh, shift onto the gravel edge as the tide builds, and keep a rod rigged for anything that shows on the bait balls if we cross paths with the whales again on the way home.

reports.headline: 4:52 AM max ebb: the only window that mattered this week
reports.subhead: Daytime current in the Canal is producing bait movement without bass commitment — the real bite is happening before the sun's up and after it's down.
reports.body_markdown:
4:52 AM. That's when max ebb hit the east end Tuesday morning, and that's when I put two fish over thirty inches in the net off the Herring Run rocks before the sky even started to gray up. Both came on an olive Savage Gear sand eel, swimming it with the current instead of against it, letting the rip do the work. By 6:15, with the sun up and the current still running strong but the light flooding the water, it was over. Dead over. That's the story of the Canal right now and it's been the story for about two weeks — the tide's doing exactly what it should, the current's got plenty of push, but the bass have gone nocturnal on us the same way they have from the Jersey shore up through the Sound.

I've fished this ditch thirty years and I can tell you the current itself hasn't changed a bit. East end still turns on hard around the top of the ebb, that rip line stacking up off the Route 6 bridge piling and running out toward the tower, same as it's done every July of my life. West end's still setting up its current seam off the Mashnee flats on the flood, pushing bait into that eddy on the inside of the bend. The mechanics are all there. What's changed is the water's warmed up enough — surface temps pushing into the low 70s the way they have coastwide — that the stripers don't want to commit to those seams under a bright July sun. They're doing what bass do everywhere right now: sliding down, going quiet in the heat, and turning it back on when the light drops out.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bite would stay tide-dependent with the best windows on max ebb and max flood as bait gets funneled through — and that's exactly what's playing out, just compressed into a smaller clock than usual. The difference this week is timing. It's not enough anymore to just hit max current during daylight. You need max current AND low light, and right now in late July those two things only overlap for about ninety minutes at each end of the day, plus the night tides in between.

Night fishing has been the better program, honestly. I had a report from a guy working the Sagamore side around midnight Sunday who did well on eels — bridled, drifted through the seam under the Sagamore Bridge on the last two hours of the ebb, three fish in the mid-30s, one that pushed 20 pounds released after a quick photo. That's the kind of quality that's still in this system. It hasn't left. It's just gone underground, or under-dark, however you want to put it.

Scusset Beach side has been decent for the bluefish crowd, and that's tracking with what's happening everywhere else on this coast right now — bunker have been getting pushed into the east end approach by the same bait movement that's got blues blitzing from the Cape Cod Bay side down through Buzzards. Guys throwing Deadly Dicks and Hopkins spoons off the rocks at Scusset during the last hour of the flood have been into blues steady, 3 to 6 pounds, occasional bigger fish mixed in. That bite's been more reliable during daylight than the bass have, which tells you something about how sun-shy the stripers have gotten.

Fluke have been a west end story, mostly around Mashnee Island and down toward Phinneys Harbor, working the deeper cuts on the tail of the ebb when the water's clean and moving but not screaming. Nothing huge — most fish 16 to 19 inches, a few keepers mixed in on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom where the current softens against the channel edge. It's a pick, not a program, but it's there if you want a change of pace between bass tides.

No albies or bonito through the Canal yet, and I don't expect them to show here first — this isn't their water, not really, though Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard corridor are exactly the kind of leading-edge zones where I'd expect the season's first scout fish to show given how the water's trending. If that happens down there in the next few days, don't be surprised if a stray albie shows up chasing bait through the east end on a hot flood tide later in the season. It's happened before. Not this week though.

Moon's swinging toward the new moon early next week, which means the currents are going to build back up after sitting on this softer neap stretch — I called that softening last week and it's held, current speeds down maybe 10-15% off a full spring tide. When the new moon current kicks back in, that funnel effect through both ends gets stronger, which should concentrate bait harder and give the bass a more defined reason to commit even during marginal light. If I had one window to fish this weekend, I'd take the pre-dawn max ebb Saturday at the east end — should be running around 5:10 AM — and I'd have an eel rigged and ready before the current even reaches full strength. Get there early, because once that rip lays down, the window's closed and you're just watching water go by.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Off Holgate Turned the Beachfront Into a Feeding Line
reports.subhead: The blitz we said was coming from Belmar finally showed up at the jetties, but stripers went nocturnal while bluefish took over the daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran the drone over the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning and the water told me everything before I even rigged a rod. Big dark ovals — bunker, thousands of them — pushed tight against the beach from the old Coast Guard station down toward the tip, and under them, that nervous, flashing chop that means blues are already in the school. By the time I got down there with a rod, the birds had found it too. Terns diving, a few gulls working the edges, and every third or fourth minute the whole pod would explode white for a second and go quiet again.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker pods pushing south from the Belmar blitz zone would funnel past Barnegat and Beach Haven on the tide changes, and that's exactly what's playing out. The bait's been thick enough that you don't need to guess where the fish are, you just need to get there before the pod moves. That's been the trick all week — this isn't a park-and-wait bite, it's a drive-the-beach-and-watch bite.

The blues have been the most honest fish out there right now. Cocktails to mid-teens crashing bunker from Barnegat Light down through Ship Bottom, and when a pod pins up against the jetty rocks at the inlet on the last of the incoming, it gets stupid for ten or fifteen minutes. Bucktails with a strip of bunker belly draped off the hook have worked, but honestly a naked white Ava 27 ripped through the school on a fast retrieve is just as deadly and you don't lose a lure to a cutoff every other cast. Guys throwing poppers into the boils off the north end of Holgate have had some of the most violent surface strikes I've seen all summer — topwater explosions that'll put a hitch in your heart rate.

Stripers are a different animal right now, and this is where I have to be straight with you — the daytime bass bite has gone quiet. Water's pushing into the mid-70s along the beachfront and that's shoved the bass off the surface layer entirely. They're down deep during daylight, probably holding on the thermocline break off the outer bars, and they've gone almost fully nocturnal. If you want stripers this week, you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark — no way around it. I worked the trough off Brant Beach at first light Wednesday with a black/purple Danny plug, slow swim through the inside slough, and picked up two schoolies in the 24-26 inch range before the sun got high enough to shut it down. Nothing to write home about, but it confirms they're still there, just working a tighter window.

Little Egg Inlet and the cut at Holgate are worth your time on the night tide — that structure holds current even when the moon's not doing much for you, and bass will slide up onto the edge of the bar to ambush bait moving through on the ebb. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5 ounce range, white or chartreuse, bounced along the bottom of the cut on the outgoing has been the most consistent producer after dark. Don't overwork it — let the current do the work and just keep contact.

Fluke has cooled off exactly like it does every year once the shallow water heats up like this. The inshore humps in Barnegat Bay that were holding fish in June have gone quiet during the day, but the channel edges near the causeway bridge and the deeper humps off Ship Bottom are still giving up keepers on the stronger stages of the tide — moving water is doing all the work for you right now. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel drop where it meets the flat, has been the pattern. Morning incoming has outproduced the afternoon for us — cooler water, more willing fish. Shorts are everywhere if you want numbers, but you've got to work the deeper edges for anything over 18 inches.

Weakfish have been a rumor more than a pattern up here — nothing consistent to report on the LBI side, though I'd keep an ear out if that Delaware Bay resurgence starts pushing fish up the coast. Kingfish have shown in small numbers on bloodworm rigs off the surf at Beach Haven on the calmer mornings, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus if you're already out there for blues.

Tide-wise, work the last two hours of the incoming at the inlets for the bluefish blitz — that's when bait gets pushed tight against structure and the blues pin them. For bass, you want the first hour of the outgoing after dark at Little Egg and Holgate, when moving water pulls bait off the flats into the cut. Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, which is keeping the surf manageable, but it's building a little haze and warming the shallows even more — expect the bass pattern to stay nocturnal as long as this holds.

Looking ahead, if the bunker keep working north past Holgate like they have been, this blitz should stay hot through the weekend — I'd bet on it holding at least another 72 hours unless a wind shift scatters the bait. Best case, the pods stack up right on the Beach Haven side and give the pier and jetty guys a shot without even needing a boat. Worst case, a stiff onshore blow pushes everything out past the bar and we're back to searching. Either way, I'd rather be on the beach at first light with a topwater in hand than sitting home wondering.

reports.headline: Sea Bright at 5 AM: bluefish choppin' bunker while the bass hide till dark
reports.subhead: The rocks are loud with blues and gulls, but the real striper bite is happening after everyone else goes home.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to five, Sea Bright rocks, and there's already a guy out on the third jetty north of the Rumson bridge who beat me there. Again. Older fella, doesn't talk much, throws a white bucktail like it owes him money. We nodded at each other the way you do when you both know the other guy isn't going anywhere. Then the water in front of us just erupted — bunker skying, blues underneath them cutting the school to ribbons, birds dropping out of a still-dark sky like they'd been shot. That's been the show all week from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach. Loud, violent, and honestly kind of a relief after how quiet the striper bite's gotten.

We called this one — said last week the bluefish blitz would keep spreading north toward Sandy Hook as long as the bunker stayed pinned along the beach, and that's exactly the picture right now. Every jetty from the Hook down to Monmouth Beach has had at least one morning this week where the water just went white. Poppers are almost unfair right now — a black-and-white Yo-Zuri Hydro Popper or anything that throws spray gets bit on the first cast if you land it inside the bait ball. Metal works too if you want distance — Ava 27s or a 3-ounce Kastmaster, worked fast enough to stay above the blues' teeth. These aren't cocktail blues either. Plenty of 8- to 12-pound choppers mixed in, the kind that'll cut you off if you're running straight mono leader. Sixty-pound fluoro, minimum, or you're re-tying every third fish.

Here's the part that's been humbling: the bass have essentially disappeared during daylight. Water's sitting warm — mid-70s off the beach, and even the deeper holes around the Sea Bright groins aren't holding much heat relief. That pushes stripers onto the thermocline and into nocturnal mode, which is exactly what we flagged happening zone-wide. I fished the Manasquan Inlet rocks three mornings this week at first light and managed one bass — a 26-incher on a 5-inch white Slug-Go, weightless, worked slow along the north jetty face on the last of the outgoing. That fish came at 5:20, right at the edge of usable light. After that, nothing but blues.

The real bass program right now is a night program, and if you're not willing to fish dark water you're going to be frustrated. Shark River Inlet after 10 PM has been the most consistent thing I've heard about or seen myself — the jetty rocks on the north side, working a black Bomber Long A or a bone-colored Gibbs Danny plug on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high. Slot fish, mostly, 26 to 32 inches, holding tight to the rocks where the current breaks. Nothing epic — two or three fish a tide if you put the time in — but it's real, and it's about the only place bass are eating with any consistency close to shore. Belmar's fishing similarly after dark, same tide window, same idea: current break, dark plug, patience.

Fluke's been the background hum it always is in late July — steady, unspectacular, and exactly what we expected with all this bait keeping things close to the beach. Shark River Inlet channel, drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp in white or chartreuse, 3/4-ounce jigheads working 15 to 20 feet on the deeper edges near the Route 35 bridge, has produced keeper counts in the 2-to-1 short ratio — meaning you're culling through a lot of dinks to find a 19- or 20-incher, but they're there. Same story off Manasquan Inlet's outer edges on the bigger tide swings — fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some push, because dead slack water in this heat just shuts everything down.

Porgies have been a nice consolation prize for anyone who wants meat in the cooler without babysitting a plug rod all night. The rock piles off Belmar and the pier areas around Spring Lake are loaded with them — squid strips or bloodworms on a high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide.

Blackfish are still weeks off — that's an autumn program, not a July one, so don't waste tide time on the wrecks yet.

Looking ahead: I don't see any reason for the bluefish blitz to slow down unless we get a wind shift that scatters the bunker, and there's nothing in the pattern suggesting that happens in the next few days. If you want blitz action, mornings on the Sea Bright-to-Monmouth Beach stretch are the play, and I'd get there before first light because once the sun's up and the joggers show up on the seawall, the bite tends to slide north out of casting range. For bass, I'd commit to a night tide at Shark River or Manasquan — pick the incoming into high, fish it dark, and don't expect volume. Expect quality, and expect to earn it. If the offshore water stays this warm through the week — and there's nothing forecast to cool it down — this nocturnal pattern holds. Plan your trips around dark water, not daylight, and you'll do alright.

reports.headline: Conimicut ledge holds after dark, bluefish tear up Greenwich Bay bunker
reports.subhead: Bass have gone nocturnal on the bay's warm water, but the blues won't let you feel bad about it.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Dominic down at the Sabin Point launch Tuesday morning, hauling his kayak up the ramp looking like he hadn't slept — because he hadn't. Told me he anchored up off Nyatt Point at eleven the night before and didn't touch bottom with the plug until almost 1 a.m. when the bass finally showed. That's where we're at now on the bay. It's July, the water's sitting in the mid-70s off Conimicut and Rocky Point, and the stripers have punched out on the daytime program almost entirely. If you want them, you're fishing the dark.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold with no big thermal shift coming, and that's exactly what happened. The bay didn't cool, didn't get a flush of fresh water, nothing changed the equation. Bass are stacked deep off the drop at Conimicut Point, sitting on that hard bottom in 25 to 35 feet, and they're not coming up to feed until the sun's been down an hour or two. Guys working the outgoing tide after 10 p.m. with eels — live or the SP Minnow in black — are getting into fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch class right off the light. Same story working the west side of Prudence, along that deep edge that runs off Sandy Point down toward the south end. Slow-trolled bunker chunks on a three-way rig, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the ebb, has been the more consistent producer than anything thrown on the surface.

Daytime, if you insist on fishing sunlight, your better play is bouncing bucktails — half-ounce to an ounce, white or chartreuse — along the rocky ledges off Rocky Point and out toward the Hope Island reef structure. You'll pick at fish, not load the boat, but there's enough there to keep it honest, especially right on the tide change when the current goes slack for twenty minutes and everything that's been holding tight to structure fans out to feed.

Bluefish are the story you can actually fish in daylight right now, and they're making up for the bass going quiet. Greenwich Bay has had bunker pushed up tight against the shoreline all week, and the blues have been running through them hard off Warwick Neck and along the flats inside Rocky Point. If you see the bunker nervous on the surface — and this week you will, they've been balled up thick off the Cove and out toward Chepiwanoxet — throw a Hopkins or a Deadly Dick, silver, and you don't need to work it much. Blues in the 3 to 6 pound range, some better, and they'll cut a light leader clean if you're not running at least 30-pound fluorocarbon up top. This bluefish push is part of the same bunker migration that's been running the whole coast, and there's no sign it's slowing down here — the schools keep refreshing every few days.

Fluke have moved into their typical mid-summer pattern, meaning the shallow flats are stuffed with shorts and the keepers have slid into deeper, cooler water. Best fish this week have come from the channel edge off Nayatt Point and down around the mouth of the Providence River near the Fields Point range markers, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Twenty-eight to 35 feet is where the better grade has been sitting. Greenwich Bay itself is loaded with shorts right now — fun for kids and a fast rod, but you're throwing most of them back.

Scup fishing stays the reliable summer program it always is. The reefs off Prudence Island and the rock piles around Ohio Ledge are stacked, and if you want a box of fish for the table there's no easier program in the bay — squid strips or clam on a hi-lo rig, bounced bottom in 15 to 25 feet, any tide stage. Black sea bass mixed in on the same structure, though you're culling a lot of shorts to find keepers this deep into the season.

No sign of the herring run mattering anymore this time of year — that's a spring story, Buckeye Brook emptied out back in May and the bass that rode that bait into the upper bay have long since scattered onto their summer program. But it's worth remembering because it tells you something about how these fish move: they follow the food, and right now the food that matters is bunker in the mid-bay and whatever bottom bait's holding on the ledges.

Looking ahead, I don't see anything changing this pattern through the weekend. Wind's been light, no fronts pushing through, water's stable and warm. If I had one night to fish, I'd be back at Conimicut on the last two hours of the outgoing, eeling the drop after dark. If I had one afternoon, I'd run Greenwich Bay looking for bunker getting nervous on top — that bite can turn on in five minutes and be over in twenty, so keep the reel ready and don't wander far from the bay-side shoreline where the schools have been holding tightest.

reports.headline: 80 feet on the Klondike lumps: bluefin in the slot, sea bass to 4 pounds on Wreck 3402
reports.subhead: Steady high pressure is holding the tuna pattern together while the bottom bite grinds on like it always does in late July.
reports.body_markdown:
Eighty feet. That's the number that's been in my book all week, written next to a set of coordinates on the western edge of the Klondike where the lumps rise up out of the mud and hold bait like a bowl holds water. Bluefin have been sitting right on top of that structure, marking thick from 50 down to 65 feet, and if you can get a spreader bar or a green machine daisy chain through that layer without a bluefish shredding it first, you're in business. Slot fish, mostly — 28 to 45 inch class — which is exactly what the recreational fishery wants right now with the trophy closure still in effect from July 3rd. Nobody's complaining about that. A 40-inch bluefin on 50-pound gear is still a workout on a July afternoon with the sun beating down and no wind to speak of.

That no-wind part matters. We called this one — said the flat-weather window would hold 48 to 72 hours out, and here we are, still sitting on glass most mornings out of Manasquan. That kind of stability doesn't happen twice in a July. It's building a real temperature break out past the Mud Hole and into the canyon approaches, warm surface water pushing into the high 70s, and that's dragging the bluefin bite further inshore than you'd expect for this time of year. Normally I'm sending guys 40-plus miles to find this action. This week some of it's showing up 25 miles off Manasquan Inlet, right on the Klondike structure, which is a gift if you don't want to burn the extra fuel and time to reach Hudson or Wilmington.

Yellowfin are still out at the canyons doing what they do when the water sets up right — Hudson, Wilmington, Washington, all producing on the troll with a mix of Ilanders and horse ballyhoo, and chunking butterflied bunker on the drift once you find the temp break. That's a longer run than most of my regulars want to make midweek, but if you've got the range and the fuel budget, it's the most consistent program on the entire coast right now. Mahi are riding shotgun on that trip too — any floating junk, any weed line drifting along the shelf, worth a few casts with a small popper or a chunk bait under a balloon. Nothing giant, mostly schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range, but they eat and they're fun on light spinning gear while you wait on a tuna bite to develop.

Back inshore, where most of my trips actually happen, the bottom fishing has been the one thing I can set my watch to. Wreck 3402 — that's one of the numbers I don't hand out easy, sitting in about 80 feet off the Barnegat Ridge complex — has been holding jumbo sea bass all month. Fish to 4 pounds coming up on Gulp Grubs in white and chartreuse, tipped with a squid strip, fished on a high-low rig with 6-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom in the current. The morning bite has been best on the last two hours of the incoming tide, before the sun gets too high and pushes the biggest fish deeper into the wreckage. Sea Girt Reef and Axel Carlson are producing too, though the average size runs smaller — good eating fish in the 14 to 16 inch range, plenty of them, but you have to sort through some shorts to find the keepers.

Shrewsbury Rocks has been quieter than I'd like this week. The porgy and sea bass are there, but the current's been running funny with these long stretches of settled weather — slack tides that don't move much water, which makes for a lazier bite. I fished it Tuesday and worked hard for a limit of sea bass, nothing like the Barnegat Ridge wrecks where the fish are stacked and hungry. If you're choosing between the two right now, I'd lean Ridge every time.

Triple Wrecks has been a mixed bag — some tog showing early, which is unusual for late July, probably fish that never left the structure through the warm months because there's enough current and bait to keep them comfortable. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up there working sea bass. Green crab on a jig head, dropped right into the wreckage, has picked at a few 3 and 4 pound tog between sea bass bites.

No bonito or false albacore reports out of our waters yet, though the water's warming in that direction and the southern New England boys are watching for the first scout schools any day now. When those show, they tend to work their way down the coast toward Shrewsbury Rocks and the reef line eventually, so it's on my radar for August.

Looking ahead, I'd bank on this high-pressure window holding through the weekend — the pattern's been stable enough that I'm not seeing anything in the setup that suggests a hard wind shift is imminent. That means the Klondike bluefin bite should keep producing on the lumps, and the sea bass on Wreck 3402 and the Barnegat Ridge wrecks should stay steady as long as the tides keep moving water through the structure. If I had one trip this week, I'd run the Ridge early on the incoming for sea bass, then swing out toward the Klondike lumps midday to see if the bluefin are still holding at 80 feet. That's the play — inshore insurance with an offshore shot on the same tank of gas.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Round the Hook: Blues Are Behind Them, Bass Went Nocturnal
reports.subhead: The bait finally made the turn at Sandy Hook, and now it's a question of fishing the blitz by day or the bass by dark.
reports.body_markdown:
I told my father Wednesday morning I was skipping the Flats and running straight to the Hook, and he looked at me like I'd lost it — July, flat calm, everybody parked on Keyport chasing porgies. But I'd been watching the bunker push north out of the Belmar stretch for a week now, and I said it right here last week: once those pods round the Hook, the blues and bass follow. That's exactly what's happening, and it's the only call to make right now if you want to be in the middle of visible, violent fishing instead of soaking bait and hoping.

I ran out past Romer Shoal Tuesday morning on the last of the incoming and found bunker balled up tight off the Hook's ocean side, maybe a quarter mile off the beach, gulls already stacking overhead before I even cut the motor. Blues came up under them in waves — five, ten pound class fish, some bigger — just demolishing pods on the surface. Didn't need anything fancy. Diamond jigs, the 2-3 ounce silver ones, cast right into the froth and let it flutter down eight, ten feet before you start the retrieve. Poppers worked too when the surface stuff calmed for a second and they were still under there sipping scraps. This is the most reliable visible bite in the bay right now and I expect it to keep building through the weekend as more bait rounds the point. If you're set up to run and gun along the Hook's ocean beach or drift the edge of Romer Shoal on a dropping tide, you're going to find them.

Stripers are a different story right now, and I want to be straight about it — daytime bass fishing in the bay has gone quiet. Water's pushing into the mid-70s on the flats and even out around Flynn's Knoll, and the fish know it. They're sliding down onto structure and holding through the heat of the day, not interested in much until the light drops. I fished the Knoll at first light Saturday on bunker chunks, soaked two rods on fish-finder rigs in eighteen feet of water on the last of the outgoing, and had one decent take — a 28-incher that came unbuttoned at the boat, which is about the story of my week. If you want bass right now, you fish the night tide or you fish the last hour of light into full dark. The Highlands bridge pilings and the mouth of the Shrewsbury have both been giving up fish after 9 PM on live bunker drifted on the current, weighted just enough to hold bottom without dragging.

Fluke have been the honest, unglamorous producer all month and that hasn't changed. The channel edges off Keyport Flats and the deeper water running along the Verrazano-adjacent structure toward the bay mouth are still holding keeper-class fish, though you have to work for them now that the shallow water's warmed through. I've been dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, right along the drop where the flats fall into the channel — 20 to 28 feet, working the drift on the tail end of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Shorts are everywhere in the shallower water, which tells you the fish are there, just not the right size until you find that depth change. Patience and boat position matter more than lure choice right now.

Porgies are still stacked up thick around Romer Shoal and the reef structure inside the bay, and if you need a box of fish to show for the trip that's your play — small hooks, squid strips, bottom rigs, anchor up and let them come to you. Blackfish season's closed this stretch so leave the tog gear home, and weakfish have been scarce here even with the better reports building down in Delaware Bay — I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish catch in this zone in weeks, so I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

Tide-wise, we're working through a slack lunar period, current's not doing anything dramatic, which actually favors the blitz conditions — calmer water keeps the bunker balled tighter instead of scattering them, and that's part of why the blues have been able to camp on them instead of chasing broken pods all over the bay. Wind's been cooperative too, nothing pushing hard enough out of one direction to break up the bait concentrations along the beach.

Looking ahead, I expect the bunker-blue show at the Hook to keep intensifying through the weekend as more bait funnels north — this is going to be the story of the next several days in this zone, and I'd rather be out there with diamond jigs than sitting on the flats waiting for something that isn't happening in daylight. For bass, I'd shift my whole game to last light and full dark this week: fish the bridge structure in the Highlands, fish the Shrewsbury mouth, and don't bother running out at 6 AM expecting daytime bass unless you're willing to go deep and slow on the Knoll and accept a long wait for a short bite window. Fluke guys, keep working those channel edges on the moving water — it's not exciting fishing but it's honest, and honest still fills a cooler if you put in the drift time.

reports.headline: Bunker schools pack the beachfront — bluefish keep the rods bent while fluke go quiet in the heat
reports.subhead: Blues are the story from Island Beach to the Barnegat Light rocks while summer fluke settle into their usual sulk on the channel edges.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a July back in the early '90s when my old mate Sal Petrone and I ran the skiff out past the Coast Guard station at Barnegat Light and hit a bunker school so thick you could've walked across it. Blues came up under it like the bay itself was boiling, and we filled the cooler in twenty minutes without ever putting a line more than three feet down. I think about that morning every time this pattern sets up again — and it's set up again right now, same as it has for weeks. We said it last week and it's still true: the bluefish are the headline on this bay, and they're not giving up the spot.

Water's sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s in the shallows, low 70s out toward the inlet mouth where the ocean water mixes in on the tide. That kind of warm has pushed the bunker schools up tight against the beachfront — Island Beach State Park, the surf line off Barnegat Light, and inside the bay wherever there's current pulling bait past a point. The blues have been on them relentlessly. I had a report from a guy running out of the Oyster Creek launch who hit a blitz right off the north end of the park Tuesday morning — blues to six, seven pounds crashing peanut bunker so hard the water looked like it was under a hailstorm. Chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig will get bit, but if you want the real fun, throw poppers or Hopkins spoons right into the melee. No finesse needed. They're not fussy when they're feeding like that.

Inside the bay, the bluefish have been working the mouth of Double Creek Channel and up around Tices Shoal on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing — that current line where the channel water meets the flat holds bait, and the blues stack up on the edge waiting for it to get pushed to them. Bunker chunks or a white bucktail with a strip of belly meat has been the ticket there. Bring a wire leader or expect to lose gear — these fish are toothy and they don't care that it's July.

Fluke are a different conversation, and I'll be honest with you — it's been a grind. Same story every summer once the shallow water heats up like this: shorts everywhere, keepers scarce unless you go looking for them in the right spots. I've been working the deeper edges of Double Creek Channel, 12 to 15 feet, and around the humps off the Oyster Creek mouth where there's still some cooler water moving through on a strong tide. Best window has been the two hours around the top of the high, when the current's still got some push but hasn't gone full ripping yet. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along bottom, have out-produced bait rigs for me this week — the softer plastic seems to draw more strikes when the fish are a little lazy in the warm water. Keepers have been coming, but you're earning them, not stumbling into them. I'd guess for every legal fluke we're throwing back four or five shorts.

Striped bass have gone quiet in daylight, which tracks with what's happening up and down the whole coast right now — warm surface water's pushed them down and nocturnal. If you want bass on this bay in July, you fish the dark. I've had better luck working the deeper holes off Barnegat Light on the outgoing tide starting an hour before sunset, live eels or bunker chunks fished on bottom. Nothing fast, but there's still fish there if you're patient and willing to be out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m.

Weakfish have been sparse on our end of things — not the story it apparently is down in Delaware Bay right now. I haven't heard of anything worth chasing at the sedges this week, which is unusual for late July, but the water's been so warm that I suspect what weakfish we do have have pushed into deeper, cooler pockets and gone quiet like everything else that isn't a bluefish.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around for the bait guys — sandworms and squid strips fished on high-low rigs off the bay bottom near Forked River and up toward Toms River have been steady for blowfish, nothing spectacular but consistent enough to keep the kids in the boat entertained.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to break. The wind's been stable, the bunker schools show no sign of thinning out, and warm water isn't going anywhere with this weather holding. I'd expect the blue­fish blitz to keep working its way along the beachfront and into the bay mouths through the weekend — that's still the most reliable card on the table. If you want fluke, go early, go deep, and be patient on the channel edges. If you want bass, set your alarm for late and fish the dark water off the inlet structure. And if the bunker schools ever thin out or a stiff northeast blow scatters them, that bluefish window will close fast — so if you've got a morning free this week, I wouldn't wait on it.

reports.headline: Where'd the fluke go? Off the beach and into the channel edges
reports.subhead: A lesson in why keeper fluke disappear from the sod banks in late July — and where they're hiding instead.
reports.body_markdown:
Got the same question three times this week, from three different anglers at three different docks, so let's turn it into a lesson. "Darnell, I fished the sod banks in Absecon same as always and all I caught was shorts. What happened to the fluke?"



Here's what happened. It's July 24th, the back bays have been baking under stable southwest wind and high sun for going on two weeks, and shallow water that read comfortable in June is now running warm enough that a keeper fluke — the mature, 19-inch-and-up female — has options, and she's taking them. She's moved off the skinny sod bank flats where you found her on the last new moon and settled into the deeper channel edges and inlet structure where the water stays cooler and the current runs harder. This is textbook mid-summer behavior. I've watched it happen every July for thirty years and it never fails to catch somebody off guard.

So class, where do you go? Three spots I'd put students on this week. First, the Absecon Inlet channel itself, working the deeper cuts along the Rum Point side on the last two hours of the outgoing. Drop a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet — chartreuse or pink shad — down into 18 to 24 feet and drag it slow along bottom, right where the channel bends. That current edge concentrates bait, and bait concentrates fluke big enough to matter. Second, the Great Egg Harbor channel off Longport, same tide stage, same depth range — the outgoing there really rips past the marina and any fluke holding on that edge is doing it because the water's moving fast enough to stay oxygenated and cool. Third, and this one gets overlooked, the Ocean City back bay channel behind the 9th Street bridge — deeper hole there runs 15 to 20 feet and it's held quality fish for me in past Julys when the flats went quiet.

Tide stage matters more than usual right now. Dead low and dead high, forget it — that's when the shallow water sits stagnant and warm and even the shorts get lazy. You want the two hours surrounding max current, either direction, when water's actually exchanging. That's when the thermal layering breaks down enough to pull a keeper up off the bottom to feed.

Now the other half of the report, and this one doesn't need a lesson plan because it's happening right in front of everybody's face. The bluefish blitz along the beachfront has done exactly what I told you it would do last week — bunker are still pinned tight to the beach by that same southwest wind, and blues have been running them from Stone Harbor and Avalon straight up through Ocean City and into Brigantine. We flagged this pattern holding as long as the wind stayed southwest and the bait stayed pinned, and that's exactly what's played out. If you're on the beach at first light with a white or chrome Kastmaster, an Ava jig, or a bucktail, and you see gulls working tight over nervous water, you don't need to think twice — cast into the edge of the school, not the middle, and hang on. Fish are running 3 to 6 pounds, some better, and they'll hit topwater poppers just as readily if you want the visual. Best windows have been dawn and again the last hour of daylight, when the sun's off the water and the blues push the bunker up shallow.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal on us, which is normal for this stretch of the calendar with surface water running into the mid-70s. If you want a bass right now, you're fishing Absecon Inlet or Townsends Inlet after dark, working the deeper structure and current seams with bunker chunks or a swimming plug worked slow along the jetty rocks. Daytime bass fishing in the back bays is mostly dead right now — I wouldn't waste a summer morning on it when the fluke and blues are both giving better odds.

One more thing worth watching closely, and it's not fully my beat but it touches the southern end of it — weakfish are showing real signs of life up in the Delaware Bay back-bay channels. That's a pattern building on warm bay water and tide-change concentration, not a one-day fluke of activity, and if it holds and pushes toward Great Egg the way these things sometimes do, I'll have more to say about it next week.

Looking ahead, if the southwest wind holds through the weekend like it's been doing, expect the bluefish blitz to keep building and possibly push further north toward Atlantic City's beachfront by Sunday. For fluke, I'd keep working those channel edges on the moving tide rather than wasting daylight on the flats — that's where the keepers are living until we get a real cool-down or a wind shift stirs the shallow water back up. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be on the Absecon Inlet channel at first light, bucktail in hand, working the last of the outgoing before the blues show up and remind me there's easier meat to be had thirty yards away.

reports.headline: Rips grinding, drum gone quiet, but Delaware Bay weakfish are the real story
reports.subhead: The ocean side is a slog right now — the back bay is where I'd spend my week.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the Rips this week: C-minus. Fishable, not fun. If you want the honest read before you burn gas and bait money, that's it right there. The bass have gone deep and nocturnal on us, which is exactly what late July does — surface water's pushing into the mid-70s off the Point and out past the Rips, and stripers don't want any part of that. We're marking fish on the meter down around the thermocline break, 40 to 55 feet depending where you sit on the tide, but getting them to eat during daylight has been a fight. I had one charter Tuesday morning working the outgoing at the Rips, bucktails and Ava jigs bounced right on bottom, and we scratched out two schoolies and lost what felt like a better fish that just came unbuttoned in the current. That's the story right now — a bite, not a blitz.

If you want a shot at something better than a schoolie, you're fishing the front of the incoming tide at first light or working into dark, live-lining bunker or eels off the drop at the Rips and along the Cape May Point bar. That's when the bigger fish will come up off the structure to feed before the sun gets high and pushes them back down. Don't waste your good bait on the middle of a bright afternoon tide — I don't care how many boats are stacked up out there, most of them are marking fish they can't buy a bite from.

Bluefish have been the more dependable ocean-side player. We flagged this pattern building and it's still running — bunker schools are getting pushed tight to the beach and the blues are all over them, working from the barrier islands right up into the Wildwood surf and out past Hereford Inlet. If you're fluke fishing the Inlet and marking bait balls getting hammered on the surface, switch over — a wire leader and a Hopkins spoon or a bucktail with a rind will get bit fast. That bite should hold as long as the bunker stay pinned against the beach, and with this warm, stable stretch of weather I don't see them scattering yet.

Speaking of fluke — Hereford Inlet and the reef sites off Cape May have been steady, not spectacular. You've got to sort through a pile of shorts to find keepers, and the better fish are sitting deeper on the channel edges and humps where the water stays a touch cooler. Five-inch Gulp in white or pink shad on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the ebb, has been the ticket. The bite windows are tight around the tide change — you get maybe 45 minutes of good current speed before it either dies or rips too hard to hold bottom cleanly.

Now for the real news, and it's not on the ocean side. Delaware Bay's weakfish are doing something I haven't seen in a few years — and we called this two weeks ago when the bay water first pushed into the mid-70s. It's holding, and it's building into a legitimate pattern, not a one-day pop. Back-bay channels around Fortescue and up toward the mouth of the Maurice River are holding weakfish mixed in with croaker and summer flounder right on the drop-offs and channel edges. Best action is coming on the tide change — that dead slack window when the water stacks up and bait gets funneled along the edge. Bloodworms or FishBites on a simple high-low rig, fished right on bottom in 12 to 18 feet, is putting weakies in the boat. Some of these fish are pushing 4 pounds, which for Delaware Bay these days is a real fish.

The black drum run, on the other hand, has gone quiet on us. That's the honest truth — May and early June were the show for drum this year, and by late July the bulk of that spawning push has cleared out of the traditional spots off Brandywine Shoal and the deeper holes toward the mouth of the bay. If you're still targeting drum specifically, you're fishing for stragglers, and I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now. Save that program for next spring.

Looking at the week ahead — if this warm, settled weather pattern holds like it's been holding, I expect the weakfish bite in the bay channels to keep climbing. That's where I'd put my time if I only had one day. On the ocean side, I'd fish the Rips at first light on the incoming, live bait if you can get it, and treat anything after 9 a.m. as bonus fishing rather than the main event. And keep an eye on those bunker schools along the beach — wherever they're sitting tight, the blues won't be far behind, and that's about as sure a thing as we've got right now.

reports.headline: Porgies pay the bills while the bass go nocturnal on us
reports.subhead: Daytime stripers have gone quiet with the heat, but scup on the reefs and a slowing Gut current are keeping the North Fork honest.
reports.body_markdown:
Old Ray Tuthill used to say a hot July sun does two things to a striper — makes him smart and makes him lazy. Ray's been dead eleven years now but I thought about him three mornings running this week, standing on the rocks off Horton Point at six a.m. with nothing showing but a few hopeful terns and water so flat and warm-looking you could've poured it over ice cream. No fish. Not a swirl. By eight the sun's up over Shelter Island way and it's plain why — that water's pushing into the 70s right off the beach, and a bass with any sense at all has gone down deep or gone home to sleep it off till dark.

That's the story this week, plain and simple. Kings Point over west is reading near 71, and even out here where New London's holding closer to 69, the shallow structure along our stretch — the boulder fields off Rocky Point, the rip lines coming off Orient — warms up fast enough by midday that the bass want no part of it in daylight hours. I've fished this shoreline sixty years and I've seen this pattern more summers than not. When it sets in, you stop being a daytime fisherman and you start being a flashlight-and-thermos fisherman, or you go find something else that bites.

Something else that bites, out here, is porgy. And thank God for porgy, because without scup this would've been a real quiet column. The rockpiles off Mattituck Inlet and the rougher bottom running toward Rocky Point have been steady — not spectacular, steady, which in my book is worth more. Anchor up on the drop where the mussel bed gives way to broken rock, drop a hi-lo rig with squid strips or sandworm on size 6 or 8 hooks, and you'll keep a rod bent most of the tide. Biggest ones — some pushing a pound and a half, nice fat scup — are coming off the deeper edge on the last of the outgoing, before the current goes fully slack. Bring enough bait. They'll pick you clean if you're stingy with the hooks.

Now the bass — and I don't want to paint too rosy a picture, because daytime effort for keeper stripers along the Sound side has been tough sledding. But work the dusk into full dark, and there's still fish to be had. I had a report from a fella working the boulder line east of the inlet who took two decent bass, one about 30 inches, working a black Danny plug on the swing right at the edge of the rocks, right as the light went out of the sky. That's the program now — last hour of light through the first couple hours of full dark, current moving, plug or bucktail worked slow and tight to structure. Daytime, you're better off dropping down with bait — clam or bunker chunk fished deep off the drop-offs — if you insist on fishing the sun hours at all.

Bluefish have been mixing into bait pods right along the beach, chopping up whatever's schooled up tight to shore. Nothing like the blitzes they're seeing to the west, from what I hear, but enough that if you're casting metal — a Hopkins or a Kastmaster — off the beach at Rocky Point in the early morning you can find a few and get your arm tired. Good practice while you wait for the bass to cooperate.

Now for the part I actually want to talk about — the Gut. We said last week the neap tide moving in around the 21st would slow the current through Plum Gut and the Race, and that's exactly what's happened. If you fished it this week you felt it — that push isn't near what it was two weeks back. Slower water means you need to adjust, and I mean it: switch down to lighter jigs, quarter to half-ounce bucktails instead of the heavy iron you'd normally need to hold bottom in that current, and slow your retrieve down to match. Guys still muscling through with the same heavy gear they used at full moon tides are working too fast for what the fish want right now. There's still bass and some bluefish working through there, particularly on the last of the ebb toward Orient, but it's a finesse game until that current builds back.

Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't seen or heard much out of our stretch. There's talk of a real weakfish pattern building down in Delaware Bay, which is interesting but does me no good standing on a North Fork jetty. If that resurgence pushes any further up the coast I'll be the first out looking for them in the back guts near the inlet, but for now I'm not counting on it here.

Fluke's been what fluke always is in late July — plenty of shorts in the shallow water, and you've got to work the channel edges and the deeper humps off Mattituck Inlet on a moving tide to find anything worth keeping. White Gulp on a bucktail, dragged slow along bottom where the current cuts a groove — that's still the ticket, just don't expect every drift to produce a keeper.

Looking ahead — that current in the Gut should keep rebuilding through the week as we move off the neap, and when it does I expect the bass and blues stacked up waiting on bait to push through with a little more purpose. If the current builds and the water stays clean, I'd plan an evening around Orient Point toward the end of the week, working bucktails on the drop as the tide starts to run harder again. Daytime, stick with the porgies. They've been honest with me all summer, and honest is worth something.

reports.headline: Penfield's ledge holds bass after dark, blues run the beach in daylight
reports.subhead: Two different games on the same water — nocturnal stripers on the reefs, daytime bluefish mayhem on bunker along the beachfront.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the call I made Tuesday night and I'd make it again: skip the last two hours of daylight at Penfield and wait for the tide to turn under darkness. Everybody wants to fish the pretty evening light. I want the ebb starting around 9:30, 10 PM, when the reef's been cooking in warm water all day and the bass finally decide it's safe to come up off the rockpile. That's the program right now, and it's the only one that's consistently working for keeper-class fish.

Kings Point is reading 70.9 — that's warm enough to shut daytime bass activity down almost completely west of Norwalk. What that means on the water is simple: the fish haven't left, they've gone nocturnal and they've gone deep. Penfield Reef, the deeper pocket on the north side around 18 to 22 feet, is holding stripers that feed hard on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood, dead of night, no moon interference right now with the cycle where it is. I've been anchoring up-current of the reef itself, not on top of it, and drifting live eels back into the structure on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom without snagging rock. Twenty-six to 34 inches has been the range, a couple pushing 20 pounds mixed in on the stronger nights. This isn't a numbers game — two or three fish in three hours is a good night — but they're quality fish and there's basically zero boat traffic to compete with at 11 PM, which by itself makes it worth losing the sleep.

Daytime, the real show is the bluefish, and it's impossible to miss if you're anywhere near the beach from Greenwich Point east through the Norwalk Islands. Bunker schools are pinned tight against the shoreline in the warm surface water and the blues are working them relentlessly — we flagged this exact pattern building last week, said it would keep spreading along the coast as bunker pushed through, and that's exactly what's happened. Now it's a coastwide story and western Sound is right in the middle of it. Poppers and metal — Ava 27s, half-ounce Kastmasters — thrown right into the froth off Greenwich Point and the outer bar at Sheffield Island are getting hit on nearly every cast during an active blitz. These aren't rat blues either, several 4- to 6-pound fish mixed into the schools, enough teeth to justify wire or at minimum a long mono leader if you don't want to keep re-tying. Best window has been mid-morning through early afternoon on the making tide, when the bunker get pushed tight against the beach and the blues pin them against the sand.

Cockenoe Reef is fishing more like a bottom spot than a bass spot right now, and that's fine — porgies out there have been thick on the Cows-adjacent structure and the reef's southern edge, 15 to 25 feet, on green crab and sandworm fished on a simple hi-lo rig during the slower midday tide stages when the bluefish and bass bite goes quiet. If you've got kids or guests aboard who just want bent rods, that's your play — steady action, nothing dramatic, but you're not coming back skunked. Blackfish season's still closed in Connecticut waters through the summer, so those Cockenoe rockpiles are strictly catch-and-release scouting for now, worth noting the spots for when the fall season opens back up.

Fluke have slid into the pattern you'd expect for this time of year — plenty of shorts working the sand between the reefs, but the keeper-class fish have pulled into deeper, cooler water. The channel edge off Sheffield Island in 25 to 30 feet on the tail end of the outgoing has been the more consistent producer, five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the bottom where the current sweeps bait off the flat into the channel. You have to cover ground here — I made four drifts Sunday morning before connecting on a pair over 20 inches, everything else was 16- and 17-inch fish going back.

Boat traffic's been the other variable to manage. Weekend pressure on Penfield and the Norwalk Islands is brutal by 10 AM once the sailing crowd and the day-trip center consoles show up, so if you're targeting the reef bite specifically, either get there at first light before the parking-lot effect starts, or better yet, lean into the after-dark program where you've got the whole structure to yourself.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this to change through the weekend. The warm surface water isn't going anywhere with this weather pattern holding, so bass stay nocturnal, blues stay the daytime headline as long as bunker keep getting pushed tight to the beach, and fluke stay a deeper-water, stronger-tide proposition. If the wind stays out of the south and the bunker schools hold their position off Greenwich and the islands, I'd expect the blitz pattern to keep spreading east toward Bridgeport over the next several days rather than break up. My money this week is on the midnight ebb at Penfield for quality bass, and first-light poppers off Greenwich Point for the sure thing.

reports.headline: Race at 2.1 knots on the neap: bass off Valiant, slack at 13:50
reports.subhead: Current's soft this week but Valiant Rock still gave up wire-line bass on the drop, and the first albie scouts are due any day now.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-point-one knots. That's what I had running through the Race on Tuesday's max ebb, which tells you everything about why the bite's been a grind instead of a slam-dunk. We're deep in the neap cycle right now, moon's past the quarter, and the current through the Race, Plum Gut, and the Sluiceway has gone soft compared to what we run during the new and full moon springs. When the Race isn't ripping four-plus knots, the bait doesn't get pinned against the rock faces the same way, and the bass don't have to commit the way they do when the water's screaming.



Still fished it. Still caught them. Slack at Valiant Rock ran 13:50 Tuesday, and I had the boat set up forty-five minutes ahead of that on the last of the ebb, wire line out with bunker spoons and a 36-ounce parachute jig working the down-current side where the rock breaks the flow. Marked bass sitting 38 to 44 feet down, right on the color line where the cold Race water meets the warmer push coming off Fishers Island Sound. Landed three keepers in the 28-32 inch range and lost a better fish — probably mid-30s — that came off right at the boat after a long fight in that heavy water. Nothing that'll make the wall, but solid, honest fish, and exactly the class you'd expect on a neap tide when the biggest fish are holding deeper and feeding more on the slow build than the max flow.



Plum Gut has been the more interesting story. Water's holding around 69 to 70 degrees on the western approach and there's noticeably more bait stacked in the Gut than there was two weeks ago — pods of sand eels and some early snapper blues mixed in, which is exactly the forage albies want when they show. I haven't had a confirmed false albacore in the Gut yet, but I said last week to watch for early sign filtering into this zone as warm water pushed east along the Sound's outer edge, and that's precisely what's setting up. The thermal gradient from Kings Point in the low 70s down through New London in the high 60s means the warm water is stacking against the eastern Sound structure, and Plum Gut sits right at that seam. If you're itching to be first on albies this season, I'd be working epoxy jigs and small Deadly Dicks off the Gut's western edge on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current compresses the bait against structure and pushes it out toward Orient Point. Nothing landed yet — but the pattern is exactly what precedes the first scout schools in this zone historically, and Montauk and Block Island are reporting the same warming trend from the east.

Little Gull and Great Gull Island have been quieter than I'd like this week. I worked the rip off Great Gull twice with bucktails — white and chartreuse, 2 to 3 ounces depending on the drift speed — and only picked up bluefish, but they were good ones, 4 to 6 pounds, slashing hard on the surface during the last hour of daylight both nights. That fits the coastwide pattern right now — bluefish are the most reliable visible story on the whole East Coast, working bunker schools relentlessly from Jersey up through the Sound, and our fish are part of that same push. If you want non-stop bent rods with less technical current work, that's your play: find the bunker schools showing on the surface off Great Gull or along the Sluiceway edge, and throw metal — Kastmasters or Hopkins — right into the boil.

The Sluiceway itself fished tough. That channel needs current to be worth the trip, and on a 2-knot day it just doesn't set up the same edges and eddies that concentrate bait. I made one pass through there Wednesday morning and didn't mark enough bait to justify staying, so I pulled out and ran back to Valiant. Lesson for anybody planning a trip this week — check the current tables before you commit to the Sluiceway specifically. It's a springs-tide spot. On the neap, your time is better spent at Valiant Rock or the Race itself where the rock structure still concentrates fish even with reduced flow.

Fluke have been a non-factor for me this week, which tracks with what's happening across the Sound generally — warm shallow water has pushed the better fish deeper, and I haven't had the bottom time to specifically target them with everything else going on. If you want fluke, I'd look at the deeper edges around Race Rock itself on a stronger tide stage, working Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to bottom, but it's not been my focus.

Sea bass on the reef structure around Valiant and out toward the Sluiceway approach have been steady and reliable — not exciting, but a good option if the rip isn't cooperating. Squid strips or clam on bottom rigs in 40-50 feet has produced consistent keepers.

Looking ahead: the current rebuilds through the weekend as we move away from the neap and toward the next quarter, and that's when I expect the Race and Plum Gut to wake back up to their full potential. Slack at Valiant next week should run a few minutes later each day — I'll have exact windows once I check the tables again — but the bigger story is the albies. Water's warming on schedule, bait's staging in the Gut, and every signal from Montauk and Block Island east of us says the first confirmed albacore should hit this corridor within the week. I'd keep a rod rigged with small epoxy jigs ready to go on short notice. When they show in the Gut, it happens fast and it happens all at once.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull holding at night, Gold Star pilings paying off at first light
reports.subhead: The Thames has gone nocturnal — daytime bass have shut down, but the tide-change windows are still producing if you know where the current stacks bait.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a spot below Fort Trumbull where the ebb current pinches down against the old ferry landing and creates a seam you can practically see from shore on a calm evening — a slick line running maybe forty feet off the rocks where the moving water meets the eddy behind the point. Twenty years of watching that seam has taught me it's a decent barometer for the whole harbor. Right now, on a summer evening with the tide dropping, that seam is showing bait — small stuff, silversides mostly, getting pushed and balled up — but it's not showing much interest from anything bigger until the light really starts to go. That tells you everything about where we are in the season.

Water's sitting in the high 60s down at New London, 69.4 on the last read I trust, and that's enough to push the stripers into the same pattern we see every July — deep and nocturnal. Daytime fishing in the harbor and up the Thames has gone quiet. I fished the flats off Pleasure Beach midday Tuesday for about two hours and had exactly one follow on a white paddletail, no commitment. That's the story right now during daylight — fish are there, they're just not feeding hard until the sun's off the water.

Where it's actually producing is the classic three windows: dawn, dusk, and full dark, and the tide change matters more than the clock right now. We called this last week — said tide-change windows would keep producing through the stretch of stable weather, and that's exactly what's playing out. The best fish I've heard about and seen myself have come on the last two hours of the outgoing, right as it starts to slack, working the current seams around the Gold Star Bridge pilings. Bass are holding tight to the concrete, sitting in the slower water on the downcurrent side, and they'll eat a bucktail — half-ounce to three-quarter, white or chartreuse — dropped right against the structure and hopped slow along bottom in twenty to twenty-five feet.
