Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, tight to the current seam below the bridge, have also been producing after dark — that's been the more consistent pattern than daylight casting right now. If you're set on daytime fish, work the deepest part of the channel bends slow, with a bucktail or a soft plastic swimbait bounced right along bottom where the current's still moving something.

White perch have pushed up out of the warmest shallow flats and into the deeper holes — Selden Creek, the mouth of Whalebone Creek, the deeper bends up toward Essex. A simple grass shrimp rig or a small piece of bloodworm on a perch spreader, fished slow along bottom in eight to fifteen feet, has been steady, not spectacular. It's a good afternoon fishery when the bass have gone quiet in the heat — not the kind of thing that fills a cooler fast, but reliable if you're patient and willing to move a little to find where they've stacked up.

Bluefish have been showing at the outer edge of the river mouth, out around the Griswold Point bar and the sandbar off the outer breakwater, chasing peanut bunker on the falling tide. It's not a blitz — more a scattered pattern of blues cutting through bait pods for twenty or thirty minutes at a time before moving off — but if you're out there on the last two hours of the ebb with a metal jig or a bunker spoon, you can find them.

We flagged it last week and it's holding up — summer flounder are pushing into the lower river now, right on schedule. I've had reports of keeper-class fluke coming off the sand flats inside the breakwater at Saybrook Point, drifted with three-inch white Gulp swim mullets on quarter-ounce jigheads, fished right on the bottom where that sand gives way to the channel edge. It's not a heavy showing yet, more a scout wave than a full push, but it's exactly the pattern I'd expect as water keeps warming through late July.

We're coming off the first-quarter moon into a neap tide cycle, which means less current overall through the next several days. That's going to soften up some of these current-dependent spots — the bridge pilings and the Point breakwater won't be ripping as hard on peak tide, which actually widens your window to fish them well past the top of the flood or ebb rather than just the hour around max current. I'd use that to my advantage this week — fish longer stretches of the tide instead of racing to catch the peak.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic change through the end of July. The river will stay warm in the coves, the bass will keep holding to the moving water and the low-light windows, and I'd expect that fluke push to build a little more as the week goes on. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at the Point at first light on the last of the incoming, eel in hand, betting on that cooler water doing what it's done for fifty years running — pulling the bass up to feed before the sun gets high enough to send them back down.

reports.headline: Neap Tide, Fat Porgies: New Haven Breakwalls Turn On While Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: Slack current on the first-quarter neap put sea bass and porgies stacked tight to the rock, but the stripers want the dark now.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, half-tide out, I dropped a two-hook rig baited with fresh skimmer clam into eighteen feet of water off the outer New Haven breakwall and felt that unmistakable thump-thump-thump before the rod even loaded up. Came tight to a porgy that pinned the scale past two pounds — the kind of fish that makes the net operator on the party boats do a double take. That's been the story all week on the rockpiles: when the current goes soft, the porgies and sea bass stack up tight to structure and forget to be careful.

We're riding into the first-quarter neap right now, and if you fish this beat the way I do — vertical presentations over broken bottom — this is exactly the water you want. Less current means less scope on your line, which means you're actually fishing the rocks instead of dragging bait across sand trying to find them. I worked the inside corner of the New Haven outer wall on the last two hours of the outgoing and never had to go heavier than a 2-ounce bank sinker. Porgies to two and a half pounds, a mixed bag of sea bass mostly in the 14 to 16 inch range with a couple that pushed past 17, all on clam and green crab fished right on bottom. Falkner Island's south side rockpile did the same thing on the incoming Wednesday morning — same depth range, same story, slightly bigger average sea bass. One of my regular dock buddies iced a sea bass out there that had real shoulders on it, not far off the class fish coming out of the eastern Sound structure lately.

Stratford Shoal is fishing well too, though you have to time it right. That current rips through there on anything but the neap, so this window is a gift — anchor up-current of the high spots on the shoal at low light, drop clam or squid strips, and let it sit. I had a triple-header there Thursday with two anglers aboard, porgies both times, nothing huge but steady enough that we never had an empty hook for more than two minutes.

Now for the bad news, or at least the complicated news: the stripers have gone quiet in the daylight. Water's sitting in the low 70s across the western basin — Kings Point read almost 71 the other day — and that's enough to push keeper bass into a strict low-light and after-dark pattern. Charles Island's sandbar, which has been money on the flood all June, is basically dead by 9 a.m. now. I fished it twice this week at first light with a white bucktail and Storm swim shad, and both mornings the bite was over in about forty-five minutes flat once the sun climbed. Got two schoolies and a fish that just cleared 28 inches on the second morning, working the drop-off on the south side of the bar right as the flood started pushing bait over it. If you want bass off that bar right now, you need to be there before the sun, or come back after dark and fish the same structure with a bunker chunk soaking on the bottom. That's the play until the water cools a notch.

Fluke have been the pleasant surprise. They're doing exactly what you'd expect this time of year — sliding off the softer back-bay mud and setting up on hard structure and channel edges where the current keeps things moving. Milford Gulf has been solid on the last of the outgoing, drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along that channel drop. Nothing giant, mostly fish in the 16 to 19 inch range, but a steady pick, and I heard of a couple pushing 20 inches coming off the harbor mouth structure near the breakwalls on the same tide stage. We flagged a couple weeks back that back-bay fluke would push toward inlet mouths and structure as the water warmed, and that's precisely what's happening now — if you're still working the mud flats expecting summer numbers, you're behind the fish.

Bluefish have been a non-event in my zone so far, which surprises me a little given how loud the bunker-driven blitzes have been to our west. I haven't seen any real bait pods pushing into New Haven Harbor or along Hammonasset yet, though the warm water and the bunker moving up the coast make me think it's a matter of time, not a matter of if. Keep a wire leader and a Hopkins jig in the boat just in case — if a bunker school wanders into the Sound proper, that bite can turn on fast and ugly.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the neap window on the rockpiles through the weekend — Falkner Island and the Stratford Shoal high spots especially, since that current relief won't last once we build back toward the full moon tides. For bass, plan your trip around dawn and dusk, not midday, and don't be afraid to fish Charles Island bar well after dark with a chunk bait if you want a crack at something better than a schoolie. Fluke guys should keep grinding the channel edges at Milford Gulf on the moving water rather than anchoring up hoping fish come to you. It's not an easy week, but it's a honest one — the fish are exactly where the water temperature and the tide say they should be, you just have to fish the right window for each species.

reports.headline: Neap's Coming to Plum Gut — Slow Your Jig Down and Fish the Dark
reports.subhead: Porgy and fluke keep the boat busy by day, but the bass want the Gut after the sun's gone.
reports.body_markdown:
My father used to say a rip has a temper, same as a man, and you learn to fish it by knowing when it's calm and when it's looking for a fight. He fished Plum Gut for forty years with nothing but a compass, a chart he'd drawn himself, and a healthy respect for the fact that the water there doesn't care how long you've been doing this. I think about that every time I idle out past Orient Point and watch the current start to build against the light. This week it's been building slower than usual, and that's telling.

We're sliding into a first-quarter neap, and anybody who's fished the Gut long enough knows what that means — the current through there and through the Race backs off, the standing waves flatten out some, and the fish that were pinned tight to the roughest water start spreading a little wider across the flow. It's not a bad thing. It just means you've got to adjust. I've gone from a three-ounce diamond jig down to a two, sometimes a ounce-and-a-half bucktail with a white pork rind trailer, because the water isn't ripping the way it does on the big tides, and a heavy jig just plows through without working right. Slower presentation, more time in the strike zone. That's the whole trick this week.

Striped bass have been in the Gut on the tide changes, same as always this time of year, but I won't stand here and tell you it's been a daylight bite, because it hasn't. The water's warm enough now — mid-to-upper 60s pushing 70 depending where you check it, warmer out toward the Race than it was a few weeks back — that the better fish have gone nocturnal on us. Dawn and dusk are your windows, and after dark if you've got the stomach for running that water at night, which I'd only recommend to somebody who already knows where the rocks are. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, drifted through the Gut on the last two hours of the ebb, have taken slot fish and a few overslot up toward 38, 40 inches. Bunker chunks have worked too when there's been current to move the scent, fished right on bottom where the rip meets the flat water off the Plum Island side.

During the day, though, it's fluke, porgy, and blackfish keeping the rods bent, and that bite has been honest and steady, which is more than I can say for the bass. Fluke are coming off the drop-offs and channel edges from Horton Point on east — Gulp swimming mullet in pink shine or white, three to four-inch, on a half-ounce bucktail, drifted with the tide over sand-to-rock transitions. Nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a keeper mixed in here and there, but a full box isn't hard if you keep the boat moving and stay on structure instead of drifting open sand. Porgy have been thick on the reef stretches off Rocky Point and around the mussel beds — small hooks, squid strips, bottom rigs, and you don't need much finesse, they'll find the bait. That bite has held up all summer without a hiccup and I don't see a reason it changes soon. Blackfish, same story on structure, though they're a touch quieter with the water this warm — green crab on a jig head, fished tight to the rock piles, still worth the trip if you're patient with it.

Weakfish have been scarce, and I won't pretend otherwise. A few showed early in the season around the inlet edges but they've thinned out with the warmth. If the evenings stay calm and settled the way they have been, I'd expect a rebuild on some of the mud-bottom stretches toward dusk — that's a pattern I've seen plenty of times, weakfish liking a quiet, warm evening more than a bright hot afternoon. Worth a cast or two with a bucktail and twister tail if you're passing through, but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet.

Bluefish have been around in patches, not the kind of blitz you'd see farther down the coast where the bunker schools are thick, but enough that if you find bait pushed up along the beach near Mattituck Inlet or off Horton Point, you'll get slammed on a diamond jig or a topwater plug fast enough to lose some tackle. They come and go with the bait, no real pattern to it beyond that.

Looking ahead, the neap should keep softening through the weekend, which widens your workable window at the Gut beyond just the peak of the tide — good news if you've been getting shut out trying to time it perfect. I'd fish the last of the outgoing at first light for bass, switch over to fluke and porgy through the meat of the day on structure, and if the wind stays out of the south and lays down like it has been, I'd try one evening drift for weakfish just to see. No promises there, but the conditions are lining up the way they usually do before that bite rebuilds.

reports.headline: Nine Hours to Atlantis, Two Slot Bluefin, and a Wahoo We Never Saw Coming
reports.subhead: The run's still long and the fuel math still matters, but the canyon edges east of Montauk are finally paying for the trip.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 0300 Tuesday, and by the time the loran numbers matched the chart plotter's guess at the Atlantis edge, we'd burned through a third of a tank and most of the coffee. That's the math out here — call it four hours running at twenty-two knots to cover the ninety-some miles, and that's if the swell cooperates. It didn't complain much this week. Three-to-four foot period swell out of the south, nothing that put anybody on the rail wishing they'd stayed home, but enough to remind you why you fuel heavy and never trust the gauge on the way back.

We found the temperature break we wanted about a mile inside where the chart said it should be — cooler shelf water running 69 degrees butting up against warmer canyon water pushing into the mid-70s. That's the kind of seam that holds bait, and where there's bait on the Atlantis wall this time of July, there's tuna working it. We set up a chunk line on the down-current side, butterfish and a handful of menhaden, 6/0 circle hooks on 60-pound fluoro, and let it soak with the current instead of against it. Took about forty minutes before the first rod bent — a bluefin right in that 27-to-under-47-inch slot everybody's fishing for since the trophy category closed on the third. Second fish came an hour later, same size class, same story. Two-fish limit filled by 0800, which on a long run like this is about as good a morning as you can ask the ocean for.

What we didn't boat was the wahoo that hit a high-speed lure on the way to the chunk spot — ran the drag down hard for maybe ten seconds and then came unbuttoned on a jump we only half saw. That's wahoo fishing for you out here; you get a look and a story, not always a fish in the box. If you want a better crack at them, the morning bite window right at first light on the edge, trolling deep-diving plugs or wahoo bombs at 10 to 12 knots along the drop where the bottom falls from 600 to 1,200 fathoms, is when they show. We'll try again next trip.

The bigger picture this week backs up what the boats running to Veatch and Hydrographer have been reporting — stable high pressure has held for the better part of ten days now, and that kind of weather window is rare enough out here that you fish it hard while it lasts. Warm eddy water has pushed in tight to the canyon edges, and it's dragging yellowfin and a scattering of bigeye up onto the troll. Standard spread — Ilanders and naked ballyhoo, cedar plugs off the shortest rigger, green machines out the back — worked at 6 to 7 knots along the 68-to-72-degree break has been putting fish in the boat at Hydrographer, with reports of similar action pushing east toward Oceanographer. Mahi have been mixed in wherever the boats find floating structure or a stray lobster buoy — nothing to build a trip around by itself, but a welcome bonus when the tuna bite slows midday.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the East Canyons were sitting within range of a strong charter push out of Montauk and the Rhode Island ports, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats out of Galilee and Block Island running to Veatch are covering the same warm-water push we found at Atlantis, just from a different angle and a slightly shorter number on the plotter depending on which slice of the canyon they're working.

White marlin sign is starting to show along these same edges — a few boats working the temp breaks near Veatch have reported tailing fish and free-jumpers around the weed lines, which tracks with what we've been watching build through the month. Nothing to plan a dedicated billfish trip around just yet, but if you're already trolling the edge for tuna, it's worth dropping a spreader bar or two into the spread rather than running a straight cedar-plug program.

The honest part of this report: it's still a long day or a longer overnight, and the fish don't owe you anything for making the run. We had two good bluefin and a wahoo bite we didn't close out — that's a solid trip for late July, not a banner one. Bring enough fuel to fish the whole window and get home with a real reserve, not a guess.

Looking ahead, the first-quarter neap settling in over the next couple days should soften the current across these shelf breaks a bit, which typically widens the productive trolling window rather than concentrating it into a short tide-driven burst. If the high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd run to the same warm-water seam we found at Atlantis and expect the yellowfin and bigeye numbers at Veatch and Hydrographer to keep building rather than fade. Watch the eddy charts before you commit a full tank to one canyon; the warm water's been stable, but it still moves.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday Run, Strong Finish: Spencer Yellowfin Take Over the Troll by Thursday
reports.subhead: A sloppy start off Cape May gave way to a building bigeye and yellowfin bite once the swell laid down and the warm water held its ground on the edge.
reports.body_markdown:
If I had to grade this week, I'd call it a C-minus Monday and an A-minus Thursday through Sunday. That's the canyon game for you — you run four different pieces of bottom out of Cape May and Ocean City, and the one that's dead on Tuesday is stacked by Friday. Early in the week we were fighting a leftover groundswell, 3 to 4 feet at a short, chunky 5-second period out past the Bight — the kind of sea state that makes a 60-mile run to Norfolk feel like a chore and turns the ride to Spencer into a rodeo. I had two boats bail on Poor Man's Tuesday morning because the ride out was uglier than the fishing was going to be worth. But the water underneath that chop never went anywhere, and once the wind backed off midweek, the bite caught up fast.

We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as the offshore water stayed put — and that's exactly what happened. The warm push riding up out of the Stream never backed off, and once the sea state settled, boats running out to the 50 and 60 fathom curve off Spencer found bait stacked and fish willing. That's the canyon that carried the week. Daytime trolling around the edge — I'm talking the drop from about 38°32'N, 73°50'W down along the break — produced yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class on a mixed spread: naked green machines and cedar plugs up front, a couple of small Islander/ballyhoo combos in the shotgun, running 6 to 8 knots right on the color change where the green Jersey water meets that cleaner blue. When you see birds working bait balls on top and the water temp needle jump a degree and a half in a mile, that's your green light to put the spread in.

Night chunking stayed the bigeye play, same as it always is down here. Anchoring or drifting on the northeast side of the canyon with butterfish chunks and a couple of whole squid mixed in, running long fluorocarbon leaders — 100 to 130 pound — down to a 6/0 circle hook, glow stick clipped a rod length up. The bite windows were tight, mostly that first hour after dark and again right before first light, but the fish that came aboard were quality, several pushing well past 150 pounds. Patience wins that game — you can burn through a slow four hours before the current line sets up right and the fish start feeding under the boat.

Bluefin mixed in right on top of the yellowfin grounds at Spencer and pushed a little into Lindenkohl too, mostly slot-class fish in that 27 to 47 inch window everybody's still working with since the trophy fish closed out July 3rd. Nothing wrong with that — a two-fish limit on 40-pound bluefin eating the same trolled ballyhoo as the yellowfin is a good problem to have, and several boats filled out mixed bags without ever switching gear.

Mahi were the wildcard, same as they always are in late July. Found some solid chicken dolphin and a handful of slammers pushing 15 pounds around any bit of floating structure — lobster pot buoys, weed lines, a broken-up patch of sargassum drifting off the edge at Poor Man's. Small chartreuse feathers and a naked ballyhoo worked when we slowed the spread down to check structure, and it's worth having a rod rigged and ready any time you spot color change or floating junk, because those fish show up fast and disappear just as quick.

Wahoo came mostly on the run — high-speed trolling with black and purple Ilanders and cedar plugs while transiting between grounds, especially crossing structure edges at Lindenkohl and the deeper contour lines south toward Norfolk. Nobody's targeting them exclusively down here yet, but enough came over the rail on the troll-through that it's worth a couple of extra rods rigged heavy while you're running.

White marlin are the story building underneath all of it. We called this one too — said the billfish migration was building through July, and Poor Man's threw a few flags this week, along with some raised fish at Norfolk that never committed. Switch-bait tactics with dink ballyhoo and a naked circle hook teaser worked better than straight dead-bait spreads; these early-run fish are still a little green and want to be teased before they eat.

Looking ahead, if the high pressure holds through the coming week like it has, I'd keep leaning on Spencer for the bulk of the day-trip yellowfin and bigeye work, with Poor Man's as the marlin play if you've got the extra fuel and daylight. Norfolk's worth the long run if Spencer gets crowded or the fish slide south with the bait — that's happened before in late July. Watch the wind forecast closer than the tide chart this week; we're sliding into a neap cycle that'll soften current on the inside stuff, but out here it's the sea state, not the moon, that decides whether you're fishing or just riding.

reports.headline: July 21 and Washington's Already Three Weeks Into Its Prime Window
reports.subhead: The eddy that pushed warm water onto the canyon in early July hasn't budged, and the yellowfin bite is proof Washington doesn't wait for August like the other boys.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock — "Wash, is it too early for Washington?" And every year I give the same answer: it's never too early for Washington. This canyon has a habit of running two to three weeks ahead of Wilmington and the Hudson, and 2026 is no exception. We're not waiting on August water temps to get a real bite going out here. We're already in it.

Here's why. That warm Gulf Stream eddy that set up against the shelf break in late June never pulled off. It's still sitting right where it was, pushing blue water up onto the canyon edge and holding bait tight against the underwater terrain instead of letting it scatter into the Slope Sea like it usually does this time of year. That's the whole ballgame for Washington in July — when the eddy holds, the fish hold, and day-boat range becomes real range. Boats running out of Ocean City and Indian River have had one of the shortest steams to blue water I've seen at this point in the season in years.

We flagged this back on the 13th — said the new moon spring tide would push hard current across the shelf break and stack bait against the structure. That's exactly what happened, and the residual effect is still paying dividends even now that we've rolled into the first-quarter neap. The current's softer this week, no question, but the eddy's doing the heavy lifting now, not the tide. That's an important distinction if you're planning your week — don't expect the ripping current of ten days ago, but don't expect the bite to fall off either.

The western wall — I'm talking the stretch running along the 50-fathom curve down through the elbow — has been the most consistent piece of structure all week. Yellowfin in the 30 to 55-pound class have been eating a mixed spread of green machines, cedar plugs, and small chugger heads pulled at 6 to 7 knots right along that break where the green water meets the blue. Water temp on the edge itself has been holding in the mid-to-upper 70s, and that thermal line is razor sharp right now — you can see it in the color change without even looking at the graph. Work the seam, not the middle of either color.

Bigeye have been showing at night on the chunk, mostly butterflied sardines and small chunks of bluefin belly fished on 50 to 80-pound fluoro leaders, drifted off the stern in that same western wall zone. It's not a wide-open bite — guys are picking off one or two fish a night, sometimes going hours between bites — but the quality has been excellent, fish pushing 150 to 200 pounds on the ones that have come tight. If you're grinding it out after dark, keep your spread thinned down and your scent trail heavy. These fish are eating out of an eddy that's concentrated but not endless.

Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure holding current — lobster pot buoys, weed lines, the occasional current seam breaking off the hook at the canyon's north end. Nothing giant, mostly schoolie-class fish in the 3 to 8-pound range, but they'll eat almost anything you throw at them — small spoons, ballyhoo, even bucktails if you're already fishing bottom structure for something else. Good fun for the crew while the bigger stuff is being patient.

White marlin have been around the temp break too, which tracks with what we've been seeing building up the coast all month — this billfish migration has been gaining steam since early July and Washington's getting its share. Most of the marlin action has come on natural bait — ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, worked slow through the color change on the troll. It's not a stacked bite, more like two or three shots a day if you're covering the right water, but the fish are there and they're eating.

Wahoo have been the wildcard. A few boats running high-speed spreads — bonito strips and dark-skirted lures at 12 to 15 knots along the deeper edges of the western wall — have picked off a wahoo or two in that 40 to 60-pound range, usually right at first light before the yellowfin bite turns on. Not a target-worthy pattern yet, more of a bonus fish if you're already out there early.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this to slow down unless the weather turns on us. The eddy's stable, the high pressure's been steady, and every report I'm hearing out of the neighboring canyons says the same thing — this bite is building, not fading. The neap tide will keep current lighter through the week, which might soften the bite window slightly on the structure-dependent spots, but Washington's not really a tide-driven canyon in July — it's an eddy-driven canyon, and that eddy isn't going anywhere I can see. If I had one day this week, I'd run the western wall at first light, work the temp break hard on the troll until the sun gets up, then switch to the chunk if the current stays manageable into the evening. Bring extra ballyhoo — you'll want options.

reports.headline: Ran to Wilmington instead of Hudson — burned less fuel, found more bigeye
reports.subhead: A chunk-all-night, troll-at-dawn trip on the east wall paid off with bigeye, a stacked yellowfin bite, and our first white marlin shot of the season.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a decision to make Tuesday afternoon — Hudson or Wilmington. Both canyons were showing decent reports, but Hudson meant another 20 miles of running each way, and with fuel where it is, that's not nothing on a 30-hour trip. I looked at the eddy positioning, saw the warm water pushing in tighter to Wilmington's east wall than it had been the week before, and made the call to save the diesel and fish closer to home. Good call this time — it usually pays to fish what's in front of you instead of chasing a rumor 40 miles up the shelf.

We ran out to the 600-fathom curve on the east side, around the corner where the canyon starts widening out past the Baby Wilmington, and found a hard color change — hard blue water butting up against a greener, cooler push off the shelf. That's the kind of edge that holds bait, and it held bait. Flying fish were nervous on the surface most of the afternoon, always a good sign, and we marked bait balls stacked from 120 feet down to almost 300 on the sounder right on the break.

We committed to the chunk that night instead of trolling into dark, and it was the right move. Set up on the edge with the current pushing us slowly along the wall, butterfish chunks in a slow drip, and by 10 pm we had our first bigeye — a fish right around 140 pounds that took a long time to get up from depth on 80-pound fluoro leader and a plain hook buried in a butterfish chunk. We picked at two more through the night, lost a couple to green mono and sharp turns near the boat, but ended up boating three bigeye by first light. That's a solid night's work for one boat — not a stacked-up, every-bait-getting-bit kind of bite, but steady enough that nobody was standing around.

Daylight, we pulled the chunk gear and put the spread back out — naked ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, a couple of small Ilanders in blue/white and green/yellow, and a spreader bar down the middle. Yellowfin showed up almost immediately working the same temperature seam, mostly in the 35- to 55-pound class, and we picked away at them trolling the break in both directions for about four hours before it went quiet around 10 am. Six yellowfin in the box, plus a wahoo that smashed a high-speed planer rig with a green Yo-Zuri bomber we had out wide — that fish nearly emptied a reel before we turned it.

We also had a legitimate white marlin shot — a fish came up on a dredge teaser mid-morning, wouldn't commit to a hookbait, but it's the first real billfish sign we've had out there this year. We flagged a couple weeks back that the marlin migration would build through July, and this is exactly the kind of thing you'd expect to start seeing right about now. Doesn't mean they're stacked up yet, but the pieces — warm water, bait, the right depth — are lining up.

Mahi were a bonus, not a target. We picked up four dolphin, biggest around 12 pounds, off a scattered weed line we crossed running between the chunk grounds and the troll spread the next morning. If you've got time between tuna stops, it's always worth a look at any floating junk or grass — a couple of small green/yellow feathers pulled fast will draw a strike almost every time there's fish under the weeds.

The bigger picture here is that this stable high-pressure stretch we've had for going on two weeks now is doing exactly what it's supposed to do — keeping the eddy water pinned up against the canyon wall instead of sliding off, and that's holding bait and fish in range instead of scattering them. We called the new moon tide would tighten bait up along the shelf break, and that's held true — the concentration we found on the sounder Tuesday night was about as tight as I've seen it this season.

It wasn't a lights-out trip. The daytime troll bite was good but not overwhelming — six yellowfin in four hours of trolling a known edge is solid work, not a feeding frenzy. If you're going, I'd plan around the chunk at night for the bigeye and treat the morning troll as the bonus round rather than the main event right now. That could flip if the yellowfin push harder onto the temp break like they were starting to Wednesday morning.

Looking ahead, if this high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd expect the pattern to keep building rather than fade. Wilmington, Hudson, Washington, and the canyons to the south are all reading similar setups. If you've got a trip planned, I'd fish the same wall we did, work the chunk overnight, and keep a dredge out during the troll in case that marlin sign turns into something more than a look.

reports.headline: A 3-Degree Break at 39°34'N Puts Yellowfin on the Chunk Line
reports.subhead: Warm-core ring water is still parked on the Hudson wall, and the numbers say it's not going anywhere fast.
reports.body_markdown:
Seventy-one point two. That's what the Bight buoy was reading before we even cleared the beach this week, and it told me everything I needed to know about the ride out. Warm surface water sitting that shallow inshore means the filament we've been tracking off the Hudson wall hasn't slid off — it's still stacked up against the canyon edge, and it's dragging bait with it. I ran the plotter out past the 100-fathom line to about 39°34'N, 72°45'W — inside edge of the Claw — and picked up a break of just over three degrees in less than a mile of water. That's the kind of gradient that piles bait against a wall and makes tuna stupid.

We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the warm filament would keep building the bite if it held position, and it held. The canyon is fishing better right now than it has all month, and the reason is written right there on the chart: warm-core ring water pushing east off the Stream, meeting cooler shelf water along the 100-fathom break, and stacking bait right where the bottom drops off hard between the Dip and the Claw.

Daytime troll has been the more consistent play this week. Spreader bars with naked ballyhoo, run at six and a half to seven knots along that temp seam, are drawing yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class, with a scattered bigeye mixed in on boats willing to push the spread out past the color change. Green and yellow machines in the shotgun, small cedar plugs and Ilanders in close — nothing exotic, just clean presentations tight to where the water goes from that milky green shelf color to the deep cobalt blue. When you see the color break, you're close. I've had my best strikes within a quarter mile of where the SST chart shows the line, not right on top of it — the fish are sitting just inside the cooler water, ambushing bait that gets pushed across.

Night chunking has been the bigger story for quality fish. Butterfish chunks fished on a slow drift over 900 to 1,200 feet of water near Texas Tower and out toward the Dip have been putting bigeye in the 60 to 90 pound range in the boat between midnight and 3 a.m. The first-quarter neap that set up around the 21st has actually helped this bite — current at the edge has softened enough that a chunk bag drifts naturally instead of getting swept off the structure, and the slower drift means baits stay in the strike zone longer. If you're running a chunk spread, keep at least one bait unweighted and let it fall naturally with the chum slick — that's where the bigger fish have been eating.

The bluefin slot fishery is holding steady, which is worth mentioning since a lot of boats gave up on it after the trophy-class closure hit July 3rd. Fish in the 27 to under-47-inch window are still showing on the troll around the 60-fathom curve on the way out to the canyon, mixed in with the yellowfin. Small green machines and Zucker rigs in the daisy chain positions have been drawing strikes from fish clearly feeding on sand eels — nothing subtle about it, just a clean two-fish-a-boat limit if you're willing to work the spread through that transition zone before you commit to deep water.

Mahi have been a bonus rather than a target — scattered fish under any floating debris or weed line inside the break, usually school-size, 3 to 8 pounds, eager for a small skirted jig dropped right off the transom. Wahoo have shown sporadically on the high-speed gear when boats run planers or a deep-diving lure through the color change at 12 to 15 knots — not a dedicated bite yet, more of a byproduct when guys are hunting bigger game. White marlin have been quiet this week, a couple of shots reported on dink ballyhoo but nothing consistent enough to call it a pattern.

Sea state has been workable — 3.9 feet at a five-second period out of the south when I checked, short and a little sloppy but nothing that keeps a well-run 32 to 40 footer off the grounds. It's the kind of chop that makes the ride out uncomfortable for an hour and then lays down once you're sitting on the edge working a chunk slick. Worth timing your run around the wind forecast rather than fighting it the whole way out.

Honest assessment: this isn't an every-drop bite. I've had trips where the troll produced steady doubles through the morning and trips where we worked the same temp break for three hours and only picked at fish. The night chunk has been the more reliable producer for quality over quantity. If the warm filament holds its position through the weekend — and right now the gradient looks stable, not eroding — I'd expect the yellowfin and bigeye numbers to keep building rather than fade. If it slides east the way these things sometimes do, I'd shift effort toward Wilmington and the Washington Canyon before I'd give up on the Hudson entirely. For now, though, the data and the fish are telling the same story, and that's rare enough to trust.

reports.headline: The Point Splits in Two: Blues Own the Bunker, Bass Own the Dark
reports.subhead: A neap tide softens the rips this week, stretching the low-light bass window while daytime bluefish carve up bunker schools off the Lighthouse.
reports.body_markdown:
Every July the Point splits into two different fisheries, and this week it's split clean down the middle. By day it belongs to the bluefish — bunker schools rolling past the Lighthouse in tight, nervous balls, blues underneath them cutting through like a chainsaw through a two-by-four. By dark, it belongs to the bass, and if you've fished this rock long enough you know that's exactly how it's supposed to go in high summer. This isn't decline. This is the rhythm the Point has kept for as long as anyone's been keeping records on it.

Water off the Lighthouse is holding around 69 degrees, which is comfortable enough to keep bait stacked tight to structure without pushing everything offshore into deep water. That's the number that matters right now — warm enough to hold bunker schools along the beach and out past North Bar, cool enough that the better striped bass haven't abandoned ship for cooler water up the Cape or into the Race. What it's done instead is push the bulk of the keeper-class bass into a nocturnal pattern. Dawn, dusk, and full dark — that's the window. Midday sun on 69-degree water and a stripers' metabolism just doesn't line up the way it did in May.

The rips are still the show. North Bar on the building tide has been giving up bass in the 20 to 34-inch range to guys working bucktails — 1.5 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse, bounced hard off the bottom on the downcurrent side where the sand drops into the trough. Cast up-current, let it sink clean to the bottom before you start working it, and keep contact through the swing. That's the Point pattern, always has been. Eels are still money after dark — rigged eels drifted through Shagwong Reef on the first two hours of the outgoing, and live eels worked off the boulder field on the south side for guys willing to fish the tide change at 4 a.m. I had a report of a bass pushing 38 pounds taken off the south side rocks on a live eel just after midnight last Thursday — that's the kind of fish this rock still produces when you put the time in and fish it right, in the dark, with nobody else around.

Daytime, if you want action instead of patience, the bluefish are doing exactly what bunker schools moving along the beach have been forcing them to do coastwide this month — and Montauk's getting its share as those pods work their way east. Diamond jigs, 3 to 4 ounces, worked through the surface froth when the blues are up busting bait, or a bucktail with a pork rind trailer bounced through the edges when they've gone under. Turtle Cove and the rip line running off the Lighthouse itself have both been holding these bluefish blitzes at various points through the week — nothing subtle about it, you'll see the birds and the surface chop from half a mile out. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these fish are shredding light mono without even trying.

With the bass on a low-light clock and the blues owning the noon hour, porgies and sea bass on Shagwong Reef have become the smart daytime move for anyone who wants fish in the cooler without burning a tide waiting for dark. Standard high-low rigs, squid strips or clam, over the reef structure in 30 to 50 feet — it's not glamorous but it's about as close to a sure thing as this Point offers right now, and it fills the hours between the real bite windows.

Fluke drifts off the south side and out toward the Elbow have been steady if not spectacular — 3 to 4-ounce bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in white or pink, dragged slow along the sand-to-structure transitions where the current sweeps bait off the reef edges. Keepers are mixed in with plenty of shorts, so it's a numbers game more than a guaranteed box, but it's a fine way to spend a slack tide between the bass windows.

We flagged the tuna building offshore last week, and the canyon boats running out of Montauk Harbor are confirming it — yellowfin and bigeye activity improving as this stable, high-pressure stretch holds warm water in range out toward the canyons. If you've got a canyon trip on the books, this is the stretch to use it.

The moon goes first-quarter this week, which means we're sliding into neap tides — softer current through the rips at Shagwong and North Bar than you'll see at the new or full moon. That's not bad news. Softer current actually widens the productive window for eel and bucktail presentations beyond the peak of the tide, so you don't have to thread as tight a needle timing your trip. What it also means is the first false albacore and bonito scouts — which typically show around the Point in that late-July stretch as water keeps climbing — haven't announced themselves yet. Keep an eye on temperature breaks out past the Point and around the Elbow over the next week or two. When the water firms up another degree or two and the bait compresses, that's when the first albie showing usually happens out here, and it can happen fast once it starts.

For now: fish the low light for bass, fish the bunker schools for blues, and use the reef for porgies when the sun's too high for anything else. That's the Point in late July. It's not complicated, but it does ask you to show up when most people are asleep.

reports.headline: The Ledge Goes Quiet at Noon — Bass Feeding After Dark, Bonito Water Building
reports.subhead: Warm surface water has pushed the striper bite into the low-light hours around Block Island, while fluke keep the rods bent through the heat of the day.
reports.body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it — walked down to the dock Tuesday morning and the air had that flat, heavy stillness that tells you the water's gone warm on top. No breeze pushing through the Great Salt Pond, glass calm out past the breakwater. That kind of stillness usually means the bass have gone smart on us, and sure enough, that's exactly what's happened.

The Southwest Ledge and the North Rip have both slowed to a crawl during daylight this week. Boats working the Ledge at high noon are marking bait and marking fish on the sounder but getting nothing to commit. It's not that the stripers left — it's that they've pushed their feeding window to the edges of the day, dawn and dusk and full dark, same pattern we're seeing coastwide right now with surface temps sitting in the high 60s to low 70s. I fished the North Rip at 5 AM Thursday, eel on a three-way rig, 20 feet down on the drop into the rip current, and connected on two fish in the mid-30s before the sun cleared the horizon. By 8 o'clock, dead. That's the rhythm right now — get there early or fish it after dark, don't waste your prime tide in the middle of the afternoon.

Night fishing off the Ledge has actually been the more dependable program. Bunker pods are holding tight to the structure after dark, and the bass are stacking underneath them in that 25-to-40-foot band where the current sweeps hard on the ebb. A live bunker on a fish-finder rig, freespooled back into the current seam, has been the ticket for guys willing to put the hours in after midnight. We're not talking blitz conditions — it's a fish here, a fish there, quality over quantity — but the ones coming over the rail have had some size to them, low 30s to high 30s, with a few reports of fish pushing 40 taken right off the rocks on the west side after dark.

Fluke have been the more honest bite this week, and I mean that as a compliment. While the bass have gone moody, the fluke haven't changed their habits one bit. Structure and moving water, same as always — the drift off Charlestown Breachway side of the island, the mussel beds south of the Great Salt Pond entrance, and the deeper edges off Southwest Ledge itself in 35 to 50 feet have all been holding fish. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing — that's been the winning combination. Nothing giant, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper pushing 4 pounds, but steady enough that you can fill a cooler if you keep the boat moving and stay on structure.

Scup fishing has been a nice consolation prize for anyone who wants an easy bag limit without burning gas hunting bass. The reef structure around Block Island Sound and the rocky patches off Point Judith are loaded with porgies right now, and a simple high-low rig with squid strips or clam will keep the rod bouncing all afternoon. Good family fishing while the bigger targets are being stubborn.

Now for the one we've had our eye on. We flagged last week that water temps pushing into bonito comfort range around Montauk, the Vineyard, and Buzzards Bay meant we should start watching the temperature breaks closely — and this week that watch is paying attention. No confirmed bonito in Block Island Sound yet, but the water's sitting right in that window where they typically show, and I'd be surprised if we don't see the first scattered fish working the rips within the next week or two. Worth running the East Grounds and the tide rips off Sandy Point with small metal jigs — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — just in case you're the one who finds them first.

We're sliding into a first-quarter neap right now, and that's going to soften up the current through the North Rip and off the Ledge over the next few days. That's not bad news — it actually widens the window for eel and swimbait presentations, since the water won't be ripping through so hard that you can't hold bottom. If I had one trip to make this weekend, I'd fish the last hour of the outgoing at first light off the Southwest Ledge with a live eel, then switch over to bucktails on the drift once the sun's up and the fluke start showing on structure. Keep an eye on that bait — where the bunker sit after dark is where the bass are going to be, neap tide or not.

reports.headline: Peconic runs hot and full — porgies stacked at Shelter Island, fluke steady
reports.subhead: The bay's ahead of the Sound again this July, and the bass have gone nocturnal while the porgies and fluke carry the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I remind people that the Peconic doesn't play by the Sound's clock, and every year it proves me right. Kings Point is sitting at 70.9, New London's still down at 69.4 — but our bay warmed weeks ago and it shows. The water off Shelter Island has that thick, green, bait-rich look it gets in high summer, and the porgies have settled into their usual haunts like they never left.

Coecles Harbor and the flats off Big Ram and Little Ram are holding porgies in the 15 to 22 foot range, and they're not shy about it. Sandworms and clam snouts on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinkers — you don't need to overthink porgy fishing here, you just need to find the sandy patches between the mussel beds and drop straight down on the last of the incoming or the first two hours of the outgoing. Same story off Jennings Point and the mouth of Coecles — bottom's holding scup in numbers, with a scattering of keeper blackfish mixed in on the rockier stretches now that the season's open. The tog bite isn't the fall show yet, but a few three and four pound fish have come off the reef edges near Shelter Island's western shore on green crab, fished slow on the slack.

Fluke are exactly where they should be. We said last week the Peconic fluke bite would carry through summer, and here we are — it has. The channels are the story: North Race, the cut off Orient, and the deeper water running past Jennings Point are all holding fish in the 20 to 32 foot range. Drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp — white or pink swimming mullet, 3/4 to 1 ounce depending on current — is still outproducing bait-only rigs, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the channel water is moving with some authority. Sizes are mixed, plenty of fish in the 16 to 18 inch range with enough 20-inchers mixed in to keep it interesting. Nothing spectacular this week, but steady — the kind of bite where a few hours on the right tide fills a cooler without much drama.

Striped bass have gone the way they usually go once the water settles into summer pattern — quiet through the middle of the day, then switching on hard around dusk and staying active well after dark. Plum Gut is still the anchor spot for this zone, and with the first-quarter neap settling in, the current through the Gut and the North Race has softened up noticeably. That's actually good news for presentation — instead of fighting a screaming rip, you can work a bucktail or a swim bait more deliberately across the edges. I've had better luck lately casting a 1.5-ounce bucktail across the deep side of the channel, letting it sink clean off the drop, and working it back slow along bottom rather than ripping it through the current. Orient Point's outer edge has been holding fish the same way — slot-sized bass mostly, with the occasional overslot mixed in on bunker schools that have been drifting through Gardiners Bay.

Speaking of which, bluefish have shown up in real numbers through Gardiners Bay and around Orient. These aren't the little snappers we saw in June — these are jumbo blues, slashing through bunker pods in open water during daylight, which is unusual enough to notice. If you find the birds working over a bait ball off Orient or the eastern side of Shelter Island, don't overthink your presentation — a bucktail or a diamond jig worked through the melee will get bit almost every cast. Just watch your fingers on the release, these fish are angry and healthy.

Weakfish have been the quiet surprise. We flagged last week that the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happened around Three Mile Harbor and the deeper holes in Noyack Bay. Nothing like the old-timer weakfish runs, but enough action after dark on bucktails and soft plastics — pink and white five-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on light jig heads — to make an evening trip worthwhile if you're patient and fishing the last of the tide into full dark.

Looking ahead, the neap tide should keep softening through midweek before the tides build back toward the coming full moon, which will get things moving again through the Gut and the Race. If the current stays gentle, I'd lean into slower presentations for bonus fluke and blackfish over the next several days — this is the window for it. Once the tides build back up, I expect the bass to tighten back onto the hard rip lines and the bluefish to keep pushing bait through the bay as long as this settled weather holds. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the Gut at last light with a bucktail in hand, watching for that first swirl in the current seam.

reports.headline: Three-Way Rig, One Eel, 38 Inches — Plum Gut Delivers on the Neap
reports.subhead: The first-quarter neap is softening the rip and opening a wider window for eels and swimbaits, while fluke keep grinding steady across the zone.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-way rig, twelve-inch eel, second hour of the outgoing at Plum Gut — I felt the take stop me cold before the current even had it, and thirty-eight inches of bass came up through the froth like it owned the rip. That's the fish that told me the neap was already changing things out here, days ahead of schedule.

We hit the first-quarter neap today, and anybody who's fished the Gut long enough knows what that means: the 5-knot freight train that usually runs through there on a big tide backs off, and instead of one violent ten-minute window at the peak of the ebb, you get a longer stretch where you can actually work an eel or a swimbait through the structure without getting swept sideways into the rocks. I fished the last two tide changes with a shad-style swimbait — a six-inch paddle tail on a three-way rig, sixty-pound fluoro leader, three ounces of dropper weight — dragged along the break where the reef drops into the channel on the east side of the Gut, worked slow on the bottom the way you'd work a jig for cod. Two fish over thirty inches in two evenings, both right on the tide change, both eating the bait as it swung off the edge and stalled in the eddy behind the rock pile.

The fluke bite has been the most dependable thing in this whole zone for weeks and it hasn't slowed down. Plum Gut structure is holding keepers mixed in with plenty of short fish — enough shorts that you grind through some throwbacks to find dinner, but the keepers are there. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, drifted slow with the current over the rock piles in twenty-five to thirty-five feet, have been the ticket. Had a client stick a sea bass in there too — 28 inches, better than five pounds, came off the same structure on a chartreuse bucktail meant for fluke. Not a fish you plan for in the Gut, but it tells you that rip is holding more than just bass and fluke right now.

Water's sitting around 69 to 70 degrees from New London out toward Montauk, which is comfortable for everything we're chasing — not so warm that the bass have gone strictly nocturnal like they have west of here, but warm enough that low-light windows are still your best bet for size. Dawn and dusk at the Race have been better than midday, plain and simple. I worked the west end of the Race at first light three mornings this week, throwing a Super Strike darter and a 2-ounce bucktail with a white shad tail through the eddies that stack along the north edge of the current, and picked up bass mid-twenties to low-thirties on the darter worked slow through the slack pockets where the rip folds back on itself. Nothing over 34 inches, but steady enough I wasn't standing there wondering if I'd made a mistake.

Bluefish are showing up along the same current edges, and when they show, they don't mess around. I've watched boils break right on the surface where the rip meets slack water off Fishers Island Sound — cast a metal into that seam, a Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster, and you're hooked up before the lure sinks a foot. These aren't cocktail blues either — some of these are jumbos, four and five pounds, slashing bait right on top. We flagged this pattern last week — called the Race and Plum Gut for sight-casting to breaking fish, and the blues are giving us exactly that right now, even if the albies haven't shown yet. If you see the boil, don't long-bomb it. Feather the cast right into the seam where the current's breaking and let it sink a second before you start the retrieve.

Porgies are still stacked on the rock piles around Orient Point and off Fishers Island in fifteen to twenty-five feet — nothing exciting to write home about, but if you want a bent rod and a bucket of dinner, a hi-lo rig with squid strips on that structure will keep you busy between tide changes. Weakfish have been scattered at best — I've heard of a few coming out of the deeper holes off Orient on bucktails tipped with squid, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Here's what I'd do this week: fish the neap while it lasts. The softer current in the Gut and the Race should hold for several more days before the tides build back toward the next moon, and that gives you a wider window to work an eel or a swimbait through the heaviest structure without it getting ripped out of the strike zone in ten seconds flat. I'd be on the water for the tide change at Plum Gut at first light or last light, working the eastern edge where the reef drops off, and I'd have a bucktail rigged and ready in case the fluke show up under the same structure — because right now, that's a real possibility on every single drift.

If the wind stays out of the south like it has been, expect the surface to stay clean enough to sight-fish those bluefish boils off Fishers Island Sound through the week. And keep an eye on the water temps ticking up — once the low seventies show up consistently out here, the false albies and bonito that have been working their way east through the Sound all summer are going to start showing on the same rips we're fishing bass and blues on right now. Not there yet. But I'm carrying a bag of small metals in the boat just in case.

reports.headline: South Swell Rebuilt the Bar Off Cupsogue — Fluke Found the New Edge First
reports.subhead: A stretch of 4-foot groundswell reshaped the inlet throat this week, and the moving water over the new structure is producing better than the old lines did.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the west end bar off Cupsogue on Tuesday's ebb and the depth finder told me something the charts hadn't caught up to yet. That stretch of south groundswell we've been eating all week — 3.9 feet at five seconds, dead out of 177 degrees according to the offshore buoy — has been stacking sand against the outer bar at the throat of the inlet. The old drop that ran roughly parallel to the training rocks has filled in a few feet, and a new scour channel has cut in tighter to the Cupsogue side. That's not a subtle shift. If you fished the old edge this week and marked nothing, that's why. The fish didn't leave, the bottom moved.

I found the new edge Wednesday on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a bucktail-and-Gulp combo — half-ounce white bucktail with a 4-inch pearl Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer — right where the new scour drops from six feet down to eleven off the flood shoal. Fluke were sitting right on that break, and it wasn't subtle fishing either. Six keepers in ninety minutes, biggest going 21 inches, with a handful of shorts mixed in that needed to go back. That's a real bite, not a rumor. We flagged this corridor two weeks back as the stretch to watch through the rest of July, and the water's backing that up — Moriches into Shinnecock is fishing as well as anywhere on the south side of the Island right now for fluke, and the reason is simple: moving water over structure, which is exactly the kind of thing that doesn't care how hot the surface temperature gets.

The timing helps too. We're sliding into the first-quarter neap, and that's softening the current through the cut noticeably day over day. Less velocity means the drift window on the fluke grounds is opening up wider than it was on the full-moon tides two weeks ago — instead of a tight ninety-minute window around the max ebb, I was still marking fish and getting bit an hour past what I'd normally call quitting time. If you're planning a trip this weekend, don't rush off the water the second the tide slacks. Stay another half hour and work the seam where the current is still trickling off the flats into the main channel.

Striped bass are a different animal right now, and anybody telling you otherwise is selling something. With the bay running warm through the shallows — that's typical for this point in July — the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime casting around Tuthill Point and the sod banks off the north side of the bay has been mostly dead unless you're right at first light. The better program has been live bunker fished on a fish-finder rig after dark, worked tight to the rocks on the ocean side of the inlet jetty where the current still runs cool over structure even when the flats have gone soupy. I had a report of two bass in the mid-30-inch range taken that way Thursday night on the incoming, right against the rocks where the tide pushes bait through the gut. If you want daytime action on bass, you're better off targeting the very edge of dawn — first hour of light, working a black Slug-Go or a bunker-imitation swimbait along the current seam where the inlet meets the ocean.

Bluefish have been the wildcard. Bunker schools are moving along the beach the way they always do this time of year, and where those pods show up off Cupsogue or Smith Point in the early morning, the blues have been slashing through them hard enough to see from the beach — birds diving, water churning white. It hasn't been a daily thing out here the way it's been reported further west along the Jersey coast, but when it happens it's fast and it's obvious. If you're surfcasting at dawn, keep a metal — a Kastmaster or an Ava jig — rigged and ready, because those windows close in ten minutes once the bait pushes through.

Weakfish have been quieter but not absent. The calm, warm evenings we've had this week are exactly the conditions that tend to rebuild that bite in the bay's deeper holes — I'm talking the channel bends off East Moriches and the deeper cuts inside Pattersquash. A bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has picked up a few keeper-class weakfish in the 16 to 18-inch range. It's not a blitz, it's a pick, but it's real and it's trending the right direction if the weather holds calm.

Looking ahead, the ocean's going to stay a factor. That south swell isn't laying down completely, which means Cupsogue's surf fishing will stay tough and the inlet bar will probably keep shifting through the weekend — I'll be back out mid-week to see if the new scour channel holds or fills back in. The neap tide should keep widening those fluke windows through the weekend, so that's where I'd put my time if I only had one trip. Bass fishing stays a dark-hours game until we get a real cool-down, and if the bunker keep pushing along the beach, don't be surprised if Smith Point sees a legitimate blitz morning before this week's out.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass Deep at the Jetty, Weakfish Waking at Ponquogue
reports.subhead: A neap tide slowed the current down, but it didn't slow down the bite — you just have to fish the right three hours.
reports.body_markdown:
By eleven o'clock last Tuesday I'd already made my call for the week: skip the day tide entirely, wait for the outgoing after midnight, and set up in the deep hole on the ocean side of the east jetty where the current pours through hardest. That's been the program all month, but it's especially true right now with the back bay running warm and the bass shoved into a strict low-light and after-dark pattern. Daytime, they're sulking somewhere cool. After dark, with the water dropping and the current ripping past the rocks, they come up to feed, and that's when you want to be standing there.

The first quarter neap landed today, which took some of the snap out of the current compared to the spring tide push we had a couple weeks back. I'll take it, honestly — a softer outgoing means the window at the jetty stretches longer instead of slamming shut in ninety minutes. I worked eels on a fish-finder rig in eighteen to twenty-two feet off the rocks starting about an hour before the tide turned, and connected on three fish in the 28 to 34 inch range between 1 and 3 a.m., all on the meat of the drop. A buddy fishing bucktails — the black-and-purple 2-ounce, slow-rolled along bottom — picked up a slot fish and lost a bigger one right at the rocks where the current seams up. Nothing epic, but three or four solid bass in a night session at the inlet this time of year is a night worth having, and it beats standing there empty in daylight heat.

We flagged this last week — said the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings — and that's exactly what's playing out at Ponquogue Bridge right now. Dusk into full dark, on the last two hours of the incoming, guys working small bucktails tipped with squid strips or 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Shrimp under the lights near the pilings have been finding weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch class consistently enough to call it a pattern, not a fluke catch. The key is fishing tight to the shadow line the bridge lights throw on the water — that's where the bait bunches up and the weakfish sit waiting. Don't overpower the retrieve. A slow lift-and-drop right on the edge of that light line has been the difference between a bent rod and nothing.

Daytime, the move in the bay is fluke, and it's been the most dependable thing going out here for weeks now. The flats off Tiana Beach and the drift lanes around Warner's Island and Cormorant Reef are holding fish in eight to fifteen feet, and moving water is doing the work — outgoing has been slightly better than incoming, probably because it's pulling bait off the flats into the channel edges where the fluke are stacked up waiting. Standard drift rig, 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow with the boat, has produced fish to 5 pounds, with a decent number of shorts mixed in that you'll have to sort through. If you want a bigger average fish, work the deeper edge of the channel drop near the Coast Guard station side of the inlet on the last of the ebb — that's where the better-grade fluke have been holding tight to structure rather than sitting out on the open flat.

Bluefish have started showing more consistently inside the inlet itself, chopping up spearing and small bunker on the surface during the morning outgoing. Nothing like the bunker blitzes happening up the coast toward the city, but if you're out there at first light with a metal Deadly Dick or a Kastmaster, you can find a few slammers cutting through bait pods right off the rocks before the sun gets too high. It's a nice bonus fish if you're already out there for bass or working into a fluke morning.

Porgies and blackfish are still a canal-and-bridge story. The rock piles under Ponquogue and the structure heading toward the Shinnecock Canal locks are holding good numbers of porgies on sandworms and clam, fished on a simple high-low rig right on bottom during slack tide when the current isn't ripping them off the spot. Blackfish season's still off out here, but I've seen a few guys picking through legal-sized porgies mixed with some decent-sized weakfish drifting the mouth of the canal on the tail end of the outgoing — worth a look if you're heading toward the Peconic side anyway.

Looking ahead, the neap tide is going to hold through midweek, which means softer current and longer bite windows both at the inlet and the bridge — good news for anyone who can only get out for a few hours instead of chasing the peak of a hard tide. If the warm, calm pattern holds like it has, I'd expect the weakfish at Ponquogue to keep building through the week, and the inlet bass to stay locked into that midnight-to-3-a.m. window on the outgoing. If a front comes through and stirs up the bay, the fluke bite on the flats might get choppy for a day or two, but structure spots like the channel edge by the Coast Guard station should stay productive regardless. My plan this week is simple: eels at the jetty after midnight, bucktails at the bridge at dusk. That's where I'm putting my time, and that's where I'd send you too.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: the bass went nocturnal on us, but the fluke never got the memo
reports.subhead: A regular asked why his daytime stripers dried up — the answer's in the warm water and the after-dark bunker bite building at the inlet.
reports.body_markdown:
Ronnie caught me gassing up at the dock Tuesday morning, already annoyed before I even had my coffee. "Mari, I fished the inlet three mornings this week, live-lined bunker off Democrat Point like always, and got nothing but a couple bluefish for my trouble. What gives?" I told him the same thing I've been telling everybody who'll listen — the bass didn't leave, they just clocked out for the day shift. Water's warm enough now, low 70s out in the ocean and not much cooler inside the bay, that the bigger fish have gone strictly low-light and after-dark. If you're fishing Democrat Point or the rips off Captree Island at nine in the morning with the sun already up, you're fishing for bluefish, not bass. That's just where we're at in July.

So here's what I told him to do instead: fish the last hour of light into full dark, live bunker or fresh chunks fished tight to structure — the rock piles off Democrat Point, the deeper cuts along the Robert Moses bridges, the seam where the inlet channel spills into the bay on the outgoing. That's where the bass are holding and feeding once the light drops off. It's not the flashiest fishing, standing there in the dark with a rod in a holder, but it's producing. A buddy of mine anchored up on the incoming tide right at dusk this week off the West End and put three fish in the mid-30s in the boat before ten o'clock, all on bunker chunks soaked on the bottom near the rocks. That's the play right now — not bucktailing the flats at noon.

The good news, and it's real good news, is the fluke haven't gotten the message that they're supposed to slow down in this heat. That bite has stayed steady all through the mid-70s water, and it's still the most dependable thing going in this bay. The Robert Moses bridges are still the classic spot — anchor or drift the pilings on the outgoing tide in 25 to 35 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid if you want extra scent in that current. We've also been picking at fish along the channel edges off Kismet and out toward the Fire Island Lighthouse flats, working the drift slow, bouncing bottom, letting the bait do the work rather than ripping it. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts to sort through, but keepers in the 3 to 5 pound range aren't hard to find if you keep moving and stay on structure. Nothing to write home about size-wise this week, but it's a bite you can count on, which counts for something in late July.

Bluefish have been the wildcard, and honestly the most fun. Bunker schools are working their way along the Fire Island beach the same way they've been pushing up the Jersey coast, and when those pods get inshore of the bar you'll see the whole surface erupt — gulls diving, blues slashing through, the water actually boiling. I had a morning last week off Cedar Beach where the blues were so thick on a bunker school you could practically walk on them. Bucktails, poppers, anything with flash thrown right into the melee will get bit instantly. The catch is timing — those schools move, and what's happening off Kismet at 7am might be off Point O'Woods by 9. Keep an eye out for diving birds and slicks on the surface; that's your tell.

Weakfish have been quietly building too, and we flagged this pattern last week — said the bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's shown up. Guys working the deeper holes off Patchogue and Sayville on calm nights with soft plastics or bucktails tipped with squid strips have been picking at weakfish in the evening slack, nothing epic, but real fish where a couple weeks ago there was nothing. If we get another stretch of settled weather, I'd expect that to keep building.

Out front on the ocean side, I'd tell you to be patient. That 44025 buoy reading is showing almost 4-foot swell at a short 5-second period, which is a sloppy, disorganized sea — not the kind of surf you want to be wading into for stripers off the beach right now. It's kicking up enough whitewater that the surfcasting has been rough and inconsistent, and honestly most of the good fish are inside the inlet and bay anyway with the thermal setup we've got. Save the beach trips for a calmer window.

We're sliding into a neap tide off today's first-quarter moon, which means softer current for the next several days. That's actually good news for the night bass bite — a slower moving tide widens out the feeding window instead of compressing it into one hard hour of moving water. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be anchored on the inlet seam at Democrat Point right at sunset with bunker on the bottom, riding that softer tide well past dark. And I'd keep the fluke rods rigged for the next morning, because that bite isn't going anywhere yet.

reports.headline: Forget the Fluke Boats — I'm Fishing the Rocks After Dark and So Are the Bass
reports.subhead: While the fleet drifts Sloop Channel at noon, the real weight is coming off the jetty rocks and bay mud after sundown.
reports.body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is out there drifting Sloop Channel at ten in the morning with a white Gulp on a bucktail, and yeah, that's still a decent way to put a fluke in the cooler. But if that's all you're doing this week, you're leaving the good stuff on the table. I've been working the rocks at Short Beach and the north jetty inside Jones Inlet from last light through full dark, and that's where the real bass have been.

Here's why. The ocean side has been sloppy — we're looking at close to four feet of swell rolling in off the Bight, short period, five seconds, ugly and disorganized. That kind of slop doesn't kill the bite, it just pushes it. Bass don't want to fight that wash in daylight when the water's warm and bright. So they've gone nocturnal on us, same as they have from here up through the Sound. Warm shallow water plus a bright July sun equals lockjaw at noon and a green light after the sun drops. I've seen this pattern plenty of Julys — when the shallows heat up, the bigger fish slide into a dusk-to-dawn feed and structure becomes the whole game.

So that's what I've been fishing. Half-hour before sunset to about ten, ten-thirty, working bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig right up against the rocks at the Short Beach jetty, fresh cut bunker if I can get it, frozen if I can't. Slack tide through the start of the outgoing has been the window — bass are sitting in the eddies where the current breaks off the rock face, waiting for whatever gets swept out of the bay. I've also had good luck slinging a black 2-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer along the inlet-side rocks on the last of the incoming, letting it swing with the current and hopping it slow off bottom. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 32 inches, a few pushing 34 — but steady enough that I'm not complaining, and a lot more consistent than what the daytime surf guys are reporting off the open beach right now.

Now the fluke. I'm not going to tell you it's dead, because it isn't — moving water over structure is still putting fish in the boat, especially through the Jones Inlet channel itself on the last two hours of the ebb, when everything in the bay gets funneled through that cut. Fifteen to twenty-five feet of water, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a three-quarter ounce bucktail, dragged slow along bottom. But it's a grind — you're picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers, and the bite window is tighter than it was in June. If you're going to fish it, fish the tide change hard and don't waste time on the slack.

The story I'm more interested in right now is the weakfish. They've been building back into South Oyster Bay on these calm, warm evenings, and I flagged this a while back — told you the comeback was real, not just a rumor from one lucky trip. Mud-bottom pockets off Wantagh and the flats behind Freeport are holding them, and the pattern's simple: quiet water, dusk into dark, small soft plastics or bucktails with a glow tail worked slow just off bottom. Nothing heavy — three-eighths to half-ounce jig heads, light drag, because a weakfish's mouth tears if you horse it. They're not huge yet, mostly 16 to 20 inches, but they pull hard and they're a welcome change from staring at fluke shorts all afternoon.

We called the spring tide right last week — said it would flush the inlet hard, pull bait out on the ebb and pull predators in tight behind it on the flood, and that's exactly what set up that jetty bite I've been leaning on. Now we're sliding into the neap around this first-quarter moon, and that changes the math a little. Current's going to go soft. Less push means the bait doesn't get flushed through the cut with the same urgency, so the bass bite may spread out over a longer window instead of firing hard right at the tide change. I'd rather fish more of the tide than chase one perfect thirty-minute stretch.

Bluefish have been a non-event for me personally this week — I haven't seen the bunker pods pushing hard enough along the beach to trigger a real blitz through the inlet, though that can change fast if a school gets pinned against the beach by an easterly wind. Worth a look at first light with a metal lip swimmer if you're already out there, but I wouldn't build a trip around it yet.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the after-dark program at the rocks as long as this warm, calm stretch holds — that's where the bigger bass are going to keep showing up. If the wind stays out of the south and the ocean settles down some, I might sneak back out to the beach for an early tide, but until then, my rods are staying rigged for chunk and bucktail after the sun goes down. And keep an eye on that weakfish bite in the bay — quiet, warm evenings are exactly what's been building it back, and I don't see a reason for that to slow down this week.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway After Dark: The Bass Went Nocturnal, So Did I
reports.subhead: With the bay running warm and the bass feeding on their own schedule, I traded daylight boat trips for midnight runs under the bridge.
reports.body_markdown:
I put the boat in at Motts Basin this week instead of launching the kayak off Canarsie Pier, and the reason's simple — the keeper bass in this bay have gone nocturnal on me, and you can't chase a night bite paddling. Once the sun's down and the outgoing starts pulling hard under Marine Parkway Bridge, that's where the grown-up fish are, not stacked up shallow at noon getting sunburned.
