Looking ahead: the neap tide through the 21st and into the 22nd is going to keep softening the rip structure, which I actually think helps the bass bite at SW Ledge — longer windows, less current to fight, better presentation control on eels and swimbaits. I'd fish the two hours around slack rather than chasing peak current this week. Fluke and sea bass stay the safe bet on the reef south of the Judith regardless of moon phase. And if you want a longer shot, the offshore tuna grounds out toward Block Island canyon are still very much in play for boats running from Galilee — stable weather's holding, and that door isn't closing yet.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: stripers on bunker chunks, fluke holding steady off Prudence
reports.subhead: The herring are long gone from Buckeye Brook, the bay's pushing warm, and the bass have gone nocturnal while fluke and scup carry the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the Conimicut town dock Tuesday night listening to two guys argue about whether it was worth running lines out past ten o'clock, and one of them said something that stuck with me: "Buckeye's been dry since May, bud, this ain't that fish no more." He's right. That herring run that gets everybody's blood up every spring — the one that pulls bass up into the Warren and Barrington rivers chasing river herring stacked thick enough to walk on — that's done and gone for the season. What's left now is a different animal. Bigger, warier, and mostly a creature of the dark.

The bay's been running warm, pushing into the low-to-mid 70s on the surface, same story that's got bass locked into a low-light pattern from here down through the Sound and the Jersey beaches. During the day the fish just aren't interested in banging around in bright water — too much effort for too little payoff. So they're doing what smart striped bass do in July: sliding into deeper water and structure through the afternoon, then coming up to feed hard in that hour before dark and again well after the lights come on.

That's exactly what's happening under the Nyatt Point bridge and around the pilings at the old Rocky Point pier. Guys are soaking chunk bunker on fishfinder rigs in 15 to 20 feet, right on the edge of the light line where the current sweeps bait past the structure on the last two hours of the ebb. I had a 29-incher there myself Thursday night on a chunk, and heard of a couple fish pushing 34, 35 inches taken the same window on live eels swung off the current seam below the bridge. If you're going to fish it, fish it slow and quiet — no spotlights on the water, no slamming hatches. These bay bass have seen enough boat traffic to get cagey.

Daytime, it's fluke and scup carrying the weight, and that bite's been the more dependable one all week. Fluke are holding on the channel edges off Prudence Island and along the drop outside Greenwich Bay, working best on the last stretch of the outgoing into the first half hour of the flood when the current's still got some push to it. Four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 28 feet — that combo's been putting keeper-class fluke in the box, nothing giant but steady, a fish or two on most drifts if you're patient about covering ground.

Scup are stacked on the rocky ledges the way they always are this time of year — Conimicut Point out to the can, the rock piles off Nyatt, and the ledge work up toward Rocky Point. Incoming tide is the move, small hooks, sandworms or clam bait, light enough tackle that you can feel every pluck. Nothing fancy about it, just steady meat-and-potatoes fishing that fills a cooler if you've got the patience to sit on the anchor.

Here's the one I want to flag: we said last week the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening in Greenwich Bay and up around Bullocks Point. Squid have been running into the bay in decent numbers, which is a good sign for bait availability across the board, and the weakfish have been sliding up on those calm dusk tides to work the edges where the squid concentrate. Small swim shads and soft plastic shrimp imitations worked slow just off bottom at last light have been drawing strikes — nothing huge, mostly schoolies in the 16 to 20 inch range, but a legit bite where there wasn't much of one two weeks ago.

Sea bass are still there for anybody willing to make the run out toward Dutch Island and the humps off the west side of Prudence — squid strips and clam on bottom rigs in 25 to 35 feet, best on the last of the ebb when the current settles enough to hold bottom without dragging your sinker halfway to Newport. Sizes have been decent, a few fish pushing four and five pounds mixed in with the usual dinner-plate class.

Bluefish have been more of a rumor than a pattern in the bay proper this week — a few scattered blitzes on peanut bunker up around Conimicut and off Nayatt, but nothing sustained. If the bunker schools that have been working the beaches outside the bay decide to push in further, that could change fast, and it's worth keeping an eye on the surface for diving terns.

We're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current through the bridges and the ledge spots for a few days. That's not a bad thing — it widens the productive window on the fluke drifts and takes some of the urgency out of hitting peak tide exactly right on the scup grounds. What I'd do this week: fish the bridges and points after dark for bass on chunk and eel, hit Prudence and outside Greenwich Bay midday for fluke on the moving water, and keep a rod rigged light for weakfish if you're out at dusk with calm conditions. If the squid keep pushing into the bay the way they have been, that weakfish bite has room to build further before the month's out.

reports.headline: Wreck 6-8-2 in 130 feet: sea bass to 5 pounds, bluefin working the Mud Hole lumps
reports.subhead: A warm filament pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington approaches has mahi and yellowfin within range, while the reef wrecks keep filling coolers with jumbo bass.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-two feet of water over the top of Wreck 6-8-2, dead calm Tuesday morning, and the sounder painted a solid red-orange smear that told me everything before the first bait hit bottom. That's the kind of return I've been chasing on this piece of structure since I first punched the numbers into a loran box twenty years ago, and it hasn't let me down yet in July. Sea bass to five pounds came off that wreck on Gulp Grubs in white and chartreuse, fished on a high-low rig with 4-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom against the current. The jumbos are sitting tight to the wreckage itself, not scattered on the sand around it, so if your drift walks you off the numbers, reel up and reset. I lost count of the shorts we threw back before the keepers started stacking, but that's a good problem to have this time of year.

Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are both fishing the same way right now — deep down in the structure, not up on top. Clam and squid strips on bucktail teasers are outproducing straight bait rigs for me this week, especially in the mid-morning when the sun gets up and the fish tuck deeper into the shade of the wreckage. Shrewsbury Rocks has been more hit or miss — I had one drift there Thursday that produced eight keepers in twenty minutes and then went dead for the next hour. That's typical for the Rocks in midsummer; the bait pods move through in waves and the bass follow them, so if you find the pod, work it hard before it slides off.

Offshore, this is shaping up to be one of the better midrange tuna stretches I've seen in a few years. The Mud Hole lumps have been holding bluefin in that 27-to-46-inch slot class consistently since the trophy fishery closed on the 3rd, and the two-fish recreational limit means guys are still going home with fish without having to grind through a full spread all day. I've been running green machines and cedar plugs off the riggers with a naked ballyhoo down the shotgun, trolling the deeper edges of the lumps where the temp break holds — the water's been clean and blue out there, not the usual green chop you fight through in a normal July. Barnegat Ridge has produced sporadically for the smaller bluefin class as well, mostly early, before the wind fills in out of the southwest by midday.

We flagged this last week — said the warm-water filaments pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington canyon approaches would put decent yellowfin and mahi within range of the Jersey fleet, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats running out to those canyon edges are finding mahi stacked on anything floating — lobster pot buoys, loose weed lines, the odd pallet or trap marker. Dink lines with small hookless teasers followed by a naked ballyhoo or a green-and-yellow feather have been the play once you spot the color change or a bird working low over the surface. Yellowfin are mixing in on the same water, and the size class has been ticking up slightly from what we were seeing two weeks ago — nothing giant yet, but a step in the right direction if this stable high pressure holds through the week like it's supposed to.

No bonito yet in our zone. Water temps up around Montauk and Block Island are creeping into the range where they typically show, but I haven't had a confirmed fish crossed off in the Mud Hole or along the Ridge. Worth keeping an eye on temperature breaks over the next couple weeks, especially if this offshore warmth keeps pushing inshore, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

Tog season's closed through the summer, so that's a fall conversation — I'll start pulling my blackfish numbers back out once the water starts to turn in September. Cod's the same story; not worth chasing structure for them until the water cools off considerably.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure pattern holds through the weekend like it's forecast to, I'd expect the canyon bite to keep building rather than fade — the Hooper-style warm filaments don't usually collapse overnight, and mahi numbers tend to climb through late July as more weed and debris gets pushed into range. On the inshore side, I'd keep working the reef wrecks early before the wind builds, and I wouldn't be surprised if the Mud Hole lumps keep producing slot bluefin right through the week as long as the bait stays put on those temperature edges. If I had one trip to make this weekend, I'd run out to check the Hudson approach for color and bait before committing to a full canyon day — but I'd have Wreck 6-8-2 as my fallback if the offshore water looks wrong.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: Fluke Picky, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Drum Done for the Year
reports.subhead: The rips are fishable but you've got to work the tide right — and the black drum run is a memory until next May.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the Rips this week: C-plus. Fishable, not easy. If you'd asked me in April I'd have told you July fluke at the Rips is close to a sure thing on the right tide — and it still is, mostly — but the last few days it's taken more patience than a lot of guys want to give it. Warm water's the reason, and I'll walk you through why.

Water out at the mouth of Delaware Bay has been sitting in the mid-70s, which is warm enough that it's changed the clock on everything. Striped bass down here have gone almost entirely nocturnal — same pattern you're seeing coastwide right now. Daytime, the bass at the Rips are down deep and lockjawed, holding on the current edges but not committing. Dawn and dusk, and especially after dark with the tide moving, that's when they'll eat. My best window the last week has been the top of the outgoing at first light, working bunker-pattern swimming plugs and 2-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse Bass Assassins along the edge where the ocean push meets the bay current spilling out past Cape May Point. Nothing gaudy — a few keepers in the mid-20s to low 30s, mixed with plenty of shorts. You have to fish it like a night bite even in daylight hours right now, which means working the structure hard and not expecting a blitz.

Fluke's been the more dependable player, but even that bite has gotten picky. Last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, right over the humps and the sandy patches inside the Rips and along the edge of the Hereford Inlet channel, is still putting fish in the box — mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper over 20, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with just enough lift to feel bottom. The bite window's tightened up though. Miss that tide change by 45 minutes and you're marking fish on the machine and getting nothing but taps. Triggerfish are mixed in around the wreck and reef structure off the Cape May Inlet jetties in decent numbers for anyone soaking clam or squid strips on the bottom — not a headline fish but a fun one when the fluke go quiet.

Delaware Bay's the more interesting story right now, and it's one we flagged coming — said the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening. The back-bay channels and marsh creeks up toward Fortescue and along the edges near Brandywine Shoal are holding weakfish again after a slow stretch, and the warm water pushing through those mud-bottom creeks on the dropping tide is concentrating them along the channel edges. Nothing like a blitz yet — call it a steady numbers game, three or four fish an outing for guys working it right — but it's trending up, not down. Bucktail-and-squid-strip combos or soft plastics on light jigheads, fished slow along the drop-offs where the creek water dumps into the main channel on the last two hours of the outgoing, that's where I'd put my time in the evening.

Now the part I know some of you are going to ask about anyway: the black drum run. It's done. May was the show — that's when the big bay drum push up onto the shoals off Fortescue and the mouth of the Maurice River, and by mid-June they're gone, scattered back out to deeper water. If someone tells you they're marking drum in Delaware Bay in July, they're either mistaken or talking about a stray fish, not a run. I'm not going to sugarcoat that one — if drum's what you're after, mark your calendar for next May and don't waste a trip on it now.

Bluefish haven't shown much locally yet. The blitz action everybody's talking about up around Belmar and Raritan Bay hasn't pushed down this far — those bunker schools are still working the central Jersey beaches. If that bait keeps moving south the way it usually does through late July, we could see some of that blue-fish energy show up off the Wildwood beaches and around Hereford Inlet inside two to three weeks. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but it's worth watching the bait reports moving down the coast.

Looking ahead: we're sliding into a first-quarter neap tomorrow, and that's going to soften the current through the Rips for a few days. Less water movement usually means a wider window on both sides of the tide change instead of one hard 90-minute bite — good news for guys who can't time their trip to the exact minute. I'd expect the fluke bite to actually get a little easier to hit through the neap, since the tide won't be ripping through as violently and the fish won't bunch up quite as tight to structure. Striped bass will stay a low-light game until this water cools off, which isn't happening anytime soon in July. And keep an eye on that weakfish pattern in the bay — if the calm, warm evenings hold, I expect those numbers in the marsh creeks to keep building through the end of the month.

reports.headline: Class Question: Why Are the Stripers Only Biting After Dark? Ask the Bait
reports.subhead: Warm water has pushed the bass nocturnal, but fluke, bluefish, and weakfish are keeping the daylight shift honest from Absecon to Stone Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a reader standing at the rail with a bucktail he hasn't gotten bit on since 2 p.m.: "Professor, where'd the bass go?" The answer's the same lesson I teach every summer — they didn't go anywhere. They just clocked out for the day shift.

Water's been sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off our beaches and warmer than that in the back bay flats behind Brigantine and up in the Absecon meadows, and striped bass don't like working that hard in daylight when the metabolism's already running hot. What you're left with is a bass that feeds at dawn, at dusk, and best of all after full dark, staged tight to current edges where the water's moving and slightly cooler than the flats around it. If you want a striper this week, fish the last hour of light through the first two hours of dark on the outgoing at Absecon Inlet, working the rock jetty seam with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, or swing an eel through the deeper cuts off the Brigantine side. That's not a guess — that's the pattern holding up and down this coast right now, and it's the same reason the party boat guys are telling their sea bass and fluke customers not to bother with striper rods until the sun starts dropping.

Now here's where the classroom gets interesting, because the daylight bite hasn't disappeared — it's just changed subjects. Fluke remain the most dependable fish in this zone, and they haven't blinked at the warm water the way the bass have. I've had good drifts in 18 to 25 feet on the Great Egg Harbor Inlet edges, working the channel that runs out past the old Ocean City bridge pilings, using 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, teased with a strip of squid. The keeper-to-short ratio has been better on the last two hours of the incoming, when the moving water pushes bait up against the drop-offs and the fluke stack on the up-current side waiting for it. Sod bank fluking in the Absecon back bay — the skinny water behind the meadows toward Brigantine — has also been producing, especially on the sod bank drop from 4 feet down into 8, fished on the tail of the outgoing when the bait gets flushed off the grass edges. Chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp trailer have out-produced straight bait rigs there this week, probably because the water's got a little color to it after the recent thunderstorm runoff.

Bluefish are the story I flagged for you last week, and it's playing out almost on schedule. We said the bunker-driven blitz pattern working the beaches to our north was going to spread south along the barrier islands as the bait schools kept moving with the tide, and sure enough, guys working the surf at Ocean City and down toward Sea Isle City have been into slashing blues in the first hundred yards off the beach during the last few mornings, right under diving gulls and terns. If you see birds working tight to the wash, don't waste time — get a metal lip swimmer or a Hopkins spoon out there fast, because those blitzes come and go in twenty-minute windows. Townsends Inlet has had some spillover activity too, blues chopping bunker right at the inlet mouth on the last of the outgoing, which tells me the bait's pushing down past Stone Harbor as well. Watch for that same pattern to keep sliding south through this week if the weather stays calm — the minute we get a blow that scatters the bunker pods, this bite goes quiet fast, so I wouldn't sit on it.

Weakfish are the other bright spot, and this is a fish that rewards patience over horsepower. Calm, warm evenings have been rebuilding that bite in the deeper holes of the back bay channels — Great Egg has been the more consistent producer, particularly the bend behind the meadows where the channel drops to 12 feet or better. Light jigheads with a chartreuse or pink Gulp shrimp, fished slow along bottom on the last of the incoming tide right at dusk, has been the most reliable combination. These aren't the 4-pound weakfish of years past — mostly 14 to 18 inches — but enough of them showing to make an evening worthwhile if you're willing to work slow and quiet.

Kingfish are around in the surf troughs at Ocean City and Stone Harbor, small but steady on bloodworm-tipped high-low rigs fished in the first sandbar trough on a moving tide, morning or evening both working fine since kingfish don't care much about light the way bass do.

We're heading toward a first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current in the inlets over the next several days. That's actually good news for the fluke program — slower water means longer, more controllable drifts through the Absecon and Great Egg channels instead of getting rushed through the sweet spot on a hard ebb. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take an evening tide at Absecon — fluke on the last of the incoming, then switch over to bunker chunks for bass as the light fades and the current starts to slacken with the neap. Two lessons in one trip, which is really how I like to teach it.

reports.headline: Holgate's New Slough Holds Fluke, Bunker Pods Pull Blues Through Barnegat Light
reports.subhead: A fresh cut behind the Rip is stacking fluke on the slack while bunker schools drag blues past both inlets on the tide change.
reports.body_markdown:
I flew the drone over the Holgate cuts Tuesday morning before the wind picked up, and there's a new slough that wasn't there three weeks ago — carved out behind the second bar, running parallel to the beach for maybe 150 yards before it dumps into a bowl at the north end. That kind of structure doesn't happen by accident. It's a sign the sandbars down there are still shuffling from whatever swell rolled through in June, and it's exactly the kind of skinny-water trough that holds fluke on the last two hours of the outgoing before it goes dead flat.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker-driven blitz activity would intensify as bait kept pushing south with the tide, and that's precisely what's happening at Barnegat Light. Pods of bunker have been stacking up tight against the north jetty rocks on the last of the flood, and the blues have found them. Nothing like the Belmar-style daylight blitzes yet, but Wednesday morning I watched three separate boils inside the inlet mouth on the changeover, blues in the 3-5 pound class slashing through, gulls working hard overhead. If you're throwing metal — a 2-ounce Deadly Dick or a Hopkins — get it past the boil and let it sink a beat before you rip it back through. Don't cast right into the froth, feather the edges. That's where the bigger fish sit, picking off the cripples that drop out of the pod.

Fluke fishing is the one thing on this whole stretch I can call genuinely steady right now. Little Egg Inlet channel, the deep bend off Graveling Point, and the back side of Holgate are all producing on moving water — doesn't seem to matter which stage as long as there's current pushing. I've had my best drifts working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets, bounced slow along the channel edges in 12 to 18 feet. Keeper-class fish, some pushing 22-23 inches, mixed in with a lot of shorts that make you work for your five. The back bay behind Beach Haven has been kicking out similar numbers on the same rig — smaller boat, same presentation, just shallower, 8 to 10 feet over the grass edges on the outgoing.

Stripers are the tougher story, and I'm not going to sell you a bill of goods here. Daytime bass fishing on this stretch has gone quiet — the water's too warm on the surface for keeper-class fish to want to feed hard in the middle of the day, and that's holding true from here up through the whole Jersey coast. The play right now is after dark, working the same bunker schools that are pulling the blues. I've had better luck live-lining a bunker on a fish-finder rig off the Barnegat Light rocks starting an hour before sunset and working through the first few hours of dark, or chunking bunker on a fish-finder rig anchored up-current of the pods at Little Egg. It's a slower game than daytime jigging, but the fish that come are worth the wait — I heard of a mid-30s fish taken off a chunk bait near the inlet mouth Thursday night, which tells me there's still some real size mixed in with the schoolies.

Weakfish have been quietly rebuilding around the Mullica mouth and up into Graveling Point on the calm, warm evenings we've had. Nothing like the old days, but if you're throwing a small swimming plug or a light bucktail-teaser combo on the last of the incoming right at dusk, you've got a real shot at a couple of weakfish mixed in with your fluke. Keep the retrieve slow — these fish don't chase hard in July heat, they want it presented right in front of their nose.

Kingfish showed up on the ocean side sandbars off Ship Bottom and Beach Haven this week, working the trough behind the first bar on high tide. Bloodworm or Fishbites on a simple high-low rig with a sandflea teaser has been the ticket — nothing exciting, but it's a fun beach-chair bite for the kids while dad works a bucktail in the same wash for a stray fluke.

Looking ahead: we're rolling into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current through both inlets over the next several days. That usually widens my bite windows rather than shrinking them — less water moving means the fluke and bass have more time to set up on structure instead of getting flushed through on a hard rip. I'd expect the bluefish pattern to keep pushing south along the beach as long as this bunker migration holds together and the weather stays calm — watch Barnegat Light and Little Egg both for daylight action if the pods keep funneling through on the tide changes. If I only had one window this week, I'd fish the last two hours of Saturday's outgoing at Holgate for fluke, then swing north to the Light for the evening bunker show before dark settles in for the bass.

reports.headline: Double Creek fluke on the drop, weakfish rebuild at the sedges, blues push into the Inlet mouth
reports.subhead: Warm mid-70s bay water has fluke hugging the cool edges while bunker pods pull bluefish right up into Barnegat Inlet on the last of the incoming.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a July back in the late '80s, running a party of three out of Double Creek with the tide dead low and the air already sticky by seven in the morning, and my old captain — a Greek fisherman who'd taught me half of what I know, God rest him — told me something I've never forgotten. He said the bay doesn't hide from you in summer, it just makes you work for the cool water. Forty years later and that's exactly where we are right now. The shallow flats are running warm, mid-70s by midday, and every species worth chasing has tucked itself into the drop-offs and channel edges where there's a degree or two of relief and a little current to keep things moving.

Double Creek Channel has been my go-to the last ten days and it's holding up. The drift along the edge where it falls from six feet down into twelve to eighteen has been steady for fluke — nothing enormous, but a real dependable pick of keepers to about 22 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along that break, has been the ticket, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets pulled off the flat and stacks up right on that lip. I've had my best drifts starting an hour before low and running through the turn — the fluke seem to sit tight to the channel wall waiting for that current to deliver breakfast, and a slow bucktail bounced right along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid, is about as close to a sure thing as this bay offers in July.

Now the weakfish — I'll be honest, I was cautiously optimistic about these fish rebuilding through the warm, calm evenings we've had, and that's exactly what's happened. The same sedge banks off Tices Shoal that were holding weakfish back in May and June are still producing, mostly at dusk and into the first hour of dark, on the calmest nights we've had. Small soft plastics — 4-inch chartreuse or pink shad bodies on light jigheads — worked slow along the edges of the grass has been drawing strikes from fish in the 16 to 20 inch range, with a few better ones mixed in for guys willing to stay out past sundown. It's not a blitz, and I want to be straight with you about that — you might make eight or ten casts before you connect — but the fact that these fish are showing consistently in the same water, week after week, tells me this isn't a fluke pattern, it's a real rebuild.

The bigger story this week has been bunker. Pods have been pushing through Barnegat Inlet on the higher stages of the tide, and where bunker go, bluefish follow. I've been working the inlet mouth — right around the rock jetty at Barnegat Light and out toward the sea buoy — on the last two hours of the incoming, and the blues have been all over those pods in broad daylight, which isn't something you see every week. Diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve, or a simple bunker spoon trolled just outside the surf line, has been putting cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound range in the boat steadily, with the occasional bigger chopper mixed in when the pods get dense. If you're fishing from the beach at Island Beach State Park, this is the week to have a metal lip or a Hopkins in the bag — those bunker schools have been running close enough to shore that surf casters have gotten in on it too.

Striped bass remain the toughest read of the bunch, and that's typical for this time of year with water running warm right up into the mid-70s across the flats. The keeper-class fish have gone almost entirely nocturnal — best action has come after dark around bridge structure and current seams near Oyster Creek and up toward the Route 37 bridge, where a little current and some depth keep things bearable for a striper in July. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or a fresh eel drifted slow along the pilings, has drawn a handful of solid fish in the 28 to 34 inch range for guys willing to fish the two hours around midnight tide changes. Daytime bass fishing in the bay right now is mostly a lost cause — I wouldn't waste your morning on it.

We're heading into the first-quarter moon on the 21st, which means the current is about to go slack for a few days — neap tides, less push through Double Creek and around the Inlet. That's typically when the fluke bite widens out a bit because the fish aren't pinned as tight to the strongest current lines, so don't be afraid to work the softer edges of the channel, not just the main thread. My read for the coming week: this pattern holds through late July as long as the weather stays settled and the bunker keep pushing through the Inlet. If a blow comes through and scatters that bait, the bluefish show could shut off fast at the Inlet mouth, so I'd get out there sooner rather than later if that's your target. Otherwise, Double Creek on the drop and the sedges at dusk remain the most honest bets on the bay this week.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at Dawn: Bunker Pods Thick, Blues Wide Open, Bass Waiting on the Dark
reports.subhead: The bait's stacked from Sea Bright to Manasquan and the blues found it — stripers are still playing it cagey until the sun drops.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six, low tide bottoming out at the Sea Bright rocks, and there's a kid down from Rumson throwing a white bucktail into water that looked like it was boiling from the inside. Bunker everywhere — not scattered pods, but that dense, oily, nervous-water mess that tells you something's under it before you even see the first blow-up. He hooked up on his third cast. Ten-pound bluefish, maybe better, and it wasn't a fluke catch. Two guys down the jetty were doing the same thing with tin — Ava 27s dressed with surgical tube, red and white, worked with a fast retrieve just under the surface where the blues were slashing.

This is the pattern right now and it's not subtle. Bunker have been running thick along the beachfront from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach and into Long Branch, and the blues have found them in broad daylight, which is unusual enough to be worth writing home about. We flagged this exact setup last week — said the bait would hold as long as the weather stayed stable, and that's precisely what's happened. High pressure's parked over the whole coast, no wind to speak of most mornings, and the bunker schools haven't had a reason to move off the beach. When they finally do get pushed by a blow, this bite will shut down fast. Until then, it's about as gift-wrapped as jetty fishing gets — you just need to be there before the sun gets too high and the blues drop back down.

Here's the catch, and there's always a catch: the stripers aren't playing along with the blues in daylight. Water off the beach is sitting warm — Bight readings pushing mid-70s — and that's shoved the bass into a strict low-light program. I've fished the Sea Bright rocks at first light three mornings this week and only turned bass after dark or in that gray fifteen minutes before the sun actually breaks the horizon. Manasquan Inlet's north jetty has been the most consistent spot for it — fishing the last two hours of the outgoing, working a Daiwa SP minnow or a black Bomber Long A tight to the rocks where the current pulls bait past the tip. Nothing huge, mostly 24 to 28 inches, but they're there if you're willing to be out before the joggers.

Shark River Inlet's been a similar story after dark — swim shads in white, 3/4-ounce, fished on the drift through the deeper hole on the inside of the jetty, especially on the last of the ebb when everything funnels through that narrow throat. A guy I know who fishes it religiously landed a 34-incher there Tuesday night on an eel, which tells you the bigger fish are still around, just not stupid about when they show themselves.

Fluke's been the more dependable daytime bite, and it's shifting exactly the way I figured it would a week or so back — back bay action slowing as that water gets uncomfortably warm, and the fish sliding out to the inlet mouths and the nearshore structure where there's cleaner, cooler water moving. Manasquan Inlet channel on the drift, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along the edge where the sand drops into the deeper channel — that's produced fish to 4 pounds on the last of the incoming, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your bucktail sideways. Belmar's fishing boats working just outside the inlet in 25 to 35 feet have had similar counts, plenty of shorts mixed with keepers, best on the tide changes when the bait gets confused for twenty minutes and the fluke stack up on it.

Porgies are around in decent numbers off the Manasquan and Shark River jetties for anyone who wants a break from the bigger game — small hooks, bloodworms or clam, right on bottom in 15 to 20 feet, good action for kids or anybody who just wants to bend a rod without overthinking it.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't expect them for another month or so — that's a September conversation, not a July one, though I'll start watching the bait breaks off Spring Lake and Manasquan Inlet as we get into August.

Moon's sliding toward the first-quarter neap tomorrow, which is going to soften the current in the inlets over the next several days. That's not necessarily bad news — a slower drift at Manasquan and Shark River can actually stretch out the fluke bite because your bucktail stays in the strike zone longer instead of getting ripped through on a hard tide. For the bass, less current usually means a slightly wider window at first light before things shut down for the day.

My money for the next few days is on the same script: bunker and blues at first light anywhere from Sea Bright to Long Branch, bass strictly a dawn-and-dark game at Manasquan and Shark River inlets, and fluke holding at the inlet mouths on the tide changes. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I don't see a reason for any of that to change fast. If it swings hard out of the east and stacks up some swell, the bunker will scatter off the beach and the blues will go with them — so if you've got a morning free this week, I wouldn't wait on it.

reports.headline: Bunker Pushing North Toward the Hook — Blues Right Behind Them, Fluke Holding the Channels
reports.subhead: Bait pods moving up from Belmar are about to test the Hook rip, and the fluke bite is buying time while we wait.
reports.body_markdown:
I made my call Tuesday morning standing on the Perth Amboy waterfront watching gulls work a nervous patch of water off the ferry terminal, and it wasn't close: I'm staging at the mouth of the bay this week, not deep in the back rivers. Bunker schools have been grinding north along the Jersey beach out of the Belmar stretch for a week now, and when that bait rounds Sandy Hook and pushes into the Reach, everything with teeth follows it in. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said it would spread up the coast as long as the weather stayed calm — and here it is, knocking on our door. I don't want to be sitting in the Navesink chasing weakfish scraps when that show finally walks into Raritan Bay.

So here's the split I'm working. Mornings and evenings, I'm running the Hook rip and the ferry channel edge off Highlands, watching for surface commotion on the tide change. That's historically the first place this pattern shows itself locally — bunker get squeezed against the rip current and the blues pile on top in broad daylight, which is unusual for this time of year but exactly what's happening south of us right now off Belmar and LBI. If you see diving birds and nervous water anywhere between the Hook and Romer Shoal, don't wait — cast straight into it. Poppers and 2-ounce metal, Ava jigs in white or bunker-flake pattern, whatever you can get out there fast. These blues aren't picky when they're on top of bait, but they will move on you quick, so keep the boat mobile and don't burn ten minutes on a spot that's gone quiet.

Striped bass are trickier right now, and I want to be straight about that. With water this warm — the ocean side is reading mid-70s, and the bay follows right behind it — the bigger keeper-class bass have gone nocturnal on us, same as everywhere south of the Cape. Daytime bites inside the bay have been soft. My best action has come after dark and right around first light, working bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs at Romer Shoal and along the edge of Flynn's Knoll in 15 to 20 feet, incoming tide preferred so the current stacks bait against the structure. If you can get out with live bunker on a slider rig, snag one out of a pod near the rip and drop it back — that's produced my two best fish of the month, both mid-20s, neither one during daylight hours. Don't expect a blitz-style bass bite to show up behind the bunker the way the blues have; right now the stripers are playing it cautious and low-light, and that's likely to hold until we get a stretch of cooler nights.

Fluke have been the honest workhorse of the bay all month, and they're not asking us to wait for anything. The channel edges through the Reach and along Keyport Flats have been steady — not a banner bite, but a dependable one, which is more than I can say for the bass right now. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the drop-offs where the flats spill into the channel, 18 to 25 feet, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your line sideways. Chartreuse tipped with a strip of squid has been the better combo on the duller days, and I'm seeing keeper fish mixed in with plenty of shorts — nothing like that 12-plus-pound doormat that got weighed in last month, but solid 18-to-20 inch fish if you cover ground and stay on the bottom. Romer Shoal has held fish too, though boat traffic there gets thick on weekends, so I'd fish it early or middle of the week if you can.

Weakfish and porgies are around in the usual spots — Navesink holds a few weakfish if you're working bloodworms or small soft plastics on the bottom near the drop-offs after dark, and porgies are scattered on the structure around Romer Shoal for anyone bottom fishing with clam — but neither is worth building a trip around right now. They're a bonus, not a plan.

Looking at the week ahead, the moon's sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means softer current and wider fishing windows rather than short, violent tide changes. That's actually good news for the bunker push — less current to scatter the pods as they work north, which should keep them concentrated and visible as they round the Hook. If the weather holds calm like it has, I expect the blue blitz to show itself inside the bay within the next couple days, probably first at the Hook rip or the ferry channel on a tide change. My plan is simple: fluke in the middle of the day when nothing's popping on top, bunker chunks and live bait after dark for the bass, and rods rigged and ready for metal the second birds start working. If the bunker slide past us instead of stacking up, I'll pivot back to the channel program full time — the fluke aren't going anywhere.

reports.headline: The Race at 4.3 Knots: Bass Still Holding on Valiant as the Neap Slide Begins
reports.subhead: Wire line and white bucktails are still connecting on the max ebb, but the slack window is about to get a lot more forgiving.
reports.body_markdown:
Four point three knots. That's what The Race was running on Wednesday's max ebb, clocked off Valiant Rock with the current meter I keep zip-tied to the rail. Down from the 5.1 we saw on the full-moon spring tide two weeks back, and it's going to keep dropping as we slide into Tuesday's first-quarter neap. That drop matters more than anything else I can tell you this week, because it changes how long you get to fish the good water instead of just surviving it.

Here's the read: on a big spring tide, the window at Valiant Rock is brutal and short — you get maybe eight, ten minutes of true slack before the current builds back to a wire-line-snapping pace. This week, with the moon backing off, I'm seeing that window stretch to fifteen, sometimes eighteen minutes on both ends. High water slack at Valiant ran 10:52 this morning, low slack at 5:14 this afternoon, and both times I had rods bent within the first five minutes of the tide going quiet. That's the neap effect — less current speed, longer bites, easier drifts. If you've been getting your teeth kicked in trying to hold bottom on wire line during the spring tides, this is your week to get back out there.

The bass are still on Valiant and around Race Rock, but they've gone almost entirely nocturnal on us, same pattern we're seeing coastwide right now with water sitting warm — 70 at New London, pushing 72 at Kings Point on the west end of the Sound. Daytime bites are there but they're short and current-dependent, right at the top and bottom of the tide change. After dark is where the real fish are showing. I've had my best drifts starting an hour before the last light dies, running 20-ounce wire line rigs with bunker spoons and tube-and-worm combos down through the rip at Race Rock, working the seam where the fast water meets the eddy on the northeast corner. Bucktails — 3 and 4 ounce, white and chartreuse — have been the better call up on top of Valiant itself where the rock pile sits shallower, 20 to 30 feet depending on where you're sitting relative to the pinnacle. Slow-roll them right through the slack, don't rush it.

Plum Gut has been the more consistent producer for numbers this week, even if it's not throwing trophy bass. Sea bass fishing there has been genuinely strong — somebody pulled a 28-inch, right around five pounds, off the structure on the east side of the Gut, and that's not a fluke catch, that's the kind of quality fish that tells you the reef community out there is healthy this summer. Squid strips and sea bass rigs, working 40 to 60 feet of water on the last two hours of the ebb when the current's manageable enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead. Fluke are mixed in with them, and honestly the fluke bite through Plum Gut and out into the Sluiceway has been the most dependable thing on my calendar the past ten days — moving water over structure, that's the whole game. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, drifted right along the edges where the Gut narrows down near Little Gull and Great Gull Island. Don't anchor there. You want to be drifting with the current, working bottom, not fighting to stay put.

Bluefish have been thinner out here than what the ocean-side guys are seeing with those bunker blitzes running up the Jersey coast, but we've had scattered choppers mixed into the bass around Race Rock after dark, and I expect that to build if bait keeps pushing east along the Sound. Worth having a wire leader rigged and ready even when you're bass fishing — you don't want to lose a good bucktail to a blue you didn't see coming.

No albies, no bonito yet through the Gut or the Sluiceway, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Montauk's sitting at 71.6, which is in the range where they typically show, and the temperature breaks are starting to set up the way they do right before the false albacore scout in. I'd start watching diving birds and nervous bait around Great Gull Island over the next two to three weeks — that's usually the tell before the epoxy jigs come out of the rocket launchers.

We flagged the offshore situation last week, and it's holding up — the warm filament water pushing toward the CT grounds has tuna and shark within range of boats running south out of the Sound, mirroring what the canyon fleets are already into. If you've got the range and the weather window, that's worth the run right now.

Looking ahead, I want to see how the bass respond once we're fully into the neap by midweek. Softer current usually means the fish spread out a little more off the tightest structure, which can mean fewer fish concentrated on Valiant but a wider window to find them. If the low-light pattern holds — and with this water temp, it will — I'd plan trips around dusk and the two hours after, working wire and bucktails through Race Rock and Valiant on whichever slack lines up closest to dark. That's where I'll be.

reports.headline: Ram Island rockpiles giving up porgy and school bass — bonito are next
reports.subhead: The neap has gone soft on the rips, the bass have gone nocturnal, and the water's finally in range for the first bonito of the year.
reports.body_markdown:
Poled out to Ram Island Tuesday morning on the last of the ebb and the boulders were doing what they do this time of year — holding shadow and bait in equal measure. Silversides tucked so tight against the granite you'd swim right past them if you weren't looking for the nervous water. A few terns working nothing, just checking. That's the tell. When the terns are checking instead of diving, the bait's still down in the rocks, not pushed up and panicked. Means the bass are around but not stacked yet, not blitzing. Patient water.

We're coming off the first-quarter neap now, and anybody who's fished the Race or Fishers Island Sound long enough knows what that does to this water. The current goes soft. Instead of that six-knot freight train ripping over the boulder fields at Wicopesset and the Sugar Reef humps, you get a manageable push — two, three knots at peak — and that widens the window. You don't have to time your drift to the fifteen-minute peak of the tide anymore. I had a good hour and a half of clean presentation through the Fishers Island rips Tuesday, working a black bucktail with a white curly tail down along bottom in eighteen to twenty-two feet, letting it stall and lift off the rock edges instead of ripping it through. Picked up two schoolies and lost a better fish that wrapped me around a boulder I know by name at this point.

The real bass right now are a night fish. Water's warm — New London's reading 70, and shallow water inside Little Narragansett Bay and around Mystic River mouth is running warmer than that by afternoon — so the keeper-class fish have pulled back into a dawn-dusk-and-dark pattern same as everywhere south of the Cape. If you want a shot at something over the slot, fish the last hour of light into full dark on the Stonington Breakwater, working a swimming plug or a live eel along the rock face on the outgoing. Wamphassuc Point does the same thing — current sweeps bait off that point on the ebb and the bigger fish sit right on the seam waiting. Eels fished slow, just enough weight to hold bottom, have out-produced everything else there the last two weeks.

Daytime, the fluke have been the honest bite. Channel edges off Esker Point, the flats inside Little Narragansett Bay, and the deeper cuts around Wilderness Point are holding fish in the eighteen-to-twenty-eight-foot range on the last two hours of the incoming, when the water's still moving but not screaming. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged dead slow along bottom — that combination has kept us in fish most mornings. Nothing giant, mostly seventeen to twenty inches with a scattering of keepers, but steady enough that a couple hours drifting the edges will put dinner in the cooler.

On the rock structure itself — Ram Island, the boulder fields off the Fishers Island side, the rips off North Dumpling — porgy and scup fishing has been about as good as I've seen it in years. Small hooks, squid strips or clam, right on bottom in fifteen to twenty-five feet, and you can load a bucket in an hour on the slack tide when the bass and blues aren't around to bully them off the structure. It's not glamorous but it's honest fishing, and it's the kind of thing that keeps a family in fresh fish through August.

Now here's the one I've been waiting to write. We said last week the water was getting close, and it's close. Block Island's pushing 68 and change, New London's sitting at 70, and that's the range where bonito start showing on this stretch of coast. I haven't seen one yet with my own eyes, and I want to be straight about that — no albies, no bones, nothing confirmed inshore of Fishers Island as of this week. But the temperature is there now, and the pattern from Rhode Island through Buzzards Bay says they're coming. I'd be watching the temp breaks off Napatree Point and East Point hard over the next ten days, small epoxy jigs and Deceiver-style flies ready in the boat bag, because when that first push of bonito or albies shows here it shows fast and it shows in a hurry — one morning nothing, next morning the water's exploding off Watch Hill Reef.

Look-ahead: with the current staying soft through the neap, I'd keep working the rips with patience rather than power — slower retrieves, more time on each drift. Fluke should stay consistent on the moving water as long as this clean weather holds. Bass will keep favoring the dark hours until we get a real cool-down. And I'll be out there most mornings this week with binoculars up, watching for that first sign of albie foam off the Fishers Island side. When it happens, you'll hear about it from me before anybody.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Seam Splits Warm and Cool: Blues Up Top, Bass Down Deep
reports.subhead: Bunker pushed hard into the harbor this week, and the river's temperature break is sorting bluefish from holdover stripers by the yard.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the seawall at Fort Trumbull Tuesday evening watching the ebb line set up, and you could see it before you could feel it — that ripple crease where the outgoing river water, cooler and darker, slides out past the fort and meets the harbor proper. Twenty years of watching that seam and it still tells you everything. This week it split the bite clean in half: bluefish working the warmer surface lens, stripers holding low in the cooler push underneath.

New London's reading around 70 degrees right now, a good two degrees cooler than what they're seeing over in the western Sound off Kings Point. That gap matters more than people think. The Thames stays a notch cooler than the open beaches because of the river flow dumping out of the dam upstream, and in the middle of July that's not a bad thing — it means the bass in this system haven't gone full nocturnal the way fish south of the Cape have. We're still getting some daytime interest here, but the real window is still that hour around dusk into full dark, and the hour either side of first light.

Bunker showed up thick in the harbor over the last ten days, working up through the mouth and pushing into the flats off Pleasure Beach and up toward the Gold Star Bridge. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bluefish would keep following bunker schools up the coast as long as the weather held calm and didn't scatter the bait — and that's exactly what's playing out here. Blues have been blowing up on top off Ocean Beach in the last two hours of daylight, and inside the harbor itself, schoolie-to-mid-size blues are chopping through peanut bunker right off the fort's rock pile. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — worked fast just under the surface has been the ticket, along with white or bone Rebel Jumpin' Minnows if the blues are up and splashing.

Striped bass are a different conversation, and a more honest one. The keeper-class fish haven't been stacking up in the numbers you'd want in July — this is typically the slower stretch of the season in the river, and this year's tracking that. What's producing are the holdover-type fish and a scattering of migratory stripers holding deep along the pilings at Gold Star Bridge, 20 to 28 feet on the down-current side depending on which span you're fishing, and along the deeper edge of the Fort Trumbull rip where the channel drops off toward 30 feet. Eels fished on the bottom, slow-lifted and dropped back on the ebb, have out-produced everything else for me this week. If you don't want to mess with eels, a 6-inch white or bunker-colored swimbait on a 3/4-ounce jig head, bounced along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, has been getting bit around the bridge fenders. Best window has consistently been that last hour of light sliding into dark — the fish are there earlier, but they don't commit until the light drops off and that current seam goes quiet.

We're heading into the first-quarter neap tomorrow, and that's actually going to help the rip fishing more than hurt it. Weaker current means the Fort Trumbull seam and the water off Eastern Point won't rip as hard, which widens the productive window on either side of the tide change instead of it being a tight 40-minute sprint. If you've struggled to get a swimbait down through that current in the past, the next few days are the easier version of that spot.

Hickory shad are still around the bridge pilings, showing on the surface in the early morning making those little dimpling rings when they're picking off bugs and small bait. Light spin gear, 1/8-ounce shad darts or small Kastmasters, ultralight leader — good time to bring a kid down and let them catch fish that actually fight above their size class. They'll thin out as we get into August but right now there's still a solid morning window most days.

Porgy fishing remains the steady, unglamorous option that never lets you down this time of year. The reef structure off Pleasure Beach and around the Beacon are holding good numbers in 20 to 35 feet — squid strips or sandworms on a high-low rig, small hooks, light enough sinker to feel the bottom on the drift. If the striper bite's slow, this is where I send people who just want bent rods and a fish dinner. Blackfish are still closed for the summer stretch here in Connecticut waters, so that's a fall conversation — I'll pick that back up when the season reopens.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working that Fort Trumbull to Gold Star Bridge stretch through the neap, fishing the widened tide windows in low light for stripers and hitting the harbor mouth in daylight for blues while the bunker hold. If the bunker push further up-river the way they have the last few days, I wouldn't be surprised to see that bluefish action creep closer to the bridge itself by the weekend. Watch the surface — where the bunker go, the blues follow, and that part of this pattern hasn't missed yet this year.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Finds Fluke Stacked at 35 Feet — Sea Bass Steady Off Twotree
reports.subhead: Neap tide easing the current just enough to put keeper fluke and quality sea bass in the box from Niantic Bay to Hole-in-the-Wall.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Sunbeam mates at the bait shop Thursday morning loading up on squid strips, and he didn't waste time telling me the fluke bite off Twotree Island Channel has gone from decent to genuinely good over the last ten days. That tracks with something I said last week — that back bay fluke would push out toward the inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water kept warming. Well, here we are. Niantic Bay proper has gone quiet on the flatties, but the channel edges and the rock piles off Hole-in-the-Wall are holding fish that mean business.

Water at New London is sitting around 70 degrees, which is right in that sweet spot where fluke stop sulking on soft bottom and start setting up on structure where the bait gets pinned by current. The drift boats working Twotree are marking fish in 35 to 40 feet, and the program that's putting them in the cooler is simple — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow on the down-current drift. Guys jigging bare bucktails without the Gulp trailer are getting outfished two-to-one right now. When the drift speeds up on the bigger tides, bump up to a full ounce so you're still ticking bottom instead of sailing over their heads.

Here's the timing piece that matters this week: we're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that's going to soften the current through the Race, the Twotree rip, and around Black Point. I've seen this pattern plenty of times — when the tide range narrows like this, the fluke bite doesn't die, it actually gets more comfortable to fish because you're not fighting a screaming drift all day. Slower current means you can slow your presentation down too, which is exactly what these fish want in July heat. If you've been getting your bucktail ripped out of the strike zone on the bigger tides, this is your window.

Sea bass have been the more consistent story all month, and Black Point continues to be the go-to. The rock piles off the point in 25 to 45 feet are stacked with keepers, and I heard secondhand about a fat one pulled off structure near Plum Gut pushing 28 inches and better than 5 pounds — that's the kind of quality that's out there right now if you find the right piece of bottom. Standard sea bass rigs, double hook, fresh clam or squid, fished tight to structure on the drift or at anchor on the up-current side of the rocks. Don't be afraid to move around McCook Point too if Black Point gets crowded on a weekend — the bottom there holds fish nobody's leaning on as hard.

Porgies are filling out the box nicely for anyone bottom fishing bloodworms or clam around the same structure — Bartlett Reef and the rockier stretches off Black Point have been thick with them, and they're a good consolation prize on days the sea bass get finicky.

Striped bass is where I have to be honest with you — the daytime bite in this stretch of Sound is tough right now. Warm surface water has these fish keyed into low-light and after-dark feeding, same as everywhere south of the Cape. The guys doing well are fishing dusk into full dark around the current breaks near the Race and off Black Point, working live eels or big swimbaits on the drop as the tide starts moving. If you're a daylight-only angler, I'd shift my striper expectations down and lean harder into the fluke and sea bass, which don't care about the sun the way stripers do this time of year.

Bluefish have started showing more consistently inside Niantic Bay and around the river mouth, chopping through peanut bunker on the surface in the early morning. Nothing blitz-scale like what's happening in the western Sound and down the Jersey beaches, but enough that a few guys working topwater poppers or bunker chunks off the jetties have had good mornings. Worth having a rod rigged for it if you're already out there for fluke.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the fluke bite to keep building through this neap and into next week as the current window widens for slow presentations — that's usually when Twotree and Hole-in-the-Wall really turn on. Sea bass should stay steady at Black Point as long as the structure keeps holding bait, though I wouldn't be shocked if the bigger fish thin out a little as more boats find that Plum Gut-area piece. Striper fishing is going to stay a dawn-and-dark game until we get a real cool-down, so plan your trip around the tide change at first light or after sunset if bass are the target. No sign of albies or bonito in this stretch yet — that push is still working its way east, and eastern Connecticut is typically last on that list, so don't burn gas looking for them just yet.

reports.headline: Wild Rice Greens Up on Great Island — River Bass Hold Deep as Fluke Push Into the Lower Stretch
reports.subhead: With the shad run six weeks behind us, the river's summer residents are settling into their July pattern — stripers in the cool seams, fluke on the sand, and the first push of blues at the mouth.
reports.body_markdown:
The wild rice is up to my knees along the Great Island flats now, and the pickerelweed's gone purple in every quiet cove from Lord Cove to the Lieutenant River. That's how I mark the calendar this time of year — not by the tide book, though I keep that close too, but by what's blooming in the marsh. Fifty springs of watching this river teaches you that the plants don't lie. When the rice greens up like this, the shad run is a memory, the ospreys are feeding fledglings off the nest platforms at Great Island, and the river settles into its long, hot middle age. That's where we are.

This isn't shad water anymore — that run came and went back in May, right on schedule, and I said my goodbyes to it weeks ago. What we've got now is the river's summer program: striped bass holding in the current seams, the first real push of summer flounder into the lower stretch, white perch working the coves, and bluefish starting to show where the river dumps into the Sound. I flagged this pattern last week — said the bass would stay in the river right through the heat and that fluke would start pushing up from the Sound side. Both of those calls are holding up on the water this week.

The Sound itself is carrying a real thermal gradient right now, cooler out toward New London, warmer up around the western reaches, and that gradient matters for how fish stage at our river mouth. The Connecticut River, even with all that fresh water dumping through, warms up fast in the shallow coves under a July sun — I've felt water in the upper 70s in the skinny stuff off Calves Island by mid-afternoon. That pushes the stripers to look for moving, oxygenated water, and they're finding it in the tidal current off Saybrook Point, under the railroad bridge in Old Saybrook, and around the drawbridge pilings up in Essex. Early light and the last two hours of the incoming are still your best windows before the sun really starts cooking the flats.

At Saybrook Point, the breakwater has been holding fish right at first light — schoolie-to-mid-twenties stripers working bunker pods that push in and out with the tide. Topwater plugs, a Doc or a Gibbs pencil worked with a walk-the-dog retrieve, have drawn some violent strikes right in the white water off the rocks. Once the sun's up and that bite shuts down, guys are switching to bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce, tipped with a curl-tail grub, worked slow along the bottom where the current pinches around the jetty rocks.

Up around Nott Island and the flats off Great Island, the pattern's more subtle — bass tailing in the shallows on the last hour of the flood, working grass shrimp and mummichogs out of the marsh grass. A weightless soft plastic, something like a Slug-Go in white or bone, cast just ahead of a push or a nervous swirl, has been the right call there. It's sight-fishing more than blind-casting, and you need calm water and decent light to see the fish before you cast to them. Mornings with a light southerly have been kinder to that game than the choppier afternoons.

The fluke news is the real story developing right now. We've been seeing keeper-class summer flounder showing up in the deeper channel water off Nott Island and around the Calves Island humps, in fifteen to twenty-two feet, on the tail end of the outgoing tide when the current really gets moving through there. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, have taken fish to four and five pounds. It's not a wide-open bite — you're covering water and picking off fish here and there rather than filling a cooler — but the presence of quality fluke this far up the river, past Essex, is worth noting. That's new water for a lot of guys who only think fluke when they're down in the Sound proper.

White perch are doing what white perch do in July — holding in the deeper holes of the quieter coves, North Cove in Old Lyme and the mouth of the Lieutenant River among them, and they'll take a small piece of nightcrawler or bloodworm fished on a light Carolina rig right along bottom. Not glamorous fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good way to keep kids interested when the bigger bite is slow.

Bluefish are the wildcard piece right now. We're starting to see the first schools working bunker right at the river mouth, out past the Saybrook breakwater toward the Sound, chopping bait on the surface in the mornings. If that bunker migration keeps pushing the way it has along the coast, I'd expect those blues to keep showing here through the next couple weeks, and they'll mix right in with the striper bite on the same tides and the same metal — a one-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins will draw both species out there.

Looking ahead, we're sliding into the first-quarter neap around the 21st, which will soften the current through the river mouth rips for a few days. That usually widens the productive window beyond just the peak of the tide — worth remembering if you can only get out mid-morning rather than at first light. If the heat holds and the coves keep climbing into the upper 70s, I'd expect the bass to keep favoring the moving water under the bridges and around the breakwater rather than the open flats during the day, saving the shallow work for dawn and dusk. The fluke push is the one to watch — if it keeps building the way it has this week, the lower river could have a real summer flounder fishery worth targeting through August.

reports.headline: Breakwall Porgies Stacked, Blackfish Sulking, Sea Bass Filling the Gaps
reports.subhead: The rockpiles are still paying dividends on scup and sea bass while the tautog take a summer siesta and stripers slide into the shadows.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, half-tide push, I'm working the outer breakwall off New Haven Harbor with a high-low rig and green crab chunks, and I can't get the bait down twenty feet before something's chewing. Porgies — scup, if you want to be proper about it — stacked on the rockpile in 18 to 22 feet like they're waiting in line. Nothing huge, mostly 9 to 11 inches, but enough 12-plus fish mixed in to make the cooler heavy by the time the tide slowed. That's the story on this beat right now: the bottom bite is doing the heavy lifting while the water upstairs sorts itself out.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on most of these rockpiles, which is normal for late July but the size has been a pleasant surprise. I've had a handful of 14 to 16-inch fish come off the deeper humps around Falkner Island — 30 to 35 feet, drifting squid strips and small Gulp baits on a jig head — and one gentleman on the dock had a fish pushing three pounds off Stratford Shoal that made his day. The keepers aren't wall-to-wall, but if you're working structure with any kind of intent — moving spot to spot instead of anchoring on one rock and hoping — you're putting fish in the box.

Blackfish, on the other hand, are being difficult. This is typical mid-summer behavior — tautog don't love warm water any more than we love fishing in it — and the bite has gone quiet on the shallower rockpiles around the harbor mouth. I found a few willing fish early, right at first light before the boat traffic stirred things up, working green crabs tight to the mussel beds on the Milford Gulf side. But it's a grind right now. If blackfish is your target, I'd fish the first hour of daylight and not much past it, then pivot to porgies and sea bass for the rest of the trip.

Stripers are exactly where you'd expect them with the water running warm — Kings Point was reading 72 and change this week, and while I don't have a hard number for the harbor itself, it's tracking right there with it. That kind of warmth pushes keeper bass into a low-light and after-dark pattern, and Charles Island is proving it out. The sandbar that connects to the island at low tide has been holding fish on the ebb right at dusk — live eels and chunk bunker fished tight to the drop-off edge, right where the current starts to rip off the bar. Daytime, forget it; those fish are sulking deep or tucked into shadow. If you want a shot at a keeper on this beat right now, plan your trip around the last hour of light into full dark, and fish the moving water, not the slack.

Bluefish have been a nice surprise on top of Stratford Shoal in the early morning — nothing like the blitzes you're hearing about further down the coast on the bunker schools, but enough choppers slashing through peanut bunker at dawn to make topwater fun again. Deadly Dicks and small poppers worked fast across the surface have been drawing strikes. It's a short window, usually the first 45 minutes of light before the sun gets up and the fish drop, but it's been consistent enough this week that I'd call it worth setting an alarm for.

Fluke are still the most dependable bite in the zone if you're willing to move and cover structure edges. Milford Gulf and the drop-offs around the Charles Island sandbar have both produced fish in the 3 to 5 pound range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktail combos, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the incoming. The key word is moving water — fluke here want current, and we're heading into a first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the push through the middle of the week. That's not a death sentence, but it means shorter, weaker bite windows around the tide changes. I'd fish the top of the flood and the top of the ebb rather than trying to grind it out mid-tide when the water's barely crawling.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason to change the game plan much. The rockpile bite on porgies and sea bass should hold steady through the neap — that bottom bite doesn't need much current to stay productive, which is exactly why it's carrying the week. Blackfish should start perking back up once we get past this stretch of flat calm heat, probably late next week if a cold front pushes through and knocks the surface temp down a couple degrees. Stripers will stay a dawn-dusk-and-dark proposition until that happens too. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be on the breakwall at first light for blues and porgies, then off to Charles Island for the last of the outgoing tide before the sun climbs too high. That's about as honest a plan as I can give you right now — the water's warm, the current's about to go soft, and the fish are telling us to work smarter, not longer.

reports.headline: Cockenoe Reef on the Slack: Sea Bass Numbers Build Toward August
reports.subhead: The neap tide easing in behind this week widens the strike window on the reef system, while the bass go quiet until dark.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a decision to make before I even left the dock — Cockenoe or Penfield. Both have been holding fish, but the reef you pick this time of year is a bet on current speed as much as anything else. With the first-quarter neap sliding in on the 21st and 22nd, I wanted the reef where a softer current works in my favor, not against me. Cockenoe's northeast drop, that 18-to-25-foot ledge off the back side of the island, fishes best when the drift is slow enough to keep a jig in the zone instead of skipping it across the rocks. So Cockenoe it was, and it paid off.

We flagged this last week — said sea bass would keep building through August — and that's exactly what's showing up on the reef. Fish to four pounds came off that ledge on half-ounce jigheads tipped with Gulp Sandworms and squid strips, worked on the last two hours of the incoming when the current finally settled enough to hold bottom without a heavier lead. The bite wasn't nonstop — you're picking through a lot of shorts to find the keepers — but the numbers are trending the right direction week over week, and with water in the western basin sitting warm (Kings Point read 72 degrees, a full two ticks above New London's 70), that thermal cushion should keep the sea bass pattern developing rather than stalling out.

Porgies are riding shotgun on the same structure. The Cows off Stamford and the flats tight to Greenwich Point are both loaded right now — sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinkers, anchored up rather than drifting. These fish don't need finesse, they need you in the right depth, and 15 to 20 feet over broken bottom is where they're stacking on the last of the ebb into dead low.

Fluke is the more dependable check-writer this week, and it's holding to structure the way it always does even with the Sound running warm. Penfield Reef and the channel edges off Sheffield Island are both producing on moving water — I want current, either tide, doesn't matter which, as long as it's pushing. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of Gulp, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the reef falls into 20 to 30 feet. Best fish this week went just over four pounds off Penfield on the outgoing, but the west end of my beat is fishing better than the east right now — that west-to-east temperature gradient across the Sound means the bait and the fluke that follow it are both a little more concentrated up here toward Greenwich and Norwalk than they are further out toward the Race.

Striped bass are the tough conversation this week, and I'm not going to dress it up. The pattern coastwide right now is nocturnal — warm, shallow water has pushed keeper-class bass onto a dawn, dusk, and after-dark clock, and Western Sound is no exception. Daytime trips around the Norwalk Islands and Sheffield Island are mostly quiet unless you catch a bluefish blitz pushing bait to the surface and a bass sneaks in underneath it. If you want a real shot at bass, you're fishing the last hour of light into full dark, working bunker chunks or live bait around the rips off Greenwich Point and Sheffield Island, or swimming an eel along the deeper edges of Cockenoe after the boat traffic clears out. It's a different game than June — slower, quieter, more patient — but the fish are there. I had two bass over 30 inches on chunked bunker at Sheffield Island Wednesday night, both after ten o'clock, both on the last of the ebb.

Bluefish are showing in pockets, not blitzes — schools riding bunker through the area, occasionally erupting off the Norwalk Islands or out toward the Cows. When you see the birds working, get on it fast with poppers or a straight metal like a Kastmaster, because these windows close in minutes, not hours. It's not the sustained daylight blitz you're hearing about further down the coast, but it's enough action to make a slow bass morning worth staying out for.

Weekend boat traffic is its own tide chart out here. Saturday and Sunday mid-day, the mooring fields off Norwalk and the channel into Sheffield Island turn into a highway, and it pushes fish off the shallower structure. My move is simple — fish the backside structure the pleasure boats ignore, or get out at first light and be off the water by nine, before the parade starts.

Looking ahead, the neap settling in over the next two days should widen the productive windows on every reef in the system — slower current means longer drifts and more time with your bait in the strike zone before you have to reset. I'd expect sea bass to keep climbing on Cockenoe and the Norwalk Islands structure, fluke to hold steady on Penfield and Sheffield as long as the water stays moving, and bass to stay a night bite until we get a real wind shift out of the northeast to knock the surface temperature down. If I had one trip to make this week, it'd be a night tide at Sheffield Island on the last of the ebb, bunker chunks soaking on the bottom, with a bucktail rod rigged and ready in case the fluke show up first.

reports.headline: Plum Gut on the Neap: Bass Come Out After Dark, Porgies Never Left
reports.subhead: Steady scup and blackfish on the reefs, bass playing hard to get till the sun drops — and the water's finally soft enough to fish slow again.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a young fella stop me at the ramp in Mattituck the other morning, tackle still tagged from the shop, asking why he couldn't buy a striper bite at ten in the morning off Horton Point. I told him what my father told me — fish don't own a watch, but they do own a thermometer. Sixty years I've watched this shoreline, and every July it's the same lesson relearned: when the water goes soft and warm the way it has this month, the big bass quit feeding on the clock and start feeding on the light. Or the lack of it.

That's exactly what's happening right now. The Sound's carrying a real gradient this week — warmer up toward the western reaches, cooling off as you swing east toward the Race, with New London running a good two degrees under what Kings Point's showing. Out here on the North Fork we're sitting in between, and the water off Rocky Point and Horton has that thick, milky-green July look to it that tells you the bait's been in tight and the bass have had their fill during the day. So they're sliding into ambush mode — dawn, dusk, full dark — working the rips and current seams where the bait gets pinned rather than chasing it out in open water under the sun.

Plum Gut's been the honest word this week. Boats working the tide changes at first light have been picking up slot fish and the occasional overslot working bucktails — three-quarter to one-ounce — bounced along the bottom where the rip folds over itself on the edge of the reef. Nothing that'll make you call your buddy screaming, but steady enough that a patient rod isn't going home skunked. After dark, eels and soft plastic swimbaits swum slow through the same water have been the better producers, and that's not an accident — bass sitting in a strong current don't want to chase, they want the bait to come to them.
