Here's the piece worth paying attention to: we're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that's going to ease the current speed through the Gut and the rips off Orient over the next several days. I've fished this pattern more times than I can count — when the tide slacks off from those big spring runs, the bite window actually widens. You don't need to be standing there at the exact peak of the moving water anymore. Lighter jigs, slower retrieves, more patience — that's the move. If you've been fishing three-quarter ounce bucktails, drop to a half. Let it hang a little longer in the seam instead of ripping it through.

Fluke, porgy, and blackfish have been the meat and potatoes out here and I won't oversell them because they don't need it — they've just been quietly good, week after week. Porgies on the reef structure off Rocky Point and out toward Orient have been thick, taking sandworms and green crab on standard hi-lo rigs in twenty to thirty-five feet, no real trick to it, just find the rock piles and drop straight down. Blackfish are mixed in on the same structure, crab baits working best, though the real tog fishing won't heat up proper till fall — right now it's a bonus fish while you're chasing scup. Fluke have been solid drifting the sand-to-structure edges off Mattituck Inlet and along the flats toward Horton, four-inch white Gulp on a bucktail teaser rig doing the damage on the moving water, better on the last two hours of the ebb when the bait gets pushed out of the inlet mouth.

Weakfish — and I say this carefully because that stock's had some lean years — have started showing again on the calm, warm evenings, a few keeper-class fish mixed in with the fluke drifts near the inlet mouths. We figured that rebuild might happen if the weather stayed settled, and it looks like it's starting to. Small sample size, but worth keeping an eye on if you're out there at last light with soft plastics.

Bluefish have mostly stayed offshore of us so far, chopping bunker pods along the beaches to our west, but I wouldn't be shocked to see that push our way — when those bunker schools finally work up the Sound proper, the blues follow, and Horton Point and Rocky Point both have the structure to hold them once they arrive.

We also flagged last week that this stretch could see some early bonito scouting activity as the water kept climbing, riding the same warmth that's been pushing albies and bonito around Montauk and the Vineyard. Haven't had a confirmed fish yet in my water, but the conditions are lining up — if you're working the Orient side and see nervous bait getting pushed on the surface in calm early morning light, don't assume it's just blues. Worth a few casts with a small metal to check.

Looking ahead: with the neap easing the current and the moon going quiet, I'd fish the low-light windows at Plum Gut and Orient with patience over horsepower, keep the porgy gear rigged for the slow stretches, and watch that inlet water at dusk for weakfish and maybe that first bonito surprise. Nothing here is a sure thing, but the pattern's honest, and honest is what this stretch of water has always rewarded.

reports.headline: Forty Miles East of Atlantis, a White Marlin Made the Whole Trip Worth the Diesel
reports.subhead: The bluefin slot fish held steady, the bigeye showed at the edge, and a marlin in the spread confirmed what we've been watching build all month.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 3:15 Tuesday morning, running dark past the Point with about 340 gallons aboard and a hundred-mile shot to the east wall at Atlantis ahead of us. Six hours at a fuel-conscious 17 knots gets you there with enough in the tanks to fish the day and still have a cushion home — that's the math I run every time, because out here the fuel gauge decides how long you get to fish, not the bite. We were rigged for tuna, dredge out, teasers up, and by 10 a.m. we were working the 100-fathom curve where the water goes from a flat green-blue shelf color to that deeper cobalt you get when warm eddy water is pushing up over the edge. That's where it happened — a white marlin came up on the long teaser, walked on its tail for what felt like a full minute, then dropped off before the pitch bait ever got there. We didn't boat him. Didn't need to. That fish told us everything we needed to know about where the season's headed.

We flagged this back a few days ago — said the billfish migration would keep building through July, and there it was, right on the edge where the warm water's pushing in. That's not a fluke sighting. Guys working Veatch and the water off Block Canyon have been seeing the same thing — marlin showing in the spread, sometimes two or three fish a day, mostly whites, occasional blue reported further south. Nothing you can plan a whole trip around yet, but it's building, not fading, and that matters when you're burning the fuel it takes to get out here.

The bluefin have been the more dependable story. Since the trophy category closed July 3rd, the slot fishery — 27 inches to just under 47 — has held up well on both sides of the canyon country. We took two keeper bluefin trolling a mixed spread of cedar plugs and small Ilanders about a mile inside the 100-fathom line at Atlantis, fish in the 30-35 inch class, both on the same spread pass on the shady side of a bait slick. Boats running out of Block Island and Point Judith toward Veatch have reported the same size class, same pattern — small bluefin holding tight to bait, not scattered out over open water. If you're headed that way, don't overthink the spread. A basic 5-6 line troll with a chunk of ballyhoo behind a bird, a couple of skirted plugs, and a naked ballyhoo way back has been plenty.

The bigger story for those willing to run the extra hour or two is the yellowfin and bigeye building at the edges — Hudson, Wilmington, and Washington have gotten most of the attention, but the east canyons are seeing spillover as that warm Gulf Stream eddy water keeps pushing bait up onto the shelf. We marked bait balls stacked from 60 to 180 feet on the sounder working the temp break where the water jumped from a shelf-typical 69-70°F to better than 75°F in the space of half a mile — that's the kind of seam that holds fish, and it's worth working slow, even trolling back over it twice, before committing to a drift or chunk.

Wahoo and mahi have been mixed in as a bycatch more than a target — a few wahoo taken on high-speed spreads run wide off the shotgun position, 12-14 knots with a horse ballyhoo or a jet head lure, and mahi showing under any floating debris or weed line you cross on the way out. Nothing you'd plan the whole day around, but worth a pass if you see color change or grass on the surface.

Weather's been the deciding factor more than anything biological. Stable high pressure has held for close to a week now, and that's the only reason boats have been able to make the run to Atlantis and Veatch on a normal schedule instead of picking weather windows. The first-quarter moon on the 21st brings us into neap tide, which doesn't move canyon fish much directly — these fish are driven by current edges and eddy structure more than tidal stage — but it does mean less push at the inlets on the way out and in, which matters more than people think when you're running Montauk or the Race in the dark.

Looking ahead, if the high holds through the weekend like it's shaping up to, I'd expect the yellowfin bite to keep building rather than back off — the bait's there, the temperature break is holding, and boats aren't reporting the eddy sliding off yet. If I had one day this week, I'd run to the east wall at Atlantis early, work the 100-fathom edge where the color changes, and keep a long teaser out all day regardless of what's happening in the spread — that marlin showed us the bigger picture is still unfolding out there, whether or not we manage to close the deal on the next one.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Slow Monday, stacked Thursday: Spencer's bigeye chunk bailed out a rough start
reports.subhead: The front half of the week had us running four different numbers looking for bait — the back half we didn't have to leave the slick.
reports.body_markdown:
Mixed grades this week, and I mean that literally spot by spot. Norfolk gets a C, Lindenkohl a solid B, Poor Man's a B-plus with an asterisk for the marlin work, and Spencer — Spencer earns the A. If you fished all four like we did, you saw the whole spectrum of what late July canyon fishing looks like right now: patchy in spots, loaded in others, and the difference came down to who found the temp break and who didn't.

Here's the why. High pressure sat on top of the Mid-Atlantic most of the week and didn't budge, and that mattered more than any single tactic. We said last week the bite would hold as long as the offshore water stayed put, and it did — that eddy of warm Gulf Stream water that's been nosing up against the canyon edges never slid off like it sometimes does when a front comes through. That kept bait pinned to the structure instead of scattering it, and it's the same reason Hudson, Wilmington, and Washington to the north have been quietly building all month. We're just getting our version of it down here.

Spencer was the standout. We worked the 100-fathom curl around 39°34'N/71°56'W starting before first light, running a standard spread — green-and-yellow machines down the shotgun, naked ballyhoo on the short riggers, a small spreader bar in the shotgun slot. Yellowfin from 25 to about 45 pounds came steady through the morning push, best window right at gray light through about 9 a.m. before the bite went quiet under the sun. That's when we switched over — anchored up on the edge in around 900 feet, butterfish chunks fanned out slow off the stern, and let it soak into the evening. Bigeye showed up reliably on that slick, biggest one we boated pushing 180. Night chunking is still the money tactic for bigeye down here, and it hasn't changed — small chunks, thin leader, patience, and staying off the spreader lights until the bite's established.

Lindenkohl fished a notch cooler and a notch slower on the tuna side, but mahi more than made up for it. We found a good weed line stacked with sargassum working the 60-fathom curve, and it was stop-and-go dolphin the whole drift — schoolies in the 5 to 10 pound range hammering green-and-white Ilanders and dink ballyhoo skipped off flat lines, with a couple better fish to 15 mixed in that wanted a pitch bait once we got baits in the water near the structure. If you're burning gas out there anyway, don't run past floating debris or a clean grass line without a look. That bite doesn't need perfect water temp, it just needs cover.

Poor Man's is where the billfish work is picking up, and it's exactly the pattern we flagged coming — white marlin migration building through July, and this week it showed. We had shots on teasers most days we ran that canyon, dink ballyhoo behind small spreader bars pulling fish up, and we put a handful of whites in the 38 to 42 inch class in the water on pitch baits before release. Nothing stacked wall to wall, but consistent enough that if marlin are your thing, Poor Man's is where I'd point the bow right now over Norfolk or Lindenkohl.

Norfolk was the disappointment, honestly. We ran down there twice hoping the deeper, more southern water would hold better numbers, and both times we found clean water but thin bait — the temp break wasn't as sharp, sitting closer to 74 to 75 degrees instead of the harder 76-plus edge we found up at Spencer. Marked some fish on the machine but couldn't buy a real bite until late in the day on the last trip, when a few smaller yellowfin came through on the troll right at the canyon's northern lip. If Norfolk's on your list this week, I'd treat it as a scouting run rather than the primary play until that edge tightens back up.

Looking ahead, the moon's rolling into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which should ease current across the board — less water moving means chunk slicks hold shape longer and anchor fishing gets a little more forgiving, which favors the Spencer bigeye program specifically. Best case, that stable high pressure holds one more week and the eddy stays glued to the shelf edge the way it has been — if that happens, I'd keep running Spencer for the double-header troll-then-chunk day and lean on Poor Man's for marlin shots. If the water slides east like it sometimes does this time of year, Lindenkohl's weed lines become the fallback and Norfolk's the one I'd skip until it resets. Either way, check the temp break before you commit fuel — that's been the single biggest difference between a great trip and a mediocre one all week.

reports.headline: July 20 and Washington Is Already Fishing Like It's August
reports.subhead: The new moon spring current we flagged last week hit the shelf break right on schedule, and now the eddy's holding yellowfin and bigeye tighter to the canyon than they usually sit for another three weeks.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock: why does Washington always seem to turn on before Hudson, before Baltimore, before the boys up north even start talking tuna. It's not luck. It's geography. Washington sits closer to where the Gulf Stream throws its meanders inshore, and when one of those warm-water eddies breaks off and slides up over the canyon, we get first crack at it while everybody else is still waiting on their water to turn blue. This year the eddy showed up early and it showed up close — inside the 100-fathom curve on the north wall, not way out on the break like a normal mid-July setup. That's a two-to-three-week jump on the calendar, and it's why boats running out of Cape May and Ocean City have had the shortest steam to warm, clean water of any fleet on the coast right now.

We called this one. Said the new moon spring tide would push hard current across the shelf break and stack bait right where the temperature line sits, and that's exactly what happened. The tidal forcing peaked right on schedule and it bait on both walls — not just the usual squid and flying fish showing on the meter, but real concentrations of small mahi holding under the pods, which tells you the whole ecosystem out there woke up at once, not just the tuna.

The fishing itself has been solid, not spectacular — and I'll be straight with you, it's been a week where the boats that worked the temperature break instead of just running numbers put up better counts. My best afternoons have come working the color change along the north wall, roughly 39°18'N, 71°42'W out to the 39°12'N line, trolling a spread of medium ballyhoo behind Islanders and a couple of naked skirted baits down the middle. Yellowfin have been running 35 to 55 pounds, mixed in with a few bigeye pushing 100-plus on the long riggers fished deep behind the pattern. Wahoo have been the bonus fish — high-speed trolling a rigged Braid Runner or a Yo-Zuri bonito along the edge of the eddy where the water goes from green to that ink blue in about a hundred yards has produced fish in the 40 to 60 pound class, usually first thing at light or right at the temp break itself.

Night bite has been the more consistent producer if you want a sure thing over a home-run swing. Anchoring up on the south wall in 900 to 1200 feet, setting up a chunk line with butterflied bunker and a few chunks of squid mixed in, has been drawing steady yellowfin after dark, especially on the tide change. That's classic Washington behavior — the current on the spring tide runs hard enough to hold the chunk slick tight and keep bait in the zone instead of blowing it out into nothing. White marlin have shown up in the spread too, mostly on the troll during daylight hours working ballyhoo skipping just off the surface — nothing stacked, but enough action on the long and short riggers that I'd keep a pitch bait rigged and ready if you're running a spread out here this week.

I won't oversell it. Some boats have had quiet mornings where the bite just didn't show even with good-looking water — that's canyon fishing, and Washington isn't immune to it just because it runs early. The days that produced were the ones where guys worked the edges patiently instead of blasting through looking for birds. Bait has been thick enough that the fish don't have to move much, which means you have to go find them rather than wait for them to come find you.

Looking ahead, the first-quarter neap hits tomorrow, and that's going to soften the current across the shelf break for a few days. Historically that widens the bite window rather than shutting it down — less brutal drift speed means baits track cleaner and the fish don't have to fight as hard to feed, so I'd expect the yellowfin and bigeye numbers to keep building through the back half of the week rather than fade. If the eddy holds its position over the canyon like it has the last several days, I'd keep working that north wall temperature break early and slide to the chunk on the south side after dark. If it slides east the way these things sometimes do heading into August, I'll be adjusting toward the deeper break and you should too. Either way, Washington's running a full season ahead of pace, and for those of us who've fished this canyon long enough to know its rhythm, that's not a surprise — that's just what this piece of water does when the Stream decides to lean our way.

reports.headline: Ran the night shift on Wilmington for bigeye — three bites, two in the boat, and a plan to do it again
reports.subhead: Stable high pressure and a warming eddy edge turned the chunk bite on after dark, while daytime trolling picked at yellowfin along the break.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Wednesday to skip the troll spread and run straight to the chunk grounds after dark, and it paid for the fuel plus a little extra. We'd been picking at yellowfin trolling the temp break most of the week — decent fish, but the numbers weren't there to justify burning that much diesel every trip. So when the reports started stacking up on bigeye holding under the chunk slicks overnight, I figured the smarter play was to run out in the afternoon, set up on the northeast edge of the canyon around 200 fathoms, and let the sun go down on us.

Glad we did it. We anchored up on a hard temperature break where the Gulf Stream eddy water is pushing warm and clean against the canyon wall — you could see it in the color change alone, that deep cobalt against the greener inshore water. Butterfish chunks on a slow, steady flow, no big globs, just a consistent trickle to keep the slick going without feeding them full. First bite came about ninety minutes after dark, second one an hour after that. Lost one at the boat on a hook pull, but we put two bigeye in the box in the 140 to 160-pound range. That's a good night by any measure, and it confirms what we were hearing — the bigeye have been sitting under those slicks consistently this week, not just a one-off.

Daytime yellowfin trolling has been more of a grind. We're still picking them off the same water — the temp break running along the 100-fathom line on the west side of Wilmington, where the eddy has set up a nice defined edge. Spreads with green machines and small Ilanders in the 6 to 8-inch range, worked well off the shotgun and long rigger positions, have been drawing strikes, but you're working for every fish. Two or three keeper yellowfin on a six-hour troll is about average right now — not bad, not the kind of numbers where you stop counting. If you want volume, the chunk bite after dark on bigeye has been the better use of your time and fuel this week.

Wahoo have shown up sporadically on the high-speed gear when we've run wire off the corners of the canyon, but nothing consistent enough to build a whole trip around. Mahi are scattered around any floating weed or debris — we picked up a pair of nice bulls, mid-teens, off a weed line about six miles short of the canyon on the way out. Worth a five-minute detour if you see color or grass, but don't expect a stacked-up school this time of year here. It's opportunistic fishing, not a target.

White marlin have been mostly a daytime troll story, and the numbers are building the way they typically do this time of July. We had two flag-raisers on naked ballyhoo skipping off the left long and short riggers — one pitch bait connection, one that just wouldn't commit. Nothing to write home about yet, but it lines up with what we expected heading into late July, and it's the kind of thing where patience pays. We flagged this a week ago — said the billfish migration would keep building through the month — and that's exactly the direction it's trending. Not a banner week, but more shots than we had two weeks back.

Water's been stable, which is the biggest factor in all of this. High pressure has held for going on ten days now, and that's let the eddy structure mature instead of getting torn apart by wind and swell. The break we've been working sits roughly along 38°25'N, 74°10'W give or take a mile depending on the day, right where the canyon wall drops from 100 to 300 fathoms fast. That kind of bottom contour paired with a stable temperature edge is exactly the setup that holds bait, and holding bait holds tuna.

Bluefin have stayed in the mix too, mostly smaller class fish inside the recreational slot, caught incidentally while working the yellowfin spread or on the troll transition running out to the canyon. Nothing worth a dedicated trip on its own right now, but a nice bonus if you connect.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this to fall apart in the next several days. The high pressure pattern isn't showing signs of breaking, and that eddy edge has had time to organize instead of getting pushed around. If it holds through the weekend, I'd keep running the same play — troll the break during daylight for yellowfin and any wahoo that want to show up, then set up on the chunk after dark for bigeye. If the wind swings and starts mixing that break apart, I'd expect the yellowfin bite to get patchy fast, and I'd lean even harder into the night chunk since bigeye tend to hold deeper and care less about surface chop. Either way, I'm planning on running back out this week — the ratio of fuel burned to fish in the box has finally tilted in our favor, and I want to see if it holds.

reports.headline: 73.6°F at Buoy 44025 — the Warm Filament Still Owns the Hudson Wall
reports.subhead: A stable eddy is holding bait right on the 100-fathom break, and yellowfin, bigeye, and slot bluefin are all working it — but you have to find the right water first.
reports.body_markdown:
73.6°F. That's the read off Buoy 44025 out in the Bight as of Saturday afternoon, and by itself it doesn't tell you much — but stack it against Kings Point at 71.6 and New London at 67.6 and you've got a picture of a coastal shelf that's still cool relative to what's sitting out past the edge. That gradient matters because it's exactly the kind of setup that pushes warm-core ring water tight against the canyon wall instead of letting it slide offshore. I've watched this pattern build for ten days now under a stubborn high pressure ridge, and it's done what I told you it would do two weeks back — the filament held, and the bite kept building instead of fading. We called that. Now it's paying off.

The run out is a hair over 100 nautical miles from Manasquan, closer to 96 out of Shinnecock, and either way you're pointed at the same target: the 100-fathom line running north-south through 72°30'W, with the heaviest concentration of life stacking up around the Dip near 39°51'N/72°32'W and pushing south to the Claw at 39°44'N/72°28'W. Boats working that stretch this week found green-blue water, a hard temp break, and bait balls thick enough to show up as a solid red smear on the sounder in 900 to 1,100 feet. That's your daytime yellowfin and bigeye zone — troll ballyhoo behind Ilanders and small spreader bars through the morning, then anchor up or drift the edge after dark and chunk butterfish once the sun's off the water. Both methods have been putting fish on the deck, which tells you the tuna aren't just reacting to one trigger — they've got bait to eat and they're eating around the clock.

The daytime troll bite has been mostly yellowfin in the 30 to 60-pound class, with bigeye mixed in on the deeper drops along the west wall where the bottom falls from 90 to 120 fathoms fast. That's classic bigeye structure — steep relief pushes bait up the water column and gives them a wall to work against. At night, the chunk bite has produced better averages on bigeye, some pushing toward the 100-pound mark, and that's not surprising given the timing — we're coming into the July 21 first-quarter neap, which softens current speed across the whole Bight. Less current means a slower drift on anchor, which means your chunk baits stay in the strike zone longer instead of getting swept out in ten seconds. If you've been frustrated by baits getting hammered on the surface before they ever sink, this is the week that problem eases up.

Mahi have been mixed in on the troll wherever there's floating structure — weed lines, a stray lobster ball, anything holding shade. Nothing giant, mostly schoolie-class fish in the 3 to 8-pound range, but they'll eat a small spreader bar or a naked ballyhoo just as fast as a yellowfin will, so don't be shocked when one shows up in the spread. Wahoo have been scarce this week — a couple of cutoffs reported near the temp break but nothing confirmed boatside — which tells me the high-speed bite hasn't fully turned on yet. If you want a shot at one, run a lure at 12 to 15 knots right on the color change itself, not fifty yards off it. White marlin have made a light appearance around the Claw, mostly on naked ballyhoo pulled slow behind the dredge, but it's a bonus fish right now, not a target.

On the bluefin side, the recreational slot fishery — 27 inches up to just under 47, two-fish limit — has held remarkably steady since the July 3rd trophy-category closure. Most of that action has concentrated closer to Block Island and the eastern canyons, but I'm seeing enough slot-class bluefin mixed into the spreader bar spread at the Dip to mention it here. If you're already running ballyhoo for yellowfin, don't be surprised if a 35-pound bluefin eats first.

Swordfish guys have been quiet on the report front this week, but the daytime drop conditions haven't changed — 1,200 to 1,800 feet off the edge near the Claw, squid strips and glow gear, same program that's worked all July. I'd expect that to pick back up once boats start committing full trips to it instead of splitting time with the tuna bite, which right now is the better bet per hour on the water.

Looking ahead: if this high-pressure pattern holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I expect the bite to keep strengthening rather than plateau. The neap tide softens current for a few more days, which favors the night chunk crowd, and the warm filament shows no sign of sliding off the wall yet. Best case, this stays a stable, repeatable Hudson pattern through the end of the month. If the eddy shifts east like these things sometimes do, I'd be ready to run a little further south toward Wilmington to stay on the warm side of the break. For now, though, the Dip and the Claw are the two spots I'd fish if I only had one trip this week.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Bass Have Gone to Bed Early — Best Water's After Dark Now
reports.subhead: Warm shallow water has pushed the big bass nocturnal, fluke are holding steady on the humps, and bonito are close enough to start checking the rips.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a particular quiet that settles over the south side of the island on these July evenings, right around eight-thirty, when the wind finally lets go of the southwest and the water off the Southwest Ledge goes flat and dark green under the last light. You feel it before you see it — the chop drops out, the gulls stop working, and for about twenty minutes the whole place holds its breath. That's when I start rigging eels. Because right now, that quiet window is where the big bass are living.

The shallow water south of the Cape has been running warm enough, long enough, that the keeper-class bass have shifted hard into a low-light and after-dark pattern, and Block Island is no exception. I've had better luck the last two weeks fishing the Ledge and the North Rip from an hour before sunset until well past midnight than I have at high noon, even on a good tide. Live eels drifted along the north side of the Ledge in eighteen to thirty feet, slow-trolled or dead-drifted with the current, have been the most consistent producer — a couple of fish over forty pounds came off that structure in the last ten days on eels fished right on bottom as the tide turned. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig at the North Rip after dark have also been drawing fish up out of the deeper water, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the current starts stacking bait against the rip line. During the day, the same water that produced all spring has gone quiet by ten in the morning — the fish are still there, just not feeding, holding deep and tight to structure until the light drops again.

Fluke fishing has been the more dependable daytime program, and it's not close. The water around Block Island runs noticeably cooler than what you find south of Montauk — we're sitting in that comfortable mid-to-upper-60s range that fluke like, rather than the warmer water that's been pushing stripers off their feed elsewhere. I've been working the humps and channel edges between the Ledge and the Coast Guard station, drifting white and chartreuse Gulp swimming mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, over broken bottom in twenty-five to forty feet on the last of the incoming and first two hours of the outgoing. That moving water is doing the work — dead slack and these fish stop showing interest almost immediately. Sizes have been solid, several to five and six pounds mixed in with a good number of shorts, so you're sorting fish but you're not starving for bites. Scup have been thick around the same structure and off the docks in the Great Salt Pond, small hooks and sandworms or squid strips doing the job for anybody who wants a bucket of dinner without much drama.

Bluefish have been scattered rather than schooled up tight around the island itself, though the bigger blitz activity building along the beaches to our west and south — bunker pods getting worked hard in daylight — tells me it's only a matter of time before that class of fish pushes up this way as those bunker schools keep moving. When it does show here, it usually shows first off Sandy Point and along the east side, and when the blues are on bunker like that you don't need finesse — a wire leader and a diamond jig or a topwater popper thrown right into the surface commotion is about all the presentation required.

Now for the one I've been watching closest. We flagged it last week — said bonito would likely show at Block Island within a week or two as water temps pushed into their comfort range, and while nobody's iced one off the island yet, the water's sitting right where it needs to be for that first wave to show up on the temperature breaks. I've had my eye on the rip lines off the Southwest Ledge and the temperature seam that sets up east of the Beacon on the last of the ebb — that's usually where the first fish of the season get spotted, working small bait pods right on the surface. If you're itching to be the first one to connect, small Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax worked fast through any nervous water or diving-bird activity out there is the move, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it just yet. Squid have also been building in numbers around the broader Rhode Island grounds, which is a good sign — that's usually the forage that pulls bonito and eventually albies in tight to structure once they do arrive.

We're heading into a first-quarter neap this week, which is going to soften up the current through the rips and widen out the productive window for both the eel bite and the fluke drift — less brutal current means you can work a spot longer before you're fighting the drift instead of fishing it. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the North Rip an hour before sunset with eels rigged and ready, working through dark into the top of the tide change. Bring a rod for fluke too and hit the humps on your way out — no reason to waste good daylight water waiting on the sun to drop.

reports.headline: Peconic pushes into the mid-70s — porgies thick at Shelter Island, bass slide onto the night shift
reports.subhead: A softening neap tide this week means slower presentations and bonus fish for anglers willing to fish the edges of daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
The Peconic runs its own calendar, and right now it's deep into the part of the summer where the bay stops being a nursery and starts being a feeding ground. Surface temps have pushed into the mid-70s across most of the system — warmer in the back coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor, a touch cooler out toward Orient where the tide from Gardiners Bay keeps flushing it clean. That gradient is doing exactly what it does every July: pulling porgies tight to structure, keeping fluke locked on the channel edges, and pushing the striped bass into a low-light pattern that's frustrating anybody who only fishes banker's hours.

Start with the porgies, because right now they're the most dependable thing happening in this bay. Shelter Island is holding them thick — Majors Harbor, the flats off Cedar Point, and the drop-off outside Jennys Creek are all loaded with scup in the 20 to 35 foot range. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, tipped with sandworm or a piece of clam, fished right on bottom on the last two hours of the incoming through the top of the tide. That's when the current is strong enough to hold the chum slick together but not so ripping you're re-anchoring every twenty minutes. Anybody complaining about porgy fishing this week either isn't using fresh bait or isn't looking at a tide chart — this bite doesn't require much finesse, just the right window.

Fluke are the other constant. We said last week this bite would carry through the summer, and it has — the channels between North Haven and Shelter Island, the cut off Jockey Creek, and the deeper stretch of Noyack Bay are all holding fish. Nothing gigantic, but a steady grade of 16 to 19 inch fluke with the occasional four or five pounder mixed in, especially on the last of the ebb when bait gets pulled off the flats into the deeper water. Three-quarter ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet or a squid strip, dragged slow along the bottom in 15 to 25 feet, is still the go-to. Drift with the tide, not against it — these fish are sitting in the current seams waiting for food to come to them, not chasing.

Stripers are where things get more honest. The warm surface water has done what it always does this time of year — pushed the better class of bass into a nocturnal or dawn/dusk pattern. Daytime fishing in the open bay has been slow and I won't pretend otherwise. But Plum Gut and the rip off Orient Point are still producing after dark and in that gray light right before sunrise, when the current is really moving through the Gut on the ebb. Eels and bunker chunks fished on the bottom, or swimbaits worked through the rip on a slow retrieve, have been taking slot fish and the occasional overslot. Jessup's Neck and the drop-off along Nassau Point are worth a shot at first light too — smaller fish, mostly schoolies and low-slot, but they'll eat a white or bone Slug-Go worked over the grass edges before the sun gets high.

Weakfish are starting to show some life again, which lines up with what we expected — calm, warm evenings have a way of waking this bite back up. Noyack Bay and the cove off Sag Harbor have both given up a few weakfish in that 3 to 5 pound range on quiet nights, mostly on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow just off bottom. It's not a bite you can plan a whole trip around yet, but if you're already out there for stripers or fluke at dusk, it's worth a few extra casts along the drop-offs.

Bluefish have been chopping through bunker pods scattered around the bay, particularly off Southold and out toward Orient, and they're a nice bonus for anyone fishing light tackle with kids aboard — poppers or diamond jigs will get bit fast when you find the birds working.

The tide is the story to watch this week. We're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means the current through Plum Gut, the Race, and the connecting cuts around Shelter Island is going to soften noticeably over the next several days. That's not bad news — it's an opportunity. Slower current means you can slow your presentations down too, which tends to produce better quality on both fluke and any blackfish sniffing around structure right now. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take advantage of that softer water to work the deeper holes around Shelter Island with a slower bucktail drift, then swing over to Plum Gut right at last light while the tide's still got enough push to hold bass on the rip.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically — the porgy bite should hold strong through August, the fluke should stay steady as long as the channels keep their bait, and the bass will keep favoring darkness until the water starts cooling down in September. Keep an eye out toward Orient and the mouth of the bay for early false albacore or bonito scouting activity as the month wears on — the water's warm enough now that it wouldn't surprise me to hear the first reports any week.

reports.headline: Bunker Boils at First Light, But the Real Bass Are Waiting on the Dark
reports.subhead: The Point settles into its mid-summer rhythm as a neap tide softens the rips and the first whispers of albie season drift in on the warm water.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a rhythm to Montauk in high summer that you either know or you don't, and right now the Point is deep into it. This isn't the frantic, everything-at-once chaos of the fall run — this is the patient version, the one where you earn your fish in the hour before the sun clears the horizon or the hour after it drops behind Gin Beach. The bunker are here in numbers I haven't seen stack this heavy since early June, rolling in tight, dark pods off the south side beaches and around North Bar, and the bluefish have found them with the kind of violence that turns flat water into a boiling mess of white water and gull screams by seven in the morning.

That blitz has been a daytime show all week — casting poppers and metal into the edges of the boil off the boulder field will get you blues to twelve and fourteen pounds, sometimes bigger, and it doesn't take finesse. A bucktail with a strip of pork rind, a Hopkins, a Deadly Dick, anything that flashes and swims erratically through the chaos gets crushed. But here's the thing about this pattern, and it's the same thing I tell every guy who calls me thinking the blitz means the bass are in it too — they're usually not, not this time of year. The water off the beach is holding in the low 70s, Montauk itself reading around 71.6, and that's warm enough to push the better class of striped bass into a nocturnal program. The blues will feed all day on bunker in the wash. The bass — the 20, 30, 40-pound fish that make this place what it is — are sliding deep into the rips at dawn, at dusk, and well after dark, and that's where you need to be if you want them.

Shagwong Reef has been my most consistent stop this week on the last two hours of the incoming into first light, working a white bucktail with a curly-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom in 20 to 35 feet, letting the current do the swimming for me. I've had two fish over 30 pounds off there in the last five days, both right at the color change where the reef drops into deeper water. The boulder field off the Point itself — the classic ground everybody talks about but few fish correctly — has been better after dark than at dawn this week, eels drifted through the white water on the building tide, weighted just enough to stay down without snagging rock. That's still the gold standard presentation out there and it hasn't changed in fifty years for a reason.

We're heading into the July 21st first-quarter neap, and if you've fished this Point long enough you know what that means for the rip-dependent spots — Frisbee's, the Elbow, the classic current seams off the Lighthouse. Weaker current means the window doesn't slam shut as fast on either side of peak tide. That's actually good news for guys who can't be out there at 4:45 in the morning exactly on the money — you've got a little more forgiveness in the timing this week than you will once the tides build back toward full moon.

Fluke fishing has stayed the most dependable thing going, and it's not close. Drifting Rocky Ground and the mussel beds off the south side in 35 to 55 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails tipped with a squid strip, has produced steady action with fish to six pounds mixed into a lot of shorts. It's not a secret bite, it's not glamorous, but it's the fallback that keeps a day from being wasted when the low-light bass window hasn't opened yet or the wind's wrong for the rips. Porgies and sea bass on the same structure — Shagwong, the reef off Frisbee's — have been thick, clams and squid on top-and-bottom rigs, easy limits for anyone who wants dinner without fighting current all morning.

Offshore, the canyon boats out of the Harbor have found their groove. Yellowfin and some bigeye activity has been building steadily on the warm filaments pushing into Block Canyon and out toward the Fishtails, and that's exactly the kind of setup we flagged as building a few days back — stable weather holding warm water in the canyons, and that same warm water is the thing to watch for early false albacore scouts working east of the Point. Nobody's connected on albies yet that I've heard of, and I'm not going to tell you they're here when they're not, but the water's doing what it needs to do. Late July into early August is when that first wave typically shows around the Lighthouse rips and out toward the Elbow, and with temps sitting where they are, I'd start watching those rips for nervous water and diving terns any day now.

Looking ahead, I'd fish the dark tides through the weekend for bass — eels off the boulder field, bucktails on Shagwong at the tide change — and keep a rod rigged with a small metal or epoxy jig in the boat just in case something with a football-shaped body and a lot of speed shows up in a temperature break. The neap should widen your workable windows through midweek before the tides start building again toward the next moon. If the bunker stay put and the blues stay on them, that daytime show isn't going anywhere either. Just don't confuse the two bites — one's entertainment, the other's the real Montauk business, and right now that business is happening after the sun goes down.

reports.headline: Outgoing at 1 A.M.: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Weakfish Wake Up at the Bridge
reports.subhead: With the neap tide softening the current, the Night Owl worked the back half of the ebb and found the bite he'd been waiting on.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Wednesday night to skip the dusk incoming and wait for the outgoing to really get moving past midnight. That's the thing about this inlet — everybody shows up at sunset, dumps bunker chunks off the jetty rocks for an hour, and clears out by ten thinking the bite's over. It isn't over. It's just getting started for guys willing to sit in the dark until the tide really starts pulling.

The first-quarter neap on the 21st has been softening the current all week, and that's changed the timing on the deep hole east of the Coast Guard station. Normally on a big spring push you get one tight window right at max ebb where the bass stack up on the sand eels getting swept through. With the current running softer this week, that window's stretched out — I had fish from about 1 a.m. through almost 3, working a 3-ounce bucktail with a white 6-inch Fin-S trailer, bouncing it slow along the bottom where the deep hole drops off the sandbar. Nothing huge — mostly 26 to 32 inches, a few slot fish mixed with shorts — but steady enough that I never went more than fifteen minutes without a hit. Live eels drifted on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current seam did about as well, and if you want a bigger fish, that's the bait I'd reach for. The bass are here on the nocturnal program right now — the back bay's been running warm, mid-to-upper 70s off the flats by Tiana, and that pushes the bigger stripers into feeding at night and staying deep and quiet through the heat of the day. We flagged this pattern building last week, and it's held — the warm water squeezed the bite into low light, and that's exactly what's playing out at the inlet.

Ponquogue Bridge is where the real story is this week, though. Weakfish had gone quiet through the hot stretch in early July, but the calm, settled evenings we've had — light southwest wind, clean water, no chop pushing through the inlet — brought them back. I had three keeper weakfish Thursday night on the outgoing, fishing bucktails tipped with squid strips right in the bridge shadow where the current breaks around the pilings. Small chartreuse bucktails, half-ounce, bounced right on bottom in about 18 to 22 feet, worked slow so the current does the swimming for you. A few guys working the same stretch with Berkley Gulp swimming mullets in pink shad picked up weakfish too, along with some decent porgies mixed in on the drift closer to the channel edge. This is the pattern we said would rebuild on calm warm nights, and it did — but I want to be honest, it's not a slam dunk yet. Some nights it's three fish in three hours, other nights you work the whole tide and get one bite. The window's real, but it's still thin. Fish the last two hours of the outgoing under the bridge lights and don't be surprised if the bite comes in one short burst rather than a steady pick.

Fluke fishing in the bay has been the most dependable thing going, day or night, and that's held true out here same as everywhere else on the South Shore right now. Drifting the flats off Tiana Beach and out toward the canal mouth in 8 to 14 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce bucktails have been putting keeper fluke in the boat, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds. The channel edges along the west side of the bay toward Hampton Bays are holding fish too — bigger baits, squid strips over bucktails, worked slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still moving bait across the structure. This is a daytime program mostly, which makes for a nice complement if you're out there grinding bass and weakfish through the dark hours — sleep in, fluke fish the afternoon flood, then go back out for the night bite.

Bluefish have been sporadic inside the inlet, nothing like the blitzes happening up around the bunker schools further west, but there's enough bait pushing through on the tide changes that you'll run into cutoffs and slashing fish working topwater plugs off the rocks at first light. If bunker schools push further east along the barrier beach the way they've been trending, expect that to change fast — worth keeping an eye on the surf reports from the west.

As for the canal — the connection to the Peconic has been quiet for stripers this week, mostly small blues and a scattering of porgies working the current there, nothing worth a special trip yet. That could change once water starts moving more with the tide building back toward full moon.

Looking ahead, the softening currents from this neap should keep stretching out the productive windows at the inlet — more time on the bite, if less raw power in the tide. If the calm evenings hold, I'd keep working the bridge on the outgoing for weakfish, and I'd keep the deep hole in play for bass after midnight. If a front comes through and stirs the water, that bridge bite could shut off fast, so take advantage of the calm while it's here.

reports.headline: The Cut Off Cupsogue Deepened Two Feet — Fluke Found the New Edge Fast
reports.subhead: A storm-carved trench on the west side of Moriches Inlet is holding fish while the ocean stays lumpy and the bass go nocturnal.
reports.body_markdown:
I ran the west bar at Cupsogue on the last of Thursday's ebb and the bottom read different than it did two weeks ago. There's a new scour hole cut into the inside edge of the bar, maybe 40 yards off the point, running eight to ten feet deeper than the flat around it — classic post-swell reshaping. That kind of groundswell we've been getting off the ocean, two-footers at 14-second intervals, doesn't look like much from the beach, but that long period pushes a lot of water and it's been quietly re-carving the inlet's throat all month. The inlet doesn't sit still. It never has. Every time we get a period like this, sand moves off the bar and drops into the channel, and the fish find the new structure before we do.

That's exactly where the fluke have been stacking. The edge of that new hole, 16 to 22 feet, has been holding fish on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood — moving water pulling bait off the flat and dropping it right into that trench. Chartreuse and white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop, have been the ticket. A few guys working the same water with strip baits on standard fluke rigs are doing fine too, but the bucktail-Gulp combo is getting more bites because it stays down in that heavier current better than bait alone. Fish have run to five and six pounds off that edge, with a lot of short-to-borderline fish mixed in — so bring the ruler and don't assume. We flagged this corridor last week as the one to watch through July, and it's holding up: Moriches into Shinnecock has been the most consistent fluke water on the whole South Shore right now, better than what the ocean-side beaches are giving up with this swell running.

Striped bass are a different animal entirely this time of year, and anyone still fishing them at noon in this bay is fighting the water temperature, not the fish. Once that sun gets up and the shallows in the back bay push into the mid-70s, bass shut down and slide into whatever depth and shade they can find. The program right now is after dark, full stop. I've had better luck working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs along the rocks at the west jetty from two hours before high through the top of the tide, and eel guys working the deeper cuts off Pattersquash Island after 9 PM have been doing quiet, steady work on schoolies with the occasional slot fish mixed in. Tuthill Point's flats hold bait after dark too — small bunker and spearing get trapped against the marsh edge on the dropping tide, and that's pulled some bass shallow right at last light. Nothing blitz-worthy, but real, catchable fish if you're willing to fish the clock instead of the calendar.

Bluefish have been the wildcard. The bunker pods pushing along the beach from the west are the same schools that blitzes further up the coast, and there's no reason that bait doesn't keep drifting east into our stretch. I haven't seen a full-on blitz off Cupsogue yet this week, but there's been bird activity — terns working nervous water just off the second bar around dawn a few mornings running, which usually means blues are underneath pushing bait to the surface. If you're walking the beach at first light with a metal — a Deadly Dick or a Hopkins — that's the window. It hasn't been consistent enough to plan a whole trip around, but it's worth having the rod rigged and ready if you're already out there for stripers.

Weakfish have been quiet, which tracks with where we are in the season — they like it calm and warm at last light, and we haven't had a full stretch of settled evenings to let that pattern build. When we do get a run of slick, glassy evenings on the incoming, that's when to work soft plastics — bone or pink shad-tail swimbaits — slow along the channel edges in the back bay behind Cupsogue and around the Moriches Bay side of the inlet. It's not there yet, but the conditions that build that bite are close.

Looking ahead: we're rolling toward the first-quarter moon on the 21st, which means neap tides through the back half of this week. Weaker current through the inlet sounds like bad news, but it's actually going to widen the fluke window — less brutal current speed means that scour hole off Cupsogue stays fishable longer instead of just the peak hour of the ebb. I'd fish it from mid-tide through the last two hours rather than trying to hit it exactly at max flow. For stripers, the softer current should also stretch the after-dark bite a little longer into the morning before the sun pushes them back down. Ocean's still carrying some leftover swell energy, so I'd keep surf efforts at Cupsogue focused on the calmer stretches between sets rather than fighting white water all morning. If that bunker push keeps sliding east, don't be shocked if the bluefish window in the early mornings turns into something worth planning a whole trip around by this weekend.

reports.headline: Captree Dock Talk: Bunker Pull Blues to the Beach, Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: Fluke keep grinding on the bridge rips while stripers wait for dark and bluefish crash bunker pods right off the barrier beach.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a guy leaning on my gunwale at the Captree dock Tuesday morning, coffee in one hand, asking why his buddy killed it on bass at 5am off Democrat Point and he got skunked at noon in the same spot. I told him what I've been telling everybody all week — you're fishing the wrong clock. Right now, this bay and this inlet run on two different schedules, and if you're not paying attention to which one you're fishing, you're going to burn a lot of gas for nothing.

Here's the deal. The ocean's been ugly — short, stacked-up swell, 2 to 3 feet at a nasty 3-second period, the kind of chop that makes the ocean side of Fire Island feel like a washing machine instead of a beach. NY Bight buoy's reading mid-70s, and that warm, wind-whipped water has pushed most of the good feeding activity off the open front and into the protected seams — the inlet channels, the bridge rips, the back bay flats where the water lays down and the current still does something useful. If you're planning a Democrat Point surf session this week, know you're fighting the ocean as much as you're fishing it.

Stripers have noticed the heat too. Water in the bay's holding solidly in the low-to-mid 70s, and that's put the bass into a low-light, mostly-after-dark pattern — same story from here to the Sound. Daytime bucktailing on the inlet seam has been a grind; the better move has been live-lining bunker after dark around structure — the Fire Island Inlet rocks, the pilings under the Robert Moses bridges, and the deep hole off the Coast Guard station. Guys running bunker on a fish-finder rig, fresh snagged and dropped right on the current break at the top of the outgoing, are still finding slot fish and the occasional overslot in that 32–36 inch range. Daytime, don't waste your good bait — save it for dusk and go park on structure.

Fluke, on the other hand, don't care what time it is, and that's been the most dependable bite in the whole zone. The channel edges around the Robert Moses bridges — both the Democrat Point side and out toward the Causeway pilings — have been holding fish all week in 25 to 35 feet, with the better drift coming on the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming when the current's still got some shape to it. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, have been the ticket, along with chartreuse bucktail-and-Gulp combos when the water's got a little color to it after a blow. Most of what's coming over the rail is in that 16 to 19 inch range with a keeper mixed in every few drifts — not a slam-bang bite, but steady enough that a patient boat puts fish in the box most days. Great South Bay flats off Nicoll Bay and out past the Sayville flats have been holding shorts in good numbers too, so if you're chasing a legal fish for the table, work the deeper edges, not the flats themselves.

Bluefish have been the loudest story on the beach this week, and we called this one — said the bunker-driven blitz pattern would keep spreading down the coast as long as the weather stayed calm, and that's exactly what's played out along the barrier beach. Bunker pods are running tight to the sand from Cherry Grove down past Kismet, and when the blues find them, it's fast and violent — poppers and metal getting hit the second they land. If you see the birds working and the water nervous, don't overthink the presentation — a 2-ounce diamond jig or a topwater popper thrown right into the boil will get bit in seconds. It's not an all-day thing, though; these blitzes are running in short, intense windows, usually first light and again right before dark, so don't plan your whole trip around chasing one pod for six hours.

Weakfish have been quiet but not dead. A few nice fish, some pushing 3 to 4 pounds, have come out of Patchogue and Sayville on warm, still evenings — the classic pattern for this fish, a soft-plastic worm imitation like a Bass Assassin or a bucktail-and-plastic combo worked slow along the deeper bay bottom right at last light. It's not a bite you can plan a trip around yet, but on the calmest, warmest nights it's been showing signs of rebuilding, and I'd keep half an eye on it heading into next week.

Looking ahead — we hit the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which should take some of the snap out of the current at the inlet and the bridge rips for the next several days. That usually means a wider window to fish moving water instead of a tight peak-tide sprint, which is good news for fluke guys who like a slower, more controlled drift. If the ocean lays down at all behind this pattern, I'd take a look at the outer beach for one more crack at those bunker-driven blitzes before the bait pushes further down the coast. And if you've only got one shot this week, I'd take it after dark on the inlet with a live bunker — that's where the bigger bass have been living, and that's not likely to change until this heat breaks.

reports.headline: Forget the Bunker Blitz Hype — Jones Inlet Bass Are Feeding After Dark
reports.subhead: While the coast chases daylight blitzes, the real Jones Inlet bite is happening on bucktails after sundown, with fluke and a rebuilding weakfish run filling the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is standing on the beach at first light this week waiting for bunker to get pushed up against the sand so the blues can turn it into a slaughterhouse. I get it — that's the sexy report right now, and it's real up in Jersey and creeping toward the bight. But that's not how you catch bass at Jones Inlet in July, and I'm not wasting my dawn patrol standing around hoping. I'm out on the rocks at Short Beach and the north jetty at Jones Inlet after the sun goes down, and that's where the fish actually are.

Here's the deal. The water's been warm right through the inlet — ocean side is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and the back bay and the flats off Short Beach are running warmer than that by mid-afternoon. Warm shallow water like this pushes keeper bass into a low-light and nighttime feeding pattern, and that's exactly what I'm seeing. Daytime soak sessions on the jetty rocks have been quiet — a few schoolies, nothing to write home about. But drop a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig tight to the rocks at Short Beach starting an hour before sunset, and let it sit through the tide change, and you're in business. I've had slot fish to 32 inches doing exactly that the last four nights running. Bucktail guys working white 1-ounce heads with a curly tail trailer, slow-rolled along the current seam where the inlet channel meets the flat, are connecting too — best window is the last two hours of the incoming tide right into the top, when bait gets funneled through the cut and stacked against structure.

We flagged this a week back — said that spring tide would flush the inlet hard, pulling bait out on the ebb and dragging predators in behind it on the flood. That's been the program almost to the letter. Now we're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means the current's going to soften up over the next few days. That's not bad news — it actually widens the bite window. When the flood isn't ripping through the cut like a fire hose, bass sit on those current edges longer instead of blowing through, and you get a longer stretch of usable water instead of one hard 45-minute window around the top of the tide.

Daytime, the fluke have been the honest bet, same as they always are here in July. Sloop Channel and the deeper cuts off the Wantagh Bridge have been holding fish in 12 to 18 feet, and the drift over the mussel bars on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the most consistent stretch. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow along bottom — that combo has out-produced bare bucktails two or three to one for me this week. Sizes are mixed, plenty of 15-to-17-inch fish getting tossed back, but I've had three keepers over 20 inches in the last five trips, including one just shy of five pounds working the deeper hole on the Freeport side of the channel.

Now the one I'm actually excited about — weakfish. They've been trickling back into South Oyster Bay for a couple seasons now, and this week the bite finally showed some teeth. Calm, warm evenings have been the trigger, same pattern we called out last week when things were still spotty. Working the flats off Freeport and the deeper bends in the channel behind Jones Beach with small soft plastics — 3-inch pink or chartreuse shad bodies on a light jig head — has produced weakfish in the 16-to-19-inch range right at last light and into full dark. They're not thick, and you're not going to load the cooler, but for a species that all but disappeared from this bay for a stretch of years, catching four or five in an outing on a calm night is worth getting excited about. Keep your drag light — these fish have paper mouths and you'll lose half of what you hook if you horse them.

Bluefish have been quiet right at the inlet itself, even with bunker pods reportedly moving along the beach further up the coast. If those pods funnel past Jones the way they sometimes do in late July, first light at the inlet mouth is worth a scouting run with a bucktail or a diamond jig — but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet. Nothing's shown here so far.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the after-dark bass bite through the neap — the softer current should stretch the productive window past what we've had on the bigger spring tides. Daytime, stick with the fluke drift in Sloop Channel and work the weakfish pattern on the next few calm evenings before any weather rolls in and stirs up the bay. If the wind stays down, this stretch has real potential to keep building.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway Bridge After Dark: Slot Bass on the Outgoing, Fluke Rule the Day
reports.subhead: Warm bay water has flipped the striper switch to nighttime — but fluke, schoolies, and a rebuilding weakfish bite keep the rods bent from sunup to sundown.
reports.body_markdown:
I picked the bridge this week, not the boat. When the bay water gets this warm — shallow flats baking all afternoon, the channels holding heat overnight — the keeper bass stop feeding on my schedule and start feeding on theirs. That means Marine Parkway. I can walk out on the pilings, fish the pilings and riprap on the Rockaway side, and be home by midnight instead of running the boat back across the bay in the dark. Access matters as much as tackle out here, and right now the access that pays is a rod holder on the bulkhead at 10 p.m., not a rod holder at noon.

Two nights out of three this week I had bass on the outgoing at the bridge — not a pile of them, but real fish, low 20s up to one push-30 that I measured twice before I let her go. Bucktails in white, 1.5 to 2 ounce, bounced off the bottom along the current seam where the tide funnels under the span, worked best. A couple guys were soaking eels on the drift and doing fine too. The pattern's simple: the water's been sitting in the high 70s across the flats all day, the bass don't want to burn energy chasing bait in that soup, so they slide out to the bridge and the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth after dark when things cool a few degrees and the current gets moving. If you're daytime-only, you're mostly fishing for schoolies and snapper blues inside the bay right now, and that's fine — it's just a different game.

Speaking of that different game — fluke have been the steadier daytime bite all month, and this week didn't change that. Cross Bay Bridge channel edges, the flats off Ruffle Bar, and the deeper holes around Motts Basin have all given up fish on the drift, five to six-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, teased with a Bonito strip if you've got it. Best window is the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, when bait gets pushed up onto the edges and the fluke stack up to ambush it. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts, but enough 18-to-20-inch fish mixed in to make it worth the drift time. I had four keepers Tuesday morning working the flats in 8 to 12 feet off Ruffle Bar, all on the incoming.

The other thing worth talking about — we flagged last week that the weakfish bite would start rebuilding as the bay kept warming on calm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening. Grassy Bay and the channel edges near the JoCo Marsh have been giving up weakfish in the last hour of daylight into dusk, mostly on light jigs tipped with a sandworm or a small piece of bloodworm, fished slow along the bottom where the mud drops into the channel. Nothing giant — most are in that 16 to 18-inch range — but a legal weakfish on a calm July evening in this bay is still a good fish, and it's a sign the bay's settling into a healthier summer rhythm.

For the kayak crowd, this is prime time to work the flats inside — launch out of Canarsie Pier or the Sebago Canoe Club ramp and paddle the shallow grass edges for schoolie bass and snapper blues on topwater or small metal. It's not trophy fishing, but it's steady action for kids and for anyone who just wants bent rods without the boat traffic.

On the ocean side, there's bunker showing along the beach from Rockaway down toward Breezy Point, and where there's bunker there's usually blues working them from below. I'd check the inlet itself on a strong outgoing — the current pulls bait past the jetty and I've seen blues follow it right through the cut. Cast bucktails or diamond jigs into the moving water at the mouth, especially around the second half of the ebb when everything funnels through that gut. It hasn't been the wall-to-wall blitz you're hearing about up the Jersey beaches, but it's there if you're willing to work the tide right.

Looking ahead — we're heading into the July 21 neap, which is going to soften the current everywhhere from the bridge to the inlet. That's usually bad news for anyone depending on a hard-running rip, but it can widen the productive window for slower presentations like eels and light bucktails, since the fish aren't getting blown off structure by a screaming tide. I'd expect the bass pattern at the bridge to hold through the week, maybe even extend a little later into the evening as the current eases. Fluke should stay consistent on the flats regardless of moon phase — that bite's been the most dependable thing in the bay all month. And if this bunker push along the beach keeps building the way it has to our north, don't be shocked if Rockaway starts seeing real blitz activity in the surf before the month's out. I'll be watching Breezy Point close for that.

reports.headline: Plum Gut Goes Quiet — And That's Exactly When the Bass Show Up
reports.subhead: A softening current ahead of Tuesday's neap is turning ripping water into a controllable eel bite, and the fluke never left.
reports.body_markdown:
Three-fifteen a.m., chest waders, standing on the rocks at the Gut with the current still hauling at four knots and a 12-inch eel swimbait on a three-way rig swinging through the seam like it owed me money. Second drift through the heaviest push, right on the tide change, something leaned into it that wasn't playing around — thirty-six inches, thick through the shoulders, came up out of the froth right where the eddy folds back against the rock pile on the west side. That's the fish that tells you the pattern's real, not just a rumor from the bait shop.

Here's the deal on Plum Gut and The Race right now: the water's still ripping hard enough to make boat control a full-time job, but Tuesday's first-quarter neap is already starting to take the edge off. I felt it Thursday night — the same stage of tide that was unmanageable two weeks ago is now giving me a longer window to actually work a presentation instead of just surviving the drift. That's the single biggest thing to know this week. As the current eases through the neap, eel and swimbait presentations get easier to control, and the strike zone stops being a two-minute burst at max flow and starts stretching into a real bite window on either side of the tide change. If you've been getting your teeth kicked in trying to fish the peak of the flood or ebb through the Gut, back off the max-current window and fish the building and softening stages instead — that's where the bass are actually eating right now, not just holding.

The technique that's putting fish on the deck is straightforward and unforgiving: 12-inch eel-style swimbaits or shad-style paddletails on a three-way rig, dropper heavy enough to hold bottom in the current, worked through the deepest, fastest part of the rip right on the tide change. You're not swimming this thing — you're letting the current do the work and controlling depth with your dropper weight. Bass are stacking on the down-current side of the rock piles and current seams where the Gut necks down, and they're eating on the pause, not the retrieve. If you're throwing bucktails instead, 1.5 to 2 ounces, same idea — cast across the seam, let it sink clean off the edge, slow rhythmic lift-and-drop along bottom. That's the pattern that's been working the hard-current edges up and down the East End this month, and Plum Gut is prime water for it because the structure creates so many defined seams to work.

Fluke haven't missed a beat. This has been the most dependable bite in the entire zone — Plum Gut, the flats off Orient, and the channel edges around Fishers Island are all holding keepers mixed into the shorts, and unlike the bass, the fluke never got fussy about the warm surface water. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift over 25 to 40 feet of water on moving tide, keep producing. I had a 28-inch sea bass — a genuine surprise, north of five pounds — come off a rock pile adjacent to the rip on the same drift as a pair of keeper fluke, which tells you the structure right at the mouth of the Gut is holding a real mixed bag right now. Worth working those humps slow and thorough instead of running through them.

Bluefish are the other story worth your time. Jumbo blues are showing on the hard current edges at both the Race and the Gut, slashing through bait right on the surface in visible boils — daylight fish, which isn't always the case with blues this time of year. When you see the boil, don't long-bomb it. Feather a short, accurate cast directly into the seam where the bait's getting pushed, because these fish are locked onto a tight ambush point, not roaming open water. Poppers and metal both work; the key is precision over distance.

Water's telling a clear story on temperature this week — New London's sitting around 70, Montauk's a touch warmer at 71.6, and that gradient is exactly why the Eastern Sound striper bite is holding up better through daylight hours than what guys are dealing with further west and south, where the warmer shallow water has pushed bass into strict low-light and after-dark patterns. Out here, the current and depth at the Gut and the Race are keeping things cool enough that fish will still eat in daylight if you find the right seam — but I'm not going to pretend it's a guarantee. I've had drifts through the peak of the tide this week that produced nothing but current burn on my line, and drifts twenty minutes later on the softening stage that put three fish on deck. Timing inside the tide matters as much as the spot right now.

Looking ahead, I expect that neap tide to keep opening up the window through the middle of the week — Tuesday and Wednesday should give the most forgiving current for anyone running eels or bucktails through the Gut for the first time this season. After that, tides build back toward the full moon and the rip gets mean again, so if you're going to learn this eel-on-a-three-way pattern, this is the stretch to do it. Fluke should stay steady regardless of tide stage; that bite's been resilient all month. Bluefish will keep showing on the surface as long as the bait stays put in the current seams, but that can shut off fast if a blow scatters everything, so don't wait around if you see a boil working — get on it.

reports.headline: Bunker Balled Up on Stratford Shoal — Blues Slashing, Bass Waiting on Dark
reports.subhead: Peanut bunker packed the mouth of the Sound this week, and the thermal wall at Stratford Shoal is sorting who gets to eat first.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching before I ever made a cast. Off the Port Jeff breakwater, a bait ball of peanut bunker the size of a swimming pool was pinned against the rocks by the outgoing tide, and there wasn't a bird in the sky touching it — which told me more than any temp gauge could. Something bigger was already underneath, holding them tight instead of letting terns scatter them. Fifteen minutes later a school of bluefish came through like a lawnmower, and that bait ball just disappeared into white water and feathers. That's the story of Central Sound this week: the bunker are here in numbers, and everybody's lined up to eat them, just not all at the same hour.

The thermal picture explains a lot of the behavior I'm seeing. Kings Point is sitting around 72 degrees, New London's still holding near 70, and that gradient means the warmer water piling up toward our end of the Sound is stacking bait and holding it — bunker, mullet, silversides, all funneling through the narrows between the Norwalk Islands and Port Jeff because that's where the Sound squeezes down and the current does the sorting for them. Predators know it too. It's why Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground Light keep producing even when the open basin looks quiet.

Bluefish are the daylight story right now. With bunker schools pushing along the shoreline from the Norwalk Islands up toward Charles Island, blues are blitzing right on the surface in broad daylight — something you don't always get once July water warms up this much. I watched three separate blitzes this week between Sheffield Island and Charles Island, all within two hours of the top of the tide. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — worked fine when you could get in range, but the bigger blues (four to six pounds, a few bigger) wanted something slower once the top-water frenzy broke up. Diamond jigs bounced just under the surface picked off stragglers after the schools sounded.

Striped bass have gone the other way. With surface water running into the mid-to-upper 70s through the day, the bass have pulled back into a low-light program — first light, last light, and after dark around bunker schools and current edges. Stratford Shoal rip is still the best bet for this, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets funneled off the shoal into deeper water. Eels drifted along bottom, and bucktails worked slow with a Gulp trailer, have been taking slot fish in the 28-34 inch range after dark. A few boats working the Norwalk Islands after sundown are finding better numbers than size — lots of schoolies mixed with the occasional overslot that comes up out of nowhere on a bunker chunk.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going, and it hasn't blinked with the heat the way stripers have. Structure and moving water are still the formula — the edges around Middle Ground Light, the rockpiles off Charles Island, and the deeper cuts through the Norwalk Islands are holding fish through the tide changes. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift in 25 to 40 feet, have been the go-to. Keeper-sized fish to five pounds have shown up consistently, with a decent short-to-keeper ratio — you're not culling all day, but you're not getting skunked either.

Porgies are stacking up thick on the reef structure around the Norwalk Islands and the rockier stretches off Charles Island. Sandworms and clam on a high-low rig, bottom fished on the last of the incoming, has been about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers right now. Nothing glamorous, but good eating and steady rods.

Weakfish have been a quieter presence, mostly showing in the back-bay mud around Oyster Bay and the Huntington side on the tail end of the ebb, when the shallow water warms fastest and pushes bait out through the creek mouths. Legal fish are mixed in with the fluke crowd there — not a targeted bite yet, more of a bonus.

We've had our eye on the bonito question since bait started concentrating through the narrows, and I haven't seen a confirmed fish push into Central Sound yet — but the ingredients are lining up. Rain bait and grass shrimp have been thick around the Norwalk Islands, and that's exactly the kind of forage that pulls bonito in behind it once water conditions settle. I'd keep a small metal rigged on a rod and watch the surface around Charles Island and the outer islands over the next week or two.

Looking ahead, we're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which should slacken the current at Stratford Shoal and the other rip-dependent spots. That's not bad news — it widens the productive window past the peak of the tide for eel and swimbait presentations, so you won't be chained to the exact top of the flood or ebb to get bit. If the bunker schools hold their pattern through the narrows, I'd fish the last light window at Stratford Shoal for bass, work the Norwalk Islands blitzes for blues during the day, and keep the fluke rods rigged on the structure edges regardless — that part of the program hasn't needed fixing.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks goes dark-hours only as bass slide into a nighttime pattern
