I've had my best luck working the outgoing tide, casting bucktails and swimming plugs tight to the pilings and current breaks under the bridge lights, letting the sweep carry the lure through the seam. The bite window tends to open an hour or two after sunset and hold through the strongest push of the outgoing water. Daytime trips around the bridge have been mostly quiet — don't waste your morning there right now.

We flagged this last week — said the weakfish bite would start rebuilding on calm, warm evenings as the bay settled into summer — and that's exactly what's starting to happen. I had two solid weakfish in the four-pound class off Ruffle Bar on a still evening, working a chartreuse soft plastic on a light jighead just as the light was fading and the water went glassy. It's not a full-blown bite yet, more like the first real signs of one, but if you can get out on a calm evening around the marsh edges — Ruffle Bar, the flats off Grassy Bay, the deeper holes near the Raunt — that's where I'd put my money over the next couple weeks.

Bluefish have been the story everywhere south and west of us — bunker schools stacking up along the Jersey beaches and pushing north, and it's worth keeping an eye on Rockaway Beach because that pattern has a habit of sliding up the coast as the bait moves with it. Nothing's blown up on the Rockaway sand yet, but if the bunker show, the blues won't be far behind, and that's a fast, violent bite when it turns on — bucktails, poppers, whatever you've got, just be ready to move fast.

Porgies are still worth a stop if you're fishing the rocks around Rockaway Inlet — small hooks, bloodworms or clam, and you can put together a nice mess of them on the bottom stages of the tide.

With the moon heading toward first quarter on the 21st, the current's easing up a bit, which usually means slower, more deliberate presentations pay off better than a fast retrieve — that's especially true for the fluke and the weakfish. Looking ahead, if the calm, stable weather holds, I'd expect the weakfish pattern to keep building on quiet evenings, the bass to stay locked into their after-dark rhythm around the bridge until the nights cool off some, and fluke to remain the most consistent daytime bet in the deeper channels. If the bunker push north and Rockaway Beach lights up with bluefish, I'll be out there — but for now, my time's split between a dawn paddle for fluke and a dusk cast for weakfish, and that's not a bad way to spend a July week on this bay.

reports.headline: Deep in the Gut: bass buried in the rip, eels doing the damage
reports.subhead: Cooler water and a hard three-way rig are putting quality bass, a 28-inch sea bass, and keeper fluke on the same stretch of bottom at Plum Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday night, max ebb, Plum Gut. I dropped a 12-inch eel off a three-way rig into the seam where the current stacks against the eastern edge of the rip, let it swing down and back like it's supposed to, and felt the rod load up like someone hooked a mooring ball. Forty seconds of pure deadlift and a 38-inch bass came up thrashing right at the transom. That's the fish that tells you everything about how this zone is fishing right now — deep, hard, and on gear built to survive current that doesn't care about your drag setting.

The pattern at the Gut and out at The Race hasn't changed much in two weeks, it's just gotten more precise. Bass are holding low, tight to the rock piles and current breaks, feeding almost exclusively when the water's ripping hardest — peak ebb and peak flood, the windows where the eddies behind Plum Island and the western edge of the Gut stack bait against structure. Shad-body swimbaits in the 6- to 9-inch range, white or bunker pattern, fished on jig heads heavy enough to hold bottom in five knots of current, have been money during those windows. When the current's screaming, I go to the three-way with a bucktail dropper and a big eel trailing behind — that combo has out-produced everything else I've thrown this month, and it's the same read that's been paying off for the shore guys working the rocks at 3 a.m.

New London's reading 67.6 degrees, which is a full four degrees cooler than what Kings Point's showing out west. That gradient matters more than people give it credit for. Western Sound bass have gone nocturnal — the water's warm enough that they're avoiding daylight stress and feeding almost exclusively after dark. Out here, with the water still in the mid-60s, we're not locked into that pattern yet. I've had fish hit at last light and again right at first light, not just in the dead of night. If you're planning a trip, that gives you two windows instead of one — work it.

The surprise this week was a 28-inch black sea bass that came off the same rip structure at Plum Gut, on a bucktail meant for bass. That's not a fluke — sea bass have moved onto that hard bottom in real numbers, stacking on the same rock piles and current breaks that hold the stripers. If you're fishing bucktails or diamond jigs down deep in the Gut right now, don't be shocked when something with a spiny dorsal fin nearly pulls your arm off. Keep a few Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged light for exactly that scenario.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing out here, full stop. The Race, the flats off Orient Point, the drift lanes along Fishers Island — keeper fluke are showing consistently in 20 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing, with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage on the drift. It's not a blitz, it's a grind — cover water, stay on bottom, work the seams where the current speeds up over the humps. But it's producing fish in the box every trip, which is more than I can say for some of the flashier bites right now.

Weakfish are worth a mention because they're some life on the calm, warm evenings — small numbers, but legal fish coming out of the same rip zones at dusk on bucktails and soft plastics fished slow near bottom. We flagged that rebuild coming on quiet evenings, and it's tracking. Not a target species yet, more of a bonus if you're already working the structure for bass.

Bluefish are the wildcard. The blitz action everyone's talking about — bunker schools getting hammered daily — is still concentrated west, from the Jersey beaches up through the western Sound. It hasn't pushed into Orient or Fishers Island Sound yet, but bunker schools have a way of migrating east through July, and if that bait shows up here, the blues will be right behind it. Keep an eye on the surface around Orient Point and the eastern flats — first sign of nervous water or diving birds, that's your cue.

Current's easing as we run toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means softer tide stages through the weekend. That's going to change the presentation game — less need to muscle a heavy jig through five knots, more room to work a slower swimbait retrieve and actually work an eddy instead of just surviving it. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Gut on the last half of Thursday's ebb, right as the moon phase starts softening the push. Have eels rigged heavy for the hard stages and a lighter swimbait rod ready for when it lays down. Bring a jig for the sea bass too — that bite's real, and it's a lot of fun on light tackle when the bass go quiet between current stages.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Into the Middle Ground — Bass Slide Into the Dark
reports.subhead: Bait's stacked thick from Norwalk to Port Jeff, but the bass have gone nocturnal on you — here's how to find them anyway.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning idling off Middle Ground Light with the sounder up and my eyes on the surface more than the screen, and here's what I found: peanut bunker balled up tight in maybe fifteen feet of water, nervous, flickering, with terns working them from above but no visible boils underneath. That's the tell. When the bait's getting pushed but nothing's exploding on it in daylight, the bass are down there working it after dark instead. Kings Point is reading 71.6 degrees this week — that's warm enough to push stripers into a thermal retreat, not gone, just smarter about when they eat.

This is the pattern across the whole Central Sound right now. Bunker schools — some peanut-sized, some already three to four inches and hardening up — are stacked from the Norwalk Islands down through Stratford Shoal and across to the Connecticut side off Charles Island. Where you find those schools tight to the bottom on the sounder during the day, you're looking at a night program. Anchor up on the drop-off edges around Stratford Shoal in eighteen to twenty-five feet as the sun goes down, soak a live bunker or a chunk on a fish-finder rig, and give it an hour either side of the tide change. I heard from two guys working the graveyard shift off Middle Ground last week who put overslot fish in the boat between eleven and one in the morning — nothing epic, two or three fish a trip, but real bass, upper 30s to low 40 inches, on fresh bunker chunks fished tight to bottom.

Daytime, the story shifts. If you want bass with the sun up, you need moving current and structure that breaks it — the last two hours of the ebb around the Norwalk Islands or the rips off Charles Island are still producing, but you're fishing the seam, not the flat. Bucktails in the three-quarter to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the current break, have been the better call than anything trolled through open water. This lines up with what I've been seeing for weeks now — the fish that do feed in daylight are doing it where the tide concentrates bait against structure, not out in the middle of the Sound where the water's just soaking up sun.

Fluke fishing is the one thing I can point to and say is dependable right now, no asterisks. Stratford Shoal and the rip lines off Middle Ground continue to hold keeper-class fish in eighteen to thirty feet, and they're not picky — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow on the drift, are doing the damage. I had a report of a six-pound fluke off the Shoal on the last of an incoming tide, which tells you these fish are still using that current to set up ambushes on the same bait pods the bass are shadowing at night. Porgies are riding shotgun on the same structure — anchor up on any rocky patch inside the Norwalk Islands with sandworms or clam and you'll fill a bucket without much drama, though nothing trophy-sized to report.

Bluefish are the wildcard piece right now. They're not blitzing the surface like the beachfront stuff further south, but they're absolutely underneath these same bunker schools, and when you find a school getting nervous with no birds working it, drop a diamond jig or a bucktail through it and you'll usually connect. I had blues to six pounds come through off Port Jefferson harbor mouth chasing peanut bunker right at the mouth of the channel — fun fish on light tackle, and they'll keep showing wherever that bait holds.

Weakfish have been quieter than I'd like to report, but a few calm, warm evenings lately have started to rebuild some activity around the deeper holes off the Connecticut shore — nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet, but worth a few casts with a soft plastic on the dropoffs if you're already out there after dark for bass.

We flagged bonito working into the Western Sound last week, and while nothing's crossed my transom yet here in the Central stretch, the bait conditions are exactly what you'd want if that push is coming — tight bunker schools, warm surface water, clean edges around Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands where bonito like to slash through. I'll be watching close over the next week, particularly on calm mornings when the water's glassy enough to spot fins.

The moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, which means tides are easing, not surging — good news for the slower bucktail presentations working the rips, tougher for anybody hoping for a hard-current blitz. If I had one trip this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb off Charles Island for daylight bass on bucktails, then come back after dark and anchor a chunk off Stratford Shoal for the bigger nocturnal fish. Bring both game plans — this water's not making it easy on you right now, but the bait's here, and where the bait goes, eventually the fish follow.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks goes dark by day — bass feeding is a nighttime job now
reports.subhead: Warm water from the Throgs Neck to Matinecock has pushed the stripers nocturnal, but fluke and porgies are covering for them in daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop this week asked me straight out — "Frank, what happened to Exec Rocks? I fished the ebb Tuesday morning, marked bait all over the sounder, and couldn't buy a bass." I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen the last ten days: the fish didn't leave, they just clocked out for the day shift.

Kings Point is reading 71.6 degrees right now, and that's warm enough to push stripers into a thermal-avoidance pattern — they're not gone, they're just smart. During daylight they're tucked deep on structure, breathing easier in whatever cooler water they can find, and they don't turn on the feed bag hard until the sun drops and the current gets moving again. I've seen this pattern plenty of Julys going back to the '90s. When the western basin runs a few degrees warmer than the middle Sound — and right now it is, with New London still down around 67.6 — the bass here get nocturnal and structure-locked. Execution Rocks, the rockpile off Matinecock Point, the drop at Stepping Stones — they're all still holding bass. You just need to be fishing them after dark or right at first light, not at 10 a.m. with the sun beating down.

I worked Execution Rocks last Thursday night on the last two hours of the outgoing, anchored up-current of the light and drifting live bunker back on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead, into the wash. Two fish over 30 inches in about ninety minutes, both came right as the tide bottomed out and the current eased to a crawl. That slower water at the bottom of the tide is when these fish commit — they're not fighting hard current, they're just sliding out of the rocks to grab what's drifting past. If you've got the stomach for a midnight run, that's still the highest-percentage bass play in the western Sound right now.

Daytime, though, is a different game — and a good one. Fluke have been steady on the reefs and humps off Matinecock and out toward Hart Island, holding in 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming and first two hours of the outgoing. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom with a slight bounce, have been outproducing bulkier rigs — the water's clear enough right now that these fish want a subtle presentation, not a big splashy teaser strip. Nothing gigantic, but a mixed bag of keepers to 22 inches with enough shorts mixed in to keep the rod bending.

Porgies are around the same structure — Hart Island rockpiles, the reef stretch off Matinecock — but I'll be honest with you, the grade is on the small side this year. Plenty of action, sandworms and clam on a high-low rig will keep you busy, but you're not filling a cooler with dinner-plate porgies like you would out east. We flagged that a week back and it's holding true — fun for a kid's rod, not a fish fry.

Bluefish have been the most reliable action of the week and honestly the most fun. They're not deep, they're not subtle, and they don't care what time it is — I've had them busting bait off the Throgs Neck at noon and again at dusk off Stepping Stones. Peanut bunker have been thick along the bridge riprap, and when the blues find them it's a five-minute free-for-all. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything silver you can chuck fast — will get bit the second it hits the water. Bring wire leader or you'll lose half your tackle box to the first pass.

Weakfish have shown up sporadically in Manhasset Bay and up into Little Neck Bay on the early morning outgoing, mostly smaller fish mixed in with the fluke crowd, nothing to build a trip around yet but worth a few casts of a bucktail-and-bait combo if you're already out there.

Looking ahead: we're running into the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the tidal swings are easing up through the weekend. That's actually good news for the rip fishing — Stepping Stones and the Exec Rocks current line fish better on that softer water because these bass, still working around the thermal squeeze, don't want to burn energy fighting a hard rip. Slow it down, fish the last hour of any tide change, and give the fish time to commit. I'd also keep an ear out for the first bonito scouts pushing into the Sound over the next week or two — that's usually a late-July story out here, and with warm water already stacked up from the city end to Matinecock, conditions are lining up right for it. Nothing confirmed on my end yet, but it's exactly the kind of summer that produces an early one. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the night bite at Execution Rocks on the bottom of the outgoing, live bunker if you can net them, and I'd have a fluke rod rigged and ready for when the sun comes up.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 6:50: keeper bass on the drop, fluke stacked on the flood
reports.subhead: No bonito yet off the Block, but the structure bite at SW Ledge is paying rent for anyone who fishes the tide right.
reports.body_markdown:
6:50 a.m. is the number I've been working off SW Ledge all week — that's when the morning slack sets up on the bigger tides, and it's a ten-minute window on either side where the current goes soft enough to hold bottom without ripping your jig sideways. Miss it by twenty minutes and you're fighting three knots of green water for nothing. Hit it right and you're marking fish stacked on the drop from 55 to 80 feet, right where the ledge falls off the hard sand into that rubble bottom south of the tower.

This isn't the October class of bass yet — I'm not going to sell anyone on giants this week. What's down there right now is a healthy population of 26 to 34-inch fish holding tight to structure, feeding hard on the last twenty minutes of the ebb and picking back up as the flood starts to build. I've had the best luck dropping 4-ounce diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid straight down on the upcurrent side of the ledge, letting it fall to the bottom, and working it up in long sweeps rather than the short jigging stroke you'd use in the fall. These fish are eating slow right now — the water's warm enough that they're not chasing hard, they're ambushing. A bucktail in white or chartreuse, 2 to 3 ounces depending on the drift speed, dragged just off bottom on the last of the ebb has worked just as well as the jig, and it's a lot less arm work for a morning charter.

Fluke have been the more consistent story the last ten days. The south side of Block, working the drift from the Coast Guard Channel out toward the deeper water off Old Harbor, has been giving up decent numbers of keepers in 30 to 45 feet on the incoming tide. Gulp swimming mullets in pink shad or white, threaded on a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a squid strip trailer, dragged slow along the sand-to-mud transitions — that's been the winning combination. Nothing giant, mostly 17 to 20 inches with the occasional 4 or 5-pounder mixed in, but enough action to keep rods bent through a tide change, which is more than I can say for some weeks out here.

Sea bass are doing what sea bass do in July — sitting tight on every piece of structure around the Ledge and out toward the humps southwest of the island, and they'll eat just about anything you drop if you're patient enough to find the right depth. Clam on a bucktail teaser rig, bounced right on bottom in 50 to 70 feet, has been steady. Not a bonanza, but a reliable fill-the-cooler bite if the bass and fluke go quiet on you.

Now, the question I'm getting at the dock every single day this week: where are the bonito? Short answer — not here yet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Water off the Block has been running in that 68 to 71-degree range, which is right on the edge of what gets bonito interested, but I haven't had a confirmed sighting or a hookup to report. What I have seen is bait starting to show heavier around Sandy Point and North Light — peanut bunker pushing through on the last of the ebb, and some silversides working the beach at Clay Head in the evenings. That's the setup. Bonito follow that bait, and historically for this stretch of coast, late July into early August is when the first scouts show off the Block, usually right around Sandy Point where the current sweeps bait around the north end. I'd keep a bag of Deadly Dicks or small metal in the boat starting this week, because when they show, they show fast and they don't stick around long enough for you to run home and get gear.

Bluefish have been filling in the gaps nicely, and I mean that as a compliment this time of year — chopper blues in the 4 to 8-pound class are hammering bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the Ledge on the tide change, and they've saved more than one slow morning when the bass wanted nothing to do with anything moving. If you're marking bait on the sounder and getting refusals from stripers, there's a good chance blues are sitting under that same bait and will eat what the bass won't.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep working that 6:50 slack window at SW Ledge as long as the tide charts hold that timing, and I'd start checking Sandy Point in the evenings for surface activity — birds working, bait nervous, anything that looks like the first bonito showing. If the water pushes past 72 off the north end like it's been trending, I wouldn't be surprised to get a confirmed report by the first days of August. Until then, the honest move is fluke on the drift and bass on the structure — steady work, not spectacular, but the kind of fishing that fills a cooler if you respect the tide.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday, Green Gold by Thursday: Poor Man's Yellowfin Bail Out the Week
reports.subhead: A short-period blow shut us down early, but squid-soaked water off Poor Man's and steady bluefin at Norfolk turned a slow start into a real week.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a split-decision week. Monday and Tuesday we sat at the dock watching 3 to 4 foot slop stack up on a nasty four-second period — that's wind swell, not groundswell, and it makes for a miserable ride out past the Baltimore Channel. By Wednesday afternoon it laid down enough to run, and from Thursday through the weekend Poor Man's Canyon flat-out bailed us out. If I'm grading the week, I'd call it a C-plus that finished like a B.

Here's the thing about running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City — you can't fall in love with one piece of water. I had three boats calling me Wednesday night asking where to point the bow, and I sent all three different directions based on what I was hearing from guys already out there. That's the whole game this time of year.

Poor Man's was the story. We worked the edge east of the tails, around 38°37'N/73°58'W, dropping down the 100-fathom curve where the water turned that milky jade-green that tells you the squid are thick underneath you. Illex and shortfin squid have been balled up out there for two weeks now, and the yellowfin are sitting right on top of them. Sizes ran the gamut — plenty of 40-to-70-pound class fish mixed with a few genuine bigeye pushing past 100 that came on the troll around daybreak. Standard spread of ballyhoo behind Green Machines and small Ilanders on the short riggers, but the real difference-maker was dropping a naked ballyhoo flat-lined off the shotgun in that green water — that's where the bigger fish were sitting. At night, guys anchored up and lit the water with underwater squid lights picked off a handful of bigeye on butterfly jigs worked slow through 200 to 300 feet. Not every boat that tried it connected, but the ones that did had a real shot at a fish over the century mark.

Norfolk, out of Ocean City, was the quiet steady producer all week — less flashy than Poor Man's but more consistent. Bluefin have been sitting on the humps in 20 to 25 fathoms working up toward the canyon edge itself, chewing on sand eels and rainbait pushed up by the same warm surface water we're seeing inshore — NY Bight buoy read 71.6°F this week, and that's roughly the flavor of water riding out over the shelf right now. We trolled small cedar plugs and green machines on the meat rig around the humps early, then shifted to jigging vertically once the sun got up and the fish went down — 200-gram speed jigs worked with a slow pump-and-wind put schoolie-class bluefin from 20 to 40 pounds in the box on three separate trips this week. Wahoo showed up as a bonus for one boat running a straight high-speed spread — 12 to 14 knots with cedar plugs and small Ilanders down the drop-off — but that was one fish, not a pattern yet. I wouldn't build a trip around wahoo at Norfolk this week, but I'd rig for the possibility.

Spencer Canyon gave us white marlin, but scattered — not the kind of week where you mark six or eight in a day. Two boats out of Cape May had multiple bites working the 50 to 60 fathom edge west of the canyon head, teasing fish up on a dredge and switching them over to naked ballyhoo on circle hooks. One boat went 3-for-5, another went 1-for-4, and a couple came home having seen fish but never converted. That's marlin fishing — you put your teasers in front of enough fish and some of them commit. Mahi showed as incidental catches around any floating structure or weed line we crossed on the way out — nothing giant, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 5 to 12 pound range, though one boat did pull a 38-pound bull off a lobster pot buoy on a small green-and-yellow popper. Worth keeping a spinning rod rigged and ready on the run out, because you never know when you'll cross a good line.

Lindenkohl I'm giving a pass on this week. The water up there hasn't been holding the same bait concentration as Poor Man's — less squid sign, cleaner blue water instead of that jade-green tuna color — and the one report I got back was a long day for one modest yellowfin. I'd rather send a boat south to Poor Man's or Norfolk right now than gamble on Lindenkohl waking up.

Looking ahead, the forecast has southwest winds building into a heat dome pattern by midweek, which usually means calmer seas but also means watching afternoon thunderstorm cells pop off the beach — standard July stuff. If that squid stays balled up on Poor Man's, I'd keep pointing boats there first; that's historically been one of the better stretches of the season for yellowfin numbers, and the second week of July has a track record of turning it on in these canyons. Norfolk should stay steady for bluefin as long as the humps keep holding bait. My plan for next week is simple — Poor Man's at first light for yellowfin, with Norfolk as the backup if the green water moves or thins out. I'd have a naked ballyhoo rigged and ready either way.

reports.headline: Captree Dock Talk: Bridge Fluke Holding Steady While Bass Hug the Inlet Seam
reports.subhead: A sloppy ocean pushed the fleet inside this week, and the fish that matter most right now were waiting there anyway.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Vinny at the fuel dock Tuesday morning, just off a half-day charter, shaking his head about the ocean. "Three-footers on a four-second period," he said, like that explains everything — and honestly, it does. That's a mean, stacked-up chop, not a rolling swell you can fish through comfortably, and it's had the open-water guys running back through the inlet by ten a.m. all week. I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen: quit fighting the Atlantic and go find where the fish already are. They're inside. They've been inside.

The water temp out at the buoy off the Bight is sitting around 71.6, which sounds warm and it is, but that short, choppy 3-to-4 foot slop with a southwest-leaning swell direction has made the surf and near-shore ocean grounds miserable to fish with any precision. Meanwhile the bay and the inlet channels are calm, structured, and full of bait. That's the story this week — not one big bite everywhere, but a handful of very specific, very productive windows if you know where to put the boat.

Fluke first, because that's been the most consistent thing going. The Robert Moses bridges — both the Fire Island span and the Captree side — are still holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot band along the pilings and the current breaks off the pilons. I've been drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current really combs bait past the structure. Doubles have come over the rail more than once when the drift lines up right — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 20 inches with a few pushing 4 pounds mixed in, but steady enough that a morning trip is worth your gas. If the current's slack or barely moving, don't bother — these fish want that pressure pushing bait to them, and dead water at the bridges is dead fishing.

Striped bass have settled into a real pattern at the inlet seam, right where the outgoing dumps out past Democrat Point and the current rips against the deeper channel edge. Bunker schools have been pushing through there on the last two hours of the ebb, and the bass are sitting underneath and behind them, picking off stragglers. I've had my best luck snagging a bunker and dropping it right into the seam, letting it sink on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — no need for anything fancy. Bucktail guys working the same water with 2-ounce white or bone bucktails, bounced slow along the bottom edge where the sand drops into the channel, have connected too, though the bunker-drop has been the more consistent producer. Sizes have been mixed — a lot of mid-20s to low-30s, with the occasional bigger fish mixed into the bunker pods right at first light or the last hour before dark. This isn't an all-day bite. It's tide-and-light dependent, and if you miss that window, you're just burning fuel.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with those bunker schools at the inlet mouth, and they've actually been the more reliable action some mornings — chopper blues in the 3 to 6 pound range busting bait right on the surface off Democrat Point, visible from a hundred yards out by the birds working overhead. Simple diamond jigs or a topwater popper thrown right into the commotion has been all it takes. If you want fast, aggressive action without overthinking the tide, that's your play right now.

I'll be straight with you on weakfish — it's been quiet. A few guys working the deeper holes off Nicoll Bay after dark with soft-plastic grubs on light jig heads have picked at a fish or two, but it's nothing like the numbers we used to see this time of year in the bay, and I'm not going to sell you on a bite that isn't really there. If weakfish are your target, treat it as a bonus fish while you're doing something else, not a dedicated trip.

Porgies have been the honest, blue-collar bite this week, and I mean that as a compliment. Anchoring up on the rockpiles inside Fire Island Inlet and around Democrat Point with sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig has produced steady, respectable numbers — not trophy fish, but a cooler full of dinner porgies for not much effort, which is worth something when the bigger stuff is being finicky about tide and light.

Looking ahead, the ocean forecast doesn't show that chop settling down dramatically through the weekend, so I'd keep planning around the inside game rather than fighting the surf. If the wind does back off and that swell period stretches out, Democrat Point and the ocean beaches west toward Cedar Beach could turn on for bass working bait pushed tight to the sand — that's the scenario I'd watch for. Until then, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet seam for bass and bunker, hit the bridges on that same dropping water for fluke, and keep a rod rigged with a diamond jig for whatever blues show up chopping on the surface. It's not a blowout week, but it's an honest one, and there's enough happening inside that a well-timed trip should put fish in the box.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier at Dawn: Fluke to Five Pounds While the Ocean Stays Angry
reports.subhead: With the surf blown out at Breezy and Rockaway, the smart money moved into the bay's channels — and got rewarded.
reports.body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Canarsie Pier at 5:40 Tuesday morning because the ocean gave me no other choice. Buoy readings off the Bight have been sitting around 71 to 72 degrees with three-foot swell on a short four-second period — that's not surf you fish comfortably from a beach chair, and it's definitely not surf you paddle into. So I did what I've done for twenty years when the Atlantic gets sloppy: I turned my back on it and went to work the flats and channels between Ruffle Bar and Grassy Bay, where the water lies down even when the wind won't.

Good call. I had four fluke in the yak before seven, biggest going about five pounds, all on a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the drop from eight feet down to sixteen off the edge of the flat. The current there was still building on the incoming, and fluke were sitting right on that seam where the mud gives way to sand. If you're working this spot from a boat, same drill — short drifts, bucktail bouncing bottom, and don't be afraid to let it sit dead still for a second before the next hop. That's usually when they eat.

The bay itself has been carrying more bait than I've seen in a few Julys — peanut bunker pushing through Beach Channel, small mullet stacked along the marsh edges by North Channel Bridge. That bait is exactly why the fluke bite has stayed dependable even with the ocean acting up. When the front is rough, forage gets squeezed into the estuary, and predators follow the food, not the tide charts. I talked to a guy at the Motts Basin ramp Wednesday who'd boxed a limit of keeper fluke in that same stretch, plus two shorts he tossed back — a good, honest morning, not a giveaway, but a real bite if you put in the drift time.

Stripers are trickier right now, and I'll be straight with you — the daytime bay bite has gone quiet the way it always does in mid-July heat. Bass don't love warm, thin water in bright sun, and Jamaica Bay's shallow flats heat up fast under a July sun. What's working is night fishing at Marine Parkway Bridge, and it's working the way it always has for me: get there an hour before the tide turns to outgoing, park tight to the pilings on the Rockaway side, and swim a white bucktail or a fresh eel through the shadow lines the lights throw on the water. I had two fish over 28 inches Thursday night doing exactly that, both within the first hour of the ebb, both right where the current started ripping off the structure. After that first hour of hard water movement, the bite shuts down fast — so don't sleep in and expect it to still be happening at midnight.

Bluefish have been the most reliable thing in the whole system. Rockaway Inlet has had blitzy pockets on the last of the outgoing, birds working tight over bunker pods, choppers in the 3 to 5 pound range slashing metal — I've been throwing a 1-ounce Deadly Dick and hooking up on almost every other cast when I find the right push of water off the Breezy Point side. If you're fishing from the rocks at Breezy, that outgoing water funneling past the point is your window; go an hour either side of the tide change and you'll likely find something busting on top, even with the ocean beyond the inlet still churned up and unfishable.

Porgies are around Cross Bay Bridge in decent numbers, nothing spectacular but steady — bloodworms or a chunk of clam on a high-low rig, fished tight to the pilings on the bottom half of the tide, will get you a nice mess for the pan. I haven't heard a single solid weakfish report out of the bay this year, which tracks with what's been happening system-wide — that fishery just isn't what it used to be here, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you want tiderunners, you're better off putting your time into bass and fluke right now and treating any weakfish as a bonus, not a target.

Looking at the week ahead, the ocean isn't likely to settle fast — that swell period and the wind pattern feeding it suggest Breezy and Rockaway Beach stay lumpy through at least the weekend. That's fine by me. It means another week of leaning on the bay's structure and current edges instead of fighting whitewater. If I had one trip to make, I'd launch out of Canarsie or Motts Basin on the front half of an outgoing tide, work the Ruffle Bar flats for fluke while the water's still moving, then slide over to Marine Parkway right at dusk to catch that first hour of ebb for bass. Two access points, one tide cycle, and you've covered both bites without burning a full tank of gas. Keep an eye on the bunker schools moving through the inlet too — wherever they stack up tight, the blues and the bigger bass won't be far behind.

reports.headline: Stellwagen Basin mud at 190 feet: haddock steady, bluefin finally chasing mack on the northern edge
reports.subhead: Cod have slid deep off the gravel with the summer warm-up, but the mud bite holds and the tuna bite is starting to build on the Bank.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-eight degrees on the surface over the Stellwagen Basin Tuesday morning, and 190 feet on the sounder before the mud showed up clean on the screen — soft, rolling bottom with just enough life on it to tell you the haddock are home. That's been the read most of this week: surface water pushing warm, mid-70s in spots on the shallower flats, but the deep basin between Stellwagen and Tillies still holds that cold cushion the groundfish want in July.

Cod have done what they always do this time of year — they've backed off the classic gravel patches on the western edge and slid into deeper, cooler pockets. I'm not finding much shallower than 140 feet right now with any consistency. The 39-42 fathom line off the northwest corner, where the gravel breaks up into scattered boulder and shell hash, gave up a handful of cod to 15 pounds on Thursday, but you had to work for every one of them. Jigging diamond jigs with a green tube teaser, tipped light with clam, is still the go-to when the current's moving. When it slacks off, switch to bait — whole clam on a high-low rig fished right on bottom, patient, letting it sit. The cod bite isn't dead, it's just spread thin and deep, and anybody telling you it's stacked up shallow this week is selling something.

Haddock are the more honest fish right now. The mud bottom in the basin, running 180 to 220 feet, has been holding solid schools — we've had double and triple headers on some drifts with fish running 2 to 5 pounds, a few pushing 7. Standard haddock rig, two hooks, red or chartreuse beads, clam or squid strips, bounced just off bottom on the drift. The current has to be moving enough to keep the bait presenting naturally — dead slack and they go quiet on you. Tillies Bank has been the more consistent producer of the two basins this week over the classic mud south of the humps, though Stellwagen's own basin ground isn't far behind.

Now for the fish everybody's been asking about at the dock. The bluefin are showing, and it's the mackerel that brought them. We've had good pods of mackerel stacked up over the northern part of the Bank, in that 60 to 90 foot range, and where you find bait balled up tight and diving birds working it, you're starting to see fish push up under it — boils, sometimes whole schools of small mackerel getting shredded from below. Nothing like the giant class fish you'll see out here come September, these are mostly school-size to mid-60-inch fish so far, but a few boats have hooked up trolling small spreader bars and green machines right through the bait schools in that stretch running from the northeast edge down toward Cape Cod Tails. If you can find fresh mackerel yourself, jig up a dozen, keep a couple live-lined off a balloon or kite rig near the surface, and drift through the bait — that's produced better than blind trolling this week.

The pattern makes sense when you think about it. Mackerel like that cooler, well-oxygenated water on top of the Bank, and where the mackerel go, the tuna follow. It's early yet for the real giant class fish that'll show later in the summer chasing sand eels and herring, but this early mackerel-driven bite is a good sign the Bank's setting up the way it should for late July and into August. Pollock have been mixed in around the wrecks and the steeper drop-offs on the eastern side of Stellwagen, taking diamond jigs meant for cod, and there's been a scattering of hake showing on the softer mud edges at night for anyone willing to soak bait after dark.

Tide's been the deciding factor more than wind lately — we've had a stretch of manageable southwest breeze, nothing over 15 knots most days, so it's really about picking your drift around the moving water rather than fighting sea state. We're coming off the new moon now, tides building toward the next push, and that stronger current should help both the haddock bite on the mud and get the cod moving again on whatever gravel they're holding to.

Looking ahead, if the mackerel schools hold their position on the northern Bank through this week, I'd expect the bluefin activity to build rather than fade — that's usually how it goes once the bait sets up. I'd spend my first hour scouting for bird activity and bait balls before committing to a troll pattern. For groundfish, I'm staying deep and patient — the basin mud over gravel structure at 180 feet-plus is the safer bet through the heat of summer, and I wouldn't waste a tide working shallow gravel hoping the cod haven't left yet. They have. Give the deep water a shot, keep an eye out for diving terns on the surface, and don't be surprised if this mackerel-tuna pattern turns into something worth planning a whole trip around by early August.

reports.headline: Billingsgate on the Flood: Bass to 30 Pounds, Cod Pushed Deep for Summer
reports.subhead: Mid-July heat has scattered the bass and sent the cod off the shoals, but the flood tide over Billingsgate and the rips off Race Point are still giving up fish to the patient boat.
reports.body_markdown:
Wednesday morning I had the boat idling off Billingsgate an hour before the top of the flood, watching the fish finder paint bait stacked tight to the bottom in eighteen feet. No birds working, no surface commotion, just that quiet hum on the sounder that tells you something's down there worth a look. I dropped a live pogie on a three-way rig, let it settle to the sand, and within five minutes had a bass pulling drag toward the deeper edge of the flat. Thirty pounds, give or take, came over the rail heavy and dark, the kind of fish that's been living on the bottom structure instead of chasing bait on top. That's been the story this month — the big ones are here, but they're not showing themselves the way they do in June. You have to go down and get them.

Water's warmed up enough now that the mackerel schools that held the bass tight to Race Point through late spring have thinned out and scattered east toward deeper, cooler water off the backside. I was out there Monday on the last of the ebb, working the rip where it breaks over the bar, and instead of the tight bait balls we had a few weeks back, it was patchy — small pockets here and there, enough to draw fish but not enough to hold a school in one spot for long. We picked up three bass in the low twenties on live mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig, twenty to twenty-five feet down, letting the current carry the bait naturally through the rip face. Slow going, but quality fish, and every one of them came right on the edge where the moving water meets the slower inside water — that seam is still the money spot, tide stage doesn't matter as much as finding where that color change and current break line up.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more about bluefish than stripers the last two weeks. Mid-morning, an hour either side of the tide change, we've run into surface blitzes — blues in the six-to-ten-pound class ripping through pogie schools, water churned white for a hundred yards. Topwater poppers and metal-lip swimmers thrown right into the chaos will get bit on almost every cast when it's happening, but it's not an all-day thing. It flares up, burns hot for twenty minutes, then shuts off just as fast when the bait scatters or sounds. If you see the birds working there, don't wait — get on it, because it won't last.

Sandy Neck and the mouth of Barnstable Harbor have been the more consistent producer for anyone who doesn't want to chase a moving bite. Fluke fishing there has held steady on the sand-to-grass edges in twelve to twenty feet, drifting white Gulp on quarter-ounce jigheads with a strip of squid for scent. Nothing huge — most fish going fifteen to eighteen inches with a few keepers mixed in — but it's a bite you can count on through the middle of the day when the sun's high and the bigger fish elsewhere have gone quiet. Best water's been on the last two hours of the incoming, when the tide's pushing bait up onto the flat edges and the fluke are sitting up to intercept it.

Cod is where I have to level with people. The shoals inside the bay — Billingsgate, the humps off Wellfleet — just don't hold cod once the water warms through July like it has. Those fish have pushed off to deeper structure, and inside the bay proper you're not going to find a real cod bite until the fall cools things back down. If someone's dead set on cod right now, I'd point them toward the deeper edges out past the bay mouth, not waste a summer morning jigging the shallow humps hoping for something that's already left.

Tide-wise, we're building toward the new moon, and that bigger swing should push more water through the rips at Race Point and give the bait somewhere to concentrate again instead of drifting loose. If that happens, I'd expect the mackerel to tighten back up and pull the bass with them — that's the pattern I've watched play out for thirty years out here, big tides reorganize the bait and the fish follow. Doesn't always happen exactly on schedule, but it's worth being out there on the days around the new moon to find out.

For the next several days, my plan is simple: mornings on Billingsgate over the flood for the bigger bottom-hugging bass, middle of the day on the Sandy Neck flats for a reliable fluke pick, and I'll keep an eye on the birds off Peaked Hill in case the blues fire up again. If the tide swing does what I think it'll do, Race Point should tighten back up by the weekend and be worth another run at the rip. Bring more bait than you think you need — pogies and mackerel have both been a little harder to net clean this month, and a dry well will end your day faster than any tide change will.

reports.headline: Mackerel Push Bass Shallow: 49-Inch Fish Off Plymouth, Flounder Working Deer Island Flat
reports.subhead: With bait schools running thick off the South Shore, I sent my week south instead of north — here's why, and where the harbor still delivered.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a choice to make Monday morning — run the harbor islands like I usually do this time of year, or point south toward Plymouth and Duxbury where word was mackerel schools have been rolling thick along the beach. I went south first. When mackerel show in numbers like they have the last ten days, big bass follow them right up onto the bars, and a fish pushing 49 inches doesn't come from nowhere. That's the kind of intel that changes a week's plan.

The South Shore didn't disappoint, but it wasn't a layup either. Duxbury Bay and the outer edge of Plymouth Beach have had pods of mackerel stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming, and where the bait bunches against the bar, the bass have been sitting underneath waiting. Best presentation has been a bare mackerel jig dropped through the school to snag a live one, then free-lined back with just enough weight to keep it down near bottom in 15 to 20 feet. No wire, no heavy leader — these fish are eating naturally and they know the difference. The 40-inch-plus class has come almost entirely on live mackerel fished this way, right at first light before the boat traffic stirs things up. By mid-morning the bite goes quiet and stays that way until the tide turns again in the evening. That's the pattern — two windows a day, tide-driven, and if you're not there for the window you're just burning gas.

Back in the harbor, Deer Island continues to do what it always does for me in mid-July — flounder on the flat and bass off the drop. The channel edge on the north side of Deer Island Light drops from eight feet down to better than 30 in a short run, and on the outgoing tide that edge holds bait that gets pushed off the flat. I've been anchoring up-current of the drop and drifting sandworms and clam bellies on a simple two-hook flounder rig for a mixed bag — nothing huge, but a fifteen-fish morning isn't unusual right now if you hit dead low through the first hour of the outgoing. Once the current really starts moving, I switch over and work bucktails — half-ounce white with a chunk of pork rind — along the same drop for bass. They're not stacked up thick, but there's a resident population working that ledge all summer and a couple of keepers most trips isn't a bad return for an hour's work.

Spectacle Island has been slower than I'd like it. The water on the flats around there has warmed enough that the bigger bass have mostly moved off into deeper water during the day, and what's left is smaller fish picking at green crabs and worms in close to the rocks. I'm not writing it off completely — an evening tide change with some current still moving can produce, but I wouldn't make it my first stop right now.

Nahant has been more consistent, especially the rocks on the east side toward the Causeway. Bass have been holding tight to structure there on the last of the incoming, ambushing whatever gets pushed against the ledges. Topwater plugs at dusk have worked well — a Danny-style swimmer worked slow across the surface has drawn some good strikes in that last hour of light. Nothing over 34 inches that I've seen personally, but a lot of mid-20s to low-30s fish, and that's a fun bite on light spinning gear.

Up on Cape Ann, the story's been about bluefish more than bass this week. Gloucester Harbor and the rocks around Rockport have had blues chopping bait on the surface during the middle of the day — not the giant class, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but plenty of them, and they'll hit anything shiny moving fast. Small metal jigs, half-ounce Kastmasters, cast into the working birds has been the easiest way to get bit. Bass fishing along the Cape Ann ledges has been quieter — a few fish coming off the deeper structure off Straitsmouth on the dropping tide, but it's been a fish here, a fish there, not a pattern I'd build a whole trip around yet.

Water's comfortable right now across the whole zone — warm in the shallow harbor flats, a touch cooler out along the open ledges off Cape Ann, which is typical for mid-July. Tides have been moving well without any big extremes, which keeps these current-edge bites predictable if you're willing to work around the clock rather than fish whenever's convenient.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep my attention on the South Shore as long as those mackerel schools hold. If the bait pushes offshore or breaks up, the big bass will follow it, and Plymouth and Duxbury could go quiet fast — that's happened before in past summers when a bait pod moves overnight. In the harbor, Deer Island should keep producing flounder on the outgoing as long as the current keeps sweeping that flat clean, and I expect Nahant's dusk topwater bite to hold steady through the week if the wind stays manageable. If you've only got one trip in you, I'd fish the early incoming at Plymouth Beach with a mackerel jig rigged and ready — but I'd have Deer Island as my backup if the bait doesn't show.

reports.headline: 3:52 Ebb at the East End: Bass on the Rip, Gone in 40 Minutes
reports.subhead: Three days past the new moon and the Canal's still running spring-tide hot, but the window at Scusset is shrinking fast and you need to be standing there when it opens.
reports.body_markdown:
3.8 knots. That's what max ebb read off the east end this morning at 6:47, three days past the new moon and still riding that spring tide push before we slide into neaps by the weekend. I stood on the rocks below the Sagamore Bridge watching the water pour out of that ditch like someone pulled a plug, and for about forty minutes — from roughly 5:50 to 6:30 — the rip off Scusset stacked up bait and bent rods. After that the current eased, the rip flattened out, and the bite went with it. That's the Canal in July. You don't fish the tide, you fish the forty minutes inside the tide.

Here's what's been happening. The bass have been sitting on the seam where the outflow meets the slower water along the beach, right where the sand drops off into that scoured channel. Guys throwing white bucktails, 1.5 to 2 ounces depending on how hard she's running, casting up-current and letting the jig swing through the seam before working it back — that's been the play. A couple of slot fish in the 30-inch range came off that rip Tuesday morning on that exact drift, and I heard of one over 36 inches taken on a chunk of mackerel fished on the bottom right at the base of the rip during the same window. Live eels after dark have been the better bet for the bigger fish — one 40-incher reported off the herring run side around 9 PM on a slow-swum eel, fished on the last of the ebb before the current went soft.

The mackerel run is done, though — that's a May-June story, and anybody still tying on tins expecting green backs is wasting casts. What's replaced it is squid. Small squid have been showing under the lights at night along both ends, and that's exactly what those bigger bass are keying on after dark. If you've got squid jigs or soft-bodied squid imitations in white or pink, work them slow near the bottom on the last two hours of the ebb, especially off the west end near Hog Island and the Mashnee flats where the current softens up before it reverses.

Speaking of the west end — that's been the more consistent water this week, if less explosive. The seams off Mashnee Island and Wings Neck have been holding schoolies and a mix of slot fish through the last two hours of the flood, when the incoming current pushes bait up against the rocks and the drop-off along the Cleveland Ledge side. Bucktails again, but lighter — 3/4 to 1 ounce — dragged slow along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid. Fluke have been mixed in on that same structure, a few keepers to 20 inches coming off the sandy patches between Mashnee and Phinneys Harbor on the last of the flood into the top of the tide, drifted with Gulp on light jig heads. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady enough that it's worth a stop if the east end rip has gone quiet on you.

Bluefish have finally shown some teeth in the mix — choppers in the 3 to 5 pound class crashing bait on both ends, mostly on the same tide stages as the bass, which means if you're marking bait busting on the surface during that ebb window at Scusset, don't be shy about throwing a wire leader and a Deadly Dick. They'll clear a school of peanut bunker in about ten casts and then vanish just as fast.

No albies, no bonito yet — too early for that, and I wouldn't waste time looking. That push usually doesn't show in the Canal until late August, once the water in the bay and Vineyard Sound climbs into the high 60s and pushes bait tight to structure. I'll start watching for false albacore signs closer to the third week of August, same as every year.

Honest assessment: this is not a wire-to-wire bite right now. The current is still strong enough off the spring tide to create real windows, but they're short — twenty, thirty, forty minutes around max ebb or max flood, and dead in between. I fished the midday slack Tuesday just to confirm what I already knew and got nothing but sunburn. If you're driving distance to fish this water, don't show up at noon and expect fish. Show up with the tide chart open and be standing on the rocks fifteen minutes before max current, because that rip line doesn't wait for anybody.

Looking ahead — we're sliding into neap tides by Sunday and Monday, which means less current, softer rips, and a quieter bite on both ends. That's when I shift tactics: smaller profile lures, slower presentations, and more patience working the seams instead of relying on raw current speed to concentrate the bait. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take Thursday's 5:40 AM ebb at the east end — still enough push off the tail of this spring cycle to turn the rip on, cool early light, and bait already staged from the last few days of squid activity. After that, I'd bank on the west end seams carrying the week through the weak tides, because that structure produces even when the current gets lazy. Watch the clock, watch the color of the water going through the pilings, and don't waste your best casts on slack.

reports.headline: Monhegan Ledges on the Ebb: Pollock Topside, Bass Chasing Pogies Into the Bay
reports.subhead: Mackerel showed thick off Damariscove this week, and where the mackerel go, the bass and pollock follow — but the groundfish still make you work for it.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-some years back, my father had a rule about mid-July: don't leave the dock till you've seen what the gulls are doing over Damariscove. If they're diving, the mackerel are up, and if the mackerel are up, everything else that eats is close behind. I still follow that rule. This week the birds were working hard off the Cove and again out toward Monhegan, and sure enough, the whole food chain lined up behind them — pollock on top, bass working the edges, and the groundfish holding deep where they always do this time of year.

Monhegan's south side has been the most reliable piece of water in the zone. Around White Head and down toward the ledges off Manana, pollock have been busting bait on the surface in the gray light before seven, then dropping again once the sun gets up. A 2 to 3-ounce diamond jig worked with a quick, erratic retrieve has taken fish steady — nothing huge, mostly 3 to 6 pounds, but enough for a fast morning. Striped bass are mixed into the same water, especially on the back half of the ebb when the current pulls bait off the ledges into deeper cuts. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a big white or bone Slug-Go worked slow along bottom, has been drawing bass up to the high 20s, occasional fish pushing 34, 35 inches. It's not a five-fish morning every time out — some days you find three or four good ones and call it, other days the bite shuts off the minute the tide turns. That's the honest version.

Eastern Egg Rock has had puffins working the surface most mornings, and where there's bait thick enough to hold puffins, there are usually bass cruising underneath looking for the same forage. Fly guys throwing olive-and-white Clousers into the boils around the rock have connected on schoolie-to-mid-slot bass, best in the last two hours of the ebb when the current stacks bait against the rock's east side.

Inside the bay, the pattern's a little different. Pogies — menhaden — have started pushing into the western passages of Penobscot Bay, and the bass are following them in rather than staying out on the open ledges. I've had good reports of fish working the mouth of the St. George River and up around the Muscle Ridge Channel on the incoming tide, right where the current funnels bait against the ledges. A big paddle-tail swimbait in bunker colors, fished slow and deep on the drift, has out-produced topwater most mornings, though the first hour of light with a popper has been worth staying up for if you don't mind a slower pick.

Groundfish are still down where they belong — the deep channels of Penobscot Bay, particularly the Fox Islands Thorofare and the stretch of water between Vinalhaven and North Haven, 100 to 140 feet on the sounder. Cod and haddock are there, but it's not stack-'em-up fishing like it was thirty years ago. You have to find the right piece of bottom — a hard edge, a hump, a spot where the current breaks — and jig it properly, or soak clams on a bottom rig and be patient. Haddock especially have been running small this year, plenty of fish just under the line that need to go back. When you do connect with a keeper cod, it's usually in that 5 to 10-pound range, occasionally better, taken on a diamond jig worked tight to bottom on the last hour of the ebb when the current slacks enough to hold your jig in the strike zone.

Down around Deer Isle and Stonington, the mackerel schools have been thick enough in the Thorofare to fill a bucket in twenty minutes with small feathered jigs — good bait for the bass runs, good eating too if you like them fresh off the grill. Striped bass around the ledges off Isle au Haut have been working the last of the ebb, and a tube-and-worm rig trolled slow along the drop-offs has taken some quality fish, a few pushing 36 inches, though the bite there has been more about timing than volume — miss the tide stage by an hour and you're fishing empty water.

Bluefish remain scattered this far east — a few showing off Boothbay in the warmer surface water near the harbor mouth, nothing like the blitzes you'd see farther south, but worth a cast if you're already rigged for bass with wire or a heavier leader.

Looking ahead, I expect the mackerel to hold through the rest of July, which means the bass and pollock ought to stay tucked in around the same structure — Monhegan's ledges, Egg Rock, the passages into the bay. If the pogies keep pushing west into Penobscot proper, I'd shift more time to the river mouths and the Muscle Ridge Channel rather than fighting open water for scattered fish. For groundfish, if the weather holds and you can get out to the deeper channels between Vinalhaven and North Haven, the cod and haddock are there for anyone willing to work the bottom instead of just drifting over it. It's a working man's bite right now — steady if you put in the time, not a gimme, and that's about right for mid-July on this water.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock on the Turn: Bass Ride the Current Edges, Groundfish Hold Deep
reports.subhead: Mid-July has the bay's current edges doing the work — stripers riding the seams, cod and haddock steady on the slack below Halfway Rock.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Peaks Island Tuesday morning, drifting toward Halfway Rock on the tail of the ebb, when I watched the water go from chop to glass in about ninety seconds. That's the tell I've learned to trust after thirty years out here — the moment the current lets go, right before slack, when the bait that's been pinned against the ledge for six hours suddenly has nowhere to hide. Terns dropped on it first, then the surface dimpled with mackerel showing themselves, and under all of that, on the sounder, the kind of soft, structured mark that means cod and haddock are holding tight to the rock rather than roaming.

That's been the pattern all week, and it's a good one if you're patient about it. Halfway Rock in 50 to 70 feet is still producing groundfish on the last hour of the ebb into slack — jigging diamond jigs and 6-ounce Norwegian jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked slow off bottom, has been the ticket. Nothing spectacular in numbers, but steady enough that a couple hours around the rock this week put keeper haddock and a mix of legal and short cod in the box for the boats I talked to at the co-op. The moment the tide starts to run hard again, that bite shuts down almost like someone flipped a switch, so timing the slack matters more than anything else you do out there.

The stripers have shifted their address a little from where they were in June. Instead of working the open water off Portland, they've tucked into the current seams around the island guts — the gut between Peaks and Long Island, the backside of Bailey Island where the tide rips past the ledges, and the mouth of the Basin off Cape Small where warm, bait-rich water pours out on the ebb. That warm water pushing out of the shallow coves and marshes is doing exactly what it always does in mid-July — it's dragging silversides and juvenile pogies with it, and the bass are stacked right on that edge where warm meets cold. I've had the best luck working white and chartreuse soft plastics, a 4-inch Slug-Go or a paddle-tail swimbait on a light jighead, cast right up against the current line and let the tide sweep it through rather than retrieving hard against it. Bucktails in the ¾-ounce range work too if the current's running enough to keep them off bottom.

Bailey Island's backside has been the more consistent of the two for slot fish — 26 to 32 inches — particularly on the first two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up against the ledges and the bass pin it there. Cape Small is more of a gamble right now; when the tide's right and the mackerel are thick, it's some of the best structure fishing in the whole bay, but I've had two trips out there this week where the bait just wasn't home and it was quiet water for three hours. That's the honest read — Cape Small is boom or bust this time of year, and you need to see bait working the surface before you commit to it.

Mackerel themselves have thinned out from the tight schools we had in late May and June, but they haven't left entirely. Small pods are still showing off Diamond Island and along the eastern side of Peaks, mostly early morning before the sun gets high. Jig with a mackerel tree, six hooks, no weight needed if they're near the surface, and you can fill a bucket in twenty minutes if you find them. That bait is exactly what's fueling both the striper bite along the ledges and, I suspect, some of the bluefish that have started showing this week — the first real bluefish reports I've had all season, mostly smaller choppers in the 2 to 4 pound range, snapping leaders off Two Lights and along the outer edge of Peaks on the last of the flood. Nothing to build a whole trip around yet, but worth having a wire leader in the box if you're working topwater plugs along that shoreline.

Water's been clean this week, no runoff issues from the rivers, and the wind has mostly cooperated — light out of the southwest most mornings, which keeps the outer ledges fishable. If that holds through the weekend, I'd put my time on Halfway Rock for the groundfish around the two slack windows each day, and I'd work the Bailey Island backside on the early flood for bass. If the wind swings onshore and kicks up a swell, the outer rock gets sloppy fast and I'd shift entirely inside to the Harpswell channels and the guts around the Calendar Islands, where the structure breaks the wave and the bass will still be working the current regardless of what's happening outside.

The next push worth watching is whether that bluefish showing turns into a real run. If the water keeps warming the way it has, and the bait stays thick along the eastern shore, I wouldn't be surprised to see bigger blues push into the bay by early August, the way they have in years when the mackerel linger into midsummer. For now, it's a solid week if you fish the tide stages correctly and an average one if you don't — which, out here, is usually the whole story.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Hour Still Owns July — Bass to 28, Blues Wrecking Higgins
reports.subhead: A dawn Danny plug bite at the Pool, a blitz that shut down half of Higgins Beach, and why the southwest wind is your friend at Prouts Neck right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-forty in the morning, first pink light over the Pool, and a bass came up under a black Danny plug like it had somewhere to be. Twenty-eight pounds, maybe a hair over, hooked on the incoming right where the channel bends past the yacht club moorings. That fish didn't chase the plug — it ambushed it, one turn from the boulder edge, and I swear my elbow's still sore. That's the thing about Biddeford Pool on the incoming: it isn't a long bite, it's an hour, hour and a half tops, but it's the best hour in Southern Maine striper fishing and it has been since before I had gray in my beard. Water stacks up through that narrow mouth, bait gets pinned against the rocks and the sandbar, and big fish sit in the current seam waiting for the buffet line to start moving. This week that seam has been loaded with pogies pushed up from the south, and the bass know it.

Higgins Beach gave me one of those mornings you tell people about at the boat ramp for a month. Birds were already working when I pulled in around 7, diving hard off the second sandbar, and it wasn't subtle — blues busting bait on top, water churned white in patches the size of a driveway. Threw a chrome Kastmaster on 20-pound braid and didn't get two full cranks before getting hit. Fish ran 3 to 6 pounds, blitz lasted maybe forty minutes before it moved south toward the Spurwink River mouth and thinned out. If you're throwing metal or a Super Strike popper at Higgins right now, keep your eyes on the gulls more than the water — they'll tell you where to be faster than any app will.

Pine Point has been a grinder this week, not a blitz spot. The current runs hard there on the bigger tides and you need to work the drop-off where the flat falls into the channel — that's holding schoolie bass and the occasional slot fish, mostly on the last two hours of the outgoing when bait gets flushed out of the marsh. Soft plastics have outfished hard baits there — a 6-inch white Slug-Go on a light jighead, twitched slow along bottom, has been the ticket over bucktails. The water's warm enough now that fish don't want to burn calories chasing something fast.

Prouts Neck has fished exactly like it should with this southwest wind we've had most of the week. That wind pushes bait right up against the rocks on the ocean side, and stripers stack in tight to structure to intercept it. I like a darter or a needlefish plug there in the last light of the evening, worked slow and parallel to the rocks — not bombed out to open water. The fish holding there aren't big-water fish, they're ambush fish, and you need to put the plug where they're sitting, not where you think the school is.

Mackerel have shown up thick off Kittery and around Cape Neddick, schools stacked 20 to 40 feet down, and that's worth knowing even if you're not targeting them directly — live mackerel on a fish-finder rig has been the best bait I've fished all month for the bigger bass holding deeper off Prouts Neck and the outer edge of the Pool. If you can jig up a few macks in the morning on a small Sabiki rig, keep three or four in the livewell and drift them past structure on the last of the incoming. That's how the 28-pounder's cousin, a fish just under 30, got landed off a buddy's boat near Wood Island Light on Tuesday.

Flounder have been steady but not exciting in Wells Harbor and up the Kennebunk River — bloodworms and skimmer clam on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished on the bottom during slack water, mostly keeper-sized fish in the 14 to 16 inch range. It's a good bite for anyone who wants dinner without fighting current or crowds, and it's about the most reliable thing going on this beat right now.

Cod fishing has gone quiet close to shore, which is normal for mid-July — the water up top has warmed enough that most of what's left has slid deeper. A few boats out of Cape Elizabeth are still finding shorts and the occasional keeper working structure in 60 to 80 feet, but nobody's calling it hot, and I wouldn't plan a trip around it right now.

Looking ahead, if this southwest wind holds through the weekend I'd be back at Prouts Neck at last light with a darter, and I'd be at Biddeford Pool at first light on the incoming with a Danny or a Doc — that combination has been the most consistent one-two punch on this whole stretch of coast this month. Higgins is a wildcard; when the blitz is on it's about as good as surf fishing gets in Maine, but it can vanish for two days at a time chasing bait south toward Spurwink or north past Cape Elizabeth. Watch the birds, not the calendar, and you'll find it.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's Ledge, 190 to 220 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, cod scratching the gravel edge
reports.subhead: Mackerel schools pushing onto the north end have the first bluefin sign showing early, but the real giant push is still weeks off.
reports.body_markdown:
Two hundred and six feet, soft mud, on the west side of the basin between Jeffrey's and Stellwagen's northern approach — that's where I found the best haddock of the week, and it's the number I keep coming back to when guys ask me where to start. Mud like that in the low 200s is haddock water this time of year. Gravel is a different animal, and the two don't mix on my chart plotter — I mark them in different colors so I don't waste a drift.

The haddock bite has been steady, not explosive. High-low rigs with clam belly, dropped straight down and worked slow off bottom, six inches at a time, are putting keeper haddock in the box in the 3 to 5 pound range, with the occasional 7-pounder mixed in to keep things honest. Best window has been the top two hours of the tide change, when the drift slows enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. I've been running 10 to 12 ounces depending on the push, more on the bigger tides. When the current really starts moving on the full flood, the fish seem to shut down for a stretch and then turn back on as it slackens toward the top. Patience pays here — chasing marks on a hard drift just burns fuel.

Cod have been tougher, and I'll say that plainly instead of dressing it up. The gravel edge on the east side of Jeffrey's, in that 130 to 160 foot band where the bottom breaks hard from mud to rock, has given up fish, but it's been a scratch bite — two or three keepers a trip in the 8 to 15 pound class, not the kind of numbers we were seeing in past Julys. Diamond jigs, 10 to 14 ounces with a bright green or white tube teaser above the hook, worked with a short lift-and-drop right on the bottom third of the water column, have outfished bait rigs for me two trips running. The cod are sitting tight to structure, so precision on the drop matters more than volume of gear in the water. If you're marking fish on the sounder and not connecting, slow the retrieve down — these cod aren't chasing much right now.

Pollock have been the saving grace for guys who want steady rod-bending action without the grind. Working the humps on Platts Bank, especially the north knoll where the bottom comes up from 180 to about 110 feet, jigging Norwegian jigs or small diamonds through the mid-water column has been putting nice fish in the 6 to 12 pound range in the boat consistently. Pollock don't need you to hit bottom — they're suspended, often 30 to 50 feet up off the structure, and once you find that band it's been fast fishing, a nice change of pace mid-trip when the cod and haddock go quiet.

Hake have shown up better after dark on the mud in Scantum Basin, which isn't a surprise — that's classic hake water once the sun drops and the water column settles. Not many of us are running out there for an overnight soak this time of year with bluefin starting to flicker on the radar, but if you've got the fuel and the patience, whiting-sized hake and a few larger ones have been coming over the rail on squid strips fished right on bottom in 250-plus feet.

Now for the fish everybody's really asking about. Mackerel have moved onto the north end of Jeffrey's in good numbers over the last week and a half, and where there's mackerel piling up, there's usually something bigger paying attention. We've had a handful of bluefin sign — a few boats marking fish and a couple of hookups on trolled spreader bars and green machines run wide off the ledge near Cape Ann's outer approach — but I want to be straight with you: it's early sign, not a pattern yet. This is mid-July. The real giant show on Jeffrey's doesn't typically load up until late September into October, when the sand eels and herring get thick and those fish start committing to the ledge for weeks at a time. Right now what we're seeing is scattered, opportunistic fish following bait, not staged fish holding structure. Worth a trolling pass if you're already out there jigging cod and haddock, but I wouldn't plan a dedicated tuna trip around it yet.

Looking ahead, if the mackerel schools keep building on the north end the way they have been, I'd expect more bluefin sign through late July, especially on calm mornings when the bait balls up tight near the surface and you can actually see it happening. For the bottom fishing, I'd keep working that mud in the low 200s for haddock — it's been the most reliable piece of the puzzle — and treat the gravel cod bite as a bonus rather than the main event until we see the water cool a touch more. Wind's been cooperative most mornings this week, laying down enough by first light to make the run out comfortable, but check the afternoon forecast before you commit to Platts or Tillies — that's a longer run home if it kicks up out of the southwest.

reports.headline: Appledore's Backside Gives Up Haddock, Stripers Chew Through the Hampton Flood
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which fifty yards of ledge to sit on — this week it was the Shoals for groundfish and Hampton Harbor for bass on the push.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to talk about. I've been running the same twenty-foot Lund out to the Isles of Shoals for going on eleven years and I can tell you thirteen miles is plenty if you fish it right. Most guys never leave the beach. I'm three miles offshore before the coffee's cold, anchored up on a piece of structure most of Hampton doesn't know exists, and I'm back at the ramp with fish in the box before the parking lot fills up. You don't need 130 miles of coast. You need to know your fifty yards.

This week that fifty yards was the north side of Appledore, out past the research station in that stretch of broken bottom where the ledge drops from 45 down to 70 feet. Haddock have been sitting tight to that structure on the slack tide, right at the top and bottom of the swing when the current lays down enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead dragging you sideways. Clam bellies on a standard two-hook rig, size 4/0 hooks, six-ounce bank sinker, and we've been picking through shorts to get to keeper haddock in the 20-22 inch class, mixed with a few cod in the 6 to 10 pound range that came up off the same piece.
