Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers — this isn't June, and the water's warmed enough that the bite window is short, maybe 45 minutes either side of dead slack — but if you're there when it turns, you're not going home empty.

What's telling is where the fish aren't. The open water between the mainland and the Shoals has gone quiet for groundfish, which tracks with what you'd expect this time of year — that water's pushing into the high 50s, low 60s at the surface, and cod and haddock want the cooler, structure-hugging water tight to the ledges where there's still some thermal relief and current to hold bait. I've stopped bothering with the mid-channel humps I fished in May. All the productive marks right now are hard structure, deeper water, close to the islands.

Mackerel showed up thick around the Shoals moorings and off Star Island in the last ten days, which is exactly the signal you want if you're chasing bass or targeting bigger groundfish, because mackerel strips and whole mackerel on a jig head are about as good a bait as exists out here in July. Snag a few on a Diamond jig or Sabiki rig before you set up on the bottom bite — costs you fifteen minutes and pays for itself.

Inshore, the story's been the stripers, and Hampton Harbor has been the most consistent piece of water in my zone all week. The pattern's simple and it hasn't changed in years: bass push into the harbor mouth on the last two hours of the incoming tide, working the deeper channel edges along the north jetty and up toward the Route 1A bridge, chasing pods of bunker and sand eels that get pushed up with the tide. I've had good luck throwing 3-inch white Slug-Go's weightless right along the rocks on the jetty, and when the current's really moving, switching to a half-ounce bucktail with a white curly tail trailer to get down into the seam where the bass are sitting on the structure waiting for bait to get swept past. Fish have run mostly schoolies and low-slot, 22 to 28 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in on the harder tide stages. Seabrook side of the harbor's produced too, particularly right where the marsh creeks dump into the main channel on the last of the ebb — that's flounder water as much as bass water, and we've picked a few keeper flounder there on squid strips fished on the bottom with light spinning gear, though that bite's thinned out compared to June.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — a few boats working the rips off Great Boars Head have run into blitzes of medium blues, 3 to 6 pounds, chopping up bait on top mid-morning. Nothing sustained, more of a here-today, gone-tomorrow situation, but if you see birds working and bait skying, it's worth a few casts with a metal lip swimmer or a Hopkins jig before you move on.

Rye Harbor's outer breakwater has held some stripers on the dropping tide in the last hour of daylight — that's been a evening pattern more than a morning one, fish sliding out with the current and feeding along the rocks where the baitfish get funneled through the gap.

Looking at the week ahead: the tides are building toward the new moon, which means bigger swings and stronger current — good news for the Hampton bite because more water movement means more bait getting pushed through that harbor mouth and more reason for bass to stack up on the structure. If the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down like it has been, I'd be back out at the Shoals working that same stretch off Appledore on the slack, and I'd have a mackerel jig rigged before I even set the anchor. The groundfish bite is thin but real if you're precise about tide stage. The bass bite in the harbor is the more dependable of the two right now — less finesse required, more about being there on the right two hours of tide.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Sachuest, Blues Crash the Shoreline While Bass Hold to the Dark
reports.subhead: Midsummer means daytime blues on bunker, night bass on the ledges, and a tog bite that's stubborn until the water cools.
reports.body_markdown:
First thing I noticed hopping out to the ledge below Brenton Point Tuesday morning — peanut bunker, thick as pepper, pinned right against the rock in that first hour of light. Not balled up tight like September stuff, more like a nervous smear along the shoreline, but it's there, and where there's peanut bunker in mid-July, something's usually working it from below. Sure enough, about twenty minutes in, the whole pod erupted about sixty yards off the point — bluefish, and not small ones either. Three, four pound choppers busting through the pod like they were late for something. That's been the story all along the south-facing shore this week, from Sachuest around to Second Beach — bunker schools moving tight to structure, blues working them hard in the mid-morning sun.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Water's warm enough on the surface — comfortable, not cold, low seventies out front of Newport most days — that the bass have pushed their feeding into the dark hours and stayed there. I fished the ledges off Ocean Drive two nights this week on the last two hours of the ebb, working a black Slug-Go and a bone Danny plug, and connected on schoolies to 28 inches both nights, with one better fish that spit the hook right at the rock. The pattern's consistent: bass are stacking on structure — the ledges from Castle Hill down through Brenton, the rock piles off Beavertail on the Jamestown side — and feeding hard right around the bottom of the tide when current compresses bait against the rock. Daytime, they've gone quiet on the open shore, but Sakonnet Point is still producing on the outgoing, especially the rip that forms off the point itself where the river current meets the open water. Sandeels and small bucktails, white or olive, worked slow along bottom in eight to fifteen feet, have been picking off keeper-class fish there on the last two hours of ebb.

Fluke have been the more reliable daytime play. The Sakonnet River, particularly the drift from the Stone Bridge area down past the old railroad trestle, has been giving up decent numbers on the incoming — four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged slow over the mixed sand-and-mussel bottom in eighteen to twenty-two feet. Nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional four-pounder mixed in, but steady enough to keep rods bent. Point Judith and the mouth of the Narrow River are producing similarly — same depth range, same slow-drag presentation, best on the top half of the incoming when there's enough push to keep the boat moving but not so much you're bouncing bottom too fast to feel the bite.

Scup are about the easiest thing going right now, and I mean that as a compliment — if you've got kids or a buddy who just wants bent rods, the Newport Bridge pilings and the ledges around Jamestown are loaded. Squid strips or clam on a simple high-low rig, twenty to thirty feet, any stage of the tide really, though the slack periods make it easiest to keep bait down where they're holding.

Tog, I'll be honest with you, has been tough. The ledges off Beavertail and out toward Whale Rock still have fish on them — I marked good concentrations dropping green crabs down in eighteen to twenty-five feet last week — but the bite in this warm water is sluggish. You'll get the soft pickup, the slow mouthing, and then nothing. It's not a dead bite, it's a lazy one. My advice right now is don't burn a whole trip on tog — mix it into a day where you're also working bass or fluke, because the real tog window opens back up as the water starts cooling into September, and that's when these same ledges turn from stingy to stacked.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't tell you otherwise. That first push into the breachways — Weekapaug, the Charlestown breachway, Napatree — is still weeks off. What I am watching is the bait. If these peanut bunker schools stick around and thicken up through August the way they're trending, and the water temps ease back a touch off their summer peak, we could see an earlier-than-usual push into Napatree and the Sakonnet mouth come late August. That's a bigger if than a guarantee, but it's the kind of bait signal that's worth filing away.

For this coming week, if I've got one morning to give it, I'm back on the Ocean Drive ledges working the last two hours of the ebb into first light, betting the bass stay locked into that dark-water pattern until we get a real cooldown. Daytime, I'd rather be drifting the Sakonnet for fluke than standing on a hot rock hoping a tog decides to commit. Wind's been manageable out of the south-southwest most afternoons, which keeps the south-facing beaches fishable but chums up a little surface chop by early afternoon — plan around it, fish the mornings when you can.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point Scup Stack Up, Bass Slide Into the Channels on the Bunker
reports.subhead: The herring run is a memory now, but Narragansett Bay's summer pattern is settling in with scup thick on the ledges and stripers working bait pods off Prudence.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning, coffee in one hand, scup rod in the other, telling me his kid brought home eleven keepers off the rocks the day before and didn't even have to move twenty feet. That's July on this bay in a nutshell — the herring's long gone up Buckeye Brook, the run wound down back in May like it always does, and now the whole system's shifted into that thick, buggy, mid-summer rhythm where the porgies own the ledges and the stripers have gone quiet and structure-bound.

Scup are doing exactly what they do this time of year — piling onto every rock pile and ledge from Nyatt Point down through Rocky Point and out toward Conimicut. I fished the rip off Rocky Point Wednesday on the last two hours of the incoming and it was about as steady as scup fishing gets — squid strips and bloodworms on high-low rigs, size 6 to 4 hooks, fishing tight to bottom in 12 to 18 feet. You don't need much weight there, just enough to hold in that current, two, maybe three ounces depending on how hard she's pushing. Guys are limiting out most mornings on the early flood before the pleasure boat traffic picks up and pushes the fish down off the structure. Same story at Nyatt — that rocky shelf drops off quick, and once the tide gets moving good you can feel those porgies stacked right on the edge where the mud meets rock.

Stripers are a tougher conversation right now, and I'm not going to sell anybody a bill of goods on it. The bay's warmed up enough that the bass have pushed off the flats and out of the upper river, and they're holding tighter to current-swept structure — the Mount Hope Bridge piers, the drop-off edges around Prudence Island, and the deeper holes off Conimicut Point where the Providence River current squeezes down. Best bite I've heard of and had myself came right at the top of the tide change, working live eels and cut bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs in 20 to 30 feet off the east side of Prudence, right around first light before the sun gets up over the water. Bunker schools have been showing up thick off Greenwich Bay and around Warwick Neck, and where you find those pods tight to the surface, especially on a dropping tide with some current pulling them off the flats, that's where the bigger fish have been sitting underneath, picking off stragglers. Nothing blitzing, but a few nice 28- to 34-inch fish coming out of that pattern on bunker chunks fished on the bottom, and on topwater plugs worked over the pods early before the boat traffic spooks everything.

Fluke are doing what fluke do in mid-July — pushing further up into the bay behind the warming water and the bait that's riding in with it. Greenwich Bay's holding a decent population right now, drifting the mud-to-sand transition zones in 15 to 25 feet with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. The fish aren't huge — mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but there's enough of them stacked in there that a slow drift on the outgoing tide will put bends in the rod. I'd also check the flats off Nyatt Point and down toward the mouth of the Providence River itself, where the current funnels bait through that channel edge — that's classic fluke water this time of year, and a few guys have been picking off solid fish there working bucktail and Gulp combos tight along the drop.

Bluefish have been scattered but present — a few schools of choppers working bunker off Rocky Point and out toward the lower bay near Jamestown, mostly in the mornings before the wind builds. If you see the birds working and the water nervous, that's your window — poppers and metal lips will get bit fast, but those pods move quick and don't sit still for long. Black sea bass are holding around the rockier structure off Prudence and out toward the lower bay ledges, decent numbers on squid strips fished tight to bottom in 25 to 35 feet, though the size has been modest — plenty of shorts mixed with a few keepers.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, have been scarce. A few reports of fish showing on the edges of the Providence River channel on quiet evenings, but nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, the tides are building toward the next moon and that usually means better current, which is exactly what this bay needs to push bait around and get the bigger bass moving again. If the wind lays down and stays out of the southwest through the weekend, I'd focus early mornings on those bunker pods off Prudence and Greenwich Bay before the boat traffic churns things up, and I'd hit the scup ledges on the incoming tide because that bite's been the most dependable thing going right now. Dog days are here — fish the edges of the day, work the current, and don't expect the bass to make it easy on you.

reports.headline: Why Do the Fluke Vanish Off the Sod Banks by 10 AM?
reports.subhead: The answer is temperature, not luck — and once you understand the split, the back bay fluke program practically teaches itself.
reports.body_markdown:
I get this question at the bait shop counter every July, and I got it three times this week: why does the fluke bite at Absecon's sod banks turn off like a switch around mid-morning, then come back to life at Great Egg a few hours later when everybody else has already gone home? It's not luck. It's thermal stratification, and if you fish the back bays long enough you start reading it the way you'd read a tide chart.

Here's the lesson. Those shallow sod bank flats — four to six feet of water over mud and grass, the kind you find along Absecon Channel behind Brigantine and up in the Rainbow Channel flats off Great Egg — heat up fast once the sun gets on them. By 9 or 10 in the morning that water can climb into the high 70s, and fluke don't like sitting in a bathtub. They slide off the flats and drop into the channel edges, the 10 to 16 foot troughs that run alongside — Graveling Point, the deeper bends of Broad Thorofare, the cuts near the Route 52 causeway. That's where they'll hold through the heat of the day. The trick is to fish the flats hard on the first two hours of the outgoing, when the water's still cool from the overnight low, then follow the fish downhill into the channel as the sun climbs. Same fish, different address.

The bait that's been doing the damage on both ends of that migration is a 4-inch chartreuse or white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the drop-offs where the flat meets the channel. Bull minnow on a simple fluke rig has been the better call in the afternoon, when the fish get sticky and won't commit to the plastic in the warmer water. Sizes have been mixed but honest — plenty of 15 to 17 inch fish to sort through, keepers in the 17 to 19 inch range showing up consistently off the outer flats at Great Egg, and a few fish pushing 4 and 5 pounds coming off the deeper edges near the Route 52 bridge on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. That's been the most dependable window all week — not the flood, the back half of the ebb, right before the bottom of the tide.

Weakfish have been a smaller story, but a real one if you're willing to get up early. The rock pile at Absecon Inlet has given up a handful of 3 to 5 pound weakfish in the gray light before sunrise, on Gulp shrimp bodies or a bucktail tipped with a strip of FishBites, worked slow through the rip on the tail end of the outgoing. It's not a bite you can set your watch by — some mornings it's two fish, some mornings it's nothing — but the class of fish has been worth the early alarm.

On the ocean side, kingfish have kept steady on the sandbars off 34th Street in Ocean City, down through Sea Isle and out to Stone Harbor Point, on bloodworm or FishBites strips fished on a simple high-low rig in two to four feet of water. The surf's had a lingering groundswell running through it much of the week — short-period, a little lumpy, enough to color the wash and keep the sight-feeders off their game — but kingfish don't care about clarity, they care about scent, and that bite has held up fine right through the chop. Best window is early, before the beaches fill and the wave runners start churning the inside bar.

Bluefish have been the reliable entertainment at both inlets — schools of cocktail blues in the 1 to 3 pound class working peanut bunker and spearing at first light and again at dusk, right at the mouths of Absecon and Townsends. Chrome spoons or a small popper worked fast across the surface will get bit fast when they're up, and they've been up most mornings this week. It's not the fall run yet — that's still a good six weeks off — but it's a fun half hour before the sun gets high.

Triggerfish have started showing as incidental catches around the inshore reef structure off Great Egg and Wildwood, mostly for guys soaking clam on bottom rigs while working the reef for fluke. Nothing to plan a trip around yet, but it's the first real sign of the pattern that usually builds through August.

I'll be straight with you on striped bass — July is the quiet month down here, and this year hasn't broken that rule. A few holdover fish have come off the rocks at Absecon Inlet after dark on eels, but it's a long, patient game for one or two fish, and I wouldn't call it a program right now.

Looking ahead, if that ocean groundswell backs off like it typically does by the weekend, I'd expect the kingfish bite on the outer bars to sharpen up as the wash cleans out. The sod bank fluke pattern should keep holding as long as that morning-to-afternoon temperature split stays in place — fish the flats early, chase them into the channels late. That's where I'll have my boat this week, and it's where I'd start if you've only got one tide to work with.

reports.headline: A Fresh Cut South of Holgate Is Rewriting the Night Bite
reports.subhead: New structure from last week's south swell is holding stripers after dark while doormat fluke stack the inlet edges on the drop.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch at dead low Tuesday morning with a cup of dock coffee going cold in my hand, and the beach had changed shape on me again. There's a new cut about three hundred yards south of the old Rodanthe-style break — a legit trough that wasn't there two weeks ago, carved out by the south groundswell that's been rolling through at fifteen-second periods. It's maybe forty yards wide, drops to four or five feet at the bar, and the inside edge has that dark green color that tells you there's a bait highway running through it. I marked it on my phone, walked it twice, and told the guys at the shop before I even had my second cup — this is the spot for the next few weeks, until the next blow reshuffles the deck.

Here's the thing about mid-July on this island: the ocean side is running warm — buoy data off the Bight has water pushing 73 degrees — and that's pushed the bulk of the keeper-class bass into a strict after-dark program. Daytime you might see a swirl or two around the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light on the last of the outgoing, but the real work is happening from an hour before high tide through the top of the flood, once the sun's down and the water in these new cuts cools a couple degrees. I've been throwing a black Danny-style swimmer and a 3-ounce darter through that Holgate cut on the incoming, working it slow across the trough, and connecting with stripers mostly in the upper 20s to low 30-inch class — a few slot fish mixed in, nothing giant, but consistent enough that I've made three trips down there this week and come home with fish twice. That's a decent ratio for July surf fishing, but it's not a gimme — you need the tide right and you need to be fishing structure, not just chucking plugs at open beach.

Barnegat Inlet itself has been the fluke story. The channel edges on the north side, that stretch running from the Coast Guard station drift down toward the rip, are holding doormat-class fish in 25 to 35 feet. I've had my best luck dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, bounced slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current really starts ripping bait off the flats and funneling it through the cut. Squid strips on the hook point add scent when the water's got any color to it after a blow. The bigger fish — I had one push six pounds Thursday — are coming off the deeper structure where the bottom breaks hard, not the flats themselves. Little Egg Inlet is fishing similarly, though it's been more of a numbers game than a big-fish game this week; lots of 16 to 18-inch fish mixed with the occasional keeper on the same bucktail-and-Gulp combo, drifted from the Holgate side across toward Beach Haven Inlet.

Great Bay and the Mullica system are doing their July thing — weakfish showing up on the evening bite around Graveling Point, mostly on the last two hours of daylight into dusk. These aren't the springtime schoolies; a few honest 20-inch fish have come out of there on peeler crab fished on a fish-finder rig, dead-sticked over the mussel bottom, with a couple more falling for a small bucktail tipped with a Fin-S worked slow along the channel edge where it drops from four feet to eight. The bay water's warmed up fast in the afternoon sun the way it does this time of year — that shallow mud and grass bottom heats quicker than the open inlet, and it's pulling bait and predators into tighter windows right around the tide change. If you're fishing Graveling, I'd rather be there on the last of the outgoing when that warm water's draining out of the marsh creeks and concentrating everything on the current seams, than sitting there at high water with nothing moving.

Kingfish have been steady but not thick on the ocean beaches — Ship Bottom and Beach Haven have both given up decent counts on bloodworm and Fishbites rigs fished in the troughs at low tide, small sinkers, light leaders, nothing fancy. It's a good bet if you want steady action for the kids or you're just killing time waiting for the evening striper bite to turn on.

Bluefish have been the wild card. Bunker schools have been moving up and down the beachfront from Barnegat Light down past Ship Bottom, and when the blues find them it's fast and violent for twenty minutes and then gone — topwater poppers and metal-lip swimmers thrown into the melee will get bit, but you need to be in the right spot at the right time, and that's mostly a function of watching for diving birds working bait balls just outside the surf line.

Looking ahead, that new Holgate cut is the thing I'm watching closest. If the south swell holds through this weekend, I expect it to hold its shape and keep producing on the night flood. If a bigger blow comes through and reshapes it again, I'll be back out there at first light re-reading the beach — that's the job. For the inlet, I'd keep working the outgoing on Barnegat and Little Egg as long as the fluke keep showing on the drop, and I'd have a bucktail rigged and ready the moment those bunker schools push back into range.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke Keep Coming on the Drift — Kingfish and Blowfish Own Tices Shoal
reports.subhead: Weakfish have slid off the sedges for the summer, but fluke, blowfish, and kingfish are keeping the rods bent from Oyster Creek to the inlet.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a July morning back when I was mating on the Point Pleasant boats, maybe sixteen years old, and the old skipper — Sal, everybody called him Sal the Greek even though he wasn't — told me the bay in high summer is a different animal than the bay in May. May, he said, the fish are moving through, hunting, hungry, and you can find them by accident. July, the bay settles into its bones. The water gets heavy and warm on top, the bait tucks into the grass, and if you don't know where the deep water runs cool you're just casting at ghosts. Forty years later I still hear him every time I idle past Tices Shoal in the middle of August and see the flat go glassy calm. That lesson never gets old, and it's exactly what's playing out on Barnegat Bay right now.

The fluke have been the most dependable thing going. Double Creek Channel is still the address — that stretch where the channel dog-legs south of the Route 37 bridge holds bait and current both, and on the last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of a new flood, the drift sets up clean. I've been running 3/4-ounce bucktails, chartreuse and white, tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in nuclear chicken, dragged slow along bottom in 10 to 14 feet. Keepers have been mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a five-minute limit, but a patient drift will put two or three fluke in the 18 to 20-inch range in the cooler for an afternoon's work. The mouth of Oyster Creek has also been kicking out fluke on the last of the outgoing, when that warmer creek water pushes out over the flat and concentrates bait right where the channel drops off — spearing and small killies on a simple fishfinder rig work there if you don't want to bother with plastics.

Blowfish are doing what blowfish do in July, which is show up everywhere there's current and clam or squid on the bottom. Tices Shoal has been thick with them on the high incoming tide — anchor up along the edge of the shoal in six to eight feet, small hooks, squid strips cut thin, and you can fill a bucket in an evening if you've got the patience for the bite-and-miss game they play. Kids on the dock at Oyster Creek have been doing the same with strips of clam and having a ball with it. Kingfish have been mixing in on the ocean side — the beaches at Island Beach State Park and the inlet jetty rocks at Barnegat Light have both given up kingfish on bloodworms and Fishbites, high-low rigs, right in that skinny wash where the sand drops off. The ocean's been running around 73 degrees off the Jersey coast the last check I had, which is right in the kingfish's comfort zone, and that water's pushing plenty of sand fleas and worms up onto the beach for them to work.

Bluefish have shown up in fits — bunker schools have been rolling through Barnegat Inlet on the tide changes, and where you find the bunker balled up tight near the surface, you'll find blues underneath cutting them to pieces. Ava jigs, the 007 size, worked with a jigging stroke right through the school, will draw strikes, and if you want cocktail blues for the kids, small Kastmasters off the bulkheads near the inlet at first light have been steady. Nothing gigantic — mostly 2 to 4 pounds — but they hit hard and they're around most mornings this week.

Now the honest part. Weakfish, which were thick around the sedge banks back in May the way they always are, have thinned way out. That's normal — they don't hang around the bay all summer the way some folks expect. A few stragglers are still showing after dark on bucktails tipped with squid strips worked slow along the edges of Double Creek and the deeper holes off Good Luck Point, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around weakfish right now. If you want them, fish the last hour of light into full dark and keep your expectations modest.

Stripers are the toughest call of the week. Summer heat in the bay pushes them out — they don't love water in the high 70s any more than we'd love a July day in a wool coat. The better play has been the inlet itself, working the jetty rocks and the deeper water off Barnegat Light before sunrise, live bunker on a fish-finder rig or bucktails worked deep along the rock edges where the current runs hardest. It's not a sure thing and it's not a numbers game, but the fish that do show are usually solid, mid-20s to low 30s, holding tight to structure where the current breaks.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down like it has the last few days, I'd keep working Double Creek on the tide changes for fluke — that pattern's been the most consistent thing on the bay all month. Blowfish and kingfish should hold steady as long as the water stays warm and clean. I'd treat weakfish and stripers as bonus fish this week, not the main event, and plan your trip around the tide, not the calendar.

reports.headline: Sea Bright to Manasquan: blues by the dozen, bass by the grace of God
reports.subhead: Dawn patrol on the rocks turned up cocktail blues and short fluke — the slot bass showed up for maybe twenty minutes a day, and you had to be standing in the right spot.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six Tuesday morning, north jetty at Manasquan, and there were four of us out there in the gray light before the sun cleared the roofline of the Coast Guard station. Nobody was talking. That's how you know it's July — everybody's saving their breath for the cast, not the small talk. A guy I've seen out there since Memorial Day was working a black Gibbs pencil popper along the tip, and on maybe his sixth cast the water just erupted. Not a bass blowup — that slow, deliberate porpoise-roll thing stripers do. This was violent, scattershot, half a dozen fish crashing at once. Cocktail blues, two to four pounds, and they stayed on top for a solid twenty minutes before the school moved off toward Shark River. That's been the pattern all week up and down this stretch — the bluefish are the ones showing up to work, and the bass are punching a very short clock.

I won't sugarcoat it. Striped bass fishing on the jetties right now is a dawn-and-dusk proposition, and even then it's thin. The ocean's sitting around 71-72 degrees off the beach — that's warm enough that the quality bass have slid off into deeper, cooler water or pushed north looking for bait, and what's left in close on the rocks are mostly schoolies in the 18-24 inch range, with the occasional slot fish mixed in if you're fishing the right two hours of tide. I had one 29-incher come off the Sea Bright rocks Sunday night on a bunker chunk fished on a fish-finder rig in about 12 feet of water, dead low tide turning to the first push of the flood — that first hour of moving water after a long slack is when something bigger will slide through to feed, and it's usually the only window you get. After that the current builds, the day boats come out, the jet skis show up, and the bite shuts like a door.

Eels are still your best bet for a real fish after dark. I've had guys tell me about 30-inch-class bass coming off the Manasquan Inlet rocks and the Spring Lake jetties on live eels, fished on the last two hours of the outgoing when there's still enough current to make the eel swim natural instead of just hanging there like a dead worm. That's a night program — headlamp, sneakers with the felt soles if you've still got them, and patience, because you might throw for two hours before one fish hits. Nobody's filling a cooler doing this. But if you want a real bass instead of a dink, that's the play right now.

The better news is the fluke. Manasquan and Shark River Inlets have both been giving up decent numbers on the drift — 4-inch white and pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, bounced slow along the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the outgoing when the current's still got some snap to it but isn't ripping your line sideways. Most of what's coming over the rail is short, 14 to 17 inches, but there's a keeper mixed in for every eight or ten fish, and a couple guys working the deeper hole just inside the Manasquan Inlet rock pile have put 3 and 4-pound fluke in the cooler this week on strip baits — squid and fluke belly combos — fished tight to bottom on the last hour before the tide goes dead.

Porgies have been thick on the jetty structure at high water — Belmar and the Spring Lake rocks especially — and if you're tired of getting skunked on bass, a bucket of clams and a high-low rig with size 4 or 6 hooks will keep a rod bending for as long as you want to stand there. Not glamorous, but it's honest fishing and the kids on the rocks with me Tuesday morning went home with a mess of them for the pan.

No albies yet — it's mid-July, too early, don't let anybody tell you different. That pattern doesn't usually light up around here until the back half of September when the bait starts pushing out of the back bays and the water starts dropping through the mid-60s. Blackfish are out of season through the summer months on most of this stretch, so leave the crab pots at home for now.

Looking ahead, the wave state offshore has been rough — 3-plus feet at a short period, which means dirty water and a harder push against the jetty faces, and that's been part of what's kept the bigger bass from committing close to the rocks during daylight. If the wind lays down over the weekend like it's supposed to and the swell drops, I'd expect the water to clean up enough that the dawn bite on top — poppers and darters worked along current seams at first light — gets a little more consistent. The moon's building toward the next new phase, which should push some extra water through the inlets on the exchange tides; that's usually good for stirring the bait and getting stripers to commit for that short window before the sun gets high. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be on the Manasquan north jetty an hour before official sunrise, throwing a pencil popper on the last of the ebb, and I'd have a bucktail rigged as backup the second the blues show up instead.

reports.headline: Channel Edges Off Keyport: Fluke Steady, Bass Working the Night Shift
reports.subhead: With the ocean side kicking up leftover swell, I'm staying inside — and the fluke on the flats are making that decision easy.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday morning before I even loaded the boat: skip the Rip, work the flats. There's still a leftover groundswell rolling off the Bight — buoy data offshore of the Hook has been holding in the 3-foot range on a short period, the kind of chop that makes the ocean side of Sandy Hook miserable for anything but the diehards. So I turned the truck toward Keyport instead, and I'm glad I did.

This time of year, the bay tells you where to go if you're willing to listen. Water out front of the Hook is pushing into the low 70s, which means the Bay itself — shallower, more protected — has been running warm and a little sleepy in the mid-day sun. The fish know it. Fluke have tucked into the channel edges where the current keeps things moving and the bottom stays cooler, and that's exactly where I found them.

Flynn's Knoll into the Keyport Flats has been my program all week. I'm drifting the edge where the flat drops from eight feet down into eighteen to twenty-two, working the transition hard on the top of the incoming tide when the current starts stacking bait against that lip. Four-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in pearl white and bubblegum, threaded on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom with just enough hop to keep contact — that's been the ticket. Picked up a stretch of keeper fluke Tuesday afternoon between 17 and 22 inches, with one heavier fish that pushed close to 5 pounds that came off the deeper cut near the Knoll's northern edge. Nothing like that doormat that got weighed in at Bayonne a few weeks back, but solid, honest fluke fishing — the kind where you keep three rods working the drift and stay disciplined about covering ground instead of anchoring up and hoping.

Romer Shoal has been a mixed bag. I got a few short fluke there Wednesday morning on the same rig, plus a couple of porgies that snuck onto a bucktail tipped with a Gulp strip — not a bad sign, means the bottom's holding bait. If you want porgies specifically, drop clam on top-and-bottom rigs right on the shoal itself around the wreck pieces; they're there, they're just not stacked the way they will be come September.

Striped bass have gone the way they always do in the heart of summer — they're not gone, they're just smarter than the boat traffic. The daytime bite in the open bay has gone quiet outside of dawn and dusk. I fished the Great Beds area at first light Thursday, chunking bunker on fishfinder rigs in about 20 feet, and connected with two schoolies and one fish that just cleared 28 inches before the sun got high and the bite shut like someone flipped a switch. That's the pattern right now — an hour, maybe ninety minutes of real window at first light, then done. If you want a better shot at bass, work the Navesink after dark. I've had reports of decent fish holding around the Highlands bridge pilings and up toward Red Bank on the last two hours of the outgoing, hitting swimming plugs and soft plastics twitched slow through the current seams. Bring a good headlamp and patience — it's not a numbers game, it's a quality-over-quantity game right now.

Bluefish have been the wildcard, and honestly the most fun I've had on the water this week. There's still bunker schools holding off Flynn's Knoll and drifting toward Romer, and when the blues find them it gets chaotic fast — birds diving, bait skying, the whole show. Chrome and green Ava jigs cast into the melee have been producing fish in the 3 to 5 pound range, some bigger. If you see the gulls working, don't wait, get on it — that window can close in fifteen minutes once the blues push the bait down or move off.

Weakfish are still around in small numbers, mostly as incidental catches on the fluke rigs in the deeper channel stretches near Keyport. I'd encourage releasing anything close to the slot — the population's still fragile enough that every spawner matters, and it's not worth the fillet to put a dent in a fishery that's been rebuilding slow.

Looking ahead, if the swell out front settles down by the weekend, I might sneak out to the Rip and see if there's a bigger class of bass holding on that current edge the way they do when bait gets funneled through there on a hard tide. But my money for the next several days stays inside — the channel edges off Keyport, the flats around Flynn's Knoll, working the incoming for fluke and putting in the early alarm clock hours for bass. That's the honest program right now: no blitzes, no fireworks, just solid tide-and-structure fishing if you're willing to be specific about when and where you show up.

reports.headline: The Race at 3.8 Knots: Bass Working Valiant Rock, Slack Ticks In at 12:06
reports.subhead: A tight thermal line from Kings Point to New London is stacking bait against the rips, and the bass know exactly where to sit.
reports.body_markdown:
Three point eight knots. That's what the Race was doing on the max ebb Tuesday afternoon, and if you've fished this water for as long as I have, you know that number tells you almost everything before you even wet a line. Anything under three and the rips go soft, fish scatter, and you're marking bait instead of marking fish. Anything over four and you're fighting the current more than you're fishing it. Three point eight is the sweet spot — hard enough to hold bait against Valiant Rock and Race Rock, slow enough that a wire line with a bucktail can actually get down and stay down.

The slack window at Valiant Rock this week has been running short — call it ten, twelve minutes on either side of the turn, with the midday slack landing around 12:06 depending on the day. Miss that window and you're fighting green water the rest of the tide. I've had boats anchor up fifteen minutes too early and sit there watching their lines stream sideways, wondering why nothing's biting. There's nothing wrong with the fish. You're just not in the water yet.

The bite itself has been solid, not spectacular. Wire line trolled with bunker spoons and umbrella rigs off Race Rock has produced stripers in the 28 to 38-inch range on the last two hours of the ebb, with the occasional better fish pushing 20 pounds coming off the north side of Valiant where the rock drops into 40 feet. Bucktails — 3 to 4-ounce, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of mackerel — have been the better call on the drift through Plum Gut itself, worked slow along bottom as the current funnels bait through that gut like water through a fire hose. The fish are there, but you have to be patient with the retrieve. Too fast and you're pulling the jig out of the strike zone before a fish can commit.

Here's the why behind it. New London's reading around 67.5 degrees right now, a good three and a half degrees cooler than Kings Point at 71.2. That gradient is exactly what's staging fish along the eastern Sound rips — the cooler, oxygen-rich water holds bait tighter, and the bass know it. They're not spread out chasing forage across open water; they're pinned against structure where the current concentrates everything for them. That's Valiant Rock. That's Race Rock. That's the north edge of the Sluiceway where the bottom breaks hard and the tide rips through Little Gull and Great Gull.

Fluke fishing off the Sluiceway has been mixed — some days you limit out on keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range drifting Gulp swimming mullets in white over 25 to 35 feet of sandy bottom, other days you grind through a dozen shorts before you find a keeper. The water's holding up fine, it's more about hitting the right stage of tide — the last hour of the incoming has been the most consistent, when the bait gets pushed up onto the flats between Great Gull and the Sluiceway proper.

Black sea bass around Valiant Rock and the rockpile structure off Race Rock have been dependable filler when the stripers go quiet, squid strips or clam on a two-hook bottom rig dropped right into the rock edges in 35 to 50 feet. Nothing huge, but steady action, and a good way to fill a cooler while you wait out a slack window.

Bluefish have been mixed into the Gut on the same tides as the bass, chopping up bucktails and forcing a lot of guys to switch to wire leader mid-drift. Not complaining — a 12-pound bluefish on light tackle in that current is its own kind of fun, even if it costs you a jig.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't expect them for another few weeks. The Gut usually doesn't see the first real push of false albacore until late August into September around here, once the water further offshore warms and the bait balls tighten up. There's chatter about squid concentrations building off Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water pushes past the high 50s and into the 60s — if that pattern holds and pushes west along the Race, it could supercharge things earlier than usual. I've seen that happen before, and when the squid show early, the striper bite at Valiant Rock gets downright violent for a stretch. Doesn't mean it's a lock, but it's exactly the kind of signal that makes me start rigging extra squid-strip bucktails just in case.

Looking ahead, if the current stays in that 3.5 to 4-knot range through the week and the thermal line holds where it is, I'd keep working the last two hours of ebb at Race Rock with wire line, and hit Valiant Rock right on that tight slack window with bucktails before the current builds back. If we get a stretch of southwest wind that muddies up the Gut, I'd shift effort to the Sluiceway fluke grounds where the bottom stays cleaner longer. Either way, know your slack to the minute before you leave the dock — out here, that's the difference between a good trip and a long ride home.

reports.headline: Ram Island Rocks Giving Up Slot Bass at First Light, Fluke Thick in the Sand Seams
reports.subhead: The boulder fields are still cool and the bass know it — but the albies haven't shown their hand yet.
reports.body_markdown:
First light on Ram Island this week, and the peanut bunker were doing what they do over the boulder field on the north side — bunching tight, nervous, ticking the surface like rain that isn't falling. That's the tell. Where the bait balls up and won't spread out, there's something underneath holding it there. I poled the skiff along the drop where the granite goes from four feet to twelve in about thirty yards, and on three separate passes I watched a bass roll through the bait without breaking the surface clean. Quiet takes. That's how they feed over rock — no crash, just a push of water and the bait scatters.

Water's been running cooler on the eastern end of the Sound than you'd expect for mid-July — New London's reading in the high 60s while the water off Kings Point to the west is already pushing 71. That gradient matters more than people think. The cooler pocket sitting over Fishers Island Sound is keeping bait concentrated and bass a little more willing to feed through the warmer parts of the day than they'd be if this whole stretch had turned into a bathtub. I'm not complaining about it. A little cold water in July off Stonington is money in the bank for August.

The breakwater has been my most consistent stop. Fished the outside face on the last two hours of the incoming tide Tuesday night with a black Slug-Go, weightless, worked slow along the riprap where the current wraps the eastern tip. Two slot bass, one at 29 inches, one just shy of 26, both came on the pause — let the plastic sit dead in the seam and they ate it sinking. Eels have worked too if you want to soak one on a fish-finder rig off the rocks after dark, but I've had better luck staying mobile with the soft plastic than sitting on bait right now. The fish aren't stacked, they're moving through on the tide, and you want to be able to follow them down the wall.

Wamphassuc Point and Esker Point have both been giving up fish on the dropping tide, first two hours especially, when the current pulls bait off the flats and funnels it past the ledges. Light tackle guys throwing 3-inch Albie Snax in bone white or bunker colors have done well working the current seams off both points. Nothing huge — mostly 22 to 26 inches — but steady enough that if you're covering water on foot or by kayak, you'll find willing fish.

Fluke have been the bright spot in Little Narragansett Bay and the sand pockets around Ram Island's southern flank. Drifting the mud-to-sand transitions in 10 to 18 feet with 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in pink shine has produced fish to 22 inches, with a decent number of keepers mixed into the shorts. The bite's best on the last hour of the ebb when the water's moving enough to keep the bucktail ticking bottom but not so hard you're dragging a brick. Black sea bass are riding shotgun on the same structure — anything with hard bottom and current, the rockpiles off Fishers Island's west end especially, and they've been thick enough that if you're not targeting fluke specifically, you'll fill out a limit of sea bass before lunch.

Tog are off the table right now with the season closed, but I'll say this quietly — I've been marking fish stacked tight on a few of the deeper boulder piles off the east side of Fishers Island, the kind of structure that always loads up before the August reopener. Worth remembering where they are when the calendar turns.

Now the honest part. No albies yet. I know the calendar says we should start watching, and I have been — glassing the rips off Watch Hill and the reef off the breakwater every morning for that first nervous bait and the boil that doesn't belong to a bass. Nothing. Water's still a touch cool for them out here, and until that gradient closes up and the whole Sound settles into the mid-to-high 60s consistently, I wouldn't burn gas looking hard. Historically for this stretch of coast, it's mid-to-late August before the first real showing, sometimes into September if the bait's slow to arrive. I'll be out there checking anyway, because that's the job, but I'm not going to tell you to go looking yet.

Moon's building toward first quarter, which means the tides are getting a little more push behind them day by day. That's good news for the boulder-field bite — more current means more bait getting worked loose off the rocks, and more reason for bass to hold tight to structure rather than roam. If I had one morning this week, I'd fish the last of the incoming at the breakwater at first light, then slide over to Ram Island for the last two hours of the ebb and work the sand seams for fluke. Bring both rods. The rocks and the sand are both paying right now, just not at the same hour.

reports.headline: Gold Star pilings holding fish on the last of the ebb, porgies stacked deep at Fort Trumbull
reports.subhead: Water's settled into a real summer pattern on the Thames, and the bite window is short but honest if you're there for it.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a spot below the Gold Star Bridge, maybe forty yards downriver of the third pier from the New London side, where the current pinches between two old dolphin pilings and folds back on itself on the last two hours of the ebb. I've fished that seam for twenty years and it still tells you something new every summer. This week it told me the fish are holding deeper than they were in June — eight, ten feet down against the concrete, not up top chasing bait on the surface like they were a month ago. That's your signal the river's shifted into full summer mode.

Water at the mouth is running around 67, 68 degrees, which for the Thames in mid-July is on the cool side of normal — there's a real gradient stacking up across the Sound right now, warmer out west, cooler as you come east toward us, and that cooler water is exactly why the striper bite here has stayed more honest than a lot of the reports coming out of western Long Island. Fish don't need to run and hide from warm water on this end. They're just settling into their summer addresses.

Stripers off the Gold Star pilings have been mostly schoolies and low-slot fish, 22 to 27 inches, taken on the drop of the tide with white bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter depending on how hard the current's pushing, tipped with a strip of squid. Let it sink to the base of the piling and hop it slow along bottom — don't rip it, these fish aren't chasing anything fast in this water column right now, they're grubbing. I had three fish in forty minutes doing exactly that on Tuesday's outgoing, nothing enormous, but steady enough that I'd call it a real bite, not a fluke afternoon.

Fort Trumbull is where the bigger story is this week, and it's porgies, not bass. The rock pile off the point, in twelve to eighteen feet, has scup stacked up thick enough that a dropper rig with two hooks, size 6 or 8, baited with sandworm or clam, is coming back doubled up more often than not on the last hour of the incoming. That's the tide to fish there — the flow pushes bait up against the rocks and the porgies tuck in tight to feed on it before the current really starts ripping. I watched a guy in a 17-foot skiff limit out on scup there in under ninety minutes Thursday morning, biggest one pushing a pound and a half, which for the Thames is a genuinely nice fish. If you want a cooler full of dinner without much drama, that's your play right now.

Bluefish have shown up in patches off Ocean Beach and out toward Pleasure Beach, chopping bait on the surface in the mornings before the wind builds. Nothing consistent — I'd call it a here-today, gone-tomorrow bite, the kind where you need to be on the water at first light or you miss the window entirely. Small metal, half-ounce Kastmasters or a Hopkins, worked fast through the froth, gets bit. Once the sun's up and the wind picks out of the southwest, which it's been doing most afternoons this week, the blues seem to scatter back down and out toward the deeper water off the harbor mouth.

Blackfish are still shut down for the season here — that's a fall program on the Thames, once the water starts dropping back toward the 50s and the tog move onto the structure around Fort Trumbull and the rock piles off Bartlett Cove. Too early to think about that yet, though I'll say the mussel beds around the fort have been thick this summer, which is usually a good sign for the fall run when it comes.

Current's been the deciding factor more than anything else this week. The Thames moves fast through the narrows by the bridge, and with these lighter July winds the tide is really running the show — fish are stacking on structure during the strong push and scattering on the slack. If you're planning a trip, build it around the tide chart, not the clock. The two hours either side of dead low, when the current is really cranking past those Gold Star pilings, has been the most dependable window for the bass. For porgies at Fort Trumbull, I'd rather have the last of the incoming pushing bait up onto the rocks than fight a slack tide with nothing moving.

Looking ahead, if this cooler, stable water holds through the week, I expect the striper bite off the bridge to stay steady on the outgoing — nothing spectacular, but reliable enough to plan an evening around. The wildcard is the blues; if that southwest wind eases up even a little in the mornings, I'd bet on a longer window at Ocean Beach before they push back out. And keep an eye on bait activity around the fort — if the porgy bite holds this thick into August, we're in for one of the better scup summers the Thames has had in a few years. I'll be out there most mornings with the tide charts and a bucket of sandworms, and I'll let you know what changes.

reports.headline: Shad Run's Long Gone — Now It's Rip Water and Bunker Pods from Saybrook to Great Island
reports.subhead: The river's shifted into its dog-days rhythm, and the fish that matter now are working current edges, not the flats at midday.
reports.body_markdown:
By the middle of July the river tells you plainly where you stand in the season. The shad are three months gone — that silver run up past Essex and the Salmon River tributaries wrapped by early June, and even the tail-end hickories that hang around into the solstice have pushed out or died off on their spawning run. What's left now is marsh grass gone chest-high on Great Island, ospreys feeding fledglings off dead snags along the flats, and bunker pods — real ones, thumb-sized peanuts pushed up into the coves — moving with the tide instead of against it. I've watched this river do this dance for fifty springs and just as many Julys, and the lesson never changes: once the shad clear out, the striper game here becomes a current game, not a structure game.

Out in the Sound proper, the numbers back up what I'm feeling at the mouth. New London's reading around 67.5 this week, a few degrees cooler than what's pushing out of our own river mouth on the ebb, and that temperature seam matters more than people think. The river itself runs warmer than the open Sound in July — freshwater flow off the Connecticut watershed heats up fast under a string of sunny days — and that warm outflow meeting the cooler Sound water right off Saybrook Point creates a real thermal edge. Bass and blues both know it. They sit right on that seam, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the warm water's pushing hardest out past the breakwaters.

The rip off Saybrook Point and the Calves Island rip upriver have both been holding fish, but it's not the easy, stack-em-up bite you get during the shad run. This is scattered, tide-dependent work. I fished the Point rip Tuesday morning on the last of the ebb into the top of the flood, and it took me forty minutes of drifting a one-ounce white bucktail with a curl-tail trailer before I connected — a 26-inch fish that came up right where the current line folded against the rock. Slow, deliberate hops along the bottom, not a fast retrieve — these fish are eating what the current brings them, not chasing anything down. Chartreuse worked just as well when the water carried a little color after Monday's rain runoff.

Great Island flats are the other piece of this puzzle, and they're producing better numbers if not better size. Juvenile bass and a growing push of bluefish are working the edges of the eelgrass beds on the incoming tide, feeding on those peanut bunker schools I mentioned. Light tackle guys — 7-foot spinning rods, small Kastmasters or half-ounce Deadly Dicks — are getting into snapper blues and schoolie stripers together in the same drifts, which tells me the size classes are still mixed and the bigger fish haven't fully separated out yet. That's normal for mid-July. The real slot-and-up bass are mostly holding deeper, working the channel edges near DEP Marina and the mouth itself, and they're not showing themselves during the heat of the day. Dawn and the last hour of light are doing all the work right now.

For those bigger resident fish, bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig, fished right on bottom in the deeper cuts off the marina and along the edge of the main channel, have been the most consistent producer for anyone willing to sit still through a tide change instead of covering water. I talked to a guy at the ramp Wednesday who'd taken two fish over 30 inches doing exactly that on the outgoing, using fresh-cut bunker he'd snagged himself off the surface schools near the railroad bridge. Fresh matters here — these fish have seen enough frozen chunk bait by midsummer that they get particular.

White perch fishing has actually been the most dependable part of the week, if not the most glamorous. The deep holes below Essex and around the mouth of the Lieutenant River are holding good numbers, and small hooks tipped with grass shrimp or bloodworm strips, fished on light spinning gear right on bottom during the slower parts of the tide, are putting decent perch — eight to eleven inches — in the cooler for anyone patient enough to sit on them. It's not a bite that makes headlines, but it's honest fishing and it's there every single day right now, which is more than I can say for the striper action.

Looking ahead, I don't expect this pattern to change much through the next week unless we get a real cool-down or a hard blow that stirs the river bottom and pushes more bait around. If the wind stays light out of the southwest like it has been, I'd fish the rips at first light and last light, work the current seams hard on bucktails, and save the bunker chunks for the deeper holes when the sun's high. The bigger bass are here — they're just making you earn every one of them this time of year, which is exactly how this river runs once the shad have gone home.

reports.headline: New Haven's Outer Wall Buried in Porgies, Bass Sliding the Charles Island Bar
reports.subhead: Scup are thick enough on the rockpiles to wear your arm out, and there's a slot-fish pattern building on the sandbar worth your evening tide.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, outer wall at New Haven Harbor, second rock pile out from the light. I dropped a high-low rig with two size 6 Chestertown hooks, seaworm on one, a strip of squid on the other, into about 16 feet on the tail end of the flood. Didn't even get the sinker settled before the rod tip started dancing — porgy, chunky one, close to a pound and a half, and that was the first of about forty over two hours before the current went dead slack and shut the whole thing down like someone flipped a switch. That's July on the breakwalls for you. When the tide's moving, it's about as easy as bottom fishing gets around here. When it stops, go home or go find moving water somewhere else.

That's really the story of the week — the porgies are here in numbers I haven't seen since early June, and they're piled onto every rockpile from the New Haven jetties out to Falkner Island. Small hooks, light sinkers, fresh bait, that's it. Seaworms are still the top bait but squid strips are keeping pace, and I had a stretch Thursday off the Falkner rocks where clam necks out-produced both for a solid hour on the last two hours of the incoming. Depth's been 15 to 25 feet depending which pile you're working, and the fish are hugging bottom tight — if your rig isn't ticking rock, you're not in the strike zone.

Sea bass are mixed in with the porgies on the deeper structure, especially out around Falkner and the rougher bottom off Stratford Shoal. Nothing giant — most are running 13 to 15 inches, right around the keeper mark — but there are enough shorts in the mix that you're culling through fish most drops. A 1-ounce diamond jig tipped with a squid strip, worked with a short hop off bottom, has been out-fishing bait-only rigs for the bigger sea bass. If you're marking bait balls on the graph over the rockpiles, that's your cue to jig instead of soak.

Blackfish are off the table right now — CT's summer closure has them shut down until September, so if you're marking tog on the same structure, let them be and come back after Labor Day. That closure's actually done the porgy bite a favor; without guys targeting the same rocks for tog, the scup have had that structure to themselves and they're piling up on it.

Stripers are the more interesting development. The Charles Island bar has been holding a real pattern on the last two hours of the flood into the top of the tide — I had three fish Sunday evening in the 26 to 29-inch range, one just under slot, working a white bucktail with a chartreuse Fin-S trailer along the drop-off where the bar falls into the channel. Water's running warm out there, and with the western Sound reading well into the low 70s, that warmth is holding bait tight against the sandbar edge — silversides mostly, with peanut bunker starting to show in pockets. The bass are using the bar as an ambush wall, sitting on the down-current side waiting for that bait to get pushed over the edge. Fish the transition zone, not the flat top of the bar, and you'll find them.

Bluefish have been spotty but real — a few blitzes off Hammonasset on bunker schools mid-week, gone as fast as they showed up. If you see birds working tight and bait skying, that's your five-minute window. Bucktails or any metal that gets down fast will draw strikes; don't waste time trying to match the hatch when they're in that mode.

Fluke are still soft. I drifted the sandy stretch off Milford Gulf twice this week with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails and only scratched out two keepers each trip, both right around 19 inches. The bottom there is clean and the current's decent on the outgoing, but the numbers just aren't what they were in June. I'd rather spend my fluke time working the edges near Stratford Shoal where there's more structure mixed with the sand — better odds of a bigger fish even if the overall action is slower.

Looking ahead, the tides build through this week heading toward the next new moon, which should push more water and more bait onto the bar at Charles Island — that's where I'd put my evening effort if stripers are the target. For bottom fishing, stick with the moving water windows on the rockpiles; the porgy bite has been consistent enough that I don't see it slowing unless we get a stretch of dead calm and slack current lasting more than a tide or two. If the bluefish schools settle into a pattern instead of running through, Hammonasset could turn into the better bet by next weekend. Worth checking both ends of the beat before committing.

reports.headline: Cockenoe Over the Cows: Working Around the Weekend Fleet for Bass, Sea Bass, and Scup
reports.subhead: With tautog closed for the summer and the Cows jammed with weekend traffic, the smart play this week is Cockenoe Reef on the early ebb — and it paid off.
reports.body_markdown:
I made a call Tuesday morning that I want to walk you through, because it's the kind of decision that separates a decent trip from a wasted one this time of year. I had two options sitting in the driveway with the boat hitched: run down to the Cows off Stamford where the porgies have been thick, or tuck into Cockenoe Reef and work the rockpiles on the last two hours of the ebb. The Cows on a Tuesday in mid-July still draws a fleet — day charters, weekend warriors who took a vacation day, paddleboarders drifting through the chum slick. I've fished that pressure before and it's not worth it unless you're first boat on the spot at first light. Cockenoe, by contrast, clears out fast once the sun's up, and the reef structure there holds fish tight to bottom regardless of who's buzzing overhead. I ran to Cockenoe. Good call.

Here's the why behind it. Kings Point is reading 71.2 degrees, which tells you the western end of the Sound has fully turned over into summer pattern — warm, stratified, with bait pushed up shallow and predators using structure and current edges to ambush rather than roam open water. That kind of water doesn't reward covering ground. It rewards picking a piece of structure, understanding which tide stage concentrates bait against it, and parking there. Cockenoe's boulder fields on the northwest corner fire hardest on the back half of the ebb, when the current funnels bait off the flats and stacks it against the rock in six to fourteen feet. That's where I found black sea bass to 17 inches stacked tight, taking squid strips fished on a simple two-hook bottom rig with just enough weight to hold in the current. Nothing fancy — this bite doesn't need it. The fish are there because the structure and the tide put the food there.

On blackfish, I'll be straight with you: it's a non-starter right now. Tautog season is closed through the end of August in the Sound, so if you're marking fish on the reef edges that look like tog, leave them be and shift your bottom rig over to the sea bass and porgy program instead. That's exactly what the Cockenoe trip turned into once I moved off the boulders into the sandier pockets between rock piles — porgies in the 9 to 12 inch range, steady action on bloodworm-tipped hi-lo rigs, best in the first hour of the incoming when the tide starts pushing warm water back over the flat. The Cows are still holding good porgy numbers too, from what I'm seeing and hearing off the dock, but if you want to fish it, get there before six, because by mid-morning the anchor lines and prop wash turn a good bite mediocer than it should be.

Striped bass have been the trickier read. The bait's here — bunker schools pushing through the Norwalk Islands, working the channels between Sheffield Island and the outer islands on the tail of the flood. I've seen bass working under those schools at first light, blowing up on peanut bunker pushed to the surface, but it's a short window. By 6:30, 7 o'clock, the sun gets up and the fish drop back down to the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet. That's when I switch from topwater and swimbaits to a slow-trolled bunker chunk or a bucktail dragged along the drop where the channel meets the flat off Sheffield. Slot fish, mostly — nothing over the mid-30s, but consistent enough that two or three fish an outing isn't a stretch if you're on the water at the right time. Bluefish are mixed into those same bunker schools, and they've been the more reliable player of the two — hit the surface blitzes hard with a topwater popper or a diamond jig ripped through the school, and you won't wait long.

Fluke have been a grind, honestly. I worked the sandy stretch off Penfield Reef on the outgoing tide with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifting the deeper cuts in 25 to 30 feet, and came away with fish, but they were short more often than not — a lot of throwbacks for every keeper. The water's warm enough that the fluke are there, they're just scattered across a wider area than they were in June, which means more drift time and less certainty per drift. If fluke is your priority this week, I'd put in the time on Penfield's outer edge rather than the shallower flats — the deeper water's holding the better-grade fish.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if this heat sticks around. Bunker schools should keep working the islands, which means bass and blues will keep showing in short windows at dawn and dusk. Weekend traffic is only going to get heavier through the rest of July, so my advice is simple: fish early, fish the reef structure that clears out fast once the crowds arrive, and don't fight for space on the Cows when Cockenoe or Sheffield's channel edges will give you the same fish with half the aggravation.

reports.headline: Plum Gut runs cold on the east end — the porgies never got the memo
reports.subhead: A steep temperature break from Horton Point to Orient is sorting the bite by degrees, and the bass know it better than we do.
reports.body_markdown:
My father used to say a bayman who trusts his eyes more than his thermometer will starve slow and confused. I didn't understand that till I was maybe forty, standing on the rocks at Horton Point watching gulls work a rip that had nothing under it. Water looked right. Tide looked right. Fish weren't there. Took me another twenty years of getting it wrong before I learned that the Sound doesn't hand you the same water twice in a week, and this week it's handing us two different oceans on one beat.

Run your hand off Mattituck east toward Orient and you're crossing a real seam. Up around the west end of my water it's pushing warm — nothing official to give you off Rocky Point, but the feel of it, the color, tells you it's tracking close to what Kings Point's been reading out west, high 60s pushing 70. By the time you're out toward Plum Gut and looking at New London's numbers, you're down closer to 68, maybe cooler in the current itself where that Race water comes barreling through. That's not a small difference to a fish. Seven, eight tenths of a degree can move a school off a rip like somebody turned off a light.

What that's meant on the water: the porgy bite off Horton Point and out past Rocky Point has been the most honest thing going. Small warm-water invertebrates, worms, spider crab bits — porgies don't ask permission, they just eat, and they've been stacked over the mussel bottom in eighteen to twenty-eight feet on the tail of the outgoing. Bloodworms on a hi-lo rig, size 6 or 8 hook, just enough sinker to hold bottom without dragging — that's been filling coolers with fish in the 12 to 14 inch range, a few pushing bigger. Nothing glamorous. Reliable, though, and reliable is worth something in July.

Bluefish have been running through in patches, mostly showing themselves in the surface commotion off Rocky Point in the last two hours of the incoming, chopping bunker pods that have been thick this month. If you see the water nervous and the terns diving, don't overthink it — a silver or blue diamond jig worked fast through the melee will connect, and so will a bunker chunk if you've got the patience to sit on it. Sizes have been mixed, plenty of choppers in the three to five pound range, the occasional bigger fish that'll make you check your leader after.

Striped bass have been the trickier read, and that's where the temperature break matters most. Closer to Mattituck and Horton Point, in that warmer water, the bass have been shallow and aggressive on the last two hours of the outgoing tide — working bucktails, half-ounce to three-quarter, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the drop-offs where the current pulls bait off the flats. Slot fish mostly, a few overslot mixed in for guys willing to work the rocks at first light before the boat traffic starts. But push east toward the Gut and that cooler water seems to be holding the bigger fish deeper and later — less willing to chase on top, more willing to eat a bucktail bounced right on bottom through the rip itself. That's classic Plum Gut behavior this time of year — the current does the work, you just need to get your offering down into it and let it ride. A friend who runs the approach regularly has been marking good bass sign on the meter down deep in that hard water off Orient, fish that won't show themselves on the surface but will eat a jig dropped and worked with the tide, not against it.

Weakfish have been a rumor more than a pattern — a few taken incidentally on bucktail drifts inside Mattituck Inlet, nothing you'd plan a trip around. Fluke have been steady but unspectacular off the drop-offs between Rocky Point and Horton, four-inch white Gulp on a light jighead, drifted slow over sand-to-mud transitions in twenty-five to thirty feet. Keeper-sized fish mixed in with plenty of shorts, which tells you the population's healthy even if the box isn't filling fast.

Blackfish, for those asking, you can leave the crab pots home — not their season and won't be for months yet.

Wind's been the other variable worth respecting. When it's been out of the southwest and built through the afternoon, the water off Rocky Point turns unpleasant fast for a small boat, and that's when I've told people to work the more protected water tucked closer to the inlet instead of grinding it out on the open beach.

Looking ahead — if that thermal seam holds where it's been sitting, I'd keep working the warmer water for the shallow, aggressive bass and save the deep bucktail work for the Gut on a strong tide, morning or evening, when the light's low and the current's really moving. If a stretch of easterly wind pushes that cooler water back west, the whole pattern could compress toward Horton Point fast, and I wouldn't be shocked to see the porgy grounds turn into a bass spot overnight. Worth checking both ends before you commit the whole day to one piece of rock.

reports.headline: July 17 and Washington's Running a Month Ahead of Where It Should Be
reports.subhead: The edge has been holding clean blue water since the Fourth, and the yellowfin bite out here is already doing what most years don't happen until August.
reports.body_markdown:
I've been saying it since May — Washingts early. Every year somebody new to the canyon circuit asks me why we're already trolling spreader bars in June when Norfolk and the Baltimore boats are still waiting on their water to turn over, and every year the answer's the same: this canyon sits right where the Stream likes to throw a filament north and pin it against the shelf edge. That happened again this year, and it happened early. We're seventeen days into July and Washington is fishing like it's the second week of August. I don't say that to brag. I say it because if you've been planning your trip around the old calendar, you're behind.

The setup right now is a warm-water push that's been sitting on the 100-fathom curve since right around the holiday, holding tight along a line that runs from about 38°22'N, 74°08'W down through the canyon head and out past the 300-fathom break. That's the edge I've been working, and it's held together better than most early-season filaments do — usually these things get chewed up by a cold eddy sliding off the shelf, but this one's stayed clean. Blue water, real blue, not that green Bight soup you're fighting up around the Hudson canyons right now. That distinction matters more than people think. Clean water holds bait, bait holds tuna, and tuna hold still long enough for you to actually catch them instead of guessing.

Yellowfin have been the story. Forty to seventy pound class fish, mostly in the morning push, trolling a standard spread — Islanders and ballyhoo combos on the shotgun and long riggers, a spreader bar with the bird out front working the middle. We've had our best runs right on that 100-fathom hook where the edge kicks north, not out in open water. The fish are using the structure of the drop the same way stripers use a rip — they're stacking where the current bends and the bait gets squeezed. I had a morning last week where we marked bait balls stacked from sixty to a hundred and forty feet on the machine right over that bend, and we didn't have to leave a two-mile stretch of water to get our fish. That's not something I say lightly this early in a season — usually we're still running and gunning in mid-July, covering thirty, forty miles a day hunting temp breaks. This year the fish told us where to sit.

Bigeye have been mixed. We're getting them, but it's a night game right now — chunking and jigging the drop after dark, working depths from two hundred to four hundred feet on the sounder over the deep canyon wall. It's not a sure thing. Two out of five trips down there after dark have produced, and when it's on, it's one or two quality fish, not a double-digit night. If you're chasing bigeye specifically, I'd rather you know that going in than sell you a bill of goods.

White marlin have shown better than I expected for mid-July. We've had shots on the color change out past the canyon rim, working dink ballyhoo and small squid chains dropped back off teasers, and the fish have been eating — not every day, but enough that I'm not surprised anymore when the reel clicks off on a long rigger with no warning. Best window's been that hour before the wind fills in, when the water lies down and you can actually see the fish come up on the teaser instead of guessing from the rod tip.

Mahi have been scattered around anything floating — pots, debris, weed lines pushed up along the edge of that warm filament. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the ten to fifteen pound range, but enough of them stacked under structure that a stop to pitch bait is worth the five minutes. Bring light spinning gear rigged with small skirted jigs or strips of squid and you can pick off a few extra fish while your spread's still soaking.

Wahoo have been the wildcard. We've pulled a couple off high-speed gear — wireline with a Wahoo Bomber style lure run fast, sixteen, eighteen knots, right on the edge where the temp break is sharpest. Not consistent, but when that filament holds tight against the shelf like it's been doing, wahoo like to sit right on that seam. Worth a couple lines in the spread if you're already out there.

Here's what I know about this canyon after enough years to stop pretending I know everything: filaments like the one we've got don't last forever. The Stream will eventually push another eddy through and either strengthen this thing or tear it apart. Right now the edge is intact, the water's clean, and the fish are using the structure exactly the way you'd draw it up on a whiteboard. If I had one day this week, I'd fish the early morning push right on that 100-fathom bend where we've been finding bait stacked, troll the standard spread, and keep bigeye gear rigged for after dark if conditions allow an overnight. If the filament holds through the weekend, I don't see a reason for this to slow down. If it slides, we adjust — that's canyon fishing. But right now, Washington's ahead of the calendar again, same as it always is, and the fish are cooperating.

reports.headline: Ran the West Wall at Wilmington — Six Yellowfin and a Mahi for the Trouble
