Stripers have been mixed in with pollock right on the surface, chasing bait balls pushed up by the current, and if you've got a light spinning rod rigged with a 1-ounce diamond jig or a Kastmaster, you can work both species without changing tackle. The pollock have run smaller than I'd like — schoolies mostly, 16 to 20 inches — but there's enough of them to keep a rod bent while you wait for something with more shoulders to show.

Eastern Egg Rock has had bait balls stacked up tight most mornings, which means the puffins are working and so are the bass underneath them — but you've got to be there early, right around first light on the last of the flood, before the wind builds and pushes the bait down. By nine or ten the birds thin out and so does the bite. I had one morning out there last week where three casts with a Doc's Sand Eel got three fish, all in the 20-inch class, then nothing for the next ninety minutes. That's July for you — short windows, good if you time them, frustrating if you don't.

Further out into Penobscot Bay, the groundfish are exactly where they should be this time of year — deep, and staying that way with this warm surface water pushing them down. The channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven, and the deeper humps out toward Isle au Haut Bay, have been holding cod and a few haddock in 90 to 120 feet. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or working a bottom rig with clam, has produced steady but not spectacular results — a few keeper cod in the 24 to 28-inch range mixed with a lot of shorts you've got to sort through. It's not the kind of bite that fills a fish box in an hour, but if you've got the patience to work the tide change slow, there's fish down there worth the trip.

Bluefish have been scarce so far, just the occasional slammer mixed in with mackerel schools off Boothbay, nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet. Deer Isle Thorofare and Merchant's Row have been quieter than I'd expect for mid-July — the current's there, the structure's there, but the bait hasn't concentrated the way it usually does by now. I'd keep an eye on that over the next couple weeks, because when it turns on out there it turns on fast.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and the water keeps warming the way it has, I expect the bass to tighten up their pattern by the weekend — probably pushing harder into the river mouths on the last two hours of the ebb, chasing that mackerel bait downstream. That's where I'd put my time if I only had one tide to fish. The groundfish out in the bay aren't going anywhere; that's a slow, steady bite you can count on right through August as long as you fish it deep and patient. Monhegan will keep rewarding early risers who fish the ebb off the western ledges. Nothing complicated about any of it — just old water doing what old water does, in its own time.

reports.headline: White Island Ledge Gives Up Haddock to 6, Bluefish Finally Crash Rye Harbor
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which six feet of it hold fish — this week it was the Shoals ledges and a sudden bluefish push at Rye Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
People from away always ask me how I fish the same thirteen miles of coast every week without getting bored. I tell them the same thing every time: New Hampshire doesn't have thirteen miles of coastline, it has thirteen miles of front door and about a hundred and thirty miles of water once you count the Shoals, the ledges, the river mouth, and every piece of structure in between. You just have to fish it like you mean it. This week meant leaving Rye Harbor before 5 a.m. with the Lund loaded light, because the haddock have been up on the humps around White Island and Duck Island, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the top of that structure by first light, you're fishing leftovers.

The groundfish bite out at the Shoals has been honest, not spectacular. White Island Ledge in 60 to 80 feet gave up haddock to six pounds on the last two mornings I ran out, mixed with a few keeper cod pushing seven and eight, all on the bottom of the tide when the current eases enough to hold a jig vertical. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid have been outfishing bare metal — the fish are picky enough right now that they want a little scent riding down with the flash. Once the tide starts to run hard past half-flood or half-ebb, that bite shuts off fast. You get maybe a ninety-minute window on each side of the slack, and if you're not rigged and dropped when it opens, you watch it close. I've had mornings out there where three of us put a dozen fish in the box in that window and then sat on a stone-cold rip for two hours waiting for the next one. That's the Shoals in July — you fish the clock, not the location.

Mackerel have finally shown in numbers around Appledore and the backside of Star Island, which matters more than people think, because that's the bait that's been pulling bigger cod up off bottom to chase. If you see the birds working tight over showers of mackerel near the ledges, drop a sabiki first, then switch over to a bigger jig once you've got a few mackerel in the well — a live mack fished on a heavy jig head near bottom has out-produced anything artificial out there this week.

Inshore, the striper story is Hampton Harbor, and it's been better than the ocean side has any right to expect given how warm and quiet the surf's been. Fish are stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming, pushing bait up through the inlet channel and holding along the edges where the current breaks against the jetty rocks. I've seen slot bass to 32 inches taken on white paddletails fished slow along that seam, and live pogies under a slip float have been money for the guys willing to soak bait instead of cast all day. The key has been fishing that inlet on the push, not the drain — on the outgoing the current rips too hard and flattens out the structure the fish are using. Give it that two-hour incoming window around the new tide change and work the drop-off just inside the jetty tips.

Bluefish showed up harder than I expected this week, cutting through Rye Harbor and pushing bait right up against the rocks at Odiorne Point. These aren't the giant choppers yet, mostly two to four pounds, but they're aggressive and they've been busting bait on top in the mornings, which makes for the kind of visual bite that gets people using words like exciting instead of technical. Topwater poppers and single-hook Kastmasters have worked, but bring wire or heavy fluoro leader — I lost three good lures in two days before I remembered who I was dealing with.

Flounder in the Piscataqua and up into Portsmouth Harbor have been a mixed bag — some days you can put together a dozen keepers drifting the deeper holes off the Route 1 bridge on the last of the ebb, other days you soak clams and worms for two hours and get nothing but hermit crabs. The river's still cold enough on bottom to hold fish, but the bite's been tide-dependent to the point where I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now. Better to treat it as a bonus stop on the way back in from the Shoals.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd keep working that White Island slack window early and expect the mackerel push to keep building, which should hold the bigger cod up shallower through the week. In the harbor, I'd fish that incoming tide hard at Hampton for another week or two before the bass start sliding out toward the open coast as the water warms further. And if you see bluefish showing at Odiorne again on a calm morning, don't wait — that bite's been unpredictable, on some days and gone the next, and I'd rather catch it than chase it.

reports.headline: Keyport's Bunker Blitzes Pull the Blues Tight While Fluke Keep Grinding the Channel Edges
reports.subhead: With a beat-up swell knocking the ocean side of the Hook around, I stayed inside all week and the bay paid me back — mostly.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday to keep the boat inside the bay for the whole week, and I'd make it again. There's a southeast swell rolling into the Bight — 2 to 3 feet at a ten-second period — and while that's nothing that'll sink you, it turns the Rip at the Hook into a washing machine you don't need to fish through when the bay itself is loaded with bait. So I skipped the ocean side entirely and put my time into Keyport, Flynn's Knoll, and the Navesink, and that's where this report lives.

The story of the week is bunker. Big pods of adult menhaden have been stacked off Keyport Flats and rolling down past Union Beach and Port Monmouth since late June, and by mid-July they're thick enough that you can see them nervous-watering from a quarter mile off — that oily slick, the gulls sitting on top waiting. Where you've got that much bunker balled up in shallow water in the heat of summer, you've got bluefish underneath it, and this week they found it. I watched three separate blitzes off the Keyport side Tuesday and Thursday mornings, right at first light before the wind came up, blues busting bunker on the surface hard enough to throw spray. Poppers and metal — I've been throwing a 1-ounce Kastmaster and a bunker-colored Super Strike popper — will get eaten the second they hit the water when it's happening like that. The trick is timing. Once the sun gets up over the trees and the boat traffic starts, the blitzes pull down and scatter, so if you want the top-water show, you need to be on the water by 5:30, not 7.

Stripers are mixed into those bunker schools but they're playing it smarter than the blues right now. This is mid-July heat — the resident bass aren't chasing bait on the surface in broad daylight, they're sitting under the school working the edges and picking off cripples. If you want them, don't fish the blitz itself, fish the perimeter. I've had better luck free-lining a live bunker on a 5/0 circle hook with just enough weight to keep it down 8 to 10 feet, drifting the edge of the bait school on the last of the incoming tide off Keyport and down toward Ideal Beach. Snag-and-drop works too if you've got the stomach for it — snag one on a treble, let it flutter down wounded, and hang on. The bass we've boated this way have mostly been schoolies and a few solid mid-20-inchers, nothing enormous, but it's honest action and it beats standing on the bulkhead getting skunked.

Fluke are still the most consistent player in the bay right now, and Flynn's Knoll has been the address. The drop where the Knoll spills into the Ambrose and Sandy Hook Channel — 25 to 35 feet — has been holding fluke all week, and the pattern hasn't changed much from June: 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, working the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your bucktail sideways. Romer Shoal has been productive too, especially on the western edge where it falls into deeper water — that's been giving up a better grade of fluke, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds mixed in with the usual 16 to 18-inch keepers. I'll be honest, it's not a five-fish-per-drift kind of bite most days — you're working for two or three keepers over a few hours — but the fish are there and they're eating with confidence when you find the right depth change.

The Navesink has quietly turned into the best-kept secret of the week. Weakfish have been showing up around the Oceanic Bridge and down toward Red Bank on the night tide, and if you've fished this river as long as I have you know that's when they show their teeth — right at dusk into full dark, on the outgoing. Chartreuse bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the bottom near the bridge pilings, have been the ticket. Nothing giant — most weakfish going 16 to 20 inches — but it's a legit bite that a lot of guys overlook once the striper run ends in spring, and it's worth the late-night trip if you're patient with the mosquitoes.

Porgies have been steady filler fishing on Old Orchard Shoal and around Romer Shoal on high-low rigs baited with clam or sandworm, decent-sized fish in the 1 to 2-pound range, good for keeping kids occupied while you wait on the tide to turn for fluke.

Looking ahead, if that southeast swell backs off like it's supposed to by the weekend, I'd take one more crack at the Rip before the bunker schools push farther down the bay — they always do eventually, usually once the water starts creeping past 78 degrees, which we're not far from. Until then, I'm staying inside: dawn blitzes off Keyport for blues, the Knoll and Romer for fluke on the incoming, and the Navesink after dark for weakfish. That's the bay right now — not blowing anybody's mind, but honest, workable fishing if you put your time in the right places at the right tide.

reports.headline: Why the sod bank drains are outfishing the open bay right now
reports.subhead: A lesson in current, temperature, and why the fluke you want are hugging the mud lines this week, not sitting out in the open sand.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a guy leaning on the rail at the ramp with a rod he hasn't wet yet: "Why am I marking bait all over the open bay and not getting bit?" It's a fair question, and it's a teaching moment every time. The answer, almost always, is temperature and current working together, and this week that lesson is on full display from Absecon Inlet down through Great Egg.

The back bays have warmed into the high 70s on the flats, and the ocean side, if the recent Bight buoy numbers are any indication, is sitting closer to 73 degrees with a lazy 2 to 3-foot swell running on a 10-second period. That's not rough water, but it's enough to keep the surf a little disorganized and push bait tight to structure rather than spreading it out. So the fish — fluke especially — aren't loafing on open sand in this heat. They're stacking where the water actually moves and cools a few degrees: the drains coming off the sod banks on the outgoing tide.

That's the pattern I've been fishing and teaching all week. Absecon Inlet's Rainbow Channel and Risley Channel edges, eight to fifteen feet, dropping tide, are the classroom. As that water pours off the marsh it's carrying grass shrimp and killies with it, and the fluke sit right on the edge of that current seam waiting for the buffet to come to them. A 3/4-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet, drifted slow and bounced just off bottom, has been the winning combination. Keep the boat moving with the current, not against it — that's the mistake I see most, guys trying to power-drift a falling tide and dragging the bait through the strike zone too fast. Slow it down. Let the current do the work. We've had keeper fluke to 22 inches coming out of that same seam three tides running, mixed in with a lot of shorts that need to go back — the size class isn't uniformly good, so expect to cull.

Graveling Point and the Great Egg back channels are fishing similarly, though I'd call that bite more moderate than hot — a few keepers scattered among a lot of teen-inch fish. If you're marking grass and mud bottom transitioning to harder sand on your graph, that's the spot to make repeat drifts.

Weakfish have been a first-light proposition only. Once the sun climbs and that back bay water heats up further, they slide off the flats and go quiet. Best window has been that gray hour right at dawn on the last of the incoming in the Rainbow Channel and up toward Longport, using a 1/4-ounce jighead with a pearl or chartreuse Gulp shrimp, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the channel edges where the mud gives way to shell. Nothing gaudy — a handful of legal fish mixed with a lot of short ones, but if you're up early it's worth the rods.

Bluefish are giving the inlet some life on the tail end of the incoming, chunked bunker fished on the bottom right along the Absecon Inlet rock jetty producing cocktail blues in the two-to-three-pound class, with the occasional heavier fish mixed in. If you'd rather cast than sit, diamond jigs worked through the same rip will connect just as well and keep you moving.

Kingfish are doing what they always do in mid-July — patrolling the surf troughs at Ocean City and Sea Isle City on incoming water, and they've been a reliable, if modest, producer. High-low rigs with small hooks, bloodworm or Fishbites, cast just past the first break. It's not a numbers game most mornings, but it's a teaching bite — good for kids and for anyone who wants steady action without needing a boat.

Striped bass are in their typical summer sulk. The resident fish haven't disappeared, but they've gone nocturnal and structure-bound. If you want a shot, fish bunker chunks on the bottom around the Absecon Inlet rocks after dark, on the last two hours of the incoming, and be patient. This isn't a volume bite in July — it's one or two quality fish for the guys willing to put in the hours after midnight.

Triggerfish have started showing on the near reef structure off Great Egg and around the outer rock piles at the inlet, which is right on schedule for this time of year. Small pieces of clam on a size 4 hook, light enough to still get bit but strong enough to handle their surprisingly stubborn pull. It's a finesse fishery — more about presentation and patience than volume — but a welcome change of pace when the fluke bite goes quiet on the tide change.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward new phase this week, which means bigger tide swings and stronger current through the inlets — good news for the sod bank pattern, since more water moving means more bait getting flushed off those flats. If the swell backs off like it's been trending, I'd expect the surf kingfish bite to clean up and the triggerfish action on the reef structure to firm up too. My plan for the coming week is simple: fish the outgoing around Absecon and Great Egg for fluke, be on the water at first light for weakfish, and save the inlet rocks for after dark if stripers are the target. That's where the lesson plan says to be.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke Are There If You Work For Them — Blowfish and Kingfish Carry the Bay
reports.subhead: Weakfish have slid off the sedges for deeper water, but blowfish, kingfish, and a patient fluke drift are keeping rods bent through the July heat.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember mating on one of the Point Pleasant boats back when I was maybe sixteen, a July morning thick as this one, and an old captain named Sal telling me, "Gus, this time of year the bay gets lazy on you. You gotta go find the fish, they won't come find you." I've thought about that line every July since, usually right about now, when the sedges go quiet and the fluke stop cooperating on the first drift and you have to actually work the boat instead of just soaking a line and hoping. That's exactly where we are this week on Barnegat Bay — not a bad bite, but a bite that makes you earn it.

Start with the fluke, because that's what most of the calls to the shop are about. Double Creek Channel is still the play, but it's not the wide-open drift you had in June. The keepers are there, we're just seeing them stacked tighter around the bends near the range markers and the deeper cuts on the edges of the channel, 12 to 18 feet, and you need to hit the tide right — the first two hours of the outgoing has been the difference between a decent box and a long, quiet afternoon. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow right on the bottom, has been outproducing bare bucktails two to one. I had a father-son pair out of Forked River last Tuesday who ground out four keepers to 4 pounds on that combo after two hours of shorts — patience paid, but it wasn't handed to them.

Weakfish are the story of the season winding down, not winding up. May and early June had the sedge banks with tide-run weakies, but by mid-July most of that school has slid off into deeper water, probably staged somewhere off the inlet or holding in the channel humps where it's cooler. You can still scratch a few keeper weakfish working the last hour of the incoming at Tices Shoal, bucktail tipped with a shrimp or squid strip fished slow along the drop, but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it right now. If you connect, treat it as a bonus, not the plan.

Bluefish have been the more dependable fireworks. Barnegat Inlet, particularly the rocks on the north side, has had real morning blitzes on the incoming — chopper blues in the 3 to 6-pound class crashing bunker pods right at first light. Metal — Ava jigs, Kastmasters in silver or chartreuse — worked fast through the melee has been money, and if you want to have some fun with it, a topwater popper thrown right into the boil will get eaten just as quick. That bite tends to shut off hard once the sun gets up over the dunes, so if you're going for blues, go early.

Stripers in the bay proper have gone to their July pattern, which is to say they've gone nocturnal on us. Water in the shallow coves and up around Oyster Creek has been running warm enough that the bass just don't want to work during daylight — I'm seeing better results after dark around the bridge pilings and the deeper holes near the inlet rip, live bunker or eels fished on a fish-finder rig right on bottom. If you're a surf guy, Island Beach State Park at first light on the last of the falling tide has been quietly productive — the ocean side is still cooler than the bay, running in the low 70s off the coast, and that temperature break has been enough to hold some slot fish tight to the bar. It's not a numbers game out there right now, more a one-or-two-good-fish kind of morning, but those fish have had some shoulders on them.

The real bread and butter this week has been blowfish and kingfish, and I say that with real affection because this is the fishing that keeps kids and grandparents happy on a hot afternoon. Blowfish are thick around the Oyster Creek docks and the marina edges at Tices Shoal — small hooks, bloodworm or squid strips, doesn't take much skill, just patience and a bucket. Kingfish have been working the sod banks along Double Creek and out toward the Barnegat Light flats on the incoming tide, sandworm or bloodworm strips fished light on the bottom. Neither of these fisheries will make the cover of anything, but they've been steady when the marquee species have made you work.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down through the weekend, I'd expect the fluke bite in Double Creek to tighten up around that same outgoing window — moving water is doing the work right now, not the bait itself. The bluefish should keep showing at the inlet as long as bunker pods keep pushing through, and I'd bet the striper bite stays a dawn-and-dusk affair until we get a real cool-down. If you've only got one shot this week, I'd take the early flood at Barnegat Inlet for blues and finish the tide out with a fluke drift down through Double Creek — cover your bases, and don't be surprised if you have to move around to find them.

reports.headline: Holgate's Reshaped Third Bar Holds Fluke on the Drop, Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: A groundswell chewed a new trough into the south end this week — fluke moved in fast, stripers are still playing it cautious until the sun's down.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch at low light Tuesday morning with the drone up before the wind picked up, and the third bar isn't where it was two weeks ago. That two-to-three-foot groundswell we picked up off a long-period east swell — ten seconds, out of the southeast — did some real work down there. It cut a new trough on the south end, maybe 40 yards off the dune line, deeper and tighter than the old one. Water's pushing through it hard on the outgoing, and that kind of current edge right up against structure is exactly what fluke want in mid-July.

So that's where I started the week, and it paid. Drifting that new cut and the flat behind it, 18 to 24 feet, on the last three hours of the outgoing — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped light, just enough to feel bottom and no more. Picked up keeper fluke to 22 inches doing that, along with a pile of shorts that kept it interesting between fish. The Little Egg Inlet channel edge, right where it necks down before Graveling Point, has been doing the same thing — same depth range, same idea, current stacking bait against a hard edge. If you're marking bait balls on the meter there on the last of the ebb, don't leave. That's the window.

Barnegat Inlet's producing too, but it's pickier. North side near Oyster Creek Channel on the incoming has given up a few nicer fluke, 4 to 6 pounds, to guys working chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp swimming mullet trailer, dragged slow along the bottom edge where the sand meets the rock rubble. That's not a drift-and-hope spot — you need to know exactly where that rubble line sits, and it moves every season. I'd rather send you to Holgate or Little Egg if you're not familiar with that structure.

Bluefish have been showing up early, and I mean early — first light, Ship Bottom and Surf City beachfront, blitzing peanut bunker and small mullet that are starting to stage up for the run. Poppers and small metal, cast right into the wash where the birds are working. It doesn't last — usually blown out by 7:30 once the sun gets up and the bait scatters — but for that hour it's about as fun as this beach gets in July. Bring a spinning rod you don't mind getting slimed.

Kingfish are on the sod banks in Little Egg and up around Graveling Point, working the marsh edges on the high tide push and pulling back off the bank as it drains. Bloodworms and FishBites bloodworm strips on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinker — these fish don't need much convincing right now, they're just not everywhere. Focus on the drainage guts where the marsh grass funnels bait out on the ebb.

Striped bass are the hard truth of this report. The resident fish are here, but July's ocean temp sitting in the low 70s and a back bay running even warmer has them doing what smart bass do this time of year — feeding at night and hiding in whatever cool water they can find during the day. I've had two decent sessions at Holgate after dark, working that new cut with a black needlefish on the slower stretches and switching to a small darter when I could hear bait getting nervous on the surface. Slot fish, nothing huge, but real bites on a real presentation instead of just soaking bunker and hoping. My plug bag right now is stripped down to three trays — swimmers for the last of dusk, poppers for when bait's showing, needlefish and darters for full dark. If you're bass fishing LBI in July and you're not out there between 9 PM and 2 AM, you're mostly fishing for the memory of spring.

Weakfish are thinning out fast. Great Bay and the deeper holes off Graveling Point still had a few respectable fish on soft plastics — Bass Assassins in pearl, worked slow along the bottom — but that bite's fading as the water climbs. The Mullica's gone properly warm and tannic, good for an hour at first light before it goes quiet and stays quiet through the heat of the day.

Looking ahead, that groundswell is backing off and the wind's supposed to swing more southwest by the weekend, which should let that new Holgate cut settle in rather than get reworked again. If it holds its shape, I'd keep drifting it on the outgoing for fluke through next week. For bass, until we get a real bait push or a cool-down at night, I'm treating it as a dark-hours program only — plan your trip around the tide stage after sunset, not the calendar.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point on the drop: scup thick on the ledges, bass working after dark
reports.subhead: The herring run's long gone, but the bay's settled into its mid-summer rhythm — bass gone nocturnal, fluke sliding onto the flats, scup piled on every rock pile from Rocky Point to Prudence.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the India Point pier Tuesday morning watching a kid with a Zebco reel haul scup over the rail two at a time, and his old man turns to me and says, "Where'd all the bass go?" That's the question I keep hearing up and down the river this week. Buckeye Brook's herring run wound down back in June, and once that bait ran dry, the bass that stacked up on it for weeks scattered. They didn't leave the bay — they just changed their address and their clock.

That's the story of mid-July here. The easy money bite off the herring is done. What's left is a bay that's warmed up top to bottom, tides running big off this new moon, and fish that have gone smart and nocturnal. If you want stripers now, you're fishing bridges after dark or you're chasing bunker schools that are holding off Prudence Island and down around the mouth of Greenwich Bay. I had a good hour Thursday night under the Mount Hope Bridge on the last of the outgoing, drifting a live eel down current past the third and fourth piling. Two fish in the 28-30 inch class, both right on the seam where the light meets the shadow line. That's been the pattern all week — small light, tight current, and patience. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off the rocks at Rocky Point have also been picking off keeper bass on the last two hours of the ebb, right around midnight to 2 a.m.

Fluke are the better daytime bet right now, and they're pushing hard into the bay off the warm flow coming out of the upper river. Greenwich Bay has been holding fish in 10 to 18 feet on the drop of the tide — I'm dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid, nice and slow along the bottom off the Warwick side. Conimicut Point is doing the same thing on the outgoing — that current sweeping around the point concentrates bait, and the fluke sit right on the edge of it in 12 to 20 feet. Nothing giant this week, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a few keepers mixed in, but steady enough that a couple hours on the drift will put fish in the cooler if you keep moving and don't marry one spot.

Scup are the sure thing right now, and that's not a knock — that's just where we are in July. Nyatt Point and the rock piles down toward Rocky Point are loaded. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, sandworm or squid strips, dropped into 15 to 25 feet right on the rocks. The bigger tides we're getting off this new moon are moving more water through those ledges, and the scup respond to it — best bite has been the first two hours of the ebb when that current really starts to rip past the structure. If you want a mess of fish for the pan without overthinking it, that's your spot this week.

Bluefish have shown up in patches, mostly chopping bait on top out toward the mouth of the bay and around Prudence Island in the early morning. I haven't seen the kind of blitz that stops traffic, but there's enough bluefish mixed in with those bunker schools that if you're throwing poppers or SP minnows at first light off Prudence, don't be shocked if something with teeth ends your leader. Black sea bass are still holding tight to the rock structure around Jamestown and the deeper edges off Prudence — small jigs tipped with squid, fished slow right on bottom, still producing a few keepers, though the season's ticking and the bigger ones have thinned out some.

Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't heard a real report on those this week. A few years back you could count on some around Greenwich Bay this time of year, but that fishery's a shadow of what it used to be around here, so I'm not sending anybody chasing ghosts.

Looking ahead, these new moon tides should keep building through the weekend, which is good news for the ledge bite — more water movement means more bait getting pushed around, which means scup and fluke both should stay active. If the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down at night like it has been, I'd put my money on the bridges again after dark for bass — that's been the more consistent program than daytime blind casting. Worth watching the bunker schools off Prudence too; if they hold position through the week, that's where the next real bass and blue action is going to break loose.

reports.headline: Wreck 3548 in 118 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds, Bluefin Working the Mud Hole Lumps
reports.subhead: A two-decade-old number still pays off, and the tuna bite on the inshore lumps is finally worth the run.
reports.body_markdown:
Wreck number 3548, sitting in 118 feet on the eastern lip of the Klondike, has been in my book since 2009. I marked it after a mate of mine snagged bottom there chasing bluefin and came up with a piece of steel plate on his jig. Took me three trips to find the actual structure with the old sounder, and it's paid rent every July since. This week it did it again — sea bass to four pounds, mixed in with enough shorts that you had to cull hard to keep the box respectable. That's the kind of number that doesn't show up on a chartplotter unless somebody hands it to you, and I don't hand many out, but I'll tell you the depth and let you find the pile yourself: 118 feet, current running southwest at the top of the tide, jigs and bait rigs both worked once we found the exact piece.

The bigger story this week is the bluefin showing up on the Mud Hole lumps again, and not just as a rumor from the radio. We had three trips out there since Thursday, connected on two of them, which for mid-July inshore bluefin I'll take. The fish are sitting on bait balls stacked over the humps in 90 to 130 feet, the kind of structure that pushes cooler water up from below even when the surface is running warm. Surface temps off Manasquan have been pushing into the low 70s, but out past the 20-fathom curve where these lumps sit, there's still a cooler pocket underneath that's holding the bait tight. Trolling small spreader bars and cedar plugs got the strikes in the early morning hours, before the sun got high and the fish went deeper. Once that happened we switched to jigging — the green-and-white Shimano Butterfly in the 150-gram range, dropped fast through the bait and worked with a short, aggressive stroke. Fish ran 30 to 50 pounds, nothing giant, but steady enough that a half-day trip out there is worth the fuel if you time it right on an outgoing tide with the current pushing the bait against the structure.

Yellowfin have been scarcer inshore, which tracks with what I'd expect this time of year — they're still holding out past the canyon edges, and the water temperature break that usually pulls them up onto the Hudson Canyon shoulder hasn't set up clean yet. A few boats working the deeper water off the Ridge picked at them trolling ballyhoo behind Green Machines, but it wasn't consistent enough to call it a pattern. I'd rather be honest about that than send you sixty miles for a coin flip.

Mahi are starting to show on the lobster and fish pots scattered between the Mud Hole and Barnegat Ridge, which is about two weeks ahead of when I'd normally expect them to stack up. We picked off a dozen fish in the 3 to 6 pound range working pot markers in about 100 feet of water, sight-casting small white bucktails and pilchard chunks once we spotted the shadow under the buoy. This is the appetizer — the real mahi bite on the pots usually locks in through August once the warm water fully settles over that structure, but if this early push holds, we could be ahead of schedule this year. Worth working the pot lines on your way out or back from the tuna grounds; costs you nothing to slow down and look.

Sea bass overall have been solid but not spectacular across the reef network — Axel Carlson, Sea Girt Reef, and the Triple Wrecks are all holding fish, but the average size has come down some from June as the bigger fish get picked over. Squid strips and Gulp on standard sea bass rigs, fished tight to structure in 60 to 90 feet, still fills a cooler if you're willing to move when the bite slows. Blackfish season's closed this time of year in state waters, so that's not part of the conversation right now, and cod have moved off entirely — too warm, they're long gone north or holding deep on structure we're not fishing this month.

Bonito have started showing on the inshore lumps and reef edges in scattered pockets, chasing the same bait that's holding the bluefin. Small metal jigs — half-ounce to an ounce, worked fast on light tackle — will connect if you find a breaking pod, but they move fast and don't sit still like the tuna do over structure.

Looking at the week ahead: if the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't kick up the kind of chop that shuts down the pot-hopping for mahi, I'd put my time on that early-morning tuna window on the Mud Hole lumps before the sun gets high, then work pot markers on the ride home. The bluefin pattern has legs as long as that bait stays stacked on the humps — if it slides off, which happens fast this time of year, I'd shift effort to the wreck numbers in 100 to 130 feet and lean on sea bass to fill the box while we wait for the next push of tuna bait to show.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips Grade: C-Minus — Fluke and Triggers Save the Week
reports.subhead: Summer water pushed the rip bass deep and cranky, but the inlet fluke and the first triggerfish of the season kept rods bent.
reports.body_markdown:
If I'm handing out grades this week, the Rips get a C-minus. That's not me being cranky for the sake of it — that's just where they're at in mid-July. The bass are there, but they're not stupid, and they're not shallow. Water off Cape May Point has settled into that heavy, warm summer stack, and every year around this time the stripers that were slashing bait on top in May and June slide down and get lockjawed and lazy. You can still find them, but you're working for every fish, not picking them off a boil.

Best window I had all week was the top of the outgoing at the Point, first light, before the boat traffic stirred everything up. Ran bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs down in 35 to 45 feet where the rip line sets up hard against the shoal, and picked at three keepers over two mornings — one a solid 28-incher that ate on the second drop. That's the pattern right now: get there before the sun's fully up, fish the strongest push of the tide, and don't expect a repeat performance an hour later. By 8 a.m. the bite shuts like someone flipped a switch. If you're trolling bunker spoons or umbrella rigs through there midday, you're burning gas for the memory of it.

The good news — and the reason this week wasn't a total wipeout — is Hereford Inlet. Fluke fishing has actually been solid, not spectacular, but honest. Drifting the channel edges on the outgoing, 25 to 35 feet, with 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in chartreuse, and we've been putting keepers in the box most trips. Nothing over 4 pounds, but steady action, the kind where you're not sitting on your hands between fish. Same pattern working off Wildwood and down toward the Cape May Canal mouth — anywhere there's current pulling bait off the flats into deeper water, the fluke are stacked up waiting for it.

Bluefish have shown up in patches along the beachfront at Cape May Point, mostly at dawn, chopper-sized, blitzing peanut bunker pushed tight to the wash. If you catch that window — and it's a short one, twenty, thirty minutes some mornings — poppers and 1-ounce metal will get bit on nearly every cast. Miss it and you're just watching gulls work water that's already gone quiet.

Now, the triggerfish. First real reports of the season came off the reef sites — Cape May Reef and the Wildwood Reef — guys bottom fishing clam and squid strips over structure in 60 to 80 feet finding a few keeper triggers mixed in with the sea bass. It's early yet, this fishery really turns on in August, but the first ones showing up now tells me the water's holding steady and warm enough offshore to bring them up onto the wrecks. Worth a look if you've got a boat that can reach the reef sites and don't mind soaking bait patiently — triggers aren't a numbers game, they're a persistence game.

On weakfish — I'll be straight with you, that fishery isn't what it used to be around here. We're not seeing the tiderunners my father used to talk about working the Bay in the old days. What we are getting is the occasional legal weakfish mixed into the fluke drift in the back bay channels at last light, usually on the same bucktail-and-Gulp combo. If you're targeting them specifically, you're going to be disappointed. If you're fishing fluke and one shows up in the mix, consider it a bonus.

And yes, before anyone asks — the Delaware Bay black drum run is done. That's a May fishery, and it wrapped up weeks ago. Fortescue and the Brandywine Shoal area are quiet on that front now; what's left up the Bay this time of year is a scattering of resident stripers around structure and current breaks, nothing worth a dedicated trip. If you're still hearing chatter about drum from somebody at the dock, they're talking about last season or they're confused.

Looking ahead, I don't expect the Rips to open up much until we get a stretch of cooler nights or a wind shift that mixes the water column — that's usually late July into August around here. Until then, my play is early mornings on the strongest tide push, fluke in the inlet on the outgoing, and keeping an eye on the reef sites as the triggerfish bite builds through the month. If you've only got one morning to fish, I'd put it on the Hereford Inlet fluke drift over the Rips right now — it's the more honest bet. But if you want a shot at a bass, first light at the Point on the top of the outgoing is still your best window, even if it's a short one.

reports.headline: Ram Island's Boulders Load with Peanut Bunker, Stripers Working the Seams on the Drop
reports.subhead: Fishers Island Sound is running cool for mid-July — the fish are pressed tight to the rock, and the albies aren't here yet, but the bait says they're coming.
reports.body_markdown:
The peanut bunker showed up in the pockets off Ram Island about ten days ago, and this week they finally pushed thick enough that you can see them nervous over the boulders on a calm morning — that flicker just under the surface, like somebody shook a jar of dimes. When bait gets nervous over rock, something's under it. I've been poling the skiff along the north side of Ram and through the boulder field off Wamphassuc Point at first light, reading the water the way my grandfather taught me to read it off the breakwater sixty years ago — not by what you see on top, but by what the water does when it hits something hard underneath.

The stripers have been there. Not blitzing, not chasing bait into the air, but working the current seams where the ebb wraps around the bigger rocks and drops bait into slack pockets. That's precision water — you're not bombing a cast, you're dropping a fly or a bucktail three feet off a specific boulder and letting it sink on a controlled count before the current sweeps it into the seam. I've had the best of it on the last two hours of the ebb, fishing a half-ounce olive-and-white bucktail with a chunk of white curly-tail trailer, working it slow along bottom in six to nine feet of water. Fly guys have done well on Clouser minnows and small peanut bunker patterns — olive over white, size 1, stripped in short erratic pulls to mimic that nervous bait behavior rather than a straight swim. Fish have run 22 to 28 inches mostly, a few better ones mixed in that we didn't measure because they went right back — this isn't trophy water in July, it's technical water, and that's exactly why I like it.

Water's running cooler than you'd expect for the date. New London's reading in the mid-60s, which is a few degrees behind where we usually sit this time of July, and that cool water is likely why the bass haven't scattered out onto the flats the way they sometimes do by now — they're staying pressed to structure, holding where the current break gives them an ambush point without burning energy in open water. That's good news for a rock guy. When the fish spread thin over sand, it's a numbers game. When they stay tight to boulders, it's a game I can win with a pole and a quiet approach.

Fluke have been steady but not spectacular in the sandy cuts between the boulder fields — the stretch between Ram Island and the Stonington Breakwater channel, and the deeper hole off Esker Point, have both given up keepers in the 18 to 21 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets, 3-inch, on 3/8-ounce jigheads, drifted slow on the last of the incoming. Nothing to write home about, but a legitimate box fish if you put in the drift time and don't rush the retrieve. Black sea bass are doing their job out around the deeper structure off the east end of Fishers Island — jigging bucktails tipped with squid strips in 25 to 35 feet has produced decent numbers, though you're culling through a lot of shorts to find keepers right now.

Blackfish are still off the table with the summer closure in effect, which is fine by me — I'd rather let those boulder-dwellers alone until the fall run anyway, when the water cools and they pile back onto the structure I've been fishing my whole life.

Now, the question everybody's been asking me at the dock: where are the albies? Honest answer — not here yet, and I wouldn't tell you otherwise. Mid-July is early for Fishers Island Sound. The real run doesn't usually light up until late August into September, when the bay anchovies and silversides get thick in the rips off Watch Hill and around the east end of Fishers. What I am seeing is the forage building the way it should — peanut bunker in the shallows now, and I expect silversides to follow within a couple weeks as the water continues to warm through the back half of July. Squid have been showing in numbers up around Rhode Island Sound and toward Nantucket, and when that squid bite pushes closer to our water it usually means the whole system is loading up for the fall pattern. It's early signal, not a bite report — but it's the kind of thing that tells you to keep your 9-weight rigged and ready.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the same program: last two hours of the ebb through the Ram Island and Wamphassuc boulder fields for stripers, working current seams tight to structure rather than open water. If we get a stretch of settled southwest wind under 10 knots, I'll be poling the skiff through the shallower boulder pockets on the last of the outgoing, since calm conditions let you actually see the bait and place a cast with precision instead of guessing. If the wind kicks up out of the east, I'd shift to the deeper structure off Fishers Island for sea bass and fluke instead of fighting a chop over the rocks — that's not a day to be running a lower unit through boulder country anyway. The bite this week has been honest work — no giveaways, but consistent enough that a patient angler willing to read the rock instead of the chart is going home with fish.

reports.headline: Valiant Rock at 4.1 Knots: Wire Line Bass Hold Through the Push
reports.subhead: A steep thermal split across the Sound is stacking stripers in the cold water at The Race while the west side goes quiet — here's where and when to fish the window.
reports.body_markdown:
Valiant Rock ran 4.1 knots on Thursday's max ebb, and that's the number that tells you everything about this week. Slack came in tight — about eleven minutes either side of 11:20 — and in that window I put three fish over 30 inches in the boat on wire line and a white bucktail worked off the north face of the rock in 38 feet. Miss that window by fifteen minutes and you're fighting current instead of fishing it. That's The Race in July — it doesn't give you much room, but it gives you fish if you're precise about it.

Here's why this window matters more than usual right now. New London is sitting at 66.4 degrees. Kings Point, forty-some miles west, is reading 71.2. That's a five-degree spread across one body of water, and it's not closing anytime soon with this heat. Stripers don't love water in the low 70s in July — they get sluggish, push deep, or bail for cooler structure. The eastern Sound, where I live and fish, is still cold enough to hold them tight to bottom in the rips. That's the whole story this week: the fish that would normally be spreading out into the Sound's open water are pinned to Race Rock, Valiant Rock, and the Gut because the current there keeps things cold and oxygenated even as the surface cooks.

The bite itself has been technical, not a blitz. I'm not going to oversell it — you have to work for these fish right now. Wire line, 60-foot drops off the downtide side of Valiant on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent producer, bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of pork rind or a Fin-S trailer when the current really starts hauling. Depths from 35 to 50 feet. The fish are holding low, right on the boulder fields, and you need enough lead to feel bottom through 4 knots of water or you're just trolling air above them. Slack itself is short and sweet — five, maybe ten minutes of genuinely fishable water before the tide turns and starts building the other way — but that's when the bigger fish, the 34-to-40-inch class, come off the rock faces to feed. I've had my best two fish of the week come in that exact window at Valiant, both on the drop of the tide right before the flood takes hold.

Plum Gut has been a bluefish story more than a bass story this week. Fresh bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 30 feet off Orient Point on the outgoing, has been putting solid 8 to 12-pound blues in the boat pretty reliably, along with the occasional bass mixed in on the same baits. If you want the bass specifically out of the Gut, work the eddy lines on the Long Island side with a 3-ounce diamond jig on the drop, tight to bottom where the current stacks bait against the drop-off.

Fluke have been steady but not spectacular on the sand flats behind the Sluiceway and off Little Gull. Drifting 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 30 feet, outgoing tide, has produced keeper-class fish to 22 inches with enough shorts mixed in that you're culling, not scrambling. Black sea bass around Race Rock and the boulder piles off Great Gull have been a bright spot — squid strips and Gulp jigs dropped straight down on structure in 40 to 60 feet are filling coolers, and that fishery's been the most dependable thing out here all month.

On false albacore and bonito — it's too early, and I'd rather tell you that straight than sell you a fantasy. The open ocean side is reading 72.9 at the NY Bight buoy with a building 2.3-foot swell, which tells me warmer water is pushing toward the Race from the south. That's the setup that eventually pulls albies through Plum Gut and into the Sluiceway, usually by early-to-mid August once the bay anchovies and silversides show up thick. I'll be running epoxy jigs and checking the rips daily starting the last week of July, but right now there's no bait signature or surface activity out there worth a special trip.

Looking ahead: the tide cycle is building toward bigger swings over the next several days, which should tighten these slack windows even further and could push more bass up onto the rock faces during the transition periods. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of a strong ebb at Valiant Rock, wire line down to bottom, and I'd have the epoxy jigs rigged and ready in case anything shows on the surface at the Gut on the way back in. The bite's there, but it's a precision game right now — miss the window, miss the fish.

reports.headline: Plum Gut Turned Over for Blues, Horton Point Still Making You Earn a Bass
reports.subhead: The Gut's running with jumbo bluefish and the first real squid smell of the summer, but the bass between Mattituck and Rocky Point are still playing hard to get.
reports.body_markdown:
Sal Petrucci's been clamming Mattituck Creek longer than I've been legal to drink, and Tuesday morning he flagged me down off the town beach holding up a bucket like it owed him money. "Water's got a stripe in it," he says. "Warm on top, cold underneath, like somebody poured two different summers in the same glass." I told him that's about the smartest thing anybody's said to me all week, because that's exactly what's going on out there — and it's why this report's going to sound like two different reports stitched together, because that's what the Sound's doing right now.

Western water's been running warm — I'm hearing Kings Point up around 71 — and by the time you work your way east toward New London it's dropped into the mid-60s. That gradient doesn't stop at some invisible line on a chart, it runs right through my zone. Mattituck's fishing like the warm side. Orient and the Plum Gut approach are fishing like the cold side. Horton Point and Rocky Point are stuck in the middle, which is about where the fishing's been too — decent, not great, and you have to work for it.

Start at Mattituck Inlet. There's peanut bunker stacked in the mouth on the last two hours of the ebb, and the bass know it. Nothing big — mostly schoolies and a few fish pushing 26, 27 inches — but they're there most evenings if you fish live bunker on a fishfinder rig, or a white 1-ounce bucktail worked slow along the rocks on the west side. I had one client stick three keepers in an hour Thursday and get skunked the next night in the same spot on the same tide. That's the warm-water pattern for you — the fish are following the bait, and the bait's moving with the temperature, not the clock.

Horton Point's been the stubborn one. The structure's still there, the current still rips off that point like it always has, but the bass have been sitting deep and picky. Clam's been out-fishing plugs and bucktails by a wide margin — cut skimmer clam on a fish-finder rig, fished right on bottom where the rip drops off into the deeper water. Guys throwing plugs through there have had long, quiet evenings. I don't know why the bass want it slow and smelly instead of something with action, but I've fished that rock pile sixty years and I've learned not to argue with what's working.

Rocky Point's given up some decent porgy the last couple weeks — good numbers of scup in the 10-to-12-inch range on the reef structure, taking sandworm and squid strips fished light, small hooks, just enough weight to hold bottom on the drift. If you want a bucket of fish for the pan without much drama, that's your spot right now. Blackfish are mixed in on the rockier stretches too, but they're still finicky this time of year — green crab's the ticket when they cooperate, which isn't every tide.

Now the good news, and it's real good news if you like bluefish with some shoulders on them. Plum Gut's turned over. The current there is doing what it does when the tide really starts to rip, and there are jumbo blues stacked on the edges of that current, blitzing bait right on the surface in spots. I had a report of fish to 12, 13 pounds taken on diamond jigs and topwater poppers worked right along the seam where the fast water meets the slower stuff off Orient Point. That's classic Gut behavior — the current does the work, piling bait against the structure, and you just need to put something shiny in front of a fish that's already worked up.

There's bass mixed in with those blues too, and from what I'm seeing they're leaning toward slot and overslot rather than shorts — bigger, more mature fish pushing through on the tide change. If you're going to fish the Gut, fish the edges of the rip, not the middle of it, and don't be afraid to let a bucktail sink clean before you start working it. That's where the bigger stripers are holding, down under the commotion the blues are making up top.

Weakfish have been a rumor more than a pattern out here this year — a few taken incidental to the fluke guys working the deeper holes off Rocky Point on bucktail and Gulp combos, nothing you could call a run. I wouldn't plan a trip around them, but keep a rod rigged light just in case.

Looking ahead, I'd watch that thermal stripe Sal pointed out. If the warm water keeps pushing east, Horton Point ought to loosen up and start fishing more like Mattituck — faster, more aggressive fish willing to chase a plug again. If it holds where it is, keep the clam rod rigged and be patient. And with squid starting to show up to our east around Rhode Island and Nantucket, don't be surprised if Plum Gut gets even better before it gets worse — that's the kind of forage that turns a good bluefish bite into a genuine bass rip. I'd fish the Gut on the next good tide change if I only had one shot this week, but I'd have the clam bucket in the truck as a backup plan for Horton Point on the way home.

reports.headline: Chicory on the Dikes, Snapper Blues at the River Mouth
reports.subhead: The shad are three months gone and the river's settled into its summer rhythm — perch in the coves, young bass on the flats, blues showing at the mouth.
reports.body_markdown:
The day lilies are done and gone along Route 156, and what's blooming now on the dikes above Great Island is chicory — that pale blue color you only see in the dog days. I've watched that flower mark the calendar on this river for fifty years now, and it always tells me the same thing: the shad run is a memory, the water's dropped to summer flow, and if I want to catch anything worth talking about, I'd better be on the water before the sun gets up over Essex.

The spring run this year came and went the way it usually does — heavy through the second week of May, tailing off by Memorial Day, a few stragglers of hickory shad hanging around the Salmon River mouth into early June for the guys who like to chase the tail end of things. That's old news now. What we've got in mid-July is a different river altogether. Low, warm, the spartina grass gone thick and green on Great Island, and the current running slack and easy except around the moon tides. The river gauge at Essex has been reading low-summer numbers for weeks, which means less push, less color, and water that warms fast in the shallows by afternoon.

That warmth is exactly why the white perch bite has been the most reliable thing going. Selden Creek, Chester Creek, up in Lord Cove behind Whalebone — anywhere the current slows and the bottom's soft mud, the perch are stacked and feeding hard in that hour before dark when the heat comes off the water. Small stuff does the work: quarter-ounce jigs tipped with a sliver of nightcrawler, or those little curly-tail grubs in white or chartreuse, fished slow along the drop-offs where the creek channel meets the flat. Nothing heroic — a lot of eight and nine inch fish, some pushing eleven — but it's steady, and on a hot evening with the kids in the boat, that's the kind of fishing that keeps people coming back to this river.

Down at the mouth, the story's about young stripers and the first snapper blues of the season. Great Island's shallow flats have been doing what they do every July — holding juvenile bass in that skinny, warm water where the grass shrimp and mummichogs are thick. I've been working those flats on the last two hours of the incoming, poling quietly and casting small paddletails — three-inch white or bone colored — up onto the edges where the marsh grass meets open water. Most of what's coming to hand is schoolie-sized, eighteen to twenty-two inches, but they're aggressive and it's good practice for anyone teaching a kid to cast.

The bigger resident bass are still working the harder current around Saybrook Breakwater, Lynde Point, and the rock piles off the DEP Marina, but you have to fish the right window. With the river running low and warm, those fish want the cooler push of the outgoing tide, especially in that gray hour right at first light before the sun heats the flats. An eel fished slow along the breakwater rocks, or a bucktail bounced through the seam where the river current meets the Sound swell, has been the play. It's not been a banner week out there — I had two solid bass over 28 inches on Tuesday's dawn ebb and then nothing but short fish and missed hits the two mornings after. That's July on this river. You work for it, and the tide stage matters more than the moon phase right now.

Worth noting — the broader Sound has a real temperature split building, running warmer to the west around Kings Point and noticeably cooler out toward New London and the eastern approaches. That kind of gradient tends to push bait and predator fish around the mouth of the river in fits and starts, which may explain why some mornings the blues show thick around the breakwater chasing silversides, and other mornings there's nothing but gulls working empty water. The snapper blues themselves — those first-of-the-year fish, four to six inches — have started showing in the lower river around Saybrook Point and off the ferry landing in Essex, which is always a sign that their bigger cousins aren't far behind out in the Sound. Small silver spoons or a sliver of bunker on a snap-swivel rig off the town dock will keep a kid busy for an afternoon, and it's the best early warning system we've got for what's coming later this summer.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change until we get a real push of cooler water or a stretch of northeast wind to stir the river up. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd take the last of the outgoing at the breakwater before eight a.m., eel or bucktail, and I'd have a backup plan to slide up into Lord Cove for perch once the sun gets high and the bass stop answering. That's how you fish this river in July — patient, tide-driven, and willing to change your plan when the light changes.

reports.headline: Penfield Reopens on the Ebb: Tautog to 6 Pounds, Porgies Stacked on the Cows
reports.subhead: July 1 flipped the switch on blackfish season, and the timing couldn't be better with the water running warm from Greenwich to Bridgeport.
reports.body_markdown:
Every July I run the same math in my head before I leave the dock: which piece of structure is going to be quiet enough to fish, and which tide window gets me there before the weekend armada shows up. Saturday I had two options — Penfield Reef on the last two hours of the ebb, or Cockenoe with a fluke drift on the incoming. Penfield won, and it wasn't close, because blackfish season flipped open July 1 and nobody east of Fairfield seems to have noticed yet.

That's the thing about Penfield this time of year — the rockpile off the lighthouse in 15 to 22 feet doesn't get hammered like it does in October when every boat out of Black Rock knows the drill. Right now it's just a handful of us who remember tautog opens back up mid-summer, and that's exactly the edge you want. I anchored up-current on the ebb, let the boat settle over the eastern boulder field, and started working green crabs on a 2-ounce jig head, snugged right into the pockets between the rocks. First fish came at 20 minutes in, a stout 4-pounder that buried the rod tip before I'd even felt the bite develop. By the time the tide laid out I had three keepers in the box, biggest going just under 6, and released a handful of shorts that were clearly feeling the same seasonal switch flip. The pattern held true to form — blackfish want that last third of the ebb when the current's dying down enough to hold bottom without a war-and-peace amount of lead, but still moving enough to keep bait working in the cracks. Slack water shuts it off almost like a valve.

While I was on tog, the Cows were doing exactly what they do every July — porgies stacked thick over the mussel beds in 18 to 25 feet. Guys anchoring up on the sandy edges around the rockpiles with squid strips and clam bellies on high-low rigs are filling coolers without much finesse required. It's not technical fishing, it's volume fishing, and right now the volume is there. Best window's been the two hours either side of high tide when the current slackens enough that you're not constantly re-baiting into a sweep. I'd rate the porgy bite as the most reliable thing happening in the western Sound right now — no asterisks, no qualifiers.

Fluke is the mixed bag this week. Cockenoe Reef and the sandy cuts around the Norwalk Islands are producing, but it's been feast-or-famine depending on which drift you land on. I worked three drifts off the southwest corner of Cockenoe on Thursday — first drift, nothing. Second drift, three keepers including a fat 4-pounder that ate a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a ¾-ounce bucktail like it hadn't eaten all week. Third drift, dead again. That's fluke fishing on structure — you're hunting for the exact seam where the sand meets the rock edge, and when you find it the bite turns on fast, but drift ten yards off it and you're wasting bait. Kings Point is reading 71.2 degrees right now, which is plenty warm to keep bait and fluke both active through the western Sound, and that thermal edge is part of why this zone is outproducing water further east — New London's still sitting in the mid-60s, a different ballgame entirely.

Striped bass have gone into the typical mid-summer pattern — daytime's tough, especially with boat traffic churning the Norwalk Islands into a washing machine every weekend. If you want bass right now, you fish the edges of the day. I had a solid hour at first light off Sheffield Island last week, live bunker on a fish-finder rig worked along the channel edge where the current funnels between the islands, and connected on two schoolies and one just-shy-of-slot fish that made the trip worth setting the alarm for. After 8 a.m. it was pleasure boats wall to wall and the bite simply shut down — not because the fish left, but because there's no such thing as a quiet drift through there once the weekenders are up and running. Same story off Greenwich Point — early morning bluefish have been showing up chasing bait pods along the flats, blitzes lasting maybe twenty minutes before they push off, so if you see the birds working, don't wait to see if it holds. Get a metal on — a Kastmaster or a diamond jig — and get it in the water immediately.

Heading into this coming week, I'd play the tide windows the same way I did Saturday. Blackfish on Penfield during the back half of the ebb, before the moon swings toward full and the current gets stronger than the bite can handle. Porgies on the Cows around high water, any day, boat traffic or not — they don't care. Fluke I'd treat as a hunt, not a certainty — hit Cockenoe or the Norwalk Islands sand pockets on a moving tide and be willing to make three or four drifts before committing. And for bass and blues, first light is the whole game right now — get out before the mooring fields wake up, because once the wakes start crossing the islands, the bite closes up shop until evening. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, I'd expect the western end to keep holding the warmer, more active water — which means Greenwich to Bridgeport keeps being the better bet over the cooler stretch east toward New Haven.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Grinding Fluke at 35 Feet While Black Point Sea Bass Bail Out the Coolers
reports.subhead: A cold pocket parked off New London has the drift boats adjusting on the fly, but structure fishing at Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall is keeping the mates busy at the cleaning table.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic charter guys at the bait shop Thursday morning loading up on spearing and squid strips, and the first thing out of his mouth was, "You believe this water?" He'd just come off a half-day trip and said the temp gauge was sitting in the mid-60s off the mouth of the river — which for the second week of July is flat-out weird. New London's reading 66.4 right now, and that's cold enough that it's basically running ten degrees behind what Kings Point and the western Sound are seeing. Whatever's pushing that cooler water in — could be an upwelling event off the Race, could just be a run of easterly wind stacking it up — it's got the fleet adjusting game plans on the fly instead of running the same drift they ran in June.

The fluke bite reflects it. Niantic Bay and the flats off Twotree Island Channel are still holding fish, but they're not as aggressive as you'd want for mid-summer. The boats that are scoring are working slower drifts in 30 to 40 feet, dragging four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid to give the bait something to chew on instead of just swat at. Bigger fish — a few in the 4 to 6 pound class — have come off the deeper edge of the channel on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Slack water has been dead in there this week. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, don't sit on it — that cool water has the fluke sluggish and they need a little current to trigger them.

Black Point has been the more consistent producer, and it's sea bass, not fluke, doing the heavy lifting. Structure in 25 to 45 feet off the Point has been stacked with keeper-class bass, and the drift boats working there are putting solid numbers in the box on Gulp squid rigs and green crab baited high-low rigs bounced right on the rockpiles. The bite's been best on the front half of the incoming tide, before the current gets too strong to hold bottom without going up in weight. Hole-in-the-Wall is fishing the same way — it's classic sea bass water, current-scoured ledge and boulder, and with the water staying cooler than normal those fish haven't scattered off the structure the way they sometimes do once things get properly hot. That's actually working in our favor right now.

Porgies are the easy button this week if you've got kids or a slower afternoon planned. The mouth of the Niantic River and the inner bay have been thick with scup in the 8 to 10 inch range, some better ones mixed in, and they'll eat anything — squid, sandworms, clam strips on a simple two-hook bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet. Good confidence-builder bite, and it's been steady through both tide stages, which is more than I can say for most everything else out there right now.

Striper action has been a mixed bag — present, but you have to work for it. Bluefish showed up in decent numbers off McCook Point and along the beach toward Black Point earlier in the week, blitzing on peanut bunker schools right at first light, and a few schoolie stripers have been mixed in with them on topwater plugs and small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Ava jigs worked well when the blitzes were tight to the surface. But it's been an early-morning window only. By 8 or 9 a.m. the bait pushes off and the bite goes quiet. If you want a shot at the bigger bass, the report from the guys running bunker chunks off Twotree has been better after dark — a handful of fish in the 28 to 34 inch range coming on fresh bunker chunks fished on the bottom near the channel edge on the last of the ebb.

Blackfish season's open now inshore, and while it's early for the structure bite to really turn on, a few boats poking around Hatchett Reef and the rockier stretches off Black Point have picked at some smaller tog on green crab. Nothing to build a trip around yet — that pattern usually doesn't get serious until the water cools back down in September — but worth knowing it's legal and there are fish there if you want to scout early.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on that New London temp reading. If it climbs back into the low 70s where it should be for July, I expect the fluke bite to turn more aggressive and the sea bass to spread off the tightest structure onto the open bottom, which usually means better numbers but a little more hunting to find them. If the cool water holds, stick with what's working — slow drifts on the fluke, tight to structure for the bass, and fish the tide stages that give you current without overpowering it. Either way, Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall are the safer bets to fill a cooler this week, with the fluke grounds needing the right window to really produce.

reports.headline: Gold Star Bridge Pilings Holding on the Ebb: Bass Deep, Blues Working the Surface
reports.subhead: Cooler water pouring out of the Thames is stacking bait against the bridge structure, and the stripers haven't left the neighborhood.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a spot about two hundred yards downriver of the Gold Star Bridge, on the Groton side, where the current pinches between the third and fourth pilings and forms a seam you can see just by watching the surface — a thin ribbon of slick water running against a wall of standing riffle. I've fished that seam for twenty years and it still tells me more than any app on my phone. This week it's been loaded with peanut bunker getting pushed and turned by the tide, and there are bass sitting right on the downcurrent edge of it, 18 to 22 feet down, waiting for that bait to get disorganized.

The water coming out of the Thames right now is running cooler than what they're seeing over in the western Sound — we're reading in the mid-60s up here compared to low 70s down toward Kings Point — and that gradient matters more than people think. It means the bigger fish that pushed west into the warmer water aren't necessarily our fish. What we've got right now up around New London and Groton skews toward resident and staging bass, mostly schoolies up through low-slot, holding tight to structure rather than roaming open water chasing bait balls the way they will once things warm through the month.

The pattern that's produced for me and for the guys I talk to at the ramp has been simple: fish the last two hours of the ebb at the bridge pilings, when that current seam is fully formed and pushing hard, then shift down to Fort Trumbull as the tide goes slack. A 1-ounce white bucktail with a small strip of pork rind or a 4-inch white paddletail trailer, bounced right off the base of the pilings and let it swing through the seam — that's been the money presentation. Don't overwork it. Let the current do the job and just keep contact. Guys throwing swimming plugs, Doc's Goggle-Eyes and Yo-Zuri Mag Darters in bunker patterns, have been picking off blues on top in the same stretch, especially in that last hour of daylight when the bunker pods get nervous and start skipping on the surface off the Groton shore.

Fort Trumbull is still doing what it always does on the tail end of the ebb — that rip off the point where the river current collides with the incoming harbor swell builds a defined edge, usually 12 to 15 feet, and it's held bass consistently through the week, though I'd call the action mixed rather than steady. Some tides you hit it right and get six or eight fish in an hour, mostly 22 to 26 inches, and other tides you stand there for ninety minutes and manage two. The difference has been wind. When we get any south or southwest breeze pushing against that ebb, the rip gets a chop on it and the bite goes quiet. Calm evenings, it's been dependable.

Down at Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach, the porgy fishing has actually been the more consistent story this week. The rock piles off Pleasure Beach in 15 to 20 feet have porgies stacked up, and sandworms or green crab on a simple high-low rig has been putting fish in the cooler steadily on the incoming tide, when clean water pushes back in off the Sound. Nothing huge — most going 9 to 11 inches — but for a guy who wants a bend in the rod and dinner in the bucket, it's about as sure a thing as we've got on this stretch right now.

The hickory shad run up through the Thames toward the Mohegan stretch has pretty much wound down for the season — that window was April into May, and by mid-July those fish have scattered or moved on. If you're still swinging small flies or shad darts up there hoping for one more push, I wouldn't hold my breath. And blackfish, obviously, are still closed this time of year in Connecticut waters, so leave the crab pots in the garage a little longer.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my expectations honest rather than excited. This isn't a blow-it-up week — it's a work-the-structure week. If the wind stays out of the north or lays down entirely through the weekend, I'd put my time on the last two hours of ebb at the Gold Star Bridge pilings and then slide down to Trumbull as it goes slack, betting that the cooler water holding here keeps concentrating bait against structure rather than letting it spread. If we get a stretch of south wind chopping up that rip, I'd skip the point entirely and just spend the tide on the porgies off Pleasure Beach — steady beats stubborn most weeks on this river.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday, Redemption Thursday: Poor Man's Turns It On After the Squid Show Up
reports.subhead: A tough start to the week gave way to a solid yellowfin bite once the Illex squid packed onto the edges of Poor Man's and Spencer.
reports.body_markdown:
If I had to grade this week, I'd call it a C-minus through Wednesday and a solid B by the time we tied up Friday. That's the canyon game in mid-July — you don't get to pick your week, you pick your day, and this week the day was Thursday.

Monday and Tuesday we ran out of Ocean City toward Poor Man's expecting the yellowfin bite we'd heard about, and instead found green, sloppy water and not much life. No birds, no showers, sparse squid on the meter. We trolled a full spread — small ballyhoo behind Green Machines, a naked bird up top, a couple cedar plugs in the shotgun — and scratched out two fish in six hours off the northeast edge of Poor Man's, working the 100-fathom curve where it kicks toward Baltimore Canyon. That's not a day I'm proud of, but it's an honest one. Water was warm on top, but there wasn't a clean break to hold anything.

Wednesday night is when it turned. We had a boat working Spencer report squid stacking up thick on the drop-off after dark, and that's the signal I've been waiting on all July. Squid show up, tuna show up behind them — that's about as reliable a rule as I've got in this business. By Thursday morning the color had cleaned up nicer along the Spencer/Lindenkohl stretch, and we found yellowfin working bait balls right on the surface starting around 8 a.m., roughly along the eastern lip of Lindenkohl where it bends toward the Wilmington side.

That day was the kind of morning that makes the whole week worth it. We put six yellowfin in the box, sizes running from a couple of "rats" in the 15-20 pound class up to two better fish in the 60s, all on the troll — same spread as before, but this time we slowed the boat to 6.5 knots and let the ballyhoo swim instead of skip. When the school got finicky mid-morning, we switched over to jigging, dropping Shimano Butterfly jigs — the 150-gram in blue/silver — down through 250 to 300 feet where we were marking suspended fish on the sounder. That's when the bigger fish showed up. Jigging produced our two best yellowfin of the day, both hooked on the pause after a long upward stroke.
