Mackerel have been thick around Eastern Egg Rock and off the east side of Monhegan, schools stacked from the surface down to about 35 feet over structure. Standard mackerel trees with a bit of bright jig on the bottom hook have been filling coolers fast on a slow bite window — you can tell when they're there because the birds are working the same water, terns diving and the puffins cutting through. That's also brought a few bluefish into the mix around Egg Rock, chopping bait on top in the early morning calm before the wind builds. Nothing giant — cocktail blues mostly — but they'll hit a small metal jig or a Deadly Dick worked fast on the surface, and it's a nice change of pace between mackerel drops.

Groundfish in the Bay have been the tougher story, and I'll be straight about it — this cold upwelled water has the cod and haddock down deep and a little sluggish, not aggressive the way they get when the thermocline sets up just right. Best luck has come from the channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven and out toward the deeper water off Matinicus, working diamond jigs and bar rigs tipped with clam belly down in 120 to 150 feet, right on bottom, slow lift-and-drop with long pauses. Pollock have actually been the more reliable eating fish this week — schooling up over the humps in 60 to 90 feet around the Fox Islands and hitting jigs worked with a bit more speed higher in the water column, 30 to 50 feet down. If you want fish for the table with less patience required, that's where I'd point the bow.

Looking ahead, this new moon spring tide peaks right through Monday, and that's the window I'd fish hardest for stripers at the river mouths — the flood-to-sunset overlap is about as good an alignment as you get up here, current, light, and bait all lining up together. If the wind backs off the northeast and lets the surface warm back up even a couple degrees, I'd expect the cod and haddock to come up a bit shallower and turn more aggressive, so that's worth checking again toward the end of the week. Mackerel should hold at Egg Rock and Monhegan for now, though once these big tides start really flushing bait out of the bay, they have a habit of pushing farther offshore fast — if you want a box of mackerel for bait or the table, I wouldn't wait too long. Plan A this week is the sunset flood at the river mouths; Plan B, if the bass don't show or the wind kicks up onshore and muddies the funnel, is running out to the mackerel schools and picking off a bluefish or two while you're at it. Either way, respect the current on these springs — it's moving a lot of water fast, and that cuts both ways for the fish and for you.

reports.headline: New moon springs push stripers deep into Biddeford Pool as bluefish crash Higgins Beach
reports.subhead: Big tides and a warming shoreline have the bass feeding on the push while blues chop bait right in the wash — but Prouts Neck cod fishing stays a grind.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat out of the southwest more days than not, which is exactly what you want along this stretch this time of year — it lays the surf down, keeps the green water tight to the beach, and lets the sand eels and pogies stack up instead of getting scattered by a northeast chop. We had a few gray, drizzly mornings mixed in, but nothing that rolled the water or dirtied it up bad. The shoreline temps have been climbing steady through the low-to-mid 60s, warm enough that the bait is thick and the fish are hunting instead of just passing through.

Now we're swinging into a new moon, and that means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger push, more water moving through the guts and creeks than we've seen since before the last full moon. That's the whole story this week. Biddeford Pool runs on tide more than almost any spot on this coast, and a new moon flood shoves a wall of water and bait through the mouth by the Yacht Club and up into the back channels. Friday through Monday, the high stand is lining up close to sunset, which is the exact scenario that gets stripers feeding hard right at last light instead of sulking off in deeper water. I haven't seen a window like this stack up since the June full moon, and if you can only fish one tide this week, make it the evening flood.

Stripers have been showing well but not everywhere — this isn't a blanket bite, you still have to find them. The Pool has been the most consistent read: fish stacking on the last two hours of the incoming, working the current seam off the rocks below the Bridge, and pushing bait up against the flats on the inside once the tide tops out. Live mackerel and eels fished on a fish-finder rig have been getting bit right at the color change where the clean ocean water meets the darker back-bay water, but the better move for most guys has been swimming a 3-ounce Savage Gear sand eel or a Game On soft-plastic paddletail right through that seam on the drift. Slow and steady beats a fast retrieve — these fish are eating sand eels, not chasing anything frantic.

Higgins Beach has had the more visible show. Bluefish, mostly cocktail-size in the 2-to-4-pound range with a few better ones mixed in, have been blitzing right in the wash on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming, chopping bait practically at your feet some mornings. Pencil poppers — the old Gibbs wood ones or a Super Strike — worked with a walk-the-dog cadence right through the whitewash have been the ticket, and if the blues are up top busting you don't need to overthink the retrieve, just keep it moving and expect to get bit. Bring wire leader or you'll lose gear all morning. The bass have been mixed in at Higgins too, but they're holding a little deeper than the blues, so if you're getting cut off on wire but not connecting, downsize to a 40-pound fluorocarbon leader and work the outer sandbar where the stripers are sitting.

Prouts Neck has fished the way it usually fishes on a southwest wind — tough but not dead. The ledges off the point have given up a scattered bass or two on bucktails tipped with a strip of pork rind or a curly-tail trailer, worked slow along the boulder fields on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Cod fishing out deeper, on the rockier bottom off Cape Elizabeth, has been a grind — you're working for every fish, jigging diamond jigs or clam bellies on a high-low rig in 60 to 90 feet, and most trips are producing a few keepers rather than a pile. The water out there stays cooler longer than the beach water, which the cod like, but it also means the bite windows are shorter and tighter to the tide change. Mackerel have been reliable filler almost everywhere along the rocks — Wells Harbor breakwater, the Cape Elizabeth shoreline, even inside the Pool on the last of the flood — small Norwegian jigs or a mackerel tree worked with a quick snap have been good for fast action and a bait bucket full of fresh strip bait for the bigger stuff.

Flounder have been steady but slow-going in Wells Harbor and the calmer stretches behind Pine Point, working bloodworms or clam strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bounced along the mud on the bottom of the tide when the current slacks off. Nobody's filling a cooler with flounder right now, but if you want a change of pace and a fish that'll actually eat dinner, that's the play on a slow-tide morning.

Looking ahead, the spring tide push through the weekend is the thing to build around. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it's supposed to, I'd be at Biddeford Pool for the evening flood Friday into Monday, working that current seam below the bridge as the sun drops — that's where I'd put my money this week. Higgins Beach should keep producing blues on top through most tide stages as long as the bait stays pinned to the beach, so it's a good backup if the Pool's slow or crowded. If a northeast wind sneaks in behind this system, expect the outer ledges at Prouts Neck to cool off fast and the cod bite offshore to tighten up even further — that's when I'd shift effort back inshore and let the rocks do the work instead of chasing open water.

reports.headline: Springs tide builds on the new moon — stripers push Hampton Harbor, groundfish hold tight to the Shoals breaks
reports.subhead: NE wind upwelling sharpened the structure off White Island while the incoming build stacked bass against the Hampton inlet rocks.
reports.body_markdown:
We're heading into the new moon, and if you've fished this stretch of coast for more than a season you already know what that means before I say it: springs tides building all weekend, bigger swings on the Hampton and Piscataqua gauges, and current at the Shoals that'll flat-out move a boat if you're not paying attention to your scope. New moon lands midweek, and the buildup through Friday-into-Monday is when I want to be on the water, not after. Last week's wind sat out of the northeast more than I'd like for comfort but exactly where I want it for fishing — that upwelling pattern pushed cooler, cleaner water up onto the ledges around White Island and Halibut Rocks, and it sharpened the edge on those breaks the way it always does. Cold water stacking against warmer surface water off the Shoals concentrates bait, and bait on an edge means cod and haddock sitting tight to structure instead of scattered over mud. That's the setup I fish for.

Water temp in the harbors has been climbing on the flood — nothing shocking, just steady summer warm-up — while out at the Shoals the bottom stayed cooler under that NE push. That thermal split matters. It's why the mackerel showed up thick around Star Island and Appledore this week, working the surface in the morning calm before the boat traffic scatters them, and it's why the groundfish stayed deep and tight rather than spreading out. Going into this week, expect the wind to back around more southerly by the weekend as the new moon springs peak — that usually softens the upwelling signal, so if you're going to fish the Shoals structure hard, earlier in the week is your window before that cold edge relaxes.

Stripers are the story inshore right now, and Hampton Harbor is doing exactly what it does on a building spring tide — pushing bait and fish through the inlet on the last two hours of the incoming. I had a report of fish to 28 inches taken right off the jetty rocks at Hampton on the top of the flood, working white and chartreuse soft plastics — 4-inch Slug-Go style baits on a light jighead — swung tight against the rip where the harbor current meets the ocean push. Same pattern's working at Rye Harbor breakwater on the same stage of tide, though the fish there have been more scattered, more schoolie-sized, mixed with the occasional bluefish that'll cut your leader if you're not running at least 20-pound fluoro. Great Boars Head has been worth a look on the outgoing at first light — bait pods of pogies pushing off the beach have pulled some bass tight to the surf line, and a swimming plug worked parallel to the beach has produced better than anything thrown straight out.

The Piscataqua is fishing the way it always does in July — you need to time the tide precisely or you're wasting gas. Stripers are holding on the current seams below the Memorial Bridge and down toward Henderson Point, and they want the tide moving, not slack. Live mackerel under a slip float, drifted through the seam on the last hour of the ebb, has been the most consistent producer I've heard of, though it's not a numbers game — one or two quality fish a trip is realistic, not a bent rod every cast. Flounder are still around in Portsmouth Harbor and up in the back channels off Pierce Island — small hooks, sandworms or clams, fished right on bottom in that softer mud current away from the main channel. Nothing to write home about size-wise this week, mostly 12-14 inch fish, but steady if you're patient and anchored in the right spot on the bottom of the tide.

Offshore, the cod and haddock bite at the Shoals has been honest work, not easy work. Boats working Sunken Ledge and the rock piles south of White Island in 80 to 130 feet found haddock stacked tight on the NE-sharpened edge I mentioned, taking clam bait and diamond jigs tipped with a sandworm strip on the drift — but you had to hit the tide right. Slack water scattered them; moving water on either side of the tide change held them tight to structure. Cod have been mixed in but smaller than we'd like this time of year, mostly short fish thrown back, with the occasional keeper in the 24-26 inch range coming off bottom bounced jigs worked slow. If I had a boat this week I'd fish the two hours around the tide change, not the middle of the flood or ebb when everything's moving too fast to hold bottom without a pound of lead.

Looking ahead — the new moon Tuesday means the biggest tides we'll see this month, and that PM flood window at Hampton Harbor lining up with sunset over the next several days is worth building a trip around. Bass tend to commit harder on that last push of light with a strong tide behind them, and if the bait stays stacked at the inlet the way it has been, I'd expect that pattern to hold through the weekend. Offshore, watch the wind — if it backs southerly like it's forecast to, that cold upwelled edge at the Shoals will soften and the groundfish will spread back out over more bottom, which usually means slower, more marks-and-miss fishing instead of the tight, predictable bite we've had. Best case, one more good push of NE wind before it shifts gives us another day or two of that sharp edge. Either way, I'd rather fish the tide change with a plan than the middle of it hoping.

reports.headline: New moon springs push Little Egg fluke into the cuts as sunset stripers return to Barnegat Light
reports.subhead: Bay water cooked into the high 70s and shoved the fluke out — the ocean side and the inlets are holding the action while the weakfish stay a no-show.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July when we get a stretch of sun and slack air — it cooked. Great Bay's shallow flats and the back stretches up toward the Mullica pushed into the high 70s, and that shut the door on the grass-flat fluke bite fast. I had two guys tell me they marked bait and structure all over the meadows off Graveling Point and couldn't buy a bite past nine in the morning. That's not bad luck, that's biology — fluke don't like soup, and once the shallow water gets that warm they slide for the channels, the deeper cuts, and eventually the inlets where there's still some exchange with the ocean. We had a couple NE wind days midweek that helped push cooler water — I'm talking mid-70s pushing into the low 70s — through Barnegat and Little Egg inlets, and that's exactly where the better fluke have been sitting since.

This week the moon flips new on the 10th, which means spring tides are building right now and peak through Saturday into Monday. Bigger swings at Barnegat Light and Little Egg — more water moving means more current in the cuts, which means bait gets flushed and predators get organized around it. That also reopens a PM window we haven't had since the June full moon: the flood tide stacking up right around sunset. Low light, moving water, and warm surf temps — that's the recipe that's been missing on the striper side for weeks, and it's back starting tonight through Monday.

Fluke-wise, the shift to the inlet and ocean side is the story right now. Little Egg Inlet on the outgoing, working the drop-off just inside the throat in 14 to 18 feet, has been the most consistent stretch — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, picking up keepers in the 19 to 22 inch range with the occasional better fish mixed in. Same story off the Beach Haven side channels and the deeper bends up toward Ship Bottom — anywhere there's current scouring a defined edge. Bay flats are mostly done for now unless you're fishing early, first light, before the sun gets on the water. Don't waste a midday tide on the meadows this week — go to the moving water.

Stripers have been a grind through late June, mostly schoolie-sized fish scattered thin, but the pattern for this weekend into Monday is legitimate. With the spring tide flood lining up against sunset, I'd be at Barnegat Light working the rocks on the last hour of light into dark — white bucktails, needlefish, or a darter worked slow across the seam where the jetty current meets the open water. Holgate's north end rip has been holding fish too, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming, with some bigger fish mixed into the schoolies — nothing giant, but 28 to 34 inch fish have shown up enough that it's worth the walk. If the wind stays light through the weekend, that PM flood-into-dark window at both spots is where I'd put my time. If it kicks up out of the east and blows the surf out, I'd shift to Little Egg on the last of the outgoing instead — dirtier water there tends to concentrate fish tight to structure rather than scatter them.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with the stripers, chopping mullet in the wash at Holgate and off the Ship Bottom beaches on calm mornings — nothing huge, mostly 2 to 4 pounders, but they'll hit the same bucktails and metal you're throwing for bass, so bring a wire leader or expect to lose gear.

Kingfish are doing their steady, unglamorous thing in the surf at Holgate and the south end beaches — bloodworm and Fishbites on a high-low rig, small sinkers, fished tight to the wash on the bottom stages of the tide. Not exciting, but it's been dependable, and it's a good one to hand a kid a rod for while you work a plug rod on the same beach.

Black drum are basically done for the season up in the Mullica and around Graveling Point — that bite peaked back in May and by now it's stragglers only, so I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

And I'll say this plainly because I think honesty matters more than hype: weakfish have been a ghost. Water temps in the Mullica and Great Bay have been in the range where weakfish are supposed to show, and they just haven't. I've heard it from enough people now that I don't think it's a fluke of reporting — the temperature threshold that used to be a reliable trigger isn't producing fish the way it used to. If you want to try, dusk on soft plastics — 4-inch pearl or chartreuse paddletails — around the deeper holes off Graveling Point is still the right idea. Just don't build your week around it.

Looking ahead: the spring tide peak Saturday through Monday is the best striper window we've had since the June full moon, and if the wind cooperates I'd fish the sunset flood at Barnegat Light first, Holgate second. Fluke will keep favoring the inlet and ocean-side channels as long as the bay stays warm, so work the moving water on the outgoing and don't bother with the flats past mid-morning. If the bass don't show at the jetty, my backup plan is always the same this time of year — Little Egg on the last of the outgoing with a bucktail, because something's usually willing to eat there even on an off night.

reports.headline: New moon springs flood the Hook at sunset as bay fluke push to the channels
reports.subhead: Big tides and warm bay water are moving fish out of Raritan Bay's flats and into the inlets — here's where to find them this week.
reports.body_markdown:
We're rolling into a new moon this week, which means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving in and out of the bay than we've seen since the June full moon. That matters more than people think. Last week the bay sat warm and mostly slack on the neaps, water pushing into the upper 70s over Keyport Flats and up into the Navesink, and the fish did what warm, sluggish water always makes them do — they left. Fluke that were happily working the flats in June are sliding out toward the channels and the ocean side where there's actual current and cooler water holding oxygen. The new moon change kicks that process into high gear. Bigger tides mean more exchange, more bait getting flushed out of the back bay, and — this is the part I'm watching closest — a PM flood tide that's now converging with sunset. That's the window. High stand meeting last light on a building spring tide is about as good a striper setup as this zone offers in July, and it hasn't lined up like this since before the last full moon.

So that's the why. Peak alignment on this new moon push is Friday through Monday, July 10-13, with the tide swings growing each day into the weekend. If you've got one evening to fish this week, that's the window — not because I'm promising fish, but because the mechanics are right: moving water, dropping light, bait getting squeezed through the Chapel Hill Channel and out past the Hook.

On the striper side, it's been a scratchy month but not a dead one. Guys working live bunker on fish-finder rigs off Romer Shoal and down along the edge of Flynn's Knoll have been picking at holdover bass in the 26-34 inch range, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming into dusk. Depths matter here — 18 to 25 feet along the Knoll's drop, tighter to bottom than you'd fish in spring. The Rip at the Hook has given up a few better fish to guys drifting live eels after dark, but it's been an every-other-trip proposition, not a sure thing. With this new moon flood-sunset window opening up, I'd be at Romer Shoal or working the edge of the Ambrose Channel with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig right as that tide turns to flood and the sun starts dropping. That's where I'm putting my evening this weekend.

Fluke is where the real story is right now, and it's a mixed bag depending on where you fish it. Inside the bay, Keyport Flats and the Highlands flats have gone quiet — too warm, too slow-moving water, and the fluke know it. But push out to the channels and it's a different world. Sandy Hook Channel and the mouth of the bay near Ambrose have been holding good numbers of keeper fluke, 18 to 22 inches, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in — there was a doormat pushing 12 pounds weighed out of the lower harbor a couple weeks back, and that tells you there are still genuinely big fish working through this system on their way to deeper water. Drift 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, 25 to 35 feet of water, timed to the last two hours of the outgoing when the channel current really starts ripping bait out of the bay. That outgoing push is the whole game for fluke right now — the fish are stacking on the current edges waiting for it to deliver food, and if you're not fishing that tide stage you're fishing the wrong two hours.

Bluefish have been a bright spot and an honest one — no exaggeration needed. Bunker schools have been thick around Romer Shoal and pushing into the mouth of the Raritan, and the blues have been all over them, especially on that same outgoing tide when bait gets pinned against the channel edges. Poppers and metal — Ava jigs, diamond jigs in the 2-3 ounce range — worked fast through the peanut bunker schools have been producing non-stop action, 3 to 6 pound blues mostly, with some bigger choppers mixed in early morning. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, this is it.

Weakfish, I have to be honest with you — they're just not here. Water's warm enough on paper, but that threshold alone hasn't meant anything the last few seasons, and this year's no different. I haven't heard of a single weakfish report out of the Navesink or the Shrewsbury in weeks. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them right now.

Porgies are steady and unspectacular off Romer Shoal and along the edges of Flynn's Knoll — bloodworms or squid strips on a high-low rig in 15-20 feet will keep a rod bent for kids and beginners, which is worth remembering in July when everybody wants an easy win.

Looking ahead: the new moon spring tides build through the weekend and peak Sunday-Monday, so that PM flood-sunset striper window is going to be at its best then — I'd fish it two nights if I could swing it, because these alignments don't come around often. On the fluke side, keep working the channels and inlets on the outgoing as long as the bay stays warm, because that pattern isn't reversing anytime soon. And keep an eye on the ocean side of the Hook — with warm water pushing up the coast and the first bonito starting to show further east, it's not out of the question we see an early Spanish mackerel or bonito flash through the Hook's rip before the month is out. Nothing confirmed yet, but that's exactly the kind of signal worth watching for.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the inlets — fluke run to the rocks as bass play it coy
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and cooler upwelled water are pushing fluke out of the bays and into Manasquan and Shark River, while the bass bite stays a dawn-only proposition.
reports.body_markdown:
Twenty-five years of standing on these rocks and I still get excited when the tide chart tells me something's coming. This week it's telling me the moon's going dark — new moon lands right in this window — and that means spring tides building through the weekend, peaking around the 11th to 13th. Bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through Manasquan and Shark River inlets on both ends of the cycle. That's the kind of setup that either turns a jetty on or blows it out entirely, depending on how much push you get and whether the wind fights the tide or rides with it.

Last week the story was heat. The back bays — Shark River especially, up past the Route 35 bridge — pushed into the high 70s, and that's too warm for fluke to sit comfortable. They did what they always do when the bay gets soupy: they ran for the inlets and the ocean front, where a little NE breeze has been upwelling cooler water along the beach, holding in the low 70s. That's a clean, predictable pattern, and it's the one I'd build a week around. The bass, on the other hand, have been more stubborn — some fish around at first light, but nothing you'd call consistent, and I'm not going to stand here and tell you otherwise.

Start with the fluke, because that's where the sure money is right now. Manasquan Inlet on the outgoing, from the Route 71 bridge down through the channel to the jetty mouth, has been holding fish in 15 to 25 feet. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, tipped with a strip of squid if you want insurance — that combo has been taking keepers in the 19 to 22-inch range, with a few better fish mixed in on the last hour of the drop. Shark River Inlet is doing the same thing on a smaller scale — work the deeper hole off the Belmar side, tight to the rocks, same bucktail-and-Gulp approach, chartreuse if the water's got any color to it from the runoff. The key is timing: you want the last two hours of outgoing, when the bait gets pinned against the structure and the fluke stack up to ambush it. Don't waste your morning on the flood — that's when they scatter back toward the bay edges.

Stripers are the harder conversation. The jetty rocks from Sea Bright down through Belmar have given up bass at dawn, but it's a short window and you need to be standing there when it opens, not showing up after the sun's already up over the water tower. Sea Bright rocks, the stretch north of the Rumson-Sea Bright bridge, has thrown a few schoolies to guys throwing white Super Strike Zig-Zag needlefish and Gibbs Danny plugs on the first light of the outgoing, right as the current starts pulling bait past the tip of the jetty. Manasquan Inlet's north jetty has done the same on occasion — bunker have been thin but not absent, and when a pod pushes through the inlet mouth on that outgoing new-moon surge, the bass show up underneath them for ten, fifteen minutes and then it's over. I had one morning last week where three fish came in twenty minutes and then nothing for two hours. That's the read right now — short, sharp windows, not a sustained bite. If you're going to fish it, fish the tide change hard and don't linger past it.

Bluefish have been the wildcard filling in the gaps — cocktail blues, mostly, blitzing bunker pods off Asbury Park and Spring Lake on calm mornings, chewing through metal lips and poppers fast enough that you'll lose a few to the teeth if you're not running wire or heavy mono leader. Not glamorous, but it's action, and it keeps the rod bent while you wait to see if the stripers show.

On the albie front — I'm watching, not promising. The pelagic window that's had bonito and Spanish mackerel showing up on Long Island's south side is closing out over the next few days, and the water temperature signatures that usually precede our first false albacore push have been building. Nothing confirmed yet at Manasquan or Shark River, but the outer rocks at both inlets are worth a look with small Deadly Dick or Albie Snax on light tackle if you're already out there for the fluke. I wouldn't build a trip around it yet — it's a maybe, not a bet.

Looking at the week ahead: the new moon spring tide peak lines up Saturday into Monday, which means the strongest current push of the month at both inlets. If the wind stays out of the northeast and light, that's when I'd put my time in — dawn outgoing at Sea Bright and Manasquan for the bass, with the fluke bucktail as backup once the sun's up and the bite window closes. If the wind swings onshore and stiffens, the surf's going to get sloppy and the jetty game turns miserable fast — that's when I'd shift entirely to the inlet channels and fish the fluke on the last of the outgoing, working the deeper cuts where the current stays manageable. Either way, don't sleep past first light this weekend. The tide's doing the work for you — you just have to be standing on the rock when it does.

reports.headline: New moon springs squeeze The Race as bonito push west toward the Sluiceway
reports.subhead: Tighter slack windows at Valiant Rock, a mixed bass bite on wire, and the first real bonito sniff east of Plum Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does after a blow — it sorted itself out slow. We had a stretch of NE flow that sharpened the breaks out past Plum Gut and put some cooler, cleaner water back into the mix after that stretch of thick, warm surface water sat on us through the holiday run. That NE push is the same mechanism that's been sharpening the 20 to 30 fathom breaks offshore for the bluefin crowd, and closer to home it did us a favor — it knocked back some of the surface warmth that had been shoving bait deep and scattering the bass off Race Rock. The bigger story, though, is the cold wall between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound falling apart. That wall has held bonito on the Block Island side for years. It just took a double-digit jump in RIS and it's not holding anymore, which means the corridor's opening up west — Newport and Point Judith are seeing early bonito, and I don't think it stops there. Little Gull and the Sluiceway are next in line if that trend holds.

This week the moon's the story that matters most for how you fish the rip. We're running into new moon springs, peak alignment landing Friday through Monday, and that means bigger exchange, faster water, and a slack window at Valiant Rock that's going to be shorter and meaner than it's been in weeks. When the tide's moving five knots through The Race on a spring cycle, the difference between fishing the turn right and fishing it forty minutes late is the difference between a rod-bending bite and a long boat ride home. High water at New London is running late afternoon into evening the next few days, and slack at Valiant Rock is stacking up right around sunset — call it 8:15 to 8:35 as the week rolls on. That's your window. Don't show up early and don't linger — spring tide current fills back in fast once it turns.

The bass bite has been honest, not easy. We've been working wire line with bucktails — the 2 to 3 ounce bucktail with a strip of pork rind or a white Fin-S trailer, dropped right on the edge where the rip meets the slick water off Valiant Rock, 25 to 40 feet down depending on the stage of tide. The pattern's been: stack up on the last twenty minutes of the ebb, hold through slack, and fish the first hour of the new flood before the current gets too strong to hold bottom without going to lead you don't want to lift. Fish have been mixed — plenty of schoolies in the 20 to 26 inch range mixed with a decent number of stripers in the high 20s to low 30-inch class, a few pushing 15 pounds. Nobody's filling a cooler with slot fish right now, but if you time the slack right you're not getting skunked either. Eels have worked too when you can find them — slow-trolled or drifted right through the seam at Race Rock on the last of the ebb has produced the better fish of the week.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player through Plum Gut and along the eastern face of the Sluiceway. Poppers and darters at first light, before the current builds, have been drawing choppers up in the 4 to 8 pound range, and once the tide gets moving they'll hold right in the rip current where the bait gets pinned. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod some mornings, that's been it.

Fluke have moved with the water temperature, same as always. Great South Bay's been running warm enough to push the better fish out of the bay and into the channels and inlets, and the upwelled water on the ocean side — clean, cooler, sitting around 71 degrees — has been the ticket. Plum Gut and the edges of The Race have both been holding fish in that 25 to 40 foot range on the outgoing tide. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, have taken fish to 5 pounds, with a decent number of shorts mixed in. It's not a wide-open bite, but it's a legitimate one if you work the drift patiently instead of running and gunning.

Black sea bass have been steady around the structure at Valiant Rock and Race Rock — jigs tipped with squid strips or just plain bucktail jigs bounced bottom in 30 to 50 feet have been producing keeper-class fish in the 16 to 18 inch range without much trouble. That's been the most dependable meat in the boat this week when the bass and fluke bites went quiet on the wrong tide.

On the bonito, I want to be straight with you — nobody's connected inside the Gut yet. The corridor's opening from the east, and with the cold wall gone in Rhode Island Sound, the fish have room to run west toward Little Gull and Great Gull over the next week or two if the warm water keeps pushing. I'd have an epoxy jig rod rigged and ready — Deadly Dicks, Hogy epoxy jigs, anything in a sand eel profile — and I'd be checking the rip edges off Great Gull on the last of an incoming tide, because that's where the bait's going to get squeezed first if the corridor keeps sliding this direction. It's not a sure thing yet. But the water's telling me it's close.

Look, the springs are going to make this week technical. Fish the slack windows tight, respect how fast that current fills back in at Valiant Rock, and don't be surprised if the bass bite stays honest-but-mixed rather than explosive. If the bonito corridor keeps widening the way it has, I think we're a week, maybe two, from the first real hookups inside our water. Until then, wire line at first light, fluke on the ocean side incoming, and keep an epoxy jig within reach just in case.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the sunset flood at Horton Point
reports.subhead: Bigger tides are stacking bait against the rocks just as the light goes down — the bass know it, even if the weakfish still don't.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the moon was working its way down toward new, and you could feel the tides building a little more push each day. Wind sat out of the northeast more than not, which is the wind that does us favors on this shore — it stacks water against Horton Point and Rocky Point instead of blowing everything flat and dead. The Sound stayed steady, not hot, not cold, just holding — the kind of stable water that doesn't spook anything but doesn't light a fire under it either. Meanwhile the bay side down toward the Peconics got up into the high 70s and pushed the fluke out of the back creeks and into the inlets and the open Sound, which is exactly the kind of thing that fills Mattituck Inlet with fish that used to be somebody else's problem.

This week the moon goes new on the 11th, and that means spring tides — bigger swings, more water moving, more current wrapping the structure. The piece that matters most for us: the PM flood is lining up with sunset now, first time it's done that since the June full moon. Peak alignment runs the 11th through the 13th. That's not a small thing on this shore. When the flood and the last hour of light hit together, the bait gets squeezed up against the rocks at Horton Point and Rocky Point right when the stripers want to feed anyway, low light, moving water, bait with nowhere to go. That's the window I've been waiting on since the solstice.

Fluke first, because that's been the most honest bite of the last ten days. Mattituck Inlet on the outgoing has been holding fish stacked up where the channel narrows down by the jetty rocks — three-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, working the seam where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper cut. Nothing spectacular, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional fish pushing 21, but it's been steady enough that a couple hours on the right tide puts dinner in the cooler. The push out of the warmer bay water is real — those fish didn't leave home because they wanted to, they left because it got uncomfortable back there, and the cooler upwelled water sitting out front of the inlet is where they're settling. Fish it on the last two hours of the outgoing, right before dead low, and don't be afraid to slow your drift down to almost nothing.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, which is the honest way to put it. Some evenings at Horton Point you'll find them working the boulder field on a strong flood, other evenings you could soak an eel for an hour and never get a sniff. What I've noticed is it's all about that current — when the water's really moving, the bass tuck in behind the bigger rocks and ambush whatever gets swept past. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right in that current break have been drawing the better fish, mid-20s to low 30-inch class, nothing enormous but solid keeper-range fish. Guys throwing swimming plugs — the bigger Danny-style baits — through the same water at last light have had shots at fish too, but you need to be working the exact seam, not just chucking and hoping. With the springs building toward that Saturday-Sunday-Monday peak, I expect this bite to sharpen up rather than fall off. More water moving through means more bait getting displaced, and displaced bait means feeding fish. If I only had one evening to fish this week, I'd take Saturday's sunset flood at Rocky Point and not think twice about it.

Bluefish have started showing in better numbers out toward the Plum Gut approach, which tracks with what I'd expect this time of year — that funnel of water moving between the Gut and the open Sound concentrates bait, and blues are opportunists first and always. Trolling small spoons or casting metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters — into the rip lines off Orient Point has been producing fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, choppy and aggressive, cutting off leaders if you're not running wire or heavy fluoro. It's not a blitz, but it's consistent enough that if you want a bent rod and don't care what species is on the other end, that's your play.

Porgy fishing off the drop at Orient Point has quietly been some of the better action on the beat — bottom rigs with sandworm or clam, fished in 20 to 30 feet where the bottom breaks toward the Gut, has been putting decent-sized scup in the bucket. It's not glamorous fishing but it's honest fishing, and on a slow bass evening it's a good fallback.

Now the disappointing part, and I'll be straight with you because that's the only way I know how to write this column: weakfish are still a no-show. Water's been plenty warm long enough now that if temperature alone triggered them, we'd have heard something by now. We haven't. I talked to enough people up and down this shore to say with some confidence that warm water is necessary but it isn't sufficient — there's something else weakfish need that just isn't here yet, or isn't here at all this year. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them specifically. Fish for bass or fluke and if a weakfish shows up, treat it like a bonus, not a plan.

Looking ahead — the new moon springs peaking the 11th through 13th is the story of the week for this shore. IF the northeast wind holds and doesn't swing around and blow onshore hard, the sunset flood at Horton Point and Rocky Point should be the best striper window we've had since the full moon in June. I'd fish the last two hours of daylight into the start of dark, bunker chunks or a swimming plug worked tight to the rocks. Plan B, if the bass don't cooperate, is the Mattituck Inlet fluke drift on the outgoing — that bite has been dependable enough to lean on. Either way, bigger water's coming through this week, and bigger water on this shore usually means something's willing to eat.

reports.headline: New moon springs push the evening flood bite right into the sunset at Fort Trumbull
reports.subhead: Big tides and warm harbor water are shoving bait — and stripers — toward the river mouth just as the light goes gold.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Thames did what it does every July — it got soft and warm on top, sluggish on the flood, and the fish backed off the pilings during the heat of the day. Harbor water up around Fort Trumbull and the state pier has been sitting in the high 70s on the surface, warm enough that the stripers that were holding tight to the Gold Star Bridge structure in June have slid deeper into the scour holes on the outgoing, or pushed out toward the harbor mouth where the water still has some backbone to it. We had a stretch of light, variable wind that let the upper river go glassy at dawn, which is nice for casting but it also let that top layer bake. Fish fed hard in short windows and shut off fast — a pattern, not a slump, but you had to be there for the window or you got nothing.

This week the moon changes the math. We're building into new moon springs, peaking July 11-13, and that's the first real PM setup we've had since the June full moon. The tides are getting bigger, the current's got more push in it, and — this is the part that matters — high stand at the harbor mouth is lining up almost right on sunset through the weekend. That's the window I'm circling. Bigger tides mean more water moving through the Fort Trumbull rip and around the Gold Star pilings on the last two hours of the flood, which stacks bait against the current seams right as the light goes low and the bass get bold. I've fished this alignment before — it doesn't happen every month, and when it does you want to be positioned before the tide turns, not chasing it after the fact.

Striper fishing itself has been honest work, not a gimme. The evening bite off Fort Trumbull on the last two hours of the flood has been the most consistent thing going — schoolies to 26 inches, with a scattering of fish pushing 30, hitting swimming plugs and soft plastic paddletails worked slow along the seam where the harbor channel current meets the eddy off the point. Olive and white 5-inch paddletails on a 3/8-ounce jighead have been the ticket, fished with a slow swing so it stalls right in the current break. Live eels, when you can get them, are still the best card to play after dark around the Gold Star Bridge pilings — drift them tight to the concrete on the outgoing, especially the pilings on the New London side where the scour is deepest. That bite has been a bit stop-and-start; some nights it's non-stop short strikes, other nights you fish two hours for one good take. That's the nature of a harbor bite riding a warm surface layer — the fish are there, they're just not committed the whole tide.

Bluefish have been mixed in but scattered, not schooled up tight yet. A few choppers in the 3-4 pound class have shown up on topwater poppers worked at first light off Ocean Beach and along the Pleasure Beach flats, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them right now — more of a bonus fish if you're already out there for stripers.

The bigger story for bait boats and light-tackle guys chasing fluke is the shift out of the upper harbor. With the river and inner harbor running warm, the fluke that were scattered through the mid-harbor channel in June have pushed toward the mouth — Ocean Beach, Pleasure Beach, and the deeper water off the New London Ledge light. That cooler, cleaner water at the harbor entrance is holding fish better than anything upriver right now. Drift the channel edge off Pleasure Beach on the outgoing with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid, and keep the boat moving slow enough to feel bottom but not so slow you're stalled in the current. Depths of 20 to 30 feet along that edge have been the sweet spot.

Porgies are doing what porgies do in July — thick around the rock piles and the breakwalls off Ocean Beach and the outer harbor structure, biting steady on sandworms and clam on light tackle almost any stage of tide, though the last hour of the incoming has been a touch better for size. Not glamorous, but it's a sure thing when everything else is being stubborn, and it's a good way to fill an afternoon with the kids while you wait for the evening striper window to set up.

Hickory shad are done for the season up in the Thames — that run wrapped up back in May, so if someone tells you they're still on them, they're either misremembering or fishing memory instead of water. Blackfish are locked up in their summer closure and the smart money's already thinking ahead to the fall reopener on the rock piles off Groton.

Looking ahead: if the new moon springs hold through the weekend and that high-stand-at-sunset alignment stays put, I'd be at Fort Trumbull or under the Gold Star Bridge with an hour of daylight left, working the last of the flood into dusk. That's the best structural setup we've had all month for a real evening bite. If the wind kicks up out of the southwest and muddies the harbor mouth, I've got a backup plan — pull back into the river proper and fish the current seams on live bait after dark, since dirty water at the mouth usually means the fish slide back upriver looking for clean current instead.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the Sound as stripers push the flood at sunset
reports.subhead: Charles Island and Stratford Shoal turn on with the tide while fluke slide out of the warm harbors and porgies keep the rockpiles honest.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did that thing it does in early July — it warmed up fast in the harbors and shallow flats, and the fish voted with their fins. New Haven Harbor and the back of Milford Gulf were running warm enough that you could feel it through your waders at low tide, and the fluke that had been stacked in there all June started sliding out toward the mouths and the deeper channel edges. Wind was mostly light out of the south and southwest through the middle of the week, which kept the surface glassy for the early risers but didn't do much to mix the water column. We're heading into new moon now — peak alignment falls Saturday through Monday — and that means the spring tides are loading up fast. Bigger swings, more water moving, and a PM flood that's timing up almost perfectly with sunset from Stratford down through Madison. That's the window I've been circling on the calendar since June, and it's here.

Here's the why: when the moon goes new and the tides get big, current speed picks up everywhere — over the reefs, through the harbor mouths, across the bar at Charles Island. Bait gets pushed and disoriented, structure fish get aggressive because their feeding windows get compressed into shorter, harder pushes of water, and predator fish start timing their moves to that current instead of just cruising. A PM flood stacking up right at last light is about as good as it gets for bass looking to ambush bait coming off the sandbar. If you've only got one evening this week, that's the one to take.

Stripers have been the story at Charles Island, and it's been honest fishing — not a blitz, but consistent if you're willing to work the tide correctly. The bar off the southwest corner is holding fish on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide, right as the light starts going flat gold. Guys drifting live eels along the drop-off in eight to fourteen feet have been connecting with schoolies mixed with a few fish pushing thirty inches. If you're throwing plugs, a black Danny or a bone-colored Gibbs pencil worked slow across the bar right at dusk has drawn strikes, especially in that last half hour before it goes fully dark. Stratford Shoal has also been quietly productive — the west side rockpile in fifteen to twenty feet is holding bass that are using the current break to ambush bait getting swept off the shoal. Bucktails with a white or chartreuse Fin-S trailer, bounced slow along bottom on the drift, have out-produced straight plugging out there this week.

Fluke are the mixed bag right now, and I want to be straight about it — the bay bite softened as that water climbed into the upper 70s, and the fish that were holding shallow in Milford Gulf and up in the harbor have thinned out. What's replaced them is a better bite right at the harbor mouths and in the channel edges where cooler water is getting pulled in on the outgoing. Drifting the New Haven Harbor entrance channel in eighteen to twenty-two feet on the last three hours of the ebb has been the move — pink or white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged just off bottom, slow enough to feel the structure. Nothing huge — most fish are running fourteen to seventeen inches with the occasional keeper mixed in — but it's steady enough to keep rods bent if you're willing to hunt the deeper edges instead of the flats.

Porgies are doing exactly what porgies do in July, which is save the day when everything else gets fussy. Falkner Island's rockpile on the north side and the rubble field off the New Haven breakwalls have both been holding good numbers in fifteen to twenty-five feet. Green crab and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, fished on the bottom during the slower current around slack tide, has been about as close to a guarantee as this beat offers. Sea bass are mixed in on the same structure — a few nice ones in the fourteen to sixteen inch range coming off Falkner and the rockpile at the east end of Charles Island, biting best on squid strips right as the tide starts to build after slack. Tog fishing has quieted down as the fish spread out and the water's warmed past their comfort zone on the shallower structure — I'd expect that bite to sharpen back up once we get into fall, but for now it's a bonus fish, not a target.

Bluefish have been running through in pockets — nothing like a blitz, but enough that if you're marking bait on the meter around the Milford Gulf edges or off Hammonasset, it's worth a few casts with a diamond jig or a topwater popper before you move on. They've been more of an afternoon fish this week, showing when the sun's high and the bait gets pushed tight against structure.

Looking ahead: if the wind stays out of the south and light like the forecast suggests, I'd put my Saturday evening into the PM flood at Charles Island — that new moon push converging with sunset is the kind of setup you don't get every week. Plan B if the bass don't show is working the fluke drift at the New Haven Harbor mouth on the same tide change, since that bite's been reliable even when the striper bite is off. Either way, watch that spring tide build through the weekend — bigger water usually means better fishing on this beat, as long as you're standing in the right spot when it turns.

reports.headline: New-moon springs open a sunset striper window on the boulder fields
reports.subhead: Fluke have abandoned the warm bay for the cuts and channels, and the cold wall that's kept bonito west of Block Island just fell apart.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — it got warm fast, and it got lazy on the moon. We were coming off the full moon push from late June, tides flattening out into the neap cycle, and the bass that had been working the boulder fields off Ram Island and Wamphassuc Point at first light went quiet by mid-week. Water in the back coves and up into Little Narragansett Bay pushed hard into the mid-70s. Bait didn't disappear, but it scattered, and so did the fish that eat it.

That's changing. We're building into new-moon springs now, with the bigger tide swings stacking up through the weekend and peak alignment landing Saturday into Monday. The piece I'm watching hardest is the PM flood meeting sunset — that's the first evening window we've had since the June full moon where high water and last light line up instead of fighting each other. When the flood floods right at dusk, bait gets pinned against structure with the light dropping, and the bass that have been sulking in deeper water all day come up onto the rock to feed instead of just cruising through. That's the window I'd build a whole evening around this week, not just a stop on the way home.

Fluke have made their move, and it's not subtle. The bay water got too warm to hold them — we're talking upper 70s in the shallow flats off Mystic and up in the coves — and the fish have pushed hard into the channels and the mouth structure where clean, cooler water is getting pulled through on the tide. Mystic River channel on the outgoing, right where it dumps past the highway bridge into the Sound, has been holding fish in 15 to 20 feet. Same story at the cuts through the Fishers Island Sound reefs — anywhere there's a defined channel edge with current moving, that's where the fluke are stacking instead of spread out on the flats like they were in June. Chartreuse and white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been the ticket. A few keepers to 22 inches, nothing to write home about size-wise, but a steady pick if you're willing to hunt the deeper edges instead of anchoring on memory from last month.

Stripers are still a rock-and-tide game right now, and that hasn't changed even with the warm water. The boulder fields in Fishers Island Sound — the stretch running from off Ram Island down toward the west end, and the rock piles tucked in behind the breakwater at Stonington — are still holding fish, but they've gone deeper and more nocturnal with the heat. Early morning, an hour before and after low, working topwater and darters over the exposed boulders has produced schoolies and a few fish in the high 20s, mostly on an incoming push. But the better window, and the one I'm circling for this week specifically, is that evening flood-sunset overlap I mentioned. Live eels and bunker chunks fished tight to structure off Esker Point and the outer breakwater rocks, right as the tide turns and the light goes gold, have been worth the mosquito bites. If the wind stays out of the south and lays down toward evening — which it's been doing — that's your night to be there.

Here's the piece that's got my attention more than anything else this week: the cold wall that's historically kept bonito and albies penned up around Block Island has broken down. Water temps in Rhode Island Sound jumped over ten degrees in a short stretch, which means that barrier between the warmer water tight to Block and the cooler water spreading west toward Newport and Point Judith just collapsed. That corridor is widening, and it's pushing toward us. We're not seeing bonito inside Fishers Island Sound yet — I haven't had a confirmed report tight to Watch Hill or the Reef — but the setup right next door has changed fast, and fast-moving warm water plumes have a way of showing up where you don't expect them. I'd be running light spinning gear with 000 Deadly Dicks and small epoxy jigs in the boat just in case, especially working the rips off Watch Hill Light and out toward the Fishers Island side on a clean tide. It's early. It might be another two or three weeks before we get a real bonito show inside our water, and the false albacore blitz everybody's really waiting for is still a September story, not a July one. But the ingredients are moving in the right direction faster than they have in past seasons, and that's worth paying attention to now rather than after the fact.

Black sea bass have been a consistent, unglamorous producer on the deeper reef structure out toward Fishers Island — 25 to 35 feet, squid strips and Gulp on a two-hook bottom rig, keepers mixed with plenty of shorts. Good action if you want dinner without overthinking it.

For the week ahead: if I've got one evening to give it everything, it's Saturday or Sunday's PM flood at sunset on the Ram Island boulder field or the outer breakwater rocks — the tide's building, the light's right, and that's the first real convergence we've had since June. Daytime, I'm running the Mystic River channel and the FIS Sound cuts on the outgoing for fluke rather than wasting time on the warm flats. And I'm keeping an eye east — if that Rhode Island warm water keeps sliding our way, Watch Hill could be the first place in our zone to see a bonito this summer, and I don't want to be the last guy to hear about it.

reports.headline: Widest thermal edge of the season lights up yellowfin on the Hudson's 100-fathom line
reports.subhead: A post-blow warm seam from Wilmington to Poor Man's put fish on the wall this week — here's where to find them before the new moon shuts the light down.
reports.body_markdown:
The blow that sat on us through the holiday weekend finally cleared out Tuesday night, and what it left behind on the shelf edge was worth the wait. By Wednesday morning I was looking at a 10.3-degree differential between the cold shelf water and the warm slope water pushing up against it — the widest thermal split I've seen all season. That's not a subtle seam. That's a wall you could practically see from the tower. The warm plume ran the corridor from Wilmington up through Poor Man's and pressed right into the Hudson's east wall, and where warm water gets shoved up against cold that hard, bait gets pinned and tuna get stupid. Wednesday and Thursday were the first real post-blow window of July, and it produced.

Looking at what's coming, the moon's going dark — we're sliding into new moon territory over the weekend, which means less light penetration at night and a different game for the bluefin crowd working the midshore breaks. The NE upwelling that's been running has sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom contours nicely, and the Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has bluefin stacked on it right now. Darkening moon plus squid on the meter is exactly the setup you want for overnight light-and-jig work — the squid come up in the dark, the bluefin follow, and you don't need much current to make it happen. That's where I'd point a boat this weekend if the canyon run isn't in the cards.

As for the canyon itself, Wednesday's bite was legitimate — not a slaughter, but real fish on real structure. We worked the temp break running along the 100-fathom curve on the east wall, trolling a spread of ballyhoo behind Ilanders — green/yellow and pink/white doing the damage — with a naked ballyhoo flat-lined down the middle. Yellowfin from 35 to low 60s, mixed in with a couple of chunkier fish that felt closer to 70 when they came tight. Nothing giant, but a solid morning bite that shut off hard by early afternoon once the sun got up on the water and the fish slid back down. If you're running out, get there for first light — that window from dawn to about 10 a.m. is where the temp break was actually holding fish, and by midday it went quiet enough that a few boats picked up and ran further east looking for green water and didn't find much better.

Bigeye have been mixed in with the yellowfin on the same water, mostly picked off on the night drift with squid strips or whole squid soaked deep off a downrigger, 250 to 300 feet, right along that same east wall contour. It's not a bigeye blitz — more a fish or two a trip for boats willing to put in a night on anchor or drift over the deeper structure — but the numbers are there for anyone patient enough to sit on it.

Mahi have been scattered but present, mostly picked up incidentally trolling the canyon edge where any bit of floating structure or a weedline held them. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range, though a few boats found a better grade under a bigger mat of sargassum out past the Dip. If you see color change or a weedline holding out there, it's worth a few casts with a small stickbait or a bucktail before you move on — dolphin don't need much invitation this time of year when the water's this warm.

Wahoo have been quieter than I'd like for mid-July, but the ones that showed came off high-speed trolled Yo-Zuri Bonito lures and cedar plugs run wide on the spread, mostly picked off along the same warm seam on the east wall in that 68 to 70-degree slot where the wahoo like to sit just under the surface temp break. One or two fish a trip for the boats that specifically rigged for them — this isn't a target-and-fill-the-box fishery right now, it's an opportunistic add-on while you're trolling for yellowfin.

White marlin are still a watch-and-wait situation. The warm plume that's been driving this whole week's action is the same signal that typically pushes marlin up onto the bank, and if that plume holds its ground or pushes further west over the next week to ten days, I'd expect the first real flag reports out of the mid-Atlantic canyons, us included. It hasn't happened yet — I haven't heard a confirmed white bite anywhere close to the Hudson this week — but the water's setting up for it, and I'd have a pitch bait rigged and ready if you're running out there regardless of target species.

If I had a boat this weekend, I'd split the difference: run out early for the dawn bite on the east wall temp break while it's producing, and if that shuts down by midday, I'd rather burn the fuel checking the Coimbra corridor at night under the dark moon than keep grinding dead water in daylight. The bluefin bite there has the better odds right now, and the squid-light program under a black sky is about as reliable a setup as this time of year offers. Either way, that shelf-slope edge isn't going to hold this wide forever — if you've got a window this week, I wouldn't sit on it too long.

reports.headline: Post-blow edge widens to 10 degrees — Wilmington to Poor Man's lights up for yellowfin
reports.subhead: The shelf break did what it does best after a blow: sharpened up and stacked bait, and the boats that made the run cashed in.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did us a favor, even if it didn't feel that way sitting at the dock Tuesday watching the anemometer spin. That kind of wind stirs the water column, and when it lays down, the shelf-slope break sharpens up instead of smearing out. By Wednesday and Thursday we had a 10.3-degree temperature differential at the edge — the widest seam I've seen all season — running from Wilmington down through Poor Man's, with the Hudson east wall showing the same signature. That's not a subtle line. That's warm water stacked against cold hard enough that bait piles up on the edge and everything with a fin knows it. Boats that ran Wednesday-Thursday found yellowfin sitting right on that 100-fathom contour, and it was the best structural setup we've had since the season opened.

This week the moon's going dark — new moon builds through the weekend — and that matters more offshore than people give it credit for. Darker nights mean better squid jigging on the drift, and the overnight guys working lights over the canyons should see it. Meanwhile the NE upwelling that's been sharpening the 20-30 fathom breaks midshore hasn't let up, and the Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms is holding a real concentration of bluefin. That's not canyon fish — that's the midshore program, closer to the beach, and it's worth a look if you don't want to burn the fuel to Veatch. Georges Bank threw a second warming surge into the mix too, which re-energized the temperature differential between Veatch and Hydrographer — that gradient had gone soft for a couple weeks and now it's back to strong. When that differential firms up, the canyon walls hold bait tighter instead of letting it spread out over open water, and that's when the marks get thick instead of scattered.

Catch-wise: yellowfin have been the story, mostly 40 to 70 pounds with a few bigger mixed in, coming on the troll early — ballyhoo behind Green/Yellow Machines and small spreader bars worked the warm seam at Wilmington and Poor Man's before the sun got high, then it shifted to chunking and jigging once the fish got tuna-shy. Butterflied ballyhoo on a long soak, 60 to 80 feet down, has been drawing bites in the chunk slick when the trolling window closes. Bigeye are mixed in but nobody's dedicating a whole trip to them yet — they're a bonus fish on the overnight drift when the squid show up under the lights. Bluefin at Coimbra have been schoolie-to-mid-size class, 40-70 inch fish, and they're eating small subsurface stickbaits and diamond jigs worked fast through the marks at 20 fathoms — that's a different game than the canyon troll, more run-and-gun, more watching the fishfinder than watching the spread.

Wahoo have been scattered — a few incidental fish on the high-speed lures pulled behind the spreader bars, nothing you'd plan a trip around yet, but the water's warm enough that I expect that to build through the month. Mahi are showing around any floating structure or weed line you can find working the edge — nothing giant, mostly schoolies in the 5-15 pound class, but a good bonus stop if you see grass or a paddy while you're running out. White marlin is still a watch-and-wait situation out here — the warm plume that's supposed to trigger the first flags is pushing toward the banks, but that's more of a mid-Atlantic canyon story right now. I'd give it another week to ten days before we see the first real flag reports out of Veatch or Atlantis. Worth having the pitch bait rigged just in case, but I wouldn't build the trip around it yet.

Fuel math on this run: from Montauk it's roughly 100 nautical miles to Veatch, more like 110-115 to Atlantis depending on where the fish are sitting on the edge — figure a 5-6 hour run each way at cruise, so you're committing to an overnight or a very long day. From Block Island or the Rhode Island ports you're looking at similar numbers to Atlantis but a shorter hop if the midshore bluefin bite at Coimbra holds — that's the play if you want tuna without burning a full tank getting to blue water. I ran the numbers this week and the midshore trip pencils out a lot better on fuel than the full canyon run, especially with diesel where it is.

Looking ahead: if that shelf-edge differential holds through the weekend — and the Georges Bank surge suggests it should — I'd keep working the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam and the Hudson east wall on the troll early, then switch to chunk or jig once the sun's up. The new moon nights this week are made for overnight squid-light trips if you've got the stamina for it — dark skies, good squid sign, and bluefin/yellowfin willing to come up under lights is about as good as canyon fishing gets. If the wahoo bite builds like I expect with this warm water sitting on the edge, by next week I'd have a couple of high-speed lures rigged in the spread no matter what else you're targeting. Best case, the differential holds and Atlantis starts producing the way Veatch did this week. If it slides or softens, I'd shift effort to Coimbra and fish the midshore bluefin instead of forcing a long run for a moving target. Either way, this is the best structural setup we've had all year — worth the trip if you can pick your weather window.

reports.headline: New-moon springs wake the sunset bass bite at Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and a fluke exodus from the warm bays are rewriting the Central Sound playbook this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in the dead heat of July — it got sticky and slow through the midday tides, then came alive right at the edges. The June full moon had worked its way out of the system, current went slack and predictable, and the water in the back bays climbed hard. Oyster Bay and Smithtown Bay have been sitting warm enough that the fluke simply left. That's not a guess — it's the same pattern we see every summer once the shallow water tips past what a flatfish wants to sit in. They don't die, they just relocate to where the current keeps things cool and moving, which this week means the channels off Middle Ground Light and the deeper cuts near Stratford Shoal.

Now the moon's swinging new, and that changes everything about how I fish the next four days. New-moon springs mean bigger tidal exchange — more water moving through the pinch points that make Central Sound what it is. Stratford Shoal, the Middle Ground rip, the gut between the Norwalk Islands — these are current funnels, and a bigger tide means more bait gets squeezed through them on a tighter schedule. The window that matters most this weekend is the PM flood stacking up against sunset. That alignment peaks Saturday through Monday, July 11-13, and it's the first evening setup like this since the June full moon faded out. When the flood tide is still building as the light goes down, bass push up onto the shoals and hold in the current seam instead of just passing through — that's your window, and it's a short one, usually 90 minutes on either side of the top of the tide.

The bass fishing itself has been honest work, not a gimme. Boats working the Stratford Shoal rip on the last few evening tides have been picking off stripers in the 24 to 34-inch range, mostly on live bunker fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in 25 to 40 feet where the rip stacks up on the drop. A few guys are doing well trolling bunker spoons and umbrella rigs along the edge where the shoal falls into deeper water on the Connecticut side — that thermal break is holding bait, and the bass are sitting under it rather than chasing it on top, at least during the brighter hours. Norwalk Islands has been more of a bucktail bite: white and chartreuse 1-1.5 oz bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the rock piles off Sheffield and Copps Islands on the last two hours of the outgoing. Nobody's filling a cooler out there, but a few keeper bass and a lot of shorts have kept rods bent, and the bigger fish have been coming right at last light, which lines up with what the tide is telling us.

Fluke have genuinely shifted. The bay water got too warm to hold them comfortably, so if you're still working the flats inside Oyster Bay or Northport, you're fishing memory, not fish. The better drifts right now are the channel edges near Middle Ground Light and the deeper humps off Six Mile Reef, 35 to 50 feet, where the incoming tide is pulling cooler water up from the main body of the Sound. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-oz bucktails, dragged dead slow, have been the most consistent producer, with a scattering of fish to 5 pounds. It's not a bay-style easy pick — you have to cover water and find where the bottom breaks, but the fish that are there are quality.

Bluefish have shown up reliably wherever there's current and bait getting squeezed — chunked bunker off Charles Island has been drawing consistent action in the 3 to 6-pound range, and topwater poppers thrown at first light off the Norwalk Islands have connected on fish blowing up on peanut bunker pushed against the rocks. Porgies are steady but unspectacular on the reef structure around Charles Island and the outer Norwalk group — bottom rigs with clam and sandworm in 20 to 35 feet, better on the last of the outgoing when the current slows enough for them to feed off bottom instead of getting pinned.

Weakfish, I have to be straight with you, are still a no-show. Water's plenty warm enough now, and every year somebody asks if this is the year they come back to the Sound in numbers. Zero solid reports again this week despite the temperature checking every box it's supposed to. Warm water is necessary but clearly not sufficient — there's something else missing from the equation, and until it shows up, I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

On the bonito front — nothing in Central Sound yet, and I don't expect it this week. The corridor's opening up to our east, spreading from Block Island toward Point Judith and Newport as that cold wall between the eastern basins finally broke down. That's still 60-plus miles from Stratford Shoal. August is when they typically push this far west, and I'll be watching bait schools off the mouth of the Housatonic and around Charles Island for the first sign of them working bunker pods from underneath — that's usually the tell before you ever see a fin.

If I had one shot this week, it's Saturday evening at Stratford Shoal, fishing the last two hours of the flood into sunset with a live bunker on a light fish-finder rig, backup rod rigged with a bucktail in case the current's moving too fast to hold bottom. Plan B is the Middle Ground fluke drift on the following morning's outgoing — cooler, cleaner water and fish that have already told us they're there.

reports.headline: New moon springs flip the switch: fluke run for the cut, bass bite the sunset flood
reports.subhead: Jones Inlet's outgoing water is stacked with fluke pushed off the hot bay, and the first real PM striper window since June's full moon just reopened.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what overheated bay water always does in July — it pushed the good fish out. Great South Bay and the flats behind Jones Beach have been running close to 79 degrees, which is bathwater for fluke, and they've been sliding off those skinny flats and into the channels, the inlet mouth, and the ocean side where the water's actually breathing. We had a stretch of light southwest wind most of last week that kept the bay glassy and warm, and honestly it made for pretty water and slow fishing if you stayed shallow. The guys who moved out to Sloop Channel and the inlet cut did fine. The guys who stayed on the flats got a tan and not much else.

This week the moon's the story. We're building into new moon springs — the tide swings are getting bigger, the current's ripping harder through the inlet, and that's exactly what flushes bait and repositions fish. More important for surf guys and inlet regulars: the PM flood is now lining up with sunset. That's the first evening high-tide window we've had since the June full moon, and it runs strongest Friday through Monday, July 10-13, with the tightest alignment right around the 11th and 12th. When the flood tide peaks as the light's dropping, bass move up into the inlet and along the Jones Beach bars to feed in that low-light window before full dark. That's not a maybe — that's a pattern I've fished for fifteen years out here, and the tide charts back it up this week better than they have in a month.

Fluke first, because that's been the more dependable bite. With the bay pushing 78-79 and the ocean side running cooler — call it low 70s where the upwelled water is mixing in through the inlet — the fish are stacking on that thermal break. Sloop Channel edges, the deeper bends off the Meadowbrook flats, and straight through the inlet cut itself on the outgoing tide have all been holding fish. Best window is two hours either side of the turn to outgoing, when the current's moving enough to make bucktails work but hasn't turned into a freight train. I've been dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets right along bottom through the deeper cuts, slow enough to feel the bottom change. Fish have run mixed — plenty of shorts, but a decent number of 19-22 inch keepers mixed in, with one 26-incher reported off the Jones Beach inlet rocks on a squid-and-spearing combo fished on a high-low rig. It's not a wide-open bite. You're covering water and culling through shorts to find your keepers, but that's summer fluking on this coast and it's better than what the bay flats gave up last week.

Stripers have been the more interesting development. Resident fish never really left after the spring run, but they've been quiet through the heat, holding deep and feeding mostly at night. With this sunset-flood alignment kicking in, I expect that to change through the weekend. The play is the inlet mouth itself — working the rocks on the Jones Beach side and drifting bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig into the current seam where the outgoing meets incoming structure. If you'd rather cast, live-lining bunker where you can find it, or working a bucktail with a curly-tail trailer through the wash at last light, has been productive for the guys putting in the hours. Don't expect blitz conditions — this is a July resident bite, not the fall bunker run — but a 15 to 20 pound fish in that inlet current on the right stage of tide is a real possibility this weekend, and worth losing some sleep over.

Bluefish have been mixed in with the fluke drift and occasionally show in short-lived blitzes off the inlet on bait pods pushed out by the tide. Nothing sustained, but if you see birds working the rips off Short Beach, throw metal — Deadly Dicks or Hopkins in the 2-3 ounce range have been getting hit fast when the blues show.

Weakfish is where I have to be straight with you. The water's been warm enough, and warm enough long enough, that on paper this should be a weakfish summer in South Oyster Bay and around the Freeport creeks. The reality on the water hasn't caught up to the thermometer. A few fish have turned up — one 26-inch, 7.3-pound weakfish came out of the bay on a light bucktail worked slow along a channel edge — but it's still one-off stuff, not a pattern you can plan a trip around yet. If you want to chase them, fish the dusk incoming around the Wantagh Bridge pilings and the deeper holes off Freeport with bucktails tipped with bloodworm or chartreuse soft plastics, but go in expecting a long shot, not a sure thing.

Porgies remain the honest bread-and-butter right now — the rockpiles around the inlet and the reef structure off Jones Beach are stacked with them, and a simple hi-lo rig with clam will keep a rod bent while you wait on bigger things. Blackfish season's closed through mid-August, so leave the tog gear home for now.

Looking ahead: if that sunset-flood window performs the way the tide charts suggest, Saturday and Sunday evening at the inlet mouth is where I'm putting my time. Backup plan is the Sloop Channel fluke drift on the outgoing if the bass don't cooperate — that bite's been consistent enough to trust.
