Keep an eye east too; bonito and Spanish mackerel have started showing at the eastern inlets on the incoming tide, and if that warm plume keeps sliding west the way it's been forecast, Jones could see its first fish of the year before the month's out.

reports.headline: New moon springs juice the Moriches cut as fluke bail out of a hot bay
reports.subhead: Great South Bay-style warm-up is pushing fluke and bait through the inlet just as bigger tides start scouring the throat — here's where to put the boat and the waders this week.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what shallow water does in July — it cooked. Surface temps in the back bay were pushing into the high 70s, and while I don't have a hard number off Tuthill Point, the behavior told the story: fluke that were scattered over the flats and eelgrass two weeks ago have been funneling toward the channels, the inlet throat, and the ocean side where upwelled water is running cooler and better oxygenated. That's not a guess — it's the same pattern Great South Bay is showing right now, and Moriches Bay is built the same way: skinny, sun-baked, and quick to push its fish toward moving water when the flats get uncomfortable. If you were still working the marsh edges last week and getting picked at, that's why.

This week the big variable is the moon. We're building toward new-moon spring tides, with the peak alignment landing Friday through Monday (July 11-13). That means more water moving through the inlet on both ends of the cycle — bigger ebb, bigger flood, more current velocity through the throat between Cupsogue and the west jetty. For an inlet system that's still settling into its post-storm geometry, that's meaningful. More current means more scour on the bar, more bait getting pulled through the cut on the outgoing, and — critically — more current lane for bass and blues to sit in and let the buffet come to them. The flip side is safety: spring tides through a shifting inlet like this move fast and standing waves build quick on the ebb against any east wind. Respect it.

Fluke are the story right now, and the pattern is inlet and ocean, not bay flats. The best drifts have been the main channel off Cupsogue Coast Guard station and down through the throat toward Pikes Beach, working 12 to 18 feet of water on the last two hours of the outgoing. Bucktails in the 3/4-ounce range, white or chartreuse, teased with a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow and bounced off bottom — that's put keepers in the box, though it's not a rip-your-arms-off bite. More like two or three quality fish per drift session if you're covering ground and staying tight to the deeper cuts where the current stacks bait against the drop. Ocean side, working just outside the bar in that upwelled 70-71 degree water, has been the more consistent producer for size — a few fish pushing 4 and 5 pounds coming from anglers working the deeper scour holes right off the jetty rocks on the outgoing push.

Striped bass are still holding at the inlet jetties, and with the spring tide building this weekend, I'd expect the outgoing to get more aggressive about pulling bait past the rocks at dawn and dusk. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig tight to the base of the east jetty has worked for the guys willing to sit through a tide change, and swimming plugs — the SP Minnow and similar — worked the seam where the jetty current meets the open bar have picked up fish in that low-light window. Nothing epic, but a consistent evening program if you're patient and pick your tide.

Bluefish have been showing in pods off Cupsogue surf, chasing bait pushed out by the bay's outgoing water meeting the ocean. Poppers and diamond jigs worked the wash line during the first two hours of outgoing have connected, though it's spotty — some mornings the blues are stacked up thick enough to keep you busy for an hour, other mornings you walk the beach and see nothing but bait skittering with nothing behind it. Worth checking at first light before the pressure builds.

Here's something newer worth watching closely: this is the tail end of the seasonal window for bonito and Spanish mackerel showing up on the ocean side of Moriches and Shinnecock, and the early signs have been there — small, fast schools working clean incoming water outside the bar. If you're a surfcaster with small metal in the bag — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce Kastmasters — this is the week to bring them along on a Cupsogue session. That window's closing fast, so I wouldn't wait past this weekend to check it.

Weakfish remain the disappointment of the summer. Water's been warm enough for a while now, and the fish just haven't shown in the numbers the temperature would suggest they should. I'm not writing them off, but I'm also not sending anyone out with weakfish as the primary target. If you pick one up, it'll be a bonus — likely a night bite around the channel markers on bucktail and a strip of squid or sandworm, not a program to build a trip around.

Porgies are steady and unspectacular in the bay proper, around Tuthill Point and the deeper holes off East Moriches, standard high-low rigs with clam. Blackfish season's closed this time of year in these waters, so that's a fall conversation.

Looking ahead: I'd fish the Friday-Saturday max ebb at the inlet throat for fluke, work the last two hours of outgoing before the tide goes fully slack, and keep an eye on wind direction — if it swings onshore against that spring ebb, the bar will stand up and you'll want to fish the inside of the jetty instead of fighting the cut. If the bonito window holds even one more week, Sunday morning at Cupsogue on clean incoming water is where I'd put my money. Plan B if that doesn't pan out: back to the fluke drift, because that pattern's proven itself two weeks running now.

reports.headline: New moon springs push bay fluke out the inlet as Great South Bay tops 78 degrees
reports.subhead: Fire Island Inlet outgoing tides are holding the best fluke of the summer while stripers set up for a sunset flood bite through the weekend.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay told us exactly what it was going to do, and it did it. Great South Bay pushed past 78 degrees — I had a thermometer reading 78.8 off my transom drifting the flats south of Nicoll Bay on Wednesday — and that's too warm for a fluke to sit comfortably on bottom mud all day. They didn't leave, they just moved. Every keeper I've heard about the last five days has come out of the channels, the bridge rips, or straight out the inlet where the water's moving and cooler. Meanwhile out front, a stretch of northeast wind did some quiet work upwelling the ocean side down into the low 70s, which is exactly where fluke and bass want to be right now. That's not a coincidence — that's a thermocline doing its job, and it's why the inlet has become the address this week instead of the open bay.

We're coming off a new moon, which means we're building into spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through Fire Island Inlet on every stage. That peaks through the weekend, with the tightest alignment falling Saturday into Monday, July 11-13, when the evening flood is stacking up right around sunset. That's the window I'm circling. A flood tide that peaks at dusk pushes bait — spearing, peanut bunker, whatever's left in the bay — right out through Democrat Point and past the bridges just as the light goes low and the stripers get bold. I've seen this setup before on a new moon in July, and it's one of the better recipes we get all season for a dusk bite at the inlet mouth.

Fluke first, because that's been the real story. The outgoing tide at the Robert Moses bridges — both the East and West spans — has been holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot band where the current rips through the pilings. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along bottom on the drift, have been drawing strikes from fish in the 3 to 5 pound range, with a few better ones mixed in — I heard of a fish pushing 7 out past the West span on Sunday's outgoing. Chartreuse and white combo bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have also been working when the current's really ripping and you need the extra scent to slow a fish down enough to commit. If you're working the ocean side, right off Democrat Point in that 15 to 20 foot depth where the upwelled water is holding, the bite's been a touch better than the bay proper — cleaner water, cooler, and the fluke are sitting tight to structure instead of spread out over mud.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, and I want to be straight about that instead of dressing it up. The daytime bite in the bay has been sluggish — too warm, too bright, fish holding deep and not eager. But the evening program at the inlet has been legitimate. Guys working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs off Democrat Point on the last two hours of the outgoing have been picking off fish in the 28 to 34 inch range, with the occasional better fish mixed in on live eels drifted through the deeper cuts near the jetty rocks after dark. That bite should only get better as we roll into this weekend's flood-into-sunset window — bigger water movement means more bait getting flushed, and stripers know how to find a buffet line.

Bluefish have shown up sporadic but violent, which is about right for July. Schools of choppers in the 3 to 6 pound class have been slashing through bunker pods just outside the inlet on the last of the incoming, and if you find the birds working you can load the boat fast on simple diamond jigs or topwater poppers before they push through and vanish. Don't overthink the bluefish — find the surface commotion, get on it quick, and be ready to move again just as fast.

Weakfish I have to be honest about: not much. The water's been warm enough for weeks now to theoretically hold them, but I haven't heard a single solid report out of the bay or the inlet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise just because the temperature checks a box. That old rule about 70-degree water bringing the weakfish back doesn't seem to be holding this year — plenty of warm water, zero fish to show for it. If you're targeting them, I'd call that a long shot right now, not a plan.

Porgies have been steady and reliable if you want an easy box of fish — working the rock piles inside the inlet and around the Captree bridge abutments with sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig, on the bottom of the outgoing, has been putting decent scup in coolers without much drama. Good option if you're bringing kids or just want dinner without chasing a puzzle.

Looking ahead, I'd spend my weekend hours at the inlet mouth chasing that flood-into-sunset striper window while the new moon springs are peaking — Saturday and Sunday evening both look good on paper if the wind stays out of the northeast and doesn't blow the water dirty. Daytime, I'd stick with the fluke drift off the bridges and out past Democrat Point where that cooler upwelled water is holding fish tight. If the bass don't show at dusk, the fluke bite is deep enough right now to be your fallback, not the other way around.

reports.headline: New Moon Springs Load The Race — Bonito Show Early Off Fishers Island
reports.subhead: Big tides and sunset stripers converge this weekend while the fluke bail out of the bay and the first Spanish mackerel show up on cold-wall collapse.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does before a new moon — it built. Wind stayed out of the northeast for most of the stretch, which kept the surface chop honest but also sharpened the thermal breaks along the 20-30 fathom edges east of us, the same upwelling that's been stacking bluefin farther out on the Coimbra corridor. Closer to home, that NE flow did something else useful: it kept cooler water pinned against the Fishers Island shoreline while the bay side of Gardiners and Peconic pushed past 78 degrees. That temperature split is the whole story of the week — bait and predators both reacting to it, just in different directions.

This week the moon takes over. New moon lands right in this window, which means spring tides building through Friday and peaking Saturday into Monday, July 11-13. Bigger tidal range means harder current through The Race and Plum Gut — I'm talking 4 to 5 knots at max ebb off Little Gull — and it also means the evening flood is now stacking up right against sunset. That's the first PM flood-sunset alignment we've had since the June full moon, and it's the window I'd build a whole trip around. When the flood peaks right at last light, bass push up onto the structure to feed on the push instead of just riding the current lane, and that's when the big fish show themselves in the white water.

Bass fishing through Plum Gut and The Race has been real but not automatic — I've had two-fish nights and skunk nights in the same 72 hours, which tells you it's tide-dependent, not a blanket bite. The pattern that's working: fish the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of high, right in the rip line off Orient Point Light and along the north side of Plum Gut where the eddy forms behind the reef. Eels are still the closer after dark — an 8 to 10-inch snake fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, dead-drifted through the seam where the fast water meets the slower back-eddy. During the day, bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked with a slow lift-drop through the same eddy pockets have put 28 to 34-inch fish in the boat. Nothing over 40 this week that I've seen personally, though there's chatter of bigger fish scattered from here out toward Block Island and the Cape — pockets, not a run. I'd treat any 40-plus as a bonus, not an expectation, until this new moon push proves it can hold bigger bass on the structure consistently.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player. Slammers in the 8 to 12-pound class are hitting hard on the same tide stages as the bass, but they're less picky about exact timing — anywhere from mid-incoming through the top of the tide off Fishers Island Race and the rip line running north of Race Rock has produced. Diamond jigs, 2 to 4 ounces, worked with a fast erratic retrieve through the moving water is still the ticket, and if you want top-water violence, a big Danny-style swimmer over the same structure at first light will get hit.

Fluke have officially left the bay. That 78.8-degree water in Gardiners and the upper bay pushed them hard into the channels and out toward the inlets, and the upwelled 71-degree water on the ocean side of Plum Gut and around Orient Point is exactly where they've relocated. The play now is outgoing tide, working the channel edges in 25 to 40 feet with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom as the current empties out through the Gut. Fish to 5 pounds have come from that stretch this week, with better numbers than size — a lot of 16 to 18-inch shorts mixed in, so you're sorting through fish to find keepers, but they're there in numbers worth the drift time.

The development I'm watching closest is the bonito. The cold wall that's normally sitting between Block Island and Rhode Island Sound collapsed hard — better than 10 degrees warmer than it was — and that's opened a corridor for bonito and Spanish mackerel to spread west from Point Judith toward us. First reports of Spanish showing on the ocean side of the inlets out east of Montauk this week fit right into that pattern, and Fishers Island Race, with its clean incoming water and structure, is exactly the kind of spot that corridor could reach next. If you're rigged for it — small Deadly Dick or Kastmaster in the 1-ounce range, worked fast on light tackle — I'd keep a rod ready any time you're running past the Race in the middle of the day. It's not a sure thing yet, but the water's right and the fish are moving in this direction.

Weakfish, for the record, are still a non-event. Water's been above 70 for over two weeks now and I haven't heard of a single fish, which tells you temperature alone isn't the trigger people hoped it was — I wouldn't burn a tide on them right now.

If I had one shot this weekend, I'd take the Saturday evening flood at Plum Gut, eel in hand, timed to hit max current right as the sun drops. That's the best alignment we've had all month. Backup plan if the bass go quiet: swing over to the fluke grounds on the ebb and salvage the trip with bucktails on the bottom.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the rips as bonito push east toward the Shoals
reports.subhead: Great Point and Monomoy are turning on with moving water while the first real bonito signal builds just west of us in Rhode Island Sound.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — built toward a new moon and let the tide do the talking. We're coming into the springs now, and you could feel the current picking up all week at Great Point, at the Handkerchief, through the Monomoy rips. Wind sat mostly out of the southwest, nothing violent, just enough to push a light chop across Nantucket Sound and keep things from going glassy and dead. Water's held steady — not the abrupt jump you sometimes get this time of year, more of a slow creep warm, which is exactly the kind of thermal pattern that keeps bait comfortable and predators patient instead of scattering everything into a panic.

This week the moon goes new around the 11th-13th, which means big tidal swings — more water moving through the rips on both the flood and the ebb, shorter slacks, and a narrower window where the fish actually sit still. That matters a lot at Great Point and off Monomoy, where the whole game is reading when the rip stands up and when it goes soft. Bigger springs mean more bait getting swept off the shoals and more current seams for stripers and blues to sit in and let the food come to them. I'd rather fish moving water over a new moon than dead slack over a full — you get shorter windows, but the windows are better.

Striped bass have been steady, not spectacular, working the structure at Great Point on the last two hours of the ebb. Guys are doing well with umbrella rigs and bucktails tipped with sea worms worked slow along the seam where the rip meets the calmer water — that color change is the whole story out there, dirty green water butting up against the clean blue, and that's where the bass are stacking. Sizes have been mixed, schoolies mostly, but there've been slot fish mixed in for guys willing to grind through a tide change instead of leaving after twenty minutes. Monomoy's been fishing similarly — the rip off the Powder Hole and down toward the Handkerchief has held fish on the outgoing, particularly right at first light before the wind fills in.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player the last ten days. Schools have been working bait pods just off Sankaty and out toward the eastern edge of Nantucket Shoals, and when you find them they don't make you work for it — poppers and metal-lip swimmers get hit on the first cast most mornings. It's not the giant class of blues you sometimes see in the fall, more three- to five-pound choppers, but they're aggressive and they're consistent, which counts for something when the bass are being particular.

Fluke are where I'd point most boats right now. The pattern's been shifting out of the shallower Sound flats and into the channels and the deeper humps around Horseshoe Shoal and the edges of the Monomoy Channel — that's typical for mid-July once the shallow water starts running warm and the bigger fish slide toward cooler, deeper structure with better current flow. Squid strips on a bucktail-and-teaser combo, dragged slow along 25 to 40 feet of water on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent producer. A few boats working the deeper cuts off Tuckernuck have reported keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of short ones, so it's worth covering ground rather than anchoring on the first fish you find.

Here's the one I'm watching closest. The cold wall that's usually held bonito penned up around Block Island collapsed on the Rhode Island side this past week, and the water out there jumped enough that bonito are spreading east across Rhode Island Sound instead of staying bottled up. That's not our water yet, but it's the signal I wait for every summer — when that eastern edge of the bonito range starts sliding, Nantucket Shoals is usually next, especially once the sand eels and peanut bunker start balling up along the rip lines off Great Point and the east side of the island. It's early. I wouldn't book a bonito trip off that alone. But it's the kind of development that tells me to start checking my epoxy jigs and small Deadly Dicks instead of leaving them in the bag until August.

No albies yet, and that's normal for the second week of July — that push usually doesn't show at Great Point until sand eels and peanut bunker start stacking up in numbers, typically late August into September on this side of the Cape. But the bonito signal moving our direction is worth logging now, because when they show, they show fast, and the guys who had gear rigged and ready are the ones who connect on day one instead of day five.

For the week ahead: I'd fish the new moon tide change hard at Great Point on the ebb, work the rip seam with bucktails and worked-slow swimmers for bass, and keep bluefish gear rigged for when you run into the blitzes off Sankaty — they've been easy to find lately. For fluke, work the deeper channels around Horseshoe Shoal and Monomoy on the incoming, squid strip and bucktail combo, and don't be afraid to move if the first drift is short-heavy. And keep half an eye east — if that Rhode Island Sound bonito push holds and the water out toward the Shoals keeps trending warm, this could be an early year for the first fish over the edge. I've seen it happen by the third week of July before. Doesn't mean it happens again, but that's exactly the kind of window I don't want to miss.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the Race Point rip as stripers and mackerel stack the structure
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and a cooling nudge from the northeast have put bait back on the bars — the bite's real, but you've got to work for it.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Bay was still shaking off the full-moon hangover from late June — slack current, warm skinny water, bass scattered instead of stacked. That's typical after a big moon pushes through; the current lanes go soft for a few days and the fish spread out looking for their own comfort zone instead of getting pinned up against structure. We had a few days of light southwest air that let the surface warm more than I like to see in the harbors, and the stripers responded by sliding out to deeper, cooler water off Peaked Hill Bars and staying down instead of showing on top.

That's changing this week. We're rolling into a new moon — peak alignment lands right around July 11-13 — and that means spring tides building fast, bigger swings top to bottom, and a lot more push through Race Point and the Peaked Hill Bars rip. At the same time we've had a few days of wind out of the northeast, which is exactly the kind of pattern that stirs the deeper, colder water up onto the bars on the Outer Cape side. When that happens the sand eels and mackerel get pushed shallow, and the bass follow. I've seen this same setup plenty of times in July — new moon current plus a northeast nudge on the water column, and the rip goes from lazy to loaded inside forty-eight hours. That's the window I'm watching hardest right now.

On the water, the Race Point rip has been the most consistent piece of structure in the Bay this week. Guys drifting live mackerel on wire, or working bucktail-and-tube combinations through the seam where the outgoing current meets the deeper water off the Point, have been finding bass in the twenty-eight to thirty-eight inch range, with a few better fish mixed in early and late in the tide. The best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the slack — that's when the bait gets funneled and concentrated instead of just streaming through. Once the tide goes fully slack the bite shuts down hard, and you're better off repositioning than sitting on dead water waiting for it to turn back on.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more of a night and dawn game. The eel bite there has been steady but not stacked — guys putting in the time after dark, drifting live eels along the edge of the bar where it drops into deeper water, have been picking off stripers in that same mid-thirties range, with the occasional bigger fish showing right at first light before the sun gets high. It's not a fill-the-box bite right now. It's a patience bite. You might make four or five drifts before you connect, but when you do, it's usually a fish worth the wait.

Billingsgate has been a mixed bag. On the higher stages of the tide, especially the last of the flood into the top, there've been bass working the edges of the flat where the bait gets pushed up against the shoal — light tackle guys throwing paddletails and soft-plastic jerkbaits have done well sight-fishing those fish in skinny water, but it's weather-dependent. You need calm enough water to see the fish working, and we haven't had that every day this week. When the wind's been up, Billingsgate has been mostly quiet.

Bluefish have shown in patches off Sandy Neck, mostly smaller fish in the three to five pound range but plenty of them when you find the school. Poppers and Deadly Dicks worked fast across the top on the outgoing have drawn some violent strikes, particularly in that hour right after the tide turns when the bait gets pushed out past the bar and the blues pile on it in the open water. It hasn't been a blitz — more like scattered pods that show for twenty minutes and then move — but if you're mobile and willing to run the shoreline looking for diving birds, you can find them.

Cod fishing has held up on the deeper structure off Race Point, sixty to ninety feet, jigging diamond jigs tipped with strips of squid or drifting clam baits over the rockier bottom. It's not the kind of numbers game you get in the fall, but there've been a few nice fish in that eight to twelve pound class coming over the rail for guys willing to put in bottom time between the striper drifts. Fluke have mostly stayed tight to the channel edges in Barnstable Harbor and around the deeper cuts near Sandy Neck as the flats warm up — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel drop, have been the go-to, with keeper-sized fish coming on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push to it.

Looking ahead, if the northeast wind holds even a little through the new moon build, I'd put my time on the Race Point rip on the outgoing, especially the couple days around peak springs when the current's strongest and the bait gets concentrated hardest. That's historically been the best combination out here — big tide plus a cool push equals bass stacked tight instead of scattered thin. If the wind swings back southwest and lays down, I'd shift toward Peaked Hill Bars at night and early dawn, since that pattern tends to hold up better in calmer, warmer conditions. Either way, I wouldn't sit on one spot all week and hope — this Bay rewards guys who move with the tide, not against it.

reports.headline: New moon springs push bay stripers to the bridges as fluke bail out to the channels
reports.subhead: Warm shallows in Greenwich Bay and the Providence River are shoving the doormats toward deeper water, while the new moon sets up the best sunset tide of the month.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July — it got soft and warm on top and started sorting fish by depth. We had a stretch of light, shifting wind out of the southwest most afternoons, which is enough to push a chop across Greenwich Bay and the upper river but not enough to mix the water down. That's the setup that bakes the shallows. Fluke that were spread across the flats off Warwick Neck and up into Greenwich Bay in June have been sliding out toward the channel edges and the mouths of the coves, looking for the cooler water stacked against the bottom structure. Stripers, meanwhile, have been doing their usual summer thing — daytime fish going quiet and deep around the bridge pilings, night fish waking up hard on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming.

This week the moon's the story. We're coming off new moon, which means spring tides — bigger swings, more current, more water moving through the East and West Passages than we've seen in a couple weeks. That extra push does two things: it flushes bait out of the coves and rivers on the outgoing, and it stacks that bait against structure on the incoming. The sunset-to-dusk window lines up with the top of the flood the next few nights, which is the alignment I wait for all summer — bass feeding right as the light goes, right as the current's still got some shove left in it. If you've only got one evening this week, Friday through Monday is when I'd take it, before the tides start easing off the neap side again.

Fluke fishing has been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about it — the upper bay bite has cooled off as the water's crept up into the high 70s in the shallows. Greenwich Bay and the flats off Nayatt have gone soft during the day. The fish didn't disappear, they moved. Guys working the drop-offs along the Prudence Island channel edge, and down around Popasquash Point where the current runs harder, have been picking at keepers in 18 to 25 feet on the outgoing tide — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. It's not a banner bite. You're working for three or four keepers over a tide instead of a dozen, but the fish that are coming over the rail have been decent, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds. If the water keeps climbing, expect more of that shift toward the bay mouth and the East Passage over the next couple weeks.

Stripers are the better story right now. The bridges — Mount Hope, the Jamestown-Newport span — have been holding fish tight to the pilings after dark, and with these spring tides pushing more current through, the bait's getting pinned right where the bass want it. Live eels drifted on the down-current side of the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing have been money, and swimming a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig off the rocks at Rocky Point and Nyatt Point has been picking up fish in the 26 to 34 inch range right at first light and again at dusk. Conimicut Point is still worth a pass on the outgoing — the flat there dumps bait right off the edge, and I've seen schoolie-to-mid-30s action for guys throwing white bucktails and swimming plugs along that drop. Nothing's blitzing. This is a tide-and-timing bite, not a run-and-gun bite. Fish the moving water around the structure and you've got a shot; fish the slack and you're just casting.

Scup have been consistent, which is the one thing you can count on in July. The ledges off Rocky Point, the rock piles around Prudence Island, and the Nyatt Point drop are holding good numbers on squid strips and clam bellies fished on top-and-bottom rigs, mostly in 15 to 30 feet. Nothing huge, but steady action, and a good way to fill a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn for bass. Black sea bass have shown up around the rockier structure near Jamestown and the Prudence Island shoreline — smaller fish mostly, a few keepers mixed in on squid and Gulp on jigheads worked slow along the bottom.

Bluefish have started trickling in — snapper blues in the coves and up in the Providence River, which tells me the bigger cocktail blues aren't far behind if the pattern holds like it usually does in late July. Weakfish, on the other hand, are still a no-show. The water's been warm enough for a while now, and that used to be the trigger, but it hasn't produced a single report I trust. I'm not chasing them until I see actual fish, not just the right temperature on a app.

Looking ahead: if the spring tides keep pushing current through the passages the way they have been, I'd fish the bridge pilings and the rocky points on the sunset flood through Monday — that's the best alignment we've had since before the full moon in June. After that the tides ease toward neap, current slows, and I'd expect the bass to spread out and get lazier, which usually means switching from moving structure to holding areas — deeper holes off Prudence and the channel bends where fish can sit out of the current and still eat. Plan B if the bass go quiet: keep working the fluke on the channel edges, because that fish isn't leaving the bay, it's just leaving the shallows.

reports.headline: New moon springs push fluke out of the back bays and into the inlets
reports.subhead: Warm bay water is doing the work for us this week — the fish are stacking where the current still runs cold and clean.
reports.body_markdown:
Class is in session, and the lesson this week is thermal geography. Last week the back bays from Absecon to Great Egg cooked — sod bank flats pushing into the high 70s on the afternoon tides, which is about ten degrees warmer than a fluke wants to work in. That's not a guess, that's basic biology: doormats are ambush predators, and ambush predators don't like being lethargic in warm water any more than we like running wind sprints in August. So the fluke did what they always do when the shallow water gets soupy — they slid to where the current still moves fast enough to stay cool. That means Absecon Inlet, Great Egg Inlet, the deeper reaches of Townsends, and the channel edges just inside Stone Harbor. If you were still working the grass flats behind Brigantine last week wondering where everybody went, that's your answer.

This week the tide chart does the fish a favor. We're coming off a new moon, which means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through those inlets on both the flood and the drain. Peak alignment lands right around Saturday through Monday, July 11-13. Bigger tides mean the inlets flush harder, which pulls more bait — spearing, mullet, small peanut bunker — out of the bay and stacks it against the jetty rocks and the edges of the channel. That's exactly where you want to be dragging a bucktail. Wind's been mild out of the southwest most days, nothing that's torn the water up, so clarity at the inlets has stayed respectable — not gin clear, but fishable, which matters more than people think when you're trying to get a fluke to commit in six feet of moving water.

The fluke program right now is an inlet program, full stop. Absecon has been the most consistent — working the outgoing tide along the rock line on the Brigantine side, three-quarter-ounce white bucktails tipped with four-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet in pearl or white, dragged slow along the bottom where the current slackens behind the rocks. Fish in the 17 to 20-inch range have been steady, with enough 20-22 inch keepers mixed in to make it worth your gas money. Great Egg has been similar — the channel edge off Longport and the drop just inside the inlet on the ocean side holding fish on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the water funnels hardest. Chartreuse and white combos have both worked; I haven't seen one color running away from the other, which tells me it's more about presentation than paint job right now. Keep that bucktail ticking bottom, don't overwork it — a fluke in moving water doesn't need much convincing once the bait's in the strike zone.

Bass fishing has been a mixed bag, and I'll be honest about that instead of dressing it up. A few schoolies and some slot fish have been coming out of the surf at night on bunker chunks fished on fish-finder rigs off Ocean City and Sea Isle, mostly the first two hours of the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the bar. But it's not consistent — some nights you get two or three fish, some nights you get sand fleas and nothing else. The bigger stripers everybody's hoping for with the mullet run are still weeks off; that push doesn't usually build until late August into September down here, so patience is the word.

Weakfish, I have to be straight with you — still nothing. The bay's been above 70 degrees for over two weeks now, which used to be the trigger everybody watched for, but warm water alone clearly isn't enough anymore. I haven't heard a credible weakfish report out of the Great Egg or Absecon systems all month. Whatever's driving that decline, it's not just temperature — I'd stop planning trips around a thermometer reading and start looking at it as one ingredient in a recipe we don't fully have yet.

Kingfish have been a nice bright spot for the surf guys working the troughs off Ocean City and Stone Harbor, small pieces of bloodworm or Fishbites on a high-low rig in three to six feet of water right off the beach — good action for anybody bringing kids or just wanting steady bites between the bigger targets. Triggerfish are starting to show around the inshore wrecks and reef sites off Great Egg, which is right on seasonal schedule; small pieces of clam or squid on a light jig head near structure will find them, though they're more of a bonus fish than something to build a whole trip around yet.

Looking offshore for a second, because it matters to guys running out of Absecon and Great Egg for tuna — the warm-water edge that set up midweek out toward the canyons was about as good a structural setup as we've seen all year, and boats working the shelf reported solid yellowfin activity on that seam. That window's closing, but if a similar edge reforms, it's worth the run.

For this coming week, I'd fish the inlets on the outgoing with bucktails, keep an eye on the new moon springs peaking through Monday for the strongest current windows, and check the eastern inlets on a clean incoming tide for any stray Spanish mackerel or bonito — the pelagic window's been open along the coast and South Jersey inlets have occasionally seen strays slip in behind bait pushes. Nothing guaranteed there, but the conditions are right enough to keep a spoon rod rigged just in case.

reports.headline: Post-Blow Seam Lights Up Wilmington-Poor Man's, Yellowfin Stack the 100-Fathom Line
reports.subhead: A 10-degree edge and clean overnight squid runs gave us the best canyon window of the year — but you had to be there Wednesday and Thursday to cash in.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did us a favor, even if it didn't feel like it while we were tied to the dock. Two days of onshore wind stacked cold shelf water up against the slope, and when it finally laid down Wednesday morning, the break between that cold inshore water and the Gulf Stream influence out past the 100-fathom line had widened to something like ten degrees — the sharpest differential I've seen all season. That's not a subtle temperature line you have to hunt for with a thermometer. That's a wall of color change you can see from the tower, green to blue in the space of a boat length, and it ran right through the heart of the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam and pushed up onto the Hudson's east wall. Bait piles up on edges like that. Predators follow the bait. Wednesday and Thursday were, without question, the best structural setup we've had all year out here.

The question now is whether that seam holds or slides. We're heading into a darkening moon this week, which is actually good news for the overnight squid game — less moonlight means the lights work harder pulling bait up under the transom, and that's exactly the tactic that's been paying off on bluefin at the Coimbra corridor, working that 20-fathom break where the NE upwelling has been sharpening things up nearshore of the canyon proper. Meanwhile out at the edge, the warm plume that fed last week's break is still pushing east, and if it keeps building toward the bank the way it's been forecast to, we should start seeing the first white marlin flags of the year inside the next week to ten days. That's the pattern we watch every July — warm water arrives, ballyhoo show up thick on the surface, and the flags follow within days.

On the water, it's been a real week, not an easy one. Boats that made the Wednesday-Thursday window scored well — yellowfin in the 25 to 45-pound class on the troll, working spreader bars and small ballyhoo rigged behind cedar plugs along that 100-fathom line between Wilmington and Poor Man's, roughly the stretch running southeast off the canyon head. Green machines and Ilanders in dark colors were the ticket in the cleaner blue water; when we crossed back into the green, we switched to naked ballyhoo on the long riggers and picked up a few more bites. Mixed into that yellowfin bite were a handful of bigeye on the chunk after dark — butterfish chunks fished on a slow drift with the current, baits set at staggered depths from 30 feet down to 150, worked over structure where the water column showed a defined thermocline. That's not a bite you can force. You sit on it, you keep the chunks going steady, and you wait for the current to bring them up to you.

Wahoo showed up as a bonus on the high-speed gear for boats willing to run the diving planers and Ilander/ballyhoo combinations at 12 to 15 knots along the edge — a couple of fish in the 40 to 60-pound range came from right around the Wilmington drop where the bottom falls off hard into the canyon proper. Mahi have been more of a grind. We found a few keeper-sized fish, 8 to 15 pounds, sitting under scattered debris and a couple of small weed lines drifting on the warm side of the break, but nothing like the kind of pot-hopping bonanza you sometimes get out here in peak summer. Small stuff mostly, with the occasional gaffer mixed in.

Here's the honest part: this bite is real, but it's not a gimme. Friday through the weekend, the wind swung around and the seam softened — the sharp color change we had mid-week smeared out, and the guys who ran out expecting Wednesday's fish found scattered, spooky tuna and a lot of empty trolling lanes. That's the nature of an eddy-driven bite. The temperature break is the trigger, and when it's crisp, the fishing can be excellent. When it relaxes, the fish disperse and you're back to grinding bird schools and hoping for a random bite window.

Looking ahead, if the warm seam re-tightens the way it did last Wednesday, I'd be back out on that same stretch between Wilmington and Poor Man's working the 100-fathom line early, switching over to the chunk once the sun gets high and the troll goes quiet. Overnight, the squid-light program at Coimbra is worth the run for bluefin while the moon stays dark — that bite has been consistent enough to plan a trip around. And keep one eye on the horizon for white marlin. The warm plume's still building, the ballyhoo are showing on top, and historically that combination means flags inside the next week or so. I wouldn't book a marlin trip on that alone yet, but I'd have the pitch bait rigged and ready just in case the first one shows early.

reports.headline: Post-Blow Window Cracks the Canyon Open — Yellowfin Stack the Wilmington Seam
reports.subhead: A 10-degree thermal break and a darkening moon set up the best two-day stretch of the young season at Washington and her neighbors.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what blows sometimes do out here — it scoured the shelf edge and left behind the kind of thermal signature you dream about in June. By Wednesday and into Thursday we had a 10.3-degree break sitting right on the shelf-slope edge, the widest differential I've clocked all season. That's not a subtle seam — that's a wall of warm water stacked against cold, and anything with a spine knows to hold on it. The wind had been howling out of the northeast for the better part of four days before that, which usually makes me groan, but this time it did the job for us: it sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom breaks north of the canyon proper and pushed a real upwelling signature into the Coimbra corridor. Cold water pushing up under warm water is a dinner bell, not a problem.

This week the moon's going dark — new moon on the calendar, which means springs building through the weekend and less ambient light for the overnight squid game. That's good news twice over. The bigger tidal push moves more water across the canyon heads, which stacks bait tighter against structure, and the darker nights make the underwater squid lights that much more effective for anybody willing to sit on anchor or drift the edge after sundown. I'd watch the wind through midweek — if it stays reasonable out of the south or southwest, this window holds. If it swings back around to the northeast and starts honking again, take the gift you got last week and don't push your luck on the run out.

We worked the warm seam between Wilmington and Poor Man's on Wednesday, trolling the 100-fathom line starting around 38°43'N, 73°47'W and running the color change southeast toward the Hudson's east wall. That wall drops from about 50 fathoms to over 300 in less than two miles — it's a real ledge, not a gradual slope, and the yellowfin were sitting right on the break where the green water met the blue, working bait pushed up against the wall by the current. Ballyhoo behind Ilanders in dark colors — purple/black and green/yellow — pulled fish in the 35 to 60 pound class, with a couple pushing bigger on the troll. Once we found the color change and marked bait on the machine at 90 to 130 feet, we slowed the spread down and let the baits sit in the strike zone longer. That patience mattered — this wasn't a run-and-gun bite, it was a find-it-and-work-it bite.

The midshore bluefin story this week is the Coimbra corridor, and it's worth the shorter run if you don't want to commit to a full canyon day. That NE upwelling I mentioned sharpened the 20 to 30 fathom breaks enough that bluefin have concentrated tight to structure there, holding around 20 fathoms. We ran into schoolies and a few mediums working bait balls just under the surface at first light, and the overnight squid-light program has been the more consistent producer once the sun's up and the surface bite shuts down. Jigging Shimano Butterfly-style jigs in the 150 to 250 gram range straight down through the bait has worked better than trolling out there — the fish are suspended, not chasing across the top.

Wahoo have been a bonus, not a target, coming on high-speed trolled lures pulled at 12 to 16 knots along the edge where the water clarity turned that deep cobalt blue — usually right where the thermal break sharpens. Nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet, but if you're already out there working the wall, it's worth throwing a couple of wahoo bombs or Ilander/ballyhoo combos on wire out the back.

Mahi have been thin so far — a few short pecks around any floating structure we found, mostly under 10 pounds, nothing like the pods you want to see stacked under a mat of sargassum. I'd keep an eye out for any grass lines pushing north with the warm plume, because that's usually where the real mahi show up once the water settles.

Honest assessment on the week: it was a good two-day window, not a season-defining one yet. Wednesday and Thursday were legitimately excellent on the yellowfin — multiple double-digit days for boats that found the seam early and stayed on it. Friday through Sunday the wind built back and the bite got patchier, more of a grind than a program. That's the nature of a post-blow window — it opens fast and it can close just as fast if the wind doesn't cooperate.

Looking ahead, I've got two things on my radar. First, the white marlin watch — that warm plume pushing toward the bank is the trigger everybody's been waiting on, and if the thermal pattern from last week holds or repeats, I'd expect the first flags in the mid-Atlantic canyons within the next week to ten days. Second, with the new moon springs building through the weekend, I'd fish the overnight squid-light program hard on the darker nights — Wednesday through Friday this week gives you minimal moon interference. If I had one day to fish, I'd run to the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam early, work the color change on the troll through midday, then shift to jigging structure in the Coimbra corridor as the light fades. Plan B if the wind kicks back up: stay midshore, work the sharper breaks, and let the bluefin do the heavy lifting while the canyon settles back down.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Widest Thermal Break of the Year Lights Up Yellowfin on the Poor Man's Seam
reports.subhead: A dirty blow gave way to the best canyon structure we've seen all season — and the bluefin found a shortcut at 20 fathoms while we wait on the first marlin flags.
reports.body_markdown:
Rough week to start, good finish — that's the short version. We had a blow roll through early, kicked up a lumpy sea and pushed a lot of the fleet to the dock for a couple days. But that wind did us a favor. It stirred the shelf water enough that when it laid down Wednesday into Thursday, we found the widest temperature break I've seen all year — better than ten degrees Fahrenheit right where the shelf drops into the slope. That's not a subtle seam, that's a wall. Boats running the Wilmington-to-Poor Man's stretch and up along the Hudson's east wall found yellowfin stacked right on that edge, feeding hard on the color change where green water met blue. That kind of break doesn't happen twice in a season, so if you missed it, don't beat yourself up — but keep the coordinates saved, because when the shelf water gets shoved around again by weather, that same seam is going to reload.

Now we're heading into a new moon week, which means dark nights and building spring tides. For us in the canyons that matters less for tide height and more for what happens after sundown — dark moon means the squid come up thick under the lights, and that's exactly when the bluefin have been showing. We're seeing a real concentration building in that 20-to-25-fathom band, a corridor a lot of guys are calling the Coimbra run, north and west of the deep-water canyons. It's close enough that Ocean City boats are making it a day trip instead of an overnighter, which is a nice change of pace after burning diesel to Norfolk all June. NE upwelling has been sharpening that break all week, and it's holding bait tight against the bottom structure there.

On the yellowfin, the program that's working is straightforward: troll a mixed spread of ballyhoo behind small green machines and Sea Witches, cedar plugs way back, running 6 to 8 knots right down the thermal edge rather than across it. The fish aren't schooled up thick — you're picking off two, three, sometimes five in a pass before you have to reset and find the seam again — but the average size has been good, 35 to 55 pounds, with a few pushing bigger out toward Poor Man's western edge where the bottom breaks harder. If you find birds working bait balls on that same color change, slow down and pitch a naked ballyhoo or a small popper. That's produced some of the better fish of the week.

Bluefin in that 20-fathom Coimbra corridor have been more of a night game. Anchor up or drift over structure once the sun's down, drop the underwater lights, and let the squid show up — they will, especially with this new moon keeping things dark. Once you've got squid marking, jig them up on a small glow jig or a Shimano Butterfly-style jig, and use a couple as live bait on a fluorocarbon leader, 60 to 80 pound, fished on a slow drift or lightly weighted downline. These aren't giants — mostly 40 to 70 pounds — but they're eating well and it's a shorter run than chasing the deep canyons, which matters when the forecast is iffy midweek.

Mahi have been scattered but present wherever there's floating structure — lobster pot warp, a weed line, a mat of sargassum holding bait. Nothing like a solid mahi bite yet, more of a bonus fish while you're trolling for tuna, but a few boats picked up fish in the 8-to-15 pound range working structure near the Norfolk Canyon edge. Wahoo showed up as incidental catches on high-speed trolled lures worked over structure and drop-offs — not a dedicated bite yet, but worth a swim over structure with a wahoo bomb if the yellowfin bite goes quiet for a stretch.

White marlin — nothing yet, and I want to be straight about that. We're watching a warm plume that's been building and pushing toward the bank, and historically that's the trigger that gets the first flags up at Spencer and Norfolk. Based on how this plume's been tracking, I'd put the window at 7 to 10 days out. Not this week, probably not next weekend either, but the ingredients are lining up. If you're planning a trip specifically for marlin, I'd hold off another week and watch how that plume develops rather than burning a trip early.

Looking at the week ahead: the new moon dark nights favor the squid-light program for bluefin, so if I only had one night trip in me, that's where I'd put it — the Coimbra corridor, lights down right at dusk, patient on the jig until the squid show. For the day boats, I'd keep working that Wilmington-to-Poor Man's seam as long as the thermal break holds. It's not going to stay ten degrees wide forever — these things relax over a week or two as the water mixes — so there's a decent window right now before it smooths back out. Wind looks manageable through the middle of the week, then there's a system worth watching for the weekend that could kick up a chop again. If it does, that's fine — sometimes it's the disturbance that resets the table. Plan A is the seam and the corridor. Plan B, if the wind wins, is staying tight to the beach edges working structure for whatever wahoo and mahi are holding there. Either way, there's enough happening right now that a well-timed trip should put fish in the box — just don't expect every drop to connect like Thursday did. That kind of day is the exception, not the rule.

reports.headline: New moon springs sharpen the 20-fathom break — bluefin show on the Coimbra corridor
reports.subhead: Post-blow canyon water opened a window for yellowfin while the inshore wrecks keep grinding out sea bass limits.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what blows do out here — it stirred the pot and left something better behind. We had a hard NE push mid-week that a lot of guys grumbled about, but by Wednesday and Thursday the shelf-slope edge had opened up to a 10.3-degree differential, which is about as wide as I've seen it set up all season. That kind of thermal break doesn't happen by accident — it's the cold shelf water shouldering up against the warm slope current, and where those two masses collide, bait piles up and yellowfin follow. Guys working the seam between Wilmington and Poor Man's, and the east wall of the Hudson, connected on some quality yellowfin in that window. If you missed it, don't lose sleep — that setup tends to rebuild after a blow, and I wouldn't be shocked to see it again before the week's out.

This week the moon is the story closer to the beach. We're running into new moon springs, with the tide building toward peak alignment Saturday through Monday. Bigger swings, stronger current, and that NE upwelling we had last week has left the 20 to 30 fathom breaks sharper than they've been in a month. That's exactly the kind of structure bluefin like to sit on when they're staging inshore of the canyons — they'll hold on the edge of a temperature break and let the current bring the bait to them instead of chasing it across open water. The Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has been the one to watch, and with the moon going dark, the overnight squid-light bite there is lining up about as well as it's going to.

On the wrecks and reefs, it's been a steady grind rather than a blowup, which is fine by me — that's the nature of bottom fishing in July. Sea bass are stacked on the Triple Wrecks and Axel Carlson Reef in 60 to 90 feet, and the jumbos are still coming out of the deeper structure on Barnegat Ridge, particularly the high-relief pieces where the current sweeps hard on the last two hours of the ebb. Standard program: high-low rigs with squid strips and green crab, or if you want to be efficient about it, a 4-ounce diamond jig tipped with a Gulp Grub in nuclear chicken worked right off the bottom. Sea Girt Reef has been kicking out mixed bags — good sea bass with a scattering of small blackfish mixed in, which tells me the tog are starting to think about moving onto structure ahead of the fall push, even though it's early for them yet.

Bonito is the wildcard this week. The corridor's been widening to our north as that cold wall up in Rhode Island Sound broke down, and the early reports out of the eastern Long Island inlets on clean incoming water have me watching Shrewsbury Rocks and the water off Sea Girt for the first stray fish to show. I haven't had a confirmed bonito in the box yet out of our zone, so I'm not going to tell you to run out and target them — but if you're already anchored on a wreck for sea bass and you see showers of bait getting nervous on top, it wouldn't hurt to have a small metal rigged and ready.

Mahi are still mostly a rumor this far into July. I know guys are itching for the pot bite to load up, but the water hasn't stacked the way it does in late summer — I'd call this the scouting phase, not the stacking phase. If you're running past floating structure on the way to the tuna grounds, throw a look and maybe a naked ballyhoo, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet. That bite typically doesn't turn on for us until the back half of the month, and this year's shaping up on the normal calendar.

For the midrange tuna guys, my numbers say the Klondike and the deeper edge of the Mud Hole are worth a look this week too — not because the bluefin have set up thick there yet, but because the same NE upwelling that sharpened the Coimbra break has been working the whole shelf edge, and bait's been getting pushed onto structure across a wider stretch than usual. I had one report of school bluefin working bait pods on the northern lump of the Mud Hole in 55 feet, taken on trolled spreader bars mid-morning — not a stacked bite, but a real one, and worth a troll pass if you're already out that way.

Looking ahead, I'm watching two things. First, that shelf-slope edge — if it holds together like it did Wednesday and Thursday, I expect another crack at yellowfin on the same seam by midweek, and it's worth the run if the forecast stays clean. Second, the springs building through the weekend mean stronger current on the wrecks, which usually pushes sea bass tight to structure and makes the drift fishing sloppy — I'd favor anchoring up on the last two hours of tide rather than drifting through it. And keep an ear out on white marlin — the warm plume that's been building toward the bank is the trigger everybody's watching, and if the pattern holds, we could see the first flags at the canyons within the week. That's a bit outside my usual water, but when it starts, the whole fleet notices.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the PM flood — bass show at Peaks and Two Lights, groundfish push deep off Halfway Rock
reports.subhead: Big new-moon tides and a lingering NE swell have the bay sorting itself out — stripers on the evening push, cod and haddock sliding into cooler water on the ledges.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat in the northeast more than I'd like for this time of year, and it did what northeast wind always does to this bay — it stacked a chop against the outer islands and pushed a slug of cooler water up onto the ledges around Halfway Rock. That's not all bad. It firmed up the thermocline out there, which matters more than people think. Surface water in the inner bay — Portland waterfront, back of Peaks, up into the Presumpscot mouth — has been running warm and a little soft on top, the kind of water that pushes bait shallow and pulls groundfish deep to find something they like. Out at the Rock and around Eagle Island the upwelling sharpened that break, and I found cleaner, cooler water sitting on the bottom structure in 70 to 90 feet, which is exactly where you want it if you're chasing cod and haddock in July.

This week the moon is the story. We're building into new-moon springs, biggest tide swing we've seen since before the last full moon, and it peaks right around July 11 through 13. That means more water moving faster through the guts between the islands, and it means the evening flood is stacking up right around sunset for the next several days — first real PM window like this since June. When the flood and the light change line up like that, bass push bait against structure they'd otherwise ignore at midday, and they do it with some confidence because low light plus moving water equals safety for a fish that doesn't love being out in the open. I'd plan around that evening tide all week, not the morning.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, honestly, and I want to say that straight out rather than oversell it. Some days you find them stacked tight to structure, other days you work three miles of shoreline and manage two fish. What's consistent is where they show when they do show — the eastern side of Peaks Island on the last two hours of the incoming, working the ledge drop where it goes from eight feet to twenty-two quick. I've had good luck there on a swimming plug worked slow just off bottom, and when that's not drawing strikes I switch to a live mackerel under a slip float, letting it work naturally in the current seam. Two Lights has also been holding fish on the outgoing, particularly around the second hour when the water's really ripping past the rocks — bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on the push, tipped with a strip of squid or mackerel belly, bounced along that rocky bottom. Bluefish have started mixing in with the bass around there too, chopping up the same bait schools, so if you're getting cut-off leaders on wire-shy stripers gear, that's your answer — the blues found the same mackerel the bass did.

Speaking of mackerel — the spring run has mostly passed through, but there are still pockets holding around Halfway Rock and off Bailey Island in 15 to 30 feet, enough that a string of Swedish jigs or a sabiki rig dropped off a stationary boat will still fill a bait bucket most mornings. That's been the real value of the mackerel right now, less as a target and more as the live bait that's making the striper program work.

Groundfish has been the harder story this week, and I won't pretend otherwise. The warm surface layer in the inner bay has pushed cod and haddock deep and made them cagey. Around Halfway Rock, though, that NE-driven upwelling I mentioned actually helped — boats working the deeper ledges, 70 to 90 feet on the northeast side of the rock, have been finding cod in the 3 to 8 pound range on diamond jigs worked with a slow lift-drop, and a scattering of haddock mixed in on bait — clam or herring chunks on a high-low rig, fished right on bottom during the slower current at the top and bottom of the tide. The bite window is tight, usually the last hour before slack and the first hour after, because once that current starts really ripping through there the fish tuck down and quit. Cape Small and the ledges off Harpswell have been quieter, more a June-style bite that hasn't fully carried into July — worth a stop if you're passing through, not worth a dedicated run right now.

Looking ahead, I'd build my week around that evening flood through the weekend while the new moon tide is still building strength — Peaks Island and Two Lights are where I'd put my time between 6 and 9 in the evening, live mackerel or a slow-worked bucktail depending on how much current you've got. If the wind backs off out of the northeast the way it's been forecast to, I'd expect that cooler water at Halfway Rock to hold, which means the cod bite there should stay steady through the week on the same tide-timing pattern — fish the slack, not the rip. Best case, the bass settle into a more predictable pattern as these big tides keep flushing bait past the structure. If they stay scattered the way they have been, I'd rather put in an extra evening at the Rock jigging cod than beat the shoreline chasing bass that aren't committing yet. Either way, the tide's doing the work for you this week — you just have to be there when it turns.

reports.headline: Haddock stack up on the mud as new-moon springs tighten the current on Jeffrey's Ledge
reports.subhead: Cod are scattered on the gravel, pollock are steady over structure, and the first real giant bluefin showings have boats working the ledge edge at first light.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week gave us a stretch of workable weather — light southwest in the mornings, building to a chop by afternoon most days, nothing that kept the fleet tied up. Water on the ledge has been doing what it usually does this time of year: layering. Warm skin on top, a hard break somewhere between 60 and 90 feet, cold and stable underneath where the haddock live. That thermocline has been getting more defined day over day, and a northeast wind component mid-week helped sharpen it further — upwelling along the steeper drop-offs on the east side of Jeffrey's and down around Platts Bank pulls cooler water up the slope and tightens the temperature break right where the bottom current lanes run. That's exactly the kind of structure that concentrates bait and holds fish tight to specific contour lines instead of spreading them across the whole bank.

We're heading into new moon this weekend, and that means spring tides building through Friday into Monday — bigger swings, stronger current at the ledge, shorter slack windows. For bottom fishing that's a mixed bag. Stronger current makes the drift move fast over the mud, which is fine for haddock because they'll still come up and eat a jig or a clam bait moving through the strike zone, but it makes it harder to hold bottom on the gravel patches where the cod like a slower presentation. My plan this weekend is to fish the early stages of the tide change and let the last hour before slack do the work — that's when the current eases just enough to control your drift without losing bottom contact.

Haddock have been the most reliable fish on the ledge the last ten days. We're finding them on the mud bottom in 180 to 220 feet between the north end of Jeffrey's and the western edge of Platts Bank, mixed schools but plenty of keepers in the 3 to 6 pound range, a few pushing 8. Standard high-low rigs with clam bait or squid strips are doing the job, but the jig bite has been better on calmer mornings — 8 to 12 ounce diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, worked with a short hop off bottom. When the current is running hard on these spring tides, go heavier and slow your retrieve down; the fish are still there, they're just not chasing far off the bottom.

Cod have been spottier, which is normal for mid-July — the bigger fish have mostly pushed off the shallower gravel onto deeper structure, and we're picking them up on the eastern gravel patches of Jeffrey's in the 130 to 160 foot range, along with a few marked on the sonar working the rockier stretches toward Tillies Bank. Nothing like the fall run, but a mixed bag of cod in the 8 to 15 pound class has been coming over the rail on clam bait fished tight to bottom, and jigging has produced a few better fish for guys willing to work the structure methodically instead of drifting through it once and moving on. Pollock have actually been the more consistent bite over structure — schools stacked up off bottom on the drop-offs, and diamond jigs or Kastmasters worked at mid-depth have been steady producers, good fun on lighter tackle and a nice change of pace between haddock drifts.

Mackerel showed up strong on the ledge this week, which matters for two reasons — they're a blast on light spinning gear with small jigs or Sabiki rigs, and they're the bait that's going to matter most for the bluefin game. We've had our first real giant bluefin sightings working bait on the surface up on the ledge edge, mostly in the early morning hours before the wind fills in. Nothing consistent yet — a few boats connected on live mackerel drifted behind the boat, a couple more marked fish on the meter and never got a bite. It's the classic early-season bluefin pattern: the fish are here, the bait is here, but the window each day is short and you need to be in position before first light with mackerel already in the tank. I wouldn't call it dialed in yet, but the ingredients are lining up — cooling upwelled water along the steep breaks, dense mackerel schools, and giants starting to show. That's usually the setup that turns into a real bite within a couple weeks once the thermal structure stabilizes.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tides through the weekend mean stronger current everywhere on the ledge complex, so I'd target the transition periods around the tide change rather than fighting max current in the middle of it. Haddock on the mud should stay the most dependable target through the week — that's where I'd send a boat that wants fish in the box. For cod, work the gravel methodically and don't expect a fast bite; it's a numbers game right now, not a blitz. And if you're chasing bluefin, get out early, have live mackerel ready, and treat every trip as scouting — the pattern's building, but it's not consistent enough yet to promise a hookup. That should change as we move deeper into July if this thermal structure holds.

reports.headline: Cold wall breaks down, bonito corridor opens from Newport to Point Judith
reports.subhead: New moon springs are loading up the breachways while bass hold the rocks and the first bonito scouts push past Block Island.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat mostly out of the southwest, nothing violent, just steady enough to keep a little push on the south-facing beaches and put some color in the wash off Second Beach and Matunuck. The moon was working toward new, and you could feel the tides start to build day over day — bigger swings through the Sakonnet and the breachways, more water moving on the ebb than we'd seen since the June full moon. That's the setup that matters this week: new moon springs peak Saturday through Monday, July 11-13, and that's going to put real current through Charlestown Breachway, Quonnie, and Weekapaug, along with a stronger rip off Beavertail and the Jamestown side of the East Passage. The other big story is thermal — the cold wall that's been sitting between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound all June basically fell apart, warming better than ten degrees in spots. That's not a subtle shift. It means bait and predators that were pinned east of Block are free to slide west, and it's the reason I'm telling guys to start checking bonito water from Newport down to Point Judith instead of just running to the island.

Striper fishing on the rocks has been steady, not spectacular. The bite windows are tightening around the tide changes rather than running all day, which tracks with warmer, calmer water — fish feed hard on the moving water and go quiet on the slack. Best sessions have been the last two hours of the incoming through the Beavertail ledges and around the Dumplings off Jamestown, working swimming plugs and darters at first light before the sun gets on the rocks. Second Beach and the Sachuest side have given up some schoolies and a few mid-30-inch fish to guys walking peanut bunker imitations — 3/4-ounce bucktails with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer — along the drop where the sand meets the boulders. With the spring tide building into the weekend, I'd target the last two hours of the evening flood at Sakonnet Point, especially around the lighthouse rocks where the current wraps and stacks bait. That's historically been the best window all season for a push of better fish, and bigger tides usually wake up the bigger stripers that have been sitting deeper on the ledges.

Blackfish season's open here through mid-October, and the ledges are still producing if you're willing to fish the slack correctly. Brenton Reef and the rock piles off Beavertail are holding tog in 15 to 25 feet, but you need to be precise about timing — fish green crabs or Asian crab right on the bottom during the 20-30 minutes of true slack at the reef, because once that new moon current gets moving hard this weekend, those fish tuck under structure and won't come out to eat until it eases again. Same story at the Jamestown Bridge pilings — good numbers of keeper-class tog mixed with shorts, but the bite is a slack-tide game only.

Fluke have been doing what they usually do this time of year — sliding out of the warm upper bay and setting up in the channels and breachway mouths where the water stays cooler and more oxygenated. Charlestown Breachway and the Quonnie side have both been giving up keeper fluke on the outgoing, drifted with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1/2-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid. Depths of 8 to 15 feet right in the throat of the breachway on the last three hours of the ebb has been the most consistent read. Weekapaug's produced some too, though it's more of a mixed bag — some keepers, a lot of throwbacks, and you have to grind through a lot of water some days to find a few worth keeping.

Bluefish have shown up in decent numbers chasing bait around the Newport Bridge rip and along the Jamestown shoreline — not the giant slammers yet, mostly 3 to 6 pound fish blitzing on scup and peanut bunker at first light. Metal — Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — has been the move when they're up top, and it's been a fun distraction while waiting for the tog slack or the striper tide to turn.

Now to the bonito. Nothing confirmed on my beat yet, but with that cold wall gone and warm water pushing west, I expect the first scouts to show along the Brenton Reef edge and the rip off the Newport Bridge within the next week or two, same water that's already given up bluefish. If you're out there working metal for blues and something suddenly hits harder and runs faster than a bluefish should, don't be shocked. I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig on the deck just in case.

As for albies — patience. That's a September program on this stretch of coast, and nothing in the water right now says otherwise. For this week, my plan is simple: tog the slack at Brenton Reef and Beavertail early, then chase the evening flood at Sakonnet Point as the spring tide builds toward its peak Sunday and Monday. If the stripers don't show in the current lane at the lighthouse, I've got the breachway fluke drift as a backup, and that's produced enough keepers lately to make it worth the trip either way.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up SW Ledge as bonito push into Point Judith water
reports.subhead: Giant-class bass are showing at Block Island's rips, fluke have pushed to the breachways, and the cold wall between the Sound and the ocean has finally broken down.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the moon was winding down out of the last quarter, current was soft, and the water did something I've been waiting on all June — the cold wall that's been sitting between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound finally gave up. That temperature differential collapsed better than ten degrees in a matter of days. For a guy who reads rips for a living, that's the single biggest story of the summer so far. It means the cold water that's been penning bait and predators against the Block Island side is spreading west, and it's opening the door for species that had been strictly a Block Island story to start showing up off Point Judith proper.

This week we're building into new moon springs — peak alignment lands the 11th through the 13th — and that matters more than people give it credit for. Bigger swings mean more water moving through SW Ledge, the North Rip, and the tide-break off Sandy Point, and more water moving means the bait gets pushed and stacked rather than just drifting lazily through. I like fishing springs at the Ledge for exactly this reason — the current builds a hard edge you can read visually, foam line and all, and predators sit right on that seam waiting for the buffet to come to them. The tradeoff is you've got a narrower window to work it before the tide gets away from you. Plan your drift around the two hours either side of the tide change, not the whole cycle.

On the striper front, the story right now is genuinely encouraging. We've had reports — and I've seen it myself on two trips — of giant class bass showing at Block Island, mixed in with a fluke run that's been building steadily on the south side. These aren't schoolie numbers. These are the kind of fish that make your drag question its life choices. The pattern has been night and dawn on the West Wall and down around the SW Ledge structure itself, working live eels on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 30 to 40 feet, current permitting. On the harder push of the springs this week, you may need up to 4 ounces to stay down. Bunker chunks fished static on the drift have also produced, especially right at the top of the tide when things go momentarily quiet before the ebb kicks in. This isn't an every-trip bite — I put two clients on fish last Thursday night and came up empty Friday with nearly identical conditions, which tells you these bass are moving with the bait, not sitting still. Find the pods of bunker or squid showing on the sounder around the Ledge and you're in business. Miss them and you're just soaking bait in current.

Fluke have made their seasonal shift, and it's right on schedule. Bay-side action has thinned out as that water's warmed into the high 70s, pushing the flatties toward the breachway at Galilee and the deeper ocean-side structure around the Harbor of Refuge and the mouth of the Great Salt Pond over at Block. The outgoing tide through the breachway is the play — a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet, bounced slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet as the water rips out toward the ocean. Fish are running mixed sizes, some solid keepers in the 20-inch class mixed with plenty of shorts, so expect to cull. The upwelled ocean water sitting around 71 degrees off both inlets is exactly the kind of clean, cooler water fluke want after baking in the bay all June.

Now for the bonito — this is the one I've been watching closely, because that cold-wall collapse I mentioned means the corridor that used to be strictly a Block Island phenomenon is widening toward Point Judith itself. We're right at the tail end of the seasonal window where the first schools typically show, and the early signs are lining up: clean water, warming trend, bait pushed tight to structure. I haven't personally connected yet this week, but I've had it confirmed that fish are starting to show off the south side of Block, working bait pods in close to North Light and down toward Southeast Light on the incoming tide. If you're rigged for it, small epoxy jigs — the half-ounce Deadly Dicks or a green machine-style tin — worked fast through diving birds is still the percentage play.
